en: Preface to the Complete Works of Master Hanshan Mengyou.
Regarding the *Complete Works of Master Hanshan Mengyou* in the Jiaxing Canon, only five volumes of his *Dharma Words* (*Fayu*) have been carved for printing. [Year] Bingshen.

In the year [of the cyclical sign], Gong Xiaosheng went to Guangdong. When the Abbot Huashou of Haitang received my letter, he struck the wooden gong and bell to announce to the assembly that they should seek out the manuscript of Chan Master Qihexi of Dinghu.
With the assistance of Mr. Cao Qiuyue and others, it was transcribed and sent back to Suzhou. I, Qianyi, personally collated the text and compiled it into forty fascicles.

The Great Master’s writings were composed spontaneously as his pen touched the paper; the prose was not... [unfinished] *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a preface or colophon concerning the compilation of the works of a Chan master. The translation reflects the extant portion.*

I have added some points; the wording cannot avoid being somewhat prolix, and there are instances where the sequence of paragraphs has been lost. During my travels to the East, I once presented the "Preface to the Heart-Dharma of the Zuo Tradition" for editorial determination.
Upon seeing it, he was delighted in countenance and subsequently discarded his previous draft. Now, as I collate and verify this work, I find it to be so.
I have ventured to add strokes and alter the text; this is truly based upon the transmitted words of the Great Master. I did not dare to overstep [his authority], for to do so would be improper.
Once the slips of bamboo were finalized, I composed a preface, saying: "The Buddhas and Patriarchs expounded the teachings by means of writing to explain the Dharma.

When Maitreya set forth the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and Nāgārjuna commented on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, their myriad gates and ten thousand paths formed an interlacing web of radiance—rich and flourishing."
How brilliant! How resplendent! It is the supreme literature of all ages. When the Great Teaching flowed eastward, the spirit of human culture gradually began to emerge.
Huiyuan and Zhi Dun developed it profoundly in the south, while Kumārajīva initiated its wide propagation in the north. Truly, they were the ones who first set the great carriage wheel in motion.
Since the Sui and Tang dynasties, the writings of Tiantai, Qingliang, and Yongming have shone like the sun in the sky and flowed like water upon the earth—how magnificent they are!

Ah! It is the ferry for crossing the waters of principle and meaning, and the deep ocean of written expression. Reaching the Song dynasty, the teachings became widespread and the texts grew voluminous;
among them, three families were most prominent. Xianjin, with his solitary loftiness, exalted the teaching; his writings are concise yet discerning.
Shimen, with his penetrating agility, supported the school; his writings are expansive and elegant. Jingshan, with his vast magnanimity, responded to the capacities of beings; his writings...
It is brilliant yet unrestrained. Now, when literature reaches the point of sophistry, it becomes ornate and unrestrained;

its fortifications and moats grow daily more secure, its branches and leaves grow daily more luxuriant, and its nets for ensnaring and its means of recruitment grow daily more extensive. How vast it is!
The flow of "cupfuls of words" pours forth daily, while the ferry-crossings and bridges grow daily exhausted. As stated in the *Xici*: "The composition of the *Yi*..."
As for that era of the Middle Ages: did not the one who composed the *Yi* (Book of Changes) harbor anxieties and tribulations? Is this not truly credible?

Our Great Master, possessed of vast wisdom and profound compassion, attained authentic realization through genuine practice. He received the transmission of the mind-consciousness-wisdom as a dream-vision from Maitreya;

he attained thorough awakening to the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm at Qingliang. Adapting to the capacities of beings and responding to their ailments, he taught both horizontally and vertically—through thousands of words and myriad verses, each and every one.
Flowing forth from the ocean of the Tathāgata’s words, those who venerated the sublime teachings at Xiantan fortified its ramparts;
those who supported the school at Shimen nourished its branches and leaves; and those who responded to the needs of the occasion at Jingshan expanded its means of gathering and guiding.
Their sole purpose was to ensure that even a single word or half-phrase might reach the sentient beings of the Dharma-ending age, so that all might [attain liberation].
Drinking from the river until the belly is full, one returns together to the ocean of wisdom before finally coming to rest. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"The King of the Golden-Winged Birds, with his pure eyes, observes the various dragons; when their lives are due to end, he flaps the waters of the great ocean with his left and right wings, causing them to part on both sides, so as to seize and devour them.
The Great Master preaches the Dharma for the sake of others, desiring to strike down the great waters of the ocean of birth and death.
To take sentient beings with roots of goodness and place them within the Buddha-dharma is likewise so.
As for the one called Ri (the Sun), the calligrapher Chen Fanghou of Guangnan, his words were stirred by sorrowful awakening; he set down his brush and shaved his head.

The Great Master grasped his profound resolve, which shone with brilliant radiance, and extraordinary marvels emerged upon the paper. Sentient beings with roots of goodness receive this teaching as it accords with their capacities; such as Fanghou, who has crossed the river...
Even after kalpas as numerous as the sands [of the Ganges], it still has not yet come to an end. Alas, how magnificent!

Both the Great Master and the Venerable Zibai possessed the extraordinary resources of heroes appearing but once in an age; at a time when the lion’s lute had fallen silent, they sacrificed their bodies for the Dharma.
Like two wheels on a single chariot, Zibai’s prose was heroic, robust, and incisive, while the Great Master’s prose was expansive, profound, and elegantly sorrowful.

In their role as torches for those wandering in the darkness of ignorance, they are one and the same. In the past, people lamented that Zhongfeng had ceased his teaching activities, wondering where he had hidden his way;
they further remarked that after Chushi and Jitan, the single branch of the "Plucking the Flower" [tradition] was nearly extinguished.
Looking at it from today’s perspective, if not to Zibo and Hanshan, to whom could it have returned? Five hundred years hence, when the hordes of demons and heretics rise up like sharp blades—
He gave birth to two masters who acted as envoys of the Tathāgata; they wore the seal of the Great Dharma and kindled the lamp of the Great Dharma.
They were truly what the Confucians call those who "appear in the world to bring fame.

Yet, there are those among the petty peddlers and plunderers who often usurp the lineage of succession and falsely attach themselves to a teacher’s transmission, busily engaging in efforts as futile as ants shaking a tree. When the Master’s collected works appear, they will be like the sun’s orb at its zenith.
The shadows of the *chimei* (goblins) have withdrawn, yet those who sleep in darkness remain muddled and have not yet awakened.
Thus, when will the Great Master’s great compassion of same-body (*samatā-kāya*)—which is like the presence of anxiety and concern in the *Yī Jīng*—ever cease?
This is truly enough to cause one to weep bitterly. When the *Mèngyóu jí* was first transmitted to Tiānjié Monastery in Wǔlín, the Venerable Juélàng saw it and sighed, saying:
The Eye and Lamp of humanity and devas has fortunately not fallen into ruin. I have hastily drafted this petition to proclaim and circulate it.

Mao Zi Zijin requested to take sole responsibility for carving the printing blocks to fulfill his private aspiration for humble instruction. After Zijin passed away, his three sons—Bao, Biao, and Yi—pursued their father’s will and thus brought the project to completion.
Those who collaborated with me in the search and compilation in the regions south of the passes were the filial and incorruptible Wan...
Tai. What do the students say? It is my clan descendant, Zhao Ding. Following him, they assisted at Huashou Monastery in collecting and retrieving what had been scattered and lost:
Fazhong of Caoxi, Yuechi of Haitang, as well as the attendants of Huashou—Jinzhong, Jinzhao, and Jinguang.
All have shared in the labor of nourishing them with the milk of the Dharma. It is fitting that this be appended to the letter.

Written on the day of the winter solstice in the middle month of winter, during the year of Kuntun, by the lay disciple Haiyin, Qian Qianyi of Mount Yu, who burns incense and bows his head in reverence, respectfully prefaces this.
The Elder Hanshan’s Self-Portrait:
Majestic and imposing, serene and profound; without defensive walls or hidden depths, entirely free of steep precipices; his spirit overwhelms heaven and earth.
His eyes gaze toward the Milky Way; though he has drifted into the gates of worldly affairs, he does not depart from the realm beyond Vairocana.

Whether layman or monk, the shoulder-pole never leaves his shoulders. If he is neither a slave nor a master of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, he must surely be a petty peddler at the site of enlightenment.
Had he not entered the red furnace of the great smith, who would have known him to be an iron man? Only when Maitreya descends to be born shall this weighty public case be settled.
Inscription for the Portrait of the Venerable Kāñcanamālā of the Kuṅ-chü Assembly, Sent to Master Hanshan (with Preface)
The Three Kingdoms was a gathering place for heroes, yet it was also a gathering place for the blades of war; therein, there was no entry point for compassion or *prajñā*.

However, when the Patriarch Kang arrived with a single staff floating upon the river, he invoked the name of the Tathāgata three times, his two eyes flowed with blood, and as he cast the *śarīra* into a jar, its radiance shone brilliantly throughout the six directions, its grace extending through a thousand ages. At that time, there were none among the sovereign and ministers of Wu who were not moved by this.
His mind was transformed and his countenance changed; he immediately verified the principle through the facts and knew that there was a Buddha without any doubt.

Once the Six Perfections were translated and the gate of *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) opened, there were those who, regardless of whether they were of noble or lowly birth, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Their number, along with those who entered the subtle depths through meditative contemplation, was beyond calculation.

All of this was initiated by my ancestor. When the Great Master Hanshan Deqing was exiled to the pestilential seas for the sake of propagating the Dharma, he skillfully employed the samādhi of compassionate heart to cause withered bones everywhere to bloom with spring.

Upon hearing of this, Layman Shenghua was moved by admiration and specially painted a portrait of the ancestor, sending it up to Caoxi to serve as the Great Master’s shadow-form and influence. Alas! This is the place where the Flesh Buddha of Caoxi resides.

Manifesting from the Tang through the Song dynasties, there has never been a lack of those who drank from the Caoxi stream and attained the Way. Lately, however, Caoxi has run dry and Baolin Temple has fallen into desolation.
Yet, by relying on Master Han, the exile became a surging wave, and the source of Caoxi was revived once more. This is the universal manifestation of the Patriarch;
his skull-eyes have opened, beyond what can be compared even to the sands of the Ganges. How could this be grasped with a mind of discursive thought?
How could one possibly fathom the depth of his merit? The Daoist Daguān does not understand how to steer a rudder against the wind;
he only knows how to push a boat downstream with the current. In praise of him, I say: [Verse follows]

When Kangzu arrived in Wu, Master Qing was exiled to Guangdong. The Great Master’s skull was like a diamond eye, protruding and piercing; amidst the horrors of the miasmic sea, his very bones pricked and his soul trembled.

Having received this penal assignment, the Great Master felt all the more grateful for the sagely brilliance [of the Emperor]. At Caoxi, the poison was so virulent that those who drank it all perished.

The Great Master drank it, and all his miasmic fevers were completely dispelled. He gathered up the śarīra relics with his fingers, yet the ancestral patriarchs’ greed was such that he did not covet them for himself;

how could such a heart feel shame? To propagate the Dharma, he incurred the risk of death, his life like a single strand of thread; across a thousand li of miasmic ridges, his straw sandals trod over every path.

The path of thunder is steep and lofty; the typhoon is at its peak. The bowl and staff travel alone; the mark of the tongue shines brightly. The *man-rang* spirits of Nan Yue clap their hands in the broad daylight.
If I were without mind, I would be a shadow or echo of the Bodhisattva; yet with this mind of peace, I am the "Dull-witted Chapter" of the Patriarch.

When a person from China wearing a ceremonial cap visits Yue, who would not doubt him? At our parting at Shitou, my innermost feelings were as cold as ice. Master Ding blew upon the fire to paint the portrait of Master Kang;
through the shadow he attained the mind, and with the extinction of the mind, his nature merged with the ultimate. Great function is impermanent—listen to the bell with your eyes.
Roots and objects, subject and object; gathering and releasing, dreaming and waking. Holding aloft the precious stupa upon the summit of Mount Lao.
Compiled by the Reverend Daguankedo as a brief record of the *Complete Collection of Dream Excursions*.
On the Human Day (Renri) of the Dingyou year, Grand Councilor Gong Xiaosheng visited Haitang and presented a letter from the Minister of Rites Qian Mouzhai.
His sincere resolve to circulate the Master’s posthumous writings was incomparably earnest. When Huashou Wuhang saw it, he too offered boundless praise.
Having already sent a selection of the texts held at Haitang to Grand Councilor Gong, he further commissioned the carving of printing blocks.

He distributed [the texts] throughout various lands as a means to seek them out widely and collect them in their entirety. Furthermore, he sent eight messengers to invite Chan Master Xihe of Duanzhou to request his complete works.
Fearing that the original manuscripts might be lost, the Master had not yet dispatched them. On the full moon of the second month, Wan Gong Lian—an former *xiaolian*—arrived.
As Mr. Qian had previously given him specific instructions, he consulted with the Provincial Governor, Cao Gong, regarding the matter.
Qiuyue sent a letter requesting [the work] once more. Thereupon, I again submitted the "Epistle to Huashou," dispatching the messenger Yu Rufa to deliver it.
Once the guest prefect had departed, the manuscript was finally released. Furthermore, Lord Cao and the Academician Qian Shugu each contributed funds to cover the costs of transcription.
It happened that the city was holding examinations at that time. All those scholars who had taken refuge with Huashou heard of this and arrived;
they licked their brushes and applied the ink, completing the work in a few days. The official in charge of grading was none other than the attendant Lingzhong.
At that moment, a Confucian scholar named Chen Fanghou was moved by a sudden realization while he was writing, and immediately requested to leave the household life. He did so on that very day.
He underwent the tonsure ceremony; his Dharma name was Guzhi, and his secular style was Qudie. I have composed this verse to serve as a supportive condition for his ordination:

The single volume of manuscripts left behind by Hanshan Was able to cause Master Chen to leave the household life. When the timing and conditions coincide, It is like drawing a thread through a needle without error.
May the assembly of fellow students present here Help him don the *kāṣāya* robe. Behold! This is but a single drop of water from Caoxi.
Within the ink-well, lotus flowers surge forth. This is not merely the manifestation of the Great Master’s heart-light gathering immeasurable beings;

it is also the vision of the various Dharma-protectors, whose single fragment of heart-light, together with insentient brushes and ink, joins before the Hall of the Flower-Crown to usher forth this monk and perform a great Buddhist service.
This monk, receiving such heart-light, acts as a catalyst for all people.
The arising of the Guide is already immeasurable; how much more so, then, can the merit of the circulation of this scripture be measured?

I have recorded this for the sake of those thousands of miles away who might hear of it with a single snap of the fingers. On the sixth day of the third month, the Bhikṣu Jīnashē (今釋) concludes his writing.
The *Dream-Wandering Complete Collection Daily Record*. Various names have been edited and cross-referenced; I hope each will be preserved.
Tonghyeong, whose style name was Gieam, served as the head seat (*śrāmaṇera*) of the Great Master. The monks of Haichang today are all his grand-disciples.
Liu Qixiang, whose style name was Zhongdang, passed the second-tier examination (*yibang*) and served as the Magistrate of Fuzhou. When the Great Master’s spirit-shrine was returned to Caoxi...
Xi and those who collected the posthumous manuscripts all contributed their efforts. Now, Shi respectfully submits this:

Volume Two of the Collected Works of the Elder Master Hanshan: Dream-Wanderings.
Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and his disciple Tonghyeung;
revised by the Disciple from Lingnan, Liu Qixiang.
In response to Zhongcheng Zheng Kunyan with these words of Dharma:
If we discuss this great matter of causal conditions, although it is inherently possessed by every person and fully manifest in each individual, nothing is lacking.

A mere hair’s breadth! Alas, how can it be otherwise? Since beginningless kalpas, the seeds of the root of craving and the conceptualizations of the deluded mind have been deeply ingrained through habitual defilement.
These obscure the wondrous luminosity, preventing one from attaining true and authentic enjoyment.

Consequently, one has always made one's livelihood within the illusory shadows of the body, mind, and world, thereby wandering through birth and death. For this reason, when Buddhas and Patriarchs appear in the world, they speak with a thousand words and ten thousand phrases.
Through various skillful means, he teaches meditation and doctrine; all of these accord with the capacities of sentient beings and serve as instruments to shatter attachments.
Originally, there is no substantial dharma to be given to others. What is called "cultivation" is merely following one's own mind to purify the shadows of delusive thoughts and habitual tendencies.
Because one exerts effort in this regard, it is called cultivation. If, for a single moment, delusive thoughts suddenly cease, one will see through to one's own [nature].
The mind is, from the beginning, perfectly full, luminous, and vast; it is primordially pure and naturally so, such that not a single thing exists within it—this is called awakening.

It is not that, apart from this mind, there is something else to be cultivated or awakened to. For the substance of the mind is like a mirror, while deluded thoughts and攀緣 (pān-yuán, clinging to objects) are but shadows;
they are merely the dust and grime upon the true mind. Therefore it is said: "Conceptual appearances are the dust; cognitive emotions..."
It is defiled by impurities. If deluded thoughts are dissolved, the fundamental essence manifests of itself. It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is cleared away, the brightness appears.
Such is the natural law (*dharmatā*). However, because sentient beings have accumulated habitual defilements over many kalpas, the roots of self-love are firm and difficult to uproot.

In this present life, we are fortunate to rely upon the intrinsically possessed *prajñā*. With internal permeation serving as the cause and external reliance on a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to trigger it serving as the condition, [the essence manifests] of its own accord.
Knowing that this is fundamentally present, one resolves to direct the mind toward it with a vow to liberate oneself from birth and death.
To uproot the very core of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas all at once—how could this be a trivial matter?

Unless one is a person of great power who shoulders the burden nakedly and enters directly with a single blade, it is truly the most difficult of difficulties. As the ancients said: "It is like a single person facing ten thousand enemies."
This is no empty talk. Roughly speaking, there are many practitioners in the Dharma-ending age, yet few attain true realization and benefit.
Those who expend effort are many; those who gain mastery are few. Why is this? It is because they fail to find the point where one can take up the practice directly and simply.

This is merely working within the realm of shadows and reflections—measuring with intellectual consciousness and suppressing discursive thoughts based solely on what was previously heard, seen, known, or understood through language.
One first stores the subtle words and wondrous phrases of the ancients within one's breast, treating them as substantial dharmas and taking them to be one’s own insight and views;
yet one fails to realize that not a single point of this is of any use here. This...

This refers precisely to relying on conceptual understanding based on others, which blocks the gate of self-awakening. Now, when practicing the *gongfu*, one must first eradicate such intellectual understandings.
One must focus resolutely upon a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*). Trust deeply that one’s own mind is, from the beginning, utterly pure and stainless, unclad by even a single thread of attachment.
It is perfectly round and luminous, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*. Fundamentally, there is no body or mind, nor is there a world; nor is there delusion.
Regarding thoughts and deliberations: this very single thought is fundamentally unborn from the beginning.
The various phenomena appearing before one are all illusory, false, and unreal; they are merely shadows manifested within the true mind.

Having investigated and penetrated it in this way, look directly and fix your gaze upon the place where deluded thoughts arise and cease. Observe where they arise as they arise, and where they cease as they cease. Just as...
Apply this forceful pressure once; no matter what kind of deluded thought arises, it will be crushed to pieces by a single squeeze, dissolving instantly like ice melting or a fortress collapsing.
By all means, do not follow its flow, nor allow it to continue. This is precisely what Yongjia meant when he said one must sever the "continuing mind.
For this empty and floating mind has no root or source from the beginning; by all means, one must never treat it as a substantial reality.
Transverse it across your chest. As soon as it arises, utter "Du! once; with one "Du!", it will vanish.

By no means must you suppress it, for if you do, it will follow your every movement like a gourd bobbing on water. You must simply cast aside the body, mind, and world, and single-mindedly maintain this one thought-moment.
Like a precious sword held across the void, whether it be a Buddha or a Mara, cut them all down at once.

Sever it completely, like cutting tangled threads; strike with vigorous force and carry it away. This is what is called "the direct mind, right mindfulness of True Suchness" (*tathatā*). As for "right mindfulness," it is non-mindfulness (*amanyana*).

To be able to contemplate non-mindfulness can be called turning toward Buddha-wisdom. At the very beginning of practice, one must first resolve the mind and have essential faith in the Dharma-gate of Mind-Only.
The Buddha taught that the triple world is Mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Much...
The Buddha-dharma is brief; it consists merely in explaining these eight characters.

To make everyone clearly believe in them is to understand that, fundamentally, the two paths of the holy and the ordinary are nothing other than the two routes of delusion and enlightenment within one's own mind.
All causes and effects of good and evil—apart from this mind—not even a single thing can be found outside of it. For the wondrous nature of us humans is innate and fundamentally not...
Since it belongs to awakening, how could it be subject to delusion? What we call "delusion" now is simply this: failing to realize that one's own mind is fundamentally devoid of a single thing;
failing to comprehend that the body, mind, and world are fundamentally empty; and being obstructed by them, which is why it is called delusion.
One has consistently taken the deluded, arising-and-ceasing mind to be the truth, and thus clings to the various illusory transformations within the conditions of the six sense-objects.
To take this as real is like setting out with a mind directed toward the goal, yet instead turning back to flow upstream;
this requires completely casting off all prior intellectual understanding. Not even a single point of conceptual insight or clever technique is of any use.
It simply requires seeing through one's own present body, mind, and world with a single glance, realizing they are entirely but floating reflections manifested within one’s own mind.
They are like illusions, like reflections in a mirror, like the moon in water.
One should view all sounds as the wind passing through trees, and view all sensory objects as clouds floating in the sky; they are all shifting, illusory, and unreal.
This is true not only of external things, but even of the mind’s own deluded thoughts and anxieties, the seeds of all craving, and the habitual tendencies and afflictions—all are likewise unreal.
This is empty, illusory, and unreal. Contemplate this deeply. Whenever a single thought arises, you must decisively examine its ultimate source;
you must never let it pass lightly, nor allow yourself to be deceived by it.
If you practice in this manner, you will gradually approach the genuine and earnest. Apart from this, do not dabble in other so-called "subtle insights" or "clever methods."
To come and gather here is entirely without connection [to the Way]. Even speaking of "applying effort" (gongfu) is a matter of necessity.

It is like employing soldiers: soldiers are instruments of ill omen, used only when there is no other choice. When the ancients spoke of "investigating Chan" and "raising the *huatou*," they all did so out of necessity.
Although there are many *kōans*, the *huatou* of "examining the reality of Buddha-recitation" (*nianfo*) is the only one.
Within the midst of worldly afflictions, it is extremely easy to gain power. Although it is easy to gain power, it is no more than a tile used for knocking at a door;
in the end, it must be cast away. Nevertheless, one cannot do without using it once.
Now, as you employ this to practice your work, you must have full confidence, rely upon it with stability, and maintain a firm grip. You must by no means waver or hesitate. Do not let it go now.
Today it is like this; tomorrow it is like that. Furthermore, there is the fear of not attaining awakening, and the resentment that things are not as subtle as they should be.
All such calculations and deliberations are obstacles. One must first speak through them so that no doubts or hesitations arise when the time comes.
When one’s practice reaches a point of power, external conditions will no longer enter; yet within the mind, afflictions will arise without cause or reason, whether as desire or...
Thoughts arise erratically; sometimes the mind becomes vexed and distressed, or various obstacles emerge, leading to mental exhaustion and physical fatigue beyond remedy.
This occurs because the seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*) accumulated over immeasurable kalpas within the eighth consciousness are now forced out by the intensity of your practice.
At this point, it is most essential to be clear about this; first, you must recognize them for what they are.
Break through! Penetrate! You must by no means allow yourself to be ensnared by it; you must by no means follow its deceptions;
you must by no means treat it as a substantial reality. Simply rouse your spirit and exert yourself with fierce vigor;
take up the head-word of your fundamental inquiry and, right at the very moment such thoughts arise, pursue them relentlessly. Herein, there has never been anything of mine.
Regarding this matter, ask him: "From where have you come? Ultimately, what is it? You must resolutely seek its ultimate point of resolution.
Pressing him in this way, you will cause even gods and ghosts to weep; they shall vanish their traces and hide their tracks.

You must strive to chase them out and kill them off completely, leaving not even a thread of them behind. By exerting yourself in this manner, you will naturally encounter good news. If for a single thought-moment...

When you have pressed through to the point of breaking through, all delusive thoughts will simultaneously fall away, like the vanishing shadows of flowers in the sky or the subsiding waves of a mirage.
Once this stage is passed, one immediately attains immeasurable serenity and immeasurable mastery; this is the place where the beginner gains strength.
Yet, do not become attached to these wonders. Even when serenity and mastery arise, one must not give rise to a mind of attachment or joy. If...
If one gives rise to a mind of joy, then the demon of joy will attach itself to the mind; this constitutes yet another kind of hindrance.

As for the seeds of the root of craving and habitual tendencies within the *ālaya-vijñāna*, which are firm, deep-seated, and hidden—where the head-word (*huatou*) cannot be applied with force, where contemplation of the mind cannot reach, and where one cannot take action oneself—one must prostrate before the Buddha, recite sutras, and repent. Furthermore, one must practice in secret.
One who maintains the mantra-heart should rely upon the Buddha’s secret mudrās to eliminate [obstacles].

Since all secret mantras are the Vajra Heart-Seals of the Buddhas, when we employ them, it is like grasping a vajra-treasure mallet to crush all things; any object encountered is reduced to mere dust.
The secret instructions on the Heart-Seals of the Buddhas and Patriarchs from antiquity do not transcend this. Therefore, it is said: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions..."

By upholding this mantra-heart, one attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. However, the Buddha spoke clearly that under the gate of the Patriarchs, there is a fear of falling into ordinary sentiments;
therefore, he kept it secret and did not speak of it. This is not because it is of no use. One must have a fixed daily practice for this.
After a long time of thorough cultivation, one gains considerable power; however, one must not seek supernatural responses.

Among those who practice the Way, there are those who attain awakening first and then cultivate, and those who cultivate first and then attain awakening. Yet, within awakening, there is a distinction between intellectual understanding (*jie*) and realized realization (*zheng*).
If one clarifies the mind by relying on the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, it is intellectual understanding; such cases mostly fall into the realm of conceptual knowledge and views.
Regarding all objective conditions, one frequently fails to gain mastery; because the mind and its objects stand in opposition, they cannot be harmoniously integrated.

Encountering every situation, one encounters stagnation, which frequently creates obstacles. This is called "semblance prajñā" and is not true investigation. As for those who have attained realization:
Proceed with sincerity from within your own mind. Press onward until you reach the point where the water ends and the mountains exhaust themselves.
Suddenly, a single thought will cease instantly, and you will thoroughly realize your own mind. It will be like seeing your own father at a crossroads—there will be no further doubt.
Like a person drinking water, the coldness or warmth is known by oneself alone; it cannot be fully expressed to others. This is the truth.
Having attained realization through diligent practice, one then uses that state of awakening to harmonize the mind and its objects.
One purifies the flow of present karma and dissolves deluded thoughts and mental anxieties, fusing them all into the single flavor of the true mind. This is realization.

Furthermore, this realization varies in depth and degree. If one applies effort from the fundamental root and breaks through the habitual molds of the eight consciousnesses, there is a sudden overturning.
The cave of ignorance is entered directly and transcendentally, with no further methods remaining; this is the realization of those with the highest, sharpest faculties, whose attainment is profound.
Others practice gradually, and their attainment is shallow. They most fear being satisfied with a mere trifle; they must strictly avoid falling into the gateway of shadows and reflections.
Why? Because the root of the eight consciousnesses has not yet been shattered; even if there is activity, it is all merely consciousness.
Regarding matters concerning the gods: if one takes this to be the truth, it is very much like mistaking a thief for one's own son. An ancient said:
"The student of the Way does not recognize the Real, simply because they have long been accustomed to recognizing the spirit. For immeasurable kalpas, this has been the root of birth and death;
yet the deluded person recognizes it as their original self. One must pass through this critical juncture above all. As for what is called "sudden enlightenment followed by gradual cultivation":
Thus, one has already attained thorough awakening; however, there remain only habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that have not yet been suddenly purified.

Therefore, regarding all objective conditions and circumstances, one employs the power of contemplative observation based on the principle already realized. By testing the mind through successive encounters with these objects, one succeeds in integrating and harmonizing a portion of the realm of experience.
To realize a portion of the Dharmakāya, to dissolve a portion of delusive thoughts, and to manifest a portion of original wisdom—this depends entirely upon diligent and continuous practice;
it is most effective when cultivated within the midst of sensory objects.

Generally, for those of sharp faculties who possess faith and courageous resolve, if they are willing to apply themselves to practice, the obstacles of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*) are easily removed, while the obstacles of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*) are difficult to dispel.
Within this context, I shall briefly cite one or two such ailments.
First, one must not crave or seek out subtlety. For this matter is fundamentally level and even, solid and plain;
it is of a single, ordinary flavor, with no further subtlety. Thus the ancients said: "Upon awakening, it is the same as when one was unawakened;
it remains simply the person of old, yet it is not the path of conduct of the past. There is no further subtlety; it is simply skillful.
If one were to arrive there, it would naturally be level and real. This is because our habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of intellectual understanding have not yet been purified.

Although internal wisdom (*prajñā*) permeates us, that wisdom is itself permeated by these habitual tendencies, giving rise to various illusory transformations. These produce many clever views that cling tenaciously to the mind.

One might think this is subtle and wondrous, yet it deeply penetrates and does not cease; it is the very essence of the consciousness-spirit, the root of discriminative false vision, also called the "thorn of seeing.
Unlike the coarse and floating deluded thoughts mentioned previously, this is a subtle, continuous flow of arising and ceasing.

It is also called the "obstruction of wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). It is precisely that which hinders right knowledge and vision. If a person takes this to be real, they will give rise to all manner of deluded views;
this is most to be dreaded.
Furthermore, one must not harbor the mind’s expectation of awakening. For the wondrous, perfect, and true mind of us humans is, by its very nature, beyond all dependence.

It was only because of the coagulation of deluded thoughts that the mind and objects, the faculties and their sensory realms, came to stand in opposition to one another; thus, confusion arose and karma was created.
Now, the practitioner need only let go of body, mind, and the world in a single thought-moment, and simply hold this single thought forward with singular focus.
Do not concern yourself at all with whether one attains enlightenment or not. Simply continue practicing step by step, thought after thought.
If your practice reaches its full realization, you will naturally behold your original face; why worry about it prematurely?

If you harbor a mind waiting for enlightenment, that very mind of waiting is itself the root of birth and death. Even if you wait until the end of kalpas, you will still not attain enlightenment, because you have failed to understand.

It is only because one assumes that the absolute, independent true mind exists separately from the relative mind. If this expectation of a separate mind is not eliminated, weariness will easily arise, leading frequently to regression and downfall;
it is like searching for an object and, failing to see it, immediately conceiving the thought of giving up.
Furthermore, one must not seek for a sublime fruit. For the deluded mind of birth and death belonging to sentient beings is, from the very beginning, the essence-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Tathāgata.

Now, while immersed in delusion, they transform the supernatural powers and wondrous functions of all Buddhas into discursive thoughts and emotional anxieties, and into discriminative cognition and views;
they transform the true and pure *dharmakāya* into the physical substance of the karma of birth and death, and transform the pure and wondrous lands into...

Regarding the six sensory objects: if, while practicing now, one suddenly awakens to one's own mind in a single thought-moment, then it is like a great furnace of glowing metal, melting away all phenomena.
This very body, mind, and world are originally the fruition-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Tathāgata;
these very deluded thoughts and mental calculations are originally the wondrous functioning of spiritual powers (*abhijñā*). To change the name does not change the essence. Yongjia said: "No..."

The clarity of true nature is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body. If one can awaken to this Dharma-gate, then the emotions of grasping and rejecting will be forgotten, and the mind of longing and aversion will cease.
Then, at every step, one is in the pure land of the Flower Treasury; at every thought, one is in the descent of Maitreya.
If, while settling the mind, one first seeks a sublime fruit, that very heart of longing becomes the root of birth and death. It obstructs right knowledge and vision;
the more one seeks, the further away one goes. When the strength of seeking is exhausted, weariness arises.
Furthermore, one must not give rise to doubts within oneself. In all practice of the Way, one should consistently set aside body and mind, severing all sights, sounds, cognitions, and perceptions.
One must cast off old habits and look toward the vast, obscure distance ahead, where there is no place to settle the body or establish one's life.

There is no new realization to be gained by advancing, yet one loses their former dwelling by retreating. If one deliberates back and forth, doubt will arise, giving birth to immeasurable calculations and speculations.
If one calculates gain and loss, or gives rise to private conjectures, activating perverse thoughts that obstruct right knowledge and vision, these must be thoroughly investigated and broken through.

Only then will one enter directly with certainty, free from further anxieties. Generally speaking, when one reaches the point where effort can no longer be applied, this is precisely where true power is gained;
if one adds further brilliance here, one will not retreat. Otherwise, one will fall into the demon of sorrow and anxiety.
Next, one must not give rise to a mind of fear. This means that through the urgency of the power of diligent practice, delusive thoughts are suppressed and suddenly cease in a single thought-moment.
Suddenly, body and mind are liberated into emptiness, and one perceives that the great earth has not even an inch of soil remaining, reaching down to the utmost depth.
One will then give rise to great terror; if one does not thoroughly penetrate this state, one will not dare to move forward.

Alternatively, one might mistake this vast emptiness for something superior and sublime. If one clings to this emptiness, one will give rise to a great false view that denies cause and effect, which is the most perilous of all.
Next, one must decisively believe that one’s own mind is the Buddha. Yet, there is no Buddha apart from the Buddha; it is simply the mind itself.

Because the true *dharmakāya* of the Buddha is like empty space, if one realizes that the source of delusion is void, then the originally existing *dharmakāya* will manifest spontaneously—radiant, quiescently illuminating, perfect and all-pervasive, lacking nothing and exceeding nothing. Do not further seek it outwardly with the mind. If...
If you abandon this mind and seek elsewhere, various and immeasurable dream-like states will arise within the mind;

these are merely manifestations of the primary consciousness (*vijñāna*). You must by no means regard them as something extraordinary. For within my pure mind, there is fundamentally not a single thing, nor even a single thought.
Whenever the mind stirs or a thought arises, it immediately deviates from the essence of the Dharma. This is the current practice of *gongfu*.
People generally do not realize that the delusive thoughts of their own minds are fundamentally illusory;

they mistake these delusions for reality and devote themselves solely to opposing them, much like a child playing with the reflection of a lamp—playing on and on, yet ever further removed from the truth.
If one plays with it for too long, one naturally becomes weary and fearful.

Furthermore, there is a class of people who fear discursive thoughts so much that they wish they could seize them by the hand and fling them to one side; yet this is like trying to catch the wind or grasp a shadow.

All day long they wrestle with these thoughts, exhausting all their strength, never finding a single moment of rest. As this entanglement persists for a long time, their faith grows weary; they can do nothing but say:
If one finds that practicing Chan yields no spiritual efficacy, one may give rise to a mind of slander, or a mind of fear, or a mind of regression and falling away;

this is a common ailment among beginners. There is no other reason for this than that they fail to comprehend the eternally abiding true mind and its nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, and instead mistake deluded thoughts for the true nature of reality. Here, one must by all means penetrate through.
[This is] past. If you wish to penetrate this barrier, there is naturally a path that goes beyond;

you need only investigate apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and seek apart from the realm of deluded thoughts. Whenever a single thought arises—whether good or evil—discard it immediately.
Do not engage in opposition with it. Have deep conviction that within your own mind, such things do not fundamentally exist. Simply take this fundamental...
Investigate the *huatou*. Exert yourself and hold it up with force, like a vajra sword that strikes down both demons and Buddhas alike.

In this matter, one requires the greatest power of courage, the greatest power of diligence, and the greatest power of endurance. By no means should you deliberate over past or future; by no means should you yield to weakness.
Simply maintain a direct mind and right mindfulness, stepping forward with resolve; naturally, you will become majestic and dignified.

When one is no longer entangled by such delusive thoughts—like a hawk released from its leather tether—one naturally ceases to be obstructed by any objective conditions throughout the six periods of day and night.
One naturally attains great pliancy and great mastery; this is the point where the initial practitioner gains power through the first step of their practice.
The foregoing points are much like painting legs on a snake; they are merely provisional expressions for a specific occasion.

They are fundamentally not ultimate, nor are they the true Dharma. This is because, while still on the road, one fears that taking even a single step outside will lead one astray onto divergent paths.

It is a waste of mental effort and a vain loss of time. One must necessarily find a truly authentic gateway that transcends the path of wondrous adornment—what is known as walking with steady and upright steps, swift as the wind.
The progress made by such practice can increase ten-thousandfold from day to day.
Ultimately, the supreme path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs does not involve traversing stages; it lies within the skillful means of the beginner's mind.
One must also penetrate through this very point before it can be attained.
To the Zen student Wusheng Lu (spoken at the monastery on a summer day in the year of Yiwei):
When ancient worthies first resolved their minds, they did so solely for the great matter of birth and death; with a firm determination to transcend them, they severed all attachments.

He took leave of his parents, went to attend upon masters and visit friends, and underwent every kind of hardship. From moment to moment, his every thought was solely for the sake of the matter beneath his own feet which he had not yet clarified;
his grief and sorrow were so intense that it was as if he had lost both his father and mother. Yet, upon meeting a true teacher, he was like an infant finding its mother.
If one could obtain even a single word or half-phrase to open and guide the ground of the mind, it would be like a sick person obtaining medicine.
If for a single thought-moment there is resonance and one attains realization within the breast, it would be like a poor person obtaining treasure.

Even if one must cast aside body and life to engage in humble, submerged labor, one never tires of the toil—just as the Second Patriarch cut off his arm to settle his mind, the Sixth Patriarch dropped his waist-belt and carried stones, and Baizhang took up manual labor. Yang...

Among those who have served the assembly at Mount Qi, all whose names are recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp) and whose light illuminates the ages for a thousand generations have come from amidst bitter struggle and austerity.
Even the Buddhas of the past, in their quest for unsurpassed Bodhi, sacrificed their bodies and lives as numerous as motes of dust;
there was not one type of existence they did not undergo, nor a single body in which they did not practice asceticism. Having cultivated the causes for ten billion kalpas, they thus moved Heaven.

Superior men have received immeasurable offerings, such that even in the age of the final dharma (mofa), their descendants shall still enjoy one portion of the merit within the light of the *ūrṇā-kośa* without exhaustion.
How could there be a Maitreya born by nature or a Śākyamuni appearing spontaneously? Alas, I deeply lament the age of the final dharma;
the time since the Sage has passed, and the disciplinary statutes of the Dharma-gate have already been swept away. We who have left the household life—[how can we remain idle?]...

Having reached the end of my life, what have I known? Since birth, I knew only to fear hunger and cold and sought only fullness and warmth. Once I entered the Gate of Emptiness, I merely followed worldly habits;
I spent all day in idle chatter, laughing heartily and indulging my passions, vainly letting the six sense organs run wild and committing every kind of evil.

Without plowing, I ate fine food; without raising silkworms, I wore fine clothing. I consumed the offerings of the faithful in vain and let my precious time go to waste, ultimately knowing nothing at all.
From where does birth come? To where does death go? How could one fail to know that cause and effect are difficult to evade, and that retribution for sins and blessings never fails?
When the great limit of one’s life arrives all at once, it is like a stone cast into water. The agonizing sufferings of the three paths are five thousandfold in a single lifetime;

even if one were to emerge from them again, who knows when another day would dawn? To speak of this with rising emotion is painful and most lamentable. Observing the currents of the times, they flow on and on, all alike.

This is so. When we look for those among us who practice [the Way], it is like sifting through sand to find gold; it is not that they are entirely non-existent, but rather that they are exceedingly rare.

Alas! Within the prison of the three realms and the shackles of the four modes of birth, scorched by the great conflagration and dwelling in the perilous house of birth and death, by what means can one moisten the fierce flames and depart from all suffering to reach the place of ultimate fearlessness?
It is not possible unless one is a man of noble character, possessing the spiritual root and harboring...
As for those with "morning bones," they are unable to exert fierce courage and leap directly forward in a single bound. You, however, have fortunately been born during the era of the Buddha-Dharma;
your bodies are clothed in the *kāṣāya*, you have early encountered an enlightened teacher, and your six sense-faculties are fully intact.

If you do not take the impermanence of life to heart and deeply contemplate this great matter—contemplating the sufferings of hell, giving rise to the bodhicitta, reforming the past and cultivating the future, and practicing with diligence day and night—you will [fail to achieve liberation]. Early [in your practice],...
Seeking liberation, you merely pass the days by habit, letting your body and mind run wild. When the great limit of your life arrives, what can you do to remedy your regrets?
Alas, as you go forth, do not forget my words of earnest exhortation at this parting; do not fail me, for that would be failing your own self-responsibility.
While traveling to Leyang by boat, I showed this to the attendant Qichi.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs teach people to suddenly realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) amidst birth and death;

yet they often lament that within this state of non-arising, one falsely perceives arising and ceasing. These words are like telling a dream to a person in the marketplace—the listener does not fail to understand them clearly.

Their eyes were wide open and their courage was undaunted; yet they had merely not realized the Truth. In essence, what they spoke was not what they had heard, and what they had heard was not what they had seen.
That the ancients prized actual realization was simply because they wished to intimately penetrate and break through the phenomena of birth and death.
It is not that there is some other extraordinary place; rather, I have often seen children who fear ghosts. Whenever they walk at night, a vague form follows them, causing them great terror.
Even when a compassionate mother tries to reassure them with skillful words that no such thing exists, the child still does not believe her.
One must wait until they have attained self-confidence and are free from doubt before ceasing [the practice].

If one has truly reached a state of non-doubt, even if one were to feign being terrified by ghosts, it would be dismissed with a single laugh. In the past, while traveling on the frontier, I was riding a horse at night together with some soldiers.
By the side of the road there was a stone. Suddenly, the horse saw it and was greatly startled, nearly falling to the ground.

"Born! All at once, they directed light from the tip of a single hair of the old man’s body, shaking the earth.
