If it is perilous, one falls. Can-can-can (Dongwen initially took Tiezui Lanfeng as his teacher; this refers to Lanfeng, who was called Shuilao He).
To establish a *śrāvaka* society for the recitation of the Buddha’s name:
Only our Buddha dwells in the world, preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings. The fourfold assembly has each attained liberation;

according to their capacities, he teaches and transforms them, employing various skillful means to cause all to obtain benefit. It is like a timely rain, which leaves no "three grasses and two trees" that does not receive its nourishment.
Moistening them, they are each sufficiently satisfied and allowed to grow according to their capacity. Thus, while phenomena differ in a thousand ways, their source is not of two kinds.
Yet, when one observes sentient beings through the lens of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), there is not a single being who cannot be saved.

When one observes Buddha-nature through the lens of one's own mind, there is not a single person who cannot practice. It is only that sentient beings are deluded by themselves and do not realize this; furthermore, they lack...
Because they were not guided by true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), they willingly fell into the depths of saṃsāra and suffered in vain.
Thus, when the Patriarch Lu first arrived at Huangmei, he was asked, "Where are you from? He replied, "I am a man from Lingnan.
Huangmei asked, "Do even barbarians possess Buddha-nature? The Patriarch said, "People have north and south, but how could Buddha-nature be dual? From this single statement, [the truth was revealed].
Like thunder startling the hibernating masses, [the teachings] were disseminated among humanity; yet those who knew them were rare, and those who awakened to them were few.
Thus, Lingnan became the source of the Chan Way and the Buddha-dharma.

Since the time the Patriarch Lu evolved this teaching and its Way covered the Central Plains, the very gateway to it has remained buried in wild weeds for nearly a thousand years. Those who discuss this all claim it was not good.

This is merely because they have not yet penetrated the meaning of Buddha-nature. I, having received the imperial grace to be dispatched to Lei Yang, arrived in Wuyang during the spring of the Bingshen year and stayed until autumn.
There, amidst the military encampments, I completed my commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
In the summer of the Wuxu year, I expounded it for the disciples who had come to me. In every session, I saw many sons of good family arriving tirelessly; as for me—
I deeply admired this. Before long, some ten virtuous gentlemen prostrated themselves and requested instruction in the method for receiving the five precepts of an upāsaka.

I joyfully accepted their request and immediately performed the *karmavācanā* ceremony for them. From then on, they turned their hearts toward the Way with daily sincerity, and their listening to the Dharma became even more earnest.
Grieved that they had not yet attained awakening and pitying that they did not understand the methods for advancing in practice and attaining self-liberation, I therefore bestowed upon them...

Regarding the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation, he taught that one should focus the mind on pure karma, feel a profound weariness toward the conditions of suffering, and turn toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss with the hope of meeting [the Buddha] monthly.
He established formal regulations, taking the practice of reciting the name, performing prostrations, and repenting at the three times of day as his conduct.

This was intended to ensure that faith becomes daily more sincere and karmic obstructions daily diminish; one must take rebirth there as a vow. If one can truly follow this path, even while remaining amidst the dust of the world...
How diligent! One may truly say that such a person’s life was not lived in vain and their death was not met with empty passing.

Is this not indeed genuine spiritual practice? Now, "Buddha" means awakening; it is the Buddha-nature inherent within sentient beings. Through delusion one becomes a sentient being, but through awakening, one is called a Buddha.
The Buddha one now contemplates is none other than the Amitābha of one's own nature (svabhāva); the Pure Land one seeks is none other than the ultimate realm of the mind-only (cittamātra).
How joyful! If people can simply maintain this mindfulness without forgetting, then Amitābha will appear in every thought-moment and the Land of Ultimate Bliss will be their home with every step.
Why, then, must they look far beyond ten trillion lands for a separate pure land to which they may return?
Therefore it is said: "If the mind is pure, the land is also pure; if the mind is defiled, the land is also defiled.

Thus, when a single thought of an evil mind arises, the forest of swords and trees of blades appear all at once; when a single thought of a virtuous mind arises, the jeweled ground and lotus ponds manifest clearly.
How could heaven and hell possibly exist outside of this mind? O sons of good family, each of you should contemplate this with earnest attention. You ought to...
Reflect deeply upon the gravity of birth and death. Impermanence is swift; once one loses this human form, it is difficult to regain it for ten thousand kalpas.

Days and months flow like a stream; time cannot be waited for. Should you neglect this favorable opportunity, you will miss it face-to-face. When the great limit arrives, what can be done to remedy regret?
Each of you should strive diligently. Cherish this, cherish this!
To show the true meeting with the Chan practitioner:
the Chan practitioner Zhenyu was born and raised in Luling. He abandoned his wife and children to leave the household life, delighting in the practice of seclusion.

With his aspirations set upon famous mountains, he traveled to visit spiritual teachers. Through the illusory karma of a phantom man, he was led by error to the southern hills and seas, where the Chan practitioner was thus able to come.
[The Master] said: "I recently took my leave to travel to Putuo Mountain to pay homage to Master Daguan, who bestowed upon me the verse of Vipaśyin Buddha. I have now brought it back to Wuyang.
Within this field of illusory transformation, I, the illusory man, perform illusory Buddhist services to awaken the illusory multitudes by preaching the Dharma-gate of illusion.
When the practitioners of Chan prostrated themselves and requested further instruction, I, the illusory man, relying upon the Illusory Samādhi, preached for them the One [Dharma]."
All phenomena are entirely like the realm of illusions and dreams; thus he revealed and taught: "Excellent, Son of the Buddha!
You should contemplate this well: all Buddhas manifest by the power of illusion; all Bodhisattvas practice by the power of illusion;
all followers of the Two Vehicles attain tranquility by the power of illusion; and all non-Buddhists [proceed] by the power of illusion."
Unconsciousness. All sentient beings undergo birth and death by the power of illusion (*māyā*). Whether it be celestial palaces or pure lands, they are established by the power of illusion.
Jade groves and jeweled trees flourish by the power of illusion. Iron beds and bronze pillars are arranged by the power of illusion.
Cauldrons of boiling water and furnaces of burning coals seethe by the power of illusion. Scales, shells, feathers, and fur likewise [arise] by the power of illusion.
Whether flying or潜 (submerged), they rely on the power of illusion; whether wriggling or soaring, they move and rest according to the power of illusion.
This encompasses all that the Buddhas of the three periods have realized and the Patriarchs of the six generations have transmitted—it does not go beyond this net of illusion.
How can a practitioner of samādhi and dhyāna escape it? You should reflect carefully: by what cause do you fall into birth and death? By what cause do you enter [into it]?
The mother’s womb. For what reason does one sink and drown within the entanglements of craving? For what reason does one vow to emerge from this submerged delusion?
For what reason does one set foot upon the path to transcend the mundane world? For what reason does one visit spiritual teachers and sages?

For what reason does one tread upon famous mountains and ascend blessed lands, penetrating the monastic groves and entering the protective communities? This year one goes to the South Sea; the next year to Mount Wutai; the following year to Mount Emei.

"You shall travel throughout the entire world; even if you pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, exhausting all the lands within the ten directions and serving all the great spiritual friends of the ten directions, none of these will transcend the gateway of illusion and transformation. This is not the ultimate, true state.
Nevertheless, though it is so, this is called 'mistaking the head for its reflection,' rather than 'seeking one's home along the path. If you can but..."
When one treads upon and severs the knots of illusion, the boundless web of illusion is instantly and completely rent asunder;

the shoreless ocean of illusion is instantly and completely dried up; immeasurable karmic illusions are instantly and completely extinguished; boundless illusory practices are instantly and completely attained;
and immeasurable illusory births are instantly and completely transcended. This is what is called "using illusion to cultivate illusion," namely, the illusory mind of sentient beings.
This refers to one who returns to and relies upon the extinction of illusion.

Should this not be the case, then even if you pass through three lives and sixty kalpas, with Mañjuśrī as father, Avalokiteśvara as mother, and Samantabhadra as teacher, and wish to rely on these karmic affinities to seek liberation from birth and death—such a goal remains exceedingly remote.
Reflect deeply; do not think of me as an illusory person, for I am not.
These are words of truth. Consider, consider!
To show that the upāsaka Yi-jin-tam possesses the roots of goodness of Buddha-nature:
it is like seeds sown in the earth; wherever there is soil, they are not absent. If they encounter the proper time...
Rain falls, and there is nothing that does not sprout. Yet, because rain falls at different times, the growth occurs sooner or later. Every person possesses the seeds of the roots of goodness;

if they encounter a great spiritual friend (*mahā-kalyāṇamitra*) who provides guidance, like the falling of timely rain, then the sprouts will suddenly emerge, sending up stalks and long trunks, flowering and bearing fruit—there are few who do not achieve success. As it is said: "When sentient beings come to sow the seeds..."
The fruit arises from the ground; there has never been a case where a fruit was summoned without a cause.

This, following the teaching gate of the Buddhas and Patriarchs above, values observing the faculties and meeting the capacities [of beings] to skillfully provide guidance, so that their own nature may reach maturity.
There is no separate dharma used to boast to sentient beings. To change the virtuous land for the True Pond, one is born in a borderland and raised amidst the dust.

I am exhausted; my mouth and body are incessantly occupied with toil, leaving no leisure. How could I have found the heart to set my mind on transcending the world? I reflect deeply on how great is the matter of birth and death.

Were it not for the fact that the roots of goodness planted in past lives were profound and deep, such that they welled up spontaneously within me until I could not help but act—how could it be that upon encountering conditions, this awakening would arise so suddenly, capable of being thus without waiting for instruction?
When I was first exiled to Leiyang and had not yet crossed the mountain ridges...
Those who speak say that the customs of the borderlands favor ghosts and involve the consumption of blood and flesh, and that there are no virtuous people at all.

Furthermore, according to the words of the Buddha, these border regions are lowly and base, classified as the Mleccha caste among the "six difficulties," because they sever the lineage of the Buddha, destroy the roots of goodness, and do not hear the names of the Triple Gem.
I believe this to be true. Recently, while passing through Dianbai, I saw Tan Xie...

A group of several virtuous gentlemen prostrated themselves with their heads at my feet; I found this most extraordinary. Upon crossing Kuting Ling, they cleared away the thatched brush to establish a tea station for the sake of creating karmic affinity.
This was the first instance of a Buddhist service being initiated at Gaitan, performed by gathering the faithful to carry it out.
Since this was done spontaneously without prior guidance, could it not be that their roots of goodness were fully ripened and the conditions of time and circumstance had already arrived? There was.

It cannot be restrained by itself; it manifests in every encounter and comes into being through conditions. Viewed from this perspective, the Buddha-nature is not necessarily entirely good, nor is the demonic nature necessarily entirely evil;

they differ only according to what one has habituated oneself to. When the Buddha spoke of the "evil seeds" of the borderlands, he was referring to those who are most heavily burdened by such tendencies.
His intent was to inspire people toward right faith, so that they might be born in the Central Kingdom and hear the True Dharma.

For this reason, I observed that Tan was pure, sincere, and profoundly faithful; his establishment of these virtuous conditions sufficiently demonstrates the vastness of the Buddha-dharma, which does not find it difficult to be practiced even in remote regions.
Thus, I composed this preface and charged Tan, together with two or three virtuous friends, to act with one heart and single effort.
Indeed, within one year the work was completed, and within three years the transformation was spread. Even today, throughout the foreign lands, travelers everywhere perform Buddhist rites.
To transform the realm of Māra and establish the realm of Buddhahood—this will surely not fail to be initiated by a single person or a single event.
From a single line of darkness comes the solid ice; from a single line of yang comes the blazing sun. Such is the mechanism of cosmic transformation (*zaohua*);

such too is the mechanism of the transformation of the Way (*daohua*). The Buddha said: "Where there is no Buddha-dharma, one must establish the Triple Gem (*triratna*); none but a Bodhisattva can do this."
"Kecheng. In Sanskrit, this is *bodhisattva*; here it means "a being of great resolve. Is Master Tan not indeed a being of great resolve?

If he progresses from this point, with his faith never regressing, his roots of goodness deepening further, and through courageous diligence suddenly awakening to his original mind, he will forever sever birth and death and leap directly to the other shore of Bodhi—perhaps even starting from this very day.
Taking one step outside the door is the first stage (*bhūmi*). If you simply possess the resolute mind of "willingness," you will certainly not be deceived. Strive on!
This was shown to the Zen practitioner Jin Gui.

As a precious person, you have made it your heart's purpose to protect the Buddha-Dharma; you have already transcribed the *Lotus Sūtra* and other scriptures in golden letters and are now soliciting [donations].
The two sacred images of Śākyamuni and Amitābha, carved from sandalwood, were completed and enshrined at Dinghu in Duanzhou.

At that time, [the donor] traveled back and forth between Wuyang, where he prostrated and requested further instruction. I showed him this: "Our Buddha has said: 'All phenomena arise from conditions; all phenomena cease from conditions.
Thus we know that all phenomena arise through the convergence of conditions. Since they arise through the convergence of conditions, they have no inherent nature..."
That which has arisen does not exist; that which has not yet arisen does not exist. Thus, although things appear to exist, their nature is eternally empty of itself.
Since their nature is empty, all dharmas are fundamentally without self-nature. Therefore it is said: "Knowing that dharmas are eternally without nature, the Buddha-seed arises from conditions.

One who can penetrate this lack of nature within dependent origination possesses the true seed for attaining Buddhahood. Excellent, O Son of the Buddha! As for those various [dharmas] you have written down...
The *sūtra* is the Dharma. The Jātaka of the Sandalwood Tathāgata is the Buddha.
Taking your power of faith as the cause and relying upon various manifestations as the conditions, the Buddha thus arises from conditions, and the Dharma likewise arises from conditions.
Within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the Dharma is the Buddha, and the Buddha is the Dharma. However, I do not know whether you have realized that this nature of phenomena is empty.

Is its nature not empty? If one were to say its nature is empty, then why is it that we presently behold the Buddha’s marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana), adorned and magnificent, with ultimate radiance blazing forth like a mountain of jewels?

Furthermore, the eighty-one fascicles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—the numinous text comprising thirty-nine chapters in their sequential order, the unfolding of the five cycles of cause and effect, and the majestic array of the forty-two stages—are all present without deficiency.
A single character. In the three cycles of prophecy in the *Lotus Sūtra*, and in the various names of the Buddhas in the ritual of repentance, there is not a single person who is not included;
they fill the eyes with brilliance, manifesting in full splendor. Can it be said that their nature is empty and devoid of substance?

If one were to say their nature is not empty, then at the moment when conditions assemble, the paper remains paper, the ink remains ink, and the gold remains gold—yet the incense [is likewise present].
Incense from itself; likewise, paper and ink are all distributed according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Such golden incense is all an adornment of evil karma.
From where, then, does the name of the Buddha-dharma arise? If one seeks its origin, it is fundamentally non-existent, and thus its nature is inherently empty.
Yet, when the present conditions now assemble, one takes this very golden incense of conventional truth and regards it as the Buddha.

Thus, using the paper and ink of the worldly convention to produce the sutras, the characteristics of the paper and ink do not differ from those of that time, nor does their substance increase compared to days of old.
Yet, once the name of the Buddha-dharma has become manifest, the distinction between reverence and arrogance becomes vast and profound.

Although the people who assisted in its production did not change from their former ways, the difference between their virtuous and evil karmic conditions is as great as that between heaven and abyss. For this reason:
Upon observation, it is clear that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are fundamentally without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), arising only through the convergence of conditions.
Thus, if one can realize that this Buddha and this Dharma are fundamentally without intrinsic nature, this constitutes the true seed for attaining Buddhahood.
Yet, as for the various excellent conditions you have cultivated, do you practice them while failing to realize their lack of intrinsic nature, or do you practice them without such realization?
Is it through action? Or does one attain the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) only after having acted?

If one acts while realizing the absence of intrinsic nature, then the Buddha-dharma resides within oneself and not in external things. If one acts without realizing the absence of intrinsic nature, then the Buddha-dharma resides in external things and not in oneself.
If one realizes the absence of intrinsic nature only after acting, then both self and things are equally devoid of intrinsic nature. To realize the self...
If there is no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), then there is no person who acts. When one realizes that phenomena lack intrinsic nature, then there are no phenomena that are acted upon.
When both person and phenomenon are empty, and right and wrong are equally extinguished, then both self and objects leave no trace. Furthermore, from what could they be distinguished?
In this way, merit is inconceivable, and Bodhi is also inconceivable. O Son of the Buddha, it is like...
To know in this way is true knowledge; to act in this way is sublime practice.
Otherwise, to perform inconceivable Buddha-activities with a conceptualizing mind is like grasping a firefly in one’s hand and attempting to burn Mount Sumeru—it only increases one's own exhaustion;
how could it ever lead to ultimate realization? Excellent, Son of the Buddha! Contemplate carefully the Dharma of the Dharma King. The Dharma King...
The Dharma is thus; it should be practiced thus, and it should be maintained thus. This may be called "skillfully transcending all realms of existence.
To the Chan practitioner Fa-jin, who said of himself that his nature was habitually prone to anger, the Old Man used skillful means to subdue him and showed him this.
Regarding the Dharma-gate of patience (*kṣānti*), he further instructed him, saying: "The Great Master Yongjia once said: 'My teacher met Dīpaṃkara Buddha;
throughout many kalpas, he was once the Immortal of Patience. From this we know that the single practice of patience is the foremost and most wondrous practice for attaining Buddhahood.
Therefore, my teacher, Śākyamuni, in life after life, served as Devadatta."

Devadatta was slandered and harmed by many; even in this present life, he committed every kind of violation of the Dharma, reaching such extremes that he did not refrain from taking human life on more than one occasion.
Yet, at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Buddha bestowed upon him the prediction of his future Buddhahood, saying:
"My thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, as well as my supreme and wondrous merits, all derive from Devadatta."

This is accomplished by virtue of having many spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Is it not, therefore, that the single practice of patience (*kṣānti*) is the essential practice for attaining Buddhahood?

Furthermore, it is said: "In the past, when King Kali cut and mangled my body, at that time I had no perception of a self (*ātman*), no perception of a person (*pudgala*), no perception of a sentient being (*sattva*), and no perception of a life-span (*jīva*). If there were perceptions of a self, a person, a sentient being..."
If one perceives the mark of birth or the mark of a life-span, Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon me.

Viewed from this perspective, all the instruments of birth-and-death suffering for sentient beings are, through the presence of a self, transformed into unsurpassed bodhi, adorned with merit and wisdom.
All arrive at this state through the absence of self. Because the self and external objects are treated as adversaries, right and wrong arise.
When right and wrong arise, love and hatred are established. When love and hatred are established, joy and anger flourish. When one's fundamental nature becomes turbid, the mind-ground grows dark.

When the mind-ground is dark, all evils increase. When all evils increase, the multitude of sufferings accumulates. When the multitude of sufferings accumulates, birth and death are prolonged. All of these—
"This is due to what I have brought about. How grave is the harm I have caused! It is like a fortified city with sturdy troops;
how could it be easily broken? Laozi said: 'The supple overcomes the rigid; the weak overcomes the strong. This is precisely the initial stage of the practice of forbearance."
Sentient beings rely upon their view of a self so firmly that it is difficult to shatter. Consequently, they cannot accept a single word of opposition;
they cannot remain at ease when confronted by a single adverse circumstance; they cannot endure even a moment of hunger or cold; and they cannot purify themselves from a single thought of desire.
All of this stems from not knowing the method of practicing patience, resulting only in the further increase of attachment to the view of a self. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching...

The disciples cultivate the practice of harmony. It is further said: "The patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna).

It is also said: "The patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is attained only at the eighth stage. Thus we know that from the patience regarding the arising of dharmas, one endures until reaching the patience regarding their non-arising;

thereby, wondrous practice becomes perfected and the fruit of Buddhahood is realized. How could this single practice of patience be anything but profound? Therefore it is said: "In all that you do, you should always exercise patience."
Thus, in every instance where the mind is raised or a thought stirs, one tests it with patience; in every instance where a foot is lifted or a step taken, one precedes it with patience;
in every instance of turning, moving, or gesturing, one sustains it with patience; and in every instance of joy, anger, grief, or pleasure, one examines it with patience.
In this way, the mind will not dare to move recklessly, the body will not dare to act recklessly, and one will not dare to engage in affairs recklessly.
There are those who dare not speak rashly; thus Laozi said, "One dares not take precedence over the world.
"Dare not" is another name for forbearance (*kṣānti*). Because one dares not take precedence over the world, forbearance is the foremost practice for attaining Buddhahood.
In this way, forbearance is great while the self is small; therefore, forbearance can clothe both oneself and all other beings. From here on...
There is no virtue for benefiting oneself and others that surpasses this. Therefore it is said: "The gentle and patient robe. This is precisely what is meant.
Since this Zen practitioner requested a discourse on the Dharma, I have titled it: "Patience as a Robe. May the Zen practitioner strive to practice it accordingly.
It is not for the purpose of serving as mere idle talk, nor is it for the sake of gaining a livelihood through it.

A Dharma Talk to Reveal the Nature for the Zen Practitioner Chun:
If one discusses this matter, it is like the bright sun in a clear blue sky; it is right there on the crossroads and the streets of Chang’an, where people come and go constantly.

Come! Who does not behold it face-to-face? How could there ever have been even a hair’s breadth of concealment? It is like the bright sun shining in the sky: the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the grasses, trees, insects, and animals;
the scaly, the shelled, the feathered, and the finned; all that flies, hides, moves, or grows—who among them does not universally partake of its benefit?
Even those born blind, though they have never seen it from the start, have nonetheless never failed to receive its advantage. Why should this alone be so?
Within your own portion, there is deficiency and obscurity.

Furthermore, you have exhausted yourself with the cost of straw sandals, climbing mountains and wading through waters, traveling vast distances to seek teachers and find companions, seeking them only in deep mountains and remote valleys before finally finding them.
It is simply that you do not understand for yourself; you must cut off the life-root at the very step beneath your heels. You have been...

For immeasurable kalpas, one has been toyed with by the habitual tendencies of various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). This is like the appearance of a person bewitched by a ghost during the day:
with eyes wide open, one utters senseless ravings toward others, not knowing from where they originate nor by whom they are being instigated.
Day and night, one remains submerged and entangled, drifting along with the waves and currents.
Through kalpa after kalpa, one knows not what deeds have been committed, nor does one know who one originally was.
When a sudden awakening occurs in a dream, one feels a profound sense of shame;

one even wrings one's hands, stamps one's feet, grinds one's teeth, and beats one's breast, lamenting that one cannot leap from the earth onto the crown of the Buddha’s head. And so it is when one encounters...
When the objective realm encounters conditions, in the blink of an eye, one unconsciously falls into the ghost-cave of the black mountains.

This is a universal malady among those throughout the world who are determined to study the Way; it is not unique to practitioners of Chan alone. However, the root of this illness lies precisely in failing to understand one's own mind;
one is merely being toyed with by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Throughout my life, I have been determined to address this very matter.
This is a momentous matter. I regret that my affinity for Prajñā is shallow and my habitual tendencies are particularly thick.
Furthermore, I lack the forge of a truly enlightened spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) like those of antiquity.

Since I first resolved to leave the household life and have practiced the Way with determination—right up until entering the mountains amidst ice, snow, and cold crags, reaching points where death and life hung by a thread—I have encountered all manner of skillful means and intellectual understandings therein.

Previously, not even a hair’s breadth of effort was of any use; it was only while lying on a cold floor with my head covered by a blanket that I suddenly glimpsed a trace of reality from before the birth of my parents.
Thereupon, I looked back upon all the various delusions of the past.
All these are merely matters within a dream. Furthermore, I reproach myself for being led astray by the karmic conditions of others, falling into various illusory realms.
Having nearly faced ten thousand deaths, I have secured this one life; it is thanks to a single point of solitary light won amidst freezing hunger that I may enjoy its benefits everywhere.
I take all manner of favorable and adverse circumstances as a furnace and a pair of tongs to smelt [my mind].

It is merely the refinement of habitual tendencies, a coarse and heavy shadowy dust that serves as an object of perception. As for the critical juncture of birth and death right now, one does not yet know what it will be like;

as for Chan, the Way, and the Buddha-dharma, one may not necessarily be able to comprehend them. However, when one truly gains faith in one's own mind and seeks not even a single point from others—this is the essential matter.
To take this as a means for passing the years—what else could one possibly say? Disciple, you shall depart now;
yet you still seek the old man’s Dharma words, like searching for Chang’an inside the Han-yuan Palace.
If you can understand it before your own feet have even moved a single step—if you can pick it up and put it down, even in the midst of daily life—[then you have found it].
When seeing forms and hearing sounds, even before the eyes have opened or the ears have been reached, one is already able to personally engage them through the ear and discern them with the eye.

One will certainly not head back into the nest of birth and death, nor wallow in the ranks of habitual tendencies, emerging and submerging therein. This is what is meant by "not traversing the journey."
A single step has already transcended [all bounds]; thus, even Buddhas and Patriarchs have no place to touch upon him. How could Old Man Yan possibly prevail against such a person?

Only by being thus can one not fail the grace of Xuelang’s guidance, nor fail the single seed brought forth through hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, remaining uncorrupted and unsullied by the habitual tendencies of the three poisons. Nor does one fail...
Today this old man shall vent his anger on your behalf amidst the field of spears and halberds.

If you do not yet realize this, then even if you were to master the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, what further benefit would there be? It would be like those people of old who, though they could clothe themselves and eat their fill, remained mere men.
What kind of person would you call him? This is precisely what the old man says today: it is like a wooden man wearing leather boots, or a stone woman wearing a hat.
An ancient said: "Traveling on foot in early autumn—each of you must go to a place ten thousand *li* away where there is not even an inch of grass.
But tell me, what is this place where there is an inch of grass? Study! Study! Study!

I show Master Miaozhan that those who left the household life since ancient times did so fundamentally for the great matter of birth and death. Even the appearance of Buddhas and patriarchs in the world was solely for the purpose of revealing this very matter;
there is no Buddha-dharma apart from birth and death, nor is there anything outside of the Buddha-dharma.
There is a distinct matter of birth and death. That is to say, if one is deluded, birth and death begin; if one awakens, saṃsāra ceases.

Thus we know that when the ancients sought through inquiry, they did so only at the very threshold of birth and death, seeking the essential point and the ultimate realization; it was not apart from this.
One should regard this as a marvelous matter, distinct from the three vehicles and twelve teachings of paper, ink, and written words.
This is why Bodhidharma came from the West not to establish written texts, but solely to bring about the awakening to one’s own mind;

for this mind is the fundamental basis of the ten realms of all holy ones and ordinary beings, including both their primary and secondary environments. To fully awaken to this mind is to become a supreme sage of the Mahāyāna.
To awaken slightly is to become a follower of the Two Vehicles; not to awaken is to remain an ordinary person.

If one awakens yet does not cling to it, and realizes yet has no attainment, this is the upward path that transcends both sage and ordinary person, and gives birth beyond birth-and-death. In recent times, students have moved further and further away from the sages;
they do not see the true practice of the ancients regarding the present conditions of daily life, nor do they face [the reality of] birth and death.
Each and every thing at the edge of the shore is penetrated; this is the very practice of daily life.

Not departing from a single dharma, yet not abiding in a single dharma—never lightly letting anything pass by in any situation—is the true and earnest work. This is precisely the case regarding all sounds and forms, favorable or adverse, currently before one’s eyes.
When one thoroughly penetrates every single instance within the realm of love and hatred, that very point of penetration is the gate of true awakening.
At this very place of awakening, every phenomenon and every dharma is the true Buddha-dharma.

It is not something that occurs only when listening to a master strike the bell or beat the drum, ascending the flowered seat to open a great mouth and mimic the howling of a jackal, or when tilting the ears, bowing the head, closing the eyes, and donning the robes. It is precisely at those times that it becomes so.

This is the Dharma of the Buddha. For this reason, the youth Sudhana traveled south through a hundred cities, visiting and paying homage to as many spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) as there are atoms in a buddha-field, thereby attaining awakening to the gates of liberation within every atom and every field.
Now, setting aside the gates of the Dharma for a moment, how could there possibly be so many spiritual friends as there are atoms in a field? One must realize that the "field" (kṣetra)...
"Every dust mote of every world-system" refers to the deluded thoughts, conceptualizations, and emotional objects that constitute our daily lives. If one can,
within the very moments of daily life when the mind stirs, at the points where the faculties of emotion are firmly bound, where love and hatred intersect and are difficult to untangle,
and where the various habitual tendencies of greed, anger, ignorance, and pride are hard to dissolve— there, one must apply the awl to the very core of the painful root, point by point.
Thoroughly investigate and penetrate each and every point; such is true knowledge.
In this very moment, one ascends the unsurpassed Dharma-gate of unimpeded and sovereign great liberation. Apart from this, what other knowledge remains to be investigated?
What further extraordinary Dharma-gate remains to be entered?
