The mountain remains eternally constant. At that time, every pore of his body was filled with a radiant and joyful serenity, like the hundred grasses sprouting in spring;

he himself did not know why this was so. Later, upon examining the teachings of the scriptures and attaining印证 (confirmation), he realized it was merely habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) arising spontaneously within him, which had permeated him without his own awareness.
Since then, as he has wandered among the clouds and waters of pilgrimage, this [state] has been as vast as the sea and as open as the sky.
The realm of empty clarity and vast brightness is, from time to time, like a great round mirror suspended between the eyebrows and eyelashes.

Recently, however, I was toyed with by illusory karma and rushed directly to the miasmic regions. Traveling by boat, I passed the mouth of Caoxi, descended the Zhiyang Gorge, traversed Little Gold Mountain, and arrived at Yangcheng.
Having had no leisure for climbing or gazing, it was only on an autumn day in the year Wuxu that I was finally able to behold its splendors. Together with...
When Master Jingxin passed through Dongpo Hall and read the poem concerning his recognition of a former life, he again felt a sudden sense of loss, as if suddenly beholding an old acquaintance.
Thus one knows that heaven and earth are a single illusory vessel, the myriad dharmas are a single illusory thicket, appearances and disappearances are a single illusory trace,
birth and death are a single illusory arena, mountains and rivers are a single illusory scene, and scales, shells, feathers, and fur are a single illusory thing— saints and ordinary beings alike.

We are but a single illusory assembly; you and I have merely met as illusions. You, Venerable Sir, have subdued your mind through the pure Dharma and recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily as your fixed practice.
Your former defilements have been instantly removed and the light of your mind gradually brightens. This is because you are willing to scrub away the grime and polish the luster;
you are not like those who drift aimlessly upon the ocean of karma. Recently, you brought this scroll seeking a Dharma discourse to serve as a support for your further cultivation.
The old man vividly recalled his past journey to Haimen; seeing Dongpo here today was as if seeing his former self.

He sighed over how the birth and death of human life are illusory transformations, coming and going like the events of a dream. If one illuminates this with the ocean-like wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, then the three periods of time and the ten directions are, from the very beginning, equal.
The celestial palaces and the pure lands are a single path, level and uniform. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—[are one].
There is absolutely no distinction between them. The cauldron of boiling water and the furnace coals are, in their true reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), cool and refreshing;

the grasses, trees, and courtyard sedges, the wind-swept sails, the birds on the sand, the shifting forms of smoke and clouds, and the rising and setting of the sun and moon—whatever meets the eye and is manifested before one is none other than the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Form Body (*sarvarūpakāyaprakāśana*).
For us who study the Way, what we value is the Vajra Eye, which pierces through the dark ignorance of delusion and causes the original nature to shine forth.

There is the radiance of wisdom. When applied to the daily activities before one, it is fully manifest in moments such as coughing, spitting, swinging the arms, raising the eyebrows, or blinking the eyes;
even in the brief interval of picking up the spoon or lifting the chopsticks, the stainless *dharmakāya* of one's own nature is suddenly revealed.
Such a person is called one who has attained liberation. This is just like when Subhūti realized *prajñā*; he wept and wailed before the Buddha, saying, "In truth, there is nothing..."
There is one who attains the name of Arhat. Among all phenomena within the entire world, could there be anything that surpasses this Prajñā?
Yet Prajñā is nothing other than the light of the mirror-like mind within our own hearts. Yongjia said: "Hitherto, the dusty mirror has never been polished;
today, it is clearly analyzed for the first time. The Master's title was Jingxin (Mirror-Mind); this is it.
Is the mind taken as the mirror? Or is the mirror used to reflect the mind? If the mind is taken as the mirror, then according to Old Lu’s way, "The bright mirror is not even a stand.
If it is not a stand, there is no mirror upon which to rely. If the mirror is used to reflect the mind, the mind is fundamentally without form;
from where, then, could one reflect it? In this way, that which is not the mind is not the mirror, and that which is not the mirror is not the mind.
Since both mind and mirror are non-existent, from what could names arise? If this is so, then the "Superior Man" (Upādhyāya) is but a provisional name;

if the name is provisional, then even the "Real" is not real. Thus, how could the Prajñāpāramitā you have been reading possess any words, phrases, or syllables residing upon the tips of your teeth and lips?
If the Superior Man can truly awaken to this Dharma-gate, then the luster of the river and the colors of the water, the songs of the birds—[all will be seen as such].
The tidal sounds all expound the *prajñā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Morning bells and evening drums escort the departing and welcome the arriving—all of which was when Śāriputra sat in meditative seclusion within his stone chamber and beheld the Dharma-body.

Thus, it is as if the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* transcribed by Dongpo and the woodblocks carved for printing by Foyin have come together with this old man today, through the karmic conditions of three lifetimes, to once again pass over this mountain and ascend [to its heights].
I, this puppet, take up this fascicle to seek further instruction. Do not say that these are merely the dream-words of a former life. As the Sūtra says:
"All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow; they are like dew and like lightning—thus should one contemplate them.
If you, O Honored One, can remain undeluded regarding your original cause even when habitual tendencies suddenly erupt, please take up this fascicle and read it; you will not fail to realize it.
Delusory thoughts, inverted views, and the dust of the sensory realms will naturally melt away like ice and crumble like a fortress.

It was once said by Ou Sheng Boyu that among all holy beings and ordinary people, there are none who do not achieve their mundane and supramundane undertakings through their aspirations; thus it is known that...

Those among us who set their will upon the nature and destiny of life aspire to transcend birth and death; those who set their will upon fame, achievement, wealth, and honor aspire to enter the cycle of birth and death.
As my Master has said: "The vast ocean of wisdom transforms into the ocean of karma that constitutes birth and death."
The wondrous nature of the luminous jewel is obscured and becomes the nature of the karma of birth and death—greed, hatred, delusion, and pride.

Viewed from this perspective, since the source of truth and falsehood in human nature is fundamentally non-dual, if one understands that one enters birth and death through greed, hatred, and delusion, then one may likewise use greed, hatred, and delusion to transcend birth and death. As the proverb says: "Do not resent small faults."
A gentleman who harbors malice is no true man of stature. I have often reflected that when King Goujian faced the humiliation at Kuaiji, he resolved to avenge the enmity of Wu.
He thus lay upon firewood and tasted gall for over twenty years; his clothing was not of double-layered finery, and his food was not of double-layered delicacies.

In the end, he extinguished Wu and established his hegemony. I am a seeker of the Way; when I look upon birth and death across kalpas, imprisoned and humiliated within the prison-cells of the three realms, how could this be merely the disgrace of Kuaiji?
Greed, anger, ignorance, and pride rob me of the light of my wondrous nature and destroy my dwelling of Nirvana;
how could these be merely the enmity of Wu? I treat them with composure as if they were sweet syrup, and I play with them in sport.
Amidst such idle revelry, they lack even a shred of shame or remorse, nor do they harbor any sense of indignation; one may say they are utterly ignorant of their own fundamental nature.
As for how they regard themselves, they might as well call themselves "great men" (mahāpuruṣa). One who possesses the will of Boyu [Bo Yi] would surely gnash his teeth in fury at this.
To Mr. Feng Wenru (Gengzi):
For one who studies the Way, the first requirement is to develop a firm and far-reaching resolve.

This must continue until the end of this present life, extending through three, five, ten, a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand lifetimes, and even through kalpa after kalpa of successive births. Directly...
This must certainly take awakening as its goal; if one does not awaken, this mind will by no means cease.
Even if one should fall into the three miserable realms of hell or pass through the wombs of oxen or the bellies of horses, one vows never to abandon this resolve to definitely attain Buddhahood.
Nor shall one lose the faith of this day because of suffering. It is, for example, like a person who has resolved their mind [to practice].
A journey of ten thousand *li* is determined by the destination one intends to reach.

From the moment one steps out the door today and takes the first stride, until one enters the gate of that destination, meets the person sought, ascends to the hall and enters the inner chamber, and exchanges joyful and intimate fellowship with them—only when one reaches such a state of total forgetfulness of self does the journey truly count as accomplished. Only in this way can it be called successful.

This refers to resolute determination. If one lacks this kind of clear and decisive resolve, merely saying "I am going out" while looking back at what is before one’s eyes—failing to let go of various attachments—or procrastinating and delaying until the mouth goes but the heart does not follow.
Or perhaps, by some fortunate circumstance, one is urged by powerful friends and relatives to set out on the road;

yet once upon the path, drifting aimlessly and listlessly, one encounters the sounds of singing and music or the fields of wealth and status, becoming greedily attached to the immediate pleasures of the senses.
They forget their original intention not to leave home; they wander aimlessly, unaware of where they are headed.

Perhaps midway, due to adverse conditions, they encounter evil friends and negative influences, leaving them with empty pockets and exhausted resources. Furthermore, being beset by chronic illness, they are terrified whether to advance or retreat, giving rise to immeasurable suffering.
Or, their bodies become weary and exhausted; having long been drenched by wind and frost, they can no longer endure the toil, and thus—
One gives rise to thoughts of turning back. Perhaps when one is about to reach the gate, one encounters a single lapse regarding a circumstance, a situation, or an event;
or perhaps due to distorted speech or mistaken hearing, one takes it as real. This causes one to fail to see the person one was about to see, or to fail to enter the chamber one was about to enter.
In all such cases, one's diligent efforts are entirely wasted, and one never reaches the ultimate goal in reality.
The reason one fails in the end is simply that at the time of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, there was no resolute will.
If this were the case, one could not even accomplish minor worldly feats of fame and achievement; how much less so the unsurpassed path of the Buddha, which brings an end to birth and death?
To realize Bodhi? Therefore it is said: "The path of the Buddha is long and distant; only after enduring diligent suffering for a long time can it be accomplished.
How could one take short-term results as the goal or seek rapid attainment? Nevertheless, even if one possesses such a resolute will, one must further possess true insight.
If one's knowledge and vision are not authentic, one will set one's will upon what should not be willed and practice what should not be practiced.
This would also be a further waste of effort. Since we seekers of the Way possess this aspiration, we must have firm faith that our own mind is, in its very essence, the Buddha;
it is fundamentally pure and devoid of things, fundamentally luminous and vast.
That which prevents us from utilizing what is thus manifest in our daily lives is simply due to these illusory delusions and the confinement and obscuration of the four elements. A mere...
Your deluded thoughts and floating mind will create obstructions, making it difficult to penetrate through them. To pass this pivotal point of birth and death is no small matter;
it is more distant than tens of thousands of kalpas across many lifetimes.

Now that you have come to know this mind and believe in it with sincere conviction, if you resolve today to take awakening as your goal, then from this very day, applying yourself to the practice of *gongfu* (meditative cultivation) is itself the way out.
The first step through the gate: today you have personally received the guidance and instruction of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), who is the one who inspires and impels you.

Once that inspiration has been aroused and you set out upon the path, all the various states encountered along the way, all the various hardships, and all the various hesitations—whether lingering or not lingering, whether falling into indolence or not falling into indolence—all reside within the fundamental nature at the very heels of the student themselves.
I have reflected upon this and concluded that none of these are worthy of being considered good spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). The gentleman Feng Wenru is resolute in his pursuit of this;
let him raise his eyebrows and look beneath his own feet at that very first step taken when leaving the gate.
The Six Symbols (of the hexagrams) were shown [to have been] produced in the past (Ren-yin).
The Sage’s use of mind is like a mirror: it neither sends forth nor welcomes; things come without adhering to it, and they depart without leaving a trace.
This is because, being utterly empty, it responds to all phenomena. Thus, Laozi said: "Without stepping out of one's door, one knows the world. How could this be false?

Can this be fathomed by the calculations of thought, the shifts of ingenuity, or the skillful conjectures of the intellect? That which is called "vast and universal impartiality" is the mind of the Sage.
Throughout antiquity and the present, those of clever intellect and ingenious artifice have claimed that there is no thought they cannot reach and no wisdom they cannot attain;

thus, they polish their cleverness while appearing ignorant. This is because the light of their minds has not yet penetrated and their fundamental substance remains unclarified; they have fallen into ignorance (*avidyā*).
To take one's place within the net of deluded imaginings and yet consider it a great wisdom is like holding a firefly and competing for light with the blazing sun.
Having once resolved to follow the Way, you should exert yourself with this in mind.
The attendant Zanzhi drew a small portrait of me, burned incense, and prostrated, requesting me to speak words of Dharma. The old man suddenly took up his staff and pursued him, saying:
"You have attended me morning and evening, yet you do not even know how to conceive a sense of reverence; how much less could you possibly understand this?"
Do you take paper and ink drawings as your models? Whenever you personally hear the teachings of the Dharma, they pass through your ears like a spring breeze.
Moreover, why do you take the words set down on paper as your standard? Since you first resolved to leave the household life, you have sought the state of liberation.
Yet you do not resolve to cultivate the practice of seclusion. Is this truly renunciation? Is this truly for the sake of transcending birth and death?

You are deluded in your own mind, rushing outward in pursuit, unaware that the sudden stilling of the wild mind is the secret essential for attaining Buddhahood. In your petty persistence, you grasp at illusions as reality;
you are like one who loses their head and recognizes only its reflection—there is no end to such confusion. This old man sits right here, facing your chest.
"In the midst [of this], you are merely conceptualizing it as a feverish illness. The Buddha said, "The deluded mind does not cease; when it ceases, that is *bodhi*.

This supremely pure and luminous mind is fundamentally not obtained from without. If one can truly act in this way, one may be called a 'seated participant' (*zuochan*); there is no need for the labor of bowing everywhere to spiritual teachers (*jñānī*)."
This is because you have entered the gate of immeasurable dharmas; this is precisely what is called "conforming to the nature of awakening. Furthermore, why do you wrap yourself up like an old man?

Reflect for yourself: throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, setting aside the times of dressing and eating, welcoming guests and attending to visitors, moving about, bowing, looking up and down, spitting, swinging your arms, and engaging in miscellaneous talk and frivolous discourse—what therein is your own original nature?
As for this "original face," if you can penetrate it here, I will grant that you have glimpsed the old man’s single eyebrow.
If not, you will be a thousand miles away even while facing me.
This is shown to the wise Chan practitioner.
In the fourth year after my exile, during the summer of the Jihai year, I was lecturing on the new commentary to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* at the Lubo Hermitage by the Green Gate in Wuyang.
A Zen practitioner traveled several thousand li from afar to visit me in this miasmic region; observing his earnest and sincere demeanor, I [was deeply impressed].

I have ordered that you be provided with vegetarian meals, intending thereby to lead you to understand the three virtues, harmonize the six aspects, unify the single mind, and cultivate the myriad practices.
You, O practitioner, have obeyed my commands and applied yourself diligently for more than half a year.

However, having recently been afflicted by illness from being drenched in the miasmic vapors, I see that my four elements are no longer sustainable and I can no longer endure the weight of communal affairs. I have therefore requested to cross the mountain pass to the north to seek a place of peace.

He took his leave, citing the need for rest and recuperation. The old man then exhorted him, saying: "How can you regard suffering and pleasure as different realms, or death and life as distinct states?
You fail to realize that the four elements are but a temporary loan, that suffering and pleasure are a field of illusion, and that death and life are merely night and day.
Furthermore, you do not understand that the mind is the source of all evils, and the body is the root of all sufferings."

Originally, the deluded mind gave rise to consciousness; clinging to the false as a self, one undergoes the cycle of birth and death in inverted fashion, appearing and disappearing within the path of suffering.
For countless tens of millions of kalpas, one has been like a person racing through a perilous road in a dream—filled with terror and agitation, seeking liberation but unable to find it.

Desiring to escape yet unable to do so, one suffers in grief, sorrow, and anguish; longing for rescue, there is no door through which to find it; the spirit is exhausted and weary, with no skill to find even a moment’s rest.
One thinks to oneself that one will ultimately fall into the depths of samsara, and thus willingly submits to being submerged.

Yet how could one have known that by calling out with all one's might and leaping up with sudden vigor, one would awaken to the Great Enlightenment? Then, all that former suffering, bitterness, and pain would become nothing but objects of laughter.
Now that you have awakened, how could it possibly differ from your former quest for liberation by as much as heaven and earth? Consider this:
your current suffering and moaning, along with your thoughts of seeking escape through renunciation or pursuit, are truly nothing more than the events of a dream.
You cannot call out to yourself to wake up; though I cry out for you, you still do not know. This is a wearying, long night, in which one never attains clarity.
The time for the eyes has come. Yet, how can you indulge in the bitter and pungent flavors of illusory falsehood, mistaking a dream for your true home?
Now that you have encountered this call and remain unaware, who else will call out to you once you have abandoned this moment? Alas!

In the long night of ignorance, delusion, and inversion, those who wish to seek the light of the Sun of Wisdom and encounter such an opportunity as today’s are among the most difficult of the difficult.
Try to contemplate this. Suddenly, through a forceful awakening, turn your head and look back; the emotional barriers of birth and death will instantly shatter.
This is precisely the moment of breaking out of the dream-house and emerging from the perilous path.
To Chan Practitioner Shuchong, who dwells in the mountains:
Chan Practitioner Shuchong is about to clear away the weeds at Mount Nanyue and requests instruction on the essential methods for mountain dwelling. The old man therefore instructs him, saying:
"The Way does not reside in the mountains; yet to dwell in the mountains, one must first realize the Way. If you see the mountains and forget the Way, the mountains will become an obstruction."
"The roots forget the mountains upon seeing the Way; wherever the eyes touch and conditions meet, there is nothing that is not the Way.

This is the renowned saying of the ancient masters and the sincere instruction of Yongjia. Now you intend to dwell in the mountains: is it that you will see the Way and then dwell there, or is it that you will dwell there and then see the Way?
If you see the Way and then dwell there, then dwelling implies a fixed abode; and if there is a fixed abode, then the Way is not the True Way.
The Way. If you wish to dwell in the mountains and thereafter perceive the Way, know that the Way fundamentally has no abode;
if it were to abide, the Way would not be in the mountains. What will you take to be the Way, and where will you dwell?

You merely regard the mountains as mountains, yet you do not realize that within daily life, the present moment, body, mind, and environment are all mountains. As the teaching says: "Birth, old age, sickness, and death are the four mountains."
It is that which is pressed upon. It is also called the mountain of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the mountain of the self and others (*pudgala-ātman*), and the mountain of *nirvāṇa*.
Now, *nirvāṇa* is the mind; the self and others are the objective realm. The body and mind of the five aggregates are the den of birth, old age, sickness, and death.

The Sanskrit term *nirvāṇa* is translated here as "quiescent extinction" (*śānti-nirodha*). The illusory and delusive states of body and mind are entirely characterized by agitation and turmoil. To investigate their origin...
When this is realized, truth and falsehood are non-dual, and movement and stillness are both as they truly are.

It is only due to the distinction between delusion and awakening that there is the differentiation between the holy and the ordinary. Through delusion, nirvana becomes birth and death; through awakening, birth and death are realized as nirvana.
Thus one knows that the mountain of the five aggregates and the self of persons is, from the beginning, the peaceful dwelling of nirvana.
This is where all sages and ordinary beings—whether being born or entering death—have never failed to reside; yet you have long been sleeping and dwelling here through the long night.
Why, then, do you now wish to dwell there? If you take delight and aversion, or acceptance and rejection, as the provisions for entering the Way, [you will not succeed].
This is like avoiding drowning only to throw oneself into fire. Therefore it is said: "I wish to escape this, but I cannot escape; for outside the Great Dharma, all is filled [with delusion].
It is further said: "If the wild mind does not cease, there is no awakening; if it ceases, that is *bodhi*.

The essential point of entering the Way lies solely in ceasing the wild mind—obliterating seeing and hearing, severing knowledge and understanding, forgetting subject and object, and stilling right and wrong—to bring this mind to a state of tranquil extinction. Indeed...
Do not hide yourself away in mountain valleys, eating to your heart's content and sleeping at will, indulging in laziness and increasing your pride, thinking this is the subtle essence of the Way.
In Sanskrit, *dhūta* means "to shake off. It is so called because it can shake off adventitious afflictions.
To simply purify the mind is the path of all Buddhas; you must strive for this.

To Zen Practitioner Jik: When the Buddhas and Patriarchs appeared in the world, they pointed people toward the Dharma solely by means of the fundamental method (*honpō*). Originally, there was no superfluous teaching, nor was there any substantial teaching.

This was simply because they wished for everyone to know for themselves that which is inherently possessed. Thus, throughout the Tripitaka, the twelve divisions of scripture, and the teachings of the patriarchs of successive generations...
This is intended solely to enable people to suddenly recognize what is inherently present, never intending to cause them to run outward in pursuit.
Because worldly people do not know that their own fundamental portion is complete, they assume there is something else and thus seek it within all verbal teachings,
investigate it within public cases (gong'an), search for it within ink and paper, and employ various skillful means, reflections, and calculations, thinking they must act in such a way.
Studying the Buddha-dharma, taking it as the practice of Zen for transcending birth and death, and engaging in various worldly activities—all these are treated as supramundane meritorious practices.
Looking at them with the correct eye today, none of them have any real connection [to liberation]. Why?

Because they are all constructed through discursive thought and deluded imagination, like events in a dream; this is because one has not yet departed from the mind and consciousness. As the ancients said: "To diminish..."
The Dharma-treasure and the merit of cessation—none of these fail to arise from this mind, consciousness, and awareness (*citta-vijñāna-manas*).
Yet, throughout immeasurable kalpas, the root-stumps of birth and death have been planted within the nesting hollows of cognitive-emotional consciousness (*vijñāna-śaitanya*).

Furthermore, they are watered with the waters of craving, nourished with the mud of desire, and incensed by the fire of ignorance, causing the sprouts of all sufferings to grow. Thus, even those who possess the Buddha-dharma’s knowledge and vision all fall [into error].
The conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of non-Buddhists merely increase the root of suffering; they are not the essential means for escaping suffering.

Disciples of the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*), being far removed in time from the Sages, do not receive the instructions of wise and authentic spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Often relying on their own cleverness, they give rise to great false pride (*mithyāmāna*).

Not only do they treat others with contempt and act arrogantly toward all things based on their Buddhist knowledge and views, but they even claim to have "surpassed the Buddhas and transcended the Patriarchs."

Secret. Furthermore, by means of the words and phrases of worldly conventions, the scriptures of non-Buddhists, and malicious views and arguments, they employ their eloquence and sharp wit to gallop about with quicksilver intelligence, treating these as the very tools for overturning the gates of heaven.

They presume that Old Man Yan cannot possibly restrain them, nor do they realize anymore the existence of the causes and effects of the mundane and supramundane realms. This is surely due to their failure to recognize [the truth].

One's own mind does not know its fundamental nature; regarding the single step beneath one’s own heels, it is utterly irrelevant. To rely merely on deluded madness only increases the inversions of a dream.

When a practitioner of Zen brings forth their own head, they then understand how to thus attend to teachers, choose friends, and engage in various causes and conditions such as ascetic practices in order to seek the Buddha-way. This is because they know what is inherently present.

Did you generate the resolve for enlightenment after [realizing it]? This would mean you were unaware of its original presence and only sought it out through the guidance of teachers and friends after generating that resolve.
If you had already known it existed before generating the resolve, then this kind of traveling on pilgrimage would not be necessary.

If you only came to know it through the instructions of teachers and friends, then there was no need for such a journey either; you would still have been a deluded madman wandering outside [of reality]. Thus:

Now, regarding the matter of secluding oneself behind closed doors to transcribe the scriptures—how about that? Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the scripture for entering the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Tell me, what constitutes the Dharma-realm, and how does one enter it?
If you can summon a heart of tempered steel and open wide the adamantine eyes, kicking over the cage of birth and death with a single stride, you will be like a lion shedding its shackles.
He wanders with sovereign ease. Observe how, when Sudhana first resolved his mind on enlightenment, upon first beholding Mañjuśrī, he broke through this pivotal mechanism;
thereupon, he became free and unimpeded. He traveled south through more than one hundred and ten cities, visiting as many spiritual friends as atoms in a buddha-field.
Only then did even the Elder Vairocana find him beyond reach, whereupon he attained equality with the Dharma-realm and with space.
It is equal to emptiness; it is equal to Vairocana; it is equal to the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.

Had he not encountered such a person at the outset to reveal such a matter, it is to be feared that it would have remained buried within a single mote of dust until this day, firmly and tightly shut like the Great Iron Ring Mountains—not merely the Zen practitioner’s "passing through the barrier" today. How could it otherwise?
The causes and effects of kalpas are accomplished within a single lifetime; thus, all former grudges and debts are settled.
If you practitioners of Zen do not believe the old man’s words, try at this very tip of a hair to pick it up and let it drop, moving it horizontally and vertically.
At that moment, look closely with your own eyes. If you truly see through with a single glance, only then will you believe that the old man does not deceive you, and you will also believe the Buddha.
Old Master Lu does not deceive you. The ancestral masters of successive generations likewise do not deceive you.
If you can immediately have confidence in your own original mind, you will not deceive yourself either. If this is not yet so, try listening to the final word.

Five years after I had fled overseas while the Chan practitioner Zongyuan was residing on the mountain, in the spring of the Gengzi year, the Chan practitioner Zongyuan and Fuzi of Qingtang came from Nanyue.
At that time, his two disciples Wuxin and Rongfo were both in attendance. The old man [Zongyuan] attended to his [the master’s] eating and resting.
Together they spent the summer retreat, having built walls for nearly half its duration. They then moved their residence to Donghua. After the retreat concluded, each took their leave.
Zongyuan bowed his head and requested a word as an essential teaching for dwelling in the mountains. The old man wiped away his sweat and showed it to him, saying:
"To enter deep mountains and dwell in an araṇya is the foremost cause and condition for entering the Way among all the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity. It is only I—"

Our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni, renounced the golden wheel, left his kin, and severed all attachments to flee into the Snow Mountains. There, amidst ten-thousand-foot cold crags, he buried himself for a thousand feet;

until a magpie built its nest upon his head and reeds grew through his knees, he remained unaware of the six years of freezing hunger and the state of his emaciated skin and bones sustained by starvation—a condition of bitter emptiness and desolation beyond description. One day, he beheld...
Awakening to the Way under the morning star, he alone illuminated the long night. Beholding him, devas and nāgas formed a protective guard, while spirits and ghosts revered him with awe.

He became the Teacher of Devas and Humans and served as the Eye of the World. To this day, his light shines across the four continents and his Way flows through billions of realms. Those who hear his name rejoice; those who behold his form take refuge.
Kings and ministers look up to him with reverence, and all who possess discernment incline their hearts toward him. His monasteries and jade palaces are magnificently adorned...
It is solemn, magnificent, and exquisite; it makes no distinction between the distant and the near, and for a hundred generations it remains as if alive.
That such a stream of grace flows without end and that such merit is transmitted without decay—all this was brought forth from six years of cold and hunger within the Snow Mountains.
Thus, even now, our descendants enjoy these four requisites without exhaustion; this is the very model for dwelling in the mountains, one who opened up heaven and carved out the earth.

From that time onward, the Way of the Dharma descended to the East. There were those such as Master Huiyuan’s Lotus Society, Sengyuan’s folding chair, the "broken-head" [ordination] of the Fifth Patriarch, Old Lu’s hunting party, Yinyan of West River, and the "withered wood" of Shishuang.

Among all those recorded in the *Lamp Records* and listed in the biographies of eminent monks, there was not a single person who did not seek out deep mountains and remote valleys to practice asceticism amidst suffering and emptiness.
It emerged from within the silence. Alas! The age has declined and the Way has become obscure; the hearts of men are no longer as they were of old.

Among all those who entrust their traces to the empty gate and lodge their forms in the *kāṣāya*, there are none who do not feign my name to seek personal ease, remaining utterly ignorant of what it truly means to leave the household life.

One might think that the four types of offerings should simply be enjoyed, without further considering the great matter of birth and death, which is the foremost essential duty for one who has left the household life.
Those of old who left home did so solely for the sake of this single point of birth and death; they traveled to consult masters and visit friends.
Having clarified one's own matter, one then retreats to deep mountains and remote valleys, wearing clothes of grass and eating food from the wood.
Using a broken-legged cauldron, one cooks coarse grain; one completely sweeps away and purifies all shadows of former karmic consciousness until not a single thread remains.
Solely and directly upholding the path above, with a body like withered wood and a mind like cold ashes, one proceeds until—
Only when you have penetrated through to the end will you be called a true son of the Buddha; only then can you repay the Buddha’s profound kindness.
Now, practitioner, you have given rise to a great spirit of valor and resolved to dwell in the mountains. You need only cast aside all external conditions and make your mind like a blank wall;
single-mindedly maintain this one thought, aspiring to equal the ancients, and must take the illumination of the great matter of birth and death as your primary goal.

I look forward to it. Do not cease until you have attained clarity; by all means, do not follow the example of your contemporaries in devising schemes for temporary ease as a means to nourish your indolence.

Go forth! Be my vanguard. Clear away the brambles at Yuelu to await the time when I, this old man, have finished settling my karmic debts, so that we may spend our remaining years together. Bear this in mind!
To the Chan practitioner Sōtō, I show this:
In the past, when Zen Master Zhongfeng resided at Mount Tianmu, he had long studied under Gaofeng; yet, as the Great Matter remained unclarified, he stood upon a precipice.
He caressed the solitary pine for seven days and then attained great enlightenment. Thus, while the cliff-side pine now stands alone, those who can truly trace its footsteps are few indeed.
A Zen practitioner named Tong went beneath the pine, cleared away the weeds, and built a hut where he resided for three years.
His daily practice was the recitation of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra; his diligent austerity was truly remarkable, yet in terms of the depth of his realization, he fell far, far short of Zhongfeng. If...
To merely clarify this matter is still not enough. Chan Master Daguan named him "Niansong" (Mindful of Pines), wishing that he would never forget his roots.
Now, this Chan practitioner has come from afar to consult me in this malarial region, and having taken his leave, he intends to travel eastward past Zhiti and north into Wutai to seek Mañjuśrī.
Amidst his ten thousand followers, may he find a companion by the side of Vajra.
"In this cave, I shall recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for a full hundred volumes to complete my remaining life. As I depart, I beg for a single word as an essential teaching.
I then raised my mustache and laughed, saying: "To hold such a view is like crossing the ocean only to seek a river bath."
To enter the vast Dharma-realm with narrow and limited habits—this is indeed difficult. An ancient worthy said:
"The entire earth is a single volume of scripture; the entire earth is the single eye of a śramaṇa.
With such an eye, one reads such a scripture until the end of the future, never ceasing for a moment. What trace of coming or going, what view of self and other, could there be?
Ah! The *Avataṃsaka* takes the equal Dharma-realm as its central tenet and non-obstruction as its gateway.

If one can awaken to this tenet and enter this gateway, there will be not a single thing that does not manifest the essence of Vairocana; not a single sound that does not proclaim the perfect and wondrous resonance;
not a single moment that does not cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra; and not a single person who is not a spiritual friend within the atoms of all lands.
This is the Samādhi of the Net of Light; with a single glance, all is clearly revealed. The True Sutra of the Universal Eye is fully present according to one's thought.

With every step raised and every footfall, one does not depart from the field of quiescent extinction. Dwelling amidst the dust of the world yet transcending it, one immediately reaches the shore of Prajñā.
Where would you seek Mount Wutai? By what dharma would you take as the Great Sutra? Therefore it is said: "I wish to flee from it, but I cannot flee."
It is attained. The space beyond the great square is entirely filled.

If you can bring this to mind and bring it to completion, why must you climb mountains and cross waters to seek companions, reciting literary texts to spend the remainder of your life? If you realize that birth is fundamentally non-birth, then you abide nowhere.
If you can awaken to the principle of non-abiding, you will naturally cease to harbor thoughts of coming and going, movement and stillness, or arising and ceasing.

The Sixth Patriarch Master, with the single phrase "giving rise to the mind while dwelling nowhere," struck down all the inverted perceptions and views accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas from the past.
You, my son, must here pluck up your eyebrows and look with eyes wide open;
you must by no means take even a single step out the door, lest you fall entirely into the weeds.
Regarding the Elder Qianshou’s Blood-Scripture Copying of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra at Mount Shifo:
Formerly, when I resided in the Nārāyaṇa Cave on the East Sea, a Zen practitioner came from Mount Wutai to visit me.

Later, when I crossed the mountain passes to the Five Oxen (Guangzhou), he followed me again from Mount Kuang to console me in this miasmic land. Upon seeing him for the first time, it was as if we were separated by an entire lifetime.
Observing that human affairs are like dreams and illusions, he then addressed his assembled disciples during the summer retreat while they were building walls.
On the day the retreat concluded, he performed a prostration and said: "I shall return to Donglin to follow in the noble footsteps of Master Huiyuan."
Emulating the pure cultivation of the Lotus Society, you wish to prick your own blood to hand-copy the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as a pure deed for adorning the Buddha-lands;
I pray that you grant me a word of instruction. I said: "Son of the Buddha, listen attentively.
What do you take to be the 'Great Sūtra,' and what do you take to be 'pure deeds'? Do you consider the paper, ink, and brush with which you write to be the sūtra? Or is it the words and phrases?"
Are characters the sutra? Is the movement of the brush in its turns and twists the pure practice? Is the distribution of dots and strokes the pure practice?
If one considers the paper and ink used for writing to be the sutra, then the ledgers and documents in the marketplace are none other than the Great Sutra.
If one considers speech and written words to be the sutra, then the talk, cries, laughter, and mundane writings of the secular world are none other than wondrous principle.
This is fundamentally without deficiency; what need is there to record it?

If one regards the movement and turning of the body as pure karma, then every ordinary daily act—whether coughing, spitting, or swinging one's arms—is none other than the perfect penetration of Avalokiteśvara entering into principle.

If one regards the distribution of dots and strokes as pure karma, then welcoming guests, attending to visitors, picking up chopsticks, or grasping spoons is none other than the practice of Samantabhadra.

Sublime practice (*sucarita*): if it is thus, then it is inherently complete from the beginning; why seek anything else? To abandon this and speak of "Dharma-practice" is like knowing that two times five is ten, yet not knowing that ten itself.
Nevertheless, throughout the entirety of the ten directions is the eternally quiescent light (*nitya-śānta-prabhā*), which fundamentally knows neither clarity nor obscurity;

to the furthest reaches of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the pure land, which originally lacks the distinction between the refined and the coarse. The myriad phenomena in their vast array are all the ocean-seal (*sāgara-mudrā*).

The spiritual texts of these beings—whether scaled, shelled, feathered, or furred—are all the true body of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The howling of monkeys and the chirping of birds are all discourses on the perfect sound of non-duality (*advaya*).
Rain falling and clouds moving are all manifestations of the wondrous function of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*). Thus, there is no turning away or facing toward;
no coming or going; no grasping or rejecting; and no beginning or end. Within this, the three periods of time do not shift, and the ten ages are perfectly realized.
A single thought-moment: this is the inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma-realm.

Yet you, desiring to find within this inexhaustible treasury, merely employ the limited mental activities of birth and death, taking the adornment of physical forms as the practice of the Dharma to seek the true cause for the Pure Land.

This is like mistaking cow dung for sandalwood, or fish eyes for the cintāmaṇi jewel. How much more so regarding the Dharma-gate of a single word, which could not be fully recorded even with the ink of the oceans!

Yet it is inexhaustible. You wish to transcribe this inexhaustible True Scripture and perform these inconceivable Buddha-works with the finite four elements, a mere drop of bodily blood, and the fleeting moments of a single *kṣaṇa*.
This is like attempting to paint the void or grasping at a flash of lightning. You must investigate this; if you have not yet realized it, try going to the summit of Mount Wulao.
Contemplate intently the colors of the mountains and the light of the lakes; listen to the songs of birds and the sounds of the streams.

What difference is there between sitting with the Elder Vairocana in the Hall of Universal Radiance, amidst the clouds of infinite bodies from the ten directions and the ocean-like assemblies within the atoms of all lands, preaching the *Sūtra of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm*, and being here now?
Investigate! Investigate!
This is a portrait of the practitioner Xuehuai, who cultivates dhyāna with a humble heart.
From Wuzhong, he traveled alone with a single alms bowl to this malarial region to attend upon me for over two years.

While I performed Buddhist rites amidst the field of spears and halberds, he maintained his cultivation with single-minded devotion; he took the lead in all manual labor, day and night without ceasing.
[The Master] was weary. From beginning to end, he remained as he was on that first day. I watched him with cold eyes from time to time; he possessed quite the air of a true monk.
Thinking that in this age of the Dharma’s decline, those who uphold this matter beneath the *kāṣāya* robe are difficult to find, I felt a deep affection for him.

Recently, he took leave of me wishing to visit various masters in different quarters. As he was about to depart, he asked: "The four great elements are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates do not exist."
"Where does the illness reside? The old man replied, "The illness resides where there is no place. He then spoke this verse to assist his journeying:

"The four great elements are fundamentally empty; emptiness itself is the illness. The five aggregates are not existent; existence arises from non-existence. When both ends are severed, there is no news.
Only then does one believe that home and mountain are everywhere one returns."
To Layman Xiqiao (a native of Jishui), [the Master] showed that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts; yet, do not suppress or extinguish those deluded minds."
"Abiding in the realm of delusive thoughts, one does not apply clear understanding; because of this lack of clear understanding, one fails to discern the reality.
This statement by the ancient masters has been frequently cited and shown to students, yet most fall into the trap of conceptualization. Only Zhongfeng added a "not" (不) to each word.
This is the *Vajramandala*.
It was shown to Mr. Chen Zifu (a native of Jishui) with reference to Confucius’s words:
"To know the *ji* (the point of transition) is it not divine? Commentators say that *ji* is the subtle movement [of things]; the student should, at this...
When you have not yet moved, fix your gaze; only then will you gain power.

"The state before joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have been aroused is called the Central" (Zhong). This is precisely the same as the Sixth Patriarch’s "neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil.
How is this the same as "What is the Venerable One’s original face? Investigate this together.
"Writing is the manifestation of the mind. If a student does not comprehend the essence of the mind, yet forcibly assembles conventional phrases, can this be called writing?
It must flow forth from within one's own breast; only then will it cover heaven and earth."

Mencius said, "Food and sexual desire are human nature. These words seem like a commentary on seventeen hundred [other] passages; they are by no means something that can be understood by mere scholars of the classics.
An ancient said, "The work lies in the midst of daily life. This is a dead word. Today, you sit here within the nest of such talk.
Within the mortar, even those who possess the will for enlightenment merely display the shadows of their conscious spirits;
this is not the fault of those who speak, but rather the fault of clinging to what is spoken.

The *Zongjing* says: "The locus of sound is entirely hearing; when one sees that there is no dharma outside, these words are not for those who have already penetrated through the crown of Vairocana’s head and ascended above.
Such people certainly do not know where the 'head of the phrase' (huatou) falls."
Confucian scholars who aspire to the Way often seek to cultivate their practice exclusively within Chan Buddhism,
yet they fail to realize that "keeping this in mind" (*nian zi zai zi*) is itself the first stage of the Supreme Vehicle.
When the night air is clear and serene, gather your mind and sit upright. Turn your gaze inward and contemplate that state of silent, non-obscured clarity;
therein you will spontaneously behold your original face. Do not deceive yourself. As Confucius said: "I have never seen one who loves virtue as much as they love beauty."
It is clear that those who are not deceived by the world are rare.
When a whirlwind and torrential rain arrive with a sudden gust, observe from where the wind comes and from where the rain arrives.
If you observe this with clear discernment, you will realize that the myriad things reside within yourself.
It is like fine seedlings that one hopes will yield a bountiful harvest; if the pestilential insects are not eliminated, their fruition will be difficult to achieve.
This is true not only in the mundane world, but likewise within the monastic community for those studying the Way.
To the Chan practitioner Zhao:
If one discusses this matter, fundamentally there is neither "upward" nor "downward. As soon as one engages in discursive thought, it becomes a superfluous dharma;
how much more so for one who enters the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) beyond words with a mind that grasps at existence? If you, practitioner, can indeed resolve this with...
Death is a momentous matter. You should now take up all those thoughts of weariness with the mundane world from the past,
as well as everything you have heard, seen, known, and understood since your ordination— including the daily practice regarding the fundamental matter for which you sought instruction,
your dressing and eating, your moving about and bowing, your activity and stillness, your leisure and busyness, and all the various conditions you have encountered before your eyes.
Investigate subtly: ultimately, what constitutes the "upward-facing" reality? Again, take this investigating mind and observe it with precise scrutiny:
ultimately, where does it land? Whenever there is a place where it lands, it becomes a habitual trap;

this is the den of birth and death, all belonging to the realm of delusive thought, not the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). As the Sūtra says: "Even if one were to extinguish all seeing and hearing..."
To have cognitive awareness while guarding the inner stillness is still merely a matter of conceptual shadows regarding mental objects (*dharmas*).

The ancients called this a "black mountain ghost cave," and it is precisely the greatest taboo in Chan practice; how much more so to employ a mind of birth-and-death with coarse and floating imaginings?
Entering the ultimate limit is to be far, far removed from it. As it is said: "To raise the mind is immediately an error; to stir a thought is immediately to deviate.
If one takes 'not raising the mind' and 'not stirring thoughts' to be the profound and wondrous, one again falls into the trap of the profound and wondrous.

A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the most profound within the profound? Zhaozhou replied, "How long has it been since you began seeking the profound? The monk said, "I have sought the profound for a very long time."
Zhou said, "Had it not been for me, you would have nearly been killed by this mystery. Look at the single word of the ancients:
it is like the Vajra-king’s precious sword, severing all the cognitive views of both ordinary beings and sages. Viewed in this way, how could this matter be expressed by lips and mouth?
How could it be depicted by paper, ink, or written characters? It resides solely within the daily activities of students, in every instance where the mind is raised or a thought is stirred."
Observe with discerning truth: even the slightest trace of emotional views, or even the most profound and subtle insights where one remains stuck or attached, are merely shadows of deluded thought;

they all fall within the realm of birth and death, and are not the transcendence of that realm. The limit of transcending limits is called the "actual limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*). The actual limit has no limit;
having no limit, it does not fall into the extremes of the holy or the ordinary. When the holy and the ordinary do not fall [into extremes], [that is the actual limit].
When the sentiments of birth and death have perished, as the ancients said: "If not a single thought arises, the past and future limits are severed.
Once severed, there is nothing more to do; only then is one called a "person of no affairs. Since affairs are already absent, where else could one seek the profound or the wondrous?

As it is said: "Simply exhaust all mundane sentiments; there is no separate 'sage's understanding'. Reaching this point is like a person drinking water—the coldness or warmth is known by oneself. Great!

It is like a mute person eating yellow-barked tree (phellodendron): it is difficult to express to others. Practitioners of Zen need only prepare a heart of raw iron and proceed straight ahead in this manner.
There is no need to wait for awakening with the mind, nor is there any need to calculate years, months, days, or hours.
You must simply take the immeasurable kalpas of past and future and, right now, bring them directly before you. Let [it be as it is].
Regarding the coming and going, arising and ceasing of birth and death, this very present single thought-moment is definitively not moved by the shifting illusions of floating light and shadows.
Even if it were a mountain of knives or a mass of fire, or even a pure land or a celestial palace, let them headlong plunge in and out as they may;
this solitary radiance of a single thought is ultimately never shaken or stolen away by anything else. Only such a state can be called "great power."
Only such a person is truly a renunciant. They are not ensnared by birth and death; they are not buried by the categories of sage and ordinary;
they are not distorted by the shifts of the three periods of time. Only when this is so can name and reality correspond; this is true transcendence of temporal limits.
Zen practitioners, holding these words, should seek verification from enlightened masters of all quarters. By no means should you treat this as mere "Zen."
In the *Dàofǎ Fǎhuì* (Dharma Assembly on the Way and the Dharma), the ancient worthy Huáiyú Xiū, the Hall Master, said:
"The entire world of the ten directions is, through and through, the single eye of the patch-robed monk. The myriad phenomena within empty space are like scales [upon its surface]."
Whether feathers and fur, vast or minute, large or small—all are but a single scroll of the *Mahāvairocana-garbha Sūtra*.
With such eyes, one reads such a sūtra, continuing without ceasing until the end of the future.
This is but a most minute and subtle fraction of the Buddha-activities within a single pore of the Great Being Samantabhadra; if one pore is thus, how much more so each and every pore? Truly.
If the retribution within a single pore is thus, how much more so for the minute dust-motes of the dependent world-realm? If a single mote is thus, how much more so for every mote?
Furthermore, since a single mote contains vast lands, how much more so for the lands within every mote, and the motes within every land?

By contemplating deeply in this way, one sees that the ocean of boundless lands does not separate self from other even at the tip of a hair; throughout the ten ages of past and present, beginning and end do not depart from one another.
In this very thought-moment, [one should contemplate] this true scripture of Samantabhadra. To be able to see this scripture is to possess the wisdom-eye of Mañjuśrī.
With this very eye, one observes the sentient beings within the dust;

every single sentient being fully expounds this scripture, causing each listener to clearly understand that all sages and ordinary beings are fundamentally non-dual and without distinction. We people...
One possesses this very eye, turns this very sutra, and delivers these very sentient beings;

though it is said that one exhausts great compassion and fulfills great vows for as many eons as there are motes of dust in a buddha-field, one never feels weariness or fatigue. Even so, this is still not the fundamental business of a patch-robed monk.
Why is this? Because within the pure *dharmadhātu*, there has never been any movement, coming, or going of the various images of ordinary beings and sages.

If even these extraordinary images do not exist, how much less so the delusive cognitions and views, the various phenomena of Buddha-dharma and the Way of Chan, or the inverted marks of grasping and rejecting—could these be anything but empty and false reflections?
Thus, one knows that when the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity pointed the way for others, they taught nothing other than to come to rest.
"Quell the wild mind; do not seek it from others. As it is said: 'Simply untie the soiled garment within your own bosom; why trouble yourself by boasting of diligence toward the external?
It is further said: 'Exhaust only ordinary sentiments; there is no separate "sage's understanding. If you form a sage’s understanding, you immediately fall among the various heterodoxies.

Because these aforementioned supernatural powers and wondrous functions are all matters of one's own fundamental allotment and possess nothing extraordinary, they are this very single flavor of equanimity."
"Constantly. Why seek the Buddha-dharma elsewhere?
Thus he instructed the Chan practitioner Liaoji (Bingwu).
When I was restoring the Baolin Chan Hall at Caoxi to receive practitioners from the four quarters, the Chan practitioner Shiliang [was there].
I made a vow to beg for alms to provide for the assembly. At the beginning of the retreat, a practitioner of Chan offered incense and requested instruction.

I therefore showed him this: "The sublime practices of the Buddhas for benefiting sentient beings are not of a single kind; the wondrous gateways of the Bodhisattvas to attain Buddhahood are fundamentally not of one path.
In the past, the Great Being Vimalakīrti performed Buddha-work with a single bowl of rice for thirty-two thousand [monks]."

There is a limited assembly; those who eat their food all enter into the practice of the precepts. Yet tell me: to this day, the alms bowls remain as they were, and the fragrant rice remains as it was.
As for those who eat it, where does their practice of the precepts reside? As for those who carry the rice, where is their spiritual power?
If you can penetrate this point, it is truly what is meant by: "That which is equal in food is also equal in the Dharma. If you cannot penetrate it, you must further...
One must visit masters for instruction and resolve all doubts until reaching the stage of non-doubt; only then does one correspond even slightly with the original ground.
If this is not yet the case, one cannot avoid being swept along by the waves. Thus, when a monk visited Zhaozhou, he said, "I have newly entered the monastic community;
I beg the Master for instruction. Zhaozhou replied, "Have you eaten your porridge yet? The monk said, "I have."
Zhaozhou said, "Go wash your bowl. That monk attained realization.

If a Zen practitioner can understand this at the point where Zhaozhou spoke and where that monk realized it, they will immediately join arms and walk together with all the superior virtuous ones within the hall of Vimalakīrti.
