*Fayu* (Dharma Words).
To Layman Rongyu (Jiachen Year):
I was residing at Sanyi Hermitage in Leiyang when the layman Wang Rongyu of Huazhou requested of me, saying:

"I, your disciple, have long turned my heart toward the Way, yet my resolve has not been single-minded. I consider that as one born within the system of names and teachings, loyalty and filial piety must be prioritized."
I feel ashamed that I have been unable to establish my fame and merit through loyalty to my sovereign, nor to acquire even a *dan-shi* of grain through filial piety toward my parents.

My mind remains unsettled, and thus it is difficult for me to fix my resolve. I replied, "Is this not so? Indeed, the substance of loyalty and filial piety is the foundation of the Great Way and the innate goodness of the human heart.
How could one abandon loyalty and filial piety while speaking of the Way, or turn their back on the nature of the heart while discussing conduct? Thus say the scholars of the world.
Generally speaking, those of our Buddhist tradition claim that one must abandon human relations and forsake loyalty and filial piety, considering them contradictory;

yet they fail to realize that what is being abandoned are outward traces, while what is directed toward is the mind. As the *Zhongyong* says: "In contemplating how to serve one's parents, one cannot afford not to know humanity."
I consider that one cannot know humanity without knowing Heaven. Humanity is benevolence (*ren*); it is the virtue of human nature.
Viewed from this perspective, to discuss filial piety without knowing humanity is not called filial piety; to discuss knowing humanity without knowing Heaven is not called knowing humanity.
To speak of knowing Heaven while failing to perceive human nature means that even Heaven remains obscure and without foundation. This being so—
The mind-nature resides within me; this is its original, innate truth. One who can know the truth of the nature of heaven is a true person.
Through the filial piety of innate truth, one is a true filial son. One should be able to cultivate oneself through the power of seeing into one's nature.
This constitutes true cultivation. To delight one’s parents with the joy of the true nature is a sublime practice; this is filial piety, the pinnacle of filiality.
To claim that reverence is what is most important while regarding the needs of their mouth and body as secondary is, indeed, a superficial view.

Yu said: "I, your disciple, shall hold these enlightened instructions close to my heart. The merit of realizing one's nature is truly great; to use this to delight one's parents is certainly what I ought to do."
This is my aspiration. Yet, like gazing at the vast ocean, I am lost and have no direction for my return. I beg the Master to point out the merit of the shortcut. I replied:
An ancient worthy said, "There is only the practice of the direct path: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. *Amitābha* is a Sanskrit term;
here it means "Immeasurable Life. *Buddha* means "Awakened One. This is the original, innate awakening that is our very own nature.
This nature is, above all, the foremost wondrous gateway for realizing one's nature. To examine its origin:

this nature was not subject to aging before heaven and earth, nor does it undergo an end after heaven and earth. It is unchanging amidst birth and death, and untransmuted through the cycles of succession. It directly transcends the myriad things, having no limit or end;
therefore, it is called "Immeasurable Life" (*Amitāyus*). This life does not belong to the longevity or brevity of the physical body.
Time may be long or short. When a person can perceive this nature, they are immediately called a Buddha. Furthermore, "Buddha" is not merely a title for a sage from the West;
it refers to one who has entered the reality of their own self-nature. As for Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang, they were the first to awaken among the people of Heaven.
Thus, while the people of Heaven must wait for conditions before they can awaken, the Sage is born with the capacity to awaken first. This...
Is awakening not precisely the awakening of the Buddha-nature? What Mencius meant when he said that "Yao and Shun were no different from other men" refers to this very same thing.
If one can awaken to this nature, then every person can become a Yao or a Shun.
Since everyone can become a Yao or a Shun, it is clear that every person can become a Buddha. Alas! The people of the world are so bound by their narrow-mindedness.

As for the views of those who follow the crooked path: having not encountered the instruction of a True Man, they are bound by conventional learning and take "eating from hearsay" as the ultimate truth.
It is no wonder that they remain茫然 (mángrán—bewildered) and do not know where their destination lies. Yu said:

"I, your disciple, have received your opening instruction and now truly know that one's own mind is Buddha and that one's own mind creates Buddha; it does not require seeking elsewhere. However, I do not yet understand the essential meaning of 'becoming Buddha. Below [is his question].
The artisan requested instruction. I said: "If we humans truly know that our own mind is the Buddha, we must examine why we become sentient beings.
Sentient beings and Buddhas are like water and ice. When the mind is deluded, the Buddha becomes a sentient being;
when the mind awakens, the sentient being is the Buddha. It is like water forming ice, and ice melting back into water. The name changes, but the substance does not."

This is the essence. To be deluded is to lack awakening; this lack of awakening is what constitutes a sentient being. To be undeluded is awakening; this awakening means that the sentient being is the Buddha.
If you, my son, wish to seek the Buddha, you need only seek your own mind. If the mind is deluded, you must simply recite the Buddha’s name. When the Buddha arises, awakening occurs.
Upon awakening, the radiance of one’s own nature (*svabhāva*) stands forth, revealed in its singular clarity. As for the preceding delusions—greed, hatred, and ignorance—they [will naturally vanish].
Below, the ice melts away. Once the defilements of karma have dissolved, one’s own mind becomes pure, liberated, and free from entanglements.
When there is no [defilement], suffering departs and joy remains; when calamity departs, fortune remains. When true joy is established, there is no state that is not joyful.
When celestial blessings manifest, everything encountered is peaceful. This true peace and ultimate joy—how could they be brought about by mouth or body?
"How attainable is such wealth and honor! This is what is meant by 'if the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. The merit of cultivating the mind does not extend beyond this;
the provisions for the Pure Land likewise do not lie outside of it. Yu said, "Having heard these teachings, my mind and eyes have been opened and clarified, as if seeing the road back home.
I am now entirely free from doubt or obstruction. However, how can taking the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) as filial piety be explained?"

"Is this what you mean by filial piety? This is not yet satisfactory; I pray that the Master will provide further instruction. I replied: "In the past, there was a filial son who had traveled far away.
His mother had a guest arrive, and as she gazed toward her son’s departure and saw he had not yet returned, she bit her finger.

The son immediately felt pain in his heart and, realizing his mother was thinking of him, he promptly returned home. Furthermore, when the mother bit her finger and the son felt pain in his heart, it was because their bodies were one and their minds were unified."
If you can clearly perceive your own mind, you will suddenly awaken to the realization that your own mind is none other than your mother’s mind.
Use your own awakening to awaken her; use your own mindfulness to wish for her mindfulness. Since your mother loves your physical form, how could she not love your mind?
If your mother were to love only your physical form, then that form would become a burden and your mind would suffer. If your mother...
As for your mind, if you forget the physical form, the mind will find joy. Furthermore, the substance of the mother’s and son’s minds is one and the same.

In the past, when a mother thought of her son, she bit her finger and the son felt pain; now, as you, the son, think of your mother while forgetting the physical form, how could your mother’s mind not be peaceful and joyful?
I only fear that your effort in serving the mind is not earnest and your study of forgetting the form has not reached its consummation, such that you are unable [to achieve this].
It is like a mother’s intense longing for her child; it is simply to move and gladden the heart of one’s mother.

Thus, the filial sons of antiquity did not exchange the nourishment of the five tripods and three sacrificial animals for the joy of playing in patterned robes while their mothers wore colorful garments.

The greatness of filial piety lies in delighting the heart of one’s parents, not in the outward form of nourishing them. If worldly filial piety were such as this, it might perhaps enable one’s mother to spend the remainder of her years [in peace].

From this point on, turn your heart toward the Pure Land; to enjoy the happiness of even a single day is superior to a hundred years of wealth and nobility, for it prevents your mother from constantly harboring sorrowful anxieties.
Thus, although one may possess wealth and status, if one’s kin do not find joy, there is a reason why that joy is incomplete.
Now, by means of mindfulness of the Buddha, you are able to bring peace to your mother’s mind.
Joyful! Joyful for a long time! Is this not indeed Infinite Life? The mother’s life is infinite, and the son’s life is likewise infinite.
This Pure Land resides within oneself and not in another; the Buddha resides in the mind and not in external traces. You, my son, must bear this in mind.
In his own hermitage, Chan Master Zhuzhai said to the assembly:
"The Buddha taught that all sentient beings wander through birth and death, with deluded thoughts and inverted views as their fundamental root."
When inverted perceptions are extinguished and one sincerely resolves within oneself, this is precisely the moment for ending birth and death and escaping the sea of suffering.
If delusive thoughts do not cease, it is difficult to emerge from birth and death; therefore it is said: "If the wild mind does not rest, it continues; if it rests, that is *bodhi*.

If we can truly and suddenly cause the wild mind to rest, we shall immediately transcend the three realms, destroy the armies of Māra, and sit upon the open ground—this is what is called [enlightenment].
A person who has attained the Way of non-action—like the Iron-Faced Old Man Yama—may possess a fierce heart and poisonous hands, yet he has no place for scheming or grasping.
Moving back and forth with ease and traversing all directions with freedom, he is a man of great liberation.
At such a time, even to call him a Buddha or a Patriarch is intolerable to hear; how much less would he consent to dwell within a latrine as a companion to foolish flies?
"Band! You are stealing the savory meat and chasing after the stench!

When the worlds of the ten directions all become pure lands, and great perfect enlightenment becomes my monastery, with body and mind filling its midst, I shall walk arm-in-arm with the Buddhas of the ten directions and attain great sovereignty.
In this state, the hermitage is oneself; oneself is the hermitage. The hermitage is the mountain; the mountain is the person. There is no [distinction]."

Within there is no without; there is neither "that" nor "this. If it is thus, then you dwell where there is nothing to dwell in, act where there is nothing to act upon, and cultivate where there is nothing to cultivate—only then can you truly be called one who dwells in their own hermitage.
If you instead nurture your indolence and foolish sleep, for sixty kalpas across three lifetimes you will do nothing but serve as a slave to others.
Reflect on this! Reflect on this!
To the Zen practitioner Qingyun, I show that a child of the monastic way must clarify the Great Matter. First, one must have a genuine and urgent concern for birth and death.
Second, one must resolve to bring about liberation from birth and death. Third, one must maintain the integrity of remaining steadfast until death, never wavering throughout one's life. Fourth...

Fourth, one must truly know that the world is suffering and develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward it. Fifth, one must associate with a most excellent spiritual friend who possesses right knowledge and vision;
one should consult them from time to time, respectfully follow their instructions, act according to their teachings, and practice with diligence and without laziness.
One must not be obstructed by the afflictions of the five desires, nor be driven by bad habits, nor be led astray by evil companions.
It shall not be diverted by adverse conditions, nor shall one allow oneself to become discouraged due to dull faculties.

By generating the mind in this way and proceeding toward its realization in this way, after a long time it will become thoroughly matured; naturally, it will accord with one’s original vows and aspirations, like a box and its lid fitting perfectly together.

Even if one cannot achieve full awakening or clearly perceive one's own mind in this present life, then for hundreds or thousands of lifetimes to come, today shall be regarded as the most significant.

This refers to the initial stage of the path. If one does not act thus, but instead relies on narrow and inferior understanding, the habitual tendencies of dullness and warmth, and complacent indolence,
seeking to take "head-mouth Chan" (verbal Zen), a狂妄 mind (reckless arrogance), defiled vapors, and the root of false views as the true vocation of a renunciant—
hoping thereby to escape the sea of suffering— it is like traveling toward Yue while heading for Yan, or taking steps backward while seeking to advance.
This was previously stated. Alas! In the age of the Dharma’s decay, those with true faith are rare.

Since you, practitioner of Zen, already know where you are headed, you ought to examine and realize your original mind, taking authentic certainty as the primary principle. Exert yourself, exert yourself!
The Buddha spoke thus to the monk Ruchang:
"One who leaves home to renounce their kin, recognizes the mind and penetrates the fundamental source, and understands the unconditioned Dharma (*asamskṛta-dharma*), is called a śramaṇa.

They constantly practice the two hundred and fifty precepts. Furthermore, it is said: 'Sever desire and eliminate attachment; recognize the source of one's own mind and penetrate the profound principle of the Buddha. Upon hearing this, he attained awakening.

Regarding unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), it is further said: "One who shaves off hair and beard to become a śramaṇa and receives the Buddha-dharma abandons worldly wealth and possessions, seeking only enough to satisfy one's needs;
eating but one meal at midday and staying but one night under a tree, being careful not to exceed these limits.

That which causes people to be deluded and obscured is attachment and desire. Such teachings, with their various earnest exhortations and words of admonition, are all essential for the purpose of [liberation].
As for the disciples of the Buddha, when they first leave the household life, they take the renunciation of desire as their primary practice.

Yet later generations, though they have left the household life in body, have hearts intoxicated by the five desires. They do not know what affliction is the dharma of distancing, nor what path is the way out of suffering;
they remain entangled and deluded, unaware of their own condition. Moreover, they falsely affect dignified deportment, deceitfully appearing to possess it.
Virtue. Outwardly one deceives others; inwardly one deceives one’s own mind. One harbors flaws and imperfections without even realizing it.

For those who wish to seek a true mind and right mindfulness, such a person is difficult to find. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "A straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
If you constantly aspire to seek the Dharma of liberation, you should take a straightforward mind as the primary principle. Be careful.
I tell you, little master Dezong:

since you followed this old man, more than twenty years have passed. Not only have you labored in service, but you have even encountered hardships and traveled to pestilential lands three times already.
Previously, I sent you back to your home mountain to serve your teachers and elders; yet your mind remains wild.

"You have not desisted; you have come here once again. Now I hear that your teacher has already become a thing of the past, yet you were ultimately unable to take up the handkerchief and water pitcher while alive, nor could you open your hands and feet at the moment of death. How can this be called being a disciple? You must return this very day.

Do you not consider how you shall repay your teacher’s kindness in the realm of the unseen? When the ancients attended their teachers and visited friends, it was solely for the purpose of accomplishing the work of the Way."
"You have now followed your teacher for over twenty years; where is your realization of the Way? Ancient sages were ashamed to appear before their parents, teachers, and friends.
Since you have achieved nothing in the Way, it is fortunate that you have no parents, teachers, or friends—leaving you with no ground upon which to cast shame. Thus spoke the Patriarch.
Sentient beings and Buddhas are no different; it is only that sentient beings have many habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), while the Buddhas and Patriarchs are pure and stainless.
You have served a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and personally heard his instructions. Your years are now advanced, yet you remain so indolent and distracted.
In the end, you do not know what face you will have when you go from here to see this old monk at some future time. What if, by some chance, the old monk were to...

Your parents feared that even in this life you would have no ground for shame. Thinking of your loyal heart and righteous spirit, they find them no less than those of the ancients. Yesterday, I read the words of Master Daguan, who compared you to Tian Guang; if this is so, how can I, an old monk, repay you for your lifelong devotion?

As it is said, "Among all forms of offering, the Dharma is supreme. Now, as we part, I shall further offer this: [Insert the specific verse or text here] I pray that you will not forget the kindness of your parents. May you be blessed with long life and good fortune. I shall wait for your return.

Sincerely yours, The Old Monk [Name] (To be sent by messenger) P.S. I have also enclosed a small amount of incense and some tea leaves. Please accept them as a token of my gratitude. I hope you will treat them as if they were from your own family. I shall await your reply. May you be well. [Date] [Place] [Seal] (Note: The specific verse or text to be inserted depends on the context of the original correspondence.)
I offer this as a tribute to repay you for your life's service. Henceforth, do not forget the words of our solemn parting today.
As we stand at the crossroads, I take your hand and earnestly charge you to cherish yourself.

The Buddha appeared in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition (ekamahākaruṇāhetu-pratyaya) to instruct the attendant Śāriputra. He desired to cause sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (buddhajñānadarśana).
Now, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is precisely the knowledge and vision of sentient beings; the knowledge and vision of sentient beings is precisely [the Buddha’s knowledge and vision].
This is the knowledge and vision regarding birth and death. Therefore it is said: "To establish knowledge within knowledge and vision is the very root of ignorance;

to have no seeing within knowledge and vision is itself Nirvana. Thus, the knowledge and vision of the sage and the ordinary person are non-dual; that there is a difference between delusion and awakening lies solely in whether one establishes [a conceptual standpoint] or not.
The Patriarch said: "If you establish even a single speck of dust, the nation will perish and the family will be ruined," for knowledge and vision are fundamentally non-existent.
Whether ordinary person or sage, as long as there is immediate attachment to a self, all obstacles will suddenly arise; when there is no self, all phenomena subside into equanimity.
Thus we know that the self is the root of birth and death. It is not only ordinary beings who create the obstacles of greed, hatred, and delusion through the self;
even for all sages and practitioners, as long as their conceptual knowledge and views have not been forgotten, they entirely belong to the obstacle of the self.

Crossing straight through with the body cast across—using the mind in this way, the Sage is not confined to the Three Dynasties, and the past and present do not depart from a single thought. There is...
He set his aspirations upon the Way. From the very moment he first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he entered therein.
He established a model for the world by demonstrating that loyalty and filial piety constitute the primary principle, saying: "Loyalty arises from filial piety and begins with serving one's parents."
The Master said: "One who wishes to serve their parents cannot fail to know other people; one who wishes to know other people cannot fail to know Heaven.
Now, Heaven is precisely the original nature inherent in us humans. In this world, all things may be feigned, but not so for human beings."
The thought of serving one’s parents alone is most genuine, for it arises from innate nature (*prakṛti*).
Since we human beings have received this nature and yet remain as persons, if we do not know the fundamental reality of our innate nature, we shall not know what it is that humans ought to value.
If one can truly know what is precious in humanity, then regarding all things that are empty, frivolous, defiled, and turbid, one will naturally [turn away from them].

How could I dare allow [delusions] to linger within my breast, thereby obstructing the innate luminosity? Once one returns to this fundamental clarity, the sages and worthies are found within oneself;
thus it is said that "the Way is not far from man. This is precisely what that means.

I show Li Zijin that human nature is inherently luminous, yet it is obscured and clouded by external objects, desires, and the dust of emotions; thus, one remains unaware of it in the midst of daily life.

Therefore it is said: "Natures are nearly alike, but habits are far apart. If we individuals are truly resolved to undertake the work of restoring our original nature, [we must apply ourselves diligently].

There is no need to seek it elsewhere. Simply, within the daily activities of seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, at those points where habitual defilements and material desires are most predominant, you must overcome them moment by moment.
Once this overcoming has continued for a long time, objects will be thoroughly penetrated and dust-like delusions will vanish, and the original luminosity will manifest of itself.

It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is cleared away, the brightness appears. Yet the essence of the mirror was originally bright; it does not come to possess brightness only because of the polishing. For anyone who is determined to apply effort toward the Way...
Indeed, one should take the subduing of evil habits as the entrance to the first stage [of the path].
Master Li Rong once cited an ancient saying:
"When cutting hair, it should reach the skin; when clipping nails, they should penetrate the flesh. This speaks to their urgency. Therefore, in studying the Way...
A person of such caliber must first establish a long-term resolve that never regresses and apply a portion of earnest, sincere, and diligent effort.
It is like ascending a mountain ten thousand fathoms high; one does not stop until reaching the very summit. One must exert effort at every step and maintain non-retrogression in every thought.
One should not be swayed by praise or blame, nor shaken or deprived by right or wrong, nor suppressed or frustrated by adversity.
It is like a single person facing ten thousand enemies; if there is even the slightest retreat or cowardice, all prior merit is utterly lost.
Furthermore, how could one reach the state of non-retrogression and peace and bliss without a mind of firm resolve?
Shi Ou said to Jiake, "There is no one who does not eat and drink, yet few are able to know their true flavor. This Way speaks of how the Dao is present in daily life;
though it is most proximate, those who know it are rare. As the ancients said: "Apart from wearing clothes and eating food, there is nothing else. This is it.
Thus, within the space between past and present, many have been deceived by the very acts of eating and wearing clothes.
Had they not been so deceived, they would have been called heroic sages. For those who study the Way, there is no need to seek something subtle elsewhere;
provided that one is not deceived by any of the circumstances of daily life, starting from the moment of putting on clothes and eating food—
To see through it all at a single glance is the true effort directed toward the upward path. Those with the aspiration for the Way should practice within their daily activities.
This was shown to Liang Tengxiao.

When scholar-gentlemen live in this world, before they have met with their destiny, there are none whose aspirations do not lie in rectifying their ruler and sheltering the people, establishing deeds of enduring merit.
Yet once they have entered the registers of office, they concern themselves only with the pursuit of fame, forgetting the very means by which such merit should be achieved.
Over time, one gradually becomes tainted by worldly customs, and the mind and spirit become turbid; without realizing it, one flows into the path of wealth and status.
In extreme cases, one even disregards one’s reputation without hesitation, such that the original aspiration can no longer be found. Why is this?
Because the initial vow did not arise from the fundamental reality, but was merely a fleeting admiration born of deluded thoughts; it was never rooted in firm resolve.
Without a firm and unshakable resolve, how can one establish an immortal legacy? Liang Sheng soars toward the heavens; his bones are strong and his spirit is transcendent.

He is by no means a man of the mundane world. Whenever he accompanies me on my travels, there is not a single word or phrase he hears that does not cause him to be startled and filled with trepidation.
On one occasion, he requested further instruction, to which I replied: "A student must certainly seek their resolve in the Way and its Virtue. As for all such resolves..."

Regarding those who cultivate the Way and its Virtue, one must first investigate our fundamental reality. This must flow forth from true nature (*bhūtatathatā*). This true nature is most vast and most great;
it is luminous and pure, sweeping away even the finest speck of dust. This is the substance of our nature, which is what is called benevolence (*ren*).
Within this substance, not a single speck of dust can be established; yet, if there arises even a single thought of delusive discrimination, it immediately belongs to the realm of existence (*yu*).
There is "I. When there is an "I," one stands in opposition to things. Once things and the self are divided, the person and the non-self are established as two.

Once the person and the non-self are established, the substance of Great Unity becomes obscured and blocked, and one cannot practice benevolence. When the fundamental substance is obscured and blocked, all manner of delusions arise.
Even if one harbors ambitions for fame and achievement, these all emerge from deluded thoughts; whatever actions are undertaken will lack true reality.
Since the root is false, one’s footing is unstable. Consequently, it is only natural that once one enters the conditions of the world, one will suddenly be tainted by worldly customs.
From this day forward, Liang Sheng, you should apply yourself to the practice of self-nature and investigate from the standpoint of ultimate reality. If, regarding self-nature—
If you have not yet been able to investigate the root thoroughly, simply take the phrase from the Sixth Patriarch—“When one neither thinks of good nor thinks of evil;
at this very moment, what is the upādhyāya’s original face?”—and harbor it within your breast. During the twelve periods of the day and night, investigate it with earnest persistence.
When you reach the state where not a single thought arises, you will suddenly recognize your original face; only then will you truly see it.
Old Lu does not deceive me.

He has shown that the essential nature of the prajñā of wandering awareness is fully possessed by every person; it is only due to the thickness or thinness of habitual tendencies that there are differences in the degree of obstruction.

When divided, there arises the distinction between the wise and the foolish. Thus we know that when greed, anger, ignorance, and attachment manifest before us, they are all occasions in which the whole body is fully revealed.
It is only because one is carried away by turbid consciousness that one fails to awaken to this; this is what is meant by "using it daily without knowing it.
Alas! The Sage is no different from ordinary people; it is only that while the ordinary person is entangled in the chaotic and conflicting states of the present world, the Sage remains aware.
At the moment of error, one must see through it with a single glance, so as not to be deceived or robbed by it.
Viewed from this perspective, the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) manifests in every thought-moment like a great mass of fire, whereby all objective realms are seen with total clarity.
I shall show you, Upāsaka Wang Boxuan.
Among the ancients, many spoke of those caught in the midst of worldly toil who yet possessed the aspiration to turn upward and seek liberation from birth and death;

this was called "a lotus growing amidst fire," for such a person is truly difficult to find. This is because all sentient beings, throughout immeasurable kalpas, have been immersed in and addicted to the five [desires].
Desire burns with the fire of afflictions, blazing day and night; not for a single thought-moment has it turned its light inward to find even a moment’s coolness.
Until this very moment, you have been able to suddenly turn your head amidst these fierce flames and instantly contemplate the way out—is this not the lotus flower blooming within the fire?
Bo-xuan is a man from Min who came to trade in Yue; he visited the Elder to seek instruction.

Regarding the Dharma of Renunciation: An old man took pity on him and conferred the five precepts upon him, instructing him in the method of mindfulness of the Buddha and directing his mind single-mindedly toward the Pure Land.
As the sutra says: "When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. For our own minds are the Buddha, and the mind alone is the land.

Purity and defilement are non-dual; the mind and the Buddha are one and the same. Observing in this way and forming such thoughts, one cultivates through every moment of thought until the single mind becomes pure.
Radiance then shines forth, and the lotus-buddha lands of the ten directions appear vividly before one.
How could it be that lotuses grow only within the burning house?
To Chan Practitioner Jijue:
Chan Practitioner Jijue is about to travel east to pay homage at Putuo Mountain. He requests a word for the weightiness of his journey. The Old Man instructs him, saying:
"When the ancients left home, it was specifically for the great matter of birth and death; therefore, they took up their staff and traveled on foot to seek out and consult those with true knowledge."
One must traverse mountains and wade through waters until one has attained illumination and thorough awakening before ceasing.
Yet those who have left the household life today merely bear the empty name of "wandering monks. This year they go to Mount Wutai or Mount Emei; next year to Putuo or Founiu.
Mouths speak of paying homage to famous mountains and visiting sacred sites with joy, yet in reality they do not know what these famous mountains are, nor what these sacred sites entail.

Furthermore, they do not know who constitutes a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). They merely record the heights and depths of mountains and waters, or the quality of the communal meals in monasteries.
Though they have traveled throughout the world, they possess not a single word regarding their home mountain. Is this not tragic?
The boundless South Sea is the surging tide of the ocean of birth-and-death suffering. The colors of Mount Putuo are the eternal abiding of the Great Being’s Dharma-body.
The sea resounds with the sound of the tide; this is the Great Being preaching the Dharma through the Universal Gate.

If a practitioner of Zen can truly cross the sea of birth-and-death, behold the Great Being at the Universal Gate, and listen to the sound of the Dharma on the cliff by the sea, they shall turn their hearing back toward themselves.
In its true nature, you need not take a single step outside your door; why must you wait until reaching Putuo Island before seeing it?

If this is not yet the case, then on your long and winding journey, you will come and go in vain—even if the Great Being were present at the crown of your head, he could not uproot the karmic roots of birth and death for you.
Zen practitioner, settle this for yourself and look into it! If there are any words or phrases from the Great Being to return to...
When you come, you should present this to the Old Man; take care not to waste the money for your straw sandals in vain.
To Liang Zhongqian (Jiayin). Liang Zisi’s courtesy name was Zhongqian.
He has followed the Old Man for many years, and the Old Man loves him for his sincere and straightforward nature.

His spirit was bold and resolute; whenever he encountered an injustice, regardless of whether it was feasible or not, or whenever there was a righteous cause for action, he would immediately risk even his own life to confront it.
The Elder often rebuked him for being coarse and impulsive, noting that despite possessing the substance of the Way, he lacked the merit of cultivation and self-possession.
It was as if he were a spirited horse without a bit or bridle; in the end, he could not avoid stumbling. The Elder—
As he was about to depart, I saw him off on a boat in Shaoyang. He requested a discourse on the Dharma to record upon his girdle, so I have written this and sent it to him.
I say that Liangzi is a man of the Way; his mind is upright and not crooked—this is the root of the Way.

His resolute spirit approaches valor, and his readiness to respond to urgency approaches compassion. To forget one’s own body in such pursuits is neither to underestimate one's capacity nor to fail to discern the proper measure of circumstances.
To fail to investigate the root while attending to the branches is entirely driven by coarse and superficial impulses; it does not arise from the power of the Way.

When the sages of antiquity engaged with the world, their essence and function were fully manifest, so that their responses never missed the proper timing—like a clear mirror reflecting beauty and ugliness, or a scale determining lightness and heaviness.
This was by no means a matter of merely following one's blood and breath. From this day forward, Master Liang...
Go. You must first wash away habitual tendencies and apply yourself wholeheartedly to the Way.
Take the phrase from the Sixth Patriarch, "Originally there is not a single thing," and hold it firmly across your chest. At every moment, keep watch over the place where thoughts arise;

whether they be good or evil, press down upon them with this very phrase, and they will vanish instantly. Maintain this state continuously and closely, making this primary koan your fundamental practice.
Command the vital breath and the *uḍḍīyāna* lock. After a long time of pure cultivation, the state of mind will naturally become empty and tranquil.

Whether in motion or stillness, in whatever actions one performs, and whatever circumstances one encounters, the *huatou* (critical phrase) will manifest before one. This is the clarity and non-confusion of illumination and function.

Sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one will naturally not fall into the realm of coarseness, superficiality, or recklessness, nor will one follow the footsteps of others. Even when reading books or composing literary works, [the practice remains present].
This does not hinder one's primary inquiry. Having read and practiced, one lets go and returns to the state where "originally there is nothing at all. Naturally, the mind becomes level and settled.
After a long time, one suddenly perceives the fundamental essence of the mindless body, as if dwelling within the Treasury of Radiance (*prabhāsvara-garbha*).
Every pore of the body is then the very activity of benefiting sentient beings; how, then, could there be any such thing as a physical life to be preserved?
Abandon it! Use your mind in this way, maintaining and nurturing it until the essence of the mind manifests before you. When reading books, your mind will then illuminate the minds of the sages;
when composing writings, they will flow forth from your own nature. This is the true accomplishment of a noble and resolute man.
What is called the pivot finding its place within the ring allows it to respond to infinity; thus, when one establishes merit and achieves great deeds, they all become imperishable.
Since Master Li possesses this fundamental principle, why should he hesitate or fear not to act?
Shown to Liu Zhongan (Winter of Gui-chou).
While I was residing in Wuyang, there were many who followed me as disciples at that time. Observing Mr. Liu, I saw that his bones were firm and his spirit was profound;
I believed he had long possessed the seeds and conditions for *prajñā* and that his vessel was close to the Way. As I was about to undertake a journey to Nanyue, Mr. Liu saw me off by boat.

In the midst of this, he specifically requested further instruction, saying: "My disciple’s aspiration for the Way is most earnest, yet because my past habits are so thick and delusive thoughts entangle me, I am unable to escape directly toward the Ultimate.
I hope the Master will provide me with guidance. The Old Man replied: "If you recognize delusive thoughts as such, then those thoughts will naturally be unable to entangle you.
Since they are called 'delusive thoughts,' they fundamentally have no substantial reality. They are, for example, like empty space."
How can a flower produce an empty fruit? It is because the seed does not realize that delusive thought (*vikalpa*) is fundamentally non-existent;
it recognizes it as a real dharma and establishes it in opposition to itself. Moment after moment, it rolls and tumbles with it, never having a single thought-moment of rest.
Thus, one takes delusive thought as the master, and one's own original substance (*ātman*) becomes buried and obscured. This is why one sees the creation of the Way.
It is merely a matter of difficulty. Have you not seen when a monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is it like when delusive thoughts do not cease?
The worthy replied, "Delusive thoughts are not evil. Under the assembly at Huangmei, the Sixth Patriarch could only say, "Originally there is not a single thing.
From this day forward, apply yourself to practice by taking the single phrase "originally there is not" as your *huatou*. Second.
Throughout the six periods of the day and night, investigate with earnest persistence. Simply observe where delusive thoughts arise; by no means follow them into their flow.
With a single, sudden pressure upon them, their tracks will naturally be swept away and their traces extinguished.
*The Dream-Traveling Collection of the Elder Hanshan, Volume Four* *The Dream-Traveling Collection of the Elder Hanshan, Volume Five*
Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and his disciple Tonghyeong;
revised by the Disciple from the South of the Pass, Liu Qixiang.
Dharma Talk for Zen Practitioner Xuanzhiyun:
A student of the Way must first see through and break through all worldly conditions, so as not to be turned by delusive circumstances.
Second, you must resolve upon the great matter of birth and death with a heart as firm as iron or stone, ensuring that delusive thoughts and external attachments do not steal away your resolve.
Third, you must completely wash away all former habitual tendencies, evil perceptions, and views, so that not even a single trace remains.
Fourth, you must truly and sincerely relinquish body and life, no longer being bound by birth or death.
The patient is obstructed by adverse conditions. Fifth, one must develop right faith and right view; one must not listen to the errors of false teachers.
Sixth, one must recognize the point where the ancients applied their minds with such earnestness and take this as the object of investigation for the *huatou*.
Seventh, one must maintain the presence of right mindfulness in all places throughout daily life, so as not to be deluded by illusory transformations; in every thought, there should be no...

In leisure, movement, and stillness, remain as one. Eighth, you must maintain a direct mindfulness that moves forward; do not harbor a mind waiting for enlightenment. Ninth, you must persevere for a long time;
until your resolve reaches the ground of the ancient masters, never settle for less and never be content with minor achievements. Do not consider a small attainment sufficient.
Tenth, in the practice of *gongfu*, one must, in every thought-moment, let go and rest. Let go again and again; rest again and again. Continue letting go until there is nothing more to let go of;
continue resting until there is no further place to rest. Only then will you naturally encounter the "good news.
If a student applies their mind in this way, they may perhaps correspond slightly with the fundamental matter. Those with the aspiration to advance upward should take this as their guide.
Exhort yourself.
To the Zen practitioner Liaoxin Hai:

Our leaving the household life is solely for the sake of the great matter of birth and death. Wielding our staff and traveling on foot, visiting teachers and seeking friends, we do so only for this purpose.

Having personally resolved the single path leading upward from within oneself, I have not ceased until clarity was attained. Therefore, the true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) points people toward this matter alone.

Lately, the Dharma-gate has fallen into decline; such a tradition is rarely heard of in various quarters. Wherever one travels as a wandering monk (paryaṭaka), there is nothing but the mere pursuit of the "fragrance of rice and gruel.
While I, an old man, was dwelling at the hermitage on Linghu, the Zen practitioner Liaoxin came to seek instruction.
Upon first entering, I saw that he possessed the core essence of a true monk; he did not seem like an ordinary eater of gruel and rice.
Now, as I am about to return to Mount Funiu, I have brought incense to offer and seek further instruction. The Elder showed me the way, saying:

"At present, throughout the Zen forests within the realm, the foremost reliance is upon the asceticism of Mount Niu; this is beyond the reach of other regions. If students of the Way can truly renounce their bodies and lives..."
Life will certainly not be spent in vain; however, for daily practice, it is most essential to maintain the single thought of the *huatou* with utmost continuity and density.

The reason one fails to attain transcendence and great mastery is that one has been consistently "deadly" in guarding the *huatou*, never letting go from moment to moment, without realizing that the foremost requirement of Chan meditation is to internally detach from body and mind and externally cast off the world, thereby leaving behind all discursive thoughts.
Attachment! Thus, by fixating the mind, one is instead bound by that very mindfulness, unable to attain liberation in the great state of self-mastery.

This time, as you enter the mountains, Zen practitioners, you should fortunately rely upon the rules and regulations and the support of the assembly; it is precisely now that you must apply yourself with effort according to the circumstances at hand.

However, within every moment of thought, observe the place where thought has not yet arisen. By remaining fixed upon this state of being free from thought for a long time, the stream of thought will suddenly snap.
Mind and object will both be forgotten, like a lion that has shed its tether, roaming with sovereign ease.
When you see the old man again at another time, his eyebrows and eyes will certainly not be as they are today—wavering and fixed.

He showed the various upāsakas of Xiangtan that when the Buddha dwells in the world preaching the Dharma, there are always four assemblies in attendance: the two groups who have left the household life—the bhikṣus and the bhikṣuṇīs.
The two groups of householders are called *upāsaka*—translated here as "male lay devotee" (*jìnshì nán*)—and *upāsikā*—translated as "female lay devotee" (*jìnshì nǚ*).
Because these householders are able to uphold the five precepts, they can serve the Triple Gem and are worthy of receiving the benefits of the Dharma;

thus, since the Buddha-Dharma came to the East, there have been those who followed its transformation at all times, never lacking for individuals. There were even those who clarified the mind and perceived its nature, entering the lineage of the Patriarchs.
Regarding those in the Master’s quarters: in recent times, the Way of the Dharma has long been submerged and the lineage of masters has lost its discerning eye.

People perform three prostrations at will and, upon receiving a single name, immediately claim themselves to be disciples. In reality, they have not yet cast off their worldly attachments nor changed their coarse conduct;
this leads to slander and brings no benefit whatsoever, becoming a major source for the corruption of the Dharma. Therefore, throughout his life, the Elder did not dare to treat them lightly.
I grant it. Observing the disciples here in Xiangtan now, their faith is profound and sincere; they are not like those who drift aimlessly with the current.

Therefore, I have reluctantly granted your request. However, I am mindful that you have not previously heard the Dharma; though you are called "good people," you do not know what constitutes goodness.
Now, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*) are taught;
however, only eleven are virtuous dharmas, while the remainder are all unwholesome mental factors. These eleven factors are: faith, diligence, shame, remorse, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
Pliancy, heedfulness, equanimity, and non-harming—when these eleven factors are fully present, one is a person of pure virtue.
However, if even one factor is lacking, one’s qualities are deficient. You should simply rely on the teachings to uphold these wholesome dharmas, investigating and clarifying each one individually.
From time to time, observe them and maintain mindfulness; regarding whichever dharma has not yet reached full maturity, apply yourself with further refinement and cultivation.
One must strive to bring all matters to perfect completion before ceasing. To apply the mind in this way is to be a truly virtuous person.
What is called a "virtuous mind" is precisely the pure, true mind (*tathatā-citta*).

Since all sentient beings each inherently possess the pure, true mind of a Tathāgata, it is only because they are defiled by evil thoughts that they act according to their passions and create karma without realizing it. Now...
If one can observe with a virtuous mind, then all unwholesome dharmas will naturally not manifest before one, and the mind will become pure of itself.
If one can apply oneself with resolve and gradually engage in deep contemplation—specifically investigating the public case (gong'an) of the Sixth Patriarch Master’s instruction to Huiming:
"Do not think of good; do not think of evil. At that very moment, what is the original face of Elder Huiming?"—then at such a time, [the mind becomes pure].
To investigate at such a time is called the path that leads upward. Beneath the heels of each of you, who does not possess even a foot of earth?

Exert yourselves and move forward; you shall certainly not be deceived. If you are willing to turn your hearts toward the Pure Land, then rely on this method and recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion.
Then, in this very life, you may sever birth and death and forever cut off the cycle of sinking and drifting. Only I fear that you will deceive yourselves with a thieving mind and be unable to do so.
This is merely performing the practice of reality. This old man has forcefully spoken such words for your sake out of pity for his three-year-old son;
he would not have spared even two strands of his own eyebrows. You must by no means interpret this as a discourse on conventional truth.
*Shifangjuezhi* (The Manifestation of the Method for Awakening), Year Yimao.

Regarding the method of awakening: although his physical form was fragmented and disjointed, his celestial mechanism (*tianji*) manifested wondrously. He visited the Old Man [Nanquan] at Mount Nanyue;

the Old Man saw that his heart-mind radiance (*xin-guang*) was brilliant and clear, concluding that he possessed latent seeds from former lives regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Consequently, he constantly pointed him toward the Ultimate.
Fangzi received this with a heart as clear as drinking ice-cold water. Now, as we were about to part, he took up incense to seek further instruction. I then showed him, saying:
"Fangzi, do not consider it a deficiency that Heaven has perfected your nature while leaving your physical form incomplete.
I know that Heaven does not burden you with form, but rather uses the formless to thicken your virtue. In the world, those with complete forms are many; yet those whose forms are damaged..."
Those who are born are many. Who among them can cast off the physical form and relinquish cognition to preserve their true nature?

The Sage regarded the body as a burden to life; thus he said, "The great affliction is that I have a body. Therefore, one extinguishes the body to return to non-existence, for when the form is dissolved, suffering ceases.
In our Buddhist teaching of sentient beings, the destruction of the self (*ātman*) is taken as the primary principle. Upon entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)...
The essential point is this: do not rely on the physical form, do not rely on the vital breaths; detach from everything, and the mind will naturally become tranquil.
When the mind is tranquil, its bliss is beyond compare. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says: "One should contemplate that this body is a provisional combination of the four great elements.

What is solid and hard returns to earth; what is moist and wet returns to water; what is warm returns to fire; what moves and shifts returns to wind. Once the four great elements have each separated, this present [body] is but a delusion."
"Body, where will you be? From this moment on, throughout the two periods of six hours each day, you should simply practice such contemplation as this.

When your contemplation reaches the state where not a single thought arises, you will see no body externally and see no mind internally. Body and mind will be tranquil and still, with not a single dharma to be found.
At that time, you will finally realize that Heaven has stripped away your provisional self and fully bestowed upon you your true nature. Then, your—
Supreme bliss does not require the forgetting of form to reach its ultimate limit. You need only apply yourself with diligence and cultivate this contemplation.
Once you have attained clear penetration, you will finally believe that the old man’s words were not false.
Record of the Elder’s Arrival at Wuyang to Preach the Dharma (Year of Yimao):
At that time, many disciples of the Dharma-nature, as well as monastics and laypeople, took refuge [in him].
This flourishing and admirable state was also due to the conditions of the time and season. Not long after, however, many disturbances arose and the Dharma assemblies were difficult to convene.
When the Elder entered Caoxi, many of those previously present at the assembly had also withdrawn; only Zhihai, An, Xiushi, and Liu Yi remained.
When [Huian] was alert and vigorous, the three men never left him to attend to his needs; even when he grew old at Nan Yue, the two disciples An and Yi followed him without ever abandoning him.

This was because their gratitude for the "milk of the Dharma" was profound and their sense of righteousness reached the highest degree. When the Elder lived in seclusion by the eastern lake, three years passed without his realizing it;
he always maintained an extreme simplicity and austerity, while the two disciples remained tranquil—this can hardly be compared to the followers of Confucius during the times of Chen and Cai.

This passed by. Shortly thereafter, Yì'àn returned home to visit his aged master, offering incense and requesting further instruction. He said, "I pray you grant me a single phrase that I may uphold for the rest of my life.
The old man thought to himself, "I am already old; the conditions for the Dharma of world-transcendence are difficult to encounter. As the Sūtra says:
'It is like a one-eyed turtle in the great ocean meeting the hole of a floating log—how easy is it not? Alas, my son, go now; you must listen attentively."

The Buddha said that all sentient beings realize perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Thus we know that the Buddha-nature is fully present within each and every person, lacking not even a single hair’s breadth.

Yet, the reason all sentient beings wander through birth and death, cycling in saṃsāra for long kalpas without returning, is simply because they turn their backs on enlightenment, unite with the sensory dust, follow the current of birth and death, and pursue the net of Māra without self-awareness.
It is known. Because one does not know oneself and does not awaken to oneself, one suffers in vain through the cycle of delusion and sinking.
This is exactly like a beggar holding a jewel who, unaware that he possesses a wish-fulfilling gem within his breast, casts it away and willingly endures a life of wandering poverty. For this reason:
The Tathāgata calls such a person one who is to be pitied. An old man constantly observes that his son’s nature is straightforward and honest; he has forgotten artifice and is close to the Way.
Yet, because his habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are deep-seated, he cannot maintain himself. He is often painfully dragged along by his past habits;
once caught in the snare of Māra, his entire being falls away, and he does not realize his suffering. When he suddenly awakens to this, he regrets it too late.

One is able to leap out of birth and death; yet, in one's frantic haste, one attempts to settle the mind for practice. Before the conditions for the Way have gathered, familiar objects appear before one, and habitual tendencies flare up again.
Unaware, one follows the waves and drifts with the current. By the time one turns back to look after oneself, much time has already passed.
Thus, rising and falling in this manner, one has relied upon an elder for twenty years, yet as for the birth and death within one’s own person—

This is a great matter; one is utterly lost and has no place of refuge. Why is this? It is because while one possesses the potential for entering the Way, one lacks the firm, unyielding, and resolute will.

Consequently, one cannot stand firmly upon one’s own feet; many evil thoughts and habitual tendencies arise within the breast, and one refuses to apply the bitter, decisive hand to cleanse them thoroughly.
To study the Way in such a way, indulging one's own whims—this is not right.

If you do not accomplish it in this life, then for a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas, there will never be a time when it is accomplished. The Buddha said: "The Buddha-dharma is difficult to hear;
a spiritual friend is difficult to encounter. Now, fortunately, you have selected a spiritual friend and heard the True Dharma. If you let this pass by face-to-face,"
He appeared once more. Who knows how much time has passed since then? It would be impossible to find such an opportunity as today again.

You have had the good fortune to meet this old man in this life; for a long time our movements and stillness were never constant, until now we have been together for two years. I rejoice that you are able to endure hardship.
One may truly call this firm resolve. Now, as we part, I fear that being separated from my elder will not necessarily be as it is today. Alas, I am old;
even if I sought to serve my elder again as I do today, it might not be possible. If I fail to achieve anything by the end of my life, [it will have been in vain].
Would this not be to辜负 (waste) the great causal conditions of this one life? My son, you are now departing. What I earnestly exhort you:
by all means do not fall again into the net of Māra. You must maintain your exceptional conduct and must not dwell long in the royal city.
If, with a heart that endures hardship for two years, you serve the Sixth Patriarch as you would an elder, and believe the single phrase "your own mind is Buddha," then...
Believing in the Elder, you shall endure and not give vent to your former habitual tendencies.
Rubbing and polishing mind after mind, examining and reflecting thought after thought, hold fast to a single phrase of the *huatou*. Bite down firmly upon your teeth; do not easily let it slip away.

If you thus devote your entire life to this, vowing never to change your resolve, then you will not only remain not a single step removed from the Elder, but will be one with the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Whether moving about, sitting, reclining, or walking, one does not step outside the precincts of the *bodhimaṇḍa*.
Not only does one thus avoid disappointing the Elder, but one also avoids disappointing oneself.
To Liu Cunchi (Year of Yimao).
Recently, as I grew old and retired to the Southern Peak (Nanyue), at the end of winter in the year of Jiayin, Liu Jizi of Chaling came from afar to pay his respects.
Amidst the snow, we sat around a brazier by night, illuminated by cold lamps. I asked him, "How have you been applying yourself lately? He replied, "In the past, I was favored by..."
The Master’s verse of instruction says: "A lotus grows within fire; the people of the world call this rare. It is not that the lotus is born from fire;
it is simply that the mind is free from defilement. Whenever I contemplate this saying, I find great benefit in its final line. The Elder was deeply pleased and said to me:
"You have gained strength from the phrase 'the mind is free from defilement. These words are not empty; they are indeed true."

It is easy to attain. As the Sūtra says: "Ordinary beings and sages are equal, without high or low; it depends only on the extinction of mental defilements, and realization is as easy as turning over one's hand.
From this perspective, sentient beings and Buddhas have been non-dual from the beginning. As it is said: "The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
It is simply that when the mind is pure, one is a Buddha; when the mind is defiled, one is a sentient being. Sentient beings and Buddhas...
The accomplishment of this is not far off; it depends solely on whether the defilements of the mind are extinguished or not.

Because this mind is originally pure, yet is obscured by the turbidity of various karmic illusions—namely greed, hatred, delusion, pride, the five desires, and afflictions—it is called a "sentient being.
If these defilements are purified, one is immediately called a Buddha. How could this depend on any external power? Alas, all sentient beings...
Sentient beings have deep-seated karmic obstructions from beginningless time and firm afflictions, making it difficult to attain purity. One must necessarily rely on the labor of refinement;
thus, there are various expedients such as Chan meditation, Buddha-recitation, and the investigation of the *hwadu*, all of which are medicines for treating the mind.

For example, the light of a mirror is originally bright, yet it becomes obscured by impurities; it must rely on the application of polishing agents to be restored. However, these agents are themselves impurities;
because they can remove the impurities, once the mirror is bright, the agents no longer remain. It is also like pure gold within ore:
amidst the sand, stones, and filth, one must employ the method of smelting and refining; once the essence of the gold is attained, the refining process is no longer required. [The multitude...]

The defilements of the mind are difficult to abandon; one must apply diligent effort to cultivate and rectify them. When these defilements are removed, the mind becomes luminous; therefore, it is said that sentient beings are originally Buddhas.
This does not mean they are already Buddhas while remaining entirely within the turbid defilements of affliction, nor is it a matter of falsely claiming to be Buddhas.

Among the various approaches, the path of Chan meditation through the investigation of the *huatou* (critical phrase) is the most essential for clarifying the mind. However, regarding those who have recently begun this practice...
Rarely indeed. This is because, on one hand, people have dull faculties and lack the "dead heart" (the resolve for liberation) of the ancients;

and on the other hand, they lack the discernment provided by true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), causing them to frequently fall into false views. For these reasons, the practice that combines the recitation of the Buddha’s name with Zen meditation is an exceptionally stable and reliable dharma-gate.

If you take even a single recitation of the Buddha’s name and harbor it within your breast, pursuing it moment by moment to examine the actual place where it arises and the place where it falls, you must certainly see its definitive point of descent.
After a long time, suddenly impurities will be cleansed and clarity will manifest; the mind-ground will open and become unobstructed.
This is no different from contemplating a *kōan* or a *hwadu*. One must exert effort and apply oneself with diligence before one can succeed.

If you pass your days in a state of drifting indifference, letting delusive thoughts rise and fall as they will, and treat this practice as something unimportant, then even at the end of your life you will find no benefit.
To take such indolence and the indulgence of delusive thoughts as true realization is to deceive yourself; it is not merely a single instance of error.
From this moment forth, until the exhaustion of kalpas, there shall be no time when you are mistaken. You have a karmic affinity for the Dharma gate of Buddha-remembrance;
try to investigate and examine it with earnestness. Indeed, even amidst the turbid defilements of afflictions, a single utterance of the Buddha’s name is like a water-clearing jewel.
To enjoy its benefits in this way is sufficient, though it does not yet exhaustively reach the ultimate source. As the Sūtra says:
It is like settling turbid water: as the sand and soil sink of their own accord, clear water appears before one; this is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*).

When the mud is removed and pure water remains, this is called the eternal severance of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). You should simply take these words of the Buddha and verify them for yourself in silence;
there will not be even one error in ten thousand attempts. If you reach the state of true detachment from defilement, it will be as the Sūtra says: "The marks of clarity are pure and refined."
One will not be obstructed by adventitious afflictions. This is not only welcomed and guided by Amitābha;

even all the Buddhas of the ten directions will likewise join their voices in praise. It is fortunate that we have spent these years together through snow and night in this style of refined, serene practice, which is rare in this world.
If you do not fail this auspicious meeting, simply proceed from now on with every thought never departing from this serenity.
Within this state of detachment lies the very path to leaving behind all defilement. If you apply effort at every step, there will surely come a time of true liberation upon reaching home.
This was shown to Zhong Hengying.
Zhong Sheng Mingxing of Chaling was born into a family with a long tradition of Confucian learning. Having fled to Guangdong due to past hardships, he came to Caoxi to meet me.
I enlightened him with the teachings on the retribution of good and evil and the law of cause and effect, thereby bringing peace to his mind so that he could return home.
His distress was ultimately resolved; this resolution was not something reachable through mere thought or imagination, but arose spontaneously when the karmic conditions coincided by chance.

I arrived. Because of this, my life was spared and I remained unharmed, treading upon a realm of peace and tranquility free from affairs. Yet, I remained utterly bewildered and ignorant of the reason for it.

Consequently, I resolved that those lifelong matters which had failed to satisfy my heart or bring me joy would henceforth be pursued with all my effort, as if reaching into a bag to pick up a blade of grass.
On the eve of the New Year in the year Jia-yin, Liu Cunchi came from afar to console me.
Accompanying me as I pass the year, the old man sighed and lamented, saying: "What you aspire to is like crossing the sea and traversing a river in search of sweet spring water.
You may not find the spring at all, yet your thirst will only grow more intense, and you shall suffer the toil of the long journey."

I previously used the principle of karmic retribution to instruct you; have you perhaps forgotten it? Indeed, the response between good and evil is as swift as a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound;
when the voice is harmonious, the resonance follows suit, and when the shape is straight, the shadow is upright. Therefore, the sages did not speak merely of cause and effect, but said instead:
"For doing good, a hundred blessings descend; for doing evil, a hundred calamities descend. For this reason, one should settle the mind and accept one's lot with equanimity.
Therefore it is said: "One who does not understand destiny cannot be considered a gentleman. The sages teach people to find peace in destiny;
the Buddha teaches people to follow conditions (*pratyaya*). Their paths are one and the same. To find peace in destiny means that not even a single hair’s breadth need be forced;

to follow conditions means that not a single thought-moment may harbor delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Thus, the Buddha-dharma teaches people with the singular principle of severing delusive conceptualization as its foundation. Delusive conceptualization...
This is the root of all various evil karmas, namely greed, hatred, and delusion.

Thus, from the Bodhisattva’s practice until the attainment of Buddhahood, the resulting supreme adornments and vast fields of merit obtained in the heavens and among humans all begin with the severing of deluded thoughts.
When deluded thoughts are severed, evil karma is extinguished; when evil karma is extinguished, a hundred blessings gather. This is what is meant by "seeking much blessing for oneself.
Therefore, it is shown in verse: All worldly affairs arise from deluded thoughts. Where the deluded mind is extinguished, karmic conditions grow light.
There is no need to seek further the path to Bodhi; It simply requires that the person take a step backward. As for "taking a step backward":
This is the supreme practice for resting the mind and severing delusions. Since the human mind is originally luminous and vast, it is the source of all blessings.
However, because it is obscured by delusive appearances and evil karma, misfortune increases daily while blessings diminish.
Now, if delusions are eliminated and karma severed, then the single nature will be perfectly radiant, and one will enjoy boundless benefit. This is the state of attaining such enjoyment.
This is true blessing. This is knowing that blessings arise from one's own actions; they truly cannot be attained through cleverness, artifice, or deception.
Furthermore, the Buddha taught that by severing the deluded mind, one moves the blessings of devas and humans. Zhongsheng originally possessed the foundation for fame, honor, wealth, and nobility.
If he can now directly bring his mind to rest, he will be able to examine from the very beginning all the karma he has created throughout his life.
Examine each detail minutely. Whatever involves a deficiency of heart or an injury to principle—any single thought that does not accord with the Great Way—is entirely a root of suffering.
Cast all of this out at once. Establish a new foundation from the beginning and apply yourself to a fresh effort.
Let "resting the mind, severing delusions, listening to the mandate, and awaiting the right time" be your sole standard. Immerse yourself in what is inherently possessed within you.
Regarding this matter of one's vocation, there is no need to separately seek out the affairs of a single moment of deluded thought to compensate for the shortcomings of previous conduct.
Once calamities have vanished and blessings arrive, fame, achievement, wealth, and honor will press upon you from all sides, leaving no room for evasion.
What use, then, is to engage in various delusions and attachments to seek elsewhere? If Master Zhong can truly believe this with deep conviction...
Do not doubt. Grasp this and put it into practice; then the fruit of Buddhahood may be expected, let alone worldly conditions. Exert yourselves, exert yourselves!

This is shown to the scholar-officials of the world, such as Yuan Datu, who have the will to advance upward and pay close attention to the study of the Buddha-dharma. Often they contemplate deeply and aspire loftily, yet remain far removed from [the actual practice].
They abandon worldly affairs and emulate the ascetic practices (*dhūta*) of withered trees as their "sublime conduct.

Little do they realize that the Buddha has already sternly rebuked such people, calling them "withered sprouts and rotten seeds," meaning they are incapable of engaging with the secular world to benefit living beings.
This is precisely what the former Confucian scholars pointed to as "voidness and extinction"; our Buddha rejected this long ago. What the Buddhist teachings value lies in self-... [text truncated]
One who benefits both self and others is called a Bodhisattva. In the Sanskrit language, "Bodhisattva" translates here as "a being of great resolve.
He receives this name because he is able to enter the realm of sentient beings and is able to sever their afflictions (*kleśa*).
A Bodhisattva abandons worldly practices that cannot be cultivated and abandons sentient beings who lack the means to sever their afflictions; therefore, the Bodhisattva relies upon sentient beings.
One must sever the afflictions of one's own nature; it is like using stones from another mountain to polish a jade gem.
These afflictions—namely greed, anger, self-love, views, pride, and various other evil habits—are the veils that obscure the luminosity of one's own nature.
They cannot be ground down and eliminated through polishing by any adverse conditions or external circumstances encountered by worldly beings. As the verse says:
This is precisely what is meant by "cutting, rubbing, carving, and polishing. Furthermore, the Five Precepts established by the Buddha correspond to the Five Constant Virtues of Confucianism:
not killing is benevolence; not stealing is righteousness; not engaging in sexual misconduct is propriety; not drinking intoxicants is wisdom; and not speaking falsely is [trustworthiness].
This is indeed true. However, what is spoken from the Buddha’s own mouth may differ in phrasing while being identical in meaning.

Nowadays, whenever people resolve their minds and vow to uphold the Buddha’s precepts, they often neglect the Five Constant Virtues (wuchang) themselves; this shows they know "two fives" but do not know "ten.

Furthermore, they promote meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as the supreme vehicle because it can clarify the mind and reveal one's nature, yet they fail to realize that Confucianism also possesses this. Take Yan Hui, for example.

Yuan asked about benevolence (*ren*). The Master said, "To overcome oneself and return to the ritual propriety (*li*) is benevolence. "Overcoming oneself" refers to the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*).

Is this not precisely the essential requirement for practicing dhyāna—first to shatter the grasping at a self? "When one day one overcomes oneself, the whole world returns to benevolence. Is this not the wondrous mystery of sudden enlightenment (*tunwu*)?
For the entire world consists of things that stand in opposition and create obstacles to the self; if the grasping at a self is once shattered, then all...
All things are already [within] oneself. Is this not the effect of sudden enlightenment through returning to benevolence? When I requested the specific details, he replied:

"Do not look, listen, speak, or act in a manner contrary to propriety (*li*). Since those things which one looks at, listens to, speaks, or acts upon are all external objects that are contrary to propriety, they constitute an obstruction to the self.
Now, 'do not' means not being turned by sounds and forms. At all times and in all places..."
To fall into such impropriety would surely not be to enter dhyāna with precepts as the foremost.

However, while the Buddha often spoke in terms of world-transcendence, when it comes to actual practice, it fundamentally does not depart from the mundane world; even the conduct of Bodhisattvas dwelling in the world does not go beyond this.
"Buddha" means "awakened. One who can awaken this very mind is called a Buddha; it is not that one seeks a Buddha apart from this pure mind.
This is because sentient beings have heavy obstructions from evil habits and their minds are difficult to purify;

therefore, the expedient means of mindfulness of the Buddha and the Dharma-gate of seeking rebirth in the Pure Land were established. It is further said, "If the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. Thus, we know that mindfulness of the Buddha...

This is truly the sublime practice for purifying the mind. Now, the essence of Buddha-recitation is precisely the purification of the mind; if one recites the Buddha’s name while the mind remains impure, what is the point of such recitation?
To observe the precepts while turning one's back on the Five Constant Virtues—what value can there be in such precepts? Mr.

Yuan possesses a sincere aspiration for the Way and has formed a fellowship with others to cultivate the Pure Land practice together. This is surely the manifestation of virtuous roots cultivated in past lives. He has visited the Elder and established a firm resolve.
"Please bestow the precepts. The elder showed him [the text] and said: "The essence of the precepts is inherently complete within you.
If you sincerely believe my words and purify your own mind, then the precepts have already been received, meditation has already been practiced, and you have already entered the Pure Land.
The wondrous practices of the Bodhisattvas and all mundane and supramundane dharmas, including both self-benefit and benefit for others, are entirely contained herein. You must strive in this."
To the Chan practitioner Shuanglunzhao, who had come for an audience, he said:
"You intend to retire to the mountains to investigate the matter beyond [the ordinary] in solitude, and you ask for the method of an elder’s mountain dwelling.
Therefore, I shall instruct you: when the ancients dwelt in the mountains, it was a place where they utterly sacrificed their bodies and lives."
This is by no means a trivial matter; it requires solely the skillful use of one's mind. As for the method of using the mind:
simply maintain the single thought directed toward the Ultimate (the "upward" direction). You must firmly plant your feet at that point where even Buddhas and Patriarchs have no place to stand.
Next, you must completely expel all the knowledge, views, subtle words, and poisonous杂毒 (mixed poisons) within your breast. Finally, you will recognize the original substance.
There is not a single dharma that can allow the shadows of delusive thoughts and habitual tendencies to give rise to various objective realms and confuse right mindfulness.
Next, you must examine the original koan, such as the Sixth Patriarch’s case: "When neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil, what is one's original face?
Exert all your strength to maintain this inquiry. However, whenever any evil habits manifest, [you must immediately recognize them].
First, you must immediately see through the fact that there has never been a single word from the very beginning. You must by no means follow along with its continuous flow;
instead, clench your teeth firmly. At this point, you must certainly maintain your ground, for only then will you not be shaken or deprived of it by it. Apply your mind in this manner.

This is precisely the point at which one must exert effort during the state of alertness. If one exerts the mind with excessive force, the mind of indolence will arise, and one will immediately fall into dullness and sinking.
At such a time, one need only quickly sharpen one's mental acuity; one must not fall into the pitfall of torpor.
One must urgently recite mantras, relying on the power of these mantras to sufficiently counteract this demon, for within the *ālayavijñāna* lie the evils of many kalpas.
Through practice, one is now driven by the *huatou* (critical phrase) into a realm of infinite transformations. All demonic realms arise from deluded thoughts;
all states of dullness arise from distraction. Precisely at the moment of applying the mind, if a single thought of distraction suddenly occurs, one immediately falls into dullness.
This must be well understood. Yongjia’s fourfold discernment regarding "stillness and alertness" is most essential.
This is essential. As for the application of mind by the ancients, they simply relied steadfastly upon a single phrase of the primary koan, as if it were an iron wall or a silver mountain.
