When one reaches the state where not a single thought arises, that too is a point of gaining strength; yet, one must not mistake this for the ultimate realization.

Only when one’s practice becomes spontaneous and no longer requires deliberate thought, and when a single thought suddenly dawns such that body and mind feel as if they have been cast off into emptiness, is the goal truly reached.
This is precisely where the practice begins, yet it is not yet the ultimate realization.
However, upon reaching this point, one naturally experiences lightness, ease, and freedom, giving rise to joy. Yet this is merely the fundamental state; it is not something extraordinary.
If one conceives of it as extraordinary, one falls into the demon of joy and gives rise to groundless, frantic knowledge and understanding. This barrier is most perilous. This...
These are all instances where elders have been tested. An ancient saying goes: "Before the withered tree at the crag, the paths of error are many;

when travelers reach this point, they all falter. This is no small matter. Even if one has the strength to strike through various states of experience, it is precisely then that one must practice and precisely then that one must protect oneself;
yet this is not yet arriving home. If you take this to be sufficient, various worldly thoughts will immediately arise.
The thoughts arising from the conditions of the five desires constitute a barrier difficult to pass; of those who do pass it, there is not one in a hundred or a thousand.
This is precisely why one does not reach the realm of the ancients: it is the fault of being satisfied with a mere trifle.

Even if you, as a student, exert yourself with bitter diligence for a lifetime and reach this stage, if you are still dragged away by such evil habits, you will nevertheless fall back into the cycle of birth and death.
In the pit, all previous merit is utterly discarded. Is this not tragic? There are many such sayings recorded in the words of the ancients;
I, an old man, have briefly extracted them for you, as it is difficult to find those who truly study the Way during the Age of Dharma Decline.

It is likely because he was once a profligate himself that he feels such particular compassion for travelers. Generally speaking, when the ancients dwelt in the mountains, it was not to indulge their indolence or seek personal pleasure;
they did so solely for the sake of the great matter of their own birth and death. Therefore, they retreated to the myriad layers of cold crags to practice their artless livelihood.
If one were to merely pass the days here in negligence and waste this precious time, would that not be even more regrettable?

How tragic! Nevertheless, once you have understood the distinctions in the application of the mind, the illusory conditions appearing before you in the mountains—the flowing water, the rustling wind, the cries of monkeys and the chirping of birds, the surging clouds and the massing mists—all these clamorous distractions will come forward.
You must thoroughly penetrate the words of Yongjia regarding "seeing the Way and forgetting the mountain. When I first resided at Mount Wutai, I was an old man.
At the time of the Dragon Gate [Examinations], beneath ten-thousand-foot cold cliffs amidst heaps of ice and snow, one is like a buried corpse.
A piercing cold penetrates to the very bones and reaches through the five internal organs; there is only a faint breath remaining, as if one were moving in and out of ice.

At this point, turning the gaze inward to observe, one seeks the place where a single thought of one's own mind arises, yet it is utterly unfindable. This state is precisely the condition that aids the Way.
Furthermore, when great winds blow, the myriad apertures roar in fury, ceasing neither by day nor night;

when the snow melts and the mountain streams flow, their resonance is like rolling thunder, resembling the surging of thousands of armies and tens of thousands of horses. Such chaotic environments are initially most difficult to withstand.
Therefore, one should reflect on the words of the ancients: "To listen to the sound of water for thirty years without turning the faculty of the mind—this may be granted."
He entered the Way. The old man then resolved his mind and sat and stood upon a single-plank bridge, listening to the sound of the water all day long.

At first, it was a constant, distracting clamor that could not be dispelled; after a long time, however, it suddenly became still and silent. From this point on, all objective realms were utterly tranquil.
As it is said: "The ten thousand objects are inherently at peace; it is only people who create their own turmoil. This, moreover, is where the practitioner dwells.
This is the foremost application of effort in the mountains. Zen practitioners, take note; do not neglect it.
To the Zen practitioner Zhuan-yu Heng (Bingchen):
The path beyond the ordinary is the fundamental duty of those who have left the household life. When the ancients set out upon their journey, they sought only to investigate this.
To clarify this matter: since recent times, people have generally failed to understand what it means to leave the household life; how, then, can they be expected to become ancients?
The Zen practitioner Zhuan-yu Heng initially relied upon Master Kongyin of Wutai to study the sutras and śāstras.

After a long time, he cast them all aside and focused solely on raising a single thought to intensely investigate the matter of one's own fundamental nature. He then traveled south for ten thousand *li* to seek instruction, passing through Cao...

Xī went to visit an old man to request further instruction. The old man said, "If you do not let go of body and mind regarding this matter, even if you exert bitter effort and investigate until you reach the point where the water ends and the mountains are exhausted, there will ultimately be no place of arrival.

Even if you do reach the point where the water ends and the mountains are exhausted, the ancients called it 'sinking into stillness' or 'dead water,' and they also called it 'the nest of subtle entanglements. If you do not turn your head and change your perspective, then..."
It stands before one like an iron wall or a silver mountain; this is merely the moment of gaining power, not the place of its actual utilization.
The application of effort by the ancients was not meant to end in death; one must bring life forth from within death.

This requires turning back the faculty and shifting one’s station. Thus it is said: "For one who sits atop a hundred-foot pole, though they have gained entry, it is not yet the truth. Hundred [feet]...
"Take another step forward from the tip of the ten-foot pole; throughout the great trichiliocosm, manifest your entire body.

When a student reaches this point, they must simply turn around and travel another path; only then will they not be obstructed by it. The Zen practitioner responded with "Yes, yes," bowed, and departed.
He then went to Mount Nanyue to practice asceticism. Before long, an old man also arrived, leaning on a staff.

Upon inquiring about the Zen practitioner, he learned that the man had been afflicted by a demonic illness and had already gone to Baqing to seek medical treatment. Hearing this, the old man sighed and said, "The Zen school is in decline."

One who practices for the sake of true reality within the cycle of birth and death is the most difficult to find. Now that this man has such an illness, could it be that the dragons and devas have grown weary of or disparaged the Dharma-gate?
On the first day of the third month of the spring in the year Bingchen, at midnight amidst wind and rain, a Zen practitioner suddenly arrived, braving the rain and wading through the mud.
Upon seeing him, the old man was greatly delighted and said, "How could this be possible for a sick man?"

Observing the radiance and refreshing spirit in his countenance, [the Master] knew that the illness was already more than eighty percent healed. He therefore offered incense once more and requested further instruction.
The Elder specifically showed him, saying: "The demonic affliction of your illness is, in fact, your great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), serving as a causal condition for assisting the Path.
Do you understand this? It should be known that the illness of sentient beings lies in the notion of 'self,' arising from attachment."
It is because of me that all the manifold diseases of affliction arise. Once disease arises, suffering inevitably follows.
From antiquity to the present day, there has never been a single person who has not suffered from this. Only those who recognize sickness as sickness are not afflicted by it.

Furthermore, these four elements are but a provisional combination; where there is an accumulation, there must be dispersal. Even if one were not currently ill, how could one ever claim not to have been ill? If...
One who understands both illness and non-illness cannot be afflicted by illness.
You know the illness of today, but you do not know that for many kalpas through successive lifetimes, illness has afflicted you until this very day.
If you do not understand the illness of today, then from now on, you will not know the ultimate end of illness. You recognize the illness of birth and death, yet you do not know how to escape it.
The illness of birth and death is far greater than the illness of birth and death itself. Why is this?

In ancient times, those who failed to emerge from the realm of the five aggregates through Zen meditation fell into the conceptual traps of consciousness and emotion; even if they attained subtle insights, these all became views of self (*ātman*).

While such an illness—clinging to the four great elements as the self—can still be cured, the present illness involves departing from the four great elements yet still clinging to a self; this illness is [incurable].

The King of Physicians has folded his hands in helplessness; this is the most difficult ailment to treat. The Buddhas and Patriarchs appeared specifically in this world solely to cure this kind of incurable disease of the gallbladder and diaphragm.
They exhausted so much mental and physical effort seeking those who would be willing to take the medicine and be healed—how few such people are there!
When the physical illness of a Chan practitioner has already been cured, one must by no means allow the "Chan-illness" to invade them. Yunmen said:

The Dharma-body has two kinds of illnesses. Even if one’s words transcend the Dharma-body, if attachment to phenomena is not forgotten and one's own views still persist, this too is an illness; it is the ultimate expression of the illness of clinging and grasping.

A Zen practitioner must spit out all the subtle phrases and elegant sayings previously accumulated, as well as the achievements and tenets maintained during the practice of Zen, all at once, until only a single point of unwholesome thought remains.
Evil habits will not remain; you shall certainly not be allowed to cultivate a root of illness. This will directly leave no foothold for Buddhas or Patriarchs.
Have you not seen how the youth Sudhana traveled south through a hundred cities, visiting fifty-three great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), each of whom bestowed upon him a specific dharma-gate?
Yet in the end, it all fell back to being equal to the Dharma-realm and equal to empty space. How could it ever have been otherwise?
Is there any attachment to real dharmas? Furthermore, one does not see Vairocana; the Dharma-body is no body, yet it takes the wondrous conduct of Samantabhadra as its body.
Samantabhadra has no conduct, but takes the conduct of sentient beings as his own conduct.
Therefore, it is said that the object of bodhi is the suffering sentient beings. If there were no sentient beings, there would be no bodhi. This is from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity.
The true exemplar for transcending the world. The old man therefore said: "The Zen practitioner’s body of the four great elements cannot be cured by anything other than a demonic illness;

the Zen illness that pierces the heart cannot be cured by anything other than sentient beings. From this day forward, if you regard your body as equal to the great earth, the demonic illness will vanish;
if your mind is equal to sentient beings, the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) will not arise. As for the view of self...
If you do not establish [anything], then the illnesses of meditation will naturally vanish. Because the mind does not take itself as mind, it is fundamentally unborn;
if it is unborn, then not a single dharma is established. If not even a single dharma is established, what dharma could there be to act as an obstacle to knowledge and views?
An ancient said: "It is easy to abandon emotion, but difficult to abandon dharmas. For a practitioner of Chan, abandoning the body is to abandon emotion; abandoning views is to abandon dharmas.
When both emotion and phenomena are forgotten, how could one not be a person of the great, unimpeded liberation? Alas, I am old;
it will be difficult for us to meet again. May you, O Zen practitioner, exert yourself.
To Li Fujing, the young Mr.
Li Yingzhen of Lingling, who requested instruction on the principles of mind and nature, I therefore showed him this: "What is mind-nature?
It is the fundamental source of all holy ones, ordinary people, and living beings. While their essence is identical, their functions differ; thus [the distinction arises]."

Due to the difference between delusion and awakening, there is the distinction between the real and the false. This is what is meant by "the triple world is but mind" and "all phenomena are but consciousness.

Because one is deluded regarding the One Mind, it becomes consciousness; thus, consciousness functions purely as a state of delusion, chasing after objects and grasping at conditions, no longer knowing the originally existing true mind.
If one realizes that the True is originally present and understands that delusion is fundamentally non-existent, then one can turn away from delusion and return to the True.
From the realm of sentient beings, one may immediately enter the realm of the Buddhas. When Bodhidharma came from the West, he transmitted the mind-seal alone;
this sudden enlightenment dharma-gate is precisely the sudden realization of this very mind. This is the principle of the true and the false regarding the nature and mind in the Chan school.
As for that which our Confucians revere—the nature and mind transmitted by Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius—

It is then said: "Only be refined and unified. Taking refinement and unification as the ultimate principle, there is a distinction between the human mind (*renxin*) and the mind of the Way (*daoxin*);
this is likewise the division between the true and the false. However, the origins of worldly teachings do not go beyond this. That which is called the "mind of the Way" [is as follows].
This is the nature that is neither deluded nor false. What is called the "human mind" (xin-ren) is when this deluded nature becomes emotion (qing).
People of the world know only how to employ emotion, yet do not know how to employ nature; they know only the waves, but do not know that the waves originate from water.
Therefore, Confucius said: "Natures are similar; practices lead to divergence. When natures are similar, it is like water having no waves at its source; when practices diverge...
Thus, one pursues the waves while forgetting the water; even the water itself is not known, let alone the realization that the nature of moisture is non-dual.
Furthermore, consider that originally there is but one water, yet when it is mixed with salty, sour, bitter, or pungent flavors, its quality of blandness perishes.
However, its nature of moisture remains fundamentally non-dual. Thus we know that the various flavors are merely transformations of delusion, whereas the nature of moisture cannot be changed.
That which cannot be changed is the Real; that which can be changed is the delusory. If one realizes that the nature of moisture is non-dual, then various forms of ignorance cannot possibly exist.
What is called Yao and Shun was merely the same as other people. That which is the same is their nature; that which is not the same is delusion.
Furthermore, it is said: "All people can become Yao and Shun. That which they can become is their nature; that which they cannot become is delusion.

This refers to habituation. Regarding what people habituate themselves to: if one were to abandon the base and lowly to pursue the lofty and sublime, then day by day one would distance oneself from what has been habituated and draw near to one's innate nature (*xing*).

That those capable of becoming Yao or Shun do so is likewise due to this habituation. When habituation draws near to the innate nature, it is precisely the practice of gradual cultivation (*jianxiu*) in the Chan school.
By contrast, the learning of worldly Confucians has not yet transcended the mundane and the near; they remain far removed from the sages.
It is not through a gradual approach that one can reach the ultimate limit. Therefore, when the Sages established their teachings, they spoke only of "practice," "attainment," and "overcoming.
Their method for entering the Way lies in gradual restoration, rather than in speaking of sudden enlightenment.

As for the Chan school, by distancing themselves from the love of wife and children and abandoning the desire for wealth and status, all burdens are already cast off, bringing them close to the Way; thus, their method for restoring one's nature—
It is easy to exert this power; therefore, it is called "sudden awakening. Because the stages in which one resides differ, there are difficulties and ease in the practice of cultivation.
In reality, the nature of mind within humans fundamentally possesses no distinction between sudden and gradual; it is merely a matter of the thickness or thinness of habitual defilements.

This is the essential point for entering the Way. If one investigates the subtle and profound nature of the mind and traces its original source, the fundamental basis of Chan lies in non-arising and non-extinction, whereas the fundamental basis of Confucianism lies in arising and extinction.
Thus it is said, "The constant process of arising and arising is called the *Yi*. This is the distinction between the fundamental tenets of Confucianism and Buddhism.
The discourse on the nature of the mind essentially rests upon this. As for the "upward direction" of the School Gate...
If one is thus attached, one transcends beyond the reach of words; furthermore, one does not rely upon the nature and mind as substantial dharmas.
To show this, when the Imperial Censor Huanran requested further instruction, [the Master] said:
"The Buddhas appearing in the world have no dharma to preach; the Patriarchs coming from the West likewise had no substantial dharma to give to people. It was only for..."
The various inverted attachments of sentient beings are struck down as appropriate to cause them to relinquish their clinging and suddenly awaken to what is inherently present.
Because the deluded and attached minds of sentient beings are so firm and difficult to shatter,
compounded by the afflictions of ignorance throughout kalpas and deep-rooted karmic obstructions that make sudden awakening difficult to attain, my Buddha spent forty-nine [days].
Throughout immeasurable eons, the Buddha has employed countless skillful means to establish the Dharma for severing delusions and realizing the Truth.

From the level of ordinary beings to that of the sages, there are fifty-five stages of progression; this was not because the World-Honored One took pleasure in such elaborate arrangements, nor did He exhaust His compassionate heart for no reason.
Because the mental illnesses of sentient beings are infinite, the remedies prescribed for them are likewise infinite.

Yet, when one reaches the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), where all knowing and seeing have completely vanished and not a single dharma is established, only then has one arrived at the ground of home.
If there remains even a hair’s breadth of knowing and seeing that is not forgotten, one is still lodging in a grass hut outside the gate. One must discard it again and again until...
There is nothing to be discarded. Even if it were so, this would still be a matter concerning the realm of the *dharmakāya*, not yet the matter that transcends the *dharmakāya*.
It is merely the ultimate point within the doctrinal schools (*śāsana*), not yet the ultimate point of the Zen school (*zongmen*).

Viewed from this perspective, how can the single matter of cultivation be treated with negligence, as if one could achieve it through mere half-baked understanding? Furthermore, as for the Zen school itself...
Prior to the Sixth Patriarch, there was no talk of the practice of investigative inquiry; it was valued solely as sudden awakening in the present moment.
From Nan-yueh and Ch’ing-yüan downward, the capacities of practitioners were not uniform, and most focused on seeking through inquiry and maintaining their cultivation.

By the time the Five Houses were established, their pedagogical methods and institutional arrangements differed, yet the fundamental principle within remained without distinction. In responding to circumstances and engaging with sentient beings, they were like—
The Qin mirror hung upon its stand, illuminating the very liver and gallbladder [of one's innermost being].

When it came to untying the knots and removing the fetters for others, pointing directly toward the Dharmakāya and the path beyond, he utterly eradicated all views and knowledge regarding the Buddha-dharma. Unless one had reached the ultimate source and the very bottom, he would by no means lightly let them pass.
During the time when the Way of Chan flourished greatly, there were many erudite masters with clear eyes throughout the land.
Monastics who study the Way seek verification and certification everywhere; thus, those who awaken do not fall into false views.

From the Song through the Yuan dynasties, although teachers were numerous, those among the students who held false views were no fewer. Failing to avoid the view of birth and death, they fell into the view of emptiness.

Having substance but lacking function, they were like the biased emptiness of the Two Vehicles. They went so far as to negate cause and effect, falling into the ranks of external paths and becoming reckless nihilists.

This is the emptiness of annihilation. Alternatively, it may be that one’s realization of the mind has not yet reached its depths; having merely caught a glimpse of its reflections, one takes a little for enough, calling oneself a Bodhisattva.
Mouth to mouth they discourse on emptiness, yet heart to heart they cling to existence. In the end, they create the karma of birth and death without realizing it.
All such cases fail to encounter a clear-eyed *kalyāṇamitra* who can examine, verify, and rouse them to awareness; thus, the Chan school has fallen into decline. As an ancient worthy said:

It is not that there is no Chan; it is simply that there are no teachers. This is why [I say so]. In this great era of the Final Dharma, many who practice Chan consider a small attainment to be sufficient.

Even if there were a truly authentic student willing to apply themselves with "deadly earnestness" in their practice, remaining steadfast in their resolve for ten or five years, they might still achieve an awakening to the fact that their own mind and all phenomena are empty—yet because they lack the seal of a true master, [they do not realize the ultimate truth].
Upon realization, one may fall into the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). Or, if the consciousness-spirit has not been shattered, one falls into the gateway of light and shadow.

Or, if habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not been purified, they are pressured by one's practice, causing various states to manifest; these are then taken to be the wondrous functioning of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
One may see Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appearing in person to preach the Dharma, or gain knowledge of others' minds and past lives, or be able to perceive the future.
Matters. Or various divergent views may arise; these are all manifestations of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
If one recognizes them as something extraordinary, one immediately falls into the path of Māra. It is a pity that the effort expended thus far will result in no small harm.

This is entirely because one has not encountered a true teacher and does not understand the skillful means for cultivating the mind within the Buddha-dharma, and so one mistakenly falls into error. There are also those who have truly investigated and attained genuine realization, seeing clearly...

When one’s own mind realizes that there is not a single dharma, yet one is unable to open the true eye at the crown of the head, one simply sits in a state that is utterly bare, naked, pure, and free from a single speck of defilement.
This is called "clinging to the tip of the staff" or sinking into the stagnant waters of death. Therefore it is said:
"The person sitting atop a hundred-foot pole, though they have gained entry, has not yet reached the truth. One must advance further from the tip of the hundred-foot pole."
The entire body manifests throughout the trichiliocosm. It is further said: "Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell; where there is no Buddha, pass by quickly.
This is precisely teaching that one must not remain settled within a state of non-action, claiming that there is no Buddha to be realized and no sentient beings to be saved.
This is truly falling into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); one is simply unable to escape this view of emptiness. Even if one reaches...
This is also a matter of the stage of the Dharma-body, but it is not yet a matter of that which transcends the Dharma-body. Have you not heard Yunmen say:
"When one reaches the stage of the Dharma-body, there is still a sense of something vaguely present; this too is because the light has not fully penetrated."
Even if you were to penetrate through it, to let it pass would still be unacceptable. These words are truly a mirror for cultivating the mind and illuminating the gallbladder.

Thus, an ancient worthy said: "The single word 'awakening' must be spat out. You should know that the Buddhas and Patriarchs preach the Dharma solely to dispel the clinging emotions of sentient beings;
as it is said: "Simply exhaust all mundane sentiments, and there will be no separate 'sage-understanding. If you form a sage-understanding, you will immediately [be bound by it]."
The various evils—the fifty kinds of *skandha-māras* mentioned in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*—are not mere empty words.

In these times, since there are no enlightened masters to provide guidance, if one does not follow the teachings and seek certification from the Buddhas and Patriarchs, what can possibly serve as a basis for reliance?

It was because sentient beings were initially attached to existence that the Buddha destroyed their views of existence; it was because those of the Two Vehicles and the non-Buddhists were attached to emptiness that...

The Buddha shattered their view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). Because Bodhisattvas cling to the two extremes of emptiness and existence, the Buddha taught that it is "neither empty nor existent" to shatter those dualistic views.
Upon entering the Buddha-dharma, he further dispels both the view of the Buddha and the view of the Dharma; thus, he leads them to a state where there is nothing further to be dispelled.
This is precisely what is meant by the statement: "Not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata. Have you not seen the youth Sudhana? He visited five...
The thirteen great spiritual friends have already entered the dharma-gate of the fifty-three stages and attained the realm of the Buddha;
they do not speak of the matter of attaining Buddhahood, but only say that they are equal to empty space, equal to the Dharma-realm, and equal to Vairocana.
Upon seeing Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, he was taught the ten kinds of practices and vows. This is the great model for practicing and studying the Buddha-way;

it does not mean that after awakening one has nothing further to do. People today who practice may, even if they are able to thoroughly awaken to the Dharma-realm, still inevitably fall into emptiness if they do not study and cultivate the great conduct of Samantabhadra as did Sudhana.

Behold the outsiders! Are they not to be feared? The preceding entanglements were spoken specifically for those who practice without the wisdom of extensive learning, who apply their minds erroneously, and thus cannot enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, I could not help but speak at length.
If you regard these words as mere idle chatter, you will not only fail the old monk but will also bring about no small error upon yourselves.
To the Chan practitioners Huiyu and Huijue of Qiyang: You two have come to attend upon the Old Man at Mount Ziyun in Huangmei.
You say that within your minds, arising and ceasing occur incessantly, moment after moment, like wild horses. You specifically seek instruction as to how to subdue them. How should you do so?
The old man pointed to his mind and said, "When a practitioner cultivates the path, it is for the sake of the great matter of birth and death.
Because the thoughts within the mind do not cease from moment to moment, birth and death are not severed.

If you truly wish to resolve birth and death, you must wholeheartedly let go of all external conditions until they are completely cleared away. Yet, there remain the seeds of beginningless habitual tendencies."
One cannot achieve purity through mere effort; one must investigate a *huatou*.

These instructions are all available on paper, yet because one does not know the skillful means regarding the difficulty or ease of applying the practice, it is essential to consult a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend). Such a teacher can reveal the expedient means, for they have traversed this path themselves and thus know the easy points of entry.
For example, when the Sixth Patriarch formerly heard the words, "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere," he immediately—
To attain awakening, people of the world do not realize that they must understand the subtle and wondrous principle. Fundamentally, it is not subtle or wondrous;
because there was formerly a state of dwelling, upon now hearing of non-dwelling, one lets go at that moment and attains awakening. What subtlety or wonder is there?
It is like the Great Master Yongming, who formerly used the mind of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) but could not penetrate it. Later, before the Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, he held up...
Drawing lots, one may attain the practice of *nianfo* (recollection of the Buddha). Regarding the study of Chan, people of the world treat Chan as if it were a mere intellectual principle;

they fail to realize that Chan is one's own mind. As the Sūtra says: "Neither arising nor ceasing" is precisely it. If you wish to clarify the great matter of birth and death, you must know that the precepts are most venerable and dare not be transgressed.
First, you must possess the power of faith and a resolute, willing heart. [Take up] the subtle principles of the world...
In dealing with human affairs, one must let go of everything. This single point of Zen meditation is fundamentally without even a thread of subtlety or marvel;
this matter is utterly plain. Will you believe this? If you truly believe it, simply cast away all former delusive thoughts at once, allowing them no room to arise in secret.
Slowly and steadily, single-mindedly hold up the name of Amitābha Buddha, relying upon it with sincerity. You must...
Observe from where this thought arises; it is like casting a line to fish in a deep pool.
If deluded thoughts arise again, it is because beginningless habitual tendencies are too heavy; you must let go. By all means, do not try to cut off discursive thoughts with the mind.
Simply straighten your backbone and do not allow your thoughts to wander east or west. Look directly at the very place where the deluded thought arises.
Stabilize your concentration. Let go, and let go again. Slowly, slowly, raise [the voice] once more with the sound of "Buddha.
In stillness, observe from where this single sound of "Buddha" ultimately arises. When you reach five or seven such sounds, deluded thoughts will cease to arise.
Then, apply the spirit of inquiry: examine closely who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. Worldly people treat this as merely a string of words, failing to realize its true significance.
To recognize this state of doubt is precisely where one gains strength. If a delusive thought arises again, simply utter a shout of "Tut!
and ask, "Who is this? At that very moment, the delusive thought will be swept away, its traces obliterated. As the Buddha said: "Constantly restrain the mind, except when sleeping."
When sleeping, one cannot restrain the mind; as soon as one awakens, one raises the *huatou*.

It is not only while sitting that one acts thus, but likewise while walking, standing, eating, drinking, moving, or remaining still. Amidst a vast crowd, one sees no people; amidst all movements, one sees no movement.
In this way, there gradually arises a point of entry. When the seven consciousnesses reach this state, they cease to function. As it is said:
Day and night, rely steadfastly upon this; do not calculate the amount of effort expended. One day, when the eight consciousnesses suddenly burst asunder, the original face will be revealed;
this is precisely the moment for resolving birth and death. Only then will you not have failed the vow of leaving the household life.
However, when practicing Chan, do not seek enlightenment. Whether Buddhas, patriarchs, or demons come, remain simply unmoved in mindfulness.

When you are about to leave for a single session of practice, do not harbor further doubts or difficulties in the interim. In this way, maintain a continuous and dense flow, with every thought uninterrupted.
Exert yourself in daily life; there will naturally be a point of realization.
To the Zen student Shimingyi:
Students do not know the path that transcends the ordinary; they merely seek to increase their intellectual views and knowledge.

Little do they realize that when knowledge and views establish further cognition, this is the very root of ignorance. Thus, failing to recognize what is inherently present, they rush outward in pursuit, desiring even more to augment it.
It is clear. If one clarifies that very clarity, then even clarity does not stand; what benefit could there be? Therefore it is said: "In learning, one increases daily.
Generally speaking, those who speak of "learning" seek a comfortable nest within the house of another.
Even if such a place is found, it ultimately does not belong to oneself. Since it does not belong to oneself, the joy is not true joy. If the joy is not true, what further...?
Does one seek peace by following along with it? To seek peace externally has been the common ailment of scholars since antiquity; it is not unique to the present day.
When the monk Mingyi requested instruction, did he wish to clarify what was useless, or did he wish to clarify what was beneficial?
If you say it is useless, then there is no need to clarify it. If you say it is beneficial, then since it is already beneficial, why would one need to clarify it?
Furthermore, why must one seek illumination? Try to examine from where this illumination comes and by what it is furthered.
If you seek to clarify that which is already luminous, you lose original luminosity; if you further seek more benefit, it conversely becomes useless.
Those who seek benefit are like a person who, having already eaten their fill, still craves the flavor of the food; they thus injure their digestion and fall ill. If one can simply follow the food...
If one vomits it, it may be cured without medication. If, however, one guards against the illness and avoids medical treatment, it will ultimately result in chronic stagnation.

For those who suffer from this condition, even Lu Ban or Bian Que could not cure them. Why? Because eating greedily and refusing to vomit is the first ailment; nursing an illness while concealing the disease is the second.
The second illness is that once afflicted, one dreads the physician; this is the third illness. Or, following this, one loathes the medicine; this is the fourth illness.
Or, seeking quick results, one does not trust the method for treating the root cause, thereby suspecting the physician and abandoning the medicine; this is the fifth illness.
Or, further following a quack physician, one mistakenly takes toxic medicine, leading to the loss of life; this is a category beyond cure. Such is the student who abandons themselves.
This is the fundamental illumination, yet people run outward in pursuit of it, merely increasing their intellectual views; for the most part, it is like this. How lamentable!
When I was young, every time I read the Parable of the Physician, I could never help but recite the Sage’s instructions three times over.

I have observed that among scholars of recent times, some are able to recite this [text] even when they are novices (śrāmaṇera), yet as they grow old, they do not know its essential principle. Consequently, there are countless who lead empty and vain lives and die in vain. This is not...

This is the fault of seeking illumination. There are also those who, in their quest for illumination, mistakenly take what is not illumination to be illumination and force themselves to appear enlightened;
this is truly the error of failing to reach the source. The Buddha said: "One who quiets the mind and reaches the fundamental source is therefore called a śramaṇa.

If a student can truly quiet the mind and reach the source, there is no need to seek illumination externally, nor is it necessary to increase one's benefits through much effort. The self-nature is inherently complete. Never...
What deficiency is there? If the Zen practitioner Mingyi can truly understand this, he will suddenly and completely vomit up all that he has previously sought.
Like one who has suffered from indigestion and now has no lingering residue in the stomach, his original vitality will naturally restore itself.
When a student sweeps away their views and knowledge, they may be called a "person of non-action. Try carefully examining the putrid and sour contents that have filled your belly until now.
"What flavor does it have? Examine! Examine! This was shown to the Zen practitioner Hui-leng. A Zen practitioner grew up in Xiuyi;
in his youth, he traveled as a merchant upon the rivers and lakes. Having grown weary of worldly dust and vulgarity, he went to Kuangshan to pay homage to Xuxiu.

When Master Fang shaved his head, the Old Man had come from Mount Nanyue to spend the summer retreat at Jinnu. A Zen practitioner offered incense and requested instruction, whereupon the Master said to him:
"You have already been able to renounce worldly affection; yet though your body has left the household life, your mind has not yet clarified the true matter of leaving the household life.
Long ago, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, relinquished the golden wheel, abandoned the royal palace, and entered the Snowy Mountains for six years..."

He practiced asceticism for six years; upon seeing the morning star, he awakened to the Way and attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). He became the Teacher of the Three Realms, revered by those in the Six Paths, and honored by devas and humans.
He universally delivered sentient beings, leading them all beyond birth and death. This is the first model of one who leaves the household life.
Looking at it in this way, how could it be a matter of seeking ease or indulging in laziness, merely seeking to enjoy a ready-made state?
If one simply acts as an ordinary person, can one truly be called a renunciant? There must certainly be a fundamental matter at hand.
Since the time of the patriarchs of old, they have taken up the great matter of birth and death as their reason for renouncing the world.

From practicing the way and traveling on foot to visiting spiritual teachers, it was specifically for the purpose of illuminating the mind-ground and uprooting, all at once, the roots of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas, thereby transcending the three realms.

To be forever free from the realms of suffering is what constitutes self-benefit. Later, when you hear the dragons and devas urge you forth to establish the Triple Gem, that is what constitutes benefit for others.
Only when these two benefits are complete is one truly fulfilling the fundamental duty of leaving the home life.
Zen practitioner, do you know today that such a thing as this exists? Do you know that there is this great matter of birth and death? What is birth and death? It is right now.
The present five aggregates of body and mind have accumulated, over immeasurable kalpas past, the various seeds of habitual tendencies of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, aversion, and attachment.
Day after day, thought after thought gives rise to delusions; yet the very mind that creates karma is fundamentally the Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata.
The seed of luminosity is now shrouded by the afflictions of ignorance; though it is used daily, one does not realize it.
Thus, to be deluded regarding this Buddha-nature is itself birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). To awaken to this Buddha-nature is to suddenly sever the afflictions and transcend birth-and-death;
such a person is a true renunciant. Viewed in this light, renunciation is the matter of a great man (*mahāsattva*) who brings an end to birth-and-death.
It is not for the sake of enjoying ease and comfort; it is only to seek self-mastery.

To be unwilling to practice and to fail to seek the enlightenment of the mind and the realization of one's nature is to squander the offerings of the faithful in vain, thereby inviting instead the suffering of retribution in future lives. How can such a person be considered a renunciant?
O practitioner of meditation: by what birth and by what conditions have you been so fortunate as to encounter an enlightened teacher who delivers you from suffering?

You dwell in seclusion at a sacred mountain monastery where the Dharma companions are in harmony. Furthermore, how fortunate you are to have met a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who provides guidance and instruction.

If you do not feel profound joy and deep shame [for past neglect], and instead fail to resolve to practice diligently for the sake of escaping birth and death, this is to abandon yourself. It would be like reaching a treasure...

To return from the mountains empty-handed—how lamentable this is! If you, practitioner of Zen, are willing to resolve to cultivate practice, your foremost requirement is to suddenly and completely sever all former afflictions, attachments, aversions, and habitual tendencies.
You must single-mindedly seek the one matter of transcending birth and death, holding the single phrase "Namu Amida Butsu" within your breast as you would your own life-root.

The mind and its objects are uninterrupted. When you reach the point where the flowers bloom and you see the Buddha, that is precisely the moment of true renunciation that brings an end to birth and death.
If you do not use the words of this old man to give rise to genuine faith, it will be like avoiding drowning only to throw yourself into fire;
you will miss this life, and when will there ever be a time for your liberation? Reflect deeply on this yourself and exert yourself; do not neglect it.
He showed him half a verse upon hearing of the Chan practitioner’s devotion.
This practitioner had studied the curriculum for the civil service examinations in his youth and harbored aspirations for transcendence.

At forty, he abandoned his wife and children to pay homage to Master Guo Qingzhan, a disciple of the Elder Zibo. He received the tonsure at Guizong Monastery, which was formerly [the site of] various...
The venerable patriarch established this Chan hermitage as a banner of the Dharma, and therein lies the *śarīra* of the Tathāgata.

Thus we know that the conditions for the Chan practitioner’s renunciation were superior, and the site where he dwelt was likewise superior; it was merely that his supreme resolve had not yet been awakened.
Guizong has long been in ruins, but when Master Zibo passed through its grounds, he was filled with sorrow and grief upon seeing a withered pine tree half-broken by the axe.
The Great Master, moved by compassion, enchanted soil and dammed up [the breach], hoping for its renewed flourishing as an omen for the reconstruction of the Dharma-assembly site.
Within a few years, the bark and bones were all restored. Thereupon, Master Zhan resolutely undertook the great revival; news of this spread far and wide.
There was no one who did not look up in wonder and follow him. The layman Xing Laici vowed his heart to lead the way.
After several years, he moved the present Emperor to bestow the Imperial Collection [of scriptures] to glorify the famous mountain. From this, the halls and pavilions were finally completed.
Subsequently, the Elder Jianyin raised funds to cast a Great Vairocana Image to establish peace and stability. Since then, the Three Jewels have been fully present there.
Second, it was because the Sangha Jewel had not yet assembled; it was insufficient to propagate the Way of the Dharma.

Eight years after the Zen practitioner had left the household life, the Old Man came from Mount Nanyue to visit. He paid homage to the śarīra at the summit of Mount Jinyun (Golden Wheel Peak) and observed how the mountains and rivers were magnificent and prominent.
He inquired about the hardships of its restoration; although the halls and pavilions were completed, the Zen residence had not yet been finished. It remained thus.
In this desolate and secluded place, Master Lai Ci has indeed endured great hardship to protect the Dharma; such diligent practice is precisely what we, his disciples, ought to undertake.

If the monastic community does not courageously proceed with this task, we shall fail the intent behind its establishment. I fear that if Master Zibo’s enlightened spirit possesses awareness, he will certainly not find peace in death.
For this reason, I have earnestly exhorted the assembly to resolve their minds, and Jianyin and Chan... [continued].

This is the guiding principle for human beings. Upon hearing these words, the Chan practitioner immediately gave rise to a superior resolve and widely transformed great donors to adorn the Buddha-land.
He then took up his staff and departed from the mountain, intending to seek further instruction as he traveled along the way.
The Old Man, wishing to strengthen his power of aspiration, joyfully instructed him, saying:

"Although you have left the household life, you have not yet heard of the practice that transcends the world. In the past, our original teacher, Śākyamuni, renounced the sovereignty of a Golden Wheel-turning King and hid his form in the Snowy Mountains.
There he practiced austerities for six years to achieve Perfect Enlightenment and become a teacher of gods and humans.

In truth, it was because he had extensively cultivated merit and wisdom throughout many distant kalpas that he could do so; thus it is said that within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, there is no one like him."
A mere mustard seed’s worth [of merit] is not the place where a Bodhisattva relinquishes body and life for the sake of sentient beings.

As for the giving of head, eyes, brain, and marrow—discarding them like nasal mucus or saliva—it was through such ascetic practices performed life after life, birth after birth, for one, two, or even immeasurable kalpas, that he finally attained this body of marks and signs, with its subtle and wondrous adornments. Now, in this age of the Final Dharma...
"A single bowl of rice for a disciple is all obtained by exchanging the Tathāgata’s own life-force, bones, and blood, left for his descendants to enjoy.
Viewed from this perspective, how can it be easy for us, who have left the household life, to consume the ready-made clothing, food, and peaceful dwellings provided for our use?

If we do not contemplate repaying the Buddha's kindness, embody the Buddha's mind, practice the Buddha's deeds, and manage the affairs of the Buddha’s household, then [we shall be guilty of ingratitude]."
Though one may be called a renunciant by name, in reality, one merely utilizes the instruments of suffering belonging to the three miserable realms.
That which is called "realizing the Buddha-mind" is the mind of great compassion. That which is called "practicing the Buddha-way" is the mind of patience.

That which is called "attending to the affairs of the Buddha" is extensively practicing the six perfections, accomplishing the two kinds of adornment, establishing the Three Jewels, and widely propagating the transformation of the Dharma. If one does not act in this way, one is not a disciple of the Buddha.
Such a person is a thief who steals the Buddha’s *kāṣāya* robe to nourish the very root of their own suffering. What benefit is there in such a form of renunciation?

As for what is called the twofold adornment of merit and wisdom: planting the seeds for the realization of *prajñā* and thoroughly comprehending one's own mind so as to wondrously accord with the Buddha-mind—this is called wisdom.
Extensively cultivating the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) as an adornment and bringing sentient beings to maturity—this is called merit.
Therefore it is said: one who is fully endowed with both merit and wisdom is called the "Bipeds' Honored One" (Dvipada-agra). Thus, I now exhort practitioners of Chan:
first, they must resolutely seek Prajñā to realize their own minds, thereby emerging from the bitter sea of birth and death;

second, they must extensively practice all deeds to universally transform the ten directions and adorn the Buddha-lands, thereby accomplishing the pure karma of a Pure Land. Apart from these two practices, there is nothing else [to be done].
Regarding "cultivation": the Buddha has said that teaching and transforming sentient beings is itself the adornment of the Buddha-land.

This is because the vast multitude of sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of suffering of greed and desire; they exhaustively create the karma of birth and death, sinking for long kalpas with no means of emerging on their own.
Thus, one encounters the suffering instruments of the three realms and the three miserable paths;

it is upon the Triple Gem that one relies as a field of merit to plant the seeds of *prajñā*, thereby creating the causes and conditions for self-enjoyment in future lives. Yet, this necessarily requires the Sangha Jewel to provide guidance.
Therefore, when we, the disciples of the Buddha, can convert a single person to resolve their mind toward excellence and break through stinginess and greed, that one person—
Purify one's own mind. To adorn the buddha-field of a single person, and to transform many people, one adorns the buddha-fields of many.
If one can transform the great earth so that every person resolves their mind [on enlightenment], then one perfectly accomplishes the buddha-fields of all people.

This is indeed the transformation of a defiled land into a pure land, and the conversion of instruments of suffering into instruments of bliss—is this not the most supreme and extraordinary excellence?
Go forth! You who practice Zen, go forth! To take even a single word from an old man and depart with it is to be a man of heroic caliber.

It is to suddenly give rise to a vast and great mind—just as the butcher of Wide Forehead laid down his butcher’s knife and immediately performed the work of a Buddha, or as the eight-year-old dragon girl attained Bodhi at the very moment she offered her pearl.
Truly, one can break open the bag of stinginess and strike it down.
Feces and soil. May those who fulfill your power of aspiration, O Zen practitioner, exert yourselves; do not be negligent for a moment.
