Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and his disciple Tongjiong;
revised by the Disciple from Lingnan, Liu Qixiang.
A Dharma discourse to show the way back to the source: Elder Jianyin Ci, while begging for alms to adorn the Buddha-land, reached the summit of Mount Kunlun’s Golden Wheel Peak.
There lies a relic of Śākyamuni Tathāgata; it is a place where the Dharma-body abides eternally.

Since antiquity, the various patriarchs have erected the great banner of the Dharma; among these thirty-seven individuals who appeared in succession, there are countless others who illuminated the ground of the mind and transcended birth and death.
Thus we know that the spiritual power of this mountain is truly the Jetavana of China.

This is Vulture Peak on the West River. As the fortunes of the Dharma have shifted and declined, rising and falling with the times, even the jade palaces and Brahma temples have fallen into neglect amidst the overgrown weeds.
When the Great Master Zibai traveled to this place, he resolved to restore it;

his sincere devotion moved the unseen realm, and the withered trees regained their luster—an omen indeed most extraordinary. Thereupon, his disciple, the Venerable Fazhan Guogong, set his mind upon [the task].
Shao-shu vowed to effect a complete renewal, his firm and unshakable aspiration being like that of Kang Hui, who sought śarīra relics at Jianchu Temple.
Before long, he indeed received a response: His Majesty the Emperor graciously bestowed a collection of sacred relics to enshrine at the mountain gate.

At that time, the śarīra appeared, emitting a great radiance; the mountains and rivers roared, and the grasses and trees displayed auspicious omens. Truly, this is a rare occurrence in the Dharma-ending age.

Regarding this matter of excellence: in the autumn of the Bingchen year, the Elder came from Mount Nanyue to pay homage to the Tathāgata’s śarīra. His reverent gaze upon these peerless wonders inspired deep reflections;
yet, looking around at the majesty of the halls and pavilions, he saw that many essential elements were still incomplete, as if his journey had been cut short by exhaustion midway.
It is no different from when it was previously amidst the wild thickets. Could this not be the intention of the dragons and spirits to provide protection?
Since the original donor who gave rise to this aspiration, Xing Laici, possessed great resolve but lacked sufficient strength, this is the responsibility of us, the śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya.

Therefore, I urge Master Jianyin Ci to resolve his mind upon the vast and great, to regard this as a rare encounter, and to prostrate his five limbs and relinquish the four elements as an act of adornment.

How much more so, when there are officials and lay devotees who were once entrusted with the teachings on Vulture Peak and who serve as kings of vows throughout the ten directions—why not universally invite them to assemble and bring this supreme undertaking to fulfillment?
In this way, you will not fail the expectations of your compassionate father.
He entrusted his family affairs to him. Upon hearing this account, Master Ci was greatly inspired with vigor and requested a word from the elder to serve as a vanguard for his practice.

The elder smiled and said, "There is no need for this. Within the ocean-like assembly of the Dharma-realm, amidst the Lotus Treasury, the infinite Buddha-lands and their subtle adornments all manifest within a single thought-moment of a Bodhisattva of Great Resolve, complete and perfect."
There is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous; it is entirely due to the power of a single thought’s inspiration. It is just as the Maitreya Tower encompasses immeasurable Buddha-lands.
This is why Sudhana could not see them when he arrived before it—he required the power of the Great Being’s finger-snap.
Thus, the old man’s words were like that slight finger-snap performed before the pavilion; its adornments [were thereby revealed].
The Buddha-land need only have its gates opened; it will then manifest all at once. What further effort is required? You, Sir, are departing;
I hope you will not be remiss.
[This was written] for Wang Zianju, who renounced his son to leave the household life.
The Prince of Xindu was originally a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*). He had a son named Yingchen, who studied Confucianism from his youth.

One day, reflecting on the gravity of birth and death, he resolved to leave the household life. He subsequently shaved his own hair and traveled to Mount Kuanglu, where he paid homage to Master Jingtang of Yunzhong.
In the summer of the Bingchen year, I came to this mountain from Mount Nanyue. The layman visited my son, and upon meeting him, [I perceived] his most profound feelings of natural kinship.

To those who find it difficult to sever their attachment, I therefore showed them this, saying: "What parents in all the world expect from their children is that they achieve illustrious fame to bring glory to their kin.
Thus, they consider the nourishment provided by the three sacrificial animals and five tripods to be the ultimate expression of filial piety.

Yet they fail to realize that the more lavish the nourishment, the deeper the suffering [of the recipient]; this burdens their parents rather than being true filial piety. Therefore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, considered such things as trivial..."
He did not exercise the power of the Golden Wheel; he abandoned his parents and left the royal palace to practice austerities in the Snowy Mountains.
Having attained enlightenment after six years, he became the Honored One of the Three Realms, revered and looked up to by devas and humans alike.

If one does not relinquish supreme nobility and sever great affection, how can one cultivate the karma that remains imperishable through long kalpas? Therefore, he is praised as the Great Filial Śākyamuni Buddha, who has repaid his debt across successive kalpas.
Regarding the kindness of one's parents: is this not the ground for repaying their grace by attaining the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*) and universally delivering all sentient beings?

When the Buddha expounded the Great Precepts, he stated at the outset that "filial piety is called the precept. This means being filially obedient to one's parents; being filially obedient to teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem;

being filially obedient to the Supreme Way; and being filially obedient to all sentient beings. Therefore, those who truly study as Buddhist practitioners shall regard all sentient beings [as their own parents].
Since they have been your parents throughout many lifetimes, how could you fail to repay the kindness of those who were your kin in this single life?

My only fear is that, having left the household life, you might not recognize their fundamental debt. Now, if you take the realization of non-arising as the root and foundation of your resolve, and if you are truly determined in that vow—
It is not only that their recompense is insufficient; even their means of sustenance are inadequate.

What the world calls filial piety is intended to win fame and achievement in order to provide sacrificial feasts and nourishment to delight one’s parents. Yet such fame and achievement are constrained by the forces of destiny (*zao wu*), and the provision of sacrificial meats depends on what one encounters.
Setting aside the fact that even if obtained, they require great toil, it is further the case that though the whole world seeks them, one may not necessarily attain them all.
One may obtain it but not necessarily be able to enjoy it. Furthermore, there are those who achieve fame and renown yet receive no emolument;

there are those whose parents do not live long enough to wait for their success; and there are those who, even while waiting, find no joy. This is because they must obey the decrees of fate rather than acting according to their own will.
Now, those who aspire to the Great Way seek it within themselves; its fulfillment likewise lies within themselves.
They employ strategies certain to achieve their goal and cherish the nourishment of supreme joy. This is something difficult for the mundane world to compare with.

Layman, if you can relinquish your son and allow him to pursue his ambition, then from this day forward, while your son hides his form in the mountain valleys, you too may bid farewell to the bonds of worldly dust.

Since the son has dwelt in the mountains, he has been able both to sever his attachments and to transcend the mundane world. As for the place where he finds joy, he wears garments of grass and eats of wood;
yet he does not exchange this for brocade or delicacies. Father and son, day and night, contemplate only the Way.

Their morning attendance and evening prostrations are beyond what even the "spotted robe" and "colored silks" could provide. Where the water flows and the wind moves, there is only the sound of the sutras and the chanting of the Buddha’s name. It is not...

The clamor of lutes and the rapid beat of pipes may be wearisome; yet bright lamps and fragrant incense, burning without ceasing from dusk until dawn, cannot be compared to the stench of meat and the filth of excrement.
A thousand-foot cold cliff and a three-bay sprout-hut appear humble compared to high halls and grand mansions.
Father and son deliberate together to accomplish the unsurpassed Way and enjoy a glory and fame that lasts beyond this age—this is a certainty.
Compared to this, the bestowal of a single official post or the praise of a single word—things that cannot be guaranteed—is like the difference between clouds and mud, or heaven and earth.
What the Layman sacrifices is small, yet what he gains is vast; whereas what you, my son, oppose is meager.
That which he has followed is profound; is this not the greatest filial piety in the world?

The layman joyfully accepted the instruction and requested that a name be inscribed for him, wishing to become his disciple. The elder named him Fuzhi (Arrival of Blessings), saying that blessings would come from this moment forward.
He gave him the style name Dailai (Great Arrival), meaning that what was relinquished was small, while what arrived was great. Therefore, this was written.
I consider this to be a dharma-gate voucher for you, presented to the Chan practitioner Lingyuan Jue.
This practitioner has resided at Guizong on Mount Lu for many years; he considers himself to be of inferior capacity and unable to achieve a single leap [to enlightenment].
"Enter directly. Simply make this vow: 'Throughout the remainder of this life, I shall recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* ten thousand times.
I pray that you will grant me your witness and seal of approval. I do not know how this practice compares to the method of investigating the mind (*cankiu*);

I wish to hear your instructions. The Elder replied to him, saying: "When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, it is like eating honey; it is sweet throughout, from beginning to end. Originally, there is nothing to be grasped."
The distinction between relinquishing [the afflictions] arises solely from the differing degrees of aspiration and aversion among those in training; thus, there is merely this difference.

For this reason, our Buddha appeared in the world specifically to reveal to sentient beings the Great Matter of Cause and Condition (mahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya). When the Patriarch came from the West, he pointed directly and transmitted alone.
It likewise serves only to cause people to realize this one great matter (ekamahā-kṛtya).
What is called the "one great matter" refers precisely to the self-mind inherently possessed by sentient beings; it is merely termed the "seed of Buddha-nature.

Thus, one should know that the Sūtras are the path revealed by the Buddha, while Chan is intended for people to follow that path. To uphold the Sūtras without awakening to the mind is like... [participating in] Chan.

To practice meditation without seeing one's nature is, in its entirety, not true practice. The Sixth Patriarch said: "When the mind is deluded, it is turned by the Lotus Sutra; when the mind is awakened, it turns the Lotus Sutra.
Is there any duality between upholding the sutra and investigating through meditation? It lies in the student’s firm, enduring, and unshakable resolve.
Upholding the sutra is itself the investigation; the investigation is itself upholding the sutra. This is the intended meaning of the Buddha within the sutra.
If one seeks those who will uphold this sutra in the final age, can this be sought among those who merely follow the lines of their texts or count the characters?

When the ancients engaged in investigation, they invariably devoted thirty years of bitter effort; even today, ten thousand volumes of scripture would not suffice without such thirty years of dedication.

If a practitioner of Zen can maintain this single thought for thirty years, remaining steadfastly in the mountains without wavering, the Buddhas and Patriarchs will surely place their hands upon his head in empowerment.
Comforting indeed! Simply distinguish the willing mind, and you will certainly not be deceived. By all means, do not interpret this as two separate dharmas.
This was shown to Zongyuan of Qiyang and Master Chang of Guizong.

Master Chang possessed the aspiration for the supreme path and was single-mindedly reciting the Lotus Sūtra. Upon hearing that the Old Man had arrived at Mount Kuang, he crawled on his hands and knees [to meet him].

I have come here to meet you at Donglin. I have personally recounted that while reciting the Lotus Sūtra, I have harbored doubts regarding the teaching that "within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), except for the Buddha’s skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), which uses merely provisional names to guide sentient beings.
I do not know what this One Vehicle is, nor what these provisional names of skillful means are. I pray that you will deign to explain them to me.
The Elder said to him: "That which is called the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is the fundamental mind of all sentient beings;
it is the self-nature of the manifest awareness in our daily activities. Because this mind-nature is the great foundation of all sages and ordinary beings, it is called a 'vehicle' (yāna).
A vehicle has the meaning of 'transporting. Therefore it is said: 'The dharmas above and below within the three realms...'"
It is created solely by this one mind; apart from this mind, not even a fragment of a thing can be found.
This is precisely what occurs at the gates of our six sense organs in daily life: seeing and hearing are unobscured, and we possess constant, clear awareness.

Unimpeded by the veils of worldly toil and deluded thoughts, the radiant light shines everywhere and spiritual awakening is manifest. This very one mind is the realm of the Buddha; thus it extends to all.

Regarding the Buddha, if one practices the six perfections extensively with this mind to gather and transform sentient beings, yet perceives no being to be delivered and perceives no Buddha to be realized—this single-mindedness is the realm of the Bodhisattva.
Thus, by transporting oneself to the state of a Bodhisattva, one uses this very mind to contemplate the Four Noble Truths;
thereby, one can sever the afflictions of craving and attachment, which are the causes of suffering, and transcend the three realms.
Realizing the bliss of nirvāṇa within the realms (*dhātu*) constitutes the sphere of the two vehicles; thus, one is conveyed to the state of the two vehicles.

If one cultivates the holy life with this mind through the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, this constitutes the sphere of the four noble ones' four dhyānas; thus, one is conveyed to the Brahma heavens.
If one can cultivate the ten wholesome paths and sever the superior grade of evil, one will experience the spheres of the various heavens of the six desire realms. Thus...

They are transported to the various heavens. If one is deluded regarding this single mind and indulges in killing, stealing, and lust, thereby severing the Buddha-nature, one will experience the severe retributions of the three paths and be transported into the three evil realms. For this reason, the Buddha taught that the triple world is mind-only;
apart from this single mind, not a single thing can be found. Since there is only this one matter and no other, he spoke of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). It is not...

Apart from this mind, there is no other dharma that can be spoken of. If there were a dharma existing apart from the mind, that would constitute the heterodox views of external paths and not the True Dharma.
If one thoroughly understands this mind, then one knows the three stages of worthiness, the ten stages of sagehood, and all sentient beings.

All are the manifestations and influences of the single mind. Since the Way is a provisional name, one knows that the three vehicles and twelve divisions of the teachings spoken by the Buddha were established according to the capacities of sentient beings;
they are all provisional names intended to guide living beings, and fundamentally there is no real dharma bestowed upon them.
All these various skillful means are solely for the purpose of revealing this mind; it is not that there is some other distinct dharma taught for sentient beings.

It is not only the Buddha who employs skillful means; even the final act of holding up the flower and Kāśyapa’s smile, as well as Bodhidharma’s coming from the West to transmit the mind-seal alone, are likewise skillful means.
As for what is called "directly pointing to the human mind so that one sees its nature and becomes a Buddha," if...
To speak of "direct pointing" is already a deviation. Students of the Dharma in the age of the final dharma fail to realize their own minds and devote themselves exclusively to seeking outwardly;
consequently, they ultimately lack any genuine realization or benefit.

Even when they have the resolve to investigate the matter that transcends the ordinary, they do not know that from the beginning there is no dharma, nor do they understand that their own mind is of a single, uniform reality. Yet they further seek some other subtle excellence. To apply one's mind in such a manner is...

It is only that their true eye is not clear; moreover, they fall into the heterodox views of external paths. Though they are called students of the Way, they do not realize that they are instead producing the seeds of hell.

How tragic this is! The old man has often told practitioners that what is truly precious is sincere application of mind, whereby one purifies the habitual tendencies of afflictions and the seeds of karmic consciousness.
To break through even a fraction of these seeds of karmic consciousness is to reveal a portion of the [Buddha-nature].
One divides the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; by penetrating one portion of the Buddha’s realm, one severs ten portions of the karmic consciousness, which is itself the tenfold realm of the Buddha.
How could there be any other clever methods outside of the mind that could be pieced together and applied to constitute the realm of the Buddha?
Practitioners of Zen, do not harbor further doubts; simply understand that one's own mind is itself the One Vehicle. If you awaken to this...
That dharmas possess only provisional names is itself the true practice. You must simply remain undeluded in all circumstances.
Exert yourself in this way in your practice; there is no need for further deliberation or calculation, for both are merely seeds of false views.
To the Zen practitioner Gu-yu:
The Zen practitioner Gu-yu came from Fu-liang to visit Jin-lun and requested instruction on practicing the *kung-an*. The Old Man thereupon asked him:
"How do you apply your mind throughout the day? He replied, "I practice the contemplation of 'mind-only' (*cittamātra*).

The Master asked again, "When you perform this contemplation, do you still perceive the existence of external objects? He replied, "At this point, I no longer perceive the existence of any objects at all.
The Elder said, "If you do not perceive the existence of objects, then with what do you maintain 'mind-only'? The practitioner said, "I simply do not forget the subject. The Elder said:
You say that it is "mind-only," and thus you employ seeing and knowing as your practice; however, in truth, you have not yet reached the realm of mind-only. As the ancient masters said:
"When one has not yet realized that objects are mind-only, various kinds of discrimination arise; once one has realized that objects are mind-only, discrimination no longer arises.
Do you still give rise to discrimination regarding the objects before you? When you engage in contemplation, does it seem as though you have forgotten them?
When encountering objects, one still discriminates; as the mind arises in pursuit of objects, even if one stubbornly insists on "Mind-Only," one will ultimately fail to attain true realization.

Even if one succeeds in forgetting external objects, if one remains attached to "Mind-Only," this means one has not yet forgotten the mind itself—it is merely forgetting that which was not yet forgotten while retaining the subject who forgets.
Consequently, the object and the mind cannot be merged in harmony; this is called "obstruction by wisdom. How much more so, if [one has not yet...]?
Having attained the forgetting of objects, you insist on asserting "Mind-Only" as if it were a substantial dharma. An ancient worthy said:

"If one has not penetrated even a hair's breadth, it is as if separated by a thousand mountains. Even if you manage to reach the point where mind and objects are both forgotten and not a single dharma is established, you still know this only from the side of views and cognition;
how much more so when you take the conceptualizing mind to be the ultimate realization—is this not to deceive yourself? O practitioner, now...
Going deep into the ten thousand peaks of Mount Nanyue, observe intently the flowing water, the rustling wind, the songs of birds, and the mountain light.
When everything that meets the eye and fills the ear is realized to be devoid of the marks of body, mind, or world, all is fused into a single whole.

Yet even these two characters, "Mind-Only" (*cittamātra*), must be cast beyond the ten directions of the world. There is still more to it; if you fall into the trap of "Mind-Only," you remain as before.
There was no way out.

He showed this to Lord Yuan Liao, who said, "All things that move and possess spirit have Buddha-nature. The *Biographies* state: "A person can become a Yao or a Shun; it is because of this [Buddha-nature] that they do so."
Yet one knows that the nature of spiritual awakening is the foundation of all things; there is no human being who does not possess it.
When I observe people throughout antiquity and the present, there have been few who were not heroes and geniuses, yet those who are sages and worthies are not seen everywhere. Why is this?

It is because they are stained by habitual biases, following their emotions and chasing after them without turning back. This is what is meant by "the common people use [it] daily without knowing it. If one could but seek it for oneself...

Once one knows this, then sagehood is not difficult to attain. Thus it is said: "He who knows himself is enlightened. Because people do not know themselves, their delusions grow ever thicker and their minds grow ever more obscured.
If there were a man of heroic caliber who could block the passions and restore his true nature, then sagehood would be within reach, and his achievements would surely endure imperishably.
The ten precepts of the Buddha, the four prohibitions of Confucius, and the single mind of Chan—all [are one].

This is the essential method for returning to one's original nature. How can those who possess the will not exert themselves? Yuan Zidao, known today as Suliang, once came to inquire after me at Caoxi;
I recognized him as one of superior capacity and keen faculties. Later, when I visited Mount Kuang, Zidao traveled from afar to visit me.

Upon reading his compositions, I saw that his natural endowment was extraordinary and his temperament acute; however, because his habits were heavy and his spirit overly haughty, I simply allowed him to follow his own inclinations.

Yet they do not perceive their true nature (*prakṛti*). If one can exert effort to distance oneself from worldly passions and restore this nature, then one will neither be arrogant nor rebellious, will not oppose the few, and will not boast of achievements.
Thus, the vessel will be broad without overflowing, the will firm and unshakable, and the chill of the mind will dissipate;

then one may advance toward this Way while sitting still. Sages and worthies are within reach—how much more so, then, are worldly accomplishments? The old man loves you and shows you how to investigate the mind.

This Dharma is much like those worn-out sandals on the embankment; therefore, I have named him Gōryō (Public Emptiness), hoping that his daily life will become as bland as something unpalatable to the palate.
This is an instruction on the essential points of Zen meditation (a small *sankan* at the Jingshan Zen Hall).
The Chan school is a single tradition established to transmit the Buddha’s mind-seal; it is by no means a trivial matter.

Beginning with Bodhidharma’s arrival in the West, he established the principle of single-lineage transmission, using the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the mind. Thus, although Chan is a separate transmission outside the teachings (*jiao*), in reality, it is through the teachings that realization is attained.
Only then does one see the non-dual path of the Buddhas and patriarchs. As for the methods of investigation and cultivation, they are also...

This emerges from the teachings. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Sitting in meditation within mountain forests, through the superior, middling, and inferior practices, one is able to perceive the flow of the delusive thoughts of one's own mind.
This is truly the World-Honored One’s direct instruction on the essential method for practicing cultivation. It further states:

"That mind, intellect, and consciousness are manifestations of one's own mind; they are the false appearances of the realm of self-nature, the ocean of birth and death, and the karma and craving [that bind one]."
Ignorance—through causes such as these, one completely transcends them. This is the Tathāgata’s sublime purport for revealing and awakening the mind. Furthermore, it is said:

"The various sages of antiquity have transmitted this to one another in succession: delusive thoughts have no inherent nature. This, moreover, is the explicit revelation of the secret seal of the mind (*cittamudrā*).
This is the most vital point for people to investigate and study according to the teachings of the "Yellow-Faced Old Man" (the Buddha), and upon reaching [this realization]...

Bodhidharma showed this to the Second Patriarch, saying: "You need only externally cease all conditions and internally allow no stirring of the mind; let the mind be like a wall, and you may enter the Way.
This was the primary essential method for investigation shown by Bodhidharma to people at the beginning.

When the transmission reached Huangmei and he sought a Dharma heir, the Sixth Patriarch simply said, "Originally there is not a single thing," and immediately received the robe and bowl. This is the manifestation of that principle.
This is the essential meaning of the transmission of the mind-seal. When the Sixth Patriarch returned to the South, he instructed Dao Ming, saying:
"Do not think of good; do not think of evil. At this very moment, who is the original face of Elder Ming?

This is the foremost instruction of the Sixth Patriarch regarding the essential method for people to investigate and realize the truth. Thus, we know that from the Buddhas and patriarchs of antiquity, they have taught nothing other than this.
A person merely awakens to their own mind and recognizes themselves. Originally, there was no talk of "public cases" (gong'an) or "critical phrases" (huatou).

However, from the time of Nanyue and Qingyuan onwards, the various patriarchs provided teachings according to the needs of the occasion, mostly striking at points of doubt to cause people to turn their heads and look back, and then let it rest.
Even for those who do not understand, although they may apply the hammer of instruction, they simply allow them to be as they are.
Regarding the causes and conditions of the times: it was not until Huangbo that people were first instructed to contemplate the "head-phrase" (*huatou*).

It was only upon reaching Chan Master Dahui that he vigorously advocated this method, teaching students to investigate a single ancient *gong'an* as the fundamental pivot, calling it the "head-phrase.
He required practitioners to maintain a constant and intense state of alertness. Why was this so? It was solely because of the "field of the eight consciousnesses" (*ālaya-vijñāna*) of the student.
Within [the mind], the seeds of evil habits accumulated over immeasurable kalpas inwardly permeate it from moment to moment, flowing in a continuous stream so that deluded thoughts are never severed;
there is nothing that can be done about this. Therefore, I give you a single phrase devoid of meaning or flavor to chew upon firmly.
First, you must let go of all internal and external mental states and deluded thoughts at once. Because they cannot be let go of, I instruct you to hold this phrase.

It is like cutting tangled threads: cut them once, and they are all severed at once, never to reconnect again. Seize and sever the functioning consciousness (*manovijñāna*), never allowing it to proceed further.
This is precisely the rule for reaching the state where "external conditions are stilled and the internal mind is without gasping, the mind being like a wall"—as taught by Bodhidharma.
If you do not apply yourself in this manner, you will certainly never see your own original face. This is not merely teaching you...
One should contemplate the words and phrases of the *gong'an* to give rise to a state of doubt, hoping thereby to seek a clear understanding. This is precisely as Mahamati taught:
he exclusively instructed [students] to "look at the head-word" (*huatou*) and apply the "deadly blow," which is intended solely to cause your "thieving mind" to die.
As he told the assembly: "In the practice of Chan, one must only empty the mind and affix the two characters 'birth-and-death' upon one's forehead."

It is like being in debt of ten thousand strings of cash. Day and night—three times by day and three times by night—in the midst of tea and meals, when walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, when exchanging greetings with friends, in moments of stillness or bustle—one must simply take up the *huatou*:
"Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, "No. One must simply look and look within this very place. Without ceasing...
When you reach the moment of "taste," it is like crashing against a wall; when you arrive at the final juncture, it is like a rat entering a cow's horn—you will then see the sudden severance.
You must prepare a long-term body and mind to grapple with this until, suddenly, the flower of the mind bursts forth in brilliance, illuminating the lands of the ten directions;
once awakened, you shall go straight to the very bottom. This upward leap is Great Wisdom.
The tongs and hammer that an old man habitually employs have but one purpose:
to block the flow of discursive thoughts within the faculty of the mind so that they no longer circulate. At the very point where they cease to flow, look directly at your original face.
This is not to teach you to seek or contemplate within the *gong'an* (public case); rather, it is to give rise to doubt and seek a clear understanding. As it is said:
"The blossoming of the mind-flower—how could this be obtained from another? Thus, the Buddhas and Patriarchs each and every one pointed the way, requiring you to investigate your own self;
it is not a matter of seeking or grasping at their mysterious and wondrous words and phrases. Nowadays, when people practice Chan and apply themselves to the work, they...
Everyone says one must contemplate the "critical phrase" (huatou) and give rise to the "doubt-mass" (yiqing), yet they do not investigate at the very root;
they merely seek within the critical phrase itself. Seeking and seeking, they suddenly conjure up a certain state of experience and claim, "I have attained enlightenment.
They then compose verses and eulogies, treating them as rare treasures and considering themselves to have achieved their goal. Little do they realize that they have fallen entirely into delusion.
To practice Zen in this manner, caught within the net of conceptual understanding and views—how does this not blind the eyes of all people in future generations?
Today’s youths, before their meditation cushions are even steady, claim to have realized the Way and then flaunt their verbal cleverness, playing with their spirits and fancies.
They treat the swift exchange of *ji* (pivotal phrases) as a mere performance, concocting several lines of groundless, senseless chatter and calling it "verses on ancient cases" (*songgu*).
This arises from within your own deluded imaginings. When have you ever dreamed of the ancients?

If awakening to the Way were as easy for people today as it is [described], then compared to the conduct of the ancients—such as Changqing sitting until he wore through seven bundles of rush mats, or Zhaozhou not mixing his mind with anything else for thirty years—the ancients would be the most [extraordinary].

For those of dull faculties, it would be useless for you people today to even carry straw sandals. As for those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), who claim to have attained what they have not yet attained—should they not stand in awe?
Regarding the practice of Zen meditation and the investigation of the *huatou*, the cultivation of the spirit of doubt (*yiqing*) is absolutely indispensable.

As it is said: "A small doubt leads to a small awakening; a great doubt leads to a great awakening; without doubt, there is no awakening. It simply requires that one skillfully employ this spirit of doubt.
If your state of doubt is shattered, then the nostrils of the Buddhas and Patriarchs will naturally be pierced through as one. It is just like contemplating the koan of "Nianfo" (Buddha-recitation):
simply investigate in earnest who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. This is not a matter of doubting who the Buddha is.
If you were merely doubting who the Buddha is, it would suffice to listen to the Dharma Master lecture that Amitābha Buddha is named "Immeasurable Light. It is not so.
One would immediately awaken and compose several verses on "Infinite Light.

If such things are called "awakening to the Way," then those who have awakened their minds must be as numerous as hemp seeds and millet grains. Alas, alas! The words of the ancients were like door-knocking tiles;
they were merely used to knock open the door so one might see the person inside the house. They were not meant for making a living outside the gate.
Consider this: it is evident from this that doubt arises based on the *huatou* (critical phrase), yet the doubt does not reside in the *huatou* itself;
its essential point lies in the fundamental root. Take, for example, when Jiashan visited Chuanshi and asked: "A thousand feet of line hanging down, the intent is in the deep pool;
three inches away from the hook, why do you not speak? As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him into the water with a single oar. At that very moment—
They boarded the boat. The Master said again, "Speak! Speak! As Shan was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him once more. Shan attained great enlightenment and nodded his head three times.
The Master said, "The line on the tip of the pole is for you to play with; yet, without disturbing the clear waves, the meaning is naturally distinct.
If it had been Jia Shan, he would have made a living upon the hook and line. How could Boatman have sacrificed his life for him? This is it.
This was the ancient way of swiftly and skillfully finding one’s own path.

In the past, when the Way of Chan flourished, there were enlightened masters everywhere, and many seekers among the monastics throughout the land received instruction at every turn. It is said that it was not that there was no Chan, but simply that there were no teachers.
Now, the Chan school has long been desolate; how fortunate it is that at this time, people have resolved their minds to practice.

Those who investigate are many; yet though they possess knowledge, some may advance through expedient means by gauging the capacities of others, or provide certification according to their own inclinations.

When the student’s mind is shallow, they immediately consider themselves to have attained realization. Furthermore, they do not trust the holy teachings of the Tathāgata nor seek the true path, but merely proceed in a state of ignorant confusion.
They take the "winter melon seal" as the definitive resolution; thus they not only deceive themselves, but also lead others astray.
How can one not be fearful? Furthermore, among the officials and lay practitioners of antiquity who transmitted the Lamp Record, there were only a few individuals.
Today, those mired in the toil of worldly dust do not cultivate even the basic precepts; their deluded thoughts are turbid and chaotic.

Relying on their own cleverness, they read a few cases concerning the karmic conditions of ancient worthies and each of them presumes to possess the highest faculties. Upon meeting a monk, they immediately engage in combat.

Regarding the "critical pivot" (jīfēng), some also consider themselves to have attained enlightenment. Although this is a contemporary malady, it is truly because our own followers are like one blind man leading a multitude of blind men.
The Old Man now follows the essential points of the true practice of the Buddhas and Patriarchs for everyone to deliberate upon.
Those of lofty intelligence and penetrating insight naturally possess the means to rectify such matters.
Take for example Dong Zhiguang;
this Master Dong was born into a household of wealth and nobility, yet at an early age he gave rise to the aspiration to transcend birth and death. Indeed, his [virtue] was cultivated from youth.

This is the power of internal cultivation through the superior conditions of practicing Prajñāpāramitā. Previously, he attended upon Master Yunqi, who bestowed upon him the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
Shortly thereafter, he visited the Elder at Shuangjing, where he requested to receive the Upāsaka precepts.

Furthermore, he confessed his own grave karmic offenses and vowed to seek the essential method for escaping suffering, asking, "By what practice may I extinguish my transgressions? In response, the Elder showed him [the following]:

He said: "The student should immediately recognize that the roots of their transgressions are deep and heavy. The ancient masters taught people to eliminate old karma at all times; by all means, do not create new calamities.
For sentient beings with heavy karma, the Buddha opened the single gate of repentance (*pratideśanā*); it is the most excellent expedient for escaping suffering. The verse says:
'All sins are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can dispel. Those who wish to repent should sit upright.'"
To contemplate the true mark (dharmatā) is what constitutes right practice; all else is merely auxiliary skillful means. The intrinsic nature of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddha;
it is fundamentally undefiled and devoid of the characteristics of birth-and-death or coming and going. It is only due to the initial lack of awakening.
Deluded regarding their own fundamental nature, they are thus called "ignorance" (*avidyā*). Because of ignorance, various delusive thoughts arise;
through various inversions, they create various karmas and falsely grasp at the suffering of birth and death within the triple world—all of this is ignorance, failing to understand one's own mind.
They revolve according to deluded thoughts. It is like a person in deep sleep who experiences various dreams—various objects and various terrors, with manifold sufferings difficult to endure.
Yet upon waking, one seeks those dream-events and finds them utterly unobtainable.
Therefore, sentient beings fall into the dream of ignorance; following deluded thoughts and inversions, they create all manner of karma and bring suffering upon themselves. Upon awakening—
Looking at it now, how could these various states of perversion possibly persist? While currently within the dream of ignorance (*avidyā*), how can one eliminate past karma?
One must use the light of wisdom to shatter ignorance and gain firm conviction that one’s own mind is fundamentally pure.
Once one is no longer driven by delusive thoughts and perversions, all karmas will lack a cause, for they arise from delusive thought.
This is the cause of all karmas. Why is this so? Because from time immemorial, one has been deluded regarding one's own fundamental mind.
Life after life, through the mind of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one creates various kinds of karma.

These karmic habits accumulate within the field of the eight consciousnesses and are irrigated by the water of ignorance (*avidyā*), causing these evil seeds to sprout as the shoots of karma. This constitutes the root of transgression. All...

Evil karma arises from this. Now, wishing to eliminate past karma, one must first give rise to the light of great wisdom to pierce through ignorance and not allow delusive thoughts to sprout or to grow secretly and imperceptibly.

If one can sever delusive thoughts at their very source with a single thought-moment, then the roots of accumulated past karma will be eliminated instantly. This is what is meant by: "Do not fear the arising of thoughts."
One only fears that awakening is late. If awakening and illumination are even slightly delayed, one will be turned by them.

If one can, in the midst of daily life, at every instance of the arising of thought and movement of mind, awaken to and observe each thought, and extinguish each thought as it arises—this is what is meant by "all sins are like frost and dew;
the sun of wisdom can eliminate them. For the darkness of ignorance can only be shattered by wisdom; this is called "wisdom being able to eliminate."
Eliminate them. If you do not abandon this throughout day and night but diligently observe, you must not allow [the mind] to proceed.
Rather, at the very place where delusive thoughts arise, investigate until you find that they have no characteristic of arising. Look and look again; ultimately, nothing can be found.

When this becomes thoroughly matured over time, your own mind will be pure and devoid of substance. This mind that is devoid of substance is the true mark (*dharmatā*). If one constantly observes thus...

In this mind, what delusive thoughts could there be to allow for the accumulation of karma, or what basis could there be for it to lodge? To employ the mind in this manner is called the Samādhi of Contemplative Observation (*vipaśyanā-samādhi*).

If the afflictions of one’s own mind are coarse and heavy, and one fails to realize the presence of the obscurations of ignorance, then one should follow the instructions of the ancient masters who taught students to engage in investigation;
specifically, one should apply oneself to the authentic public case of "Investigating the Buddha-Recitation."
With all your might, bring up a single invocation of the Buddha's name and hold it across your chest. Immediately investigate: "Ultimately, who is this one reciting the Buddha’s name?
In this way, raise the name and investigate simultaneously; do not let it become empty or vacant. Hold this knot of doubt across your chest as you would your own life-root, never letting go of it.
Whether moving or still, at leisure or in haste, coming or going, sitting or standing—do nothing but this.
This is the one thing; there is no other matter. When you apply the mind in this way and the moment a delusive thought arises, press upon it with this *huatou* (critical phrase).
It will then be instantly pulverized, and all delusive thoughts will naturally have their tracks cleared and their traces extinguished.
With this *huatou*, it is like the sun’s orb suspended in the sky; there is no darkness it does not illuminate.
One only fears that the power of the mind will become lax and one is unwilling to maintain the inquiry with genuine earnestness, and thus cannot overcome delusive thoughts.

If you can overcome them, the very moment delusive thoughts dissolve is precisely the time when your old karma is extinguished. To abandon this single point and seek elsewhere outside the mind is to turn away from the Buddhas.
It transcends the world and there is no place for repentance; this depends on one's own power and cannot be substituted by the power of another.
If one's evil habits are so strong that one's strength cannot overcome them, there was a clear instruction from the Buddha of old:

"If a practitioner’s habitual tendencies are not eliminated, they should single-mindedly recite the Heart Mantra spoken by me, the Unconditioned Heart-Buddha. This is truly a method beyond the ordinary.

This is indeed so. Because the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) flows secretly within each person and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are so profound that the power of ordinary intellect cannot reach them—this "unreachable ground" must necessarily rely upon the Buddha’s Mind-Seal (*citta-mudrā*) to be broken through by means of the Esoteric [Teachings].

It is like a difficult-to-defeat enemy, for whom one must request the Sword of the Upper Direction. This requires that, during the two periods of morning and evening, you personally employ skillful means, taking only the practice of investigative inquiry as your task.
This is the ear of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The old man points this out for him, much like giving a staff to a blind person;

yet, in reality, practice lies within one's own person and cannot be substituted by teachers or friends. Because the layman’s aspiration is to return to the Dharma-gate, I have named him Fojue (Awakening of Merit).
This is because awakening and illumination must be taken as the foundation of practice. I have given him the style name Zhiguang (Wisdom Light); it is not merely the light of intellectual wisdom.
Furthermore, how does one shatter the darkness of ignorance? It requires only awakening and illumination without obscurity;
when the light of wisdom manifests before one, that is precisely the moment for resolving karmic obstacles and transcending birth and death.
I have heard that you, the layman Vimalakīrti, reside in the city of Vaiśālī; having cleared away all your possessions, you lie alone in a single room, manifesting illness to preach the Dharma.
Even Mañjuśrī and the other thirty-two great beings, with all their eloquence, were unable to equal you.
To keep one’s mouth shut in total silence—this has been, since antiquity, the foremost way for laypeople to perform Buddha-work. Old Pang completely dispersed his family wealth;
having attained the Great Meaning of the West from Mazu, he said: “I only wish to empty all that exists; by no means should you reify what does not exist.
This, too, was an excellent emulation of Vimalakīrti. You, Layman Dong, should take these two...
Is it that old age acts as a kinsman?

To the Chan practitioner Hanyou Hai, Hall Master of Jingshan, I show that the Buddhas and Patriarchs are of one mind and that the teachings and Chan are of one principle. The "separate transmission outside the teachings" of the Zen school does not exist apart from the mind; there is nothing else besides it.
There is but one Dharma that can be transmitted; it simply requires that people abandon language and written words to realize, in solitude, the meaning beyond words.
Yet those who practice Chan nowadays often disparage the teachings, failing to realize that the teachings elucidate the One Mind, which is the very foundation of Chan.

The Buddha spoke only of "one mind," yet he explained it thoroughly in terms of the two paths of delusion and enlightenment. In the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), the direct pointing to one mind does not belong to either delusion or enlightenment;
it requires that people awaken to it thoroughly. In reality, ultimately there is no duality.

Within the *tathāgatagarbha*, one cannot find even the slightest trace of coming or going, delusion or enlightenment, birth or death. How could this possibly belong to delusion or enlightenment? As the Second Patriarch said: "I have sought the mind..."
It is unobtainable. The Sixth Patriarch said: "Originally there is not a single thing.

This refers to the Prajñā in which the five aggregates, the sense bases and their objects, consciousness, and even the supramundane dharmas of the Three Vehicles are absent. Because there is nothing to be attained, one attains Bodhi;

this is no different from the statement that when seeking the mind, it is utterly unobtainable—how could these be two separate teachings? Thus we know that while the teachings speak of the One Mind, what differs is merely the distinction between ordinary sentiment and the state of a sage.

"Understanding through the ear" refers to the sudden shattering of ignorance through Zen meditation; this is the severing of mundane sentiments. "Awakening" likewise involves spitting out [conceptual understanding]; this is the severing of sagely interpretations.
Thus, while Zen rebukes intellectual understanding, the Teachings (the Sutras) have never failed to do so as well.

Nowadays, those who practice Zen by turning their minds away from the Teachings cannot forget their knowledge or sever their interpretations. When they take up the *huatou* (critical phrase), they cannot forget their emotions or eliminate their traces. All of these...
This is what is being censured. Why disparage the teachings by claiming they are not worth adopting?

Those who now abandon the teachings to practice Chan must first understand that fundamentally there is neither ordinary nor sage, and that one does not belong to either delusion or enlightenment; this constitutes the "ground of seeing.

Relying on this to investigate, if at the moment of a person’s single thought there remains even a thread of emotional views or a trace of subtle intellectual understanding, it all indicates that one has not yet penetrated through; these are all the states of birth and death.

Matters concerning the extremes—how could these be taken as attainment? Now, without the seal of approval from an eye-opening spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), if you do not use the teachings to seal the mind, you will ultimately fall into the ranks of demons, heterodox paths, and outsiders. However, you must not cling to the words and letters spoken by the Buddha.

Furthermore, regarding the wondrous words and phrases of the Patriarchs, you should take them as your own realization and insight. You must investigate them with diligence until you reach a state of resonance. As a sutra says:
"All afflictions, when brought to mind, are transformed into unsurpassed awakening. This is precisely what sudden enlightenment looks like.
You must not allow the habitual tendencies of affliction to intermingle with your realization; rather, you should treat them as wondrous.
This is awakening. It is not that there is something else; it is simply the exhaustion of the habitual tendencies of affliction (*kleśa-vāsanā*), whereby one reveals one’s original face.
Thus it is said: "Having awakened, one is the same as when unawakened; still, one remains the person of old, without changing one's former conduct.
Have you not seen how, before Jia Shan had met the Boatman, he ascended the hall and a monk asked him:
"What is the Dharmakāya? Shanshan replied, "The Dharmakāya is without form. He asked again, "What is the Dharma-eye? Shanshan replied, "The Dharma-eye is without flaw.
At that moment, Daowu, who was sitting in the assembly, could not help but let out a laugh.
After meeting Chuanzhi, Daowu sent a monk to ask him the same question: "What is the Dharmakāya? Shanshan again said, "The Dharmakāya is without form. He asked again, "What is..."
"This is the Dharma Eye. Shan then said, "The Dharma Eye is without flaw. When the monk returned and reported this to Daowu, Daowu said, "This fellow has only now reached full penetration.
This is the manner of a clever master of the teachings who abandons the scriptures to practice Chan. Haitang had long been intimately familiar with the Vehicle of the Teachings;
now he abandons what he has practiced to seek solely the path that goes beyond. Observe how Jia Shan [responds]."

The two turns of speech, preceding and following, are generally the same. Why is it that Daowu approves of the latter but not the former? Try to see where he does not approve and where he does approve.
If you can reach a definitive conclusion here, you will surely cause both the meaning of the patriarchs and the meaning of the Buddhas to be spat out all at once.
On another day, you will be able to swallow the entire Great Canon in a single gulp, transforming every character into reality.
This is the Treasury of Radiance (*Prabhāsa-garbha*). There is no small amount of entanglement here. Take care, take care!
Regarding the words spoken by Zen practitioner Lingjian Zhi of the West Hall at Shijing Mountain, who received this teaching:
"I say that all phenomena are unborn; this is the meaning of the momentary (*kṣaṇika*). That which is first born immediately possesses cessation. Not...
This is spoken for the sake of the ignorant. An ancient sage said: "Only one who realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*) perceives the momentary (*kṣaṇa*).
Now, once non-arising has been realized, how could there still be a momentary [existence] to be perceived? If one perceives a momentary [existence], then one has not realized non-arising.
Why, then, do you now say that one who realizes non-arising perceives the momentary? Are non-arising and the momentary one and the same, or are they different? The Buddha...
If one speaks of moments (*kṣaṇa*) based on non-arising, then they are not different. The Patriarch said: "Only those who realize non-arising see the moment.
Thus, non-arising and the moment are also not one. If one seeks them apart from being either one or different, then the very notion of non-arising is merely a tethering stake for a donkey.
Guishan said: "When people today suddenly comprehend their own mind in a single thought-moment, this is called 'awakening' (*wu*)."
One immediately uses what has been realized to purify the flowing consciousness of present karma; this is called cultivation.

Now, as for "flowing consciousness," it refers to subtle arising and ceasing—that is, the momentary mind (*kṣaṇika-citta*). To say that one cultivates after realization means that one sees [the truth] after having realized it.
Furthermore, it is only after awakening that one perceives the *kṣaṇa* (moment); thus, it is clear that what was previously awakened to was not truly non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Now, when practicing Chan by holding the *huatou*, although one speaks of applying effort, subtle arising and ceasing continue to flow and circulate secretly, like grass being suppressed by a stone.
It fades away and is no longer seen. If one does not sever arising and ceasing, how can one realize non-arising? If it were not non-arising, how could one withstand birth and death?
If one sees [the truth] only after realization, then the World-Honored One spoke of non-arising based on the *kṣaṇa* (moment).

Furthermore, this serves as a supplementary teaching. Xitang has thoroughly mastered the doctrines of the teachings, yet now he abandons what he has practiced and holds up solely the path that transcends all.
You should examine him closely to test his realization here. However, you must not attempt to reconcile it through intellectual reasoning, nor seek it within conceptual understanding.
If one can suddenly perceive non-arising within a single thought-moment, then the nostrils of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—[are grasped].
He threaded them together.

He showed this to Master Xishi, who had long resided at a lecture hall and had followed the various patriarchs at Shaolin to investigate their karmic conditions; now, having completely set aside all that he had studied, he was single-mindedly...
Pointing toward the upward path, he stood alone at the Double Peak (Shuangjing). When the Old Man arrived, he took up the incense and requested instruction.
The Old Man showed him, saying: "This matter is fundamentally without deficiency in every person; it is perfectly complete and fully endowed.
That you do not recognize it in your daily life and cannot enjoy its benefits is solely because the seeds of beginningless evil habits have been steeped for kalpas, their roots deeply entrenched."

It is already difficult to extricate oneself from this; now, moreover, one is further burdened by newly acquired verbal teachings, written texts, the *gong'an* of the patriarchs, and various forms of intellectual understanding, which add yet another layer of obstruction.
Thus, although one seeks to clarify one's own nature, the more one seeks, the further away one becomes. Why is this so?

It is simply because one has obscured one’s own nature that one seeks it from others. Due to the accumulated habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśa-vāsanā*) over many lifetimes, these are called the "affliction-obstruction" (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Because they obstruct wondrous knowledge and vision, they are called the "obstruction to the known" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). If these two obstructions are eliminated, the fundamental essence manifests of itself.
Now, in investigating the matter of the "upward direction," you must first set aside all previously learned texts, words, and language that obscure wondrous knowledge and vision.
Rationality is called "mixed poison. Vomit it all out with your whole heart and single-mindedly uphold the original *kōan*.
Deepen your state of doubt to sever the very root of delusive thoughts and afflictions, so that they cannot emerge from within nor enter from without.
Cut off the past and future; in the interval, you stand alone. Let there be only this single mass of doubt as your own life-root. Doubt until you cannot doubt.
Go! When you cannot find a place to apply force, gaze fixedly for a moment and see what it ultimately is.

As you look and look, pressing and pressing, there will naturally come a time of decisive breakthrough. However, if even a hair’s breadth of intellectual view remains, it will immediately create a separation of thousands of miles.
Just consider what the First Patriarch said: "A mind like a wall can enter the Way. This is it.
This is the primary path home. If the mind is unwilling to die and one’s doubt is not acute and appropriate, then for a thousand births and a hundred kalpas, one will remain forever on the road.
Master of the Mountain, simply direct your spirit toward this;
you can be certain that the place you attain in the future will surely be something more than a mere "is it so? Strive with all your might.

Master En Shan (Sōng Puk) of the ancient past taught people to practice Chan meditation by first requiring them to "internally detach from body and mind" and "externally cast off the world. One must let go of everything,
leaving not even a hair’s breadth of attachment behind, and single-mindedly hold up a koan or *huatou*, such as Zhaozhou’s “Wu” (the dog has no Buddha-nature).
"Is there also Buddha-nature? The Master said, "No. Or, "When the myriad dharmas return to the One, where does the One return? Or, "Examine with precision:
who is it that recites the Buddha's name? Take one such case and hold it across your chest like the Vajra King’s precious sword.
Sever all discursive thoughts and delusions at once, as if cutting tangled threads, so that nothing may emerge from within and nothing may enter from without.
Seize the vital passageways and block the throat, not even permitting the breath to escape. Exerting yourself in this manner, gaze with a single eye:
"What, after all, is this 'raising the head-word'? Cast your doubt in this way, and let the doubt persist.
Let go of doubt. Let the mind of doubt become like a wall, no longer permitting a second thought to arise.
As soon as there is a subtle flow of discursive thought, look at it directly; upon seeing it, immediately exert all effort to raise the *huatou* (critical phrase) once more.

Again apply the state of doubt, examining and doubting further, and press down upon this mass of doubt until it is stifled. When mental thoughts do not arise and discursive imaginings do not function, that is precisely [the moment].

This is the place where power is gained. Relying firmly in this manner, throughout all walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, and amidst movement, stillness, leisure, and busyness, one must clench the teeth with determination and never let go.
Even within sleep and dreams, one must not let go. There is only this single thought of the *huatou*, which is the very life-root of a person.
It is like a dead man who still has breath; one must apply such a deadly blow to tear it apart.

Only then is one truly a person who applies effort in the practice of Zen. When one exerts oneself to the utmost, disregarding days and months, there will suddenly come the moment—like a bean popping in cold ashes—which is the occasion of great joy.
If you remain indolent and arbitrary, practicing for a day and neglecting for ten, I fear that in the end you will never find the time when you gain true efficacy.
Master of the Mountain, as you possess the aspiration for the supreme matter, you should encourage yourself with these words.
This is shown for the daily practice of practitioners of the Esoteric Vehicle and those studying Chan:
contemplate the four great elements as shadows; contemplate what is before you as dream-events; and contemplate the mind as a rushing torrent.
Contemplate physical movements as being like mechanical wooden puppets; contemplate sounds as being like echoes in a valley; contemplate sensory objects as being like flowers in the sky.

When practicing this contemplation, there is no self and nothing belonging to a self; there is no agent who moves, nor is there any agent who acts. Whether going or coming, sitting or standing, [all are thus].
Without arising and without ceasing, one should contemplate non-arising; this is called entering the Samādhi of Non-contention.
As for the Chan practitioner Tanyuan:

when he was young, he frequented lecture halls and studied the doctrines of the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Characteristics of Dharmas) school. After a long time, however, because he did not perceive his own nature, doubt arose within him.

The elder then showed him the way, saying: "The ancients said, 'I do not value your conduct; I only value your realization. As for what is called 'conduct'—"
This refers to the practice of diligent cultivation. As for "ground of insight" (*jendi*), it means thoroughly realizing that one's own mind is the foundation of practice.

If the foundation of practice is not clear, then one’s efforts will lose their essential purpose. Therefore, students of the Way take the ground of insight as primary. Regarding what is called the "ground of insight":
Thus, one gains faith in one's own mind: it is fundamentally pure and devoid of even a single thing. Not only are ordinary emotions absent, but even the state of a sage does not exist.
It is only because of beginningless ignorance that one’s own wondrous luminosity is obscured;

consequently, various inverted states arise, along with deluded thoughts and discriminations, leading to the creation of all manner of karma. This is like a sober person who, having no affairs, suddenly experiences various dreams while asleep.
In a dream, experiences such as suffering and pleasure appear vividly before one; yet upon waking, when one seeks them, they are utterly unfindable.
This is called "existence arising from non-existence"—how could it be a real phenomenon? It is merely that deluded people, through their inverted views, cling to it as being truly existent;

this is simply a failure to see through to the truth. Furthermore, when a Buddha appears in the world and teaches various dharmas, these are but the instruments for shattering the dream. It is also...
It has no fundamental basis. Yet, those who study the Buddha-dharma further cling to it as a reality that truly exists within themselves;
this is merely adding a dream to a dream. Now, the method of Zen meditation has no secret or marvelous formula other than directly shattering the delusions and inversions of one's dreams.

If one thoroughly understands that [dharmas] are fundamentally non-existent, and gains firm conviction that one’s own mind is pure and devoid of substance, then one realizes that deluded thoughts do not exist.

Once one realizes that delusion does not exist, one knows that even the Buddha-dharma—which is intended to destroy deluded thoughts—is itself fundamentally non-existent. The Buddha-dharma is the medicine, and deluded thoughts are the illness.
If neither medicine nor illness is established, then the fundamental essence remains in tranquil stillness. In this way, one knows that both medicine and illness are...
Illness. Now, the investigation of the ancient public case (gong'an) regarding the word "Mu" (No) that is presented is precisely the medicine for attacking the disease of medicine.
This is called "using poison to remove poison. If one knows that fundamentally there is no thing, then even the single character "investigate" (can) becomes yet another dose of poison.
How could one possibly take this as a subtle and wondrous meeting? If you do not believe in your own mind, even if you practice, it is like mistakenly ingesting poison.
Can a Chan practitioner believe this? You should investigate at the place where not a single dharma is established.
I am staying at Jizhao on Mount Shuangjing.
Layman Gushanzi came to visit me for an audience. When I inquired about his occupation, he said he practiced geomancy (*xingjia*).

He subsequently went to Huacheng, where we pointed out the features of the mountains and waters and discussed the subtle wonders of the creative transformation (*zaohua*), which transcend both form and vital energy (*xingqi*).
It appears that he grasped the essence while discarding the coarse; therefore, I questioned him about it. He replied that he had once seen the essay "On Awakening.
This essay was composed by my disciple Zhouzi. I previously wrote a preface for it, stating: "The One is the root of the myriad things and the treasury of creation.
Thus it is said: 'Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; the Sage attains the One...'"
This is taken as the standard for the world. When one is correct, one is not confused by depravity, and thus one solidifies the root.
Now, human and thing, principle and vital energy (*qi*), mind and form—all are one. Once this One is attained, all principles converge upon it. As the saying goes:
"If you recognize the One, ten thousand matters are finished. Therefore, we practitioners of the subtle thread must say: "The myriad things return to the One; to what does the One return?"
As for their ultimate destination, it can be known as the One; yet the destination of that One cannot be known.

Now, people are entangled in myriad affairs and assailed by myriad anxieties; they are in a state of constant turmoil and find no peace at all. This is because they fail to recognize the fault of not knowing the One.
Layman, you are already able to perceive that the creative transformations of heaven and earth return to the One, yet you do not recognize [the unity of] your own body and mind.
The destiny of nature and life returns to one. This is like knowing the two fives but not knowing they constitute ten.
If one truly knows that the destiny of nature and life returns to one, then the myriad transformations are fully contained within oneself. How can one not apply oneself to this?
I tell you, Mr.
Tan Liang, that your spiritual capacity (*indriya*) is most sharp; it has indeed emerged from your long-standing cultivation of *prajñā*.

Now, *prajñā* is the Buddha-nature inherent within all sentient beings, fully possessed by each and every one. Yet, the reason why capacities differ as either sharp or dull is truly due to the habitual tendencies of the five desires.
It is merely that their dispositions vary in degree, being either thick or thin. Those of sharp faculties, having long practiced Prajñā, have purified and eliminated defiled habitual tendencies;
thus, in this present life, they possess keen intelligence and clarity.

Yet, people do not recognize this and instead turn away from it, using their sharp faculties and brilliance as resources for defiled and evil habits—this is what is called "inversion. Because Prajñā internally permeates them, at times...
At that time, there was a resolve to transcend the mundane world. He said, "I shall wait until a certain time for my worldly affairs to be concluded, and then I will go to study the Way.
Such views and understandings are common throughout the world;

because they harbor thoughts of the future, the various circumstances and conditions encountered in the present are regarded as unworthy of concern and are treated with disdain due to their preoccupation with lofty ambitions for the future.
By means of such empty imaginings, one instead increases arrogance and conceit, claiming that others lack this mind and are all merely commoners.
Consequently, one lets the present moment slip away; losing both the mundane and the supramundane, one vainly wastes time.
By the time the future arrives, it is uncertain whether one’s original resolve will still remain as it was. Furthermore, the mind fails to examine its own subtle conduct.
To harbor such negligence while considering one’s own views to be lofty is an even greater error.
To call this "possessing ambition" is to be surpassed by the common farmer in a village of three households;
he has no other thoughts, yet his livelihood is secure year after year—should you not feel ashamed? The Sage taught people not to leap over stages, saying: "Act according to your station."
Laozi said: "He who leaps over things does not walk. Now that you already possess this aspiration for the Way, from this very day forward, apply yourself with earnestness and meticulous care.

Mr. Tan, please look directly at the present moment; do not let even a single move slip away, and you will immediately see where your lifelong efforts have truly landed.
It is shown that for ordinary people like Cao Shiju, daily life does not depart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; the same is true for the sage.

Since their functioning is identical, the distinction between the sage and the ordinary person lies merely in the interval between knowing and not knowing. Therefore it is said: "The common people use [it] daily."
Yet they do not realize this. For the student who seeks the work of sagehood, it lies precisely in the midst of daily life where one is unaware;
one must seek that innate knowing. If one perceives this inherent knowing, then all sounds, forms, wealth, and profit will clearly fail to move the mind.
Thus, when encountering circumstances and conditions, it is like a mirror reflecting images—there is not a single thing that can stir within. This...
This is the essential gateway for entering the Way.
To show the student Feng Yanying how to turn toward the Way:
first, one must fear birth and death; second, one must know the root of birth and death. As for the root of birth and death:
It is precisely these various activities of hatred, attachment, grasping, rejection, pride, greed, anger, and delusion that manifest before us in the present moment.

Since these are the very roots of the suffering of birth and death, one must resolve to sever them; there is no other method. At the very moment they arise, one must directly perceive them so that they cannot continue to emerge.
When they are met at the point where they do not arise, they are extinguished right where they stand. At the time of their extinction, they do not further interact with one another.
Continued: If you apply your mind in this way—moment by moment without negligence, thought after thought without obscuration—then that which knows is inherently numinous.
If this knowing is numinous, then when encountering objects, the objects will not entice the mind; when contemplating the mind, the mind will not attach to objects.
When mind and objects do not reach one another, there is no room for birth and death to lodge. To apply the mind in this manner, there is no need to seek anything else profound or wondrous.

Those who hold the view of a self cannot enter [this path]. If one perceives a self, then one regards the Buddhas and Patriarchs as merely human forms.
When the person and the self stand in opposition, there will ultimately be no person from whom one can escape, nor any place where one may find rest.
If you do not rest yourself, there will be no ground for rest. If you are willing to rest, then you shall rest right now. Let go of everything.
Below. This is the great rest. In this rest, both Buddhas and sentient beings alike avoid their shadows; there is no ground left to accommodate them.
Your quest for the "path above" may be called extraordinary, yet it is not as well as simply letting go and settling into peace.
An ancient said: "When the realm is settled and people are few. If you reach the state of total settlement, even a Buddha would not act. Furthermore...

[the Master] showed that for those who do not understand the great matter of birth and death, the ancients would go into the mountains to dwell alone, like a solitary shadow, solely to investigate it.

It is like a gourd on water: it cannot be suppressed and merely rolls about. This is the most difficult point at which to apply effort. When one cannot apply effort, one beats a retreat.
It is understood. Such a person is one who lacks willpower and strength; what need is there to speak of "investigating Zen"?

Now, those with a beginner's mind should simply set aside all internal and external principles, knowledge, views, as well as deluded thoughts and deliberations, putting them down completely and putting them down again until there is nothing left to put down. The *huatou*. For example, take Zhaozhou’s “Mu” (No) held across one’s chest. Why does he say “no”? Re-apply the state of doubt (*yiqing*).
If this state of doubt gains strength, then deluded thoughts will not arise. If they do arise, you must by no means confront them;
do not attempt to sever them with the mind, nor try to suppress them, nor allow them to continue. Simply...
As soon as you perceive it, let it go; with one letting-go, it vanishes. Immediately seize the *huatou* (critical phrase) and look deeply into it.

rather, it is simply a point from which one may effectively apply effort. For a practitioner of Zen who abandons the teachings to follow the path of meditation, this initial stage is the most difficult.

The elder then showed it to him, saying: "The Buddha appears in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition.

This is the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by all sentient beings. Now, however, it is shrouded by ignorance and obscured by deluded thoughts and false perceptions;

thus, in their daily lives, they perceive, hear, know, and sense according to their passions, creating karma that leads them to undergo the sufferings of birth and death without realizing it themselves.

this is called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), and not the deluded knowledge and vision of sentient beings.
If one awakens to this knowledge and vision, then every phenomenon and every dharma is the true application of the mind. Whatever...

"Even raising a single hand, or slightly bowing the head, even with a single incense stick or a single flower—by making such offerings to the Buddha, one has already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Even minute causes and small virtues are all true causes for attaining Buddhahood; how much more so when one’s body undertakes manifold tasks?
To sacrifice one’s life for the sake of the Dharma—is this not the true seed for attaining Buddhahood?

If you do not enter this Dharma-gate, even if you can maintain hundreds of thousands of millions of sutras, you are merely an enemy to their meaning;

This is fixed as the mind of birth and death; one cannot resolve to sacrifice one's life to the very end. Furthermore, there is the fear that the evil habits, knowledge, and views of past lives will create obstacles midway, causing one to flow into the net of heterodoxy.
