by no means should you let it pass with a casual or indifferent attitude.
To illustrate the nature of the field of cultivation for practitioners who traverse the ocean of toil:
if one surveys the heroes and sages of antiquity who encountered hardships and suffering yet maintained a long-term, indomitable resolve, such individuals are generally not seen in great numbers.
Such persons include the Five Ministers of Jin, who followed Duke Chong'er in his exile abroad for nineteen years without ever flagging.
As for the mind, it likely yearns day and night for a fief of but a few inches, seeking to leave an imperishable mark upon bamboo and silk.
This is because fame and profit entice the heart, leading one to forget oneself in service; such is the common sentiment of people throughout past and present.
Yet as for the practitioner Tian Dao, he has followed Master Da for over twenty years, neglecting both sleep and food, never once slackening for even a single breath.
Whenever he committed even the slightest transgression, he was severely rebuked and punished with heavy canings; consequently, his two legs were often as black as ink.

Yet, throughout it all, he never gave rise to a single thought of resentment nor uttered a single word of complaint. Even when faced with grave offenses that made death seem imminent, while dwelling within the gate of solitude, suffering, and emptiness, what did he seek?
That he could remain so steadfast and indomitable in his diligence—observing this, one cannot help but marvel.
That which was extremely rare among the loyal ministers and righteous scholars of antiquity is now seen in this man of the Way.
Furthermore, that he may follow the Master in death to be interred at Shuangjing—this single mound of earth, I say, is not easily obtained even by monastics, let alone laypeople;
it is as if he has already received an enfeoffment of "máo" and "tǔ" within the land of the Dharma. This is not merely the sacrifice of one's body.
A bloody battle. Why did this occur at the moment of death? He entrusted this scroll to his disciple, the Daoist Zhu.
Now, Master Tan has given it the name "Ocean Plowing" (Hǎi-gēng); it is also a deed-certificate for the ancestral legacy of the Dharma gate. How could this be a minor connection?
Addressing Zhu Sunchen, a scholar studying the Way:
Many people believe that reading books is an obstacle to the Way. The old man said, "How can reading books hinder the Way?
It is simply that when one does not read, one is often disturbed by groundless discursive thoughts. If, during moments of leisure, one can gather the mind into one—"
In all circumstances, sever the flow of delusive thoughts so that they do not arise; let every thought dwell within the Way, never forgetting it for a moment.

If you act in this way, your time spent studying the Way will be much greater than your time spent reading books. The Old Man has often instructed students: whenever a thought arises, you must see through it immediately;
do not give rise to them recklessly before circumstances have even presented themselves. If you can truly apply your mind in this manner, delusive thoughts will naturally be severed.
External affairs will naturally cause no disturbance; the power of the Way will naturally strengthen; and the practice will surely be easily accomplished.

This is shown to Shen Zhi: the Way does not desire complexity. Complexity leads to multiplicity; multiplicity leads to disturbance; disturbance leads to anxiety; and anxiety leads to non-entry. As the ancients said: "Study..."
The path of the will must return to the One. What I call "the One" refers simply to unifying one's will.
Now that you already know the method of investigation through inquiry (*kanhua*), you should take the *gong'an* you are investigating and hold it across your chest.

Whether in leisure or busyness, movement or stillness, whether receiving guests or attending to others, and in all the activities of daily life, you must maintain mindfulness at every moment without letting it slip away. If you let it slip, you will be disturbed by external conditions.
If one is disturbed, weariness arises. When weariness arises, there is only a desire for seclusion, and no mind intent upon the Way.
When the will is unified, then all matters can be accomplished. In every instance where the mind is applied, one must exert effort precisely at the point where a thought arises.
As soon as it arises, one must see through it; once seen through, it vanishes instantly and does not continue. Not being manipulated by it—this is *chan* (investigation).

This is the ultimate secret of the method. Therefore it is said: "Plan for the difficult in the easy; accomplish the great through the minute. This refers precisely to the easy and minute points where one applies oneself;

then, one will immediately feel that effort is saved. If you set this aside and wait for leisure time or a quiet moment before finally beginning your practice, then even if you live out your entire life in this way, there will never be a time when you enter the Way.
Mr. Shen, simply apply yourself within a single thought-moment; it is not necessary—
To seek outwardly, one then pays homage to the Buddha and recites mantras; this too is accomplished solely through the power of faith in a single thought-moment.
In short, all various skillful means are simply methods for gathering the mind.
To Master Guanjū Kai:
Among the loyal and righteous men of antiquity, none could undertake great affairs without possessing great power. This power consists of both mental power and vital energy.
As the saying goes: "The will reaches its goal; vital energy follows. It is further said: "Maintain your will, and do not let your vital energy become violent."
If the form is over-exerted, it withers; if the essence is over-exerted, it is exhausted; if the spirit is over-exerted, it falters. Zhuang Zhou said:
"To pursue the infinite with the finite is already perilous. To do so while claiming to possess knowledge is doubly perilous.

This speaks of excessive use without knowing how to nourish oneself. Therefore, Laozi said: "In governing people and serving Heaven, nothing is better than frugality (*se*). Frugality means having..."
Yet they did not exhaust their resources in its use. Nourishing the physical form is called "governing people"; nourishing one's nature is called "serving Heaven.
This is precisely what our Buddha meant when he said that the six sense organs rush toward the realms of the six sense objects until, over time, they become exhausted.
Thus we know that among the ancients who undertook great affairs, there were none who did not employ what was in surplus when engaging with worldly matters. For example, Emperor Gaozu of Han...
To seize the world by force, one may lose a hundred battles without ever winning; yet once victory is achieved, the great task is accomplished.

Is this not because those who excel at defense have more than enough to manage what is insufficient in governance? Our late Master entrusted the great matter of the Dharma-gate to you alone, and you bore it upon your shoulders without withholding any of your strength.
Faced with the brunt of a hundred setbacks, you exhausted every faculty and exerted all your power to respond, down to the finest detail.

This is because his aspirations were so abundant that he had no leisure to concern himself with the fact that his physical form was prone to exhaustion. Now, the body is easily transformed and time passes such that it is difficult to recover;
one must therefore take advantage of the present moment to cultivate restorative care in order to preserve the harmony of Heaven.

This is what is meant by "the foundation being established, the Way arises. Given the lifelong studies of your honor, you have taken the clarification of the mind as your standard; yet if the mind is expansive while the form...

If you remain aloof, your strength will be preserved and your capacity will have a surplus; thus, the unfinished task remains as if one were to reach a destination of a thousand-li journey after a brief rest.
You must surely have a way to settle yourself in this regard. What do you think?
An Exposition on the Essential Points of Mindfulness of the Buddha (Spoken at Yunqi for Wenzi and Jiangzi, together with their mother):

The single gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha to seek rebirth in the Pure Land is fundamentally intended to resolve the great matter of birth and death. Therefore it is said: "Mindfulness of the Buddha resolves birth and death.

Nowadays, people develop the aspiration to practice only because they wish to resolve the matter of birth and death; it is precisely for this reason that they are willing to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. It is simply a matter of the Buddha...
This can bring an end to birth and death. If one does not know the root and trunk of birth and death, toward what ultimately will one direct one’s mindfulness?
If the mind that recites the Buddha’s name cannot sever the root and trunk of birth and death, how can one bring an end to them?
What is the root and trunk of birth and death? An ancient said: "If karma is not heavy, one is not born in this Sahā world; if craving is not severed, one is not born in the Pure Land."
Thus we know that the root of craving is the very trunk of birth and death. That all sentient beings undergo the suffering of birth and death is entirely due to the fault of craving and desire.
Tracing back this root of craving, it is not something possessed in this present life, nor was it possessed in one, two, three, or four lifetimes;
rather, it has existed from the very beginning of time, since the first occurrence of birth and death, throughout every successive life.
Life after life, from one body to the next, we have all been transmigrating through the flow of craving and desire up until this very day.

Reflecting back upon the past, when has there ever been even a single thought that momentarily departed from this root of craving? Such seeds of craving have accumulated over kalpas, becoming profound and deep;
therefore, birth and death are endless. Only today have you finally resolved to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, yet you merely hope for rebirth in the Western Land by means of empty wishes.
Furthermore, you do not even know that "continuous attachment" is the name for the root of birth and death. When has there ever been a single thought-moment that severed this clinging?
Since you do not know the root of birth and death, you simply recite the Buddha’s name on one side while the root of birth and death continues to grow unchecked.

Thus, as you recite the Buddha’s name in this manner, it remains entirely unrelated to birth and death. No matter how much you recite in such a way, when you reach [the point of... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
At the moment of death, one sees only the root of attachment to life and death manifest before them. Only then does one realize that the Buddha was of no help at all;
one then resents the fact that reciting the Buddha’s name lacked efficacy. By then, it is too late for regret. Therefore, I exhort those who currently recite the Buddha’s name:
first, you must understand that attachment is the very root of birth and death. As you recite the Buddha’s name now, in every thought-moment you must sever this root of attachment. Thus...
In daily life, as it manifests before you, when a layperson recites the Buddha’s name, they see their children, grandchildren, household affairs, and property;
there is not a single thing that is not an object of attachment. Consequently, there is not a single matter or a single thought that is not a calculation for birth and death.
It is as if one’s entire body were within a pit of fire. One does not realize that while reciting the Buddha’s name, the root of attachment has never been set down for even a single thought-moment.

It is as if, while reciting the Buddha’s name, one merely says that the recitation is not earnest, failing to realize that attachment is the sovereign master and the recitation of the Buddha’s name is but a superficial facade.
In such a state, the Buddha hears only the recitation, while attachment grows unchecked. For instance:
When feelings of attachment toward children and wife manifest before you, turn the light back upon yourself and look: can this one invocation of the Buddha’s name truly withstand this love?
Can it truly sever this love? If you cannot sever this love, how will you ever ultimately resolve the cycle of birth and death?
Because the conditions of love have been familiarized through many lifetimes, while the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name is but newly initiated and remains extremely crude. Furthermore—

This is not genuine; therefore, it will not be effective. If you cannot maintain this resolve regarding the objects of attachment before your eyes, then you will ultimately be unable to maintain it at the time of death.
Thus, I exhort those who practice Buddha-recitation: first, you must realize that your mind is urgent in its concern for birth and death;
second, you must sever the mind of birth and death with urgency; third, you must cut down the very root of birth and death in every thought-moment. Only then will your recitation be...
To maintain mindfulness is the very moment for resolving birth and death. Why must one wait until the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month before finally accomplishing it?
That would be the ultimate in lateness. As it is said: "Everything before one's eyes is the matter of birth and death.

If one can resolve the emptiness of birth and death right now, then with every thought truly earnest and every stroke of the blade seeing blood—should one still fail to transcend birth and death with such an application of mind? It is impossible.

If that were so, all Buddhas would be guilty of speaking falsehoods. Therefore, whether lay or ordained, simply knowing the mind of birth and death is itself the moment of transcending birth and death. How could there be any other sublime dharma?
In the *Shi Yunqi Shizhe* (Account of the Attendant at Yunqi),

it is recorded that before the Great Master entered parinirvāṇa, for nineteen years prior, his daily activities— whether rising, resting, eating, or breathing— were attended to by his attendant day and night. Consequently,
there were no secret practices he did not witness, no subtle words he did not hear, and no responses to those with karmic capacity that he did not perceive.
This is not understood. There is nothing regarding the mind and affairs of all beings that he does not know;

thus, the entire physical form, color, and voice of the Great Master are clearly manifest within the space between one's heart and eyes. Even if one were to attend upon tens of millions of followers, none would possess a true knowledge and realization equal to that of the attendant.
Thus, even now, every member of this great assembly perceives the Great Master as having entered parinirvāṇa. It is only...

Only the attendant did not conceive the thought of his passing into extinction. In practicing the Pure Land during the Dharma-ending age, one must necessarily contemplate the wondrous marks of Amitābha;
yet, because one has not yet personally beheld his countenance, even such contemplation is not truly authentic.

One must hear Amitābha preaching the Dharma, for otherwise, even such reflection is not truly authentic. I observe that the Great Master was an emanation of Amitābha, and the attendant served him with devotion.
"It has been a long time. How could I possibly forget the Great Master? Furthermore, how could I seek instruction on the Buddha-dharma from another house?
I told my attendant: 'There is no need for any other thoughts; simply contemplate the Great Master’s every scale and model of dharma as they were when he was alive.'"

Regarding sounds and speech, activities and deportment, meditative cultivation and contemplation, and compassionate acts for the benefit of living beings—contemplate each of these minutely from head to foot, one by one, throughout the day and night.

If you do so, every moment of such contemplation is itself the manifestation of Amitābha. To have even a single thought of forgetfulness is to fail the Buddha’s benevolence and enter the realm of birth-and-death.
At the time of my death, I, this old man, have no further words to speak. I shall simply place my entire body within your heart;
you must not expel it. This is precisely my "old man’s samādhi of invisibility. Contemplate this deeply.
Show the attendant Dengyu how to practice mindfulness of the Buddha within one's own mind:
mindfulness of the Buddha is mindfulness of the mind; mind and Buddha are non-dual. Moment-to-moment, there is no abiding; even the one who can practice mindfulness does not exist as a fixed entity.

That which is contemplated is empty of intrinsic nature; this emptiness of intrinsic nature is quiescent extinction. When both subject and object are forgotten, this is called "attaining the Buddha of self-nature through the very mind.
If one misses it for even a single thought-moment, one immediately falls into the karma of Māra.

Shi Xuanzhinhe served under Master Jingci, who was the site where Chan Master Yongming proclaimed the Way. When he first shaved his head, he paid homage at the Yongming Pagoda amidst the overgrown weeds.
In all matters, he followed the master’s legacy; he personally compiled a record of his deeds and selected a new location for the relocation of the master’s pagoda.
In the Zongjing Hall, he subsequently vowed never again to solicit alms, but instead solely practiced the *Lotus Sūtra* Repentance Ritual, steadfastly maintaining his vow.
Those who gathered there were like clouds. Once the construction of the pagoda was completed, he renovated the Zongjing Hall and built three ponds as a pond for releasing living beings;
these were all the original vows of Yongming. When I went to visit Master Yunqi and was about to proceed to Jingci Monastery, the Master attended to the affairs of the Zongjing Hall.

It served as a place for his temporary residence. Upon entering the gate, I paid respects at the stupa of Master Yongming. Observing its exquisite and meticulous craftsmanship, the layout was executed according to the Dharma;
even the finest details were perfectly proportioned. I remained there for ten days, surrounded by a multitude of hundreds and thousands, each person fully satisfied with the joy of the Dharma.
Nothing was neglected, whether internal or external; everything was orderly and well-arranged, managed with effortless ease as if it had not been planned.

I thought to myself: "In my view, your talent is capable of governing the world, and your compassion is sufficient to benefit living beings. It is not merely that you possess a profound mind; you truly embody boundless, wondrous conduct.
Were it not for the power of past vows, such a thing would not be easily achieved. Now that I am departing, I request your guidance as I see you off. Thereupon, I showed him this:
"Among those who are disciples of the Buddha, there are the true and the false; in their practice, there is the conventional and the ultimate; and in their talent, there is the..."

Regarding essence and function, although the mind may vary in its breadth and narrowness and all are equally called "monks," there are differences among them as vast as those between heaven and earth.
Thus, the bodhisattva’s gateways for benefiting sentient beings are manifold. The Buddha rebuked the śrāvakas as being "name-only arhats," rejecting them as not being genuine.
That which the Buddha values most highly is those who protect the life of wisdom in the final age; such individuals are extremely rare.
Living in this world of stubborn strength and turbidity, one has no leisure even to save oneself; how then could one serve the Dharma-gate?

If one lacks the means to provide for one's own body, how can one be expected to cherish and protect sentient beings? Throughout all the Mahāyāna teachings, those who are able to protect the Dharma are called true disciples of the Buddha, for they are capable of fully bearing their family legacy.
The Buddha, fearing that after his parinirvāṇa there would be no one to seek out and uphold the sūtras, [entrusted them to others].
This is difficult. However, the sutras are the Buddha’s Dharma-body and his life of wisdom; they are not merely paper, ink, or written characters.
Furthermore, since the Dharma-body flows through the five realms of existence as sentient beings, one who can protect these sentient beings is thereby protecting the Buddha’s life of wisdom.
Therefore, in the Prajñā teachings on the Bodhisattva path, saving sentient beings is primary, and not dwelling upon the marks of sentient beings is the sublime practice.
This means that although immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings are brought to parinirvāṇa, in reality, there is not a single sentient being who is saved.

This is to realize that the characteristics of sentient beings are empty. Yet, I am the very "sentient being" of sentient beings. Since sentient beings are empty, how could there be a self? Both self and others are empty;
as for the activities in between, who performs them and who receives their results? When both object and self are forgotten, [all is resolved].

In the interim, there is spontaneous stillness. If the three wheels are empty, then the true mark is suchness; it is a single, equal illumination. Bodhi and nirvana are both like illusions and dreams.
How, then, could there be any Buddha-dharma to be taught, any path of Chan to be cultivated, or any myriad practices to be performed?
Therefore, in the assembly of the Lotus Sutra, when praising those who uphold the sutra, it is said: "Lifting a hand or bowing the head, all [attain enlightenment]."
One has already become a Buddha. Thus, by means of the mind of one who has already become a Buddha, one performs all present practices;
therefore, every single practice is a Buddha-practice. There is nothing more sublime than this among the wonders of practice. One who acts in this way is called a true disciple of the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "The object of compassion is sentient beings who suffer. If there were no sentient beings, there would be no bodhi."
Therefore, the Bodhisattva possesses a mind like the great earth, for he bears the burden of sentient beings; he possesses a mind like a bridge, for he ferries sentient beings across.
Vairocana takes Samantabhadra as his body, and Samantabhadra takes sentient beings as his body.
If one takes sentient beings as one's own mind, this constitutes bearing the burden of the Tathāgata. You, sir, should examine my words and verify them against your own mind. If...
When one perceives one's own mind and its fruit accords with the Dharma, then there is no dharma outside of the Dharma; it is like there being no space outside of space.

If there were even a blade of grass, a speck of dust, or a hair that did not entirely return to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), then there would be dharmas outside the mind and a mind outside the dharmas;
the distinction between self and others would remain vivid, and right and wrong would not have been extinguished. Apart from this Dharma-gate, where else could one seek the direction?
From beginning to end, the Buddha never had a single dharma to give to others; the Patriarchs likewise aspired only to save themselves.

If you harbor the view that there is even one dharma, it means your own mind has not yet been saved; if you cannot save yourself, what use is seeking out Buddhas and Patriarchs to become a slave carrying manure for them?
From this point forward, you must keep your eyes wide open and examine yourself closely; do not speak of "Old [Shan]"...
The monk was loquacious.

The Buddha said that one who has realized the profound state of meditation is like a person whose mind is as straight as a string; such a person can enter the Way. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "A straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment."
The Sage also said: "The birth of a person is straightforward. Thus we know that there is no other marvelous place in the Buddha-mind;
it is simply the person of straightforward mind among all sentient beings. Being straightforward means being free from the appearance of deviousness.

As for what is called "straightforward," it is when not even a single speck of dust is established—only then is it called straightforward. For example, how much can a straight bowstring contain? As soon as there is a single thought—
Lack of straightforwardness is precisely an error. If one can maintain straightforwardness in every thought-moment, then in every thought-moment not a single thing will find entry.
Where no thing is established, the fundamental substance manifests of itself. Thus, the Great Master Huineng said: "Constantly see your own faults.
These very words are the essential secret for a patriarch to become a patriarch. What is meant by "faults" here is not a failure in performing specific tasks, but rather—
It is merely the delusion of one’s own mind. Since this mind is fundamentally devoid of a single thing—level, even, and settled—the moment a single thought arises, it becomes a transgression.
If a single thought constitutes a transgression, how much more so for various evil habits that manifest in every thought-moment?

If one does not realize them, how can one avoid transgression? When a student applies their mind, if they do not exert effort upon each and every thought, they will spend their entire life in mere study.
In their study, they are unable to attain true realization because they take deluded thoughts and reflected images as their practice; thus, they go astray to the very end.

When this Chan practitioner first visited me at Mount Jing, I named him Liaowu (Realizing Nothingness), wishing that he would apply his efforts to the principle that "originally there is not a single thing.
As we parted on the boat, I wrote this to encourage him.
To the Chan practitioner Xueling Jun who studies the Way:
First, one must have resolute bone and spirit; second, one must have a vast capacity for understanding; third, one must have a pressing sense of birth and death.

Bone and spirit, as well as capacity for understanding, are matters of one's prior cultivation and innate disposition; however, if the mind of birth and death manifests before you, these three matters will naturally be established.
This is what it means to be fully endowed with the path. As for applying the mind to investigate:

when the ancients taught people how to first apply themselves, they insisted that one must depart from the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*) to study the way beyond both the mundane and the sagely. This statement is known by all students;

yet, when they actually apply their minds, as soon as a single thought arises, they immediately fall into the trap of the intellect and consciousness. How can they ever depart from it? It is because of the habitual tendencies accumulated over many lifetimes.

The vital energy (qi) has consistently made its livelihood within the world of body and mind. It has fallen into the domain of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) and is ensnared by them, unable to transcend or escape.
When one applies oneself to spiritual practice, the manifestation of various strange phenomena is entirely due to this fault.
This requires that one’s capacity for discernment be vast and one’s perspective be transcendent. First, cast aside the body, mind, and the world;
then raise up the original koan as if it were a stake driven into empty space. After a long time, when empty space suddenly shatters, this is the field of vision of a great man.
It is certainly not comparable to the ordinary, misguided Zen of silent illumination. This...
To exert such power, one must possess a piece of adamantine bone; only then can one stand firmly upon one’s heels.

As for those whose habits are soft, warm, weak, and full of the "gruel-and-rice" temperament, how could they dare hope for even a fraction of this? Furthermore, when contemplating the *huatou*, one most fears falling into the trap of subtle and wondrous intellectual views;
this is what is called the "ghost cave of the Black Mountain. As soon as there is even a hair’s breadth of the subtle...

If you harbor wondrous knowledge and insight within your breast, or if you cherish the words and phrases of the ancients without letting them go, you will fall into the heterodox views of external paths.
Within this [state of awakening], not even a speck of dust can adhere; the very point where nothing can adhere is precisely when one gains true power.
One must simply break through the lacquer bucket to its very bottom to be truly real. Furthermore, one must not use the mind to wait for enlightenment.
This is for making the railing-head boards. Zen practitioners, simply apply yourself with effort; on another day, you will personally believe that this old monk does not deceive you.
To Layman Liu:
You have left home for the sake of birth and death. Sitting alone atop a solitary peak for ten years—how truly earnest this is!
It is heard that he was harmed by Māra dozens of times, yet his mind remained unmoved. The assembly all urged him to go elsewhere to avoid it, but in the end, he did not leave.
What kind of power of patience is this? This must mean he has attained great mastery over the fundamental nature of things.
Since he can act thus in a single thought-moment, one should regard the four elements as empty flowers or the moon reflected in water, and view birth and death as a dream or an illusion.
If one truly attains liberation, one will simply sit and pass away.

If one cannot do so, one should remain unmoving for even a single thought-moment, regardless of whether others cut one with a blade or smear one with fragrant incense, or dismember one limb by limb; only when one remains ultimately unmoving for a single thought-moment is this true right view and right practice.
Now, hearing that you wish to die by abstaining from grain is to be seen as being possessed by Māra; you must immediately see through this.

This mindfulness must certainly not be recognized or grasped in such a manner. Not only would it be a pity for oneself to suffer in vain due to the cycle of birth and death, but one must also fear that it might cause others to fall into the net of false views.
I show this to the Chan practitioner Feishi Yu:
in the Dharma-ending age, many students of the Way still value superficial habits and do not reach the ultimate reality.

Consequently, regarding the teachings and path of the Buddha-Dharma, they merely cling to names and terminology without attaining the profound intent. They increase their intellectual views and give rise to great arrogance. This is furthermore due to the Buddha...

The fetters of the Dharma are the root of birth and death. This is truly because, from the very first moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), one does not set foot upon the path beyond birth and death, nor does one know what birth and death actually are.
Believing that they have no concern with oneself, one wanders blindly through the night; thus, the path of correct practice cannot be found.
Furthermore, every word and every phrase of the Buddha’s teaching is a method for transcending birth and death. Yet, how could one have expected that people today—

On the contrary, one falls into error. This is not the fault of the Buddha; the fault lies with the student who lacks right faith and right view, and who has not yet approached a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to have their understanding pointed out and broken through.
The student Fangyu once attended upon the Old Man (Linji Yixuan) beyond the mountain ridges.
Truly simple and unadorned. The Elder traveled east to the regions of Wu and Yue, where he carved a new commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Lotus Sūtra*.

He commissioned Yu to proofread and collate them, and through careful deliberation and refinement, Yu attained the meaning beyond the words of the Elder. Now the Elder has returned to Mount Kuanglu to retire in his old age.
On another day, when you are able to accompany me in the midst of empty leisure and solitude, investigate the matter that transcends [the mundane].
Then, you shall not be hindered by the habitual tendencies of words and letters as cognitive obstacles. The old man departs;
on the peak of Seven Sages Mountain, there is fire from cow dung to bake taro for you—bear this in mind.
He showed Layman Shen of Wujiang that all sentient beings take self-grasping as the root of birth and death. Because there is a self, there are objects.
When objects and the self confront one another, conflict arises. By inviting conflict through the self, all manner of opposition returns; once there is opposition, it becomes [suffering].
It is therein that they are deluded. Thus, the eye is deluded by forms; the ear by sounds; the nose by odors; the tongue by flavors; the body by tangibles;
and the mind by mental phenomena (*dharma*). To be deluded is to be disturbed; to be disturbed is to be disordered; and to be disordered is to lose one's correctness.
Once its correctness is lost, those who are harmed by it will be many. The people of the world are all deluded by it without realizing it;
they are wounded by it without knowing the pain. How utterly foolish they are!
Moreover, they take it as their own resource, and furthermore, they cherish, cling to, and grasp at it—this is the foolishness of the foolish. Only the wise truly understand this.
Since these do not benefit me, I distance myself and avoid them. If one must avoid them, it is better to forget the self.

Truly, if one can forget the self, then even amidst a multitude of enemies, they will be like many arrows shot into the air—there will be nothing upon which to fix them. This is the resolve of those who aspire to the Way.
Let us begin from this point.
I shall show Prince Yong that worldly people have, from birth until death, made their livelihood solely upon the illusory realms of body and mind. They have never...
If one were to once awaken to the mind’s own original face, one would realize that it is due to a lack of such awakening that the root of the illness remains unknown.
Because water and fire oppose one another and the four elements attack each other, this constitutes physical illness; likewise, there is the false conceptualization of grasping at objects.
Attachment and aversion, acceptance and rejection—these are the maladies of the mind. While physical ailments can be treated with medicinal stones and herbs, mental illnesses have no such medicine.

The Buddha is the King of Physicians for the world; in treating the mental maladies of sentient beings, he employs various skillful means, yet ultimately relies solely on awakening to shatter the naturelessness of deluded thoughts as the wondrous medicine that restores life. Those who study must seek peace and happiness.

Regarding this Dharma gate: one must first recognize and break through the notion that the body is not "mine. Simply observe that before the parents were born, where did this flesh-and-blood frame ever exist?
Furthermore, when the four great elements separate, where will this present body be established thereafter?
If one observes in this manner from time to time, after a long period, one will suddenly awaken in a single thought-moment and will no longer be afflicted by this body.
This is the wondrous medicine for treating physical illness. The source of all illnesses arises entirely from the deluded mind;
it is simply necessary to observe moment by moment throughout daily life. Whenever any thought—whether wholesome or unwholesome—arises, that very place is the root of the disease.
Upon discovery, you must apply effort within the present moment of thought. Observe it right where it arises;

see exactly from where it ultimately arises, and who it ultimately is that arises and ceases. Furthermore, when the deluded thought ceases, you must certainly investigate where it ultimately goes to cease.
Pursuing the matter in this way until arising is found to have no place of arising, and ceasing is found to have no place of ceasing—this is called...
When arising and ceasing have no source, the substance of the mind is tranquil and one attains great mastery.
By thus seizing the essential pass, the past and future do not continue; the single thought in the interim stands alone.

At this point of solitary independence, through long-term cultivation until it becomes pure and mature, the diseased root of delusive thoughts is uprooted, and all mental defilements find no place to lodge. This is called...
This is the wondrous medicine for curing the disease of the mind. You, Ziyong, are earnestly intent upon matters directed upward;
however, your error lies in seeking within words and letters, rather than seeking within the ground of your own mind.
Since the delusive thoughts of your own mind are already the root of the disease, to further take the words of others as substantial dharmas is to add yet another layer of obstruction.
From now on, simply and directly perceive and shatter the delusive thoughts of your own mind so that you are no longer driven by them. Merely observe the place where delusive thoughts arise;

they shall certainly not continue. The Buddha said: "If the frantic mind ceases, that cessation is itself Bodhi. This supremely pure and luminous mind is fundamentally not to be obtained from without.
If you apply your mind in this way without regressing, then this very mind present before you is itself great peace and bliss.

This is the Dharma-gate of Liberation. Because the old man requested instruction, [the Master] named it "Fujiao" (Awakening of Blessings), for this awakening constitutes the foremost immeasurable merit. May you exert yourself in it!
He showed that Layman Shen Yuchang was born into a family of the ten wholesome deeds and dwelt in a chamber of wealth and honor; he took Bodhisattvas as his parents,
spiritual friends as his kinsmen, those of common practice and vow as his servants, and the manifestations of the power of compassion as [his attendants].
Though surrounded by children, he stood amidst them like a blue lotus emerging from the water, upright even within the mud.

Having conceived faith, he cultivated various merits; everything accorded with his wishes. Around his residence were lakes and ponds spanning several *li*, filled with fish as numerous as the sands of the lake.
When the Tripitaka Master first requested the scriptures and passed through the Reed Isle (*Luzhou*), the fish in the full ponds, riding upon red light at night, [followed him].
They were all reborn in the heavens. The excellence and vastness of the meritorious conditions they encountered were such as this.

However, they felt remorse for not having practiced the Way with sufficient vigor and requested further instruction from the Elder. The Elder then showed them the way, saying: "This is indeed something to be regretted. Why?
Because external giving is easy, while internal giving is difficult; it is simply that the mind of renunciation is not as easy to relinquish as material objects. Nevertheless,"
This is what men find difficult. Because the roots of emotion from birth and death throughout kalpas have become deep and firm, they are hard to uproot;
unless one arouses a spirit of great courage and resolute determination to seek practice in accordance with the Dharma, it is truly not easy.

If an elder were to look upon it with the correct eye, it would certainly not be difficult. Layman, believe this earnestly: if you can truly contemplate the body as a material object, then the body will easily become light.
If one observes the mind by means of the body, the mind is easily forgotten. If one observes feelings by means of the mind, feelings are easily broken.

If one observes the nature by means of feelings, the nature is easily clarified. If one observes contemplation by means of the nature, then thoughts do not arise. When thoughts do not arise, the Way resides within oneself and not in external things.
If this is so, how does it differ from the fish in the pond that gazes at the reflection of the Dharma and suddenly sheds birth and death?
How extraordinary! Layman, you are able to believe without doubt; thus, you dwell at home yet enter the homeless state, and remain in the world yet are able to transcend it.
Since all wealth, resources, and kinsmen have entered the Samādhi of Illusion, how could any path be difficult to practice?
How difficult it is to uproot the faculty of attachment! Layman, if you wish to enter the Dharma-gate of non-duality in Vaiśālī, you should enter from this point.
Śākyamuni Buddha showed that among the blessings of the world not a single dharma is solid; he spoke of dharmas such as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows, they arise and perish swiftly; all such phenomena of impermanent birth, death, and decay are thus.
Only the seed of Buddha-nature, though existing within the cycle of birth and death, remains indestructible throughout kalpas; this alone is truly firm and solid.
Yet worldly people mistakenly perceive the impermanent as permanent and take the non-firm to be firm; this is called the "perverted view. However...
The root of perversion is the nature of evil; what merit could there be in it?

Now, if one awakens for a single moment within the laws of impermanent birth and death, and resolves to seek the seed of Buddha-nature, then one can discard insubstantial wealth to exchange it for the wealth of the Dharma, and discard the insubstantial body and life to seek the substantial life of wisdom. This—
This is indeed a merit that transcends the world; it is the greatest of merits. Therefore, in accordance with your faith in taking refuge, I shall name you "Fujian" (Firm Merit).
This is intended solely to inspire a firm resolve—what is called "seeking much merit for oneself.
How could a mere empty name be worthy of esteem?
I showed this to Gu Rupi.
Rupi had served the Elder Zibo for the longest time. Formerly, when I was imprisoned during my period of persecution, I sent a letter to Zibo while Rupi stood by my side;
I immediately entrusted the letter to him, instructing him: "Hold this; in the future, we shall surely meet again."

At that time, I took this as my formal pledge. Twenty-two years later, in the year of Bingchen, during the month of the longest day, I traveled from Mount Nanyue to Shuangjing to attend the occasion of Zibo’s entry into his stupa.
Ruyi Ping welcomed me at Songling, leading me to the residence of Yan Shengsheng in Louxiang.
There, while paying my respects and seeking further instruction, he brought forth this scroll; therein I beheld the traces of Zibo’s own hand and [the writings of] my former self.
Epistle. Alas! Within the ocean of the Dharma-nature, the emergence and submergence of sages and ordinary beings are like bubbles upon the great sea;
their arising and ceasing have no source, and their coming and going have no location. Thus, birth and death are but dreams and illusions, utterly unfindable within profound stillness and silence.
Furthermore, since my former death was not a true death, this present life is not a true birth. Neither dying nor being born, there is a single, vast expanse of serene stillness.
Thus we know that Zibo’s death today—how could it truly be death? The traces of his hand remain vivid; his *dharmakāya* abides eternally.

When Zibo looked at me in the past, he saw me as clearly as the hairs on his eyebrows and eyelashes. You now behold Zibo’s heart from those days, its solitary radiance shining forth like the sun and moon.
Since life is not separated by physical form, how much less can it be obstructed by the grave?
"Clear and leisurely indeed! The Buddha said, "To contemplate that which is far distant is as if it were this very day.

Not only I and Zibo, but all ordinary beings and sages alike, are like bubbles upon the great ocean; they are but flashes of lightning in the sky. You, Pingjiao, have long entered the chamber of Zibo.
Regarding this Dharma-gate of ultimate equality, you must surely enter the great ocean for a bath, so that the hundred rivers [shall flow into it]."
This water soaks through every pore of the body. Perhaps the Elder Zibo has not yet broached this point;
therefore, I have specifically pointed it out so that he may gain confidence in this Dharma and attain great benefit from its use.

If this is not yet the case, try looking with a fixed gaze at the time before your parents were born. After a long while, you shall know that there is no difference between seeing me now and not seeing me.
This concerns the past and future limits [of time].
It shows that Yan Zhongxian, a lay practitioner who maintained the Cundī-dhāraṇī,
possessed a thick abundance of the five desires and deep-rooted afflictions that manifested daily, intermingling before him.

It is like boiling water surging and bubbling; how can one attain a single moment of cool clarity? Even if one resolves to practice, it is difficult to find a way to apply oneself to the cultivation of the Way.
Those with clever intelligence who study the scriptures merely acquire some intellectual understanding to serve as material for conversation, which is utterly devoid of practical utility.
They regard the recitation of the Buddha's name as something ordinary and refuse to apply themselves with a "dead heart. Even if they were to do so, they would gain no power, because—
However, while one may recite the Buddha’s name amidst floating thoughts, in reality, the habitual tendencies within the *ālaya-vijñāna* flow on secretly, such that one perceives nothing at all.

Therefore, from the very beginning of reciting the Buddha’s name, not a single thought has ever fallen away. If reciting the Buddha’s name is effective, how could one seek something else as "subtle and wondrous"?

Nowadays, there is a certain class of people who, being fond of loftiness and longing for the extraordinary, hear of the sudden enlightenment of Zen meditation and immediately consider themselves to be of superior capacity.

This is a failure. Do not practice; I fear you will fall into gradualism. Regarding the recorded sayings (jiyuan) of the ancient worthies, you merely memorize a few "catching-the-head" phrases and chatter recklessly, seeking only the convenience of using them as "critical edges" (jifeng). These people are most pitiable.
Looking at it, if one has truly resolved to leave birth and death behind, it would be better to enter the path through the recitation of mantras, for this is the method used first.
Because it arises from a single heart of sincere earnestness, it is easily attained. When Yan Sheng Fochi asked about the essentials of practicing while remaining a layperson, I showed him this.
Those who observe this must by no means understand it through intellectual reasoning; for such reasoning has misled people far too often.
Thus, this Dharma-gate is especially superior even to investigating the "pine tree" or the "dry dung pellet."
The *Sūtra on the Hall Master Lingyan of Jiahe* states:
"The seeds of the Buddha arise from conditions. That is to say, if one wishes to understand the meaning of the Buddha-nature, one should contemplate the causes and conditions of time and season."

Thus we know that the Dharma-realm takes dependent origination as its fundamental principle. When one observes the mundane and supramundane worlds with discerning insight, there is not a single phenomenon that does not arise from causes and conditions.
The ancient monastery of Śūraṅgama was first established during the Tang Dynasty; it has been here for a long time that the Longshui commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra has been expounded.
Because it is situated in the midst of the city’s bustling marketplaces, it has previously been encroached upon by those who use force. Five...
Master Lu of the Terrace received the entrustment of Mount Ling on this land; from birth, he made the protection of the Dharma his heart’s intent.

Chan Master Daguan appeared in response to the times and shared a profound karmic affinity with Master Lu. Upon their first meeting, their minds were in perfect accord, and they immediately discussed restoring the monastery.
However, it was difficult to find one capable of bearing such a responsibility. Master Kaizang, having cast aside his scholar’s robes to leave the household life, relied upon [Master Lu].
Master Da was a入室 (入室) disciple [of the Master]. Hearing that there were discussions regarding the restoration of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*, he took full responsibility for it.
Once the meditation hall was completed, he proposed carving the *Tripitaka* into printed volumes to broaden the circulation of the Dharma.

Furthermore, by imperial grace, he was granted a set of the *Tripitaka*, yet the Great Hall had not yet been finished. Unfortunately, Master Kai withdrew from the project before its completion. Later, Master Weng of Mount Wutai...
In later generations, when Master Cai Huaiting arrived as the Prefectural Governor, the temple was suddenly revitalized.

With the lay practitioner Bao Xinian serving as its leader, the hearts of the people gathered in harmony like an echo responding to a sound. Before a year had passed, the blue-roofed halls stood majestic and the golden images shone brilliantly—how magnificent!
When measured against the initial proposal for its restoration, nearly twenty years had elapsed; such was the power of the timing and conditions.
Because of these conditions, there exists that which is inconceivable. I came to Shuangjing to perform the *pindapāta* (cremation) rites for Master Da;

on my way back, I passed through Lengyan. Observing its vast scale and grandeur, it is truly a pure land amidst the mundane world; its meditation hall is so refined and pure that it is truly a Brahma palace within the illusory sea.
Upon meeting the abbot, Master Lin, I found him upright, refined, and elegant, possessing great patience.
Compassionate and harmonious, he may truly be called a leader of the monastic community (*saṃgha*). I have often harbored a secret sorrow for this world of five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*):
even Bodhisattvas, to whom the Buddha’s work was entrusted, dare not venture into it to benefit sentient beings, let alone ordinary people of the mundane stage.
Because Master Lin is so upright and elegant, all who see him cannot help but revere him; because Master Lin is so compassionate and patient, all who return to him...
I am not pleased that you have used a mind of universal reverence and joy to accomplish a task that is neither yet perfected nor fully realized.
It is like sailing with the wind at one's back and the sails unfurled across calm waters; what difficulty could there be in reaching the other shore?
I say that the lute strings of the lion were about to fall silent, yet fortunately you have succeeded them—this too is a matter of karmic affinity. It rests solely upon your steadfast endurance.
By the power of your vow to uproot [delusion], you maintain this dojo that is difficult to achieve and not easily realized, intending it to become a Buddha-activity that is infinite and imperishable.
The circulation of the Great Dharma is precisely the pervasion of your own mental radiance.
Furthermore, why do you not cherish this body of flesh and blood as the Triple Gem does?
The Chan practitioner Langyai Yao of Jinsha Dongchan Temple was shown [this place].
It was originally established by the Grand Historian Wang Nianxi of Dongchan Temple and entrusted to Langyai Yao to oversee.
Recently, having heard that the Elder was traveling to Shuangjing, he specifically sent his successor, Master Nanrong, to request the scriptures.
He established a summer retreat (*varṣā*) with the intention of using it as a place of rest for the Elder Forest. On the day after the full moon in the ninth month, the Elder arrived;

he saw that the assembly was solemn and orderly, pure and reverent, and that they were exclusively devoted to the practice of reciting the Lotus Sūtra from memory. This had been their commitment for seven years.
More than thirty people achieved mastery in recitation; this was a rare occurrence indeed. Not long after, he departed for Mount Jing.

When his affairs there were concluded and he was about to return to Mount Kuanglu, bidding farewell to the world with a long bow, the Duke earnestly entreated the Elder to remain, his resolve not yet satisfied.
As they parted, the Elder bestowed this upon him as a teaching, saying: "Within the nature of the Dharma-realm, how could there be any marks of coming or going? This is wisdom."

The eyes have not yet opened, and thus the sensory objects remain separated from the mind. The perception of separation and union ceases within the heart, while the conditions of gathering and dispersal bind one's thoughts.
Were it not for one who realizes that the three periods of time do not shift and that the ten directions are without interval, it would not be easy to reach the realm of non-duality.
Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* takes the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its central tenet; the Prabhūtaratna of the past still exists, and Śākyamuni of the present is no different.
Extinction is eternally abiding within one mind, never obscured throughout kalpas. The causal conditions of Prince Mahābhijñājñāna continue unbroken until this very day;
the karmic connection of the prediction by Dīpaṃkara is naturally manifested through realization. Viewed from this perspective, how could there be even the slightest trace of change or error?
Observe, for instance, how a single ray of light from the white tuft of hair illuminates all things without obstruction—the beginning and end, the causes and effects of all sages and ordinary beings.
It is manifest before one's eyes: the coming and going of the old man is like the bright moon over the long river; though it travels east and west, the moon itself remains serene.
If even a single thought is pure and true, then the radiance of the mind will interpenetrate and shine through.

Do not, therefore, allow worldly conventions and common sentiments to become a habitual view of birth and death. I pray that you, by means of the Lotus Samādhi, will reach the ultimate realization of the future, and thus—
The old man’s eyebrows are knitted together; we shall return together to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). For kalpas we have relied upon one another, remaining inseparable for all eternity.
Why, then, do you concern yourself so much with this illusory and empty body—a mere reflection of the moon in water or an image in a mirror—giving rise to such deluded thoughts of self and other?
Old man, go forth! May you exert yourself!

He showed the King that the two types of Buddha-nature—sacred and profound, original and deep—exist within humans, just as water exists on high ground: where there is one who digs and excavates, there is none from whom it cannot be obtained.
This is because the roots of affliction in us are deep and the sentiments of love and hatred are firm; they are no less than the soil of a high plateau. If one can exert effort...
Delving deeply to seek [the truth], one must persevere in the application of effort. The endeavor lies in uprooting the afflictions (*kleśa*) and tearing asunder the net of attachment and aversion.
Thus, the spring of the *dharmatā* will flow forth in an inexhaustible stream, irrigating the spiritual roots and nourishing the sprouts of wisdom.

Not only can the fruit of the Path be anticipated, but the hidden currents shall also be deepened to moisten the parched and withered, universally benefiting both humans and devas as they all return to the ocean of Dharma.
"A single drop shares the same essence as the vast Bohai Sea; how could this be sought from without?
The brothers Shengchong Yuanshen have long entered the chamber of Zibo. Now that the sage has passed away, I fear that the clear flow of their nature-water might encounter obstructions.
I, the Old Man, have just arrived to unblock it; now the source has been opened, and from this point forward, it shall never again run dry."
Do not take the dry earth of afflictions and cast it in to turbidify [the water].

I show you, Sun Xin, that the root and trunk of birth-and-death ignorance reside solely in the present moment of thought. It is like a person traveling throughout the ten directions for their entire life.
Those who exert their strength without ceasing may believe they have traversed thousands of miles of road, yet they do not realize they have not moved even a single step from their own heels.

Thus one knows that the wandering through deluded thoughts across kalpas and the revolving cycle of birth and death have, in truth, never departed from the single thought-moment of the person themselves.
If you can apply effort at the very point where each thought arises within your daily activities—within seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—then [liberation is attained].
If you see through this—that the place of birth is itself unborn—then the emotional roots of birth and death throughout kalpas will be severed instantly and completely.
In truth, this does not rely on any external power. The Buddha said, "As long as the wild mind does not cease, once it ceases, that is Bodhi. How could these words be false?
Strive with all your might to investigate the phrase "before the parents were born" which the Old Man has pointed out; one day you shall surely attain self-confidence.
It was the right time.

To show this, Jiang Yanghui—Jiang Sheng—was a youth of brilliant talent whose spirit and character were extraordinary; it was not that his spiritual roots had been planted long ago, nor that the seeds of *prajñā* were deeply sown within him.

"Excellent! It is not easy to find such a fine character. When I was young, I once met the Great Master Zibo, who immediately named me Xinguang (Light of Faith), intending that it signified the light of *prajñā* inherent in one's nature.
Recently, while attending to the Elder for instruction, he bestowed upon me the courtesy name Yanghui (Nurturing Obscurity).
In our daily lives, all seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are the radiant manifestation of the light of wisdom; it is only that they are obscured by ignorance."
Obscured, it transforms into emotional consciousness; thus, it is dark and does not manifest.

If one can have confidence that the true light is inherently present, remaining unclouded by the phenomena before one, then within the darkness of the critical juncture of love and hatred, the numinous light shines alone, unobscured by the roots of emotion.
This is to nurture [the light] amidst obscurity; thereby, the essence of light becomes ever more luminous, and the true source—

It can be restored. By employing its light, one avoids the calamities that afflict the body. If Master Jiang embodies this principle, then vast and brilliant radiance will manifest amidst his every movement and action.
The establishment of merit and fame will all become enduring and magnificent achievements;
how could he allow himself to remain in darkness and lack faith? It is simply that when the banner of self-conceit is toppled, the light will reveal itself spontaneously.
I address the assembly:
Lately, there are many young people from all quarters who are determined to practice Zen meditation. Yet when they meet me, they are all nothing but deluded people;
they take the stubborn maintenance of delusive thoughts as their vow, they take the nurturing of laziness as their diligent effort, and they take the growth of arrogance as their path.

They are solitary and aloof. They take the flapping of lips and tongue as their "critical pivot" (*jīfēng*). They regard the clinging to ignorance as the "higher path. They consider turning their backs on the Buddhas and Patriarchs to be self-evident correctness.
They rely on their own cleverness as "wondrous enlightenment. Consequently, whenever they arrive at a monastic community (*sōnglín*), their physical actions cannot integrate with the assembly;
their speech and mind cannot harmonize with the assembly. They indulge their passions and follow their whims, failing to cultivate the three karmas. They treat ritual recitation as...
They are base and inferior; they treat the gateways of practice as menial labor, regard the Buddha-dharma as an enemy, and take conventional clichés for their own realization.
Even if there are those who can look at the *huatou* and apply themselves to the work, they first seek awakening within the mind.

Consequently, before their meditation cushions have even been stabilized and before their drowsiness has been dispelled, they have not yet seen anything even in their dreams. Yet, they already harbor self-importance and arrogance, rushing off to visit so-called "good teachers."

Consciousness. To speak of the subtle and speak of the wondrous, to present one's awakening and present one's understanding, yet then take a few words that have no foundation and speak recklessly in search of a seal of approval—if you are one with the karmic affinity, you will meet an enlightened spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who will immediately shatter your conceptual nest;

this may be called great good fortune. If, however, it is unfortunate, you will run into a blind, ignorant Chan practitioner who, with a single stamp of the "winter melon seal," will deliver you straight to your doom.
They have entered the treacherous pits of external paths and fallen for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, with no time of emergence in sight.
Are they not truly objects of pity? These deluded ones have lost the true cause for themselves and have further encountered the poison of heterodoxy;
even if they were to meet Linji or Deshan, they would still be unable to resolve their delusive attachments. Are they not most pitiable?
The decline of the Chan school has reached this point. If one observes the ancients of old with discernment, they were certainly not like this.
Just look at Baizhang serving Mazu; whenever he was working in the fields, such as when planting his spade, that became the occasion for the "wild ducks" kōan.
This was precisely where he engaged in the genuine work of verification. For this reason, there is the saying: "If for one day you do not work, for one day you shall not eat."
The admonition against eating [without purpose]: Yangqi served Ciming for over twenty years. He personally attended to the gates of practice and performed hundreds of thousands of tasks with toil;
he never shied from labor. Thus, he attained a brilliance so vast that it illuminates both the present and the past.
Consider the case of Lanrong carrying rice and Huangmei at the rice-mortar room; observing the ancients, there was not one who did not emerge from amidst hardship and toil.
Come! Why is it that these youths of today, having barely entered the monastic groves, immediately take "investigating Zen" (chanzhen) as the ultimate goal?
They seek only to sit upright and enjoy a state of ready-made attainment; with hands tucked in their sleeves, they do not unfold their efforts, nor do they pluck even a single blade of grass.

Such is their meager merit, utterly devoid of a sense of shame. Even if they possess wondrous insights, they result only in solitary melodies, completely lacking the offerings of devas and humans—let alone [the offerings of] men.
Are you one who practices in truth, or one who squanders the offerings of the faithful and willingly falls into the depths of saṃsāra?

If you are truly a seeker of liberation from birth and death, you should contemplate how our Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, throughout the trichiliocosm, did not leave even a space the size of a mustard seed where he did not sacrifice his head, eyes, marrow, and brain in pursuit of Bodhi. Contemplating in this way, you should resolve to do the same.
With valor, he relinquishes his single, wretched life and offers this stinking skeleton as alms to the ten directions.

He made offerings to the great assembly. Regarding all gates of practice, he maintained them with diligent effort; what was difficult to perform, he performed; what was difficult to endure, he endured.
If, within the daily activities of the six sense faculties, one can penetrate through each and every instance, then one attains liberation in every dharma.
As the ancients said: "Those who enter through conditions correspond most swiftly. If one applies the mind in this manner without changing for thirty years, even if one does not attain awakening—
The Way. To emerge once more from it is surely to be a man who stands firm with his head touching heaven. The Old Man used this to instruct him and announced it to all his fellow practitioners.
