Revised by the Disciple from Lingnan, Liu Qixiang,
based on the Dharma Words shown to Chan Attendant Zhigui of the Jingzong Monastery.

Gui-zong was the site where ancient venerable masters expounded the Dharma. Master Da-guan initiated the project to restore it, and subsequently, Master Zan exerted his entire being and strength until the original properties were finally returned.
Now, more than twenty years have passed since Master Zan passed away; his disciple Xiu-ci has taken up the responsibility.
In the summer of the Bingchen year, I came to pay homage at the Golden Wheel Śarīra Stūpa and beheld the monastery, its scale and design preeminent among those in Kuang-jong.

Regarding the excellence of this mountain, I reflected that one truly capable of serving as a counselor and assistant was indeed difficult to find. Among the assembly, I observed a Zen practitioner who was wise, whose countenance was refined and prominent, and who possessed a striking spirit of integrity.
Consequently, I entrusted him to the administrators and appointed him as the Chief Administrator (Jansae). This Zen practitioner excelled in secret practice.

Whenever there were matters that the multitude had failed to attend to throughout the day, he would examine what required attention and would surely remain awake all night, personally managing each detail.
When dawn broke, there was nothing that was not settled. I sighed and lamented, saying:
Is this not so? I have often seen young monks in the monasteries who generally lack a sense of shame and remorse;
they indulge solely in idleness, fail to restrain their three karmas of body, speech, and mind, and do not cultivate ritual prostrations or recitations.

They even sleep soundly during the day—how could they possibly remain awake all night through, personally undertaking the toil to attend to the affairs of the great assembly? Formerly, among the Buddha’s twelve hundred disciples, only Rāhula was singled out for praise.
Hou was foremost in secret conduct; therefore, he became the Buddha’s eldest son.

The patriarchs of the preceding generations in this land—exemplified by Baizhang’s maxim that "one day without work is one day without food"—thereby established a thousand-year-old archetype for the monastic community.
Yongming practiced one hundred and eight daily observances; thus, his image is enshrined and venerated within the Hall of King Yama. The Buddha spoke of the three thousand great...
In a thousandfold world-system, there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed that is not a place where a bodhisattva has sacrificed their body and life for the sake of sentient beings;

thus they are moved to become the God among Gods. It is known from this that from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity down to the present, there are none who have not established the merit of the worldly field of blessings through the gate of practice.
A Chan practitioner can, with this very mind, relinquish body and life to shoulder the burden of the monastic community.
The forest is precisely the establishment of the Triple Gem. The permanence of the Triple Gem is the continuation of the Buddha’s life of wisdom.
That this life of wisdom remains unbroken is the repayment of the Buddha’s profound kindness. To recognize kindness and repay it is to be a filial son to one’s compassionate father.

Having undertaken such conduct and vows, throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, contemplate with focused mindfulness: from the beginningless cycle of birth and death, I— (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
Come! Since beginningless time, you have discarded bodies whose bones would equal Mount Sumeru, and you have drunk as much mother’s milk as the waters of the four oceans.

Thus, discarding one body to take up another, you have performed only karma that leads to the suffering of birth and death. When, for even a single day, have you used this life and body to cultivate supramundane practices?
If you had indeed done so, my son, you certainly would not now remain in the state of an ordinary person as you are. Now...

Fortunately, having obtained this body, you have resolved to cultivate that which is difficult to attain. If you devote your entire life and exhaust your very being without abandoning your fundamental practice, then in a single lifetime you will surpass the efforts of a hundred or a thousand lifetimes.
Only by doing so can it be said that your birth has not been in vain.
From this point forward, O practitioner of Zen, exert even greater diligence; at all times, simply take up the koan of Zhaozhou’s "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? and internalize it.
Within your breast, go directly to the place where you practice and investigate with every thought. Ultimately, why does he say "no"?
One day, when you strike it and rub it away, the knot of doubt will burst asunder in a single moment. Your former cycle of birth and death will be instantly brought to an end.

This may be called the dual adornment of merit and wisdom accomplished in a single lifetime. As the ancients said: "When you move the flowers, the butterflies arrive; when you buy the stone, you gain more clouds."
The first thirty-six ancestral masters are all together upon the eyebrows of this practitioner, turning the Great Dharma Wheel.

To the practitioner Nian, who belongs to our own school, I show that as a disciple of the Buddha, one cultivates the supramundane Dharma through two kinds of sublime practices: self-benefit and benefiting others. As for benefiting others:
Cultivating merit is called benefiting oneself; cultivating wisdom is called benefiting others.

When a Bodhisattva resolves their mind and diligently seeks unexcelled bodhi, although they know that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is empty and quiescent, they do not abandon conditioned activities (*saṃskṛta-saṃskāra*). Knowing that the nature of phenomena is empty is called self-benefit;
not abandoning conditioned activities is called benefiting others. Among the Buddhas and patriarchs of the past, there has never been one who did not proceed by means of these two practices.
One who attains this is one who has transcended birth and death. For this reason, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni diligently practiced difficult and painful austerities throughout successive kalpas.
Since the beginningless vast kalpas, we have emerged and submerged in the ocean of birth and death, discarding and assuming bodies in an inconceivable manner;
all of this has been a life lived in vain and a death met in delusion. What single hair’s breadth of genuine practice has there been? If there were such genuine practice, then...
"Truly, this present life is not like that former one. This refers to the head and face. Turn the light inward and reflect; contemplate with urgency: is it not a tragedy?
Now, by virtue of past affinities, you practitioners have fortunately been able to leave the secular world at an early age and forever depart from the sea of suffering.

Furthermore, you have found a place of peaceful dwelling in a famous mountain—a site where the patriarchs preached the Dharma and where the supreme path was realized. This is an affinity difficult to encounter in ten thousand kalpas; it is precisely [like] hunger...
To encounter the King’s provisions and to meet a Physician-King when ill is itself a cause for immeasurable celebration.
To exhaust this present life and body, sacrificing one lifetime to cultivate such merit, is already superior to passing a hundred kalpas or a thousand lifetimes in vain and without benefit.
You practitioners of Zen should believe the words of this old man; from this day forward, generate a firm and non-retrogressive resolve, and maintain a courageous and steadfast spirit.

This is the resolve. Exerting all one’s physical strength, weighing one’s own talents, and cultivating a heart of sincere commitment, one should follow conditions and fulfill one’s vows with patience and endurance—enduring hardship and labor.
Thus, accomplishing even a single merit in a single day surpasses a lifetime spent in vain.
A practitioner may say of themselves that their body is weak and their spirit exhausted, unable to undertake such tasks; yet the ancients valued...
It depends on the strength of one's mental power and the greatness of one's vow; it does not depend on whether physical strength is robust or weak.

Although you currently have a slight ailment that does not constitute great suffering, if you were to create evil karma and fall into the three miserable realms, you would not be able to seek the benefits of a field of merit with this body and mind of minor illness and minor affliction even if you sought them today. The Buddha instructs sentient beings to contemplate the earth.
The suffering of the hells has prompted me to resolve upon Bodhicitta; this is precisely the day to raise the banner of diligent effort (*vīrya*).

As the ancient masters said: "It would be better to die with the Dharma than to live without it. Even if one must sacrifice this body and life to perform such sublime practices, they still serve as a vessel of Prajñā to reach the other shore.
If one fails to exert oneself and strengthen one's resolve, it can be said that one has lived this life in vain. Now that we have arrived...
To return empty-handed from a mountain of treasures—how regrettable! If you can settle the mind in non-action, then the mind becomes empty.
When the mind is empty, the spirit does not exhaust; when the spirit does not exhaust, the body does not weary.

This is what is called the wondrous practice of non-action. Encountering conditions, one immediately realizes the source; thus, one will certainly not be turned by daily activities. In every instance, one achieves the great gate of liberation.
Indeed, you should contemplate this carefully.
To General Lu (personal name Shi-xian, style name Zhen-hu):

the General is a scion of the lineage of Hao-liang; by nature he is heroic and outstanding, and the capacity for the mechanism of killing was surely bestowed upon him by Heaven. In his middle years...
Knowing he was heading toward the Way, [Zhaozhou] entered the room of Master Zhou. The Master took up the words of an ancient, "I urge you to recognize the true host," and showed them to him.
The Elder retired to seclusion on Mount Kuang. [Zhaozhou] went to visit the Elder at the foot of Mount Jilun and, realizing his own karmic burden from killing had been too heavy, requested to repent.
The Elder rejoiced in his straightforward nature and lack of pretense; he was indeed a man of ancient heroism.
They are those who possess noble loyalty and righteous courage. However, throughout the ages, many have been endowed with this natural disposition, yet they have all misapplied their minds;

thus, they have taken the seeds of Buddhahood and transformed them into the instruments of suffering in hell. The Buddha-nature is non-dual; there is not even a hair’s breadth of separation between sentient beings and Buddhas.
Sentient beings who realize their nature are Buddhas; Buddhas who do not realize their nature are sentient beings. It is like [the water of] purity...
Cold water: when offered to the Buddha, it is pure; when used to wash away filth, it is turbid.

Thus, the compassion of the Buddha is precisely the mechanism of killing for sentient beings. An ancient worthy said: "To protect life, one must employ killing; only when killing is exhausted does one dwell in peace. He also said:
"The Sanskrit term *arhat* translates here as 'slayer of thieves. A sutra states: "[He has conquered] the demon of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-māra*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*)."
The Māra of Death. He fought against the Māra of Death and achieved great merit; he extinguished the three poisons, emerged from the three realms, and shattered the net of Māra.
At that time, the Tathāgata was filled with great joy. This Elder Śākyamuni is the model for encouraging people to kill.
Because the Buddha was able to "kill" in this manner, he is titled the Great Hero (Mahāvīra). World-Honored One, worldly people are ignorant and possess only brute strength.
The Buddha-nature is fierce; yet instead of slaying its own thief, one uses it to kill others.

From kalpa to kalpa and birth to birth, one repays this with the sufferings of hell, yet considers oneself to have achieved great merit. Is this not the height of folly and delusion—to employ one’s Buddha-nature in such a perverted manner?
As the saying goes: "When one general achieves his success, ten thousand bones lie parched. Since antiquity, there has been no sin greater than this.

This is worse than killing living beings. To take the killing of humans as one's merit, or to kill for food and meat, indulging the mouth and belly to satisfy one’s own ignorance—such people are equal to the foolish.
General, you are able to turn your mind toward the higher path and seek great blessings for yourself.

From this day forward, use the very courage you employ in killing to slay your own desires. The Buddha said that greed, desire, and anger are worse than hateful enemies; you are able to [subdue them] yourself.
To sever it is to be a slayer of thieves; to be able to destroy the afflictions and emerge from the suffering of birth and death is to be a Great Hero.
To seek the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood directly by means of this is the great reward.

Such are the benefits of this slaying, yet to abandon it oneself and fail to plan for it—can this be called wisdom? Nevertheless, while killing others is easy, killing oneself is difficult; hence it is said: "To go forth..."
"This is the great task of a householder; it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. Elder, my entanglements have come to this.
This is what is called the compassion of the gift of Dharma. If you, General, believe in this, that is true repentance."
Shi Hui Cheng was the Head Seat (Shouzuo).

In his middle years, he abandoned his wife and son to leave the household life. He had studied under both the two great masters Daguan and Lianchi, and even spent time in seclusion at Mount Nanyue and Hudedong.
When the Old Man (Yunqi Zhuhong) was about to settle his residence at Mount Nanyue, Hui Cheng broke through the retreat enclosure to meet him.

He welcomed him and subsequently attended to his needs, providing handkerchiefs and shoes. One day, he performed a prostration and said: "I am fortunate to have encountered the final dharma as a disciple of the Buddha.

My resolve is to transcend birth and death. I have personally seen the three great masters appearing in this world of five turbidities to protect the Dharma-gate, practicing what is difficult to practice, enduring what is difficult to endure, and taming those who are difficult to tame.
Whenever I encounter the teachings within the Tathāgata’s dispensation regarding the methods for instructing bodhisattvas..."

"I had thought these were but empty words; now that I have personally received the conduct and exemplary models of the three great masters, I can from this moment forth rely upon them for as long as my life lasts.
It would truly be difficult to abandon this and seek another source of refuge. Thereupon, he painted the portraits of the three great masters.
"I shall wear and uphold this throughout my life. Furthermore, from birth to birth and age to age, I shall hold fast to this wheel of vows.
Whether coming and going among gods and humans or circulating through the six realms of existence, I shall never grow weary or tired. I beg the Master to bear witness for me.
The old man heard this and smiled, saying, "This is indeed your profound inner resolve and original vow. Although it is so, it still does not yet probe the root. Please try to observe."
Now, our original teacher, the Venerable Master, is Vairocana. His Dharma-body is no body;
it is formed through the practices of the three great bodhisattvas—Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and Samantabhadra. Mañjuśrī is wisdom, Avalokiteśvara is compassion, and Samantabhadra is conduct.
If these three are abandoned, the Dharma-body would be desolate and have no basis for manifestation. Thus, the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is like...
Regarding his wisdom, it penetrates the principles and phenomena of the Dharma-realm, as well as cause and effect;

even down to blades of grass, dust, and a single hair, there is nothing whose source and bottom he does not exhaustively fathom. He thoroughly penetrates the roots and origins of every thought and mental state within the entire realm of sentient beings.
Regarding his compassion, he regards all sentient beings as his own body; for all the hunger, cold, suffering, and illness of sentient beings—
From physical pain and itching, up to the intense sufferings of the three miserable realms, the Bodhisattva accepts them all with his entire body as one.
Therefore, he is able not to abandon even a single sentient being. If one were to describe his conduct, it would exhaust the entirety of empty space and penetrate the Dharma-realm;

there is not a single blade of grass, speck of dust, or hair’s breadth that is not a place where the Bodhisattva has sacrificed his body and life. Thus, each of the ten vows of Samantabhadra speaks of "empty space."
The realm of space is inexhaustible; the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible; the karma of sentient beings is inexhaustible; and the afflictions of sentient beings are inexhaustible.
My practice and vows are likewise without end. Therefore, the Original Teacher Vairocana, by means of these three dharmas, accomplishes a single body.
If even a single dharma is lacking, the Dharmakāya is not perfected; if there is even one sentient being who is not oneself, then the Dharmakāya is not all-pervasive.
Even down to a speck of dust, a hair, or a blade of grass—if there is anything that is not thoroughly penetrated, then ignorance is not yet exhausted.
If one’s conduct and vows were to end at the very limit of space, then the Dharmakāya would be subject to annihilation. Nevertheless, within the nature of the Dharmadhātu, one contemplates...
These three are like the three eyes of Śiva: they are one and yet three, neither three nor one.
Within the ocean of quiescent extinction, they are merely like bubbles appearing and vanishing.

If there were a truly eminent and immeasurable Great Being who could walk upon the crown of Vairocana’s head and look back at these three types of practitioners, it would be much like calling a servant by the name of "Master. For such a person, these [distinctions] are...
If one were to compare the conduct of such a person to that of the three great bodhisattvas, it would not even be like that of a slave or a servant;

how could such a person ever exhaust the measure of the Buddha’s Dharma-body? If one can, from this point on, give rise to a firm and resolute mind, sacrifice body and life, and establish the Triple Gem, then every act—no matter how slight—that benefits the Dharma-gate or assists sentient beings is the virtue of the entire substance of the Dharma-realm.

Its application is such that, just as one atom pervades all atoms, or as a single hair is merged into many hairs, so too from this life until the furthest reaches of the future, throughout kalpa after kalpa and birth after birth, never shall this mind decline;
it shall endure until the realm of space itself is exhausted, as in the vow of Samantabhadra.
Yet their practices and vows are inexhaustible. Throughout every birth and life, whether eating, resting, rising, or moving;

walking, standing, sitting, or reclining—they never depart from outside a single pore of their original teacher. These three great elders, within the ocean of the Dharma-nature, emerge and submerge together;
they do not exit the illusory samādhi. Adapting to circumstances as they perform, they carry their staffs with them, preaching the illusory Dharma to awaken the illusory multitudes.
This is indeed so. How could such a person suffice to be a teacher? It would be appropriate for them not to limit their minds and thus narrow themselves from the realm of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya.

In the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the Buddha addressed the practitioners of dhyāna who possess self-awakened wisdom, saying: "O bhikṣus, every morning at dawn, you should rub your own heads. These words are most intimate and profound.
The old man reflected on this repeatedly: "Our Buddha’s compassion penetrates to the very marrow of my bones.

He often spoke of how monks in the age of the Dharma’s decline would receive many provisions, being provided with the four requisites during the summer retreat; each of them considered these things as their rightful due."
Furthermore, they do not consider who they are, from where things come, or for what purpose they are received;

thus, those who recognize kindness are rare, and those who repay it are few—indeed, not even one has ever rubbed their head. If only they would turn their light back upon themselves and rub their own heads.
Then, startled by this, he thought to himself: "Why have I shaved my hair and beard, and why do I not associate with worldly people?
If I truly know that my form differs from the mundane, then I shall not dare to draw near to the mundane, nor dare to enter the mundane, nor dare to think of the mundane.
Thus, he delighted in the practice of seclusion; without waiting for the instruction of a teacher, he spontaneously gave rise to courageous effort.

Having entered the mountains, one fears only that they are not deep enough. How could one endure mixing with the common folk of the marketplace, letting the body and mind drift aimlessly, acting as a person without shame and performing useless deeds?
A practitioner of self-awakening through Chan came from the human world to Mount Kuang to pay respects to the Elder.
He vowed to wither his heart while dwelling in the mountains to cultivate world-transcending practices. The Elder thereupon instructed him in the dual cultivation of merit and wisdom.
The practice of wisdom lies in contemplating the mind; the practice of merit lies in the myriad deeds. Contemplating the mind, nothing surpasses the recitation of the Buddha’s name;
among the myriad deeds, nothing precedes making offerings. These two are the universal retention (*dhāraṇī*).

All that we do in our daily lives—every arising thought and every movement of the mind—is but delusive conceptualization, which serves as the root of birth and death and thus invites bitter fruits. Now, by means of this delusion...
If one transforms the mind of conceptualization into mindfulness of the Buddha, then every thought-moment becomes a cause for the Pure Land; this is the fruit of bliss.

If mindfulness of the Buddha continues without interruption from thought to thought, delusive thoughts will be extinguished, the light of the mind will be revealed, and wisdom will manifest before one, whereby the Buddha-dharmakāya is realized.
Yet, the reason sentient beings are impoverished and lack merit and wisdom is that, throughout birth after birth across successive lifetimes, they have never...
To offer worship to the Triple Gem for a single thought-moment in order to seek merit and virtue is already for the sake of this body of suffering within birth and death.
Yet, moment by moment, one greedily seeks the pleasures of the five desires, thereby nourishing the very root of suffering.

Now, turning that mind which seeks only for oneself toward the worship of the Triple Gem, one uses this limited body and life to offer worship to the ten directions according to one's heart and capacity—even with a single incense offering.
A single flower, a grain of rice, or a stalk of vegetable is like a drop of water entering the vast ocean;

a single speck of dust falling upon the great earth—though the sea may dry up and the earth reach its end, the merit thereof is inexhaustible. Thus, it evokes the fruition of Buddhahood and the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha) Adornment as one’s own future ground of enjoyment.
Were one to abandon this, there would be no sublime practice for attaining Buddhahood. If a practitioner feels weary...
"Disgusted! You should rub your own head; then you will spontaneously give rise to immeasurable valor.
To Zen practitioner Longhua Tai, I said:
"In the past, when I was begging for alms in Chang'an, I passed beneath a Dragon Flower tree. My host there, Master Ruian, recognized me."

I was greatly delighted. It seemed as though there were many causes for our mutual affinity. When I observed those dwelling within the city of Rājagṛha, they were for the most part superficial and habituated to worldly ways;
yet the Master alone was solitary, firm, and pure in character. He never affected his speech or countenance toward others, and I knew in my heart that he was no man of the mundane dust.
Thus, we became inseparable friends, coming and going from one another’s presence repeatedly. Among his disciples, there were likewise none who did not [share this sentiment].
Because he was my kinsman, there was no distance between us. When the Master passed away, his grandson, Master Tan, looked upon me as he had looked upon the Master.
When I was exiled to the regions beyond the passes, I felt ashamed that throughout my life I had ultimately been unable to repay his kindness.

Recently, when I emerged from the passes at Mount Nanyue, my Dharma-descendant, the monk Tai, came from afar to inquire after me. Upon seeing him, I could not help but feel a piercing pain in my five viscera. In the past...
The voice and appearance of this master remained vividly before my eyes. When I reached Shuangjing, I fully understood the circumstances surrounding the Great Master;
the Zen practitioners attended upon him, and subsequently, when I returned to Mount Kuang, I brought these Zen practitioners along with me back there.
I keep in mind the virtue of your ancestors and hope to help you, a practitioner of Zen, accomplish your work for transcending the world; this is my way of repaying the kindness of the land.
After residing there for a year, due to the labor of clearing the wilderness, my body and mind had not yet found rest. Recently, I have been instructing you, a Zen practitioner.
Only when the initial resolve is awakened does one truly begin to move toward the goal. My father sent a letter summoning him, but due to other circumstances, he could not comply;

I made a concerted effort to keep him, yet it was impossible. As the practitioner was about to depart, he requested further instruction, whereupon I showed him this: "I am a member of the monastic order."

First, one must urgently address the matters of primary importance and briefly set aside those of minor significance. What is meant by "great"? It is birth and death. What is meant by "small"? It is worldly conditions.
As the ancient masters said: "Setting aside the true great matter of birth and death, everything else is merely a subject for discussion.
This is because sentient beings have been submerged in the sea of suffering and drowned in worldly conditions from the accumulation of kalpas until this very day.
I have never, even for a single thought-moment, turned back to reflect. Now, fortunately, I am a disciple of the Buddha;

I wear the *kāṣāya* upon my body and have encountered spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), possessing the conditions for entering the Way. Yet, I do not renounce worldly attachments, nor do I apply myself with a diligent mind to investigate the matter within my own person.
I fear deeply that you may miss this present life; even if you emerge from it, I do not know if you will be able to have all conditions as complete as they are today.
You, Zen practitioner, now dare not disobey your father’s command; though you must go, you should regard the thought of life and death as urgent.
Do not lose the opportunity to cultivate the Way. Once your affairs are concluded, return immediately. I, the old man, hope for your well-being.
Even if I am buried alive in a desolate mountain, as long as my remaining breath lasts for a single day, I shall have the merit of refining the Great Matter with you, my fellow practitioner.
I, the old man, shall take the end of my life as the deadline; you, my fellow practitioner, shall serve me with a deathly resolve.

Should you but allow the light of that one thought-moment of true humanity to shine forth, not only will you, my fellow practitioner, bring an end to the cycle of birth and death accumulated over kalpas.
This is a great matter; it is also the way for an old man to repay the land of his ancestors and not fail the karmic conditions of this world.
You who practice Zen, depart now; do not linger long in a foreign land, lest you further increase the burdens of birth and death.
To the Zen practitioner Cuilin, [I say]:
The Buddhas and Patriarchs teach people that only a true mind and actual practice constitute the essential means for transcending birth and death.
When the mind is true, then in all movements, speech, and conduct, there is not a single act that is not true. When practice is real, then in all that one says and does, [there is no discrepancy].
There is not a single practice that is not real; therefore, true reality is like a fine seed. All other activities and various established practices are the conditions for its growth.
For this reason, from the sprouting of the shoot and the development of the trunk, to the blossoming of flowers and the ripening of fruit, it is ultimately not in vain.
Thus, the Buddha taught that generating the mind of awakening and engaging in practice is like sowing seeds, and the attainment of Bodhi is considered the final fruition.
"Result. "Result" means reality (*satya*). This is because from beginning to end it is entirely true and real.
Therefore, when the Buddha rebuked the followers of the Two Vehicles as being "withered sprouts and rotten seeds," it was because their mental conduct was not true and real.

From the successive patriarchs above, they have taught people that one must practice the essential inquiry and attain essential awakening. Thus we know that all sentient beings are born in vain and die in vain because of their delusions.
The perversion of perception functions as an active force; throughout kalpa after kalpa and birth after birth, not for even a single thought-moment has it been true.

Thus, one drifts within the ocean of birth and death, finding it difficult to reach the other shore. This is what is meant by the "vast expanse of karmic consciousness," having no fundamental basis to rely upon.

How much more so for a disciple of the Buddha, whose body is clad beneath the *kāṣāya*—how can one allow a lifetime to pass in a state of wandering, with every thought-moment consisting of deluded perceptions and karma?
Consciousness flows on, yet not for a single moment has it turned back in self-reflection to seek and practice the path of true reality.

This is to have lost one's human form beneath the *kāṣāya*; it is most pitiable. Since you, O practitioner of Zen, have not come from a distance of a thousand li, [you must not let this opportunity pass].
Those who come to consult an old man must give rise to a single piece of sincere faith.
Since this desolate mountain is not a place for empty pretense, for what purpose have you come? Once sincere faith has been given rise to, it will not be resolved by a single meeting;
nor will it be in vain if one does not seek a single piece of genuine practice. If you seek that which is genuine—

Practice. This arises directly from the mind of true reality. If there truly exists a mind that is authentically real regarding birth and death, you must thoroughly investigate and examine, one by one from the beginning, everything from your previous births until your renunciation of the household life:
when was there ever even a single thought or a single action that was a matter of true reality? All that has passed before is already empty and gone. Thus—
From this day forward, give rise to a single mind of world-transcendence.
Cast away at once all worldly attachments, deluded thoughts, and攀緣 (pān-yuán) [clinging to objects]. Abandon this bundle of bones all together.
Entrust this very life-force to the vast mountains and great marshes, letting it be scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind; let all things rest in peace.
Cast aside all thoughts of ease, comfort, and warmth; set them all aside with total resolve. Single-mindedly and directly hang the single thought of life and death upon your eyebrows.
Take a single ancient kōan and harbor it within your breast, investigating it day and night.

Observe that the moment a single thought of worldly mind arises, you have already fallen into the realm of birth and death; you must decisively sever it, allowing not even a hair’s breadth of it to remain.
Investigate in this manner, never ceasing until awakening is attained. This very point is the true mind regarding birth and death.
With this very mind, throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, engage in all manner of activities and various practices:

from prostrating before the Triple Gem and making offerings to the ten directions, to harmonizing the assembly and attending to the elderly and the infirm—engaging in every such practice with this mind.
There was no service he performed for his master’s person that he did not carry out with all his might, nor did he give rise to even a single thought of weariness or fatigue.

He never entertained a single thought of conceit regarding self and others, or of right and wrong, gain and loss. Nor did he harbor a single thought of seeking rest or contentment. He was just like the Great Master Yongming.
Daily perform one hundred and eight expedient practices, never altering them for as long as you live; this is precisely what constitutes true practice.
If you maintain such resolve and establish such conduct, you will penetrate through to the luminosity of your original ground.
Then, all seeds of habitual tendencies—of greed, anger, ignorance, and attachment—accumulated over countless eons will be dissolved one by one, transforming into the reality of Buddhahood.
This is the seed. To apply the mind in this way may be called not wasting this life, not failing one’s renunciation, and not having traveled in vain across wind and waves to visit spiritual teachers.
If you continue as before to engage in emptiness, merely acting out habitual sentiments, then the seeds of karmic defilement and sinful defilement will simply follow along with your deluded thoughts.
Not only will you fail this life, but you will truly bring upon yourself the three miserable realms for kalpas beyond measure.
It is merely suffering.
To demonstrate compliance is easy for practitioners of Chan, śramaṇas, and sons of the Śākya;
they are people who have emerged from the dust of the world. To draw near to the Buddha-dharma is to draw near to a dharma that transcends worldly sentiments. Truly, it shatters [delusion].
Regarding my own implements, those who study today learn extensively and possess much erudition, yet they merely increase their views of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*).
Few are able to partake of the flavor of the Dharma to nourish the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom; is this not the height of perversion?

It is easy to dismiss those who practice meditation on the grounds that extensive learning is of no benefit, for those whose resolve lies in pure cultivation are already far removed from such views. Nevertheless, to take mere pure cultivation as one’s practice, while failing to...

To deliberately exhaust the very roots of birth and death, yet fail to profoundly penetrate the ground where neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs have reached—this indicates that one’s initial resolve was not far-reaching.
Consequently, one accepts the price of a single day as the ultimate gain; can this not be considered failing to realize what is inherently possessed?
That which is difficult for us disciples to attain is weariness with the mundane world; that which is most difficult to attain is weariness with birth and death. Now, the Zen practitioner knows this.
One feels weary, yet does not know to investigate the reason for that weariness; this is like one who runs fifty paces and laughs at another who has run a hundred.

Alas, I am old, with few days remaining; the great affliction of birth and death hangs before my very eyes. I fear that my weariness will not reach its ultimate limit. This Zen practitioner is also advanced in years;
he should be able to use the old man’s weariness to weary himself. If he cannot weary himself by means of the old man’s weariness—how can he be said to have truly become weary?
Together, amidst thousands of crags and ten thousand gullies, we shall transcend all forms and forget words, cultivating the practice of wearying detachment from the world.

From this point on, we shall take our final leave of the five turbidities and forever depart from the four modes of birth, traveling together to the vast and boundless land of Ultimate Bliss. Is this not the most supreme of causes and conditions?
How could it merely be compared to one who packs provisions for a journey of a thousand *li*, looking down upon those who roam only among the elm and locust trees? It is certainly so.
Such a person is not yet fit for the Way.
To those practitioners of Chan who possess the capacity, he showed that taking the recitation of mantras as their primary practice was appropriate;
yet though they engaged in this for thirty years, there had been no breakthrough in the state of their minds.

The petitioner requested the elder’s instruction. The elder then pointed it out to him, saying: "The Buddha taught that there are many gates to the path of cultivation, yet they are non-dual in their return to the source.
Thus, investigating Chan through the use of a *huatou* and reciting the Buddha's name while upholding mantras are both the same, non-dual Dharma."
As for those who do not apply their minds skillfully, they do not know to borrow [this practice] to refine habitual tendencies and shatter delusive thoughts;
instead, they use a mind of attachment to reinforce ignorance. Thus, they exert great effort yet achieve little result.
This matter is like using a tile to knock on a door: one only seeks to have the door open, without needing to calculate the quality of the tile in one's hand.
Because we have accumulated the seeds of greed, hatred, delusion, and craving through immeasurable kalpas, they lie hidden within the *ālayavijñāna*,
deep, firm, and remote, such that no one can break through them. The Sages provisionally established skillful means,

instructing people to take a single koan as a *huatou* (critical phrase), to intensify their state of doubt, and to block the gateway of discursive thought so completely that not even a hair’s breadth remains.

Let go. After a long time, you will gain power. It is like a dog being cornered that leaps over a wall; suddenly, the *ālayavijñāna* bursts open, revealing one’s original face—this is called "awakening to the Way.
If it were merely a matter of suppressing discursive thoughts through sheer pressure, what need would there be for a *huatou*?

Even the old woman who counted the charcoal lumps attained awakening through single-minded concentration on one thing alone; how much more so for those who practice both mindfulness of the Buddha and the recitation of mantras?
When a Zen practitioner who has maintained the vidyā-mantra for thirty years sees its efficacy, it is not that the mantra lacks spiritual power.
It is merely that the mind with which you hold the mantra has never gained power. It is like pushing an empty cart down a slope;
the mind simply rolls along, for how could it ever apply force? With such an application of mind, not only will there be no efficacy in this life.

Even throughout the exhaustion of kalpas, it remains exactly thus. When the realm of the five aggregates manifests before you and the moment of birth and death arrives, you will once again find your vision blurred and disoriented.
To then blame your practice for lacking a firm foundation—is this not merely to deceive and err yourself?

From this day forward, meditators need not seek change; simply take the mind that maintains the mantra as the *huatou* (critical phrase). Focus with all your might on every single syllable and every thought.
Grinding and Rubbing. It is like pushing a heavy cart up a slope; one must exert all the strength of one’s entire body, not daring to relax by even a hair’s breadth.

Inch by inch, step by step, the heels must never lose contact with the ground. When exerting effort in this manner, it merely forces the flow of discursive thoughts to cease and blocks the life-root (*mūla*).
When one reaches this point and no further progress can be made, one should remain precisely at that place where the effort is applied.
Deepen your state of doubt and scrutinize it profoundly. Interrogate this very person who exerts effort in reciting the mantra: "What exactly is this, after all? Look and look again;
doubt and doubt further, like a rat entering a cow's horn, until you reach a point where you cannot turn back or draw a breath.
This is precisely the moment when you gain true power; by no means must you allow yourself to rest.

Do not consider it difficult to give rise to the thought of withdrawal and rest. When you reach the point where a single thought-moment is suddenly opened and cleared, this is the "Lightning Flash Samādhi.
You must by no means entertain thoughts of subtle joy. From this point on, exert even more vigor and devote your very life to the practice.
Until the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) suddenly bursts asunder and empty space is pulverized, you shall certainly not [rest].
Let go. If one can hold the mantra in this way, how could there be two distinct dharmas between this and the practice of Zen?
Therefore it is said: "Juzhi merely recited the three-line mantra, yet he was named as one who transcends all others. This can be verified; it is to personally behold the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Nor is it easy to dispute the words of the Old Man.
The novice Shami Shizhi is truly a contemporary monastic who, in this age of the Dharma-ending period when strife is rampant, has resolved his will upon the great matter of birth and death.
He single-mindedly upholds the one supreme point, taking full awakening as his goal. Such a person of the highest capacity is indeed...
It is not easily seen. Even now, there are those who investigate this matter;

yet, because their evil thoughts and habitual tendencies are thick, and because they have not yet stabilized upon the meditation cushion, false views arise recklessly, and many fall into demonic paths—this is the difficulty. An ancient worthy said:

"If you are not yet able to investigate the 'upward' [transcendent] path, then apply your mind to the teachings; in this way, your time will not pass in vain. Regarding this application of mind to the teachings:

There are two types. The first consists of those whose faculties are somewhat sharp, who exhaustively investigate the principles of nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*) until they penetrate deeply to their source.

Through the power of cultivation based on extensive learning, they enter *samādhi* via hearing, reflection, and meditation. Such individuals not only personally realize the nature of the mind, but also serve as teachers for others;
this is how one repays the profound kindness of the Buddha and does not fail the resolve of leaving the household life. Up to this point...
If one’s faculties are somewhat dull and one cannot extensively cultivate the teachings of the Vehicle, then the practice of recitation and chanting a single gate is especially essential.
Therefore, the Great Master Tiantai took reading, reciting, receiving, and upholding the sutras as the foremost of the five grades of contemplative practice (*pañcavidha-pratipatti*).

This is precisely what the *Lotus Sūtra* describes regarding the Dharma-master who upholds the sutra: "In this very life, with the physical body born of one's parents, one immediately attains the purification of the six sense organs."

This merit of upholding the sutra—how could it be considered inferior practice? Once a śrāmaṇera has come to know the weariness with the suffering of birth and death and has left home to join the Buddha, if he does not possess single-minded dedication to one practice, will he not be failing this life? By upholding the sutra as a single practice, one can concentrate the mind and unify the will;
like the ancients who immersed themselves in mental contemplation until, in a single moment, they forgot words and attained realization, thereby grasping the essence of the Buddha’s mind.
It is through Wenzi that one attains *dhāraṇī*. This is what is called the "Gate of the Revolving Dhāraṇī. By means of this, one enters realization;
the roots and sprouts of birth and death throughout kalpas are severed all at once by relying on this Dharma-gate. Is this not the path to unsurpassed *bodhi*?
If one lets the years pass aimlessly, wasting one's time and falling into the common stream of those who merely consume their meals, [what benefit will there be]?
Is this not to waste the offerings of the faithful in vain and to further increase the burden of karmic retribution?

What, then, is the purpose of leaving the household life? To the practitioner Xingjue, I show that the original purpose of leaving the household life is for the great matter of birth and death. Yet now, those who have left the household life do not know what birth and death are; they merely...
One knows that as one drifts with the waves, the karmic consciousness is vast and茫然 (mángmáng), having no foundation to rely upon.

In ancient times, those who traveled to various regions on pilgrimage sought out spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*) solely to investigate and clarify the matter within their own person. Today, people travel across the world and traverse every monastery, yet they do nothing but drum up the habitual tendencies of food and drink;
in the end, they do not know how a true teacher acts for others. It is truly a pity to be so奔波 (bēnpō) in vain toil.
Throughout one's entire life, in the end there is no trace of attainment; such a person is truly pitiable.

There are even those who harbor a single thought regarding the mind of birth and death, yet do not know the essential point of practice. Some take ritual chanting and the recitation of the Buddha’s name as their practice;
they toil throughout their lives, yet in the end, regarding the matter of their own very selves, it remains like a lacquered black bucket—utterly dark and opaque—in the face of birth and death.

This has no bearing [on the matter]. A practitioner who resolves their mind with sincerity for the great matter of birth and death must take the investigation of the "point above" as their true practice.
First, one must cultivate a resolve that is long-term, firm, and determined never to retreat.
For two or three decades, the ancients held up this single thought-moment, refusing to rest until they attained awakening. Above all, one must not point to...
I pray that you may quickly achieve success. Did not the Elder Śākyamuni refine his body and mind for three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas?

How could he have been of dull faculties? Although there are many opportunities for investigation through the encounters of the ancient worthies, the single phrase "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?
is the most effective for gaining power when examined with sincerity. If you, as a practitioner of Zen, resolve today to investigate this, simply take up this one...
Regarding this koan, you should bring it to mind from time to time.

First, completely set aside all deluded thoughts and chaotic mental states, both internal and external, within your body and mind, until there is nothing left to set aside. Then, deeply and firmly utter the name "A-mi-t'o-fo" once.
Let these four characters be vivid and distinct; look at them with an urgent gaze. If your looking lacks power, call out the name again.
At the sound of "Buddha," if you possess the power [of resolve], immediately cast down your state of doubt. Question yourself: "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?
Examine this again and again; ultimately, who is it? As soon as you perceive dullness or distraction arising, quickly sharpen your mental acuity.
Again bring it up and examine it; again question and doubt it. Doubt until you reach a point where you can no longer doubt, until your chest feels like a silver mountain and an iron wall.
It stands between the mind and the eyes. This is precisely when the *huatou* (critical phrase) becomes effective.
Once you have reached this point of efficacy, it is right to deepen your state of doubt (*yiqing*).

At all times and in all places during daily life, let not a single thought waver, even until after a long time, it is as if within dreams one is still awake. If you apply effort to this extent, you will certainly [attain realization].
One may fall back and regress; yet, suddenly, the mass of doubt shatters, and one naturally and instantaneously perceives one's original face.
If you are willing to give rise to this resolute will and a mind that never retreats, simply proceed directly with a single thought-moment.
You must by no means seek quick results, nor must you harbor a mind waiting for enlightenment. If your practice is continuous and subtle, there will naturally be a breakthrough.
This breaks the conventional notion of "time and occasion. As explained above, the section on "investigating with single-minded resolve" is most easily practiced and requires the least effort.
It is essential to be able to let go, to be able to take up, to rely with stability, and to doubt with intensity. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;

whether moving, still, at leisure, or in haste—these are all occasions for applying the mind. The Sixth Patriarch said: "If one speaks of this matter, it is like entering the fray brandishing a wheel-bladed sword."

This is precisely what can be accomplished. This is what is meant by that. If a Chan practitioner is resolute and truly seeks to resolve the matter of birth and death, they should set foot upon this very path.
[End of] "Showing the Treasure-Treasury Aspect. The Chan practitioner bows at Putuo.
The Great Being Avalokiteśvara has realized the fundamental root of perfect penetration. With his Dharma-realm body, he manifests in response to conditions; how could he remain fixedly at Potalaka?
The ocean is a metaphor for birth and death, and the mountain is a metaphor for nirvana. The Great Being universally responds within the ocean of birth and death with his Dharma-body;
thus, the ordinary daily activities of all sentient beings are all manifestations of the Great Being’s majestic spiritual power—serene and quiescent.
It is extinguished. It is like a mountain of jewels; therefore, it is likened to Potalaka in the midst of the ocean.

Because [the Bodhisattva] dwells within the ocean of sentient beings' afflictions, whatever suffering sentient beings have is itself the Great Being's (Mahāsattva's) suffering. Thus, by reciting his name even once, one immediately attains liberation.
This is for sentient beings to awaken their own minds to the Great Being. When the Great Being manifests before them, then quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa) manifests. Quiescent extinction is...

Suffering cannot reach it; therefore, the mountain is situated within the sea, where waves and tides cannot shake it. For this reason, it is said that the Great Being (Mahāsattva) constantly dwells at Potalaka.
This does not mean that the Great Being’s abode is restricted to a mere fist-sized rock in the ocean.

Sentient beings, deluded by ignorance, do not pay homage to the Great Being within their own minds, who personally resides upon the site of the Path of Quiescence (śamatha-vimokṣa-maṇḍala), majestic and immovable like the ocean.
Zhongshan is right here. Yet you must traverse mountains and rivers for several thousand li, enduring the hardship of stumbling and struggling as you seek it elsewhere;
how deeply deluded you are! Nevertheless, as the Sutra says: "The return to the source is non-dual, though the expedient means are manifold."

Now, all sentient beings of this great earth believe that the Great Being is in the Southern Sea. You should harmonize with their capacities and lead them forward, causing them to cross the seas and climb the mountains.
If they but once call out to the Great Being, they will have a sudden awakening to their own minds;

then, upon contact with every sight, the waves and tides will all enter the gate of perfect penetration. You must ensure they attain self-confidence before you cease. Among those practicing together in this way, if there is even a single person...
If you can believe these words of an old man, then you will not have failed in this one journey of pilgrimage; otherwise, you will have merely wasted the money spent on your straw sandals.
Thus he instructed Minghui to pay homage to the Patriarchs at Shaolin.
If we discuss this matter: before the Buddha appeared in the world and before the Patriarch came from the West, it illuminated heaven and earth, lacking nothing and leaving nothing behind.
Even when the Old Man with the Yellow Face appeared in the world and spoke at random for forty-nine years, shaking his lips and stirring his tongue all day long, he never uttered a single word.
Yet, at the very end, when he held up a flower and Kāśyapa broke into a smile, [the Buddha] said: "I have..."
"The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana—this I now entrust to you. It is much like an empty fist deceiving a small child;

from this point on, it is called the 'Specially Transmitted Way Outside the Teachings. It is as if placing a handle upon a bowl. One person transmits what is false, yet ten people transmit it as true.
Bodhidharma’s coming from the West further spoke of a 'direct pointing to the single transmission,' and his nine years at Shaoshi Mountain were nothing but a deception."
The Divine Light (Shenguang) was of dull nature; he stood in the snow and severed his arm, yet one might think there was something truly extraordinary about it.

When traced to its ultimate conclusion, it was simply that he sought the mind and could not find it. From that point on, people have merely inherited empty echoes, all building towers and pavilions in the air and establishing their own gateways and courtyards.
Though there are two lineages and five schools, they have ultimately never brought forth [the truth] for the sake of others. Until... [as in the original text]... like Rujing.
Nowadays, the great earth is as black as lacquer, causing those who are deluded and frantic to ply their wits within the ghost-caves.
Claiming to transmit the Chan of Shaolin and asserting themselves to be the descendants of our lineage, they thus deceive and mislead the ignorant. Is this not truly a matter of great pain?
"Today you, practitioner of Zen, come to visit this old monk. Here, I have no Buddha-dharma or path of Zen to give to people;

what need is there to speak of 'dry dung'? You practitioner of Zen wish to go on to Shaolin to pay homage to the Patriarchal Founder, seeking Buddha-dharma and the path of Zen while abandoning the inch of soil beneath your own feet.
Why do you seek it further beyond thousands of mountains and ten thousand waters?"
To search for it within one’s own house—is this truly wisdom? Zen practitioner, try to investigate this for yourself:
look at whether you are the same or different when you have not yet taken a single step out the door compared to when you have arrived at Mount Kuang.

Furthermore, look at whether you are the same or different right now as you take a single step away from Mount Kuang, travel back and forth to Shaolin, and return home. If they are different, then [the self] before you have taken a single step out the door...
It has already been missed long ago; how much more so over a thousand or ten thousand miles!
If you, practitioner, do not believe this old man, try going to Shaoshi and ask the pillar before the Hall of Single Transmission: "Look, what is this?"
Regarding the instruction on the Dharma-realm for Chan practitioners:
Chan Master Chansheng was born in Jianchang. Since leaving the mundane world, he has long wandered beyond the secular realm.

He once paid his respects to Zibo and the Old Man (Zhaozhou) in the capital, more than thirty years ago; he has now again come to visit the Old Man at Mount Kuang, and thus [the Old Man] instructed him.

It is said: "The monastics of antiquity all undertook the great matter of birth and death; they climbed mountains and waded through waters to seek out spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) for decisive discernment.
Beneath a single word or a single phrase, they severed the life-root (*jīvamūla*).

They instantly and completely cut off the defiled habits of hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, like a hawk released from its leather tether. From that moment on, they were no longer subject to human constraints. Thus it is said.
One can cast off one’s arms at the head of the road of birth and death, never looking back.

If one carefully examines how the various patriarchs of the *Chuan deng lu* extracted nails and pulled out wedges for the sake of others, what profound mystery or secret is there? It is simply that students have consistently focused solely on birth.
This one matter of death dwells within the breast; it cannot be swallowed and cannot be spat out, choked and obstructed as if one had lost an elderly mother.
Yet, when the time and conditions ripen, one suddenly encounters the staff of a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), and with a single push, it is turned around.
What further doubts could there be? It is simply a matter of believing with certainty that one’s own mind is inherently present.

Nowadays, people travel on pilgrimage, wandering to the ends of the earth and entering every monastery; wherever their eyes fall upon something warm and bustling, they consider it a fine place of practice (*dharma-cakra*).
Seeing the rice and gruel pure and clean, and eating a full meal until they snore contentedly, they take this to be a true spiritual teacher (*kalyāṇa-mitra*). From meeting those with clear vision...

Consciousness is entirely deceived; one misses the mark right before one's eyes. To travel on pilgrimage and visit various teachers in this manner, yet fail to attend to one’s own fundamental task, is nothing but wandering through birth and death.
One’s entire life passes in vain, and the money spent on straw sandals is wasted. Is this not truly a matter for deep lamentation?
Zen practitioners leave the household life and travel on pilgrimage for the sake of birth and death; they visit teachers and dwell in famous mountains to practice.
Ascetic practices and various dharmic conducts—having experienced each one in turn—tell me now: regarding the matter of birth and death, what is its ultimate nature?
Tell me: when you previously saw the Elder Zibo and now see the Elder, what difference is there from the time before you had seen him?
Tell me: being here now at the summit of the ten-thousand-fathom peaks of Mount Kuanglu, deep within the white clouds, compared to being in the city of Rājagṛha—what is the distinction?
Within ten thousand staffs amidst the red dust, is the realm one or is it different?
If you say they are the same, yet they are separated by three thousand *li* and there is no connection. If you say they are different, where are the eyes of the wandering monk?
If you can reach a definitive conclusion here, then thirty years is this very day, and this very day is thirty years ago. The red dust is...
White clouds. White clouds are precisely the red dust of the world.

All birth and death, afflictions, karmic actions, and various differentiated realms—there is nothing that does not, upon meeting the eye, become quiescent extinction (*śānti*). If this is not yet so, today you shall once again set out on foot;
starting from the beginning, you shall go to Mount Wutai and Mount Emei to meet Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, and ask them: "What is equality?"
This dharma-gate of ultimate quiescence awaits someone capable of understanding it; come again to meet this old monk.
To the Chan practitioner Chongguan, who travels between Wu and Chu, having journeyed from over several thousand *li* to seek instruction: upon seeing him once, I knew he possessed [the potential].

He has set his will upon it but has not yet achieved it. The old man, pitying him for having come from so far and having nothing else to point out, took his name and bestowed upon him the style "Jianwei" (Perceiving the Subtle).
This is because the root-stalks of sentient beings' birth and death flow on subtly and minutely; they are deluded by false thoughts and remain unaware of this themselves.
Therefore, our Great Teacher, the Buddha, established contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to illuminate it. Indeed, it is precisely because it is subtle that it is not [grasped by] ordinary observation.

Without illumination, one cannot perceive the greatness of the power of birth and death; without contemplation that does not involve even the slightest [conceptualization], one cannot manifest the efficacy of the power of illumination.
If one can penetrate the subtle and profound, then one may emerge from birth and death. This is specifically the ultimate standard of the teaching school.

As for the realm of the patch-robed monk (śramaṇa), there is naturally a hammer beyond the ordinary: simply being able to make a single thought as firm as an iron wall or a silver mountain, blocking it off completely.
There is no place from which to exhale through the throat; one must reach the point of death and then return to life before there can be even a slight degree of resonance.
For the time being, you practitioners are merely drifting in the ocean of consciousness and have not yet severed the life-root.
If, at some future time, you are able to spit out the various poisons and let go of body and mind, you will have the opportunity to come again and seek instruction.
Sixth, regarding Reverend Kun:

following the various patriarchs of antiquity, he taught people to engage in *chan* (meditation). Although there were discussions of "surpassing the Buddhas and transcending the patriarchs," the actual intent was simply to lead people to become Buddhas and patriarchs themselves.
There has never been one who sought to become a Buddha or a patriarch without following the words and teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs.
To set aside the teachings and speak only of practice is like discarding the compass and square while seeking to produce a perfect circle or square.

Furthermore, the Buddha taught Ānanda that as soon as one opens the mouth, one should speak with a straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*). The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

The Great Master Aśvaghoṣa, in revealing the essential points of cultivation, stated that one must give rise to three kinds of minds: namely, the straightforward mind, right mindfulness of *tathatā* (suchness), and... [the Dharma-mind].
Therefore, the profound mind is for the purpose of gathering all wholesome practices; the great compassionate mind is for the purpose of vowing to rescue all sentient beings from suffering.
Among the successive patriarchs of old, there has never been one who did not give rise to these three kinds of mind.

Students know only to go blindly to investigate the *huatou* (critical phrase), seeking only the subtle and wondrous through deluded thoughts and craving; yet they do not realize that this is precisely the direct mind.
To maintain right mindfulness of *tathatā* (suchness) is the expedient teaching of the Patriarchs.

If one were to speak of the two characters "true-suchness," students would immediately try to grasp them through intellectual reasoning; who would then be willing to apply themselves with the effort of death?

If one simply instructs them to observe the *huatou*, and they observe that *huatou* until it presses upon and grinds away the emotional faculties accumulated over kalpas, then at the moment of sudden severance, all former deluded thoughts and attachments—

When all deliberations are extinguished in the present moment, one seeks even a single thought of arising mind, yet finds it utterly unobtainable. Reaching this point is precisely the realm free from conceptualization.
This is what is meant by "right mindfulness is non-mindfulness. If one reaches this state of non-mindfulness, there is no longer a need to seek union with True Suchness (*tathatā*);
one naturally accords with its essence through direct encounter. This is the manner in which the Buddhas and Patriarchs instruct people to follow their direct mind.
My son, you should know that in the practice of Zen there is no other clever method; it simply requires that one truly and earnestly practice until reaching such a state.
How could there be any secret or clever artifice? This is the first: the cultivation of the straightforward mind.
Second is the profound mind, which seeks to gather all merits and virtues. Regarding these various merits and virtues—
This is not something conditioned that exists externally. As the Great Master Bodhidharma said to Emperor Wu: "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect;
its essence is inherently empty and still. This is true merit. Thus, we know that what Bodhidharma spoke of as "pure wisdom, wondrously perfect" [is this very reality].
This is precisely Aśvaghoṣa’s direct mind, right mindfulness, and true thusness (tathatā).
All the merits spoken of by Aśvaghoṣa consist of applying this direct mind and right mindfulness to bring true thusness universally to fulfillment within all conditioned phenomena.
If you seek to realize true thusness today, do not seek it within the ghostly cave of a fixed, staring gaze; rather, you must seek it within every day.
One seeks upward through the myriad practices of the conditioned. The reason for seeking upward through practice is not to seek out a separate, subtle, and wondrous *tathāgata* within phenomena;

rather, it is simply to take direct mind and right mindfulness and examine them within all matters to see whether they accord with or do not accord with direct mind and right mindfulness. If, in every matter and every phenomenon...
When one is in accord with the direct mind and right mindfulness, then not a single phenomenon or event before one's eyes fails to be the realm of True Suchness (Tathatā).

This is why Mazu and his disciples, including Baizhang, during their daily activities—whether carrying firewood and drawing water, weeding fields and planting rice, or lighting fires and cooking meals—would confront and examine them at every turn. In their ordinary words and phrases, they constantly tested one another.
Whether spoken coldly or warmly, all these words are intended to lead disciples through the gate of realizing *tathatā* (Suchness).
Only when you have investigated until you truly reach a state where you are not deluded in any circumstance may you be granted the capacity to benefit others.

If there is even the slightest thread of doubt remaining in your breast, and you have not yet reached the realm of non-thought (*amanyana*), then the mere arising of a thought will cause you to be turned by karma and fall into the pit of birth and death. Therefore, [it is said that]...
The light seal is correct. These seventeen hundred cases of the *Chuan deng lu* are all words that have been truly sealed as correct;

they are not merely subtle, wondrous, or sharp-edged utterances. Yet nowadays, practitioners all treat them as subtle, wondrous, and extraordinary phrases, storing them within their chests and taking them to be their own understanding.
In their daily lives, at every turn, they have never once seen through even a single hair’s breadth of them. Is this not a grave error?

Third is the mind of great compassion, which vows to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings. As a student of the Way today, seeing oneself uprooting the suffering of sentient beings is the work of a bodhisattva.

One might wait until becoming a perfected bodhisattva in a future day to deliver sentient beings, yet one does not realize that it is precisely at the moment one is able to deliver sentient beings that one is a bodhisattva.
Delivering sentient beings from suffering is not something that occurs only when one possesses supernatural powers and wondrous functions. It begins right now.
To go forth and deliver sentient beings is, in fact, the state of direct mind and right mindfulness; it is the very locus where all merits are gathered, which is the activity of delivering beings.
For instance, the World-Honored One taught Subhūti that although one must deliver all sentient beings, in reality, there are no sentient beings to be delivered.

Extending even to the extensive practice of the six perfections, there is not a single dharma that can be practiced. Extending even to the supreme seeking of Bodhi and the fruit of Buddhahood, there is likewise nothing to be attained.
Yet, in saving sentient beings, is this not the accumulation of all merits? Truly, there is not a single dharma that can be obtained;
is this not the direct mind and right mindfulness of True Suchness (*tathatā*)? Such wondrous function is none other than the spiritual power of one's own daily life.
Pervasive; taking it is without restriction, and using it is inexhaustible. Thus, what dharma could be other than an act of merit?

Since the various activities and dharmas used daily by sentient beings are all the active manifestations of afflictions (*kleśa*), if one now seals and breaks through each and every phenomenon with a single thought of *tathatā* (Suchness), they are entirely transformed into the wondrous functioning of *tathatā*. This is precisely to deliver the multitudes within one's own mind.
To study in this manner is what is called being a true seeker who investigates with sincerity.
It is not to sit idly in a state of complacency for three or five years, then boastfully declare, "I have practiced Chan for so long; I have realized how many wonderful points.
Such a level of understanding is that of one who will receive an iron staff before King Yama; it is actually inferior to... [the former].
The young man from the village homestead has indeed been spared the karmic debt owed to his faithful lay donor.
When I, an old man, examine this, the Buddhas and Patriarchs taught people with complete clarity; it is only that later generations have misunderstood, and thus erred.
Since you, Zen practitioner, have turned your heart toward me, you must believe my words. From now on, you shall carry and guard a crystal bottle.
Crush it all to pieces with a single squeeze. Take everything you have previously investigated and shift it entirely onto this one body and mind.
At the gateway of bringing sentient beings to maturity, cast away your very life. Experience each point with earnest reality and give rise to the vast, universal mind.

To be able to inspire even a single sentient being to resolve upon Bodhicitta is to uproot the suffering of that one being, to shatter a portion of one’s own ego-clinging, and to diminish a portion of one’s afflictions.
To eliminate a portion of the afflictions of self-view is itself to realize a portion of the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
If, from this point onward, one further develops a long-term resolve, then within three lifetimes or ten kalpas—

Throughout kalpa after kalpa and birth after birth, one practices until reaching the point where afflictions are completely exhausted; this is precisely the place where all sentient beings are delivered.
If the afflictions of sentient beings were to be exhausted all at once, what further Buddhas or Patriarchs would there even need to be?
In the West, Master Jinggong was shown to have been dedicated to the exclusive cultivation of the Pure Land.

In recent times, many among the scholar-officials have favored oral tradition and superficial learning; they indulge in mere talk and universally revere the practice of Chan meditation as the supreme pursuit.
Neglecting the Pure Land without cultivation, our followers—those who prioritize reputation—have mostly practiced the ready-made phrases of ancient masters merely to facilitate their own eloquence.
Holding this in high esteem, the Dharma gate has consequently declined day by day;
not only is genuine practice entirely absent, but even Mahāyāna sūtras are slandered as mere words and forbidden from being approached. This world is devoid of wisdom.
The eye-consciousness is such that, in the end, one can never turn back its wild torrent; this is truly to be feared.

Generally, they have not delved deeply into the teachings of the Vehicle (Śāsana) and do not understand that our Buddha’s means for delivering sentient beings involve many doors, though their ultimate aim in returning to the source is non-dual.

Worldly people know only that under the Gate of the Patriarchs, awakening is held supreme. The original intent of awakening the mind is to transcend birth and death. [Yet they neglect] the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name.

Is this not the very method for escaping birth and death? While many who practice Chan meditation may not necessarily attain liberation, those who practice *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation) will undoubtedly escape birth and death.
The reason for this is that Chan meditation requires one to abandon discursive thoughts (*vikalpa*), whereas *nienfo* focuses exclusively on such thoughts.

Since sentient beings have long been submerged in delusive thoughts, it is truly difficult to abandon them. Therefore, rather than rejecting defiled thoughts, one transforms them into pure thoughts; this is like using poison to [counteract] poison.
Investigating the poison is merely a method of broad exchange; therefore, it is difficult to attain awakening through such investigation, whereas reciting the Buddha’s name is easy to accomplish.

If one truly possesses a sense of urgency regarding birth and death, and recites the Buddha’s name with that same mind used for investigation, what cause for concern would there be that one would not resolve the matter of birth and death within this lifetime?
It is only because of this Pure Land Dharma gate that worldly people regard it as provisional; they fail to realize that it is, in fact, the most authentic Dharma gate of all.
Contemplate Samantabhadra: taking the Dharma-realm as one’s body and cultivating the ten great vows, one will inevitably find ultimate refuge in the Pure Land.

Master Vasubandhu, the patriarch who transmitted the mind-seal, followed the teachings of the hundred Mahāyāna treatises and composed the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*; its final conclusion likewise points toward the Western Paradise.

Although the various patriarchs who transmitted the lamp in this Eastern land did not explicitly mention the Pure Land, once the mind is awakened and one has transcended birth and death, one cannot but return [to that source].
How could the Pure Land be subject to annihilation? Yongming [Yanshou] compiled the entire Tripitaka and pointed back to the single mind, yet he also subsumed it within the Pure Land.
As for Chan, by the time of Zhongfeng, the era was in its final stage, yet he exerted all his efforts to praise the Western Paradise.

How much more so this Dharma gate, which was spoken spontaneously by our Original Teacher without being asked and is praised together by the Buddhas of the ten directions; how could the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...
"Great Patriarch, would you rather not speak falsely like those practitioners of the present day who defile sentient beings with their defilements?
Master Jing renounced worldly attachments in his middle years to enter the monastic life. He first studied under Great Master Zibo, who gave him instructions on the practice of Chan meditation.

Now, regarding the single gate of the Pure Land, he has made a vow to cultivate it but remains undecided. The Elder therefore said to him: 'There is no need to ask others about this matter; simply observe for yourself.'"
As for your own mind regarding birth and death, how is it? If you truly possess a mind regarding birth and death, it must be like saving one's head from fire;
your resolve must be to accomplish this in a single lifetime. It is like a person suffering from a terminal illness who finds someone seeking an elixir of immortality that can save them.
Another person then grants them a simple prescription from the sea that is sufficient to raise the dead and restore life. This depends entirely upon the patient having a resolute mind.
Believe this and you may take it; there is no need to wait for or seek out the elixir of immortality (*rāsandana*).

Simply taking this single prescription will cause the entire body to break into a sweat, and only after death is one restored to life. At that time, one will finally realize its wondrous efficacy. One need only believe this method with earnest faith and single-minded devotion;
when the moment of death arrives, one will know its benefits for oneself. Why, then, must one ask others? Strive!
Go and practice it; you shall certainly not be deceived.
When the śrāmaṇera Xing’ai came to attend upon me and requested instruction from this old man, I named him Jianren (Firm Patience). May the Buddha show his grace to this disciple.
It is said: "Donning the garment of patience is called the armor of firmness.

Taking this armor as a means to ward off calamities is like a great general who, when facing the enemy, does not suffer the afflictions of arrows and stones, yet is able to preserve his body and life, achieving the merit of certain victory."
This is the power of armor. Furthermore, we śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākya, tread upon the field of birth and death and encounter the great enemies of the five desires and various māras;
were it not for the firmness of the power of patience, one would be insufficient to overcome them. Therefore, it is said: "Endure form; endure desire.
Only by being able to endure what is difficult to endure can one preserve the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom, thereby reaching the realm of ultimate bliss. This is the teaching of our Buddha.
This is also called "enduring various hardships," all of which one must be able to endure. How much more so in the perilous path of the Dharma-ending age, where calamities and difficulties abound;
if one lacks the power of firm endurance, how can one possibly complete the task of transcending the world?

Compiled by the Disciple Tonghyeung;
Re-edited by the Disciple from the South Land, Liu Qixiang.
*Fayu* (Dharma Words).
In the "Eulogy on the Night Terrace Chan Master," it is stated that Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva dwells on Mount Qingliang, where he constantly expounds the Dharma to a retinue of ten thousand followers;
thus, śramaṇas from the Western Regions pay homage to this mountain from afar as the Golden World. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Mañjuśrī is present in all places."
