"Mañjuśrī, you have come from the world-system of Universal Golden Light. Considering this, does Mañjuśrī truly dwell permanently on this mountain?
Generally speaking, within the realm of sentient beings, the accumulation of afflictions constitutes a land of burning anguish.

If a practitioner can open the eye of wisdom, reach the fundamental source so that deluded attachments are forgotten, and realize that the essence of mind is in harmony with its ground, then they will immediately attain coolness and clarity. It is thus."
Thus, everything one encounters is none other than the transformative realm of Mañjuśrī; every step taken does not depart from the Qingliang Bodhimanda.
This is what is meant by "the golden world of Mañjuśrī in all places. As for the practitioner Yetai, he resided for a long time at Mount Wutai;
because he used to roam there at night, he received this name. Now that he has come to the south on pilgrimage to pay respects to spiritual teachers, he will surely encounter Mañjuśrī in person.
He points the way as he comes, like Sudhana’s journey southward; though he has passed through one hundred and ten cities, his feet have not moved a single step.
It is as if he had previously traveled throughout the worlds of the ten directions without ever leaving the Golden World-realm.

Every spiritual friend encountered along the way, and every dharma-gate—whether encountered with favor or opposition—is none other than the wisdom-eye of Mañjuśrī. Now, he sees the Elder atop Mount Wuyú, bestowing [instruction] upon...
Whether the Golden World is the same as or different from this place—if you can discern this here, I grant that you have personally seen Mañjuśrī.
If this is not yet the case, buy another pair of straw sandals and go forth on pilgrimage. Study! Study!
Shisheng Ranjue, a Chan practitioner whose nature was awakened through Chan, left home at the age of middle years. He traveled from afar to Mount Kuang to seek the bestowal of full ordination.

Because he suffered from a chronic ailment and could not remain in attendance for long, he took his leave to return home and requested further instruction. The Elder showed him this, saying: "The body is the root of great suffering."
This is a gathering place for all sufferings, the cycle of birth and death within the six realms. First, one must recognize this cause of the suffering of birth and death:
namely, that the root of all sufferings is craving and desire. If craving and desire are extinguished, there will be nothing upon which they can depend.
Therefore, the Buddha taught the Vajra Precepts as a Dharma-gate of the mind-ground; these are the tools for severing desire and the boat or raft for escaping suffering. You are now fortunate...
Upon hearing this Dharma, one should keep it in mind without forgetting and maintain an uninterrupted state of mind without slackening; this itself is the essential point of practice.

As the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* Sūtra (*Nengxian Chuanxingshi Jing*) states: "One should contemplate that this body is a composite of the four great elements. I now observe that what is solid and hard returns to earth."
Moisture returns to water; warmth returns to fire; movement returns to wind. Contemplate these four great elements (*mahābhūta*): each has its own place of return.
Where, then, shall this deluded body now abide? Observe in this manner, maintaining mindfulness without interruption, with every moment of mind remaining unclouded.

After a long time, when [the practice] becomes thoroughly matured, one will suddenly perceive this body as empty and detached; the four great elements will be like space, and all sufferings will be instantly cast off.
This very method of cultivation is the foremost sublime secret for transcending birth and death.

Among the patriarchs of the past, there was not a single person who attained enlightenment regarding the nature and mind without coming through the process of investigation and inquiry. There has never been anyone who attained it without practicing.
Those who are able to attain benefit should reflect further: although this body is suffering, as long as even a single breath remains, one may still seek the means to escape it.
If you lose this [opportunity] even once, your body will have donned the *kāṣāya* in vain, and you will suffer the pains of the three miserable realms in the future.

One may wander through them for many eons; though one desires to seek deliverance, it cannot be attained. Therefore, it is said: "Contemplate the suffering of the hells and give rise to the bodhicitta;
exhort yourselves and do not be indolent."
He explained that those who study the path of Chan are called practitioners of the Way.
He went to visit the Elder at Caoxi specifically to clarify the essential purport of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
He taught that for us practitioners, if we do not rely on the fundamental wisdom of *prajñā*, it is difficult to escape the cycle of birth and death; yet this *prajñā*—
It is not to be sought elsewhere outside; it is the very essence of one’s own mind, which has been inherently complete from the beginning.
Therefore, in current practice, one seeks only one's own mind and does not further search for branches and leaves. The Buddhas and Patriarchs taught people only to turn back and seek their own minds;
thus it is said: "Recognize the mind and reach the source; therefore, one is called a śramaṇa. It is also said: "If a person can recognize [it]..."
Mind. Throughout the great earth there is not an inch of soil [of one's own]. My own mind is fundamentally the radiance of *prajñā*;
it is originally devoid of all things. Yet, due to a single moment of delusion, one uses it daily without knowing it.
One merely knows this illusory and false provisional self, and thus fails to know the originally abiding *dharmakāya*. If you now wish to awaken to this original *dharmakāya*, then...
In the midst of daily activities, when thoughts and mental movements arise at the gates of the six sense organs and one clings to a locus of self, one must immediately illuminate and shatter this.
Fundamentally, there is no self. Where there is no self, there is no person. Where there is no person, there are no sentient beings.
Since sentient beings are empty, the root of birth and death is severed. Once birth and death are transcended, there is no life-span. Thus, the four marks [of existence] are eliminated.
With the single mind having no place of attachment, is this not the wondrous practice of non-abiding?
If you cannot achieve immediate and thorough awakening, simply take the Sixth Patriarch’s words, "Originally there is nothing," and place them before you.

Whenever you perceive any circumstance or condition and a dualistic mind arises, that is precisely self-grasping. If you can, at this very point of grasping, apply a single moment of insight to shatter it, then, in that instant—
When emotions are forgotten and the mind of dualistic opposition ceases, this is precisely non-self. Where there is no self, there is no person.
Once both person and self are empty, the body and mind in daily life are entirely free from obstruction.

Since the circumstances of daily life—whether adverse or favorable—are all pathways to birth and death, if these circumstances are seen through and one is free from obstruction, then the very roots of birth and death will likewise be severed from the ground up.
Thus it is. Is this not indeed the excellent cultivation of the wondrous practice of non-abiding Prajñā?
If a practitioner of Chan is resolved to transcend birth and death, they must take this as the primary principle. To seek anything else besides this is to fall into the deviant paths of externalists.
To Wei Shengqi, Layman Shengqi. Recently, you sent a letter requesting further instruction, saying:

"Lately, although I have been struck with a sense of urgency regarding the great matter of birth and death, and desire liberation wherever I am, whenever adversity suddenly befalls me, I am unable to accept it in the present moment. Although [you] immediately...

One can perceive that the master has already been ensnared. Observing the intent behind these words, it is clear that this person is truly and earnestly committed to the great matter of birth and death;
however, because they have not yet encountered a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to point out the practice of the "ground of the mind" (cittabhūmi), they lack a firm handle.
Indeed, from time immemorial, we have only identified deluded thoughts as the mind, unaware of the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu) that is inherently present. Part 1.
Hitherto, you have merely given rise to likes and dislikes, hatred and love, and all manner of discriminatory views and perceptions regarding the favorable and adverse conditions of worldly life.
You have failed to realize that these emotions of hatred, love, joy, and anger are entirely the very root-stocks of birth and death.

Among all people in the world, there is not one who has not been tossed about within this cycle throughout their entire life. The ancient masters taught people to practice Chan meditation in order to...

Birth and death do not consist in departing from these [conditions] to find some other subtle wonder; rather, it is simply to see through the mind of aversion and attachment within these very realms, and that is what constitutes the ending of birth and death.

Since these delusions of aversion and attachment have been habitually cultivated since time immemorial until they are thoroughly matured and deeply rooted, how could one possibly overcome them without a skillful method? This is why one engages in *chan* meditation by observing the *huatou*.
This teaching is precisely the sharp instrument for destroying afflictions. The reason one is entangled by them is simply because one lacks this "head-word" (hua-tou) to exercise mastery over.
For instance, when a monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does even a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou replied, "No.
One should take this single word "No" and carry it within one's breast as a head-word, bringing forth doubt.

Maintain this with constant mindfulness; let not every thought be obscured. Amidst all circumstances—whether in leisure or busyness, motion or stillness, social engagement or sudden urgency—simply hold fast to this single phrase.
Deepen your state of doubt and interrogate it thoroughly. As you continue to doubt and doubt, there will come a time when only the *huatou* (the critical phrase) manifests before you.
Even if you are reading a book, as soon as you set the volume down and turn your head to look, immediately apply your state of doubt.

This doubt must be firm and solid; by no means should one attempt to resolve it through intellectual reasoning or conceptual understanding. One simply requires that this single thought of doubt be sincere and earnest.
After a long period of cultivation until it becomes mature, whenever a delusive thought arises in the mind, simply pose this question once, and it will dissolve instantly like melting ice.
Whatever anger or joy arises in the mind is nothing more than a false conception. First, take up this *huatou* (critical phrase) as your practice.
When the sovereign [mind] and its objects encounter one another, as soon as they meet, you must see through them; they will then vanish like ice melting. Do not exert any effort at all.
Practice in this manner, and you will not only overcome and shatter external objects, but will also reach the moment of awakening.
However, you must by no means engage in conceptual deliberation regarding subtle and wondrous principles, for fear that it may instead lead you astray.
To the Chan practitioner Fudun and the Chan practitioner Xin'an:
You have traveled from afar to Mount Kuang to seek the bestowal of the precepts. Your name is Fudun; your courtesy name is Dukur.
"Duke" means earnest and sincere; it is the state of being pure and single-minded without artifice—the ultimate height of refined sincerity.

Now, we śramaṇas, the sons of the Buddha, who wish to transcend birth and death, realize the true and eternal, and seek the blissful fortune of unsurpassed nirvāṇa—if it were not for this single thought of refined sincerity, [it would be impossible].
To be pure and free from delusion, one must exert the power to shatter the demons of affliction and suddenly uproot the seeds of attachment and aversion;
yet, to desire to enjoy the blessings of non-action all at once is difficult. A journey of a thousand li begins with the first step; from this point on, the precepts serve as the foundation.

This is the first step toward awakening. Thus, with every thought moving forward and every mind never retreating, one seeks but a single moment when the root of the passions of birth and death can be traced to its source;
yet, in the end, it cannot be found. That which cannot be found is precisely the place where birth and death are unattached.
One need only fear that one’s resolve is not firm and one’s practice is not vigorous. If you fear it is not vigorous, simply...
Take the four characters of Amitābha Buddha and place them horizontally across your chest as if they were a sharp axe;
after a long time, the roots and trunk will naturally be severed. To apply effort in this manner is called "sincerity. Exert yourself! Exert yourself!
The Chan practitioners Fuhou and Xin'an came to visit Mount Kuang to request the bestowal of the precepts. His name was given as Fuhou, and his courtesy name was Jiru.
For those who have left the mundane world, merit is accumulated gradually until it becomes substantial; only upon reaching Buddhahood is it fully perfected.
It is like the accumulation of minute particles of dust to form the great earth—the ultimate state of thickness.

Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, from immeasurable kalpas past, has sacrificed his head, eyes, marrow, and brain, accumulating merit and practicing deeds until he attained Bodhi. Bodhi is the peaceful dwelling of Nirvana and the source of all bliss and fortune.

This is the ultimate point. If one does not accumulate [merit and wisdom], how could one reach this state? However, that which is "as-it-is" (tathatā) is the Buddha-nature, which we all possess inherently from the beginning.

It is simply because we have been afflicted by the encroachment of afflictions (*kleśa*) throughout countless kalpas that the dust of emotional afflictions has grown ever thicker, while the Buddha-nature as-it-is has become thin.
Now that you know the Buddha-nature is inherently present and need not be sought elsewhere, from this moment onward in your daily life...

In every thought-moment, know where one returns. Whenever the dust of the emotions arises, illuminate it with the light of wisdom. After a long time, through constant practice, the Buddha-nature will become thick while afflictions grow thin;
as afflictions grow thin, karmic obstructions become light; as karmic obstructions grow light, birth and death are severed.
This is achieved by accumulating *tathatā* (suchness) to cut off birth and death, seeking to realize *bodhi* (enlightenment), and enjoying the bliss of permanence, self, purity, and bliss.
Abundant fortune—how could it not arrive through accumulation? Thus it is said: "If the accumulation of water is not deep, it lacks the power to support a great ship.
May you, O practitioner of Zen, exert yourself!
On the Chan practitioner Tongchen Rui of Dīnnán:

The Chan practitioner Tongchen Rui of Dīnnán traveled from afar to the Great Capital, where he personally attended the lecture halls. Subsequently, he completely abandoned his prior studies and traveled south to seek out spiritual teachers.
He visited Mount Huángshān in Xīn'ān; finding its seclusion and excellence inspiring, he eventually settled there in humble retreat.
Traveling with only a single almsbowl, he had no fixed place of residence. Nevertheless, he took the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as his regular recitation.

In the middle summer of the Renxu year, he came to Mount Kuang to request the bestowal of the full precepts (*mahā-śīla*). Holding incense, he requested instruction. The Elder (the Master) therefore showed him this, saying:
"You take the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as your constant recitation; are you able to know the fundamental principles and essential tenets of this sūtra? It is solely because of our Vairocana..."

Vairocana, throughout kalpas of causal practice, cultivated the conduct of Samantabhadra by means of the Dharma-realm mind (*dharmadhātu-citta*). Having realized the ultimate extent of the Dharma-realm, he is named the Reward Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) and titled Vairocana.
He possesses marks and embellishments (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields; this constitutes his primary retribution (*pratyaya-vaipākya*).

The twenty-layered Flower Treasury World (*padma-garbha-loka-dhātu*), with its inexhaustible adornments, which he has elicited, serves as his environmental retribution (*āśraya-pratyaya*). He dwells therein, abiding in the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgara-mudrā-samādhi*).
It is called the Wisdom of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka-jñāna*).

For the Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), this sutra is expounded as the *Sūtra of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm*, a dharma-gate that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which is manifold, subtle, and inconceivable.
Such a dharma-gate is the realm of self-realization of all Buddhas; it is fully present within the deluded thoughts of the daily activities of sentient beings, moment after moment.
Manifestation. A sutra states: "For example, within a single mote of dust there exists a great scroll of scripture, inscribed with the events of the trichiliocosm.
There is a wise person who clearly perceives this scripture; he splits open the mote of dust and brings forth this great sūtra, bringing infinite benefit.
Now, that single mote of dust is the deluded mind of sentient beings; the great scroll of scripture is [the Dharma]."

This scroll [reveals] the inherent nature and virtues possessed by sentient beings from the very beginning. That these remain hidden and do not manifest is because sentient beings employ them in their daily lives without realizing it.
When the person of clear-sighted wisdom breaks through the dust to bring forth this scripture, it is the ultimate realization of all Buddhas;

thus, the revelation of this Dharma to sentient beings serves as a great benefit and joy. It should be understood that what is taught in this scripture is the deluded mind of the daily activities of sentient beings.
Listen! How great is the mind of sentient beings! It possesses vast and inconceivable power, and its wisdom and function are boundless;
yet it is obscured by a mere moment of deluded thought. Is this not to be lamented? Our Buddha appeared in the world specifically for this matter; thus he said:
"I have appeared in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition. For the Buddhas have realized this Great [Dharma].
It is for this matter, by reason of this, and on account of this, that he has appeared in the world specifically to preach it for the sake of sentient beings; there is no other matter.
Because sentient beings are deluded regarding this great matter and thereby undergo birth and death, birth and death are themselves treated as the great matter. Viewed from this perspective:
This is the magnificent text consisting of eighty fascicles. That which it reveals is none other than the deluded mind of a single thought-moment of our own.
Therefore, it is said: "I now attain equal and perfect enlightenment within the minds of all sentient beings.

This means that the sentient beings within the hearts of all Buddhas attain the Way at every moment, and the Buddhas within the hearts of sentient beings realize the Truth in every thought. Thus, the *Banzhou*... [text continues]
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said: "When inhaling, one does not dwell within the aggregates or realms; when exhaling, one does not involve oneself with external conditions.
One constantly turns this sūtra hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of times.

If one can, with such an eye, turn this sūtra until the end of the future, without interruption—speaking in every dust mote, speaking in every world-system, speaking with blazing intensity without ceasing—this is indeed..."
This is the great purport of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the True Scripture of the Dharma-realm.

If a practitioner of Chan awakens to this Dharma, then even before unrolling the scroll, they will see through to the boundless Dharma-realm within the mere interval of fanning the fire, picking up incense, clearing one's throat, or snapping one's fingers.
Although it is thus, one must still pierce through the ox-hide before success can be attained.
To the Chan practitioner Haiyang,
who has come from afar to Mount Kuang to seek the conferral of the precepts and request the name Shen-yu (Profound Ignorance), I offer this incense and grant his request.

Yi said: "I, your disciple [Name], have made a vow to seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land. I have gathered a group of several fellow practitioners to assemble in one place to cultivate pure deeds exclusively.
I pray that you will compassionately grant us instruction on the essentials of the Dharma. The Elder thereupon instructed them, saying:

"The Buddha taught many skillful means for the practice that leads to transcendence of birth and death; yet among them, there is none superior to mindfulness of the Buddha to seek rebirth in the Pure Land."

The Pure Land is the most swift and essential path. Just as the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and other perfect and wondrous Dharma-gates, as well as the sublime practices of Samantabhadra, ultimately point toward the Pure Land as their final destination;
so too did the great patriarchs such as Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and those of our own land including Yongming, Zhongfeng, and others.
All [the masters] advocate for the Pure Land gate with utmost vigor. This dharma-gate was spoken by the Buddha spontaneously without being asked;

it universally covers those of the three faculties and gathers the fourfold assembly alike. It is not something established as a provisional teaching for those of inferior faculties. As the Sūtra says: "If one wishes to purify the Buddha-lands, one should purify one's own mind.
Thus, when practicing the pure karma today, one must take a pure mind as the foundation. One must purify oneself...

Regarding the mind: first and foremost, one must ensure that the roots of the precepts are pure. Through the three actions of body, four of speech, and three of mind—these ten unwholesome karmas are the causes of suffering in the three miserable realms.
Now, the essential point of upholding the precepts is that one must first purify these three types of action; then the mind will naturally become pure.

If one refrains from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, then the karma of the body is pure. If one refrains from false speech, frivolous talk, divisive speech, and harsh words, then the karma of speech is pure.
If the mind is free from greed, hatred, and delusion, then the karma of the mind is pure.
Thus, when these ten unwholesome paths are forever severed and the three types of karma are as clear as ice, this constitutes the essential method for purifying the mind. Within this pure mind—

Within this world, one should cultivate weariness toward the sufferings of Saṃsāra and make a vow to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). One must establish the correct practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (nien-fo).

However, this mindfulness of the Buddha requires that one’s resolve regarding birth and death be urgent. First, sever external conditions and single-mindedly maintain the thought of the Buddha. Take the single phrase "Namo Amitābha Buddha" as the very root of one's life.
Never forget it from moment to moment, maintaining an uninterrupted continuity of mind throughout the two periods of day and night, whether walking, standing, sitting, or...

Whether lying down, picking up the spoon, raising the chopsticks, turning or bending, looking up or down, moving or still, at leisure or in haste—at all times—one is neither deluded nor obscured, and there is no other distraction.

If one applies the mind in this way for a long time until it becomes thoroughly proficient, such that even in dreams one does not forget or lose it, and waking and sleeping are as one, then the practice will be continuous and unified; this is what is meant by "the time of attaining power."
If one’s mindfulness reaches the state of single-mindedness without distraction, then at the time of death, the realm of the Pure Land will manifest before one.
One will naturally not be detained by birth and death, and will be moved by Amitābha Buddha to emit light to welcome and guide one.
This is the definitive efficacy for attaining rebirth there. While single-minded recitation is certainly the primary practice, it must also be supported by the cultivation of visualization.
Furthermore, one may see its stability and secrecy. For the sake of Vaidehī, the Buddha taught the sixteen sublime contemplations; thus, one can achieve completion in a single lifetime.
The present *Contemplation Sūtra* still exists. If you form a pure assembly to practice together, you may each follow your own aspirations among these sixteen contemplations.

Select any one visualization at will. One may visualize either the sublime marks of the Buddha or the Bodhisattvas, or contemplate the realms of the Pure Land, such as the jeweled ground of lotuses described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. Contemplate these according to your inclination.

If the visualization becomes clear and distinct, then throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, you will be present as if in the Pure Land—whether sitting, lying down, or walking—and whether with eyes open or closed, it will be as if before your very eyes.

If one achieves accomplishment through such visualization as described above, at the moment of death, a single thought will arise instantaneously. This is what is meant by: "As for birth, it is certainly born;
as for departing, there is truly no going. This is the sublime instruction on the Pure Land of Mind-Only. One should apply the mind in this manner.
If one upholds the precepts with diligence, the six sense faculties will become pure. If one forever severs evil karma and afflictions, the ground of the mind will become pure.
If mindfulness and contemplation succeed one another, wondrous conduct will easily be accomplished. There is nothing superior to this as the true cause for rebirth in the Pure Land.

If one merely speaks of reciting the Buddha’s name while seeking birth in the Pure Land, yet fails to maintain pure precepts, does not sever afflictions, and leaves the ground of the mind defiled—[such a person will not attain rebirth].
The Buddha said that such a person will never achieve success. Therefore, for a practitioner, the foremost requirement is to take the observance of precepts as the foundation;

making vows serves as the auxiliary cause; and the recitation of the Buddha’s name and meditative visualization constitute the primary practice. If one practices in this manner and yet fails to attain rebirth [in the Pure Land], [it is impossible].
Then the Buddha would fall into falsehood.

Regarding the instruction that the essential point of mindfulness of the Buddha and Chan meditation is to examine the public case (gong'an) of the Buddha's name: it means to single-mindedly hold up the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha" as the *huatou* (critical phrase), and then—

Regarding the point of raising [the inquiry]: this refers to the doubt raised below. To investigate thoroughly, one asks, "Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? One raises it again and investigates again;
investigating and investigating further, one asks, "Ultimately, who is it that recites the Buddha’s name?

By thus relying firmly upon the *huatou* (critical phrase), all deluded thoughts and miscellaneous discursive thoughts are instantly severed, like cutting tangled threads. They can no longer arise; wherever they might attempt to arise, they are immediately dissolved. Only...

There is a single thought, vividly and clearly solitary and luminous, like the midday sun in the sky. Deluded thoughts do not arise, and confusion naturally recedes. It is a state of profound stillness and alert clarity.

Master Yongjia said: "Profound stillness with alert clarity is correct; profound stillness without awareness is not. Alert clarity with profound stillness is correct; alert clarity with distracted thoughts is not.
This means that while being profoundly still, one does not fall into dullness or indeterminate consciousness (*avyākṛta*); while being alertly clear...
Do not fall into deluded thoughts; let the states of alertness and stillness flow as one, and abandon both sinking and floating.

When you see the place where not a single thought arises, the past and future limits are severed, and the middle is naturally solitary. Suddenly, having broken through the lacquer bucket, you will instantly behold your original face.
Then body, mind, and the world sink away instantly, like the falling shadows of flowers in the sky.
The ten directions become perfectly luminous, forming one great treasury of radiant light. Only at such a time is one truly "at home"; it manifests in daily life, vast and brilliantly clear.

There is nothing further to doubt; one begins to believe that one's own mind has been thus from the very beginning. The ground of self-realization of all Buddhas and patriarchs since antiquity is non-dual and without distinction.
Upon reaching this realm, one must not grasp it as a view of emptiness. If one grasps it as a view of emptiness, one falls into the evil views of external paths (*tīrthika*).

Nor should one form a view of existence, nor should one form a subtle or wondrous view of knowledge. It is simply this: *Note: The character [糸-八] (miāo) appears to be a variant or error for "wondrous" (妙).*
To have such views is to fall into false views. If, while in the midst of practice, various states of experience manifest, you must by no means become attached to them;
a single "Hah! will cause them to vanish. Do not fear evil states, nor do you need to rejoice in good ones. These are the demons of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
If you give rise to sorrow or joy, you will fall into the power of Māra. You should contemplate that these are merely manifestations of your own mind and do not come from without.

One should know that [the mind] is originally pure; within it, there is not a single thing. Fundamentally, there is neither delusion nor enlightenment, and it does not belong to the category of the holy or the ordinary.
How, then, could there be various objective realms? Now, because one is deluded regarding this original mind, one must apply diligent effort to wear away the habitual tendencies of ignorance.
If one awakens to the fact that the original mind is fundamentally without substance and is fundamentally luminous and vast, [all such realms vanish].
It is pure, serene, and tranquil; if one were to let it proceed spontaneously in this manner, what effort would there even be to perform?
People today merely believe that this mind is originally without any substance. They now apply effort solely because they have not yet seen their original face;
therefore, they must undergo a period of "deadly" effort before the time comes to arrive home. From...
Simply proceed directly in this manner; naturally, there will come a time when you suddenly see your original face.
Then, you will certainly transcend birth and death without any doubt.
This was written for the Chan practitioner Haike, who had pricked his own blood to transcribe the sutra.
The Chan practitioner resolved his mind to transcribe the five great divisions of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and specifically traveled to Mount Kuang to seek instruction.

The Elder then showed him this: "Vairocana dwells in the Ocean-Seal Samādhi and manifests inexhaustible clouds of bodies throughout the ten dharma-realms, preaching the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, which is named the *Sūtra of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm*. As for his primary retribution body, from every pore..."

In the midst [of this], light was emitted and it was said: "If one relies upon the world of retribution, even down to blades of grass, weeds, and minute particles of dust, then every particle speaks and every land speaks.
Such preaching continues until the end of the future, without interruption or rest.

Such sutras fill the entire Dharma-realm—namely, the Dharma-gate of a single word—which could not be exhausted even if written with the ink of the oceans. Now, you, with your limited body and mind, [are like] a mere drop..."

Even if one were to shed drops of blood from one's body, how could one ever finish writing it all? Nevertheless, if this sutra truly cannot be written down, then all sentient beings would be cut off from their share [of the Dharma].
Furthermore, it is said: "The sutra of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) means that everything within the Dharma-realm is none other than this sutra.
If one awakens to Vairocana and takes the Dharma-realm as one's own body, then one's own body and mind are likewise identical to the Dharma-realm.

This is precisely what is manifest in daily life: whether moving or still, speaking or silent, picking up the spoon or lifting the chopsticks, coughing, spitting, or swinging one's arms—all these are the great functioning of the Dharma-realm. Thus, when is it not a time for transcribing this sutra?
If the body is identical to the Dharma-realm, then every single pore is entirely pervasive. In this way, raising a single drop of blood [is equivalent to...].

It shall wither away together with the ocean of nature. Therefore, the Great Being Samantabhadra flayed his skin to make paper, split his bones to make pens, and pricked his blood to make ink, with a volume equal to the Dharma-realm.
Thus, the entire scripture does not issue from a single character; yet, when one character is written, it is the whole.
This is true even for a single complete scripture, let alone a hundred fascicles of text.

If a practitioner of Zen can contemplate in this way, then those who transcribe the text, those who see or hear it, those who prostrate and offer praise, those who present offerings of a single incense stick or a single flower, and even those who perform manual labor and exert physical effort—all will return together to the Dharma-realm. How could such merit ever be measured?
It is inconceivable. If a practitioner of meditation lacks such an eye yet engages in such practice, they will likewise fail to escape seeing flowers in the sky by pressing upon their eyes;
will this not further increase their inverted perceptions?
In the *Shi Caoxi Shamisheng Nenghua Shuhuayanjing* (Letter to the Śrāmaṇera Nenghua of Caoxi), it says:
"The Buddha-seed arises from conditions; therefore, the true cause of sentient beings—Buddha-nature—is inherently possessed.

Yet, because ignorance is so firmly entrenched, if one does not encounter virtuous conditions, it will ultimately never be awakened. It is like a seed in the earth, which requires the dew and rain [to sprout]."
Only through the conditions of the harmonious spring can sprouts emerge and stems develop, eventually leading to the blossoming of flowers and the ripening of fruit.
Before I, this old man, arrived at Caoxi, the novices practiced only worldly occupations; they did not even know there were Buddhas or monks, so how could they have known the Buddha-dharma?
It was only after I began to transform them through various skillful means—inducing, guiding, and instructing them—that they first came to understand.

He became a monk. Subsequently, considering that the Buddha-nature is difficult to clarify, he first taught the copying of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, so that people might know how to draw near to and accord with the Buddha-dharma.
Once faith was awakened, they could then be led into the Buddha-wisdom. Initially there were only two or three such individuals;
from then on, everyone vied with one another to resolve their minds [on enlightenment]. Within less than ten years, those who had copied this great sūtra already...
It formed more than ten schools. A thousand years have passed since the Sixth Patriarch entered nirvana; what occurs today is unprecedented in history.
Buddha-nature is inherently present in every person, and the merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are fundamentally possessed by all.

Yet, because they lack the guidance of wise teachers, everyone creates evil karma through their innate nature and incurs the bitter retributions of the three miserable realms. If one awakens to this Buddha-...
By nature, one transforms evil karma into the adornments of immeasurable pure lands. Now, this śrāmaṇera is able to transform;

he can take the very mind that creates karma and transform it into the adornments of a pure land, making it the true cause for attaining Buddhahood. This is what is meant by the "seed of wisdom" contained within the ground of the mind:
when it encounters the conditions of the rain of Dharma and the sun of wisdom, it is able to sprout the bud of bodhicitta and grow the roots of goodness.
Pluck the branch of merit and open the flowers of the myriad practices; in the future, you will surely attain the wondrous fruit of Bodhi.
This is precisely what is meant by "the seed of Buddhahood arises from conditions.

Whenever the Elder reveals the teachings of Caoxi to his disciples, if each person therein exerts themselves with vigor, gives rise to the unsurpassed mind, and possesses the resolve for the Buddha-dharma to investigate and clarify the great matter of their own person, then—
When the Sixth Patriarch dwelt in the world, those who realized their own minds among the thousands—how could they have been limited to merely thirty-odd individuals?
This was due to the merit of their successive transmission and instruction of the Dharma.

A Letter to the Zen Practitioner Xingchu Yuan The Zen practitioner Xingyu Yuan came to visit Mount Kuang. The Old Man gave him the name Xingchu. He made a vow to transcribe the Great Sutra (the Mahāyāna scriptures).
Thereupon, the Old Man instructed him, saying: "In the practice of leaving the household life, the Buddha taught many expedient means; it truly depends on each individual."
Each person’s resolve is simply different. The first type turns upward toward Chan meditation, seeking to clarify their own mind and resolving to end the cycle of birth and death.
The next type profoundly explores the ocean of the teachings, with the aspiration to propagate them widely, protect and uphold the True Dharma, and continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom.

The following type deeply loathes birth and death, focusing single-mindedly on pure karma and vowing to be reborn in the Western Paradise. These are all matters of principle and practice, and are considered the most superior.
As for this: although various forms of ritual practice exist, even the transcription of scriptures is one of the six types of Dharma-preachers praised by the Buddha.
Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states that a Dharma-preacher who upholds the sūtra attains purity of the six sense faculties in their physical body in the present life;
how could such a thing be compared to mere ritual acts? Furthermore, it says that "raising a hand or bowing the head, all have already attained Buddhahood. This...
How could such practice, which accords with the true nature (*dharmatā*), possibly be achieved through mere brushstrokes and ink marks?

In the past, when I, an old man, resided at Mount Wutai, I once drew blood and used gold leaf to transcribe the Great Avataṃsaka Sūtra. During the process of transcription, I did not restrict myself to the strokes, dots, sizes, or lengths of the characters;
rather, for every single stroke I laid down, I would recite the Buddha’s name once. In this manner, I continued dot by dot.
Painting, painting. The light of the mind flows forth, uninterrupted and unforgetting from moment to moment; it does not err and does not fall away.

After a long time, it no longer depends on whether one is writing or not writing, even unto the midst of dreams, where everything becomes a single seamless whole. Consequently, all objective realms [are thus transformed].
Amidst movement, turmoil, and clamor, his mind remains profoundly still, attaining the gate of liberation that is sovereign and unimpeded regarding all objective realms;
even all that is seen and heard is none other than the True Sutra manifesting before him.

To take this as proof, the practice of copying sutras is wondrously centered on a single, undistracted mind. How could it compare to children smearing vermilion ink, seeking merit merely through the act of copying?
Virtuous one, let the practitioner attempt to practice in this way: by writing thus and upholding thus, there may be some slight correspondence with the Dharma.
If, however, you consider mere calligraphy to be sublime conduct and seek fame and renown as a means to acquire offerings, then you are no better than an ordinary monk who subsists on rice gruel;
you would be a monk of no purpose. Strive diligently!
To the Chan practitioner Zhao Fanyong:
When you previously visited the Old Man at Wuyang, he once showed you the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Recently, you came to pay your respects at Mount Kuang;
I observed that while your resolve for the Way has become increasingly earnest, your work of investigation and cultivation has not yet reached full maturity, as you have not yet grasped it.
"It is merely to accomplish one great matter of reality. The old man then showed him, saying:
"When the ancients studied the Way, the first requirement was an urgent sense of life-and-death; it was not a matter of seeking subtle and wondrous principles. What is meant by 'life-and-death'?
It refers to the various realms of worldly toil that are present in our daily lives, where we encounter circumstances and conditions. If...

Whether contrary or compliant, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) within the inner mind draw forth active manifestations, giving rise to various deluded thoughts of discrimination—such as love and hatred, or grasping and rejecting.
Because one clings to objects of perception moment by moment, one initiates various karmic actions, both wholesome and unwholesome, which together form the roots and trunk of future birth and death.
Since deluded thoughts are boundless, birth and death are likewise without limit. Thus it is that sentient beings...
To wander through the ocean of birth and death for long kalpas without a time of emergence is truly due to the fault of not knowing one's own mind.
Thus it is said: "If you do not understand your own mind, how can you know the right path?

Throughout antiquity and the present, those practitioners who aspire to transcend birth and death seek nothing more than to clarify their own minds. Because this mind is consistently coarse and floating, it is like boiling water.
The flames of affliction are fierce; there has never been a single moment of cool clarity.

Therefore, the ancients established skillful means, using a kōan to teach practitioners to maintain it in every thought and investigate it. For example, when a monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?
or as Yongming instructed people to examine thoroughly, "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"—this very word "No" (wu) serves this purpose.

The word "Who" (shui) is the sharp sword that severs the life-root of birth and death. However, this investigation and examination of reality consists simply in scrutinizing this word "No" (wu) and this word "Who" (shui):
from where does it arise, and toward what does it fall? One must simply observe the place where this single thought arises and falls, seeking to see the root-source of its arising and ceasing.
If you investigate until you reach the ultimate point, take this single thought— [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated here.*
The delusory thoughts of arising and ceasing are severed; the lacquer bucket is shattered, and one suddenly beholds one’s original face.
Upon reaching this state, the nostrils of the Buddhas and Patriarchs above are all entirely within one’s own hands.
From this point on, one recognizes the person of the original source and no longer harbors doubts regarding Zhang San or Li Si. It is precisely one’s own natal destiny and primal spirit. Thus it is.
What subtle marvel is there to be sought? Furthermore, why must one seek it within the house of another? Yet, regarding this single point:
if it is not the initial resolve born of the urgency of birth and death, then no matter how many skillful means you employ, they are all the livelihood of ghosts.
Even if you possess a fragment of knowledge or insight, it is all the teaching of Māra. Whatever you do will be nothing but the work of Māra.
It is a pity that throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, such a great matter of causal conditions is so difficult to encounter.

If a practitioner of Zen truly aspires to this matter, they must take the clear, sharp, and wise insights from within their own breast, which have been cultivated through the truths of past lives, and apply them directly.
All various delusive thoughts are simultaneously brought together and resolved, returning to the single moment of thought.
Take a single phrase of the *huatou* as a precious sword suspended in the void to sever all prior delusions, like cutting through tangled threads.
If you can truly apply such a "poisonous hand" and exert such earnest effort, yet still fail to attain genuine awakening, then even the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past—[would be at fault].
This falls into falsehood. What is most to be dreaded is precisely the lack of a sincere heart;
it is merely using the practice of Chan as a mask to speak pleasant words.
Regarding the Chan practitioner Lichu Chong:

he was born and raised in Yuzhang and had long possessed an aspiration for the ultimate path. Having heard that the Old Man [Zhaozhou] was living in seclusion on Mount Kuang, he abandoned worldly attachments and came with a purified mind to attend upon him.
Consequently, he was retained to join the assembly, where he entered the room at regular intervals. After some time, [the Master] observed that he was... much.
His habitual tendencies were soft and warm, yet his bone-marrow vigor was not firm; thus, his resolve to enter the Way was not fierce.

He habitually exhorted himself for his shortcomings, and one day, while offering incense and seeking instruction, the Elder pointed this out to him, saying: "You possess the aspiration to turn toward the Way."
As for those who lack the spirit of resolute emergence, it is because their mental power is not pure; therefore, their bones are not firm.
Because their bones are not firm, they lack the will of steadfastness, courage, and valor. This is what is meant by "if there is no master within, one cannot stand.
The reason there is no master within is that, first of all, their mind of birth and death lacks reality; thus, they lack the determination to remain long-term without retreating.
As for resolve: since there is no resolute will, all one’s pursuits and conduct lack distinctive excellence.
Consequently, one follows old habits, drifting through the days and months, merely maintaining a state of leisure and idleness, taking it as self-evident that one is free and unrestrained.
Since one does not know how to examine the mind, one likewise lacks the strength to sustain this illusory body of the four elements; thus, in daily life—
At present, there is absolutely no genuine effort, nor is there any genuine realization.
From this day forward, you must first give rise to a sincere resolve for the sake of birth and death, establishing a firm and enduring vow never to retreat.
For the remainder of this life, you must resolutely investigate and clarify the great matter within your own person, ultimately reaching equality with the ancients.
A person who truly does not wish to辜负 (disgrace) this life must follow the ancients and take a single koan as the focal point for investigation.
Among these, the koan of Master Yongming’s "examining the reality of Buddha-recitation" is the most stable and reliable.
One should immediately cast aside all former habitual tendencies, views, deluded thoughts, and calculations from within the mind, letting them go completely until they are exhausted.
There is nowhere to let go; simply raise the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha. Then, examine the place where this thought arises, scrutinizing who it is that recites the Buddha’s name.
Recite while examining, and examine while reciting. Rely firmly upon this single thought.

When you thoroughly examine the point where power is gained, you will suddenly perceive the mind as being like a wall or a barrier. When you investigate until there is nowhere further to investigate, that is precisely the moment you gain power.

If you investigate in this manner for a long time, until the mind reaches a state of no further use—like a rat entering a cow's horn—then when a single thought suddenly bursts apart, that is the moment of liberation from birth and death. If you can do so, my son...
Apply your mind in this way and exert yourself with such diligence that your bones naturally become firm and your spirit fierce; such a person is called a preeminent man (*dhīra-puruṣa*).
Compared to the previously mentioned state of softness and warmth, the difference is truly many times greater than a day compared to an eon (*kalpa*). You must strive for this.
To the Zen practitioner Huijingxin:

When our Buddha preached the Dharma, he took the one mind as the fundamental principle. Regardless of the hundreds or thousands of dharma gates, they are all nothing other than practices for realizing the one mind.
Among these, the most essential are simply the practice of Zen meditation and the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Now, regarding Zen meditation, it is the method of this land...
The methods for awakening the mind established by the patriarchs of old consist of this very gate of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation).

This was taught by our Buddha to the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages and Ten Grounds as the essential means for attaining Buddhahood through *nien-fo*. Although Bodhisattvas of the Ten Grounds have already realized *tathatā* (suchness), is this not itself awakening?
Yet they all say: "Do not depart from recollecting the Buddha, recollecting the Dharma, and recollecting the Sangha. Thus did Sudhana...

He visited fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). The first was the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī, who bestowed upon him exclusively the gate of liberation through mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-vimokṣamukha*).
Finally, he met Samantabhadra as his spiritual friend for entering the state of *samyak-saṃbodhi*. Thereupon, he focused solely on dedicating his merit toward the Western Pure Land, saying:
"I shall personally behold the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Light, who will bestow upon me the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of Bodhi before my very eyes."

Viewed from this perspective, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra is the supreme One Vehicle, and its cultivation of practices in accordance with the Dharma-dhātu never departs from mindfulness of the Buddha from beginning to end.
Even the noble ones of the ten stages, who have already realized True Suchness (tathatā), do not depart from mindfulness of the Buddha;

yet, how can those deluded people of the final dharma dare to slander mindfulness of the Buddha as an inferior practice? How, then, can one doubt that meditation and mindfulness of the Buddha are different?
This is due to a lack of extensive learning; they do not understand the Buddha’s intention and merely give rise to false discrimination.

If one considers the Pure Land of Mind-Only, then when the mind is pure, the land is pure. Therefore, when first practicing Chan before attaining awakening, there is no way to purify one's own mind except through the recitation of the Buddha's name.
However, the purification of the mind is precisely the awakening of the mind. Once a Bodhisattva has awakened, they do not abandon the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).

Thus, without mindfulness of the Buddha, it is impossible to achieve perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). How could one know that the Patriarchs did not awaken to the mind through mindfulness of the Buddha?

If one practices mindfulness of the Buddha until reaching the state of "single-mindedness without distraction," afflictions (*kleśa*) are eliminated and one clearly realizes one's own mind; this is what is called awakening. As [it is said]:

This means that reciting the Buddha’s name (*nien-fo*) is itself the practice of Zen meditation (*chan*). If one is like a Bodhisattva, it means that after awakening, one does not abandon the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

Thus, the various patriarchs of the past all did not forsake the Pure Land in this manner; therefore, reciting the Buddha’s name is itself Zen meditation, and Zen meditation leads to birth in the Pure Land.
This has been a doubt unresolved since ancient times, but this teaching has completely shattered it; thus, Zen and Pure Land [are one].
Discriminatory views are thereby completely eliminated. Even the appearance of all Buddhas in the world does not differ from this teaching.
If one abandons this to produce other false discourses, these are all the teachings of Māra and are not the Buddha-dharma.
When I first crossed the mountain pass and arrived in Wuyang,
my disciple Xiuliuyi Gong immediately led his peers to take refuge [in the Triple Gem] beneath the Bodhi tree.
Even as we traveled south of the pass to Mount Nanyue and journeyed through Wu and Yue, he followed me through all hardships.
Amidst these hardships, twenty-five years passed from beginning to end without a moment’s respite.

When I retired to seclusion at Mount Kuanglu, Master Gong—whose resolve for the matter of life and death had always been urgent and whose aspiration was directed toward the sublime—also followed me to the summit of Mount Jinlun.

There he closed the "death-gate" for three years, single-mindedly upholding the one thought. Fortunately, he attained a ground of self-confidence. Now, with the Master Xing returning to his native mountains, I record this.
Holding up incense, he requested instruction. The elder then showed him, saying: "Leaving home is for the sake of birth and death; seeking the path that goes beyond is one's fundamental duty.

That a Zen practitioner remains at the 'dead gate' for three years—to let go of body and mind, to shake off adventitious dust and afflictions, and to wear away habitual tendencies—is the very first step.
Once you have gained confidence in this, simply continue your investigation."

The root of the disease of death has not yet been uprooted all at once. In the practice of Chan meditation, one must first recognize the root of the disease of birth and death before one can apply medicine for its treatment.
What is meant by the root of the disease of birth and death? Greed, anger, ignorance, and pride all take the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as their fundamental basis.
For all noble ones and ordinary beings alike, both types of birth and death arise from clinging to this self; yet, this self depends upon the view [of self].
To establish such views is deluded vision; it is the root of self-clinging and is called a thorn in the Dharma-body.
As long as this thorn of vision is not extracted, it is difficult to escape birth and death. Therefore, all ordinary beings cling to views of body and mind, self and others, and right and wrong;

all non-Buddhists perversely cling to false views; and the noble ones of the Two Vehicles cling to birth and death versus nirvana, indulging in preferences for the one and aversion to the other, and engaging in acceptance and rejection.
The views of all bodhisattvas consist of the perception that there are sentient beings to be delivered and a Buddha to be sought.
Even enlightened sages have not yet forgotten the view of a Buddha and the view of dharmas; thus, they possess two types of ignorance.

Furthermore, among the patriarchs' disciples, beginners who practice Chan meditation mostly first give rise to the view of awaiting enlightenment, and within their state of non-enlightenment, they falsely claim to have attained what they have not attained.

As for these views: when there arises even a single moment where the wild mind briefly subsides, one immediately clings to it as a sublime awakening and gives rise to the view that "having attained a little is sufficient.
One then seizes upon the words and phrases of the ancients, twisting them to fit one's own interpretations and clinging to them as subtle and wondrous views.
Accumulating these within the breast and refusing to spit them out, over time they ferment into a toxic medicine, leading to...

One may mistakenly fall into false views; even if one should have a single thought of sudden awakening that one's own mind is fundamentally devoid of any thing, one will again fall into the gateway of shadows and reflections, taking this to be the ultimate view. Therefore, Yunmen said:

"Even if you manage to reach the Dharma-body, because your attachment to dharmas has not been forgotten and your own [subjective] view still persists, you fall into the side of the Dharma-body—this is called 'clinging to the pole.'"

If one possesses even a trace of attachment or views, there will never be the realization of transcendence. In short, as long as even the slightest emotional or conceptual clinging has not been eliminated, it is all subsumed within the realm of arising and ceasing;
it is entirely the root of the disease of birth and death. Even if one were to attain awakening, it would still belong to the domain of birth and death.

Therefore, it is said that even the single word "awakening" must be spat out; how much more so when one has not yet attained full realization, but remains merely in a state of vague and hazy uncertainty?
They give rise to views and knowledge, considering themselves to have attained realization; they then take the ready-made words of the ancients and treat them as their own wondrous enlightenment.
All of this is falling into self-deception and is entirely not the work of true investigation and earnest study.
To apply the mind in such a manner is the fault of failing to recognize the root of the disease of birth and death. Therefore, an ancient worthy said: "Do not seek the truth; you need only..."
Cease the view. If you know that views have vanished, what need is there for "reality"? Therefore, the Buddha showed Ānanda:
"When the seeing sees, that seeing is not [the ordinary] seeing; even seeing is detached from seeing, such that seeing cannot reach it. This is the ultimate exhaustion of the source.
To take "seeing" alone as the root of the disease of birth and death is because false seeing arises from the Dharma-body;

by seeing the existence of body, mind, and the world, one sinks into birth and death. Therefore, to now eliminate seeing is to transcend birth and death and realize the ultimate principle of the Dharma-body.
Master Aśvaghoṣa showed people that the true cultivation and actual realization consist in the elimination of thought, for it is because of thought that [birth and death] exist.
If one perceives [the object], and upon its passing away one reflects on one’s own detachment, delusion will naturally subside.
Thus we know that while the disease-roots of afflictions such as greed and anger are shallow, the disease-root of the thorn of views alone is deep and most difficult to extract.

Therefore, through the practice of investigation, afflictions are easily severed, yet habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are difficult to eliminate. If habitual tendencies are not eliminated, deluded views will secretly nourish themselves; if deluded views nourish themselves, then...

Even if you have moments of awakening, they will all become habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), thereby forming demonic views. For this reason, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that the demons of views are the most profound, as they remain hidden and difficult to discern.
If a practitioner of Chan has the resolve to engage in genuine inquiry and authentic investigation, they must see through them directly;
by no means should one fall into the net of intellectual views. When it is time to apply yourself to the practice, simply take Zhaozhou’s [“Wu”].
The word "wu" (無). This is to be studied alongside the Sixth Patriarch’s “originally there was not one thing.
Before the word is even raised, first let go of body and mind, both internally and externally, all at once. Let go again and again until there is nothing left to let go of.
Then, look through to the bottom of this word "wu": ultimately, what scent or trace does it have? As soon as a single thought arises, at that very moment—
Look! Look closely at him. What, after all, is he? Thus settle yourself and establish your life. Rely firmly upon the *huatou* (critical phrase).
Drive deep and strike with pain. Do not shift for a single thought. It is like a rat gnawing at a coffin; there will naturally come a time of breakthrough.
You must by no means harbor the ancient *gong'an* cases and their words within your breast, only to bring them out later for comparison.

To speculate—to use the calculating mind—is immediately an error; it is by no means the realization of the ancients. As for ordinary moments when responding to conditions, simply rely firmly on the *huatou* (critical phrase);
with a vivid and solitary clarity, you will naturally not be shaken or snatched away by the winds of external objects.
Even when engaging in conversation with others, you must by no means take the ancient *gong'an* (public cases) as your own intellectual views to bolster yourself.

Idle chatter. This is a root of affliction that is most deeply entrenched. When one is in the midst of speaking, one seeks only immediate gratification, completely unaware that this is not one's own fundamental duty.
Thus, one lets the mind run wild and speaks recklessly, never once turning back to reflect or examine oneself.
For this reason, one does not realize it is a disease. If this ailment is allowed to fester, it will become the great demon of *māna* (arrogance). It is...
They are possessed by mad demons. What we see before our eyes today among the monastics and laypeople who favor Zen is everywhere like this;
one cannot help but be afraid. When the ancients practiced Zen, there was no other subtle mystery.

It was simply that they were willing to sweep away both worldly sentiments and saintly understandings all at once, leaving their chests empty and vacant, with not even a hair’s breadth of knowledge or views to act as a master.
When the executive officer [of the mind] no longer harbors cognitive views, true vision radiates its light, and one naturally realizes that not a single thing exists.
At such a moment of letting go, one's own single thought is like a great mass of fire;

all defiled emotions and habitual tendencies are incinerated upon contact, like a flake of snow on a red-hot furnace, leaving no trace behind. Looking back at all peripheral matters of cognition and view, they are likewise consumed.
It is as if one were merely dreaming. Thus it is said: "In the practice of Zen there is no secret method; it simply requires letting go.
If you let go for a single thought-moment, then that moment is true. If you let go in every thought-moment, then every moment is true.
If you let go thoroughly, then until the end of the future, you will be thoroughly true. You are now on your way; do not forget this instruction.
When he spoke these words, they were as if the eyebrows of the old man were knotted together; there was never even a hair’s breadth of separation between them.
Alas! The old man is aged; if he should fail this karmic connection and miss this lifetime, it is unknown how many millions of kalpas it would take before such a connection could be sought again.
Master Hye-gyeong demonstrated his wisdom by coming to the Eastern Sea, a land where the Buddha-Dharma had not been practiced.
Since Master Gwibong of Mount Lingshan began his work of transformation there, those who have abandoned heterodoxy to return to the orthodox path have been numerous.
When I, this old man, formerly resided at Haerin Temple, I marveled at the flourishing success of that master’s Dharma-benefits; his various disciples...
My son, those capable of preaching the Dharma are numerous. Now that you, a student of later years, have arisen, you are truly my legitimate grandson.
It has been twenty-eight years since I departed from Vulture Peak. Since the year of Xinyou, I came to Mount Kuang; after the new year, I took my leave to return to my old mountain.
You requested instruction on the essential methods for cultivating the mind, whereupon I showed you this: "That which the Buddha most censures is mental affliction."

The two kinds of obstacles—the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*)—constitute the root of birth and death. Among them, the obstacle of afflictions consists of greed, hatred, delusion, and craving;

these are the root of birth and death for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). The obstacle of the objects of knowledge consists of [obstructions regarding] the Buddha-dharma’s knowledge and vision; it pertains to the noble ones (*ārya*) of the three vehicles.
This is the very root of birth and death. If these two obstacles are not eliminated, there is no way for one to escape from the manifold sufferings. Alas!
It is certainly not surprising that those people of the present age who do not know the Buddha-dharma remain ignorant;

however, even among those who study the Buddha-dharma, some fail to sever their afflictions (*kleśa*), and moreover, they take the very dharma they have studied as an obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This causes the growth of self-conceit (*māna*) and further increases their afflictions, leaving their minds and hearts [defiled].
Defiled, with seeds activated and manifesting heedlessness, body and mind are utterly unrestrained; to act according to one's whims and create karma—is this not a great error?
Now that this student has heard the elder’s instruction, he realizes it concerns the momentous matter of birth and death, and has resolved to seek the fundamental practice.
This is indeed a most supreme power of aspiration; yet, regarding the current practice of inquiry: not...
Seek it separately. Simply take those habitual seeds already existing within your breast and cleanse them one by one until they are thoroughly purified.

Do not allow them to manifest as active states (*samudācāra*). Whenever you encounter objects or conditions in daily life, at the very moment a thought arises, see through it immediately and do not permit it to continue.
As for the application of the mind and the method of practice, it is exactly as described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

It is said that Avalokiteśvara’s faculty of the ear is the perfect penetration (*avivarta*). By reversing the mechanism of hearing and returning to hear one's own nature, this single gate of contemplation is the most excellent for applying the mind.
If, during daily activities in the midst of seeing and hearing, one can truly reverse the gaze to contemplate one's own nature, then one will not flow along with external objects.
If one thus reverses the stream moment by moment, then every thought-moment is a path returning to the truth. Thus should it be applied.
Regarding the mind: if habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not eliminated, they will manifest as active outflows (*samudācāra*), and one will certainly fail to gain power.

This entirely depends on the single point of opposing current karma; this constitutes the supreme practice. However, it is also essential that one’s concern for birth and death be urgent, for only then will one be willing to apply oneself with "deadly effort.
It is only when a student truly seeks liberation from birth and death and applies their mind with earnest sincerity that there is actual benefit. This is not mere talk.
To understand and then let it rest is to form a kind of Buddhist view and knowledge.
When the Elder went to the Wu region, he visited the layman Jingxin; Jingxin paid his respects and requested instruction. The Elder instructed him with the practice of mindfulness.
Regarding the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation: because it is like a "water-clearing pearl" that can purify turbid water, I have taken "Purifying the Mind" as my dharma-name for several years now.
In a letter you have recently sent, you say that your Buddha-recitation has not yet achieved single-mindedness, and you again request further instruction. In response, I tell you:
the foremost requirement for cultivation is a sense of urgency regarding birth and death. If this sense of urgency regarding birth and death is not keen, [cultivation will not succeed].

How can one dare claim that their recitation of the Buddha’s name has reached a state of continuity? Furthermore, for immeasurable kalpas, sentient beings have been possessed by delusive thoughts in every moment, their emotional faculties firmly shrouded.
Even though they have now attained birth in this world, they have never for a single thought-moment felt genuine pain regarding birth and death.

Day after day, moment after moment, they follow their emotions without ever reflecting back upon themselves. Now, wishing to sever the cycle of birth and death accumulated over many kalpas with such a superficial and floating faith—how could this possibly succeed?
To say that a single drop of water can extinguish a fire of piled firewood—how could such a principle exist?

If one truly feels an urgent sense of urgency regarding birth and death, and maintains at every thought-moment the intensity of someone whose head is on fire, one will only fear that once this human body is lost, it will be difficult to regain it for hundreds of kalpas.

One must firmly bite down upon this single sound of "Buddha" and resolutely confront delusive thoughts. When all manner of sufferings manifest before one’s mind at every moment, one must not be overcome by them.
Deluded thoughts act as obstructions. If one applies such diligent and earnest effort over a long period until it becomes thoroughly matured, it will naturally accord with reality.
Thus, without seeking to form a continuous state of mind, it spontaneously becomes one. This matter is like a person drinking water: whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves;
it cannot be told to others. It depends entirely on one's own exertion. If one merely takes the recitation of the Buddha’s name as a mere facade...
"Leather! Like this donkey's age, there will never be a time for its use. You must simply be courageous; do not hesitate any longer.

To the venerable elder Rentian, who upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—the Venerable Rentian who had recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for over twenty years—the Master spoke these words as he was about to go seek his instruction:
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the supreme One Vehicle, is the essential secret long preserved by our Buddha; it is the certificate for bestowing predictions upon his disciples.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "When the mind is deluded, the *Lotus Sūtra* revolves [around it]; when the mind is awakened, the *Lotus Sūtra* revolves [with it].

To recite the sūtra without understanding its meaning is to act as an enemy to its true significance. The Twenty-seventh Patriarch said: "Inhalation does not dwell within the realms of the aggregates; exhalation..."
Traversing through manifold conditions, one constantly turns such sutras as these, numbering hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, just as the two preceding patriarchs have described.
"O Benevolent Heaven, how ultimately do you uphold this sutra? The sutra says: "This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination.
If this is so, then even though the Sixth Patriarch may grant that he understands the meaning, he still has not yet upheld it. Furthermore, it says: "This sutra opens..."

This is a gate of skillful means to demonstrate the true mark of all dharmas. Thus, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, tiles, and stones are none other than the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Even the twenty-seventh patriarch could not maintain it apart from the inhalation and exhalation of breath.
If this is so, then how ultimately does benevolence sustain the heavens? As the Buddha taught in the "Chapter on Sustaining" (Dhāraṇī-paṭala):
even if one transmits and teaches this sutra to a fiftieth person through successive transmission, the merit is inconceivable.

Viewed from this perspective, the merit of transmitting the teaching does not depend on whether one understands the meaning or not, nor on whether one is free from or not free from worldly distractions; it requires only a single moment of faithful mind.

Knowing that one possesses this from the beginning, the life of wisdom is never severed. For this reason, the Elder most highly praised the Lotus Dharma Society, regarding the upholding of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as the sublime practice.
By hearing this sutra but once, one immediately plants the true seed for attaining Buddhahood.
Since Ren Tian used this to teach many others, enabling them to act as the Buddha praised—what dharma could possibly surpass this?

To show that the two practices of Chan and Pure Land are fundamentally not two separate dharmas: the Great Master Yongming demonstrated this long ago. It is established that the essence of Chan is the departure from discursive thought;
yet, regarding the Pure Land, there is the "Highest Grade of the Highest Birth," which is never practiced apart from this very departure from discursive thought. If...
It is said: "Recite the Buddha's name until you reach the state of single-minded non-distraction. Yet, how could there still be "recollection" (nian) present?

Although this state is indeed non-dual, when it comes to applying oneself to the practice, there is no lack of distinction between skill and clumsiness; for the point at which one applies the mind through investigation is most subtle and most profound.
When one is engaged in investigation, there is the state where not a single thought arises. If one speaks of "reciting the Buddha's name," then a thought of recitation has already arisen.
In this way, there would be no small amount of duality. By bringing the act of recitation into the very place of investigating recitation, they are forged into a single path.

Only when one desires that which does not arise to arise, and that which arises is itself non-arising, is this the true practice of Yongjia’s "the simultaneous flow of alertness and stillness. Why is this so?

If one discusses the practice of investigating the kōan by blocking the faculty of the mind and demanding that not a single thought arise—though this is indeed a method of investigation, the ancients called it "clinging to a post and rocking the boat. That very thought which one seeks to prevent from arising is itself already arising;
how could it truly be non-arising? It is just like the recitation of the Buddha’s name: if one takes a single utterance of "Buddha,"...
Keep this in mind; do not forget it for a moment. Is this truly "one mind undistracted"? The ancients taught people to investigate the "living word" (*huoju*) rather than the "dead word" (*siju*).
It is precisely at the point of arising that one perceives the non-arising of thoughts. As the Sūtra says: "Only those who perceive the *kṣaṇa* realize non-arising.
By means of these very words, the investigation of the Buddha-name can, in this very moment, become a single path.
Listen attentively, O practitioners. This method of investigating through *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) is prone to confusion and error; it must not be treated with negligence.
How is it that investigating is itself *nianfo*, and *nianfo* is itself investigation?

To investigate now, take the single phrase "Amitābha" as the *huatou* (critical phrase) and apply rigorous, authentic practice. Regarding one's own body and mind, the world, and all that has arisen from...
Completely set aside all worldly conventions, common parlance, and the intellectual views of the Buddha-dharma.
From within this state of empty emptiness and profound stillness, exert yourself to bring forth the single invocation of "A-mi-tuo-fo," making it vivid and distinct.
At the very moment you bring it forth, look directly at it; examine with certainty who it is that is reciting the Buddha’s name. Cast your doubt deeply once more.

Examine it again and again; doubt it again and again. Like a donkey looking down a well—looking and looking, doubting and doubting—doubt until you reach a place where the paths of thought are cut off, like a silver mountain or an iron wall, with no room to turn the body or draw a breath.
At that moment, suddenly bumping into it or touching it, the true state of non-arising manifests abruptly. At that time, all is penetratingly clear.
Sweat flows from my body; it is like awakening from a great dream. Only upon reaching this point do I believe that arising is non-arising, and non-arising is arising.

To investigate (*can*) is itself mindfulness (*nian*); mindfulness is itself investigation. Looking back with a turn of the head, I finally realize that all along I have been like someone seeking Chang’an while inside the Han-yuan Palace.
When practicing in this manner, one fears most of all trying to use the mind to seek enlightenment. As soon as there is a desire to be enlightened...
This very mind is the headboard itself. Simply continue practicing straight ahead without calculating the progress.
Even when you reach a point where you can do no more, rouse your spirit and begin anew from the start.
You must by no means crave subtle wonders; even if a thought momentarily ceases and there is a sense of stillness and joy, you must never regard this as a state of excellence.
You must simply spit it out. By all means, do not take the subtle words and wondrous phrases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and use them as proof, treating them as the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, you must not fall into the trap of "nothingness," taking this to be attainment. In short, regarding all holy ones and ordinary beings:
Neither delusion nor enlightenment is of concern; one simply pursues the point where the single thought-moment falls away.
Pursuing until one reaches the point of total exhaustion and eradication, after a long time, one will spontaneously see one's own original face. It is like seeing one’s father at a crossroads;
one no longer seeks him out by questioning others. Look at this matter: it is originally the fundamental duty of every person, and there is nothing more to it.
A Remarkable Place. The practitioner should, with true sincerity, take up the great matter of birth and death; if you attempt to begin from this point, you will certainly not be deceived.
