From the *Dream Travel Collection* of the Elder Master Hanshan, Volume Nine.
The Dream Travel Collection of the Elder Hanshan, Volume Ten.
Compiled by the attendant Fushan and the disciple Tongjiong. Section on Daily Records.
Revised by the disciple from Lingnan, Liu Qixiang,
based on the Dharma words shown to the Zen practitioner Yin.

In the past, at the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, our Buddha, wishing to entrust the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to those who would uphold it, commanded that it be received, maintained, and widely disseminated during the final age.

Although hundreds of thousands of beings, both humans and devas, immediately received their predictions of enlightenment, not a single one among his disciples dared to circulate this Dharma within the Sahā world; it was necessary to wait for those who would emerge from the earth.
To be able to shoulder and uphold this Dharma is by no means easy. In this world of five turbidities, sentient beings possess meager merit;
their natures are stubborn and they are most difficult to subdue. Therefore, in my Buddha-dharma, I teach that those who uphold this sutra must take patience as their foremost practice.
Thus it is said: "After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who wish to preach this sutra for the fourfold assembly..."
One should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat before one may extensively expound this sutra for the sake of the assembly.
The Tathāgata’s chamber is the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings. The Tathāgata’s robe is...
"A mind of gentleness and patience is it. That which is the Tathāgata’s seat is the emptiness of all dharmas.
Abiding therein, one may then, with a mind free from indolence, preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of the assembly.

Therefore, the Buddha personally recounted his own past conduct in seeking the Dharma, such as the enmity and harm caused by Devadatta throughout successive lifetimes, as well as [the story of] Sadāparibhūta.

They prostrate themselves before him. Whether the fourfold assembly reviles and insults them, or subjects them to various forms of suffering such as blades, staves, tiles, and stones, they joyfully endure it all without a single thought of weariness or retreat.
This is the true teaching for Bodhisattvas; it is the most supreme practice for upholding this sutra in the final age.
We, as disciples of the Buddha, if we lack the practice of patience, how can we uphold the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom? Let [it be so].
It is unceasing. Furthermore, regarding the Bodhisattvas who receive this entrustment and uphold the sutra, they take a vow, saying: "I shall be able to endure all manner of hardships.

For this reason, the Buddha taught that throughout the trichiliocosm, there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed where a Bodhisattva has not sacrificed their body and life in pursuit of bodhi, nor where they have not offered their head, eyes, marrow, or brain.

There is stinginess and attachment. Therefore, I teach those who uphold the sutras to first practice patience. Seeing that this is the final age of the Dharma, how else could one protect the Buddha-dharma and sustain the life of wisdom without the power of great patience?
An old man like me repeatedly instructs practitioners of Zen through the practice of patience.
If a Zen practitioner can have deep faith in an old man like me and likewise maintain themselves through the power of patience, they will not only be able to preserve it at the end.

The site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is where one also accomplishes one's own practice; one must by no means regard it through the ordinary perspective of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), nor seek any other dharma of birth and death apart from this.
Furthermore, this sutra was brought forth into the world by our Buddha, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the "one great cause and condition" (*ekamahā-kṛtyahetu*).
This "one great matter" is precisely the Buddha’s primordial wisdom and insight (*jñānadarśana*) that all sentient beings inherently possess.
Furthermore, "the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers to the ability to perceive the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

Because sentient beings are deluded regarding true knowledge and vision, they merely identify with the illusory and false body and mind composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), and thus fail to see the true reality. If one were to see this true reality, then throughout the three realms, from the highest to the lowest, not a single dharma would exist;
how, then, could birth and death have any place to lodge? If this is so, how could it be that [this realization] belongs to the practitioner alone?
If Chan can bring an end to birth and death, could the upholding of this sutra not likewise bring an end to birth and death?

If those such as Nanyue and Tiantai—both great masters who realized the ultimate reality (bhūtatathatā)—were among the practitioners of this dharma community reading and reciting this sutra, might there not be even one person [among them]?
For one who, like Tiantai, awakens to and enters the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, this single assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly as if it had not yet dispersed.
Thus, the person who protects and upholds this Dharma possesses inconceivable merits as vast as the sands of the Ganges.

For the sake of this Dharma, the Buddha has sacrificed his body and life through kalpa after kalpa and birth after birth; the practitioner of meditation is likewise able to sacrifice this single lifetime to achieve great realization.
This is the benefit of the Dharma. Why then should you look outward or seek elsewhere for the Buddha-Dharma?

Even if you cannot currently resolve the matter of birth and death, you may rely upon this Dharma as a vessel and sustain it through the power of your vows; thus, within the ocean of birth and death, you will certainly reach the other shore in the end.
This is far superior to the empty living and aimless dying of the past. Since you, O practitioner of Zen, have now placed your trust in the words of this old man, from this point forward—

One should give rise to the power of great patience and the power of great diligence; this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata, by which one accomplishes the Great Practice of Samantabhadra.
One must by no means give rise to a mind of arising and ceasing, establish views of self and person, or conceive thoughts of regression and decline.
I introduce the Chan practitioner Yuanben Jue of Xinxian Yangshan.
For over thirty years, Yuanben Jue has revitalized the Yangshan Dharma center, manifesting various kinds of magnificent adornments through the power of his own mind.
He has also recited the *Nirvana Sūtra* and the *Brahmacarya Sūtra* for more than twenty years, maintaining pure conduct with great diligence. All of this—

Following his long-standing practice of Prajñā, he now paid homage at Kuangshan to request the bestowal of the full precepts (*upasampadā*). He offered incense and requested an exposition on the profound meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (the *Yuanjue jing*).
The Elder then instructed him, saying: "The Buddha taught that all phenomena within the three realms, whether superior or inferior, are created solely by this one mind."
That which is called Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa) flows forth all pure *tathatā*, bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the *pāramitās*, instructing the Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, for a disciple of the Buddha, if one realizes the Dharma-gate of Mind-Only, then all causes and effects of defilement and purity will manifest before one;
they transform from moment to moment. Thus it is said: "If the mind is pure, the Buddha-field is pure. Directly...

As in the case of the causal conditions of Yangshan, what was previously nothing but perilous crags and steep precipices, overgrown with wild brambles and thick grass, has now, in a single day, been transformed into this Dharma-hall as if it had descended from heaven.
All of this results from that initial single thought of firm, resolute faith;
thus such vast and magnificent Buddhist activities are brought to fruition. Viewed in this light, how could the Western Pure Land possibly be attained outside of the mind?
I, this old man, now bestow upon you, practitioner of Zen, the Vajra Jewel Precepts of the Brahma Net Sūtra.
These precepts are known as the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground of Vairocana. As the Sūtra states: "If one receives the Buddha-precepts, one immediately enters the rank of all Buddhas.

Thus we know that a single thought of faith immediately opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and all Buddha-lands manifest before one's mind in an instant. Therefore, the pure lands of all Buddhas...
All lands are established from the adamantine ground of the mind.

If a practitioner of meditation can truly understand this dharma-gate, then from this point forward, in every aspect of daily life and all activities, they will clearly and vividly know that everything flows forth from their own mind.
Thus, every phenomenon (*dharma*) becomes a true cause for the Pure Land.

Furthermore, if one can chant "Namo Amitābha Buddha" with such mindfulness that it is never forgotten and the mind remains ever-awake, until the point where thought and movement are non-dual and waking and sleeping are as one, then every step taken in the present moment is treading upon the Pure Land.
Walking upon the jeweled ground with this very body and mind, one has already sat within the womb of a lotus flower. Directly...
When the time comes to end one's life, as soon as this body is cast off, one will see the Buddha upon the blossoming of the lotus flower, like awakening from a dream.

Only upon reaching this state does one finally realize that birth and death are like dreams and the Pure Land is like an illusion. Within a single thought-moment, one dwells forever in the stage of non-retrogression.

Beyond this, what other method could there be for transcending birth and death? Although you, practitioner of Zen, have long cultivated pure conduct, you have merely not yet personally heard the teachings of the One Who Knows Well.
Consciousness! Break through the delusive dreams of the past; simply realize that all phenomena are but mind. What need is there to seek the Buddha-dharma elsewhere?
Strive with diligence and cherish this!
Thus it was shown to the good man Chen.

The region of Chu and Mian is renowned as a distinguished commandery; it was formerly a land of literary excellence and constitutional virtue. However, those who were transformed by the presence of virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) within the Dharma-gate were rare.

Now, the Chan practitioner Guanzhi has arrived here with his monk’s staff and remained behind closed doors for three years, during which time many have been moved to follow his transformative influence.
This recently arrived virtuous person is, in fact, a long-standing disciple who took refuge in him with faith. He has traveled from afar to consult the Elder of Mount Kuang, seeking his instruction.
He showed it and transmitted it to the great assembly. The elder then pointed to it and said:

"When the Buddha dwelt in the world, men and women at home who were able to uphold the five precepts—namely, not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking alcohol or eating meat—"
They are always present at Dharma assemblies as upāsakas and upāsikās—terms translated here as "male and female lay followers"—because they are capable of drawing near to and serving the Triple Gem.
As for their practice, they diligently observe the five precepts to avoid falling into the miserable realms of the three evil paths.
This constitutes the merit of devas and humans. Therefore it is said: "If one does not uphold the five precepts, the path to the realms of humans and devas is cut off.
If one upholds the five precepts, first and foremost, one must clearly believe in cause and effect. The retribution for good and evil follows like a shadow follows a form.

This means that by creating a virtuous cause, a fortunate result will certainly arise in the human or heavenly realms; whereas by committing an evil cause, an evil result will inevitably lead to a fall into the three miserable paths of suffering. Furthermore, observe the world...
Those who hold high offices and noble titles, and who possess wealth, honor, and prosperity, must have cultivated merit in previous lives by making offerings to the Triple Gem,

providing vegetarian feasts for the Sangha, practicing charity, printing scriptures, casting images, repairing temples, building stupas, relieving the poor, and uprooting suffering. As for those who enjoy longevity and many sons,

whose fathers are kind and sons are filial, whose husbands lead and wives follow, and whose elder brothers are friendly and younger brothers are respectful— these are likewise the results of such virtuous deeds.
This must surely come from practicing the release of living beings and abstaining from killing, and from observing the precepts of fasting.

Among those living as householders, if there are those who can uphold these five precepts, then the Five Constant Virtues are complete within them: namely, not killing is benevolence (*ren*); not stealing is righteousness (*yi*); and not committing sexual misconduct is propriety (*li*).
Not speaking falsely is faith. Not drinking alcohol is wisdom. A Confucian who can achieve this becomes a gentleman of perfected virtue.
Is observing the fast not something beyond one's ordinary duties? Among them are those of superior intelligence and lofty brilliance;

having already maintained these precepts, they further contemplate that human life is impermanent, like a candle in the wind. They dread birth and death, for once one loses this human body, it is difficult to regain.
Ten thousand kalpas may pass before such a state can be restored. Reflecting thus and contemplating the suffering of birth and death, one should develop an earnest resolve to seek liberation.

Furthermore, it is fitting to arouse the bodhicitta and recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. One should hold this single phrase of the Buddha’s name across the chest, maintaining it without interruption in every thought.
Never forgetting this in mind, they worship the Buddha and recite the sutras morning and evening, dedicating their merit toward the Western Quarter and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.
If one recites the Buddha’s name until a single thought becomes pure and matured, and the mind remains undistracted, then at the moment of death, one will behold Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddha emits light to welcome and guide them; they entrust themselves to a lotus flower, taking it as their parents.

When the flower opens, they behold the Buddha, and from this point on, they forever transcend the suffering of the cycle of birth and death, taking a long farewell to the three realms. This is what is called a Bodhisattva.

This practice of mindfulness of the Buddha has been undertaken by laypeople, both men and women, throughout the past and present. Many have achieved their goal in a single lifetime and been reborn in the Western Pure Land. Therefore, it is said: "Only..."
There is a direct path of practice: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. To seek anything else besides this is entirely a wrong view and a wrong practice.
If virtuous people uphold this and convert their kind—whether it be one person, one family, one village, one district, or a great capital—it shall become a Buddha-land.
One need only strive in practice; provided that one’s faith is sincere, even a single thought-moment [is sufficient].
Practice accordingly; there is no need to seek elsewhere for the wondrous Buddha-dharma.
As it was said to Laozi when he was flourishing in the lotus-born state: "My great affliction is that I have a body. If I had no body, what affliction would I have?"—thus it is perfectly complete.

The *Jue jing* (Sutra on Awakening) says: "This body of mine is a composite of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). One should contemplate that within the body, what is solid and hard returns to earth;

what is moist and wet returns to water; the warmth returns to fire; and the movement and transformation return to wind. When these four elements have each separated, where will this deluded body now abide?
If one contemplates in this manner until the mind becomes long-term and thoroughly matured, the physical form will suddenly become empty, and various afflictions...

Afflictions all arise from deluded thoughts and inverted views. Just as dreams and inversions are fundamentally non-existent, when afflictions arise, one should directly contemplate this mind’s deluded thoughts:
from where do they arise? By tracing them back to their original state of non-arising, deluded thoughts will not arise.
When deluded thoughts do not arise, afflictions become empty. When body and mind suddenly become empty, then all afflictions [will likewise vanish].

The lower [afflictions] will be extinguished. By maintaining mindfulness, one shall immediately enter the Cool and Utterly Blissful Land. This contemplation is of vital importance; it is the wondrous medicine for liberation from suffering.
However, this contemplation is not easily accomplished by a beginner. One should simply take up the phrase "Amitābha Buddha" as a rigorous *huatou* (critical inquiry).
Be earnest and never forget this. When delusive thoughts arise, raise up the *huatou* (critical phrase) and apply pressure; then the delusive thoughts will extinguish themselves of their own accord.

Because one lacks right mindfulness in ordinary circumstances, one exclusively pursues delusive thoughts, flowing and turning through them, with攀緣 (*pān-yuán*, clinging to objects) never ceasing, thereby nourishing suffering.
All phenomena arise from the mind; there is no dharma outside the mind. If you do not contemplate the mind, yet seek [enlightenment]...
To escape the path of suffering is like taking a step backward while seeking to move forward; one need only arouse a mind of courageous vigor.
By no means should one say "I cannot," for that is merely self-defeat.
I address Wu Qi and Gao Qi:

You have long since taken refuge in the Triple Gem and maintained a vegetarian diet for many years. Now you have come to Mount Kuang to seek the conferral of the precepts and become a disciple of the Dharma, thereby establishing the conditions for liberation in future lives.
For this reason, I have named you Fuchang and titled your residence Jingxin (Pure Mind).
The gentleman was then conferred the Upāsaka precepts. He further offered incense and requested further instruction. The Elder thereupon showed him, saying:
"All the various karmic activities of the mundane world are impermanent; they all serve as causes for suffering.

Consequently, one is reborn in the Sahā world-system, which is a gathering place for sentient beings and is thus named 'Endurance' (Kṣānti). Foolish and deluded people take suffering to be pleasure, thereby further nourishing their greed."
Craving further increases the root of suffering; not knowing the essential means for escaping suffering is what constitutes perversion (*viparyāsa*).

Therefore, if there is even a single thought among the people of the world that recognizes this as impermanent, suffering, and empty, and gives rise to the resolve to seek liberation, such a person is one of great wisdom.
If there is but a single moment of introspection that awakens a mind of wearying revulsion toward suffering, that itself is the path out of suffering.
If one possesses even a single thought of the aspiration to seek birth in the Pure Land, this is itself the root of attaining Buddhahood.
Therefore, the Buddha taught the precepts, instructing people to cease evil and cultivate goodness. When evil is ceased, the mind becomes pure; when goodness is cultivated, suffering is extinguished.
When suffering is extinguished, merit increases; when the mind is pure, it becomes the cause for the Pure Land; when suffering is extinguished, it becomes the foundation of Sukhāvatī.

When merit increases, it results in the fruit of eternal bliss. Thus we know that by giving rise to the thought of receiving the precepts for even a single moment, all sufferings can be severed, all merits can be accumulated, one can escape from birth and death, and one can be reborn in the Pure Land;

all of these proceed from that initial single thought, as the resolve to awaken serves as the causal ground. Since you, Layman, are now able to understand this matter and give rise to this mind, therefore—
Whatever you do is itself a practice that transcends the world. Although you have not yet left the household life, you are already called a child of the Buddha.

From this moment on, by means of the fruit [of the path], recite the Buddha’s name with a mind of upholding the precepts. Purify the latent defilements within the mind—the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, and craving—and thus the ground of the mind will become pure.
With this pure mind, recite the Buddha’s name without ceasing; let it not be forgotten from moment to moment, maintaining an uninterrupted continuity of thought after thought.
They manifest immediately in the present; every single thing is a cause for the Pure Land.
Thus, all the various offerings of the four requisites made to the Triple Gem serve as the resources for adorning the Pure Land. As it is said: "When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.
This land of the mind is the self-nature of Amitābha, which is fundamentally not separate from one's own single thought-moment. This is the reality.
This is the practice of the Dharma, which is what is called the merit of true permanence; it arises from a pure mind, and for this reason it is so named.
Lay brother, if you can indeed believe with certainty and without doubt, what need is there to seek the Buddha-dharma elsewhere? You must simply not engage in ordinary worldly affairs;
if you keep this in view, your aspiration for the Way will naturally become firm and your faith will grow day by day. Take care, take care.
To the Zen practitioner Wuzhijian, who has left the household life:
First, you must understand that leaving home, severing attachments, and bidding farewell to kin is fundamentally for the purpose of seeking liberation from birth and death.
Regarding this great matter of birth and death, you must know that all phenomena in the world are the root of suffering, and the body itself is suffering.
To gather [the conditions for liberation], it is essential to resolve to practice and seek the path out of suffering. First, one must see through the current state of body and mind.
One should contemplate this body as a provisional form composed of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind.
When these four elements separate, where will this delusory body then be? Once seen through in this way, one will no longer strive for the sake of this body.
One must next penetrate through and see through the various pleasures of sensory enjoyment. Whatever is presently seen, heard, known, or perceived is entirely the functioning of deluded thoughts;
it is not the true mind at all. By means of this deluded mind, one creates all manner of karma. Every stirring of thought and every movement of intention is nothing other than karma;
it is nothing other than transgression. This very single thought-moment is the root of the suffering of birth and death. One must by no means follow it.
His delusive thoughts flow on incessantly. Day by day, he should closely and secretly observe the very place where delusive thoughts arise;

as soon as they appear, he must see through them and extinguish them instantly. By no means should he follow their continuity, allowing his攀緣 (pān-yuán—clinging to objects) to go forth without returning.
If his observation is unstable and he lacks a firm grasp, he should simply take the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha" as his *huatou* (critical phrase), holding it fast and securely.
Maintain this mindfulness at all times. With this *huatou* as your master, whenever you perceive a delusive thought arising, immediately bring forth the Buddha.
This is for the sake of bringing right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) to the fore; then, delusive thoughts will vanish of their own accord without needing to be dispelled.

In this manner, throughout the two-and-six periods of the day and night, apply yourself with constant and subtle diligence, making this single thought your sovereign. All other delusive thoughts [will likewise subside].

This is for the sake of the guest. When guest and host are distinguished, and after a long time this becomes thoroughly matured, deluded thoughts will naturally vanish and the true mind will naturally manifest.
If a practitioner of Zen truly has the resolve regarding the great matter of birth and death, they should take only this single thought as real;
all other worldly arts and skills—composing poetry, calligraphy, and even pursuing sensory objects, socializing, or wandering about—are all [delusions].

This is the work of perverse delusion. If one does not aspire to actual practice but devotes oneself solely to empty frivolity—indulging the six sense-faculties and engaging in groundless chatter—one will vainly waste one's time;
not only will one live and die in vain, but one also fears that evil karma will be difficult to escape.
For a thousand lifetimes and a hundred kalpas, there will be no time of emergence.

To Xu Qingzhi, he showed that the Buddha’s teaching on the upper and lower realms of the three worlds is created solely by the one mind. He said that what is called the "upper" of the three worlds is precisely the transcendence of the world.
The four types of noble ones refer to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.

Those below the three realms are the ordinary beings of the six paths, namely the three wholesome paths of devas, humans, and asuras, as well as the three unwholesome paths of hell-dwellers, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Thus, within the ten dharma-realms, all noble and ordinary beings, the causes and effects of good and evil, and the adornments of the primary and secondary [realms], all arise from one [mind].
It is created by the mind. Yet this single mind is not something separate; it is the very mind of discrimination and cognition that is present in our daily lives.

Since everything arises from the mind, it is not produced through a gradual sequence, but rather consists of the karma performed in every thought-moment as it manifests in daily life, causing one to circulate through the ten realms of existence.
If even a single thought is produced by greed, hatred, or delusion...
The ten unwholesome paths of action—three of the body, four of speech, and three of the mind—are the causes for rebirth in the three miserable realms.
If one turns these ten unwholesome acts into the ten wholesome ones in a single thought-moment, they become the cause for the sublime bliss of humans and devas.

If, in a single thought-moment, one forgets both good and evil, seeing neither a self within nor another person without, and the single mind is tranquil, this constitutes the [cause] of the Śrāvaka...

Hearing the causes for escaping suffering, if one contemplates that the present joys and sorrows, adversities and favors, arise and cease through causes and conditions, and undergo the cycle of transmigration and cessation,
this constitutes the cause for becoming a Pratyekabuddha. If, in a single thought-moment, one realizes that persons and phenomena lack selfhood (*pudgala-nairātmya* and *dharma-nairātmya*),
that their nature is empty and devoid of an agent or recipient, yet without obstructing the actual practice of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience within the six realms—
To practice the transformation and deliverance of sentient beings constitutes the cause for becoming a bodhisattva.

If, in a single thought-moment, one suddenly awakens to the fact that one’s own mind is originally luminous and vast, encompassing all without exception and saving all without exception, and realizes that not a single dharma exists to engage the mind, such that the states of birth and buddhahood are equal, this constitutes the cause for attaining buddhahood. Therefore, this single mind is vast and without exterior; it is originally pure.

This is the perfection of luminosity. If one awakens to this in every thought-moment throughout the day, then even while dwelling amidst the dust and toil of the world, one becomes a person who has transcended the world.
This is why Vimalakīrti called it the "Dharma-door of Non-duality.
If a layperson can embody this in their conduct, then all enmity and favor, right and wrong, self and other, as well as afflictions and the roots of emotion, will be transformed in an instant.
This is the Treasury of Radiance. In all circumstances encountered in daily life, try to observe this; remain alert and aware in every thought-moment.
If you cannot maintain patient endurance, you will be obstructed by afflictions (*kleśa*).

As soon as you perceive their arising, immediately bring up the Sixth Patriarch’s phrase, "Originally there is nothing," like the Vajra King’s precious sword; then all afflictions will instantly freeze.
It vanishes; the body and mind are transformed into a pool of cool clarity.
If one practices with such vigor and can persevere without retreat, then one will suddenly realize the field of great liberation. What need is there, then, to seek the Buddha-dharma elsewhere?
He instructed the practitioners of Chan, saying:
"Practitioners of Chan, let us gather our like-minded companions at East Chan Monastery by the Golden Sands to establish the Blue Lotus Society.

Our primary practice shall be the recitation of the Lotus Sūtra. All who wish to join the society must first master this sūtra through thorough reading and be able to recite it from memory before they may enter."

Within a few years, there were several dozen who were able to uphold it; though their comings and goings were not uniform, only the Chan practitioners remained single-minded and unwavering, eventually making this their practice for as long as they lived.
When they requested further instruction from the Elder, he showed them [the scripture] and said:
"This sutra is that which our teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, specifically revealed to sentient beings—the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—for the sake of attaining Buddhahood."

Because they possess the true seed, their past causes are recounted: namely, that at the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, they were sixteen princes who heard this sutra and transmitted it from one to another.
Consequently, all those who have ever heard it from them will surely be born together in the same place throughout every lifetime, for they take the upholding of this sutra as their practice.
Those who received transformation in the past continue until this present life at [the site of] Ling...
At the mountain assembly, each was granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood; he then specifically revealed that this sutra is the true seed and the direct cause for achieving Buddhahood.
Therefore, he explained in detail the method for upholding the sutra: namely, that within the six sense organs produced by one's parents in this present life, [the Buddha-nature resides].
One will certainly attain purity, as clearly elucidated in the sutra and personally proclaimed by the Golden Mouth; it is no empty word.
Since this sutra entered the Middle Kingdom, many have received and upheld it, yet among them, only the Great Master Sita of Mount Nanyue attained a profound and subtle realization.
When the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai recited this sutra, he beheld the assembly on Vulture Peak as if still present and undispersed. Master Si...
It is said: "This is the Lotus Samādhi. None but you could realize it; none but I could recognize it.

Therefore, Tiantai relied upon this to establish the wondrous gate of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight), elucidating the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses.
Those who have since awakened to and clarified the one mind by relying on *śamatha-vipaśyanā*—such as Yongjia and others—are not merely one person. Thus, we know that this sutra..."

It is clear that this is the sublime practice for attaining Buddhahood. Only the Sixth Patriarch said: "When the mind is deluded, it is turned by the Lotus Sutra; when the mind is awakened, it turns the Lotus Sutra.
This further demonstrates the gate of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*) for those who uphold this sutra.

Now, as you practitioners uphold this sutra, try to suddenly open the true eye at the crown of your head before even unrolling the scroll, thereby piercing through ignorance and [realizing] the reality of all phenomena.
When the sensory spheres are illuminated through clarity, one perceives forms and hears sounds as direct realization before one’s eyes.

If one can thus recite this single scroll of the True Sutra, the seeds of attachment, aversion, and affliction accumulated throughout kalpas within the field of the eight consciousnesses will be instantly transformed entirely into the Treasury of Radiance.
To uphold it in this manner is true diligence; it is the clear and true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata.

If one considers mere paper, ink, and written words to be the wondrous Dharma, and regards the recitation of a few characters as the upholding of a sutra, yet the mind-ground remains unpurified and afflictions remain unemptied—how is this different from mistaking water bubbles for mani-jewels or steaming sand for the basis of rice?
In such a case, the ox-hide has not even been pierced; how could it be anything more than a mere attempt to shield one's eyes?
To the Chan practitioner Xue Dao-ren, who contemplates with the wisdom of clouds:
Make a vow of equal mind to die for the sake of the primary meaning of transcending birth and death. Furthermore, letting go is the essential requirement for entering the Way.
As the ancients said: "The will should return to one point; if one does not retreat after a long time, one will surely know the wondrous Way on another day."
The place of refuge. These five dairy products are the site where the old man returns to truth. Zen practitioners take refuge in the mind of the old man; one lifetime is spent here.
Now, fortunately, there is this place for planting a single awl—this is precisely where you all shall lay down your bodies and lives.
While alive, practice together; when dead, return together. You should let go of all external conditions and remain single-mindedly tranquil. At...

I have gathered two or three like-minded companions here. The elders shall focus their minds on the recitation of the Buddha’s name and diligently cultivate the practices for the Pure Land, vowing to persevere until death.
In this way, the Way of the Dharma will endure and the life of wisdom will not be severed; thus, they will not fail the thought of taking refuge.

You should reflect that your ancestor, Lord Rokuhō (Yoshida Kanemitsu), shared a bond spanning three lifetimes with the Elder. You ought naturally to take righteousness as your foundation and remain steadfast in this. There is absolutely no [room for doubt].
Second, mindfulness. If one maintains only a single thought, one is not truly a person engaged in the cycle of birth and death.

In ordinary daily life, one must strive to take the Dharma as one's core concern, acting as the guiding pillar of the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), harmonizing the assembly, making the internal and external one body, and ensuring that guest and host share a single mind.
Furthermore, forget both self and others; utterly sever right and wrong. To realize that afflictions are fundamentally empty is itself the path for transcending birth and death.
This very state of mental clarity and coolness is the essential gateway to the Pure Land. Strive in this! Exert yourselves!
To demonstrate the essentials of the practice of Buddhas and Patriarchs for those who have accumulated and mastered Chan, there are only two gates: Chan and Pure Land.
Adorned with the myriad practices, these constitute the path of correct cultivation. Lately, among students, those who study Chan are many; yet they are led astray by the errors of false teachers.
To see such dense thickets of delusion, to fall under the sway of the demon of self-conceit (*asmimāna*), and to increase the ranks of the heterodox—this is truly a cause for great concern.
How much more so when not one in ten attains the state of liberation! This is not merely a matter of self-deception; it also leads others astray. Is this not something to be feared?

For this reason, I, an old man, exert all my strength to advocate for the true cultivation of the Pure Land. Yet the people of the world do not understand this, treating it with utter contempt as if it were something ordinary.
It is because they do not understand the subtlety of nianfo (reciting the Buddha's name) that many errors arise. Furthermore, nianfo is itself the practice of Chan meditation;

there are no two separate dharmas. When practicing nianfo, one must first cast aside all afflictions, delusory thoughts, greed, anger, ignorance, attachment, and all manner of chaotic mental states within one’s own breast.
One should let them go until there is nothing further to be discarded, and then focus solely on—

Simply bring forth the single invocation of "Amitābha Buddha. Let it be vividly clear and uninterrupted within the mind, like beads strung on a thread, or like the nock of an arrow resting upon the shaft.
With not even a hair’s breadth of gap between them, exert yourself in this way and remain steadfastly settled.
At all times and in all places, do not allow yourself to be led astray or lose your focus by external conditions. Practice in this manner throughout daily life, remaining undisturbed amidst movement.

Without confusion amidst the manifold, remain as composed in dreams as in waking. Applying the mind in this manner, when the time of death arrives, to maintain single-mindedness without distraction is precisely the moment for transcending birth and death and attaining the Pure Land.

If one merely speaks the name of the Buddha with the mouth while the heart remains impure and delusive thoughts are not eliminated, claiming that the practice of *nien-fo* is ineffective—then even if such a person reaches the sixth rebirth after three lifetimes, [the goal will not be attained].
Even after ten kalpas, there would still be no prospect of emerging from it; therefore, you must exert yourself.

In response to the inquiry of King De, the messenger conveyed the King’s instruction, asking: "I have heard that the mountain monk practices a direct and swift Dharma-gate. May the King already be able to..."
He observed the precept against killing and maintained a vegetarian fast for three years. He thought only that his final moment was the most urgent matter.

"What Dharma should be practiced so that one may meet death with peace and ease, and not be deluded in future lives? This, indeed, was due to the Great King’s past habituation; his roots in Prajñā were deep.

Having cultivated these practices over many lifetimes, you now occupy a position of wealth, honor, and authority. Yet, do not obscure that original single thought-moment; earnestly seek the essential Dharma.
This mountain monk is dull and inferior, yet I dare speak with sincerity: when the Buddha preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, it was like medicine prescribed according to the ailment;
the skillful means were manifold and not of a single kind. Since the teaching flowed into this land, it has been relied upon and honored by those of all ages as they have practiced it.

Regarding the practitioner, there are two approaches: meditation (*dhyāna*) and instruction (*śāsana*), through which all people pass. As for meditation, the various patriarchs of the "transmission of the lamp" valued only the direct realization of one's own mind.
Their method of practice involved single-mindedly maintaining a *hwadu* (critical phrase) to investigate it, continuing until they clearly perceived their own mind, at which point they would cease.
This was intended solely for those of the highest faculties, who enter directly with a single leap; furthermore, they must be skillful...

If one constantly disciplines, protects, and rouses oneself through wisdom, only then will one find the correct path. Among kings and ministers of old, there were indeed those capable of this, yet such individuals were not many.
This is because it is easier for those who have left the household life to practice; now, Your Majesty dwells in profound seclusion.
It is not easy to meet with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); therefore, I did not dare to urge you on by means of this.

As for those who practice according to the teachings, there was formerly the Tiantai Master Zhiyi, whose *Great and Small Calm and Contemplation* (*Mohe zhiguan* / *Xiaozhiguan*) constitute the essential gateway to attaining Buddhahood.

While the text of the *Great Calm and Contemplation* is extensive and difficult to comprehend, the *Small Calm and Contemplation*, though concise and simple, provides a clear and lucid explanation of its essential points.
The "Easy Mind-Settling" (Shouxin Anxin) is likewise not easy to enter. Even if one can understand it and practice it, it is difficult to attain its intimate realization.
When it comes to daily life, it is frequently of no use in the face of adverse or favorable circumstances; how much more so regarding the great matter at the end?
This Dharma is not something that even Your Majesty can easily practice, and I do not dare to recommend it. Now, there is only the Buddha’s teaching of the Western Pure Land.
This single gate exclusively takes the single practice of mindfulness of the Buddha as its essential core.

It takes the contemplation of the pure realm as its primary practice, the recitation of Mahāyāna sūtras as its catalyst, the making of vows as its direction, and the giving of alms as the adornment of the field of merit.
This is indeed a path traversed by all throughout ancient and modern times; regardless of noble or humble status, or wise or foolish, all are capable of applying themselves with genuine diligence.
Thus, when ten thousand people practice, ten thousand experience its efficacy. May Your Majesty take heed of this.
I have respectfully set forth the rules for daily practice as listed below.
Our Buddha, in order to rescue and deliver the suffering sentient beings of this Sahā world, exclusively taught the Dharma-gate of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
One need only single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha and resolve to be reborn in that land.
There is one fascicle of the *Amitābha Sūtra* which serves as the proof; everything described within that sūtra concerns that land and its environment.
The reality of the dhātus is most clearly evident. Regarding the method of practice, there is also a sequential order.
As for the ritual of monastic recitation, one need not be bound by rigid formalism; simply take the recitation of the Buddha’s name as the primary focus.

Every morning upon rising, pay homage to the Buddha, then recite either one scroll of the *Amitābha Sūtra* or one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Thereafter, take up the prayer beads and recite the name of Amitābha.
Recite the Buddha’s name three, five, or ten thousand times. Upon completion, immediately dedicate the merit before the Buddha and make a vow to be reborn in that land.
The words for this are found in the *Gongke Jing* (Sutra of Daily Recitations). This constitutes the morning recitation; the evening practice is the same.
Practice this daily as a fixed routine; it must never be omitted. Teach this method to all members of the palace retinue so that they may practice together according to the Dharma.
Cultivation becomes even more sublime. This is precisely what was practiced by our Holy Ancestor, the Benevolent and Filial Holy Mother, who established this method within the inner palace;
that it remains unfailing to this day is because it constitutes a constant practice. As for the final, ultimate matter, the application of effort therein must be even more intimate and direct.
Apart from the two periods of daily liturgical recitations, throughout the twelve hours of both day and night, one must apply oneself with earnestness.
Simply take the single phrase "Namo Amitābha Buddha" and place it across your chest. Never forget it, keeping it constantly present in mind without a moment's lapse.
Do not think of any worldly affairs; instead, take this single phrase of the Buddha as your very life-root.

Bite down on your teeth and resolve never to let go. Even while eating, drinking, rising, or reclining—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—let this single invocation of the Buddha’s name manifest before you at all times.

Should you encounter circumstances that are adverse or favorable, joyful or vexing, or when your mind becomes unsettled by the conditions of affliction, take up that single invocation of the Buddha and press it upon yourself with force; immediately, you will see the afflictions vanish on the spot. By means of this mindfulness...
Contemplate that afflictions are the root of the suffering of birth and death. Now, by means of mindfulness of the Buddha, one extinguishes these afflictions;
this is precisely how the Buddha delivers one from the realm of birth and death. If mindfulness of the Buddha can eliminate afflictions, one will then be able to bring an end to birth and death;
there is no other method. If, through mindfulness of the Buddha, you attain mastery over the afflictions, you will likewise attain mastery even within your dreams.
If one can maintain mastery while dreaming, one will maintain mastery amidst the suffering of illness.
If one maintains mastery amidst the suffering of illness, then at the moment of death, one will know with perfect clarity where one is going.
This matter is not difficult to practice; it requires only that one’s resolve for life and death be urgent and single-minded, relying solely upon the single sound of the invocation.

The Buddha further instructed him not to engage in discursive investigation. After a long time of pure cultivation, he naturally attained great peace, bliss, and mastery, as well as the enjoyment of great joy;
this is truly incomparable to the pleasures of the five worldly desires. May Your Majesty pay close attention to this Dharma;
it is the authentic practice. Apart from this, there is nothing more direct, simple, or effortless than it.

Furthermore, you must by no means allow yourself to be deluded by heterodox views or false teachings. Moreover, Great King, if you wish to know your destination at the end, there is yet another sublime method;
please listen as I describe it. This method lies within the mind of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation).
At all times, silently engage in contemplation, visualizing a great lotus flower appearing before you—whether blue, yellow, red, or white, its form is unrestricted.
Visualize the form of the flower as clearly as a large chariot wheel. Then, imagine yourself sitting within the flower, poised motionless upon the filaments and the pericarp.
Visualize the Buddha emitting rays of light that shine down upon your body. While forming this visualization:
Regardless of whether one is walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, and without regard for years, months, days, or hours, one need only ensure that the visualization of the object is clear.
Whether with eyes open or closed, it must be vivid and unmistakable;

even within dreams, one should see Amitābha Buddha together with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta within the lotus flower, as clearly as seeing them in broad daylight. If this visualization of the flower is perfected in this way, it is then complete.
This is the timing of birth and death. Until the moment of passing away, this flower will appear before one’s eyes;
one will see oneself sitting within the lotus flower, whereupon Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta will come together to welcome and guide one.
In a single thought-moment, one shall attain rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression, never again to undergo rebirth.
The suffering of death—this is truly the practical efficacy of practicing throughout one’s life to achieve completion.
This Dharma gate is not mere monastic talk; it is a direct and straightforward path revealed everywhere within the Buddha’s sutras. As it is said: "There is only this path of practice:
simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Apart from this, there is no other sublime Dharma. I have heard that such is Your Majesty’s mind.
Do not seek longevity; simply wish for clarity at the end. Apart from this, there is no other method for attaining clarity.
If you fear illness and wish to study breath regulation and the circulation of *qi* (energy) to ward off disease, this is not a wholesome method.
If the *qi* is not properly circulated, it may instead lead to a grave illness that becomes incurable. You must by all means not be deluded by such things. If it is...
Regarding the single practice of Buddha-recitation, one attains intimacy; as for all other matters, there is no need to concern oneself with them.
I pray that Your Majesty will believe this with sincere earnestness and by all means refrain from harboring doubt.
Furthermore, on the twenty-seventh day of the first month, the monk Yunzhen, having received the Imperial Decree and bearing the Sage’s words, was sent down to inquire about certain matters.
As this mountain monk has read them over and over again, it is evident that Your Majesty is investigating the great matter of birth and death. I wish for—
I clarify the nature of life, the faculties, and the fundamental source; I have thoroughly understood the intent and purpose of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' Chan and teachings.

This mountain monk is ignorant and does not dare to speak recklessly. I have carefully consulted the scriptural canons and have recorded each point of your inquiry in its proper order, providing clear responses as set forth below.
I humbly request your imperial perusal.
First, he asked about the Way of the Three Vehicles, the source of nature and life, the teachings on Chan, and the path of Bodhidharma:
"What is meant by the 'Wordless' (Wu)? Where does one apply effort within the mind-ground? What is the ultimate destination of human life? Furthermore, you say..."
Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, what is the ultimate reality? Furthermore, you speak of a state of stillness wherein there is neither self nor person, being like the great void;

how is this, in the final analysis? I would wish to hear a detailed analysis and explanation of each point, drawing upon the teachings of the upper, middle, and lower vehicles, as well as the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' intention to deliver sentient beings.

Answer: The fundamental tenet of the Buddha’s teaching takes the single mind alone as its core principle. If one traces the origin of this mind, it is fundamentally perfect and complete, luminous and vast, utterly free from even the slightest speck of dust;
it is pure and devoid of all things. Within this, there is originally no delusion or enlightenment, nor birth and death;

neither sage nor ordinary person is established. Living beings and Buddhas share the same essence, being non-dual and without distinction. This is precisely what Bodhidharma came from the West to point directly at.
The original, inherent true mind constitutes the Chan school; therefore, he said to Emperor Wu, "Vastly empty, there is no sage.

If one can suddenly awaken to this mind, then birth and death will be forever severed. It depends solely upon one's own single thought of sudden awakening; at that moment, one is called a Buddha of Suchness (*tathatā*).

This does not belong to the stages of cultivation and realization, nor does it belong to the gradual progression of the Three Vehicles. In the Chan school, this is designated as "Directing Toward" (*xiang*).
The aforementioned path, which has been transmitted by the patriarchs of old, takes this very mind as its ultimate principle; this is what is called Chan.
This school does not establish written texts, but values only the clarification of the mind and the realization of one’s nature. Regarding the methods of cultivation and progress:
when Bodhidharma first instructed the Second Patriarch, he asked, "What are you doing? The Second Patriarch replied, "I beg the Master to pacify my mind. Bodhidharma said:
Huineng said, "Bring forth your mind so that I may settle it for you. The Second Patriarch replied, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly ungraspable.
Bodhidharma then certified him, saying, "I have finished settling your mind for you. These words, "this mind is ungraspable," are precisely the pointing-out instruction from the West.
The Second Patriarch asked again, "Is there no further expedient? Bodhidharma said, "You need only cease all external conditions; let the internal mind be without..."
When one’s breathing is labored and the mind is like a wall or a barrier, one can enter the Way. This is precisely the very first point of effort for beginning the study of Chan.
Such is the entirety of the Way of Bodhidharma. Beyond this mind, there is no other method.

Later, as the Chan tradition developed over time, practitioners were unable to achieve sudden enlightenment; therefore, the teaching of "investigating Chan by means of a *huatou*" (critical phrase) arose. Its...
It does not matter who provides the *huatou*. Simply take a single ancient *gong'an* and harbor it within your breast as the *huatou*, giving rise to the spirit of doubt.
Even the single character "wu" (no) is itself the *gong'an*. To directly doubt this point is precisely what constitutes investigation.
By investigating again and again, after a long time, the mind-ground will suddenly burst open like awakening from a great dream; this is then called [enlightenment].
Awakening: To investigate through inquiry is itself the application of effort. At the moment of correct inquiry, not a single thought arises in the mind, and there is nothing at all;
thus one speaks of no-self and no-person, which is like the great void. This state of awakening is the true point of descent.
Once one has attained awakening to one’s own mind, the emotional roots of birth and death accumulated over kalpas are severed all at once. Having awakened to this mind—
Furthermore, it is said that when one is profoundly identical with the Buddha and sentient beings, from this point onward one transcends the three realms;

one comes and goes at will to deliver living beings, forever severing all suffering and no longer being detained by birth and death. This is what is called a Bodhisattva. This is precisely the ultimate destination of Zen meditation;
here, life and nature are brought to their final consummation. If one does not awaken to this mind, then one is merely acting as a commoner for a lifetime.
Dragged by the karma of good and evil, one revolves through the six realms of existence amidst all manner of suffering, ultimately finding no place of rest.
This is precisely what is meant by the so-called "sea of birth and death," which has no further shore.

First: A question concerning the Way of the Three Vehicles. This is indeed the Buddha’s means of delivering sentient beings; it is a dharma-gate of skillful and expedient means established according to their capacities.
The entire Tripitaka is based on this principle. To trace the origin of the Dharma of the One Mind: the living being and the Buddha share the same essence, fundamentally devoid of body and mind.
It is merely because of the initial movement of a single thought of delusion that one becomes confused regarding this mind, and thus [karmic bonds] are formed.
The formation of this illusory and delusive body and mind refers to the physical frame of flesh and blood that every person possesses today, which is called the *rūpakāya* (form-body).

That which presently perceives, cognizes, and deliberates is *vikalpa* (delusive thought); as stated in the *Heart Sūtra*, these are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). The five aggregates are form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The physical body is the aggregate of form; the mind consists of the four aggregates of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. By means of the body and mind...
Knowing suffering, pleasure, and so forth is sensation (*vedanā*). The continuous, uninterrupted mental activity of conceptualizing and craving is perception (*saṃjñā*).

This uninterrupted succession of such perceptions constitutes volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). These three are precisely the mind that cognizes, perceives, and deliberates. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

When one was initially not deluded, it was simply called "nature" (*prakṛti*); once the true mind became deluded, these illusory and false body and mind arose, and consciousness maintains their continuity.
This body is therefore called "life. This life is the source of the mind. When the Buddha first appeared in the world, he taught nothing other than for people to awaken to this mind.
Because they had been deluded for so long that they were unable to achieve such awakening, the Buddha established skillful means.
First, one teaches people that this body is the root of suffering. This suffering arises from the accumulation of afflictions (*kleśa*), having greed, hatred, delusion, and craving as its causes.

Therefore, one must first cause people to sever these afflictions so that suffering may be transcended. There are those of middling and inferior faculties who, relying on this teaching, practice and sever their afflictions;
they truly succeed in escaping the suffering of birth and death. These are called *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.

For those of the two lower and middle vehicles, because they rely on others and can only deliver themselves but cannot deliver others, they do not understand the meaning of the same essence (*samatā-sarvadharmas*) and obtain only half [of the path];
therefore, it is called the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). Furthermore, there are sentient beings with the Great Mind who are able both to deliver themselves and to deliver others;
benefiting both self and others, they extensively cultivate the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), namely: giving (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), and diligence (*vīrya*).

Advancing in meditative concentration and wisdom—possessing these six practices, one’s mind becomes vast; this is called a Bodhisattva, and thus it is named the Mahāyāna (Great Vehicle). It is also called the Supreme Vehicle (*Agrayāna*).
This Dharma of the Two Vehicles is entirely explained within the Great Canon of Scriptures; it seeks only for people to awaken to this mind.
Ultimately, when all is realized as returning to the One Mind, it is then named the Most Supreme Vehicle. This is what is meant by...
The Buddha: This is the ultimate principle within this teaching. The methods for the practice of the Three Vehicles are exceedingly numerous; they cannot be fully described.

Yet, by practicing according to even a single dharma, one may transcend the suffering of birth and death. It does not stop at a single approach; various skillful means are simply for the purpose of awakening to and realizing this mind.
Only when one has realized this mind is it the final place of rest. As long as one has not awakened to this mind, one remains entirely within the cycle of birth and death.
Within the ocean of death, one revolves according to good and evil deeds. If one performs good, one is immediately reborn among devas or humans;

if one commits evil acts, indulging in greed, hatred, delusion, and craving, one falls into the three miserable realms and undergoes immeasurable suffering. Regarding these Three Vehicles of the Dharma:

if one studies and practices the Middle or Lower Vehicles, one will invariably remain attached to this body, craving its enjoyments, and the mind of false conceptualization will be unable [to transcend].

Because they have severed [these roots], they are unable [to achieve it]. If those who study the Supreme Vehicle practice, although they may be able to practice giving and uphold the precepts, they cannot fully accomplish the latter four practices, nor can they immediately transcend birth and death.

Even if they cultivate wholesome dharmas and are born in the heavens, when their merit is exhausted, they fall back down again, like a waterwheel drawing from a well, never reaching the bottom. If one seeks to awaken to and clarify this mind, it is possible.
Having understood the nature of birth and death, one is nonetheless beset by the entanglement of present affairs and phenomena.
Furthermore, one is unable to apply oneself with earnest resolve to investigate the Way; even if one does investigate, one fails to receive the guidance of a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).

Fearing that one will misapply the mind and instead fall into deviant paths, how can one avoid spending this life in vain? Though one seeks a definitive resolution, in the end there is no resolution. Thus it is said:
Receiving blessings in the heavens does not exempt one from the cycle of saṃsāra; therefore, the Buddha has established a distinct, direct, and expedient method:

the single gateway of reciting the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. This is a path that achieves fulfillment in a single lifetime, and at the moment of death, one will certainly find a place of descent.
I shall now set forth for Your Majesty this Dharma-gate of reciting the Buddha’s name and the Pure Land.
First question: For what purpose was the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land established? It was because the Buddha established the teachings of the Three Vehicles to require people to practice;
these cannot be perfected in a single lifetime. Fearing that one might fall into the ocean of birth-and-death suffering and find it difficult to escape suddenly, [the Pure Land method was taught].

If one wishes to engage in Chan meditation, one may attain enlightenment in a single lifetime and escape birth-and-death. Furthermore, because of the proliferation of delusive thoughts and habitual tendencies...
It is profound and vast, yet difficult to investigate and penetrate. If one has not awakened to and clarified this mind, one cannot avoid the cycle of saṃsāra.

Therefore, a separate gateway to the Western Pure Land was established. This does not distinguish between those of superior, middling, or inferior faculties, nor between the wealthy, the poor, the noble, or the lowly;

provided one is willing to rely upon it and practice accordingly, one may achieve accomplishment within a single lifetime. As it is said: "There is only the direct path of cultivation; simply recite the name of Amitābha."
Amitābha Buddha, there is nothing more skillful [than this]. Why is this so? Because the world in which I currently reside is named Saha, a place of extreme suffering.
This refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, and even the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
it includes the gathering of enemies and all manner of sufferings that cannot be fully described. Though one may be a king, a noble, a general, or a minister...
Wealth, nobility, enjoyments, and all manner of pleasant things are all causes of suffering.

Because it is difficult to escape from such extreme suffering, the Western Pure Land is called the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). It is named "Ultimate Bliss" because within this land one experiences only various forms of happiness;
it is named a "Pure Land" because that Buddha-land is utterly free from defilement. There are no women there.
Because one is born through transformation from a lotus flower, there is no suffering of birth. Because one’s lifespan is infinite, there is no suffering of old age and death.

Because food and clothing appear spontaneously, there is no suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. Because all superior and virtuous people assemble in one place, there is no suffering of encountering enemies.
Because that land is adorned with the seven treasures, there are no shards, thorns, or impurities.
Pure. It is variously pure and entirely different from this world. Everything described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* is a reality.
Now, for all people who seek rebirth in that land, there is no other method than to take the single-minded recitation of the Buddha's name as the primary practice.
One should daily dedicate the merit and, furthermore, visualize oneself sitting within a lotus flower. Therefore, at the time of death—
At the time of death, one immediately beholds Amitābha Buddha, who emits light to welcome and lead one forth.

One sees a great lotus flower suddenly appear before oneself, and sees one’s own body seated upon that flower. In a single thought-moment, one is reborn there. Having been born in that land, from this point on one shall never again fall into the miserable realms of birth and death;
such a person is called a Bodhisattva of the Stage of Non-retrogression. This constitutes the completion of cultivation in a single lifetime.
The results will clearly manifest as a downfall in future lives. Apart from this, any other claims regarding what kind of state one experiences at the moment of death are all heterodox teachings.
If you do not practice mindfulness of the Buddha, then at the time of death, as you follow your own accumulated evil karma, evil states will appear before you;
by then, it will be too late for regret. This is the most concise, essential, and direct method of practice; it is the Buddha’s special [instruction].
This is established as a skillful means for guiding [practitioners].

First is the cultivation of the Pure Land, which does not necessarily require seeking awakening or clarifying the nature of the mind; it takes exclusively the practice of Buddha-recitation and visualization as its primary path.
Furthermore, one should use the merit of making offerings through almsgiving and cultivating various fields of blessings as an aid for adorning the Buddha-land.
Although one makes vows for rebirth within the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, it is essential to know that one must first sever the root of birth and death.
Only then will there be swift efficacy. What is the root of birth and death?
It is this very present attachment to the various enjoyments of the world, as well as beautiful forms, licentious sounds, and flavors for the mouth and body—all of which are the source of suffering.
Furthermore, it is all hearts of anger, resentment, and indignation, and hearts of clinging, delusion, and craving; these, along with all demons, heterodox paths, and false views—[are the root].

The teachings spoken by the Master [concern] the doctrines of heterodox sects, such as those currently propagated by a certain class of heterodox individuals who falsely claim them to be the Perfect and Sudden Dharma (Yuantun Daomo) and other teachings, as well as the falsely established doctrines of Nanyang Jingkong’s “Non-action” (Wuwei) and the "Verses on Returning Home.
Every one of these is a fabrication recently concocted by heterodox persons out of thin air. Such words are methods for deluding and confusing the people of the world. All of them...

One must exhaustively cast it all out until reaching the state of complete truth. Such techniques as the extraction of yin and yang, as well as the doctrines of inner and outer elixirs (*neidan* and *waidan*), are all heterodox teachings;
none of them are to be trusted. One should simply and single-mindedly place firm faith in the single gate of Buddha-recitation (*nianfo*).
Each day, recite two scrolls of the *Amitābha Sūtra* and chant the Buddha’s name a certain number of times, or even without counting, provided that one’s mind remains focused on nothing else.

Forget the name of the Buddha; this itself is the *huatou*. This is the very root and source of one's life and nature (*xingming*). There is no need to further inquire as to what this "life and nature" is.

Such talk regarding one's original face, or the theories of the three souls, seven spirits, and primal spirit (*yuanchen*), all belong entirely to the realm of the fleshly body—they are merely false identifications and pointing fingers that have no ultimate foundation. If you ask:
What happens while one is alive? What happens after death? For those who commit evil while alive, when they pass away, evil realms will manifest before them.
For those who recite the Buddha’s name while alive seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, when they pass away, the realm of the Buddha in the Pure Land will manifest before them;
thus their aspirations are fulfilled, which is indeed a good thing. However, if that which arises from within the mind is not what was sought, it is entirely the work of demons.
In matters of practice, one must by no means place misplaced trust, lest one waste hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes. Look simply at what is clearly explained in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
if it says that all phenomena with marks are false, these words belong to the school of Chan meditation.

There, one seeks exclusively for the pure true mind, allowing not a single thing to remain; therefore, it is said that all phenomena with marks are false. This is because of the purity of the Buddha-recitation [practice].
The land is originally intended for the accomplishment of the mind. As the Sūtra says: "When thought becomes clear, the land is formed.

Because it is most difficult to sever the mind of false conceptualization through the practice of Zen meditation, one now replaces defiled thoughts with pure ones. That the lotus flower manifests before one is precisely the accomplishment of visualization.
Furthermore, why do you dismiss this as a mere false appearance? The paths of cultivation each differ according to their respective gateways.
This cannot be discussed in a one-size-fits-all manner. All that has been answered above is based on a point-by-point verification against the sutras and teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
it is not mere idle talk. If one practices Chan meditation, then clarifying the mind and seeing one's nature (*citta-darśana*) is the primary focus.

If one follows the single gate of reciting the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, it is not necessary to clarify the mind and see one's nature; one simply recites the Buddha’s name. "Buddha" means awakening (*bodhi*).

Furthermore, if you do not forget the Buddha from moment to moment, then every thought-moment is clear awakening (*prabodha*). If your own mind forgets the Buddha, that is non-awakening (*aprabodha*).
If your mindfulness reaches the point where you can remain mindful even within dreams, this is constant awakening without obscuration.

If this mind is unobscured in the present, then at the time of death, this mind will likewise be unobscured. This state of the mind being unobscured is precisely where one finds one’s ultimate destination.

"Virtuous King, with the myriad affairs of state as they are today, you will certainly be unable to engage in seated meditation. There is nothing better than the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (nien-fo).

It is not restricted by leisure or busyness, nor by movement or stillness; it can be practiced everywhere. It requires only that you maintain single-mindedness without forgetting; there is no other clever method.
As for the aforementioned knowledge of the future, that belongs to the realm of supernatural powers (abhijñā); you need not seek this, for the Buddha did not permit its study."
If one practices this matter and achieves Buddhahood, supernatural powers (ṛddhi) will arise spontaneously without needing to be sought.
As for the prescience of ghosts and spirits, these are not things that can be acquired through human learning; one must by no means harbor thoughts of such matters.

If one recites the Buddha’s name until the time of death approaches, one will naturally know in advance that the end has come; this too is simply the accomplishment of the power of constant mindfulness and must not be forced.
Thus it is. The above several points are respectfully submitted for the Worthy King’s detailed examination and careful consideration.

A Dharma Discourse in Response to the Question of Monk Haiyin of Huzhou:
Regarding those who have already received the single transmission and direct pointing of the ancients, yet further cultivate the practice of purity with the desire to be reborn in the Pure Land.
Is this after awakening, where one initiates practice according to one's vows? Or is it before awakening, where both types of practice are cultivated concurrently?
If they are cultivated concurrently, one falls into a thieving mind and a divided mind; how then can one’s spiritual effort become a solid mass?

If one has already awakened, then every dust mote is the Flower Treasury World (Huazang) and every location is a lotus sprout; nothing in the ten directions would be unsuitable. Why then focus exclusively on the Western Pure Land?

Answer: According to the teachings, there are three pure lands: the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light (*nitya-prabhāsvara-kṣetra*), the Land of True Reward Adornment (*vipāka-vyūha-kṣetra*), and the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-kṣetra*).

If all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the ancestral patriarchs who have attained realization through the direct transmission from above, all experience the Dharma-bliss of their own nature (*svabhāva-dharmasukha*), there is not one among them who does not return to the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light. This is what is called the "Pure Land of Mind-Only" (*cittamātra-purī*). If...
That every particle of dust and every land is a pure land refers to the Flower Treasury Adornment (Avataṃsaka) realm of true recompense; this, too, is merely a manifestation of the mind.
As for those who seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land, this is called the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder;

it is but a single land within the lands and particles of the Flower Treasury. This is for those who desire to seek rebirth there. As the Treatise says: "When sentient beings first begin their practice, they are afraid..."
Faith is difficult to establish. For those whose minds wish to retreat, one should know that the Tathāgata possesses a supreme skillful means to protect and sustain that faith;
namely, by single-mindedly recollecting Amitābha Buddha in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss and dedicating the roots of goodness thus cultivated.
One will immediately attain rebirth as desired and constantly behold the Buddha upon whom one has taken refuge; thus, there shall never be any regression.
This refers to those who practice while not yet having attained awakening, in accordance with Yongming’s statement: "If one can simply see Amitābha, why worry about not attaining awakening?
If one practices this method concurrently, it is as stated in the treatise: "If one contemplates that Buddha’s True Suchness Dharma-body, one should always be diligent..."
Through cultivation, one ultimately attains birth and abiding in right concentration; how, then, could this be a "thieving mind"?
This is because [such a person] has not yet reached the essence of mindfulness of the Buddha and does not understand the meaning of the Pure Land.

Thus we know that those who have already awakened do not need to seek it for birth to occur naturally, while for those who have not yet awakened, birth cannot be achieved through a "thieving mind" of mindfulness of the Buddha.

Question: In the study of Chan, it is valued that not a single thought arises; in the recitation of the Buddha’s name (nienfo), it is valued that pure mindfulness continues uninterrupted. Now, in this method of investigating through nienfo, the intent lies in attaining wondrous awakening and thereby achieving rebirth in the Pure Land. Yet, at present, when one recites the Buddha’s name, the mind and the Buddha are distinct and clear; however, when investigating, both are completely severed. Consequently, the power of investigation gradually increases while the recitation of the Buddha’s name gradually diminishes. What is the reason for this? Answer: It is because the principle of Chan is to sever all thoughts, whereas the principle of nienfo is to maintain continuous mindfulness. When the power of investigation is strong, the continuity of mindfulness is naturally weak. This is why, in the stage of "investigating the Buddha" (kanhua), one must abandon the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name. Furthermore, when one investigates the "Who is this? (shishen shui), the mind is already focused on the Buddha; thus, there is no need to recite the name separately. However, if one does not investigate the "Who is this? but instead merely recites the name, then the mind and the Buddha remain separate. Therefore, the ancients taught that one should abandon the practice of reciting the name and instead investigate the "Who is this? If one can investigate with vigor until the very moment of death, one will surely attain rebirth. If one cannot investigate with such vigor, then one should simply rely on the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name. Thus, the ancients said: "If you wish to attain rebirth, you must investigate the 'Who is this? If you do not investigate the 'Who is this?', you will not attain rebirth. This is the meaning. It is not that the power of investigation is superior to the power of recitation; rather, it is because the power of investigation cuts off the continuity of mindfulness. Therefore, the ancients said: "When the power of investigation is strong, the continuity of mindfulness is naturally weak. This is the reason. Furthermore, if one investigates the "Who is this? with vigor, one will naturally attain rebirth. If one merely recites the name without investigating, one will not necessarily attain rebirth.
