As for the various mental afflictions of us ordinary people, only the Buddha has revealed them exhaustively—such as the states of ascent and descent among the seven realms in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the forms of the fifty kinds of demonic hindrances (*skandha-māra*), and the false views of the non-Buddhists and the two vehicles in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
If it were not for the Buddha’s detailed explanation, from what source could one know these things?
Are you afraid? What I call "sealing the mind" is precisely this: it simply requires using the teachings to illuminate the mind; it does not lie within the path of conceptual meaning.
Even if one reaches the path of meaning, it is still not the ultimate. Furthermore, the various kinds of habitual tendencies from past lives do not even abide within the path of meaning.
The Fifth asked Chengkuan: "The Dharma-gift is great; the Dharma-offering is supreme. Because you have awakened to and sealed the teachings, you immediately seal Chengkuan as well.
This seems to accord with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, turning the Great Wheel of Dharma. Yet, this awakening is not true awakening."

To rely on one's own "seal" (interpretation) is for that seal not to be a true seal. To propagate [one's views] while claiming sole authority, to erase all commentaries, and to display only one's own brilliance—is this the mark of a lion or a fox?
It is easy to disparage oneself; it is difficult to recognize whether one is propagating the truth or slandering it.
We pray you will deign to provide a discerning judgment, which we shall forever revere as our divining stalks and tortoise shells.

Answer: As disciples of the Buddha, we recognize that the Buddha’s kindness is difficult to repay. To truly repay his kindness, there is nothing better than to propagate the Dharma on the Buddha’s behalf.

Therefore, among the great masters of the past who propagated the Dharma, there were three distinct types. First, those who realized their own original nature and wondrously accorded with the Buddha’s mind;
regarding the Buddha’s teachings, it was as if they flowed forth from within their own chests, possessing the four unhindered powers of eloquence. Furthermore...
There are those who have entered deeply into the ocean of the teachings, where the waves are vast and immense; such are the great ancestral masters of the Qingliang, Guifeng, and Tiantai schools.

Second, there are those who, though they have not yet awakened to their own minds, rely upon the Buddha’s verbal teachings to seal and confirm their own minds. They extensively explore the ocean of the teachings, and as they explain them, they do not err from the Buddha’s intent.
Although these individuals have not yet transcended words and mental images, they do not dare to arbitrarily employ their own views.
To speak broadly, there are those who expound according to the teachings, such as the great Dharma masters of former times.

Third, there are those who possess the seeds of *prajñā* from past habituation; having cultivated the work of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they have personally clarified their own minds and wondrously accorded with the Buddha’s intent.
Although they have not extensively engaged in broad learning, their correct view is unerring. While they may have the fault of taking the shallow for the profound, they do not slander the Dharma.

Regarding these transgressions, those who propagate [the Dharma] all take the gift of the Dharma as their primary intent, seeking neither worldly fame, profit, nor honor—just like the venerable masters Jiyin and others of former times at Wénlǐng.
These are all instances of the greatest gift of the Dharma.

There are even those of keen intelligence and sharp faculties who rely solely on their own views, claiming them to be correct; they reject the teachings of the past and present, speaking recklessly and indiscriminately, and claim only to propagate...
To claim that the Dharma is for one's own benefit not only destroys the Buddha-Dharma, but furthermore leads later generations into error and downfall.
How, then, can such a person be said to propagate the Dharma? This is clearly and easily seen; it requires no further inquiry to understand.

Sixth, regarding the verses on ancient cases (songgu): After attaining awakening, the ancients composed verses on ancient cases like painting the void; they did not fall into the realm of forms and appearances.
Nowadays, those whose awakening has not yet reached thorough penetration rashly compose verses on ancient cases; their phrasing stems from poetic fancy, and their intent is akin to mere wit.

To take these as words of awakening and states of awakening has become so popular it is like minced meat on the tongue; yet with a single turn, one falls into the fox’s den, remaining complacent and unaware of the fear.

Is this not the degenerate corruption of the Dharma-ending age? We of our generation are easily prone to fall into this pit; I pray you will provide the necessary acupuncture and cauterization, universally bestowing your profound compassion.

Answer: Verses on ancient precedents (*songgu*) originate from those above; they do nothing more than expound the strategic maneuvers of the ancients and briefly demonstrate the arrangements of the school’s gate to manifest great capacity and great function.
Furthermore, they allow one to bring forth one's own self, wielding the hands that bestow, take away, kill, and give life.

They are not merely for the purpose of venting one's mouth or indulging one's passions, nor are they for the sake of constructing clever schemes for gain. These two matters—verses on ancient precedents and the elucidation of the teachings—are both beyond the reach of beginners.
Urgent! Why must you make such preliminary arrangements? An ancient worthy said: "Once you have attained realization of your own mind, do not worry about being unable to preach the Dharma.
For those at the beginning of their practice, the only thing of urgency is to investigate the mind and seek clarity regarding the great matter of one's own person.
You must by no means harbor such views. If we can truly realize our own minds, even if we do not expound the teachings or chant the ancient cases (gong'an), that too is sufficient.
This is true renunciation; one does not bring shame upon those beneath the *kāṣāya*.

*The Dream-Travel Collection of the Elder Hanshan*, Volume Twelve.
Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and his disciple Tonghyeong;
revised by the Disciple from Lingnan, Liu Qixiang.
In the *Fayu*, Master Jizhao Kei requested instruction on eight points of inquiry.
A sutra states: "Unimpeded, pure wisdom arises entirely from meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). How then did Nanyue refer to Master Ma?
The Patriarch said: "If you study sitting meditation, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down. If you study becoming a Buddha, a Buddha is not a fixed form.
Regarding the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject. As for these two statements, which is right and which is wrong?"
Answer: Under the gate of the Patriarchs, one does not concern oneself with sitting in meditation to become a Buddha; one values only the seeing of one's nature.
If one sees one's own nature clearly and distinctly, there will naturally be no grasping or rejecting. As soon as there is grasping or rejecting, one falls into right and wrong.
Question: The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "Now these four elements of mine—namely solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion—each return to earth, water, fire, and wind;
therefore it is said that the four elements are each separate. As for this deluded body of the present moment, where does it reside?
I do not yet know whether this body is already separated from the elements before death, or whether they become separated only after death.
Answer: It must be cast off before one dies; thus, at the time of departure, one is not burdened by it.

Yet when that moment actually arrives, to achieve such detachment is as difficult as a living turtle shedding its shell—the most difficult of difficulties. As the ancients said: "Prepare in times of leisure to use in times of urgency."
This is precisely what is meant.

A question is raised: The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that Ānanda said to the Buddha, "By what means should one subdue the mind on the path of its original aspiration, so as to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?
The Buddha replied, "If you wish to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully examine the ground of practice (*ādhāra-bhūmi*)."

Is the initial aspiration identical to or different from the awakening of the stage of fruition? If, at the causal stage, one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation while seeking the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing, such a thing is impossible. I do not yet know:
is the very mind with which you now seek to transcend birth and death through Zen meditation and the study of the Way a mind subject to arising and ceasing?

Answer: When a practitioner of the Way engages in Chan meditation, they first sever the mind of arising and ceasing. Upon the manifestation of illumination, they then perceive the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.
If one engages in Chan with a mind of arising and ceasing, one merely follows after deluded thoughts and transmigrates; this is not true investigation.

He asked Chan Master Baizhang Hai: "To seek even a partial understanding after having visited a virtuous teacher (kalyāṇamitra) is the 'demon of the virtuous teacher,' because it gives rise to verbal views.

If one makes the Four Great Vows, vowing to deliver all sentient beings before attaining Buddhahood, this is the 'demon of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-wisdom,' because of the vow not to abandon them. If..."
Observing the precepts, practicing dhyāna, and studying wisdom are outflowing roots of goodness (*sāsrava-kuśalamūla*).

Even if one sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to achieve perfect awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), delivers beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and causes them all to realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, these are roots of goodness that are demonic, because they give rise to craving and attachment.
If, regarding all phenomena, there is no defilement whatsoever and only the principle of dhyāna remains—this profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*)...

One does not advance; this is the demon of samādhi. Because one has long indulged in its playfulness, how may those who today practice Zen and study the Way escape this demon and enter the path of correct cultivation?
Answer: All practitioners of the path are moved by the net of Māra solely because they do not forget their mental perceptions.
If mental perceptions are eliminated and forgotten, then even "Buddha" cannot be established.
Question: Regarding the refutation of attachment to the four great elements and the five aggregates (*skandha*), is there a sequence of priority?

Answer: According to the teachings, the five aggregates are refuted gradually; one must first refute the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). However, if one breaks through the "lacquer bucket" through Zen meditation (*chan*), then the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is first broken.
Once the aggregate of consciousness is broken, the four great elements have no basis to rely upon; thus, it is like cutting through water or blowing out a light—everything is realized as empty.
They do not touch one another.

Regarding the four propositions concerning the Vajra, there has never been a clear explanation of them from ancient times to the present. Some point to form, sound, fragrance, and so forth as the four propositions;
some point to the four of eye, ear, nose, and tongue; some point to the various marks and the absence of marks; or some point to...

Regarding the existence of truth and the non-existence of truth, and so forth, when it came to Vasubandhu, he said: "I ascended to Tuṣita Heaven and requested further instruction from Maitreya, who replied:
'There is no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-spanner. This is what is meant.
The Sixth Patriarch said, "It is this Mahāprajñāpāramitā.

The Great Being of the Twin Trees further said, "In the sutras, one should uphold these four lines so that they never leave one's person: 'The fool sees them as a dream; the wise man sees only the truth.
From antiquity until now, why has there never been a fixed formulation?"

Answer: The Buddha taught that Prajñā is like the myriad herbs on the Snowy Mountains; each and every one is medicine. To take them up and apply them immediately will certainly eliminate all ailments.
Therefore, when the ancients pointed out what constitutes the "four lines," they were each merely taking up a single blade of grass from the Snowy Mountains.
Question: An ancient said, "Even if one attains pure clarity free from a single speck, it is still the flow of true permanence.

Even if one attains a state where not a single dharma confronts the mind, one is still subject to Yangshan’s scrutiny. Even if one attains a state where the entire body is illumination, one is still merely extending a hand within the community of patch-robed monks.
Even if one attains realization prior to the seven Buddhas, beyond the era of Wei-yin, it is still just talk."
"Will they? Do the scholars of today truly reach this state?
Answer: "The ancients offered these words merely out of fear that people would fall by the wayside. Even if a student were to reach such a state, it would still be a matter of being on the path;
how much more so for those who have not yet reached it, yet immediately open their mouths to speak of Chan—this is all nothing but deceiving one's own mind."
He asked Great Master Yuanwu: "Since the time of the Patriarch, the sole endeavor has been that of direct transmission.

Using words to dispel words, using function to seize function, using poison to counteract poison, and using activity to break through activity, it is for this reason that branches and schools have proliferated."

Each must excel in their own family tradition; one must possess a superior capacity (*indriya*) and the resolve to perpetuate the Buddhas and Patriarchs before they can penetrate the innermost depths and receive certification.
Apart from this, you should strictly treasure [the teachings] and not treat them lightly.
Observing students today, many fail to examine their own capacities and immediately seek to investigate the ultimate matter; if they truly do not...
Question: Does one judge a person’s capacity? Answer:
The Patriarchs judged people by their capacity; this is what the Buddha in the scriptures meant by "discerning spiritual lineage.
If one does not possess such a lineage, one will ultimately remain stuck on the surface of the skin and bone. People today have impure capacities and are certainly cut off from this matter.
If you are willing to apply yourself earnestly to this matter and do not regress from it, you may eventually be permitted to make progress;
this belongs to the category of those with indeterminate nature. At the request of Wang Ji’ān and Zhu Báimin.

Question: The Buddha spoke of sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*) and gradual teaching (*jian-jiao*), and Chan opens the gates of the sudden and the gradual. Are these two teachings and two gates the same or different?

Answer: When the Buddhas and patriarchs appear in the world, fundamentally there is no dharma to be spoken. Since the dharma is fundamentally unspeakable, how could there be distinctions between the sudden and the gradual?

They are distinct. To speak of "sudden" and "gradual" is merely a designation established for the sake of specific capacities (*indriya*); it does not pertain to the Dharma itself. Nevertheless, as for the existence of sudden and gradual teachings:

when Vairocana first attained perfect enlightenment, he preached the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at the site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), suddenly revealing the dharma-gate of the mind-ground within the equal dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
He showed it directly and exhaustively, like the sun first rising and illuminating the high mountains before others. Thus, the distinction is made.
As for the teaching, it is called the Perfect and Sudden Dharma-gate; this is the Buddha’s sudden dharma.
However, this sudden dharma is intended only for those among the great-rooted beings on earth. Within it, the forty-two stages are deployed; this is precisely the gradualness within the sudden.
As for the others with inferior faculties who were seated there, they were like the blind or the deaf, having no share in it whatsoever. Thus, although the dharma...
Though great, the means of gathering sentient beings are not extensive; that is to say, there is only a single gate, and it is moreover so narrow and small.

How could the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma be intended for a single person alone? Therefore, he manifests transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and adapts to the three faculties to establish the teaching of the Three Vehicles.

Initially, one proceeds from gradual cultivation toward realization—this is what is called the gradual teaching. Later, one arrives at the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Nirvāṇa*...

The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* suddenly reveals the seed of the Buddha-nature; this is what is meant by "sudden" arising from the "gradual. This refers to the division of the teachings into the gradual and the sudden.

As for the single gate of Chan (Dhyāna), it is mentioned everywhere throughout the teachings: among the Bodhisattva’s six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), there are the two perfections of meditation (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

The Bodhisattva of Doctrinal Classification [states]: "By means of two gates, one opens the two doors of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), which serve as the foundation for practice.
Within this teaching, one employs the sudden [approach] while practicing gradually; thus, this Chan represents the gradual within the sudden.
As for the Chan of Bodhidharma, it is the 'Treasury of the True Dharma Eye' shown by the World-Honored One at the end of his life, when Kāśyapa broke into a smile upon the lifting of the flower."
The wondrous mind of enlightenment thus became the essential purport of the "separate transmission outside the teachings. It was transmitted twenty-eight times in the Western Regions;

then Bodhidharma came to the East, and after six transmissions it reached Caoxi. The various patriarchs recorded in the *Lamp Records* thereafter practiced a Chan that is a direct pointing to the single mind through single-lineage transmission;
this is not comparable to the Chan of the Six Perfections. Because this single mind is shown directly without any other method, it is called "single transmission."

To see one's own mind directly and instantaneously, without belonging to the categories of cultivation and realization, delusion and enlightenment, or cause and effect, is to manifest specifically that single point prior to the appearance of the Buddhas in the world;
this is called the "Path Above" and is named the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna. This is the "sudden" aspect of Chan.

As for the successive patriarchs of the various dynasties who attained sudden awakening to this mind—even their single word or phrase, their single blow of the staff or shout—[is the direct transmission].
"Lower [grade]: Direct and immediate awakening. This is generally because one has cultivated for many lifetimes, such that the roots of *prajñā* are deep;
when the conditions ripen, it reaches maturity today. There are also those who investigate in this life and attain awakening only after twenty or thirty years of effort.
In such cases, although it is sudden, it nonetheless arises from the gradual. As Guishan said: 'If a student can awaken in a single thought-moment...'"
To recognize one's own mind as being inherently possessed from the beginning is called "awakening" (*bodhi*).

Yet, because there still remains the subtle, continuous flow of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), one uses that which has been awakened to purify the flowing consciousnesses of present karma; this is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).

There is no cultivation other than this. Viewed in this light, within the sudden (*tun*) approach, the gradual (*jian*) is never absent. I have often observed the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and its divisions...
There are four gates concerning the sudden and the gradual: first, the sudden-sudden; second, the sudden-gradual; third, the gradual-sudden; and fourth, the gradual-gradual.

One must understand that these cannot be discussed by adhering to a single perspective. Although there is sudden awakening, one does not abandon gradual cultivation. The minds of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are fundamentally no different.
Question: The Buddha taught all the various sūtras as discourses that accord with the nature of reality (dharmatā) and as teachings of definitive meaning (nītārtha).

Why, then, did Bodhidharma repeatedly praise the *Laṅkāvatāra* saying, "This sūtra is the essential core of my mind," while at Huangmei he pointed to the *Vajracchedikā*, and other sūtras—what difference is there between them?

Answer: Although the various Mahāyāna sūtras spoken by the Buddha are discourses that accord with the nature (*dharmatā*) and reveal the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), they nonetheless function as gateways for the establishment of transformation;

they do not transcend the opposition between delusion and awakening, nor the relative nature of phenomena. They invariably require the turning back from the false to return to the true, all of which involves a process of reconciliation before the single truth can be revealed.
As for the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* alone, it points directly to the one mind; although it distinguishes between the true and the false, this is done to demonstrate the nature of consciousness.
The "Treasury" (garbha) is the Tathāgatagarbha; it need not be reconciled with other systems. It solely reveals the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

Simply realizing that the delusive imaginings manifested by one's own mind are devoid of intrinsic nature is itself noble wisdom; there is no need for further transformation. This is its very practice:

merely observing directly the flow of one's own mind, the immediate perception (*pratyakṣa*) of delusive imaginings, and thereby suddenly attaining realization of one's own mind. Furthermore, no stages or gradations of attainment are established.
Therefore, those who classify the teachings designate this as the "Sudden Dharma Gate. For this reason, Bodhidharma took it as the "Mind Seal" (*citta-mudrā*).

By means of this sutra, he revealed the essential key to the Chan school. Because this sutra is difficult to clarify and hard for those of inferior understanding to enter, when its transmission reached Huangmei, he used the *Vajra* to seal the mind.
This *Vajra* is one of the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and its text consists of six hundred fascicles.
Only this fascicle alone accords with the mind-seal of the Patriarchs. This is because Prajñā is the initial gateway for entering the Mahāyāna, just as is taught in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
"A Bodhisattva takes the mind that is neither arising nor ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation.
Now, Prajñā is the fundamental, ultimate wisdom of the Buddha, and it is precisely this mind that neither arises nor ceases. This sutra takes non-abiding as its central principle.

Its function is to sever doubt. Because those of the Two Vehicles falsely give rise to views of sentient beings, views of Buddhas, and views of dharmas, they become attached in various ways and repeatedly harbor doubts.
This sutra completely uproots these seeds of doubt, leading one directly to the ground beyond doubt, where all knowledge and views are extinguished.
Not establishing a single dharma, one completely dispels the mind that dwells in attachment; this is identical to the methods of the Chan school for "untying the sticky" and "removing the bonds.
Severing the conceptualizations of mental discourse is precisely what the Chan school does not permit—namely, conjecture or dwelling upon thought.
When the conscious mind is withered away, one penetrates the Dharma-body and moves beyond it; this is precisely why Huangmei used this to seal his heart.
While other sutras contain various attachments and entanglements, this sutra alone cuts them off completely. Once one has realized this through Zen practice, entry [into the Way] becomes easy.
Question: It is said that there is Tathāgata Chan and Patriarchal Chan. Do these two types of Chan actually differ from one another? Xiangyan had an awakening upon striking a bamboo;
he presented the verse "Last year’s poverty was not yet true poverty" to Yangshan.

Yangshan said, "I am glad, elder brother, that you have understood Tathāgata Chan; as for Patriarchal Chan, you have not even dreamed of it. Based on these words, it appears that [the two] are distinct.

The Tathāgata-dhyāna and the Patriarchal-dhyāna are different. If one follows from Kāśyapa down to the First Patriarch’s coming from the West, and the patriarchs have transmitted it to one another, then the original founder of all schools is none other than Śākyamuni; how could there be any difference?
Answer: Tathāgata Chan and Patriarchal Chan are fundamentally non-dual. However, Tathāgata Chan speaks of awakening within the midst of delusion;
it requires cultivation before one enters it. Patriarchal Chan points directly, belonging to neither delusion nor awakening, and does not depend upon artificial cultivation.
The essential point is for one to directly and suddenly realize one’s own mind. Any falling into the threshold of delusion or awakening is already the secondary meaning.
Therefore, as the ancient masters said: "Cultivation is not non-existent; yet, what can be done about defilement?
Thus, regarding the upward path of the Zen school, one must be a person of this very caliber to succeed. Among the four types of dhyāna in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, this is the supreme vehicle.
Chan is precisely the Chan of the Patriarchs; in reality, there is fundamentally no difference between them.

If one’s faculties and vessel are impure, yet they recklessly display their cleverness and intellectual views, claiming to have realized the Chan of the Patriarchs—then such a person has not even dreamed of the Chan of the Tathāgata.
It is like a poor man who falsely claims to be an emperor and brings about his own execution. Is this not something to be feared? Is this not something to be feared?
To Master Xiao Xuanpu, Minister of Rites (This is the final writing from the sixth day of the tenth month in the winter of the Guihai year of Tianqi):
To enter the Way, one must first realize that the substance of the human mind is originally luminous and vast, encompassing all things without limit.
All-pervading and pure, where neither sage nor ordinary person is established, one is not constrained or obstructed by body, mind, or the world.
This is the single path leading upward; it is the Heart-Seal of the One Who Came from the West, and nothing more than this.

Once one has attained thorough realization of this mind, then in daily life, as one responds to conditions, all objective realms are like images appearing in a mirror: they come without attachment and depart without a trace.
In this way, whatever actions are performed all flow forth from the true mind, the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Each and every one is a genuine and imperishable undertaking; they do not merely vie for brilliance with the sun and moon.

Compared to the petty delusions and mechanical contrivances of those ignorant and confused people, how can they possibly be spoken of as being of the same order? This light is present in every person.
They were complete and originally lacked nothing; yet, because their views of self were so firm, whatever they did was necessarily claimed as their own achievement.
They clung to their own perspectives as being invariably correct, resulting in a confusion of right and wrong with no final, settled doctrine.
The reason for this is that it is difficult to establish a thousand-year, imperishable legacy without a mind of vast and universal impartiality.
Furthermore,
the essence of our own mind is originally perfect and luminous; yet, because we have been unable to realize this suddenly and thus fail to experience it directly at present,
it is due to the fact that throughout immeasurable kalpas, various afflictions— greed, hatred, delusion, and craving— have obscured it.
Therefore, the merit of gradual cultivation must not be slighted. Guishan said:

"If a student can suddenly awaken to their own mind in a single thought-moment, they should simply take what they have awakened to and purify the flowing consciousnesses of present karma; this is called 'cultivation.
It is not that there is some other cultivation apart from this. If a student of the Way merely seeks sudden awakening and considers that sufficient, they will assume there is no need for effort."

This may be used [as a practice]. However, these habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) lie deep and hidden; when they encounter external conditions, they erupt surreptitiously. If this continues for long, one will eventually flow into the realm of demons.

Nevertheless, the merit of gradual cultivation does not require a fixed sequence; it simply requires that during daily life, you direct yourself toward the state where the mind has not yet given rise to thought or movement.
Firmly establish the foundation of your practice. Turn back to observe and illuminate within. At the very moment a single thought arises, immediately investigate where this thought originates.
Trace it back to the source of its birth; there, you will find it is fundamentally unborn from the beginning. Thus, all deluded thoughts and mental anxieties [are seen as empty].
At that moment, it will melt away like ice. However, what is to be feared is a lack of courageous power;
if one cannot seize the throat [of the mind], one will not realize the continuity [of delusion], and thus it will flow on without returning.
To Zhou Ziyin (the following is appended the *Haoyin Gao*):
Today the assembly has entered the retreat at Mount Ju. I, Haiyin, am presiding over the seat to preach the *Lotus Sūtra*.

At that time, a letter arrived from you, accompanied by fine fruits. From these signs, it is evident that you, too, are among those who attend this Dharma assembly; indeed, you shall be the first to attain the Way.

As for "fruition," this is not something achieved through mere ritual or effort. As stated in the previous writings at length, daily practice must be precisely aligned with this principle without fail;

only then can one gradually enter the gate of non-duality. However, within that daily life, every instance and every thought is still a mental activity of arising and ceasing—how, then, can one find the bliss of quiescent extinction?
If you seek a genuine experience of the mind-ground, you must further apply yourself to reading and writing.

When you have already understood this, you should settle firmly upon whatever various conditions arise. Suddenly turn back to look within and observe these various activities of the mind as they arise and perish:
ultimately from where do they arise? And right now, toward what place do they go when they cease?
Contemplate deeply in this manner for a long time until you gradually enter into a subtle and dense state. If, within this state, all habitual tendencies...

At the place where the hidden current flows, because afflictions are absent, it arises. Look intently and fix your gaze upon this very reality: see what it ultimately is, and from where it arises and ceases.
Pursue it until its tracks are swept away and its traces are utterly extinguished, like a single flake of snow falling into a cauldron of boiling water.
Practice in this manner throughout daily life; do not let go of even a single thought for even a moment. As soon as there is the slightest...
When thoughts of indolence, laziness, and negligence arise, or when the mind gives rise to a desire for ease, comfort, and self-indulgence—this is precisely the moment the root of the illness erupts.
At that very instant, you must suddenly raise your eyebrows here and not allow yourself to be entangled and bound by them.
As soon as you see yourself being entangled and bound, you must by no means lie down with the body and roll around with them;
take great care, take great care! Above all, at the moment of death, rely firmly on a single invocation of "Bodhisattva" or "Buddha," and grapple with it.
Whenever various evil habits arise, immediately lift this *huatou* (critical phrase) with vigorous effort and brandish it toward the void.

Whether it be demons or Buddhas, the habitual tendencies of afflictions, the deliberations of good and evil, or all sensory objects—cut them all off at once and completely, like severing a tangled skein. If you practice in this manner, it will not hinder your reading nor your composition of essays.
When reading, observe where this book is being directed; when composing an essay, observe from where this writing arises.
From where does it flow forth? It is not hindered by welcoming guests or attending to visitors, nor by drinking tea, eating meals, defecating, or urinating;
in all such places, there is not even a hair’s breadth of a seam or gap. To settle the mind in this way is precisely what Yongjia described:

"When the mind is applied, it is precisely when the mind is not applied; when the mind is not applied, it is precisely when it is applied; that which is constantly applied is precisely the absence of the mind. This is it.
"Ordinary? It is not ordinary. Do you not know that you can trust the Elder Haiyin? Is he not free from falsehood? Please test this for yourself.
If you find my words to be unerring, only then will you realize that Yanzi’s three months of 'heart-fast' were truly laughable.
As for the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, read it thoroughly; recite it every morning and evening as your daily practice. Wait..."
When we meet next spring, let us deliberate together. My usual correspondence with you cannot help but be somewhat tinged with intellectual consciousness;
I am ashamed that it has not yet reached you, though it is not that I have failed to reach you—it is rather that I fear your faith has not yet reached its full depth.
Now that I see your faith gradually increasing and becoming increasingly pure, if I do not at this time gouge out this very heart of mine and give it to you...
My dear friend, when will you reach through to the bottom? If you remain complacent and fail to penetrate it, then the Sea-Seal (Haiyin) will simply pass away on its own.
How tragic! How tragic! Human life is pitiable; this Way is pitiable; but looking at your heart, my friend, it is even more pitiable.
Furthermore, your letter requesting further instruction is most sincere. However, you have not yet attained a definitive understanding of the two terms "emptiness" and "illusion";
consequently, there remains some obstruction regarding the relationship between mind and objects. This is why your practice is difficult to advance. I shall now explain this for you.
Then one will clearly understand and no longer have any doubts. What is called "emptiness" (śūnyatā) is not an emptiness of absolute non-existence.

It is precisely like the common expression "acting as if there were no one beside one"; does it mean that there truly is no one there? Rather, it means that while the person is present before one's eyes, they do not exist [as a substantial entity].
What is called "illusion" (māyā) is not an illusion of strange transformations; it refers to that which exists but is not real. For example:
It is like a market magician who, from a hollow tube, conjures forth a multitude of figures as if they were being pulled out;
yet within this tube there was originally nothing at all, and these things appear suddenly. Although they exist, they are not real. Since they are not real, they are fundamentally non-existent.
Because they are fundamentally non-existent, they are said to be empty. Therefore it is said: "For example, a person created by illusion is not non-existent as an illusory creation."
A person is like a conjured illusion; they are not a true person. Since a person is not real, are they not empty?
When the Buddha spoke of the word "empty," he meant to shatter the worldly attachment to things as being substantially existent; it did not mean absolute non-existence or annihilation.
Fearing that people might fall into the view of annihilationism, he further spoke of the word "illusion" to dispel that notion of annihilation.
Thus, all phenomena of body and mind are empty because they are illusory; it is precisely because they are empty that they are said to be like illusions.

When these two terms are contemplated as mutually dependent, one suddenly perceives their wondrous nature. What is called "emptiness" is the contemplation of emptiness through the perspective of illusory existence.
It is called "true emptiness. That which is called "existence" is but a phantom existence of that which is fundamentally non-existent;

thus it is called "wondrous existence. Because of true emptiness, the mind is not annihilated. Because of wondrous existence, objects are unborn. Since objects are unborn, what is there for the mind to grasp?
Since the mind is not annihilated, where can deluded thoughts abide? When deluded thoughts do not abide, with what mind could one grasp?
Objects. Objects are fundamentally illusory; by what object could one be dragged by the mind? This is simply that the mind does not grasp at objects, yet the mind is not annihilated.
Objects do not drag the mind, yet objects remain as they are (*tathatā*). When mind and objects are both *tathatā*, why should one not rejoice?
This is what is meant by: "The mind is originally unborn, arising only because of objects. If the preceding object does not exist, the mind likewise does not exist. One need only observe this.
To shatter that which is unreal like an illusion is called "non-existence. Yet, when the numinous mind shines alone and the deluded mind suddenly ceases, this is called "also non-existence.
That which is non-existent is merely the deluded mind; how could it mean the total absence of the true mind? What constitutes the deluded mind?
It is that which clings to objects and fails to transform them. What constitutes the true mind? It is that which does not grasp at the body, the mind, or external objects.
This is its characteristic: to know it clearly and constantly, as that which is numinous, tranquil, and illuminating. When one uses the mind in this way, what hindrance could there be?
Therefore it is said: "The self-mind grasps the self-mind; through non-illusion, illusory phenomena are formed. If one does not grasp, there is nothing that is non-illusory.

Since even non-illusion does not arise, how can illusory phenomena be established? This is precisely what is meant by: "In objective conditions there is neither good nor evil; good and evil arise from the mind."
If the mind were not designated as "strong," how could love and hatred arise? This means that it is merely emotion that does not attach itself to objects;
how then could objects obstruct the person? Since objects cannot obstruct the person, how could the person, in turn, obstruct objects?

The reason worldly people fail to attain self-mastery is simply that they do not realize that the mind and its objects are non-arising, like illusions and devoid of reality. If one thoroughly understands this—

If you contemplate that all things are unborn and like illusions, then all suffering and pleasure, grief and anxiety, gain and loss, love and hatred, and the states of grasping and rejecting will instantly dissolve and vanish like ice melting into water.
Therefore it is said: "To know the illusion is to leave it; no expedient means are required. To leave the illusion is to awaken;
there is no gradual progression. This is what is meant by reaching the Buddha's house in a single thought-moment—it is no empty word. Yours truly.
Simply observe that wherever all deluded thoughts arise and cease, and wherever all objective realms arise and cease, there is nothing that is not an illusory transformation and lacks reality.
Then the mind will naturally not rush toward objects, and objects will naturally not pull the mind.

As you respond to conditions in coming and going, a single thought is empty and luminous, shining alone with spiritual clarity. You perceive the body and mind before you as being like an illusion and a transformation.
It is like the moon in water, like a reflection in a mirror, like clouds in the sky, like a mirage in the wild.
Grasp it firmly with the adamantine eye; do not let it move again. Let all objective realms encounter it and they will immediately vanish.
Relying on what deluded mind could it possibly exist? A single glance causes it to be extinguished. If you apply the mind in this way, what delusion could there be? The mind can be [thus realized].
Why trouble yourself? Furthermore, what delusive objects are there that could disturb the mind?
These words are spoken by Haiyin with all his might, to reveal himself entirely for your sake and to overturn everything to its very bottom. Do not harbor further doubts;
you must by no means engage in retrospective calculations or various deliberations. All such reflections are evil thoughts and evil habits, and they are all causes that obstruct the Way.

It is a matter of conditions. If it were truly as this old man says, then those before one's eyes would be people of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Trustingly, I have taken up my brush and written these words;
I did not realize they have become so disheveled. With such great compassion, I have let slip these words in this manner. Take care.
Furthermore, we have been separated for several months in a state of sudden parting. Time flows swiftly; days and months deceive us.

Whenever I hear that you are practicing with redoubled diligence than usual, it fills my heart’s field with the nourishment of joy. My original intention was to wait until after your departure before entering the mountains myself.
In a single meeting, we shall mutually verify our past efforts and reach a definitive resolution. This thought was truly sincere; I did not realize it had manifested in the form of a dream.
It is laughable that you, a man of the Way, have fallen so far into emotional views. As stated in your letter:
"To seek stillness through sitting, and to seek the mind through stillness"—this is indeed the primary gateway for entering the Path and is most appropriate. However, as for sitting...
The essential points have not yet been clarified therein; hence one grows weary after sitting for a long time. This is because one has not attained mastery over the subtle nature of the mind.
Thus, after prolonged stillness, there arises a desire to hear more, accompanied by doubts that seem diffuse and lacking a point of return. This is truly due to the seeking mind itself.
Not having yet obtained the secret instructions, you have sought them with a single thought, only to find that this very effort becomes a source of weariness.

Thus, seeking the mind with the mind is exactly like a thirsty deer chasing a mirage. The *Zhongyong* says: "Only after knowing where to rest does one attain stillness. Because the mind beneath your feet does not yet know where to rest, it cannot attain stillness.
Regarding the items for governing the mind that you requested—such as the "four things not to do" and the "three reflections"—[these are the means].
Draw this mind in and hold it steady through concentration. This is the point where you must apply your refined spirit with earnest diligence;
it is precisely in this that I, your humble servant, place my greatest hopes in you. Now that you have willingly granted your consent, why do you instead remain secretive and stingy?
I fear that you have only recently entered our Buddha-dharma and have not yet attained extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).
Consequently, amidst your discourse, you have for the most part merely turned [your words] into the stale habits of what you previously saw and heard.

This prevents the nectar-like medicine from producing the effect of restoring one's youthful complexion through immediate application. Although the methods for teaching people by the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past are numerous, they do not go beyond—

The three trainings of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—namely, that concentration arises from morality and wisdom is produced from concentration—their detailed exposition does not exceed the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
As for the words of the Patriarchs, none are equal to the single work, the *Yongjia Ji* (The Collection of Yongjia).

You should read and savor it thoroughly. Regarding the secret instructions on the application of mind during entry into concentration, it says: "Precisely when the mind is being applied, precisely..."

Just as there is no mind to employ, the mindless state is precisely what is employed; that which is constantly employed is precisely the absence of mind. It is further said: After forgetting conditions, there is profound stillness; the nature of numinous awareness is vividly clear.

Where there is the dullness of non-recording consciousness, there is instead brilliant clarity; where there is the adherence to ordinary reality, there is instead the perfect realization of fundamental true emptiness.
This is the divine talisman for the cultivation of the mind. As for the "four things not to do" and the "three reflections," these are precisely the precepts;
all of this is fully detailed herein. In reality, the specific items for the practice of cultivating the mind do not go beyond the three gates of *śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, and *samādhi*.
Within this collection, *śamatha* is tranquility (*zhi*); *vipaśyanā* is insight (*guan*); and *yuganaddha* (or *ubhaya*) is the simultaneous application of both tranquility and insight.

Samādhi and prajñā are held in equilibrium. For now, let this suffice as a response to your request. As for those items marked with red circles in the *Zhongjing*, please pay close attention to their indications.
If you do not understand them, do not hesitate to send inquiries repeatedly.
Regarding the methods for the swift path of śamatha and vipaśyanā, I shall allow myself to write another sheet of paper to repay my debt from today.
Furthermore,

regarding these causal conditions, even the transition from the easy to the difficult has been practiced so deeply and thickly through the impure cycle of birth and death for immeasurable kalpas. Yet,
in this very moment, a single thought of faith has begun to sever it.
Morning and evening, one seeks to stem the long-flowing current of eternal kalpas; this endeavor is indeed no easy task.
Even this single thought of turning back is profoundly difficult to arouse. This is the sprout of spiritual roots accumulated over many kalpas;
it meets its time and begins to bud and stretch forth, eventually blossoming and bearing fruit entirely through constant cultivation and protection. Otherwise—
Suddenly one sees it withered and parched. When encountering circumstances and conditions, one deals with matters as they arise;
after a long time, through such mastery, one further applies the power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, whereby one may gradually reach liberation.

Yet, because we are fundamentally liberated from the very beginning, the reason our afflictions (*kleśa*) are not liberated is not the fault of the Dharma, but rather that our own minds are bound and attached, failing to attain liberation. This is truly because...
Hitherto, worldly sentiments have been deep and habitual attachments have become thoroughly matured; what is familiar is difficult to forget, and thus it arises as soon as one encounters it.

Therefore it is said: "I have never seen one who loves virtue as much as they love beauty. If one were to exchange that for this, then what was born would naturally become matured, and what was matured would naturally become born.
What is born becomes distant; what is distant becomes remote; what is remote becomes insipid; what is insipid leads to forgetting; and when one forgets, [the attachment] ceases.

Seeking liberation while remaining unbound—after a long time, when this mind attains great tranquility (*samādhi*), then the myriad forms and states before one’s eyes will be viewed as being like flowers in the sky, the moon in water, a mirage, or a frozen river;
fundamentally, there is nothing to bind or cling to, so what is there to seek in liberation?
It is said that Master Sengzhao gained strength from the words "things do not transmigrate. This would not be possible unless you possessed a vessel of great capacity.
One may be able to enter the threshold of this "gate of old age," yet remain alone unable to penetrate the phrase "the sun and moon shining in the sky.

If one cannot penetrate this, then know that Master Sengzhao has not penetrated it; if he has not penetrated it, then he has not truly attained mastery. This saying has been a source of doubt for me for several years.
Ultimately, within my own mind, I have realized it for myself alone. Since then, whenever I have encountered conditions and attained mastery, [it has been through this realization].
I have frequently relied upon the words of this old man. That you received his letter immediately upon leaving the gate is truly no small matter.
The old man did not begrudge explaining it to you in full; however, I fear that one day you might come to revile this old monk. You should simply take these words...
Transverse it across the mind. In all movements and actions; in all instances of sound, form, wealth, and profit; in all circumstances and conditions, whether adverse or favorable;
in all states of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure; and in all instances of love and hatred, acceptance and rejection.
Regarding all states that are in flux, seal them with this very seal.

Observe how there is a place that does not shift, how there is a place of constant stillness, how there is a place that does not flow, how there is a place that does not move, and how there is a place that is not all-pervasive.
Looking and looking in this way, suddenly—*bò!*—you will see through it.
Upon hearing these words, you will know that the old man does not deceive you, and you will finally believe that the fundamental truth is not something one deceives oneself about.
To Mr. Huang Weiheng:
although you are said to be turning toward the Way, the eye within this [teaching] has not yet attained clarity; you often mistake worldly dharmas for...
Regarding the Buddha-dharma, its essence and its teaching cannot help but be spoken of as two separate pieces.

If they are spoken of as two separate pieces here, then all things—love and hate, opposition and compliance, grasping and rejecting, good and evil, success and failure, motion and stillness—and so forth, would naturally each become two separate pieces.
I, Haiyin, have repeatedly told you that the Buddhas and Patriarchs fundamentally have no substantial dharma to bestow upon others.
It merely serves to reveal to people the matter that is inherently present within each and every individual’s own portion. The *Zongjing* says:

"Taking the one mind as the school and illuminating the myriad dharmas as the mirror. It is precisely because we are unable to know the one mind that the Buddha preached the teachings to point toward it;
it is because we are unable to see our own minds that the Patriarchs provisionally used Chan to demonstrate it. These two [approaches]—

All of this is simply unavoidable. Your recent statement—that practicing the teachings inevitably leads to mental exhaustion, whereas following the fundamental principle (zong) is like riding with a favorable wind—demonstrates that you possess deep-seated habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) for *prajñā* from many lifetimes.

Within such a major section as the "Ocean Seal" (*Sāgaramudrā*), both [approaches] are equally illusory; there is, in truth, no talk of difficulty or ease. If you do not realize your own mind, then...

The various schools are characterized by erroneous understanding and defilement; all fall into the conceptual traps of consciousness. Likewise, the teachings involve false knowledge and false views, entirely reducing them to the handles of verbal discourse.
None of these are the ultimate, true state. Little do they realize that the teachings are the Buddha’s eye and Chan is the Buddha’s mind;
the two are not two different things—how could there be any distinction between them? Haian instructed people to study the teachings and practice Chan, for both are...
This is not the kind of knowledge and vision you have today; by forming such an interpretation, you not only fail the Haiyin (Ocean Seal), but you also fail your own spiritual nature.
I recall an ancient person who was once asked: "When the ancients were hungry, they ate."
"Beating sleep when weary is itself the Way. People today eat when hungry and beat sleep when weary; why is this not the Way?
He replied, "In the past, when the ancients ate, they simply ate; when they beat sleep, they simply beat sleep. Therefore, it was the Way.

Today’s people do not simply eat when they eat, nor do they simply beat sleep when they beat sleep; instead, they engage in distracted and confused calculations. Therefore, they turn their backs on it."
This is the Way. Looking at it from this perspective, in your daily life, simply raise your eyebrows and let out a shout;
let it cause gods and ghosts to tremble with fear, shatter the courage of celestial Māras, and dissolve the souls of dark spirits.

With one roar, drive them all back, so that you may settle into the stillness and quietude of your original ground—unclad by even a single thread of silk, starkly vivid, pure and naked. Take this very segment...
This is our family tradition: if you wish to study, then study; if you do not, set it aside and do not allow even a single character to hang upon your mind.
If you wish to compose a literary essay, then compose one; if you do not, set it aside and do not permit yourself to engage in idle speculation.
Even when drinking tea or eating a meal, simply drink the tea and eat the meal. If you wish to sleep, then sleep. If you wish to defecate or urinate, then attend to those needs.
When you must defecate or urinate, do it immediately upon feeling the urge; do not allow yourself to dwell on it afterwards.
Be like a wandering ghost—utterly empty, pure, and stainless—and yet do not remain stuck within that emptiness or purity.
Thus, entering directly with a single blade, advancing with a single thought, you will, when reading, personally encounter the ancients, and when composing, [you will truly create].
It is simply to spit it out from within one's own breast all at once, with no before or after. The moment of containing and nurturing is itself the moment of spitting it out;
the moment of spitting it out is itself the moment of containing and nurturing. In this way, one is not turned by movement or stillness, light or darkness.
One who is not moved by various arts and stratagems—this is what is called a preeminent great man, a person of immeasurable capacity.
Do you truly believe this? If you indeed find it credible, then immediately rouse yourself and enter into this very state. Take care, take care!
To the Layman Ma who studies the Way:

First, you must have a sense of urgency regarding birth and death. Second, you must recognize that the body is the root of suffering, and the mind is the source of deluded thoughts and the creation of karma.
Third, you must truly and thoroughly see through worldly fame, achievement, wealth, and honor.
Sound, form, wealth, and profit are all empty and insubstantial.
Fourth, one must fear that by committing evil karma in this life, one will fall into hell in the future and undergo various sufferings with no one to provide rescue or protection.

Using the mind in this way throughout the twelve periods of the day and night—whether moving or still, at leisure or in haste—one remains as such, unmoving. Whether encountering adversity or favor, good or evil, enemies or kin, one regards them with equality.

'If one renews oneself on this day, one should renew oneself day after day, renewing it yet again day after day. Now you have resolved to cast off your former self and renew yourself greatly."
It is not only that your son’s name is vulgar, but his mind as well. A name is the guest of reality; the mind is the substance of virtue.
If one does not strive for substance but prizes empty fame, this is not virtue.
Viewed from this perspective, it is not only that your son is vulgar in name, but also vulgar in mind. What is called vulgarity does not refer merely to dress, speech, or appearance.
This refers to those who, through habitual intimacy with defilements, corrupt their innate nature. The innate nature of our humanity is fundamentally luminous;

yet, as we gradually become stained by sensual desires, the eyes are obscured by perverse forms, the ears by licentious sounds, the nose by foul odors, the tongue by unwholesome flavors, the body by false tactile sensations, and the mind by perverse thoughts.
These six faculties mutually obscure one another, causing turbidity and confusion within. Thus, through long-term cultivation, they gradually [corrupt the nature].
Through the habituation of defilements, these have become one's nature; one regards them as inherently existing and considers them to be the natural order of things.

Consequently, one gallops wildly through the realm of delusion, and the virtue of fundamental luminosity is instead viewed as a foreign object. How could one know that there is a "former self," a true former self?
That which the sages lament lies precisely here. Therefore, one casts oneself into the waters of the precepts to wash and cleanse it. Now, these precepts are not some external thing;
they are the light of wisdom inherently present within one's own mind—what the Confucians call "illuminating virtue" (mingde).

At present, people’s light of wisdom is not bright, and thus their illuminating virtue grows ever more obscured. By now restoring this illuminating virtue, one returns to the original truth of nature.

One must radiate the light of wisdom to shatter the darkness and obscurations. When the darkness and obscurations are shattered, the fundamental reality manifests; when the light of wisdom radiates, all hindrances dissolve.

This is why our Buddha enjoined the precept against killing to perfect benevolence (*ren*), the precept against stealing to achieve righteousness (*yi*), the precept against sexual misconduct to establish propriety (*li*), the precept against false speech to strengthen trustworthiness (*xin*), and the precept against intoxicants to clarify wisdom. When these five precepts are complete, and...
The five constants were fulfilled, the six faculties were restrained, and the three karmas were purified. This is what is meant by washing away old defilements and advancing toward daily renewal;
casting off the former self and creating a new transformation. Thus, the illusory person also changed his name to Yan and styled himself Zilun.
I entrust these Buddhist precepts to you as if they were your sovereign’s command; may you exert yourself in them.

they traverse the marketplace of the Great Dharma and gather the unsurpassed *amṛta* and the wondrous flavor of clarified butter.

If you do not harbor a grudge so deep as to gnash your teeth, and forget the resolve to sleep on firewood and taste gall, being unable to exert yourself by suspending your beam or piercing your thigh, then how will you fulfill your original ambition and wipe away this great disgrace?
I have heard that according to the Grand Being (the Daode Jing), first one establishes virtue, next one establishes merit, and next one establishes fame. You...
If those below can truly encourage themselves with the example of the Supreme (Taishang), then even in poverty one may find joy. What else, then, need occupy the mind? Confucius said:
"If a scholar sets his will upon the Way yet feels ashamed of coarse clothing and poor food, he is not fit to be discussed. The ancients also said:
"If one possesses the joy of the Way and righteousness, then the physical form may be cast aside. Once the physical form can be cast aside, what more is there beyond this?"
Thus, there is nothing to be done; how could one allow the mind to be entangled by it? How could one dwell therein without being at ease?

It has often been said that among the myriad things created by Heaven, only man is most intelligent; this is an ancient saying. I, however, maintain that it is not so. Why?
Because both man and the myriad things possess the nature of spiritual awareness (*ling-jue*). This nature is equally bestowed and shared by all.
How could there ever be a distinction between man and thing? Ultimately, that which distinguishes man from things is because [man]... [is endowed with... things.
To possess [the nature] and yet not know it—such people merely know what they possess. To know that it is inherently possessed and to exhaustively realize it is called being a sage (*śramaṇa*).
To know that it ought to be exhausted but to be unable to exhaust it all at once is called being a worthy one (*bhadra*).
To know this and be willing to seek its exhaustion is called being wise. To know this but be unwilling to turn back and seek it is called being foolish. To know it but not truly...

To seek with excessive intensity is called "madness. To possess knowledge yet lack clarity, clinging to a single perspective as if it were necessarily correct, is called "narrow-mindedness" (or "self-restraint").

It is simply a matter of things. Alas! This lies between man and thing, between knowing and not knowing, between seeking and not seeking.

Though the difference may be but a hair’s breadth, the resulting error is a thousand *li* away. I have observed the gentlemen of the Three Qi: who among them does not feel indignation in their hearts and struggle for words in their mouths?
They look back upon a thousand ages with a far-reaching gaze, and their every sneeze or spittle stirs the winds and clouds. Even those like Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou—
Their religious activities were hardly worth observing. When questioned about their mental nature, they stared blankly with tongues tied.

Yet, when discussing the subtleties of the mind, they could not help but sigh with appreciation and nod in agreement. However, when it came to speaking of the Buddha, they looked away in disdain and paid no heed.
Alas! To know the mind but not the Buddha is like knowing that two fives make ten, yet remaining ignorant of the number ten itself.
Consequently, the Way and its arts remain obscure, and even men of brilliant intelligence and heroic talent cannot avoid being hindered by this.

As for those who instruct others: by employing sincere hearts and truthful words morning and evening, they should gradually cultivate and influence them.

Although the recipients may not yet attain self-confidence, they will nonetheless be transformed along with their instructors. For the gentlemen of the world, what they hear and see from birth are the constant objects of their ears and eyes;

As for me, I shall dissolve into the long waves—what regret could there be? This was written by Wang Sheng Muchang and Zhou Sheng Shifu.

Rather than using *yujinzi* (Gardenia) and *yumu* (Leonurus), he used *baimu* (Fritillaria), which further caused the large and small intestines to lose their function; the constipation grew increasingly severe day by day.

An incompetent physician mistakenly administered *rūkṣa* (meat-cour), which further increased the heat; he was on the verge of suffocating to death. Fortunately, licorice (*yaṣṭimadhu*) resolved it and removed the *rūkṣa*.
When *jīraka* (pepper) was added to harmonize the condition, perspiration broke out over his entire body. The practitioner fortunately assisted with *śuṇṭhī* (dry ginger), and he was restored.

As for those suffering from the same ailment, they were unfortunately struck by *vatsanābha* (aconite); even a skilled physician was at a loss. Fortunately, their vital essence (*prāṇa*) had not yet been depleted; [they will surely recover].

Do not harm your life-force; you must regulate it slowly and gradually. Once the true yin-water arises and the heart-fire gradually descends, the adventitious pathogenic influences will be eliminated and subdued, and the True Lord will become serene.
Only then can you preserve and restore your original qi and fulfill your innate nature. I am deeply grateful for your compassionate concern in inquiring from afar about the origin of my illness.
Its symptoms are as described above; I rely solely upon the distant illumination of your white tuft of hair. Since I first fell ill...
Although the fierce flames of a great fire scorch his body, his five internal organs remain cool and refreshing; he lacks even a single moment of weariness or fatigue.
He regards the prison of the triple world and the shackles of the four modes of birth as nothing more than celestial light reflected in clouds.

The Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*) he previously entered has thus become a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) where all is like the moon in water, and a Buddhist service (*buddhakārya*) where all is like flowers in the sky. Fortunately, he has reached the gate of emotion...

The [knots] burst asunder; the fetters of consciousness are suddenly cast open. Now, taking the elephant-king of long-term strategy to pursue the golden-haired [lion], I turn my steps toward the sandalwood forest.
Hungry, I shall feast upon the purple cypress; thirsty, I shall drink from Caoxi. My life’s aspiration is hereby fulfilled.
I dare not trouble you to move your steps to Vaiśālī to bestow the nectar once more; I only pray that the Nāga remains at peace and enters deeply into the boundless.
I shall wait until they have completed three circumambulations. Please return. I respectfully offer these words to comfort you and convey my compassionate regards.

Furthermore, the phenomena of the world are like flowers seen by those with cataracts; their distortions are beyond the need for discussion. Yet, through the cycles of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, beings continue to come and go in succession.
Thank you. Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are thus; the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*) is serene and still—what further addition or subtraction could there be?

It was only that I reflected my Dharma-affinities were not yet widespread and my power of vows (*praṇidhāna*) was not yet complete, previously hindered by intellectual obstructions. Now, with a single clap of thunder from within emptiness, all manner of illusory transformations and cloud-like obscurations have been utterly cleared away.
Furthermore, I am fortunate that from this day forward I shall truly be a man of the Way who is free from affairs. This is precisely the conflagration and the sword-blade...
Mountains! You have achieved the cool, illusion-like liberation; this is truly the holy grace of the Sage, which has not been slighted by me.

All other matters of right and wrong have vanished and are almost entirely exhausted—what more is there worth saying? If one can achieve the power of the unsurpassed Way, [all else is of no consequence].
One may be reborn in any buddha-field according to one’s vows; how much less so within this trivial space of a mere fist-sized rock and a spoonful of water?

Knowing that your love for me, as we share the same essence, exceeds that for one's own flesh and bone, and your concern for me, as we share the same heart, penetrates my very marrow, I venture to offer this consolation.
It is no empty word. My lack of wisdom means the time for my departure is not far off; yet if there remains some karmic affinity to sustain us, I shall still hope to receive your favor.
He ascended Mount Yunshan and spent his final years in leisurely ease; as for the joy of the Dharma he experienced therein, how could it be described?
This, moreover, was sent by the devas and nāgas, accomplishing a merit most rare and supreme.

Furthermore, my lack of wisdom and the karmic conditions obstructing me have been deep and heavy. I am humbled that you, Master, have accepted me through the compassionate power of our shared essence.

The exertion of your spiritual faculties and your various most subtle and profound insights truly transcend the realm of ordinary emotion; how could they ever be contained within words or metaphors? As we part at this temporary sojourn, I bid you farewell with my horse-hair banner hanging down.
He traveled westward, arriving at Tongjiang on the fifth day of the New Year. Braving the snow, he went to pay his respects at Jianzhai and met with Master Tai.
He inquired after the well-being of Xiulang, who replied that he had already packed his bags for departure the following morning, bound for Jiujiang.

Shortly thereafter, a letter was sent to Jishui inviting [the author] to Tongjiang to join him on the boat, where they joyfully discussed their pasts as if they were old acquaintances from many lifetimes.

He was one who roamed among those who practice the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). When Erzhan heard of this, he immediately went to welcome him into the Tiexie Buddha Hermitage where they met;
their spiritual dialogue was most harmonious. This gentleman’s faculties were sharp and keen, and moreover, he had the support of Xiulang as his vanguard.

Thus, before even a single word had been spoken, the previously fortified walls and the banners and drums fell of their own accord; the case was suddenly overturned, and he was no longer the person he had been before.
Mr. Zhou of Rizhou was not particularly wise; he had merely surpassed others in his youth. Later, while traveling to Luling, Huilang escorted him there, where they met Wang Xinghai.
This gentleman possessed a natural bone of the Way; one could not have expected such superior faculties and sharp intelligence to exist amidst the defilements of the Dharma-ending age.
In the future, your affinity for the Dharma will not be slight. Having lingered for two days before parting, Xiulang immediately set sail eastward.
If you wish to fully understand the circumstances of this connection, you may do so by looking at Zhi’en. On the third day of the second month, I passed over Mount Yuping;
suddenly, upon the wall of my lodgings, I beheld the Master’s inscription. It was as if I were facing the Dharmakāya while gazing into a precious mirror.
Filled with joy and exultation, he composed a verse, saying: "When you reached Caoxi, I did not come; when I reached Caoxi, you had already departed.
Coming and going, there is fundamentally no mind—whom could have known we would meet upon this narrow path? Having eaten his fill, he departed.

On the sixth day, he arrived at Caoxi and paid homage to the true likeness of the Sixth Patriarch. Shortly thereafter, he left the mountain and traveled to Wuyang, where he went to visit the Commander-in-Chief, Lord Wang.
He appeared before him dressed in prison garb; this lord was of exceptionally noble character and personally descended from his steps to release his bonds, saying:

"You are a transcendent man beyond worldly affairs. Moreover, you have brought about this extraordinary calamity for the sake of praying for blessings upon the Imperial Court. What crime could there possibly be?"
"We are deeply moved by our feelings for you. How could we meet as mere ordinary people of the world? We firmly decline your refusal. Eventually, they stayed to converse for a long time;
after partaking in a meal, they took their leave. Furthermore, they dispatched guards to escort him to his place of exile.
The journey spanned fifteen hundred *li*, where corpses lay scattered along the road; even children of three feet in stature were brandishing spears and carrying blades. It was truly extraordinary.

They could not distinguish between those who were thieves and those who were not. Upon reaching Dianbai, the journey was still half complete. To the south lay dense forests where one lost one’s tracks at every step;

across the vast wilderness and high plateaus, there was not a single smoke from a hearth. For days on end, they did not have a grain of rice to eat, and for the entire morning, they did not sip so much as a drop of water.
The famine in Leidi was especially severe, having persisted for four years already. Miasmic fevers broke out violently, and pestilence spread through the land.

They roam横行 (wildly), their poisonous vapors suffocating the heavens and their scorching heat obscuring the sun. With empty bellies, they suffer calamity; those who die or are wounded exceed half the population.

The state of such misery and tragedy is beyond description. How much more so when one encounters the stinking winds of the seacoast, the miasmic smoke, and the blazing sun—these strike the nose and pierce the heart.

The spirit is clouded and the mind is intoxicated; this is a realm of sin. Truly, it is not established in vain. I privately consider that were it not for one whose very bones are as cold as ice, how could one endure such bitter poison?

I look up to the protection of those capable of subduing all things. On the stage of *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patience of non-arising), even bearing arms in the ranks of an army is no different from a *bodhimaṇḍa*.
Yet, when the springs run dry and the grass withers, there are no *wei* plants to gather; my sustenance is no longer provided by meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
How could I not become a starving man of the Western Mountains? It is only that my wisdom is insufficient and I am ashamed before the virtue of my predecessors;

yet, having encountered this era, I have surpassed them. This is overcome by the power of karma, so what need is there to dwell on thoughts of death and rebirth? I feel shame and remorse only because my original vows remain unfulfilled and the Buddha’s grace remains unpaid.
I privately reflect that the Buddhas, through their inconceivable spiritual powers, subdue sentient beings—this is no [ordinary matter].

By employing a single expedient means, you have both subdued and gathered them, wishing for their passions to wither and their intellects to be exhausted, so that they may know the ultimate limit and the source of reality.
This profound benefit for those of dull faculties demonstrates that your true compassion is not shallow.

If there is indeed a karmic affinity for the Dharma, and if in the future Heaven grants us the opportunity for a meeting, when we discuss together the Dharma-gate of dreams and illusions, will this not serve as a true verification of today’s conditions? I pray only that you, Master...

The light of wisdom shines perfectly and universally; though ten thousand *li* lie to the south of heaven, not even a hair’s breadth separates them. I look up and pray that the power of your unconditioned compassion will at all times sustain me.
Furthermore:
Since our parting at the riverbank, three years have passed in the blink of an eye. There was no moment when my thoughts were not directed toward the vast heavens.

At the beginning of winter in the year of Dingmao, Jueyin arrived, and I was able to receive your handwritten letter; I am deeply grateful for your compassionate kindness, as your precious Dharma-treasures fill my basket—a manifold merit indeed.
He sprinkles the nectar of truth upon the parched and withered, and spreads the clouds of compassion over the burning house.
This is the encomium of Kangzu. It pierces open the adamantine eye within the skull; reading it causes the pores of one’s entire body to bristle with joy, an ecstasy beyond description.
How could this be achieved were it not for the power of unconditioned compassion? Jueyin said: "Holding my staff, I have the intention to travel afar. From [this point]—
You do not know what I am pointing at. This mind pursues after deluded thoughts; whenever I meet with Youwu, we never fail to discuss the wondrous sounds and forms of the Dharma.
Youwu is truly an extraordinary man. When we parted last winter, it was as if a needle had pierced the crown of my head.
He himself said that the pain pierced all the way to his heels. Suddenly, he overturned his previous case. I, the Unwise One, therefore presented him with this verse:

"The Layman Juefei has now become a person vastly different from his former self. After this gentleman had departed, time passed in long, silent intervals. Fortunately, all external conditions were severed;
the four elements were light and at ease, free from any affliction or distress. Thus, I was able to close my door within my tent and bring to completion that which had remained unfinished.

Kōan. Fortunately, I have already escaped the weeds of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. Last summer, I led several beginners to expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* at Wuchang to repay my Master’s great vow.
There were several sheets of notes taken by those who clapped their hands in approval; these are all merely fragmented dregs and are by no means the power of true knowledge and vision.
Yet, reflecting on this remainder of my life as I remain within the armor of non-action, I am moved with even deeper gratitude.

The sagely grace is difficult to repay; I shall merely pass my years by means of this. Furthermore, relying upon the spiritual power of the Buddhas, I maintain it to wash away the transgressions of the defiled teachings;
thus, I do not begrudge its circulation within the realm of worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*). Having just received the Dharma-intent, I could not help but fall down in joy.
Beholding the Vajra Stūpa is like facing the Dharmakāya; reading the encomiums to the Patriarchs is like hearing Brahma-sounds. I sip...
This Yangxian spring tea is like pouring clarified butter (ghṛta) into one’s mouth. Considering this malarial region, by what karmic conditions could such a thing be obtained?
May all who see or hear of it rejoice and receive its benefit. That the Great Master has come once more—this man is indeed a "Chengying" among the monastic community.

This disciple’s roots of faith are originally deep, yet his habitual tendencies (vāsanā) were not shallow; now, fortunately, they have been cast off and greatly diminished. Furthermore, he is sustained by the power of the Master’s Dharma.
"Maintain this! This very state can be expected to advance further. Jueyin’s arrival has greatly shaken what was within my breast, and there is indeed a ground of joy.
It is a pity that while his aspiration is abundant, his strength is insufficient; yet he has not failed this life and may serve as a seed for the Vajra.
When he emerges again, he will surely not fail the ground of his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). He heard that the Master was at Mount Kuanglu."
