I wish to see you in person; therefore, I have sent you back first to report this. Calculating by the great principles of the matter, you should arrive by summer. When that time comes, I shall provide you with full details once more. Furthermore, [Note: The source text provided ends abruptly with "Furthermore" (又). The translation reflects the fragmentary nature of the input.]

When Da Yi arrived previously to receive the Dharma-sound, my joy was immeasurable. Knowing that his movement and stability were appropriate to the occasion, it greatly comforted my long-held aspirations.
Regarding recent matters concerning Caoxi, I imagine you will surely clap your hands with great delight upon hearing them.
My original intention was still to have Master Yi travel from Yan to Jin; yet as he was about to depart, I reflected that for twenty years he has wandered through foreign lands, and now—
The Master passed away more than two years ago. How could I bear not to offer a pinch of incense and a handful of soil?

For this reason, I have resolved to hasten my return to the mountain of my home. Traveling from Hupeh back, I was unable to prostrate myself at the feet of the Venerable [Master]. This summer, my illusory body has fortunately been free from major illness;
however, I was afflicted by the "maggot-demon" of lychees, resulting in scabies and sores all over my body. Furthermore, I have been living on the rice and gruel of Caoxi as a guest.
The "monk-demon" (saṃgha-māra) falsely manifests as a spectral apparition; for this reason, one dwells in a temporary shelter to nurse an illness.

At this time, you were precisely about to enter the mountains, yet fortunately Master [So-and-so] has given rise to the mind of the Great Way and wishes to act as a donor (*dānapati*). However, that person is as pure and tranquil as water; his resolve is great, but his strength is slight.
You, Master, can by means of your wondrous power of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) extend your right hand from afar across more than one hundred and ten cities to raise this golden [banner].

O Gangdang, I do not know on what day the Tathāgata Ratnatejas will preach the Dharma for sentient beings in the Buddha-land above, so that I may hear from afar the sound of his clearing his throat and snapping his fingers.
Having received your letter three times during the New Year, my heart is comforted by its profound sincerity;
I am deeply moved by our shared bond of the Way and our common essence. I know you should travel by carriage, and I calculate that you may arrive at Jimen by the middle of autumn.
Please take this to heart as you sit at my feet. The youth Feng Changli, a filial and upright scholar (*xiao-lian*), is the foremost among the disciples here.

He recently sent a letter saying that he has already entered the Master’s chamber; how fortunate I am! However, I do not yet know whether this young man’s future conduct will be such as to warrant praise or reproach.

If he happens to be at the capital gate, I hope you will grant him timely rescue and deliverance. I know that you two patrons possess great and courageous power, and that you will surely move [the spirits] to respond.
It is appropriate; one should simply listen to the timing and conditions.
Furthermore, regarding the various illusory transformations within the Sahā world-system, it is precisely fitting to view them with the Dharma-eye. If one enters the realm of Śāriputra...

Even this categorization cannot entirely avoid the perception of purity and defilement. Yesterday, Yongshun brought me the *Fayin* (Sound of Dharma), from which I learned that you were carrying your staff toward the Sacred Peak (*Lingyue*).
I have already sent a reply directly to inform you. Regarding the causes and conditions of the Sandalwood Tathāgata, I have fully understood your previous inquiry;
it is simply because the Buddha’s spiritual power does not depend on anything else. I have taken the notes from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* with me and respectfully presented them to Hui[...].
I, [Name], of inferior capacity, deeply understand that this great matter of karmic conditions has been sent by the Tathāgata and bestowed as a sacred grace.
This itself may serve as the ground for repaying his kindness.

I only pray that this Dharma may pervade all lands as numerous as motes of dust, so that all who see or hear it may together enter the direct perception (*svasaṃvedana*) of their own minds. Thus, I shall not fail to diligently fulfill my obligations.

If one can reach this point, then for this life, one will have all that is needed and more than enough; what further cause for regret could there be? However, I do not yet know whether there is even a small portion within it that corresponds to my own condition.
I pray that you will grant me the great gift of the golden probe to strip away and clear the cataracts of my ignorance. My good fortune would lie not in mere trifles.

Furthermore, in the third month of spring, Cujiao Yin returned from his illness. At that time, I was still thinking of Zibo, who was contending for supremacy with the Five Elders, so I dispatched Baxing to inquire after him.
Suddenly, Chan practitioner Shun arrived bearing a letter written with a hair-pen; from this, I knew he had already been mired in the mud.
Water. He has gone ten thousand *li* into a place where not a single blade of grass grows. Why does this old fool laugh? For what reason is he so busily occupied?
Yesterday someone said that on the road to Chang’an there is a man who knows no restraint;

he has stolen a handful of soil from the imperial domain and molded it into a sixteen-foot golden body, causing immeasurable people to give rise to inverted perceptions. Furthermore, taking that sixteen-foot [body]...
The Golden Body is cast onto a crossroads, causing the donkeys and horses passing by to trample it. If Old Zibo were as deluded as this, what would he have done?

I often recall how Old Zhaozhou took a single blade of grass and made it a sixteen-foot Golden Body, while Old Lei Yang took that sixteen-foot Golden Body and made it a single blade of grass. Are these two public cases the same?
This is a distinction. To know it atop a ten-thousand-fathom peak, one must surely let out a laugh.
Old Red Helmet, recently smothered by a toxic miasma, has become deaf, his eyes blurred, his nose congested, and his throat stifled; he knows not when he shall turn over in the realm of white silver.
This was the first instance of him casting off this evil habit.
Furthermore,
when Hongkui was ten thousand *li* away from Zibai, he heard the sound of the Dharma being preached amidst the clamor of drums, kettledrums, and gongs, as if it were right before him.
Poisoned lacquer enters the ear, yet it is transformed into miasmic smoke and toxic mists, which are further transmuted into nectar (*amṛta*). One feasts upon this day and night until satiated;
thus, though one ought to die, one does not. Furthermore, one beholds mosquitoes and gnats crawling along the rim of the bowl, their greedy saliva overflowing across the great trichiliocosm.

When will the fires of the three calamities arise to burn all to ashes? When will the *Vilambana* wind blow away the dust and the rains of the *Ābhāsvara* heaven fall, washing away the kalpa-ash until nothing remains?

This is the remainder. Caoxi was formerly known as the Precious Forest of the Western Heaven; recently, it has been treated as a palace of demons and a den of ghosts—a truly laughable state of affairs.

It is pitiful that the Elder Zibai’s spiritual power was not great enough to secure even a single night’s lodging there. Now, Heaven has dispatched the "Red Helmet" (the military) specifically to sweep and cleanse the site.
Within eight years, they have exerted their utmost power to wash away [the defilements] almost entirely; the demonic factions have been driven out. Now, it will...

He transformed a defiled land into a pure land and converted an ocean of karma into a lotus pond. Mazu Daoyi, who had lain buried for a thousand years, today finally regains his breath and turns his body;
having passed away only to revive again, he suddenly beholds a radiant and magnificent brilliance.
However, as the gate remained firmly closed, he was unable to suddenly manifest the infinite adornments of the Buddha-land.

He merely waited for Mañjuśrī to extend his right hand from afar, passing over more than one hundred and ten cities; by the mere act of snapping his fingers, he beheld layer upon layer of inexhaustible realms.
Even if every single Sudhana throughout the worlds of the ten directions were as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field...
When sentient beings pay their respects, may each one be enabled to enter instantaneously into the Dharma-realm of Vairocana.
This is indeed the Buddha-work of the old Red-Helmeted Spear-Wielder, who exerts his efforts beneath the banners and drums;

it is equal to the time when the old Zibo, dwelling serenely in the Pure Land amidst lotus flowers, extended his broad and long tongue to preach the Dharma-gates for benefiting living beings to the various emanated Bodhisattvas.
How have you been? A certain Zen practitioner has come from afar to inquire after you. It is no less than Qi Shun who has traveled to Huiyang to bestow his kindness upon me.
Old Hongkai lacks the refined character of Juefan; he merely rivals Hu Qiangzhong in his coarse habits.

From time to time, the purple Dharma-body of the Elder appears at the tip of my tongue, standing vividly before my eyes. I respectfully hold this bowl of fragrant incense to extend my offerings; may you look upon me with compassion.
I, [Name], a disciple of Chan Master Miaofeng, reflect deeply upon myself:
my faculties are dull and inferior, and my habitual defilements are thick and heavy. Yet, by virtue of karmic conditions from past lives, it was a heavenly fortune that I encountered my teacher.

I have been honored by your true compassion, which has rescued and uplifted me. You have exhausted every ounce of your mind and strength through skillful means, instructing me face-to-face and guiding me by the ear without ceasing day or night for several years.
In my daily life, I have constantly observed my Master’s silent, transformative heart;

yet I regret that I cannot leap entirely into his heart, suddenly causing my own vision to become steady and clear. Were there not some numinous sage, I would remain nothing more than mere earth, wood, clay, or a hollow shell.

In the end, it is difficult to effect a transformation. Nevertheless, because my prayers have been long-standing and my entry [into the practice] has been deep, there has not been a lack of resonance and a hidden response.

Although my disposition is coarse and uncultivated, that which has secretly nourished and subtly transformed me has never failed to arise from the power of the grace bestowed by our Master’s *māyājāla-samādhi*.
Like clouds gathering over the Cool Grove (*Sītavana*) and the moon shining brightly in the realm of space, from this point on, my form shall divide and my shadow shall disperse.

Appearance and disappearance occur simultaneously; though the sound of your wondrous voice resounds, its power is obstructed by mountains and passes. Yet your true marks and real body remain solemnly present within the waters of the mind.
Though five years have passed, it is as if it were but a single day; though the Way transcends three thousand worlds, there is not so much as a thread’s breadth of separation.

Thus, dwelling in profound stillness by the secluded shore, one enters ever deeper into the realm of perfect penetration (*yuantong*). It may be said that while outward traces become increasingly sparse, the inner mind becomes increasingly dense;
as superficial sound daily dissolves, the true reality daily manifests. My own body and spirit have never for a moment departed from a single thought of my Master.
Yet, I am aware that my physical vessel is filthy and turbid; I consider these decaying bones to be such that their foul vapors pierce the heavens, far from being anything serene.
The vast valleys are insufficient to contain it; the dust and toil that block the heavens cannot be washed away except by a boundless, immense ocean.

Therefore, with a willing heart and at the cost of my life, I have cast myself into these remote mountain villages and placed myself in a land of utter isolation, intending never again to return to the world of men.
Unbeknownst to me, I have silently received the protection of the Dharma-protecting Bodhisattvas, who have mobilized the treasury of jewels to suddenly cause—
A single ray of light shines eastward, utterly shattering the profound darkness; this may be called a merit and virtue rarely encountered in ten thousand ages.
Tracing its origin, both the giver and the receiver have emerged entirely from the Perfect, Wondrous, Pure, and True Mind of our Master.

Last winter, when I received the Dharma instructions brought by someone, I read through some ten or so scrolls and perceived the Master’s heart so deeply that, without realizing it, my tears flowed freely.
I sigh. As it is said: "The heart of joy turns into such extreme distress that one sobs with tears soaking the collar.
Yet, that which I lament does not belong to mere emotion; rather, it lies in that which transcends ordinary sentiment. Looking around, all is desolate and sparse—how could one bear to see so much?
This is something that cannot help but move me to grief and pain. Alas! My life here is at its end; in the end, I shall be no different from the withered grass and trees.
There is no doubt. As for my heart’s desire to serve at your side, my long-held wish has not yet been fulfilled.

I only pray that my Master’s true compassion will not abandon me, but will embrace me with a mind of perfect illumination, so that this deluded child may not enter the path of inverted madness, but may walk steadily back to the Way of Perfect Enlightenment.
At present, I am fortunate enough to rely upon this single branch, which is quite secluded and excellent; should the Ocean of Wisdom...
Pocheng: I believe that my teacher’s mind-moon is able to voluntarily withhold its radiance and not cast its reflection here.
Furthermore, throughout my life, I have constantly disciplined myself with this thought: that to encounter my teacher during this long night may truly be called a second meeting.
You are my close friend. Therefore, since our meeting thirty years ago, I have known that there is a matter directed toward the Ultimate.
For twenty years, I have constantly and diligently cleared away dung; this single thought of bitter urgency has never been removed from the space between my eyebrows and eyelashes.

My only regret is that because my accumulated habits are so deep-seated, I have been unable to suddenly purify the flowing consciousness of present karma, thereby failing to repay the Dharma-compassion of my teachers and friends. This is truly a great shame.

I feel shame and remorse. Since our separation, fifteen years have suddenly passed. In truth, I have already been lying on wooden chips and tasting gall, urging myself on with such bitter pain that I have not dared to slacken even slightly.
Yet, because the cataracts of illusion have not yet cleared away, I still remain submerged in the net of delusion; though my mind knows I am bound, [the fetters persist].
My strength is not free; it is truly because the sword of wisdom is not sharp that I cannot suddenly rend [the veil]. Knowing this point of pain, how could I dare deceive my Master?
Now, fortunately, by taking the Dharma as a condition, I know how to repay the Buddha’s grace. I shall take the net of illusion as a Buddhist service.
My heart in bearing this burden is truly like holding up nine tripods, yet the malady of attachment to the Dharma increases by seven layers. I had thought...

To venture to follow the sages despite my own failings is truly an act of madness and folly; it is not a matter of wisdom. Fortunately, I am aware in my heart that this is not the correct path, like dreaming of crossing a river.

Yet, mindful of the profound grace bestowed by Your Majesty, the Holy Sovereign, who has granted me the Vajra-flame to incinerate the deep darkness, causing the roots of worldly passion accumulated over kalpas to be shattered in a single stroke, I look back upon my former wanderings as nothing more than dream-events. Therefore—

I am not wise. Because of this, I have found joy and fulfillment throughout my life. In my heart, I knew that my Master would surely offer me congratulations. Although I now cast myself far away into this miasmic sea, it is as if I were sitting within a *bodhimaṇḍa*;

though I drink deeply of the scorching heat, it is like partaking of sweet nectar (*amṛta*). In the leisure moments between bearing arms, I have done nothing but face the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to investigate the mind-seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Only now do I realize that everything prior to this had fallen into the gateway of shadows and reflections—it was not true knowledge.
The power of vision. This is to know that the spiritual powers of all Buddhas, in taming sentient beings with whom they have a karmic connection, do not employ only a single kind of expedient means.
Whether through adversity or favor, there is nothing that does not cause them to enter the cool gate of great liberation.

Even the mass of fire and the mountain of blades are nothing other than the ultimate site of the ground of quiescent extinction. From this day forward, one may truly say that one has not failed one's own spirit; it may also be said—
This means that I have not failed my teachers and friends. At moments when the mind was awakened, I recorded these thoughts as they arose.

Now that I am about to complete this work, although it is not a formal or orthodox commentary on liberation, I have taken pleasure in the Dharma for my own amusement; it is sufficient to show that my time has not been spent in vain.

I believe that upon hearing this, my Master would surely let out a laugh. You have traveled ten thousand *li* for the sake of the Great Meaning, and you take joy in having heard the sound of the Dharma.
However, I reflect that this disciple has been entrusted with a single word from my Master by the one of little wisdom [myself] for fifteen years;

my heart remains as it was on the first day, and I have endured myriad forms of hardship. Yet, regarding the Way of Chan and the Buddha-Dharma, I have ultimately not yet opened my mouth to speak. This—
A true world-transcending man and a marvelous phenomenon of the Dharma—now you have once again come here from ten thousand *li* out of deep dependence [on me].
How could this not be something my wisdom can bear? Moreover, since both your teacher and kinsmen are old, why should I alone be the one to do so? For this reason, I urge you to return.

Furthermore, I offer my own conduct and concealment as consolation for your wise compassion and concern. However, while conditions involve gathering and dispersing, the Dharma is without arising or ceasing; it lies in correctness.
I gazed upon it with my eyes, yet there was not a single trace to be found. The oceans of lands were not separated; eons and moments were perfectly encompassed.

How, then, could there be any marks of coming or going, or of self and other? My teacher has dwelt here for a long time; I trust you do not consider this a crime against a foreign land that would weary your meditative contemplation.
If Heaven grants us further years, we shall still return together in our white-haired old age to fulfill our original vow. May we find nourishment solely in the joy of dhyāna.
The Divine One loves himself through the Way.
Furthermore, the Master takes the Dharma-realm as his mind and makes his vows and practices his body; thus he completely encompasses the dust-like adornments of the Flower Treasury World.
Land. You should not grow weary or fatigued. Although this remote and desolate region is far away, it does not lie outside the pores of my Master.
His heart of gathering-in [sentient beings] is like an interlacing net of jewels, where light shines upon light, leaving no room for delusive thoughts to enter between them.
Having been of dull faculties, I have spent these years sitting in this malarial region; yet the Buddha-work I perform likewise does not go beyond my Master’s illusory net.
I am dim-witted. It is simply because the arising of emotional attachments creates a barrier to wisdom that I am unable to partake in the joy of the Master’s Dharma-nature.

Nevertheless, I rely upon this very practice to dispel my feverish afflictions and create a ground of cool clarity. Would you, Master, consider this to be delusion? The ancients spoke of "reaching home on the mountain."

Following conditions, one finds joy in the ground; yet without wisdom, one cannot embody it as a whole, being merely sufficient for one’s own amusement. The four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* truly serves to seal the mind.
My teacher Hui-mu has purified himself with solemnity; he must have deeply illumined and thoroughly penetrated its source.
Although in this life there will be no opportunity for us to meet face-to-face, may we always be dharma-companions throughout successive lifetimes.

Furthermore, since entering these pestilential regions six years ago, I have not known what the frost and wind were like. On the sixth day of the first month this year, I set out on my southern campaign and stayed overnight at an inn in Xinzhou.
The cold wind lashed against my face, no less piercing than that on the northern frontier. Deep into the night, wrapped in my robes, my dreams were filled with [the sight of] the snow.

Amidst ten thousand feet of ice and snow, someone suddenly pushed open the door and knocked; this was a matter of great significance. He was struck with such joy and astonishment that he collapsed in laughter.

Opening first the master’s box among the letters from old friends brought from the north, it was as if he were sitting face-to-face within the Zhudi Hermitage on Mount Wutai, sharing midnight talk while leaning his head upon the master’s knee.
His joy was beyond measure. He then further inquired about various matters concerning the master.
Your meritorious virtues and manifold adornments are matters of common knowledge in this household and need no further praise.
Yet, when I formerly read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and saw Ānanda’s plea for the Buddha to bestow upon him the samādhi, I took it to be mere empty talk.

Looking back now, not only while sitting amidst the miasmic sea, but even were I to enter the Iron Ring Mountains, I would surely have been first illuminated by the light from my Master’s feet. This is what is meant by "the cause."
The convergence of conditions is such that even if kalpas were exhausted, it would not wear away; how could this be a false word? This year, at fifty-six, I have not noticed old age arriving;
my physical form has transcended the mundane, and my mind-ground opens day by day. I often speak to myself:

"If this form does not dissolve, I shall be content enough to dwell within the sea of suffering, acting as a bridge and a resting place for humans and devas. Such a narrow and inferior view has only just begun.
It was my teacher who expanded upon this; now I have finally seen its true essence.
My journey to the pestilential regions was indeed a hardship, but now that I am sent back home, I can rest from my frantic mind and attend to the task within my own person.
I hope for my teacher’s fierce and bitter hammering to melt away my habitual tendencies; thus, I shall not fail my fellow practitioners, nor shall I fail the original intention of our ancestors.

Furthermore, though the unwise, by the power of their karma, have shifted and corrupted [the teachings] and cast them beyond these mountain ranges, it is no less than Mañjuśrī being present within the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa).
Your compassionate light, Master, shines and protects us from time to time; this is no less than being in the Place of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa) at the moment of first attaining Perfect Awakening.

Furthermore, Great Master, you have come; we are fully grateful for your compassionate guidance. Our gratitude is beyond words. We only pray that your wheel of vows may expand daily and your samādhis deepen day by day.
As for this humble and defiled body of mine, how could I ever hope to again enjoy such close proximity and compliance as in the past?
Having been in this land of karma for over three years, though I am of little wisdom, I know not what my progress in dhyāna and liberation may be like; yet, this alone is what I rejoice in.
This person is a student who has become a truly worldly man. Those days and months he has spent have only served to further increase his vulgar habits of literary composition;
these are all the accumulated obstacles of many lifetimes that have manifested today. I know not what day I shall be able to circumambulate the seat three times and seek repentance.
First, please provide me with several examples for my study, which you, Master, may then verify and correct for me. I recall from afar the wondrous stupa of Prabhūtaratna surging forth.

It appears as empty space; yet, in the past at the assembly on Vulture Peak, when all the emanations of Śākyamuni had gathered and the stupa door opened to reveal Prabhūtaratna, when will the emanations of our Master likewise assemble?
This causes those who hear of it from afar not to be restrained by their longing to behold him.
Even if there were flowers fit to be scattered, there would be no supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) with which to dispatch them.
To the late Master Lianchi:
When I formerly dwelt in the Golden World, my teacher came there to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.
By the power of his unconditioned compassion, he gathered me into his care amidst the ice and snow, enabling me to sit and gaze upon the radiant form, which deeply consoled my long-held aspirations.
After staying for two nights, we parted. Since then, my yearning heart has been filled with constant devotion.
I, [Name], was about to leave Mount Tai to travel south through a hundred cities, intending to attend upon you at your seat; yet, I was once again drawn eastward by the power of karma.

This was because I became enamored with a state of barren stillness and consequently placed myself in a remote corner, a land of *mleccha*. Thereupon, I vowed to establish the Triple Gem as a way to repay my debts of gratitude.
O Buddha’s grace! For ten years now, I have remained here with body and life at stake.

For half that time, because my power of the Way was feeble, I was greatly disturbed by Māra, thereby bringing disgrace upon the Dharma-gate and being rebuked by the wise. Even now, I still lack self-awareness;
I remain lingering in this pit, placing my arm across the ruts of the chariot, my mind never once wavering from its resolve. Could this be due to the persistence of past habits?

Ah! I reflect deeply that the Dharma is approaching its autumnal decline and the True Lineage has grown faint. It is thanks to our Master, who, mounting the wheel of great compassionate vows, has loftily raised the banner of the Dharma.
He has mastered both the essence and the exegesis of the teachings; he practices both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in tandem; he uniquely upholds the *vinaya*; and he specializes in the Pure Land.

Thus, he enables wayward children to know where to turn and allows the pure customs of old to be drawn upon once more. Whenever a practitioner of Chan comes from the south, there are none who do not inquire in full detail after your well-being.

Knowing the essence of the Dharma, he is serene; his physical body is robust and healthy; he possesses unhindered eloquence in joyful preaching; and he tirelessly adapts to the capacities of sentient beings.
His subtle regulations do not fall short of those established at Kapilavastu. How fortunate that, in this degenerate age and its final flow, we encounter such a grand model!

Whenever I reflect upon this, my five limbs leap with joy and every pore is filled with fragrance. I feel deep shame that, bound by karma, I am unable to advance and have yet no leisure to behold him in person. Now, his disciple...

As a successor to the lineage, I have specifically sent these inquiries. I respectfully offer incense of three varieties as an offering for the occasion of the recitation of the precepts, so that its fragrance may universally pervade the fourfold assembly.
I humbly hope for your compassionate acceptance.
Furthermore, our Master alone occupies the field of quiescent extinction; by means of the precepts of Buddha-nature, he plants the seeds of the vajra for sentient beings of the final dharma age.
Such supreme causes and conditions are the aspiration of Vairocana and the praise of Śākyamuni; they are indeed appropriate.
They are revered by the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas.

If those lacking wisdom, with their defiled and turbid natures, stain the Dharma-gate, and through the conditions of their karmic burdens, incur such sinful impurities, they truly suffer the reproach of all Buddhas and bring disgrace upon my Teacher’s compassionate protection.
Is this not because he regards all sentient beings with impartial great compassion? Otherwise, what would his kindness be?

The sound of your voice has reached this place without obstruction. That you have deigned to send a humble letter from a malarial region is, as it were, like the light of the Buddha’s feet illuminating the Iron Ring Mountains;
it first confers benefit upon those with the karmic affinity who slandered the Dharma.

I, of dull wisdom, was previously submerged within the illusory net, but now I am fortunate to receive the spiritual power of the Buddhas, which consumes and melts it away with the fierce flames of the vajra. Now, the nature of my transgressions is clearly manifest. Furthermore—
Relying on this as a ground for repentance, amidst the exhaustion of my travels over recent years, I have composed several works on Buddhist practice.
These are intended to serve as tools for breaking through obstacles by means of the luminous mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Yet, with such solitary and limited views, dwelling in a remote and secluded region, I do not know whether these fruits correspond even slightly to this Dharma. I respectfully present them at your feet, beseeching you, Master, [to examine them].

May the Dharma-eye grant me its seal of approval; if I do not fall into the slander of reification, perhaps I may slightly appease my long-standing transgressions and repay my boundless debt of gratitude.
[Written] to Master Yuechuan of Wutai.

I am unworthy and of dull faculties; I have drifted with the current upon the ocean of illusions, like flowers falling into the cold void. It is more than a matter of merely dragging my tail through the mud;

I have long been content to flee and hide away. Yet, when I look back at those in the Golden Realm, who dwell serenely within that single assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, and see how the light from the white tuft of hair flows eastward, illuminating even the most remote and secluded places—I cannot help but observe this dhūta practitioner thus delivering sentient beings while practicing the path of Bodhi.

I have been honored by your repeated compassionate thoughts and your persistent inquiries. Because I have been deprived of both my person and my environment, I have had no words with which to repay you;
yet, I trust that as one who knows me, you view us as one body, and certainly do not regard our hearts and mouths as different.

Previously, I received your critique regarding the non-transmigration of things, and I thought to myself that you had merely composed these words in the course of a casual diversion. I shall now attempt to enter this "game" to test it.
Because of this samādhi, I did not dare to offer a reply, fearing that it might cause the true Dharma to be spread abroad. In an instant, three autumns have already passed.

Now that you, Master of Illusions, have come from afar to this remote corner, I am deeply moved by your inquiries after my well-being and by the expression of your sorrowful longing; my gratitude for this is boundless.
Furthermore, you have produced the draft of your esteemed critique, which I did not expect would be so incisively piercing. I am but an unworthy and ignorant person.

Although this is not like Yang Xiu’s critique of the "Young Lady," upon a single reading I perceive its subtleties quite well. However, I am ashamed that my own capacity is insufficient to meet your standards.
Because you have shown me such profound trust, I dare not fail the expectations placed in me; thus, I shall briefly set forth my views. In my humble opinion, regarding what has been refuted:
if one examines names against reality, even if Master Zhaoming were to rise again, he could not alter those words. But if one forgets words to realize the ultimate meaning...
The purport is this: Qingliang’s reappearance was surely intended to emulate his (Sengzhao’s) prowess. The saying goes, "A team of four horses cannot overtake the tongue"; how truly profound it is!
Yet, when he composed his treatises, engaged in deep reflection, established his positions, and gave names to his concepts, he did not claim to be without insight.

Furthermore, he took the non-transmigration of phenomena as the conventional truth and regarded what is not ultimately real as the ultimate truth. Viewed from this perspective, what he spoke of was the non-transmigration of things, rather than the non-transmigration of ultimate reality itself.

Because things undergo transition and flux, it is now shown that non-transition is the subtle excellence. If things were truly already non-transitory, what would be the point of speaking of non-transition?
Thus it is said: "These dharmas abide in their dharma-positions; the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. How excellent is this purport!

If one were to judge by your lofty views, every passage of the treatise you have cited consists entirely of words regarding transition and flux, yet your refutation of them is word-for-word without error.
Every word has its basis; even Master Zhao, when confronted with these words, lowered his head and remained speechless. Yet he himself explained it thus:

"That which is created is never different, yet that which is perceived is never the same. I fear that you may have rebuked him for his words while failing to understand his intent, or perhaps that what he perceives is not the same as yours.
Therefore it is said: "Right words seem contrary; who would believe them?"
If you, sir, still do not believe this, then who is it that does? Moreover, Master Sengzhao clearly pointed out that non-transmigration resides within phenomena;
yet you seek to investigate it through the perspective of the "True" (the ultimate). Thus, our gates differ, and so our paths are distinct.

It is only natural that our views should differ. I heard that you initially cited my humble words regarding Qingliang—specifically the statement that "all things each abide in their own nature within a single world"—and, misinterpreting them as being equivalent to the Hīnayāna, proceeded to refute the doctrine that one may proceed from here to other realms.
However, the reason I cited this was because I had a specific purpose in mind; it was simply because, in ordinary discourse, I [treated] things...

The meaning of "non-transmigration" (bùqiān) has been scrutinized by the great virtuous ones of all quarters; they generally maintain that while phenomena transmigrate, the True [Nature] does not transmigrate. Consequently, everyone speaks of this as two separate points.
However, within the *Qīngliáng Shù* (Chengguan’s Commentary), there are actually two intended meanings. It first states: "The manifest text appears similar to the Hīnayāna," and so forth;
yet its actual intent lies in the Mahāyāna. Birth is non-birth; cessation is non-cessation; transmigration is non-transmigration. This is the original [principle].
The Master Qingliang’s intention was this: he feared that later generations, upon seeing this treatise, would fall into the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) view of arising and ceasing and of constant flux.
Therefore, he specifically highlighted this point to manifest it, desiring that everyone would deeply understand the purport of the treatise and realize the profound mystery of non-transmigration.
However, the *Chao* text merely cites the Small Vehicle and refutes it with a single intent, without yet exhausting the [discussion of] the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).

This is merely the concluding phrasing of the argument; it simply states that, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is no transmigration. As for the meaning, however, length and brevity are relative to one another;
it is only that the phrasing is somewhat obscure. In the past, when I raised this point, I did so precisely because I feared you might encounter such a situation today.
At that time, we parted with our arms interlaced; it has already been eight years since that snap of the fingers.

I had presumed that your strength was exhausted and you would not proceed further, yet you have thoroughly perceived the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. I did not expect such a development as this.
I venture to say that your current view not only fails to capture the intent of Master Zhaolun’s treatises, but also completely misses the intent of Master Qingliang’s commentary. It is not so.
I alone have not attained the heart of clear and cool realization, nor have I yet reached the state of a humble, settled mind.
Thus, between you and Master Zhao, it is precisely as you have said: that what has been cultivated is never different, yet what is perceived is never the same. Such is my limited view;
I do not yet dare claim it to be definitive. Having recently devoted myself to this for some days, I have gained a degree of self-confidence.
This is simply to lift up [the matter] time and again, out of the sentiment of one who, though once a profligate, feels particular compassion for travelers.
With my unworthy and foolish mind, I wish that you would be kind to yourself and, for now, set this aside without contention.
Rather, try to exert effort toward all phenomena and observe them closely: as for whether they shift or do not shift, it is truly like the rushing currents of rivers. It is not—
The flowing wild horses are buffeted by the wind; yet they are truly immovable. See it directly, right now! Do not allow yourself to grasp at or cling to the emptiness of nature.
If this is indeed so, then Master Zhao’s treatise here is entirely superfluous.
Why then do you laboriously dispute over mere inches based on the tip of a snail’s horn? This is sufficient to show that I am not one to blindly conform or provide forced proofs. Hehe.
Accompanying Dharma Master Kongyin of Wutai to the far-off lands of the south was truly like being cast into a furnace.

Whenever I recall our former travels, a thousand-foot expanse of ice appears vividly before my eyes, and I suddenly experience a refreshing coolness that penetrates to the very marrow of my bones. Yet, as my gaze reaches to the clouds, there is the golden-maned lion.
It does not manifest; it merely causes people to become so thoroughly familiar with it that they find it difficult to forget.

Formerly, when Devadatta pushed down a mountain to crush the Buddha and his body was afflicted by intense pain, he was asked about it and replied, "It is like the fourth dhyāna heaven. Only today do I realize that this was no empty boast; it was truly his own natural state.

Furthermore, while those within the burning house find coolness by recollecting the Pure Land, how could those already within the Pure Land fail to increase their afflictions by recollecting the burning house?

I am ashamed of my own inferiority; having followed in the footsteps of the dragon-elephants of the Dharma-gate, I vowed to achieve some measure of accomplishment, even if only by taking up a single blade of grass to offer to the ten directions.
Yet, I did not realize that fixed karma is difficult to escape, and so I have remained submerged in samsara until old age.

Since Master Da’s transformation, this mind of mine has already perished; there is no longer anything left in the human world. Master Miao has cast off his hands and returned to the source, outshining those before him and surpassing those who come after;
he may truly be said to have no regrets. Now, as the eyes and the standard for the human and celestial realms, you alone stand as a pillar of radiant light.
If I am granted a few more years, I shall rely upon the power of the Dharma to fulfill the karmic connection of meeting you once more, thereby bringing this life to its end. Truly...
I am deeply fortunate. Had our karmic conditions not coincided, I would likely have departed this world long ago, and we would already be parting forever;

thus, my only hope lies in the three assemblies at the Dragon Flower (Nāgapuṣpa) tree. Though I am but a person of singular ignorance, I have long harbored the aspiration to take up the path of a son [of the Buddha]; it is a pity that I have fallen ill.

Should I be able to recover, I shall surely become one of the "white eyebrows" (the most eminent) among those seated beneath you. I have recently carved three types of woodblocks and send them for your inspection and correction. However, I am old...

I have written this single volume. There has been no excellent commentary on it since antiquity; having labored over it for fifteen years, I believe it may serve as an introduction for later students.

As for the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-viniścaya* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-pariccheda*, if they happen to accord with your mind, I would be grateful if you would circulate them; this too shall be an act of Dharma-giving.

Last year, when my elder brother Xuelang’s attendant came from the south, he brought your earnest letter. You instructed me that the Dharma-gate is of primary importance. I am of dull faculties and inferior capacity;

I have long been addicted to withered stillness, sinking daily into solitude and narrow-mindedness. Although the thought of birth and death has remained vivid within me, it has not yet been extinguished.
[Your] younger brother is dull-witted. Because my habitual defilements are so deep-seated, I have been unable to suddenly realize non-arising (*anutpāda*).
I feel inward shame for failing to emulate the ancients and am burdened by the failure of my initial resolve. Lately, I have observed that the Dharma-gate has fallen into decline.

If even we, who are brothers by nature, remain separated like the stars Venus and Jupiter, unable to frequently sit side-by-side to investigate the mind and spread the drumbeats of this Way, what need is there to mention those who are merely indifferent? Your younger brother.

Since receiving the teachings, my aspiration to benefit others has also gradually unfolded. Yet, I have often reflected that my realization of the *Sūtra* (the doctrine) is lacking clarity and my study of the *Vinaya* (the teaching) remains unrefined.
Furthermore, as a student of limited learning whose understanding is superficial, I am prone to value hearsay over direct observation; thus, it is not easy to inspire confidence in others.

My desire to transform customs and reform social mores seems difficult to fulfill all at once. I have long pondered deeply how our Buddha established his teachings, taking the Three Trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) as their foundation.
Master Zong said: "Whenever I see junior students, those things my elder brother spoke of as most difficult to establish are often neglected at their very root.
Even among those with one or two sharp faculties, they are frequently possessed by mad demons, leading them to treat the Dharma with arrogance and their teachers with contempt.
To the point where body and mind lack even the slightest restraint, their foundation is not firm; how then can one hope for their branches and leaves to flourish?"
This is precisely what my elder brother meant when he said that among a thousand people, not even one or two can be spoken with.
It is for this reason alone that tears have never failed to fall from my eyes. Your younger brother has followed my elder brother’s great teachings for nearly twenty years;

it was only this spring that I began to reluctantly open the hall and lecture for the assembly as usual. At the very beginning of opening the hall, the first incense offering was made to the Original Teacher.
Venerable Master Shouyu, my brother, I often reflect on the beginning of my tonsure and ordination, when I was unworthily entrusted with the Dharma seat of the *Avataṃsaka*.
My late teacher’s affection for me was no less than that he felt for you, yet the ways in which I have repaid my late teacher amount to not even one ten-thousandth part.
I recall that many years ago, when I first set out on my travels as a wandering monk, I parted from you at Xuelang and once inquired of him: [...the rest of the text...]

Regarding my elder brother’s aspirations, he once said, "After the Master has passed away, I shall erect a stele and build a stupa to repay the milk of the Dharma and bring my life's journey to fulfillment;
this is my fundamental vow. As for all other matters, they may proceed according to conditions without hindrance.
These words still ring in my ears. I, your younger brother, have clearly recorded them in my heart, and from time to time I have mentioned this matter to those I know.
I simply do not know whether my elder brother’s vow has already been fulfilled. I reflect deeply that both you and I have reached the age of fifty;

such is the nature of illusory transformation. Even in the years before death, one gradually inclines toward decay. Although the vow to benefit sentient beings may not yet have ended, the desire for worldly involvement has long since turned to ash.
If, at this time, we establish a superior connection, it will not only extinguish the legacy of our late teacher...

This is regrettable. It suppresses and diminishes the light of the Dharma-gate, leaving later students without a foundation and ignorant of its origins. A distant source and a long-flowing stream are what the virtues of antiquity valued;

that one's family reputation is not spread abroad is what the sages of old felt shame for. If even brothers such as ourselves, whose names are renowned throughout the universe, remain so silent and obscure, how much more so must it be for others?
I pray that my elder brother will exert himself with urgency while there is still time. I respectfully submit this humble note.
I have prepared one incense stick of fine fragrance and a certain amount of funds for stone materials to serve as an offering for this initial undertaking.

Since my elder brother is currently unable to manage the circumstances and I fear that constructing the stupa might prove difficult, I suggest that we instead carve a square pillar with eight facets; this would appear even more ancient and elegant. Furthermore, there is no need to entrust the inscriptions to another hand;
it is my greatest hope that my elder brother will personally undertake this task.

Furthermore, I, your unworthy younger brother, am a sinner of such a nature that I have brought disgrace upon the Dharma-gate and caused anxiety for my teachers and friends; I am deeply burdened with shame and remorse.
Previously, I intended to return to my home mountain to prostrate myself fully, relying upon your compassionate power for acceptance, and to perform the *karmavācanā* for the confession of my sins.

It is an honor that my venerable elder brother has briefly emerged from *nāga*-samādhi to step forth upon the riverbank. Out of compassion, he has instructed me, allowing me to feast fully on the nectar of immortality.
Suddenly, my five internal organs feel refreshed and cool; both body and mind are transformed, and both sin and merit are seen as empty. This is the virtuous journey southward of Sudhana.
Therefore, I began my journey from before the Great Stūpa. After our parting, on the sixth day of the new year, I arrived at Tonggang.
Zou Nanlao came to meet me at Tiefo Monastery; he first brought out the scroll of the karmic encounters of the various patriarchs written by my elder brother.
Upon unfolding it, its brilliance was dazzling, illuminating both mind and eye. The colophon, with its纵横 (zōnghéng) [free-flowing] mastery over killing and giving life, stood there in solemn dignity.
Sitting, he brandished his fly-whisk. Master Zou treasures this; it is indeed the Dharma-body constantly serving as the host within the hermitage. Master Zou’s faculties are most sharp and keen;
fortunately, there is a karmic affinity between you and your younger brother from a former life. With a single word that strikes the vital point, all previous cases will be overturned.

He has vowed to welcome my elder brother to propagate the teaching in the West River and provide great guidance for others. This truly reflects his sincere heart and gallbladder. Should there be any questions—
[He] arrived. You, elder brother, should skillfully guide and subdue him, causing his right faith to increase and flourish so that it may become the true seed for attaining Buddhahood;

the causal conditions for this are not slight. He passed through Wangtang on Mount Luling, where he was hosted by an old man whose care for him was excellent. That man’s devotion to the Pure Land was singularly earnest;

yet judging by his expressed views, they seem to deviate from the fundamental intent [of our school]. On the third day of the second month, he crossed the Yuling Pass; on the sixth day, he visited Nanhua Temple.

I paid my respects to the Sixth Patriarch and observed that the topography and geomantic features of the mountains and rivers were exceptionally magnificent; it is no wonder that seventeen hundred people have flowed forth from this place.
It was fitting that we, his disciples, should not fail to pay him our respects. On the nineteenth day, I arrived at Guangzhou and visited Chen Yishan, who had already passed away.
I first heard that the elder Oulun was still alive, and when I was about to purchase a boat to go to his residence, [I found that...]
The reply stated: "He passed away three months ago. That the distant regions have lost these two intimate friends is truly a cause for profound sorrow and lamentation.

Previously, it was reported that life-spirits flourished in the South Seas and the local customs were pure and wholesome; now, however, they have become excessively frigid and thin, meeting with a famine more severe than usual."
Grain prices have soared, and the people can barely survive. From the seventh month of last autumn until now, there has been no rain;

the fields are devoid of farmers, and every household harbors thieves. This is especially severe in Lei Yang. The road from the provincial capital to the military garrison passes through fifteen hundred li.
Lei has already suffered misfortune for three years, its people and resources ravaged; now, pestilence breaks out violently once more, and the dead and wounded exceed [all count].
Half the road was strewn with corpses, its tragic horror piercing the heart. In the late spring, the scorching heat was like the falling stars;

yet my younger brother privately remarked that, had he not encountered the conditions of the Way, he would have known nothing of the cold of the northern snows. Now, were it not for the power of karma, how could he have known the heat of this southern land?
These two paths of worldly existence—my brother has now experienced them both to the utmost. Yet, were it not for the former, the latter could not have been shattered. My brother...

Upon arriving, he immediately joined the ranks and took up residence in an ancient temple, appearing exactly like a *dhūta* practitioner; yet when bearing a halberd at the military gate, he was manifestly a cavalryman.
Only then did I realize that a master of illusion creates all manner of forms through his artifice. Furthermore, regarding the perils of birth and death, why should my heart feel any unease?
I simply reflect that we share a karmic affinity from many kalpas ago, and having fortunately met again now, our past conditions have not yet been exhausted.
I fear only that we may sink into the miasmic sea, forever separated from the long journey ahead. If we should happen to meet again on the crossroads of life, how could it be as it was before?
I am certain that you, my brother, with your wisdom’s perfect illumination, will surely embrace me through the power of impartial compassion;
you will certainly not abandon these sentient beings of karmic illusion merely because of their defilements. What else remains to be said? I lament this age of the Dharma’s decline.
I bear in mind my debt of gratitude to the Buddha and pray that you, brother, will exert yourself for the sake of the Dharma, cherishing and protecting yourself.

Furthermore, from the moment we stayed one night by the riverbank, I was sprinkled with the nectar of the Dharma; even as I entered the malarial regions immediately thereafter, it was entirely thanks to this that I was able to drive away [the afflictions].
This is to dispel the heat and affliction of the sweltering summer. How profound is the samādhi bestowed upon me by my elder brother!

Your younger brother has always had but a thin karmic affinity for the Great Dharma; hearing nothing in his youth, he knows nothing now in his old age. Recently, during the intervals between bearing arms, I have diligently investigated the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and recorded it as a commentary.
I intend to use this to atone for the transgression of slandering the Dharma. Relying on my own solitary and humble views, I have already—

I have not followed conventional clichés, yet I have not yet been able to request the certification of the True Dharma Eye; in the end, I have merely used fine wood for the sake of making a fine object.
This may be called "the galloping horses cannot overtake the tongue. I respectfully entrust this to the attendant to hold and request its correction.

I do not know whether, within it, there might be even a small portion that corresponds [to the truth]. Should I, by chance, scoop up a single drop of flavor from the ocean of nature, or allow the light of true emptiness to penetrate the pores of a mustard seed?
I can say with some confidence that I have not failed my lifelong vocation, nor have I brought reproach upon the Dharma-seat.

Should there be even a single word that is inappropriate, I shall immediately consign it to fire and water; I most certainly dare not trade this for empty fame, increase the seeds of karma, obscure my own wondrous clarity, or further obstruct the vision of future generations.
Alas, in this age of the Final Dharma, those who possess the true cause are rare. Fortunately, you and I, brother, were born together in this world.

Worldly beings alike tread the same path; if one’s mind is certified within this Dharma, then one need not claim to be a biological sibling of Māyā, for it is sufficient to establish the karmic affinity for sharing a seat with her in Tuṣita.
I, a humble follower of the Silent School of Shaolin, reflect that as autumn deepens at the ancestral temple, all around is desolate and silent; there are many reasons for which one might shed tears.

Fortunately, you have come here by virtue of your vow to shoulder this great responsibility with all your strength. This is precisely the time to brandish the halberd to stay the sun’s course. Last autumn...
By the grace of Heaven, we met through auspicious conditions in the royal city; yet, parting with but a single word, I returned to lie upon the sea.

Beholding the phenomena of the world thus, all my thoughts were reduced to ashes, and I no longer had any intention of resuming the work of saving sentient beings. I remained only in silent solitude within the empty mountains.
Together with this illusory assembly, we shall till the fields and seek our sustenance, merely passing the daylight hours and spending the remainder of our years.

Lately, I have heard by report that the rain of the Dharma has moistened all things and the fourfold assembly has gathered like clouds; I imagine that the mechanism of thunder and lightning will soon shatter profound darkness and awaken the masses from their ignorance.
I deeply lament that the ways of the world are in decline and that people are generally lacking in faith, failing altogether to regard the fundamental as important.
I am deeply concerned. Furthermore, if the vessel of the mind is impure, how can it possibly receive the nectar of immortality to heal the great illness?

I only pray that you, seated here, will reflect deeply upon these words of your final testament and extensively expound the original regulations. Thus, let those of beginner’s capacity follow the wind to be harnessed and take great strides following the hook.
Only then shall you spread the true breeze across the sky of nature and disperse the clouds of delusion from the valley of the aggregates.
This is merely my ordinary practice, like driving a light carriage on a familiar road. As for these words of a mad fool, what do you, O Illustrious One, think of them?

To Master Yuan'an, who was forty *li* away from the Buddha’s preaching, I say: those who do not hear the Dharma incur the sin of slandering the Dharma; as for me, a humble person, I know that the Dharma seat is but a few inches away.
Even if one does not personally hear [the teachings], one still falls into this transgression; it is not due to one's original intention, but rather because obstacles hinder these conditions.
Yesterday you deigned to visit me; at first sight I was greatly pleased, yet subsequently I was moved to sorrow.

That you endure such suffering beneath the seat of the Dharma is indeed a testament to your firm and resolute diligence, which is surely the hallmark of a great propagator of the Dharma. Nevertheless, to abandon the root for the branches is not the mark of wisdom.
This is the first [point]. For the body is the foundation of the Way, and gravity is the root of lightness. Yet you, seated here, because of a single meal, wish to diminish your life;
you would rather assume a form of suffering to pursue fame. This is truly the height of folly. Is this not precisely a failure to understand what is weighty and what is light? An ancient said:
"If one possesses a single thought of pure sincerity, using a measure of gold daily is not beyond one's capacity. You, seated here, see...
If one understands it in this way, how could one not abide in pure truth?

Regarding Vimalakīrti’s teaching that "those who are equal regarding food are also equal regarding the Dharma," does the assembly below take this to mean that equality consists in being impartial toward the multitude?
If equality were merely impartiality toward the multitude, then even those who make offerings to me would not be called fields of merit—what, then, is the meaning of this? Yongjia said:
"The illusory, transformed, empty body is itself the Dharma-body. By damaging it yourself beneath this seat today, you have impaired the life of wisdom.
Can such a person be called one who knows the Dharma? To preach the Dharma without knowing it—how can this serve as a model for devas and humans, or provide a standard for future students?
Those who claim there is no partiality of intent point to Caoshan’s refusal of food; yet if we observe your conduct, sir, [it is otherwise]."
If one intends to practice the words of Caoshan, how could it be right to treat them as being on the same footing as Bo Yi and Shu Qi?

It is truly laughable that those beneath you preach the Dharma without knowing the Dharma, acting for yourselves rather than for others, recognizing the light while ignoring the heavy, and calculating loss rather than preservation—all of which are merely inverted views. What I, this humble man, say of this is that it is very much like snow.
A frost has fallen upon the world above. I now respectfully present this meager offering for your sustenance to serve as a requirement for your breaking of the fast.

Were you not to partake of it, I would not have dared to appear before you in person. Furthermore, being unable to go in person, I have specially dispatched Rusana to represent me in performing three circumambulations and exhorting you to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, this humble person offers words of comfort to your honor with such bitterness because of the profound depth of my reverence for the Dharma.

I grieve that this age of the Final Dharma (*mappō*) is so desolate, that one looks around and finds no true kin. Fortunately, I rely upon your honor, who harbors the resolve to brandish a halberd to stay the sun; I can only sigh in admiration.

Please forgive me. However, the pathos within this matter is not something ordinary feelings can comprehend; it is simply that I, being someone accustomed to traveling, am particularly sympathetic toward travelers.
I beseech you, sir, to bear this burden upon one shoulder through the power of the two kinds of giving, for time passes and life is impermanent.
Physical strength has its limits; however, I fear that if one’s spirit is insufficient, the joy of the Dharma will not be fulfilled.

How then can one satisfy the beings of the human and celestial realms? That the body is the foundation of the Dharma is no idle talk. Your heart surely knows the secret meaning behind these words, which lies precisely beyond verbal expression.
Even at the gateway of illusory transformation, one must rely upon the vigor and robustness of physical strength as a dominant condition.

Among the ancients, there was none who did not rely upon medicinal herbs and stones to nourish the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the vital energies (*rōei*). This is because these four great elements are illusory things; they are merely the furniture of one's own house.
Reading the *Fayan* (Words on the Dharma), one sees that amidst the chilling frost and snow, the pine and cypress maintain their dignified form.

Yet, it is only when the snow melts that the pine and cypress display their full luster. Is this not a manifestation that does not depend upon the warmth of spring? I only wish that the "springtime" might fill your quarters.
Thus, it would cause all plants and trees to flourish in spring. This is because I have great expectations that you, seated below, will become a pillar of the Dharma-gate;
therefore, I venture to speak at such length. Furthermore, [the following].

It has been four years since we last met; how time has slipped away. Truly, though we are ten thousand *li* apart, our hearts are but a single inch’s distance. For a thousand autumns, it is but a single day.
It is fortunate that while my hair grows white daily, my heart grows red each day; as my physical form ages, my worldly thoughts fade away. As it was said of old: "When the great fire burns..."
"In this land of mine, there is peace and security. Now that I behold the Old Barbarian (the Buddha), I truly see that he does not deceive me.

Since entering this malarial region, in less than a few days, I have thought of the *Laṅkāvatāra* as my very food and sleep. Amidst fierce flames and poisonous mists, to possess such a teaching is like a water-clearing jewel;
it makes this body and mind like *huashan* cloth [fire-resistant]. Whenever I sit beneath the Bodhi tree, I deeply contemplate the Old Barbarian."

Carrying this single branch and its seeds, I crossed the seas to come here. Fortunately, I encountered a wood-gatherer who cultivated and irrigated it, allowing it to grow lush and provide shade for humans and devas.
For two thousand years now, no one has tended to it again. Alas! In the intervals between my military duties, I have taken up residence beneath it;
at dawn I cleared away the weeds and filth, and with the moon still rising, I returned home bearing my hoe. Gradually...
The sprouts of awakening have naturally begun to take root and flourish. Since the source of Caoxi was choked off, I have once again cleared and deepened its course;

my intention is expressed in these few words, which I entrust to you, Fayan, for your illumination. It is sufficient to see that I, this sinner, dare not forget my ancestral vocation nor betray the supreme grace [bestowed upon me].
On the day I was formerly dispatched, the Elder Zibai was at Mount Kuanglu, facing the three...
Baoli made a vow, wishing to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* one hundred times to seek divine protection. Now, he has returned this [merit] to the person [who requested it].

Consequently, leading his disciples, he fulfilled his vow within a felt tent (*qōnglú*). Beyond the mere recitation and upholding, he expounded the text for the assembly, setting forth its essential principles under the title *Jíjié* (Striking the Beat).
I request correction of these points together, so as to perceive the burning house at the edge of the world and the stratagems for rebirth beneath the red helmet.
[He] heard this and laughed.

This [incident] brings shame upon me, an old man burdened by transgressions, as a disgrace to the Dharma-gate. I am filled with self-reproach and have no ground upon which to repent. Fortunately, those who know [of this]...
Through the power of the加持 (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of his consciousness, he was able to live for a long time in this pestilential region.

Whenever I recall his countenance, he sat amidst a retinue of ten thousand fingers, emitting the sound of the ocean tide and letting out the lion’s roar to universally awaken the deluded masses; wherever his voice and radiance reached, there were none who did not receive benefit—how much more so for those of us who are spiritual kin and possess a karmic affinity?
Recently, Da Yi returned to his home mountain and heard that you, sir, were still residing at Mount Zhongtiao.

I shall surely obtain the opportunity to behold your radiant countenance. I have carved several small pieces [of wood] to present before your enlightened gaze; may they serve as a slight glimpse into my sentiments from ten thousand *li* away.

Should you deign to grant me liberation, I still hope to clasp your arm beneath the moon on a solitary peak, sharing a smile across the vast sky to wash away the dust and exhaustion of this half-life.
To the Venerable Yinan:
Our Buddha used birth and death as metaphors for the ocean and the river; thus, I dwell by the seashore while you dwell by the riverside.
Yet, the waters of the sea are boundless and the currents of the river are swift. I have already observed the ocean here for ten years, but I do not yet know if you have observed it.

How long has it been since the river? I constantly think of my late teacher passing away and never returning; it causes me unending grief and sorrow. I observed the three-year period of mourning for him in spirit.
Furthermore, I do not know whether you still remember your late teacher as I do. My desire for you to remember your late teacher is not a wish for you to conform to worldly sentiments;
rather, it is because I wish for you to regard life and death as being like that river. As Confucius said: "Those who have passed away..."
It is even so. Day and night pass by; upon what do you rely to cross the torrent? Pray tell me this, to comfort my anxious longing.
I have taken this opportunity to send three kinds of famous incense; I pray that you will use it to perfume the root of faith at your feet.
Once this incense has perfumed them, sweat will immediately flow down and soak your back—this shall suffice as an offering to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Haiyin holds such high expectations for you. How will you repay me?
You have kindly bestowed upon me, the monk Jingxiu, the hat of your late grandfather; it is so exquisite that it is beyond compare. I wear it constantly, as if it were heaven itself. Although...
Even when dwelling in a small room, one should always keep [the Buddha] before one's eyes. Does Master Dai regard the legacy of his ancestors as I do?
We have been separated from the Buddha by three thousand years; yet today, if we maintain our minds and fix our gaze, it is as if we were beholding the golden countenance face-to-face.

If our contemplation is not sincere and our reliance on the teachings is not earnest, then we are not disciples of the Buddha. You have been able to maintain such contemplation of your ancestors for thirty years.
As for why we should conceive of the World-Honored One in this way: it is easy for a humble person like me to see the Buddha, but difficult to see you gentlemen.

It is not that my body is unable to reach the human world; rather, it is because your minds are unwilling to be like the ocean. Because the seal [of the Dharma] separates body and mind, it is difficult indeed.
Human life is fleeting and fragile, and the passing of time is swift. Are you able to brandish a halberd to arrest the white sun?
One may perhaps allow oneself not to fear impermanence or to die in vain; yet, amidst such idle chatter and laughter, what ultimate purpose can there be? Reflect deeply upon this.
Sent to Master Songgu.
"If a Sage does not appear in the world, ten thousand ages will be like a long night. Although these words have circulated for a long time, those who have witnessed them are rare.
In the past, while I, this unworthy one, was convalescing in a remote valley, I frequently saw a ray of light shining from the east; it never failed to emanate from between the eyebrows of my Master.
Thus, those from the ten directions who sought the light and arrived here all found a place of refuge. This is why they scatter flowers.

As for those who make offerings, they shall fully accomplish the work of a Buddha. Yet, since this Dharma-gate possesses such auspicious signs, how could the Buddhas of the ten directions not all together give rise to joy and offer praise?
Now, in this spring, I, the unworthy one, sit amidst an evil kalpa; the sounds of manifold sufferings pierce my innermost heart.
Furthermore, I hear that our Master, weary of being a ferryman across the stream, has cast aside his arms and departed. This is a place of pain where even a single pinprick would be unbearable.
I privately maintain that although our Buddha resided in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, the old woman to the east of the city was unwilling to see him.
Later, those who possessed the complete and correct instructions declared that this "old lady" (pó-zǐ) possessed the marks of a great person (*mahāpuruṣa*).

Now, observing the world of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), this land of manifold sufferings, one cannot find a single person with clear vision. I, though unworthy, also say that the sentient beings of this land likewise all possess [these marks].
"This is a mark of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa). When it comes to this, what do you, my teacher, think? My karmic conditions are deep and heavy;
recently, they have again dragged me into this noisy fray. Alas, my narrow and inferior habits are not yet forgotten, and the Great Bodhicitta has not yet been awakened.
Yet, while I do not see my teacher before me, sons of the poor from other regions are piling up at the gate of the Elder."
[This is] the gate. Those who have no one to rely upon are just like the stars when the bright moon is absent. Thus, the ten directions are shrouded in darkness;
it is not that the Buddhas and Patriarchs alone lack radiance, but that they have truly caused the site of awakening to become so desolate.
The great earth is frozen with cold—will this not freeze the Dharma-body to death? It causes people to grieve incessantly; how could this be merely a lament for the long night? This...
My mind has no ground upon which to rest; I shall merely join my palms in praise within the water-moon light of our Master.
Gazing afar at the Bright Moon Mountain, before the Radiant Stone, he speaks of the Dharma-gate of self-realization to the assembly of the presiding mountain deities.
It causes those who hear it to go deaf and those who see it to go blind; this is my teacher’s own nature—the joy of the Dharma.
He surely spends his days and months in this state, shattering the solitary inner ear.
Having met Master Jingtang after ten years, we were joined for but a single arm’s length before he was lost to me again. Yet this moon of my heart remains desolate;
how could it fail to hang beneath the tall pines at the foot of the steps? I recall my master always leading his disciples to wander freely and find rest.

In the midst of this, would these not become a distraction for chanting and a hindrance to meditative concentration? I imagine the Great Master’s seamless stupa has already taken shape. Who will compose his *Xingshi* (Account of Conduct)? When it is completed, I hope you will send it to me. As for what I have written since we parted: [The following verses follow: The autumn wind rises from the west; The moonlight shines upon the eastern peak. The white clouds drift across the sky; The green mountains stretch far and wide. The myriad phenomena are all empty; The ten directions are entirely still. The nature of reality is originally pure; The mind-ground is fundamentally tranquil. The Dharma-body is without form; The Nirmanakaya appears according to conditions. The Great Way is beyond words; The True Principle transcends thought. The three realms are but a dream; The six paths are like an illusion. Birth and death are like a flash of lightning; Samsara is as fleeting as a bubble.

If one does not cultivate the Way now, When will there ever be a time of peace? The sun sets in the west; The night dew falls thick. The years pass by like an arrow; The seasons change with the turning of the wheel. Do not wait until old age to repent; Do not let the opportunity slip away. Awaken to the truth within yourself; Seek liberation through your own effort. The Buddha’s teaching is vast and deep; Its benefits are immeasurable. If you can practice with single-minded devotion, You shall surely attain the fruit of enlightenment. I pray that you will always remain diligent; Do not allow your resolve to falter. May you quickly transcend the world of suffering; And together reach the shore of Nirvana. I offer these humble verses; May they serve as a small offering. Respectfully submitted. [End of text]

I only wish that you would write upon paper a hundred feet long, so that I may immediately enter the light of my Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*) and become a companion to this illusory person.

Together with the Venerable Wuan Weigong, you serve as a pivotal mechanism for the Dharma-gate; the burden you bear is exceedingly heavy, and it is truly not due to mere superficial merit, but rather through the power of your long-accumulated vows.
Ever since parting from Qingliang, although this decayed man has falsely been born into the human world, I have never once ceased to feel affection for you, Master.
What I feared was not for your person, but rather for that which your person depends upon; this is no empty talk.
Yesterday, on account of a momentous matter, I entered Śrāvastī and saw you for the first time; my joy was beyond measure, and my heart was set at ease like ice melting away.
Only now do I realize that the wandering of dragons and elephants cannot be measured by narrow paths. Words fail me in expressing my gratitude and consolation.

Having associated with you for over a month, I have observed the mist and clouds within the space between your brows and eyelashes; you appear truly joyful, possessing a spirit that regards the defilements and husks of this turbid world as mere dross.

Whether speaking or remaining silent, your demeanor shines brightly with the brilliance of samādhi. This is surely because you have planted spiritual roots in past lives, and the Prajñā has internally permeated you.
This is what has been brought forth. What is lacking are external conditions, which merely serve to assist in manifesting the supreme ultimate meaning. Truly, this is lamentable.
For that which humanity is endowed with—our unique spiritual nature among all things—is it not for the sake of merely providing comfort and satiety to the mouth and body?
There is indeed a true, great wealth and nobility; in seeking this wealth and nobility, one finds it within oneself, existing independently of others. That is to say:
That which is illustrated by the analogy of the *maṇi* jewel is this: because our Buddha, the World-Honored One, perceived this long ago, he did not cling to security, wealth, nobility, or honor.
Instead, he willingly dwelt in cold caves and, through six years of ascetic practice, acquired vast and sublime attainments.
Thus, upon seeing the morning star, it was as if it were already held in the palm of his hand—something inherently possessed by us all, yet [previously] unobtained.
Seeing this, one would willingly pursue it, exchanging a life as precarious as a single breath for immeasurable suffering and affliction.

Thus, as soon as an object of attachment is encountered, it is discarded like spit or snot. To weigh their relative value is no different than using a pearl from the Lord of Sui to strike a sparrow ten thousand feet high.
How do you compare yourself to such a thing? I hope you will hold yourself in high esteem.
Maintain this state. By all means, do not disparage or abandon yourself. Be wary of becoming so steeped in indulgence that you become an object of concern for your friends and kin.
This decrepit man reflects upon himself and sees that he is as useless as a rotten piece of wood, unfit for any craft; thus, he has never dared to cast his shadow upon the world.

Yet, he considers how difficult it is to meet with one such as you, and he is moved by your noble character—how singularly generous and profound is your regard for this wretched man. For these reasons, I venture to offer these words.
I reply: fleeting light is difficult to tether, and the sun and moon deceive us. I only wish that you would exert yourself in every moment of time and hold yourself in high esteem and self-love.

I, [Name], a disciple of the late master Mei-weng, reflect upon the origins of my own transgressions; I do not presume to offer formal repentance, for I have received this body from my parents and am thus their recipient of grace.
To my sovereign, I owe instruction; to my teachers, I owe knowledge; to my friends, I owe understanding; to my spiritual mentors, I owe the Dharma;
and to my donors, I owe sustenance. For these acts of grace and virtue, were I to sacrifice my life in retribution, it would not suffice to repay even a fraction of them.

Were I to pluck out my own hairs to count my transgressions, I could not calculate even a small portion of them. Even now, though I am cast into the wilderness ten thousand *li* away, I still remain within the protection of Your Majesty’s governance.
During this period of the four-month summer retreat, we rely above on the Holy Sovereign and below on the donors so that we do not fall into hunger, distress, or wandering exile;
