all of this is due to a portion of the merit from the Tathāgata’s white tuft of hair between his brows. Although this place is called a land of sinners, we have equally received the benefits of his creative nurturing.
While these human rewards may still be escaped, I fear that as for the true causes for the hells, how could they be avoided?
I am relieved. This has been the source of my corroding heart from night to day. Since parting from the Master, four years have passed in a blur.

Although I have sat amidst the fields of spears and halberds, I have never for a single thought-moment forgotten my original practice. Previously, I could not read even a single phrase of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*;
now, fortunately, by relying on this place, I shall be able to thoroughly investigate the mind. Upon first arriving at the garrison, I sat in a śītavana (cemetery) and immediately felt at peace.
I contemplated this with my mind and recorded it as it arose, until the scroll was completed without me even realizing it.
This summer, I expounded upon it once for the assembly; those who heard it did not encounter many errors. I am personally confident that I have not spoken falsely.

Thus, I do not dare to claim that this is intended as a formal treatise, yet it may suffice as a means for repentance. Furthermore, it shows that even in moments of haste or distress, I— [The text continues: —...also [maintained this practice].
I dare not forget the Buddha’s work; I respectfully present this copy before my teacher as an offering to repay the kindness of his instruction.
I pray that you will keep it within your chamber as a treasure for your descendants, and as a source of conversation for future generations.

I entrust these words to you, my disciple; go forth. Be good at comforting yourself. Do not let a small matter damage a great one. Do not reject a word because of who spoke it. These words are clear and distinct; they shall serve as a basis for your trust.
If you seek that trust, may its fruit truly be as I have trusted. You must exert yourself in this; do not follow your impulses, and do not rely on them.
Resolve is essential; yielding to the breath causes injury, and relying on one’s will leads to madness. If one cannot endure small matters, they will bring disorder to great plans.

If a person lacks far-reaching foresight, they will surely have immediate anxieties. Minor matters must be corrected; every detail of conduct must be diligent. The mandate of Heaven is to be feared; the words of the sages are to be revered. Stabilize your resolve and concentrate your spirit;
do not treat this as something easy. Let the mind be ever cautious and trembling; guard the mouth like a sealed jar and defend the senses like a fortified city.
Only through learning does one accumulate daily; only through virtue does one renew daily. When worldly customs have become deeply entrenched, one seeks friends among the ancients.

The gentleman guards against the unmanifested; he does not dwell in the midst of suspicion and shame. Like a bird choosing its tree, like a tiger relying on its mountain—the paths of the world are most treacherous, and every step ought to be taken with caution.
Therefore, the sage is born from anxiety and hardship, and dies through negligence and indulgence. One must inquire with earnest urgency.
Reflect deeply. Be widely learned and firm in your resolve. Appear as if you were ignorant when meeting others; dwell in this world as if it were a temporary lodging.

Do not rely on your eloquence, nor adorn yourself with fine clothing; remain tranquil and detached. Let your body be like an empty boat and your mind like a hollow valley. This is what I believe, and what I trust in; you must strive toward this.

Dear Venerable Xiaochen, do you still remember our time perched upon the lion’s seat at Mount Tianmu—clinging to the precipice by the palm of the hand, caressing the pines, and standing amidst the snow?

I imagine that on the solitary peak and highest summit, you have found the traces of the ancient practitioners’ footsteps. If you should carry even a fragment of cloud with you, it will not hinder you.
Scattered throughout this vast and desolate wilderness, it serves as nectar to clear away feverish afflictions.

*The Dream-Traveling Collection of the Elder Hanshan*, Volume Fourteen.
Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and his disciple Tonghyeong;
revised by the disciple from the South of the Mountains, Liu Qixiang.
In this letter, I address Master Lan’an of Qixia:
My teacher has long lain in repose amidst the mists and clouds, burning pine needles and boiling deer-spring water for over thirty years. As for his view—
They are like the insects that infest a bowl; how much more so this guest exiled to a malarial region!

This "Lengqie Notes" was written while living a life between donkeys and horses beneath the Red Helmets, merely to discharge the poisonous vapors within me as offerings to the Great Beings of the mountains.
May those gathered here imagine it and break into a great laugh.
Yesterday at dawn, Master Mìzàng Kāi and I finished circumambulating the stupa and immediately withdrew to chant the sutra. When we reached the passage, "How wonderful!
This treasury of the Lotus Sutra is profound, firm, and remote; no one can reach it. Within it, countless emanated Buddhas may find accommodation," it was as follows:
Therefore, as we sport amidst these woods, our clearing of throats and snapping of fingers must surely shake the great trichiliocosm;

it is only that the sentient beings herein do not perceive or know it. If your karmic conditions for the Dharma are exhausted, you may come and sit with us for a meal’s duration; if they are not yet exhausted, [you must remain].
This is the ultimate reality; do not grow weary or disheartened by fatigue.
The Dharmakāya is immovable—how could one not find joy therein?
My humble salutations. To Chief Seat Wuxin.
In the past, when Devadatta attempted to harm the Buddha, the Buddha gathered him in through the samādhi of loving-kindness; in the end, this served to perfect the Buddha’s power of patience.
When Dharma first arrived at Shaolin, he was poisoned five times; Master Si was harmed seven times for propagating the Dharma.

These are but a few instances of what can be seen regarding the Buddhas and patriarchs; how much more so for us, who are born in the Dharma-ending age and feel ashamed that our virtue and conduct fall short of theirs?
The Buddhas and Patriarchs—how much more distant they are from that time! What is there to marvel at? However, the old man’s fundamental intention was for the ancestral temple of Caoxi.

Throughout his life, he took the Sixth Patriarch’s words, “I do not owe you my life,” as a *māyopama-samādhi* (the samādhi of illusion-like wisdom) to contemplate his fixed karma, desiring to repay it so that he might remain free from even the slightest hindrance on the path of birth and death. Truly, if he had owed him...
As for past debts, one should simply repay them as they come. If there is no debt, it is like following someone with courtesy; it is simply that the person does not accept it.
Within this Great Treasury of Radiance, not even a speck of dust can stand; this alone is the place of true and great enjoyment.
"You, my son, must set your mind at ease and exert yourself to fulfill the Way.

Together with my junior disciple Tixuan and this decrepit old man, we have cast ourselves into a burning house; it has truly become a sea of poison. Were it not for hearts as firm as iron and stone, and minds as pure as ice and frost,"
Why sit idly away the bright days? All that one is capable of is but a fleeting, fragile form, a phantom of birth and death.

One does not know if it might be possible to preserve even a single breath to await my children. Would you, with your beard bristling in a long laugh, find leisure amidst the high void and the bright moon?
Yet considering the habitual tendencies of many kalpas, there is nothing but this that can refine them. If I may rely upon the spiritual power of the Buddhas, then—
Through this process of refinement and cultivation, may the vajra-seed manifest its essential radiance, causing even the subtlest conceptual shadows to be utterly cleansed away.
Having accomplished this supreme causal condition, you will deeply feel the grace of the Sages; how could you begrudge a single death?
You must by no means regard it with ordinary sentiment as a mere waste or a cause for grief.
To the Chan practitioner Wuxiang, the Buddha said:
"A human body is difficult to obtain; birth in a central land is difficult; the arising of right faith is difficult; hearing the True Dharma is difficult.

Now, though you are born amidst the dust and toil of the world, you possess this right faith. Approaching the end of your life, you have become a disciple of the Buddha and encountered a virtuous friend."
Knowledgeable one, it is fortunate that you have heard the True Dharma; this is the most difficult of difficulties.

It is because the seeds of roots of goodness cultivated over immeasurable kalpas have been stimulated and ripened upon meeting with the right conditions—it is not by mere chance. From now on, you shall take the *huatou* (critical phrase) of "Nianfo" as your very life-root, never letting it slip for even a single breath.
Whether in leisure or toil, motion or stillness, do not lose it at any time, until you have mastered it through recitation.
When you have become thoroughly proficient in dreams, then, at the time of your great destiny, upon the threshold of birth and death, you will attain a small measure of correspondence with the truth.

It is essential that you completely sever all worldly afflictions and habitual tendencies from the past. During the two periods of six hours each day (the twelve periods), you must absolutely not allow them to arise arbitrarily.
Even if they do arise, you must immediately penetrate them with insight and never give them a second thought, lest you again bind yourself to the karma of birth and death. Furthermore...
This sows the seeds for rebirth in hell.

I have heard from the Master of the Dragon Flower Assembly that there was once a Bodhisattva who gave his body to feed a tiger and cut off his flesh to feed a hawk; when the moment came to give it up, it was truly difficult to part with.

Thus, one practices various gateways of contemplation—namely, contemplating the body as an illusion and the world as empty—and only after employing hundreds of thousands of skillful means does one relinquish [the body].

Why is this? It is because ascetic practices are difficult to perform. Now, this worthy master and disciple have abandoned the flesh, hands, and feet of this body to feed the greedy tigers that are the bodhisattvas, and to nourish the hungry hawks that are their spiritual friends. This...
The body is limited, yet those who eat are infinite; moreover, they take delight in it without satiety.

Without relying on expedient means and without giving rise to a single thought of falling back, if one seeks the Unsurpassed Way other than as a virtuous teacher or disciple, this is to come into this age of Dharma-decline to repay karmic debts from former lives.
If the repayment exceeds what is due, one will instead be required to pay for the surplus. This is because...

The masters and scholars coming from all directions will surely become the hosts of the present Dragon Flower Assembly, while Master Xian and his disciples will surely become the great masters and scholars themselves.
These are the sincere words of the Buddhas; they are not empty speech. It is only Haiyin alone [who is an exception].

Fearing the incurrence of debts for future lives, one should constantly calculate and repay them in the present. One should aspire to make offerings through the Dharma to settle these accounts accordingly.
This is what is meant by "that which is equal regarding food is also equal regarding the Dharma"—this is the original intention.

However, at this time, the power of the Dharma is not yet sufficient and one is poor in the wealth of the Dharma; therefore, wait until after three years of accumulation to sit with legs outstretched beneath the Dragon Flower Tree.
Below, he forms the lion’s snarl. With the sound of his coughing, he causes the three thousandfold world system to tremble.
At this time, it is like burning incense or setting one's finger ablaze: the karmic debts accumulated since beginningless time must, by necessity, be repaid all at once. Ha ha!
Regarding the arising and ceasing, coming and going, gathering and dispersing, and starting and stopping of the Venerable Yueqing: these are all like flowers in the sky seen by diseased eyes.

As long as the illusory cataracts have not been removed, such inverted perceptions will inevitably persist. Throughout my life, this decayed man has set his mind upon the supreme matter; amidst the bone-chilling ice and snow, he has died.
It is not a matter of unity. It is simply to gain a state of being without affairs within the breast; beyond this, there is nothing else.

One might think that spiritual practice lacks efficacy, but upon passing through these various circumstances, at the point where the pain pierces to the very marrow of the bones, one shatters the old pivot from before.
Standing before the altar of birth and death, it is as if entering Huangbo’s chamber, or like traveling ten thousand miles away to drink the miasmic smoke.

Patiently enduring hunger and emptiness, he sat daily within the Śītavana forest, reading only the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. Suddenly, he beheld the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past, realizing that they did not possess such a view as his own.
Only then did he know that all his previous efforts had been submerged within the gateway of illusory transformations and shifting shadows;

he realized that this alone was sufficient to surpass thirty years of wandering as a pilgrim. Looking back, one sees that when the ancients left the household life, their goal was not merely to await [the end].
This is no trivial matter. One who acts as a true disciple of the Buddha is likewise no ordinary person. To speak of Chan, the Way, and the Buddha-dharma is also no mere plaything.

What this old man calls "entering the Buddha-dharma by means of the royal law" is to know that the spiritual power of the Buddhas in subduing sentient beings does not rely on only a single expedient. Today, it may be said: "Offer this body and mind..."
Throughout the dust-motes of all lands—this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
Since there is nothing that can serve as a token of faith across ten thousand miles, I merely report this to you for your joy; what else could be said?
When I was with Dharma Master Yin’an in the prison cell prior to his departure, our mutual gazes and the expressions of sorrow and joy remain vividly before my eyes.

Since parting, although I have sat in this miasmic region and drunk from the poisonous fogs, I have repeatedly used this noble spirit of yours to dispel my feverish afflictions. As for this sinner, during these recent years here...
The flavor of the Dharma is not meager. An ancient said, "Though the iron wheel turns upon one's head, one must not lose samādhi and prajñā.
How could a sinner like myself dare to possess such? It is simply that throughout thirty years, I have undergone this practice; the progress can be seen therein. You, sir, know me well;
you will surely not consider this to be false.
Together with Master Yun of Fangshan, you have occupied the chamber of the *Zaobo* (Jñānapāda) for ten years amidst the rocky ravines of Mount Fangshan.

There, receiving the offerings of devas and humans, you have drawn from the waves of the ocean of nature and propelled the oars of the flower of compassion. The Dharma-joy you have enjoyed therein has surpassed—
Even while dwelling in the fourth dhyāna, one still uses the eye of wisdom to behold the traveler lost in the wilderness;

yet how much more so when this unworthy person stands before the miasmic ravines, the mind entering the cold void, hearing from afar the resonant and piercing sounds of the Brahma-voice, nearly falling into the state of non-conception?

Had it not been for the sound from beneath your seat shaking the dust-motes of the world-systems, this unworthy person would never have heard the ten directions with their ears. This unworthy person has fallen into this scorched and desolate wilderness, no less formidable than Mount Cakravāḍa.
I have heard that in the past, Bodhisattvas also performed great Buddha-work within this very place.
Now, the Tathāgata’s light shines through the darkness between the two mountains, transforming it all into a pure land. This is no empty boast of the Buddhas.

Recently, regarding the public case enacted within the felt tent, I have taken up a single leaf as an offering for the assembly of the nine assemblies. May the Buddhas of the ten directions behold this.
This is a rare occurrence; once again, I marvel at its wonder! To the south of heaven, the wild geese do not fly, and a single foot of silk cannot convey my message.
Only the right hand of Mañjuśrī can be extended so as to reach here. If you will not abandon those with whom you share this karmic affinity, I pray only that you take hold of me.
Master Huan Yi once said:

"When shaving the hair, it is appropriate to reach the skin; when clipping the nails, they should be close to the body. This is because hair and nails are distant from the self, whereas the skin and body are intimate.
I recall the time when I, a lowly being, was struck by calamity: the Dharma-gate trembled and shook, gods and ghosts wept in alarm, and those beneath my seat abstained from grain.
He drank water and circumambulated it four times more, wishing he could substitute himself for it. If there were nothing that pierced his very flesh, how could he have reached such a state?
This is what is called the dharma-gate of "concerning oneself," wherein one shares in the joys and sorrows of another as if they were of the same body.
Therefore, I take the Dharma as my heart's concern and wish to express my gratitude through the Dharma. This single volume of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* shall suffice as my recompense.

I respectfully address the assembly of the Caodong Lineage and the *pǔnsào* (rag-robe) *dhūtas* of Yuan Tong Temple on Mount Lu. To the entire assembly of Yuan Tong Temple on Mount Lu: it is only we of Caoxi who...
The Dharma-way of the Great Master Sixth Patriarch was widely proclaimed by Nanyue and Mazu in Jiangxi.
Reaching the Song dynasty, it flourished most greatly at Mount Lu, where the Yuan Tong Monastery stood preeminent among all temples as the foremost center for propagating the Dharma.

The stern integrity of Master Ne and the lofty spirit of Da Jue have endured for over five hundred years until now; even the waterfowl and trees, the sounds of the streams, and the mountains [bear witness to this].
The physical appearance is no different from when those elders of former years ascended the hall and entered the inner chamber.

Moreover, the temple buildings stand majestic and lofty, and the bells and drums resonate together as they have been for ages without harm. It is a pity, however, that the Sage has long since departed and this Way is no longer heard. You all—
They have fallen into worldly conformity, knowing only the breath of rice gruel and unaware of the matters beyond the former Buddhas and patriarchs;
their dark karma deepens, the light of their minds is buried, and consequently, the dragons and devas manifest wrath while the Fire God (Agni) gives rise to anger.

Thus, in a single day, they are reduced to ashes, causing the jade palaces and Buddhist temples to be abandoned as overgrown brambles. Although this is brought about by the five cycles of destiny, it is truly...
Because you have been scorched by the fires of your own karma, this pure land has been transformed into a house of fire. Are you able to realize this?
Fortunately, the Buddhas and Patriarchs possess spiritual power; having first attained *dhāraṇī*, they act as your refuge.

They cause you to forget self and others, and to harmonize differences with strength, so that each of you may abandon greed and delusion and share a single life together according to the path of the Dharma from before.
In its prime, it was merely a matter of uniting ten million people as one body.
Now that things have reached this state, why worry that the monastic groves will not flourish again, or that the Way of the Patriarchs will not be revitalized?

If from now on you maintain this resolve in every heart, remaining undaunted in every thought, advancing straight forward until death without wavering, you can transform this defiled land into a Pure Land. Change...
If a burning house can be transformed into a lotus pond, how much more so for a mere tile or a beam? All have emerged through the power of the ten directions;
what difficulty could there be? The only great concern is that minds are not equal and vows are not firm.

Elder Zongchi has come to Caoxi and fully recounted the earnest intentions of the assembly, desiring that I, an old man, might temporarily serve as your guide. Although this is what the Dharma-gate requires...

This is a matter within the proper domain of those like us; however, as this old man’s past karma has not yet been extinguished and the roots of his transgressions have not yet been uprooted, how could he dare to act recklessly and arbitrarily, becoming once again a source of ridicule for the Dharma-gate?
Should he be graced by the secret assistance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and if the Sage’s bounty be vast and boundless...
May the crown of this old man’s head radiate light at this moment. This first incense offering is to pray for the long life of our Sage Emperor.
This second incense offering is to repay the profound kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. This third incense offering is to make offerings to the great masters of Nanyue and Mount Lu;
it shall surely permeate to Yuan-t'ung, so that when you all hear its fragrance, you will know it fully.
This is the time of the Elder Hanshan’s descent and birth from the womb. You all must exert yourselves; do not hesitate.
Take care, take care!
To the Chan practitioner Zongxuan.

Your Reverence has long cultivated the spiritual roots and has not lost the true cause. To close the gates for secluded cultivation and sever all external conditions is precisely the authentic practice of our kind.
However, I do not yet know whether you have received the instructions of a virtuous teacher (kalyāṇamitra) and attained the Dharma-gate for the correct cultivation of the mind.
Within the cloistered retreat, this is certainly not like the passage of idle years. Your letter states clearly that because of reading the Elder...
In the *Renjingang jueyi* (The Vajra of Humanity Resolving Doubts), it is recorded that at night he dreamed that the flesh and bones of his entire body were completely replaced;
however, when he sought to replace his heart, it could not be found. This was because the Master had long practiced Prajñā, and his numinous faculty had burst forth.

Through this, while in stillness, deluded thoughts were subtly extinguished, and he was unaware that such a state manifested within his dream. Although it was but a dream, it was precisely the point where his cultivation attained power.
If you take this dream and investigate it from time to time, exerting effort to look and observe at that place where the mind cannot be found;

as you look and look again, after a long time, the true light will naturally manifest in its own right. Have you not seen how the Second Patriarch attended upon Bodhidharma and requested the Master to "settle his mind"?
Bodhidharma said, "Bring forth your mind and I shall settle it for you. The Patriarch replied, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unfindable."
"Attained. Mazu said, "I have finished settling your mind for you. Under these words, the Patriarch attained great enlightenment and subsequently received the robe and bowl brought from the West.
Your request to ask an old man to exchange your heart is precisely what should be studied alongside this public case (*kōan*).
Right now, the old man asks you, "Bring forth your heart so that I may exchange it for you. How will you respond? Will you understand this as mere talk in a dream? Or will you not?
Do you take the words spoken in a dream to be reality? Have you not seen that the Buddha said both birth-and-death and nirvana are all like a dream from yesterday?
I only fear that you are taking the affairs of a dream and treating them as real dharmas.

The *Vajracchedikā* uses six metaphors as the profound gateway for entering Prajñāpāramitā, and the dream is the first of these six metaphors. If you can use this matter of the dream as an analogy to contemplate all dharmas, then—
All phenomena are like dreams; ultimately, they cannot be apprehended. This state of non-apprehension is the ultimate destination of Prajñā.

If you have not yet realized this, simply take up the kōan of the Second Patriarch questioning Bodhidharma and investigate it from time to time. There will naturally come a moment when the dream is suddenly shattered.

I, an old and decrepit man, have looked up to the Great Master from the assembly at Yunqi Monastery for over thirty years. Hitherto, due to the constraints of my karma, I have not yet been able to visit his chamber once.
I regret that throughout my life I have lacked the necessary karmic conditions. Yesterday, holding incense, I paid my respects before the shrine;

you appeared as if still present within the *saddharma-nirvāṇa* light, conversing and exchanging greetings with your fellow practitioners. I imagine the Great Master must have broken into a joyful, smiling smile.

Since I, this old man, returned to Mount Kuang, I have longed for the days when the Great Master was alive; his preaching of the Dharma was no less than at Vulture Peak, and his manner of harmonizing the assembly...
The regulations were established by adapting them to specific circumstances, precisely following the principles of the Vinaya according to the times.
Since the Venerable Elders have long been immersed in this transformation, their roots are already mature; moreover, as the mere branches and leaves have vanished, only the reality remains.

Thus, the monasteries enjoy peace and security, and the four requisites are abundant. It is exactly as if the Great Master were seated upon his lotus throne, lacking not even a hair’s breadth of difference. Therefore, the assembly...
Body and mind are tranquil and serene, like a clear mirror or still water; how could they admit even a speck of dust, such as deluded thoughts or discursive imaginings?
It is truly as the World-Honored One said: "A bhikṣu of the final dharma who can uphold the *Prātimokṣa* is no different from my own presence.
From this it may be known that the Dharma companions in the mountains, from this day forward until the end of the future, shall enjoy the Great [Dharma].
Even a single portion of the merit within the Master’s white tuft of light cannot be fully exhausted; what, then, is lacking?

That which is lacking is nothing more than a mind of rest. If every person were to let go of body and mind and each simply sought the ground of great rest, then within this Great Enlightened Land, there would be no further need to seek out Buddha-dharma, Chan, or the Way. Within this, not even a speck of dust remains.

He could not remain standing. Had he given rise to even a single thought of shamelessness or lack of remorse, he would not only have betrayed the kindness [of his teacher], but would have brought great reproach upon himself.
Hearing that Dharma Master Huiren was in the mountains, he went to join him and the Venerable Dharma Master as two companions, together supporting and assisting the monastic community.
I harmonize the great assembly. Just as when attending the Great Master on the day of the formal proclamation (*paṭaha*), I simply wish that you all contemplate the Dharma of the Dharma King.

This single phrase, "The Dharma of the Dharma King is thus," is manifest before one’s face without obscurity; it is none other than the Great Master emitting light and shaking the earth day and night.
I am old and worn out; there will be no further meeting. Thus, my grief increases, and words cannot fully express my intent.
The two Dharma masters Chao Song and Yi Yu have recently arrived.
I learned that you have closed your retreat and been reciting several fascicles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. You still have the capacity to study the commentaries and sub-commentaries;
such dedication of spirit to enter the ocean of the Dharma-nature places you one step ahead of everyone in the world. I reflect that I am already old and worn out.
Dwelling in the empty mountains, my gaze meets only vast silence. For this reason, I cannot leave the memory of these two brothers from my waking hours nor my dreams.

I lament that though born in a flourishing age, I have ultimately failed to witness its full splendor—not only because it is difficult to encounter a Buddha before or after his appearance, but now that the sages have all passed away, leaving behind only a decaying object like myself.
Yet, I am fortunate that these two brothers remain; moreover, they each dwell in different heavens.
I long for a single word or smile, yet it cannot be obtained; I fear that for the rest of my life there may be no day of seeing you again.
At this moment, all the thoughts of this old man have turned to ashes, save for those concerning you, my elder and younger brothers, which I cherish because what is most important is the Dharma-gate.

While the old man has been in the mountains for months amidst continuous snow and rain, wrapped in his robes upon a stone seat, he was compiling the essentials of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* up to the "Ten Stages" chapter when he dreamed—

Within this, there happens to be a single verse that is most worthy of public consideration. Perhaps through the Buddha’s spiritual power, he has temporarily assumed the guise of an old man to inspire the compassionate vows of you, my brothers.
I have recorded it separately for your perusal, hoping to provoke a smile; let it be regarded merely as the rambling of a dreamer.

Recently, while examining the first volume of the *Lengyan Tongyi* (General Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra), I found that within the section refuting attachments, the text seems difficult for beginners to comprehend. Should...

Within this, there are points where my understanding of the fruition is incomplete; I pray that you, sir, will clarify them for me. To forget emotions through the Dharma is precisely what precludes the views of self and other.
The scenery of Mount Kuang is most pleasing to the heart, yet it is difficult to find the necessary conditions to support it.
Recently, at the foot of Seven Sages Peak, I have constructed a thatched hut amidst the lotuses—a place of extreme seclusion and wonder. I long for you both.
That you and I have conversed face-to-face is a joyous event for all eternity. My longing cannot be restrained; I have scribbled this hastily by the lamp.
It has been a long time since I first beheld the heart-light of Zen Master Wunian of Huangbo.
Though I, of little wisdom, am honored to belong to the Dharma gate, my realization does not overcome my habitual tendencies, and I remain adrift.
Throughout my life, I have established nothing. Although Caoxi became the site of the Sixth Patriarch’s monastery, I was unable to complete my studies there due to heavy karmic obstructions.
Later, when I received my Master’s profound concern for the ancestral Way, I entrusted Lord Mei with the protection of the Dharma.

At that time, I, the unwise one, had already departed for Mount Nanyue; our karmic conditions did not coincide, and I have failed to live up to his compassionate thoughts. Now that I have come to Caoxi, I shall simply attend to human affairs.

I do not dare to harbor presumptuous thoughts of active cultivation, much less so as my years have already declined and the time has passed; even if I possess past vows, they must await a future life.
Yesterday, when I passed through Luling, the various gentlemen there were all deeply distressed by the unresolved case of Qingyuan.

Recently, hearing that Lord Mei has been appointed to the Prefecture of Qianzhou, everyone raised their voices in celebration, intending to rely upon his wisdom to extend [the resolution] from afar, like Mañjuśrī.
With his right hand, he once touched [his] crown and caused him to swiftly realize this Great Liberation Gate of Adorned Buddha-Lands.
Now, although Caoxi and Qingyuan were father and son of direct bone-descent, it was only you, Master, who—because Caoxi’s vow had not yet been fully exhausted—bestowed it upon Qingyuan.
You took up the burden of this Way as your heart’s purpose and dwelt peacefully in the equal Dharma-realm; you certainly would not have begrudged even a single [teaching].
"A mere snap of the fingers—how is that?
He replied, "Master Wuyi of Boshan, I am ashamed of my own decrepitude.
My realization does not overcome my habitual tendencies, and I have contributed nothing to the Dharma-gate. Formerly, I was driven by karmic forces and drifted astray across the sea."

As for those abroad, it has been twenty years since you entrusted yourself to a distant foreign land. Had I not heard or seen reports of you, I would have commanded my master to erect the Dharma banner on a grand scale;

yet, in the end, not a single word of news reached me. In the summer of the Bingchen year, while seeking refuge from the heat at Kuangshan, I was able—by means of a stubborn stone—to gain a partial glimpse of the subtlety of your Way, and I regretted that I had not yet been able to meet you in person. Recently, I have heard that your master has entered *nirvāṇa*. How lamentable!
The Dharma-gate has lost its protector. I mourned for a long time. Recently, I learned that you were expounding the Dharma at Boshan; my joy was beyond measure.
Honored by your letter and gifts reaching me from afar, you have entrusted me with the composition of an inscription for your late teacher’s stupa. Joy and trepidation mingle in my heart.

Out of principle, I did not dare firmly decline, yet I reflected that over the past two hundred years of our Ming dynasty, the Way of Chan has been desolate and the records of the *Lamp of the Dharma* have been incomplete.
How fortunate it is that you have been able to cause our Master to rise from the decline of his generation; what is at stake here is no small matter.

Had you not been able to open the orthodox eye and the essential principles of the school, it would have left later students without a way to receive the resonance of the Dharma. It was for this reason, after repeated and earnest deliberation, that I did not dare to act rashly.
Nevertheless, in my old age, I trust myself to believe that I am not an unknown friend to our Master; therefore, I have delved deeply into his [teachings].

I have abridged the coarse details of his samādhi; how much more so, then, could I exhaustively record them in the style of a literary composition? In this inscription, I have merely set forth his primary instructions;

as for his other actual practices, it would be appropriate to compile them into a separate record. I am deeply ashamed of my lack of literary skill, yet I have written this to express even a fraction of the truth.
Not a single character herein has been written with negligence, for I fear that future generations might have it included in the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).
There are those among us who possess the eye of wisdom; I trust you will instruct your disciples that they must not arbitrarily alter or replace [the text].

Not only would this damage the literary style, but it would also diminish the brilliance of our Master. This is something to be feared. I hope you will grant me your understanding. For one as aged and infirm as I, it is the duty of the Dharma-gate to offer praise and exaltation.
To have been honored by your repeated visits has filled me with great humility. I respectfully [offer this] for the adornment of the Three [Jewels].
I am not yet fully sated by your sincere offering of the milk of the profound Dharma.

Furthermore, we are within sight of one another, as close as the eyebrows and eyelashes; our voices reach each other without being separated by even a hair’s breadth. It is therefore a great honor that you have deigned to send me this inquiry.

With utmost diligence, you have further received the far-reaching illumination of the torch of wisdom, which has shattered my darkness and ignorance. Facing you, my mind is stilled, and my samādhi is further enhanced.

There is none who excels you in the depth of your Dharma-love. Reflecting upon this age of the Final Dharma, when the Gate of the Patriarchs has fallen into decline, we rely entirely upon you for its preservation.
I lament that my juniors are shallow and insincere; those who possess true integrity are few, while many indulge their cleverness and their thieving hearts grow even more extreme.

Unless there is a great furnace of red-hot metal, such base habits cannot be melted away. I further pray that you will not weary in providing the ferry and the bridge, but increase your forging and hammering—this is my utmost hope.
As for what was said regarding "such a person," because I am an old and decrepit member of the Dharma-gate, I have previously committed verbal karma.
"It is no wonder that it is so. Samantabhadra’s use of the tongue of space to praise all Buddhas is indeed his fundamental practice;
how could it be a matter of karmic retribution? You should remain silent and need not speak of this again."

The single lineage transmitted from the West by Chan Master Yunmen Zhenran reached our Ming dynasty some one hundred years ago; for a long time, it had been on the verge of extinction, and no one of sufficient power had yet appeared to revitalize it.
How fortunate that you have arisen in the southeast, erected the great Dharma banner, and alone proclaimed the Way of the Single Transmission.

By opening the way for the ignorant masses, you have enabled those who follow in the later generations of the Dharma-gate to suddenly abandon their debased habits and turn toward it, like water rushing into a valley;
this is truly a magnificent achievement for the age. Last year, while traveling through Wu and Yue, I had the good fortune to behold your radiant presence.

I rejoice in the flourishing of the Dharma-path, and my praise cannot cease. I, an old and decrepit man, am ashamed that I have brought no benefit whatsoever to the Dharma-gate, and moreover, I am now advanced in years.
Recently, I have retired to Mount Kuang to spend my remaining days. I have closed my door to sever all worldly ties, awaiting the end of my life with a single breath.

Mount Lu has long been renowned as a scenic wonder of the Western River; it is not only where the Lotus Society first took root, but also where Guizong established his mountain monastery since the Jin dynasty.
There was the Chan Master Red-Eye of the Tang dynasty, who greatly propagated the spirit of our school.

From him down to the great elders such as Foyin and Zhenjing, thirty-seven individuals in all have been illustrious transmitters of the lamp. Yet for over a hundred years, these sites had fallen into overgrown wilderness.

Recently, following the causal conditions initiated by Master Da, they have been restored for more than twenty years; yet they still remain as they were before. As for this old and decrepit one, I possess only...
I can only sigh in lamentation. Master Wang, the Protector of the Dharma, and Layman Xing intend to welcome you to their presence to bring glory to the monastic community.

Upon hearing this, I, an old man, rejoice and offer my praise. At a time such as yours when the True Teaching is flourishing, it is certain that you would gladly accept the invitation to these famous mountains and sacred sites where the earth is numinous and the people are eminent;
for surely the karmic conditions have converged. May you certainly bestow upon us the fruit of your guidance throughout the great thousandfold world-system.
He did not let the distance of mountains and rivers weigh upon his mind.

In response to the four points, he informed me that he had retired to Mount Kuang to spend his final years; there, with his door closed, he was nursing his ailments until only a single breath remained. He then dispatched a letter by hand, [containing] two sections on the Sūtras and Śāstras.
I have received the commentary you have graciously presented for me to preface. Having been afflicted by decline and illness for many years, my vision has grown dim and my head heavy with dizziness;
I do not dare to unroll the scroll and gaze at it for long. Day after day I am overcome by drowsy sleep, and thus I have been unable to read it from beginning to end.

Without having grasped its subtle instructions, how could I dare to venture a reckless conjecture? For this reason, I am unable to comply with your command. Should Heaven grant me further years and my ailments diminish, [I shall endeavor to fulfill your request].
I must still praise the portion of fortune.
Master Youguan’s practice with Master Liu Sixi was a source of confusion yesterday;
I imagine it has now settled. This matter cannot be accomplished through mere pretense. One must...
You must take up the blade where the life-root is to be severed and proceed straight ahead. Do not concern yourself with "how he is" or "how I am.
As soon as even a hair’s breadth of existence remains in your breast, you will be played with by him.
This present circumstance is something that could not have been found even after seeking for hundreds of thousands of kalpas. Had such a circumstance as today existed earlier, then—
We have not wandered aimlessly until this day. Today, fortunately, there is this great cause and condition;
how could we lightly let it pass? A hundred-year lifespan is but a fleeting moment. To steal these three years of effort—once they blink by, they are gone.
Clench your teeth with determination; the turning point is right here. Do what you can do now; wait until after three years, and see what happens regardless of what others say. Even if...
To realize the Way is to fulfill the initial resolve of this study of the Way; it is the very first step in transcending birth and death.
How could one possibly turn back as soon as one has stepped out the door? From this point forward, you must truly let go and no longer concern yourself with what others may say.
Even in the midst of spears, halberds, swords, and lances, you must cast aside your body and life; how much more so when seeing ghosts and going mad on level ground in broad daylight?
Is it inverted perception? Do not harbor any doubt at all; you must simply cut it off decisively. Exert your full vigor and do not allow yourself to be entangled by it.
Furthermore:
The long rain has been distressing to people; I have been unable to send inquiries. This mind of mine has not for a single moment let go of its concern.
Knowing that you dwell in peaceful seclusion, your body and mind must be at ease, and delusive thoughts will naturally have subsided over time.

However, within the midst of this subsiding of delusive thoughts, there arises a natural lightness and well-being; one must not mistake this lightness and well-being for a state of sensory enjoyment. If one were to...
If you seek to attain [realization], you will consequently fall into the sickness of indolence; you will merely plot for a state of deep, lingering stagnation, regarding "non-action" as sublime.
Little do you realize that this sickness is most virulent: if you harbor and maintain it for a long time, there will be no progress whatsoever, and ignorance will grow in secret.
The karmic consciousness that flows on continues as long as the life-root (*jīvitendriya*) is not severed; it is ultimately like rubbing dead mercury with saliva—it is utterly useless.

When these deluded thoughts begin to dissolve, this is precisely the time to exert effort in maintaining the *huatou*, investigating it with earnestness, and deeply applying the state of doubt (*samsaya*).
If the power of doubt gains ground, rely firmly upon the *huatou* and examine it day and night; the more you investigate, the deeper it becomes.

In the end, there will surely come a time when cold ashes explode with beans. If you settle for thinking there is nothing to do and fail to give rise to the spirit of inquiry, it will never be true spiritual practice.
The *Recorded Sayings of Gao Feng* is precisely what you should take as your teacher; furthermore, do not interpret it through the lens of abstruse or mystical principles.
Exert yourself! Exert yourself!
I heard that Master Han Yuecang exerted his utmost effort for the sake of others regarding the path above [the ordinary], which is most difficult to encounter in this age of the Dharma’s decline.

However, the habitual patterns of sentient beings are deeply entrenched; if practitioners take mere intellectual reflection as their investigation and regard profound subtlety as awakening, they will fail to realize it.
I fear you will be unable to pass through the Patriarch’s Barrier, nor will it be easy for you to emerge from the thicket of delusive thoughts.
If you truly wish to benefit others, do not, by any means, use verses to incite beginners; rather, directly cause them to die their last death as a thief and extinguish all views and knowledge.
This is my foremost concern; I hope only that we may not fail this present karmic connection. As for such questions as "What is Tathāgata Chan?

What is Patriarchal Chan?"—these are all merely culinary garnishes. To hear that you dwell together with those who have attained the "cold ashes" state is truly a blessing; I trust we shall encourage one another in this very endeavor.

Answer: Regarding the person of the Venerable Wanshi, a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), he was like a lion taming its cub; even when the cub merely yawns or stretches, the lion must exert his full strength.
When I, this old man, acted as his official attendant, I truly did not spare my eyebrows. Fortunately, I entered the chamber of Mount Bosan, and I thought that I had finally escaped.
Our very selves have been transformed together. I have just received your letter; you are still the same person as before—how tragic! This clearly demonstrates the difficulty of entering the Way.
If this furnace and bellows do not transform you, you will become but an inauspicious metal. May you exert yourself with diligence!
What I require is insufficient to match the Dharma-eye; let it be set aside for now. My hope is simply that you will exert yourself in your fundamental duty.
Regarding the Eastern King of Virtue, His Serene Highness the Prince:
your intelligence is Heaven-endowed, your wholesome fruits were cultivated long ago, your compassionate virtue is inwardly integrated, and your benevolent grace—

Externally manifesting [in the world] yet dwelling deeply within the palace harem, you maintain your contemplation upon the mountain forests. This is truly because the cause of your *prajñā* is profound; you are indeed one who is fully endowed with both merit and wisdom.

I, this poor monk, am but a rustic from beyond the clouds, yet I have repeatedly been graced by your compassionate favor. Your solicitous regard has moved my heart again and again, and my gratitude is exceedingly deep.
I am ashamed before you, having no ground on which to stand. Yesterday, I was fortunate enough to behold your majestic radiance in person; I look up to you, wearying your jade-like virtue.
Master Ti asked about the Way and discussed the mind; transcending the mundane and detaching from the secular, this was truly a rare encounter for a thousand years and a blessing for three lifetimes.
Although it lasted but a fleeting moment, it already surpassed many kalpas. Furthermore, my faith grew ever more profound, and I received his words without doubt.
Every sentence struck the vital point, and every thought dwelt upon the Way. Moreover, I took finite birth and death as a source of fear, and impermanence, illness, and suffering as...
I reflect: that which the wealthy and noble do not deign to consider is precisely what the Wise King has made his sole focus.

This truly transcends the mundane world and constitutes the gateway to taking refuge in the Pure Land. Were it not for the roots of goodness accumulated over many lifetimes, how could one be capable of such a thing?
I have humbly received your inquiry regarding the practice of daily cultivation. I respectfully set forth my response as follows:
abstaining from killing can prolong one’s lifespan; curbing lustful desires can ward off illness; quelling discursive thoughts can clarify the true mind;
severing afflictions can lead to liberation from the realms of suffering; and reciting the Buddha’s name can bring rebirth in the Pure Land. Be broad-minded...
Benevolence can govern a state; repentance can extinguish karmic obstacles; compassion can nourish ministers and subjects.
The sound of singing filling one’s ears is not equal to reciting the Buddha’s name a thousand times. Amusing oneself throughout the entire day is not equal to sitting in stillness for a single day.
The merits described above are the sublime Dharma for dispelling illness, prolonging life, and ensuring many descendants and eternal prosperity.
The true mind is originally pure, yet because it is defiled by deluded thoughts, suffering and affliction arise in turn. The Buddha-body is fundamentally one's own mind;
because it is obscured by ignorance, its radiance does not manifest. This very mind is the Buddha; this very mind becomes the Buddha. Mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of...
Mind. Contemplating the mind is contemplating the Buddha. When a single thought of deluded mind arises, a Buddha becomes a sentient being.
When a single thought of an evil mind arises, a Buddha immediately creates karma. When a single thought of an awakened mind arises, a sentient being is transformed into a Buddha.

When a single thought of a wholesome mind arises, hell is transformed into heaven. Therefore it is said: "The three realms are only mind; all phenomena are only consciousness. The mind creates heaven; the mind [creates hell].
One creates hell. If the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure; if the mind is defiled, the Buddha-land is defiled. Apart from this mind, not a single thing can be found.
Therefore, when mental conceptions are turbid and impure, one dreams of inverted things in the night; when mental conceptions are pure, one dreams of traveling through sublime landscapes.
Yet birth and death are like night and dawn, and the objective world is like a dream or an illusion—all arise from one's own mind.

This is what is manifested through transformation. If a person’s mind and every thought recollect the Buddha and every thought purifies the Pure Land, then the visualization will be accomplished before one's eyes.
Past karmic offenses will be eliminated, and at the time of death, one will not be entangled by the suffering of illness.

With a single thought, one will be reborn in the Pure Land, where one immediately beholds the Buddha and hears the Dharma, drawing near to Amitābha and the great bodhisattvas of the An-yang (Peaceful Nourishment) World of Ultimate Bliss.

One shall join the assembly at the Lotus Pond to roam together. In the future, through the power of compassionate vows, one will travel throughout the ten directions to deliver sentient beings, no longer detained by birth and death, and attaining great sovereign mastery in coming and going. This is the direct and expedient Dharma-gate for cultivation;
apart from this mind, all else is demonic illusion and false dharma. Therefore it is said: "There is only the direct path of cultivation; simply recite the name of Amitābha."

Homage to the Buddha. One must by no means mistake the pleasures of the defiled five desires for true happiness, thereby obstructing the inherently existing pure true mind and losing the inherently existing pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Together with Prince Shan-yin of Pu-zhou, he recalled the past:
when begging for food among the people and approaching the gate of a great donor with his alms bowl, he was immediately honored by being gazed upon by the Master of the Dharma Eye.
Forgetting one’s form and yielding one’s status, I have caused this rustic man to toil in vain, unaware of his own stubborn ignorance.

Entering and exiting the vermilion gates, and standing by the side of jade-like countenances, it was as if I were wandering among thatched huts and familiarizing myself with gulls and herons. Were it not for those who are true masters—having deeply realized non-arising and forgotten both self and others—such things would not be possible.
The fragrance of such virtue permeates people so that, without their realizing it, it colors the very marrow of their hearts and bones. Since our last meeting...

Ten years passed as if they were but a moment. Even when dwelling in a cold place where my very marrow was pierced by frost and ice, or when subtle forms and sounds of color occasionally arose as latent, obscure delusions, they appeared clearly within the mirror of my mind.
Since entering Mount Tai, I have deeply relied upon the power of Master Miao’s polishing;

though I am ashamed before the ancients, I have at least not lost my original resolve. I feel quite... (Note: The final character "頗有" (pǒ yǒu) suggests the sentence is incomplete, likely leading into a description of self-reassurance or further reflection.)
On this ground of faith, I have not dared to betray my benefactor. Since then, clouds have dispersed and the Cool Grove (Qingliang) has become serene;

Master Miao has established his traces at Luya, while I have hidden my form in the mountains and wilds by the Eastern Sea for several years. Daily I sit within the light of the Sea-Seal (Haiyin), dwelling in a world of crystalline tranquility.

As the realm of dust and defilement grows ever more remote, my body and mind drift further away from it. Thus, in response to the inquiries of the Great Donor, I have ultimately returned to stillness.
"It has been extinguished. The aged monk Dashiwang Gu happened to be wandering at sea according to conditions when he entered my excavation.
When I inquired about the Dharma-gate realized by the Great Donor, he said: 'Day by day it deepens; the Samādhi of Illusion renders all existence empty, and the mind has no dwelling place.

I, this mountain recluse, was filled with joy beyond measure. I have often heard that people would rather discard a light jade arch and four fine horses than value sitting and advancing in this Way; yet here we have reached such a state."
As for one who skillfully enters the realm of worldly toil to perform the Buddha-work, such a person has not yet been seen;

it is now that we behold this Great Donor, whose feet do not fail those of us who consider him a true知己 (zhiji—intimate friend/understanding companion). Although mountains and rivers lie deep and far away, his heart’s radiance shines brightly, with not even a hair’s breadth of separation between us.
It is only to be feared that when emotions arise, they create a barrier of their own own accord. Alas! This life is already at its end; words and laughter shall no longer be shared.
I pray that you, Great Donor, may settle your mind in a single state of stillness and view birth and death with equanimity.

This would mean that we shall join hands at the field of tranquility and reach the ultimate limit of the inexhaustible—how could it be compared merely to the saying of "the same wind blowing a thousand miles apart"? Since I have not yet had the opportunity to touch your feet in person, I entrust this silent sound to strike upon your profound silence.
I hope that the divine pearl will shine with brilliant clarity, without the need for many words.
Furthermore, it has been fifteen autumns since I last beheld your radiant countenance. Human life is but a long, lingering dream or illusion—is it truly like this?

Only through wondrous resonance can one transcend words; in truth, the conventional and the ultimate are non-dual. Such is the relationship between you, the donor, and we, the poor monks. This is the Dharma.

Between close kin, one’s gaze is fixed upon the other; such a person is difficult to find again. Whenever a delusive thought arises, the light of the mind flickers for an instant, and the Dharmakāya suddenly manifests.
Thus we know that even at a distance of three thousand *li*, there is not a single thread of separation—this is surely no empty word.
When the Venerable Longhua Tan arrived and I was granted his Dharma words, I read them three times over with my own hands; it is evident that he has deeply entered the station of the *Anantārtha*.
However, this poor monk’s "yellow waxwood" meditation—advancing an inch only to retreat a foot—is such that he does not know his own measure.

Having happened to drop some words into the human world, they were subsequently exposed by those who seek out the extraordinary. Unwittingly, my distant dust has reached Your Celestial Eye; I am truly filled with shame and remorse.

How could I dare again to trouble you for a seal of certification? Such over-praise is beyond measure. If you do not begrudge me your Dharma-love, may it flow on endlessly, so that for a thousand years...

I bow. I hope you will look upon me with the same spirit as our shared tradition; how could it be that we merely harmonize our voices? Master Miao has brought the Dharma-treasury to Jizu Peak—this is truly a single blow that serves a double purpose.
Yet, as you travel ten thousand *li* on your cloud-like journey, this mind of mine cannot help but be filled with longing.

Previously, there was no one to ask about you; now I know that Master Da is the contemporary Lion among men. You previously mentioned traveling your eyes across the Three Qin regions; I entreat you to pass by my humble gate for a meeting.
I do not yet know whether he has arrived. However, this master’s character and spirit are truly like a precious sword sweeping across the void;

were one to merely brush against it, the roots of attachment would be severed forever—how could he possibly merely treat ten thousand households with contempt? I have often thought that in the Age of Images, there might well be no Linji or Deshan.
Yet, in this age of the Final Dharma, we cannot do without such an elder.

Furthermore, as we have not communicated for several years, I imagine that you, my patron, have likely not left behind even a single written word. Such is the dream-like and illusory nature of human life.
Does this not cause you to increase your sorrow and lamentation all the more? The Venerable Master has fashioned a seamless stūpa and already presented its model;
it must surely be kept within the secret treasury of the donor. Should he happen to visit in the future, I wonder how he will extract it from there.
As for me, dwelling in the Nalāṭa grove, I lack the power to practice and am being manipulated by mountain spirits, who have raised such a clamor that they have shaken the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven itself.

This caused the Heavenly King to be so startled that he fell into a rage; he cast [the being] into a great forge and smelted his entire body through one process, causing both body and mind to be transformed and his flesh and bones to be entirely consumed.
Consequently, his family was ruined and his kin perished, until now he has been cast into the miasmic sea.
Traveling alone across ten thousand *li*, I am filled with joy at having cast off the shackles of fire; I celebrate this wandering life, intending to resolve the unfinished case of thirty years past.
I trust that when you, my patron, hear of this, your heart will feel a keen sense of urgency.
Now that I have set out upon the long road, I fear that if your attachment does not cease, you will surely be tossed about from the south to the north, your dreams inverted and your mind disturbed.
I offer these greetings out of delight in the joy of meditation (*dhyāna-prīti*); this is to report glad tidings, not sorrow.
May you, the donor, and Master Miao, have the radiance between your eyebrows illuminate eighteen thousand lands; yet even these ten thousand *li* remain as close as the hairs on one's eyelashes.
I know not how you might further receive and sustain me.
Furthermore, as for the matter of last night’s dream, it was fully detailed in my previous letter. Since all such things are fundamentally inverted illusions, what more need be said?

At most, they are but worldly appearances subject to increase and decrease; they neither add to nor subtract from the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). With the eye of wisdom clearly illuminating, one may truly remain undisturbed by them within profound meditative stability (*samādhi*).

I have heard that you, Mountain Wildman, cast this illusory and empty body into the midst of barbarian mists and poisonous fogs, as if sitting upon a thousand-foot cold cliff amidst ten-thousand-year ice and snow;
even if your bones were not yet melted, they would surely be consumed by such conditions.
I wonder where Your Excellency the King will seek out Śūnyatā-janman on another day? Mountain Wildman is currently in Wuyang and has been able to receive your instructions.

Having read this, I deeply appreciate the earnestness and intimacy of your compassionate concern. Upon carefully examining your various compositions, I see that they all emerge from a refined mind; they shall naturally shine brilliantly for a thousand ages.

Comparing them to the official gazettes, I observe that the "Memorial on Severing the Hair" and the "Letter of Admonition" are truly the result of Your Royal Highness’s bodhicitta-habitual tendencies cultivated over kalpas, which have been stirred by these circumstances.
They are also sustained by the power of your vow to take up the burden of sentient beings. Mount [Name]... [End of fragment]
The world considers you a worthy king. If you can indeed regard birth and death as being like a single hair, then you will surely be able to draw a thousand-jin weight with that single hair.
To use this for the sake of the state above and the common people below, bringing your sovereign to the heights of Yao and Shun—what difficulty could there possibly be?

This does not require transcending the three realms to attain Bodhi. If, however, one were to cultivate and give rise to loyalty, using that loyalty to support one's practice, one would not avoid appearing deranged.
Though one might gain a broad reputation and high standing, it would be difficult to reap actual results;

thus, one would lose both worldly and world-transcending dharmas. I believe Your Majesty must surely have a way to position yourself; I pray you will graciously instruct me. [I remain] waiting with uplifted mind.
Your virtuous voice from the capital brings comfort to our pressing distress here in this county.

Furthermore, though the north of the barrier and the south of heaven are separated by ten thousand *li*, when viewed through the perfect observation of the eye of wisdom (*jñāna-cakṣus*), there has never been any interval between them; yet, due to deluded sentiments—

You have concealed yourself; could you truly be without thoughts of coming and going? I wonder whether, in recent times, you, my patron, who find delight in the Dharma, have been free from decline or affliction.
I have heard that the Buddha, for King Prasenajit, pointed out the vision of non-transience, sealing it with the analogy of the river.
Yet, although our worthy King gazes upon the flowing water all day long, wagering that "that which flows away is like this," he perceives that nothing has ever departed.
Is it not so? Formerly, whenever I listened to those who spoke, they held that while the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are impermanent, the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is truly eternal;

this was regarded as their secret seal. Now, however, I say this is not the case. Why? Because the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) pervades even insentient things, and every phenomenon (*dharma*) is truly real.

Thus, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are fundamentally empty; what more could be added to or subtracted from the four great elements? Observe the Buddha’s bone-relics, which are adamantine (*vajra*).
The light of Śāriputra’s relics is such that the thought of non-arising perfumes this body of outflows, thereby perfecting the Buddha-nature as eternally abiding and indestructible.
Beholding the entire body of the Sixth Patriarch, one truly believes that the Buddha’s words are not false.

When the Virtuous Prince views this illusory body in this light, is it not like the moon reflected in water or an image in a mirror? Indeed, if one seeks it therein, it cannot be found; thus one turns back.
When one observes what lies before one’s eyes, all is said to be illusory transformation; thus, the sentiments of anxiety and distress find no place to lodge.
Those of dull faculties who have not yet entered this great furnace and forge cannot avoid falling into the view that things are half-arising and half-ceasing.

Now, having entered the ocean of the *dharmatā* of the *Laṅkāvatāra*, one thoroughly penetrates former knowledge and views, realizing they were truly like the "precious fish-eyes" (pearls). From this, one comes to know the ancients.
If a person does not wish to treat others lightly, they must reach the place where the source is exhausted and traces are severed.

This is certainly not a matter of using intellectual views to dominate things, nor is it the doctrine of "holding fast" or "letting go. All such [distinctions] are merely frivolous arguments (*prapañca*).
If one observes Yongjia’s meeting with the Sixth Patriarch, all doubts will suddenly melt away like ice. What do you think of this, Worthy Prince Zhizhao?
The Notes from Yelengga: These are all records of my repentance over the years, as one of dull faculties. I have sent them to the Noble Prince for him to examine together with Master Miao.
If there were even a space here large enough to insert a needle, then I, of dull faculties, would surely be cast further into the Iron Ring Mountains.

Furthermore, it has been nearly thirty years since my last parting from you, Layman Lao; yet in truth, it was but a fleeting moment. This truly confirms that a single thought-moment and an eon are identical in time.
However, I fear that in this ephemeral world of man, how long can these illusory reflections last? It is my dread that such noble friends and superior conditions may not be encountered again.

It is so; how much more so now that we have diverged onto different paths, as if separated by an entire age? Though our spirits may penetrate one another, our physical traces no longer follow each other.
To speak of this makes one feel nothing but sorrow and lamentation. Previously, Da Yi came from the River Region bringing the purport of the Dharma;
now, suddenly counting on my fingers, three years have passed. Days and months deceive us until they reach such a point. Having read your letter, I know the state of the Dharma.
He endures old age; his sinews and bones grow ever stronger. This elderly layman has, throughout many kalpas, been perfumed by Prajñā, taking the diamond-seed as his embryo.
How could he not be robust, for he acts as the true sovereign over those things subject to the shifting flux of the Creator?

I am deeply comforted. This illusory body of mine, dwelling in the mountains and wilds, has entered this furnace and crucible; it is solely by relying on Your Majesty’s grace that my dross is gradually being refined away.

As I reflect upon this with a heart full of gratitude and shame, there is nothing with which I may repay You. Though I sit in this malarial region, I dare not for a single thought forget the bounty of Your Majesty and the compassion of the Buddha.
Furthermore, human life between heaven and earth is as fleeting as that of a traveler on a distant journey;

how much more so for one with but a breath’s worth of remaining life, bearing this fragile body as a guest among guests, amidst this scorched wilderness and pestilential sea where toxic vapors seethe? Thus one should know.
The Worthy King thinks of me with this [thought], yet he does not know that I think of the Worthy King with this [thought].

Having entered the land of transgressions, I have thrice received the sound of the Dharma, which rings clearly in my ears. When I reflect upon our former travels, not even a hair’s breadth separates us.

Thus we know that the ancient sages’ principle of non-transmigration resides precisely within the daily activities of the person here and now. In recent years, I, this mountain recluse, have [experienced] the flavor of the Dharma herein.
It is not shallow; it simply must not be shared with those who are merely acquaintances. Yesterday, so-and-so arrived, and I learned in full detail of your Highness’s well-being.
I have thoroughly examined the state of the Crown Prince, whose benevolence and filial piety are pure and ultimate. These qualities arise from the very nature of *prajñā*.

Moreover, having now entered the "sacred womb" (*āryagarbha*), he further receives the power of nourishment and cultivation. Why should one worry that he will not attain its wondrous perfection? Furthermore—
To nourish one’s will through poverty and to nourish one’s wisdom through tranquility—this is attained only through the power of aspiration.
Within this blazing house on fire, how easy is it to find a person who seeks such cool serenity? Only you, O Virtuous King, wander as an illusion through this floating world;
of all things, there is nothing that can satisfy the heart, save for the flavor of this simple detachment. The Master Miaoxin’s seamless stupa is supported by a single hand.
Its form appeared once more, even at the corner of the crown of the Virtuous King’s head, as if suddenly emerging from the earth.

As for the assembly of emanated bodies, it is not yet known whether they have gathered; nor is it known who snapped their fingers to open the doors of the precious stūpa, so that humans and devas might assemble universally and all behold the entire body of Prabhūtaratna.
Furthermore, it is not known whether sentient beings dwelling in darkness will be able to see him all together.
Is this light not so? It is like that which I once saw in the Venerable Master Zhai Taichang;
his faith was profound and sincere, and his aspiration for the Way was genuine, far surpassing anything comparable to mere sounds or forms. As for...
You have cultivated the practice of the two benefits in the profound darkness and harbored a heart dedicated to protecting the Dharma, taking this Way as your responsibility.
If you and my fellow gentlemen do not decline this out of excessive modesty, it would be a blessing for the age of the Final Dharma; how fortunate could it be! Such is my private reflection.
To act as a master amidst the dust is the most difficult thing for a person to achieve;

for while dwelling within the deep pit of the five turbidities and afflictions, one now wishes to set out on the path home and realize *bodhi* without leaving this very place. Unless one is a courageous man, one would not dare to consider oneself capable of this.
If you truly regard the great matter of birth and death as paramount, the first requirement is to possess the adamantine right eye (*vajra-cakṣus*) and penetrate through to the truth.

At present, amidst all manner of illusory transformations, do not be led astray or toyed with by the jester of the five desires; do not be obstructed or obscured by right and wrong, or by self and others;
do not be deluded or distracted by fame, achievement, wealth, or status; do not be caged or confined by the body, mind, or the world;
and do not be entangled or bound by the attachments of delusive thoughts, such as hatred and love. If you act thus, then you abide—
The world is like space; dwelling amidst the dust of the mundane without being defiled—this may be called skillfully entering the gate of great unimpeded liberation.
This is precisely what is meant when Ānanda manifested drowning while the World-Honored One alone revealed it through the *māyopama-samādhi* (the illusion-like samādhi).
You, sir, are uniquely urgent regarding the matter of birth and death; I pray that you will attempt to enter this samādhi. If you enter and attain its truth, it will be like a great fire.
The assembly is gathered; the place of contact is brilliantly clear. What thing would dare to obstruct its side?
When people of the world study the Way, they all abandon what is before their eyes to seek something else profound and mysterious. They do not realize that the mystery is right before them;

consequently, they create many obstacles and fail to attain true realization. Furthermore, they give rise to countless arbitrary views, speaking recklessly and at random, yet remaining unaware of this.
That is to say, within the midst of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, one need only recognize and break through their falsity, so as not to be deceived by them.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs’ preaching of the Dharma is like the art of riddle-guessing; they merely use empty fists to show people.
Those who are deluded do not understand and claim there must be some extraordinary object therein, giving rise to immeasurable conjectures. If a wise person sees through this, it is quite different.
A laugh escapes me. Viewed from this perspective, even the Buddhas and Patriarchs possess nothing extraordinary; they are simply those who have not been seduced by various illusions. Thus it is said:

You must not attempt to understand it through intellectual reasoning or abstract speculation, nor should you try to remove what is before your eyes to seek some other "better" state. Mind and object are fundamentally one and the same; they cannot be spoken of as two separate fragments.
Nor can it be said that the mind is inside the physical cavity, dark and murky. The ancients called such a state a "black mountain ghost"—a mere excavation of delusion.
If one falls into this state, it is most difficult to emerge from it. If the substance of the mind is free from thought, that is itself the land of eternal tranquil light;

what need is there to seek a separate pure land? If for a single moment the mind is perfectly luminous and its substance is free from thought, one encounters the source at every touch—this may be called being a person of great mastery.
If you truly believe the mountain monk’s words, then the three doubts mentioned previously will be severed all at once.
There is no need to divide things into stars or split them into two parts. If you search for and arrange each thing one by one, you will only increase your deluded thoughts of seeking and grasping.
Since your commitment to the Way is sincere and earnest, I simply wish that from this day forward, you would set aside all previous skillful means and intellectual views;
furthermore, you must set aside all intellectual views regarding the Buddha-dharma, such as seeking the profound or searching for the wondrous. If [you do so], all...

When the sentiments of both the holy and the ordinary are exhausted, what is it other than the Real? As it is said: "Simply exhaust the sentiments of the ordinary; there is no separate 'holy' understanding.
