Letter to Grand Censor Lu Wutai: I humbly address you, Elder Layman.
Having personally received the entrustment of Mount Lingyan, you have appeared in this age of Dharma-Decline in the form of a high official to rectify the world.
Upholding the Image-Teaching for several decades, when the nine tripods of the Dharma-gate hung by a single thread, it was solely this Elder Layman who bore the burden alone.

This mountain monk, dwelling in constant solitude within the mountains and forests, has always been moved by the profound kindness of this Dharma protector; there have been times when he could not help but weep with tears streaming down his cheeks.
Previously, I felt it was a deficiency that I had not yet obtained the opportunity to pay my respects. Now, having briefly faced him at Jetavana during the spring, I am filled with joy.

"May you live long! Shortly thereafter, I returned to the sea to the east. Again, I heard that the icchantikas were creating great obstacles to the Dharma, which filled my heart with profound alarm and fear.
Fortunately, it was thanks to our venerable layman who covered [the texts] with his robes;

not only did this ensure the peace and stability of the Dharma-gate, but it also allowed the Great Canon to be revealed, so that humans and devas no longer harbor doubts or fears. Whenever I face the Triple Gem, I burn incense and cauterize my arm."
This is to requite the spirit of his gift of Dharma; my gratitude is immeasurable.
Regarding the circumstances of the Taishan Tripitaka, it seems that Master Puji has not yet heard of them. I trust that his resolve to uphold it will become even more steadfast.

With Zhongcheng Li Kuōān, we once reminisced about the moonlit nights in Cháng'ān, when we pressed our knees together to converse on the heart’s core. At that auspicious time at Xiāngjí Temple, we satiated ourselves with the "Non-Duality" (Advaya) meal.

Looking back upon the winds and dust of this world, we have been separated from that moment ever since; it has been nearly several decades since we last met. Yet, as I reflect on his loyalty and the bonds of our shared path, my mind remains bright and steadfast.
He was brilliant and discerning; his gaze was ever fixed upon the Milky Way in the high heavens. Alas, alas! In this turbid world, the Way runs contrary to the times.
Beings of meager merit cannot behold the auspicious signs of the qilin and the phoenix. It is as if the Elder had lost the pearl from beneath the chin of the black dragon;
not only is the Nine Abysses left without light, but he has also brought shame upon those who rely on him for aid. How, then, could one hope to reach the ultimate?
How could one enjoy the abundance of the four requisites in the Land of Ultimate Bliss?

Moreover, with the hordes of Māra roaming at will and yakṣas appearing from all directions to devour the flesh of the living, it may be said that there is no peace, much like a house on fire—not only in the burning lands of the south.

I humbly reflect upon you, O Elder: you concentrate your spirit in tranquil detachment and wield the blade of wisdom with ease within the profound void. You draw in the pure breeze of pines and bamboo and manifest a lofty resonance like ice and frost;
you are no less than the Great Antiquity of the Age of Fuxi and Huangdi. As for this mountain monk, my past deeds have brought heavy transgressions, and I have fallen into this sea of miasma.

I have merely sustained my life for a single breath, barely reaching four years. From the snowy north to the fiery south, we are separated by ten thousand *li*. Recalling our former travels, how could they ever be regained?
Though it be a remote frontier or a vast wilderness, even plants and trees possess sentience; how could they ever forget the benevolent grace of the "Vernal Sun" for even a single day?
I know not whether, within the light of the white tuft of hair, you have once shone upon this head-shaven mendicant stained with defilements, due to his karma.
"Does one practice the Buddha-way through causes and conditions?

He replied, "I am fortunate that you have honored me with your inquiry regarding the Dharma through these several verses. I am but a person of dull faculties and mediocre character; how could I possibly meet your lofty expectations? For now..."
I exhaust my powers of inference to offer a response to your inquiry. Regarding what you call "the meaning of the West's arrival": ultimately, what was the purpose of that arrival from the West?
If, indeed, this meaning had come from the West, then before the Patriarch had arrived, did the people of this land all lack Buddha-nature?
You simply do not realize that this meaning is inherently complete within every person, lacking not even a hair’s breadth—just like the lining of a garment.
A bright pearl has always been one's own possession; the Buddhas and Patriarchs merely pointed it out once. Originally, there is no substantial dharma to be given to others.
If you interpret this as a substantial dharma, you will be far, far removed from the truth. As for what is called "sitting in meditation," even meditation does not belong to sitting.
If you take sitting to be meditation, then what would become of the other four modes of conduct—walking, standing, and so forth? Little do you realize that meditation is the mind itself.
Regarding these different names: if one realizes that the essence of the mind is quiescent and fundamentally unmoving, what need is there to be constrained by sitting or walking?
If one does not penetrate one's own mind, even sitting is merely a superfluous practice, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is likewise not something that can be entered.

If there were anything to be entered, it would not be the Great Concentration. As it is said: "The Nāga is always in concentration; there is no time when he is not concentrated. How, then, could there be entering or exiting?
It exists. The mind is fundamentally without marks; if it has marks, it is not the true mind. These are all matters of deluded thoughts,攀缘 (pán yuán—clinging to conditions), and shadows.
How could they be taken as real? What is called "reciting the Buddha's name" is precisely recollecting one's own mind.
If the mind is pure, then the Buddha-land is pure. If the mind and the land are pure, there is neither birth-and-death nor coming-and-going. As for what is called "investigating the phrase":
Regarding those who can enter the Way through the *huatou*: if the Way were merely attached to the *huatou*, then everyone could easily enter it.

Yet there are still those who look at it and do not enter; they simply do not realize that this was a provisional expedient of the ancients, like a tile used for knocking on a door—merely borrowing a path to pass through.
How could it be the ultimate reality? Nevertheless, to guide beginners, one must indeed proceed from this.

Only when you have penetrated through this point can you truly begin the work of practice. The ancients had their own expedient means: they simply took the single-minded maintenance of the one thought as the primary focus.
It is like a precious sword held across the void; both Buddhas and demons are severed, so how could the dust of worldly emotions dare to obstruct its side?

If you apply yourself with such a mind, and if that single thought becomes pure and refined, all conditions will be suddenly cast off. This is what is meant by "entering deeply through a single gate" and continuing for a long time.
You should indeed have confidence in this.
Since you share the same native land as Kong Yuanzhi, how could we merely share the same five-turbid, defiled world? When one traces back to our original homeland, it is truly...
We have come from the same pure land of the Dharma; you, mountain man, know the path of return yourself.
How could I bear to leave you at my feet? Why not take me by the arm? Yesterday, as I was about to depart, I composed a few words to entrust to Bi-sheng to leave with you.

I also cited Wang Wei’s verse, “If one wishes to know how to eliminate old age and illness, there is only the study of non-arising. This was intended to strike at the most painful point of a literary man.

If you, my friend, are unable to attain awakening through this, I pray that you take refuge before the Triple Gem and receive and uphold one scroll of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*).
Recite it with a refined mind until it is thoroughly mastered, not forgetting a single character. Meet me, the Mountain Man, three years hence;
this shall serve as your offering. I have heard that your spiritual companions possess pure faith; I hope you will instruct them in the practice of Buddha-recitation (*niàn fó*).

Regarding the Dharma gate: the single path of seeking rebirth in the Pure Land can lead one to profound entry. As the time for your selection to a high office approaches, I hope you will take good care of yourself when the matter arises.
Furthermore, in this world of five turbidities, it is impossible to cause sentient beings to rejoice unless one embodies the great compassionate mind of a Bodhisattva.
I pray that you, my worthy friend, will take this to heart.

I have received the command from the Grand Historian Guo Meiming to compose an inscription for the stupa of Master Mian. Having already drafted it in a hurried manner, I have merely copied the model like a monkey drawing a gourd;
I did not dare to arbitrarily add or subtract anything. However, regarding the few words of yours concerning [Master Mian] being moved by compassion for the Dharma, I have poured forth my heart here.
The Duke’s heart and liver were filled with bitterness; he merely exhorted the Master not to offer excuses, though at that time he could not help but sigh with tears.
I, a humble man, have specially set this forth in a memorial so that future readers may likewise be moved by the Duke’s state of mind today.
Would the Duke consider me thereby increasing his infamy? His inscription is thus delivered with detachment.
A Rebuttal. I dare not refuse this request from you, sir.

You have shown me the correspondence from the renowned official, Inspector Wu Cheng, desiring that I, a mountain monk, provide certification. Generally speaking, those in the secular world who study the Buddha-dharma...

Abounding in errors and inconsistencies, it lacks refinement and makes it difficult to fixate upon its characteristics or definitively distinguish right from wrong. Unless one has long applied oneself to the Buddha-dharma and the path of Chan,
studied under authentic spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to wash away impurities and cleanse habitual tendencies,
yet instead merely seizes upon vague resemblances to learn superficial phrases for the sake of conversation or to act as a "grass for a shadow-body," this is absolutely impossible.

The ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is difficult to perceive. To claim that there is a true mind for the sake of the great matter of birth and death, while simultaneously clinging to the view of self and erecting walls and moats, is to fail entirely in the essential connection. Today, those called "distinguished gentlemen" are many;

as a wild man from beyond the clouds, how would I dare to rashly speculate upon their relative merits? Fortunately, the Dharma-eye of the lay practitioner Guan Dongming remains. Dongming previously...
Master Chuye served under Master Chutong Gong. Observing this work now, one sees that he strove to remedy the defects of the "Chulao" style, not shying away from the threat of the axe or halberd.

This is precisely what is meant by "when it comes to benevolence, one does not defer even to one's teacher. One who does not possess the Eye of the True Dharma, who does not wield the Sword of Wisdom, and who cannot be called a heroic and valiant man would be incapable of such a thing.
I, this mountain monk, have glanced through it briefly and already grasped its general purport.

However, although Master Guan has seen his nature, he has not yet attained a thorough and penetrating realization. In essence, he upholds the teachings and practices them with diligent effort and deep reflection;
every word has its source and every matter has its master, such that it is by no means idle talk. Yet, even within this, one cannot yet perceive Master Guan’s ultimate excellence.
If you, sir, would truly apply yourself to this Dharma, I request that you read the *Nirvana Sutra on Perfect Enlightenment* a million times.
Each word will penetrate and harmonize with the mind-ground, leading to a realization that transcends words. There will naturally come a moment of resonance;
at that time, you will understand for yourself. You need not seek the Buddha-dharma extensively, nor need you give rise to many views and knowledge.
You will certainly no longer follow in the footsteps of others. As an ancient saying goes: "A man of true character possesses a will that soars toward the heavens. It does not...

To act according to where others act—this is no empty talk. If you truly intend to pursue this matter, you must earnestly and authentically regard it as the one vital point of the great affair of birth and death.
By all means, do not treat it as a mere plaything or increase your verbal transgressions.
Because you treat the Triple Gem with a sincere heart, I, this mountain monk, have likewise bared my liver and exposed my gall, disregarding criticism and suspicion,
solely for your sake.
To Huang Ziguang.
At that time, he came and sat peacefully within the light of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi. Together with the various phantom assemblies, he brandished his whisk and spoke in silence.
Shortly thereafter, the venerable brothers appeared vividly before me in their samādhi. Dwelling in seclusion far from the marketplace, they closed their doors to investigate the mind;

mountain colors met their eyes and the sound of streams filled their ears. It is certain that they were not failing to face the Dharma-body while listening to the long tongue [of the Buddha]. Spring has arrived and movement stirs.
Samādhi is superior and eternal. Know that by sitting and progressing in this Way, one’s joy shall be immeasurable.
As for what you said—that within this state there is something difficult to express to worldly people—this is indeed so. It depends entirely on self-knowledge and self-confidence;

it is just like a mute person tasting sweetness or bitterness. How could its true nature ever be articulated? I have sent you a copy of the *Recorded Sayings of Dahui*; I hope you will take the time to read it.
*Pei*. I hope that Your Reverence will from time to time join this old man in walking together arm-in-arm, so that even Buddhas and Patriarchs must yield ground by thirty paces.
For some days now, the "moon-palace" of the Way and the "flower-of-emptiness" of the Buddha-work have been performed; let them follow as shadows and echoes as they appear.

Once the preparations for the adornment are complete, we shall welcome your staff and sandals to ascend together to the Dharma Hall. My right arm has long been numb and useless, such that I cannot spread [the teachings] publicly.
I have composed this letter to address you, Venerable Huang Wushan Weizu, with these general words:
You have long planted the roots of spiritual merit; however, their maturation is as yet not deep. It is to be hoped that the power of your faith remains firm and steadfast.
Shaken by the various demons of affliction, we were just now beginning to rest our shoulders from the miserable realms;

it was precisely the time to halt our chariots and take the lead, using our whips to stride across ten thousand miles and mount this bridge of salvation. Unforeseen, the celestial banner of the Dharma has been toppled;

in a single day, all has crumbled and fallen apart, leading us to this state. From the perspective of an old man with the eye of the Dharma, there is not a trace of dust to be seen; that which causes suffering is precisely...
As for my fellow practitioners, their power of the Way is frail; they have lost this refuge and thus grieve with longing.
Though I am but a decayed man, my sole vocation is to benefit living beings. If I were to forget you all, I would be forgetting my own vow. These words are not false.
Having traveled ten thousand li, I have spoken these parting words to you all, each illuminating the other. I hope you will all read them together.
At Mount Huangbo, our Buddha appeared in the world;
this was entirely due to the depth of the karmic conditions between the teacher and the responsive capacity of the disciples, which manifested the longevity or brevity of the Dharma.

When the resonance is deep, the teaching abides for a long time; when the conditions are shallow, it is easily destroyed. This principle is indeed certain. Now, the Haiyin Monastery is located in the East.
It is simply like the light of the sun and moon in a deep valley; amidst the long pines, massive boulders, and dense forest shadows, one may not see them for all eternity.
That they cannot remain forever is likely not because the Buddha-sun does not shine upon them with sufficient depth;

rather, it is truly because those who perceive it—the sentient beings—are obscured by the thick forest of afflictions. Furthermore, why discuss their formation and destruction through ordinary sentiments?
It is so. As you have wished, all obscurations have been suddenly removed. What cause for concern is there that the light of wisdom would not shine brightly?

For this old man, this journey across the ten-thousand-li vast sky—where wind and moon are one and the same—possesses no marks of coming or going. I am merely concerned that you, my honored friend, may be well;

that your son Guang has found his place, which is sufficient to put your mind at ease. In another day, when our paths meet through mutual resonance, it will remain the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi).
Together with Jiang Wuyu and good spiritual friends,
he appears in the world, wandering with sovereign ease like a great lion. All that he does is to carry out the commands of the Tathāgata,
taking it as his task to teach and bring all sentient beings to maturity, even for the sake of a single assembly.
I am born into this world without avoiding the intense sufferings of the three miserable realms; even mountains of blades and masses of fire I do not consider afflictions.
Judging by my own situation today, I simply wish to find one person who can never retreat from the bodhicitta and who can bring about the most supreme causal conditions;
if such a person is found, I would truly be content. Otherwise, even adornments of the seven treasures all belong to the realm of outflowing karma.

It is because of this. And what more could one take from it? Now, this decayed man has cast his body into the realm of Māra for barely a decade, yet many have developed faith and come to know that this Way exists;
it is simply that their conditions were not yet ripe. Viewing the present in light of the past, the eastern borderlands seem as different as distinct eras.
Furthermore, among those who followed me at that time, you alone were the most deeply steeped in worldly attachments.
I have now received your letter, in which you have suddenly changed your course. This truly does not belie your heart; though we are ten thousand *li* apart, it is as if we were face to face.
How could you not joyfully set out upon the path?

Regarding the sentiments of parting and reunion with the elders of Jimo, sorrow and joy have existed since long ago; the thoughts of our past departures and present arrivals have been a labor even in my dreams.

This is because the heart suffers for those who understand it, and the longing is keen for those with whom one shares a karmic bond. It was thus even for the ancient sages and worthies, let alone for ordinary people. I have heard this from one source... [end of fragment].
Every sip of drink and every grain of food belongs entirely to prior conditions (*pūrvapratyaya*). Whether one is noble or base, it is in their mutual conduct that true friendship is revealed.

As for my relationship with you gentlemen, the joy we have shared over twelve years has not diminished the affection of bone and flesh; and the dispatch of this message from ten thousand *li* brings with it the heavy anxiety felt for a brother.
Is this not what is meant by being a "companion known for a thousand ages" or having a karmic affinity (*sahaja-pratyaya*) from many lifetimes? As the proverb says:

To attain the glory of a single lifetime is not as good as attaining the fame of a single lifetime. Just as the mountains and wilds cannot compare to the seas and rivers, [the former] certainly cannot spread a fragrant reputation;
it is merely enough to invite derision. Yet one does not know how many hundreds of years children have been reciting these words, passed down from father to son.
How much more so when one spreads the clouds of compassion over the frontier lands and illuminates the sun of the Buddha amidst the thick darkness, opening the nature...
The source of the ocean turns the axle of the pivot of literary expression; it sows the seeds of Buddhahood below and nurtures the embryo of the sages.
Those with mountain-like hearts and wild natures understand this case: they have deep faith in the workings of Heaven, wherein there exists that which is inherently without sound and without scent.
Furthermore, why discuss the withering of empty flowers or compare gain and loss through the eyes of one afflicted by cataracts? If one truly knows how to depart...
He has taken this up; thus, these gentlemen may be called world-transcending intimates.

Not only does its merit for the state extend its bounty to ten million generations, but the achievement of the Dharma-gate shall stand as tall as Mount Sumeru.

Alas! Now that the Dharma-banner has been broken, upon what shall the fourfold assembly rely? Who will permit the great donor to mount the white ox-cart for the sake of this single benefit? My grief lies in the Dharma.
This news is truly enough to cause one’s heart to break in grief. Fortunately, you, Layman, are a son capable of upholding the family;

you shall not only perpetuate your ancestral lineage, but also continue the illustrious reputation of your clan’s founding patriarch. My sorrow lies in that former matter, while my joy rests in this present one.
Dwelling in the remote wilderness, far from civilization, and burdened by the weight of my own transgressions, I regret that I cannot hold incense and visit your funerary chamber.
I shall perform *brahman* chants to praise your meritorious virtues. Yet, in this single thought-moment, your karma has already transcended the vast blue seas and the long reaches of heaven.
Holding this half-verse from afar as an offering before the True Presence, I imagine that you must joyfully accept it within the realm of *sambhogakāya*.

I pray that you, Lay Brother, will bear this humble sincerity in mind; please have an attendant lead me around your seat three times as a token of circumambulation. I trust you will not consider this to be frivolous or far-fetched.
And so he rejected him.

Together with Wang Zhongjia, they reminisced about the past, when they followed their worthy elder and younger brothers while still children; it had been more than thirty years since they last parted, and they did not know [what had become of them].
"Where have the sun and moon gone? Recently, I was blown by the winds of karma and fell into the land of the rākṣasa demons.
Yesterday, coming from the south to Zhenzhou, we met unexpectedly; it was as if I were dreaming. Viewed through the lens of worldly emotion, there is no lack of sorrow and lamentation.
Yet viewed with the eye of Dharma, one does not perceive even a hair’s breadth of coming or going, movement or stillness. I, this poor monk, sit here in this malarial region."
A single breath contains a thousand days. If one had cultivated the Way in this manner from the outset, would they not have surpassed the ancients?
Now, intending to wash away all prior transgressions, I dare not fail to exert myself and urge myself forward. Thus, while bearing the halberd, I investigated this mind with all my might.

Only then did I realize that my previous views and insights had mostly fallen into the gateway of shadows and reflections. Had I not been graced by the Sage’s great mercy and bestowed upon me the tongs...
A hammer! Who would have known that such a thing would happen today? Looking back at the Emperor’s own "claws and fangs," they were no more perilous than Huangbo’s staff;
yet I am ashamed that my dull faculties do not match Linji’s, who received three blows and a slap on the spot.
I recall sitting together with the Censor Guan Dongming in our mountain pavilion, listening to his profound discourses. At that time, I was still in a state of ignorance;
though I did not understand the secrets within Vimalakīrti’s chamber, I knew in my heart that he was an inconceivable man. It has been thirty years since we parted.
A few years have passed—perhaps as long as it takes to eat a meal. Do you believe that the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, from beginning to end, never departed from the *kṣaṇāntika-samādhi*?
I, this poor monk, constantly reproach myself for having been born in vain in this world and having entered the Gate of Emptiness in vain.
Although my aspirations are equal to those of the ancients, I regret not having encountered the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of old, such as the venerable elders Linji, Deshan, and Yunmen.
As for those who take me as their master and model, they may indeed use the fire of *prajñā* to smelt the gold of Buddha-nature;
yet, those who wish to seek the true countenance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs will find this difficult.

Therefore, for over twenty years, I have practiced with bitter earnestness in the mountain forests, never daring to let even a single thread of laxity enter my midst. All manner of illusory conditions have been entirely cast away into the void.
Regarding the Buddha’s work, he likewise refused to allow the flowers of emptiness to obscure his vision.

This solitary radiance of a single thought can only be fully known and seen through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata’s divine eye; it is a truth that can only be shared with those who truly understand.

Recently, having been favored by the compassionate power of the Buddhas, I have been gathered in by inconceivable means. Having personally encountered these worldly upheavals, I have immediately [retreated] in private...
I rejoice within myself, thinking that these heavy gates of the Iron Ring Mountains cannot be shattered by any other tongs or hammers than this.

Since undergoing these hardships, I have viewed them solely through the eye of the Vajra; from beginning to end, my heart of joy has not diminished from what it was before, but rather increases day by day.
Thus, I am moved all the more by Your Majesty’s sacred compassion and deeply feel its grace.

The power of the Buddha—this mind can be known only by a Buddha. This humble monk has often said that while ancient and modern eras differ and the paths of sages and ordinary people diverge, although their ways of emerging from seclusion or remaining in it vary and their deeds and practices differ, each possesses its own intent.

None of these fail to proclaim their intent through words or reveal their mind through actions. Thus, the *I Ching* was expounded at Youli, the *Sageo* was composed on the banks of the Yangtze, and the Way and Virtue were manifested.

Regarding the departure from the pass, Zhuangzi of Nanhua composed his work on "Retreating from the World. Although their temperaments follow different paths, their underlying intent is one and the same.

In all such cases, the mind relies upon verbal expression, and the will is manifested through events. As for this humble monk, he knows that his habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are concentrated in loyalty and righteousness.
It is my constant private reflection that once a man of stature lives in this world, if he cannot uphold the fundamental social norms and fulfill his duties...
Regarding human relations, I am fortunate that my body is entrusted to the *kāṣāya*. I must therefore be a loyal minister to the Dharma-King and a compassionate son to the Father.
For this reason, for thirty years, I have applied myself to this matter with bitter earnestness, even amidst thousand-fathom cold cliffs and ten-thousand-year ice and snow.

It penetrates to the very marrow of my bones and the core of my heart. As for those who have nearly died nine times in a single lifetime, such instances are not limited to what has happened today alone.

What I regret is that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) accumulated over kalpas are difficult to eradicate entirely within a single life; this is indeed a hardship. Nevertheless, I know for myself that there is a subtle awakening, though I most certainly dare not hope to equal the ancients.
Yet, this single thought of pure sincerity shall never retreat, even through the exhaustion of kalpas; this is no falsehood.

I speak with deep sorrow, reflecting on how I was born into this degenerate age of the Final Dharma. Having been unexpectedly buffeted by the winds of karma, those who seek to do good immediately begin to count me among the ranks of the Dharma.
I am ashamed that my realization is not yet full and my practice is not yet complete; thus, I am insufficient to inspire confidence in the world and future generations.
Furthermore, I have encountered these adverse conditions and, like others, have fallen into worldly categories. Since my outward traces have become so faint, my mind grows all the more [distraught].
Subtlety is indeed difficult to see and believe in at once. As for the great matter of birth and death, it truly rests upon one's own person;
how could there be no ground for repaying the Buddha’s profound kindness? I have heard that when a son serves his parents, he is called filial if he does not bring disgrace upon his body.
Now, this poor monk has severed his hair and altered his appearance; since I can no longer be a filial son in the worldly sense, I have incurred sin.
To engage in such disgraceful conduct is insufficient for completing the work of transcending the world; truly, both monastics and laypeople would lose their way.

Would this not render this life lived in vain? It is my sincere desire that, during this critical juncture where the nine tripods hang by a single thread, I may, with the resolve of Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu, uphold the life-vein of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, so as not to fail in being a loyal minister to the Dharma King. Therefore:
Amidst the blows of the cudgel, cast into this land of pestilence and miasma, he did not dare for a single moment to forget the work of delivering sentient beings.
Once he entered the region of miasma, within a few days he took the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* as his primary Buddhist practice. Within three years, he composed various treatises with his own hand;
amidst the desolate wilderness and barren sands, he did not dare to slacken for even an instant. This was because he urgently desired to bring his work to completion.

Regarding this koan: I reflect that I have long dwelt in the north of the passes and traveled to the far south of heaven. Among the extremes of heat and cold in the human world, I have experienced them all.
Looking upon this wretched little body, when shall it ever endure such burning and boiling?
My will remains, yet my form is already wasting away; though the days are long, my life has already become short. If I do not strive to maintain even a single breath through the Dharma...
This is for the sake of my life. I truly fear that were I once cast into a ditch or a ravine, I would wither and decay along with the grass and trees.
Moreover, once one loses this human body, it is difficult to regain it for ten thousand kalpas.

Should circumstances diverge and we take different paths, changing our faces and altering our heads, I would then wish to use this present body to perform the deeds of today, maintain the words of today, and seek the realization of today.

Once consciousness has ceased, how could it ever be recovered? For this reason, I feel no shame and do not deliberate over what is permissible or forbidden; I simply allow things to proceed according to causes and conditions.

Should a single word of mine happen to accord with the mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and I am recognized as one who understands the essential truth, then even to die at twilight would be sufficient.
What leisure have I to concern myself with the praise or blame of others, or to judge gain and loss in order to satisfy the discernment of the masses? Your Excellency knows this.
As for "I," would it not be a delusion to claim such a self? I have heard that only a sage can penetrate the wills of the world and accord with the sentiments of the multitude;
I have never heard of the world being able to penetrate the will of a sage, nor of the multitude being able to accord with the sentiments of a sage.
It is simply a matter of what is received by the mind, without depending on external things. Having carefully read your letter, I find its praise to be excessive.
I feel a profound sense of gratitude for your dedicated protection of the Dharma and a deep compassion for our shared essence; I dare not measure this by worldly standards.

I am truly honored by your kindness in entrusting such high expectations to one as inferior as I. It is like a mute person eating yellow-barked tree (Huangbo) bark—it is difficult to describe to others.
If you would be so kind as to verify and correct this at your Lankavatara desk, then we shall face each other across a thousand miles. Furthermore...
He asked: "I do not yet know whether, in the years before my death, I might be able to receive your guidance and fulfill my aspirations as we have discussed today.
[This was said] to the Imperial Historian Feng Jiqu.

I recall sitting together beneath the Dragon Flower tree in the past; now we have been parted for more than twenty years. That human existence is but a phantom dream—this is sufficient evidence to observe.
This humble monk was recently submerged in the net of illusion, but has now been graced by the True Edict of the Dharma King, which wields the Vajra-jewel sword.
I have torn [the bonds] asunder. Otherwise, how could there be this day? For this reason, my gratitude for the Sage’s profound grace is no small matter.
For years, I have sat motionless in a humble hut in a malarial region, devoting myself solely to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to investigate the patriarchs’ seal of the mind.
Fortunately, as my intellect was exhausted and my emotions withered, I have found a slender thread of a path within this Dharma-gate, following wherever my eyes wander through my own mind.

I have recorded these boundaries in writing, yet I am unaware that I have fallen into the obstacle of superimposition (*samāropa*). I intend to take this as a ground for repaying my debt of gratitude.
Having long been immersed in the inferior, the eye of wisdom has not yet been cleared; I do not know whether I can correspond even slightly with this Dharma.

The ancients traversed a hundred cities along this path of the "upward direction," lamenting that they could not advance further due to being bound by their karma; they were unable to [complete it] in three...
At the foot of the seat, I respectfully dispatch this attendant to present this formal invitation.

I look up with hope that your wisdom-light may shine through clearly, penetrating the Secret Adornment (*Guhyasamāja*), and that the Great Gate of Generosity may open to suddenly reveal the Treasure Store—this is truly my deepest aspiration.

I am deeply honored that Your Excellency, the Grand Historian, has graciously shared in my true compassion and protected me with manifold concern. Previously, I heard that the Southern Lands were truly like a house on fire, where those starving from famine lay prostrate upon the roads.
In my private reflections, I considered that even these most remote and desolate frontiers serve as the crucible for the conditions of the Way; if—
If one can employ this as a crucible for smelting, so that defilements and impurities vanish and the pure essence alone is revealed, this is truly a gift bestowed by Your Holiness’s sacred grace.
It would indeed not be a waste of this life, and would suffice as a way to repay those who know me.

Furthermore, how could I dare allow my emotions to arise in pursuit of sensory objects, thereby once again bringing blemish upon the Dharma-gate? I pray you will convey these thanks to my old friends and look upon me with compassionate care. I further wish that—
The Master Daozong cherished himself and loved himself.
He once told Wang Zhongbai, the Court Historian, that all sages and ordinary beings alike abide and are sustained by illusory karmic forces; thus, they come and go and arise.
Cease! Gathering and dispersing, concealment and manifestation—all are nothing but dream-events. My current journey of ten thousand *li* into the mountains and fields is sufficient to verify this.

When wisdom’s light shines perfectly, not even a thread’s breadth is obstructed; yet when a momentary delusive thought arises, the vast expanse becomes like a cloudy sky, such that one knows not where one is or what direction one faces.
What is said—that "when emotion arises, wisdom is obstructed; when thought changes, the essence becomes distinct"—is no empty talk. Thus says the Mountain Man.

I look up and rely upon the reach of your compassion; I hope that all is well with you. However, here in the south, we have suffered successive years of famine, suddenly exposed to scorching heat, a situation truly comparable to treading in boiling water or leaping into fire.
While I, a mountain dweller, can endure these conditions, my illusory and ephemeral body finds it difficult to withstand this consumption and decay;
I fear I shall soon fall into the ditches and ravines, unable to behold the sun and sky again. I trust you will convey my thanks to my old friends on my behalf.

Strive to honor yourself through the Way. As for the various masters of the Jade Discourse (Yupan), I have not yet had the opportunity to offer them separate editorial arrangements; I pray only that you will compassionately guide me from afar.
Furthermore, worldly phenomena are like empty flowers, and sentient beings are deluded. That which agitates the eyes can only be clearly seen by the eye of wisdom, which remains upright and tranquil.
This is merely the realm of cessation. As for the merit of the profound realization attained through distinct contemplation, it has already entered deeply into the boundless.

Hearing this, which is the object-condition of Bodhi, one contemplates all realms of suffering. Recalling the past in Chang’an, when we met before a lamp one night at the depth of the night, it was as if I were born again.
Observing the expressions of surprise and joy upon the assembly, one can sufficiently understand the longing of those who have not yet seen you, as well as the sentiments cherished since our parting.
Although the ancients said that reason subdues emotion, when it comes to emotion and reason, there is much that cannot be subdued by reason.
This is the sorrow of shared essence, which enters the realm of true knowledge—like the moon reflected in a cold pond, or a person facing a precious mirror. It arises spontaneously.
One cannot escape its reflection. In recent times, the Dharma community in the royal capital has declined; as those who know the Way have scattered like stars, how could one not feel desolate?

Having observed closely your recent entry into the capital, I imagine that you will once again meet old friends with whom your minds resonate in silent accord—there are things that simply cannot be put into words.
As for this inferior person, in recent years I have dwelt in this malarial region, relying on your compassionate protection for my four great elements.

It is cool and refreshing, free from all feverish afflictions. Formerly it was said that purity and defilement follow the mind, and that suffering and joy reside within oneself; now I have realized this in truth.
When one illuminates it with the ocean-like wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, even these lingering traces vanish entirely.

I have received High Sire Sima Cheng’s affectionate bequest of his draft; it is a profound honor that truly reflects the sincerity of a true friend, such as one encounters but once in a thousand years.

However, I am but a rustic man who does not wear the cap of office, and my words do not concern the refined winds of statecraft. I fear only that they might tarnish your illustrious virtue. Reflecting upon myself from early on...

I have abandoned my brush and inkstone, having devoted myself for many years to exploring the profound principles and investigating the ultimate source of human nature. As for poetry and prose, these were never my primary vocation;
even the few informal remarks I have made were merely intended to respond to the traces of manifestation and transformation, and by no means represent my own mastery as a writer.
Regarding the writings of the Chan school, I have drafted several works, which I intend to carry with me on this journey to the south to take up arms.

In my leisure time, I have compiled these writings into this volume and respectfully request your inspection and correction. If even a half-verse may be offered to you, I would be fortunate if it were appended to your enduring legacy;
then the grandeur of this Dharma-gift would surely flow from the sincere heart of a noble benefactor.

This was like the time when I, along with the late Grand Minister Tseng, were together on the river during a snowy night; one evening felt like a thousand years. As we parted, he gave me these words: "The Great Mountain and the Nine Cauldrons.

Not only did I feel the sincerity of his righteous affection, but I was truly indebted to his compassionate and earnest concern, which enabled this withered and decayed person to take root once again.

That those dwelling amidst the pestilential miasmas of the southern lands are not shaken or led astray by the winds of their environment is entirely due to the power of a single word from you, the Elder Layman.
I respectfully hear that your physical health is growing stronger day by day; this is a blessing bestowed by Heaven upon you, a man of venerable age with white hair.

I pray that you will continue to cherish yourself and maintain your well-being, being careful in your daily conduct, temperate in food and drink, and sparing in thought and concern. This is the supreme means of prolonging one’s life.
Regarding the art of longevity, focusing solely on the single gate of *nenbutsu* is especially the secret method for concentrating the spirit on the Land of Ultimate Bliss in one’s later years;
it is the supreme strategy for transcending the world. Although you, O Elder, occupy the pinnacle of ministerial rank, you have already regarded the phenomena of this world as mere floating dust.
If you were to apply even a slight degree of attention to this practice of transcending the world, it would surely not fail to bring your life to ultimate fulfillment.
This concludes the *Jingludi* (The Land of Ultimate Joy).
Together with King Xinghai, we have extensively discussed the price of rice in Luling;
in the end, there is nothing with which to repay you. Having already deeply established the superior conditions for the Pure Land, we are now satiated by the joy of Chan.

"Eat! You must not fail the trust placed in you by the one who wanders with an empty bowl. After our parting, I arrived at my military post. The land was shrouded in miasmic smoke and beset by famine;
encountering only such realms of suffering, my heart was filled with grief at every sight, the pain piercing to my very marrow.

I lamented that I could not have every pore of my body emit the four requisites for sustaining life, just as they do from the one who wanders with an empty bowl. This indeed accords with the Bodhipakṣa-dharmas of this humble monk.

The Dharma serves as the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Entrusting you with my vision of the *Laṅkāvatāra*, I await the time when this illusory body finds its proper place and may briefly rest from the toil of worldly dust.
I shall certainly exhaust the depths of the spirit and will by no means fail the karmic conditions of this entrustment.
Furthermore, the monk Qianfeng from the north, who previously came to inquire after your health, also presented a note on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and requested your seal of approval.

Since you and this Dharma heir share a karmic affinity, it seems as though there has been a waiting for this matter. This sutra has entered China for over one thousand three hundred years; moreover, regarding the sutra itself—
Regarding the hands that have translated [the scriptures] three times: among the masters who have propagated the Dharma since antiquity, there have been no few such as Qingliang and Guifeng.

Their commentaries and sub-commentaries are so numerous they could fill the houses and exhaust the ox-carts [of their transport], yet this alone was not reached by them, causing the Heart-Seal of Bodhidharma to remain obscure and unmanifest until today.
Now, it has been brought forth by you, sir; with a single word, you have shattered [delusion] amidst the rushing torrent. You have entered the mountains...
That this hand of mine, dull and obtuse as it is, should have played with these matters—this is truly no small matter.
How could it be that I am to receive the same entrustment on Vulture Peak as my fellow disciples, and strike the harp of this Dharma to rescue the world from the evils of the final age?
Otherwise, why would such an inconceivable event occur? As for what its ultimate significance may be, I do not know; yet all at once, by means of it—
This great treasure is presented upon a platter, its radiance illuminating humans and devas; it is surely not without the employment of supernatural power.
I pray you will point out any flaws—like the seizing of the jade disc from the court of Qin—this depends entirely on the courage and skill of those present.

As I reflect upon this journey of ten thousand *li* with you, Attendant Censor Fu Jinsha, it is because I have had the honor of your constant guidance that I may directly ascend to the other shore. How could this not be the power of the Dharma?
This sense of gratitude is beyond words. Since entering these miasmic lands, I have known my own transgressions in my heart and have practiced repentance with diligent effort day and night.

I repent. I dare not presume to fail the Sacred Grace above or to betray the trust of those who know me. Seated amidst a poisonous mist, I have cherished the Dharma in my heart, never flagging day or night.
Recently, the venerable Master Qianfeng arrived; fortunately, I was able to receive his Dharma voice, a joy beyond words.

I have fully heard that Your Holiness has directed this dedication of merit, so that the Wheel of Dharma may turn greatly and its radiance pervade the world, while the profound pivot operates silently—relying upon [this power].
Your wisdom and power are preeminent; how can I but rejoice? As for my humble self, bearing the burden of the Candana Tathāgata, the state of such hardship cannot be fully described in detail.
Now, having been rescued from sinking into the depths by your hands and eyes of great compassion, I am made to no longer lose my way regarding the Dharma-body.
Yet, with this inferior mind, I have attained liberation and no longer harbor the thought of attaining Buddhahood. Furthermore, why is this so?
Coming and going, one sees the Tathāgata. To dwell upon signs while practicing giving is to seek the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions—all of which are matters within one's own domain;
it is only to be feared that one might miss the mark right before one's face.

Furthermore, the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world does not arise from a single cause or condition; it necessarily occurs through the mutual resonance of response and stimulus, manifesting only when the capacities of beings and the Buddha's intent meet in profound harmony.
How could this apply solely to the Buddha-realm? It is so for every phenomenon (*dharma*). This is illustrated by the single instance of the Candana Tathāgata.
Upon examining this, there truly exists that which is inconceivable. Yet, before the Buddha-Tathāgata appeared from the mountain wilds, it was not possible for the disciples under his seat to emerge;
and after he had already emerged from the mountain wilds and sat upon his throne, it was not possible for the disciples under his seat to emerge.

Thus, this work of the Buddha could not have its beginning without the mountain wilds, nor could it have its end without those under his seat. If one scrutinizes this causal connection closely, should it fall among the masses...
If one is but a raw hand, one cannot avoid being like withered wood or rotten stumps; ultimately entering Danxia’s furnace, one’s eyebrows and beard—the marks of an elder—will surely fall away.

What benefit would there be in that? Furthermore, how could one manifest in Tuṣita Heaven or descend to the imperial palace to cause immeasurable devas and humans to conceive a rare and extraordinary mind, serving as a bridge and raft across the sea of suffering? Observing all phenomena from this perspective, [one realizes their emptiness].

Indeed, it is impossible for the conceptualizing mind to fathom the realm of the Tathāgata. Previously, I sent a letter to Observation Commissioner Zhu of Nanxiao, requesting him to protect the Dharma.
Yesterday, I received news that he has already issued an order for Nanxiong to escort [the relics] across the mountain pass.
However, the messenger was vague, and the accompanying attendants seem to be merely following his every step; I do not know when they will arrive.
At the capital gate, the light of the white tuft between his eyebrows protrudes, illuminating eighteen thousand worlds to the east.

Within that light, regarding those who practice the bodhisattva path through various causes and conditions, even if Maitreya should harbor doubts, by relying on Mañjuśrī’s eye of wisdom, they will surely be penetrated one by one without exception;
there is no need for the weary to chatter at length. I respectfully entrust this to you, [the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*].
I offer this single leaf of the *Gāthā* as an offering for the eye of wisdom. This sutra profoundly clarifies the present, everyday realm of our lives, enabling immediate and actual realization;
it is what is known as the "Sudden Teaching. I pray that you, in your daily life throughout the six periods of the day and night, shall never for a moment forget this Dharma.

Since the time of our various hardships until the present, I have sought within my own fundamental mind with the elder Zhang Daxin, yet not a single stirring thought or thought of regret can be found.
How much less could there be any views of right and wrong, gain and loss, gratitude and resentment, or formation and destruction?— the Elder.
Since leaving the mundane world, I have known the great matter of birth and death at the age of seven.

For thirty years, I have endured all manner of frost and ice and exhausted every hardship, solely to win this single thought-moment. Alas, how can it be that it now lies submerged within the net of illusory transformations?
Had it not been for the Sage’s grace, which shattered [my delusions] with a single blow, I would not know where I would have ended up by now—perhaps lost for donkey-years.
For years I have sat amidst the miasma of the swamps, yet I dwell upon the ground of purity; daily I take the *Laṅkāvatāra* as the seal of my heart. This is truly a gift bestowed by the Sage’s grace.
I imagine that when you, Layman, hear of this, you will surely feel great joy. As for you, Junfu, how have your virtue and practice fared over these recent years?
I offer these hundred admonitions: maintain purity and minimize desire; do not give rise to thoughts of excessive greed or restless pursuit beyond your station.
In the future, you will naturally find vast abundance for your enjoyment. In your leisure, withdraw and collect your body and mind, making study your primary concern.
When you achieve success and stand before others in the future, you will be able to look back with no cause for shame. As I, an old man, reflect upon my own past, it truly seems as though...

Within the dream, there is no longer even a single thing; this is surely because it resides within the great mind. Whatever true merit one possesses, one will certainly not retreat from the original resolve.
A reply to Ke Fuyuan, the Xiaolian.
I have heard that your illness is severe; my mind has been preoccupied with this concern day and night without ceasing. As our Buddha taught, all illnesses arise from deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).
Since deluded thoughts are the root of all ailments, one knows that severing these thoughts is the singular, wondrous medicine.
You possess the resolve to resolve the great matter of birth and death; it is a pity, however, that you have not yet entered deeply into this Dharma-gate. Previously...

At the time of our meeting, we were too casual and let the matter pass; we thought that the conditions for our encounter were still pending, little realizing that birth and death would press upon us so swiftly.
You are thin and gaunt, standing like a mere skeleton; even without illness, you bear the marks of sickness, let alone having been ill for a long time.
I reckon that your recovery will be extremely difficult. If you do not take the pivot of life and death and bite down with a single firm resolve, all worldly thoughts will persist.

At this time, let go all at once of emotional defilements, delusive thoughts, and discursive reflections; do not seek immediate results, for it is like a flickering lamp flame that only reveals its own exhaustion.
At such a moment, nothing is more effective than the single application of "deadening the mind" (sixin), which is the most effortless method.
Other skillful means are of no use; all learning and texts will prove ineffective.
If one were to completely expel everything previously held within the breast, then the root of the illness would be entirely uprooted, and branches and leaves would naturally cease to grow.
As the Elder Pang said: "I only wish to empty all that exists"—this is a true word.
Furthermore, the Buddha said: "To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty is to transcend all suffering and calamity.

All sufferings—that which can be suffered—consist solely of the five aggregates of body and mind. If the five aggregates are all empty, what suffering could there possibly be? Yet, as for these five aggregates of body and mind...
It is originally and inherently empty; it is only that we have not personally seen through this. If one sees through it directly, then all that exists is like flowers in the sky.
One who can perceive this body and mind as being like flowers in the sky is named Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
All those who are amidst the suffering of illness should practice such contemplation. If you are oppressed by distress, [then contemplate] the mind...
The ground will not yield its coolness; rather, one must confront that which is pressing and unyielding.

With a single glance, fix your attention upon this point and exert your strength here, as if you were facing off against Old Yan himself. You must resolve to see through it completely. If you can penetrate this point, [all else follows].
Then the mechanism of birth and death throughout hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas will be shattered all at once.

Walking with such nonchalance—casting aside one’s arms—is what is called being a person of great sovereign freedom. The ancients all achieved this at the critical juncture of illness, calamity, and the cycle of birth and death;
therefore, they attained such stability, confidence, radiance, and vastness. Strive with all your might to realize it.
In the past, before I had met you face-to-face, Dīng Nányǔ already perceived your mind; now that I have met you at the riverbank, I behold your spirit.
The Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions, and the patriarchs of successive generations, have emitted radiance from within a single hair-tip of yours.

The earth shook; it was no wonder that this occurred. Previously, the Great Being bestowed upon me the *māyopama-samādhi*, and I have constantly been sprinkled with its nectar, which instantly caused my feverish afflictions to become cool and refreshing.
Shortly thereafter, Jueyin arrived, bringing the portrait of the ancestral path of Kangzushi.
To expose [this] amidst miasmic fogs and poisonous mists causes one’s blood and tears to gush forth from every pore of the body.
Master Kang was my ancestor at Changgan; the śarīra is the flesh and bone of my teacher.

I have exerted myself with diligent effort. Furthermore, within these past three years, I have attained a slight degree of correspondence with the Way;

this makes it evident how difficult it is to navigate the world and how the state of the Perfected Person is not easily learned nor easily reached. I have shared this solely with you. When compared with this matter, [all else seems trivial].
It is entirely accomplished amidst adversity; furthermore, its benefit is more manifest and its merit is greater, increasing day by day and kalpa by kalpa.
This must be undertaken by a person of great power and capacity. An ancient said: "One may have the skeletal constitution of a general or a minister, yet lack the karmic fortune for renunciation.
These words are not superficial. However, the difficulty of renouncing the world is likewise no small matter. Throughout my life, I, this poor monk—

The suffering [I endure] is not merely ten thousand times greater than yours; yet, in terms of the resolve to undergo such suffering, it is as vast as the distance between heaven and earth compared to yours.
Since I entered the monastic life, whenever I have been addressed by others, I have never once spoken of us as "brothers."
Why is this? Because his resolve was to walk alone and stride independently, not to associate with the mundane world;
this is the aspiration for transcendence and upward progress. Now, within these three years, he has finally begun to socialize and call others his brothers;
this is precisely the first step of effort in "blending with the world and harmonizing with light. Thus one knows that the Bodhisattva’s mind in responding to the world is subtle and wondrous.

To be without direction and without abiding is the Supreme Vehicle. When the Sixth Patriarch heard [the verse], "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere," he immediately awakened to his original nature, and the wheel of birth and death through kalpas of eons was instantly stilled. How could this have been the act of a petty man?
This is something I, this poor monk, know for myself. Previously, we both dwelt in a state of biased, stagnant emptiness;
this is no different from worldly people dwelling in the sea of afflictions. Since you were previously dwelling in existence, there was no distinction between you and my own dwelling in emptiness.
Now that you have been able to turn over completely with a single step and break through [that state], you have immediately surpassed me by thirty [stages].
This can be called "transcending directly and entering at once" after years of effort. This is not a matter of casting aside present phenomena to seek another way out.
If one were to abandon what is before one's eyes to seek liberation elsewhere, one would be either a fool or a madman.

Yongjia said: "To discard existence and cling to emptiness is likewise a sickness; it is like avoiding drowning only to leap into fire. This refers precisely to this point. As for [your] letter to me...
It is difficult to meet in person. My previous letter was already written beforehand; yet, upon opening it and reading your letter once more, my gratitude overflowed.

Thus, facing the messenger at my desk, I drafted this in haste, unaware that such tangled complications had arisen. This is surely because, having long been accustomed to being a companion, I feel a particular affection for you as a guest.
That you have given rise to this unsurpassed resolve is a karmic condition for transcending the world; how could it be otherwise?
I have responded to you with such superficiality; therefore, I have laid my heart bare in this manner. You may take this note as a point of inquiry to pass the days and months;
it may well serve as a "Clearing Powder" (Qīngliángsàn) for you.
Furthermore, I previously received your letter, in which you spoke of turning your heart toward the Pure Land. Such is your fierce resolve!

Consequently, I have written this hastily upon my desk for the messenger, filling a full page without knowing what I was saying. For the most part, I have spoken with utmost earnestness to exhort you to practice with reality.
Amidst adversity, seek a place of peace and joy. When encountering circumstances that are difficult to manage, simply let go of body and mind right within those difficulties.
Let others call you an ox or a horse; as for me, there is nothing acceptable and nothing unacceptable.
This kind of enjoyment is something only Laozi could achieve; even Confucius, had he not attained this Dharma-gate, would have found it difficult to navigate the world.
After meeting Laozi, he was struck by a sharp probe at his vital point that pierced straight through to the very bottom; at that moment, he attained immeasurable benefit.

As for his subsequent instructions to his disciples—“Do not be arbitrary, do not be compulsive, do not be rigid, do not be self-centered”—and the statement “It is empty and void like space,” these are all words spoken after full realization; they certainly did not come before that.
This is speech. The impurity within our minds consists merely of these notions of self and other, right and wrong; we cling to our emotions and cannot let them go.
We harbor fixed intentions and a stubborn sense of self, insisting that things must conform to our own views before they can be considered good.
Yet, while we insist on following our own will, how could others not likewise follow their own? All of this belongs to the affairs of the bitter sea and the defiled land. One need only let this go.
The mind: within the mind, it becomes utterly pure and clean. Its joy is beyond compare. What could there be that is not possible? It is level, vast, and open;
this very state is in resonance with the Buddha-mind. To recite the Buddha's name with this mind, every thought is Amitābha.
Every thought-moment is itself the Pure Land.

Furthermore, regarding the various dream events that occurred while he was in the province prior to his departure: according to what he related, they were as clear as if before one's eyes; although I did not yet fully believe them.
Beyond these words, you have already grasped their subtle essence; this is a matter of great joy.

Since ancient times, men of integrity have feared that their character might remain unsettled, and those who suffer calamity have feared that their merits and faults might not be clearly discerned. I, a poor monk, have now attained both of these—how fortunate!
Even if I were to die old and decrepit in a ditch, what regret would there be? For this reason, I have retired to rest at Caoxi.
Xī’s resolve became even firmer. He thought, "If I may invoke the spiritual power of the Sixth Patriarch and borrow a single scoop of earth to cover these withered bones, what more could I desire?
Although this act of veneration is of great merit, its completion shall not be measured by years or months.
With this, my mind feels quite at ease; moreover, the affairs of the Dharma are like clouds in the sky, originally devoid of fixed form."
It is like praying for rain during a period of excessive drought: when one’s sincerity reaches its ultimate limit, there is nothing that does not receive a timely response.

The conditions of Heaven and the affairs of men are, in their essence, one and the same. Master Xiaoxiao was by nature sincere and earnest—a loyal and truthful gentleman, the sort who is difficult to find even within the sphere of the Name-and-Teaching (mingjiao).
It is a pity that his spirit was overly impetuous while his heart was overly compassionate; thus, regarding the words of petty men, he was easily moved and lacked decisiveness.
This poor monk, grateful for being encountered by one who understands him, has acted for the merit of the local region.
He cast himself before the hundred-fold edge of the blade to eliminate the greatest harms for the common people. Fortunately, he has barely managed to escape with his life; now, in this district—
My strength is already exhausted, yet the task ahead is boundless. How could one use finite spirit to navigate a boundless sea of poison?
Would any wise person willingly endure such a fate? Had it not been for me being here last year, there would have been great cause for fear in this region.
This autumn, they earnestly wished to invite me to go; therefore, I declined their request with all my might. I, the poor monk—

Daozi regards this body as being bound by the Dharma-gate; he intends to seek the spiritual power of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and entrust it to serve as a source of merit for ten thousand generations.
Since there is something far more significant than this, how could he not cherish himself? Thus, he now employs various skillful means and circumlocutions.
I have already begun to carry out my plan of concealing my traces; how much more so from this point forward? Therefore, I am not far away.
How could I bear to be defiled by impurity, even to the point of bringing disgrace upon the Pure Land? Birds do not weary of the heights, nor do fish weary of the depths;

Caoxi shall become a mere mound and corner. You who know me—what do you think of this? I have received your instruction that one must hold a rosary when practicing the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
This practice of focused mindfulness is most intimate and essential. Previously, I did not dare to mention it, fearing that you might feel a sense of shame.
Now that it is required, I respectfully offer this single string of agarwood beads which I have personally maintained.
Although they have been held for a long time and lack fragrance, their spiritual potency is already full. I trust that upon receiving these, you will surely be able to attain sudden realization.
This is the entry into the Treasury of Joy.
In response to Yang Yuanshu, Yuanrong, it is said by the ancients:
"In the midst of the field of feverish turmoil, cold eyes are difficult to withstand. For the Three Realms are without peace, like a burning house.

Those who enter and exit within it are all without exception scorched and boiled. If one can find even a single patch of cool ground amidst these fierce flames, it is not one with cold eyes who can attain it.
If one can, in a single thought-moment, attain this coolness, one will suddenly see the entire earth as ice;
thus, one no longer makes the world of body and mind one's dwelling place. This is from the Great Master [Shigong].

A person of power who sports within the field of birth and death, able to transform worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) into Buddha-work and transmute delusion into Bodhi—this relies solely upon their single cold eye and their single cold heart. What other supernatural powers or wondrous functions could there be?
These words are very easy to understand, yet very difficult to see. For instance, when the Buddhas and Patriarchs employ only all phenomena...
The single teaching that "it is like a dream" is the essential path for transcending the world; yet, among the wise and the foolish of this world, all alike can say that human life is like a dream.
Although their words seem similar, their meaning is not so; in reality, they have never truly grasped it with authentic clarity.
With a single glance, one perceives that human life is like a dream.

If one truly penetrates this insight, one will naturally be able to pass by all occasions of honor and disgrace, profit and loss, gain and failure, right and wrong, as if shaking off dust from one’s sleeves.
Who then would dare to encounter such a person? In truth, there is nothing particularly mysterious about it; however, regarding the very first step, there is certainly a method for it.
As we dwell in this world, we must first take the events of our dreams and present them before our eyes, examining them minutely.
We must resolutely see, with absolute clarity, that point where we involuntarily break into a great laugh.

Upon reaching this state, the ordinary "dream-talk" of the mind will suddenly become entirely different from what it was before. Immediately, even while in the midst of daily activities, turn a single thought back toward the present moment.
Regarding these objective realms: place them within a dream and observe them minutely.
When you see them becoming drowsy, heavy, and inverted, a sudden and fierce awakening will arise. In this way, turn back and contemplate your entire life;

all the various realms you have previously experienced, when sought with earnest scrutiny, are utterly unfindable. This state of total unfindability is precisely the True Teacher of all Buddhas and Patriarchs.
This is the foremost gateway for escaping birth and death.

*The Dream-Traveling Collection of the Elder Hanshan*, Volume Sixteen.
Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and his disciple Tonghyeong;
revised by the Disciple from Yeongnam, Ryu Giseong.
Regarding this correspondence with Inspector Zhou Haimen,
I have been sprinkled with the nectar of his head-dhūta practice, which has cooled my heart and bones and suddenly cured my chronic ailment. Such is the karmic connection of these events.

This is truly no small matter. My sentiments since our parting are much like those of Śūnyatā when he sat in meditation within his stone chamber, perceiving that the Dharma-body is not separate from the space between the mind and the eyes.
I have often said that for this matter, one must be such a person. The Way of the Dharma has long been submerged in the South of the Pass;

fortunately, we have encountered the hand and eye of Great Compassion to bring it forth and propagate it, so that even those of the icchantika class may suddenly give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.

Regarding these supreme roots of goodness, although those who have entered the inner chamber are rare, those who know [of them] are many; those who take refuge increase day by day and become ever more excellent.
Just as beneath the Bodhi tree, among the monks of Caoxi, those who were most difficult to tame have, in recent times, turned their hearts toward faith in two or three out of ten.
This singular current of true wind all proceeds from the Great Radiance.

That it has emerged from within the [Tripitaka] Canon provides sufficient proof that this gentleman’s current journey of official service was truly sent forth by the dragons and devas, proceeding as one who rides the wheel of his great vows.
Now that the *Record of Caoxi* has finally been completed for carving, I would be grateful if you would deign to provide a word to place at the beginning of the volume.
May we manifest the radiance of the Sixth Patriarch and open the eyes of humanity and devas, so as not to fail this auspicious assembly.
Furthermore, I met with the Licentiate Ke in the provincial capital during the fifth month; it was like being born again. This gentleman’s spiritual capacity is sharp and keen.
One who can, at the critical juncture of sorrow and illness, suddenly shatter the nest of birth and death is a true hero.
As the Layman [Zhaozhou] once said: "Everyone possesses the highest capacity; it is simply that they lack the great furnace. This gentleman is no ordinary disciple.
How could one be so capable of such awakening? Were it not for superior faculties, how could one be so fiercely courageous?

In the future, the life-vein of the True Dharma beyond the seas will truly depend upon this person. I pray that the Buddha’s power may sustain him with robust physical vigor, so that he does not suffer from being inferior to those of old.
For years, when I have preached the Dharma in the mountains and wilds, it was as if I were speaking to a wooden man; such is my disciple outside the mundane world.
Among those close to me, I have recently gained one or two individuals who are somewhat capable of being refined through instruction.

While there were those who momentarily believed and turned toward the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the one who truly practices and realizes it is none other than Mr. Feng Changli of Shunde. This youth possesses remarkably deep spiritual roots (*indriya*);
he is held in high esteem by his community, and regardless of age, all who enter his gate serve him as their teacher. His sincerity truly moves others.
Therefore, my sincere instruction is as follows: observing this son’s determination, it is clear that he will not regress in the future and can continue the lineage of Jiangmen.
This is truly a convergence of karmic conditions for the Dharma-path in the regions south of the Ling Mountains. Recently, I heard that he has been traveling with the Grand Historian Tao Shikuai;
this gentleman possesses a heart as pure as ice and snow, having come from a state of pure precepts for generations, and he is a companion to this mountain monk.
When we met, it was only because our karmic conditions had not yet deepened; had we been able to associate more closely, it would have been a most exhilarating matter.
Recently, Tu Changqing has joined forces with De-yuan as fellow practitioners, and he too should be guided at this time into this supreme path.

General-in-Chief Zheng Kunya is truly one who seeks liberation from birth and death; he is currently retired in the forest, and I know deeply that he will find great satisfaction in this. However, with him—
When this mountain monk contemplates it, this uppermost aperture has not yet been opened.

That you, Layman, were able to inquire after me with such detailed courtesy and offer words of consolation is a profound manifestation of your deep compassion. Here, the conditions for the Dharma are gradually unfolding;

as mentioned in my previous letter, you have already heard of those among my disciples who are ready to be transformed. Yet there are still two or three whose capacities have not yet matured. Should...
If Heaven grants me three years, there may be some slight possibility of accomplishment, sufficient to not bring this mission to naught.
Protected by all Buddhas and commissioned by the Tathāgata, it is my hope that this Dharma-gate will fulfill the aspirations of those who know me.

Answer: To cultivate and observe this section of practice as you have directed requires that one act with directness and swiftness amidst the surging current, within the flash of a spark or a streak of lightning;
only then is it a matter of great power. Having received your instruction, I have attained great coolness and peace therein, which is itself the sudden realization of Bodhi.
This is the primary meaning. I only fear that the power of your illumination may not be steadfast, such that you are carried away by the flow of phenomena without realizing it.
If you do realize this, then the clouds will disperse and the rain will cease; with radiant breezes and a clear moon, its joy will be beyond compare.
To General Zhu Xincun (byname Yibin):
I have heard the Buddha teach that all conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows. I recall in the past following his instructions as I moved through the world.

Now it is all as vague and fleeting as a dream. Since our parting at Caoxi, everything has been according to my destiny; all manner of things have been like illusory phenomena, and now I view them as mere bubbles.
Yet within the mind of deluded thought, they are but shadows. Only through the observation of Great Wisdom—how could anything exist outside of this?
This entire episode of the restoration of Caoxi, down to its smallest detail, has emerged from the Samādhi of Compassionate Heart. Thus it is with the mountain.
The immeasurable suffering of the wilderness was entirely sustained by his compassionate vows.
Although his work remains unfinished, its general framework may serve as a pioneering undertaking for the revival of the ancestral Way in this age.

While such deeds in the mountains and wilds are surely not worth chronicling, the radiance of your venerable compassion in protecting the Dharma must never be extinguished. Therefore, we disciples have recorded here a brief account of the actual events.
I have arranged this into ten sections and venture to request that you, as a donor of the Dharma, provide a preface to serve as a Vajradhvaja pillar.
This shall exist eternally alongside the Dharmakāya of the Sixth Patriarch, truly constituting a great causal nexus for the renaissance of the teaching a thousand years hence.
I pray that you will extend your broad and long tongue to cover the entire trichiliocosm, so that all who see or hear it may universally enter the Great Treasury of Radiance.

This karmic connection between Great Councilor Ding Youwu (style name Juefei) and this mountain recluse is indeed naturally extraordinary; even among those who understand within the realm, there are none who do not marvel at it.
This is truly because we both fall into the two kinds of views—mundane and supramundane—and are hindered by the great obstacle of ego-inflation (*māna*). We have become habituated to...

The seed of vital energy (*vāyu-bīja*) obscures the luminosity of innate wisdom. Because Gong fell into this, his wings were clipped mid-flight, and he could not unfurl his feathers to strike the wind.
Because Shan-yang fell into this, the banner of the Dharma was broken in the middle, and he was unable to uphold the reputation of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Relying upon the vast and true compassion of all Buddhas and their inconceivable spiritual power, they together [sound] the swift thunder of the Dharma.
They were struck down and shattered. Though the human affairs of each side differ, the furnace they encounter is the same; subsequently, the miserable realms into which they are cast are the same;
and ultimately, their lives and natures are dependent upon one another as equals. How could they not desire to transcend birth and death together, and to realize Bodhi together?
Therefore, they bind them all with a single strip of bamboo and cast them all at once into the great ocean of the East, desiring nothing more than for us—

In an instant, all the coarse and floating habitual tendencies accumulated over kalpas—such as pride and prejudice, right and wrong, enmity and gratitude, gain and loss—all manner of defilements, are washed away almost entirely.
Otherwise, how could it be that we share the same death and the same life, yet reach such a state?
