I have often said that for this koan, those whom the ancients found difficult to subdue all employed this single device; it is like the Eastern [teaching] of Changli...
Slope: "The various elders of our school, such as Juefan, were all like this. If it had not been for Dadian, the stubbornness of Changli would not have been transformed;
if it had not been for Dan’er, the arrogance of Dongpo would not have been dissolved; and if it had not been for Qiong and Ya, the habitual views of Juefan would not have been extinguished.

Yet, while these several masters were identical in their refinement and cultivation, the circumstances they encountered were different; therefore, they are not ranked among the immortals of a thousand ages."
How extraordinary! Although you, sir, are certainly not Māṇikya (Changli), this mountain recluse dares not hope to reach the heights of the old master [Fengxue].
Although this mountain recluse feels ashamed before Juefan, you do not yield to Dongpo. Thus, by the conditions of today, you surpass the predecessors of the past;
truly, this is a once-in-a-thousand-years moment, and my joy is great. If you, sir, had no inclination toward the delight of Chan, this mountain monk would have none...
Having received the seal of the mind of Laṅkā, I shall still return following the old path; would this not be to betray such a favorable opportunity and to fail the mandate of Heaven?
This is why, though we have dwelt together for years, I have not dared to slightly reveal even a glimmer of this "one stroke above" [the ultimate teaching].
With your superior faculties and sharp instruments, you are naturally capable of transcending directly and entering [the Way] at once.

This is just like the butcher Guang'e at the assembly of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, who, upon laying down his butcher’s knife, immediately performed the work of a Buddha; this is truly not comparable to those of limited capacity.

For the conditions for entering the Path surely have their own appointed seasons. I did not expect such a sudden parting; I truly feel that even after a hundred kalpas it would be difficult to meet again.
Now that we have fortunately encountered one another, how could I possibly let you go so lightly?
Therefore, though I am aware of my own rustic and humble nature, amidst these turbulent waves, I hope to receive your joy and settle the matter of life and death once and for all.

Without the violent awakening at the Three Rivers or the firm vow at the Return-to-Qi, I shall certainly not retreat even a single step; I will surely pursue you to the very source of Caoxi, until the waters run dry.
Only when the mountains are exhausted, through great rest and great repose, does one finally come to an end.

The reason for this is that you alone, sir, have with faith the heart of a Bodhisattva toward me, Shan-yeh, and have treated my body as your own flesh and bone. Among those who know you within the seas, all regard the meeting between you, a world-transcending figure, and me, Shan-yeh, as extraordinary.
If I, Shan-yeh, were not to [respond] to this karmic connection of a momentous matter by carving into my heart...
To extract my gallbladder and present it to you—how could this possibly satisfy the expectations of one who knows me well, or repay your extraordinary affection?
You do not regard the task of shouldering the Tathāgata’s legacy as your own most urgent personal concern, nor is this the way to show love for these mountain recluses or to requite a true friend.
This stage of practice is by no means difficult; it lies solely in the essential nature of your own sincere mind, which is *prajñā*.
His radiance is majestic and uniquely manifest; thus, his breast encompasses the stars and constellations, and his vital energy overwhelms heaven and earth.
Yet, because the habitual tendencies of coarseness, frivolity, anger, and arrogance occasionally emerge, they obscure his own wondrous clarity.

Therefore, I have laid bare my very heart and liver, yet people may not find faith; I have exhausted my compassion, yet people may remain unmoved. You, sir, must reflect deeply upon this: what else remains?
What is there to feel ashamed before others? Our Buddha has said: "When a single thought of anger arises, a million gates of obstruction open.
This is the great taboo for the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra in benefiting sentient beings, for anger and compassion cannot coexist.
Now, I only wish that by eliminating even one part of my habitual tendencies, ten parts of luminosity may be revealed; by removing even one part of anger—
Pride. Thus, one establishes a hundredfold merit. As the ancients said: "One need not seek the Truth; one must only cease [conceptual] views.
It is also said: "There is no need to seek elsewhere; simply letting go is it. And again: "If you can see through it, you may even become a Buddha. Yongjia said:
Following the slander of others, one may occupy the earth as one pleases, yet it is not right; to hold fire and burn toward heaven is but a wearying of oneself in vain.
When I heard this, it was like drinking nectar—melting away and suddenly entering the inconceivable. From this, we can clearly see that the ancients had no other special talent;
they simply were willing to let go of everything within their chests that was contrary to their will. It is precisely what people find unbearable to endure.

In these circumstances, one must first cultivate patience toward beings (*sattva-kṣānti*) so that one can endure them personally. If one’s patience reaches the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*), then one immediately ascends to the stage of Buddhahood;
what subtle or wondrous skill could there be then to smear upon the ears and eyes of others?

Previously, there was a couplet which said: "When a thought arises, see through it at once; before a matter arrives, do not give rise to it falsely. Though these words are small, they serve as a parable.
Great! From this point forward, I exhort you, sir: first, enter the Dharma-gate of patience; apply yourself to the practice of mental ease; engage in the work of letting go.
Look back upon all your travels during the first half of your life and realize they were but dream-events.
Spit them out all at once, leaving not even a hair’s breadth behind. Leap forth with naked strength, rouse your spirit, overturn the old nest, and reveal a brand-new day.

To establish a separate life-path for oneself—only when one reaches this state does one truly become a great man (mahāsattva). One covers both heaven and earth, not failing the spirit of one’s entire life.
Naturally, devas and nāgas will fold their hands in reverence, and demons and spirits will hide their tracks.

This is precisely what it means to cultivate the "noble rank of Heaven" (deva-pada), whereby the "noble rank of men" (mānuṣya-pada) follows of its own accord. Compared to this, how can empty and floating conceptualizations compare to performing deeds of true and imperishable merit?
Your virtue is indeed as vast as heaven and earth. To call you "Master Juefei" (Awakened-Non-Worldly) would be an extreme oversimplification.

What do you, O Illustrious One, think of this? If you consider me not to be deceiving you, then even orchids and frankincense cannot compare to our affinity, nor can metal and stone suffice to match our covenant.
This is truly the seed of the Vajra, unpolished through kalpas; I pray that it may be shared with you throughout your life.
"From life to life, we shall together serve as bridges for transcendence and act as compassionate kin, delivering all sentient beings without ever parting from one another.
The words of this mountain recluse today reveal my very heart and soul, transcending ordinary sentiments."
This is a world-transcending covenant, established here. If you truly place your trust in it, I beg that you burn all previous letters sent to you to ashes, leaving not a single character remaining;
thus, my hundred anxieties shall turn to dust. From this day forward, I pray that whenever I write to you, I shall send nothing but words of medicine and stone.
May every word be an imitation of the true speech and real speech of our Buddha—neither false nor deceptive.

This is Qi’s admonition. It is what Your Reverence has taught me. I only wish that, regarding our daily practice since we parted, we might mutually stimulate and encourage one another concerning where effort is spared and where it is expended, and where progress is easy and where it is difficult, so as to achieve a great feat for the age.
I pray that Your Reverence first acts as a gatekeeper at the critical juncture of birth and death;

once this gate is penetrated, one may then cast off all concern and wander freely. *Gao* (戈) [Note: This character appears to be a scribal error or variant for *yóu* (遊) or *xiá* (暇), or perhaps part of a name or title.]

Amidst the field of halberds and within the thicket of right and wrong, at every place and at every turn, light is emitted that shakes the earth. Manifesting in the body of a high official, he performs great Buddhist rites.
Such a one may truly be called a world-transcending, heroic, and courageous man; he is by no means comparable, even in the slightest degree, to the worldly heroes of past or present.
Parting is not yet far, yet the sentiments of life and death are deep. Gazing longingly toward our respective heavens, we are entangled in the vines of separation.
Throughout the land, I pray that you will brandish the sword of wisdom once and leave not even a hair’s breadth remaining; I beseech you, O Illustrious One, to strive diligently toward this end.
Furthermore, since our parting, day after day has passed without any news. As the person who departed grows ever more distant, my longing for him grows ever deeper. Every time I see...
I have never ceased to be struck with alarm and wonder, questioning you as to what causes and conditions could cause our communication to be suddenly severed in such a manner.
Suddenly, I received your letter, which arrived slowly from amidst the clouds; opening the envelope, I was startled to see your countenance.

Moreover, every word flowed forth from the true mind and the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Grief and joy welled up within me simultaneously. When I observe and contemplate this mind, it manifests whether walking, standing, sitting, or...

"Not departing from it even while lying down"—these few words caused my heart to overflow with joy beyond measure. I never imagined that, at this very moment, I would suddenly hear such a rare Dharma.
I have often said that this Way is inherently complete within every person; it does not matter whether one's faculties are sharp or dull, nor is there any restriction on the speed of awakening.
It depends solely upon the individual’s own self-confidence and self-acceptance. This is what is meant by "a single thought turning back."
Light is identical to that which has existed from the beginning; how could one seek it elsewhere? It simply awaits its own proper time and conditions for manifestation.
Regarding the letters received from my old friends throughout the Three Wu regions, I long for you, Layman, to enter this Way immediately, for my thoughts of our shared essence are most earnest.
Therefore, there are many concerns. It seems that for lay practitioners (*upāsaka*), habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) tend to predominate, making this [path] difficult.
However, as for the mountain recluse observing you, Layman, your being is transparently lucid, like the "chicken-startling" *rishi* horn;

even if there is some partiality, it belongs entirely to the influence of adventitious delusions and is not your original nature. Entering the Way is like a single arrow piercing three barriers; it simply requires a willing mind.
Once he has struck out, there is truly the momentum of a single man at the pass who cannot be resisted by ten thousand men;

how then could one dare to compare their speed or distinguish between their sharpness and dullness? Thus, those who worry for the layman are like those who worry that a person from Jiao or Handan will fail in their martial prowess.
Since antiquity, there have naturally been men of extraordinary caliber and immeasurable capacity; how can they be compared [with ordinary men]?
Generally speaking, this matter depends entirely upon valor and courage; one must simply step right through to the very bottom.

If habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) should suddenly arise, one must simply apply a forceful pressure with the power of a hegemon—like pulling up a mountain or lifting a cauldron—exerting every ounce of strength at once.
Or again, it is like a single shout of defiance that causes a thousand men to collapse. If one acts in this way, what worry need there be that habitual tendencies cannot be overcome?
Exhaust it. As soon as there arises even a hair’s breadth of a thought that one cannot exhaust it, one falls into cowardice and immediately realizes one lacks the spirit of a true man.
The crux of this matter lies in the attachment and aversion of the mind; this is the most difficult point to break through. Strike it with a single blow of effort.
If this single point is broken through, then hundreds of thousands of millions of crucial mechanisms will all be broken at once.

If this difficult point is not broken, then even if one were to swallow up with a single gulp hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhist teachings, insights, and principles, there would be not even a trace of practical utility;
it would be of no benefit whatsoever, whether in the mundane or the supramundane world. Why is this? Because the root of the illness has not been extracted.

It is like the poison of a rat: it erupts upon encountering a thunderclap. If the root of illness erupts, then no matter how many deeds of fame and merit one performs, or what various skillful means one employs, they are all merely the conduct of a disease;
they are by no means the conduct of a valiant and heroic man. Since one is acting contrary to the way of a hero, [one is not a hero].
Furthermore, why is he called a "great man" (zhàngfū) who bears a capacity that transcends the world?
I privately admire the layman for his human qualities, literary talent, fame, achievements, innate aptitude, and learning—every single one surpasses others.

Yet, if the root of his illness is not uprooted, he may only dominate his own generation, but cannot dominate the ages. If he were willing to take the intelligence and strength he has cultivated throughout his life...
Gather everything together; concentrate your spirit and focus your mind upon this single great cause and condition.
Once you break through it all at once, then all the various grudges and favors, honors and insults, right and wrong, gains and losses from ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes will vanish.
The afflictions and karmic obstructions are all simultaneously transformed into the unsurpassed bodhi, the seed of radiance.
From this point, upon emerging once more, whatever one does or undertakes—every subtle activity—is manifested from within this very seed of radiance.
Every matter and every dharma becomes imperishable. This is what our Elder Śākyamuni abandoned.
He abandoned the royal palace and severed the bonds of affection; he practiced austerities for six years in the Snowy Mountains to attain the ultimate realization.
Yet, a mere layman once swept it all away and wrapped it up in his sack. Is this not truly a great, heroic, and courageous man?
He constantly mocked Goujian for the humiliation at Kuaiji, who spent over twenty years lying on firewood and tasting gall, yet whose ambition was limited to swallowing the state of Wu.
This is all there is to it. How vulgar! I, this mountain recluse, often say that the thieves of affliction have, throughout kalpas, invaded my right faith—not merely once in the state of Wu.
Because of them, the pure land of the Dharma has been ruined, the city of Nirvana destroyed, and we have cast ourselves into the sea of suffering, drifting without end—not merely the shame of Kuaiji.
If we can truly gnash our teeth and establish the resolve of Goujian, [then...]
Furthermore, the enmity of birth and death spanning kalpas need not necessarily require twenty years of effort to resolve.
Since that [enmity] is something done by others, whereas this [resolution] is something done by oneself; now that it is something done by oneself, what is there to fear in not doing it?
Furthermore, having received your message, I am greatly delighted that you have found great benefit even amidst these adverse conditions.
Generally speaking, to derive such great benefit from adversity is the very task of a true man of character; it is merely a matter of daily life and nothing particularly extraordinary.

This "special place" is simply that which is present in daily life; it is the point where, when encountering favorable conditions, one becomes accustomed and habituated, such that [the truth] manifests without one's awareness, and one is deceived by them.
This is what makes this point difficult. For instance, consider right before our eyes, regardless of whether the matters are great or small, those things that do not accord with our wishes.
This is an adverse condition. As soon as one is touched by it, anger arises; thus, one is moved by others. Once moved, there is suffering, and one is unable to enjoy [the state].
This is precisely what is meant by "it is difficult to forget that which is familiar. The mechanism of birth and death lies solely in this single turning point.
If one can turn [the mind] at this point, one becomes a sage on the spot. If one cannot turn it, one remains fallen into affliction (*kleśa*).
Within this nest, at this place of the swift current, a single turn of the pivot is the very power that shifts the celestial gate.
Unless one is a person of great strength like you, with a diamond-like mind-ground, it is truly difficult to manifest such capability.

What the ancients called "the Buddha-dharma is not much" refers precisely to this. Generally speaking, it is only when one attains the joy of utilization amidst the midst of afflictions that one is truly free.
This is true enjoyment of the ears. Throughout his life, a layperson’s afflictions may have been immense, yet his moments of joy were likewise great.

If, at this very moment, he can strike the nest of his afflictions with a single blow until it is shattered to pieces and leap whole into the field of joy, looking back upon the habitual tendencies of hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes as nothing more than saliva to be spat out in one gulp—this is truly heaven.
Above heaven and below earth, he is the foremost sovereign, a man of immeasurable and great joy. Can you, Layman, consider this to be mere recklessness?
Today the dharma-assembly is complete; there are immeasurable matters of joy before our eyes that I wish I could share with you, but for now, I shall briefly use this to report my well-being.
Furthermore,
this ten-thousand-li journey of mine has relied upon the compassionate power of the Buddhas and the vast grace of the Holy Sovereign.
To have attained this great matter while dwelling in this malarial region is truly the most supreme causal condition for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
"Consider this, Layman: you share these joys and sorrows with me; how can you not also share this flavor of the Dharma?
There is a proverb that says, 'When the sun rises, affairs arise again. Amidst the vast and boundless ocean of dust, there is ultimately no end.
When one finds a moment of leisure, one should seize it. Reflect on this body of a man: it supports heaven and earth. If one sets aside worldly matters, there remains the transcendence of the world."
The realm of infinite leisure and joy—how could one mistake the illusory transformations before one's eyes and the deluded thoughts of this world for the ultimate?
It has been two years since you left; I imagine that at the point where you have seen through things, you must have gradually entered a refined state, taking a step forward from the very foundation.
To your diamond-like mind, this [my letter] is but a mere cough or a spittle. How do you find it?
It has been ten years since I last parted from Master Tang Hai’ruo, Director of the Shrine Department, in the blink of an eye. Yet the radiance of his *śarīra* remains vividly before my eyes;

thus, all these various conditions of illusory transformation are but the empty-flower activities of the Buddha. As this mountain monk sits here in this malarial region, I rely upon the truth of the Triple Gem.
Through the power of being sustained by loving-kindness, one is free from all afflictions and may spend the years simply taking the Dharma as an object of focus.

A signal gong is no different from a broken-legged cauldron; yet, alas, the habitual tendencies of literary expression accumulated over lifetimes erupt uncontrollably even within this state of non-action.

During this period of a thousand days, apart from the intervals spent running about in military ranks or performing corvée labor, I have composed various writings totaling no fewer than several hundred thousand words.
Although these offer no contribution to the Ultimate Way, they serve as a modest manifestation of my single-minded, solitary light, which remains unclouded even within this land of rākṣasa demons.
I trust that those who truly know me will not consider this endeavor to be迂 (extravagant or pedantic).
With Liu Cunchi, we have both accumulated karmic afflictions over many lifetimes. The mire of the five desires and the fires of the seven emotions are deep and fiercely blazing;

there is no man of talent or heroism who has not been submerged, scorched, or boiled by them. Even when seeking a single moment of turning the mind toward awakening, it is utterly impossible to find. How much more so...
One should aspire to give rise to a mind of detachment, seek the path to escape suffering, and single-mindedly fix one's thoughts upon the Pure Land.
This is not merely like a lotus emerging from the mud; it is even more extraordinary, as its roots spring forth from fire. How joyful this is!

Those of us who wish to transcend birth and death must understand the root of birth and death; those who wish to seek the foundation of the Pure Land must realize that [the root of birth and death] is none other than the mind.
The foundation of the earth is precisely the root of birth and death; it lies within this very mind, in the space of a single thought-moment’s transformation.
Do not spare any effort in this regard. I pray that you will examine with clarity the present conditions of daily life, even during moments when your wife and children are gathered together.
In the midst of social interactions with friends, at the point where righteousness and profit clash, and before joy or anger has yet been provoked—look ahead and fix your gaze in advance.
With absolute sincerity and perfect clarity, you must discern what constitutes the very root of birth and death.
One must then exert all effort to uproot it. However, my mind is fundamentally pure; that which defiles and turbidizes it is truly the corruption of these root-stocks.
If one can successfully uproot them, then the Pure Land will arrive of its own accord without being sought.
This is precisely what is meant by the saying: "Once one faculty returns to the source, the six faculties achieve liberation. If...
If one penetrates through to the root in a single thought-moment, then every aspect of daily life will be nothing other than a field of liberation, entirely returning to the realm of Ultimate Bliss.
This truly means that although the body has not yet reached within the lotus flower, the mind has already been sent back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

I, the impoverished and lowly monk Zheng Jinwu, am utterly unworthy; I am but a withered stump. When the thunder shook and roared yesterday, those who looked on were like people standing by the fires of the kalpa’s end.
Yet, beneath your seat, you freely cast aside all concern for your person and, rolling up your sleeves, reached out to rescue me through various means.
I have thus sought to rescue them, resolving that I would not rest until they were all reborn, no less than the elder’s concern for his children within the burning house.

Since parting from you, I have sat alone in this malarial region; whenever weariness and fatigue arose, my thoughts turned toward your presence, and I found myself suddenly swelling with immeasurable courage and the vow to deliver sentient beings.
Now, by the grace of Your Holiness, the remaining years granted to me shall be spent accordingly.
The Dharma thus expounded and the beings thereby benefited all emerge from the Vajra Ground beneath this seat;
their practices and vows are inexhaustible, and their merit is likewise endless. Having fallen into these pestilent lands as one of inferior capacity, I have spent over a thousand days in an instant.
I am ashamed that my causes of outflow are insufficient to repay your signless bestowal. I pray to express my gratitude through the Dharma; I respectfully present what I have recently [composed].
The Buddha-works performed are of various kinds according to the Dharma. I offer these words of consolation and compassionate thought as a way to repay your kindness. Please examine them further;
they are like glimpsing the tracks of birds in the sky, intended merely to follow the path of a wandering practitioner, which never departs from amidst the dust of carriages and the hooves of horses.

I, He Jinwu, have often recalled the words of the ancients: "White-haired, yet as strangers; meeting under a spreading canopy, yet as old friends. There are those for whom the Way exists spontaneously without words;
yet when it comes to the moments of hardship, calamity, life, or death—when one gazes upon the bonds of fetters and shackles—it is not so.

Those who speak while harboring such thoughts in their hearts are indeed rare. Why is this? It is because people are easily moved by emotional appeals, yet it is difficult to bestow kindness upon those who do not repay it.
In the past, I, this mountain dweller, through my own recklessness, provoked Your Majesty’s wrath from above and was subjected to interrogation and suppression from below.
At that time, with thunder and lightning looming overhead and the cauldrons of hell before me, my clear and steadfast intentions could find no way to be made known.
The officials respectfully received the imperial decree to oversee the execution. Yet they lingered in hesitation amidst the whips and staves;
even had his body been as hard as metal or stone, how could it have withstood the furnace and bellows?

Fortunately, it was decided by your single word—truly like pouring a drenching rain upon a blazing fire, or casting sweet nectar into a parched throat, instantly bringing coolness to the five internal organs and causing one to leap for joy.
Yet, when one is about to undergo physical punishment, one does not even realize that one is amidst the blades and saws. Under the laws of the imperial court, there has been no leniency shown;

however, observing from the side the compassion in Your Honor’s heart, which naturally manifests upon your brows and eyelashes, I have already come to know deeply that you are a benevolent man and a gentleman.
I merely cherish this gratitude in my heart, yet I do not know how... [the text ends].

I have long wondered who you might be. Having retreated deep into the mountain wilds and pestilential regions, surviving the aftermath of famine and on the brink of death nine times over, I have never ceased to keep your noble character in mind.
Only recently, upon being questioned by your esteemed colleagues, did I first learn that you are the honorable gentleman [so-and-so].
I have therefore respectfully composed this brief letter to express my private devotion to your virtue.

In response: I, Zheng Kunyai, Governor-General, have from afar received the white tuft of light shining upon the eighteen thousand lands. Within that radiance, I beheld the ascetic practices of a dhūta practitioner, as if personally paying homage to the compassionate countenance and hearing the wondrous teachings in person.
Furthermore, I am indebted for being sprinkled with the nectar of the Dharma, whereby my habitual defilements were suddenly emptied; my heart leaps with joy.
It cannot be fully conveyed by words. I, this poor monk, have heard that the sublime practice of a Bodhisattva lies in testing the mind through successive objects of experience.
When afflictions are seen as empty, there is no need to seek Prajñā elsewhere; when the various sensory dusts are penetrated, this very state is the Gate of Mystery.

I humbly recite the single phrase of "Ultimate Reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*); it is truly a golden probe for those with cataracts. Having personally received your vow, I long to attend at your feet at all times, yet my deluded emotions...
With deep longing, my devotion increases ever more. I pray only that your true compassion may embrace me, never forsaking one who shares this karmic affinity.
I further hope that you will extend a hand from afar; this is what I most reverently yearn for.
Furthermore, for a long time it has been said that the Five Sheep (Wuyang) were Mlēcchas; the fortifications where they dwell are not *ārāmas*.

Relying on the sagely compassion, this poor monk has treated ten thousand *li* as a place for subduing. Tremblingly, he has served among the crucibles and hammers, fortunately using poison to eliminate poison. Its...
My base and inferior habitual tendencies seem to be gradually melting away, truly like drinking water; yet in the end, they are but the froth of a landlocked fish.
Caoxi in Lingnan is the place where the Sixth Patriarch transformed and taught, the "Zhusi" of the Chan school, where his physical body still resides.

This humble monk secretly wishes to take a handful of soil from there to invoke its spiritual power within the realm of quiescent light, so that my past karma may be secretly extinguished. At first, I did not dare...

I have set aside my body and mind, fearing only that I might lose my place in the ranks. From time to time, I have wandered through the intervals between the rows; now, I rely upon the generous concession of the Dharma Hall, where it seems I may finally rest my shoulders.
Recently, while begging for food along the river, I suddenly received a jade casket descending from the heavens, like the sound of the celestial drum.

Having read your compassionate instructions three times over, I realize they are truly the manifestation of boundless great compassion—not abandoning those with whom one has a karmic connection, even within a single speck of dust or a single pore.

Your single phrase, "Hunting the Hidden," truly strikes the painful core like a driven awl; it moves my heart with profound gratitude, for which I offer boundless prostrations of thanks. Regarding your instruction on finding peace of mind wherever one is:
this is precisely liberation in every dust mote. I pray that you will skillfully subdue [the mind] so as to broaden the vessel of the Dharma—this is my highest hope.
I reply to Ge Zixiu regarding what you have shown me.
Since childhood, I have known my own inquiry as to what this mind is. I used to think that the physical lump of flesh was the mind;

yet after death, the body remains, so how is it that it no longer possesses sentience? At these few words about seeking the mind and not finding it, I could not help but be struck with wonder and admiration.
It is finished. Since I entered the mountains and turned toward the Way on my own accord, more than thirty years have passed since I began practicing in the mountains.
Among the monastics and laypeople throughout the realm whom I have encountered, I have never seen anyone with such an awakening of the initial resolve to seek the Way as those here.
This is truly because the Buddha-nature of all sentient beings is identical; it is only due to their past habitual tendencies regarding *prajñā*...

The conditions of one's affinity vary in depth; they differ according to what has been cultivated through proximity over many lifetimes, the seeds of knowledge and auditory permeation, and the distinctions between the false and the correct, or the sudden and the gradual.
Therefore, the resolve to enter the Way varies accordingly, manifesting as differences in being false or correct, sincere or hypocritical, and slow or swift.
What you have said is that, having for many lifetimes drawn near to true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), the seeds of the unsurpassed *prajñā* were perfumed by hearing;
thus, through the internal emergence of these habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), I unconsciously revealed them from my youth, for these seeds are deeply rooted.
Therefore, it presses insistently within the chest; constricted and blocked, one cannot let it go for even a moment.
For this reason, one cannot swallow it down nor spit it out, as if a large object were obstructing the interior. It is simply that one cannot find it, precisely because one treats it as a thing.

Yet, though he sought it, he could not find it. Throughout his life, his reflections failed him; unable to trust himself or reach a definitive resolution, he would merely seek it from others whenever he met them.
When he saw someone point toward empty space, he would take that pointing as a realization of empty space itself. Upon hearing a shout, he would again take that shout as the realization.
Now, empty space is form, and a shout is sound; this is because for many lifetimes he has wandered and transmigrated within the realms of sound and form.
Through habitual practice, you are now once again being led away by them into transmigration.
The reason you are led away by them is simply that you treat this mind as a thing and regard sounds and forms as mere sounds and forms;
thus, in your daily life, whenever you see forms or hear sounds, they immediately become adversaries to the mind. This is precisely what is meant by "seeking Chang'an within the Hanyuan Palace."
How can one escape this cage? Have you not seen the ancients say: "To call it a thing is already incorrect"? And again:
"Be most careful not to seek it from another; to do so is to distance yourself from me. And yet again: "Seeing form is not related to form."
"Hearing sound is not hearing sound," and it is also said, "The locus of sound is entirely hearing; there is no dharma outside of seeing.
Such words and phrases can cause people to die, yet they can also cause people to live. Generally speaking, they cause the living to die and the dead to live.
You yourself claim that when you seek the mind, it cannot be found; this is precisely the most intimate point.
Why then do you not believe in your own mind, but instead give rise to various further deliberations and seek elsewhere?

Have you not seen when Bodhidharma sat with his face to the wall, and the Second Patriarch, Shen Guang, said: "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to pacify my mind"? Bodhidharma replied: "Bring forth the mind."
"I grant you peace. After a long silence, Huineng said, "When you seek the mind, it is utterly unattainable. Mazu said, "I have finished granting you peace.
From that time forward, these words circulated among people and were called the "Direct Transmission of the Single Lineage" (Dānchuán Zhízhǐ). This was from the Sixth Patriarch downward.

From Nanyue and Qingyuan down to the five houses and the seventeen hundred cases, throughout the heavens and across the earth, those who have explained Chan and the Way and attained liberation from birth and death are beyond counting.
All of these have come from seeking the mind from Shen Guang [Huineng], yet finding not a single word that could be grasped.
You must surely believe that the mind is a thing that can be sought from others, and that such a relationship between teacher and disciple is possible.
Regarding the one who offered his hand: Observe what it was that Bodhidharma personally handed over to Shenxian, and what it was that Shenxian personally received.
Furthermore, the words "People everywhere look on; seeking the mind, it is ultimately unattainable" are identical to your own words.
How is it that you do not believe that Shenxian himself was [the recipient]? If you say this is because of your own resolve...
If there were two [aspects] to Shen Guang, then the Buddha-nature of sentient beings would likewise be twofold.
If there is no duality between him and Shen Guang, why did Shen Guang not doubt, while you yourself continue to doubt?
If you claim that this very state is unattainable, then that itself is awakening. Why, then, did Shen Guang awaken once and for all, while you, upon hearing the shout, spoke of a "doubting mass"?
I do not know where to go. Why is it that today, regarding the *gong'an* of the Patriarchs, you still do not penetrate them, while written words again act as an obstacle?
Simply look and see where they reside. Furthermore, when hearing the shout of "No-thought" (*wunian*) correctly, how can the knot of doubt be suddenly dispelled?
What do you see that allows you to attain such carefree ease? Today, for your sake—

"Why is it not free and unobstructed? Immediately look at that place where it is not free and unobstructed. Who is binding you? At the point where the mechanism of words and thoughts does not penetrate, who is creating the obstruction?
You need only apply effort; strike the hammer right where it hurts. When the hammer reaches the point where there is no further place to descend, you will suddenly see through it with your own eyes.
Only then will you believe that this mind is not a thing and does not require seeking from without; only then will you know.
In the past, there was error; error went to the very bottom. There was no error; no error went to the very bottom. At such a time, you will finally believe the words of this mountain monk.
It is much like raising one's voice to stop an echo, or painting a snake and adding feet to it. My words do not reach my meaning;
I have written this hastily with my brush, and before I knew it, the undergrowth of complications had spread everywhere. Once you have read this, spit upon it and burn it. Furthermore—
It may be preserved for future generations as a subject for discourse and a source of inquiry.
Regarding the plan for Vice-Minister Hu Shun’an’s return to the East, I know your integrity and resolve; you will surely leave no strategy untried. This is merely my humble wish. However—
Human life’s fortune and rank are all predetermined by one's past lives; how can one presume that human effort can surpass destiny?

Even if this were not the case, how could one merely wait for liberation before being able to advance on the Path? Rather, while outwardly dwelling amidst the trappings of office and honor, one should inwardly harbor the Buddha-mind;
such that when encountering objects or facing critical moments, one gives rise to kindness and exercises compassion. This is what is meant by "everything encountered before the eyes is [the Path]."

The seeds of Buddhahood and the inexhaustible field of merit—were one merely to apply oneself with even slight attentiveness, the merit produced within a single day would exceed that of the aforementioned by ten millionfold.
Furthermore, your honor’s authority is like heaven and earth; it is the locus of both life and death.
The pivot of good and evil can surely be discerned through clear investigation; yet, within the interval of a mere hair’s breadth, what is at stake is exceedingly great.

The strategy for managing affairs—whether to bring peace or to quell disorder—resides within Your Great Wisdom, though it remains but a single thread. Simply take compassion as your root and use pity to save all beings;
practice expedient means extensively, remaining tranquil within the state of Great Samādhi. To act in this manner is precisely to manifest the governance of a ruler.
To perform Buddhist rites while holding official rank—how can this be compared to those who seek the glory of a single body?

By means of these shackles and fetters, one may instead transform them into instruments for spiritual transcendence; why then be so anxious to withdraw from the world and flee the physical form, merely to sit idly watching the passage of days and months?
My thoughts from a thousand miles away have no gift to offer; these worn-out words are used simply to provoke a response from you, sir.
"Spittle! How is it?
Furthermore, throughout his life, Shansheng made the direct realization of birth and death his sole concern for over twenty years. If he set his will upon the mountain forests, then—
I have been unable to realize the ultimate truth and equal the ancients. Yet, regarding the critical juncture of birth and death, I possess genuine self-confidence:

that all demonic adversaries and grievances are ultimately *bodhi*, adorning the fruit of Buddhahood. As for other calamities, gains and losses, right and wrong, praise and blame, I leave them to their own natural course;
what need is there to disturb my tranquility? Thus, since encountering this hardship, my mind has remained cool and serene at every thought-moment.
The earth has never for a moment shifted. Since last winter’s tenth month, when I stood at the head of my horse facing south in Jicheng, my very bones were chilled by the ice and snow;
yet by the twelfth month, I had reached Baixia, where I joyfully took leave of my elderly mother on the riverbank. On the eighth day, I hoisted sail and headed west.

Relying upon the fact that my worldly emotions have withered and my intellect exhausted, such illusory reflections have entirely vanished; like a bright mirror or still water, I am but briefly [at peace].
I shall find contentment within myself. These circumstances have been forged from the furnace of the Great Smith; fortunately, do not trouble yourself on my account.
I only wish that you may nurture the harmony of Heaven in tranquility, so that we may together reach ultimate joy.
Should Heaven grant me a return to life, I shall still plan to settle our unfinished karmic ties and spend our remaining years together.

Furthermore, since this humble monk first entered these difficulties, I have truly been on the brink of death nine times. Yet, when I look directly with the right eye, I do not perceive even a hair’s breadth of movement or stillness;
though we are separated by ten thousand miles, in reality, we are not more than a few steps apart. I am mindful of dwelling together with you.
The scholar has forgotten his physical form for half his life; he must surely have entered this Dharma-gate long ago.

How could he again conform to ordinary sentiments, racing after thoughts of coming and going, and with a fluttering heart experience the bitterness and sorrow of a dream? This present circumstance of mine is not merely a matter of transcending thirty years of wandering as a pilgrim;
it is sufficient to transcend the cultivation of kalpas. The heat and steam of Lei Yang are like a cauldron of fire.
The marshes where those who die of pestilence are like the Wuo-chiao abyss. This poor monk sits motionless in the Śītavana forest;

drinking the miasmic smoke is as if pouring down nectar, and enduring the emptiness of hunger is as if satiated by clarified butter. Were it not for my intellect being exhausted and my passions withered, how could I endure and receive this?
Recently, having obtained the Great General as a protector of the Dharma, I have already borrowed a portion of his quarters within the walls of the capital city.

In the intervals between bearing my spear, I remain seated in silent meditation with my door closed, suddenly severing all external conditions; I do nothing but peruse the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and investigate the Mind-Seal transmitted from the West.
Having resolved the kōan of "the realized and the unrealized," your mind of merit and goodness has already been transformed into a Banner of Radiance;

you truly do not disgrace the lineage of our master. As the ancients once said, "If the ancestors do not resolve [the matter], the calamity will reach their descendants. Fortunately for me, I have avoided falling into such words.
The Buddha said that giving the seven treasures as alms to fill the sands of the Ganges is not equal to upholding even four lines of this sutra. Know that you dwell [in this state].
The scholar does not forget the impoverished son; I venture to offer this to bring him some comfort. What else remains to be said?

Furthermore, as I sit amidst the miasmic fogs of the barbarian lands, I am glad that my karmic conditions for life are diminishing daily, while my karmic conditions for the Way are increasing daily. As for this physical frame—
The more suffering there is, the more joyful the mind becomes. In this regard, what place is not the grace of Your Majesty? And what is not the power of the Buddha?
This may be spoken of with those who share one’s inner knowledge; it is difficult to explain to worldly people. I wonder how your health is. Mañjuśrī once said:
"If you wish to know how to eliminate old age and illness, there is only the study of non-arising. How much more so when considering the fleeting light of a hundred-year life?
It is like snapping one's fingers—how long can it last? Layman, your years are many and your remaining days are few.
You have experienced every flavor of this turbid world until they are exhausted. As the proverb goes: "In the end, salt is as salty as ever, and vinegar is as sour as ever.
When all is said and done, what ultimate conclusion can there be? An ancient said: "The coming was quite fine; one only fears that the departing will not be as good as the coming."

This is no empty talk; lay brother, reflect deeply upon it. From your past achievements and undertakings, down to your plans for children and grandchildren—all these are merely the livelihoods of others.
What, then, is your own true livelihood? If you can experience a moment of intense awakening to this point—
Unconsciously, he let out a cry and naturally became urgent, straightening himself up to attend to the great matter of life and death beneath his own heels.

Had he not become urgent and straightened himself up, he would still not have achieved a sudden, forceful awakening; without such a sudden awakening, one is far from being a true lay practitioner (*upāsaka*).
These are the affairs of heroic men and women. Twenty years ago, I myself realized what this lay practitioner has said.

Having once resolved upon this, I have not begrudged my own body or life, wishing to roam with him. Although half of my accumulated merit has been for the sake of nourishing my own person, it has all merged into what I am today;
yet within this, that single point of sincere heart is much like Zhang Liang’s intention to serve the House of Han from beginning to end.
I have conversed and laughed with you, lay brother, for over ten years; it has been nothing but a realm of empty flourish—mere human sentiments and Buddhist rituals.
In truth, we have never yet shattered our livers and gallbladders [in a moment of profound intimacy].

Yet, a single span of heart between us has shone brightly upon one another, and I have never failed to know this innermost secret of yours, mountain recluse. We had hoped to reach our white-haired years together, returning as one...
Having understood this matter, how could it be that in a single day they have fallen apart and become estranged, even reaching such a state?

From this, one can observe the nature of birth and death. How much more so now, when we all dwell within the same heaven and earth; though separated by ten thousand *li*, viewed with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), we are still like neighbors.
We cannot even once receive their countenance or look upon their features with the joy of former days, let alone face the long journey of birth and death.
Once separated from you in the realm of the profound darkness, when shall we meet again? If this mountain recluse cannot return to life, it will be a permanent parting from you, Layman.
Were I to emerge once more, I do not know if it could ever be as it is today in this very life. To speak of this brings forth a great sorrow and bitterness.
Having received from you, Layman, the honor of being a true friend, there is nothing that would suffice as a repayment for your kindness.
Xin Shan-yue has never reached this place, nor would it be appropriate for him to respond to one who considers himself a true friend.

Although I, Zhou Li-zhai, have long privately admired your noble magnanimity, I had not yet had the opportunity for deep conversation. Yesterday, while carrying my alms bowl through the royal city, I was fortunate enough to meet you.
Beneath the Dragon Flower tree, I beheld his path of contemplation—pure and sincere—and my joy permeated the depths of my heart.

Indeed, when the ancients held a single promise more precious than a thousand pieces of gold, it was because the gentleman’s true worth lies in being known by one who understands him. From this day forth, this mountain monk shall devote his life to the mountains and seas;
he shall have no further longing for anything else. Relying on your Dharma-eye, which is perfectly clear and bright, how could I ever again reproach those who are deaf? (Private note.)
I contemplate the literary fortune of the East, which was inaugurated by our late Lord; might the fortune of the Dharma now indeed belong to this humble person?
That the mundane and the supramundane interact and serve one another is a marvel between heaven and earth. This is no idle talk;
it is precisely what I hope for you, my Lord, who honors yourself through the Way.

Answer: Zhou Ziyi, Shibo, Zhongshi, and others, the gathering and dispersing, the arising and ceasing, the formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness within the realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are naturally so;
why should they be a cause for grief? That which is truly lamentable is that, within the dark and obscure long night, one loses this torch of wisdom, leaving the sons of the Buddha without refuge.
Take refuge! The sacred sprouts of the seeds of wisdom are daily scorched and withered by the fierce flames of the five desires, such that they cannot bring forth the supreme fruit.
Only the six sense-objects obscure the sky of one's nature, and the weeds of craving overgrow the field of the mind.
Afflictions shroud the forest of merit, and greed and hatred assault the dwelling of Nirvana. They are felled by the axes of wine and lust, and let loose—

If left trampled by monkeys and horses, it will surely be seen to fall into ruin and eventually become a wasteland. I pray that you, in every thought and every moment of your heart, shall take this as a cause for personal sorrow;
thus, cultivate and till it, restraining it with the bridle of precepts and guarding it with vigilance.

In this way, may the flowers of awakening bloom in abundance to adorn the precious ground, and may all devas and humans alike harbor the seeds of wisdom, while even the wriggling insects and winged creatures together ascend the shore of enlightenment.

Since you have not only sustained your family’s reputation for all time, but have also sufficiently washed away the present-day shame of the Dharma-gate, what else could there be to hope for from one among your esteemed peers?
You have traveled ten thousand *li* on official duty; may you take care of your health.
It is merely like that of neighbors.
Together with the Grand Historian Jiao Congwu, I reflect upon this desolate age of the Final Dharma (*mofa*).
The Dragon Gods and Heavenly Beings have entrusted you, sir, to manifest in the body of a lay official (*zai guan*) to erect the great banner of the Dharma. To this end—
You are the eyes of the world for your contemporaries; this is no small matter. Having been separated for many years, we met yesterday beneath a tree, yet you appeared as if from another age.

Human life is so vast and fleeting; such are its dreams and illusions. Moreover, beholding your countenance and celestial form, it is truly as if you have not arisen from the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) while manifesting all manner of dignified deportment.
Were it not for the secret turning back of the light of your mind, how could you illuminate everything so perfectly?
How could it be grasped through sounds or forms? My joy is immeasurable. I, [Name], am ashamed of my dull faculties and inferior nature;
for twenty years I have toiled in the mountain forests, yet I remain like one sitting atop a pole, with no ground upon which to find release.

Nevertheless, the causal conditions for the Great Matter are truly not easy to attain. To receive even a single word of the Teaching at another time fills me with boundless gratitude. Returning home, I sit in a state of dazed stillness.
Yan: "Each mind shines alone; how could I dare betray my enlightened friend? At times, when the ocean is tranquil and the sky is clear, the Dharma-body suddenly manifests.
Is this not, within this state, the mutual resonance of the Way? While I idly don the wings of Laozi and Zhuangzi, I have thereby synthesized the great achievements of all schools.
Although many commentaries and sub-commentaries are steep and difficult, they are merely the 'Lao-Zhuang' of each individual, not the true Lao-Zhuang. Only you, sir, have entered into this."

This samādhi is profoundly deep; why has it not been thoroughly overturned? I have often discussed this. You, sir, were born in a world without a Buddha, and you may be considered akin to a pratyekabuddha.
However, if you remain within the confines of worldly convention (*zhuāng*), your attachment to dharmas has not yet been forgotten.

Once you have entered the play of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), your transformations will be manifold, dazzling the eyes of men. Unless one walks hand-in-hand with you, few will not be played with by such displays. If...
Upon examining the underlying essence, there is indeed a distinct gate of liberation. This elder, across ten thousand generations, may be said to have met you as if at dawn or dusk.
In the past, while traveling on pilgrimage, I once had these two elders as companions.
I observed their conduct from time to time and found it quite resonant with my own mind, though it was difficult to describe in words. There were several instances in the Inner Chapters...
The character *diǎnduō* has not yet been transcribed; I shall request its correct interpretation on a later occasion.

This preface for reading the *Tongzhì of Caoxi* with Vice Minister Yang Fusu consists of every word flowing forth from the great compassionate true mind—unlike what is seen and heard by ordinary people.
There was none who did not feel great joy; how much more so those a thousand years hence—how many people from within their dreams will this awaken?
Only our Patriarch Lu, dwelling in the Great Samādhi, must surely manifest a joyful countenance, join his palms, and offer praise.

Huang Sheng has arrived and presented further words of the Dharma, yet he says there are still points that remain unsettled for him. However, as for the way he extols this mountain recluse, it seems already sufficient.
This is already excessive. Only Master Haimen is one who has entered the chamber of Caoxi; I venture to seek a single word from him to further augment its brilliance.
[The reply is recorded by the Palace Counselor.]
I have received your exposition on cause and effect; it is perfectly clear and leaves me without doubt. It is without the slightest error and is truly what is meant by "shadow and echo.
However, regarding the previous discussion on the knowledge of evil persons, this principle is most profound and difficult to clarify, yet it is also easily believed to be an absolute certainty.

The mind of the Sage is profoundly clear and luminous; looking back to the beginningless past and forward to the endless future, it is like a great round mirror that reflects throughout the ten directions.
All realms, whether subtle or coarse, appear as distinct reflections without exception.
Even matters spanning eighty thousand kalpas would not be considered extraordinary to it, let alone those of several hundreds of thousands of years. As for what is called "good" and "evil" people...
When one performs deeds of good or evil, this principle of direct cause and effect is manifest and easy to believe.
Yet, even if a wicked person has not yet been born after hundreds or thousands of years, that person’s evil karma has already been fully formed over many previous lifetimes;
the retribution for their grievances has already been clearly determined in prior existences. It is simply that the karmic causes have not yet ripened and the adverse conditions have not yet arrived.

Although that person wanders in the cycle of samsara amidst the inversions of the worlds of the ten directions, remaining unaware of it, the Sage has long since perceived them within the Treasury of Great Radiance;
and when the conditions of evil ripen, they encounter their karmic enemies.

The fruition of evil is accomplished; this is the end of the evil fruit, just as it was the beginning of the evil cause. Without waiting for the arising of a thought or a movement of the mind, one naturally understands it.
This is what is meant by: "Observing that distant past, it is as if it were today. This is the true and eternal mind of the sage.
Furthermore, cause and effect are without discrepancy, not obscured by even a hair's breadth. As it is said: "Even if it be hundreds of thousands of kalpas..."
"Actions performed do not perish. When causes and conditions meet, one must personally experience the retribution. This is an inevitable principle.
Can you, Illustrious Sir, believe this with true conviction? Viewed from this perspective, those who act unvirtuously are not predetermined by Heaven;
rather, they have created their own [fate] through their own deeds."

It has been two years since I parted from you, Officer Yin. I have heard that you have recently joined the military campaign and are currently still at Li. The sweltering heat of summer has now passed;
I trust your noble body remains free from ailment. These people are not clever rats; they are all subjects of Heaven. To slaughter them beyond measure—this is excessive.
I fear this may harm the harmony of our relations. I am certain that you would never consider this an act of great merit. Yesterday, Liu Qinghai, the Commander of the Garrison, departed;
I have already instructed him repeatedly on this matter. By no means should killing be regarded as a feat of achievement. When we meet, we shall surely find full accord.
I previously saw your humble composition titled "Gazing at the Sea of Pearls," which speaks of the Li people as being the subjects of the Great Antiquity. I have inscribed it upon the head of my fan.
In response to your letter,
which you, the Honorable Zheng,
recently deigned to send, I see that you have devoted your heart to this Way. You further mention that, within your daily life, wholesome thoughts manifest before you.

The nature of human beings is inherently good from the very beginning. However, because it is defiled by the habitual tendencies of sensory dust, its luminous intelligence is obscured within our daily lives;
we employ only emotional habits rather than the true essence of our nature. This is why ordinary people live their daily lives without knowing [this truth].

If you understand this, then sages and worthies can be expected at any moment. When wholesome thoughts arise in daily life and you remain undeluded, that is precisely when your original face manifests.

If these thoughts manifest constantly and you maintain awareness in every moment, until your awakening reaches the ground of pure goodness, then the true nature will spontaneously return and the luminous essence of the fundamental body will naturally be revealed.
In response to Imperial Censor Zou Nangao:

Previously, I, this rustic of the mountains and fields, was already in a state of total seclusion. Lately, moreover, illusory illnesses have persisted one after another; I have been recuperating in deep retirement, and my conditions for contact have become even more severed.
Truly, it is by the grace of Heaven that I have become a man of leisure. Looking back upon the mundane world, its bustling toil and labor—how few are those who can attain the state of non-action?
I imagine that those who understand me must surely clap their hands in approval from time to time.

Relying on this Dharma-protector, I am able to dwell in peaceful meditation within the *Laṅkā-samādhi*; my entry therein grows ever deeper. Recently, Minister Wang Guanglu and Grand Councilor Ding [visited].

I went to the Governor’s residence in Duanzhou according to our appointment. I received a letter stating that there were many rumors circulating within the governor's administration, causing great harm to this mountain recluse.
The two gentlemen exerted themselves in my defense, to such an extent that their hair stood on end and their eyes nearly burst from indignation. What indeed does this mean?

By this, one knows that the defiled land of Sahā, with its earth, stones, and mountains, cannot be compared to the pure lands—which are as level as the palm of a hand—even in terms of their basic nature.
As for those followers who have come from the north, since they have no door through which to beg for alms, I now dismiss them all to return home.
I, a solitary mountain recluse, find this place of temporary lodging particularly refreshing. The withered trees and cold cliffs are no different from those of old;

it is here that one may dispel the stifling heat and eliminate the miasmic toxins. At a time when state affairs are fraught with difficulty and the common people look toward you for guidance, may you, O Greatly Compassionate One, serve as their bridge and ferry.
I pray that you will exert yourself and take nourishment, cherishing yourself for the sake of the nation. For...
I have always cherished the Way.
Furthermore,

I have repeatedly received your handwritten letters, which honor me with your earnest and compassionate concern, reaching every detail with such thoroughness that it could not be anything other than the great compassion of our shared essence.

How could one who cherishes worldly things be so earnest and persistent? Though I dwell in these mountain wilds amidst such hardships, I have fortunately been able to associate with those who possess true knowledge within the dust of the world;
thus, I maintain myself with vigilance, and the Dharma-gate I have entered is not shallow. Yet, for years, I have been immersed in the bitterness and emptiness of solitude.

He did not diminish his seclusion in deep mountains and remote valleys, severing all external ties and never setting foot among the laity. Among those who knew him in the city, there was only Wang Xun, the Vice Minister;
even over the course of years, he passed by his gate no more than three times. His only frequent visitor was the Right Military Commissioner, with whom he occasionally exchanged visits.
Truly, we are as close as flesh and bone to one another across the ends of the earth; I have not forgotten you even for a single meal.

It is not only that our paths and principles mutually benefit one another, but even the provisions I supply involve the reduction of my own allotted rations. Our lives are thus dependent upon one another; this particular circumstance is by no means trivial.

This gentleman’s gallantry and sincerity illuminate others like the mirror of Qin; meeting things and responding to circumstances, he penetrates the depths of the five viscera. In his capacity as a vehicle for the Way, he is most highly praised.
Those of superior faculties and sharp instruments have been forged by the celestial virtue of this occasion; their progress is exceedingly great and not like that of ordinary people.
In the future, they will adorn the Buddha-lands and bring sentient beings to maturity in an inconceivable manner. When that time comes, you should imagine that their joy will be immeasurable.
Furthermore, since the year of Gengzi, the world has undergone a single transformation; daily we witness the treacherous and perverse, and the waves of the sea of suffering appear boundless.
This humble monk has drifted with the winds, finding no peace or rest. Only now do I realize that the ancients spoke of "acting amidst the dust."
Master, this is no small matter. Liberation in accordance with conditions is truly not easily attained.

Every time I recall your earnest instructions during our parting, and upon receiving your recent letter, I have repeatedly emphasized this point with great urgency. As the proverb goes: "If you wish to know the path down the mountain, ask those who come and go.
Were it not for your having deeply entered the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi), how could you have penetrated to such a depth?
Such is the nature of the Dharma. I have often heard it said that the fierce flames of affliction (*kleśa*) are precisely the crucible of the sages and worthies;
various habits of attachment cannot be melted away without this. Were it not for Your Holiness’s sacred grace, how could I have reached such a state?
As time passes, I see ever more clearly that this great kindness is difficult to repay. Within this, I transform worldly toil into Buddhist practice, and thus become a true Sixth Patriarch.
Caoxi has performed immeasurable meritorious deeds; these surely arise from a heart of earnest and sincere suffering.
Compared to those of former days who relied upon the Aśoka tree and partook of the communal meal, this is indeed as different as heaven and earth.
The source of the ancestral Way at Caoxi was once choked with filth and long served as a den of demons; now it has been swept clean. Yet there remains an unfinished public case—how regrettable!
My strength here is exhausted, and I was just about to dispatch someone to convey my most respectful greetings. Yet, you have honored me by sending this messenger;

could this not be an act of compassionate reception from the Patriarch himself? Out of respect for these circumstances, I shall describe the general outline of them, so that they may be held and brought into the illumination of wisdom.
If one reflects that we now dwell in the Dharma-ending age and this Way has become desolate, I hope you will sound the drum of thunder to universally announce to all who have the karmic affinity:
"Awaken to this as but a dream and an illusion. How does this sound?
Furthermore, human emotions such as sorrow and anxiety are all fundamentally the essence [of reality].

Were it not for grasping the seal of ultimate truth, how could one transform afflictions into bodhi, and transform birth-and-death into nirvana? That you, Layman, have lived in this manner for years is sufficient proof.
There is truly much that has been transformed here. Were it not for this, what else could dispel [the delusions]?

Those who have studied the Way since ancient times have all passed through the gateway of birth and death with nonchalance; this was not fully understood by our predecessors. In recent years, however, there have been those such as Luo Jinxi.
As for that person, though this poor monk’s body resides in a malarial region, my mind dwells with you; there is no moment when we do not move together in harmony.
For this reason, the various samādhis of the Layman are perfectly clear to me, with nothing hidden. Since the passing of Huineng of Caoxi in Lingnan...

The great sound of Dadian has ceased, and the gate of Jiangmen has not been raised again. Now that we have found the Elder Yang Fu, he has raised the banner of the Nature School (Xingzong) like a great tree.
It is my good fortune to sit upon this very ground; my joy and praise are inexhaustible. May the various students gradually break through their worldly habits and attachments.
This, too, is the foundation for their transformation and edification. Yesterday, I again wrote a preface for Old Man [Lao]’s *Record of Caoxi*;

it was truly with every bit of my sincere heart—truly what one might call "a tongue long enough to drag upon the ground. I present this for your perusal; I do so only because of the joy it brings to these many ignorant ones.
Since parting from you at Yue-shi [馬*凡], I have twice received your letters.
I learned that there was a conflict in the region of Zou and Lu. Alas! When the direct Way is no longer tolerated at court, it is further cast aside by one's own village.
The state of the world can be known from this. I heard that you sought refuge in the capital city; yet even this was not...
I have long been aware of this. I have heard that Bodhisattvas subdue sentient beings by entering deeply into the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*);

fundamentally, these are not substantial dharmas. You, sir, have long entered this Dharma-gate; I hope you will not harbor deep resentment. There will surely be those who mediate, and it may be resolved with a single laugh.
I, the mountain recluse, have chosen seclusion on Mount Kuang, which is most suitable for me. As for what you call "protecting the Dharma," there are those who shoulder this burden.

My heart! The gate of giving has not yet been opened; I have not yet seen you exerting yourself. If only Mañjuśrī would extend his right hand from afar, then the gates of the multi-storied pavilion could suddenly be seen opening. How can you, sir, remain indifferent to this?
Furthermore, your recent visit to the prison of the Minister of Works was no less significant than when Ānanda questioned Devadatta regarding the Iron Ring Mountains.

At that time, you poured *sarpis* (clarified butter) into my mouth and sprinkled *amṛta* (ambrosia) upon my heart; thus, you have performed a marvelous feat for the sake of both worlds. I count this on my fingers as a momentous event.
Huan: How could I have expected to see you again? Just now, while sitting here, I beheld the blazing flames of a vajra flickering before my eyes.
Having been parted for some time, I could ultimately not restrain my impatience and have come forward to disclose this.

I do not know whether, within the ocean of nirvana, bubbles are still repeatedly arising and perishing. This humble monk has fled into the miasmic lands; I rely solely on the spiritual power of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to sustain me.
I take the dust of chariot wheels as my flowered seat and the horsewhip as my fly-whisk.
At times, I travel toward the realm of rākṣasa demons to discourse on the teaching of non-arising, causing countless skulls to open their eyes and their light to shatter the darkness.
Truly, I do not know whether this is driven by the power of karma or brought about by the power of my vows. Those who truly understand me will surely let out a single spit upon hearing this.
[The Master] said:
"Together with the Minister of Personnel Yu De-yuan and the Layman Yao-wang,
I sit upon the Lion Throne of Mount Tianmu, barking at the white ox in the open field, and sport in the West."

Between the three *zhú* of Lake [Huang], there is abundance of water and abundance of grass; how much more so for one who takes Maitreya as teacher and Asaṅga as younger brother, who hears the precepts of nature and beholds the light of the flowers!
As for the bliss of their nirvāṇa, even the mark of the broad and long tongue could not proclaim even a ten-thousandth part of it.
As for a person like this poor monk, he seeks empty fruits with empty flowers; he holds onto a thicket of transgressions and enters the realm of sin.
Although there is no deficiency in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), those who harbor deluded thoughts are not without inverted views.

As for a householder viewing me with the Dharma-eye, how much could it possibly reach? Jueyin has arrived, bringing a letter of profound words exceeding a foot in length; I am deeply grateful for the utmost kindness of your compassionate concern.
Beholding your sincere devotion to the protection of the Dharma truly makes the hairs on my body stand on end with a sense of poignant sorrow. Alas for this age of the Final Dharma!
The Buddha-nature within us disciples is like a divine jewel in a latrine: not only is its radiance concealed, but its foul stench even oppresses those nearby.
How could it be anything less than a night-blooming flower or the child of a courtesan?

I have received several volumes of your successive letters from the Honorable Official Fan Youxuan, through which I am fully informed of your well-being. Since Mr. Ke arrived, I have further learned that you are in good health, peaceful, and at ease.
This internal state of samādhi is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, one knows it for oneself. It has been a year since Mr. Ke departed, yet he is also able to—

Your progress has been such that it is evident that all anxieties, calamities, and hardships are merely aids to the path. That you have obtained this excellent friend in this malarial region is surely a divine providence.
Regarding the causes and conditions for this new commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, they all arise from the manifestation of merit within the mind of non-characteristics (*animitta*).
Now, relying upon your empowerment, as my work is nearing completion, I first offer one volume to seek correction. I trust you will do so in the stillness of your retreat.
I have cast my gaze upon this work; it is not without its merits, yet I beg for your guidance with the golden probe, that it may become once more a great gift of Dharma.
I have heard that the various disciples under your guidance are progressing daily. I recall that the Tathāgata did not abandon a single sentient being, making great compassion his foremost principle.

Now, as you occupy the seat of authority in this malarial region—a land of your compassionate vows—I hope you will never grow weary of acting as a bridge and ferry for them; this would be a blessing for the Way.
Together with the licentiate Xing Meiyang, you have served as a patron for the various ancestral temples of Mount Kuang in Jiangzhou. Here, the seeds of Prajñā are particularly abundant;
though many have scorched them, only you have managed to sprout shoots and grow trunks, blossoming with flowers and bearing exquisite fruit that stands out among your predecessors.
This is not merely due to the depth of his vow-power; nor could the roots of the mountain be so firmly established without him.
As Master Da traveled back and forth between Chéngyún and Wǔlǎo, it was not through your companionship that the mountain spirits were made to flourish.
I have long admired you, Master, yet I regret that there has been no opportunity for us to clasp hands.

Accompanied by my two friends, Qu Dongguan and Zhongfuwenqing, I entered the capital. Master Miao has already arrived; there, you will surely find joy in the Dharma and enjoy its depths, rather than feeling desolate.
Reflecting on this age of the Final Dharma, where no one upholds the Two Truths, it is truly said that you alone manifest in the body of a lay official to preside over and lead this Way.

The gift of Dharma is inexhaustible. I pray that through your boundless great compassion, you may deliver those yet to be delivered, enabling them to gain benefit from seeing and hearing [the teaching], so that they may plant the seeds of wisdom in this life and realize Bodhi in future lives.
At that time, looking back at past causes, it need not necessarily have begun other than from this very day.
As for the gentlemen previously mentioned, all were those whose faith was sincere and earnest; I pray that you, sir, will likewise act at this time.
By means of the water of the Dharma, you irrigate the sacred sprouts; thus, you shall not fail the seeds sown long ago.

This requires entering his person through the *māyājāla-samādhi* (Illusory Net Samādhi) and skillfully transforming [him] with all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*). Is this not your task, who else could it be?

I am deeply aware that my writing is superficial and that I have presumptuously donned the *kāṣāya*. Nevertheless, I dare not harbor arrogance; it is a great fortune that you have condescended to take me into your heart.
I understand. Our true aspiration is non-dual; how can I express my joy and consolation? Upon returning, all thoughts have been reduced to ashes, and my single mind has no further reliance.
As the sun sinks into withered stillness, these few words at our parting are truly for my own sake.

At this time, when the house of fire is ablaze and the five heats are fiercely burning, I pray that you will restrain yourself for the sake of the Way and never grow weary of ferrying others across. This is my highest hope.
Furthermore, having been graced by your compassionate gaze, you have provided me with the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (The Compendium of the Five Lamps), which is indeed the bestowal of samādhi upon me.

I, this mountain monk, constantly study and inquire into it, yet I am deeply ashamed that my faculties are dull and inferior, preventing me from personally encountering the ancients; nevertheless, I have gained a rough understanding of it.
I have eradicated [delusions] and gained insight into the limits of phenomena; I only regret that I did not let out a roar of power upon the ground, which would have brought lifelong joy.
From this point forward, I shall take up the pivot of the koan. Perhaps one day there will be someone who understands my realization; how could I dare forget the ground from which it arose?

I consider you, Master, to be one who presses his finger upon the dust of the mundane world until the Ocean-Seal Samādhi radiates its light; wherever he encounters things, he raises them up as nothing other than Buddha-work.

Yet I do not know whether among those who have newly resolved their minds, there are any capable of undertaking this great matter. I pray that you will not forsake your original vow, but tame beings according to their needs, so that they may plant the seeds of the Vajra.
Whenever I contemplate the lingering grace of Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranādin and the remaining traces of Jñānavijaya, [I am moved by this thought].
To have encountered this assembly on Vulture Peak by chance—had the intent not been of such a kind, who would have been a worthy recipient for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world?
Thus, those of the future looking upon the present are just as we of the present look upon the past. What do you, in your venerable compassion, think of this?
I have often come to the Many-Jeweled Stupa to inquire after the World-Honored One: "Are there not many sentient beings here who are arrogant and jealous? This inquiry alone should suffice.
Below. I pray that you will, from time to time, protect and cherish me for the sake of the Way.
Furthermore, since our parting at the Dragon Flower Tree until the present day, looking back upon this world, it truly seems like a dream. I long to meet you again and exchange words of Dharma-seal.
