As for the mind, how could it ever be recovered as it was at the first assembly? Only you, Layman, have seen your vow to benefit sentient beings expand daily, while your entry into the gateway of principle has grown ever deeper.
With both merit and wisdom fully realized, your practice of benefiting both self and others has advanced directly into the adamantine ground of the mind.
As for me, I have been tossed about by the winds of karma until I have reached this state; yet, fortunately, through the samādhi of illusion, I have been uprooted [from delusion].
This pit of the obstacles to principle; now, by the spiritual power of the Buddhas, a bridge has been provided for me. I imagine that you, Layman, who know me, must feel great joy at this.
In the winter of the Bingshen year, when I was released from confinement and set my staff toward the south, I parted from Layman Tianchi at the capital gate.
I had previously intended to take the road through Huanggang to enter the chamber of Vimalakīrti, but unexpectedly, at the head of the path—

Circumstances having changed, I have finally passed through Nankang and entered the miasmic regions. Relying on the mantle of your compassion, I am able, with a heart as cool as ice and snow, to endure the vapors of the pestilential mists.
By the end of three years, I shall likely be spared from the fluctuations of the four elements. I recall once discussing the essence of the Three Teachings with you,居士 (layman), at night;
using the doctrine of Consciousness-Only to verify the principles of the other two schools, we were honored by the mutual resonance of our mind-seals.
At this time, returning to the seashore, I happened to pen these thoughts into a book titled *An Examination of the Influence and Reflections of Laozi and Zhuangzi*.

Now, for the first time, I have carved them into woodblocks. Minister Yang has praised this as a definitive judgment for all ages. As for the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, I have often read it with deep emotion yet could not master a single phrase;

My friend, believe that in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is fundamentally no distinction between self and other. I have often said that the difference between the mundane and the supramundane lies merely in the distinction between birth and non-birth.
Nevertheless, the various illusory karmas manifesting in daily life and all those who undergo transmigration are all causes of birth and death.
If one is not turned by external influences, does not forget the objective realm, and possesses forbearance, this is called "patience toward beings" (*sattvākṣānti*).

When one perceives neither that which is to be endured nor the one who endures, it is "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*). If patience reaches the state of non-arising, then there is no non-forbearance.

When mind and objects are thus in suchness (*tathatā*), they are also in cessation (*nirvāṇa*). Furthermore, what is termed "the work of Māra" does not occur solely through hostile adversaries; it applies to all ordinary [phenomena] as well.
Whenever a person gives rise to thoughts that do not accord with liberation, that harms the Dharma-body, or that oppresses the true nature, they belong to the faction of Māra.
When we people are determined to practice *gongfu* in order to transcend birth and death, we cannot endure such things;
otherwise, how could we be called powerful great beings? We have been born and dwell in this Sahā world; if we do not break through at this very place, there will be no [liberation].

That which can be refuted must certainly be addressed directly through the power of great patience and the power of great diligence, taking the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) as the standard, regardless of whether one’s spiritual conditions are favorable, whether prior determination has been made or not, or whether one’s efforts are equal or unequal. Do you not believe this to be so?
It is difficult to meet face-to-face; thus, I have unconsciously let my words flow out to this point.

Furthermore, in the past, you received the illumination of the Flying Light (Fei Guang) which descended upon Haiyin. This was a truly peerless and auspicious condition, suddenly forming the seed of the Vajra, which shall never be worn away throughout eternal kalpas.
It will ultimately penetrate to the very marrow of your bones; this is the great feat of a true Mahāsattva, not merely that of a lay devotee.
A man of such power, bearing the burden upon one shoulder—whom would dare look him straight in the eye? Since our parting, the circumstances have been beyond my full knowledge;
as for your well-being, I am certain you have long since entered the Samādhi of Illusion, wherein movement and stillness are non-dual.

This humble monk was recently toyed with by a mountain spirit, and further compounded by the karmic obstacles of past lives, resulting in this severe reprimand. Although this has brought a stain upon the Dharma...
Furthermore, it is fortunate that by the power of the superior path, what was called "being burned by a great fire" refers to this land being secure; it is no false speech.
Ancient sages often took hardships as superior conditions for aiding the path, and the very point where they gained strength lies precisely here.
Upon hearing this, the layman thought, "Is this a 'poison-coated drum'?

Now that I have already borne my spear for half a year, it coincides with a season of great misfortune, where pestilence breaks out in succession and both people and things are withered and ruined—truly a matter of deep pity.
For this reason, my resolve for the bodhicitta has become even more exalted. Yet this illusory and empty body remains within the burning house. [The Dharma of Vaisālī...]
I understand. To engage in dialogue on non-duality—when will that day truly arrive?
It is only out of compassion for our shared essence that this withered and decayed dhūta-monk occasionally allows delusive thoughts to briefly arise.
I have been traveling with the venerable scholar Feng Qinan for nearly twenty years. It is as if we are walking amidst moonlight upon the water;
all circumstances, whether adverse or favorable, are but shadows within that light. That while the sons enter together, their experiences and enjoyments differ, is precisely like this.

Heavenly beings and humans share a single vessel for receiving food, yet what they receive differs in refinement and coarseness; this is because their Buddha-nature depends upon the conditions of their respective seeds.
That an old man like me should encounter your sons is a rare occurrence, like a timely rain. Each seed will then sprout and produce its own fruit, depending entirely on the person.
Now that I am departing from Yue, it is as if the time has not yet come; I hope you will [cherish this opportunity].
That you have provided irrigation for it so that it does not wither and dry up—this circumstance is truly no small matter.
Those of the Two Vehicles merely fear that sentient beings are difficult to deliver, and thus they sever their connection to Bodhi. Do you, however, hold sentient beings in your eyes?
Fundamentally, this matter depends on one’s own consent; where there is consent, that is the point of entry. The ancients...
To sacrifice one’s body and life is simply a matter of a single act of affirmation. I only wish that you, sir, would affirm it for the sake of others;

then there will be no one who does not affirm it. Just reflect on how this present life has been missed: once the human form is lost, it is difficult to recover for ten thousand kalpas. Thus, there is no room for non-affirmation.
This old man knows in his heart that the conditions for the Dharma are difficult to encounter; this current endeavor is surely due to the narrow habits cultivated in mountain forests.

I have sent this message. Now that my frantic mind has suddenly ceased its turmoil, I contemplate the spiritual power of Mount Nanyue, which was once graced by the extraction [of the Dharma] by the various Patriarchs;
today, that vitality is exhausted, making it difficult to sustain the life-force there. I am currently staying in Hudu (Hudong), much like when Master Sheng resided at Tiger Hill.
My disciple Shansun has returned from the north and will soon join Chun Chan in entering Guangdong; you may learn more about this in detail. I know that you are prone to illness, and thus—

Your Reverence is well-versed in the Dharma-gates; I pray that there will be no shortage of lion-thrones within your chamber, so that all who come may together enter the Samādhi of Illness as an Illusion.
Thus, this illness shall become a banner of diligence.
When the old man Longyuan Wen first entered Guangdong, you were the very first to enter the Dharma-gate and became the elder among the lay devotees.
For twenty years since we have traveled together, we have never been apart from the realm of sound and form. Now that the old man departs from Guangdong, I rely entirely upon you.
You are the leader of the Dharma-gate. May you, sir, protect the Dharma with a mind as steadfast as a vajra-banner, holding the entrustment of the teachings close to your heart.
Through various skillful means, guide and gather those with whom you have a karmic affinity, ensuring that the life-force of wisdom remains unbroken; this shall be your primary aim.
The subtlety lies in the finger that points beyond words, for you naturally possess nostrils that reach toward the heavens—how could you be reduced to a mere single hair of an old man?
"Did you pierce through the eyebrows? Formerly, the World-Honored One did not permit Ānanda to listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind;
the Gate of the Patriarchs does not permit the turning of correct [truth] through words and speech. This was intended merely to manifest the essential function of the person of the present moment.
Why then use real dharmas to bind people? I am moved by your earnestness for the Dharma and your diligent, sincere efforts; how could I bear to remain indifferent? I only wish that this Way..."
If it does not fall, then a thousand years will be as a single day; how, then, could there be any coming or going?
The numinous power of Mount Nanyue has already been exhausted, and all the sites of practice have been abandoned to overgrown brambles—this is truly heartrending.
Even if the various elders were to rise again, it would not be easy to restore them. Alas! The Way and the times—how can one force them to coincide?
Together with Yuan Wenqi,
I recall my late father’s interactions with his sons over the past eighteen years; it was much like a magician performing various illusions at a crossroads—
though there were all manner of appearances, whether beautiful or ugly, joyful or sorrowful, they all ultimately resolve into one.
This illusory person—observing it today—is yet another dream-event. When the old man first set out, he falsely imagined Mount Nanyue to be a place of great rest.
Upon arriving, however, he realized that the mountains were not suited for an old man; all manner of hardships became burdens to his body and mind.
Furthermore, being decrepit and lacking the equipment necessary for traveling or excursions, he could do nothing but let go according to circumstances and make the best of the situation.
To the east of the lake, I have fortunately received the assistance of one or two patrons to help establish my retirement home. Last winter, I cleared away the brush and constructed a thatched hut;

by the final days of the year, I had already settled into a period of meditative seclusion (*an-ga-ju*). Thereupon, my wild mind was suddenly stilled. That which I had aspired to throughout my life was, in a single moment, attained.
The hardships and toil I endured for twenty years have been transformed into a realm of supreme, wondrous bliss. Truly it is so!
Purity and defilement follow the mind; suffering and joy reside within oneself. In every place, there is nothing that is not the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the serene light.
Most joyful of all is that I have already received the vast and boundless grace of the Sage, which has restored my original face; henceforth, I shall have no further longings for anything else.
As for the reception of guests at the mountain gate, I rely upon Master Zhan to shoulder this burden. From now on, I shall close my door, eat my fill, and sleep soundly.
All paths of dhyāna and the Buddha-dharma have been set high upon the shelves. Today, I am but a person of no affairs amidst heaven and earth;
this single day’s peace is far superior to a lifetime of bustling toil. Sons, upon hearing this, would you not feel great joy for me?
While residing together with Master Xiu, he constantly reminded me of this matter, lamenting that he could not [share it] with me.
All sons share in this. The ancients said that while the paths each take may differ, the way they support their parents is the same.

If all sons are indeed able to apply this daily in every situation, taking the happiness of their elders as their own happiness, then whatever the elders possess shall belong to the sons as well, and whatever the elders lack shall likewise be lacking for the sons. This is what is meant by "one body, one mind."
Wisdom, the power of insight, and fearlessness are likewise so. How could these words have been spoken by the "Yellow-Faced Old Man" himself?
Do not say that the old man’s affairs today are severed from those of his sons;

rather, within the very place where daily delusions intersect and afflictions are firmly knotted, this is precisely the moment the old man manifests before you. If you miss him face-to-face, you will be separated by distant mountains.
This is the Chu River. This year marks precisely the time when the vow-power (*praṇidhāna*) of all these sons has reached maturity.

I recall that within the Mañjuśrī Cave, among the ten thousand members of the retinue, dozens of seats were often empty; moreover, beneath each person’s feet was a cloud—how could they have been willing to let others ride upon them?
It is only those who grow weary of serving as ferrymen and bridges [for others] who depart. For the sake of the great assembly, the Elder Qinan should take their place.
[The Master] struck the gavel and said:
"In response to you, the Grand Historian of Li Xiangzhou:
Since I entered the Gate of Emptiness, I have harbored the aspiration for the Ultimate Vehicle. At nineteen, I donned the black robes and consequently abandoned my brush and inkstone."
He devoted himself to investigating the matter within his own person for ten years, yet he had not attained awakening.

He then withdrew into the ice and snow of Mount Wutai, where he subjected his body and mind to rigorous austerity—even in places where not a single character was known. Suddenly, the four elements fell away and he became independent of them;
looking back upon the mountains, rivers, and world of former times, he saw them all as matters of a dream. From this, he attained great bliss. (1)

All things should be perceived as conditions, like reflections in a mirror, entirely free from obstruction. For eight years I practiced in this manner; previously, I had not yet fully mastered the various sutras.
However, upon contemplating the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I realized that its essence lies in the threefold contemplation within a single mind. Previously, I had been hindered by literal texts;

now, I have clarified my mind and observed with precision, making contemplation of the principle (*li*) the primary focus. Once the contemplation of the principle is thoroughly mastered, the remaining textual details can be understood.

[Omitted]. He succeeded to the lineage in Donghai and applied his mind with hidden diligence until he suddenly attained realization. He then composed this book directly, believing it would certainly be trustworthy;

yet, there were not a few who harbored doubts within the Dharma-gate. Having long admired his profound understanding, they specifically requested that he verify and correct [their views], for there were matters they wished to resolve face-to-face.

At that time, however, he was suffering as demonic illness manifested its influence. If the autumn becomes clear and cool, he intends to close his door for ten days [in retreat] and [discuss these matters].
On this day, I have finally resolved upon my lifelong vow. May this Way, though sparse, not remain solitary within heaven and earth. At dawn, I shall trace back the current;
looking back, there is only a lingering sense of reverence and reliance.
I address this to you, Governor Gao Yingtai.
Recent events have been heart-stirring. Your noble spirit remains undaunted; having read your esteemed draft, I am fully informed of your recent circumstances.

Yet, while it is indeed the fundamental duty of a ministerial subject to manifest loyalty for the sake of the state, such action at this particular juncture seems to contravene the admonition regarding when to serve or retire. Moreover, at this time...
To face the affairs of advanced old age while dwelling in a place of fixed poverty—this is precisely a time when even a man of great strength would lose color;

how could it not be a great burden to one’s body and mind? Regarding the weighing of such heavy and light matters, the wise Du must surely have a single principle by which to deliberate and settle them.

I, this mountain recluse, am nearly eighty years of age; my decline and illness increase day by day. Fortunately, I have hidden my traces in these empty mountains, merely prolonging my life for a single breath, awaiting death.
Thus it is. My withered and decayed heart has no one to whom I may entrust the Way.

If you, sir, could lower your mind to the realm of stillness and enjoy the joy of pure cultivation, thereby creating a single karmic connection toward transcendence, it would be a most extraordinary thing. As the ancients said:
"The infinite sorrows and regrets of a lifetime—where else can they be dispelled but through the Empty Gate? This is truly what my heart hopes for.

In response, within the span of a brief conversation, I occupied a plot of land east of the lake and constructed a thatched hut in the shade of a flowing stream. My work has fortunately reached completion;

on the eighteenth day of this month, I entered the room and lay down to rest, whereupon my dreams and thoughts suddenly became empty. This is sufficient to delight me in my old age, and I rejoice that it has turned out as you wished.
Those below who follow the Way communicate with one another through their spirits; it can truly be said that they are not left desolate.
When the practitioner came, he spoke of the words from your letter, which seem to involve applying effort upon the level of cognitive views (*jñāna-darśana*).

This reflects the depth of your sincere faith and inclination. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "To establish cognition within cognition is the very root of ignorance. This refers to the gateway of all calamities.
It is further said: "To know seeing as non-seeing is itself nirvana; this is called the gateway to all wonders.
Herein, what is termed "knowing and seeing" is by no means an ordinary state of mind, nor is it within the realm of conceptual thought or intellectual calculation.

It is entirely produced from the actual practice of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), emerging from the point of genuine inquiry and true awakening. It is absolutely not a matter of verbal sophistry; one must treat it as the Buddha-dharma itself. Your faith...
Gu Du has not yet entered deeply into the Dharma, yet he already utters various words of "knowledge and views" (jñāna-darśana); these all constitute frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Regarding his standing as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), he does not treat the Buddha-Dharma with favoritism, nor does he grant approval by means of the "winter melon seal.
What the Elder said—that the knowledge and views of sentient beings are themselves the knowledge and views of the Buddha—was merely a deduction from the fundamental source.

This was merely said from the perspective of those who are deluded; it is not that the deluded, false conceptualizations and views of the ignorant should be taken as the knowledge and vision of a Buddha.
If one were to take false conceptualization as the knowledge and vision of a Buddha, then all sentient beings in this great earth would already be Buddhas—what need would there be for cultivation?
If one were to take ordinary, mundane conceptualizations and emotional anxieties as the realm of enjoyment, then... [one would be lost].
If one interprets it thus—that all those in the world who have not yet eliminated lust and killing, and who are greedy, wrathful, and negligent, are all Buddhas—this is the teaching of Māra.
How could one take such a perverse view to be right awakening? Whatever various words you may bring forth, none of them constitute a place of true practice.
You need only completely eradicate all your former knowledge and views, leaving not even a hair’s breadth behind.
Only when one perceives even a slight trace of influence within the state where not a single thought-moment exists can one speak of the matter therein.
If you take clever, sharp intellectual views to be the correct understanding, it is just like mistaking donkey dung for a bright pearl.
If such views are maintained under the guidance of a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), then that spiritual friend would likewise become a type of demonic being. Old [Master].
My friend, you have conceived a great attachment to dharmas; thus, you do not begrudge your eyebrows to repay my intention.
You should examine this for yourself: what actual reality is there within your views and knowledge? You must not fall into this arena of frivolous conceptual proliferation.
Consider this to be the true seed for entering the Way; reflect upon it deeply and with earnestness.
Furthermore, regarding the upward path, those who draw near to it are rare; were one not a truly extraordinary man, one could never wield the single blade alone.
Enter directly. This matter is by no means something that can be grasped through worldly cleverness or wit; nor is it the "zhi-huo-ye" (pedantic scholasticism) of conventional learning and views.
It must be realized as a sublime awakening. Nor is it a matter of memorizing the profound words and eloquent phrases of the ancients and taking them for one’s own understanding.
One need only engage in genuine investigation and earnest inquiry until [the truth] flows forth from within one's own breast.
Only then does one truly cover heaven and earth. If you have the resolve to investigate this matter, you must simply cast out all prior knowledge and views with total abandon.
Even the characters "Shang Daren Kong Yiji" (The Great Master Kong Yiji) are not permitted to remain within your breast.
Continue casting them out until it is utterly clean and pure, until not a single thing remains. Put it down, and put it down again, until there is nothing left to put down.
This is precisely the moment for entry. At this time, it is exactly right to apply effort and practice the work.

When you reach the point where you can do no more—standing as if on a wall ten thousand fathoms high—that is the very moment you gain true power. Applying the mind in this way is like driving a dog over a wall;
there will certainly be a flash of insight that bursts forth from within. This is the place of true utilization; it is truly not otherwise.
One may reach this place by drifting along; however, were it not for a true man of great resolve, one could not arrive here.
How many clever and quick-witted people in the world have surrendered their banners within the field of the five desires!
Those of superior capacity are led onto the path of fame and achievement; it is nothing more than this. How could there ever be any personal livelihood for oneself?
Given your spiritual faculties, combined with your sincere faith, you have already established the foundation—this is most rare and difficult to find.

If one merely imitates the "oral drum" Chan of the present age, relying solely on the chime of eloquence without investigating ultimate reality, would this not be to bring shame upon one's own spirit?
Since you trust in this old man’s heart with absolute certainty, I dare not fail the hope of your devoted reliance.
My previous letter was presumptuous and reckless; because I relied on our mutual understanding, I did not spare my own eyebrows, yet it was not for the sake of mere display.

I peel away what lies beneath your feet. I pray that you will reach the true limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), rather than merely heading toward the threshold of the gate or falling into the ranks of the common herd.
You claim to have received the transmission under the blows of the staff and shouts; this clearly shows a place of great power.

Yet you must know that the ancients did not lightly bestow their staffs and shouts; even receiving them requires that one not act with casual negligence. I pray that from this day forward, you will...
Comprehend all knowledge and views; exhaustively practice letting go. At the very point of letting go, apply focused attention (*tisi*), and you will immediately perceive true enjoyment.
Because my expectations for you are no small matter, I do not begrudge this distress; it is precisely because you possess such great power of capacity.
Therefore, I have placed this burden of a thousand catties upon your shoulders. Beneath these words of my reading, I request that you, Great Wisdom (Mahāmati), examine the written inquiry;
then you will see that this old man does not bestow [his teaching] lightly.

I, Mu Xiangxuan, have long harbored the aspiration to retire in old age at the Southern Peak (Nanyue). Last winter, I arrived here carrying my staff, yet the conditions for a mountain retreat had not yet been fulfilled.
Recently, I stayed briefly at Hudeong in Hengyang, which is also a site of the ancient Way. Master Qin has now come.
I have learned that you, Illustrious Sir, have recently performed great deeds of Buddha-work, suddenly opening the eyes of the human and celestial realms.

Hearing this, I am filled with joy beyond measure. I have often remarked that the single radiant light of *prajñā* possessed by the heroes and sages of past and present has mostly been shrouded by worldly conditions;
they exhaust their efforts at the gateway of fame, achievement, wealth, and honor, yet are unwilling to turn toward the fundamental source of their own life and nature.

Those who can set foot upon the path that leads upward are exceedingly rare to find. This great matter and its underlying conditions constitute the ultimate place of rest and homecoming for a true man of great capacity.
That you, Illustrious Sir, have suddenly been able to turn toward this—looking back upon fame, office, and worldly achievements as nothing more than dust, dross, and chaff—is a joy beyond compare.
My only regret is that I am unable to join you in resolving and discerning the matters that transcend the ordinary.

This is a deficiency. I have heard that Your Excellency diligently upholds the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. Recently, I obtained a copy of *Jueyi* (Resolving Doubts) and offer it to you as a gift of Dharma.
In response to Liu Yushou, Secretary of the Ministry of Works.

Fortunately, I entered the chamber of Vimalakīrti at Wuguan. Since then, our correspondence has been frequent; however, that I have not yet fulfilled your intention to take refuge in the Dharma remains a source of shame.
After departing for Mount Kuang, I lived there in retirement for six years. In the first month of winter of the *Renxu* year, I again set out on a journey to Lingnan.
I received the letter you sent during the intercalary month of the *Xinyou* year, and it was only in the second month of the *Guihai* year that I was finally able to open it.
Recite it. One instance of its transmission reaching such a state is like this; how much more so for the karmic conditions of many lifetimes for a human being?

As for the medical records you sent, I have read them carefully. Although they describe symptoms of illness, they must arise from the investigation of one's own habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), rather than being the result of karmic retribution.
Within them, I see that you possess no small measure of joy; however, it would be premature to regard this as a genuine realization (*sākṣātkāra*). Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* clarifies...

Xun: "If this arises from genuine investigation within meditative concentration, I still dare not claim realization. Were one to take this as a holy attainment, they would immediately fall prey to various demonic influences;
how much more so in the case of a pathological state? Nevertheless, after passing through this stage, you, sir, should have confidence in your own mind."
Sweep away all prior views and insights; you need not worry about not reaching home, for the ground will be level and smooth.
[The Master] replied:
"I, Shanyue, am ashamed of my own meager abilities and consider myself a sinner against the Dharma. For over twenty years, I have drifted upon the miasmic sea until my bones..."
His spirit has perished and his body is wasting away; only a single breath remains. He intends to conceal his shadow in the remote mountains to end his life in this world.
However, for the sake of the Dharma, he feels bound by the bond of life and death with Master Da and mourns that Master Lian’s sun of wisdom has set.

For this reason, he has traveled more than several thousand li, carrying a fragrant incense offering to pay his respects. Having now fulfilled his vow at Shuangjing, he plans to pass through the remainder of the winter.

On my journey to Yunqi, I was bound to take the route through Qiantang. Having entered the chamber of Vimalakīrti, what could have been more humbling than for the great elders to first extend their compassionate greetings?
I met with Dharma Master Xuanjin and learned in full detail of the grandeur of this Dharma assembly. How fortunate that in the remainder of my life I may witness such a day once again!
My gratitude is beyond words; I am filled with shame and find no ground upon which to stand. I hereby offer these thanks, and shall [respond] accordingly.
I respectfully accept this admonition to eliminate my narrowness and inferiority.
To Prince Gongwei, the Worthy Prince of Jingzhou:
Your sagely virtue is perfected by Heaven, and your spiritual roots were planted long ago. You inwardly harbor true compassion and outwardly manifest...

O Lord of the Nation, though your person dwells amidst the dust and toil of the world, your mind is fixed upon the Pure Land. For a long time now, the withered mountains and forests have looked up to your virtue and admired your reputation;
yet I, being personally without such fortune, have not once received the honor of your gracious inquiry. Last autumn, while traveling my eyes over Mount Kuanglu, I was on the verge of departure.

Just as I was returning to the old monastery of Guizong, I received the Imperial Decree brought by this messenger. I have humbly received the bounty of the Incense Accumulation (Xiangji) Monastery; however, being in a hurried state of pilgrimage, I have not yet had the leisure to offer my thanks.
This summer, I returned once more to Mount Kuang, intending to plan for my retirement in old age. It is my good fortune that my old friend, Minister Wang, has [extended his kindness].

We regard one another with the Dharma-eye. We wish to form a covenant of the Ten Worthies and enter the Lotus Society together. We intended for the Worthy King to serve as our leader and previously entrusted your attendants with this message;

we suspect it may not yet have reached Your Majesty’s hearing. However, since Mount Kuang is none other than Vulture Peak and Qihuang is like Śrāvastī, how could we exclude the Worthy King from the Dharma-gate?
We merely hope that you will remain our bulwark and protection from beginning to end. Recently, we received your envoy.
To receive such an honor from you is a source of great shame. Having received this gift of the Dharma, I am deeply moved by your compassionate concern and offer my boundless gratitude.
Furthermore, having heard of the变故 (catastrophic change) concerning your eldest son, I know that Your Majesty, due to the profound affection of a brother, cannot avoid suffering and grief.

Yet, the longevity or brevity of human life each has its fixed lot; these belong fundamentally to prior karma. Since what has passed cannot be retained, one must still look toward the future with high hopes. How could one—?
To use a soul that does not act to injure the nature of one who lives—this is something a person of realization should dispel through principle.

By no means should you, out of deluded thoughts, further weary your noble body. I only pray that the Three Jewels will look upon us with compassion, which is sufficient to benefit both the living and the deceased.
I wish that Your Highness will preserve and cherish yourself most deeply.

I reply: Since the late King ascended the throne, the affairs of state have been fraught with many hardships. Your Highness, being of such tender age, is currently devoted solely to your studies. Thus, the responsibilities of both internal and external affairs rest entirely upon the shoulders of the Queen Mother alone;
how great must her sense of anxiety and toil be! As for this mountain-dweller, I— (Note: The text provided ends abruptly. This translation reflects the full extent of the available passage.)
This must not be forgotten from the heart. However, you must know for yourself to cherish [yourself], tempering sorrow and reducing vexation;
sustain the mind with stillness, govern those below with compassion, and secure the favor of Heaven. In this way, you will surely avoid transgression or injury and satisfy the hopes of the multitude.

As for the practices of mindfulness of the Buddha, reciting the sutras, and prostrating, these are matters of vital personal importance; furthermore, one must not allow the mind to retreat due to hardships, nor abandon these.
I reflect that there is nothing capable of moving the Buddha or invoking heavenly protection except for utmost sincerity, which alone can reach Heaven. I respond to the noble thoughts of Mr.
Gong Zhaogji of Wuxi, a teacher of public morality whose devotion is pure and refined;
he desires to instruct those who come to study him, urging them to engage in genuine inquiry and earnest investigation. I shall not...
To fall into the gateway of shadows and lights and take that for the primary meaning—this is generally the case with those of the holy learning tradition.

Only when one is truly able to investigate the methods of the Chan school will there be actual realization. Furthermore, those who study superficially often delight in discussing the clever and awakened phrases of the Zen school;
this has become a great source of corruption and has misled many. Because these words remain merely on the tongue, they do not constitute true knowledge and insight. As for the *Laṅkāvatāra*...
The *Śūraṅgama*, *Vajracchedikā*, and *Tripiṭaka* [sic: *Tathāgatagarbha*] Sutras reveal the most supreme, primary meaning. Yet to regard them merely as words is not the correct perspective.
I hope you will apply your mind to them and investigate them from time to time; you shall then find the true path.
For those in this degenerate age who lack the eye of wisdom, they serve as a seal of authentication.
I share with you, my dear friend, the resolve for the mind of birth-and-death. It must be as true as if one were putting out a fire on one's head.

Within the mire of the five desires, it is truly difficult to uproot them all at once unless one possesses such firmness and valor. If, amidst this burning affliction, you can give rise to even a single thought of coolness—
This is indeed like a lotus growing from fire. However, I regret that while your physical constitution is weak, your mental strength and bone-marrow are firm;
it is simply that your physical vigor is insufficient. You are often ill. Do you recognize the source of this illness?
The illnesses of others arise from worldly greed and delusion; your illness arises from greed and delusion regarding the Way. Although the illnesses differ, they are both [illnesses].

The illness is the same for both of us. Your indignation is driven by the desire to transcend birth and death; you believe that by shedding the net of worldly dust, you will achieve liberation from birth and death.
Yet you do not realize that it is by leaving the net of delusive thoughts that one truly transcends birth and death. Moreover, the kindness of your parents has not yet been fully repaid.
If one were to depart as a result [of their efforts], it would only increase the grief of one's parents; this would be returning suffering to one's kin.
What reward could there be? Because they cannot escape, they remain in a state of delusion day and night, feeling that their aspirations have not been fulfilled.
Thus, while the Way remains unaccomplished, the sprouts of suffering have already begun to grow. Is this not the height of folly? You should reflect upon this for yourself:
delusive thought is the very root of birth and death; yet, within the midst of illness, one should examine this delusive thought and find it utterly devoid of root or foundation.

Thus, in every thought-moment, one suddenly uproots birth and death. By sitting in this very way and advancing upon this path, the Dharma-body grows ever stronger and the mind-ground grows ever clearer;
liberation comes spontaneously without waiting for a formal release. I, an old and infirm man, have been moved by your faith and have never ceased to think of it.
Hearing that you are still not at ease due to illness, I offer these words of consolation.

In the past, when men of heroic stature who possessed the talent to govern the world—such as Vice-Censor-in-Chief Jin Shengwu—knew only how to establish meritorious deeds and achieve enduring legacies, they did not realize what constitutes a truly imperishable legacy.
Because they failed to comprehend that which is inherently present, they abandoned their own nature to follow others; thus, their achievements [remained limited].

Success is not necessarily achieved; even if achieved, it is not necessarily imperishable. Even if one possesses a hollow reputation that is handed down to posterity, its survival is of no benefit while black karma follows in its wake.
Among those whose causes and effects are manifest to the ears and eyes of men, the generals and ministers of antiquity mostly fell into this trap.
Who, then, can be like the great elders such as Pei, Zhang, Bai, and Yang—those who transcend both the mundane world and the world beyond? This is so.
There are those who, knowing that the true nature is primordially complete, pursue the remnants of worldly fame and achievement;

yet there are also those who, upon the completion of their tasks, withdraw from the world and return to the root of their own nature and destiny. Although they differ in the timing of their realization, they are one and the same in being transcendentally self-attained and beyond comparison with the common world.
It is precisely because you, sir, were able to let go of all attachments on the very day your achievements were fulfilled and your body withdrew from public service.
To immerse oneself in the ground of ultimate truth—that which is called the supreme joy within oneself—is something for which even the Nine Cauldrons could not be exchanged;
is this not the mark of a great hero? May you, O Elder, exert yourself precisely at the point of letting go, until you reach the state where there is nothing further to let go of.
One will naturally not be bound by the karma of birth and death. Thus, one should practice the single gate of the Pure Land.

It is most essential to let go of defiled conditions; only then will pure karma be accomplished. However, while letting go, one seeks rebirth in the Pure Land; this is merely exchanging that for this.
This is merely a method of exchange. At Yunqi Monastery, the monastic regulations are solemn and still, like a vajra-ring.
I only wish that the assembly will be single-minded and practice according to the teachings; then the Dharma-body of Master Lien (Nianfo) will be majestically seated upon the lion throne.
It is only for the sake of the assembly’s Dharma-protecting great patrons to provide constant empowerment so as to increase our diligence—what more need be said?

After returning to the mountains with Yan Tiancheng and Zhong Han, I have already reported the details in full. I offer my condolences for your compassionate concern. As for my mountain retreat, the site selected is most secluded and excellent.

With diligent toil, I cleared the brush and constructed several thatched huts; they were completed after the full moon of the tenth month, and I have been settled there for nearly three months. Now that the year draws to a close—

There was nothing that did not reach his mastery. Only there, amidst a thousand peaks of accumulated snow and the pine-surfacing waves of ten thousand ravines, filling the ears and dazzling the eyes, sat a solitary old man with disheveled hair and beard.
He sat hunched and upright, wrapped in a monastic robe by a hearth, burning pieces of firewood.
He remained far removed from the knowledge of human society, and yet the world of men likewise knew not that within the vastness of heaven and earth there existed such a being.
The afflictions accumulated over kalpas of dust can be washed away almost entirely; how much more so the scorching miasma of twenty years?
I imagine that upon hearing this, the elder layman will surely not once clap his hands in joy.

In conversation with the lay practitioner Wang Jihé, I remarked that lately my days have been filled with much indolence and a lack of the power of diligence; this is a clear self-awareness. As the Sūtra says:
"To know them as empty flowers is to be free from saṃsāra. Since I recognize this state as indolence, I shall certainly not allow myself to be turned by it.
An ancient worthy said: "When the mind does not harmonize with worldly sentiments, this is true diligence. Recently, I heard that Tongyuan was initially studying in the mountains of Dongting.
Far removed from the dusty world, his six sense-faculties had no point of attachment. He placed himself amidst thirty-six thousand qing of vast, cold waves;
it was as if he were sitting within a great circular mirror, conversing face-to-face with a superior friend.

It is non-dual. Within this, where else could there be room for indolence? I only fear that deluded thoughts do not cease, like dreaming during broad daylight, whereby one spontaneously gives rise to inversion.

The Magistrate and Layman Gu Lichu possesses the natural bone of the Way and has been endowed with a disposition that transcends the mundane. Cultivating his essence amidst the mountains and forests, he is truly called noble and eminent;
yet, regarding the fundamental source of life and nature—the single step for transcending birth and death—it seems he has not yet applied his mind. Layman, your faculties are already...

I am fully equipped [with what I have]. As for the knowledge that remains lacking, I hope to refine it through discussion with others; perhaps it is simply because the time and conditions have not yet arrived.

I have taken up residence in the mountains south of Mount Kuanglu, at the foot of Seven Sages Peak, facing the Five Elders. There, we bow to one another amidst the clouds, while swallowing and spitting out the waters of Lake Pengli.
Its ripples and cloud-reflecting shadows are no less magnificent than those of Lake Taihu. Although its flowers and fruits cannot compete with those of Dengwei, its seclusion...
He excels them all. As for me, Shan-ye, I am fortunate to have found refuge here in my retirement;

I wish to emulate the legacy of Master Huiyuan at Donglin Temple by inviting eminent worthies from within the realm to join me in renewing the covenant of the Lotus Society. Will you, Layman, deign to devote your attention to this endeavor?

It would be fortunate indeed if we could agree with our esteemed companions to each set forth our aspirations, so that when the construction of the *dōjō* is completed and we return on another day—like long-traveling guests returning home—we may grow old together amidst the mists and clouds and return as one to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Would this not be the most supreme of causes and conditions?
If you, Layman, would truly be so gracious as to act as our guide, there will be no need for this mountain recluse to speak further at length.

I went with Yu Suxin, the Minister of Personnel, to have an audience with the Master at Dongchan Temple. Beholding his countenance and celestial form—so sincere, earnest, and dignified—I knew in my heart that he was a man of great influence.
What I regretted for him was that, while possessing the vessel of the Way, he had not yet heard the Way; I feared that when faced with momentous affairs, [he would falter].

It is simply that man cannot overcome Heaven. If one does not rouse a genuine faith and apply oneself with a focused mind within the Buddha-dharma to profoundly investigate the study that transcends birth and death, this will be the true foundation. Mundane talk and hearsay are neither ultimate grounds.
For supramundane authentic cultivation, there is only the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; for wondrous application to the world, nothing surpasses the *Daodejing*.
Letter. I hope you will quickly give rise to faith and apply yourself with diligence here; after a long time, there will surely be a state of self-attainment.

While passing through Wuchang before meeting with the Imperial Censor Xiong Zhigang, I was fortunate enough to behold his radiant countenance. He did not treat me with disdain but honored me with great kindness, providing me with a full meal of fragrant rice. Deeply...

Having received these profound words, he recounted a segment of his experiences from his time in Liaodong—a spirit such that his majesty extended even to the barbarians and his will was such that he desired to swallow the Hu tribes.
He laid down his weapons and brought the fierce invaders to submit like infants; every deed emerged entirely from the Treasury of Great Radiance within the Vajra-mind.

Listening to this, one could not help but feel one’s pores bristle with joy. I privately remarked that this must have been a Bodhisattva manifesting in the body of a high official to stabilize the state and bring peace.
The entire realm belongs to the playful mastery of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita*). I have long heard his words; now I see the man himself.

To attain Buddhahood with this very mind—this is truly a "leap-over" direct entry. How truly a heroic and valiant man he is! Since our parting, his radiant countenance has occasionally appeared in my mind-mirror.
Recently I have heard that he is immersing himself in Buddhist practice; this is yet another step beyond the mundane world. As the ancient saying goes: "To be born..."
To settle infinite matters of grief and sorrow, where else can one turn but toward the Gate of Emptiness? This Gate of Emptiness is truly the place for heroes to retreat.
If you are willing to let your body rest within it, use the fire of great wisdom to melt away your prideful spirit.

Possessing this sharp weapon of non-arising, you may be called a Master; relying upon it as a sword, it is a celestial longsword that secures the eyes of heaven and earth. In days to come, your spiritual powers will manifest.
Looking back at what occurred previously, it was merely a single spittle; this is truly what I have long hoped for. Do you, O Illustrious One, intend to do so?
I have long had a karmic affinity with the Magistrate Cai Wuyue;
upon first beholding your radiant countenance, I was immediately honored by a spiritual accord within the Dharma-gate. I understand that you act as a protector of the Dharma for the Sixth Patriarch.
Although the icchantikas created obstacles, the diamond-seed had already been ground no further. Subsequently, the circumstances at Caoxi were also devoured by lion-insects;
ultimately failing to fulfill his original vow, he instead became a public case for the future. I, the Mountain Man, also departed in relief.
Not long after, I was graced by imperial favor to cross the mountain range. Initially, I planned to retire in old age at Mount Nanyue, but that was not to be; I returned once more.
He possessed the practice of the Double Path (Shuangjing) and thoroughly understood the causes and conditions that even his teachers had not yet mastered.

Throughout the monasteries he visited, he was everywhere illuminated by the light of his public mind. Regarding the "one further step" of the Chan school, there were none who did not recommend him as their preeminent leader.

Among the officials of the Dharma-ending age, those capable of true inquiry and diligent investigation like his are such that one need not point a finger a second time. It is evident that over the years his practice has been profoundly sincere.
When passing through the pass, one should cast off the arm; meeting with conditions, one acts with sovereign ease. All illusions and transformations are illuminated by the lamp of Prajñā wisdom.
[The Master] replied to Wang:

Regarding the arrival of Master Fantan, I have been honored by your gracious letter. You hold the single matter of birth and death most earnestly in your heart and have given rise to this great resolve.

This is truly rare. To claim that while there are gradual stages in the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), one seeks instead a doctrine of sudden enlightenment—this is merely a modern trend among scholar-officials who study the Buddha-dharma.
They delight in preparing "palatable food," rather than providing "medicine suited to the illness. For they lack a genuine sense of birth and death;
they merely discourse on abstruse and subtle principles, claiming in their speech alone that they are concerned with birth and death. Furthermore...
Furthermore, one does not know what constitutes the root of birth and death.

That which is called the root of birth and death is precisely the various deluded thoughts in our daily lives—such as the notions of self and others, hatred and love, greed, anger, and ignorance, along with all afflictions and karmic actions.
If even a single thread of this karma is not severed, it remains the very foundation of birth and death. As it is said now, one must practice Zen meditation to achieve sudden awakening.
As for birth and death, please examine this for yourself: can you truly sever the afflictions accumulated over kalpas in a single thought-moment, as if cutting through a tangled skein?
If you cannot sever these afflictions, then even if you achieve sudden awakening, it will merely become a demonic activity. How could you possibly regard this lightly?
The sudden enlightenment of the patriarchs of old also arose from the gradual cultivation accumulated over many lifetimes;

therefore, this matter of sudden enlightenment seems easy when explained, yet in reality it is difficult. If one lacks twenty or thirty years of effort directed toward "deadening the mind," how could one achieve sudden enlightenment in a single thought amidst the heat of affliction?
It ultimately depends on knowing for oneself what one’s own capacity is like.
As for the single gate of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation), people of the world do not know its subtlety and regard it as shallow and mundane. In reality, however, every step is taken upon solid ground.
Why is this? Because since birth, human beings have, in every thought-moment, given rise to deluded thoughts and attachments, thereby creating the karma of birth and death.
When has there ever been a single thought that turned the light back to reflect upon one's own mind? When has there ever been a single thought that was willing to sever the afflictions?
Afflictions! Now, if you can transform this mind of deluded thoughts into mindfulness of the Buddha, then in every thought-moment you will sever afflictions.
If in every thought-moment you can sever afflictions, then in every thought-moment you will transcend birth and death.

If this single thought remains undisturbed, then at the time of death, evil karma will be extinguished and the realm of the Buddha will manifest before you; with a single thought following the Buddha, you shall be reborn in the Pure Land.
One will forever transcend birth and death and ascend to the stage of non-retrogression. As it is said: "If one merely attains the sight of Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment?
Furthermore, what need is there to debate sudden versus gradual, or to concern oneself with the three grades and nine levels? It is like ascending the imperial examination list in this world;
even being the very last name on the list is sufficient. Why must one necessarily be among the top three? If it is as stated, then practice accordingly.
If one penetrates to the very beginning and the very end of Chan, then the five turbidities and the ten directions are nothing other than the Pure Land. These words are indeed most incisive.
However, I fear one might not be able to achieve this; would that not lead to self-destruction in this life and cause one to fall back into the cycle of birth and death for long kalpas?
If one can truly maintain the single thought of Buddha-recitation without shifting and with a mind undisturbed, it will have a deeper realization than even the study of Chan. In short:

It depends solely upon being sincere and earnest in a single thought-moment. However, in the essential practice of Chan meditation, one must resolve to die to the worldly mind and allow not a single thought of delusion to arise.
As for the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation), it involves replacing defiled thoughts with pure thoughts; it is a method of exchange where thought is used to eliminate thought.

This is easily accomplished according to the capacities of our own faculties. In reality, one should recite the Buddha’s name in every thought-moment, ensuring that every thought remains unclouded. This...
My heart feels a wondrous joy that is beyond words. I beg Your Reverence to try composing one for me; please do not consider me an old man of inferior understanding.
These are no deceptive words—may you take them to heart. This concerns the teaching on the three grades of rebirth in the Pure Land.
I have previously prepared a discussion on the Pure Land teachings within my *Jingtu huiyu lun*. May you not harbor doubts regarding heterodox doctrines; I ask that you examine it closely.
There is no need for further elaboration.
With gratitude, I submit this to the State Councilor Wu Shugou.
Recently, I have received your letter, in which I learned that Your Excellency has long taken the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* as the seal of your mind.

Formerly, Zhang Fangping happened to obtain a copy of it and was struck with the realization that it was a manuscript from his own previous life; this, too, is surely an old possession from within your own breast.

However, the text of this sūtra is perilous and its meaning profound. Without modesty, I, a mountain recluse, have ventured to provide annotations, yet I am unable to bring forth even a fraction of its full significance. In response to your inquiry:

Why does this sutra not establish nine consciousnesses? It is because the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma accords with the capacities of his listeners; his teachings possess both provisional and ultimate aspects.
When he first appeared in the world, those to be converted were not yet mature and were incapable of receiving the Great Vehicle.

Thus, for the sake of those with inferior faculties of the Hīnayāna, he taught that the six consciousnesses and the three poisons are the root of birth and death, while the secret of the eight consciousnesses was not yet revealed. It was not until thirty years later that their faculties...
When their faculties gradually matured, he then taught the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), taking the eight consciousnesses as the root of delusion, awakening, birth, and death.

Fearing still that they might not believe in the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), he established a ninth consciousness outside of the eight, named the "Undefiled Consciousness" (*amala-vijñāna*), in order to lead them forward.

This also does not yet exhaust the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the Mahāyāna. Following this, once [the Buddha] perceived that the capacities [of sentient beings] were fully matured, he then taught the *Laṅkāvatāra*.

It directly points out that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is itself the Tathāgatagarbha, serving as the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna. This sutra does not establish gradual stages of cultivation, realization, names, or ranks;
rather, by realizing the non-arising of a single thought-moment, one suddenly becomes identical with the body of the Buddha. Therefore, although the sutra contains various expressions...

These [teachings] are all intended to shatter the afflictions of attachment held by non-Buddhists and followers of the Hīnayāna. They teach only the departure from verbal conceptualization so that one may suddenly realize the fundamental mind.
Therefore, when Bodhidharma came from the West, he took this sutra as the "Mind Seal" (citta-mudrā), which is entirely different from the explanations found in other sutras.
Your Excellency need only observe the phrase within the sutra, "The consciousness-store (*vijñānālaya*) is itself the Tathāgatagarbha," and it is the ultimate truth.
This is the ultimate limit; there is no need to further seek the nine consciousnesses as substantial dharmas.

Generally speaking, this sutra merely intends for one to depart from verbal conceptualization as the foundational practice for entering the Way. Upon opening the scroll, "all is neither" (*sarvam na*)—this is the true mandate of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
My conjecture is thus; I pray that you, Illustrious Lord, will take heed.

In reply: Last year, when I heard that you, Prefect Yuan Danyu, had hung up your official cap and returned to the east, my joy and consolation were immeasurable. Indeed, the salvation of sentient beings is the fundamental practice of a Bodhisattva.

During the age of the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the impurities of sentient beings are heavy; even Śākyamuni could not avoid frowning in distress—how, then, could he exhaust his power of vows?
As for the white clouds on Mount Jing, the pure blessings of one's later years are far more abundant there.
If one cultivates the Pure Land practices with diligence to bid a long farewell to this world of endurance (*sahā-lokadhātu*), it shall be the most supreme condition for a man of purpose.

*Questions and Answers*.

After parting from the Imperial Censor Wang Xingdong in the winter of the Renzi year, I suffered a severe illness the following year that nearly cost me my life; though I was restored to health, by that winter I set out for Nanyue across the mountain passes.

Initially, I had intended to retire there in old age, but due to various circumstances, this did not come to pass. Furthermore, Master Da had a karmic case yet to be resolved, so I proceeded to Bing... [text ends]
In the summer of the Year of the Dragon (Jinxi), I set out on a journey to Wu and Yue to seek news of you, but in the end, it was impossible to find.
I first arrived at Mount Lu to observe the summer retreat; seeing its secluded beauty and excellence, I conceived the ambition to spend my final years there.

Upon completing my studies under Master Liao Da, I returned to Mount Kuanglu in the fifth month of the Ding-si year. I selected a site beneath Wuru Peak on the southern side of the mountain—a small hill and a valley—sufficient for my needs.
I have been reborn here. All the conditions for this structure’s construction relied upon the protection of the Dharma; now, fortunately, it has found its place of rest.

What I have longed for over twenty years has finally been fulfilled at the end of my life. This is sufficient proof that the blessings of living among the mountains and forests are not easily obtained.

Last summer, when Master Ruo arrived, he kindly sent me a letter, through which I first learned that you were observing mourning for your parents at home. I calculate that the period of mourning will soon come to an end. Upon entering—
All things may be expected. As my boat passes Luoxing, I raise my head to see the clouds and mountains within the distance of a "cow-bellow" (one *niuming*);

I have long gazed upon this auspicious occasion day and night. Whenever I contemplate the Dharma-way of Lingnan over the past millennium, although I, an old and infirm man, have not greatly revitalized it, I rely on your entry into our community.
The flourishing state of our sons at this time is such that, with the two masters Feng and Long serving as exemplars, everyone is worthy of admiration.

Alas! Two disciples have passed away in succession; this Way lies desolate and vast. We rely solely upon your strength to bear its burden, yet it is regrettable that you were unable to remain long to guide the younger disciples.
Now they are scattered without a central authority, which is deeply lamentable. I did not expect the rise and fall of the Dharma to be so swift.
You alone possess an abundance of Heaven-endowed talent; my only regret is that you were unable to penetrate deeply into the Dharma-gate, such that your protection of the teachings—
The mind, however, has not yet truly broken through its attachment to a single point of letting go; thus, there remains a boundary between worldly dharmas and Buddha-dharmas.
If one can open the heavy gates wide so that both inside and outside are transparently clear—like raising the sun and moon in the midst of the sky—then all is resolved.
Then how could the robe and bowl of Caoxi be allowed to become stale?
If you, a man of such great capacity, do not resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, then this profound darkness will never see the torch of wisdom. I am old and worn; my remaining days are few.
I have constantly contemplated this sequence of causes and conditions and feel profound sorrow. Do you, sir, reflect upon this?
To practice the Six Closures at the summit of Mount Jinyun is a matter of great hope. If you remain in these mountains for now, let us merely engage in some discursive debate;
meanwhile, it will allow you to enter the gate of wisdom. In days to come, your two sons shall find you as a protector of the Dharma and greatly propagate this Way.
Thus, I shall simply grow old and die, for there is no immortality. Yet the karmic conditions across many kalpas will not be in vain. What more need be said?
Though ten thousand li separate us, it is as if we were face to face; may you, sir, bear this in mind.
In response to Chen Wuyi:

Your mountain retreat as a *sacivā* (Cibù) is far removed from the world; yet whenever you hear of current affairs, your heart is startled and your pain pierces to the five internal organs. I did not expect that things would change to this extent.
Now that the Son of Heaven, [Emperor] Chongzhen, presides over the realm, governance issues from many doors—what is called "many physicians and disordered pulses. It is no cause for wonder.
This is indeed so; even Lu Ban and Bian Que would have to fold their hands in helplessness. What can be done? Recently, the chariot ahead has already overturned;
now we must simply act with caution and maintain vigilance to strengthen our defenses. To cultivate the primal qi (*yuanqi*) is the supreme strategy.

If one is fixated on repairing a broken vessel while insisting it be whole, or prizes that which gratifies the palate and delights the senses, then what is called "illness not killing the person" will come to pass.
The physician has declared him dead. Beyond this, what other artifice remains?

Though there were many gentlemen at court at that time, even if they could consult the classics and examine the pulse, it is feared that despite devising ingenious and manifold schemes, they would not necessarily have been able to achieve a swift success. Your Excellency’s period of mourning is drawing near.
One should immediately step forward to fill the vacancy; it is not necessary to let the state of disorder determine whether one acts or desists.
As it is said: "When the great fire burns, this land of mine remains peaceful and secure. Worldly affairs are like a game of chess; those in the midst of the game are lost.

If there is a clear-eyed observer looking on from the side, they can point out a single move that secures the overall victory. What need is there, then, for them to engage in the game themselves? It is simply inappropriate to roll up one's sleeves and interfere.
In the interim, it causes the player to grow weary; this is what our Buddha taught—valuing only the practice of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

How is this so? You have shown that the solitary luminosity occasionally manifests again. However, your taking it up (*abhyupagama*) lacks vigor. If you say it "manifests," it is the clarity of self-knowing;
if you say you "lack the vigor to take it up," it is simply that you do not yet possess sufficient self-confidence. Yet, as for this manifestation...

It manifests through every thought-moment; it is not merely a matter of occurring at certain times. Simply observe that at the point where it breaks through and manifests, there is fundamentally nothing at all.
Thus, that which appears before you in every thought-moment is your original face.

If you apply effort in this way moment by moment, remaining in the state of non-arising, the whole body will manifest—how then could there be any question of "accepting" or "not accepting"? This is because the person themselves possesses one-pointed self-confidence.
Consequently, one gives rise to the notion that there is a separate mind apart from this, thereby missing the mark face-to-face and claiming instead that one’s resolve was not courageous enough.

This ailment lies in the mind that seeks elsewhere. All who turn toward the Way err in this way. You must simply look directly at the moment when a single thought manifests and see through it as non-arising.
When there is no arising, there has been nothing from the very beginning. This is the state of being far removed from [deluded] existence.

At the very beginning, before even a single thought has shifted, from this moment forward, there is only this one thought; what else could you seek? Since it is solely this one thought, whom else could you be asked to take charge of it?
The Sixth Patriarch said: "If we discuss this matter, one may even succeed while facing the enemy with a whirling blade.
I pray that you, Master Gong, will have true faith in this mind and see through the point where every thought is manifest; then, every thought will be refined.
Proceeding in this manner, there is nowhere that is not the great field of liberation; how, then, could there be any distinction between order and chaos?
Because the moment of face-to-face encounter is difficult to grasp, I have inadvertently let it slip.
In response to Mr. Cao Nengshi, Minister of Justice:
Since my youth, I have admired the sublime beauty of Mount Lu. Now that I am advanced in years, I have finally set out for it.

Upon ascending this mountain in the year of Bingchen, I learned of the presence of great officials and spiritual friends acting as banners of protection for the Dharma. Furthermore, upon reading the fundraising prefaces for the Dragon Canon, my heart...

In Zhe, there was Moqie (Vimalakīrti), who possessed the divine power to grasp the great trichiliocosm; here, we have immediately cleared the brambles at Wuru (Five-Milk) as a plan for our retirement.
Thus, beneath the peak, we lean against the Seven Sages of the Horizon while gazing upon the Five Elders in the Clouds;

they appear vividly before our very eyes, acting as protectors of the Dharma for our mountain gate. Master Zang has labored tirelessly for the site of this practice hall, his feet never resting. How joyful!
I am ignorant and lack the capacity for such a task. However, Your Reverence possesses great power of aspiration and intends to establish this Dharma assembly;
this is a vast and auspicious cause and condition for Mount Lu. It is essential that you, as the Dharmakāya, personally preside over this gathering, so that the great Dharma drum may be sounded.
Otherwise, how could a mere *dhūta* practitioner clad in rags bestow fearlessness upon this ocean-like assembly of followers gathered from the ten directions? This—
Within a vast and expansive mind, one is surely able to accomplish such a rare and marvelous feat.
In my reply to Sima Xu Mingheng, I wrote:

"I am honored that you have deigned to visit this desolate mountain. At the first sight, your wisdom-light shines forth uniquely; both within and without, you are transparently clear, like a crystal pitcher or jade."
Jian was, from the outset, one among those who have realized Prajñā; he was not someone whose roots of goodness had been cultivated over merely one or two lifetimes.
Upon hearing the profound discourse uttered [by the Master], a single fragment of his adamantine mind-ground manifested as a loyal heart and a righteous gallbladder.

Possessing only the single thought of loyalty to the sovereign and love for the nation, he no longer knew how to concern himself with the interests of his own family or person. Truly, he had come by the power of his original vow to rescue suffering sentient beings.
Truly, you manifest as a magistrate to perform the Buddha’s work. I am grateful for your kind letter, in which you inform me that your physical health has long been frail;
you even say your mind is strong while your bones are weak. This is but natural, for this defiled physical frame is inherently unstable and fragile by its very nature.

Reflecting upon this body of flesh and blood, it is originally a concretion of deluded thoughts; through the constant steaming influence of every moment of thought, it is only natural that it occasionally fails to maintain proper regulation and harmony.

Thus, even those of great stature do not recognize the grace [of the Buddha], let alone those whose external desires are coarse and whose hunger is insatiable; these only serve to increase the root of their illness.

Only the Buddha alone, through the single-minded application of the adamantine mind-ground (*vajra-citta-bhūmi*), perfumes and transforms every thought-moment, thereby causing this body to become entirely solid and firm, so that the *śarīra* (relics) remain indestructible.
I have heard that the true essence of the Holy Path is used to cultivate the person, while its dregs are used for the governance of the world and the state.
This is a discourse on the fundamental and the derivative. Now, your aspiration is to benefit others; therefore, you must first establish the foundation.
Once your cultivation is firm and profound, you may then forget yourself in your endeavors. As Laozi said: "By placing oneself last, one comes first;

by regarding oneself as external, one survives. There must surely be a way to this. Since your resolve and vows are great, O Honorable One, your mind must likewise be great, and so too shall your person.
Only after becoming refined can one succeed; this requires maintaining internal composure while testing oneself externally through affairs. Thus, one gradually enters an excellent state.
It is like constructing a multi-storied pavilion: one must first rely upon its foundation. It is my humble wish that you, Venerable Sir, will resolve your mind from this moment forward.
Simply uphold one mantra—be it that of Cundī or Vajra-Vimala—and hold it within your heart. Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, do not let it be forgotten from moment to moment.
After a long time, a powerful and resolute spirit will arise; through natural permeation, you will become strong of your own accord without needing external force.
Knowing that your intelligence is lofty and your faith is sincere and profound, I venture to speak thus.
In response to the Honorable Magistrate Wang Dongli:
Since our parting, it has been as if we were always conversing under a moonlit night in a frosty sky. Such scenes and such moments have all been within my dreams;

who could truly awaken from them? Only with those beyond the mundane world can one share tea in the bowl and incense by the brazier to discuss the discourse on non-arising. I acknowledge your kind message.

Recently, while reading the *Laṅkāvatāra*, I reached points that resonated with my own mind. I was greatly delighted. According to this sutra, one must transcend the marks of words and transcend the marks of mental objects;
only through the wondrous resonance of forgetting words can there be an entry point. From this moment on, I shall have no doubts and shall surely attain profound realization.

In another discourse, it was said that a single illumination is itself awakening and can even transform the objective realm. To say that [subject and object] have been forged into a single piece is still like being separated by the Iron Ring Mountains;
this one must know for oneself. If they do not become a single piece, where does the fault lie? This teaching of the ancients regarding "a single piece" is no small matter.
From the very first moment of resolving to practice Chan, one takes a single koan as a *huatou*, such as Zhao...
The words, "The dog of this province has no Buddha-nature," "The myriad dharmas return to the One," and "Where does the One return?
were held crosswise in his chest, blocking the faculty of thought so that it could not function again. With a profound state of doubt, he bit down on his teeth day and night.
Do not abandon it for even a single thought-moment. Only after a long time of complete mastery will it finally be forged into a single piece. This may take ten or five years;
this is the "thought-subject" (hwadu) becoming a single piece, but it is not yet awakening into a single piece. Although you, Master, have sincere faith in this matter...

There is already a point of understanding, yet one has not yet applied the "deadly effort. As with the ancients who investigated the *huatou* (critical phrase), even if they understood this principle, they remained within the realm of mere appearances;
their minds of arising and ceasing had never for a single thought-moment been temporarily stilled.
Therefore, when at leisure and without affairs, they perceived the presence of principle, but as soon as they encountered circumstances or conditions, they were immediately swept away. Thus we know:
This matter cannot be attained through the practical utility of intellectual understanding or views. It is further said:

"Cultivate the contemplation of the 'unified totality' (yīhéxiàng) to destroy views with views, to detach from marks by means of marks, to eliminate consciousness by means of consciousness, and to shatter attachments by means of attachments.
While these words certainly possess their own logic, the "unified totality" is not something that can be entered by joining two ends together; for it involves both mind and object...

"Forgetfulness" is precisely awakening to a single state of being, where not even the slightest phenomenon is perceived as an obstacle within the mind. Everything returns to its source, and every dharma is revealed.
Only when this occurs can one enter the "single unified mark. If, at this point, you attempt to use consciousness to break through appearances, you will fail.
It is like oil mixed into flour; how could it ever break through? Furthermore, seeing consciousness is the root of the illness, not a tool for destroying an enemy.

To practice contemplation in such a manner seems to involve confusion and error. If one enters according to the scriptural teachings, it must be like the six metaphors of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*;
once a single contemplation is mastered, there will naturally be full correspondence. If entering from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, then simply regarding...
In quiet sitting, being able to perceive the continuous flow of one's own mind’s delusive thoughts is precisely where the work begins.
It is further said that gaining strength from the single phrase "delusive thoughts have no inherent nature" allows them to be dissolved and returned to their source moment by moment.

If you practice according to the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), simply rely on the Sixth Patriarch’s question: "Before you think of good or evil, what is your original face? This is most direct and authentic.
Apply yourself to practice in your daily life. In this way, do not forget it from moment to moment.
There is no need to seek a "single unified state" (*yixiang*). If, suddenly, a single thought accords with reality, you will unexpectedly fall into that very unity.

Therefore, Master Yuan, you need not seek a single unified state, nor need you fear the shifting of circumstances; simply, at all times, let your mind follow this one phrase as your core focus throughout your daily activities.
If you look directly at the very place where a single thought arises and bite it off on the spot, it will be dissolved.

If delusive thoughts are thus dissolved, you will no longer be turned by any external circumstances. If the eight consciousnesses are shattered and you achieve a great penetration, then there will be no objects left to turn.
When there are no objects to turn, mind and environment become one; this is the true "single integrated mark."
Furthermore, as you travel eastward, it is fortunate that you have met a true man of the Way; one may say your journey was not in vain.

I, an old man of the mountains and fields, dwell amidst green peaks and white clouds, growing ever more distant from the world. Your vow to benefit sentient beings is being widely propagated; it is a joy to converse with you.
It has not been many days since I heard that you have been applying yourself with such keen vigor to the practice of the Way; truly, you are advancing a thousand li in a single day.

However, while it is easy to exert oneself in cultivation, it is difficult to forget one's efforts and sever all signs of attainment. For if you become attached to the profound and subtle, or sink into the habitual patterns of stillness, after a long time—
Unaware, they fall into the demonic net of false views and knowledge; this is the first difficult pass on the path of learning since antiquity.

If one passes through this pass, it is to take a further step from the top of a hundred-foot pole. Reaching this state, there is only a single flavor of ordinariness, with nothing particularly extraordinary.
As it is said: "It is still just the person of old, yet it is not the sphere of activity of the person of old."
Thus, the pores of one’s entire body radiate light everywhere; this is by no means a realm of intellectual deliberation, nor does it involve dwelling within the gateway of shadows and reflections.
