In this matter, it is simply a matter of clearing away step by step, so that one may naturally arrive at great rest.

Furthermore, I have received your letter, for which I am deeply grateful. Your sincere affection for the Dharma moves my heart; our spirits are in perfect accord, separated by not even a hair’s breadth.

Within the Treasury of Radiance (*prabhāsa-garbha*), there is fundamentally nothing that physical form can separate—truly, this is no empty word. I am fully aware of your recent practice; day by day, I see it becoming increasingly stable and serene.
Having already stepped into the realm of effortless ease and bliss, this is sufficient evidence of the power of great diligence. As it is said:

"The nostrils of the old man cannot tolerate even a hair’s breadth of attachment"—this is precisely where one gains strength. Yet, within that very state where not even a hair’s breadth of attachment can remain, there is further mystery and difficulty;
one must simply pass right through it. As the ancients said: "Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell; where there is no Buddha..."
Pass quickly! I fear you will sit within the armor of "nothingness. If you do not penetrate this, it will be even more difficult to turn yourself around in the future.
Have you not seen Yunmen say: "There are two kinds of light that do not penetrate through: first, when one is not clear in all places, as if there were an object before one's face;
second, when one has penetrated such that all dharmas are empty, yet there is still something lingering, as if an object were present."
This, too, is a case where the light does not penetrate. The Dharma-body also has two kinds of illnesses.

When one reaches the stage of the Dharma-body, if attachment to dharmas is not forgotten and one's own views still persist—this is the first. Even if you manage to penetrate through it, you must not let it pass unexamined;
if you scrutinize it closely, what trace of vitality remains? This, too, is an illness. In the past, people initially considered the realization of the Way to be difficult, but as for...

Upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is most difficult to dispel; many fall into this very trap. As the saying goes: "To remain attached to what one recognizes is still not it.

Although there may be no particularly brilliant moments of progress in this stage of practice, one must certainly understand the point of relinquishing the single attachment to views regarding phenomena (*dharma-dṛṣṭi*).
What do you, O Illustrious One, think? In the past, I have abandoned [all things] moment by moment, until I reached the point where there was nothing further to abandon. Furthermore—
Not sitting at the edge of that which cannot be relinquished, one is naturally not bound by views; thus, the entire body becomes like a great mass of fire.
[This was written] for the Gentleman of the Ministry of Rites, Bao Zhongsu.
Mount Huang and Mount Bai have long existed within the vast primordial chaos.

By what cause did the spirits of these mountains manifest auspicious omens, moved by the Great Dharma-Protector, so that in a single day the azure cliffs and verdant crags were transformed into Buddhist temples and pearl palaces, and the wondrous golden forms descended from the void?
The true exegesis on palm-leaf manuscripts descended from heaven, instantly causing the land where there was no Buddha to overflow with the splendor of the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*).
You have gathered and transformed immeasurable humans and devas, leading them together into the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Such wondrous efficacy flows entirely from the single thought of your compassionate and true mind. How could its merit and benefit be anything but vast? I, this mountain recluse, pay my respects.
I have heard from afar your words of praise; my only regret is that, burdened by old age and decline, I am unable to pay you a visit and offer my prostrations.

Lately, I have chosen a secluded valley on Mount Lu to spend my remaining years. It is my good fortune that Master Chishih has become the patron (*dānapati*) of this mountain gate, intending to invite eminent worthies from across the land to once again strike the lotus-leaf water-clock.
In his letter, he writes: "I am grateful that you, Elder, have been the first to sing the praises of Jetavana, and I am mindful of Mount..."

This hermitage is a place of renown; it has earned the approval of eminent worthies, bringing luster to its crags and valleys. However, I, a rustic of the mountains, am ashamed to compare myself to Master Yuan;
I simply cannot bear to serve as the presiding host of the Donglin community.

Furthermore, at the start of the new year, I received the messenger from afar, who brought your earnest and compassionate concern, desiring that this mountain monk travel once to form a bond of Dharma-joy.
My initial heart was delighted, as I had already fully understood your intent. Recently, however, I have received a letter from Minister Wang, which says: "Liao..."
The alarm is most urgent. Yesterday, on the twentieth day of the second month, the army set forth. Of the four generals leading the routes, three have already perished;

eighty or ninety thousand living beings have been ground to dust in a single day—a sight truly chilling to the heart. Only General Li remains on one route, yet Liaodong is extremely difficult to sustain;
I fear he may press forward in a long march, which is a matter of great concern. The court is in turmoil, lacking any unified strategy.

Conscripting soldiers and transporting grain are as urgent as a shooting star or a spark from flint. What time is this? We, who rely on the mountain forests for our livelihood, depend upon peace and stability.
Considering that the hearts of the people are now in a state of tumultuous alarm, we have no leisure even to conceal our tracks or offer our sincere prayers;

how, then, could we dare to engage lightly in wandering excursions? This is the first reason. Furthermore, I have heard that the capital is in a state of agitation and that monks are being prohibited from traveling between the north and the south.

For those who wander about seeking food, there is no place to set foot. Should they hear that you have arrived in the mountains and wilds, they will likely hasten toward you at the mere scent of the wind;

it is difficult to guarantee they will not come, and I fear this may cause inconvenience for the local area. This is the second reason. Initially, one might take such an excursion as a pleasure, but subsequently, there may be matters of concern.
Therefore, I do not dare to proceed lightly. I have written this letter specifically to inform you; I humbly beg for your compassionate understanding and pray that you will plan to proceed slowly.
I await a later time for this.
Furthermore, I have received your recent account of your practice, noting that you are gradually gaining entry into the fundamental ground. You seek a single word of secret instruction.
They take this as a shortcut. To examine the origin of this matter, it is fundamentally neither secret nor non-secret;
it simply depends upon one’s own single thought-moment. Even the practice of "examining the critical phrase" (kōan) is employed only as a last resort.
One must simply recognize that the consciousness manifesting in daily life is entirely the activity of deluded thoughts, even if there be profound principles or mysteries.

These wondrous insights and views are all but shadows of the *vijñāna* (consciousness-spirit); they are all matters pertaining to the periphery of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manas-vijñāna*).

In sum, one has never realized that which is detached from mind, intellect, and consciousness by even a single hair’s breadth; therefore, whenever the mind is raised or a thought stirs, it invariably falls into the trap of delusive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
Thus, the Buddha said: "All sentient beings, because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind, employ various delusions..."
This perception is not true; therefore, there is cyclic existence. This is precisely what Aśvaghoṣa stated:

"All sentient beings, from the very beginning, have never been free from thought. Thus we know that the various deluded thoughts used daily by sentient beings are ultimately nothing but a single deluded thought.
Yet this single thought is the source from which delusion first arose, extending back to the beginningless past.
Up until now, there has been only this single thought, with no second. This very mind, intellect, and consciousness all arise within this one thought.
If, by practicing the cultivation of mindfulness right now, you can see through this single thought, then all delusive thoughts and emotional anxieties will instantly become as pure as ice.
This is what is called the state of being free from the marks of thought; it is equal to the realm of empty space. However, because of sentient beings...
One gives rise [to this view] merely by perceiving that the deluded thoughts within the mind are numerous and chaotic; in reality, one does not know that they are but a single thought.
Now, being unable to free oneself from these proliferating thoughts, the ancients taught people to take up a "critical phrase" (huatou) as their practice.
Upon investigation, even this critical phrase is itself a deluded thought; it is simply that one takes this single thought of the critical phrase [as the object].

Block off discursive thoughts and bring them back to a single point. If you thoroughly investigate this one thought and look deeply into it—looking and looking again—you will find that it originally has no place of arising;

it is fundamentally unborn from the very beginning. If, at once, you awaken to the fact that this one thought is unborn, then the emotional faculties of kalpas upon kalpas will be instantly liberated in this very moment.
This is what is called awakening; it is not that there is some other mysterious or subtle state to be awakened to.
Furthermore, when you, Elder Layman, apply yourself to the practice by taking up a *huatou*, focus your efforts solely on this single thought-moment.
Pursue it deeply and profoundly until, suddenly, you see that this single thought-moment has no place of origin.
If you realize that this single thought is unborn, then from this point forward, all successive thoughts will likewise be unborn. This is what the Sixth Patriarch meant when he said:
It is the arising of the mind from non-abiding. If one seeks the profound and mysterious, that is itself abiding. In such a direct and straightforward state, it is most powerful;
there is no need for extensive seeking after knowledge and views. Not a single word has any use here;
one must simply first cast away all deluded thoughts and conceptual knowledge within the breast, putting them down all at once, until the mind becomes utterly empty.
"Clear and unobstructed, not a single thread remains. Observe the very place where a single thought arises, and immediately apply your strength to investigate it.
This is what is meant by 'entering directly with a single blade,' allowing no room for calculating before or after, nor for any kind of scheming.
As soon as there is calculation, one is far, far removed. Layman, you have set your mind on this matter; try taking up the practice in this way—how does it seem?"
I have accepted these coins, for which I, the humble mountain recluse, feel deep shame;
it is a blemish upon the Dharma-gate. Moreover, having long been submerged in the sea of pestilence, I would rather gladly fill a ditch or a ravine than endure this.
I did not expect to be granted another life, yet here I am today. Previously, because of my decrepit age and many ailments, I intended to hide away in the remote mountains;
however, as there were still unfinished karmic conditions at the Double Peak (Shuangjing), and since the matter of righteousness involves life and death, I could not neglect this single journey.

Therefore, I have come here with faltering steps. Although I do not dare say that I have followed Sudhana’s journey southward in search of the Dharma, I am fortunate to have been able to visit various spiritual teachers (kalyāṇamitra).

For a long time I have heard that you, Layman, are the contemporary equivalent of Pei Xiu and Yang Jie, serving as a bulwark for the Dharma-gate; furthermore, I know that your compassionate concern for me has been most earnest.

I had intended to visit your chamber; however, as you mentioned yesterday that Master Cihang was previously waiting for me at Mount Xi, we missed each other face-to-face, which left me deeply regretful.

Now, I have been honored by your kind message reaching me from afar, along with various Dharma offerings. Having reverently read them over and over again, my feelings of gratitude grow ever deeper, causing my deluded thoughts to soar beyond bounds.
My feet can no longer endure the delay. Yet, as rain and snow fall incessantly, I shall wait for a brief clearing before departing the mountains.
I still have a journey to Yunqi; I shall not linger long upon the lakes. Upon my return, I will surely enter the chamber of Vimalakīrti at Wumen.
I offer these thanks in advance. Sincerely yours, [Your Name] (Not signed)

Furthermore, as I dwell constantly in the mountains and wilds, I have always been concerned that the Dharma-gate would fall into decline. It is difficult to find a person of genuine sincerity who can serve as a true protector and defender of the teachings.

Yesterday, I was fortunate enough to meet you, Layman; this brings great solace to my long-held aspirations. Though you manifest in the body of a high official, you raise the banner of the True Dharma.
At this time, there is great hope for him. As for myself, I am but a withered stump in the mountains, a discarded thing by the Dharma-gate.

Yet, owing to the depth of my affection for the Dharma and my own confidence in our long-standing karmic affinity, our meeting at Mount Yu was too brief for me to fully express what I harbored in my heart. I am honored that you have joined your boat to escort me so far.
I am further moved by your earnest concern. Since our parting, I arrived at Mount Kuang after the full moon of the midsummer month.

I have chosen a dwelling among the Seven Sages and Five Nipples peaks on the southern side of the mountain, clearing away brush to build a few thatched huts for a temporary place of rest. When I previously sent you my letter, I had not yet settled upon a permanent residence.
Lately, old age and illness have assailed me; this illusory body has long suffered from chronic rheumatism, which has recently begun to manifest its pains since the onset of winter.
It is a minor matter. When compiling the *Hufa* (Defending the Dharma), I read through the various old epitaphs for patriarchal towers; every word points toward the ultimate path.
Having attained the true eye of the Chan school, the Dharma destiny of our Ming dynasty has flourished greatly, and we rely on these as a standard and mirror.
If they are carved and circulated, the benefit to the Dharma will not be slight. As for the manuscript, I shall wait until next spring to present it specifically.

Furthermore, regarding the notes on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* previously submitted: this scripture is the true main artery of the Mind School (*cittamātra*). I do not know whether you have given it your attention.
Lately, among the monastics of the southeast, many are investigating the ultimate reality; yet, alas, there is a lack of enlightened masters with the "clear eye" to guide them.
I show you: throughout the world, people dangle their conscious spirits at the gateway of shifting shadows and lights, yet they are branded and ruined by the "winter melon seal.
Furthermore, they refuse to draw near to the teachings of the scriptures to seek authentic knowledge and vision; truly, such people are difficult to find.

Among the officials, there have been many with the great resolve to protect the Dharma over the past thirty years, yet those who seek the true truth and apply themselves deeply to the fundamental practice are rare indeed.
Such individuals are also not easily found. For the most part, the scholar-officials (*shidafu*) are far too clever.
Whether it be Chan or the Teachings (*jiao*), they take everything at face value. One can see this generally among those who were previously renowned in their own eyes.

At this time, it is difficult not only in worldly affairs, but even more so within the Dharma-gate—speaking of it brings tears to my eyes. Now that the ways of the world have grown corrupt, the Dharma...

In these desolate autumn days at the gates [of the Dharma], were it not for a person of great power and resolve to emerge, who would provide rectification and support? I have often said that to rectify the ways of the world, one must rectify the human mind;
to protect the gates of the Dharma, one must rectify knowledge and vision. Yet, rectifying the human mind must take rectifying knowledge and vision as its foundation.

This is what is meant by being unbiased and impartial, whereby the Way of the King flows vast and wide. Were it not for a heart of ultimate public-mindedness and selflessness, how could this be achieved?
The collective will is determined by the sentiments of a single group. However, the study of non-self must involve diligent practice within the Dharma;
one must undergo a thorough transformation of body, mind, and the world to reveal the great treasury of original luminosity.

Only then can one naturally regard the world and self as like flowers in the sky or bubbles and reflections in water, and view fame and fortune as like dreams, illusions, or the moon in the water. Thus, all things are equalized.

Birth and death; right and wrong; transcending praise and blame—only when one acts in this manner can they dare to say that they view the world as a single family and all living beings as their own body.
To be vast and impartial in this way means that the human mind becomes naturally upright and the ways of the world may become pure.

Thus, the effect of serving the sovereign and benefiting the people does not exceed this. If one observes the learning of Master Lou of Song (Zhou Dunyi) with discernment, it truly emerges from [this principle].
Thus, he was able to serve as a winged support for the Holy Ancestor and open the way for the enterprise of ten-thousand-year peace.

Reading the *Fuhufa bian* (Compilation on Protecting the Dharma), there is no page one does not turn over with a sigh. In this degenerate age, there are many corrupt practices that cannot be turned back;
it must be through such a person as this that the governance of a Great Peace can be spoken of. Furthermore, the Way of Heaven operates without ceasing—how could this world alone be an exception?
Truly, such a person as this does not exist! I, the mountain recluse, am ashamed to be a discarded object of the Dharma-gate;
though my life has contributed nothing to the world, my concern for the Dharma is as if it were my own. Therefore, what I hope from you, Layman, is both weighty and great.

I earnestly pray that you will seize this opportunity to nurture and sustain [the Dharma] deeply, so that you may together receive the favor of Heaven. Regarding the state, the altars of soil and grain, and the common people, they look toward you with bated breath.
Standing on one foot has reached its limit. How could you not give rise to a profound resolve and solemn vow through patient endurance?

Regarding the *Fahufa bian* (Compilation for Protecting the Dharma), there is no need to add further critical annotations to the prose. However, if I were to briefly develop even one or two points concerning where the "right eye" was opened within the epitaphs of the various patriarchs, it would already be redundant.
I hope you will expedite its publication. Furthermore, my recent humble work, the *Lengyan tongyi* (Comprehensive Treatise on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra), has already been sent for your perusal.

This sutra is vast and comprehensive, encompassing the holy teachings of an entire lifetime; its principles regarding the causes and effects of delusion and enlightenment penetrate all things without exception.
Previous commentators have not fully elucidated its meaning, yet this work by this mountain recluse does not follow the old tracks and seems more accessible to entry.

Furthermore, the general meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has also been completely overturned from previous cases. Without knowing the *Lotus Sutra*, one will not know the Tathāgata’s salvation of the world.
I have exerted great effort in this matter. If one does not understand the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, one will not know the pivotal point regarding the delusion and awakening of mental cultivation.

If one does not understand the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, one will fail to distinguish between the right and wrong of correct and erroneous views. Regarding these three sutras, you, Layman, should investigate them with a deep and earnest mind.
On another day, there shall be further requests.

Furthermore, the *Hufa lu* (Record for Protecting the Dharma) is the *Chanzong chuanteng* (Transmission of the Lamp of the Chan School). Its primary concern lies in possessing the "Dharma-eye" of the school.

Examining the individuals therein, one observes their spiritual capacities as teachers and disciples, their gates of awakening, their conduct, and their achievements—particularly their final, decisive breakthrough.
The vastness of what has been taken up is now fully expressed within the tip of a single hair. It is not only that his literary skill is marvelous;

rather, regarding his profound resolve to protect the Dharma, there is not a single character that does not flow from the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Concerning the sources of the teachings and the lineages of transmission for both the Exoteric and Esoteric traditions, he has treated them exhaustively without omission.
This book is a peerless masterpiece of past and present, far beyond the reach of mere compilations by others. Now, however—
Regarding the epitaphs for the various great patriarchs of the Zen school, they primarily emphasize right view and right practice;

as this is largely consistent with the lay practitioner’s own perspective, I have not dared to add further defilements. As for the inscriptions and prefaces on the steles, these are merely literary compositions and are therefore unnecessary.
I am now sending the original manuscript for your review; if it were carved even one day earlier, then...

This Dharma gate has already received the grace of a single day. I, this mountain monk, have previously read the collected writings of the Great Emperor (Gao Huang) concerning Buddhism, as well as the prefaces to various sutras, including those for Tianjie, Baoen, Linggu, Nengren, and Jiuming Monasteries in Nanjing.

The five [monasteries] established within the imperial palace each have their own records. As for the essential and significant deeds recorded in these registers, my intention is to compile them into a single work to demonstrate the Imperial Founder’s heart of protecting the Dharma.

If this record were combined with those others into one volume, it would sufficiently illustrate how, in this illustrious era, the sovereign and his ministers are of one body—an achievement unprecedented in ancient or modern times.
Only... (Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "惟居" (only/residing), suggesting the source material was incomplete.)
If you, sir, would mount this and apply your attention for even a single *xun*, it would be the most excellent matter; indeed, it is the very aspiration of this mountain monk.

Furthermore, I am honored by your letter, which fully informs me of your recent circumstances, and you have also cited the final phrase from Master Mei’s note. As for this mountain recluse, for a long time...

This is a matter of urgent concern; it cannot wait for the present moment. Regarding the establishment of a society for the support of the elderly, it was originally through the aspirational power (*praṇidhāna*) of the head seat Huicheng that the mountain monk [myself] offered words of praise, merely wishing that he would relinquish his current residence. What time is this? We are already pressed for time seeking mere security;

why then trouble ourselves with such further affairs? Moreover, as the years have passed, my decline and illness have increased daily; my feet suffer from chronic dampness, making my movements increasingly difficult.

Dwelling in the mountains in a state of rustic simplicity, I have merely settled here for the time being. Furthermore, fearing that my remaining days are few and with a sense of urgency regarding birth and death, I have closed my retreat and severed all external ties.
Holding fast to a single thought, I await nothing but death. Yesterday, on the Mid-Autumn Festival, I finally began this practice.

Having contemplated it for over twenty years, the winds and waves of the sea of suffering and the green mountains and white clouds have often appeared in my dreams; now, fortunately, they have been realized all at once.

How could one possibly regard this as a trivial matter? Nowadays, all the Chan teachings and Buddhist Dharma in Guanzhong have been cast aside on high shelves; everyone has adopted a single flavor of "guarding against cleverness.

I often reflect that the ancients would recite the name of Amitābha Buddha one hundred thousand times day and night. Today, I am ashamed of my own decline and old age, for my physical strength is no longer sufficient.
I test myself and find I can usually manage at least half of that number. I specifically emulate Master Huiyuan’s practice of the six periods of the day, using the lotus-water clock.

I offer incense in place of flowers. For several months now, my body and mind have naturally attained the state of ultimate bliss. Knowing the depth of your compassionate concern, I venture to inform you of this.
Furthermore,
The attendant has returned with the news of your realization of the Dharma-sound. It is evident that your mind-ground has recently attained liberation;

this is not something easily achieved without genuine effort. I am deeply comforted, truly comforted. I have received your instructions on the essentials of the Gate of Non-duality; there is nothing that surpasses the single pivot of the High Seat, for it is not merely a single dharma.
Regarding my preface to the *Heart Sūtra*, it was indeed a rash and superficial discourse; I am honored that you, with your great hand, have corrected it.

These words form an excellent discourse; they are truly the work of an alchemical elixir that transforms the base. I do not dare say they must be transmitted, but I merely preserve this one Dharma-gate.
You have observed that state affairs are difficult and arduous, and that none are willing to exert their utmost strength for them—this is indeed true.
However, when observing those who have sacrificed themselves for the sake of the nation since ancient times, it was never something they did impulsively or by chance. For such people...

This chapter contains many causes and conditions that cannot be easily conjectured. First, when sentient beings face great calamities, there are certain Bodhisattvas of great compassion who come forth by their own vow;
all of their activities are manifested through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

He has appeared not from within the realm of deluded thoughts, speculations, or calculations. Whether looking back to the past, even the heroes who were contemporaries of my Holy Ancestor were such as he.
Furthermore, he is one born by Heaven’s decree to respond to the destiny of the times and to uphold the Way of the world.

Internally, they possess the spiritual root of *prajñā*; externally, they wield the means of adaptive response. Having first established this foundation, when it comes time for practical application, it is as if reaching into a bag—hitting the mark every hundred times.
Liu Bang (the Marquis of Huaiyin), Zhuge Liang, and the various lords such as Zhongding of Pingyuan were precisely such individuals.
Furthermore, these three also emerged from the power of their *prajñā* vows, bearing loyalty and righteousness throughout many lifetimes.
Those who possess resolute habits, who are firm, upright, and centered, and who are steadfast and unshakable;

those who deliberate upon great matters and maintain their resolve without wavering—such as Wen Xingguo and the various worthies like Xu Xiaoru of the Ming dynasty—who are individuals whose innate nature is fixed and cannot be taken away—are precisely such people.
Looking at the persons of the world today, is there anyone who possesses even one of these qualities? Observe!
In their speech and discourse, can they truly possess the insight and vision necessary to decisively quell chaos and support those in peril?

To seek practical results without possessing the underlying foundation—is this not an error? Therefore, the loyal ministers of antiquity possessed a fixed talent and integrity, as well as the means by which they could inevitably act;
if not employed, they remained still, but once employed, they invariably produced results. This is just like the talents of the present age.

Who is it that possesses both [qualities] in their entirety? Therefore, those of antiquity who established unshakeable achievements all had their plans predetermined within their hearts, like Fan Li, Zhang Liang, and Zhuge Liang;
they moved with ease and composure. How could they have treated empty talk as actual deeds?
Even someone like Dongpo was merely one of literary talent and moral integrity. It is only you, Layman, who are currently...
As for those who place their hopes in me, I simply examine my own endowments: how do they compare with those of you gentlemen?
What I possess is merely a single heart of sincerity. If my talent and equipment were not sufficient, how would I dare speak of the great affairs of the world?
This is precisely what I, this mountain recluse, have earnestly hoped for in the profound cultivation of you, Layman. From my perspective as an old man, I observe your...
The mind carefully deliberates upon various public undertakings that ought to be performed;

once one has resolved to accomplish them, as for the task of quelling chaos and supporting those in peril, by what means does Cao intend to achieve it? Is this something that can be mastered through gradual refinement from within?
The current affairs are merely minor matters; there are others even greater than these. I only wish that you, Layman, would prepare yourself early.
Regarding your preparations, I hope you will not entrust your life to them; this would be the complete strategy. The whole world is lost in delusion—how could it be awakened by a single call?
Knowing that you, Layman, intend to emerge from the mountains, I have sent this inquiry specifically. I hope you will delay your departure for now.
Cao prepares to await the opportune moment. Heaven surely has its own intent for the accomplishment of this great enterprise. By all means, do not act with reckless haste.
If your long-term cultivation is complete, then emerge when the timing is right; act decisively upon seeing the opportunity, like a blue hawk seizing a rabbit, leaving no trace behind.
Only then is it the strategy of a great hand. How could one consider it a gain to merely follow others out of courtesy and surrender one’s life and destiny to them?
What do you, Gao Ming, think of this?

Furthermore, I have received a letter from the Layman Zide, sent by hand last autumn when he left the mountains, which contains several lines concerning "nurturing the body through dependence. This has brought great comfort to my humble self.

I am deeply grieved. I did not expect that the destiny of the nation would encounter so many calamities, with external threats and internal anxieties leaving both the court and the commoners in a state of terror.

Your Imperial Majesty stands alone; it is difficult for such great shoulders to bear this burden. Fortunately, at this time, the assembly of eminent ministers like Kui and Long is numerous. Above, you rely on the spiritual protection of the imperial ancestors; below, you comfort the hopes of the common people.
It is precisely now, Layman, that you ought to firmly maintain your power of aspiration, taking the bearing of this responsibility as your core intent, and turning back the obstacles of madness.

Lan. It is absolutely impossible to rely on impetuous spirit or haughty temper. Furthermore, it is difficult to adapt to changing circumstances or fluctuate with the times as a skillful means (*upāya*).
This is the disposition for the wild vegetables and bamboo shoots of the mountain forests; within the Great Radiant Treasury (*mahā-āvabhāsagarbha*), there must surely be a way to rest and dwell.
What is called the mystery of the Great Way is simply difficult to transmit through words. As for this mountain recluse, I have been afflicted by decline and illness in recent years.
Written on this day. My mind is not one that will remain long in the human world; there will be no further time for us to meet in this life. To speak of it brings such bitter sorrow;
what the mountain recluse laments is not merely the affairs of the age, but rather that the Way of the Dharma has become so desolate.

Among those who rely upon me with a heart to protect the Dharma, as you, Layman, do, there are no more than a few fingers’ breadth remaining. How could it be only the *Vajradhvaja*? I, the mountain recluse, [sit] amidst the peaks...
Among his disciples in the south whom he had initiated into the seal of the mind (*yixin*), there was one named Feng Changli; he was one of the "lost writings" of the Four Masters.
Alas, it is to be regretted that he passed away prematurely (several lines are missing at the end of the text).

I have received your detailed account of recent circumstances from Xu Qingzhong, Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat, which deeply comforts my earnest thoughts. As the Sage said, "Only after the cold of winter does one know the pine and cypress.
For a man of integrity to live in this world, his will is fulfilled through many hardships. Having experienced such a trial as this, your resolve—your *gǔ*—is surely strengthened.
A firm spirit becomes supple; a strong mind and robust strength thereby perfect the late-career practice of merit and longevity.

Thus, those who encounter adversity and hardship are all means by which Heaven brings one to completion; they are all my spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). In this way, there will be more than enough cause for celebration.
Furthermore, how could there be any cause for resentment? As the saying goes: "There are things a person can forget and things they cannot forget.

That which has conferred a virtue upon me cannot be forgotten; that which has brought me grievance may be forgotten. Moreover, regarding the blessings and fortunes of human life, even the finest details are all predetermined.
Any loss or gain does not stem from others; it is all that is inherently one's own. From this point forward, you ought to maintain the Way with diligent precision.

He exerts effort to distance himself from friends who are of no benefit and to economize on expenditures that are of no benefit. In all his thoughts, he directs his mind solely toward creating merit for the future.
Truly, this is a person of immeasurable greatness. How remarkable! How remarkable!

Furthermore, I have received a series of personal letters from the Censor Huànrán, in which I clearly perceive the old layman’s concern for the state and the people, as well as his anxiety for the Dharma.

Moreover, regarding the matters you have humbly inquired about concerning this mountain monk—how could such feelings reach such a depth? Though this mountain monk is but a mere blade of grass or tree, he has long harbored [such intentions].
To aspire for transcendence is to be a loyal minister to the Dharma King and a filial son to the Compassionate Father; this is no empty talk, for it is based on what has been tested.
As for following the instructions of the Buddha’s settled vocation, I have done so throughout my life for many years. Now, unfortunately, I am approaching old age and witness the chaos of the world;
this is because I have encountered the calamities of the kalpa. How could one possibly escape the completion of one's karma? Looking back, I see no way to flee.
That which cannot be avoided is called "fixed karma" (niyata-karma). If one can escape it yet does not do so, that is merely ignorance.

How much more so when one does not regard the Dharma-gate as important, but stubbornly clings to ignorance—is this not wisdom? Having repeatedly received your enlightened instructions, I am deeply moved by your fervent resolve to protect the Dharma;
this is certainly not for the sake of this mountain monk alone. However, regarding what you have taught: if one hears even a single word of disorder, then immediately—
He overturned the meditation seat, shouted to disperse the assembly, and then withdrew. This state of frantic confusion and loss of composure is not something befitting a wise person;
this is the first reason why I, this mountain monk, cannot do as he did.

If it is said that traveling alone with a single bowl is indeed noble and eminent, yet I am nearly eighty years old and feel ashamed before Zhaozhou; this is the second reason I cannot. If it is said that the autumn moon...

If you go there to support your aged parents, you will simply be fleeing from your reputation. I have heard that the mountain ranges of the autumn moon extend for several dozen *li*, where fruits and all manner of nourishing provisions abound.
Yet, fearing that you might be unable to maintain them, you instead offered them as tribute to the royal court and sought to distribute them among the high officials.
Since they are so fond of fame in this way, how could this be a place suitable for avoiding it? If you go there, they will—
"I am a rare commodity. Furthermore, an old cow does not conceive; these four things I cannot do. Moreover, to seek fame by avoiding it is a contradiction;
when people come to me, I am like a sacred tortoise dragging its tail—these five things I cannot do.

Although the old layman’s love and concern for me are indeed earnest and deep, as a mountain monk, there are five matters in which I cannot comply with his instructions; therefore, I hesitate and do not [accept]."
One must decide for oneself. What was said previously—that even Caoxi cannot be hidden—is true if one speaks in terms of location; indeed, it cannot be hidden there.
However, if one evaluates it from the perspective of principle (*li*), this is something that the old layman has not yet understood. Nevertheless, as for saying it "cannot be hidden":
One might worry about pirates from the sea; however, Caoqi is nearly a thousand *li* from the coast, and ships do not reach there—this is the first reason for having no cause for concern.

Furthermore, although the mountains are not deeply secluded, the location is one of relative security; even if the world were in great turmoil, it would not necessarily be a place of contention—this is the second reason for having no cause for concern.
Moreover, this site of practice has already stood for a millennium and has undergone numerous changes of dynasties.

The great chaos did not exceed that of the Five Dynasties of the Tang, yet Huang Chao’s reign was the most惨烈 (catastrophic). Furthermore, when the imperial guards reached this place, they were moved by the spiritual power of the Sixth Patriarch;

they relinquished their military campsite to serve as fields for offerings and sustenance. To this day, it is known as "Huang Chao’s Estate. Thus, even a demon king served as a protector of the Dharma;
this is the third reason for being free from anxiety. Moreover, the ancestral temple and meditation hall are monastic communities established by this mountain monk.
Master Lin, throughout his entire life, this single matter alone remains as his enduring achievement. All phenomena are inherently my own; going there is like returning home.
There is no need for the arduous flight to Mount Zhongnan. This is the fourth reason for being free from worry.

Furthermore, the descendants of Caoxi are all disciples nurtured by this mountain monk; now they think of me as a compassionate father, and my going there will be like a father looking upon his children.
There is no need to rely on others; this is the fifth freedom from worry. Furthermore, as for one’s sustenance, it does not depend solely on former patrons;
even the mountain fields can be cultivated now, and vegetables and fruits can be eaten. There is no need to seek far away in the world, nor is there any need to wait for others;
this is the sixth freedom from worry. Moreover, the Sixth Patriarch’s physical remains are as if alive; he is the Dharma...
The body is eternally abiding. If one relies upon this [Dharma-body], then one takes the Dharma-realm as one's life;
if the Dharma-body perishes, then sentient beings die. This is the seventh instance of being free from sorrow.

Having heard that those who are loyal sacrifice their bodies for their country, and if they die on the frontier, they shall not perish even in death—now I, this mountain monk, vow to be a loyal minister to the Dharma-King, for the sake of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The life of wisdom is what is most important. If you remain at Mount Kuang, it is truly not a place for an elderly man seeking leisure.

Even if you maintain your fixed practice there, it would be of no benefit when death arrives. If, however, you stay at Caoxi, you may use even a single day’s leisure to instruct those who come to study, thereby continuing the life of wisdom.
To ensure that the Buddha-dharma is not interrupted, even if this mountain monk encounters great chaos, his fixed karma cannot be avoided; though he dies, he shall not perish in vain.
It would be as if one were sacrificing oneself for the state—dying for the borders and frontiers, one’s death would then be a fitting end.
How unfortunate it is! Moreover, while distancing oneself from the five things to be feared, one attains the seven things free from sorrow.

Since these are obtained within what is inherently possessed, why hesitate not to act? The local governors and provincial inspectors have already sent three letters requesting your return to the mountain for three years.
Now, this prefecture has prepared a letter and issued an official notice, dispatching a monk to invite you; they sit and wait here at the mountain.
The Sangha, having no choice but to comply, has accepted the invitation and gone.

Fearing that the elderly layman might hear of this and believe me to have violated the Great Teaching, I venture to set forth each point in detail to console his profound resolve as a protector of the Dharma.
By all means, do not be alarmed by rumors; I pray only that you will understand my heart.
I have received several letters from you, Magistrate Yuan Cangru, and I know that your heart is turned toward the Pure Land with absolute certainty. When there is no doubt, there is decisive faith.
I am most grateful, most grateful. Furthermore, you said that regarding the distance of the Pure Land from this world, the analogy of imagining India remains undecided.
However, this analogy is fundamentally not apt; the analogy of a dream is the most appropriate.
Moreover, it does not distinguish between pure and impure perceptions, which is why the principle of "mind-only" remains unclear. Only the Buddha has taught that all phenomena are like [dreams].
It is like a dream or an illusion. Furthermore, it is said that birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday.

It is also said that purity and defilement follow the mind, and that during the day one acts with the conceptualizing mind, while at night these take form in dreams. Therefore, the dream is used as a metaphor for the principle of "mind-only. Please attempt to explain this.
However, whether thoughts are defiled or pure, they are all the root of birth and death; hence it is said that "all worlds are sustained solely by thought.

Yet, while the essential point of Chan meditation is to transcend thought, the essential point of the Pure Land method is to focus exclusively on thought. This is because using thought to eliminate thought is a method of broad exchange.

Since sentient beings in their daily lives are moment-to-moment immersed in defiled thoughts, they merely create the karma of suffering within birth and death. Now, if one wishes to escape this suffering...

Therefore, in every thought-moment, one should cultivate pure perceptions and contemplate the Buddha’s Pure Land. When pure perceptions are superior, defiled perceptions vanish; when defiled perceptions vanish, pure perceptions become predominant;
and when pure perceptions are predominant, the defiled land is transformed into a Pure Land. It is like a person who, while thinking of sexual desire, dreams of lustful acts.
Although those lustful acts are illusory, they are not non-existent within the dream, and one takes them to be real. If a person [is pure]...

If one focuses exclusively on contemplating the Pure Land during the day, then at night one will dream of the transformed terraces and jeweled grounds—the realm of Ultimate Bliss—wherein one enjoys sovereign mastery;
this is then a reality. Thus, the Pure Land exists only in the distinction between dreaming and waking; how could there be any actual distance or proximity?
This is why the Buddha spoke of the "Pure Land of Mind-Only": it refers solely to the transformations evoked by a single moment of pure contemplation.
Therefore it is said: "Perceptions crystallize into a land. Yet this Sahā world, a defiled land, is entirely the result of the binding of the defiled perceptions of sentient beings;
it is purely foul and evil. Nevertheless, when the Brahma King Śikhin beholds it, he sees it as a purely pure land.
It is just like the Ganges: humans see it as clear, cool water, while hungry ghosts see it as fire. Thus, when those of the Two Vehicles behold it...
Saha is a defiled land; one feels deep aversion toward it because one does not realize that what is defiled is itself pure.

Therefore, during the assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the Buddha transformed Saha three times into a pure land. This was intended to point out that within one's daily activities and conduct—step by step, moment by moment—all is pure land.
If this is so, how could there be a distance of ten million billion lands away? Nevertheless, the sūtra says:

The phrase "ten trillion" refers to the Buddha pointing toward the Flower Treasury World (*Huāzàng Shìjiè*). To the west of this Sahā world, beyond ten trillion buddha-lands, lies the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Jílè Guó*).
This is the land of true recompense where Amitābha Buddha resides, intended merely to let people know where to turn for refuge.
If one says that all is "mind-only," then the Flower Treasury World is also mind-only; how much more so the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Please consider this through a proximate analogy.
Regarding the principle of "Mind-Only," when I was a youth in the mountains and countryside, I heard the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speak of Mount Wutai, where ice and snow remain for ten thousand years.
Consequently, I felt a deep and persistent longing to dwell on this mountain. Thus, day and night I contemplated it until, after a long time, I saw only a single snow mountain before my eyes;
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, I was always within it. Even when passing through a bustling marketplace, I did not see a single person.
Although he was traveling through the Snowy Mountains, when he later arrived at Mount Wutai, it was exactly as he had previously imagined.
Observing this, one can understand that the distance to the Pure Land is relative. Yet, while Mount Wutai requires the physical body to reach, the Pure Land requires only the mind to reach.
If one recites the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion and contemplates the realm of the Pure Land in every thought, after a long time, [the realization will become] pure.
When this is matured, it manifests in daily life; at every step and in every situation, one is as if sitting, reclining, or walking in the Pure Land.
Thus, even when hearing all manner of sounds with the ears, they are all the sound of reciting the Buddha’s name. Reciting in this manner until the end of one's life—
Then all worldly discursive thoughts will not manifest at all; there will be only the single thought of Amitābha Buddha.
Thus, one’s diligence remains undisturbed, and before one’s eyes, only the realm of the Pure Land appears.

Either lotus flowers manifest, or Amitābha Buddha and the various Bodhisattvas personally come to welcome and lead one. With the spirit and consciousness remaining tranquil, one follows the Buddha directly to be reborn there, immediately.
One immediately ascends to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, no different from the previous dream-vision. If this is so, how could there be a distance of ten million billion lands?
This is what is meant by "being born, one is certainly born; going, one truly does not go.

This is the ground of ultimate reality, not a mere matter of intellectual reasoning. It simply requires that the pure thought of a single moment reach full maturity, thereby effecting a vast exchange.

If one transcends the perception of impurity, then that defiled land will naturally transform into a pure land. Furthermore, the teaching that birth in the pure land is like a dream is not a mere metaphor;
it is a literal truth. For from the time a bodhisattva begins their practice until the seventh stage, they have not yet shattered the dream of ignorance.
Thus, all their efforts to teach and transform sentient beings and to perfect a pure land are entirely [within the realm of that dream].

Buddha-activities within a dream: thus, a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage is like one crossing a river in a dream; they have not yet attained awakening. Only upon reaching Buddhahood is one called "Greatly Awakened.
This is a clear statement, fully recorded in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, providing manifest evidence.
Yet those who have spoken of this in the past have never brought it to light. If you, Elder Layman, understand this in this assembly, then as for the distance to the Pure Land—[it is near].

All doubts have been completely purified and exhausted without remainder. However, regarding the Dharma gate of Buddha-remembrance as taught in the *Amitābha Sūtra*, "single-mindedness without distraction" is the ultimate expression.
In reality, this state is not easily attained. Elder Layman, test it within your own mind:
whether or not rebirth in the Pure Land will be realized depends solely upon observing whether or not your single thought is distracted. Thus—
Be silent and have confidence in yourself; like a person drinking water, you will naturally apply yourself with diligence.

It is said that you have long been established in the Tiantai school, yet now you seek the Pure Land teachings of the Tiantai school and the unification of the three contemplations (*sanguan*). Regarding this matter, the *Miaozong chao* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) is the most clear.

As it says in the "Household Matters" of the Tiantai school: "Although there are sixteen contemplations, when one speaks of the Buddha, all is complete. Therefore, the contemplation of the Buddha is the universal contemplation.
This very practice of contemplating and recollecting the Buddha involves maintaining the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

That is to say, at the precise moment of practicing the contemplation of the Buddha, one must completely set aside the body and mind, both internally and externally, without retaining even a single thread of thought. When the ground of the mind is like empty space and not a single dharma is perceived, this is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
Within this state of an empty mind, one utters the name of the Buddha; as soon as the thought is raised, it is the [contemplation of] provisionality (*pratītyasamutpāda-vipaśyanā*).
Contemplating the Buddha image as if it were before one’s eyes, vividly clear and unmistakable, is the contemplation of the provisional (jia-guan).
However, while in the state of correct contemplation, one reflects back upon the essence of the mind that contemplates and recollects; this essence is empty and tranquil.

Within this emptiness and tranquility, one continues to contemplate without forgetting. When one is thus neither forgetful nor attached, the single mind is luminously present; this is the contemplation of the Middle Way (zhongdao-guan). Furthermore, this...

Regarding the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*): do not employ artificial arrangement; simply raise the thought, and the three contemplations will be one mind, with a single thought fully encompassing them all.
Furthermore, within this context, you must not apply the old-fashioned arrangement of the three contemplations; to direct the mind in such a manner would not be subtle.
I ask you: how is it that you apply yourself to this? Please try it.

Furthermore, it is known that this elderly layman has resolved with great urgency upon the single matter of his own fundamental self. He realizes that the affairs of birth and death are of paramount importance;

it is precisely when such matters are urgent that one must apply oneself to the practice of investigation. Generally speaking, the method of cultivation consists solely in taking up a kōan as the focal point of inquiry. If [the mind] is great...

Master Hui advocated this most strenuously. It is known that those who attained realization in the Chan school in the past all achieved it through the practice of "raising the critical phrase" (*huatou*).
However, within this practice, there were many differences in how the mind was applied. Nowadays, the way people speak of raising the *huatou* is even more erroneous;
their application of the mind is far removed from the truth, for they know only to raise it, but do not realize that letting go is the essential subtlety. The ancients...
To let go of one thing is the most essential teaching for entering the Way. Thus, we know that the single character "to lift" (*ti*) refers to the very act of letting go;
it does not mean merely to fixate on the *huatou* (critical phrase) as "lifting. As Aśvaghoṣa said: "The essence of mind is free from thought."
It is equal to the realm of empty space. Furthermore, it is said to be a realm beyond thought, corresponding only to direct realization.

Since the essence of mind is fundamentally free from thought, people today do not recognize this freedom from thought as right mindfulness; instead, they grasp and exert themselves with a single mind.
Consequently, their confusion and distress only increase. Why is the state of letting go considered "exertion"? It is simply like taking Amitābha Buddha as...
Regarding the *huatou*: Before bringing up the word "Buddha," one must first set aside external objects;
next, one must completely set aside all internal discursive thoughts; then, one must set aside even this very thought of setting things aside.
Once you have reached the point where there is nothing further to set aside, you may then exert effort within that state to bring forth the sound of "Buddha. Then, observe this very sound.
"Where did the Buddha come from? Where does he go now? Fix the adamantine eye with total concentration and gaze intently. Gaze until there is no place to land;
then, lift it up and gaze again, pursuing it back to the point where a single thought is unborn, and you will see your original face.
At first, apply the mind to gaze and pursue; pursue until the two ends of a single thought are severed.
In the midst of this, you are alone. Turn toward this state of solitude and exert your full brilliance to pursue it directly.
Suddenly, the knot of doubt will burst asunder, and your original face will manifest of itself. This is precisely the true state of non-arising within a single thought-moment.
If a student can bring this single thought-moment of non-arising before them, they will attain great utility in all circumstances; this is indeed [the Way].

This is also the time to transcend birth and death. In recent times, people have failed to understand the point of letting go; they seek a single point of detachment from thought and stubbornly cling to the *huatou* (critical phrase) until death.
Consequently, this only increases their obstacles. Furthermore, they give rise to all manner of discursive thoughts, pre-existing with mysterious and subtle views and insights.
This is the very root of obstructing the Way. Thus, although this elderly layman’s investigation of the mind is earnest, [he is hindered by these factors].
This is because one has not yet been instructed to let go of this single point. It is merely due to the shadows of habitual tendencies toward the profound and mysterious that they act as obstacles;
thus, one is unable to enjoy its benefits. Among hundreds of thousands of skillful means, there is only this single point of letting go that is most effortless.
If one acts within this place where effort is saved, then every thought and moment of daily life is the true enjoyment. May those of lofty intelligence reflect upon this.
[Sent] to Yuan Gong Liao.
I have often remarked that those heroic men of antiquity who were able to establish great achievements and found great undertakings all emerged from within the practice of endurance.

Even for the attainment of Buddhahood, the practice of patience (*kṣānti*) is considered foremost; hence it is called "the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Among all sages and worthies, there has never been one who did not succeed through patience and fail through a lack thereof. Thus, this old man, even in his youth, read the histories.
Commentary: Upon reaching the biographies of Han Xin and Zhang Liang, one sees that these men were able to establish great undertakings; yet, observe from where they ultimately came.
By examining their deeds in detail, one suddenly encounters the humiliation Han Xin suffered at the hands of a young bully in the marketplace of Huaiyin.

Han Xin gazed intently at him, then stepped out from beneath the bully's crotch. In this instance, one sees the character "shu" (intently/gaze) in the historian’s brushwork, which captures the essence of the moment completely.
Throughout my life’s studies, when I advanced three steps upon the broken bridge, the old man finally approved me; yet at Bo-lang, my hammer was shattered by a single straw sandal.
Thus one knows where the ancients found their strength. In my old age, I have entered the Buddha-dharma through this very principle;
hence what I wrote in my previous letter—these are merely the words of a commoner from the marketplace of Huai, a mere sandal on a broken bridge.
It has been twenty years since I parted from you, the Grand Secretary Zhou Haimen. We have not exchanged news for over ten years.
Although our spirits remain undivided, nothing compares to the joy of beholding your countenance and hearing your voice. Last spring at Yunqi, I made preparations...
Having received your instructions on the lake, I waited for a long time without your arrival; thus, I returned to the mountains with a sense of regret.

By the grace of Heaven, this poor monk has been granted a remaining span of life, allowing me to await my death at Mount Kuanglu—this is a profound and great blessing. Reflecting upon this age of the Dharma’s decline, you alone, O Layman, stand as a banner of light.
This poor monk is old and the day when I may again receive your instructions has passed; all I can hope for is to meet you at the future Dragon Flower Assembly.

I understand. This poor monk has been graced by Your Majesty’s imperial bounty, which has permitted me to travel ten thousand *li*. Yet, I have contributed not even a hair’s breadth to the Dharma-gate;
as for that supreme point beyond, it is likewise unfit to be mentioned to others. Fortunately, through the eye of the teachings, I have realized the school of direct pointing.
In the three sutras—the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Śūraṅgama*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—the conventional shackles of words and letters have been thoroughly overturned.
All have already been carved into printing blocks. I entrust them to you to definitively request certification. Only within the mountains of Langye does the wild fox still hide its tracks;
I venture to beg for the Eye of Vajra to once and for all illuminate and shatter the darkness. Furthermore, this shall serve as a great auxiliary condition for this Dharma.

Preface to the Miaoming Hall of Bodhi Hermitage:
While I was residing at Bodhi Hermitage, I newly constructed a chamber for my quarters. The host requested a name for the hall, and I inscribed it as "Miaoming" (Wondrous Clarity).

The great assembly requests an exposition. The old man’s intention is to take up the two phrases from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "the nature of awareness is wondrously luminous" (*xing jue miao ming*) and "original awareness is luminously wondrous" (*ben jue ming miao*).
This is because when Pūrṇa heard that the preceding sense organs, bodies, and the vessel-world were each "pure and originally so," he gave rise to a doubt, saying:
"If they are pure and originally so, how is it that mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena suddenly arise?"

This was a challenge to the Dharma. He thought that within the pure realm, there could not possibly allow for the arising of such things. Since the World-Honored One had reached this point, it was truly difficult to find words;

therefore, he raised two phrases commonly spoken—“the nature of awareness is wondrously luminous” (*xingjue miaoming*) and “original awareness is luminously wondrous” (*benjue mingmiao*)—to interrogate him by means of a double entendre.
However, the former phrase does not pertain to delusion or enlightenment, for the innate, wondrous nature is inherently spiritual. Thus...

The phrase "the nature of clouds is wondrously bright by its very awareness" refers to that which is cultivated and perfected without being lost amidst delusion; hence it says, "fundamental awareness is bright and wondrous.
This means that although it is now perfected through cultivation, it is not obtained from without, but is rather the inherent awareness possessed by each individual.
By interrogating [the interlocutor] with these two statements, the Buddha’s intention was to use the pivotal juncture between delusion and awakening to bring about his enlightenment.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra mistakenly takes the single phrase "the original enlightenment is luminous and wondrous" as his attainment.

He assumes that the fundamental awakening is inherently spiritual, wondrous, and luminous, requiring no further illumination. This view, however, possesses only the "luminosity that illuminates," yet lacks the "awakening that is illuminated.
His intention lies in an awakening that has something to be illuminated; this is precisely where he errs. Little does he realize that the moment there is something to be illuminated...
Once there is this "awakening," the infinite illusory phenomena of subject and object in mutual opposition arise from it.

Because all sentient beings undergo birth and death after death, every phenomenon arises from within the pure realm; yet, without cause, they forcibly give rise to a single thought, seeking to clarify that awakening.
However, because there is both clarity and awakening, subject and object remain distinct. Therefore, what follows is the elucidation of this subject-object duality.
When delusive phenomena are clearly and distinctly perceived, one profoundly exhausts the source of the Dharma-nature. This monastery is named Bodhi;
"Bodhi" is a Sanskrit term, which here means "Awakening. While everyone knows of the Buddha realized through cultivation, they do not know the Buddha that is inherently possessed.

The old man’s intent lies in true cultivation, which first requires the realization of the nature that is never deluded. Therefore, although one cultivates the myriad practices, [the goal is this awakening].
To not fall into ordinary sentiments is to not depart from the present moment and yet suddenly realize Bodhi.
This lies in first awakening to the wondrous luminosity as one's initial resolve; therefore, it is used to name the hall.

Preface on the Circumstances of the Reconstruction of Tiansheng Temple in Huzhou The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* describes the Buddha-lands of the ten directions as being like the interstices of Indra’s net suspended in space.

Whether in a state of formation, abiding, destruction, or emptiness, they all share the same single limit (*ekānta*). All Buddhas and the ocean-like assemblies of Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma therein, providing instruction.
They transform sentient beings. Their various supernormal powers and wondrous functions fill every place simultaneously, like the interlacing light of pearls on a net;
each shines with the others without confusion and without obstruction.

Yet, within the wisdom-light of all Buddhas' minds, all sentient beings—whether adorning Buddha-lands and taming beings, or committing the ten evils and the five heinous crimes within the three realms—are [contained therein].
The six realms of existence and the performance of good and evil karma are not known by those within them;
hence it is said that the realm of the Buddha is inconceivable, and the mental activities of sentient beings are inconceivable. Now, at Tiansheng Temple by the lake, all of this is clearly seen.
At the end of the Jiawu year, the temple monk Zuding visited me at the Maitreya Pavilion in the capital and we happened to discuss the history and circumstances of the temple.
It is said: "Its hall is vast and expansive, like empty space; yet its adornments are dense and intricate, with bracket-capitals clustered together and tiered eaves overlapping like a net.

On its two central pillars, dragons were carved from wood; their heads, horns, whiskers, eyebrows, claws, and fangs appeared so lifelike and dynamic that they seemed like living dragons.

Carrying a heavy broken stele, he opened it and read it. It was from the Zhonghe era of the Tang dynasty, concerning how the lay practitioner Wu Yan donated his residence to become a temple.

Viewed from this perspective, the formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness of that Buddha-land are already inconceivable; yet, by examining the individuals therein, one further perceives the donors and the makers.
Those that have been formed, those that abide, those that are adorned, and those that are destroyed— the various and differing mental activities of good and evil—
all suddenly manifest with brilliant clarity within the great light of the Buddhas' wisdom, like images appearing in a mirror, without the slightest detail being obscured.

The relationship between cause and effect is manifest; in sum, all of it is inconceivable. At the outset, the mind of one who is forming does not know that there will be a mind of one who is destroying;

Thus, the former formation is the cause of the subsequent destruction, and the former destruction is the condition for the subsequent formation. If one contemplates the mind by directly observing its objects, this is precisely so.

You have already reached the age of sixty; what more is there to wait for? If you were to pass away now, would you not regret it later? Moreover, the Buddha’s teaching is vast and profound, yet its essence is simple and direct. It is like a person who has lost their way: they need only find the correct path and follow it. What else is required?

Do not let your thoughts be distracted by external circumstances. If you can maintain a single thought of mindfulness without interruption, that itself is the Way. This is the most urgent matter for you at present. He then took leave of me and returned home. Soon after, he received the precepts from Master Zhixu and subsequently passed away peacefully. He was reborn in the Pure Land. This is truly a case of "the merit of a single thought being greater than the merit of a hundred years of practice. How could this not cause one to rejoice? This is recorded here to encourage those who seek the Way. *Recorded by the monk Yinyuan.* *Postscript:* I have heard that the layman Tang Yangxing was originally a man of the world who enjoyed wine and women. Later, he encountered the teachings of Master Yunqi and began to cultivate his mind. He eventually became a disciple of Master Zhixu and attained the Way. This is truly a rare example of transformation.

It is said that when he first came to see me, he had not yet renounced worldly life. I told him: "If you wish to attain liberation, you must first sever the roots of desire. If you do not cut them off, you will never be able to escape the cycle of birth and death. Even if you study the scriptures and treatises extensively, it will be of no benefit. You must first resolve to abandon all worldly attachments and devote yourself solely to the practice of the Way. He followed my advice and subsequently left the household life. This is indeed a testament to the power of the Dharma. May this serve as an inspiration for all.
In the past, the Buddha had no son, yet he regarded all sentient beings of the triple world as his only child; thus, to this day, everyone calls him the "Compassionate Father.
Layman, why do you not apply the same mind with which you think of your own son toward all sentient beings?

If you do so, the title of "Compassionate Father" will fill the worlds of the ten directions in the future. For now, you should instead contemplate those who have already been delivered, who dwell in the three...

Master Tan, you are able to build a protective barrier to guard [this place]. If you cause the sentient beings within it to be like those in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, then all present here will call you their "Compassionate Father.
What need is there then to wait for the future? We pray that you, Layman, will lead the way.
Yet those who wish to become compassionate fathers are many. This, then, is the celestial palace and the pure land; why abandon what is before one’s eyes to seek elsewhere?
Upon hearing this once, every wise person will be moved by ten thousand feelings, without waiting for the words to end.
The old man has great expectations in this regard.
