Preface for the Bestowal of the Title of *Senglù Juéyì* upon Master Wújìn and His Appointment as Abbot of the Jìngtǔ Chányuàn in Píngyáng (Composed within the Circle).
In the twenty-third year of the Great Sage Emperor’s reign of non-interference (*yíròu*), due to famine throughout the four quarters and many disturbances in the east and west, the Ministry...

The granaries were reported to be exhausted. An edict was issued to grant a great amnesty, decreeing that among the common people of the countryside, anyone possessing talent or skill who wished to offer their services for a single cut [of the sword] might, according to established precedent, remit grain as tribute and be granted an official post of varying rank.

This applied regardless of whether they were within or outside the orthodox fold; even followers of the two [Buddhist and Daoist] traditions were included therein. The monk Wujin was of the Yang clan of Pingyang in Jin.
In his youth, he shaved his head at Jingtu Temple in the prefecture. Always aspiring toward the ultimate, he carried his staff across a hundred cities to visit and consult various masters.
He refined his practice at Niufeng and realized the enlightenment of Shaoshi. He withdrew to Zhongnan Mountain, where he received the transmission from Wuding.

He established a Dharma society of fifty-three members and exhausted the twelve divisions of the ocean of teachings. Having thoroughly investigated the single mind and fully traversed the myriad practices, he happened to pass through his native village.
There, the local magistrates, elders, lay devotees, and the fourfold assembly requested that he preach the Dharma.

They each contributed gold, following the imperial precedent of making offerings, and he was granted the title of *Jueyi* (Enlightened Meaning) in the Office of Buddhist Records (*Senglü*) and appointed as the abbot of Jingtu Temple.

Abbot: It is our supreme reliance that the state’s prestige and authority serve as the ground for protecting the Dharma, so that the bridge of salvation may be widely spread and the path to enlightenment fully opened.
The eminent monasteries and masters of the capital, such as those like the Venerable Jingzhan and Jie Shangren, all offer congratulations upon this singular method and Way.
I beg you to grant me your wisdom by composing a preface to present to them, saying: "I have heard that when the Great Hero (Mahāvīra) governed the world..."
His traces appeared in Kapilavastu, and his Way spread throughout the three realms. In establishing his teachings, he took as his principle pure transcendence of the world;

through its vastness and perfect fusion, there is nothing it does not encompass. Thus, he manifests bodies without discriminating among classes of beings, benefiting others according to their respective regions.

The resonance between his capacity and their response reflects one another like the moon appearing when the water is clear, occurring without the intervention of discursive thought—just like Avalokiteśvara’s Universal Gate, as seen by Sudhana.
By universally honoring these [deities], one observes that the Dharma which transcends the world is indeed detached from the world.

Therefore, to explain the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) without destroying conventional designations (*prajñapti*) lies in the wondrous realization of the single mind (*ekacitta*), whereby all phenomena (*dharmas*) are suddenly integrated.

One realizes *tathatā* through the very truths of worldly convention (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and attains the ultimate fruit by means of manifold practices; certainly not by sitting idly in non-action or becoming mired in the intoxication of silent extinction.
Cessation is attainment. Since the transmission of the Dharma flowed eastward from Han times until the present, more than two thousand years have passed.

Regardless of how far the teaching of the Elephant Vehicle has spread, those who have practiced according to the Dharma—employing both provisional and ultimate truths in tandem to manifest its Way—have not been few.
Consequently, throughout successive dynasties, the rulers of the realm have honored the Teaching and esteemed its practitioners; their regulations, however, have varied.
It was our Sage Ancestor, the Divine Founder, who established the enterprise and transmitted the legacy. His laws and institutions were detailed and exhaustive, encompassing every minute point.
As his followers multiplied, he established offices to govern them: the *Senglü* (Registrar of Monks) was appointed in the two capitals to oversee all prefectures and counties;

each prefecture and county established its own *Senggang* (Monastic Head) and *Zhenghui* (Ecclesiastical Administrator) to lead the various monasteries. Their ranks differed according to their selection based on spiritual practice.

Regarding those who excel in both [worldly and spiritual matters], they are granted their offices in succession, each with its specific domain of responsibility. The reason for this is that one relies upon worldly laws (*saṃvṛti-dharma*) to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma;
the essential point is precisely to realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) by means of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Those entrusted with these duties generally take the propagation of the Dharma and the benefiting of sentient beings as their primary task—just as in antiquity, those who spread the Way throughout a region were appointed to such roles—and it is certainly not for any other purpose.

Renown and status are matters of worldly glory. Now, as for the Venerable Master Wujin, his aspirations transcend the dust of the mundane world and his traces surpass those beyond the conventional realm.
That which he has used to illuminate the supreme truth of the Ultimate Meaning (paramārtha-satya) is surely something to be kept secret;

yet, the sincerity with which the fourfold assembly looks toward him is like the resonance within a bell—its sound issues forth. How could this be so without substance? There must certainly be something extraordinary about him.
In human conduct, how could one compare those who grasp at provisional names while remaining ignorant of the true nature of reality? As the Sūtra says:

"If one seeks the Dharma through sounds or physical forms, one does not see the Dharma. Therefore, I say: if these fourfold assemblies now seek Bodhi through sound and form, they fail the Superior One;
and if the Superior One preaches the Dharma while clinging to provisional names, he too fails them.
The fourfold assembly has heard this: those who fail their teacher fall; those who fail the assembly are arrogant.
If one possesses even one of these faults, how can they clarify the sun-like Buddha and repay the kindness of the imperial court for protecting the Dharma? My elder brother is now departing.

Should his path lead him through the Golden World (Suvarṇabhāsa), may he take the words of this sick old man from Vārāṇasī and verify them with Mañjuśrī, so that they may be proclaimed to the great assembly.
"May each of you, by means of these provisional names, realize the true nature of reality. By relying on this bridge, may you all suddenly transcend to the other shore.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they paid their respects and departed.
Preface to Sending Master Jian on a Journey to Bāgūi The Master has been a renunciant for many years.
It was originally through attending upon an elder that he gave rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta.
Recently, together with several fellow practitioners, he invited Mr. Ouyang Boyu to jointly establish the Dharma-flower Society at the Bodhi Tree, seeking its protection and shade.
Day by day he attained the joy of cool serenity. Every half-month, he would invite the Elder to sit beneath a tree upon the Bodhi seat;
there, waving his fly-whisk, he expounded for the assembly the Dharma-practice for advancing toward the cultivation of unsurpassed Bodhi. Thus it continued from spring until summer.
Four months have already passed. The Master of the Mountain bows and says that he intends to depart for Bāguì to visit an old friend amidst the green mountains and white clouds.
Furthermore, he wishes to travel as a wandering monk, following circumstances wherever he may encounter them to deliver beings, so that all who hear of him or see him may be inspired.
They all gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled bodhi. This is the first step upon the bridge leading out of the mundane world.
The old man spoke to them with joy, saying: "Excellent, O sons of the Buddha! You should know that whatever the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do, they always act for a single purpose;
namely, to teach and transform sentient beings through this bodhicitta—this is the one great matter."
This is to emerge from birth and enter into death; for this reason and by this cause, there is nothing else besides this single matter.

Even if one must traverse perilous paths and undergo all the tribulations of the three miserable realms, as long as one can cause even a single person to resolve upon Bodhicitta, one will willingly endure all such manifold sufferings.
Therefore, the conduct of the sages is not in vain; their deeds are entirely real, whether pertaining to the mundane or the supramundane.
At rest, there is not a single dharma that surpasses this bodhicitta. It is that which practices this bodhicarya and performs these bodhisattva deeds.
That which is called "bodhi" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "awakening" (jue). Awakening is the buddha-nature inherently possessed by all sentient beings;
it is numinous awareness, tranquil and illuminating, and is therefore called "true awakening. Because it is clearly and spontaneously realized, it is so named.
He is named the Solitary Realizer (*pratyekabuddha*). Because he has attained a brilliant and great penetration, shattering the dense darkness, he is called the Great Awakened One (*mahābuddha*).

Yet, though it is used daily, one does not know it; thus it is called "non-awakening" (*abodhi*). To be in a state of non-awakening is to be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); an ordinary person is precisely a sentient being (*sattva*).

This is because every sentient being possesses this nature of spiritual awakening (*jñāna-dhātu*), yet they do not know it while using it daily. Alas! Though they possess it, they do not [realize it].
Do you understand? Is this not to be pitied? If one does not know, one cannot apply it;

if one cannot apply it, it is like holding a jewel while acting as a beggar, or carrying treasure while lost in a foreign land—needlessly enduring hardship, rushing through birth and death, and willingly falling into the ocean of suffering. Is this not to be pitied?
Therefore, the Sage does not pity that which is not to be pitied, but specifically pities that which is worthy of pity; for this reason, he appears in the world.
At leisure, he employs various skillful means to guide them. This is what is meant by being self-awakened and able to awaken others—that is, the previously awakened awakening those who awaken later.
Now, one who is self-awakened is not deluded regarding phenomena; one who awakens others does not abandon phenomena. Being undeluded, they integrate phenomena into themselves;
not abandoning them, they relinquish themselves to follow others. Because they integrate [phenomena] into themselves, they do not...

When one perceives external objects, one fails to see the self within them. If there were no objects, then all things would be wondrous; if there were no self, then this single self would not be real.
Knowing that the self is not real, the self is identical to objects. Knowing that all objects are wondrous, objects are identical to the Real.
When objects are identical to the Real, then objects are not objects and the self is not a self. When both object and self are non-existent, they are transcended.
Coming into the signless, all conditions are darkly tranquil and the single Way is empty and at ease;
this is the heart-essence of the Great Awakened One and the sublime practice of all Bodhisattvas. Thus, the two types of awakening are complete and the two benefits are fulfilled;

this is what is meant by manifesting various dignified demeanors through the practice of quiescent extinction, benefiting others according to circumstances, and thereby constituting the sublime practice for Bodhi. Otherwise, [one would merely] drive...
Rushing along perilous paths, wading and climbing through mountains and rivers, one exhausts the muscles and bones and brings hardship to the physical form;

this increases feverish affliction, damages the roots of goodness, and prolongs existence in the realms of suffering—it is not the means by which to accomplish Bodhi or the work of transforming sentient beings.

As for the superior man’s practice: when tracing the current upstream, amidst the vast, azure clouds and mountains, everything before one's eyes is a realm of truth; where monkeys cry out and cranes shriek.
All that fills the ears is the True Scripture; the Man, Yao, and Orang-utangs encountered are all the True Buddha; the flowing water and swaying winds are all the broad and long tongue;
the azure sky and white moon are all the Pure Body. To awaken thus is for every place to be a site of Bodhi.
Step by step is the Land of Ultimate Bliss; thought after thought is true cultivation; matter by matter is true practice.

Why, then, calculate the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane, or differentiate between self-benefit and benefiting others? Can you, Venerable Sir, believe and accept these words of an old man?
If you have any doubts, when you pass through Mount Xiang, I ask that you consult the Buddha of Infinite Life regarding them.

Preface by the Head of the Sangha, Mount Ilsan, Venerable Gyeong, in the fourth year of my exile to the coastal regions of the mountain ranges, on the full moon of the seventh month in the autumn of Jihai (1459).
At that time, the Head of the Sangha residing at Beopseongsa Temple was Mount Ilsan, Venerable Gyeong, sixty-one years of age. At that moment, the civil officials were residing within the city.
The lay devotees and the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus each held incense and flowers to make offerings, offering prayers for the Venerable Master.

At that time, it was the period of the summer retreat’s *pravāraṇā*. The Venerable Master also established a *Ullambana* Dharma assembly to feed the monks of the ten directions, following the precedent set by Maudgalyāyana, thereby repaying his filial debt to his parents and requiting their boundless kindness. At that time, I was lecturing on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* for the assembly.
The *Gaxin jing* (Sūtra on the New Year) concludes; it is precisely for this reason that it is considered a Buddha-work (*buddhakārya*).

Hearing that the Venerable One has given rise to such a mind, I rejoice and praise him, saying: "As for the lifespan of worldly people, it does not transcend the marks of self, person, sentient being, or life-span—these are what are called the 'marks of a self' (*ātmagrāha*).
Our Buddha did not accept them, nor do the Saṃgha abide in them. Yet, what the Buddha accepts is the life of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*)."

"Abiding" refers to *dharmavarṣa* (dharma-ordination age). Thus, eminent monks of antiquity spoke of both "worldly age" (*shishou*) and "dharma-ordination age. This does not depend on the number of years;

rather, it is based on the initial reception and upholding of the precepts. Completing one three-month period of *an-shu* (rainy season retreat) with the essence of the precepts (*jieti*) remaining intact constitutes one *varṣa*.

Because it is by *kaṭhina* robes and not by years that seniority is determined, there are those who are advanced in years yet have few *kaṭhina* robes, and those who are young in years yet possess the longevity of the aged.

In all cases, the *kaṭhina* robe is honored because it takes the precepts as its foundation. Since the precepts are the foundation, they are what sustain the Buddha’s life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*).
Therefore, when the root of the precepts is pure, the life of wisdom is radiant; when the foundation of the precepts is firm, the life of wisdom is long. As the Sūtra says:
If a person receives the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the number of the Buddhas.

Furthermore, since the lifespan of a Buddha is immeasurable, yet it is said that one attains this all at once upon ascending to the stage of the precepts—is this not because one takes self-nature purity as the Buddha and realizes self-nature purity as the Sangha?
This is precisely what is meant by "continuing the Buddha's life of wisdom. It is for this reason alone that our Buddha preached the Dharma for forty... [years].
In the nineteenth year, at the very end, he held up a flower and transmitted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Mahākāśyapa.
After twenty-eight transmissions, it reached Bodhidharma. Bodhidharma came by sea;

when he first arrived in Wuyang, it so happened that previously, during the Song dynasty, Guṇabhadra had brought four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to this place and established a precept platform there. When Bodhidharma arrived, he necessarily...
He relied upon it. Furthermore, when the Second Patriarch was transmitted [the Dharma], he pointed to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* as the "mind-seal.

Later, when Zhiyao brought a branch of the Bodhi tree and planted it beside the altar, he said: "In one hundred and sixty years, a Great Being in flesh-and-blood will renounce the world beneath this tree and expound the Supreme Vehicle.
When the Sixth Patriarch subsequently manifested his origins here, it was as if two tally-sticks had met. This continued until...
Today, our school is divided into five branches, and its Way covers the entire world; all take this temple as their primary ground.

Thus, the Dharma of Bodhidharma has not perished, and the true body of the Sixth Patriarch still remains. Is this not because the root of his precepts was firm and the life of his wisdom was prolonged?
From antiquity to the present, it shall endure forever and ever. Therefore, a sutra says: "The sons of the Buddha dwell here."

This land is where the Buddha himself enjoyed his realization. Now that you, O Superior One, dwell upon this ground and preside over this Sangha, beholding the Sixth Patriarch as if he were alive—how could this be anything less than a minor cause?
When I first entered Guangdong, I arrived at that temple and knocked upon its gate; though I called out a second time, there was no response.
Yet now, less than three years since I have resided here, the monks are gathered in great numbers, all harmonious and united at once, regardless of their age.
The young ones all gave rise to the bodhicitta; their ears and eyes were suddenly and brilliantly renewed.

Is it that the buddha-nature of these people was non-existent before and only now exists? It is simply that the buddha-nature is inherently possessed by every person, yet they lack the guidance of a teacher.
As for the merit of such guidance, it depends on the leader’s diligent practice; then the fourfold assembly will respond with joy and gratitude, like the falling of seasonal rain. Oil...
Yet it flourishes and thrives, though he himself is unaware of how this comes to be. Now, at the age of sixty-one, the Master has suddenly given rise to such a mind and undertaken such practices:

he repays his parental kindness through Buddhist service, takes pure precepts as the foundation of his longevity, and is further able to draw near to spiritual friends and practice in accordance with them.
If future disciples were merely to observe the Master’s state of mind...
If you emulate the conduct of the Master from youth until old age, and pass it down from son to grandson, then this transformation will be infinite and this source inexhaustible.
Should a "Sixth Patriarch" ever arise and suddenly restore the former glory, the opportunity for the renaissance of this Dharma would likewise lie in this very day.
The Master’s merit is immeasurable; indeed, it is the very life-force of the Dharma.
It is inexhaustible. How could it be compared to the trivial span of a worldly life?

Thereupon, he commanded his disciples, including the layman Tong’an Ou Qihong and others, each to hold incense and flowers, to once again proclaim this meaning as a long-life offering for the Venerable Master.
Preface to the Return of Chan Practitioner Yunsu Wenyu to Mount Jinshan:
Since my youth, I have harbored the ambition to travel afar, yet illness has prevented me from doing so. In the Jisi year of the Longqing era (1569), I purchased a boat and visited Mount Jinshan.

I have long cherished this ten-thousand-li river flow, where a fist-sized rock props up the void, standing solitary and independent like a true man, possessing a majestic air of towering toward heaven and standing firm upon the earth.
Master Shanzhu, along with Masters Tong, Min, and Zhi, welcomed me; I resided there for two years.
My disciples who followed me were numerous. Whenever I had finished my meals, I would join one or two eminent gentlemen to shake out our robes and wash our feet by the stream.
Beneath the bright moon high in the sky, the autumn waters and the vast heavens form a single expanse of empty void;
it is truly as if one were treading upon crystal while gazing into a suspended mirror. Since our parting, more than forty years have passed; when I recall it now, it seems as vividly as a dream.

For twelve years in the deep and stagnant miasma of the frontier, I have drunk the smoke of barbarian lands and eaten the poison of the mists, rushing through the burning house and sitting amidst the scorching heat.
Whenever I harbor such thoughts, my skin breaks out in goosebumps and my very marrow feels a refreshing coolness.

Thus, I have long used this stone by the flowing stream as a pillow and for rinsing my mouth amidst the thatched huts and earthen walls, serving as an efficacious remedy for dispelling the dust of the world and unraveling my vexations.
How regrettable that we are separated by ten thousand *li*, our kin and old friends having withered away and grown sparse, while news and correspondence have become distant and rare.

I often wonder whether the moonlight and the sound of the tide atop Mount Miaogao, upon the Stone of Sudhana (*Sudhana-śilā*), can still evoke the flavor of those years; yet there is no way to inquire after them.
Toward the end of spring in the year of Dingwei, I was graced by the Emperor’s clemency and traveled to Duanzhou to pay my respects to the Regional Commander (*Zhifu*), receiving his official decree.
In Lei Yang, having concluded the aforementioned matters, I returned to Wuyang to pay my respects to the Provincial Judicial Commissioner and await further instructions.
While my boat was moored on the banks of the Zhujiang River, a venerable monk arrived from Yuzhang bearing a letter from Grand Councilor Ding Gong.

Opening the envelope and reading it with urgency, I learned that he was the grandson of Jinshan Xuzhou Yin Gong. Moved by old memories and stirred by nostalgia, I truly felt as the saying goes: [The text here would continue with the poetic sentiment.]
His heart was so overwhelmed with joy that he wept until his sleeves were drenched with tears. Alas! A lifetime passes in a world where years and months shift and change;
when one looks back upon this human realm, it is but a dream and an illusion. Once my affairs are concluded, I shall return to the mountains, and Master Wen will accompany me to Caoxi.
Now I shall speak of my return. I have thus recounted past events and recorded my sentiments since our parting, to express my gratitude to my old friends.

Furthermore, I entrust these greetings to the spirits of the mountains and the Lord of the Sea. I am about to turn my oars toward the head of the Yangtze River to once again visit the ancient sites of the Three Mountains.
I pray that you will drive away the Wind Earl to clear the river's currents, sweep away the floating clouds to release the bright moon, and welcome me.
Upon the Terrace of Mount Sumeru, sitting within the Laṅkā hall, he expounded the dharma-realm of the ocean-like storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
He resolved the unsolved kōan concerning Master Su and Zhang Fangping; if Steady Master (Wenyi) maintains this, he will surely not suffer any loss amidst the rice basket and the clay alms bowl.
Should anyone ask about me, report this for me: my beard and hair are now already white with age. There is no more.
It is as if one were once again smelling the "gruel-and-rice" air of his youth.
Preface to the Return of General Wu to Yue:
When the General was young, he followed his father’s service into Guangdong, his ambition set upon the frontiers. Having traversed mountains and seas, he struck down and pacified bandits and rebels.
There was no service he did not undertake; there was no battle he did not conquer. He viewed precipices as level ground and returned from deep abysses as if ascending a hill.

Regarding all the chieftains of the islands, their circumstances were fully detailed. When the Eastern Japanese (Wakoku) incited the rebellion, those who discussed it regarded the vast ocean as if it were the Ninth Heaven, and viewed its flames as if entering a mass of fire.
The Commandant of the Two Yue (Guangdong and Guangxi), Lord Sima, consulted daily with his subordinates, yet they were all rendered helpless.

There was no strategy. At that time, the General was recommended to go and scout the situation; he obtained a full understanding of the matter from beginning to end, and the eastern campaign was subsequently pacified.
Upon his return, he reported that his former master had already been lost. The General’s merit remained ultimately unable to proclaim itself;

he could only follow in the ranks of the common soldiers, never again daring to speak of the affairs of the world. Nevertheless, both superiors and subordinates all recognized the General’s capability, yet in the end they were unable to bring him to prominence.
He was a general. Whenever he encountered the entanglements of bandits and rebels, those in authority would all insistently say, "General!
General!"—regretting only that they did not have the General seated upon the seat of Duke Wei. Once the matter was settled, they would say, "It was not that I lacked the ability.
If anyone at that time spoke of the General, they would all say, "The General, the General indeed! Thus, the General’s reputation was established through these very circumstances.
I loathe being born [into this world], for it can bring about calamity; indeed, there have been several occasions when I nearly failed to escape it.

At such times, those who were previously called "General" or "General"—they all prided themselves on their adherence to the rules and standards, yet they feared that their penetration into the nature of the General was not deep enough. Alas!
Such are the affairs of the world; how could I dare again speak of the matters of a great man?
When the southern barbarians violated the mandate of obedience, the faces of all those who eat the meat of office turned dark with anxiety. At that time, you, General, were within the prison cell.

I considered who might shoulder the burden of the frontier, and found no one else but you, General; thus, I repeatedly entreated for your release and provided every means of protection to establish you there.
As the vanguard, the General breached heavy surges and ascended steep ridges, engaging in successive battles as far as Huafeng. He attacked nests and destroyed lairs.
General Yang knew the General well; thus, he did not conceal his abilities, and the General’s achievements in decapitating, slaying, and capturing were foremost among the ranks.
Ultimately, the General perished from illness after completing the task, having exhausted both body and mind in a single, selfless undertaking.
How rare such a person has been! From this, one knows that the General’s destiny is likewise extraordinary. When the General reached this point, he also deeply realized his own misfortune;
thus, he carried his wife on his back and wore his son upon his head as he returned home, intending to wander the Five Lakes. The General is but a man of the dusty world;
it was not out of personal admiration or shared spirit that I permitted myself to acknowledge him. It was merely because of the ant that rouses its arms in defiance.
To oppose a chariot track with one's bare hands—who would not know their strength was insufficient? Yet, to meet it with a single burst of wrath is not a matter of physical force.
By this, I know the General to be like Jiufang’s appraisal of horses: how could one exhaustively judge a horse's true nature by its gender or its color—black or yellow?
It is for this reason that I lament those in the world who judge by outward appearance alone, who are so narrow-mindedly preoccupied with the superficial.
It was not because of my hair color that I addressed you as "General. When you were passing by Caoxi and were about to part from me, we happened to meet again on the river;
we stayed together for two nights and three days, and I composed this poem to express our farewell. It was not because the General was capable of soaring high that I did so.
My words fall short of my meaning, and my laughter does not reside in the speech itself.
Preface to Zhouzi’s "Wu Yipian" (One Chapter on Awakening).

Zhouzi, styled Hiyen and surnamed Ruyu, was a native of Taishan County. For three generations his family had been orphaned and impoverished; he was profoundly filial and devoted himself to the study of geomancy (kan-yu) with great diligence.
Among the renowned dukes and great personages within the realm, there were none who did not humble themselves and incline their hearts [toward him].

His credibility was like an echo in a valley, for his words were verified and his affairs never failed. Thus, they listened to him as if to a voice; his extraordinary manifestations were not limited to one.

At the end of autumn in the year of Jia-mao, following the commission of Ren, the Prefect of Shao, he entered Caoxi. Caoxi is the dwelling place of the Dharma-body of the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch. Its...

Mount San was first opened at the beginning of the Liang dynasty. The divine monk, Master Jiaye, declared it to be no different from the Jewel Forest (Ratnavana) in the Western Heaven—a world-transcending site of practice.
Because it had fallen into decay, I privately harbored doubts about this. I questioned Zhouzi on the matter, and Zhouzi said: "It is because the Yin and Yang do not follow the proper course.
Since it comes from the left and departs to the right, it begins large and ends small; this is precisely why [the decline occurred]."
With a single word, all doubts and stagnations were instantly resolved. From this, we know that Zhouzi’s discourse on the "Form School" (Xingjia) was not merely about physical form.

Upon reading the various chapters such as "Awakening to Oneness," one sees even more clearly that Zhouzi attained the truth of his own nature (*svabhāva*), and merely used form as a means to reveal its profound mysteries.
I once read a poem by Wang Wei which says: "Mountains and rivers are within the eye of the celestial deity; the world is the Dharma-body."

Furthermore, the eye cannot cling to even a speck of dust, yet it is said to "contain mountains and rivers. The Dharma-body cannot be characterized by physical form, yet it is said to "encompass the world.
Viewed from this perspective, how can it be described in terms of form or color? This principle is subtle;

it is cautioned that it cannot be transmitted through words, but must be realized through wondrous awakening. Thus, when Zhouzi discussed mountains and rivers, he necessarily rooted his argument in [the *Zhongyong*].
True Qi. True Qi gathers to form shape, much like the human body, which necessarily possesses a network of blood vessels throughout.

Where these vessels converge, they form orifices (xue). Thus, when a person is born, if a disease is treated by needling at the correct orifice, it is sufficient to open the way between life and death.
When a person dies, if the burial site is chosen such that the "thousand-path" (qian) hits the correct orifice, it is sufficient to transform misfortune into good fortune.
This is indeed its underlying principle. As the saying goes: "Heaven and earth share a single root; the myriad things are one body. Thus, the great earth is a single form;

yin and yang are a single breath; death and life are of one essence. To view the great earth through the lens of a single breath is like seeing the ox as a whole before the butcher's knife has been applied;
to view death and life through the lens of a single pore is like seeing the pulse without missing a single hair. If one proceeds from a single leaf...
Behold the Yang-spring (the season of spring): therein the work of transformation does not require so much as a single thread.

From this, we know that Zhouzi’s observation of form does not reside in the form itself, but in that which causes the form to exist. To trace its origin: the four great elements each pervade everywhere, and the five phases mutually integrate.
All things are rooted in nature and emotion (*xingqing*). From the obscurity of nature arises emptiness; this is the Supreme Ultimate (*taiji*). Emptiness, being dark, coagulates into form;

thus do the four elements and the five physical forms undergo transformation. This is the basis of form. Nature transforms to produce form, and heaven and earth thereby find their positions. The *Zhuan* says:

"When one attains the perfection of centrality and harmony, heaven and earth find their places and the myriad things flourish. This is the ultimate of principle. Internally and externally, the five...
All phenomena originally arise from one source; the sentient and the insentient share a single substance. When a person is born, they move and possess consciousness.
Those who attain the center of Heaven and Earth will, within their own bodies, be intelligent, sagacious, and successful. Therefore, when they die...
When one is still yet possesses spirit, and attains the harmony of mountains and rivers, then blessings, longevity, and well-being will be bestowed upon their descendants.
That Heaven and Man possess unified virtue is a principle of extreme subtlety. Is this not precisely what is meant by the saying that "burying [the dead] rides upon the vital energy" (*shengqi*)?
By this, I know that those in the world who are deluded by geomancy (*kan-yu*) and recklessly propound theories of calamity and fortune all fail to recognize this One.
This is for that reason. Zhouzi’s realization of the One was not merely for the sake of geomancers (xingjia), nor was his method intended as a discourse for those seeking auspicious forms.
Rather, it was fundamentally rooted in the person and sought the nature (xing) within. Therefore, he titled it "Realizing the One" (Wuyi).
How profound! Thus, regarding theories of form, there was none before Zhouzi who could reveal the secrets of the ancients, and none after him...

Master Zhou was unable to grasp the true nature of yin and yang. I, however, maintain that his writings are worthy of transmission; therefore, I have read them repeatedly with deep immersion and focused my attention upon them.
I have specially composed this preface to bring them to light.
Preface to the Gift for the Elder of Tàihé The elder’s origins are unknown.
With a magnificent beard bristling upward, he carries a staff across his shoulder and travels throughout all quarters.

He performs Buddhist rites wherever he goes and points the way to liberation wherever he arrives. Those who see his form turn their hearts toward the Way, and those who hear his voice are released from their bonds; the number of such people is beyond reckoning.
They numbered in the hundreds of millions. Moving like clouds and birds, they drifted across the ridges to visit the region of Yue.
I observed their hair, disheveled and wild; their twin pupils were bright and piercing, radiant as brilliant stars. Their voices resonated like bells.

Listening to their discourse, it was as wind-born and as swift as a flash of lightning. According to what was appropriate for each, they manifested their bodies and preached the Dharma, examining their faculties.
Regarding human nature, he delivers beings according to the specific means by which they should be liberated. Toward the Confucians, he reveals the principle of exhausting one's nature;
toward the Daoists, he opens the pivot of the profound and mysterious; and toward the Buddhists, everything he does is nothing other than a Buddha-act.
Even as for the various heterodox spirits and external paths, those with iron bellies and the swamps of water—there were none whose blades did not meet his edge or whose points he did not crush;
they would merely look upon his banner and cease their drums. Thus, his Way was never bestowed in vain, and his words were never uttered in vain.

Like the archery of Yang You or the lute-playing of Shi Wen—drawing the arrow to meet the string, or the tuning pegs emerging from the water—for such instances, one could not even calculate the number of hundreds of thousands of followers. Moreover,
His mind was vast and open, entirely free from obstruction; he did not bring anything with him when coming, nor did he leave anything behind when departing.
Is this not what is meant by those of old who attained the liberation of non-obstruction? I have roamed and played with this elder in the midst of the vast, boundless wilderness.
He roamed at ease through the vast wilderness, unaware that this body existed within heaven and earth, nor that external objects existed within this body.
His spirit was tranquil and his mind intoxicated; he was as if dazed or as if in a stupor.

Just as the old man was about to drag his staff and wander into the infinite expanse, I suddenly awoke from my trance and pursued him to the riverbank, whereupon I sang this song to see him off: The clouds are his banners.
Ah! As I journeyed forward, the thunder rolled yet made no sound. The wind wafted lightly, blowing my robes; the trees stretched far away, imbued with emotion.
Your heart, alas, does not give rise to love; that which I long for is pursued only by the spirit. Gazing toward the horizon, it is beyond reach; I return once more, startled from my dream.
Preface for the Eighty-first Birthday of Master Donghu Xian, Former Abbot of Caoxi.
Master Donghu Xian, former abbot of Caoxi, was born in the previous Dinghai year; thus, four hundred and eighty sexagenary cycles have now elapsed.
The twenty-third day of the seventh month is the anniversary of his birth. The great disciples within the mountains...

My son, you alone have praised the Master as the most venerable elder. Moved by his virtuous teachings, which have long been trusted by the hearts of the multitude, each person rejoiced, burning incense and scattering flowers as an offering.
At that time, they all prostrated themselves and requested me to compose a discourse on the causes and conditions of longevity to honor the Master.
I joyfully spoke these words for the sake of the assembly: "As for the mark of longevity, it arises from..."
These are the notions of self, person, and sentient beings; therefore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, rejected and did not permit them.

Furthermore, he spoke of "Childlike Longevity" (Dongshou) and "Immeasurable Longevity" (Wuliangshou). Why are these names used exclusively? It is because "Childlike Longevity" refers to possessing the virtue of the aged while remaining in the state of childhood;
thus it is based on virtue rather than years. As for "Immeasurable Longevity," it is based on the mind rather than physical form.
Because this mind precedes heaven and earth yet does not age; follows heaven and earth yet does not end; transcends the four seasons yet does not change;

encompasses the ten directions yet is immeasurable. Therefore, when the True Persons of antiquity awakened to this mind, it was not worn away for ten thousand ages and remains as if from a thousand autumns past.
For this reason, our Buddha said of himself: "I dwell on Vulture Peak Mountain, always present."

Yet it does not perish. If my teacher, the Sixth Patriarch, possessed a spiritual bone that was steadfast and a Dharma-body that is eternally present, how could he have been constrained by his physical frame or evaluated by his outward appearance?
Therefore, for us disciples who are the descendants of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, the essential point lies in awakening to and clarifying this mind;
we do not measure our time by the duration of worldly years. Having observed the lineage of transmission throughout history...
The one thousand seven hundred people recorded in the *Denglu* all emerged from the single stream of Caoxi; they were all those who awakened to and clarified this mind.
Thus, they transmitted mind by means of mind, like continuing the lamp through the long night, to realize the fruit of non-arising and non-extinction.
This truly consists in entering the birthless through birth, and reaching the unextinguished through extinction. When there is no extinction, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is eternally arising.
Non-arising is true, eternal, and quiescent extinction. This is extinction that gives rise [to phenomena]; thus, there is neither arising nor non-arising.
It is extinction within arising, yet extinction that does not extinguish. This is truly the authentic transmission of the thousand sages and the essential tenet of the one mind.
Viewed from this perspective, it is beyond doubt that people share this same mind, and the mind shares this same lifespan.
You, sir, were born at Caoxi, grew up within the Dharma-gate, and have spent your life in Buddhist affairs.

Because you previously took your own body to be the body of the multitude, you are now able to take the lifespan of the multitude as your own lifespan. Furthermore, among the thousands of people on this mountain, each possesses their own mind; yet the mind—
Each [person] possesses their own lifespan. Truly, by using the lifespans of the multitude to sustain the Master’s life, one then uses the Master’s life to sustain the multitude’s lives.

In this manner, they pass the benefit on in succession through infinity, just as one lamp transmits its light to a thousand lamps; lamp after lamp continues in succession, without end and without exhaustion.
Thus, the longevity of the multitude’s hearts is certainly inexhaustible, and the Master’s own longevity shall likewise be immeasurable.
By this, one knows that eighty years of age are but a single hair on a horse’s body, or a single grain of millet in the Great Granary.

Now, we gather the hearts of the multitude to offer felicitations to you, Master; we pray that you may take this very heart as your longevity, so that for every year of your life, each year shall be like this.

Now, the followers of Master Shou are no fewer than they were before; it seems that the day when the World-Honored One held up the flower is not remote, and the time when the Sixth Patriarch brandished his fly-whisk is not far off.
To compare those of childhood with those of venerable virtue is like comparing the eye of a mosquito to the vast ocean.
When the assembly heard this, they rejoiced and prostrated themselves, holding this [teaching] as a blessing for their longevity.
Preface to the Gift of the Good Physician, Master Liang of Xingshan:
I have been exiled to the frontier of Linghai for eighteen years. Driven through the scorching wilderness, I have drunk deeply of the miasmic vapors.

Looking upon this leaking physical frame, which is not of gold or stone, I see it daily decaying as various ailments arise in succession. In the sixth month of summer in the year of Gui-chou, I happened to fall ill.
When a carbuncle on the back is as large as an inverted basin, the agony is unbearable and physicians are at their wits' end; in such cases, everyone recommends Master Liang.
By nature, Master Liang loves to drink; yet when informed of an illness, he never calculates profit at the outset nor boasts of his success at the conclusion.
Living in his village, he conducts himself with steady humility and courtesy, possessing the air of an ancient sage. When I was critically ill, a townsman told my servant, saying: "I have heard..."
"Venerable sir, you are unwell; if you obtain Master Liang, you will recover immediately. Before he had finished speaking, the Master arrived as if summoned by a spirit.
He was invited to examine the patient and said, "This is a 'bee-hive carbuncle. Its shape is like a bee's nest. From each opening, three larvae are born daily;
if this continues for long, they will layer upon layer and invade the bone, at which point it will be incurable. It is fortunate that medicine can be administered early."
I have no worries. The Master’s methods for treating illness are manifold. He says, "The pain shall cease," and the pain ceases; he says, "The swelling shall subside," and the swelling subsides;

he says, "The necrosis shall suppurate," and it suppurates accordingly. His responses to each ailment are as swift as his hands; there is nothing that does not yield immediate efficacy. His medicines contain no minerals or metals; they are all derived from various herbs.

When I observe the Master treating a malignant ulcer, he perceives the internal organs with perfect clarity. His skill is like that of one juggling balls; he achieves results according to a fixed schedule, as if by divine inspiration.
How divine! Initially, after the Master had treated him for several days, someone suggested another physician; the Master joyfully yielded to him without any sign of reluctance.
Subsequently, when the other physician’s treatment failed, the Master returned without any words of complaint. From this, one knows that his skill was high yet his mind was humble.
At that time, as the medical treatment remained undecided, prayers were offered repeatedly, but he alone granted permission [to proceed]. Truly, this was a divine favor. How moving!
While my teacher was treating my illness, I reflected on an ancient saying: "When a man lives in this world, if he succeeds, he becomes a worthy minister;
if he does not succeed, he becomes a skilled physician. Today, the ailments of the world are as numerous as a thousand sores and a hundred wounds—not merely those of my own person.
Who is there to heal them? Even if one possessed the hands of Lu Ban or Bian Que, people would not necessarily trust them; even if they were trusted...
Yet they do not necessarily employ them; how much more so when one avoids illness and shuns medical care?

To seek the restoration of the Great Harmony and primal qi under such conditions makes it difficult to achieve the merit of reviving life. Your Eminence’s saving of people has been as if by divine power, and your merits in restoring life have been manifold.
From the beginning, you have not sought recompense, accumulating these as deeds of hidden virtue (*yin-de*). I pray that your Eminence’s sons and grandsons will propagate your art...
In governing the world, the state, and the family, you have been swift and effective at every turn; thus, the grace of your former life flows on without end, not merely saving me today.
Such a person as you—when you had not yet fathered a son, I treated you on the second day of the second month, and you gave birth to a son;
all say this is a reward for your hidden virtue. Therefore, I rejoice to congratulate you, Master, and present this gift.
Regarding the words:
"Separately recorded, the Preface by Shengming Zhan was composed at the beginning of the Wanli era.
During my years begging for alms in the Chang'an market, I encountered Master Chen of Yishan; upon seeing him in the crowd, immediately—"
He regarded me as an eccentric person and subsequently became my inseparable friend. At that time, I already knew Ou Zhenbo in Lingnan;
he and the Master were both guests in the capital city of Yan. Since then, I have retired from the world of men, while the Master has traveled on official tours of duty without further news of him.
In the year of Bingshen, I was dispatched to Lingnan by imperial decree; arriving in Wuyang in the second month, I went to visit the Master.

Thus, he has achieved immortality through the ages. Ming-zhan was my younger brother by adoption. Master Yi-shan was a man of bold and extraordinary conduct, possessing a light and airy spirit that transcended the mundane world.
Ming-zhan, however, was refined, sagacious, and profound; he was modest and elegant in his demeanor, serene and tranquil, utterly devoid of any worldly affectations.
I held him in high esteem; whenever I saw him, he remained silent without uttering a single word. Furthermore—

There was no one among those who heard my words who did not rejoice. When my elder brother, Minister Hun-gyeong (Veakp’ong), retired from office and returned home, he selected the West Garden at Longjin as his residence.
It was situated in close proximity to the Floating Hill (P’u-ch’u) of the Palace Commissioner (Kwangnok) Yi Wui-wang.

From time to time, he would invite me to take meals between the two gardens; whenever we ate, I invariably placed Myeong-jam first. Myeong-jam followed the two elders and never traveled abroad. Only...
The filial piety and righteousness of these two elders stand as the pinnacle of human relations for this age; they do not merely hold such virtues in high esteem in Lingnan.
Mingzhan was born in Chong, grew up in Chong, and was schooled in Chong; he did not merely know what was worthy of esteem, but firmly held it in high regard.
At eight years of age, Mingzhan was able to master the classical curriculum, and by ten, he could recite ancient prose and poetry. When his father passed away, [he mourned at] Caifeng...

The Duke regarded him as his own son. When Ming-zhan grew up, while the Duke was occupied with state affairs and found leisure time, he would daily discuss with him the people of antiquity and the present, from the highest to the lowest, and would select those whom he esteemed to entrust to Ming-zhan’s care, thereby refining his character and habits.
Thus, Ming-zhan was nurtured by one who understood what is truly important. It is no wonder, then, that Ming-zhan does not deign to concern himself with the trivialities of the vulgar world.
The Master said: "If the gentleman is not grave, he will lack dignity; if he does not study, his learning will not be firm.

Thus we know that for the learning of the gentleman, firmness is rooted in gravity. Let us attempt to discuss this: the nature of human life is fundamentally upright and substantial, devoid of artifice.
However, because prior knowledge guides the emotions and superficial splendor tempts the will, the original nature is lost and the substance is corrupted; clarity fades and...

This is a long period of darkness. Thus, not only has the root lost its ground, but that which it clings to is not its kin. Consequently, the sun flows into low-lying hollows where it stagnates in filth and turbidity;
this causes the body that should be unblemished by friction to be gradually worn away, and the substance that should be unstained by mud to become darkened and soiled.
Those who remain in profound ignorance without awakening, and who gallop like fire toward the abyss without returning, are indeed numerous. This is why the Sages value [the cultivation of the self].

To associate with the benevolent is why Śākyamuni and Laozi both placed such emphasis on severing desire. I have personally witnessed this with clear vision; for ten years it has been as if it were but a single day.

From beginning to end, he remains as one in mindfulness; amidst slander and praise, he remains as one in heart. He does not allow his feelings to differ based on separation or union, nor does he allow his will to be divided by coming or going.
That he undergoes such austerity and consumes only the bland, and that his filial piety and fraternal duty are so sincere and earnest, is surely due to the natural goodness of his innate nature.
In truth, this is rooted in the practice of cultivation. The *Zhongyong* says: "Heaviness is the root of lightness; stillness is the lord of agitation.
Therefore, in the learning of the sages, they attain heaviness and lightness follows it; they concentrate on stillness and agitation is transformed by it.
This is why Confucius regarded unrighteous wealth and honor as floating clouds, and Laozi considered ten thousand *zhong* of grain as no more than worn-out sandals. If one can simply...
Once one attains this gravity, then failure and success are of one essence, life and death share the same category, and past and present are unified.
By this, it is sufficiently proven that the study beyond the secular world is no idle talk, and the school transmitted from the West is no eccentricity or absurdity.
I have been acquainted with Ming-zhan for twelve years, yet he never once spoke a word of Chan; since Ming-zhan has long cherished his own worth so highly, how could he [have spoken of] Chan?
That which exists is now spoken of as distinct; it does not lie outside of this. To clearly observe and comprehend its intent, one must look to the sequence of the game.
Regarding the "Postface to the Subtle Sequences of Fang Zhenyi":

When I was young, I knew Fang Zhenyi; he was already renowned for his skill in the game during his childhood, yet I had never met him. It was only when I went to beg for food in Chang’an that I encountered him.

Throughout the city, everyone he encountered praised him without exception; there was no one at all who spoke of his shortcomings. I personally recognized that he truly lived up to what the Grand Historian Li Ben-ning had said—not only regarding Yi, but in general as well.
When I was exiled to the coastal regions of Linghai, in the late autumn of the Bingwu year, Zi-zhen arrived in Guangdong together with Observation Commissioner Xiao.
He came to visit Caoxi, and upon meeting me, it was as if a mirror of the mind had been suddenly polished.
How extraordinary! This man has recently produced with Huang Shi-fu a subtle treatise on *weiqi* (Go). I was certainly unable to fathom it;
yet, upon observing his game against Master Xiao, I realized that Zi-zhen’s approach to *weiqi* advances beyond mere skill through the Way (*Dao*).
Allow me to attempt an analysis: the Way resides in Heaven and Earth. All those who grasp its essence and spiritualize its transformations are said to [possess it].
As for the Sages, their moral virtue is beyond question. As for those of artistic talent: Ma Yuan was a sage in painting;
Zhong Yao and Wang Xizhi were sages in calligraphy; and Zhang Zhi and Wang Xun were sages in cursive script. Why limit this to the arts? It is the same with technical skills.

Take, for instance, the ball-games of Shi Liao, the archery of Yang You, and the Go of Qiu—all of these have their own accounts. Go is a contest of paths. In all contests, one competes for reputation.

When things are forced and strained, the vital energy (qi) prevails while true virtue is meager. Master Zhen alone was not like this; he was steady, refined, and elegant, never boasting of his own excellence.
At the chessboard, he appeared as if lacking intent; when facing an opponent, he seemed as if unaware. Yet, when the opponent was vulnerable, he would invariably reveal the truth to them.
Occupying a position of superiority yet appearing as if not contending, his demeanor is relaxed and leisurely; he smiles and laughs with self-composure, his inner being serene.

His strategic position is like a clear wave, his mind like the bright moon. He determines his moves before the opportunity arises; when the spirit moves, Heaven follows. When an opponent departs, he does not pursue;

when an adversary approaches, he responds in accordance with the situation. Through this, one knows how subtle and profound it is. Commentators have used the game of *wei* (Go) as a metaphor for this.
As for military strategy, I further maintain that *weiqi* (Go) can be analogized to Chan Buddhism; it is that which abides in the unmoving while operating through movement.
I have long maintained that Master Zhen’s *weiqi* advances from the Way toward technical skill. Upon observing Master Zhen, I see that he possesses not merely technical skill.
The man was likewise so. As the Master of Lao said: "Only by not contending can none in the world contend with him.
His character was thus extraordinary, and his skill was truly divine. How could those who merely hold their knives with prideful intensity ever be compared to him?
Although I am ignorant of the game of Go, having now witnessed Mr. Zi-zhen’s match against Lord Xiao, I feel ashamed that my own play does not even float above the water [in comparison].
