Preface to the Ordination of Master Ciyin Jiān as Abbot of East Chan Temple in Jīnshā.
East Chan Temple in Jīnshā is an ancient monastery. Since its restoration by Grand Master Dáguān, his disciples, the Sūn brothers...
He initiated the undertaking. The Grand Historian, Duke Wang, brought it to completion. First, Master Langyai Yao took up residence as abbot.
Once the sacred precincts were fully adorned, he joined with his fellow practitioners to form the Blue Lotus Society (*Nīlotpala-saṃgha*).

They recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* from memory and observed the three trainings of precepts, concentration, and wisdom as their pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). Before many years had passed, more than thirty people were able to recite the sutra from memory. [They] went to Yao...
The Duke, together with various donors, specially constructed the Buddhajātīya Hall to welcome me for my retirement. In the winter of the Bingchen year, I traveled eastward and arrived;
I beheld its regulations as elegant and solemn, its quarters peaceful and pure, and its four requisites abundant and exquisite—both the environment and the people were excellent.
"It is the most supreme place of practice for the Dharma-ending age. He praised it for a long time.
Having understood the master’s final circumstances, I immediately retired to Mount Kuang. Master Yao wept and tried to detain me, but I could not stay.
Two years after I entered the mountains, Master Yao departed due to obstructing conditions. At that time, all the donors looked to me, hoping I would send someone to preside over the monastery.
Before long, Master Jianyin arrived. The entire assembly rejoiced and made earnest requests. Initially, the Master had considered Mount Guizong unsuitable as his home mountain and had returned there;
now, he was responding to their invitation. Upon passing by Wuru, I greeted him with joy and said to him:
"How magnificent is the Dharma-realm! It takes dependent origination as its fundamental principle. Therefore, all phenomena are entirely dependent [on conditions]."

The establishment of a buddha-field, whether pure or defiled, is brought about by the mind; it transforms according to what the mind perceives, and its formation and destruction likewise depend upon this.
Therefore, when our Buddha first attained perfect enlightenment at the site of Bodhi, that ground was firm and solid, composed of diamond.
This refers to the bond produced by the resonance of the vajra-mind; therefore, when a bodhisattva practices, they must take this mind as the foundation of their practice.
What is called the "vajra-mind" is precisely the Vajra Jewel Precepts taught in the Brahma’s Net Sūtra, which is named the Dharma-gate of the Buddhas’ Mind-ground.
For this reason, [the Buddha] commanded the thousand billion Śākyamunis to propagate this Dharma, namely, for the sake of the one...
A great causal condition has appeared in the world, specifically to transmit this Vajra Precept alone.
This single precept is the very condition for attaining Buddhahood; hence it is said: "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions.

For us, the disciples of the Buddha, if we do not observe this precept, then whatever we establish—whether mundane or supramundane dharmas—will all fail to be accomplished, as we would lack a foundation.

It is for this reason. This very monastic code follows the regulations of the Three Studies (*tri-śikṣā*). Among the Tripiṭaka, the Sūtra-piṭaka takes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as its core; the Vinaya-piṭaka takes the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* as its core;

and the Śāstra-piṭaka takes the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* as its core. Thus, these three are all the most supreme One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which elucidates the principle of the one mind and constitutes the essential method for attaining Buddhahood.
There is nothing that surpasses them; they are the ready-made public case (*kōan*) manifest before one’s eyes. Now, sir...
Go forth! If you uphold the Buddha-mind as the presiding master, that very ground will be composed of vajra; body and mind will be tranquil—this is what it means to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber.
If you take the Lotus Sūtra as the seed of the Buddha, then every single glance, every single prostration, every raising of a hand, and every bowing of the head are all sublime practices.
Thus, every cause and condition is nothing other than the work of the Buddha; there is nothing that is not so.
If one becomes weary and exhausted, yet uses wisdom to illuminate the single mind and thoroughly penetrates ignorance, then afflictions will not arise and all obstacles will naturally subside.
In daily life, every single thing is true liberation. Furthermore, you have long maintained the practice of the "Universal Gate" chapter and the "Dharani of Vows" chapter to purify your karma.

If you take great compassion as your core intention, you will regard all beings as having the same essence and observe enemies and kin with equal vision, realizing that there is no distinction whatsoever.
Regarding the marks of self and others: if one takes the conduct of Samantabhadra as one's practice, then one relinquishes body and life to provide for the great assembly;

when even a drop of water is shared universally, how could there be any private interest for oneself? If one takes Great Perfect Enlightenment as one’s monastery, then in gatherings from the ten directions, every individual is non-active (*wuwei*);
how, then, could there be any concern for the affairs of descendants? You, sir, should dwell in this manner. As...
This is upholding [the precepts]. To dwell in *an-śū-kia* (summer retreat) in this manner is to immediately transform the defiled into the pure;

the three trainings are perfected within a single mind, and the myriad practices are accomplished in a single thought-moment. As it is said: "When a son of the Buddha dwells in this stage, he is the very enjoyment of the Buddha;
he is constantly therein, whether walking, pacing, sitting, or reclining. In this way, one does not fail the donor (*dānapati*), nor does one fail oneself.
This is a great cause and condition for the world. One should take these words and inscribe them upon the Hall of the Buddha-seed;
it may well serve as the mark of the broad and long tongue.
This is the preface to the consecration of Master Wuyuan Dao as abbot of Shaolin.
The World-Honored One departed from India and sat upon Vulture Peak, taking the *utpala* flower as the seed of Bodhi.

Since the Dharma reached China at Shaolin, it has been considered the first stage of Bodhi; the inexhaustible flow of the Dharma from the ten directions has issued forth from this source in an unending stream.
Yet, as the branches have multiplied while the source became turbid, our Great Master Xueting unified these various currents and—
They returned [to him]. His mind was vast; his merit was truly eminent. From that time on, he became the true progenitor of the lineage, with descendants being born generation after generation.
By means of non-arising, he made his dharma his hereditary occupation, such that no one could speak of him as merely a public monk.

He inherited the dharma-stream of the Great Master Huànxiūrùn of the twenty-fifth generation, causing devas and humans to honor and support him as he presided over the monastery. The great bhikṣus and kṣatriya rulers...

The official and the lay devotees were all filled with joy and offered praise. I, having come from the eastern land of Nārāyaṇa-kūpa, also joined them in sympathetic joy, pressed my palms together, and said:
"Before the Buddha appeared in the world and before the Patriarch came from the West, the household enterprise was already manifest and fully possessed by every person.
Yet, because they possessed it, they did not realize it; thus, the Yellow-Faced One and the Blue-Eyed One could not restrain their brilliance and appeared specifically for this purpose."

To reveal one's origin for others is to cause the million in the assembly on Vulture Peak and the seventeen hundred who transmitted the lamp to all turn their heads at a single call and suddenly realize what is inherently possessed.
This, then, is the single word "knowing," the gateway to all wonders. Alas! Buddhas and patriarchs originally had no substantial dharma to give to people;
yet how could they have expected that everyone would mistake empty flowers for their own diseased eyes, and furthermore, invite those flowers to bear fruit?
The hearts of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are indeed thus. This single word "knowing" is the gateway to all calamities.
If we do not vigorously polish away the golden blade, how can we perpetuate our ancestral legacy? Alas, how difficult this is!

Yet, the Buddhas and Patriarchs take the Dharma-realm as their home, the great earth as their vocation, and empty space as their measure. If they did not establish even a single speck of dust, they would be unable to manifest [the truth].
Body. If one were to establish even a single speck of dust [of conceptualization], one would be unable to deliver sentient beings. Now you, sir, with this bare body, fully shoulder this task;
you drag the hundred rivers back to their source—how could this be easy? Sir, proceed! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and contemplate it well.
If you do not establish a single speck of dust, you fail the Buddhas and Patriarchs; if you establish a single speck of dust, you are not what the Buddhas and Patriarchs are.
Regarding those who look toward you, O Master, may you exert yourself.
Preface to the Painting of the Portraits of the Patriarchs by the Dharma Master Changye Gyeong.

Formerly, when the World-Honored One resided in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for three months, King Udayana could not cease his longing for him; he therefore commanded an artisan to take [the Buddha’s likeness]...

They carved his image out of sandalwood. Śāriputra, fearing that ordinary craftsmen would be unable to fully capture its exquisite beauty, employed his supernatural powers to manifest thirty-two men, each of whom was assigned to carve one of the marks.
Once the marks were completed, he invited the image back to the royal city; those who beheld it regarded it as equal to the living Buddha.
When the World-Honored One descended from the celestial palace, [Śāriputra] prostrated before him and said: "After my parinirvāṇa, I rely upon..."
When you were saving immeasurable beings, your image likewise extended its hand to respond to them.

Thus, all carvings, paintings, and various forms of adornment that pervade the worlds of the ten directions originated with this sandalwood [image]. Alas! How could it be that only the Buddha was thus?

In my view, the various patriarchs are all of one and the same body and one and the same wisdom; their powers and fearlessnesses are likewise so. Therefore it is said: "The mind is like a craftsman..."

A painter can depict various forms and images. While such forms and images may indeed be painted, how could one possibly paint spiritual powers, wondrous functions, or the work of delivering sentient beings?

I have long felt this deficiency. However, upon reading Master Da’s preface to Ding Sheng’s painting of the portraits of the patriarchs, as well as his letter accompanying the request for a portrait by Master Qing, I realized that spiritual powers, wondrous functions, and the deliverance of sentient beings [can indeed be conveyed].

All such activities are nothing other than the Samādhi of the Tip of a Single Hair. Alas! While Śāriputra exhausted his supernatural powers and required many people to complete a single image, now Mr.
Ding, by means of the wondrous power of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), manifests many bodies from a single hand.
Master Qing accomplishes the work of saving sentient beings within a single thought-moment, while Master Da [achieves it] with a mere snap of the fingers.
In an instant, the Dharma-body is made to spread everywhere, like clouds rising in the cold sky, its reflections interlacing upon the autumn waters.
Is such wondrous function simply the natural functioning of spiritual powers (*dharmatā-abhijñā*)? Or does it arise from the convergence of causes and conditions?
If an observer can, perhaps, behold this face-to-face without doubt, they will finally believe that the self-nature of each and every person is inherently complete in this very way. Master.

Go! Do not grow weary of this manifold manifestation. Even if one were to manifest many bodies from a single body, filling the void of space and streaming light across the great earth, it would still not depart from a single hair-tip of this very moment. You must uphold this and convey it to me.

Preface to the Ordination of the Monk-Registrar, Left Superior Worldly Virtue Chao Ru Ying, as Abbot of Daci’ousi Temple At the beginning of the reign of the Sagely Son of Heaven, his age was yet tender.
His Imperial Mother, out of supreme devotion, nurtured him with diligent care.

Reflecting that the ancestral temple, the altars of the land and grain, and the great vessel of the empire were entrusted to him, he pondered how best to repay her profound virtue and bestow blessings upon the common people below.

Upon his birth, [the Emperor] provided meager offerings and reduced his own provisions, then disbursed funds to establish the Dacijsou Temple (Great Compassionate Longevity Monastery), intending to rely on the Triple Gem for its broad protection and to secretly shelter the impoverished regions.
When the temple was completed, he selected the monk Guzhen as the abbot. After three years, Guzhen passed away;
the Emperor then appointed his grandson, Benzai, as the Left Supervisor of the Sangha Registry (Senglü Zuoshanshi) to succeed him in the affairs of the monastery. This was Master Zai.
He served in office for twelve years. Above, he offered prayers for the Emperor’s ten-thousand-year longevity; below, he welcomed the four classes of beings.
Without weariness from morning until night, he was like the clouds of compassion and the rain of Dharma, filling the entire realm; there was nothing that did not flow forth from him.

Yet the Master exerted his loyalty and contributed his strength, exhausting his person and toiling to the end, so that through the heavy and urgent nature of his duties, his body grew weary and his spirit withered, until the four elements fell into disorder and he became emaciated.

Reduced to a mere skeleton of bone, he still could not bear to abandon his affairs. When Chan Master Daguan was passing through Cishou Monastery, he saw him and said in astonishment, "Why have you come to this state?
Though we practitioners surely value the Dharma even at the cost of forgetting our own bodies, what can that avail against the great matter of birth and death?
The Master wept silently, shedding many rows of tears, and said, "It is not that I am attached to fleeting fame; it is simply that I am mindful of the Emperor..."

The master’s kindness was profound and weighty; having no one to whom he could entrust the incense and lamps, he merely continued to linger on. The Zen Master then asked who was capable of bearing the affairs of the temple.
The master immediately recommended his disciple, the Chief Administrator (Jiansi) Chan Master Yuanying.

When [the Master] was invited to see him, he was greatly pleased and said, "Is this not one who has come by the power of his original vow? He ordered him to disrobe and sit at ease, just as Jiu Fang inspected horses, saying, "This is it."
"You shall surely travel a thousand *li*; fortunately you have this son, so what need is there for further concern? Having heard this, the Master reached a clear resolution.

The following day, he reported the matter to the Holy Mother, who approved it. An imperial edict was issued to the Grand Minister of Rites, commanding that he be appointed as the Left Supervisor of the Sangha Registry (*Senglǔ Zuòshànshì*) and serve as the third-generation abbot. The eminent masters from all the great mountains each...
Upon hearing this, he was filled with joy. He then addressed the humble writer, praising him, saying:

"Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, takes the Dharma-realm as his home, takes precept, concentration, and wisdom as his vocation, and takes the propagation of the Dharma and the benefit of sentient beings as his task.

He takes kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity as his model, and takes teaching, principle, practice, and fruition as his governing framework. With the three trainings complete and the four immeasurable minds perfected, the four quarters are brought into order; thus the Teaching flourishes."
Prosperity! Now, as for this family [of practitioners], they abide in a state of no-mind and maintain themselves through non-self.

They advance or retreat according to causes and conditions, and subdue others in accordance with their capacities. This is the mastery of the Perfected One; how could it be attained by ordinary people?

Therefore, in an era of the True Dharma, the four quarters are extended and the Way of the Dharma flourishes. Observe the various patriarchs: regardless of whether they were young or old, a single word...

Following this, he was able to carry on his predecessor’s work. During the age of the Semblance Dharma, the teachings spread to the Eastern Land. From the Han through the Tang dynasties, there have been worthy individuals in every generation;
branch after branch has flourished, bearing abundant flowers and fruit. Yet it is said that there are now no fruits. Reaching the age of the Final Dharma, those who produce fine fruit are rare.
This is because while the doctrine and principles remain, the practice of the fruits is lacking; the net is already half-loose—how can one hope to maintain order?

This is the family vocation: to rescue and ferry across those among humans and devas. Now that we have entered the Age of Dharma Decline (*mappō*), more than six hundred years have passed since the World-Honored One was about to enter *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, sixty trillion bodhisattvas vowed to exert their influence and ensure the circulation [of the teachings] during the Age of Dharma Decline;

furthermore, he entrusted the Buddha-dharma to kings and great ministers. Thus, it has been transmitted through successive generations. It is only in our own nation that this teaching is held in such high esteem.
Valuing this person, the sovereign and his subjects became one in purpose. Reaching down to our Holy Mother, she propagated the Three Jewels with a breadth that transcended previous dynasties.
While monasteries and temples were spread out like a chessboard across the stars, this temple alone stands as a grand spectacle for all under heaven, a treasury of the Dharma that is inexhaustible.
From this all virtues emerge; into this all enters. It is the pivot of the Dharma-gate and the raft of those who possess knowledge.
One who assumes this responsibility upholds the mainstay of the Great Teaching and serves as a model for the four seas; it is by no means a trivial matter.
Yet at the age of only twenty, Master Ying already held the office of *jian-si* (monastery supervisor), overseeing all the affairs of the mountain gate.
He bears this burden with his body. He does not treat himself as private property; he does not shrink from toil; he does not decline resentment.

He is unaware that the body has a world, and he does not know that the mind has a body. Without conscious recognition, he responds universally without artifice. This is what is meant by being "young in years but mature in virtue."

Substantial on the outside and hollow within, he forgets artifice as if possessing no mind; he responds universally as if possessing no self; he disregards profit and harm as if leaving matters to conditions.
This is the true capacity for maintaining the Dharma. Is this not what Master Guan referred to as "one who has come by the power of his vows"?
I have privately remarked that, in relation to the Master, Master Ying was the water. If the accumulation of water is not deep, [the boat cannot be supported].

Thus, one who lacks the strength to carry a great ship cannot fulfill the task. Since Master Ying has already been able to carry his teacher for ten years, how could he not be capable of carrying himself?
Master Ying, exert yourself! I pray that you shall realize the Truth and practice the Reality, becoming a true son of the Buddha and maintaining his household.
With this body and mind, I offer prayers for the compassionate longevity of our Sacred Sovereign, that it may be as vast as heaven and earth, universally covering all.

It is inexhaustible. If this is indeed the case, then the fragrance of the banner flutters, the sound of bells and drums flies forth, the pagoda and hall span the void, and the chimes and gongs resound—day and night without ceasing;
all these are moments when the broad and long tongue turns the Wheel of Dharma. You must exert yourself in this endeavor.

Preface to the Bestowal [of the Title] upon the Venerable Dàlún Duān as Abbot of Guǎngjì Temple North of the city of Rājagṛha, there is a great vihāra called Guǎngjì. It was the place where the Great Knowledge-holder, Master Bǎozàng, preached the Dharma.
Initially, the Master lived in seclusion at Zhōngnán, where he realized the Seal of the Mind. Later, he took his disciple Shuāngsōng with him...
Master Ping and his peers stopped there. They raised the great banner of the Dharma, and the multitudes of humans and devas gathered.

The Upādhyāya occupied the lion’s throne, and Master Ping immediately took charge of the affairs of the monastery, receiving disciples from all quarters; his fame spread throughout the land for over thirty years.
When the Upādhyāya reached eighty years of age, his spiritual influence grew as great as the rising sun. Then, Master Ping withdrew from his illusory conditions and departed. Furthermore—

Because his disciples, including Duan Gong, Jishi, the Elder of the Mountain Gate, the elders of the capital city, and the venerable masters of Longhua and Rui’an, were all filled with joy, they requested a word of praise for him.

I have heard that when the Buddha resided at the Jetavana Monastery in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, among his assembly of twelve hundred disciples, each was designated according to their particular excellence; thus, he was honored with the title of "Elder" (Thera).
Śūnyatā-jāti. Śūnyatā-jāti asked the Buddha where he dwells. The World-Honored One then told him that he should give rise to his mind by dwelling nowhere.
He should not dwell on form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas when giving rise to the mind. Furthermore, he said: "One should dwell in this manner;
in this manner, one subdues the mind. But what is it that he actually dwells upon? Nevertheless, how could one take non-dwelling itself as a dwelling? Moreover, it is heard that the Buddha dwells...
Within the Great Luminous Treasury (*Mahā-ābhāsagarbha*), together with the twelve great bodhisattvas, he secretly expounded the gateway of the Perfect Sūtra, saying:
"I take Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery (*ārāma*); body and mind dwell in tranquility within the wisdom of equanimity.

This is what is meant by abiding in the field of quiescent extinction (*śamatha-viṣaya*) and practicing non-conditioned conduct (*anabhisaṃskāra-caryā*). Furthermore, how could one abide by means of having something to abide in? Nevertheless, the Superior One [personally...]
He transmitted the Dharma to Master Baozang; Master Baozang received the Dharma from Chan Master Dachu, who upheld the true mandate of Linji.
Within a single brow-raising, a glance, or a staff-blow and a shout, he encompassed the five teachings and suddenly realized the thousand gates.

Subject and object were both stripped away, and principle and phenomenon were simultaneously forgotten. How could this be contained within a monastery in the royal capital or a *gālayana* of Perfect Enlightenment?

Is it not to deliberate upon their essence and coarseness, their excellence and inferiority? If you, Venerable One, indeed maintain the Dharma through this method, you will be able to continue the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom and offer a true repayment for the grace of the State.
This is truly what is meant by "a Son of the Buddha maintaining the Dharma, skillfully transcending all realms of existence.
Upon hearing these words, the elders were all greatly delighted; they immediately took up this single leaf to inquire after the Venerable One’s well-being. The Venerable One—
Let it not be said of me that I am a sick man of Vaiśālī; I am no one who has snatched away an alms-bowl. This serves as the preface.
Preface to the *Phantom Journey* Sent to Dharma Master Fangshan Yingchuan:
A phantom person went to travel through the capital city and encountered the son of Mount Fang within the Great Field of Illusions. They became inseparable companions, free from all opposition.
After a while, the illusory person departed along with illusory conditions. Fāngshānzi immediately entered the Great Gate of Liberation that is like an illusion;
abiding in the field of quiescent extinction, he manifested various illusory phenomena, revealing the Great Treasury within the Dragon Palace and receiving the sublime offerings of devas and humans.
The illusory man was just now avoiding his shadow in the Eastern Sea; occupying the vast void and great valleys, he contended for mastery with the mists, clouds, and deer.
Upon hearing this, Fang Shanzi was delighted and immediately came forth, leaning on his staff.

He searched for me in the land of the hairless people (Qiongfa), where the illusory man and I clasped arms and roamed together. We ascended the Peak of Vajra and entered the Cave of Nara; we boarded the raft of firmness and floated away.
The light of the Ocean-Seal (Sāgarāmudrā) probes the void and directs the myriad phenomena. When weary, one spreads upon jade grass and lies beneath the long forest;
when hungry, one drinks the refined nectar (sarpis) and eats the thorny chestnuts. At times, one pats the belly and rests the chin upon the hand, or slaps the thighs with a bird-like leap of joy.
They inhale the waves of the leviathan and swallow the vast blue sea; they rebuke the Great Mass (the universe) and belch forth the long winds.

They cause the ten thousand apertures to resonate in unison and diverse currents to surge in competition, yet remain utterly unaware that "you" and "I" exist within the cosmos, nor that morning and dusk constitute the sun and moon.
Furthermore, how could these floating lights and illusory shadows, these wild horses and dust motes, possibly stain the vast measure of the Great Clarity?
Fāngshānzi was so delighted that he forgot to return; he did not realize that two watches had passed and the four seasons had shifted in a mere instant.

At that time, Fāngshānzi sprang up and said to the Illusory Man: "I have heard that the Land of the Immortals is not something that ephemeral insects like mayflies can even conceive of. It is the Vast and Desolate..."
"It is a wilderness beyond the knowledge of a mayfly. It is indeed so. I wish to die here with you. Since the conditions of our illusion have not yet ended, I shall leave you for now;
in the end, we shall surely go back together hand in hand. The illusory man then advanced slowly and said, "Heh!"
Is this so? Do you harbor thoughts of coming and going? Try, for a moment, to observe how when a single cloud arises, the great void is pervaded;
or how when a speck of dust is lifted, the entire earth is encompassed. Without being divided, it is omnipresent, and thus the drenching rain pours down;
without being dispersed, it is all-encompassing, and thus the mountains vie in their splendor. Viewed from this perspective, all phenomena have never been separate from arising.
This is merely a provisional station. You, my son, must exert yourself; do not harbor thoughts of coming and going.
Nevertheless, it is like empty flowers forming fruit—deluded by a cataract in the eye; or like bubbles piercing pearls—misled by a foolish child. You shall go now; try striking and scraping them.
If the pearls are broken and the cataract removed, do not forget our covenant made at our side-by-side meeting. I vow that I shall [be with you].
The Master died at Nārāyaṇa-kūpa.
*The Dream-Wanderings of the Elder Hanshan*, Volume Twenty-one;
*The Dream-Wanderings of the Elder Hanshan*, Volume Twenty-two.
Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and his disciple Tonghyeong;
revised by the disciple from Lingnan, Liu Qixiang.
Record of the Stele for Master Wǎn’s Monastery at Shíjīngshān in Zhuōzhōu.

In the past, while perusing the scriptures of the Tripiṭaka, I encountered the *Pranidhāna* (Vow Text) of the Great Master Sī of Nányuè, in which he vowed that his physical body (*rūpakāya*) would remain eternally present. Upholding this...

To wait for Maitreya within the Buddha-dharma is already most rare; yet, having beheld the Great Capital and traveled my eyes through the "Little Western Heaven," I see these stone scriptures—how magnificent they are!

It was during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty that the venerable Śramaṇa Jingwan of Zhiquan Monastery in Youzhou, enduring the calamities of the kalpa of destruction, feared the submergence of the Great Dharma and desired to cause the Buddha’s...
The lineage was not severed, and he first carved the printing blocks for the stone-stored canon (shijing), sealing them at Mount Baidai to the west of Zhuozhou.

The mountain has seven caves, each of which was filled [with the blocks]. From the Daye era until the twelfth year of the Zhenguan period of the Tang dynasty, his vow remained unfulfilled when he passed away.
His disciples—Dao, Yi, Xian, Fa, and four others—succeeded him through five generations, yet even the canon remained incomplete. Throughout these years...

From the Tang through the Song dynasties, there was never a lack of worthy individuals. Reaching the Yuan dynasty, during the Zhengtong era, the Great Master Hwaeul (Huiyue), a śramaṇa from Goryeo, had still not completed his studies.
The full details of these events are recorded in the various steles erected at Yunju.
Yet, in our Ming dynasty, nothing of the sort is heard of. Why is this? Alas! If there is not the right person, the Way does not manifest in vain; the seeds of the Buddha arise from conditions.

This is precisely what is meant by "arising. When the Great Master Daguanken first arrived at Narayana-kutsa in the autumn of the Wuli period (1606), he traveled north to Yunju and reached the stupa of Master Wan. Upon seeing it for the first time, his tears fell like rain.
When Wangzi saw his parents’ thatched hut at their tomb, he embraced the banner and wept bitterly; after lingering there for a long time, he departed.
He traveled south to Mount Emei and returned to Jintan, where, to repay the kindness of his parents, he personally transcribed the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* until they were complete.
Six years later, in the sixth month of the Renchen year, he went to the capital and commissioned Mr. Xu Yan of the Court of the Imperial Stud to craft a precious casket.
He was escorted to the Wunfo Pagoda at Luyaya.

While resting briefly at Tanzhe, Empress Dowager Cisheng heard of this and dispatched her attendant Chen Ru with provisions for a vegetarian feast to offer to him. Chen Ru followed the Master back to Yunju.
The Stone Sūtras were enshrined at Raeyunsa Temple. At that time, a sudden light illuminated the cliffs and valleys. Upon opening the stone case within the hall for veneration, there was a casket;
inside the casket was found a silver box, which contained a golden box. Within this was a golden vessel holding three śarīra relics.

It was as brilliant as a diamond, yet appeared as if it were an ancient relic; the entire assembly marveled at its wonder, their hearts filled with a mixture of grief and joy. Thereafter, they paid obeisance once more to Master Wan.
At that time, the pagoda complex had already been sold by the monastery monks to a wealthy family, and the Master’s remains were on the verge of sharing a nest with foxes and hares.
The Teacher was deeply moved by sorrow and immediately used the gold provided as an offering for the monastic meal, granted through Imperial benevolence, to redeem them.
It was incomplete. The high-ranking eunuch Yang Ting commissioned his disciple Xu Fading to assist in completing it.

The Master was then staying at Shangfang Mountain to escape the summer heat, and Daoqing also arrived from the East Sea to pay his respects to the Master at Doushuai Monastery; they discussed this matter.

He struck his palms together in painful lamentation. After the time it takes to eat a meal, the Master’s senior disciple, Monk Mikazō Kō, arrived with the deed for redeeming the monastery, accompanied by Tōen.

The Master leaped for joy; he immediately invited Seishin to go to Ungyo-ji together to pay homage and offer praise. Braving the rain and wading through the mud, they reached their destination at the end of the day.
They circumambulated the site three times, silently contemplating the Master’s solemn presence. His vital spirit was so vivid and imposing that they sighed, saying, "The Master will surely not..."
How transient is all! Moved by this sentiment, I, together with Master Yan, contributed gold to purchase several mu of land as a means for maintaining the incense and lamps.
I requested Master Da to record these matters in writing. But who am I, Gu Qing? Only after much hesitation did I finally speak these words:
The entire earth is the eternally abiding Dharmakāya; only the person of ultimate realization can know it. Within a single mote of dust lies a great thousand-fold scripture;
only the eye of wisdom can see it. With such a body, he preaches such a scripture. This Dharma is most profound and subtle; few are able to believe it.
For those who do believe it, how difficult this is! Therefore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, within the vast expanse...

Throughout kalpas, one observes the worlds of the ten directions and finds not even a space the size of a mustard seed where this Dharma was not sought by sacrificing body and life for the sake of sentient beings;

having sought it with such persistence, it is attained. Thus, within the tip of a single hair-pore, a Jewel-King Buddha-land appears, and within a single mote of dust, the Great Wheel of Dharma is turned.
This refers to all that is spoken in the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures; every word and every character is [the Dharma].
This is the very bone, blood, heart, and marrow of my Buddha-nature. Therefore it is said: "Wherever this sutra is found, one should erect a stupa and make offerings;
there is no need to enshrine relics therein, for within it already resides the complete body of the Tathāgata.
Thus, those who can uphold this Dharma repay the profound kindness of the Buddha. At the assembly on Vulture Peak, the Buddha desired to entrust this Dharma [to them].
There were those present at that time—ten million humans and devas—not a single one among them dared to breathe out a sigh of burden while shouldering this task.

Looking upon this great assembly, are they not indeed heroic and eminent men? Yet, having personally received the Buddha’s teachings and inwardly grasped the Buddha’s grace, they still remain so hesitant and timid.
They must surely wait for the sixty-two billion assemblies, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to emerge from the earth. This...
Why is this? For it has been granted that [the Dharma] shall endure for but five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa;

how much more so when one must wait for Maitreya, enduring through the three calamities and passing through the exhaustion of kalpas? This sufficiently demonstrates that upholding the Dharma is as difficult as this.

Viewed from this perspective, anyone who can give rise to even a single thought of the profound resolve to protect the Dharma will be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas. This is truly because...
If there were no Buddha, the Dharma could not bring about perfect enlightenment. If there were no Dharma, there would be no means to deliver sentient beings.
If sentient beings were not the Dharma, there would be no means to clarify one’s own mind. If the mind were not clarified, there would be no means to protect the True Dharma.

If the Dharma were not protected, how else could one repay the Buddha’s kindness and be called a disciple? It is because when the Buddha passes away, the Dharma passes away; yet if the Dharma endures, the Buddha’s body dwells eternally.
The Buddha, by means of his eternal body, presides over the dharma-realm and establishes the great enterprise. As for those who guard the boundaries of the realm, their methods are indeed manifold.
Yet, regarding the *dhāraṇī* of vows, it is not as evident in the deeds of Master Nanyue as it was in the case of Master Yuan.

Nevertheless, while the Buddha’s enterprise is vast, it would not have been able to uphold its fundamental principles without Nanyue; and while Nanyue’s vows were indeed profound, they could not have been realized without [the Buddha].
Master Wan lacked the means to carry on his legacy; Master Wan was indeed eminent, yet none but Huìyuè could succeed to his resolve. Alas!

It is easy for those who practice based on an existing foundation, but difficult for those who initiate a new undertaking. Throughout the ages, there have always been individuals who continued the flame and transmitted the lamp.

As for one who, amidst the towering vastness of the *dharmadhātu*, regards the beginning and the end as one, shares in both joy and sorrow, and with diligent heart and profound reflection succeeds in perpetuating the lineage of the Tathāgata—such a person is rare indeed.
Setting aside Ānanda and excluding the Venerable Maitreya, there is only I, the Master Yuan, alone. Alas! The Master’s merit is vast; sentient beings throughout kalpas receive his bounty.
Were it not for the Master, even the Buddha would have worn his robes with the lapels turned outward. Did he come as one who had personally received the secret seal?
Or was he one among the sixty-two billion [bodhisattvas]? How is it that his power of aspiration is so immense? How lamentable!
In this turbid age, those who know you are rare; thus, one who knows you is noble. As for knowing you as you truly are, there is only my Great Master Daguan alone.
Only you and the Master may truly be called a meeting of morning and evening across a thousand years.
Alas! If the world does not know you, it does not know the Buddha. Yet, if it does not know the Master, how can it know you?
I, the fool, say that your mind is the Buddha and your bones are the Sūtras. The mark of the broad and long tongue is neither extinguished nor born;

the Dharma of the Buddha is imperishable, yet it relies upon the preservation of your bones. Your bones and the Dharma-realm are mutually the beginning and the end. Now, as for the Master and you, [in the matter of] birth and death...
That the work of flesh and bone, once past, is now restored—this is to re-open a single speck of dust and bring forth the scripture of the Dharma-realm.
How could this be a minor cause? Alas! The Master’s bones are entrusted to you, and the Master’s heart is engraved upon this stone.
Hereafter, those who read these words and do not shed tears are like people who hear of their parents’ blood, heart, and bones [without being moved].

To remain unmoved by such colors [of worldly phenomena] would be utterly inconsistent with being a true disciple. I, Qinggu, say that among our followers there must surely be tears, which shall certainly be shed upon the remains of Master Wan.
Record of the Relics at Leiyin Qu of Shijing Mountain in Western Zhuozhou In the twentieth year of the Wanli era of the Ming Dynasty,
the year of Renchen, on the fifteenth day— the gengyin of the first month— of the fourth lunar month,
Daguank'e Chan Master arrived from Mount Wutai to escort Longzi back to Tanzhe. [The] Holy Mother’s Compassion...
When the Imperial Empress Dowager heard of this, she dispatched her close attendants, Chen Ru, Zhao Yun, and others, to provide offerings for the ritual retreat.

On the twelfth day, the *xīnwèi* of the first month of the fifth lunar month (the *gēngshēn* new moon), the Master, accompanied by his attendant Dàokāi Rúqí, Xu Yán of the Court of the Imperial Stables, and others, arrived at Lèiyīn Qū on Shìjīng Mountain.
This site was where the Venerable Jìngwǎn had carved stone tablets during the Dàyè era of the Sui dynasty.
At the Tripitaka Repository, the Master observed that the statues and furnishings within the excavation were obscured and the stone scriptures were eroded by corrosion.
He consequently ordered Mingliang, the abbot of Dongyun Monastery, to clear away the debris. On that day, light shone like torches upon the cliffs and valleys, and wind and thunder shook the earth.

The following day, they opened the cave and paid homage to the stone; beneath the stone was a hollow, and within the hollow was a stone casket one chi in length and breadth, its face inscribed with large characters.
In the twelfth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, the year being Bingzi, on the eighth day of the fourth month, a Jiazi day, three grains of Buddha-relics were enshrined within this casket.
May they remain and sustain [the Dharma] for eternal kalpas. This inscription consists of thirty-six characters.
Inside, four or five sheng of sacred bone were stored; it was like stone marrow, emitting a wondrous and fragrant scent. Within that was a silver casket, one square inch in size.
It was granted. Inside [the box] was a small golden casket about half an inch in size, within which was stored a small golden flask like a pea.

Inside that was placed the Buddha’s śarīra, three grains in number, the size of millet seeds, purple-red in color, and as hard as diamond. The attendant opened [the box] and invited [the relics] to the Master’s quarters.
The Master joyfully prostrated and offered praise. Thereupon, he dictated a letter and entrusted it to Zhao Yūn, instructing him to present it to Xu Fǎdēng and request an imperial edict.
The Empress Dowager, the Holy Mother, was delighted and joyful. After fasting for three days, on the first day of the sixth month, the *jichou* day, she was welcomed into the Cining Palace.
She was venerated there for three days. Furthermore, outside the small golden casket, a small jade casket was added;

this jade casket was in turn encased by another small golden casket, measuring about one *cun* square. These were placed within a silver casket to serve as an adornment. Funds were then withdrawn from the treasury.
Fifty taels of silver were used to construct a large stone casket, which was used to enclose [the relics] entirely.
On the twentieth day, the *dingwei* day, of the eighth month of the *renchen* year in the twentieth year of the Wanli era (August 1592), they were reinstalled in the stone crypt.

May they remain for eternal kalpas, so that through the convergence of conditions in life after life, they may be beheld again. He commanded the śramaṇa Deqing to record these events. Deqing, with single-minded devotion, [did so].
Joining his palms, he spoke, saying: "As for the *śarīra*, they originate from our Buddha’s stage of practice (*bhūmi*).

It was first produced by the arousal of the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*), which radiated the light of morality, concentration, and wisdom (*śīla-samādhi-prajñā*) to permeate and transform the impure and impermanent three karmas (*trikarma*).

Through these transformations, there arose the distinction between the physical body (*janmakāya*) and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). From the initial awakening until the exhaustion of all habitual taints (*āsrava-kṣaya*), [the process continued] through the three..."

Because his virtues are perfected, the physical body manifested according to conditions—its marks and signs of excellence and its radiance—is as brilliant as a mountain of jewels, a mass of purple-gold light from Jambūnada gold.
His three karmas and six sense faculties are translucent both internally and externally; thus, this impermanent body has realized the adamantine essence.
Therefore, at the Great Parinirvāṇa, the various great disciples and the great assembly of devas each held sandalwood and aloeswood...

Water is accumulated to cremate his body; then his skin, bones, flesh, blood, hair, fur, nails, and teeth follow the flow of the flames, each transforming into a vajra seed, most extremely firm and solid—entering fire it is not burned, entering water it does not drown.
Just as mercury conforms to the ground, each of its droplets is perfectly round; this is called *śarīra*, which in this [language] is translated as "bone-born.

This refers to the physical body (*jāti-kāya*). It is perceived only in fragments; therefore, its colors follow those of the skin, bones, blood, flesh, hair, fur, nails, and teeth, appearing in various hues such as red, yellow, white, and black.
They differ in color, some being small and others large, some round and others straight, resembling dewdrops.

The pearls are like millet or beans. Furthermore, due to the perfuming of three factors—meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the practice of the Way, and the power of vows—they may be mobile or immobile, manifesting in various forms or remaining unmanifest.
As for meditative concentration, it is perfectly still and eternally quiescent.
As for the practice of the Way, it revolves like a vase or a basin, never ceasing throughout all eternity. As for the power of vows, whatever is sought is necessarily fulfilled. If one says, "I..."
Abiding on Vulture Peak, it is ever-present and never extinguished; is this not the entire manifestation of the Dharma-body? Alas!
What Yongjia said—that the illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma-body—is no empty talk.
Viewed from this perspective, all sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet, they are merely conditioned by deluded thoughts, ignorance, and karmic actions.
One forms a body that is impermanent and subject to decay; yet, in the very midst of daily life, it manifests before one.
Moment by moment, it flows secretly, and the true light alone is revealed, gushing forth from the eighty-four thousand pores. Each and every ray of light shines boundlessly.
By means of this very impermanent body and mind, one becomes the eternally abiding vajra. If this light is extended to universally illuminate the great earth, then—

All mountains, rivers, grasses, and weeds, even down to the finest motes of dust, are none other than the true body of the Buddha; they are ultimately firm, immovable, and indestructible. Each and every one is a relic of the Dharmakāya—how could there be any limit to them? It is only because they are perceived according to the power of the conditions of sentient beings' minds that the entire physical body of the World-Honored One was seen to yield only eight *hu* and four *dou* of relics when divided.

Furthermore, let us distinguish this: The relics of the Tathāgata are of two kinds: first, the relics of the *dharmakāya*; second, the relics of the *rūpakāya*. What is meant by the relics of the *dharmakāya*? It refers to all phenomena within the triple world, from the great earth up to the summit of existence (*bhavāgra*). All these are the relics of the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya*, for they are all the Tathāgata’s own nature. Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya* is omnipresent, and all phenomena are the Tathāgata’s own nature. Therefore, it is said that "all things are the Buddha. This is called the relics of the *dharmakāya*. What is meant by the relics of the *rūpakāya*? It refers to the relics obtained after the Tathāgata’s *rūpakāya* has entered *parinirvāṇa*. These are the relics of the *rūpakāya*.

Regarding these two kinds of relics, the relics of the *dharmakāya* are immeasurable, while the relics of the *rūpakāya* are measurable. Why is this so? Because the *dharmakāya* is eternal and unchanging, whereas the *rūpakāya* is subject to birth and extinction. Furthermore, the *dharmakāya* is the ultimate reality, while the *rūpakāya* is a manifestation for the sake of guiding sentient beings. Therefore, the relics of the *dharmakāya* are immeasurable, while the relics of the *rūpakāya* are measurable. This is why, although the entire physical body of the World-Honored One was offered, only eight *hu* and four *dou* were obtained. This is merely a portion [of the whole].
There were three [copies]. Heaven, the human realm, and the dragon palaces each took one to erect as stupas and offer worship to them.
As for that which spread among humans, King Aśoka, by means of his great supernatural powers, dispatched spirits and deities to erect *stūpas* throughout Jambudvīpa;
in our land of Zhendan (China), those that can be counted by sight number nineteen, including the one at Mingzhou.
Your Majesty, you have just now occupied the preeminent position; is this not perhaps due to being permeated by the two kinds of wisdom?

As for me, Jīnlíng Chángqiān, I was sought out by the divine monk Kāṅhuì—could this not also be due to the permeation of his vows? This is especially true of the eminent monks of successive generations.
Generally, those who have perfected the three trainings are many; yet they are merely called "sons of the steadfast.
It has been said that China was formerly known as Chixian Shenzhou (the Divine Land of the Red Pass).

Moreover, since the people of that land possess largely the faculties for the Mahāyāna, and there are countless relics of our Buddha, how could their influence possibly be limited to only ten or so? I harbored these doubts within myself until I read the *Śā*... [text fragment].
Record of the Response to Merit: It is seen that the Divine Nun Zhixian of the Sui dynasty obtained a single *śarīra*.
When Emperor Wen was first born, the nun took him up and raised him. When Emperor Wen grew up and bore the great responsibility of state affairs, he desired to repay the divine nun.

The nun simply entrusted him with the *śarīra* she had preserved, saying: "My child, you shall become a compassionate father to all under heaven and cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish once more. For this reason...
"It would suffice to build stupas everywhere; what need is there for me to offer a reward? The Emperor accepted this as his command.
Consequently, among all the famous mountains and their respective pagodas and temples throughout the realm today, those of the Great Sui dynasty predominate. I, a fool, wonder:
are these śarīras enshrined here those that Master Yuǎn personally received from Emperor Wén’s own hands, or are they sustained by the power of our World-Honored One’s vows?
The Sūtra-piṭaka intends to reveal a small portion of the true body (*dharmakāya*); does it not desire that sentient beings suddenly perceive its entirety?
Now, as soon as our National Preceptor arrived, the śarīra immediately emerged and was thereby transmitted to the Queen Mother.
Is this not perhaps due to the convergence of karmic conditions from former lives? Otherwise, how could such a profound resonance between the Way and its response be so manifest? I venture to say:

During the Three Wu period, the Buddha-dharma had not yet reached the region south of the Yangtze River. Yet for what reason did these śarīras previously exist within the earth, their radiance soaring through the heavens?
Senghui followed the light and arrived; the people of Wu regarded this as extraordinary.

When he spoke of these śarīras and requested that they be sought with earnest devotion for twenty-one days, the people of Wu consequently transformed their view of the strange and miraculous into one of reverent faith. Thus, the Way of the Dharma was spread.

It was from this point that it began, handed down through successive generations for over a thousand years until our Sacred Ancestor, the Divine Sovereign, who revered and honored these matters beyond those of a hundred ages.
Furthermore, it was by relying on this that the capital was established at Jinling, laying the vast foundation for ten thousand generations.
To this day, the light of the stupa shines brilliantly; its solemnity and exquisite beauty are equal to the Buddha’s own body—how could this be a trivial matter? Moreover,
These stone scriptures are the work of my master, Master Wan, who, riding the wheel of aspiration from Mount Nanyue, awaits Maitreya.

Having passed through the three calamities and traversed kalpas beyond measure, how could they have been encountered even in a hundred million lifetimes? Yet these śarīras have been buried for a long time; now that I, Shi Yi, have come as his disciple.
Appearing without being sought, it is my Holy Mother alone. Residing in the ninefold palace, she arrived of her own accord without expectation.

Is this not because our Buddha, through the power of his great vows, extensively protects the Triple Gem, manifesting at the opportune moment to extend the longevity of our imperial house and to bless all living beings with eternal and boundless fortune?
Thus, he causes the True Dharma to circulate and ensures that the lineage of the Buddhas remains unbroken.
Is it not so? Furthermore, if we examine the stone scriptures carved by Master Wan, which spanned more than six hundred years from the Sui to the Yuan dynasties, they had barely completed even half.
By the time of our Ming dynasty, there was suddenly no further record of them. Could it be that our World-Honored One revealed only this small portion?

Like a single petal of a flower revealing boundless spring, [this work] seeks to cause sentient beings to extend the wisdom-life of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body from this treasury of scriptures far into the exhaustion of kalpas. Is it not so? How easy its appearance has been!
Therefore, I, Qing, have been able to record its beginning and end in detail to illuminate future generations, so that those who see or hear it may know that the Sage—
A response that is empty must surely have its cause; how could it be in vain? This serves as a record.
In general, the Stele Record of the Permanent Endowment of Mingyin Temple states:
It was only our Buddha, the World-Honored One, who descended his spirit to Vulture Peak to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, whereas his various disciples did not.
Those of noble lineage and pure conduct do not cross over; those who have entered the state of non-arising do not abide. Therefore, that which they dwell in is impermanent.

He merely cautioned them, saying: "Eat but one meal at midday; lodge but one night under a tree. This was to demonstrate that his remaining life was like a temporary sojourn, passing once and never to return, having from the outset no intention to remain among the affairs of the human world.
It was not for the sake of what is called high and spacious dwellings or the abundance of mouth and body. Thereafter—
The city of Rājagṛha was benefited by the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada, who, intending to invite the Buddha to preach the Dharma, requested Prince Jeta’s grove to construct a vihāra to welcome him.
He did not begrudge covering the ground with gold coins, and thus the multi-storied lecture hall was inaugurated.
The communal residence for the Great Assembly also began from this point; yet, [the Buddha] still went on alms rounds day after day, and the four requisites were never lacking.

It was originally intended for the abundance and well-being of the community. Later, because [the monks] were unable to go on alms rounds due to old age and illness, the permanent endowment (sanghārāma) was established.

Thus, this permanent endowment was indeed established for the sake of those who were aged or infirm; how could it have been conceived for the affairs of today? Since the teachings flowed eastward, magnificent palaces and great monasteries have arisen.

The monasteries were scattered like stars, with smoke from their hearths and fires visible to one another, and the sound of bells and drums heard from afar. Yet, as time distanced them further from the Sage, they deviated greatly from the original intent.
Therefore, Master Baizhang arose to vigorously revitalize the tradition; he established the Pure Rules (*qinggui*) to support and supplement the Vinaya, hoping to return to the original regulations.
Alas! Those who dwell within these gates—how could they all have been of noble lineage or have renounced worldly glory? By practicing pure conduct, they sought to harmonize with the Unconditioned.

Is it not so? Therefore, those who establish [a monastery] do not fail to provide for the *anāthapiṇḍada* (the "solitary mendicant"); yet those who respond to this invitation are not necessarily like the Buddha.
Those who dwell therein are not necessarily all free from old age, sickness, and birth. Thus it is said: "If guest-monks are not received, my Dharma shall perish.
This is not only no land of merit; rather, it turns instead into a sea of poison. Thinking of this, I cannot help but weep.
The dew moistened his breast. To the south of the capital city is a temple called Mingyin (Bright Cause), formerly known as Sāngshèng (Three Saints).

It was founded by the Great Master Yúnyá. The Master was born in Bǎoding; at the age of seven, he donned the black robes of a monk. At eighteen, he began his travels to visit various masters, studying under them all.
Initially, the sacred site of Wǔtái was seized by a band of rebels who throttled its vital arteries, and [the Master] sought refuge there.

[This record] is concluded. Previously, there was the Great Master Wu-zhu, who, following the old path over the mountain ridges of Shaolin’s domain, cleared away a bandit’s nest and established a monastery called Longquan Temple to provide rest for travelers. Thus, the Dharma-way of Mañjuśrī flourished greatly.
When the Great Master [Wu-wei] reached the age of twenty, he assisted Master Wu-zhu in its expansion; his merit was truly great. How could this be...?

Was this not his long-cherished vow? Having resided at Longquan for ten years, he first entered the capital, ascended the altar to receive full ordination, and immediately established San-sheng Monastery to welcome practitioners from all quarters.
Another five years passed before he was selected as a Grand Master (Dazongshi). Receiving an imperial decree, he ascended the honored seat and transmitted the Vinaya teachings for many years;
his Way flourished ever more greatly. In the third year of the Wanli era, he once again restored and clarified [the tradition].
Ten years later, the Great Master entered nirvana. Five years after that, his grandson, the Venerable Yang-ya (Aṅgāra), inherited his legacy.
The Venerable was esteemed for his learning and conduct in his time; residing at Longquan, he preached the Dharma.
Moved within by a sacred mother, she donated gold to rebuild the temple, naming it Huguo Mingyin (State-Protecting Clear Cause). Thus, the merit originated from the imperial lineage.
Master [Yunqi] Zhuhong. In the autumn of the Renchen year of the Wanli era, I followed my karmic conditions to the royal capital and met Chan Master Daguan at the Great Cishou Monastery.
Master Qinggong came to visit me and said: "Mingyin was indeed founded by our patriarch.

Yet, as I observe the various Buddhist monasteries throughout the land, those who dwell within them often fail to embody the original intent behind the establishment of these sacred sites by the former sages."
As for those who sell themselves yet maintain the fundamental precepts, what can they do against the accumulation of karma? I pray that this [monastery] may remain as a permanent dwelling forever.
From this day forward, all meals at the mountain gate shall be shared equally with the assembly;

the worthy may dwell here, the aged and infirm may find peace here, and travelers may be welcomed within. Regarding all necessities for the regular residence, the administrators are authorized to increase the provisions.

No damage shall be permitted. To all my descendants: their residence is permitted, but partitioning [the estate] is not permitted; all profits and benefits are permitted for public use, but private appropriation is not permitted;
all fields and property are permitted to be maintained, but sold they may not be.

May the incense and lamps be bright as the sun and moon through every generation, so as to perpetuate and honor the Triple Gem and repay the Buddha’s kindness. May the Emperor’s life be long and enduring. No end.
[The petitioner] entreated me to record these events. Having heard them, I was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and I praised him, saying:

"The Master takes the mind of the Tathāgata as his abiding and the mind of Baizhang as his permanent residence. He causes those who dwell hereafter to take non-discrimination as their sublime practice.
If all under heaven were to hear of this wind and be inspired to arise, there would be no place where the Jetavana Grove is not replicated."
The sublime precepts of the True Dharma may perhaps be seen manifested this very day. How could the meritorious virtues of the Honorable One be measured?
With a sincere heart, I have briefly engraved these words upon this enduring stone to illuminate future generations.
Epigraphic Record of the Opening of Guanyin Cave at Jinping Mountain.

Among the many wondrous and sublime sites of China’s famous mountains, Mount Taihang serves as the overseer of heaven and earth. Stretching from Shouyang to the coastal mountains, it commands the vast expanse.
Refined spirit coalesces within the capital. Thus, along the western mountains of the old capital, jade palaces and Buddhist temples are as numerous as fish scales set in a mosaic;
all are embellished by human effort upon the handiwork of Nature. Yet there are those of natural wonder and beauty that require no carving or polishing.
That which transcends ordinary perception is found solely in the single realm of Guanyin Cave on Mount Jinping.

The mountain lies about one hundred li west of the capital. The cave occupies the breast of the mountain, consisting of three interconnected recesses like the eyes of Maheśvara. Within, the formations are crystalline and dense, shaped like water and milk mingling;
their myriad forms and infinite appearances are beyond description. The mountain’s terrain encircles it in a protective embrace. It is named... [name of the site].

The flowers differ from common blossoms; when they bloom, they resemble a brocade screen. A single stream, its source deep in the valley, winds and meanders before pooling at the foot of the mountain.
Thus, the surrounding peaks stand tall and dense, like blue lotuses emerging from the water.
According to local tradition, elders often report seeing the Great Being Avalokiteśvara appearing amidst the clouds and mist; it was for this reason that the place was named. In the year Guiwei...
In the spring, I traveled with my staff to various famous scenic sites and practiced the art of abstaining from grain within Sanxue Cave.
Wang Gongyue, the Duke of Feimuchang, came to visit me; when we discussed this matter, I went there to see it for myself. Upon seeing it once, I fell deeply in love with it.

The Duke then requested that I develop the site, first donating thirty mu of land to serve as a preliminary offering for the incense and lamps, and constructing a tea pavilion to provide for travelers.
Come! At that time, I was weary of wandering in the human world and had no leisure to manage affairs;

thus, I entrusted the Dharma-heir Jiufeng Zhenyu Shanshi with its governance and immediately set out eastward across the sea. Subsequently, an official of such-and-such rank arrived by imperial command to supervise the affairs of the monastery, serving as a devoted patron (*dānapati*) for its founding.
The administrators of the monastery and others joined heart and mind in assisting its completion, expanding [the site].

The local people were mobilized to labor. They excavated the hollows and filled the voids, leveling the high ground to the low. Over several years, they created cliffs and embankments tens of feet high.
Outside the cave, they further constructed a meditation hall of two bays. What was once overgrown with thorns and brambles is now a sacred ground.
In the autumn of the Renchen year, while carrying my alms bowl through the royal city, I passed this site again and sighed deeply, saying: "Truly, the environment follows [the mind]..."

The mind undergoes transformation; the Way depends on human effort. I have often heard that the Great Being Avalokiteśvara is universally responsive through perfect penetration, manifesting everywhere.

This is because he dwells within the convergence of resonance and response, appearing like the moon reflected in clear water. Furthermore, since every person is inherently a Buddha, one cannot achieve this without cultivation;
and since every place is a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one cannot perceive it without diligent application. This mountain is certainly...

This is a miraculous wonder. Had it not been for the sovereign and these lords, who relied upon causes and conditions to establish this with fervent dedication, even if it were adorned with the seven treasures, it would all have been abandoned amidst thorns and brambles;
how then could one dare hope to transform such thorns and brambles into a grove?

Now, the sound of bells and the resonance of the *brahman* chant together discourse on Prajñā; the azure cliffs and stone walls all manifest the *dharmakāya*. Those who hear this are not deluded, and those who see...
Those who attained awakening thereby, and those who realized perfect penetration through this ground, are beyond counting.

The merit of the patrons, the donors, the creators, and the assistants shall all endure forever without end. This is intended to pray for the longevity of the Sage and to spread the breeze of compassion so that it may continue endlessly.
The practitioner Haiyin, not forgetting the beginning and disregarding the end, has thus composed this inscription.
The inscription reads:
"The Dharma-body of the Great Earth originally possesses not a single inch of soil; the towering azure cliffs are visible to all who have eyes. So too is the resonant, perfect sound."
Fundamentally there is no sound; yet as the waters flow with a surging roar, all who have ears hear it. At every place of practice (doctrang), he is present without ever departing.

To those of great power, he manifests as a golden *yū* (a ritual vessel); the Great Being of Universal Pervasion (*Samantabhadra*) appears in forms according to the capacities of beings—how could he be limited to this alone?

Out of special compassion for sentient beings, I reveal that the interior of the cave is fundamentally void; its myriad wonders and transformations are, by their very nature, perfect penetration—the original form.
When the time had not yet arrived, it was long buried under dust; now that the season has come, it opens at the mere slightest intention. Its sound resounds through the gates of heaven.
Its radiance surges across the great earth; the merit of seeing and hearing it is inconceivable.
May it pray for the imperial domain above, securing the stability of the altars of soil and grain, and may the Sage’s life-span be boundless for a thousand autumns and ten thousand years.
Epigraphic Record (with Inscription) for Daci Xuanwen Temple at Fangshun Bridge,
the Lower Monastery of Fenglin Temple on Mount Wutai Mount Wutai is the sacred site of Mañjuśrī. Within it, ten thousand bodhisattvas preach the Dharma, manifesting transformations without limit.

Miraculous manifestations were manifold. Beginning with the arrival of Kāśyapa Mātanga during the Yongping era of the Han dynasty, and continuing through the Three Kingdoms and Six Dynasties, and across the successive dynasties of Tang, Song, Yuan, and Ming, the records of imperial devotion by emperors, empresses, consorts, and rulers are clearly traceable.
Our Emperor Chengzu, the Wenhuangdi, invited the Great Dharma King (Nagawang) to reside here; since then, the monasteries and temples have flourished year after year.

The [veneration of the Buddha] increased year by year. Upon the accession of our current Sovereign, during the early years of the Wanli era, our Holy Mother, Empress Dowager Cisheng Xuanwen Mingxu, performed great Buddhist rites for the benefit of the late Emperor and to protect the person of the present Sage.
Beginning with Mount Wutai, she invited twelve eminent monks from famous mountains throughout the realm; among them was the Chan Master Erhu of Fenglin Temple.
The Master served as the head seat (śrīpāda). His name was Deyin, his courtesy name was Chetian, and he was a native of Taiyuan in Shanxi.

From his initial emergence until the end of his life, his practice was centered on Mount [Yun]shan, where he became renowned both at home and abroad. The Holy Mother built Fenglin Temple for him to reside in.

Once the temple was completed, considering that Mount [Wutai] was a thousand li from the capital and its deep valleys spanned several hundred li, she further established a residence for him in Mancheng, Baoding Prefecture.
The County authorities then established a reception temple by the side of Shun Bridge, with the plaque inscribed "Daci Xuanwen" (Great Compassion Proclaiming Culture).

Furthermore, they granted over ten *qǐng* of land for the temple’s support to protect the incense and lamps so that they might endure for all eternity. They also ordained the novice Mingli as an attendant.
The Master’s Way was esteemed beyond the secular world, and his fame reached the inner court; thus, the Imperial Grace bestowed upon him was profound and surpassed the ordinary.
As for those who served Master Xu, such as Prince Qingming, the various gentry and scholars, and Grand Marshal Lord Wu, they all held the Master in profound esteem;
consequently, his meditation halls flourished into monastic communities wherever he stayed, with the morning bells and evening chants resounding through them.
With incense and fire-crystals, we offer these prayers for the Emperor’s boundless longevity and for the preservation of the Imperial Realm for ten thousand generations.
This is entirely due to the vast and compassionate grace of our Holy Mother; indeed, it is truly because of her that she has been moved.

Now, this site shall serve as sustenance for the physical bodies and the wisdom-lives of the assembly of monks, ensuring their steadfastness. How could the merit and blessings thereof ever be measured by number?
How profound! The compassionate grace of our Holy Mother is as vast and thick as Heaven and Earth; may these meritorious virtues likewise endure for all eternity.
There must surely be spirits and deities providing protection therein, so that those who approach this place in the future—

Those who protect this land, how could they fail to trace the source of the Sage’s mind? How would they dare forget the kindness of their sovereign and parents, only to incur the retribution of ghosts and spirits?
When the temple was completed, he commanded the śramaṇa Qing to record these events. With humble prostrations, I have composed this inscription, saying:
[The Inscription] says:
How sublime is the primal power of Kun! All things derive their life from it. Lofty is Mount Taihang, serving as the main axis of heaven and earth.

Exalted is Qingliang, the sacred site of the Sage. It is the dwelling place of myriad spirits, situated as a pillow to the north; it serves as a protective bulwark without while reverently supporting the Divine Capital within.
Jade palaces and Brahma temples abound everywhere in these monasteries. It was solely our Holy Mother who nurtured the imperial virtue;
whatever she undertook was nothing other than for the sake of the nation. She established this renowned monastery to welcome fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life.

Arriving from the ten directions like clouds or walls, they seek to cultivate their spiritual lives, which must necessarily rely upon the physical body. Without the need to labor for alms, the fragrant provisions are overflowing—there is land here.
