The construction began in the [month] of the [year] and was completed in the [month] of the [year].

It was formerly called Nanshan (South Mountain) and is now named Jingtu (Pure Land), reflecting its fundamental cause. The official’s surname is Sūn, his given name is Yúnyì, and his courtesy name is Túnán. He is of the Jin [dynasty].
Recorded by the monk Deqing of Changgan, below the White Gate (Bai Xia).
Regarding the Record of the Huiliang Mountain Society:
When I was formerly traveling as a wandering monk, I passed through the hamlet of Pingyang with Master Miaofeng and settled at the southern slope of Mount Huo. From afar...
Gazing upon the myriad peaks, lush and verdant, rising majestically toward the Milky Way, with misty forests dense and flourishing, one feels there must surely be a sacred site of the sages here.
The Master said, "This is Mount Xiuliang (Mount of Ceasing Grain). In the past, there was a practitioner who subsisted on cypress here; it was named for that reason.
Later, a Buddhist monastery was built called Ciyun (Cloud of Compassion). I passed by here before I had the opportunity to ascend and visit. I now reside at Wutai, located to the east."
It has been thirty-seven years since the time beyond the ridges of the sea; I have often felt a sense of dazed wonder within my mind and eyes.
In the spring of the Renzi year, Master Kongyin of the Bamboo Grove at Qingliang sent his disciple Wuci to deliver a letter and inquire after me in this miasmic land.

I inquired about the flourishing state of the Master’s Dharma and Way, and he further remarked that those disciples who had long received the benefits of the Dharma had all dispersed to live in seclusion, selecting famous and beautiful sites to cultivate their spiritual conditions.
He then presented me with the Master’s "Pact for the Society at Mount Xiuliang" along with the preface by the Imperial Historian Li Benning.
Upon reading them, I sighed deeply and said: "Alas! How magnificent are these mountains and rivers; they wait for someone to realize their potential."
Yet it arose; for were it not for the right person, the Way would not have been practiced in vain—how could this be said without significance?

I reflect deeply upon Śākyamuni’s descent of his spirit into Kapilavastu, where the most eminent and heroic arhats gathered at Gṛdhrakūṭa; there, through the conditions of dependent origination, he proclaimed the Way at Jetavana and Kukkuṭārāma.
These are all traces of manifestations in accordance with conditions; this is precisely how the Dharma-society was initiated.
Since the Way and its Teachings spread to the East, every famous mountain within the realm has served as a place for proclaiming the Way.

Among the sages of antiquity, there has never been one who could perpetuate the transformation of the Dharma without occupying a magnificent site and relying on a spirit-infused landscape. National Teacher Qingliang Guan first expounded the *Huayan* [Avataṃsaka Sūtra]...
He was venerated at Mount Wutai, and his Way spread throughout the world; he served as the preceptor to seven successive emperors of the Tang dynasty.

Since that time, over a thousand years have passed in relative silence. Now, Master Kong has once again opened the Bamboo Grove and extensively propagated the Sudden and Perfect Teaching (*yuantun-jiao*).

Disciples from the ten directions have gathered like clouds, surrounded by tens of thousands. Is this not the great flourishing of an era? Today, his disciples are able to take the realization of the Way as their...

Huai’s aspirations were set upon secluded dwelling, and his mind was fixed on pure deeds (*śukla-karman*). He followed the legacy of those who abstained from grain and spread the rain of Dharma from the clouds of compassion.

He gathered a multitude of eminent monastics and laypeople to open the gate of non-duality and establish assemblies of equality. Throughout the six periods of the day, he maintained the lotus-hour clock and cultivated practice with single-minded diligence.
By day, he expounded the teachings to clarify the fundamental principle; by night, he sat in meditation to still discursive thoughts. Regarding the precepts...

I pay homage to Upāli. As you practice in accordance with Prajñā, you have suddenly caused the cragside trees and courtyard sedges, the cries of monkeys and the calls of cranes, all to manifest the Dharma-body and proclaim the wondrous meaning.
What was once a region of profound gloom and ultimate stillness has now been transformed into a place that illuminates both past and present.
Is this not because the spirit of the mountains awaited its human counterpart, and because the Way moves in accordance with the times, such that the karmic conditions have finally converged?

Is it not the case that the resolve to consume cypress wood has not perished even unto this day? Having once passed through that region and gazed upon its scenic splendor, I now dwell in a land of miasma;
hearing of this undertaking from afar, my heart feels cool and refreshed as I imagine that auspicious assembly.

I have briefly recorded the general outline of its decline and restoration to establish a karmic connection for future generations. As for the regulations for its establishment, they shall be governed by the presiding authority according to the established laws.
*Record of the Reconstruction of Haihui Xuan (Along with Inscription)*
Lingnan borders Chu. From Caoxi to Nanyue, the distance is a thousand *li*, across which stretch lofty mountains and steep ridges, with rolling hills and peaks winding and dense;

everywhere there are fine mountains and waters. Since the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch, caused the Way to flourish throughout Lingbiao, his disciple Master Rang has propagated the Dharma at Nanyue.
Consequently, these places have become sites for renowned monks and great virtuous ones who have retired in seclusion, existing in every location.

Whenever a place became a site for solitary habitation, over time it would eventually become a blessed ground (bǎofáng) and a sacred site (fódì), serving as a point of veneration for the surrounding region;
such places were found wherever conditions allowed. Yichang lies between two mountains, near Shaoshi Peak and under the jurisdiction of Hengyang.

It is a necessary thoroughfare for those traveling back and forth. About five li from the administrative seat, there is a mountain named Houpei, whose peaks and ridges are remarkably beautiful and lush with forests.

Lush and flourishing, it is truly a preeminent site for the Way. Recently, Li Junye, a local resident, donated it as a hermitage and invited Zhenrun, a disciple of Dayong, to reside there, establishing it as a temporary resting place for eminent practitioners from all directions who wander like clouds and water.
It was named Haihui (Ocean Assembly). Construction began in the Jiamao year of the Wanli era; from then until the present Gui Mao year, it has again been ravaged by wind and rain.

It had been neglected and dilapidated, but the group of those who sought its restoration, like Yao, renewed it once again. Above, there is a Buddha hall and a mountain gate, each consisting of three bays;
to the left and right are the abbot’s quarters and the refectory and kitchen. Everything is fully provided for. There are one hundred *mu* of fields, which can yield two *shi* of grain.
Its cultivation can provide for more than ten people. For those who come and go as wandering monks, they need seek nothing outside here for a single meal or a single night’s stay;

this is truly like one of those "Transformation Cities" (化城). I have lived beyond the mountain ridges for eight years, when I was invited by the local authorities to enter Caoxi and serve as an attendant to the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch.
When the monk Ruyao visited me and requested a record, I therefore recorded it directly as follows.
Thus, he composed an inscription to commemorate it. The inscription reads: "Ah, the Southern Peak!
It is established there between Jing and Xiang. From its roots it draws forth branches and trunks, spreading its lineage to the distant wilderness. Winding for a thousand li..."
The Yuling Ridge winds high above, while the Precious Grove stands aloft. The waters of Caoxi are cold; these waters of Caoxi trace their source back to Western India.
There, a Supreme Being washed his bones of the Way. Those bones of the Way remain as if alive, and the flow of water never ceases, dispersing itself as *amṛta* (clarified butter).
Bringing forth rain and moisture upon the southern slopes of Mount Zhang and at the foot of Mount Houpei, a transformation-city (nirmāṇakūṭa) has surged forth as a blessing for these people.
This city of transformation is not far away; the place of jewels is near at hand. May those who are weary find rest here, and may they all come together to take refuge. We take refuge in our Teacher.
I have been granted the honor of beholding Your true countenance. I pray that You will protect this land, so that its blessings and prosperity may be inexhaustible.
This is the Record of Long’an on the West Bank of the Water at Nanxiong.
From Mount Heng, the main axis rises up; it extends eastward down to the southern marshes, embracing the Yangtze and the Huai rivers as they flow northward to pay homage to the source.
The Ling River flows backward and away from it; entering the Southern Sea Commandery (Xiongfu), it occupies the upper reaches, encompasses the Hundred Yue territories, and seizes their vital throat.
Acting as a bulwark for the Central Plains, it is truly a metropolitan center of the southeast. It governs the hundred rivers like a vessel tipping a jar, and this is its strategic essence.
The prefectural city leans against the ridges and embraces the river; with two rivers encircling it like arms, it stands majestically towering, overlooking the vast ocean.
If it were like a city of Gandharvas in the sky, or like climbing to heaven or touching the clouds— visible from afar yet unattainable—
then these mountains would fly and these waters would run, with no pools remaining to collect. Thus, the principles of life would not endure,
and people would live in constant anxiety, chasing profit as if chasing waves, seeking only to accumulate substantial stores to prepare for the uncertainties of the year.

Such people are rare indeed. Therefore, the heavens, the earth, the mountains, and the rivers—like the four seasons that do not appear simultaneously—are difficult to maintain in their integrity and stability;
they must necessarily rely on human agency to fashion and perfect them. Thus, the legend of "repairing the heavens" is not a falsehood.

Observing those who governed this commandery in the past, if they possessed even a slight degree of the "Dharma-eye," they could not avoid the distress of gazing helplessly at the weeds [of disorder], yet they were able to pull back the surging waves and stem the hundred [calamities].
As for the ambition of the rivers, one must inevitably employ human labor to supplement them.

Whenever there is business concerning these waters, one must invariably construct temples and shrines, erect stupas, and install bells and drums to confront them; thus, victories are often achieved as swiftly as the sound of a resonance.

Yet people ultimately do not know the reason for this. Allow me to attempt an explanation. Generally, among all things, those that are spiritual and whose transformations are unfathomable are dragons.
Therefore, the sovereign takes them as a model; the Sage is like a dragon, moving like clouds and raining down blessings, upon which all things depend.
As for the claims of geomancers—a tradition not even ranked among the Nine Schools—they speak of "seeking the dragon" and "pinning its [vital point]."

The Cave. Once attained, it blazes forth with brilliant splendor like a great conflagration. Why is this? It is because when one applies acupuncture and moxibustion and strikes the correct vessels, one possesses the power to raise the dead and restore life.

For instance, when a person’s ailment resides in the *gao-huang* (the region between the heart and diaphragm), where medicinal decoctions cannot reach, it is necessary to penetrate it with needles and moxa.
Thus we know that when the dragon of wind is severed and the terrestrial veins are infused, one must surely establish a temple and erect [a monument].

The setting up of bells and drums by the Buddha is like treating a chronic ailment of the gallbladder or diaphragm with acupuncture and moxibustion. Furthermore, heaven and earth constitute a single body;
yin and yang are a single breath. Mountains are its bones and rivers its veins. As for one who possesses the virtue of a dragon yet remains hidden, his fiery nature cannot be restrained.
Those of old who raised dragons must have possessed a specific art; by employing that art, they could [subdue them] at the mere sight of their shadow.
I prostrate myself. Generally, that which is efficacious in the arts must be essential. Those who do not understand it regard it as something miraculous;

yet, for every thing there is that which is liked, there must also be that which is disliked. It is as when a human being dislikes dampness while an eel dislikes dryness, or as water and fire mutually restrain one another, or cold and heat mutually grind against each other—this is surely their inherent principle.
What difficulty could there be in this? Now, dragons delight in concealment and loathe manifestation; they fear metal and iron, and...
It fears the sound of bells and drums; thus, when the body touches it, it trembles; when the ears touch it, it quakes; and when the mind touches it, it submits.
Therefore, when the ancients sought to subdue dragons, they invariably used iron-bound bowls. Thus they were able to tame their nature and conceal their forms.
By following them into their realm through sound, one undergoes transformation; this allows them to be held in the palm of one’s hand, to accompany one’s form and shadow, never departing.
This is it. Its secret lies in nothing else but attaining its fundamental nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, the land is also governed by this. I have often observed the power of this great commandery:
its mountains and rivers leap forth like soaring dragons; how could they be easily constrained?

Thus, at the upper reaches of the East River, a needle was applied at the Yanxiang Pagoda—this is the *baihui* (hundred-meeting) point. At the right armpit of the West River, a needle was applied at Renhe.

The pagoda is located at this waist-vessel (yaoshu). As for the western side of the water, it corresponds to the Gate of Life (mingmen). The hermitage is named Jilong; how could this not have significance?
It is as if the meridians throughout the entire body are integrated at the Gate of Life, encompassing the Sea of Qi and channeling its essence—this is the most vital point.
Alas, the scale of this site is too narrow and insufficient to match it; it is like having a large physical frame but a meager vital energy.
The illness is deep while the medicine is slight; moreover, with the Tailgate (Weilu) discharging its waters, how could it be easily resolved?

Thus, the reason why [the Dharma] was nearly extinguished in the past and was subsequently revived was due to the force of circumstances. Now, the water-mouth of the Three Peaks is like that Tailgate;

the construction of this pagoda and monastery to suppress it is like erecting a defensive gate. Alas! This undertaking was not possible for one who lacked the Dharma-eye and the power to subdue [obstacles].
As for the art of the dragon, why is it associated with this? The offering of this stupa is like blocking the Tailgate (Weilu) to gather the Gate of Life (Mingmen);
it fills the essence and preserves the primal qi. It is truly a matter where life and death are interrelated in this great commandery.
How could it concern itself merely with matters of joy and sorrow? If one were able to expand its foundations, enlarge its scale, and restore its bells and drums, and [cause] sutras to be recited...

Chanting the sounds of this sutra, one offers forth sincerity to reach the divine spirits, so that dragons may hear it and submit, the heavens may hear it and rejoice, humans may hear it and be transformed, and all creatures may be moistened by it and flourish.
May rain and sunshine arrive in their proper seasons; may calamities and portents be utterly extinguished.

May blessings be bestowed upon the people in numbers of billions, and may prayers be offered for the eternal stability of the Imperial Realm and the preservation of these lands without limit. Viewed from this perspective:
It is a gathering of blessings and a congregation of dragons; thus the hermitage is named Jilong (Gathering Dragons), for it is here that dragons have gathered.
The origins of the hermitage’s founding cannot be traced. At the beginning of the Longqing era, the monk Zhenliang dwelt there in austerity.

With funds from his recitation of sutras, he purchased several mu of land to provide for the sustenance of the monks. Not long after, he passed away, and his disciples were unable to maintain the endowment. I have resided there for five years.

The sheep and the disciples were like mirrors. Arriving here, he rested; kneeling, he recited the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*. For three years, he applied himself with such arduous devotion that the people of the commandery came to believe in and revere him.
When he wished to depart, they earnestly entreated him to stay, whereupon he renovated the site extensively. After another three years, the work was finally completed.
In the winter of the Gui-mao year, I went to Caoxi to serve the Sixth Patriarch and personally passed by this hermitage; I knew it was not merely for the sake of one person.
This district is a vital hub; furthermore, it serves as a gateway for the monastics from beyond the passes.
I intend to gather these monastics here to serve as the lifeblood of the dragons and the spiritual essence of the mountains and rivers, so that they may assist in its governance.

Moreover, by spreading the rain of Dharma across worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and nourishing the roots of enlightenment through vast eons, the merit and benefit thereof shall not be established for the sake of this single district or this single person alone. Thus it was decreed.

Having surveyed this land, I grasped its general outline within ten days. Taking the smallness of this hermitage as a metaphor for the vastness of the mountains and rivers, I have directly revealed its hidden depths to inform those who have not yet heard them.
The Dream-Wandering Collection of the Elder Hanshan, Volume Twenty-Three;

Daily Record by the Attendant Fuxian.
Compiled by the Disciple Tonghyŏng;
Revised and Recorded by the Disciple from the South, Liu Qixiang.
Record of Exploring the Wonders of the Qiongxi Sea:

Ten years after I was exiled, in the third month of spring in the year Wuli (1605), I set out on foot from Leyang for a southern journey to Tianchi, to explore the wonders of the Qiongxi Sea and fulfill the appointment made with Lord Wang, the Minister of Rites, and Mr. Xu, the Palace Attendant. I stayed there...
As for the Mingchang Pagoda Courtyard, it was established by Lord Xu to compensate for the deficiency in the northeast quadrant of the prefectural city.

Standing alone in the center of heaven, its lofty pinnacle reaches the Milky Way; from it one may ascend to look out in all directions, as if riding the cool winds and wandering through the vast void.

The tidal sounds stir the heavens, and the color of the water clarifies the void; it is as if the music of the celestial realm were mirrored in a clear mirror—a magnificent and singular spectacle indeed.
After staying there for ten days, my disciples made daily progress. While lingering upon the pavilion, we discussed the Way at our leisure.
At that time, Chen Shengyu invited me to seek out the Golden Grain Buddha of Vaiśālī and to visit the White Dragon of Su Dongpo.
Having fully attained the truth, he delighted in it so much that he forgot to return. After several more days, Officer Liu went for a stroll at West Lake to view the Jade Dragon Spring;
thereupon, with joyful heart, he urged his mount. This was the tenth day of the first month of summer. The lake lies about twenty li west of the prefecture;
its ridges and hills stretch out in succession, appearing verdant from a distance. Traveling twenty li south toward Mount Shishi, he emerged from the city walls.
For about a *li*, village gardens and vegetable plots extend in continuous, orderly succession. Stones are piled high and wide to form ditches, while the earth is split to create furrows;

their skeletal structures are exposed while their flesh-like soil is concealed. Though appearing lean on the outside, they are rich within. Sorghum, millet, beans, wheat, fine vegetables, and small grains—all five types of grain are fully present.
Everything before one’s eyes is brilliant and radiant, appearing almost like the Western Hills at Jimen. Winding and meandering, one gradually enters deeper.

The forest stretched for several li, its dense foliage obscuring the landscape so that one could no longer distinguish the high from the low. Piercing the clouds and treading upon stones, I emerged at a small stream;

its clear current reflected the person, allowing even the finest hairs on the head to be seen. My heart and spleen were washed clean, and the stifling heat was instantly dispelled. It was not even a dozen paces before—
Thus, he approached a large stream and crossed a stone bridge. Looking down at the flowing water, he washed his hair; his flesh and bones were covered with goosebumps.

He then leaned on his staff and took a leisurely stroll, hearing dogs barking from within the clouds yet seeing no smoke or fire. Turning slightly, he entered a village hamlet where the inhabitants lived in square-walled huts built entirely of piled stones;
their forms were simple and their colors ancient. Pale moss and green vines spread and entwined across them like strings of pearls.
He was wearing a celestial crown. Delighted, I forgot my fatigue and leaned on my staff as I entered the gate. After a long while, an old man emerged.
With long eyebrows and a shaggy head, he wore a cow-hide loincloth, tattered clothes, and a grime-stained face; his sleeves were tucked up so that his elbows were visible.
He appeared as if he did not see me, and when questioned, he did not respond. He seemed absent-minded, shaking his head as he walked back inside. From this, I knew him to be a person of Qin.
While at Wuling, I stood still for a moment. With my beard bristling, I let out a long whistle and emerged from the western side of the village house.
The rocks gradually grew larger and the forest became deeper. As stone banks flanked the stream, I beheld fertile soil and level fields where grain and rice spread like clouds;

flowing water poured through them, swirling and eddying on all sides, much like the Wei River or the Qi and Ao valleys—only I regretted the absence of tall bamboos reaching the clouds. Coconut, *zōng*, and betel-nut trees...
The *nang* trees stand everywhere, supporting the heavens; such things do not exist in this world.

What is difficult to change about the banks of the Qi River is that I dragged my sandals along the current, wading through fields and crossing over ridges until I could no longer distinguish east from west. After traveling several more *li*, I crossed a small stream and ascended a level ridge, where I realized I had turned westward.
Thorns snagged at my clothes and forest grasses blocked the path; I pushed aside clouds and brushed away mist, climbing over creepers and treading upon them.
The steps were steep; my spirit was at ease and my feet grew strong. After traveling over ten li, the path was lined with boulders serving as moats—shaped like balls, fists, spheres, and tables;
large and small, tilted and leaning, square as if cut, and slanting like walls.

They were piled into embankments, as dense as woven silk patterns, naturally rising in sharp, orderly rows, none of which failed to conform to the proper proportions. Some were as large as a chamber of one *zhang*. The cliffs...
Like the walls of a palace, there were some so massive that ten thousand men could not lift them; they hung in heavy, drooping clusters, appearing as if wrought by spirits.
Climbing high to look afar, these stretches extended across the fields for miles, existing everywhere in this manner. How extraordinary!

As one wandered about gazing, they emerged faintly from the tops of the thickets, arranged in jagged tiers like a layered city. Looking around in all directions, it was desolate and silent, devoid of human sound—how secluded!
It was deep and secluded, unlike any world of human habitation. Turning slightly to the north, I saw from afar a stone monument amidst the clouds;
my attendants identified it as the Stone Lake (Shihu). I privately harbored doubts about this, for the stones were spread across the ground, as level as a palm, with a color like ancient iron.
Their shapes were ingeniously formed, resembling lotus platters on a large scale and bee-hives on a small scale, displaying a myriad of wondrous and extraordinary forms as one walked along them.
Following its traces, one turns slightly and enters a stone gate. A winding path leads upward, where one first realizes it is a natural formation of rock.
It spans several tens of *li* in circumference, with high ridges on all four sides and a depression in the center containing a lake.

It is like a bright mirror reflecting the heavens, or as if placed within a living basin of water, appearing like a crystal cup; one does not know who carved it. Tradition says that this place was formerly...
The residents once experienced a great storm of wind and thunder. A dragon emerged from the rock, and the waters surged and boiled until the houses were completely submerged, turning into a lake.
When the drought subsided and the water receded, the rock remained in the shape of a dragon. During a severe drought, it appeared in a dream to the Prefect, saying, "I am the Dragon of Stone Lake;
if you pray to me, rain shall surely fall. Whenever the Prefect went there to pray, his requests were immediately answered, and he subsequently constructed a temple to enshrine him.
This has been the established practice until the present day. Entering the Stone Gate for a hundred paces, one crosses a small bridge and comes upon a series of ponds.
Above the ponds, ancient trees spread like a canopy; beneath them stands an ancient hall of three bays, its beams and rafters all made of stone.
Behind the hall is another pond, titled "Jade Dragon Spring" (Yùlóngquán). Upon the pond stands an ancient temple of three bays, housing an image of the Jade Dragon’s Goddess. To the left is...
Longquan (Dragon Spring) emerges from a fissure in the rock; it gushes forth like pearls, as large as carriage axles, and pours into a square pond.
Upon the pond there is the site of a pavilion, and beneath it is a long bay; both possess historical significance, though they have now vanished.

To the east of the pond, separated by a small stone ridge, lies a stream called Huangxi below the ridge. Looking down at the stream from afar, the terrain is rugged and precipitous, with hollowed-out rocks.
In the center, there is a pond like a basin that is most wondrous and extraordinary.

Forests and grasses grow so thickly as to block the way, yet the waters collect and flow, winding and hidden, before converging into a single opening. It is said that the water emerges from the stone bridge of the village ahead;

following it, one circles the base of ten thousand mountains, passes through fields and across gorges, emerges outside Shitashan Mountain, enters southward through the prefectural gate, and crosses the Xiangshui (Resounding Water) Bridge.
The bridge leads directly east to join the great river, which flows down and pours into the Gulf.
There, I and the military aide, along with the two young men Tang and Huang, washed our feet in the clear current, loosened our hair, and opened our robes as we lingered by the pool.

A pure breeze came from all directions, making my very marrow and bones feel cool and refreshed, as if I were sitting in the Hall of Broad Cold (Guanghan), facing a crystal pitcher and gazing upon a jade mirror. Little did I know that this was the sweltering wilderness and the pestilential marshes of the south.

As evening fell, I turned my horse back and followed the waterway to gaze upon it. From its source, it emerges from the valley, winding westward before sweeping south and then heading straight east into the river;

it appears to have no connection whatsoever with the provincial capital. Having exhausted the day’s journey, I returned home and lay upon my high pavilion, where I felt as if I were wandering in a dream.
Upon waking, I recorded this and commented: "This is the mountain range that extends from the Central Plains."
From Mount Nanyue it turns toward Western Yue; its branches extend downward to Guilin. To its left and right, the two rivers flow southward in a continuous stream.
Reaching Cangwu, it passes the Gui Water through the gorges, winding and emerging at Lingqin before entering the sea as the Penglai and Hu islands.

Turning toward Zhuya, it suddenly surges upward, with five peaks piercing the heavens. Facing north toward the Central Plains, it serves as the lock and key for the Southern Commandery, encircling three thousand li.
Truly, this is a great marvel of heaven and earth! The Imperial Founder once said: "The Southern Ocean is vast and boundless;

within it lies a wondrous land spanning several thousand *li*. Is this not indeed the work of the Heavenly Eye? Having personally surveyed the geography from the Southern Range downward, I see that its ridges divide into the Five Ridges (*Wuling*).

The mountains and waters turn their backs on the Central Kingdom and rush southward into the sea. Thus, when one examines the grand configuration of the encircling seas, the left side faces the court.
Xian lies to the right of An-nan, like its two wings. Japan, Luzon, Siam, and various other islands are arrayed on the periphery.
Qiong-dian appropriately serves as a defensive screen for the Hundred Yue regions; it is truly a great metropolis beyond the seas.

The Five Fingers Mountains encircle and converge, rising prominently from the center of heaven as the "Azure Dragon" (Zu-long) of Qiong. The mountains face northward, and the waters flow northward, their waists bound by the Ding [Mountains].
The waters flow peacefully to the left, turning rightward and following the dragon’s course as they extend across the eastern part of the prefecture before plunging directly into the estuary.

The mountains then rush to the right, following the western estuary and coalescing into Shishan (Stone Mountain) in the north. Raising its head and opening its mouth, it exhales the true pulse [of the land], which coils and flows eastward, falling like a cascade.
Looking back, it resembles the bright pearl beneath the chin of a roaming dragon, forming the prefectural city; Stone Mountain serves as its head.

To the left, the lips of the land stretch toward the estuary, forming a rear support; a small stream follows this. To the right, long ridges extend for several tens of *li*, with Stone Lake (*Shihu*) situated within them, winding southward.
A transverse ridge forms the county seat. Behind the ridge lies White Water (*Bai-shui*), which tightly encircles the main dragon axis.
From the stone pagoda, it winds around the southwest corner of the city, passes through the gate to the left, and pools at a low elevation to form Southern Lake (*Nan-hu*). And so on.
The waters of the Shihu flow outward, enclosing the interior. According to the measurements, the Xiangshui Bridge was anciently located at Mapo, extending northeast and winding around Chunniu Guan.
It gathered the waters of Donghu, which turned northwest, and from Xin Qiao, it joined the Baishui River, embracing the eastern side of the city before swirling back.
Now, however, the current has reversed and flows straight in; the river is like a bow, with its back turned toward the prefectural seat, showing no regard for it.
It was as the geomancers say: "The vital energy (*qi*) has dissipated. Duke Xu constructed the Mingchang Pagoda in the northeast (*gen* direction) to block the water-mouth.

It was proposed that the waters of Shihu be diverted to wind around the south of the city, embrace the eastern suburbs, join with the Bailong and Jinsu rivers, pass by the Mingchang Pagoda before finally entering the main river, thereby completing the vital energy.
This would have truly been a work of divine creation; yet it ultimately did not succeed. Was this not...?

"How oppressive it is for people! While I was sitting atop my pavilion, I ascended the tower every night and gazed upon the mountain ranges and rivers; their vital energy (qi) had become utterly depleted.

Pointing this out to my traveling disciples, I said: 'Jiong will surely meet with calamity. Because the mountains and rivers are so desolate and the city appears as empty as if no one were there, it is devoid of vital energy.
At that time, they considered me delusional. Now, on the first full moon of the early summer month, I have crossed the sea to return north."

Before many months had passed, the earth shook violently. The ground split at the eastern gate and the city wall collapsed; all the houses fell down, leaving both officials and commoners exposed to the elements.
The stupa also tilted by half its height, and the pavilion where I resided likewise swayed and trembled uneasily for half a year.
To this day, those who record my words do so as a testament; therefore, I have recorded them here together.
*Record and Inscription on the Jin-su Spring of Qiongzhou* The Qiong Prefecture is about ten *li* from the sea.
At the northeastern corner of the city, where the ridges meet the waters, there is a spring that gushes forth grains of millet. Each grain—

The grains were brilliantly radiant, like pearls floating upon the vast ocean. People took them and tested them; when they removed the husks to reveal the kernel, it resembled the *bùgǔ* (cuckoo) bird of the north.

When winter arrived and the atmospheric energies contracted, the water in the spring became warm, and the millet sprouted like rice seedlings piercing the surface of the water. Thus, these were indeed real grains and not produced by illusion.

The people of the time marveled at this wonder, not knowing where they had originated, and called them generically— [Note: The original text ends abruptly with "概呼" (generally called), suggesting the remainder of the passage was omitted.]

For Susquan. In the third month of spring in the year Wuli Bisi (1585), I crossed the sea from Leiyang to visit the Grand Minister of the Court of Ceremonial, Lord Wang, and the Palace Counselor, Lord Xu, while also exploring the wonders of the Qiong and Hai regions.
Chen Sheng Yuchen is a scholar of broad learning and refined elegance.
I visited him at the Mingchang Pagoda Courtyard. He invited the Lord of the Ministry of Rites to join me in passing through to the abbot’s quarters of Tianning Temple.
During our tea conversation, this matter was mentioned, and so we took up our staffs to go and observe it. I had my servant probe into the sand and mud; indeed, he found several grains of millet.

When the husks were crushed, the kernels emerged looking as if they had been recently harvested. I marveled greatly at this and thus named it Jingu Suquan (Golden Millet Spring), intending to take its meaning from the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
The Tathāgata Maki-ku (Golden Millet) was said by Li Bai to be his own future incarnation; perhaps this is now being realized in the person of the Minister of Rites and Academician.

As he draws water to brew tea, the flavor is exceptionally clear and pungent; upon drinking it, one’s hair and bones feel refreshed and cool, as if one were in the chamber of Vimalakīrti partaking of the food from the Gṛdhrakūṭa Hall.
The young man Chen harbored doubts and rose from his seat to ask: "Millet is produced in the northern lands."
The spring gushes forth from the southern heavens; it is separated by ten thousand *li* and divided by the vast ocean. Why has it come here?
This is what the wise must surely doubt and what ordinary minds cannot fathom. I venture to ask the reason for this. I replied: "Alas!
This is something difficult to discuss with those of the common world. Allow me to attempt an explanation. The great earth floats upon the waters like a single leaf. As for the water—"
It flows secretly through the four continents like the blood vessels circulating throughout a person's body.

Originating from the heart, it nourishes the five viscera, extends outward to the four limbs, permeates the skin, reaches down to the涌泉 (yǒngquán) [the "fountain-head" of the feet], and ascends as far as *nirvāṇa*.

There is not a single hair, pore, nail, or tooth that it does not fully sustain; were it not so sustained, there would be no benevolence (*rén*). Viewed from this perspective, heaven and earth are but a single finger.
Indeed, all things are one body. Water and fire oppose each other; mountains and marshes communicate their vital energy;

wind and clouds breathe together; tides ebb and flow; heaven and earth open and close; day and night come and go—there is not a single moment when the mechanism ceases, just as a person’s daily eating, breathing, and rising and sitting.
What cause for wonder is there? Formerly, a divine monk came from the Western Regions and drank at Caoxi.
The water was fragrant, beautiful, and sweet. Startled, he exclaimed, "This is the water from the Jewel Forest (Ratnavana) of my West Heaven.

At Zhongshan, there is the Great Compassion Hall (Dabei Ge). The hall is a hundred feet high, and the statue within is eighty feet tall. A strange monk from the Tang dynasty traveled everywhere to solicit gold, money, copper, and wood;

wherever he collected these materials, he deposited them into wells. When he returned to retrieve them, they all emerged from the wells, thereby fulfilling his needs. This remains so even to this day.
A single piece of wood remains there. From this we may observe that the waters of the great earth have never failed to flow through, and no object has ever failed to reach its destination;

this is indeed a fact. Formerly, when Su Changgong resided in Danni, he once appraised the waters of three mountains and declared them to be interconnected with those of Huishan, thereby naming it "Huītōng (Whitewater) Spring.
Thus, the Great Void is vast and expansive, and the myriad phenomena are interpenetrating. Man—

It is merely that there are mental limitations and obstructions. I have observed that the land of the Jade Sea (Qiong Hai) originates in the northwest and its vital energy (qi) coalesces in the southeast;
it is like the nail of a single finger. The nail is the remnant of the sinew. Blood nourishes the sinew, and when the sinew is firm, the nail is thick.
Generally, those whose nails are thick are long-lived. Thus, where the soil is deep, there will surely be many resources. So says the commentator.
Everyone says that the soil of the Central Plains is rich and fertile; therefore, generals and ministers mostly emerge from among them. I, however, say this is not so.
Qiong dwells in the South, which corresponds to the Trigram Li. Li has the essence of Qian; it absorbs one Yin line, being firm on the outside while yielding within, empty yet radiant.
This is the symbol of civilization. The earth floats amidst the ocean; fire and metal give rise to water. Thus, there is scorching heat by day and cold by night.
Because the true qi of Qian and Kun reaches its ultimate here and concentrates here, the mountains and rivers abound with gold, silver, and bright pearls.
Exquisite birds and famous incenses, rare and extraordinary beasts, and precious treasures arise here; all things are complete within it.

Among its people, there appear those of immortal spirit and literary fame, as well as loyal ministers and righteous scholars, emerging from time to time. This is but a single corner of heaven and earth, like a mote of dust in the vast void.
The subtle transformations of the Creator pass by unnoticed by the ignorant; I have merely used this single grain to illustrate it for you. As if following one...
"Leaves serve merely to distinguish the spring and autumn; what is there to marvel at? When the Minister of Rites heard this account, he leaped with joy and sighed again, saying, 'How extraordinary!

At that time, Shen Shengde and others who were seated there led one another in prostrating themselves and requested an inscription to enlighten those who had not yet heard it. Thus, he composed this inscription for him:"
The great earth is but a single speck of dust; the vast ocean is but a grain of millet. Filling the ten directions, what could possibly be lacking?
Like hair upon the body, like blood circulating through the limbs—seen at every touch, how could anything not be real? The trigrams Kan and Li, water and fire, Qian and Kun—all reside within me.
When the interaction of the trigrams Jiaogou gives rise to [this phenomenon], what is there that is not possible? The terrestrial qi originates from the north but concentrates in the south;
all things follow suit, surging forth amidst it. People wonder at these grains and do not know their source. When the place of origin is unknown, how can one clarify the fundamental principle?

The subtle transformations of creation do not belong to the realm of hearing or seeing. I shall borrow a single grain to observe its changes. If one understands this single grain, one will see that a mustard seed contains the void;
fire and water circulate everywhere—how could they not be mutually accommodated? The vital energies permeate the entire body, from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet.
Moving upward and downward in a continuous cycle, it ends and begins again. The Great Way revolves in a circle; there is no departure that is not followed by a return.

The pulse of the Way flows subtly, like a single grain of millet; from its deep spring it gushes forth incessantly, emerging from time to time. The pulse of the Way comes from the south; herein one may divine its presence.
Record of a Visit to Jingtai Temple:
The mountains and rivers of Yue originate from Mount Heng; they turn toward the Yuling Pass and descend, their mid-section binding Caoxi.
Winding southward, they flow directly to the Five Rams. The principal mountain of the Five Rams is called Yuexiu; the ancestral dragon of Yuexiu is called Bai.
Yun: White Clouds (Baiyun) is indeed full of wonders and excellences, yet Jingtai is the most sublime. It occupies the belly of the White Clouds while overlooking the city of the Immortal Dragon.
Its two wings embrace it like an aged oyster holding a pearl. Solitary peaks and precipitous ravines abound; deep forests are lush and verdant.
Exotic flowers and strange herbs flourish as mist and clouds emerge and vanish. Starwort grows from the crevices of rocks, and *tso-wen* palm fronds drape the woods.
The inscription reads: "The great ocean is like a mirror, standing upright between the brows; the bright moon is like a pearl, its radiance flowing from the lips.
Truly, this is a wondrous sight in heaven and earth, a magnificent splendor of the South Sea. Originally, the temple was named after the mountain.
During the Jingtai era of our Ming dynasty, a petition was submitted to grant it its former title. Governor Ma Gong’ang led his subordinates to renovate it. I..."
I resided at Wuyang for three years. In the year Wuxu, I took my fellow practitioners on an excursion to view the site, which was exceedingly magnificent and superior.

In the second month of spring in the year Dingwei, I returned to the mountains by imperial decree. The monk Zhengyi of this temple brought this painting to request a record; I have thus composed this brief account for him.
Record of the Baoyue Terrace in Duanzhou:

According to the local gazetteer, one hundred and fifty paces north of the prefecture lies the Baoyue Terrace. It rises abruptly from level ground, two zhang in height and approximately one li in circumference.
Viewed from afar, it resembles a terrace; thus, it is a natural formation rather than a human construction. It is unknown who gave it this name.
In the beginning, there were high cliffs and deep valleys, subject to constant change and transformation. Today, they have become a vast, level lake and embankment.
It seems as though someone with great power has carried them away and departed; the mountains and rivers remain as they once were, yet their true master is no longer present.

In the Jiachen year of the Wanli era, while Governor Chen of Lingxi was at leisure from his administrative duties, he traveled to survey the scenic excellence of the region. Climbing to a high vantage point to gaze into the distance, he sighed with profound emotion, saying:
Only now do I realize that the Terrace of the Precious Moon lies at the very heart of the level lake. According to the principles of geomancy (*xingjia*), a dwelling must rely upon its surroundings;
thus, Xingyan Peak serves as the protective screen for the prefecture, pressing forward in front while receding behind—a configuration created by Heaven for this land.

It serves as the throat and tongue of the region south of the ridges and is a vital thoroughfare for the Hundred Yue peoples. Considering its climate and topography, how could it be so sparse and leaky?
Thus, one knows that this terrace’s relationship to the prefectural city is undoubtedly what geomancers call a "ghostly entrustment. How could such a thing be allowed to remain forever in ruin?
Consequently, he proposed constructing an embankment at the heart of the lake and building a terrace upon it to fill the void. He then mobilized the laborers and gathered the materials.

The project was completed in no time. Feng Yuancheng, the former Governor of Zhejiang who had been transferred to this region as the Chief of the Provincial Judicial Commission, ascended the terrace for a panoramic view and remarked, "It is beautiful indeed, yet it is not yet complete.
Furthermore, using an embankment as a terrace means the name does not accord with the reality.
A circle is round and a square is angular; such shapes lose their true essence. This is because man has not yet harmonized with Heaven. Moreover, the mountain possesses immortals..."
Thus it is named. When water possesses a dragon, it becomes numinous; this means it has found its master.

Therefore, those who establish enduring and unshakeable merit must rely on human effort while being protected by the divine. By depending upon a constant master and not losing their sacrificial rites, they are able to coexist with Heaven and Earth in eternal duration.
The Duke then donated his stipend to construct a Great White-Robed [Buddha] within the central pillars of the hall.
The portrait of the Master: draped in pearl necklaces, he gazes upon the void and waters; seated within the house of fire, he dispenses coolness and serenity.
He stands upright like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon. I was honored by the Master’s invitation, and thus I consulted with him on how to remedy previous omissions.
Subsequently, a pavilion of five bays was constructed, preceded by two towers for bells and drums; this was designed to take a circular form symbolizing the moon, its height imposing.

If this terrace relies upon the spiritual power of a Great Being (Mahāsattva) to preside over it, one may say that the virtues of Heaven and Man are united, thereby restoring the full efficacy of the creative transformation.
The Duke, filled with resolute inspiration, donated his stipend and oversaw the commencement of the work.

It began in the tenth month of winter in the *dingwei* year of the Wanli era and was completed in the seventh month of autumn in the *wushen* year. Its scale is magnificent and its expanse vast, rising loftily toward the center of heaven.

The painted rafters reach toward the clouds; the vermilion pillars reflect the sun. At that time, as I ascended to survey the view and gazed upon the scenery from all sides, my thoughts soared beyond the mundane, and I exclaimed:
"How magnificent are the defenses of these mountains and rivers! How extraordinary is this marvel wrought by Heaven! Thereupon, I reflected upon the original naming of the terrace.
Those who possess the dharma-eye of geomancy must have observed that the coming dragon from Dongyue occasionally surveys the landscape; its distant lineage honors Mount Heng as its source.
As it descends, it branches out and flows toward Huai, with Dinghu serving as the ancestral dragon for the prefecture. It rises majestically into the clouds and mists.
Winding westward, the mountain ranges open out in broad display. The Hall of Light (Ming-tang) spreads vast and wide, its perimeter corresponding to the Purple Microcosm (Ziwei).

It coalesces into the seven stars; its wondrous peaks and cavernous halls manifest in a thousand forms and ten thousand shapes. Inscribed cliffs and brocade-like stones steam like clouds and shimmer like dawn mists; rounded pebbles and fragments of stone lie scattered about.
It truly serves as a treasure of the world; it is the refined essence of creation and the profound secret of the mountains and rivers.
Star-like crags stand in array, while spider webs and wandering ants dot the level plains. Turning eastward, one reaches the Lingyang Gorge, which forms a grand defensive gateway.

Following the river upstream to the left from Huanggang and heading west, the city of the prefecture is established. Examining its form and discerning its principles, it is like a coiling dragon looking back toward its ancestral source.
Turning my gaze toward the Seven Stars, my aspiration is named after this terrace. Rising abruptly from the plain of Pingyang, is it not like the pearl beneath the chin of the black dragon?
Its meaning is derived from the "Moon-Bright Pearl" (Mingyue-zhu), taken as the ultimate treasure of the world; thus it is named "Treasure Moon" (Baoyue). How profound!
Furthermore, that natural ingenuity can be captured and imitated is already marvelous enough. Yet, once the divine pearl is lost, even the "Wangxiang" spirit must search for it in vain.
To recover what was lost from the deep abyss and thereby return to the work of transformation—this is yet another marvel.

To fill what was deficient and extend what was drawn out, clarifying it through the spirit and making it a constant practice—this undertaking alone has caused the various scholars and gentlemen of this age to gather their finest talents.
In the space of a single glance, their excellence will flow for ten thousand generations. This is what is called "arising in dependence upon others," the true realization of benevolence and wisdom.
How could this be a mere coincidence? Water possesses dragons because it is numinous; dragons possess pearls because they are divine.

One who would mount a dragon, grapple its horns, seize its jaw, and strike its scales to take [the pearl] from it—such a person is he. Thus, the spiritual power of this land has long been established.

The two pagodas of Tai and Yi stand to the left and right, like the sun of wisdom and the moon of tranquility, alternating day and night to illuminate those lost in the dark and shatter deep ignorance.
As the sounds of bells and drums mingle and the tide-like chants alternate, they offer prayers for the longevity of the Emperor above and bestow blessings upon the people below.
That loyalty, filial piety, integrity, and righteousness flourish in accordance with the times is truly due to the spiritual power of the Great Being (Bodhisattva).

As for enshrining this image to stabilize both the Chinese and the barbarians, and spreading the breeze of compassion to assist the Imperial governance—this is indeed a benefit that will endure for ten thousand generations without end;
how could it merely be valued for the beauty of a scenic sight? This is the record.
A Record of Dreaming of Duancan:
Midsummer of the Jiyou Year of the Wanli Era. On the twelfth day of the fifth month, I went to the city of Duanzhou to procure timber for the reconstruction of Baolin Monastery.
I traveled back and forth for a full year; when the work was completed and I returned to the mountain, it was the height of the humid summer, and torrential rains fell heavily upon the river.

The waters overflowed; on both banks and the islands, one could not distinguish oxen from horses. Thereupon, we boarded a drifting boat and descended through the Lingyang Gorge, passing the mouth of Duanxi.
In an instant, clouds gathered from the four mountains and wind and rain came rushing down. The waves surged and roiled, and the boat could not advance.
We moored it to take shelter from the storm. My spirit was shaken and my eyes grew dizzy; leaning upon my armrest, I dozed off and dreamed.

There I strolled. Looking up, I beheld peaks and ridges of extraordinary beauty, reaching toward the highest heavens; strange crags rose steeply and precipitously, while below there was no ground beneath one’s feet.
Listening afar, the mountain streams roared and surged, crashing through crevices and rushing against cliffs like the striking of great bells or the beating of dragon drums;
the sound came from the sky, deep and resonant, its source unknown. One might have thought it the dwelling place of dragons and sea-monsters.
It is the secret grotto of gods and men, the sound of footsteps in an empty valley. My heart leaped with joy;

I called out to the fisherman, who rowed his boat into the stream so that we might feast our eyes upon the scene. After a short while, the wind and rain ceased momentarily; the mist cleared and the mountains brightened.

I then tucked up my robes and went barefoot, leaning on my staff as I wove through the clouds. Turning slightly along the stream for over a hundred paces, I reached the foot of the mountain, where there was—

There was a shrine altar. I entered the midst of the overgrown brushwood and rested for a short while upon a rock. After walking several dozen paces, I suddenly heard an extraordinary sound as if it were emanating from the air.

I stood waiting for a long time; looking around in all directions, I was utterly bewildered. Peering at the overhanging cliffs and gazing down into the deep ravines, I finally investigated the source from which the sound originated.
The fisherman said, "This is the Small Cliff of Duankui, the very place where the famous ink-stones are produced. It was a cliff.

The hollows are filled with water; a single aperture is like a mouth. Suddenly one hears its sound, like the roar of a lion. A multitude of voices mingle and clash, like a crowd crying out and running.
The great and the small sounds are like thunder and lightning, like a landslide and a galloping herd, like bamboo flutes and *sheng* pipes.
The ringing of metal and stone is like the nocturnal chiming of the imperial carriage bells—this is the sound of the gurgling spring flowing within the cavern. I...
Standing on tiptoe, leaning his ear to listen, he raised his beard in delight and said, "Aha! Is this not what Zhuangzi called the 'whistling of the earth'?

How extraordinary and wondrous its unique tones and marvelous resonance! He lingered there for a long while, then ascended the layered peak to the left and gazed toward the waist of the mountain, which resembled battlements;
it was the site of the stone-quarry office. Crossing a small ridge to the east, after several..."

A hundred *bu* away, a mountain stream winds through the valley, flanked by two ridges like outspread wings. On both sides of the ravine, jagged fragments of rock lie scattered like a constellation of stars.
Those that resemble torn silk trailing in disarray are the sites where stone was quarried.
Among them, there are pieces small and large, shaped like palms, fingers, ears, and teeth; like bees, butterflies, wings, and tails—so many that one cannot even count them.
Tens of millions fell. Observing their forms closely, they were like pieces of black jade cut from a branch of jade, or like clouds and mists sheared away to scatter fine silks;
they were the discarded tears of the vast and the dregs of the perfected, fit for contemplation but unfit to be grasped.

Lovely yet impossible to gather; beholding it with one's own eyes brings joy to the heart, and treading upon it fills one with divine vastness. Climbing eastward, I waded through brambles and traversed rugged peaks.
Descending the ridge, I entered a stream where the clear water was like a mirror, so transparent that even a single hair could be counted; a single expanse of azure embraced the void.

The reflections of the myriad peaks fell into the water. Clutching at the creepers, I looked down; steep cliffs rose up toward the current, their depths profound and silent, as if a divine dragon were coiled beneath them.
A fisherman pointed and said to me, "This is the Great Cliff of Duankui.
One sees only verdant vines and green bamboo shading its summit; it is secluded and mysterious, its entrance impossible to discern. The fisherman said, "This is the gate."
It dwells at the bottom of the water, sealed by chaotic rocks. Even when the government extracts it, one must wait for the waters to recede during the three months of winter before opening it.
Its depth is unfathomable; once the hollow space is excavated, it becomes a pool of accumulated water several tens of *zhang* wide, so profound that it cannot be crossed.
Above, it communicates with numerous apertures; below, it connects to the Tailgate (*weilu*). Its tides ebb and flow, waxing and waning in accordance with the seasons. Although—

The strength of ten thousand men is not easily exhausted. When work was undertaken here to drain the water using carts, labor began at midnight and continued until noon, at which point the edge of the cliff was barely visible.
The stone workers had to weave bamboo mats to extract it; it was not easy to obtain.
From this, we know that the inkstone which holds water but is not drunk from is born of water.

On the face of a cliff, two mountains embrace like arms; the space between them is like the palm of a hand. From afar, it resembles an ancient tomb. Unable to ascend to its height, he ordered a youth to go and inspect it.
There was a stele covered in moss, its date indistinguishable, though it identified it as the tomb of Chen Mengfu. Thus it is transmitted.
It is said that a high official of a former dynasty was summoned for service and died while on duty; he was subsequently granted burial here so that his spirit might guard the site.

Reflecting on this, I sighed: "The mountains and rivers remain as they were, yet how brief is human life? This is the very proof of it. I called out to a fisherman’s boat and crossed the clear stream to explore beneath the cliffs.
The jumbled rocks piled up at the bottom of the water are the entrance to a cavern. The ripples of the water shimmer and sway.
If drifting mists disperse their colors upon the surface of the water—something that may be beheld but cannot be grasped—it is the lingering majesty and residual radiance of the Stone.

I cast off my robes and sat in contemplation; opening my breast and loosening my hair, I washed my feet in the clear stream. As I rowed the boat forward a short distance, the collapsing waves and surging rapids struck the rocks, spraying pearls of mist.
The spray splashed against my face and soaked my hair; my hair stood on end and my skin broke into goosebumps. The water was shallow yet the boat was large.
The glue could not hold; he consequently abandoned his boat and entered the stream. Wading through the murmuring waters, he climbed over several clusters of rocks to frolic and wander among them.
The jumbled stones were like ants—jagged and serrated. The large and the small were like sheep, like oxen, like pigs, and like dogs.

Some resemble winnowing baskets or measuring buckets; others resemble fists or hands. Among them, the larger ones have had their flesh eroded until the bone is exposed, yet they remain naturally smooth and rounded.
The smaller ones are the remnants of hammering and chiseling, polished to a brilliant luster. Those that share the same nature as common顽石 (unrefined stones) are difficult to describe in words.
All are stroked, caressed, and played with, washed and scrubbed; their hair is pulled out and their grime scraped away, revealing a rich, tender, and charming luster that shines forth brilliantly.
It was worth beholding. I sighed with melancholy and said: "Truly, the Creator cherishes such exquisite vessels.
One thus knows that the essence of mountains and rivers and the brilliance of cultural artifacts are forbidden by Heaven; they cannot be seized or appropriated by ordinary people.

Fishermen have their nets and traps, and woodcutters have their axes and hatchets, yet when the time has passed, they remain oblivious and fail to notice [such things], because they have no use for them."
Furthermore, there are those among the inked ministers and court chroniclers who seek them but do not find them, or admire them but find them difficult to encounter;

this is because they have placed themselves far beyond reach, making it hard for them to be known by the world. There are also those who capture their outward likeness, yet their utility does not match their office.
When names do not accord with reality, yet one proceeds to disparage them, it is like purple dye usurping the place of vermilion.

Therefore, I exerted myself in commanding the youth to sift through the sand and dig out the mud, selecting and simplifying [the text]. The large pieces were so solid they could not be lifted; the small ones filled my hands, numbering about ten fragments.
I tucked them away and returned home, as if gathering purple *zhī* fungi or picking up clouds of refined essence—truly a source of joy. However...
These are all remnants of what was pared away or slanted; they cannot withstand carving or polishing.

Knowing them to be useless, yet I treasure them because their quality accords with that of a gentleman—possessing the essential form though on a small scale—and they are just sufficient to lodge my mind and offer a glimpse of a single stroke of the Creator’s artistry.
Recently, however, wind and rain arrived suddenly, driven by thunder and rolled up by lightning; I knew then that the spirit of the mountain would not grant me [these treasures].
He then followed the current down the stream and returned to his boat. Suddenly, a violent thunderclap split the mountains, and he was startled awake;

everything he had previously possessed had vanished. Pushing back the sail-screen, he sighed deeply and looked around at the myriad mountains. Enveloped by mist and veiled by clouds, the peaks rose to the heavens like dense halberds.
Wandering and hesitating, he thought that those who seek the extraordinary might still wish to speak of the traces of fish and birds.
I have been unable to recall the details of my mourning speech, so I have committed them to pen.
This is the "Record of the Reconstruction of the Hall of the Sixth Patriarch at Guangxiao Temple in Guangzhou.
Formerly, before the Buddha had appeared in the world, Prince Jeta of King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī possessed a garden that was lush and magnificent. It was sufficient...
It was prepared for excursions and sightseeing. When the Buddha appeared in the world, he divined that this site should be opened as a lecture hall and subsequently selected it to be a vihāra;
to this day, it is called the Jetavana Garden, a name derived from its excellence. When Zhao Tuo served as the Governor of Nanhai, he selected the Hālindā forest to serve as his garden.
Later, during the Long’an era of the Eastern Jin dynasty, the Venerable Dharmayaśas, a śramaṇa from the kingdom of Kaśmīra, [arrived].

He came from the Western Regions; because he loved the excellence of this land, he requested permission to establish a Buddhist monastery there, naming it Wangyuan Monastery (Monastery of the King’s Garden).
At the beginning of the Yonghe era of the Jin dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra arrived from the western lands carrying the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*;

he established a precept platform at that monastery to await a holy personage. At the beginning of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta from India arrived carrying the *Bodhi*...

A branch from that tree was planted beside the altar and inscribed with this record: "One hundred and sixty years hence, a flesh-body Bodhisattva shall expound the Dharma here, delivering immeasurable beings.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the royal garden was renamed Faxing Temple.
At the beginning of the Longshuo era under Emperor Gaozong, our Sixth Patriarch Master received the robe and bowl of Huangmei and remained in seclusion for over ten years.

Five years passed. At the beginning of the Yifeng era, he emerged from obscurity through his discourse on the wind and the banner, truly shaving his head beneath a tree and ascending the altar to receive the precepts.
He was promoted as a teacher for humans and devas, in accordance with a cryptic prophecy.

From then on, the banner of the Dharma was raised at Caoxi, and the transformation of the Way spread throughout the realm; even today, this place is called the Root Ground. Thus, as for the Buddhas and Patriarchs—

The Way originates from non-duality; thus, the Jeta Grove, the Garden of the King, is likewise one. Is it not the case that a place is made eminent by its people, just as a person is made eminent by the Way?
I have previously read Xuanzang’s *Record of the Western Regions*, which states that the Jetavana Vihāra is now a field of thorns and brambles.

Yet, seeing the Bodhi tree at the Ahalya Forest today, I still hear the resonance of bells and the chanting of the *brahman*. How could the spiritual wonders of Nan Yue be less than those of the West?
"O Celestial One! Is the Way of the Ancestors superior to the Buddha-dharma? The Sages transmit it to one another, appearing in the world in accordance with the movement of the times;

at the moment of transmission, there is no space for even a hair’s breadth of delay. However, because their vows have varying depths, the duration of their transformative influence varies—prolonged or brief.

It is like the four seasons: when their work is accomplished, they withdraw. Thus, the sounds of transformation await one another; they wait, yet there is that which waits, and within that waiting, there is further waiting."
This is a matter of waiting. If there were no waiting, the traces of responding to conditions would have almost ceased.

Now, a thousand years have passed since our Sixth Patriarch Master; among the seventeen hundred people recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu*, the sites where they transformed and taught have flourished and declined according to the times, and many have fallen into ruin in every location.
Of the Buddhist monasteries in Yue, not even one in a hundred remains—just like the stream of Caoxi.
Yet it does not dry up; the Bodhi tree flourishes and never withers. Is this not because this Way has something upon which to rely?

This, moreover, shows that the earth exists by means of the Way, and people abide by means of the Dharma. In my youth, I devoted myself to arid meditation and was consequently censured for following the Dharma.
In the early spring of the year Bingshen, I visited the Great Master Huineng at Caoxi and beheld the Bodhi tree at Guangxiao Temple, seeking out his remains.
The traces of his deeds are far-reaching, yet people did not recognize the monk [Huineng]. After one year, he began his alms-rounds; after three years, he practiced the precepts and fasts;
after five years, the release of living beings was instituted; and after ten years, the teachings were widely propagated, and the new ordination platform at Caoxi was restored.
Believers in the Way, it is indeed the nature of the great cycles of time. In the past, people designated the site beneath the Bodhi tree as the place where the Great Master shaved his head;
consequently, a hall was constructed there to enshrine the Dharma rites, a tradition that dates back far into antiquity.

Though weathered by wind and rain and subject to periods of prosperity and decline according to the times, the monk Weitong has now led his disciples, including Xingpei and others, to solicit contributions from the masses to restore it anew. For this, I [have written this].

To cleanse their countenances and expand their courtyards, so that the dignified appearance of the Way may become manifest after its period of obscurity, and the lamp of wisdom may shine brightly without dimming—this further depends upon people for its realization, as it is through such matters that the significance of those people is underscored.

Yet, the Buddha gathers sentient beings through the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), among which the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is foremost; moreover, that which is not adornment is itself called adornment. If indeed...
When phenomenal appearances and the nature of reality (dharmatā) are interfused, then conventional truth and suchness (tathatā) penetrate one another.

In this state, even the burning of incense and scattering of flowers become sublime practices. If one understands this principle, then why would the carving of rafters and the ornamentation of eaves not serve as resources for the Pure Land?

In the past, when the altar was established and trees were planted, they already waited for the Sixth Patriarch; now that the traces remain while the rites are performed, though the person has passed away...

Yet the Way remains; how could it not depend upon those who come after? Moreover, as for the excellence of King’s Garden compared to Jetavana, that was there while this is here—there is indeed a distinction. This serves as the record.

Record of the Circumstances of Kāifú Monastery in Héngzhōu Prefecture Kāifú Monastery is situated about one *lǐ* south of the Xīngjiāng River within the city walls of the prefecture. During the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty, Chan Master Wúzhù established the mountain monastery here.
The lineage of this master is recorded in the *Chuán-dēng-lù*. Initially, he formed a connection with Chan Master Fǎzhào.
The Nianfo Society was established at Huedong; later, they both traveled to Mount Wutai, where they personally beheld Mañjuśrī, as recorded in detail in the *Qingliang Zhuan*.
The Master and his younger brother, Wu Jue, jointly established a place of practice. The Master founded Kaifu Temple, while Jue established Dabeisi in Jinlan Village of Xiangxi.
This was truly a momentous occasion. When Kaifu was first constructed, its scale was vast and grand during the Chunxi era of the Song dynasty.
At one time, Chancellor Zhao Zhongding Gong (Zhao Ruyu) was exiled to Yongzhou. While passing through Heng, he fell ill and was harassed by the local governor Qian Mou;
he died suddenly and was interred here, whereupon a shrine was established and offerings were made to him annually.

Later, the prefect Xiang Zi, who possessed benevolent governance, saved tens of thousands of people from starvation during a famine. The common people were moved by his kindness and likewise established a shrine for him.
In this place, the temple fell into ruin after a long period. In the first year of the Yuan Emperor [Hongwu], Chan Master Fuhai restored it and newly established Beibi Temple.
During the Xuande era of our Ming dynasty, the temple was again destroyed. Laypeople built a small hermitage on the desolate site;

the land occupied only a single plot, and a few remaining monks have guarded it until the present day. Fortunately, it has not been lost among the common people. This was in the Renshen year of the Longqing era.
The virtuous men of the district, Qi Xia and others, reconstructed his hut and appointed the monk Rulu to guard it.
In the gengxu year of the Wanli era, Du Junyougui, a distinguished scholar (xiaolian), lived as a neighbor to the temple. One night, he dreamed of an old man who urged him to mount a horse, saying:
"I am the Earth Deity of Kai-fu Temple. This year, Du Jun-jun passed the provincial jinshi examination.
He then related his dream to his relative, Minister of Rites Zeng Jinjian. The Minister said, 'Consulting the local gazetteers, Kai-fu was rebuilt by Chan Master Fu-hai.
Your current sobriquet is Fu-hai; could you be a previous or subsequent incarnation? You should restore this temple to commemorate that one's original nature is not obscured.'"
This was the cause. Master Du was delighted and made an agreement with the local virtuous gentleman Liu Zilan, Qi Xia, and the scholar Liu Mingluan to join their efforts in a grand renovation.
The District Commandant, Lord Yin, who held the Triple Gem in high esteem, took charge of the project as its patron.

Since the site had long been abandoned, much of it had fallen into private hands; the foundations were cramped and narrow, and the two shrines had also fallen into ruin, leaving no one capable of restoring them.

He restored it to its former state. After five or six years of planning and construction, he first built a three-bay Buddha hall. It was situated at Kaifu Temple on the east side of the lake, only a few paces away from the other.
When Master Zeng rebuilt the temple on the east side of the lake, he invited me to serve as its abbot. In the winter of the Gui-chou year, I arrived from Guangdong.
The virtuous patrons who were managing the reconstruction of Kaifu came to request that I go there to oversee the work; I took pity on their sincerity and admired their efforts.

Zhi then composed a record for it, saying: "Since ancient times, wherever a Buddha or patriarch has preached the Dharma, the site where a *bodhimaṇḍa* was established to form a *vajradhātu* has always been guarded by dragon deities and spirits who protect the Dharma; thus, even through the exhaustion of kalpas, it shall not perish.

Long ago, when the World-Honored One was traveling with Śakra, he pointed to this ground and said: 'This is the place where the seven past Buddhas preached the Dharma; one should establish a Brahma-palace here.'"
At that time, the Elder Xian immediately planted a stalk of grass in the ground and said, "The construction of the Brahma-shrine (Brahma-kṣetra) is complete; this is its proof.
Since the Dharma first arrived in China, the monasteries throughout the land and the jade palaces have been spread out like stars or arranged like chess pieces.
Even when they fall into overgrown wilderness, their names remain imperishable; whenever there is one who revives them, they reveal what was hidden in obscurity. Just as...
Beholding these ancient objects, one realizes that cause and effect can never be obliterated. For example, Xu Xun built a stupa, but he passed away before its completion.
Later, when Pei Du served as Chancellor, he visited the temple. Upon seeing him, the custodian said, "Xu Xuandu, why have you not come for so long?
The stupa from days of yore remains just as it was. Upon hearing these words, Pei Du restored it. Indeed, there was an inscription carved upon the stone within the pagoda.

Regarding the prophecy concerning the Chancellor in Crimson Robes: observing this, we see that although Kāifú had remained desolate and abandoned for over a thousand years, Master Yǐn and the two masters Cēng and Dù initiated its restoration;
they all possessed a profound karmic affinity with this Buddha-field, which was no mere coincidence.
In the past, both Wúzhù and Fǎzhào set out from Hūdōng and traveled to Wǔtái, where each was able to behold [the sacred sites] in person.
Mañjuśrī, I have now set out from Wutai and am spending my final years in Hudu. Coincidentally, I have arrived on the very day Kaifu Temple was restored.
These people come and go, snapping their fingers as they appear and disappear;
yet they have never left the Bamboo Grove Monastery of Mañjuśrīśrī or the Diamond Pit. Three before and three after—how inconceivable is this convergence of causes and conditions!

Ah! O sons of noble family, that the Master Shizu served as the temple administrator at this monastery, and furthermore, that he would become the future Xuandu—this is corroborated by the omens of Lord Du Junfu’s sea-voyage and the "circle of Sangzhong. These signs are all the more evident and unerring.
Therefore, I have recorded the beginning and end of these events in their entirety to inform those who come after. As the proverb says: "A thousand-year field has eight hundred owners. Now...
As for those who offer praise and sympathetic joy, are they not the protectors of the Dharma in the future? The merit of the field of blessings (puṇyakṣetra) surely endures without perishing;
how can one not believe this?
Record of My Excursion to Mount Zhi I was living in seclusion at Linghu in Hengzhou when someone spoke to me of the extraordinary beauty of Mount Zhi in Yongzhou; my heart yearned for it.

In the ninth month of autumn in the year of Yimao, Lord Feng, the Minister of State Affairs, was transferred from Wuling to govern Hunan and established his headquarters in Yongzhou. He invited me [to join him].

I set out on a journey to the Nine Doubts (Jiuyi) Mountains. Arriving on the final day of this month, I beheld the clear and magnificent scenery of Yong County, which resembled a celestial palace or a hidden grotto;
it could not be regarded as merely an ordinary part of the mundane world.

I took up residence at the Small Pavilion atop a Rock on the western bank of the Xiao River, where I sat and surveyed the splendors of the mountains and rivers as if they were spread before me upon a desk. On the ninth day of the tenth month of winter, Tang Xiaolian...
Returning to harmony, I was invited by the scholar Lü Xugu, along with Zhou Bokong of Tanzhou, Zhang Hancha of Siming, and my disciple from Lingnan, the monk Chao Yi, to tour Mount Zhi.
Cold rain had persisted for several days, but at that time it had cleared slightly.

We then took up our staffs and followed the bank of the West River; after traveling about one *li*, we ascended the winding slopes at the foot of the mountain, and after another *li*, we reached the summit.
At the small ridge, one gazes upon a multitude of peaks towering and steep, impossible to climb. Descending the ridge and entering the valley for two hundred paces, one turns slightly to the west;
there, a singular peak rises majestically, with overhanging cliffs sharply carved and a Buddhist temple with soaring eaves nestled against the crags and interstices of the rock.
It is called Zhishan Temple. It was established by the bhikṣu Mingjue in the year Wanyili Bisi (1605).

There was no extra space in front of the temple, as it was blocked by the head of a dragon-shaped ridge, making it impossible to have a full view. Turning westward, there is the Guanyin Pavilion, situated beneath a high cliff;
