from there, the view is open and vast, with the various mountains arrayed like hairs on one's eyebrows or eyelashes. Below, the ground is level.
The fertile soil stretches out; the mountain streams wind and meander like the nine bends of a sheep’s gut, as if celestial robes with flying sashes were drifting into one’s embrace.
From the foot of the mountain, the water enters the river. Turning westward for a few paces, there is a single hall where three Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) have been sculpted since ancient times.
It was destroyed by icchantikas; its location is most secluded and excellent. Behind it is a cavernous chamber that can accommodate several people.

Turning westward again, one passes through a stone fissure and ascends through a crevice; after winding for dozens of steps, one reaches the mountain’s waist, where there is a level ground several *zhang* across.
Formerly, the Governor Wang constructed a solitary pavilion here, where travelers may sit when they arrive.
They took delight therein. Extraordinary peaks and strange rocks stood in dense array on both sides, manifesting a thousand moods and ten thousand forms beyond description.
They resembled the clustered stones of Lake Tai, piled and stacked like layers of brick; there were jade-like flowers and crystalline buds, with dense leaves in full bloom.

To the left of the pavilion, one ascends along the cliffs, a sight that stirs the heart and startles the eyes, as if one were peeling back a blue lotus to sip its jeweled nectar—so numerous they cannot be counted. Ascending further still...
There are two stones shaped like hands, known as the Palms-Joined Rock (Hepalgyan). Below it is a cave entrance, naturally pierced through.

Ascending through this gateway, one reaches the Hall of the Jade Emperor (Yuhwang-dam). Upon reaching this point and looking out, the mountains and rivers on all four sides are entirely visible at a glance.
The city walls and suburbs spread out like a painted scroll; the entirety of Yong’s supreme beauty is revealed here without exception. I venture to say that Master Liu...
Horses have inhabited this place for over ten years; there is no hidden corner they do not explore, yet their hooves have never reached here—how utterly insignificant it seems!
Some point to this as Mount West Mountain (*Xishan*), for which there is a record by Liu Zongyuan stating that one proceeds west from Dyed Brook (*Ranxi*) and that it stands out prominently;

this appears to be what is currently called True Pearl Ridge (*Zhenzhu Ling*). Others point to it as Mount Clustered Jade (*Qunyu Shan*); the local gazetteer says that below this lies the Abode of the Immortals Cave (*Zhaisandong*).
That the mountain lacks a hermit’s cave—both of these are deficiencies. I say that it is the mountain’s misfortune not to have met with Liu;

yet it is also Liu’s own failing that he did not come to this mountain to exhaust its every secret. Perhaps the Creator has guarded it in secrecy, awaiting this very day? I and my companions sighed in harmony, saying:
"The mountains and rivers preserve their sublime traces, and we, our generation, have come once more to ascend and gaze upon them. How we linger here in leisurely delight!"
Walking slowly, he followed the willow cliffs back home.
Regarding the Record of the Scripture Hall at Gaoyun Mountain in Yizhang:

Among the famous mountains within the realm, those that concentrate the quintessence of Heaven and Earth are characterized by their heroic spirit and extraordinary beauty; of these, the Five Peaks occupy the position of honor, while others branch out from them.

There are four branches of the lineage. Yet the source and root of Caoqi lies at Nanyue. Nanyue and Caoqi are separated by over a thousand *li*, with their peaks stretching continuously like a constellation of stars.
Since the Sixth Patriarch initiated the transformation of beings and Master Ruangong branched off the stream, the lineage of the Way has pervaded the world.
Throughout the regions above and below Shaoyang, there have been several dozen *mahāsattvas* in their physical bodies;
that some remain as if alive even to this day is surely because the mountains and rivers harbor such profound mysteries, such that the lineage of the Way has found its special resting place therein.

Thirty *li* to the west of the seat of government in Jiayang, situated between Mount Cao and Mount Heng, lies a mountain named Gaoyun. It is a descendant of Mount Zhurong and has long been a site of spiritual power. In the *jiawu* year of the Jiajing era...

In the year Wuxu, the local resident surnamed Ouyang established a small hermitage and invited Master Shajin Hai to reside there. He expanded the Buddhist temple to provide a place of rest for the broad assembly.
The inhabitants of the entire district took refuge in him as a field of merit; he was provided with eight pecks of grain for incense and lamps before long.

Afflicted by the calamity of Hui-lu (fire), Master Hai departed and lived in seclusion at Zhiti Mountain in Min. His disciples, including Wu-dan and others, rededicated themselves with single-minded effort to the restoration.
In the year Renwu, the construction was completed; they erected a stupa at Longshou and invited the sacred remains of Master Hai back for interment.
He is thus the founding patriarch. His disciples advanced daily, and those traveling from the ten directions to Cao-heng were beyond measure.
He stopped there and did not proceed further. A local resident of the village, Mr. Yuan Wenxian, donated thirty mu of land to provide for the rice gruel and meals of the traveling monks (*yunshui*).
Consequently, people from all quarters praised him. Once the monks had assembled, even the commoners of the deep mountains and remote valleys came to know that there were Buddhas and monks.
However, they had not yet heard of the Dharma. There was one named Sun Xingcheng who was devoted to it.

He sought the Tripitaka at Jinling for twelve years with great diligence. When his vow was finally fulfilled, in the sixth month of the summer of the Jiyou year of the Wanli era, he welcomed the Tripitaka back home.
The fourfold assembly beheld it with joy, as if a white horse had come from the West.

His hermitage is situated atop a mountain where the forest trees are lush and dense, and the mists rise in humid vapor; fearing that the Tripitaka would not endure for long, his Dharma-grandson Zhen...

Gui and others deliberated and proposed constructing a pavilion at the foot of the mountain, naming it Nanzhuang (South Manor). At that time, Grand Magistrate Zheng Gong and Military Governor Tong Gong acted as patrons (*dānapati*) to initiate the project.
They issued a circular of faith to inform the four quarters; those who heard of it rejoiced, and those who came to offer their support gathered like a marketplace.
Construction began in the [month and year] and was completed in the [month and year]. A Dharma assembly was then to be inaugurated.
The ritual for the Water and Land (Shuilu) was performed to proclaim universal salvation; it was truly a great site of practice (*dharma-cakra*).

When the ceremony was successfully completed, the Master’s disciple Wushao, who followed me at Caoxi, requested that I provide words to record this event, saying: "An ancient worthy said, 'The entirety of the ten directions is the land of eternal quiescent light;
throughout the whole earth is the true scripture of the Universal Eye. This means that the Buddha-land requires no cultivation."

And it becomes pure of itself. Without unrolling the sutra scrolls, they become clear of themselves. Nevertheless, this is truly because the land appears when the mind is pure, and the Dharma manifests when the eyes are clear.
This is what is meant by "it is man who can propagate the Way; it is not the Way that propagates man. At Gaoyun Monastery, the Great Canon arrived from the East.
It was not solely through Master Hai’s initial accomplishment, but through his descendants’ succession of the legacy and the patrons’ [support].
The end is thus accomplished. Furthermore, how could one otherwise cause thorns and brambles to become jeweled trees, and transform sand and gravel into Brahma palaces?
Once the Dharma-banner is raised and the course of the Way is grandly opened, then amidst green mountains and white clouds, the Dharmakāya dwells eternally;
as monkeys cry and birds chirp, sublime verses are constantly proclaimed. Thus, with the flowing water and swaying winds, the broad and long tongue naturally emerges, [harmonizing] with this realm.
Ordinary people sing its praises as inexhaustible; all who have seen or heard it and rejoice in it are like Sudhana entering the Adorned Pavilion of Maitreya.
How could the measure of this merit ever be encompassed by even the tip of a single hair? This is the record.
Lijiang’s Mu Liugong, a devotee of the Buddha, recorded this for me:
I was about to retire in old age to Mount Nanyue, intending to dwell in seclusion at Linghu on Mount Heng. At that time, Mr.

Feng Yuancheng, who had been transferred to serve as Governor of Hunan, visited Yongzhou. During our conversation, he spoke of my former travels through the various scenic sites of Yunnan and presented his *Wuleng Gao* (Manuscripts from Wuling). I—[continued].
Having read the *Biographies of the Six Lords*, I learned that to the west of the Golden Horse and Azure Cock mountains there lived an extraordinary man, the Sixth Lord Mu.
This lord governed Lijiang and possessed its territories; as he was the sixth in descent from his ancestors, he was called the Sixth Lord.

His forebears, at the beginning of the dynasty, rose to prominence through loyalty and obedience, their military achievements being most renowned. Upon reaching Lord Xueshan, the family became celebrated for their literary talent and refined song.
His poetic compositions were elegant and possessed a soaring, transcendent spirit, which the Imperial Historian Yang Yongxiu greatly admired and praised.

It is said that his calligraphy and literary style reached a peerless excellence, comparable to those of Yulong Songhe. As for his pure cultivation within the Lotus Society, he set out upon the path of awakening;

by the time he reached these six masters, they had far surpassed their predecessors and stood uniquely beyond the mundane world. By nature, the Master was simple and unassuming toward worldly flavors.
He had no personal indulgences; his heart was devoted to loyalty, filial piety, compassion, and love, cherishing only the salvation of others and the benefit of all things.

He placed his trust in the Triple Gem and applied himself earnestly to *dhyāna*. He delighted in welcoming spiritual companions from beyond the mundane world, with whom he exchanged greetings and practiced cultivation with refined diligence.

He appeared humble and unassuming, like a *dhūta* ascetic clad in rags, yet he was especially generous in the practice of giving (*dānapāramitā*). These qualities were difficult for those of wealth and status to achieve, yet the Master uniquely possessed them.
Regarding his daily conduct: is this not the manifestation of one who, having planted roots of goodness over many lifetimes, responds to and transforms others through the power of compassionate vows?
When I first entered the gate of emptiness, I did not know the vastness of the Buddha-dharma;

I thought that dwelling alone like a solitary shadow in remote mountains and deep ravines, wearing clothes of grass and eating from trees, and maintaining a withered meditation would constitute the supreme vehicle. However, when...

My devotion to the Great Teaching deepened day by day. Reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and contemplating the sublime practices of Samantabhadra, I saw that there is not a single form that does not manifest itself, nor a single activity that is not the work of the Buddha.
Because he never abandons even a single sentient being, I thereby perceive the vastness of the Buddha’s compassion.
Without discarding even a single speck of dust or a single hair, one may then recognize the profound depth of the *dharmadhātu*.

For this reason, whenever encountering officials with whom one converses, one does not further exhaustively investigate the mysteries or embody the subtle; rather, one simply realizes one's own mind and extensively practices the myriad deeds.
Thus, even mundane speech and worldly activities for livelihood all accord with the True Dharma. This is what is meant by: "In the ground of ultimate reality, nothing is received."
A single speck of dust. Now, regarding the gateway of phenomena (*dharmamukha*), not a single dharma is abandoned.

As for those who harbor superficial aspirations and empty pretensions, who discourse loftily on "shedding the shoes" [of worldly life] while remaining stubbornly attached to greed and delusion, and who are entangled in mundane affairs—they differ from those who, though dwelling within the net of the world, set their wills upon transcending the dust of the mundane.

With the mind settled in profound stillness, one is like a lotus emerging from the mud—pure and untainted. How could such a being be considered of the same root or stem [as those still mired in defilement]?
Thus we know that although the Buddha-nature is one, there are differences between delusion and awakening due to the varying thickness of habitual taints.

Therefore, regarding the discussion of seeds: those that arise from greed and hatred nourish greed and hatred; those that arise from *prajñā* nourish *prajñā*. When *prajñā* is deep, greed and hatred become thin;
when *prajñā* manifests, greed and hatred are eliminated. It is like a miraculous power transforming the foul and corrupt into the sublime, or the foul and corrupt being transformed into the sublime.
Their essence is one, yet their functions differ; it is by this that the distinction between the sage and the ordinary person is made. Thus it is understood.
When the mind is vast, the physical form cannot constrain it; when one contemplates the emptiness of the *dharmadhātu*, the myriad existents cannot obstruct it.
Thus, those who have attained realization are untainted by worldly emotions because their wisdom is supreme and their habitual tendencies are thin.

Therefore, when the sages of old who awakened to the mind took up the long river and turned it into cream and curd, or transformed the great earth into gold—what other artifice was there? It was simply the power of their realization.
One realizes only the wondrous nature of one's own mind, which fills the expanse of the Dharma-realm, for there is no phenomenon outside of the mind.
You have carved the Great Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra at Mount Jizu; surely you must have attained this realization.

However, because the roads were perilous and there was no great master of the school to open the eye atop your crown, your aspiration turned toward the life beyond the secular world, leading you to desire a long journey to seek out and consult the wise.
Consciousness is entangled by worldly dharmas and thus cannot be apprehended. My humble opinion, however, is otherwise:

if you, sir, can sit in stillness and observe the mind until the six sense faculties are dissolved and restored, then empty space will perish; if you can penetrate and observe the Dharma-realm, then mountains and rivers will no longer create separation.
One will behold the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*) upon the tip of a hair, and encompass the Pure Lands within a speck of dust. Without moving a step, one traverses the ten directions;
without rising from one's seat, one serves all Buddhas. This is the natural state of one's own nature, fundamentally and inherently complete, never requiring anything external.
Furthermore, you, sir, possess a land. Given the vastness of its mountains and rivers and the multitude of its people— (End of excerpt)
He inferred their Buddha-nature and transformed them through teaching. As the saying goes: "When one family practices benevolence, the whole state flourishes in benevolence.

You, sir, have moved all things with your refined sincerity and transformed the people through Buddhist rites, causing every household to know of it and every person to recognize the Buddha within themselves.

Each heart came to know compassion; thus the people followed without being commanded and submitted without being coerced. All were joyful and content, living in harmony while nourishing themselves on the food of the world.
Pounding their bellies in the remote wilderness and frontier borders, they encounter the vast wind of the Buddha-land. You, sir, sit as if upon a lotus flower, dwelling serenely in Sukhāvatī;
the governance of the Great Antiquity rests between your palms and thighs.

Why then labor over traversing mountains and rivers to regard the world as floating light and bubble-like reflections, thereby performing the ultimate work of a Buddha? It is through you, sir, that I have come to know your dwelling in such a distant place.
Born in a remote land of the eight difficulties, you have certainly manifested as an emanation body in response to your compassionate vows.

My only regret is that I am old and cannot carry a single alms bowl southward to seek your counsel. I view the chamber of Vimalakīrti as if it were between my eyebrows; I hope to form a karmic bond with you in another life.
During the three assemblies under the Dragon Flower tree, I have already determined that you are a government official and a son of the Buddha within the Final Dharma age of Śākyamuni.
Do you have no intention [to accept this]?
The Record of the Origins of Dīpaṃkara Buddha with Long Ears at Faxiang Temple.
The mountains and waters of Hangzhou are preeminent throughout the world. Where ancient sages have manifested their traces, the temple banners stand as densely as a forest;

indeed, there is no peer to this within the realm. Faxiang Temple is situated at the foot of Nanfeng Peak; it is secluded, profound, and vast, where the trees and forests are lush and verdant, and the springs—

Shi Qingqi (Stone Clear and Strange). This was a place where human traces were rarely found in ancient times. During the Five Dynasties period, an extraordinary monk took up residence here in seclusion, and it subsequently became a site of spiritual practice (*daochang*).

The Master’s name was Xingzhen; he was the son of the Chen family from Quanzhou in Min. His mother dreamed of swallowing the sun before conceiving him. From birth, the Master had an extraordinary appearance:
his two ears hung down to his shoulders, reaching as far as his chin. Everyone marveled at this. At the age of seven, he did not speak. Or...
The finger was pointed out, saying, "Is this child mute? The Master immediately opened his mouth and said, "Had you not encountered a true master, you would have merely broken your skull for nothing.

He left home at a young age and attained awakening under Chan Master Xuefeng Congzhen. He subsequently traveled on foot to Siming, where he lived in seclusion in the mountains, preaching the Dharma to ghosts and spirits.
The devas scattered flowers, and monkeys and birds offered fruit. Later, he emerged from the mountains and arrived at...
In Qiāntáng, he lived in seclusion at Yǐngxiù Wǔ on South High Peak. Originally there was no water; when the Master arrived, he planted his monk’s staff, and a spring gushed forth.
At that time, he went to beg for food in the marketplace, and everyone marveled at him. Children gathered around and chased him;

seeing that the Master’s ears were long, they pulled them from both sides, and as they did so, the Master simply turned with them, smiling and laughing indifferently. When people asked him what it would be best to do, the Master replied: [The text ends here.]

It is said: "The cultivation of merit can shield one from a hundred deformities. In the third year of the Qianyou era, on the birthday of the King of Wuyue, Zhongyi, monks were fed at Yongming Temple.
At that time, Chan Master Zhijue Shou was expounding the Great Dharma; when the Master attended the assembly, his entire body was covered with scabies and sores.
He went straight to the head seat of the assembly, which everyone detested. When the King saw this, he was greatly displeased and dismissed him.

He immediately returned to his mountain retreat and sat in meditative composure within a single room. After the midday meal, the King asked Shou, "Did any holy monk descend today when we made offerings to the Sangha?
Shou replied, "The Monk Long-ear is the manifested body of the ancient Buddha Dīpaṃkara. The King repented and hurriedly went in person to pay his respects, saying:
The disciple was a common person with fleshly eyes who did not recognize the ancient Buddha. He prayed for repentance. The Master said, "Amitābha is being too talkative.

Having finished speaking, he sat and passed away. The King returned to pay his respects to Shou, who then entered parinirvāṇa. Consequently, the King built a monastery and preserved the Master’s physical body.
These [teachings] survive to this day. King [Wu] was moved by faith and treated the two masters as his teachers; he submitted a memorial requesting posthumous titles for them.
The master [Huiyuan] was granted the title *Dazhi Yongming Zongzhao*, and the other master was granted the title *Dazhi Zonghui*. Alas!

When the Buddha preached the Dharma, he often remarked that during the final five hundred years, the Semblance Dharma (*xiangfa*) would have already declined, and sentient beings would be so turbid and evil that they were most difficult to transform. He further said: "I shall dispatch emanations..."
This person, everywhere for the sake of all sentient beings, reveals and expounds this Dharma to deliver them.

Thus we know that both "contrary conduct" and "conforming conduct" are manifestations of great skillful means (*upāya*) for benefiting others; whether through speech or silence, everything is nothing other than the exposition of the supreme Dharma.
By observing the simultaneous appearance of these two masters, this can be clearly understood. Yongming [Yanshou] felt compassion for the final dharma age.

The nature and characteristics [of reality] are difficult to clarify; therefore, he established the Mirror of the Fundamental Teachings (*Zongjing*) to reveal the principle of the One Mind, so that all who see or hear it would not fail to leap with joy into its realization.
As for the one with long ears, he benefits sentient beings through his extraordinary form; from beginning to end, there is no dharma he can speak.

He transforms and gathers sentient beings solely through the samādhi of compassionate heart. Since the root of sentient beings' birth and death is craving, and since [he addresses them] by means of the male...
Women are the root of desire. To use desire to treat desire, she causes those beings who are childless to find that their prayers are invariably answered.
To this day, those in the world who lack heirs do not fail to seek her aid; and when they pray, she surely responds as swiftly as a shadow follows a form or an echo follows a sound.

This is a teaching that is not explicitly taught, yet its influence blazes forth while the site of enlightenment remains serene. As the incense and lamps have continued for so long, she brings relief to the most destitute of sentient beings.
The realms remain; though the roots of craving are not yet exhausted, the sound of the Dharma constantly persists. How could one not believe this? This is the record.
Record of the Dading Hall at Jinming Temple in Jiahe: Jinming was once a renowned monastery in Jiahe.
Later it became Fanli Lake, and now it is the seat of the prefectural city. The tides have turned, and the mulberry trees have grown where the ocean once was.
It is a field. The temple was first established during the Qiandao era of the Song dynasty by Chan Master Jinghui, who opened the mountain.

Although it has undergone various cycles of prosperity and decline, the grounds of the monastery have been protected by spirits and deities; thus, they have never become overgrown with weeds. While the halls and buildings toward the front have fallen into ruin, [the site remains preserved].
The monastic community has not lacked for offerings. Recently, in the year of Gengzi, the Venerable Xuan of Qiutan began the reconstruction of the Buddha Hall;
however, he passed away before it was completed. The Chan monk Daoxian, in accordance with his vows as a disciple of the deceased, took up the task of continuing the work.

The hall was eventually finished, and the Buddha Hall, the Avalokiteśvara Pavilion, and the Heavenly Kings Hall were all renovated anew. He then invited Dharma Master Yexi to lecture on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

The monastery subsequently flourished into a great monastic center (conglin). To the right of the temple, there was a plot of land measuring about ten mu that had formerly served as the site for the meditation hall (candian).
It had been occupied by those with influence, but the lay practitioners Bao Xinxian, Shen Runa, Wang Jichang, Shen Erhou, and Zhongzhen contributed funds to redeem it.
Subsequently, they invited Dharma Master Xuanjin to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Yuanjue-jing*, and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
The number of those who took refuge in and believed in the various sutras increased. Furthermore, he constructed a meditation hall, a refectory, a kitchen, and storehouses;

those things previously lacking were all at once made complete, becoming a magnificent sight for the site of practice. When I came to Shuangjing and Yunqi to pay my respects to the two great elders, [I witnessed this].

Previously, while passing through Wumen, I met Master Yexi. Observing his dignified and weathered countenance, I rejoiced that there was a teacher in the Dharma-gate who served as a model for the southeastern region.
Later, when I went to reside at Mount Nanyue and completed my *Lengyan Tongyi*, it was carved and published in Gusu.

When the Master arrived there in accordance with his lecture schedule, he saw the work and sighed, saying: "This lifts the heavy clouds obscuring the study of doctrine. I wish to request that you complete it."

Master Jie extensively bestowed the Dharma through teaching. Upon concluding his lecture and returning home, he passed by Jinming Temple. Master Xian had previously attended his Dharma seat and served him as a disciple.
The Master then expressed his wish to propagate and expound the teachings there. However, ten days after his return to the mountain, he passed away. Alas!

Life and death are like dreams and illusions; how could they be restricted to human beings alone? Observing that one departs with their aspirations intact, we know that there exists that which does not depart.
Dharma Master Xuanzhin was the legitimate successor of Master Jie; he was truly one who inherited his master’s will and carried on his legacy.

While I was residing at Jingci Monastery, Xuanzhin served as the host for the guest quarters (*danguo*). When I returned to Mount Kuang, Xuanzhin escorted me as far as Jinming. There, I visited his temple.
Moved by this account, I then instructed Xian to invite Xuan so that his former aspiration might be fulfilled. Consequently, I inscribed the name "Great Samādhi" (Dading) upon his hall;
this is the name for the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama. Here it is called "firm, solid, and indestructible.

Indeed, when the Buddha first sat at the site of enlightenment, the ground was firm and composed of vajra; therefore, it is named Araṇya, the place of true cultivation. Thus, [I have named the hall after] that.

This land has undergone five hundred years of each of the periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness; thus, many kalpas have already passed. Yet, it shall ultimately become a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
When its flourishing begins, it will take the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* as its starting point; now that it is established, it will conclude with the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.

However, the cultivation and realization of the *Śūraṅgama* takes the adamantine mind-ground (*vajracitta-bhūmi*) as its fundamental beginning; as for that which is realized, it is realized precisely through this. For...
Contemplate this: whether it be the mind or its objects, they are all equally adamantine, eternally abiding and indestructible;
therefore, I have named this hall "Great Samādhi. It is certain that those who dwell in this hall abide with this mind;
those who preach the Dharma speak with this mind; and those who listen to the Dharma listen with this mind. Thus, when the bells and drums resonate together, the *brahmā*-chants...
They harmonized with one another; even the clamor of the marketplace and the laughter and play of men and women all entered the gate of Great Samādhi.
How, then, could there be any distinction between stillness and turmoil, or any separation between mountain forests and cities?

The disciples escorted me as far as Linxi to attend the vegetarian feast hosted by the layman Shen Erhou; this was indeed a convergence of conditions that brought both beginning and end to fulfillment. Therefore, I have composed this record.
Thus it is.
*The Dream-Travel Collection of the Elder Hanshan*, Volume Twenty-four;

Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and the Disciple Tonghyeong;
Revised by the Disciple from Lingnan, Liu Qixiang.
Record of Fayun Temple on Wuru Peak of Mount Lu.
Mount Lu derives its vital energy from Nanyue; it turns westward across the borders of Xiangshan into the region of Xiyue, and turns northward toward Xingzi and Linwu.
To the east of the realm lies the province of Yue. Reaching the borders of Guiyang, it branches from the Wu and Chu regions at Mount Yuping.
Its trunk extends eastward, passing through the Wugong area for over two thousand li, reaching directly to Xunyang.

With Lake Pengli before it and the Nine Rivers behind it, it sprawls for over two hundred li like an emerging blue lotus, its peaks piercing the Milky Way. To the south it overlooks Wu and Yue; to the north it gazes across...
The Central Plains directly vie for supremacy with the Five Sacred Peaks; it is truly one of the most magnificent wonders within the realm.
Its geomantic source flows through Yuan Tong Gorge, where it rises abruptly as the various peaks, including Ma’er Peak.

Winding eastward for over twenty li, it gives rise to a singular peak called Peach Blossom, which leans against the high heavens and serves as the primary sovereign of this mountain range. From this point, the range divides into two great branches.
The first branch extends eastward, arranged in nine odd-numbered peaks like a protective barrier, reaching the mouth of Hanpo.

There it turns north to rise as Qiangang Ridge, with the guest [branch] yielding to the host [main peak]. Its influence extends fully to the northeast, where the Yangtze and the Lake embrace one another in a winding and meandering circuit.

From the summit of this ridge, a great primary branch shoots out toward the southeast, forming Wulao Peak. Looking back toward Penghu, it serves as the gatekeeper for the West River. This completes the third [section].
Diequán (Falling Water) is the most extraordinary and sublime spot. Among the various monasteries at the foot of the peak, it is pure and exquisite.

Five li to the east lies Báilùdòng (White Deer Grotto), which serves as the Huì'ān Academy. Tradition holds that there was once a study hall here belonging to Lí Qīnglián (Lǐ Bái), though this cannot be verified.
The Five Elders Peak first drags its ridges and hills along, following the Hénpó watershed, winding west and then south until reaching Xīngzhǔ, where it forms the territory of Nánkāng Prefecture.
This is the southern face of the Five Elders (*pañca-vṛddha*) Peak. Proceeding northward from this Qian Ridge, one reaches Songguang Ridge, which divides into two branches.
The northeastern branch forms Lotus Peak (*padma-śikhara*); its lower extension becomes Wu Zang Mountain, which runs directly to the mouth of the lake.
Within it lie various *ārāmas*, such as Huiri; outside, the level ridges spread for over ten *li* to the tomb of Zhou Lianxi, which faces south toward Lotus [Peak].
From Huafeng, after another twenty-odd *li*, one reaches the city of Jiuyang Commandery. The northern trunk of that ridge turns west to become Wulong Tan.
From there, it extends downward for a branch-like stretch of over ten *li* before entering the plains as Taiping Gong. It then winds and turns to the left.
After traveling some ten li or so, one arrives at the site of Master Huiyuan’s Lotus Society at Donglin.
Looking back toward Mount Xianglu, Bai Xian’s thatched cottage is there; its foundations still remain.

Proceeding west from Wulong, one passes through Shishi, Dalin, Shuikou, Yubeiting, Zhulin, Foshouyan, Jiangjingtai, and the various scenic spots such as Xianglu, until reaching the confluence of Tianchi. Turning back, one gazes upon Taohua.
Therefore, it is the principal monastery of the mountain. Beneath the cliff is a stone gate, which is the very water-mouth of the entire range.

In the center of the mountain lies the Yellow Dragon Pool (Huanglong Tan), like a single pistil at the heart of a flower. The various monasteries and hermitages are arrayed around it like the fragrant banners of its filaments.

This concludes the description of the topographical features of the eastern branch. Its peach-blossom peak emerges from the southern main trunk and runs westward against the direction of the incoming dragon.

Between them lies a valley, the highest point of which is called Dahan yang Peak (Great Han Yang Peak). It serves as the principal mountain on the southern face, standing majestically in the midst of heaven.

It faces and encompasses the two lakes, while from afar it gazes upon the Jiangnan region. A range of peaks stretches across the horizon, arrayed like— (Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)
The stars arch toward the North; with a single glance one can see for a thousand *li*, reaching as far as Lake Kǒu.
It winds back to embrace Wǔlǎo Peak; this is truly a grand vista of the southeast. At the westernmost extremity of Hányáng lies Gùlián Spring.

Descending from there to the level plains is Cháisāng, the birthplace of Yuánmíng. From the midpoint of the range, a branch extends southward, where a single peak rises prominently from its waist, standing solitary and tall.
It stands several hundred *chi* high, like a stūpa floating in mid-air, and is called Jīnlún (Golden Wheel).

During the Jin dynasty, the Indian master Venerable Yaśas carried iron to construct the pagoda and enshrined the Buddha’s śarīra at its summit. About two *li* below it lies Dōngfèng’s Apricot Grove, which is still celebrated to this day.
The plain at the foot of the peak is Guīzōng Temple; it was originally the residence built by Wáng Yòujùn while he was serving as the Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
Later, he encountered the Brahmin Bhadrata here and consequently donated his residence to establish a monastery.

Today, there are the "Ink Pond" and the "Goose Pond," so that this ancient temple vies for preeminence with Donglin. Since the time Chan Master Chiyen of the Tang dynasty preached the Dharma here, more than thirty successors have followed him.
In the past, the Dharma path flourished uniquely here in Jiangxi; thus, it became the foremost monastery of this mountain. This is Kuang...
It is the great bulwark of the south. As for its five breasts:

from the very center of the face of the Great Han Yang Peak, one branch extends upward in particular, rising and falling in several sections to form a great barrier. To its left, with its back to the Peach Blossom Peak, is the Stone Man;
various peaks run eastward down to form Qixian externally, facing the Five Elders, and then descend and wind around the Hengpo watershed.

Qixian is called Yuyuan Tan (Jade Abyss Pond). The waters converge here to form a river that flows into Xingzhu. To the left, the terrain forms an inner embrace like a lotus flower turned upside down.
Within it stands a stone Buddha. This is where the three aranyas—Xizhang, Baoping, and Baoqing—are located;

among them, Baoping was the former dwelling place of the great elders Dahui Zonggao, Ying Shaowu, Yue Gonghui, and Baofeng Chuyue, as well as the first seat-holders and other eminent masters. It has been so for a long time.
[The previous structure] was abandoned; it has now been reconstructed. To the west is Sleeping Dragon Ridge (Wòlónggāng). Below the ridge is a valley, within which stands a hermitage.
During his tenure as Governor of Nánkāng, Zhū Húiwēng frequented this place and carved the "Memorial on the Expedition to Wú" (*Chūshībiǎo*) into stone.

The hermitage has fallen into ruin, yet the stone inscription still remains. This constitutes the left protective barrier of Hányáng. Its right barrier consists of the peaks of Guǒzǐzhài and others, extending to Huángyán.
A waterfall descends from the sky, pouring into a pond. Upon the large rocks of the pond are many inscriptions by famous figures of antiquity.
In front is Kaiguang Temple, which was originally a monastery purchased and built by Li Zhongzhu as a place for the various patriarchs to preach the Dharma.
Yangming Wang inscribed the verses of the Seven Buddhas upon the cliff face. To the left of the temple, one passes over a ridge.
This is Wan-shan Temple; it forms the rightward bulwark before Han-yang. At the very center of this bulwark, a single branch rises alone, like a horse’s mane hanging down.
From the flank of the peak, one summit rises prominently, shaped like a unicorn’s horn, called Hu-bi. To the left, the range stretches out like a screen;
seven peaks stand side by side, their summits piercing the high heavens, called the Seven Sages. Formerly, the Tang dynasty scholar Liu Ke read his books here.
At the foot of the peak, later Master Huì-ǎn brought his son along with his disciples Chén Zhèngsī, Chén Yànzhōng, Yú Jìqīng, and his nephew Wèi Yú to visit this place;
it was therefore named after them. The local people commonly call it "Seven Peaks" (Qījiān), which is an error.
Below the Seven Worthies (Qixian), there are five peaks resembling breasts, hence they are called the Five Breasts (Wuru).
They are connected from top to bottom and reach the Wulong潭 (Dragon-Lying Pond) in the east, where the waters divide and flow downward; this is the Dragon on the left of the Five Breasts.

From the Hubi (Horse-Nose) Peak, which bows in respectful greeting, a single peak rises in succession called Shigum (Stone Drum). It descends gradually, winding like a dragon roaming among the clouds, its zigzagging ridges extending for several [li].
The village is situated such that, when one raises both arms and encircles it, a single palm’s space opens up at its center as the site of an ancient temple.

Leaning against the Seven Sages and facing the Five Elders, it is like a lotus stalk amidst branches. The temple is deeply hidden, like the fibrous core within a lotus; it occupies the most secluded spot on the mid-slope of the southern mountain.
Within it, various waters converge into a ravine and flow down around the temple, emerging from a stone crevice after approximately five li to reach [the valley].
At the foot of the mountain, it meets the Yuyuan River. It winds inward around Mount Yujing and enters Lake Mountain, which was the former residence of Yuanming (Tao Qian).
As his poem says: "In the past, my home was at Yujing. At the mouth of the Wuru Water, there is a stone peak several *zhang* high.
Above is a square zhang square of flat rock, known as Liu Ke’s Reading Terrace; it is still so called by the local people today.

The records state that there was once a library (shuyuan) here, which was later converted into Lingyun Hermitage. Located below the Seven Peaks, the ancient temple was destroyed by war, and its history cannot be fully verified;
however, its foundation stones remain. Later, an inscription on a cliff was seen, recording that the restoration work was carried out in the fourth month of the Ren-shen year of the Zhizheng era.
[End. As for the mountain fields and arable lands of this temple, they first became private property during the early years of the Jiajing era.
In the year Wancheng Bingchen (1616), I traveled east from Mount Nanyue and stayed at Jinnu to escape the summer heat; venturing into its seclusion, I reached this place.
Admiring its hills and valleys, I intended to rest there and eventually settle my residence. It happened that Xing Maoxue, a distinguished scholar from Huangmei, purchased it for me.
It was established as a place for my retirement. At that time, the Grand Marshal of Huangmei, Mr. Wang Keshou, volunteered to serve as the patron (*dānapati*) for its construction. Mr.
Chen Dashou, the Shangbao of Fuliang, coordinated with [myself and] others to contribute funds and gather materials, whereupon the temple was completed.
Mr. Gong Yuli and the layman Mr. Miao Xiuyong donated land for the incense and lamps; thus, the community was able to dwell there in peace.
The construction began in the year Ding-si and was completed in Ji-wei. County Magistrate Yuan Gong Mao-zhen composed a text to record it.
Consequently, monastics from all quarters arrived in increasing numbers, and it eventually became a great monastic center (conglin), truly like a single petal upon a lotus flower.
To the left of the temple is a ridge where there was formerly the Wanghu Pavilion (View-of-the-Lake Pavilion), built by Huian; its foundations still remain. In that valley, there is...

There are two *araṇyas*. One is at the foot of Shigufeng Peak and is called Chongmo Zhai (The Studio of Profound Silence). I have composed an inscription for it. It is most secluded and magnificent, lofty and spacious;
from there one gazes upon the various mountains beyond the lake, spanning a thousand li at a glance, arrayed before one like sitting upon a lotus pedestal.

It is as if the Buddha had extended his broad and long tongue, and the multitudes from the ten directions were gathering like clouds to hear the Dharma. The other is at the foot of Qixianfeng Peak and is called Furong An (Lotus Blossom Hermitage). Its facade...
In his fifth year, he sat upon the Sleeping Dragon Peak (*Wolong*). The surrounding peaks are arrayed like items on a desk or mat.
Entering several li from the hermitage, one reaches the Great Valley known as Fragrance Valley (*Xianggu*). There is a stone screen, before which stands a large rock with a surface like a table.

Beneath this rock is a cave from which a wondrous fragrance emanates; it drifts slowly, enveloping the person without ceasing. Nearby, at the cliff of Long Water (*Longshui*) close to the temple, there is a place called Wood... (the text ends here).
"Seokam" (Stone Hermitage) signifies one's aspiration. I have also composed an inscription for it; both are within the precincts, like the heart and filaments of a flower.
To the left of the temple, amidst the valley, lies the ruins of Gwaneumam (Avalokiteśvara Hermitage). The record states that there were two ancient wells whose locations were unknown;
they have now been found among the overgrown brambles. Furthermore, its left arm serves as Gwigiam (Return-to-One Hermitage), which connects to Worongbunsi (Dragon-Lying Water-Dividing).
They all converge into the great river; this is yet another district. Dongpo said: "I have not seen the true face of Mount Lu, for I am situated within its midst.
Because the mountain resembles a lotus flower and those who dwell there are as if sitting amidst its blossoms, its true face is visible only from the south of the mountain.
Among these, the Five Elders and the Seven Sages are the most magnificent. Their temple is situated within a valley, leaning against the various peaks of Mount Hanyang.
The peaks serve as a natural screen. Looking back, the Seven Sages and Five Elders appear seated amidst the clouds. Penghu Island encircles it from without;
beyond the lake, clouds and mountains extend for a thousand li, bowing inward and arrayed in solemn silence before us. It is truly like a Huazang (Flower-Treasury) mystic capital.

Daily, the fellow monks chant the Avataṃsaka Sūtra with clear, resonant voices. The tolling of bells and drums intermingles with the sound of pine waves and spring torrents, together performing the tide of Dharma.

The sounds, moreover, lend a fresh luster to this mountain. However, I have been unable to emulate Master Huiyuan by carving out a lotus-drip water clock to perform the rituals of the six periods of the day.
*Record of the Zongjing Hall at Jingci Temple on the West Lake*
In the West Lake of Wulin, there is a mountain called Nanping. Upon it stands a temple named Jingci.

When Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty fled southward, he honored the Five Mountains and Ten Monasteries, placing this one at their head. The temple originated in the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty and was built by Qian Zhongyi, the Prince of Wuyue;
initially it was the Yongming Monastery, where he invited Chan Master Zhijue Shou to serve as its first founding patriarch.

He served as the abbot in succession and changed the temple’s name to its present title. The Great Master received the Dharma from National Teacher Shao of Tiantai and was a direct descendant of Fayan.

He perfectly realized the single-transmission mind-seal and was extensively versed in the Tripiṭaka. He thoroughly mastered the Buddha’s entire great canon of teachings, specifically elucidating the principles that the triple world is mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only.
Following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he was one of the masters who propagated these teachings in the Western Regions.

Based on the principles of "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) and "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), two schools were established regarding the nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of reality; these schools clashed like ice and fire, even to the point of parting rivers and drinking from separate waters, thereby destroying the True Dharma.
Less than three hundred years after the Great Teaching arrived in the East, Bodhidharma came from the West.

He did not rely on written words, but directly pointed to the human mind, asserting that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha. This is the Chan School. Thus, there subsequently arose the notion of that which is "outside the teachings" (*jiao-wai*).
The Way of the Separate Transmission was transmitted six times down to Caoxi, branching into Nanyue and Qingyuan, which subsequently became the Five Schools.

From the Tang through the Song dynasties, this Way flourished greatly; consequently, Chan and the doctrinal schools (Jiao) criticized one another, much like the conflict between the schools of Nature (Xing) and Characteristics (Xiang).

This was because they all failed to grasp the essential principle of Mind-Only and Consciousness-Only, instead establishing their own sectarian gateways. From the Liang dynasty through the Tang to the Song, four hundred...
In recent years, scholars throughout the realm have been clamoring and vying with one another in debate, yet they were ultimately unable to rouse the Great Awakened One to serve as an arbiter.

Thereupon, the Master, lamenting that the sun of the Buddha’s teaching was growing dim, assembled over a hundred individuals from the three schools—Xianshou, Cien, and Tiantai—who were masters of the study of doctrine and refined in the principles of the Dharma.
He provided them with lodgings in two pavilions so that they might extensively survey the ocean of meaning and engage in mutual discussion.
When faced with challenges and objections, the Master resolved them using the standard of the Mind-essence (cittadharmatā).

Furthermore, he compiled sixty Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras, along with three hundred works by sages and saints from India and this land, to establish the doctrine of Mind-only (*cittamātra*). He composed one hundred fascicles for this purpose.

It is titled the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Source-Mirror), and for this reason, it was used to name his study hall. Its intent is to take the One Mind as the source and the illumination of the myriad dharmas as the mirror.
It tears down the barriers of the three schools and reveals the profound meaning of the One Mind; it is like hanging the image of the Dharma over the celestial realm of intrinsic nature.
Gathering the extraordinary currents back into the ocean of Dharma, it is not merely that nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*) are fused as one;

even the nine schools and hundred masters, as well as the arts and means of livelihood, are all led back to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). How, then, could there be any inconsistency between teaching and Chan, or any failure to extinguish false views?
This is truly because sentient beings have long been mired in delusion; yet, although nature, characteristics, teaching, and Chan are distinct, they all manifest the single mind.
Excellent! Yet, the Buddha’s opening and closing of the gates of mind—his final act of holding up the flower—is a self-spoken paradox that ultimately cannot be reduced to a single unity.
Consequently, those who cling to the fishing trap mistake the finger for the moon; who is able to correct this? Two thousand years have passed since the World-Honored One entered *parinirvāṇa*.
Were it not for a Great Master to arise and bring about universal penetration, I fear that these delusions will persist through all eternity. How can one investigate this to the end?
In the end, there was no day of returning to peace. Thus we know that the Great Master’s merit was immense. He gathered the great completion of our Dharma;
even if Śākyamuni were to arise again, his merit could not exceed this. Is this not because the Master was far more worthy than Yao and Shun? Someone may say:
"The various patriarchs of the past all attained realization of their own minds," yet it is said, "Regarding that which transcends..."
"A single attachment! The Buddhas of the three periods do not permit even a glance at it. Furthermore, he said, "The entire Tripitaka is merely worn-out paper for wiping scabs and pus.
He saw the World-Honored One at his birth pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, and immediately wished to strike him dead with a staff.

Even when ascending the hall to instruct the assembly, there was never a time he did not bitterly denounce written words and forbid any intimacy with the teachings and their meanings. The Great Master now...
To forcibly unify the mind by attempting to harmonize its nature and its characteristics—does this not contradict the intent of the Dharma Master’s coming from the West?
Or do the ancient worthies themselves contradict the meaning of the one mind? It is said: This is precisely because the great purport of the [Dharma] that came from the West was not understood;

thus, through the mutual arising of biased views, they merely produced matters for this present life. Indeed, the recorded encounters and conditions of the ancient worthies all manifest the suchness [of reality].
The great function and great activity manifested by those who have come [into this world] have never ceased to be the strategic expedients of the Buddha.
For example, when Mañjuśrī gave rise to views of Buddhahood and views of the Dharma, he was banished to Mount Cakravāḍa. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī once held a sword and threatened to kill the Buddha.

When his various disciples entered the chamber of Vimalakīrti, they were subjected to all manner of rebukes. These were all the functional manifestations of the patriarchs; they were merely intended as a means of concealment.
It is merely a medicinal herb for subduing sentient beings; it is not the ultimate reality.

However, those with initial resolve and shallow wisdom do not realize the Tathāgata’s impartial dharma-realm, and thus cannot penetrate the principle of being free from marks. It is only through the Tathāgata’s teaching that [this is understood].
By means of the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*), one seals and determines all phenomena. That is to say, empty space is like a sapphire (*indranīla*); it is void and luminous like a mirror.
The great earth, mountains, forests, grasses, weeds, humans, animals, and the myriad phenomena of the universe—all without exception—manifest their reflections within this empty mirror.
When the waves of the great ocean are stilled and its void-luminosity is transparently penetrating, the reflections in the empty mirror appear within the sea, just as...
Just as with the impression of a seal, when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he uses the great wisdom of equality to perfectly illumine the dharma-realm.
He knows the number of every sentient being’s thoughts and knows the number of every drop of rain falling upon Jambudvīpa. This is called the Ocean Seal Samādhi (*Sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
Viewed from this perspective, there is not a single thing that is not the Buddha-mind; there is not a single dharma that is not a Buddha-activity;
there is not a single practice that is not a Buddha-practice. Among all dharmas, how could there be even the slightest fraction that exists outside of the Mind-only?
Thus we know that the title "Mirror of the Source" (Zongjing) signifies using the One Mind to illumine all dharmas, and merging the myriad dharmas back into the One Mind.

Then what dharma would not be the heart-seal of the Patriarchs? And what distinction could there be between the teachings on Nature (xìng) and Characteristics (xiàng), or between the doctrinal teachings (jiào) and Chan?
Thus, those who disparage characteristics do not comprehend the Dharma-nature; those who reject the teachings do not comprehend the Buddha-mind.

Failing to grasp the wondrous function of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, they cling to them as substantial dharmas. This is why the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is so difficult to clarify. Is this not tragic? Now...
The temple faces West Lake. The lake water is like a mirror; the four mountains stand in array; flowers and willows line the six bridges; multi-storied boats come and go;

people of both beauty and plainness pass by; songs and flutes resound from near and far; bells and drums mingle together. Throughout the six periods of day and night, from ancient times to the present, there has been an unceasing flow of activity upon the lake.
Yet within the hall, the Tathāgata remains serene and silent, as if having entered the *Sāgaramudrā-samādhi*.
Not even a hair’s breadth has ever strayed from the Mirror of the Source (Zongjing).

Even now, the sound of pines and wind, the flow of springs, the chirping of earthworms, and the croaking of frogs are still the time when the Great Master sits in the Hall of the Mirror of the Source, waving his whisk to assemble for the exposition of the meaning of the Dharma. What need is there, then, for brush and tongue?
Thus one knows that the site of this mountain is preeminent among the central provinces; its temple is foremost among all monasteries; and its Dharma transcends the teachings.
Chan: the supreme state of mind and object. Having reached the Hall of the Mirror of the Source, one shall share in the beginning and end of the lakes and mountains with the Master.
More than four hundred years after the Great Master entered *nirvāṇa*, his bone stupa was lost amidst the wild brush.

In the [blank] year of the Wanli era, the temple monk Dahe sought it out and recovered it, relocating it behind the hall. This was truly the Great Master’s *dharmakāya* manifesting once again after having been hidden.
This hall shall remain eternally present and imperishable. The hall lacks an inscription.
Hege requested that I record this for him.

According to the records of Lingxiao Peak at Mount Jing, the Longyou Pavilion sits atop Mount Cuifeng; its painted eaves and ornate plaque receive the clouds and embrace the sun, yet it remains empty.
Outside the eaves is what is called the Lingxiao (Soaring to the Clouds) Pavilion; this refers to a pavilion atop the peak.

Furthermore, the records state that five-colored rays of light were occasionally seen at the summit, and for this reason there was a Baoguang (Precious Light) Hall; it appears there was a hall in front of the pavilion, but both have now fallen into ruin.

In the past, Chan Master Yuanzhao resided on the summit for ten years. There is a saying: "He has sat and cut off Lingxiao for already ten years; he follows along to uphold the school and support the teachings."

Regarding the phrase "due to this": subsequently, Master Guding also resided there for ten years. Observing from this, one sees that among those who dwelt on mountains in previous generations, there were none who did not cherish its solitude and seclusion.
However, because the mountain peak lacks water and is exposed to high winds and total isolation, it is not a place for hidden cultivation.
Dharma Master Yueting also once preached the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for the assembly here, as this peak is...
It is the sovereign of the Five Peaks and the ancestral dragon of the Double Path (Shuangjing). Recently, the Venerable Huaihui constructed a hermitage upon its summit;

he has resided there for thirteen years. Previously, they suffered from a lack of water, but the Master excavated the rock and discovered a spring capable of supplying a hundred people, which does not exhaust even during great droughts.
He personally planted "pathway pines," hoping they might transform into dragons. I ascended it during the New Year of the Ding-si year and gazed out in all four directions.

Vast and expansive; with a single glance, one sees for a thousand li. I therefore inscribed his hermitage as "Dwelling in Emptiness" (Kōngzhōngjū), signifying that his aspirations transcend the mundane world.
At that time, I composed a poem to record it. The water of the spring is sweet and clear, emerging from within emptiness like celestial nectar;
thus, I named the spring accordingly.
Record of the Zunseng Hermitage in Haiyu.
Haiyu lies in a remote corner of the eastern region; it was certainly not easy for the Buddha’s transformation to reach it.

Recently, I passed by to observe it, and found that those who devote themselves to the Triple Gem there were uniquely flourishing compared to other places. Neighbors vied with one another in emulation, for the district abounded in former scholar-officials.
Sheng was originally a protector of the Dharma. There were those who, through spiritual resonance and inspiration, were moved to arise [in practice];

they truly believed that Buddha-nature is inherently present and that the transformation of the Dharma is universally pervasive, such that even grasses, weeds, and minute particles of dust all possess the seed of Buddhahood—it depends solely on how the one who guides them acts.
Now, Zunseng Xian was founded by Master Minggong, the Dharma Master Yuehui. This Master was the son of the Chen family of this district; he was young...

He immediately began chanting the names of the Buddhas in a low murmur. When instructed in various ritual practices, he was unacquainted with them all; his sole aspiration was for transcendence from the world.
At the age of seventeen, he paid homage to Master Yiyuan at the Yufeng Hermitage and took him as his teacher. He then received the full precepts (upasaṃpadā) from the Great Master Yunqi.

Subsequently, he traveled to the Southern Capital to attend the lecture hall of Dharma Master Xuelang, where he studied the doctrinal meanings of the Xianshou school. He applied himself with arduous dedication for seven years.
In the autumn of the year Hai, I returned to visit my mother. At the Yangloutai on Mount Yu, I closed my door for three years to investigate the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West.
In the year Renyin, I traveled again to various regions; wherever I went, I saw those who were aged and infirm, yet the monastic communities mostly refused them admission.
Having no place to rely upon, I made a vow: "If I am ever to possess even a patch of thatch, I shall share it with the aged and infirm of the ten directions. Alas, this has not yet been fulfilled.

Thus, it remained neglected for ten years. In the autumn of the Renzi year, the local *xiaolian* (honorable scholar) Weng Zhaoji offered ten *mu* of vacant land in front of the temple to establish a Chan monastery for the ten directions and a quiet chamber for the elderly.
The Master was delighted, considering that he had finally found the site to fulfill his long-held aspiration.

According to the local gazetteer, there was once a Zunseng Hermitage that had long been abandoned; when they excavated the foundation to a depth of over one *zhang*, they discovered ancient [remains].
There is a single well; its water is exceptionally sweet and clear. I suspect this is indeed the original site. That the vast ocean has become fields—how could this not be the turning of kalpas?
Construction began in the summer of the *ding-ji* year of the Wanli era and was completed in the autumn of the *wu-wu* year.

Because the Master had throughout his life maintained the practice of the Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī, the temple was named after it. He sent a letter requesting me to write a record for it, saying: "The sentient beings of the great earth have no..."
There is not a single person who lacks the Buddha-nature; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single speck of dust that is not a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

It depends solely upon the convergence of karmic conditions and the mutual resonance between the seeker and the response. Thus, by a mere snap of the fingers, the manifestation appears. Given Master Weng’s donation of land, why need one wait for Jetavana?

Given Your Excellency’s establishment of this transformation, why need one wait for Baizhang? One may immediately settle the dharma companions therein for their summer retreat, practicing the six periods of daily service.
In the chanting of liturgy, the sounds of the sutras and the names of the Buddhas mingle with the tolling of bells and drums.

May this cause the elderly to find ease, the sick to find peace, the ignorant to gain wisdom, the indolent to become diligent, the weary to find rest, the hungry to eat, and the thirsty to drink. What among these is not a mark of supreme merit?
May the pure regulations of Yunqi not fall into decline, and may the Dharma-way of Vulture Peak endure forever. If the Lord of Devas were to take up [this practice]...
To take a single blade of grass and make it a Brahma-world is something that can by no means be grasped through thought or calculation.

Furthermore, may this serve as an upper blessing for the longevity of Your Majesty, and a lower boon for all these people to ascend together to benevolence and long life. Moreover, it shall become a hidden current within the great ocean, providing inexhaustible moisture and nourishment.
As for me, being of dull wit, what name could I possibly deserve?
Record of the Bronze Aśoka Śarīra Stūpa Commissioned by King Zhongyi of the Qian-Wuyue Kingdom:

Long ago, when the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, his body was cremated, yielding eight *hu* and four *dou* of śarīra relics. These were divided into three portions, each enshrined in a stūpa for veneration:
one in the heavens, one among humans, and one in the dragon palaces. At that time, King Aśoka personally received one portion and distributed it throughout Jambudvīpa.
In Jambudvīpa, nineteen stupas were obtained in the land of China (Zhendan), of which the Aśoka Stūpa in Mingzhou is one.

Its design likewise originated from the Western Regions. The śarīra relics within are brilliant and radiant, manifesting transformations that each person perceives differently according to their own capacity;
some even fail to see them at all, for this depends on the thickness or thinness of their karmic obstructions. Two thousand years hence... [the text continues].
In the past, during the era of the King of Qián Wúyuè, Zhōngyì, who inherited his ancestral legacy, reverently served the Triple Gem.

He fashioned eighty-four thousand small bronze stupas according to ritual specifications and buried them within the famous mountains of his kingdom; for generations, no one had known of their existence.

In the early years of the Wanli reign of our Ming dynasty, Gù Gěngguāng of Chángshū excavated one such small [stupa] from the burial grounds of his father, the Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
A copper stupa, approximately five inches in height, fashioned in the style of King Aśoka’s stupas. Inscribed within are nineteen characters reading:
“The King of Wuyue, Qian Hongchu, reverently constructed eighty-four thousand precious stupas. Recorded in the year of Yimao.
On the four exterior sides are engraved the life stories and manifestations of Śākyamuni’s past causes; on the front is the scene of King Viśvantara cutting his own flesh to feed a hawk.
On the back is the rescue of the pigeon; further back, King Maitrībala cutting off his ear to light a lamp; on the left, Prince Sattva leaping from a cliff to feed the tigers;
and on the right, King Candraprabha sacrificing his precious head—these four events are rendered with meticulous detail and texture, inlaid with gold ornamentation.
Mr. Gu was the maternal uncle of the Court Historian Qian. Because Mr. Gu was a descendant of the Prince of Zhongyi, he subsequently entrusted the stupa to him. Having received this, Mr.
Gu styled himself the Layman Jusha (Gatherer of Sand), taking it as a sign of his spiritual cause. He then sent it to the Xingfu Aranya.
When I traveled east to visit the Court Historian, I passed through Dongwen and saw the stupa; finding the matter extraordinary, I recorded it thus: "The Buddha..."
Taking the Dharma-realm as one's body, even blades of grass, leaves, and threads are all the true essence of the Buddha; how much more so for those who rely upon images?
This is because sentient beings are deluded regarding their original Dharmakāya, which transforms into the three poisons and constitutes the eighty-four thousand afflictions.

The Buddha, by means of his wisdom of universal radiance, perfumes the three poisons to become the secret treasury of the three virtues; thus, he transforms afflictions into the eighty-four thousand [virtues].
The four thousand merits were established by King Aśoka; this was likely intended to represent the quantity of his meritorious deeds.

The Kings of Wu and Yue fashioned bronze stupas according to that same number and buried them entirely within the earth, intending thereby to signify that these merits are stored within the minds of sentient beings.
I hope that by opening a single stūpa, one may perceive a particular kind of merit—that is, beholding the entire body of the Dharma-realm.
It is like seeing boundless space through a single crack; how could this be viewed as a mere physical form? The Dharmakāya is firm and solid, remaining unpolished throughout kalpas;
it manifests in response to conditions. As for this stūpa, O Grand Historian, is it not a crack revealing the emptiness of intrinsic nature from within the ground of practice?
Record of the Buddha’s Birthday, the 45th Year of the Wanli Era.

Reading the *Account of Extraordinary Dreams*, it is said that the Man of Illusions traveled east through Wu and Yue, then returned west to Mount Lu. As his boat passed the Wuguan Pass, the gatekeeper Yu received him from Mr. Liu.

He invited [the master] to stay for one night. It happened that Guan Maocai Xizhi of Wumen was coming by a different route. The following morning, Xizhi arrived at the boat first and inquired about the "phantom man" (the master).
He immediately spoke of the matter of Yu Shou’s extraordinary dream, which left Xizhi astonished.

When he questioned Yu Shou, the latter produced his *Qiancheng Youcao* (Drafts from Travels in the City of Dryness), and upon reading it, the record of the extraordinary dream was found to be very detailed. Initially, Yu Shou had accepted an invitation to serve in Qianzhong.
While traveling, he lay ill at the post station of Xiajùn. During the night, he dreamed of a magnificent man with a long beak who burst into the room as if seeking something;
his demeanor was haughty and resentful. Yǔ Shòu bowed to him and invited him to sit, then asked after his clan and lineage.

The man raised his voice and replied, "I am General Cao Han of the Song dynasty. Because of my excessive killing of the innocent during the campaign against Jiangzhou, I brought this calamity upon myself;
what more can I say now? When Yujue received the dream, he did not yet fully understand the origins and details of the Jiangzhou incident.
He merely recalled that Han had served as a general alongside Cao Bin, and said, "You were under the command of the State Councilor Cao;

he was benevolent and did not kill. Why should you have cause for grief? The man replied, "I was enraged that Jiangzhou had long resisted the royal decree, so I first killed the defending commander Hu Ze and subsequently slaughtered the city.
I sought only momentary gratification; how could I have known that in death I would suffer the retribution of the underworld? My colleagues at the time—"

"O people! You have all fallen into heterodox paths, while I alone have become a pig. This is likely because during my previous life my nature was prone to anger and abuse, and the sharp edge of my tongue was fiercely poisonous.
Having now received this retribution as a pig, my cries are loud and incessant; when I am captured, my shrieks pierce through the four quarters.
The punishments meted out by the underworld do not err by even a hair's breadth. I beg you, sir, to rescue me. Yu listened to him with trepidation and said, "I still..."
"Ordinary person! Why have you escaped, sir? The man replied, "Sir, you are compassionate by nature; whenever you see us, you always treat us with deep pity.
You may recall a dream you had in years past: 'The one who has been reborn because of you is this very person.

This was because, during the spring of the Wushen year, when my master was receiving his share of the harvest, a house servant used several pigs to pay off his rent arrears. That night, I dreamed of a man—"
He begged for his life, whereupon the man ordered his servant to keep him. After more than a year, he died of his own accord.

In a dream, he clearly recalled past events and replied, "It is indeed true, but I did not know it was you. Now, where else could I have found you? The other man said, "Karmic retribution is not fixed.
Yesterday I repaid a debt to a person from a nearby county; I never expected that, through such a connection, I would encounter you again here."
This time again, I do not know where my karmic destiny lies. At these words, he wept most piteously. Slowly wiping away his tears, he said:

"I was fortunate enough to serve as a minor official during the reign of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty. There, I heard a Dharma Master preach the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections* and made offerings to him.

As a result, I was reborn for successive lifetimes as a high-ranking official. However, at the beginning of the Song dynasty, when my merit was exhausted, I suddenly committed evil deeds and fell into [a lower state]."
I am receiving this retribution; yet, fortunately, due to roots of merit planted in former lives, I have now encountered you, sir. From this day forward, I beg of you:
whenever you encounter those like us—whether seeing us being seized, hearing our cries, or seeing the remains of our flesh being eaten—please recite the Cundī Dhāraṇī or invoke the name of Amitābha.
By doing so, I may temporarily endure my suffering and will surely be liberated from this retribution to be reborn among humans. I vow never again to commit such deeds.
The man said, "To fail in one's duty is a grave offense. Yu Shou replied, "This has been my long-held intention; moreover, having received your instruction, how could I dare breach our agreement?
The man was delighted, bowed in thanks, and departed. Alas! How extraordinary! The retribution of karma is so manifest that it does not err in this way. Consider Cao Han:

beginning as a minor official, he heard the Buddha-dharma and performed the meritorious deed of providing a single meal for a monk; consequently, for generation after generation, he received [the rewards thereof].
As his merit and the resulting good retribution were about to exhaust, he served as a great general and indulged in the karma of killing.

How could it be that evil habits increase along with the maturation of merit? This is truly to be feared. Because of the cruelty of his karmic deeds of killing, he underwent the suffering of the blade and the chopping block for over six hundred years.
Yet, by virtue of the roots of goodness planted in the past, he appeared twice in dreams to Lord Liu, ultimately requesting release from [his suffering].
The realm of suffering. Yet, was Master Liu not originally a Dharma-master who preached the sutras?

Observing that Cao Han’s evil retribution was unfailing, one sees that Master Liu’s roots of goodness likewise have their origins. When I, this illusory person, first heard his account, I was struck with wonder;
upon examining Master Liu’s *Record of Extraordinary Dreams While Wandering in the Grass*, I have therefore composed this narrative for the sake of all. *Pu* (Universal).
I address the humans and devas to extol the virtue of releasing life and refraining from killing—a matter that is clear and manifest.

Now, if even those who merely hear the sound [of the rite] or see the flesh, yet maintain mantras and recite the Buddha’s name, may still hope to endure and escape their retribution of suffering, how much more so for those who manifest true compassion by observing the precept against killing and releasing life?
I have felt a profound resonance with this at the放生所 (Life-Releasing Center) of Yunqi; thus, I respectfully record these words.

This is to inform the administrators of our own temple: you must act in accordance with the established rules. Generally speaking, for all those who have been released [from their bonds], there are those with whom one has a karmic connection;

at such times, one should provide diligent care and nourishment, preach the Dharma to instruct them, and perform recitations to escort them through death—all of these are matters of true reality. I trust you will not grow weary or indolent in this.
If one observes through the lens of the Buddha-nature, then even those who possess the requisite accumulations (*sambhāra*) should have their share;
may they not suffer from lack, nor be left hungry and empty.
This is the record of Zhenru Hermitage in Taihe County.
Forty *li* to the northwest of Tahe lies Zhaoheshi. There is a temple called Zhenru-an, which was established by Guangguo, a disciple of Yunqi.
Guo was a native of Jixian; he observed the vegetarian fast from his youth and served the Triple Gem with reverence.
In middle age, he brought his wife and children to leave the household life, shaving his head at Jingye Hall on Mount Lu and receiving the precepts from the Great Master Yunqi.
Furthermore, having received complete training under the late Master Guxin, he returned to his hometown and arrived at Tahe.

There, the filial and incorruptible Luo Shao Kui donated five mu of land to establish a hermitage and invite him to reside there for the purpose of receiving visitors. Eight years have passed since then.

Over time, practitioners gathered like clouds until the assembly grew ever larger; consequently, two main halls were constructed, along with a lecture hall, a refectory, and a kitchen, so that all facilities were fully provided and the site stood in solemn dignity.

It was a single site for religious practice. Fearing there would be no means to provide for the assembly, he gathered those with faith to establish a "Hundred Sons Lamp Assembly" (Bai Zi Deng Hui) and set aside its funds to purchase several mu of land as permanent property (*changzhu*).
This was intended to provide for the assembly perpetually, ensuring that the four requisites were never lacking.

"You may now dwell in peace and cultivate pure karma with diligent application; there is no need for external solicitation. Once his affairs were settled, he indeed went to Mount Lu to request that I write a record for him.
I therefore said to him: "I have often heard that the Pure Lands of the ten directions are transformations of the mind alone.
When the mind is pure, the land is pure. It is like the events of a dream: when a person of noble status dreams of suffering, they groan; when a poor person dreams of gold..."
One treasures it and rejoices; though it is empty upon waking, during the dream it was never non-existent.
What is called birth-and-death and nirvana is like a dream from yesterday; how much more so the conditioned adornments and merits of conventional truth?
Formerly, Bodhidharma said to Emperor Wu: "Conditioned practices truly possess no merit. Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect, its essence being inherently empty and quiescent. Nevertheless—

To fail to realize the essence of the ultimate truth (*wu kong zong*) while abandoning the practice of conditioned phenomena (*you wei xing*)—is this not like an empty stomach waiting for a royal feast, hoping thereby to satisfy one's hunger?
As it is said: "Though conditioned phenomena are artificial, if they are abandoned, merit and practice will not be accomplished;

though non-action (*wu wei*) is true, if it is merely sought as a goal, the fruit of sainthood is difficult to attain. If one can penetrate the emptiness of nature (*xing kong*) and yet establish the myriad practices, this may truly be called [the Middle Way].
The simultaneous cultivation of principle and phenomena is the realization of the oneness of the true and the deluded. Furthermore, why establish this as "active practice"?

If one were truly a Chan practitioner, they would be no different from an ordinary layperson. Yet, in his middle years, he brought his wife and children out of worldly toil and suddenly cultivated the pure precepts;
before ten years had passed, he had established a place of practice. Is this not the truth that the Pure Land is but the mind? Moreover, this hermitage—
What was once a wasteland and salt marsh has now become a site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa). This is truly accomplished in a single thought-moment.
Viewed from this perspective, the Western Pure Land is not separate from before one's eyes; how could one not believe it?

The *Qichang Qiji* records that Jingkou is a metropolitan center of mountains and rivers, yet Qu’a is an especially extraordinary and secluded region. Mount Huishan lies behind the city walls and rests upon flowing waters;

its forests are lush and verdant. The lake’s light reflects boundlessly, a single expanse of azure as clear as a mirror. The ridges and hills wind along in succession, where tens of thousands of pines cluster in deep green.
The celestial winds blow at intervals, and the myriad pipes of nature sound in unison, penetrating the mind and reaching the ears; this is the most excellent place among the mundane.
