The Layman Tunan cleared away the weeds and built a cottage there, where he sat in meditative repose. He named it "Pure and Refreshing" (*Qingchang*), intending to capture the spirit of Xu Miao of the Jin dynasty—his frugality and pure cultivation.
In the early summer of the Ding-si year, I visited Huishan; the Layman attended to me and inquired about the Dharma.
When I returned to Mount Kuanglu, the Layman sent a letter requesting a record of my visit. I therefore said to him: "Now, 'relief' (*chang*) is the opposite of 'oppression' (*yu*).
Thus, when heaven and earth are oppressed, a violent vapor is released; when manure and soil are oppressed, poisonous fungi grow; and when human emotions are oppressed, a hundred ailments arise.
From this we know that relief is the harmony of the vital breath (*qi*) and the fulfillment of emotion. Alas for those who are submerged..."

To be immersed in wealth and honor, to indulge excessively in sensory desires, and to seek gratification for a fleeting moment as one’s sole pleasure—this is what is meant by "suppressing the distress only to achieve a momentary exhilaration.
It is like eating poison that pleases the palate; one fails to realize that after a long time the poison will manifest, destroying one's life.

Formerly, there was an official serving in Western Yue who was fond of the taste of *shébùgū* (partridges). Because the region produced many of them, he could fully satisfy his craving. It was not... [text fragment ends].
He did not eat this [meat]. Later, upon returning from his official duties, he fell ill; his entire body swelled and broke out in ulcers. Even a skilled physician was at a loss.

One who possessed discernment said, "This is the toxicity of *pinellia ternata* (banxia). The partridge feeds on *pinellia*, and by consuming it for a long time, its poison has filled the five viscera;
it is likely beyond salvation. Those in the world who indulge in delicious delicacies and thereby trigger such toxicity are all of the same class as the partridge.

The layman regarded official rank and robes as shackles; he viewed wealth and honor as floating clouds. Widely learned and possessing a powerful memory, he immersed himself in Buddhist principles, investigating the source of nature and destiny and penetrating the mysteries of life and death.
He released his spirit into the vast heavens and found inspiration amidst the clouds and forests, roaming with the Creator.
That which he enjoyed was the unimpeded flow of the six supernatural powers; he intended to broaden the great void to serve as his dwelling and to submerge himself in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
He has made this his home. Furthermore, it is not merely for the sake of frugality and pure cultivation that he dwells here to approximate the subtle principles of the spirit;
rather, while instructing his son to study within these precincts, he intends thereby to perpetuate his legacy in the world. I have therefore specially composed this record for him.
The Record of the Merit of Releasing Living Beings:
The Buddha taught that the Dharma-body is no-body, for it takes sentient beings as its body; the sublime practice of a Bodhisattva is to take the liberation of sentient beings as their practice.
Thus, all myriad practices are subsumed within the Six Perfections, with *dāna* (generosity) placed at their head. However, giving that dwells upon signs is what the Tathāgata [rejects].

Alas! Because they have not yet forgotten the distinction between self and others, they are unable to view all things with equal regard. Thus, the merit they produce mostly becomes tainted (*sāsrava*).

It is only natural that such efforts are like an arrow shot upward into the sky; they inevitably fall back down. Only when one’s practice is free from conceptual marks (*lakṣaṇa*) can its essence accord with true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Among all manner of adornments, none surpasses the merit of releasing living beings as being supreme. Why is this?
Because whether they be born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or by transformation—whether wriggling, crawling, or flying—one regards them with the Buddha-nature.

One takes pity on their sinking into the path of suffering and must rescue them from the blade, the block, the fire, or the cauldron, ensuring they are not cast upon a place of scorching or putrefaction. Once they are released from their cages and bonds, one places them where they may fly.
Emptiness dwells in the abyss; one wanders freely in the land of ultimate bliss. Compassion arises without conditions; pity is not born of attachment or biased views.

Through the contemplation of the equality of the same essence, there is not a single thought of hoping for recompense. Therefore, the measure of its merit and blessings is like empty space—inconceivable.
Is this not the most supreme and extraordinary sublime practice? Yet, as for humans and things, though they differ in magnitude...

It is extraordinary. Such is the nature of Buddhahood (*buddhatā*). Now, consider an ordinary person: if someone provides them with a single meal worth a thousand pieces of gold, or offers a jar of broth when they are on the verge of death, that person will surely feel gratitude and cherish the virtue [of their benefactor], never forgetting it.
How much more so, then, for one who has been rescued from the fires of the cauldron in a place of certain death?

If one bestows gifts while contemplating the Buddha-nature, the response will surely accord with the Dharma-nature. Cause and effect are as clear as the distinction between black and white; this is indeed the natural order of things. How much more so, then...
Human life is limited, while material things are inexhaustible. Now, by forgoing a single meal, one can save the lives of hundreds of millions.
How could the merit of such an act possibly be measured? Therefore, followers of the Buddha take the protection of living beings as their supreme practice.

This is still strictly within the context of transcending the world; however, when it comes to engaging with the secular world—where one unifies the noble and the lowly, and distinguishes the wise from the foolish—nothing compares [to this].
The release of living beings is a sublime practice. In recent times, Yunqi specifically highlighted this practice;

he recorded the karmic responses to the merit of abstaining from killing and releasing life in written chapters, which have been widely adopted throughout the land. When I previously visited Wancheng, I observed that the local customs largely honored the Buddha, a state brought about by the official Lord Wu, who personally led the way.
It was proclaimed from house to house and understood by every family, such that the influence of the Buddha’s teachings was vast and pervasive.

This is the custom of our nation; it may serve as a mirror for Master Zhan. By upholding the Dharma of Yunqi, he has established a society for the release of living beings and set aside permanent endowments to perpetually turn the inexhaustible wheel of Great Compassion.
Upon hearing this, I was filled with joy and said: "In the past, the Great Master Zhizhe took the sea as a pool for releasing living beings.
Subsequently, the Tiantai school flourished throughout various foreign lands. Those who discerned the significance remarked that..."

This is the realm of retribution experienced by those beings who were released. Master Zhan cited the example of a contemporary official and layman who followed the Dharma-stream, delivering immeasurable sentient beings so that they might together return to the ocean of nature.
If one truly maintains constant clarity and non-delusion, then those who receive this grace will undergo transformation and become human beings;
it shall be seen that loyal ministers, righteous scholars, filial sons, and compassionate grandsons will gather in one place, uniting their hearts to protect [the Dharma].

The Dharma is like a city with its moats; it establishes the great banner of the Triple Gem. Furthermore, it does not merely stop the various barbarians from following the Dharma, but can indeed be verified within one or two decades.
Its success will be realized before long, and there will surely be those who witness its efficacy with their own eyes.
How could there be any deficiency in such merit?

This record of the resurgence of pines at Guizong Temple reflects the Buddha’s teaching that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, thickets, and forests are all the true body of the Buddha, together turning the wheel of Dharma. This is the intended meaning.

This reveals the principle that the three realms are mind-only. As for the attainment of Buddhahood by insentient beings—a matter difficult for the world to believe—it is simply a failure to comprehend the meaning of "mind-only.
Mount Lu’s Guizong Monastery was the place where Master Chiyen preached the Dharma;
there, thirty-six enlightened masters followed in succession. Situated amidst the splendors of Mount Kuang, this site has long been a locus of spiritual power.
After it had been abandoned, the palatial halls and Buddhist temples were left to the weeds; only a single ancient pine tree before the monastery stood tall, reaching toward the heavens.
Its roots had been gnawed away by woodcutters until half were gone, and its branches were withered and frail, on the verge of breaking.
At that time, Chan Master Daguan passed by and asked about it, sighing, "Of all that once belonged to Guizong, only this remains."
"It is merely a single *kṣa* staff. Alas, it has encountered the axe! Were this not so, the traces of the site of enlightenment would have vanished.
Thereupon, he led his disciples to transport stones and construct a perimeter wall, piling earth around it and performing incantations and prayers.

He made a vow, saying: "If this temple is destined to be restored, may this pine tree grow back as it was before. After lingering there and composing the "Fu Lei Wan" (Ballad of the Old Man), he departed. Not many years passed.
The fruit was heavy and large; its bark was intact and dense, and its branches and leaves were lush and flourishing. Before long, a great famine occurred.
There were some surviving monks in the monastery who used pine nuts to exchange for rice for their sustenance. A master carpenter eyed the tree with intent to fell it.

Just then, a beggar took shelter beneath its shade and wished to redeem it by offering rice. Moved by this, the carpenter desisted. Within a few years, the water from the fruit became clear and limpid.
The Duke restored the temple, ultimately moving His Majesty to bestow the Tripitaka. At that time, the local authorities constructed halls and buildings, transforming rubble into a pure land.
Was not the catalyst for this transformation already foreseen in a single withered tree?

If one were to say that insentient things can act thus, it is nevertheless due to the power of sincere devotion. Though grasses and trees lack consciousness, it is through such earnestness that they respond.

Through such responsive transformations, the principle that "all is but mind" is clearly manifested. Consider how Meng Zong wept over the bamboo until it sprouted shoots in winter, or how Master Sengsheng preached the Dharma until the stones nodded their heads.
Since phenomena are not outside the mind, these transformations arise from the person. This is just like the story of the withered tortoise that foretold good and bad fortune for others;
though it was drilled seventy-two times without a single error, the result depended solely on the sincerity of its intent, and the response followed like an echo.
It is said that if one can master external objects, they are identical to the Tathāgata; when person and object are of one essence, they may together turn the Wheel of Dharma.
This is what was verified here. Therefore, I record this to inform future generations: know that this pine tree is the eternally abiding Dharmakāya.
Should anyone in later ages damage even a single hair of it, they commit an injury to the Dharmakāya and sever the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom—how could they not be mindful of this?
Ah! This is the Record of the Śarīra Stūpa of Śākyamuni Buddha on Mount Lu’s Golden Wheel Peak.
Since the Dharma first entered China during the Yongping era of the Han dynasty, in the Wucheng era of the Wu state, the Western Region Dharma Master Kang Seng...
He arrived at Jiankang, where he established images and performed circumambulations. He sought śarīra relics at Changgan-li, and the Wu king erected a stūpa to enshrine them.

He founded Jianchu Monastery; this was the beginning of monasteries and stūpas in Jiangnan. During the Xiankang era of Emperor Cheng of the Eastern Jin, the Dharma Master Dharmatrāta arrived bringing the *Dhyāna-sūtra*.
At that time, Wang Xizhi, the Right General of the Secretariat, was serving as the Governor of Jiangzhou.
Seeing this, he marveled at it; he then donated his own residence to establish Guizong Temple and settled there.
During the Yixi era, Master Huiyuan arrived at Mount Lu and established the Lotus Society at Donglin. When the Venerable Yaśas arrived, Master Huiyuan invited him to join the society.
He then took the Śākyamuni Buddha’s *śarīra* that he had brought with him and constructed a stūpa atop Mount Jīnlún at Guīzōng;
he personally bore iron to build the pagoda, which became the first of the monasteries in the Western River region.

During the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty, the Chan Master Chìyǎn Cháng received the mind-seal of Mázŭ and established the Dharma at Guīzōng, [thereby becoming the progenitor] of the famous monasteries throughout Kuāngnán.
All were eminent disciples under his guidance, the preeminent figures of their time, renowned as the "Dharma Pit" (Hofuku). Here, the single-lineage transmission of the West was greatly revitalized;
from this point on, more than thirty individuals followed in succession to preach the Dharma, all of whom are recorded in the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).
By the Five Dynasties and into the Song, the Way gradually declined and the temple fell into ruin. During the Jingshi and Huangyou eras of the Song dynasty, it was reconstructed once again.
During the Yuanfeng era, the monk Wenjing once again revitalized it; however, by the end of the Yuan dynasty, it was destroyed by war.
From that time on, the stupa and temple fell into ruin, and the mountain lands and fields were entirely taken over as private property by the common people.

In the *guichou* year of the Wanli era, Master Da’s disciple, Master Guoqing Zhan, while paying respects at the stupa, passed by and sighed in lamentation. He subsequently resolved to restore the site and visited various officials and patrons to seek their support.

In the same year, through their unified efforts, they moved the Imperial Sovereign to issue an edict bestowing a complete set of the Tripitaka upon the monastery and appointing its disciple Xiuci as the abbot.
Local officials constructed halls and buildings, while the Huangmei scholar-official Xing Maixue donated funds to redeem all the monastery’s mountain lands and fields;
thus, it became a magnificent center for the Dharma. In the Gui-chou year, Master Zhan wished to renovate it.

Regarding the stupa: he purchased tens of thousands of catties of iron, but before the work was completed, he passed away. In the year Jiayin (1054), Xiuji built a great image of Vairocana in Wuzhong.
Upon his return, the stupa’s śarīra emitted light on three occasions, illuminating the mountains and valleys.
Behind the temple, five pine trees produced cones shaped like stupas, each approximately eight inches high and consisting of thirteen tiers; everyone near and far marveled at this.
In the spring of the year Yi-mao, following the final instructions of Master Cibing, iron was smelted to cast a thirteen-tiered stupa.

The relic chamber was reopened, where several hundred grains of śarīra were discovered, emitting five-colored jewel-like radiance that dazzled the eyes of onlookers. All who beheld them paid homage with profound reverence and joy.
In the ninth month of the autumn of that same year, at the time of the enshrinement, the mountains and valleys roared like thunder for seven days.
Next, all who heard of it knew it to be an auspicious sign of the *śarīra*.

Fearing that iron might easily corrode, he protected it by pounding together magnetic ash and rice gruel to coat the exterior, so as to ensure its durability and long-term preservation. In the summer of the Bingchen year, I came from Mount Nanyue to pay my respects;
I beheld its wondrous peak rising steeply and loftily, standing alone to prop up the void, its form resembling a *stūpa*. As for the peak—
The summit is about two *zhang* high, with a stone cavern several *chi* deep, barely large enough to house the stupa; it is clearly a creation of Heaven and Earth, not a mere accident.
I have recorded this, saying: "Long ago, when Śākyamuni Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, his remains were cremated and eight *hu* and four *dou* of relics were obtained.
These were distributed and enshrined in stupas throughout the heavens, among humans, and in the palaces of the nāgas. King Aśoka then distributed them throughout Jambudvīpa."
Regarding those in our land of China, there are nineteen. Among them, only those from Mingzhou and Jiankang are most renowned;

the others remain obscure and unremarked. Could this [relic] be one of them? A śarīra is the residual fragrance of precepts and meditative concentration, formed by the condensation of the four great elements.
Because it is composed of various elements such as flesh, blood, hair, teeth, and bone, it exhibits the differences of five colors.
Its substance is firm and rigid, capable of piercing metal and stone; its radiance dazzles the eyes, surpassing all worldly treasures.
Among those that are solid and motionless, and those that flow up and down with various changing forms, each arises according to its respective conditions.
Alas! Buddhas and sentient beings alike possess this same mind; yet sentient beings, through ignorance, the three poisons, and delusive thoughts, [fail to realize it].

Because it is permeated by [defilements], its substance is foul and stinking, and it ultimately becomes ruined and decays. The Buddhas, however, are permeated by the diamond-like mind, precepts, and meditative concentration;

therefore, their substance is firm and solid, radiating brilliant light, eternally abiding and indestructible. Such is the nature of their primary retribution (*sambhogakāya*); their secondary environment (*bhājanaloka*) is likewise so.

As for the secondary environment of sentient beings, they evoke a world of the five turbidities, filled with various impurities. The pure lands of the Buddhas, however, [are endowed with the seven...]
Because it is adorned with jewels, the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra* states: "That ground is firm and solid, composed of vajra; this is what is called 'transformed by mind alone.
How could it be produced by other power? A Buddha does not dwell apart from a pure land; therefore, śarīra relics are not enshrined except in superior lands."
This Golden Wheel Mountain stands majestically to the south of Mount Lu, towering above the clouds and mists and overwhelming all surrounding peaks with its grandeur.

It is an empty abode in the human realm, yet the Dharma-body and śarīra relics of the Buddha dwell eternally within it; how could this be the result of minor conditions? Although it is true and eternal, indestructible, it remains so.
Yet, as worldly phenomena undergo change, the rise and fall of these Buddhist edifices have not been uniform.

To ensure their endurance for all time, one must examine the original intention of those who first established them and the resolve of those who later restored them; therein must surely lie the power of their vows. This is the record.
Record of the Śarīra Stūpa of King Aśoka at Mount Mao in Mingzhou.
In the Sanskrit language it is called *śarīra*; here it is translated as "body-bone.

Our World-Honored One, throughout vast eons, cultivated the Vajra-samādhi with a vajra-like mind until he attained Buddhahood, never for a moment harboring divergent thoughts. Thus, the five [aggregates] born of conditions were transformed...
The illusory body of the aggregates is perfected as the vajra-body; this is the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, eternally abiding and indestructible, forever free from birth and extinction.
Among the ten bodies of the Buddha, this is one: the Body of Sustaining Power.

When the Tathāgata manifested in the Sahā world, he appeared in Kapilavastu, preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, and having completed his work of transformation, [passed away] in the Śāla grove at the city of Kuśinagara.
Between the twin trees, he entered Great Parinirvāṇa. At that time, the king of that country performed the cremation according to the Dharma and obtained eight *droṇas* of relics.
These were divided into three portions: one for the heavens, one for the human world, and one for the dragon palaces, each of which erected stupas for worship.
In the human world, they were divided among eight kingdoms. King Ajātaśatru of the kingdom of Magadha received one portion, which consisted of eighty-four thousand grains.

Upon reaching the time of King Aśoka, who possessed great supernatural power and was able to command spirits and deities, he ground the seven precious gems into powder and constructed eighty-four thousand stupas, which he distributed throughout the four continents.
Since the continent of Jambudvīpa in the south served as the land for the Buddha’s physical teachings, the number of stupas there is the greatest.
Those that came to Zhendan numbered nineteen; among them, only those at Changgan in Jinling and Mount Mao in Mingzhou were most prominent and renowned.
Having left home at a young age at Changgan, I frequently witnessed various miraculous omens beyond description.
Although I had not yet traveled to Mingzhou, I had long heard of the signs of its spiritual responses. Now, having seen Master Li’s *Record of Mount Yuyang*, I am further enlightened.
Having read this, he was moved and sighed, saying: "This is the place where my Original Teacher currently dwells in the world, preaching the Dharma.
Now, what is the *śarīra*? It is the one true *dharmadhātu*, the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of vast and great radiance.
The Buddhas realize it as the pure *dharmakāya*; the Bodhisattvas cultivate it as the adamantine ground of the mind; sentient beings, however, are deluded by it."
That which is thus [transformed] becomes the *ālaya-vijñāna*. That which is indestructible constitutes the seed of Buddha-nature, termed the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
Because this is inherently possessed by sentient beings, the Buddhas appear in the world specifically to reveal and demonstrate it, enabling them to awaken and enter into it.

When the Patriarch came from the West, he pointed to it as the "Mind-Seal" (*cittamudrā*). Thus, one knows that sentient beings and Buddhas are non-dual and without distinction; there is only the difference between defilement and purity through perfuming (*vāsanā*).

The difference lies merely in their transformation. Because sentient beings’ karma of ignorance perfumes and steams [the mind] moment by moment, they give rise to a body composed of the four great elements and five aggregates—a body that is foul, putrid, stinking, impure, impermanent, and subject to decay.

That which does not decay is the karmic fruit of saṃsāra, which is never forgotten throughout kalpas. The Bodhisattva takes this very [karma] as the basis for concentration and wisdom; through such cultivation, they attain the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*).
Taming sentient beings and purifying Buddha-lands, those indestructible, subtle, and wondrous merits achieve adornment;
only the Buddha realizes this, which constitutes the pure Dharma-body, eternally abiding in the light of quiescence. Body and land are non-dual.

When it manifests a great body, it possesses immeasurable radiance and marks of excellence, dwelling within the Adornment of the Flower Treasury; this is called the Body of Real Reward. When it manifests a small [body]...
The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)—the sixteen-foot golden body—manifests birth in the human world and shares the sufferings of commoners;
yet sentient beings who behold it see only a Buddha born of conditions and do not perceive the true essence of the *dharmakāya*.

To reveal that the Dharma and its manifestations are non-dual, and that impermanence is itself permanence, he enters parinirvāṇa and leaves behind relics (*śarīra*) to gather in and sustain sentient beings. This is called the "body sustained by power," demonstrated for their sake.
The indestructible Vajra Dharma-body eternally abides in the world; fundamentally, it is devoid of the characteristics of birth and death, or coming and going.
Therefore, the manifested light-forms and various auspicious responses are inconceivable, appearing in response to the minds of sentient beings as they are moved by them.

This is the Dharmakāya preaching the Dharma in response to the capacities of sentient beings. By means of the Samādhi Beyond Words, it points directly to the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by all beings, desiring that those who behold it may immediately awaken to their own minds and suddenly perceive the non-arising and non-ceasing nature of the Dharmakāya.

How does this differ from the Buddha sitting upon his seat at Vulture Peak, holding up a flower at the very end? Therefore, the Buddha’s appearance in the world and his preaching of the Dharma are nothing other than this.
He pointed to this great matter of one great cause. Thus, within the single assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra*, he revealed to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Since this knowledge and vision is precisely the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body, it is said: "Wherever this sūtra exists, one should erect a stupa made of the seven treasures.
How much more so for the Buddha’s knowledge and vision! Yet, it is further obscured by written words. When it comes to the Patriarchs directly pointing this out to people, however—
It is manifested amidst blows with staffs, shouts, rebukes, and scoldings, yet people characterize it as "critical wit" (jīfēng), believing there must be some other profound mystery therein;
thus, those who awaken to it are rare. Now, one personally beholds the Dharmakāya and the Tathāgata face-to-face, who proclaims the Dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing;
yet people fail to realize it within themselves, regarding it instead as mere radiant auspicious signs. This is truly...
This means that one passes by the truth face-to-face; how lamentable! Alas! We have been submerged for many kalpas, wandering through birth and death.
Now, by what fortune and by what cause have we encountered this rare and difficult-to-find event? Yet we still mistake our own head for its reflection.
Is this not to fail upward toward true compassion and to obscure our own inherent nature? Can this not be called a matter of great sorrow? In the past...
At the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, the Buddha himself spoke of the lifespan of the Dharmakāya as being eternally abiding and imperishable;

yet this remains merely a hollow claim, for there has not yet been anything like this—something seen through the profound, clear, and manifest reality of actual practice. It is only Samantabhadra who, by means of the ten great vows, reveals the Dharmakāya, saying:
"I entreat the Buddha to remain in the world, exhorting him to turn the wheel of Dharma, and to always follow the Buddha."

The meaning of these three aspects of study is clarified herein. Initially, when Senghui arrived at Changgan, the Ruler of Wu, Sun Quan, commanded him to seek śarīra relics, setting a deadline of seven days.
When there was no response, he extended the period to twenty-one days. Still, by midnight, there was no sign. Senghui prostrated himself and pleaded with sorrow, saying:
"The Buddha takes compassion as his heart; if there is truly no response, it would cause the sentient beings of this region to fall into annihilation."
"The Buddha-seed has been planted! Thereupon, he wailed aloud, invoking the name of the Buddha three times.

Blood and sweat gushed forth from every pore of his body, and suddenly a metallic clanging was heard within the jar, its light illuminating heaven and earth. Upon opening it, the śarīra were found to be perfectly intact within the jar.
Liu Sahe had fallen into the hells with no prospect of escape; thus, he followed the instructions of a foreign monk to seek the śarīra.
Because it served as a ground for repenting one's transgressions, a precious stupa emerged from the earth. Thus we know that Kang represented others and Liu represented himself;
both were in accordance with the intent of Samantabhadra’s exhortation.

As for those who provide various adornments and offerings, and who protect and praise [the Dharma], are they not surely those who follow and study alongside the Buddha? Furthermore, the Buddha-nature within sentient beings is indeed its...
How deluded you are! As for the radiance of Prajñā, which shines eternally without ever being obscured, it manifests through deeds.

Thus, when those such as loyal ministers and filial sons, or men of ambition and benevolence, perform their actions to serve their sovereign and benefit the people, accomplishing works of enduring merit—could these not be the outflow of the Dharmakāya? This is why the emperors of successive dynasties have revered it.
Its flourishing—is this not indeed the "beneficial appearance" of the Dharma King? In short, there is not a single sentient being who does not possess this nature.
Therefore, those who see, hear, rejoice in, prostrate to, or make offerings to it, are no different from those who personally receive his feet;
they immediately offer their bodies and lives, exhausting all that they possess, giving both internal and external gifts to serve as adornments, specifically for the enjoyment of its own nature.

Earth-Ear. Now, as for those who, upon a single glimpse of the *śarīra*, suddenly shatter ignorance (*avidyā*), fully realize the *dharmakāya*, take a long farewell to birth and death, and forever emerge from the path of delusion—it is not that such persons do not exist among those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom who have long possessed the permeation of hearing and whose conditions have ripened in the present moment.
Viewed from this perspective, the successive generations of kings and ministers who initiated these works in the past, the Grand Chancellor...
Master Lu revived the tradition in the past; Master Sima Guo has revitalized it once more in the present.
Furthermore, they entrusted their Dharma-bodies to the Samādhi of the Hair-tip to ensure their imperishability; this, too, is sustained by the wheel of Samantabhadra’s vows.
Is it not reasonable that the Buddha addressed Śāriputra as "Empty-born" (Kūṭadanta) and as an "Elder"? I personally believe that the assembly at Vulture Peak remains vividly before my eyes.
Previously, the sound of his preaching the Dharma blazed forth without interruption; therefore, I have specially recorded this to inform all who see or hear it.
Those who rejoice in it, prostrate, or make offerings must not seek him through physical form or appearance.

Record of the Hall for the Great Compassion Repentance at Mount Lu:
Only the Buddha’s Dharma-body is boundless, yet it manifests as a whole to become sentient beings.

The deluded thoughts of sentient beings are boundless, yet they manifest as a whole to become the false karma of birth and death. Because this false karma is not extinguished, the ocean of suffering of sentient beings is likewise boundless. And...

In the end, none know how to escape. Were it not for the power of the Great Compassionate One’s vow, there would be no way to exhaust the ocean of suffering, to eliminate deluded karma and emerge from birth and death to realize the ultimate limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). Therefore, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is called the Mind of the Dharma-realm;
he practices the conduct of great compassion, secretly entering the sea of the false conceptualizations of all sentient beings to deliver them, and establishes *dhāraṇīs*.

It causes practitioners to maintain the recitation and cultivate it through practice, desiring to lead sentient beings out of the ocean of suffering, to behold the original Dharmakāya, and to ascend to the shore of Nirvāṇa;
this is the origin of the Great Compassion Repentance Method. Its mantras originally derive from the Abhiṣeka Section (Guandingbu) and flow forth from the Dharmakāya of the Middle Way;
they constitute the Heart Seal (Hṛdayamudrā) of Vairocana. It began with the Venerable Master Siming, who followed the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*.
Its establishment dates back to ancient times. It is because the profound gateway of the *ālayavijñāna* within sentient beings cannot be shattered without the secret seal of the mind (*cittamudrā*).
This is the excellent medicine for liberation from suffering. Master Man was directly instructed by Yunqi;
he retired to Nan Yue to cultivate his practice, making the method of repentance his primary Buddhist activity. Those who placed their faith in him were numerous. Subsequently...

He went to Mount Lu, where he lived in seclusion and dwelt alone. Wishing to propagate this Dharma to deliver the fourfold assembly, he constructed a hall for repentance to demonstrate the ritual of cultivation.
Once the hall was completed, he requested a record from the Elder (Zongmi). The Elder said to him: "All sentient beings are originally the Dharmakāya.
Having become deluded, they have fallen into the ocean of karma of birth and death; therefore, cause them to be sealed by the mind-seal of the Dharmakāya."

This perfumes and transforms the nature of karma; it is like pouring water into water, or space merging with space. Those who possess even a modicum of faith will, amidst the sufferings of birth and death, emerge from them without even intending to do so.
You, sir, with a heart of great compassion, serve as the kind oars for the vessel that crosses the ocean of suffering.

By means of the Dharma inherently possessed by every person, he points it out to them; like sprinkling nectar upon that which is parched and withered, he cools the ground of the mind, so that one comes to know it spontaneously without waiting for further instruction.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inexhaustible, and the realm of sentient beings is likewise inexhaustible.
This Dharma is likewise inexhaustible. Furthermore, why should one harbor plans for eternity?
This is the inscription for the Ten Directions Permanent Endowment (Shifang Changzhu) at Yunzhong Temple on Mount Lu.
Zen groves are spread like chess pieces across Mount Lu; at its summit, beneath the Nine Wondrous Peaks, this site is the most secluded and sublime. It is commonly called...
Yangtianping (Looking-up-at-Heaven Plateau). Because it is so high that nothing stands above it, it was formerly the den of tigers and wolves.
There is Yunzhong Temple, which was founded by Master Zhonggong. The master’s name was Fazhong; he was originally a native of Shexian.

At the age of nineteen, he took the Venerable Daji of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou as his preceptor and served as a kitchen assistant for three years. He reflected that the Great Matter remained unresolved.
He subsequently attended lecture halls and studied various sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Yet, he still regarded words and letters as obstacles.
He crossed the river to Shaolin, where he relied upon Master Dajian to investigate the purport of Bodhidharma’s arrival from the West. After residing there for ten years, he traveled to the capital.
Fulil also visited various great spiritual mentors (*mahājñānin*) to have his essential insights confirmed. Thereupon, he traveled to Mount Wutai, where he met me and Master Miao;
he recognized them both as preeminent talents within the Dharma-gate. When I departed for the Eastern Sea and Master Miao returned to Luya, Fulil invited the Master to go with him.
He resided there for three years, consulting him on many matters concerning the establishment of monastic institutions. Shortly thereafter, Fulil again left and entered Niushan. [The text ends here.]
After some time, he moved to Kuangshan. Initially, he built a hut at Jingangtai (Diamond Terrace) to lecture on the sutras; he resided there for three years.

Finding the constant coming and going to be a distraction, he moved again to Wulao Peak. After another four years, he reached Yunzhong; admiring its sublime loftiness, he cleared away the brush and bound together rafters to dwell there.
Clad in grass and subsisting on wood, many eminent and spiritually gifted monks from the ten directions gathered around him. The Master cast off his physical form, remaining without self-attachment.
I have forgotten self and others through the Way; I establish no rules or regulations and impose no constraints. Each person governs themselves, without using worldly standards for display.

Regarding the four requisites, I leave them to conditions: if they are lacking, I personally go begging to provide for them. Even down to a single thread or a grain of rice, I always keep the community in mind.
I refined my three karmas and cultivated a clear, unified mind. After residing there for twenty-two years, it eventually became a monastic center.
In the forest, he later built a thatched hut to provide a place for rest and recreation. He inscribed the name "Among the Clouds" (Yúnzhōng) upon the mountain gate; his ambition was most lofty.
The Master delighted in planting pines, totaling over one hundred thousand trees, hoping they would transform into dragons to mark the passing of years.

Having come from Mount Nanyue to visit this mountain, I engaged in a night conversation with the Master, who said to me: "I am old now; as for the illusory transformations of the human world, I leave them to their course."
"I have resided on this mountain for thirty years. My remaining time is not long. This very site is a *bodhimaṇḍa*;

though it is formed through illusory conditions, my original intention was to establish it for the 'elephants and dragons' (great bodhisattvas) of the ten directions, not for the sake of this single, petty individual.

I beg for a word from the Master to serve as my guiding resolve. The Master rejoiced and sighed, saying: "How great is the Master’s heart! As the Sūtra says: 'By means of the Great Perfect Enlightenment...'"
To establish my monastery, one must abide peacefully in body and mind; this is the wisdom of equality, for it is the Buddha who takes the ten directions as his concern.
As the saying goes of West River: "The assembly gathers together from the ten directions; each and every one studies non-action. This is the field where Buddhas are selected;

with an empty mind, one returns having passed the imperial examination. Thus, the Patriarch took the ten directions as his heart. It is only you, Master, whose lifelong aspiration has been rooted in selflessness.
Therefore, whatever has been established is entirely without self. Now, to entrust this all at once to the ten directions is the ultimate absence of self.

As for those who can truly inherit this enterprise and shoulder its burden with bare hands—those who take the Master’s mind as their own mind—if they are sincerely resolved upon the Way, how could there not be heroic figures who have "passed the examination" by realizing the emptiness of the mind? This is like the mountain colors and lake...
The light, the flowing water, and the moving wind all proclaim the Dharma-sound of non-self. The Master’s broad and long tongue-mark remains eternally present and never perishes.
As for the details of this eternal presence, there is a separate document which I have not recorded here.
I have briefly noted the beginning and end of the Master’s life to inform those who come after.
Record of the Adorned Buddha Images at Wanshou Monastery on Mount Lu.
To the south of Mount Lu, monastery banners stand in view; among its great valleys is that called Qixian. Its cliffs and ravines are steep and precipitous.
The forest trees are lush and verdant. Mount Taiyi, Hanyang, Taolin, and the various peaks stand in dense array amidst the clouds.

Numerous streams converge in a great ravine, within which lies a temple called Wanshou (Ten Thousand Years of Longevity). It was originally built by the Tang dynasty monk Deying as a Chan hermitage. After many years, it fell into ruin.

He bequeathed these three fields to them. When these three are complete, the worldly and supramundane life-force truly depends upon them.

If those who later guard these three fields do not cultivate them with diligence and allow them to become overgrown and desolate—neglecting respect is like committing an act of hostility; neglecting compassion is like committing theft;
and lacking merit means that the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom will be severed. It is not considered a transgression for anyone who has not yet reached the point of reflecting upon this.
Such a person is not even a disciple of the Buddha. Nevertheless, those who consume the fruits of this field should also know to cultivate this mind;
then the spiritual sprout of the seed of wisdom will flourish day and night, and the fruit of Bodhi may be hoped for. Otherwise, one will fall into the state of a withered sprout and a ruined seed.

Once the hermitage was completed, he traveled to Mount Lu to recount these matters and to ask me for a name for it.

Suddenly these people were established in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once the transformation through the Way had flowed forth, the literary era truly flourished. May these far-reaching blessings be firmly settled, as enduring as high mountains and long rivers.

*Record of the Miraculous Responses of the Portrait of Master Baozhi of Mount Yang in Xin’an*.
Mount Yang in Xin’an is a secluded and magnificent peak that stands preeminent among the wondrous sights of the southeast; it was founded during the Liang dynasty.
It served as the site of the Dharma-center for Master Baozhi. During the Tang dynasty, it was renowned by the name of Chan Master Ji; however, it had long been abandoned and fallen into obscurity.

The local populace were originally ignorant of Buddhism, yet they venerated Master Baozhi with particular solemnity. Whenever they prayed for rain, sought progeny, or invoked blessings against calamities, their petitions were immediately answered.

Consequently, the offerings and sacrifices continued without interruption. At the beginning of the Longqing era, Master Shoujing Xuan practiced the dhūta austerities with such extraordinary diligence and purity that he stood out from others.

He was constant in his influence; those both near and far were transformed by him. The prominent clans within the region gathered their families to deliberate and requested that the Master restore Mount Yangshan.
The Master complied. Upon entering the mountain, he saw the old foundations fallen among the weeds and brambles, yet the mountain terrain within the precincts remained intact.
All [the land] was returned to those with power. The Master then first recruited commoners from the foot of the mountain to exchange for that land.
Leading his disciples Xingyu and Xingjue, he dwelt amidst the wind and bathed in the rain, clearing away weeds and thorns to establish it.

In less than ten years, the old was demolished and the new was built; thus, a great place of practice (*dharma-āyatana*) was completed, as if descending from heaven or springing up from the earth, throughout the four borders.

Within [the community], everyone knew of the Three Jewels. Once the temple was completed, the elders passed down the tradition that there were three scrolls of Master Zhigong’s portraits that had circulated among the common people, though their whereabouts were unknown.

they were the handiwork of Zhang Sengyao of the Liang dynasty. These scrolls were...
He harbored the desire to return home. This man was of the Li clan of Jixi, Xin’an. He had three sons, each of whom inherited one [portion].

The two masters received it, regarding it as a divine object. After some time, a fire broke out at the eldest son’s house; he hurriedly sent word to his family...

Several years later, while returning from a long journey, his elder son lost his way and mistakenly arrived at a roadside inn at the foot of a mountain.

Dōkō pointed to him. The guest was moved and asked his name. Dōkō replied, "Jōkō. The guest was astonished, while Dōkō did not understand the reason for his reaction.

The guest said, "My late father was a stonemason. While repairing the Baoen Pagoda, he obtained three scrolls of a painted image of the Great Being Zhigong.

It was merely that [the name] had been combined with the previous two. When Guang received it and unfolded it, he saw that the forehead bore the inscription:

"Bestowed by Imperial Decree upon the Great Being’s Disciple Jingguang for his veneration. Thus he came to know that what he had previously marveled at was the strangeness of the name being identical.
In the first year of the Taichang era, during the month of Jiaping, Jingguang came to Mount Kuang to confer the precepts; he fully understood the circumstances thereof.
I heard of this and found it most extraordinary. While the Great Being’s manifestations are immeasurable, they all transform after a single appearance;

The Great Being then tore open the skin of his face with his finger, revealing the countenance of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Thus one knows that he was a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The biographies record that during his lifetime, he frequently traveled between Mount Qian and Lake Tai;
however, there is no mention of him being at Mount Yang. When the Great Being entered *parinirvāṇa*, Emperor Wu used two earthenware jars as a funerary shrine.
He was buried on the southern slope of Mount Zhong. When our Holy Ancestor established the capital at Jiankang, he personally selected a site for a mausoleum within the mountains;
the Emperor himself determined it. Upon breaking ground, a ceramic sarcophagus was discovered.

Upon opening it, the flesh-body was seen as if alive, with hair grown long and reaching his shoulders, and his hand resting upon a wooden tablet inscribed: "Liang Dynasty’s Master Baozhi. Our Holy Ancestor marveled greatly at this and subsequently moved [the remains].
He was buried at Linggu Valley in Shandong, where a pagoda and temple were constructed to enshrine him.

A statue was established in the city at Jiming Temple, where sacrifices were offered during the spring and autumn seasons using flour as the sacrificial victims. The rites performed by the Grand Master of Ceremonies have remained unchanged to this day.
It is not surprising that amidst the wild thickets and brambles of Mount Yangshan, light was emitted and auspicious signs manifested;

Furthermore, he ordered the carving of the hall’s architectural style, and when Emperor Wu personally arrived to offer incense, the Great Being [manifested] for all...

Thus, these three images originally did not reside in a single place. Nevertheless, from the Liang dynasty until the beginning of our current dynasty, more than a thousand years have passed.

One will take upon oneself the intense sufferings of the three miserable realms, from which there is no means of escape for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.

For instance, when one takes the life of another and consumes their flesh and blood to satisfy one's own appetite, within the space of a single meal and inside a single vessel, one injures hundreds of thousands of lives.

The suffering of ten thousand lifetimes is already immeasurable; how much more so the karma created in a single lifetime? A single type of karmic action involving killing is already boundless, let alone many types of karma.
