Only our Buddha has realized this, and out of compassion for those creatures who are deluded, he has appeared specifically in the world to reveal it universally, enabling them to awaken and enter [the Way].

While there are many gates of skillful means (*upāya*), recollecting the Buddha (*nien-fo*) is the most simple and direct. Yet, recollecting the Buddha is none other than invoking the innate, true nature.
This is the Buddha. To awaken for a single thought-moment is to be a Buddha for that one thought-moment; to awaken in every thought-moment is to be a Buddha in every thought-moment.

If one is constantly aware and never deluded, one becomes a permanently abiding Buddha. No means of self-benefit surpasses this. Yet, once one has awakened oneself, one takes pity on those who remain lost.
As for all things—whether flying, submerged, or wriggling insects—how can they be made to awaken by themselves? Therefore, [the Bodhisattva] extends [this awakening].
I shall uproot them through compassion that shares their same essence and sustain them by relying on the true kindness of the Buddha. Thus, by recollecting many Buddhas, one generates many births;

yet, upon relinquishing a single birth, one immediately becomes a Buddha. In this way, one suddenly causes immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings—born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or by transformation—to all enter into *nirvāṇa* without remainder. Truly, there is not a single being left behind.
Those who have attained nirvana through birth—would this not be the most supreme practice for the dual benefit of self and others?
Thus, relying upon the power of the Buddha through my own vow, I have established images of those who welcome and guide, and constructed pavilions to enshrine them.

May all who see, hear, or rejoice in this, through a single gaze or a single prostration, give rise to the mind of universal salvation; thereby, may their compassion for those of the same essence increase ever further.
Extensive and profound, the true seed of Buddhahood is further deepened. How could such merit and virtue be fathomed by thought?
This is the record.
Record of the Ten Directions Permanent Endowment for the Reception of Guests at Beihaitai Hermitage, Gaoyou Prefecture.
The three Great Bodhisattvas manifest their bodies throughout the ten directions to universally deliver sentient beings, reaching everywhere without exception.
Within our land of Zhendan, they have established the three great sacred mountains as perpetual *dharmakāya* sites for the Way.

While Mount Emei is situated in the remote western province of Shu, far off in a corner, only Mount Wutai and Mount Putuo stand facing one another in the north and south, serving as [the abodes] for the monks of the ten directions.

Those seeking lodging and those traveling to and fro were as continuous as a single thread. Located at a strategic pass between Huaiyang and Gaoyou, along the banks of the Grand Canal, the county was isolated in the middle of its course;
as clouds and waters passed by, no one’s feet could rest for even a moment. The road was long and the people weary.
When the day ends and the path is exhausted; when the wind blows at dawn and the rain falls at dusk; when treading through snow and walking upon ice—this leaking body is beset by hunger and thirst.
The sufferings of the physical frame are beyond counting. There has not been a single traveler, nor a single day, who has gone forth on pilgrimage without being destitute.
There was a lay practitioner named Lu Xiong, who resolved to construct a guesthouse for travelers as a place for temporary rest.
Concerned that providing for visitors would not be constant, he solicited the public to establish one hundred and eighty mu of farmland, taking the harvest to fill the alms bowls.
Thus, for the monastics who came and went, those weary found rest, the hungry found food, and the thirsty found drink; consequently, those who arrived felt as though they were returning home.
This person was the foremost and most excellent field of merit in this world. I, [the author], am a retired elder from Kuang...
Shan, a lay practitioner (*gṛhapati*), came to me and requested that I compose a record for him. I joyfully spoke these words to him: "All sentient beings cling to the mark of self (*ātman*).
With nothing but their own benefit in mind, they regard even a blade of grass or a single leaf as being as precious as the Nine Cauldrons.
There is none who does not plan for their descendants; who, then, can maintain even a single thought of benefiting and saving others? Only our Buddha has taught *bodhi*..."
The Bodhisattva’s Great Mind takes solely the benefit of others as its mission. Among the six perfections he practices, giving is foremost. This giving is distinguished by three types:
internal and external, and exhaustive. External refers to material wealth; internal refers to one's body and life. "Exhaustive" means leaving nothing remaining.
Were it not for the ultimate state of selflessness, who could perform such a deed? In these present times of the Final Dharma, the multitude...
One born with meager merit finds that stinginess and greed increase day by day; thus, this practice is difficult.
If there is one who can, for even a single thought-moment, extend their resolve to this point, they are a Bodhisattva of great mind. I say that these three grades of giving are all of one mind.
Since sentient beings regard wealth as their very life, to relinquish wealth is to relinquish life. If the greedy mind is not exhausted, then it is as difficult to pull out a single hair.
As soon as the mind of renunciation arises, it is utterly exhausted without remainder.

Yet, since the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three—are without distinction, a single thought of renunciation encompasses the full extent of the Dharma-realm and constitutes the very essence of attaining Buddhahood.
It enables the recipient to likewise enter the Dharma-realm through a single thought of joy; thus, this mind is one with the Buddha and...
The realm of sentient beings is entirely equal. Thus, giving is the very foundation for attaining Buddhahood.

If one can employ this mind of relinquishment to benefit others, without interruption from moment to moment, then in every such thought-moment, one is simultaneously attaining Buddhahood together with all sentient beings.
As a Great Sūtra says: "I now attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment within the minds of all sentient beings. This is what it means.
Therefore, the myriad practices of a Bodhisattva are subsumed within the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). Furthermore, giving (*dāna*) serves as their comprehensive retention (*dhāraṇī*);
because its mental resolve is vast and difficult to achieve, its virtue is broad and ever-increasing. This is why the wisdom of Mañjuśrī and the conduct of Samantabhadra [are so named].
That the compassion of Avalokiteśvara is equal to the entire dharma-realm is, in truth, the ultimate realization of the mind of non-self.

Thus, although this hermitage is small, it is sufficient to contain the dharma-realm; the Three Great Sages dwell perpetually herein, and how could the benefits of this field of merit ever be fathomed?
Therefore, I have bestowed upon the Layman the name "Field of Merit" (Futian), intending—
This constitutes the record of his travels.
*The Collected Works of Old Man Hanshan from His Dream-like Wandering*, Volume Twenty-six;
*The Collected Works of Old Man Hanshan from His Dream-like Wandering*, Volume Twenty-seven.
Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and his disciple Tonghyeong;
revised by the Disciple from Lingnan, Liu Qixiang.
Epitaph for Chan Master Daguan Ke of Mount Jing:

Now, throughout the great earth, birth and death constitute a long night of delusion; the gates of emotion are firmly closed, and the shackles of consciousness are difficult to open. There are those who are able to overturn [this state]...

To rise up and shatter [the world] with a single blow, or to cast aside one’s arm and go forth alone—this is not easily achieved by anyone who is not a heroic and courageous man endowed with a capacity that transcends the world.
Looking back through the various elders of the *Chuan deng lu* (Transmission of the Lamp), they were all such as these;
now, I have seen them in Master Daguan. The Master’s name was Zhenko, his courtesy name was Daguan, and his late title was Zibo. His disciples addressed him as...
"Venerable Sir, it is because he reveres the Dharma. He was originally from Jiuqu; his father was Shen Lian, who had lived for generations on the shores of Lake Tai in Wujiang.
The Master was the youngest son. His mother dreamed that a strange person gave her a large, fresh peach with its stalk still attached;
upon waking, the fragrance filled the room, and she subsequently conceived. When the Master was born, he did not speak until the age of five. A strange monk passed by his door and stroked [his head].
His father said to him, "This child shall renounce the world and become a teacher for humans and devas. Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished. The Master was then able to speak.
Previously, a giant's footprint had appeared in the courtyard, but from that time on it was no longer seen. From his youth, his character was fierce and bold;
he was noble and spirited, with a majestic appearance beyond compare. Even as a weakling, he did not enjoy playing, and throughout his life he took no pleasure in seeing women.

He was not permitted to bathe first. One day, his elder sister mistakenly went ahead to bathe; the Master was greatly incensed, and from then on, not even his own relatives or women dared to approach him.
Changzhi’s ambition grew daily greater, and his parents could not restrain him. He once wrote a poem that said: "The heroic spirit of one who slaughters dogs is not easily extinguished.
This was indeed a factual record. At the age of seventeen, he finally took up his sword and traveled far away to the northern frontier.

They traveled to Changmen in Suzhou and were walking through the marketplace when it began to rain heavily. There they encountered the monk Mingjue of Tiger Hill (Hūqīu), whose appearance struck them as noble;
they looked at him with admiration, and he sheltered them with his umbrella. They subsequently returned to the monastery together, where they partook of an evening meal with great joy.
Hearing the monk reciting the names of the eighty-eight Buddhas at night, their hearts were filled with immense delight. At dawn, they entered Mingjue’s quarters and said, "We two..."

"There is great treasure. Why is it defiled here within this [place]? He untied from his waist more than ten pieces of gold and gave them to Jue, instructing him to prepare an offering and request the tonsure.
He then prostrated to Jue as his teacher. That night, he sat upright in meditation until dawn. Every time they spoke in private, he sighed three times, saying:
"Looking at it, there is no meat; eating it, there is flavor. Jue wished to smelt ten thousand catties of iron to cast a great bell. The Master...
He said, "I shall assist you. He then went to a large household in Pinghu and sat cross-legged outside the gate. When the master of the house brought food forward, the Master did not eat.
The master asked what he required, and the Master replied, "I need ten thousand catties of iron to cast a great bell; if you have it, I will accept the meal.
The host immediately went out and brought ten thousand catties of iron to the gate. The Master smiled. Having finished eating, he went straight back to Huqiu with the load. Upon his return, he...

He shut his door to study, remaining within its threshold for half a year. Upon seeing a monk who drank wine and ate meat, the Master said, "For one who has left the household life to act in such a way is truly despicable.
All the monks were struck with awe and trepidation by him. At the age of twenty, he received full ordination from a lecture master.
He once traveled to Changshu, where he met the State Councilor Yan Yangzhai; the latter recognized him as a man of extraordinary talent and kept him for over a month before he departed.
At Dongta Temple in Jiaxing, he saw a monk copying the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. He knelt to observe it for a long time and sighed, saying, "For us, this alone would suffice.
He then went to Jingde Temple in Wutang and remained in seclusion behind closed doors for three years.

Upon returning to Wumen, he took leave of his teacher Jue, saying, "I shall now go forth on pilgrimage to various regions to visit and study under spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), in order to thoroughly investigate and clarify the Great Matter. Thereupon, he set out, staff in hand.
One day, he heard a monk reciting the verse by Zhang Zhuo on realizing the Way. When he reached the lines, "To sever delusive thoughts is to increase one's illness;
to advance toward True Suchness is likewise a deviation," the Master said, "That is wrong. It should say, 'Only then is there no illness; it is not a deviation.

The monk replied, "You are wrong, but he was not. The Master became deeply perplexed by this. Everywhere he went, he wrote these two phrases on the walls, his doubt persisting until it overwhelmed him.
Both [his head and face] were swollen. One day, during a meal, he suddenly attained awakening; his head and face immediately subsided.
From then on, he traveled throughout the various regions, once saying, "If I had been under Linji or Deshan, a single slap would have awakened me; what need was there for all that 'how, how'?

Later, he went to Mount Kuang and exhaustively investigated the profound meanings of the Abhidharma school. One day, after traveling twenty li, his feet ached; the Master ground his feet with a stone.
Traveling two hundred *li* per day, he finally stopped. While wandering the Five Terraces (*Wutai*), he reached a steep cliff and an empty cavern where an elderly master was sitting alone.
The Master paid his respects and asked, "What is it like before a single thought has arisen? The master held up one finger. He asked again, "What is it like after thoughts have arisen?
The master extended both hands. At these words, the Master realized the essential meaning. He followed the master's tracks, but lost him.

He traveled to the capital and visited the great master Bianrong. Bianrong asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "I have come from Jiangnan. Bianrong asked again, "For what purpose have you come here? He replied, "To study the lectures.
Bianrong asked further, "What do you mean by studying the lectures? He replied, "To penetrate the essential meaning of the scriptures and propagate the Buddha's teachings on his behalf.
Bianrong said, "You must preach the Dharma with purity. The Master replied, "Right now, I am untainted by even a single speck of dust. Bianrong then commanded him...
He stripped the Master of his formal robe and gave it to a nearby monk. Looking back at the Master, he said, "Having shed one layer, you must offer up another.

The Master accepted this with a smile. Consequently, the robe was left hanging in the stupa. The master Zen teacher Xio Yan, as well as masters such as Xian Li and other great teachers, all became his disciples.
After nine years, he returned to Tiger Hill to visit Jue, and subsequently went to Songjiang, where he remained in seclusion for a hundred days before proceeding to Wu.
In Liaoche County, Master Fu Guanzhai served as the magistrate. His son, Ligeng, requested the Master’s guidance. The son was dissatisfied.
One day, the son took two flowers in his hand and asked the Master, "Are these one or two? The Master replied, "They are one. The son opened his hand and said, "These flowers are two;
why do you say they are one? The Master said, "I speak of their root; you speak of their branches. The son—
He then performed a prostration and went to Tianchi, where he met Guan Gong Dongming. Upon hearing his words, Dongming held him in high esteem.
The Master then took a single cluster of roses with two blossoms and asked the official about them. The official said, "These flowers grow from the same root. The Master then separated them into two.
De asked Gong about this, but Gong had no words; consequently, he was fined one offering for the midday meal, and they thereafter became inseparable friends.
At that time, the third year of the Emperor’s reign, Dàqiānrùn opened the hall at Shaolin. The Master formed friendships with Cháolín, Jièrú, and others, and went there to seek instruction.
Upon his arrival, he saw the abbot ascending the hall to lecture on *gong'ān* (public cases), using oral transmission as the seal of the mind and using a silk scarf [to pass the lineage].
The disciple claimed this was the true transmission, which the Master found shameful. He sighed and said, "Is the meaning of the West's coming truly like this?
Thereupon, he withdrew from the assembly and soon returned south. Upon reaching Jiahe, he met the Grand Chancellor, Lord Lu Wutai; their minds were in great accord.
Previously, there had been one named Dao Kai of Miza, a native of Nanchang, who had abandoned his scholar’s robes to leave the household life and received tonsure at Nanhai. He heard—
The Master’s reputation spread like the wind, and people flocked to him for refuge. Recognizing that he was a vessel for the Dharma, the Master kept him as his attendant.

The Lengyan Temple in the prefectural city, where Changshui had once commented on the sutras, had long been in ruins; powerful interests had encroached upon it to convert it into a garden and pavilion. The Master composed a poem to lament this, saying: [Poem omitted per instructions]
"A single bright moon, cold outside the curtain; at night it has often shone upon those who sit in meditation.
With the desire to restore [the monastery], he entrusted Master Kai with the task of restoration and requested that the Grand Minister serve as the protector of the Dharma (*dharmapāla*).

The Grand Minister’s younger brother, Lord Yuntai, donated five bays of space to construct a Zen hall. Once it was completed, he invited the Master to inscribe a couplet for its pillars. The Master composed the following verse: "If..."
If one does not investigate the mind, sitting in meditation merely increases the suffering of karma. If one can maintain mindful protection, even reviling the Buddha benefits true cultivation.
Thereupon, he drew a needle and pricked his arm; the blood flowed until it filled a bowl, which he used for writing. From then on, he received visitors and travelers.
More than twenty years later, the Prefect Huaiting Cai Gong was finally able to restore [the temple], for this was sustained by the Master’s power of aspiration. The Master saw...
In these degenerate times, the Way of the Dharma has declined; I have made it my lifelong concern to propagate the teachings and benefit sentient beings.

Considering that the volumes of the Great Canon are so numerous and heavy, and that there are those in remote and secluded regions who will never even hear the name of the Buddha-Dharma, I wish to carve them into printed books to facilitate their circulation.
May all who see or hear them plant the seeds of the Vajra. If anyone should slander this endeavor, I shall take their transgressions upon myself.

Consequently, he deliberated with Grand Chancellor Gong, Minister of Education Feng Mengzhen, Minister of Justice Zeng Tongheng, and Director of the Court of Imperial Appointments Qu Rujì, and they reached a consensus.
They commissioned Master Kai to oversee the project. In the *Jichou* year of the Wanli era (1589), carving began at Mount Wutai.
After four years, due to the bitter cold of ice and snow, the work was moved again to Jizhao Monastery on Mount Jing. Once the labor had commenced...
[The project] proceeded. Master Kai retired due to illness. Those who subsequently completed the work were his disciple Hanhui Ruqi, Ruqi’s son Hanyu Benji, and finally his disciple Danju Kai.

Initially, Wu Gongxian of Tongcheng, serving as a Minister of Rites, entered the Master’s inner chamber and spoke leisurely regarding the matter of carving the Tripitaka. The Master replied abruptly, "You and this Dharma..."
There was a great cause for this. After the Master passed away, Lord Wu was appointed as the Governor of Zhejiang.

Following the initial proposal of Professor Feng, he restored Huacheng Monastery as a subordinate branch of Jing Shan to house the printing blocks of the Tripitaka. This was due to Lord Wu’s profound faith, but it was also because the Master had previously made a prophecy.
Having reached an agreement regarding the carving of the Tripitaka at Jiahe, the Master returned to Wumen to visit his preceptor, Master Jue.
After his awakening, Gong returned to secular life and became renowned as a physician. When he heard that the Master had arrived, he was struck with great trepidation.

The Master disguised himself as a merchant and lay prostrate in a small boat, requesting that Gong come to examine him. Upon seeing the Master, Gong was greatly alarmed. The Master wept and said, "How have you become so deluded?
What shall we do now? Gong replied, "I shall obey whatever you command. The Master immediately ordered him to shave his head and take him away.
Jue was moved by shame and wished to attend upon him as a disciple. On the day the Master arrived, Jue was having his evening meal when his rice bowl suddenly fell to the ground and shattered;
such was the power of his sincere devotion. When the Master first crossed the Wujiang River, the families of the Shen and Zhou clans gathered their kin to pay him homage.
Upon reaching Jinsha in Qu’a, the families of the He, Sun, Yu, and Wang clans likewise joined together to offer him their respectful service. The Master...
In Yuyuan Garden, he transcribed the Lotus Sūtra to repay his parents. The place where Yan transcribed the scripture is called the Ink Radiance Pavilion (Moguang Ting);

it exists there today. Hearing that Master Miaofeng had constructed an iron pagoda at Luya, he sent the scripture to be enshrined within it and consulted with him regarding the management of the treasury.
He then returned to the capital gates and visited me at Donghai in the seventh month of autumn in the Bingxu year of the Wanli era.
It is the month of Yue. Because of my connection with Mount Wutai, which had reached the inner court, I sought seclusion from fame in the Narayana Cave by the Eastern Sea.
For the protection of the Imperial Person and the prolongation of the national destiny, the Empress Dowager Cisheng commissioned the printing and distribution of fifteen sets of the Tripitaka.
The Emperor had issued an edict to all famous mountains within the realm, with the Eastern Sea being the first mentioned.

When I went to Chang’an to offer my thanks for this imperial grace, Master [Dao]xuan took Kāi with him and traveled by sea to Jiaoxi. There, the autumn waters were swollen and overflowing; everyone judged that they would certainly be unable to cross.
The Master removed his robes and waded across first, calling out urgently to the assembly. The water had already reached their shoulders, yet the Master leaped forward.
Once they had all crossed, he looked back at his disciples and said, "At the gateway of life and death, one must pass straight through to succeed. The assembly was filled with deep admiration.

While I was in Chang'an, I heard of this and hurriedly packed my belongings to return home. Traveling by double stages, I arrived at Jimo, only to find that the Master had already left the mountain and was staying at Jueyuan.

On the following morning, he was about to set out for Changfa. That night, they met once more and shared great laughter. When dawn broke, he requested to return to the mountains, staying for ten days.
Their minds were in perfect accord; the Master regarded me as one who understood his words and granted me his lifelong friendship.

Upon returning to the capital, the Master visited Shijing Mountain and paid homage at the stupa of the Sui dynasty’s Master Wan, reflecting on how Master Wan had foreseen that the three calamities would destroy the world and cause the True Dharma to fade away.
He carved the stone Tripitaka and enshrined it within a mountain cave; moved by the profound sincerity with which he protected the Dharma, his tears fell like rain.
The grounds of Master Yuan’s stupa complex had already fallen into the hands of powerful local families; he vowed to reclaim them but did not succeed.

Thereupon, he resolved to travel west to Mount Emei, proceeding through the Three Jin regions, across Guanzhong, and over the Zigzag Bridge Road to reach Shu, where he paid homage to the Great Being Samantabhadra before descending downstream.
Passing through Qutang Gorge and Jingxiang, he ascended Mount Taihe and reached Mount Kuanglu. Seeking the ruins of Guizong Monastery, he found nothing but a single ancient pine tree.
A temple monk was selling five bushels of rice, and a master carpenter intended to cut it down. A beggar, moved by pity, begged for the rice to ransom the tree.

In order to preserve the traces of the temple, the Master heard of this and was moved by a sense of inspiration. The roots of the tree had been gnawed and hacked by woodcutters' axes until they were on the verge of breaking;
the Master piled stones and filled in the earth, and through his incantations and vows, the tree grew back to life. This served as an omen for the future restoration of the temple.

Thereafter, the tree grew day by day, and the temple was eventually rebuilt. Such was the firmness of his power of aspiration. Later, Xing Moxue, a filial and upright scholar from Jiangzhou, invited the Master to reside at Changsong Pavilion. The Master...
He preached the Dharma for them; they were named Changsong Ruitui, Imperial Censor Zuerzhan, and Grand Councilor Ding Shoyuan.
They intended to remain at Mount Kuang, but as their plans did not materialize, he departed. Passing through Anqing, Mr. Ruan Zihua invited him to visit Mazu’s Hermitage on Mount Wangong.
The Master rejoiced in the site’s transcendent excellence and commissioned the construction of a Buddhist monastery there. The layman Zhao Woen from Jiangyin [also supported this endeavor].
He requested to leave the household life and subsequently shaved his head in the mountains; the Master named him Fagai (Dharmavarma), who was said to be the very last disciple.

The Master then traveled north to Tanzhe. Upon hearing that the Master had arrived, Empress Dowager Cisheng ordered her attendant Chen Ru to present offerings of vegetarian food and specifically bestowed upon him a purple *kāṣāya*. The Master firmly declined, saying, "I am ashamed that my poor bones are [unworthy of it]."

Wearing purple robes, he bestowed [the relics] upon eminent practitioners, whereby their merit was doubled. When the Confucian scholar followed his master to Yunju, he paid homage to the Stone Sutras at Leiyin Temple.
He opened the stone chamber and found beneath the Buddha’s seat a golden casket containing three śarīra relics, whose radiance illuminated the cliffs and valleys.
Consequently, he requested that the śarīra be brought into the Imperial Palace for a three-day offering. He then provided treasury gold to re-enshrine them within the stone cave.

The surplus funds from the offerings for the Saintly Mother’s fast were used to redeem the pagoda of Master Wan. He subsequently invited me to go together to pay our respects and requested that I compose a commemorative inscription.
Upon returning to my lodgings at Cishou Temple, we resided together in the garden of the Western Suburbs for forty days and nights, conversing without closing our eyes;
I truly consider this the most joyful event of my life. As Master Bianrong had already entered nirvana, I composed a text to mourn him, which includes:
Regarding the saying, "One may succeed to the lineage, but not necessarily to the Dharma": When the Master was at Tanzhe, he habitually waited until after prostrating to the Buddha before eating.
One day, a guest arrived, and the Master inadvertently ate a meal first. He then said to the administrative official (zhishi), "Today there has been a transgressor of the precepts;

I order you to administer thirty blows of the staff as a severe reprimand, or else he must make restitution. The official was startled, not knowing who had committed the offense. Shortly thereafter, the Master handed him the staff.
He prostrated himself on the ground and received his reprimand from before the Buddha exactly as prescribed. His two thighs became as black as ink, whereupon he said:

"The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of sentient beings since beginningless time are like oil mixed into flour; they are firm and cannot be broken. If one does not break their passions until they feel pain, it will not be easy to subdue them."
The Master consulted with me regarding the compilation of our dynasty’s *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).
Concerned that the Chan school was in decline, I made an agreement with the Master to travel to Caoxi in Jun to revitalize the Dharma lineage; the Master arrived first at Mount Kuang to await me.
This was the seventh month of autumn in the year of Gui-si. Three years later, in the year of Yi-mu, I presented the Tripitaka bestowed by the Holy Mother and established Haerin Temple.

It was accomplished. Due to a separate circumstance, [the Emperor] became incensed; he issued an edict for his arrest and cast him into prison. Though interrogated, [the Master] offered no further words.

By imperial grace, he was spared from death but was dispatched to garrison Lei Yang. His monastery was demolished. When the Master learned of this news at Mount Kuang, he vowed to recite one hundred volumes of the *Lotus Sūtra*, hoping that its blessings would prevent his death.
He immediately traveled back to Caoxi, intending to go to the capital to rescue me. However, he heard that I had gone south.
He was released. He then waited by the riverbank. In the eleventh month of that year, they met at Ryuhaku-an in Shaka.

The Master took my hand and sighed, saying, "You have borne the great Dharma upon your shoulders even unto death. The ancients who acted for the sake of the Dharma possessed the resolve of Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu;
what person am I compared to you? Since you do not return alive, I shall no longer have a day of birth. Thus he comforted me.
He repeated this two or three times. As he was about to depart, the Master instructed him, saying, "In the future, even after my death, the affairs of the deceased shall belong to you.
Thereupon, they parted for good. Five years after I had crossed the mountain pass, in the year Gengzi, the Emperor, due to the construction of the Three Palaces, began levying taxes on mineral mines.
An imperial commissioner was stationed at Hukou, and the Governor of Nanchang, Wu Baoxiu, impeached him in a memorial and was subsequently arrested. His wife grieved...
Wu became enraged and died by hanging himself. When the Master heard of this while at Kuangshan, he remarked, "When affairs have reached this state, what can be done about the ways of the world?

He then took up his staff and proceeded to the capital gates. Wu was in prison; the Master provided various forms of protection and bestowed upon him half a verse from the Buddha Vipaśyin, instructing him to recite it until it reached one hundred thousand times, at which point he would be released from prison.
Wu recited it to eighty thousand times when the Emperor’s favor was won and his case was resolved.
He attained the final decline. My teacher, because I had not yet returned to my original robes, often sighed, saying: "The Dharma-gate has no one left.
If we sit idly by while the banner of the Dharma collapses, then where shall those who uphold and flourish the Triple Gem direct their efforts?

He said: "If I, the old Hanzhi, do not return, it is one great failure in my mission to appear in the world; if the mining taxes are not abolished, it is another great failure in my mission to save the world."
"If the transmission of the lamp is not continued, it will be a great failure for my life of wisdom. If these three failures are avoided, I shall never again wander through the city of Rājagṛha.
In the autumn of the Gui-mao year, while I was at Caoxi, I sent a letter by messenger to my disciple Ji-xie, inviting the Master to join me in the mountains.
In his reply, he stated directly: "I shall simply cast aside this set of poor bones. Not long after, a strange letter suddenly arrived.

The news spread, shaking both the inner court and the outer world. Envious rivals took advantage of the opportunity to impeach the Master, and he ultimately met his end because of this. Previously, His Majesty—the Wheel-Turning Monarch—had out of the power of his vows revered the Great Dharma and had personally transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. By chance, sweat fell and soaked the paper; suspecting it should be replaced, he sent his close attendant, Lord Cao Zhi, to consult the Master. The Master offered this verse in response: "The Buddha’s true body is not made of flesh and bone; It is the Dharma-body, which is eternal and unchanging. If you wish to honor the Tathāgata, You need only revere the Dharma-scripture. Lord Cao returned with this verse and presented it to the Emperor. The Emperor was deeply moved and said: "The Master speaks as one who has truly realized the Way. He is indeed a great teacher of the Dharma. He then issued an imperial decree bestowing upon him the title "National Teacher" (*Guoshi*). The Master declined the honor, saying: "I am but a humble monk from the mountains. He requested the Master to preach the Dharma. The Master said, "I follow illusory conditions and exert my strength for the sake of the Great Dharma, constantly keeping the great matter of birth and death in mind.

how could one consider the mere movement of lips and tongue to be attainment? You all should encourage yourselves in this. I shall now depart. After a short while, he passed away.

He manifested a slight ailment and sat upright for three days and nights, conversing and laughing as usual. At midnight, he passed away in silence. This was the fourteenth day of the sixth month in the Ding-si year of the Wanli era.

From birth, the Master had been composed and dignified; he spoke and smiled rarely. He was strict in disciplining himself yet lenient in governing others; his majesty was awe-inspiring even without severity.
For over thirty years he preached the Dharma, and thrice expounded the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. Although he ascended the flower-adorned seat, [he remained humble].
Surrounded by ten thousand fingers [of disciples], his mind remained as if he were alone. Celestial food arrived daily, yet he remained content with coarse and simple fare.

He constantly devoted himself to contemplation of the principles, his side never touching the mat. Deeply profound and silent, even in old age he showed no sign of indolence. His disciples who received the Dharma numbered in the thousands;
those who emerged from his gate were for the most part honest and simple, devoid of superficial habits, for they were truly guided by the example of their master.

In his lectures, he grasped the essential principles and frequently introduced novel insights. When comparing the flourishing state of the Dharma seats in the north with those of previous generations, none could surpass him.

He authored works that circulate in the world, including *The Correct Contemplation of the Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, *The True Eye of the Vajracchedikā*, the *Prajñā-Prakāśatattva-Śāstra*, as well as commentaries on the *Hetuvidyā*, the *Aśvabhāva’s Commentary on the Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda Śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and the *Yongjia Collection*. The Master was born...
In the *dingwei* year of the Jiajing era, at the age of seventy-one and with a monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*) of over fifty years, his entire body was interred to the left of the Bamboo Grove.
Upon hearing of the Master’s passing, His Majesty granted treasury funds to construct a stūpa, which was inscribed with the plaque:
"Stūpa of the Incarnate Body of the Great Dharma Master Kōngyìn. Indeed, since the beginning of our dynasty, many masters of both the Chan and Exegetical schools have initiated [this tradition].
The Imperial Heart has been graced with such profound favor as has not been witnessed for two hundred years.
Is this not because the Master is an emanation of Mañjuśrī who has come forth, or perhaps the influence of Qingliang?
Among those who received ordination from the Master were seven disciples, including Wei-dong and others; those who received the Dharma were Yuan-qing and others.

There were several hundred such people, many of whom were able to transform and enlighten their respective regions. The Dharma-body is formless, yet it manifests in encounter with things; the light of Prajñā shines forth through written words. Therefore, those who uphold this sutra entrust their life of wisdom to it.
Having thoroughly realized the emptiness of nature, they speak that which is unspeakable. From India to this land, there has never been a lack of such individuals throughout the generations.
Therein lies the Cool and Refreshing [Land], where the transformation body resides in a vast chamber. The waves of the ocean of nature surge forth, and the stars of its meaning shine brilliantly.

The Dharma-realm is perfectly interfused, manifesting clearly and simultaneously. Dwelling in the Golden World and seated upon a jewel-flower throne, he extends his broad and long tongue, scattering a profusion of various flowers.
A thousand years later, the Great Master was born. His noble regulations were inherited from afar; like a lion cub, he sat loftily within his den and let out a great roar.
All beasts were struck with terror and fled at the sound. He simultaneously grasped both nature and characteristics and fully opened the precious treasury.
A single rain universally nourishes all; the three faculties respond according to their measure. His fame reached the Nine Palaces, and he was favored with profound imperial grace.

Thus, the Brahma-realm flourished and the banner of the Dharma was erected high. For more than thirty years, he taught others without weariness, employing the power of his knowledge and vision in accordance with skillful means.
He disciplined his person with rigorous austerity and withdrew his spirit into profound serenity. He turned back the wild winds of passion and returned to the essence of purity and simplicity.

Manifesting this illusory body as a model for gods and men, he was truly a Jewel of the Sangha amidst the Dharma-ending age. As the shadow of his stupa supports the void, his Dharma-body stands revealed alone.

As the wind moves and the waters flow, the perfect sound spreads everywhere. Amidst thousand-fathom cold cliffs and ten-thousand-year ice and snow, the sun and moon are inexhaustible and their radiance never ceases.

Epitaph for Chan Master Wuming Jing of Xincheng Shouchang The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is like the vast void;
it has been so from antiquity and cannot be made bright or dim by the alternation of day and night.
Only those who attain it are like those who have obtained a wish-fulfilling jewel, whose application is inexhaustible. Its inconceivable power is innate...
One is inherently complete; one receives illumination within the mind, without depending on the external. Among the patriarchs of antiquity, there were none who were not thus.

Why is it that in recent times they have become so rare? It is not that there is no Chan; it is simply that there are no teachers. If there truly were none, I have found such a person in Master Shaokang.
According to his biography, the Master’s name was Huìjīng, his style name was Wúmíng, and he was of the Pèi clan from Chōngrén, Fǔzhōu.

He was the son of [Surname], whose father was [Name] and mother [Name]. At his birth, there were complications; his grandfather recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and he was subsequently delivered.

Consequently, he was named "Jing" (Sutra). From birth, the Master was exceptionally gifted and stood apart from the crowd; his appearance was solemn and ancient, like a wild crane soaring through the air.
By nature, he was serene and free from worldly attachments. At the age of nine, when he entered the local school, he immediately asked, "What is this so-called 'vast and sublime qi'?"

His teacher regarded him as extraordinary. He lived his life as one who seemed indifferent to the affairs of the human world. At the age of seventeen, he abandoned his brush and inkstone, and with a sense of profound resolve, set his mind upon the Way.
At twenty, he entered the residence of a layman (jushi) and saw the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* on a desk;
upon reading it, he finished the entire scroll at once, rejoicing as if he had recovered a long-lost possession. He immediately spoke of his intention to the layman, who marveled at him. From this...

He renounced the consumption of pungent vegetables and alcohol, firmly resolved his intent to transcend the world, and his parents also granted him permission. When Chan Master Zhongyunkong was preaching the Dharma at Lingshan, he went there to rely upon him.
Upon inquiry, the master’s original name was revealed as Huijing. He attended upon him for three years; regarding all that he heard taught, he followed it without deviation, as if he were a fool.
He once harbored doubts concerning the four-line verse of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. One day, he saw the Great Master Fu.

The verse says: "If one discusses even a single four-line stanza, it should never leave one's person. Upon hearing this, his teacher was moved to a state of profound realization and composed a verse containing the line:
"Light radiates throughout the entire realm. From this, it is known that his prior habituation to Prajñā had been awakened.

At the age of twenty-four, one day while perusing the Tripiṭaka, he reached the "Chapter on the Eye of the School" (Zongyan pin) and only then learned of the "separate transmission outside the teachings."

Regarding the intent of the *Chuan* (Biographies), I harbored doubts concerning the distinctions between the Five Houses. For eight months, I was mired in confusion and perplexity, as if I had lost all capacity for hearing and seeing;
at times, I even considered it a case of delusion. After a long while, I attained a realization and developed a resolute will to investigate the truth.

Consequently, I took my leave of Lingshan, intending to go into seclusion. I then visited E-feng, where I found the groves and valleys secluded and profound; there I cleared away the brush to build a dwelling and vowed not to [leave].
He resolved that he would not descend from this mountain until he had clarified this great matter. After three years had passed, no one knew of his purpose.

While reading the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), he came across a monk asking Xingshan, "What is the Way? to which Xingshan replied, "A truly fine mountain. The Master was at a loss;

a state of profound doubt suddenly arose within him. Day and night he maintained this inquiry, forgetting even to sleep or eat. One day, while moving a stone, it proved so heavy that it could not be lifted despite his utmost effort.

As he pushed his inquiry further, he attained a sudden and great awakening. He immediately composed a verse, saying: "If you wish to study the Way of Unsurpassed Bodhi, Hurry to clear and open the Great Good Mountain.
Only upon knowing the Way do you realize the mountain is not good; Turning your body around, you leap out through the Patriarchs' Barrier.

He presented this to Namsan, who recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma. The Master had been frail since birth, barely able to wear a robe; yet once he took up residence on the mountain, he became exceptionally robust.
He applied himself with diligent effort. He personally engaged in cultivation, quarrying stone to clear fields, undaunted by toil and hardship, unconcerned with his physical appearance.

Whenever he heard the sounds of clamor in the midst of the empty mountains, he would say, "An old monk does not gather what is inexhaustible. Thus, he lived without closing his door; he would walk alone through the mountains at night.
At the age of twenty-seven, before he had yet shaved his head, someone urged him to do so. The Master replied, "I shall wait until I have attained the status of a monk (*śramaṇa*)."
The circumstances were such that it was only at this point that he finally shaved his head, donned the dyed robes, and received full ordination.
For twenty-four years, he remained in the mountains without venturing forth, as if a single day had passed. Baofang in the district was the former monastery of Chan Master Songshi Bao;
he was invited to restore it and thus accepted the summons. First, he went to Lingshan to sweep the master’s stupa before proceeding there. In a mere instant, thirty years had elapsed.
He forgot the words of his journey’s beginning. At that time, the Master was fifty-one years old; it was the Wuli Xushen year (1618).
While residing at Baofang, the Master increased his power of diligence day by day. In all matters requiring effort, he always took the lead with his own person.

His body became withered and skeletal, yet he never grew weary of his labor. Within a few years, hundreds of walls were renovated anew, several acres of fields were reclaimed, and the Buddha Hall and the three gates were restored.
The hall and kitchen were fully equipped. Monastics from the four quarters who heard of his reputation arrived day by day.

A monk asked the Master, "Since residing on this mountain, whom have you ever met? The Master replied, "I have not yet traveled anywhere. The monk prodded him, saying, "How can one view the world as small from a single corner?
The Master appreciated these words and subsequently took up his staff to travel afar, eventually crossing the South Sea to visit...
From Yunqi, he returned to the Central Plains and entered Shaolin, where he paid homage at the stupa of the First Patriarch and inquired about the meaning of the single transmission from the West.
He subsequently traveled to the capital to visit Chan Master Daguan, who held him in high esteem. He then went to Mount Wutai to study under Master Duanfeng;

although the Master’s gate was austere and formidable, the Teacher attained resonance with him upon their first meeting. He then requested further instruction, saying: "I, this humble one, regarding the ancient masters..."
"Regarding these several koans, I have doubts. I beg the Master for instruction. Feng said, "Please speak.
The Master said, "Linji said, 'Buddha-dharma is not much. Ultimately, what is it? Feng said, "You say it is 'not much'; yet, what is it?
The Master said, "Xuansha said to Lingyun, 'I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the bottom. Where is he [at fault]?"

Regarding the point where he had not yet reached full penetration, Feng said, "In fact, Xuansha himself had not reached full penetration. The Master asked, "Zhaozhou said, 'The old woman at Mount Tai—I have seen through her for you.
Where exactly did he see through her? Feng said, "It was actually the old woman who saw through Zhaozhou.
The Master requested further instruction, to which Feng replied, "When you know it is a matter such as this, simply let it be. The Master bowed and they subsequently became companions.

Regarding the mudrās, Feng asked a series of challenging questions, and the masters each answered with verses; these words are recorded in a separate document. At the end, Zhaozhou’s verse says: "The spring colors are hidden in the dark;

the autumn light is revealed in the bright. Though one has eyes, they cannot discern it; though one employs wisdom, it is difficult to measure. Having reached home, one does not ascend the road to Chang'an;
let the wind, flowers, snow, and moon rise as they will. Feng deeply approved of this, observing that the Master’s words avoided total completion.

The pivot of the teaching lies in its mutual interplay; its subtlety perfectly accords with the five ranks. Thus, it is known that the spiritual style of the Dongshan school will surely flourish from this point forward.
From then on, the Master grew weary of his travels and returned his staff to Baofang, where he first opened the hall to preach the Dharma.

He appointed Master Lai of Boshan as his First Seat; teacher and disciple were in elegant accord, sounding the bellows of this Way and vigorously upholding the fundamental tenets for the patch-robed monks from all quarters.

Those who came to him upon hearing the news increased by the day. On the wu-shen day, the Shouchang Monastery in the district—which had been founded by the Indian Master Zhuxian—had long been in ruins.
The community requested that the Master reside there. According to an old tradition, there was a prophecy concerning this; the Master shared the same hometown and the same surname as Zhuxian.
Everyone considered the Master to be a second incarnation of Zhu Fashen. While residing at Shouchang, he did not seek external support nor solicit patrons for fundraising;
he simply acted according to circumstances as required. Within a few years, expenditures reached tens of thousands, yet the adornments of the monastery became brilliantly magnificent.
Everything suitable for a monastic community was provided in its entirety; within less than ten years, he was surrounded by a thousand disciples.
Could this not have been brought about through the Master’s power of wondrous non-action? Indeed, from birth, the Master was endowed with a straightforward nature;

his temperament was gentle yet his will was firm, his mind harmonious yet his conduct rigorous. Although he did not cultivate outward formalities, his demeanor was dignified and solemn, like the addition of a harsh frost.

He was majestic without being angry; upon seeing him, even seasoned monks lost their composure. Furthermore, he skillfully guided others according to their capacities, so that each attained what was appropriate for them.
Whenever he encountered a sick monk, he would invariably prepare his medicine and food himself. Upon a monk’s passing, he would personally carry the firewood for the cremation.

Regarding all matters within the monastic community, whether great or small, he applied his mind with thoroughness; without needing consultation, his actions accorded with the proper measure. He made no distinction between the pure and the impure, always exerting his full strength and heart.

He acted accordingly; his inner spirit was vast and serene, as if his ears and eyes perceived nothing at all. Even upon reaching seventy years of age, he still mingled with the common laborers, never ceasing his plowing and digging.
He would always leave before others and return after them, personally leading the way in clearing fields.

The annual income from his three monasteries could support three hundred monks; thus, throughout his life, his engagement with the Buddha-dharma never departed from the side of the mattock. For over forty years, he had...
There was not a single moment when he sought ease for himself. Even when presiding over vast assemblies, he never assumed the airs of a teacher.

As for his social interactions, his verses, recitations, and Dharma discourses flowed like a river and surged like clouds; truly, this was what is called the radiance of Prajñā, responding without thought, like a mani jewel shining in perfect clarity.
Although the various elders who have transmitted the lamp since antiquity each possessed unimpeded understanding, [he surpassed them all].
Among those who have not grown weary of ten thousand practices, there is but the single individual Yongming. Yet even he did not reach the master’s coarseness [of endurance].
One such as the Master may be said to have had his Way accord with the single transmission and his mind harmonize with the myriad dharmas; how could he not exert such vigorous and diligent effort?
King Yi, drawn to the Master’s virtue and conduct, praised him deeply and remarked: "The time since the Sage departed is remote; it is fortunate that this old man has been left behind."

His work was esteemed in such a manner. On the seventh day of the twelfth month of the Ding-si year, returning from the fields, he said to the assembly, "From this point forward, I shall no longer lay stones.
The assembly was astonished. On the eve of the New Year, he ascended the hall and said, "This is the only time remaining this year.
Let me ask you all: do you know it or not? His admonitions were earnest and repeated; he concluded by saying, "This is the final instruction of this old monk."

This final word was entrusted to the assembly; you must all cherish it with utmost care. On the third day of the New Year in the year Wu-wu, he manifested a slight ailment and consequently ceased eating, saying, "I am not ill;
it is time for me to depart. The assembly surrounded him in attendance, yet they were as joyful as if it were their usual state.
The assembly was unsettled. He addressed them with a verse, saying: "In the life of man there are experiences that are not requitals; do not be distressed by old age, sickness, and death.
On the seventh day, he presented a verse to Boshan, in which he sequentially recorded the "Precious Methods" and the final testament of Shouchang.

He then said: "The ancients protected and cherished the communal property (sangha-āraṃbha) as their own life-force. This old monk does not spare his life-force for the sake of securing the communal property. On the fourteenth day...
He wrote letters to monastics and laypeople far and near, urging them all to strive forward on the Path. On the fifteenth day, Xiao Xiaolian of Jishui came to pay his respects;

the Master gave him instruction, telling him simply to contemplate "the myriad dharmas returning to the One," and exhorted him to investigate this with diligent effort. On the sixteenth day, he entrusted the arrangements for his cremation.
He himself composed a verse for the lighting of the pyre and commanded his attendant, Chezong, to chant the verse while the fire was lit. The following morning, he took water to rinse his mouth.
He washed his face and wiped his body, then instructed them, saying, "There is no need for further bathing; it would merely waste the monastery's resources for water and firewood.

He admonished the assembly, "Do not follow worldly customs by feigning mourning. Those who do so are not my disciples. He then took up a brush and wrote in large characters: "Today I have clearly pointed the way.
Having cast down the brush, he sat upright and passed away on the seventeenth day of the first month in the Wumu year of the Wanli era, at the hour of Wei.
Furthermore, when his body was cremated, the flames were of five colors; the heart-flame was like a lotus flower, its fine petals resembling bamboo leaves.
His cranial bone and teeth remained unburnt; the rest were as white as jade, heavy as gold, and marked with five-colored patterns.

He was buried at [Location], and a stūpa was erected there. The Master was born in the Wushen year of the Jiajing era; his worldly lifespan was seventy-one years, and his monastic seniority was forty years.
He was extraordinary. He had several disciples who attained the Dharma; their leader was Yuanlai, who now propagates the Dharma at Boshan.
The others maintain the permanent residence at the Three Mountains. There are three volumes of his recorded sayings (*yulu*). Long ago I heard of the Master’s reputation.

In the year Bingchen, while seeking refuge from the summer heat on Mount Kuang, a disciple brought me a portrait of the Master in the *yuanxiang* (circle) style. Upon unrolling it, I immediately recognized that the Master belonged to the "beyond-the-pattern" (*gewai*) tradition.

I regretted that I had not lived long enough to meet him in person, and thus composed a eulogy for him. It contained such lines as, "A towering, magnificent mountain emerges, visible from afar across a thousand li.
When Boshan saw it, he took me to be one who deeply understood the Master within our Dharma lineage;

he then provided a detailed account of the Master’s life and requested that I write an inscription for his stupa. I lamented with deep sorrow the desolation of the Chan school, which had never before witnessed such a state.

Regarding this "arousing [the dharma]": the lion’s string was on the verge of snapping its final note. Now, as for the Master’s conduct: his realization is stable and profound, and his skillful discernment is sovereign.

Not only is his Dharma-eye perfectly clear, reviving the collapsed纲 (gāng, "guiding principles"), but his austere integrity and solitary style are truly sufficient to stir the customs of the degenerate age.
As for his great diligence and power of endurance, one must seek them among the ancients; even in his shadow...

Without leaving the mountain, his reputation and brilliance reached afar; was this not what is meant by "dwelling in stillness like a corpse yet appearing like a dragon," or "silent as a deep pool yet sounding like thunder"?
Observing how clearly he illuminated the nature of birth and death, his practical realization can be known. Therefore, I shall arrange his actual deeds in order and compose an inscription for him.
The Inscription reads:

The Great Way is vast and open, like the great void of space. The illusory leaves of sages and ordinary beings cast their shadows therein. Yet, though one seeks them, they are ultimately unobtainable;
to deliberate or reflect upon them is like rowing a boat or wielding a staff to strike at the moon. Gautama was frantic with feverish agitation; Bodhidharma came in haste.
In the end, it results in nothing but a single leather shoe. Jian strikes the drum of lethal poison, fully manifesting the true command.

Should anyone strike it, they shall lose their body and forfeit their life; for those who do not value their lives, he strikes once when the time comes, leaving them deaf for three days—a thunderclap in the clear sky.
Body and mind were shattered together; the traces of both Mara and Buddha vanished. The light of the mani-jewel shone forth, penetrating through all eight directions with empty clarity.
Only I, Shouchang, mistakenly fell under its influence; from every pore of my body, samadhi emerged and dissolved, transforming the cave of birth and death into a mass of radiant light.
In daily life, at every turn, there is nowhere that is not so. Raising the hoe is like wielding a vajra sword; amidst the dense forest of afflictions, Buddhas and patriarchs appear.
For over forty years, I have tilled the soil and dug the earth, yet the rubble and thorns are entirely paved with the seven treasures.
The world of body and mind is shattered into fine dust; in every particle of dust lies a Buddha-land where one sits, reclines, or walks.
Setting aside the Buddhadharma and the Way of Chan, when someone comes to inquire, point directly to what is before them, like a great round mirror upon which the five colors arrive all at once.
Neither emerging nor entering, they sport within birth and death; yet they fall into it themselves and do not abide eternally in the world. They act right now, and yet have never departed.
Do not believe me—just look! Among blades of grass, weeds, and even the finest specks of dust, what single thing is not this entire body?
The shadow of the stupa against the green mountains; the long tongue of the pines and wind—these sounds of the Dharma discourse never cease for a moment.
This is the inscription for the stupa of Master Wugou Lian of Jiuhua Mountain.
His name was Xinglian, and his courtesy name was Wugou. He was the son of the Wang family of Xianyuan in Taiping. From birth he was extraordinary; in his youth, he delighted in...

He performed the work of a Buddha. From an early age, he harbored the aspiration for world-transcendence. When the Buddha-dharma had not yet spread to that region, various non-Buddhist practitioners gathered there to propagate their doctrines.
The Master would frequently go to observe and listen to them. One day, he said to the crowd, "These are but the ravings of dreams;
what can they do against birth and death? Thereupon, he resolved to leave the secular life. At the age of twenty-two, he abandoned his wife and children and dissolved his household.

He dispersed his possessions and departed for Qixia Temple on Mount She in Jinling. There, he received the tonsure and full ordination under the Dharma Master Suanan Jie and resided within the lecture halls.
He studied the meanings of various sūtras and śāstras; however, as he closed his scrolls, he sighed, saying, "I left the household life for the sake of the great matter of birth and death.
Can this truly resolve that great matter? He then abandoned them and departed. He subsequently obtained [the teachings of] Niu from his hometown.
At Mount Tou, he cleared away the weeds to rest and practiced "sword-plowing and fire-seeding," focusing his thoughts exclusively on the matter of his own person.
After a long time, however, he had made no progress and eventually abandoned that life. He traveled to Qinghe to visit Master Fatang, who transmitted to him the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation;
he then entered into it with deep faith. Subsequently, he went to the capital to attend upon the elder Bianrong, who, upon seeing him once, recognized his potential and took him under his care.
He remained in seclusion for a long time. Later, when Master Miaofeng was expounding the Dharma at Luya, the Master went specifically to visit him and underwent great refinement under his guidance.

He then returned to his hometown at Dayuan Mountain, where monastics and laypeople from all quarters came upon hearing of his reputation, exclaiming: [...]* *Note: The original text contains an ellipsis indicating that the quote continues beyond the provided fragment.*
"I am one who has left the household life. How could I, for the sake of a few drops of water or a flowing wave, use a blade of reed to obstruct this entire lifetime?

He again abandoned his search and vowed to travel through all famous mountains, to visit and study under virtuous teachers (kalyāṇamitra), and to journey extensively in many directions, undergoing every kind of hardship.
Thus he spent seven years. Once, while crossing a river in winter, the ice cracked with a sound; he fell into the water, and the cold pierced him to the marrow. Suddenly, there appeared—
He pondered this and said: "The eyebrows have always been horizontal; the nose has always been straight. To drink when thirsty and to eat when hungry—what else is there?
Thereupon, the doubts of his entire life dissolved like ice melting. He immediately returned to settle at Shanshan in Chiyang, where monks from the ten directions arrived day by day.
He subsequently established a Buddhist monastery, making the reception of guests his primary concern; those who came were for no other purpose.

His skills were limited to the meticulous preparation of gruel, rice, tea, and soup; he possessed no realization of Chan or the Buddha-dharma. Yet, those who observed him believed him with absolute conviction and without doubt.

At the sacred site of Jiuhua, the ground of the Path, they welcomed the Master to serve as the head of the monastery. He disciplined himself with rigorous austerity and sacrificed his own comfort for the sake of the community.
Whenever he sought to transform those of ill-nature, he invariably employed skillful means through humble prostrations and deferential conduct, even enduring their insults and abuse.
He would certainly wait until great faith was established before ceasing his practice. People of the time called him "Never-Disparaging" (Chángbùqīng).

For nearly twenty years, monastics and laypeople alike from far and near turned toward him with devotion as if he were a Buddha or a Patriarch. Consequently, for whatever necessities he required, he never once sent out a monk to the streets as a solicitor for alms.
Responding to the times like an echo, wherever his footprints reached— whether at a place where he ate a single meal or stayed for a single night—
all became sites of the Way (bodhimaṇḍas). These included Shanshan on Chiyang, Jingangfeng on Jiuhua,
Jintang on Guanyinshan, Ca’ān on Dàshān, the quiet chamber on Liánlǐng, Huashān on Jīnlíng, and others such as Qīntóufēng and Pósuō.

At Long, Cenfengdong, and Baisha Mountain, as well as at the various auspicious celestial sites, dozens of *āraṇyakas* (hermitages) were established in each location for those who practice seclusion and tranquility to reside in.
Each has its own disciples who maintain these establishments; is this not truly forgetting oneself for the sake of others?

Is it not that transformation is accomplished without deliberate intent? In the second month of the middle spring of the Bingshen year, at the request of the assembly, he went to Mount Xuan of the Third Patriarch.
Within a few months, all neglected matters were restored, and the influence of his virtue stirred both far and near. He returned once more to Jiuhua.
The following year, the fourfold assembly of Mount Xuan earnestly requested him to depart. He nodded his head and said, "If I must go, then I shall go; however, it is still necessary for three..."

On that day, he happened to pass through Kowloon the following morning and visited a hermitage master. Looking around with joy, he said to the assembly, "My great task is finished upon reaching this mountain.
The assembly did not understand his meaning. Two days later, he manifested a slight illness and passed away there.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the right of the *ārāma* on the third day of the ninth month of the Dingyou year of the Wanli era. This is the Master’s birth [and passing].

On the eighth day of the fourth month in the Jiachen year, at the age of fifty-four and with twenty-five years of monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vaṣa), his public disciples were very numerous, each taking charge of their respective monasteries.
As for his lay followers (upāsaka), those who came to seek the Buddha-dharma...
Only Shao Jigong’s brothers, Cha Ruding and Xiao Bogu, were in perfect harmony with one another, forming a bond of life and death beyond the mundane world.
Less than a month after Gong passed away, Ruding hurried to Lingnan to visit me amidst my travels, bringing Gong’s biographical record and requesting that I compose an inscription for it.
As I read it over and over again, I was moved by Gong’s integrity and self-possession; he may truly be said to have been consummate in his self-effacement.
Thus, the inscription says:

To forget one's own body for the sake of others is like insects gnawing at wood; to regard others as oneself is like water not washing water. When both self and other are forgotten, [true non-action is realized].
He does not encounter the sharp edge of calamity. The stone man dances by day; the golden sun shines by night. As for the Master’s person, it drifts like a passing cloud;
as for the Master’s mind, it rests like the spirit of the valley. Neither coming nor going—who dies and who lives? The Nine Flowers reach toward heaven.
The onlookers are deaf; Mount Wan strikes against the Han River. The listeners are blind; a solitary pagoda stands tall, towering above the void.
To seek the Master’s path, ask the Nine Peaks.
Epitaph for Master Zhu of Xiexiang Yingzhai.

Since the founding of Mount She by Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, it flourished during the Tang era. In the past, many renowned virtuous masters preached the Dharma there, but it has long been in a state of ruin and desolation.
During the Jiajing period, Lord Lu of Wutai, upon beholding the site, was filled with solemn resolve; he commissioned the Sangha Superintendent to request the former Yun... [text continues].
Master Gu practiced meditation therein. Master Shan of Mount Song restored the temple, inviting Dharma Master Suan-an to extensively open the seat of the Dharma.
Scholars from throughout the realm gathered like clouds at that time; among his disciples were several dozen, the foremost of whom was Master Zhu of Yingzhai.
Master Zhu was the son of the Li family of Anlu; he was exceptionally gifted from birth. His father, Jing...
He served the Three Jewels. When Gong was young, he accompanied his father to a temple and was moved by hearing a monk reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
He subsequently requested to leave the household life and took Master Yue of the district as his preceptor. After serving him for several years, he developed a desire to travel far and so departed.
He went to Qixia in Jinling, where he received full ordination from Dharma Master Xi, a disciple of Suanan.

He listened to lectures on various sutras and treatises, exhausting the fundamental tenets of both the Nature (Xing) and Characteristics (Xiang) schools. For fifteen years, he applied himself with a focused mind to the teachings and contemplative practice.

One day, he questioned his master regarding the meaning of the "Special Transmission Outside the Teachings. The master replied, "This is a matter of the higher realm; it possesses its own lineage of transmission. As for Elder Huanyou..."

"The rightful master of the Dharma is at Shaolin; you should go there to consult him. The Master (Dongshan) then went to Shaoshi to see Xiu. He immediately asked, "What is the matter that transcends [the ordinary]? Xiu replied, "The moon atop Wuru Peak; the lamp within the Hall of Single Transmission. Dongshan did not yet attain realization, so he requested to be enrolled as a resident monk. After long training with the assembly, he entered the master's room.

One day, while discussing the public case of Shishuang, he attained awakening and presented this verse: The moon atop Wuru Peak, The lamp within the Hall of Single Transmission— I have now seen it clearly, And my former doubts are all gone. Xiu said, "You have finally arrived. Dongshan bowed. Later, when he returned to his own mountain, he visited Xiu again. Xiu asked, "How is it now? Dongshan replied, "The moon atop Wuru Peak; the lamp within the Hall of Single Transmission. Xiu said, "This is the same as before. Dongshan said, "Before, I was like a man facing a wall; now, I am like a man facing a mirror. Xiu said, "Though you have attained it, you must not forget to protect it. Dongshan bowed and departed. He then composed a verse:

The moon atop Wuru Peak, The lamp within the Hall of Single Transmission— Before, I was like a man facing a wall; Now, I am like a man facing a mirror. Xiu said, "You have truly attained it. Dongshan bowed and left. He returned to his own mountain and lived out his life there. His disciples numbered over a thousand. At the age of eighty-four, he passed away. He was posthumously titled Chanshi. His stupa was named "Jingzhuang" (Pure Adornment). His dharma heirs included Fayan Wenyi, Yunmen Wenyan, and others. His teachings were widely propagated throughout the world. Thus ends the record of National Teacher Dongshan Liangjie.
It is said: "Stepping out the gate, it is all weeds. In the cold forest, flowers bloom; spring returns early.

How laughable that those who lack feet understand how to walk, yet they take Mount Sumeru and trample it sideways. Cease! That single phrase before sound is wondrously harmonized in hidden penetration. The true wind beyond kalpas is profound, subtle, and dense.
This is the matter of hand-to-hand transmission from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old; it is not something reachable by the calculating intellect or the conscious mind.
Furthermore, it is not a path that can be traversed by the profound; you must not propagate it according to worldly conventions. The Duke paid his respects.

Having served in these duties for four years, he returned once more to Qixia. From then on, his mind no longer engaged with external conditions and his traces did not enter the secular world; day and night he practiced with refined diligence.

With single-minded devotion and without slackening, and for one day without illness, he requested a bath, changed his robes, and passed away with solemn composure on the [day], [month], and [year] of the Wanli era.
His worldly lifespan was approximately [number] years; his dharma-ordination age was [number] summers; he had [number] disciples who received ordination under him;
and his entire body was enshrined in a stupa at a certain location on the mountain. When I was young, I served Great Master Yungu, and every...

Passing through Xiqia, he admired Master Gong’s rugged and imposing physical presence and knew him to be a vessel for the Dharma. In the end, he did not fail his lifelong aspirations and attained the ultimate core of the Way.
How could such a person be spoken of on the same level as those who, bound by ordinary scholarly learning, remain shackled to birth and death?
Thereupon, he inscribed this eulogy:

"The quintessence of mountains and rivers has manifested here as human culture; the subtle pulse of the Way flows on, like clouds gathering and rushing into the valley. This is the spiritual power of this monastery."

The wondrous essence had long been accumulated; then there appeared a man of wisdom who pierced through a single aperture. The transformation of the Dharma thus became manifest, and the profound breeze fanned out daily.

Just then, Master Zhu was born, his lofty character as brilliant as rosy clouds. A dragon of meaning within the ocean of teachings, a divine colt of the ancestral school, he could gallop a thousand li with a single glance.

Swift as a flash of lightning and galloping like a shooting star, he grasped the supreme talisman and held aloft the banner of truth. Concealing his brilliance and veiling his light, he penetrated deeply into the boundless.

Embracing the Way and concentrating his spirit amidst the azure crags and verdant cliffs, he passed away while seated; his solitary radiance blazed forth, and the shadow of his stupa now supports the void.
The true wind wafts and fans; the Dharmakāya stands majestic and imposing. Amidst clouds and mists appearing and vanishing, this is the Stele Inscription for Dharma Master Yexi.
His name was Zhìruò, with the courtesy name Yexi. He was the son of the Yao clan of Shanyin; his mother was of the Yan clan. Initially, she prayed to the White-Robed Avalokiteśvara...
Yin. Once, while dreaming, he was told by a dhūta who was washing his feet, "I shall become your lion cub. Upon waking, he became pregnant; when born, he possessed sharp faculties.
From childhood, he delighted in sitting cross-legged and reciting the Buddha’s name. His father died early, and his mother remained a widow. When he was just seven years old, his mother fell ill.

He wept in sorrow day and night. When his mother was at the point of death, she entrusted him with these words: "You have been a monk since your youth; do not fail your original vow. Having spoken, she passed away.
In accordance with his mother’s final instructions, the Master sought out Venerable Xian of Huayan Temple in Kuaiji to receive the precepts and leave the household life.

At the age of seventeen, he first shaved his head and donned the robes. Constantly reflecting deeply on the great matter of birth and death, he went to Niutou Mountain to resolve to practice under a teacher.
After some time, he followed Dharma Master Jingshan to Mount Tiantai to hear the *Lotus Sūtra*.
He then withdrew into the mountains, where he applied himself with resolute effort for six years in solitary retreat. One day, upon encountering a particular circumstance, he attained a realization.

At the age of twenty-six, hearing that Master Xuelang En had begun preaching the Dharma in the Southern Capital (Nanjing), he set out carrying his water gourd and staff. First, he studied under Dharma Master Su’an at Qixia.

He received full ordination and subsequently became a disciple under Xuelang. He pursued his studies for twelve years, exhaustively investigating various sutras and śāstras until he attained profound mastery of their subtle mysteries.
In the Jichou year of the Wanli era (1589), Shen Sima and Yue Shuibu established the Huihuā Ān in Zhuili and invited the Master to reside there.
In the Gengyin year (1590), when the Master was thirty-six years old, Lu Taizai Wutai and Guan Qianxian Dongming [also joined him].
Liu Zushi Ziwei requested that he lecture on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in Wumen. In the year Renchen, he lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* at Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou;
the following year, he lectured on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* at Jingci Temple. In the year Rentyin, he took up residence at the northern foot of Feilai Peak in Wulin.
There was the site of the former Yongfu Temple, which had been abandoned and absorbed into private dwellings; Pan Taichang redeemed the land and constructed a Buddha hall and a Chan meditation hall.
He established a hermitage there. Throughout the three Wu regions and two Zhe provinces, all followed his teachings;
wherever he was, he opened and expounded various sutras and śāstras at more than thirty locations, convening over fifty sessions.
He is thus called a master of the age. I and Xuelang were brothers of the same school; when my venerable brother opened the Dharma in the Southern Capital, the Master was his foremost disciple. I...
I have heard of his early realization for many years. In the year Ding-si, while on my way to Shuangjing due to certain karmic conditions, I passed through Wumen and met Master Gong at Ruyi.
Beholding his weathered, skeletal countenance of one on the Way, I rejoiced that the Dharma-gate still possessed its traditional standards of conduct. When Master Gong returned, I...
I went to offer my condolences at Yunqi. Upon arriving in Wulin on the ninth day of the month, the Master had already manifested slight illness. He wrote a letter to me by hand, saying:
"My original intention was to follow the Great Master back [to the Pure Land]. Now I am about to depart for eternity; I cannot wait any longer. He then instructed his disciples, saying:
"I shall reserve this final offering and surely present it to him. The next day, he requested a bath; he rose, changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away.

Alas! Master Gong possessed innate wisdom from birth; he left the household life in his youth and immediately resolved to pursue the supreme goal. Upon attaining enlightenment, he made further breakthroughs.
Exhausting the depths of the scriptural teachings, he served as a teacher for humans and devas; was this not indeed due to the power of his vows?

Throughout his life, he maintained his integrity with self-restraint, remaining untainted amidst worldly affairs. Possessing nothing beyond his three robes, he passed away with a sense of liberation, free from all attachments.
This was because his roots in Prajñā were deep, making him difficult for others to discern. Alas, I, an old and decrepit man, have admired the Master for over thirty years.
