On one hand, he did not forget [his resolve] even at the very end; was this not due to past karmic conditions? Thus, I have related the general outline of the Master’s conduct and composed for him this inscription, saying:
"Birth and death are as firmly bound that none escape their entanglement; how is it that you, O Master, regard them with such utter detachment? By means of the seed of Prajñā..."

Through the continuous perfuming of successive births, one proceeds through past and future lives without exerting any effort at all. Like the moon of precepts, the flower of compassion, the cloud of loving-kindness, and the rain of Dharma, one benefits oneself and others, remaining pure and free from the slightest defilement.
In profound accord with the Buddha-mind, one extends the broad and long tongue; when the sound of the Dharma reaches the ears, it transforms all who hear.

The retribution for his merit shall endure through many kalpas. Alas for the age of the Dharma’s decay! You, sir, stand as a banner of the Dharma; may you long remain in this world, so that demons and heretics may naturally submit.
Amidst the coming and going of birth and death, the Dharma-body is quiescent and extinguished; you, sir, are truly serene—this is true liberation. Your stupa rests upon a solitary peak.
The sound of pines never ceases; day and night, the perfect sound resounds, constantly preaching with fervor.
This is the Stele Inscription for the Founder and First Abbot of Yunzhong Puxing Chan Monastery, Master Gujing Xuan.
The sun and moon adorn the heavens, bringing benefit even to those born blind; spring returns to the great earth, and warmth arises in the secluded valleys.
Thus, the Dharmakāya of our Buddha, the World-Honored One, pervades all; every sentient being possesses it fully.

Even those in remote borderlands or the Mleccha tribes, provided they encounter the necessary conditions, are all led to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, where their foul and impure realms are transformed into a Pure Land. This is so.
It depends entirely on the merit of one’s transformative enlightenment. I am deeply moved by Master Hyun-gong. His name was Uisang;
his pen-name was Gogeum (The Ancient Mirror). He was the son of Ja of the Yunjung clan; his father was Lin and his mother was Lady Yi. He possessed extraordinary signs at birth.

In his youth, he grew weary of worldly life and took refuge under Monk Dingsheng of the local monastery, vowing to pursue the supreme path. Later, he bid farewell to his teacher and set out upon his travels. At first—

He arrived at the capital and received full ordination (*upasampadā*) at the Wanshou Precept Platform. He traveled extensively to pay homage at famous mountains throughout the realm and visited various spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*) to resolve matters concerning his own practice.
Having attained certain insights, he reflected that his merit and wisdom were not yet perfected and his cultivation and conduct incomplete;

thus, in middle age, he returned to his hometown to perform extensive Buddhist services. He established karmic conditions for providing meals to the Sangha beyond counting and commissioned the creation of gilded [images].
He fashioned images to adorn the Buddha-lands; he painted scenes of the waters and lands to deliver those in the dark realms of the netherworld; he constructed bridges to aid those crossing over;
and he erected stūpas to mark the way for humans and devas. He knelt and recited the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha* mantra three hundred and sixty thousand times to support his pure karma.

In all matters of benefit, he applied his whole heart and exerted every effort to guide and profit many people. Consequently, the fourfold assembly took refuge in him, and kings and ministers looked up to him with reverence.
Even among those in the borderlands and remote regions pressed by barbarian incursions—whose people were fierce and violent—he transformed them through his teaching.
To transform the mechanism of slaughter into the seeds of goodness—is this not precisely what one does when manifesting in the body of a bhikṣu to preach the Dharma?

Your Excellency possesses a robust physique and a gentle nature; those who see you rejoice in your teachings and follow you like a shadow. You have thoroughly mastered both Buddhist scriptures and secular classics;

your learning is vast and your conduct is lofty. Thus, you were moved by the Prince of the State of Dai, who honored you with reverence for three generations, as did the Princes of Jiyang, Duanhui, and others.
He served as their external protector and established the Puxing Chan Monastery, subsequently becoming its founding first abbot.
The Master was born in the Dinghai year of the Jiajing era and entered parinirvāṇa in the Yisi year of the Wanli era; he reached an earthly age of eighty and a monastic seniority of over forty years.
His stupa is located outside the outskirts of Yunzhong. In the month of the winter solstice during the Bingchen year, I went to pay my respects to the Elder Zibo.
At Shuangjing, the old friend from Longhua, Master Yue Qingtan, dispatched a letter and presented a formal petition requesting an inscription for him.
I have therefore composed this inscription, which says:

“The Dharma-body is all-pervasive, reaching everywhere without exception; like the moon appearing in water, it flows equally through both the clear and the turbid. Therefore, for all sentient beings...”
All sentient beings possess [this nature]. Although good and evil differ, their fundamental nature is non-dual. The mechanism for transformation depends upon skillful guidance.

When water is poured into water, that which was not wondrous becomes wondrous of itself. Therefore, the Perfected One manifests in every place; yet if there is no karmic affinity, [the teaching will not take root].
It cannot be seen face-to-face. Yet, if its wondrous function enters the minds of sentient beings, it is like the moon reflected in water—becoming ever clearer and ever deeper.

If one can transform through goodness, one may turn the mechanism of their murderous intent. Because it is devoid of self, those who know it are rare; it is like the sun shining at the center of the sky.
Spring returns to the great earth; when the time comes, it is present everywhere. Your Eminence manifests through conditions and perishes through conditions;
birth, death, coming, and going are ultimately ineffable. The pagoda spire reaches into the void, and the Dharma-body dwells eternally. Thus we know, O Great Master:
The true mechanism is uniquely revealed.

The Imperially Bestowed Stele Inscription for Chan Master Da Fang Qian of Longgang Temple, as recorded in the *Chanzong Chuandeng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp of the Chan School), is entirely based on the five houses [of Chan]. The length of their dharma lineages varies, and their systems are not uniform. Since [the beginning],...
The late Master Xueting was the proclaimer of the Dōngshàng (Cave-Mountain) school, which had reached its twenty-fourth generation at Shaolin.
It was restored by Master Dazhang Shu, and the present Master Qian is his direct successor. The Master’s name is Rujian; his courtesy name is Dafang;
his alternative style is Songgu. He is a native of Qishan in Fengxiang, Shaanxi, of the Li clan. His father’s name was Duo, and his mother was surnamed Zhang.

He was surnamed Shi. The Master was born in Luoxing Village. From his youth, he took delight in Buddhist affairs; whenever he reached a Buddhist temple, it felt like his old home, and out of such affection, he would forget to return.

He entered the local school at an early age to practice the Confucian curriculum, but his heart did not find joy therein. He frequently said to his parents, "I have heard that the Buddha-dharma is the cause for transcending the world;
my aspiration is to leave the household life. At the age of seventeen, his parents could not turn him from his resolve.
He then abandoned his original precepts; leaving his native province with no fixed trace, he took Master Ben as his teacher and underwent tonsure and ordination.

After residing there for three years, he resolved to cultivate his character and principles, traveling far to seek out spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to resolve the matters concerning his own person. He first visited Venerable Xue’an Xi, from whom he received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and was instructed in the path beyond the ordinary.
Subsequently, he entered Mount Qingfeng to dwell alone in solitude, where he attained a realization. Having heard of [Master] Da...

Master Zhang Zhongshi opened the hall at Shaolin, and [the author] went there to seek certification. In the *Xinyou* year of the Jiajing era, he visited Master Zhang in the "Courtyard of Standing in the Snow" (*Lixueting*) and subsequently remained there to rely upon him.
Morning and evening, he entered the inner room to undergo refinement through the karmic conditions of the ancestral masters; thus, he received the seal of approval (*yinke*).

He was entrusted with the instructions to guard and preserve the "jade thread on the tip of a needle" and the "iron ox at the bottom of the sea," despite his diligent toil day and night. From this point onward—
The essential teachings of the Dongshan school regarding the five ranks of orthodoxy and deviation had not yet faded even by this time.

After the Master received the Dharma, he packed his robes and bowl and traveled throughout the famous mountains within the realm. Upon returning to the capital, he frequented various lecture halls to thoroughly investigate the fundamental tenets of the Xing (Nature) and Xiang (Characteristics) schools.
Later, he arrived at Huaiqing, where Prince Zheng Rang, having abdicated the throne, was secretly cultivating pure deeds; hearing of the Master...

Upon his arrival, he performed the rites of formal greeting and consultation; they were deeply in accord with one another. He then established a vihāra at Longgang to invite the Master to dwell there in peace.
At that time, scholars from all quarters heard of his reputation and came from afar. In the Dinghai year of the Wanli era, he accepted an invitation to the Ciyun Hermitage in the capital.
He proclaimed the essential tenets of the school. In the year Wuzi, he was invited by Qianfo Temple to lecture on various sutras; each day, the assembly numbered in the tens of thousands.
In the year Gengyin, by the gracious decree of the Empress Dowager Cisheng, he opened the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land at Cishou Temple;
those present in the assembly numbered twelve hundred. He was honored with the casting of a large gilded Buddha statue and granted the Tripitaka, which he protected.

The Imperial Calligraphy of the four characters "Dàfǎbǎozàng" (Great Dharma Treasure Storehouse) was bestowed [upon him]. In the spring of the Jiawu year, he was invited back to Longgang, where he founded a temple and established offerings.
On the eleventh day of the eighth month in the autumn of the Wuxu year, he first manifested a slight ailment and passed away with a dignified countenance.
He was born in the Wuxu year of the Jiajing era; his worldly age was sixty-one, and his monastic seniority was slightly over forty years. His entire body was interred at...

Twenty-two years after the Master’s passing, in the *Jiwei* year of the Wanli era (1579), his disciple Haiyun traveled to Mount Kuanglu to visit me and requested an inscription for the stele of his pagoda.
In the past, when I met the Master at Cishou Monastery in the capital, I saw that his solitary bearing was majestic and imposing, like a tall pine standing amidst the snow.
When monastics came to seek instruction, he would not employ any artifice of word or expression; he simply brought forth and upheld the essence of the School.
His teaching invariably pointed toward the ultimate as its final goal. In responding to sentient beings and engaging with others, he was consistently single-minded and sincere;

in his every movement and stillness, he never for a moment showed laxity, embodying the exemplary model of the former masters. When I conversed with him for ten days and nights, there was not a single moment when we did not clap our hands and strike our palms in approval.
I have long maintained that Master Han is the true eye of the Chan school for our generation.

When I was exiled to the regions beyond the passes and the Master returned to his native mountains, he spoke of me to his disciples with a sense of longing spanning ten thousand *li*. Thus, his memorial inscription was intended for me.
Moved by the fact that the Master was a true confidant of the Dharma-gate, I have composed this inscription for him, saying: [The Inscription]

One flower with five petals; two branches and five schools. Each established its own pedagogical methods, each excelling in its own family style. The true source of the Dongshan lineage values the mutual interplay of spiritual mechanisms;
like jade thread and golden needle, it dwells in neither the orthodox nor the deviant. Xuefeng the Elder took up this theme once more, and the Master of Calligraphy (Fayan) inherited his legacy.
Reaching our Master Qiangu, he personally inherited the very marrow of the lineage. Like an iron ox at the bottom of the sea, he was decisively certified by the seal of the occasion;

whenever conditions met him, he established the school. Fully upholding the correct command, he pointed toward all directions. Like a bright mirror set upon its stand, beauty and ugliness were not hidden; with the eight characters wide open, he revealed all.

For over twenty years, he mixed mud and entered the water, working with his hands for others until he completely forgot himself. His fame reached the Nine Palaces, and his Dharma light shone during the final age.
The Dharma-treasury descended from heaven; dragons and spirits revered him. Having forgotten his achievements and ceased his labors, he retired to the forests and springs to grow old.

Body and mind are stilled; the light of wisdom is perfectly round. Illusory conditions have come to an end; with a letting go, one simply departs. Originally there is no extinction, so how could there be birth?
The stupa is locked at Longgang; the Dharma-body dwells eternally. When asked for the final word, at daybreak it is not revealed.
Epitaph for the Stupa of Master Gongqian Jingsheng at Qianfo Monastery on Mount Lu.
The Master’s name was Renjing; his courtesy name was Gongqian, and his alternative appellation was Huanshi. He was the son of the Wu clan of Xiangyang. From birth, he was unlike the common crowd.
From his childhood, he harbored the aspiration for transcendence. At Futián Monastery on Mount Fúniú, he paid homage to Dharma Master Gāo’ān, shaved his head, and received full ordination.

There, he listened to lectures on the sūtras and śāstras, investigating the fundamental tenets of both the Nature (xìng) and Characteristics (xiàng) schools until he had exhausted their depths. For three years, he was diligent day and night, gaining profound faith and acceptance in the teachings and contemplative practices.
His teacher said, "The aspirations of a student should be vast and far-reaching; do not limit yourself to the narrow perspective of one peering through a tube or measuring with a ladle."
Seeking self-sufficiency, he eventually proceeded to the capital. There, the great Dharma masters Dongyuan Xian and Lilu were both preeminent teachers of their time.
The Master attended their lecture halls and mastered all their profound meanings. Later, the Great Master Zhang opened up the principle of the Single Transmission of Bodhidharma at Shaolin;
the Master completely set aside his previous doctrinal studies and went there to investigate further. Having stayed for over ten years, he sighed and said:
"This is merely a matter of mouth and ear; the Way is realized within the mind. What is the use of empty words? Having said this, he departed for the Vow Ox (Funiu) site of refining demons.
Within the great furnace, he cast off both body and mind and practiced the "long seven" for three years, until he attained realization.

He traveled extensively to visit various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in search of confirmation of his realization. Upon reaching Jinling, he met Chan Master Shouxin, who lived in seclusion at Hongji.
Shouxin’s conduct and secret practices were highly esteemed by his contemporaries; upon seeing [Dongshan], he marveled at him greatly and said to him:

"The Way is realized through the mind; its preservation lies in stillness and secrecy. To climb mountains and wade through waters is merely to waste the money for straw sandals. He then invited Dongshan to remain.
He closed himself off from the world. Together they refined one another’s understanding, daily advancing into the profound depths until all their mystical interpretations were completely swept away.
This continued for three years. Upon breaking his retreat, he resolutely entered Mount Lu, intending to establish a life of seclusion for the remainder of his days.
It was the year Ji-mao of the Wanli era (1579). When the Master first entered the mountains, he selected a site at Jinzhu Ping; seeing its vast and expansive terrain, he sighed in admiration.

He said, "This is the place where five hundred people enter the summer retreat. Therefore, I have made a vow with the mountain spirits, wishing to offer my very body and life here to establish a karmic connection for the monastics of the ten directions.
He then cleared away the brush to bind together a thatched hut and dwelt there alone, like a solitary shadow.

He took up the labor of carrying grain and performing manual service, while his disciple Zhilian assisted him. Thus, the Master was able to remain in seclusion for three years. The following year was Geng...

In the year of the Dragon (1652), Chan Master Daguanke came to visit. Upon seeing him, he marveled at him, saying, "Since you are able to settle your mind in such profound stillness, your future progress must be immeasurable.
They subsequently became inseparable friends. After lingering for over a month, Daguanke departed.

In the year of Guiwei (1663), [Zhixu] accepted an invitation from Wuzu Monastery in Huangmei to expound the *Lotus Sūtra*. Three years later, in the year of Yiyou (1665), he accepted another invitation.

At the request of Mr. Wu Guolun of Xingguo, he lectured on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. That region was long known for its fierceness and martial spirit, yet many people were moved and transformed by his influence.

Mr. Wu took the lead in initiating the construction of a temple hall. After five years of diligent effort, in the year of Jichou, the three main halls, the meditation hall, the kitchen, and the storehouse were completed.

Mr. Wu then traveled to Nanchang to solicit donations for the creation of a thousand-petaled precious lotus and a Great Image of Vairocana. [The text continues: ...the Great... (Note: The source text provided appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the available portion.)

The official Dingyu Deng served as the presiding master for the ceremony. Before his work was half-finished, Master Gong manifested slight illness and passed away on the seventh day of the sixth month in the nineteenth year of the Wanli era, the *xinmao* year.
He was fifty-one years of age and had been a monk for over thirty years.
I hurried from the mountains to attend the funeral, wailing so bitterly that I felt no desire to live; yet Master Deng exhorted me to carry on.

In recording these events, I have fulfilled my master’s wish to complete the Great Image and carry his sacred remains back to the mountain to be interred behind the temple on a certain day of a certain month in the year Wanshi Bingshen (1608). Master Gong had nine disciples who received ordination under him;
only Lien attended him for the longest time, serving as the vessel upon which his master’s vows were entrusted. Twenty-eight years after his parinirvāṇa, in the year Ding...
Thus it was. Each of the grandsons donated their robes and alms bowls to construct a stūpa and requested me to compose an inscription for it.

The inscription reads: The Great Way is like space; there is nowhere it does not penetrate. Only by leaving behind obstructions can it embrace all things. Deep as the ocean, it is vast and unfathomable.
The hidden current flows through the great earth; whoever digs it will surely reach the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Thus, that which carries the Way resides in physical forms and vessels.
If the mind’s capacity is as empty as space, the Way is naturally complete. I observe my lord: he forgets himself for the sake of others, spreading his heart like the earth.
His vow was thus fulfilled. Beholding that empty mountain, he gathered a handful of thatch grass, intending to cover the ten directions. He left it for whoever might come;

though his aspirations remained unfulfilled when he departed this life, his son succeeded him in the family estate and ultimately revitalized his father’s work. Thus, the Buddhist monastery was established.

The assembly gathered like clouds; the hungry ate and the weary rested, none knowing the reason for it. The Master’s mind abides eternally, his Dharma-body is imperishable, reaching directly to the end of the future.
Though stones crumble and oceans dry up, the shadow of the stupa stands tall as a landmark; amidst the sound of pines and the resonance of springs, such is the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
In the appreciation of those who understand the music, this is the Stele Inscription for the Venerable Master Zhong of Jingtang at Yunzhong Temple on Mount Lu.
The Buddha, through countless skillful means, tames sentient beings; the Bodhisattva, through various causes and conditions, seeks the Buddha.

This is the Way. To know this is to be a disciple of the Buddha and one who continues the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom. It is not merely sitting upon the flower-throne, brandishing the mallet, or holding up the whisk that constitutes the supreme matter.

Even those who direct their aspirations toward the misty peaks and practice in secret, their subtle applications have never failed to take the sound of spring water and the rustling of the wind as their broad and long tongue.
Is one such as Master Zhong of Yunzhong not, indeed, within the light of the white tuft between the Buddha’s brows?
Is it one who seeks the Way of the Buddha by sitting in quiet contemplation amidst mountains and forests? The Master’s name was Fazhong; his courtesy name was Jingtang.

He was the son of the Cao family of Hexian in Xin’an, and his mother was of the Cheng clan. From birth, he was exceptionally gifted; even as a child, he preferred to sit upright and did not join in play with other children.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, he grew weary of Confucian studies and took no pleasure in managing worldly affairs. Early on, he harbored the aspiration for transcendence. At the age of ten...
9. While traveling to Lingyin Temple in Qiantang, he encountered the monk Da Ji, a master of Yunshan, and immediately requested ordination.
Da Ji shaved his head and conferred the precepts upon him. He served as an attendant for three years; at the age of twenty-one, he ascended the platform to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).

He then relied upon lecture halls, where over time he studied under many masters. Nevertheless, he had not yet attained self-confidence. He subsequently set out on a pilgrimage to Shaolin, where Chan Master Daqian Run was presiding over the hall.

He expounded the Dharma, and the Master relied upon him to investigate the essence of the single-lineage transmission. Before long, he traveled to Chang’an to pay his respects to the two great elders, Bianrong and Yuexin, receiving their instructions on the essentials of the mind.
He subsequently returned to Wutai Shan. I was then residing at Longmen on the Northern Terrace together with Chan Master Miaofeng;
the Master came to visit us amidst the ice and snow, and upon seeing me, our minds were in perfect accord. He then remained there for a period of time.
In the year of Renwu during the Wanli era, Master Miao parted from me and went to Luya. I invited him to go with me, where he subsequently established a monastic community;
he contributed greatly to all these new foundations. After residing there for three years, he departed and entered the fire-enclosure at Mount Funiu to refine his three karmic faculties.
Upon returning south, he ascended Mount Kuanglu; finding its seclusion and beauty inspiring, he eventually cleared away the brush to build a hut upon the Jingiang Terrace and settled there.
After three years, he returned to Wulao Peak. For four years, he dwelt there alone, his shadow his only companion.

One day, while ascending Aoyanting—indeed the summit of Mount Kuang—he was filled with joy at its sublime loftiness and took up residence there. Remaining a solitary practitioner for several years, he gradually constructed buildings.
Over time, disciples began to gather. The Master personally planted over one hundred thousand pine trees, hoping to establish a great monastic community. Throughout his life, the Master...

He was straightforward and simple, without artificial embellishment. In governing the assembly, he did not establish formal rules; rather, he led by personal example in all matters, great and small, never tiring until his old age.
He lived according to circumstances, maintaining himself with nothing beyond a single robe. Even a grain of rice or a stalk of vegetable he would invariably share with others.

He regarded the community as one, practicing compassion with impartiality regardless of whether they were wise or foolish, virtuous or unworthy. Through long association, he transformed them through silent influence.
Yet he was unaware of this himself; thus, those who came to him were like returning home to serve their parents.

Whenever he uttered a word or phrase, it was filled with such profound lamentation and poignant sincerity that there was no one among the listeners who did not grasp its meaning at heart and intuitively understand it.

For this reason, although he did not ascend the hall or enter the inner chamber, the entire assembly remained solemn and dignified, like a great furnace and bellows—this was because he taught through his person. In the year Ding-si, I retired from public life and...
Wuyuru visited the Master while he was at Yunzhong. The Master joyfully recounted their past history. One day, the Master came to my quarters, and we conversed through the night on adjoining beds.
He requested that I compose a record for the "Ten Directions Constant Abode" (the monastic community). Three years later, in the autumn of the Gengshen year, he manifested slight illness.

At the time of his passing, he sat upright and said to his disciples, "I see the red sun suspended in the sky and golden lotuses covering the earth; it is time for me to depart. Having spoken these words—
He passed away in serene stillness on the twenty-first day of the seventh month. The Master was born in the *Xinchou* year of the Jiajing era;
his worldly age was eighty, and his years of ordination (*dharma-vassa*) were sixty. In his later years, he ordained three disciples:
Nenghuan and Nenggui, both from Heshi, and Nengcheng from Qianzhou. Nenggui oversaw the Master’s cremation, collected his sacred remains, and enshrined them in a stupa at Taohua.
At the foot of the peak, he presented a formal petition requesting an inscription. I sighed with a sense of serene admiration and said:
"When you first visited Mount Wutai, I saw you soaring like a solitary crane riding the wind; my heart deeply admired your lofty spirit. I tried to detain you firmly at that time, yet you said:"
"Could you have been buried within this very place? The Master replied, "Where there is affinity, there must be fulfillment. Afterward, they parted ways;

it was thought that there would never again be an occasion for meeting once more. Who would have expected that in their old age they would return together? Shall I now recount the Master’s life? The inscription says:

The Great Way is like space; the essence of the myriad dharmas is identical. Those who can employ it skillfully take it as their fundamental principle whenever they encounter conditions. Whether responding to circumstances favorably or unfavorably, they act as is appropriate, remaining entirely without deficiency.
This is the work of the wise, employing all manner of expedient means: even the sound of pines and the resonance of springs issue forth as the broad and long tongue of the Buddha.

How much more so for those who are ready to receive the teaching; how could this not be a skillful exposition? Therefore, the Perfected One uses the body as his teaching; his secret practices are fully manifest, and every action is wondrous.
Whether tilling the soil, digging the earth, carrying firewood, or drawing water, the Great Function is ever present—how can one be restricted by distinctions of self and other?
Meeting through conditions, acting without intention—every dharma, every instance, is entirely liberation. Solitary as a shadow amidst layered cliffs, yet as if facing a vast assembly;
for over twenty years, he has remained majestic and unmoving. From every pore of his body, he pervades the ten directions.
There are those who enter this state: their entire being is cool and refreshing; the world-system is established amidst the clouds, and the Sangha arrives from beyond the mundane age.

Their morning gruel and evening meal are as if drawn from the world of Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha). This is our Master’s effortless, wondrous power—functioning yet not concealed. With a single toss from the void, it is all cast forth.

Before his great vows had reached their end, the illusory conditions dissolved. He walked away with a dismissive wave of his arm, utterly silent. A single stupa now supports the void, serving as the locus for this sacred trace;
the Dharma-body abides eternally throughout the bounds of the future.
Epitaph for the Venerable Dado, the Practitioner of Huayang Mountain in Xuancheng.
His name was Dado, his courtesy name Fazhen, and he was the son of the [surname] family of Wanling. From birth, he transcended the common crowd; his spirit was pure and his tone resonant.
When he was young, while attending the local school, he read the *Analects* and reached the passage: "If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die in the evening.

He then asked, "What thing is this 'Way'? How can one hear it and yet be ready to die? Consequently, he became deeply skeptical of it. Time and again he questioned his seniors about this, but none of their answers satisfied him.
One day, he encountered a wandering monk and asked, "What is the Way? The monk replied, "This is our Buddha's..."
The supreme and wondrous Way is not merely the benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom of the world. Because of this, Gong came to have profound faith in the Buddhist Way;

he subsequently paid his respects to a monk and had his hair shaved. At that time, he was only twenty years old. The monk instructed him, saying, "I am not your teacher; you should go to consult Yunqi.
Gong went directly there and received the śrāmaṇera precepts. After relying on the community for a short while, he followed Xuelang.
He attended various Dharma assemblies to study the principles of the teachings. Constantly seeking realization of his own mind, he failed to grasp its essential point.
He returned once more to Yunqi Monastery to receive full ordination and requested instruction on the essentials of cultivating the mind.

[The Master] showed him the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation, taking "one mind without distraction" as the core objective, and entrusted him with the *Chan-guan ce-jin* (Exhortation for Progress in the Zen Barrier) as the secret manual for investigation. The Master received these instructions with deep reverence and returned to his original home.
At Seoknangnyan in Gun, he closed his quarters for three years, single-mindedly maintaining a single thought. After a long time, he attained realization.

He then went to Yunqi to seek formal certification (*kengyō*), whereupon he remained with the assembly for several years to refine his practice. Departing, he returned to Hwaryang-san in his native district; clearing away the brush, he took up residence there.
Hwaryang is ancestral to Huangshan Baie, spanning one *yojanas* in length and breadth, and encircling four districts. [This was his] hermitage.

Situated amidst ten thousand mountains, it was the most secluded and remote place. The Master resided there, planting taro and tea, gathering acorns and chestnuts, and picking pine pollen to sustain himself.
He ultimately severed all ties with the secular world; he was attended only by a single śrāmaṇera named Zhihao.

When Hào was reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he reached the section on the investigation of the mind (*citta-vicaya*). He asked, "In the sevenfold investigation of the mind, it cannot be found anywhere.
Ultimately, where does the mind reside? The Master struck the desk once, then after a long silence, asked, "Do you understand? Hào replied, "I do not understand."
He then presented the "Ancestral Master" (Second Patriarch) kōan. After a long time, he told Hào to go and study under various masters elsewhere, while he himself remained in solitary residence.
Laypeople and monastics requested that the Master explain the essential meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Master took up the passage: "Whatever has marks is entirely illusory.
If one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. He asked the assembly, "Do you understand? The assembly said they did not understand. The Master said:
"All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow; they are like dew and like lightning—thus should one contemplate them.
He then said, "The assembly, each of you, take care of yourselves. I shall now depart. Thereupon, he bathed, changed his robes, sat upright in mindfulness of the Buddha, and passed away.
This was on the eighteenth day of the seventh month in the Wuli (1598) year of the Wanli era. The Master was born in the Jiashen (1574) year of the Wanli era.
Xushen year, the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month. His worldly age was forty-five, and his years as a monk were twenty-eight.
He was buried at a certain location within the hermitage. When Zhihao returned from his travels to visit him, the Master had already entered nirvana for three years.
Zhihao then crawled on his hands and knees to Mount Kuang and requested that I compose an inscription for the stupa. Upon reading his account, I learned that the Master first sought the Way...
Upon uttering the single word "death," he immediately renounced the mundane world. Although he was well-versed in the teachings and their meanings, he did not prize mere words;
he resolved his will upon the desolate shores of the empty mountains. Holding fast to a single thought, he regarded birth and death as the great matter.
His conduct was solitary and peerless, transcending all like that of the ancient hermits of Mount Yan. Such is something difficult to achieve in this age of the Dharma’s decline. Alas!

If the influence of your virtue could cause those among us who are greedy to become frugal, the mad to find rest, and the restless to attain tranquility, what need would there be for you to occupy a magnificent seat to preach the Dharma?
Being moved by this thought, I have composed this inscription: [The Inscription]
The numinous root of *prajñā* is like a seed planted in the earth; it sprouts when it encounters the right conditions.

If nourished by the timely rain of hearing a single word of the Way, one’s long-standing cultivation naturally manifests upon even a slight touch, appearing before one in an instant. Since death is already acceptable, what attachment could there be to life?
Suddenly casting aside worldly ties, he entered the mountains to practice cultivation. He did not concern himself with speech, single-mindedly upholding the "Upward" direction.

With a single thought of solitary luminosity, both self and ego were lost. Using acorns, chestnuts, and pine blossoms to sustain his withered body, he regarded floating clouds and illusory transformations as if they did not exist.
In the desolate, empty mountains, solitary wind and no companions—do not seek its guest; look instead at the Lord of Lords.

Unchanging through birth and death, like a flash of lightning in the great void, it dwells in the silence of extinction within the sky, transcending emotion and leaving behind all views. To stir and depart immediately is as if one had never come at all.
Empty flowers clouding the eyes; wild horses and dust motes. The shadow of the stupa circles; mists steam and clouds lock the sky. When asked for the final word:
green mountains, cluster upon cluster.
Epitaph for the Bhikṣu Xingci:

The Bhikṣu Xingci was the son of the Pan family of Piling. By nature he loved seclusion from the world; while still a child, having heard the Dharma Master Yuezhu lecture on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he resolved to leave the household life.
He paid homage to the Dharma Master Yuguang at Mount Hua to seek ordination, who then conferred upon him the precepts.
Through the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, he cultivated the holy life with single-minded devotion. He took pleasure in caring for the elderly and the infirm, his heart never weary.
He practiced the Buddhist rites of chanting and music. Later, he met the monk Xingyu from Duan-nan;

they traveled together to the South Sea and lived there for over ten years, dwelling together in a thatched hut. When Yu fell ill for many years, he attended to him with diligent compassion, as if serving his own parents. Briefly...

She maintained a composed and tireless demeanor. By the end of the Wanli period, she was free from ailment. In the Jiwei year of the Wanli era, she received the full precepts (*upasampadā*) together with Cí on Mount Kuāng.

Upon returning to Putuoshan, Yù’s illness flared up again, and Cí redoubled her efforts to nurse and protect her. In the Gengshen year, feeling the deep gratitude for the Dharma-milk, Cí came once more to visit Mount Kuāng.
While traveling by boat to Dígǎng, she suddenly felt a slight indisposition and subsequently passed away while seated in the boat. She entrusted [her final instructions] to three companions...
The person was cremated at Zishazhou on the first day of the fifth month in the Gengshen year of the Wanli era.

Upon hearing this, Yù rushed to carry the sacred remains back to Putuoshan for interment. He then traveled to Mount Kuāng to recount the circumstances in detail and requested that they be recorded in a commemorative inscription.
Upon hearing this, I was moved and said: "The Classic of Poetry says, 'Brothers quarrel within the walls. In this world, there are many who, though bound by blood, act as enemies;
how much more so between two different surnames? Yet as for [Master] Ci and [Master] Yu: they met unexpectedly, drew close through the Way, and shared a single mind free of discord.
For ten years they attended to each other’s illnesses as if it were but a single day. Ci was able to exert his full heart and strength during the master's lifetime, while Yu..."
Thus, gratitude for one’s kindness is realized after death; this is truly what is meant by the saying, "In one life and the next, one sees the true nature of friendship.
I have therefore arranged these events in sequence and further set forth the principle of the Dharma-gate: that attending to the sick should be regarded as the foremost practice.
Chiseng was born on the seventeenth day of the first month in the Gui-si year; her worldly lifespan was twenty-eight years. Yu.
He was the son of the Xu family of Kunming in Dīnnán. As his family had been engaged in the Confucian profession for generations, I have recorded this here as well.

Thus, I compose this inscription: "From past lives he possessed the karmic affinity for the Way, meeting it spontaneously and without design. Though their forms differed, their hearts were one; they were brothers who shared the same hardships. They regarded each other’s bodies as their own."

Death and birth are non-dual; one transcends the emotions within emotion, and thus it is so. The bones are buried beneath white flowers, while the mind coalesces within the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
I venture to ask the Great Being: where, indeed, do you come and go?
Epitaph for Master Yuan’an of Zhibo Monastery on Mount Huang in Xian’an The Master’s name was Guangji, with the style name Yuan’an.
He was the son of the Yu family of Kaitua, Quzhou. From birth, he was intelligent and possessed a resolve to transcend the mundane world.

At the age of fifteen, he informed his parents that he wished to leave the household life; they granted him permission. He then entered the service of Master Wúwéi at Mount Zhanggong in the prefecture.
As a śrāmaṇera, he was fond of learning and possessed many skills; broad-minded and elegant, he excelled in the arts.

He constantly traveled between Xiu and Wu, where no scholar-official of the time failed to hold him in high esteem, delighting to form lifelong friendships with him regardless of age. At the age of twenty-four, he sighed and said:

Human life passes as swiftly as a horse's hoofbeat in a crevice. Floating aimlessly like this, what is the purpose of leaving the household life? He thus resolved to travel abroad to visit and consult with spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Although he attempted several times, he was detained by his relatives and acquaintances and did not succeed. Thereupon, he fled under the cover of night, carrying only a single ladle and a solitary staff.
He went directly to Yunqi. Upon seeing him, the Great Master recognized his potential and conferred the full precepts upon him. He revealed the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation, saying:

"In Buddha-recitation, there is no other skill; it lies solely in single-mindedness without distraction. The Master [Wang] took these words to heart and subsequently served as the *karmadāna* (Venerable).

In his daily life, he applied himself with earnest cultivation, maintaining the single thought of recitation, strictly restraining the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, and solemnizing his deportment. He regulated...

He was harmonious toward both those within and without, and his conduct delighted the hearts of the multitude. One day, the Great Master addressed the assembly, saying: "The court establishes officials so that they may fulfill their duties;
this applies not only to the state, but likewise to the monastic groves. In Sanskrit, *karmadāna* means 'one who delights the assembly.

If one entrusted with the office of *karmadāna* can truly be said to fulfill their duty, then they are worthy of the title. Consequently, the entire community came to honor him, and he remained in that position for eight years.

He returned to his native mountains to visit his teacher and remained in seclusion for three years. In the *gengxu* year of the Wanli era, he entered the Changxiang Plains of Mount Huang, where he cleared away the brush to establish a retreat for cultivation.
He exhorted himself with diligent effort, never wavering from a single thought, as if having forgotten the world of men.
After some time, many among the clergy and laity in that region placed their faith in him; Mr. Wang Tunan built a hermitage for him to dwell in. He sat there for ten... [years].
For two years, he happened to be afflicted with a serious illness, yet he never spoke of it; his movements and conduct remained as usual, and no one was aware of it.

After some time, his illness grew critical, and a local man requested a physician to examine him. The Master said, "Life and death are like guests; when it is time to depart, one simply departs. What more is there to do?
He ultimately refused any medicine, remaining only in a state of serene composure, sitting upright as if he did not possess a body. One day, he summoned his disciples and said:
"I am departing. You must recognize this as my final task. Having spoken these words, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away.
This was the second day of the second month in the first year of the Tianqi era, the Xin-you year. At first, the disciples did not expect the Master to pass so suddenly;

they had not yet prepared the funerary chamber and had merely placed his seat upon a table. Fearing that his physical form might undergo change, they hurriedly gathered firewood for cremation. It happened that it was snowing heavily.
He could not be moved for seven days. Monastics and laypeople from near and far heard of this and broke through the snow to rush to his funeral.

Seeing that the Master’s countenance was as if alive, his joyful expression full and inviting, the color of his lips unchanged, and his hands as soft as cotton, everyone said, "This is a man who has truly lived;
how can we bear to see him pass away? They firmly refused to allow the cremation and instead borrowed a Buddhist shrine to receive his remains, which were enshrined in the hall they had renovated.
In his chamber, the snow ceased to fall. His disciples said to one another, "Could this be the final event? Thereupon, they also did not dare to cremate him.
Through the heat of summer and autumn, his physical form and vital energy remained unchanged. They intended to wait three years before performing the burial.
In the third month of the following year, Renxu (1622), the disciple Dashi went to Mount Kuang and reported the matter in full, requesting that I compose an inscription for him. I—
Upon hearing this, he sighed and said: "The practice of us śramaṇas values genuine cultivation and actual realization;

it does not lie in flaunting one's reputation or establishing a school of thought as a mark of attainment. Given your high intelligence, manifold talents, vast learning, and extensive knowledge, once you have entered the Dharma-gate..."

He immediately severed all worldly ties with total sincerity and applied his mind single-mindedly to the Way. He appeared as if he were a fool or one who was speechless; dwelling constantly in a single thought, he remained dense and continuous.

When meeting others, he would not utter a single word; when questioned, he would do nothing but smile. Even when living among his fellow practitioners, he forgot self and other and cast aside the concerns of the physical body.
There was no one who did not love and revere him. Was this not the manifestation of his majestic deportment and the cultivation of his vital energy? It was indeed correct.
Can one truly understand how things are such that there is dharma-preaching without words? Alas!

That you, sir, regarding birth and death, had your spirit depart while your form remained, transforming the foul and corrupt into the marvelous and divine—was this not due to the cultivation of precepts and meditative concentration, and the profound, penetrating integration of your refined mind?
Even the indestructible diamond-like nature of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, their eternal and imperishable state, is likewise brought about by this; otherwise, it would not be so.
It did not last until morning. It was like a piglet feeding at its dead mother; regarding this, I was moved to reflection, and thus I composed this inscription:
"The myriad phenomena of the three realms are created by the mind. Whether they perish or do not perish, all are contained within a single aperture. [Like] the glow-worm and the pearl in the oyster."

Although this light is small, it is nonetheless a subtle and wondrous, perfectly luminous jewel; how much more so is the Buddha-nature! This precious, awakened, and enlightened mind is inherently possessed by me;
how could it not be profoundly deep? Perfumed by precepts and meditative concentration, it is the diamond seed; therefore, it is called *śarīra*.
That cluster was like ants; since there is an illusory form, how could one avoid illusory illness? The bonds of fruit remain present, for karma is predetermined from before.
Just as your physical frame has not yet decayed after so long, it is likely that within it the light of the mind remains stainless. From this point on, you shall refine yourself with purity.
Life after life, they shall not regress; they will certainly reach the stage of Vajra. Whether burned or preserved, it matters not.
Wait for three years, then return to inform me. I have composed this inscription not for the sake of the public alone, but to announce it universally to all people.
Everyone, exert yourselves!

The Master’s name was Fakai; his courtesy name was Renzhi, and his sobriquet was Dangu. He was a native of Jiangyin, surnamed Zhao, a family renowned for generations as a prominent clan.

Magnanimous and transcending the common crowd, he studied the curriculum for the civil service examinations as an adult, achieving a brilliant reputation for his talent, yet he regarded worldly affairs with the indifference of mere dust.

Yong was dedicated to the study of the nature and destiny of human life (*xing-ming*). Although his parents arranged a marriage for him, he ultimately did not consent. After his father passed away, he took up his staff and traveled alone.

He ascended Mount Taihe, where he encountered a Daoist priest who taught him the arts of longevity. Later, passing through Wuchang, he met those who lectured on the doctrine of "innate knowledge" (*ling-zhi*);

He returned to Fushan, where he sat in the Three-Bend Cave and wrote out the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety) with his own blood. In the year Gui-si, he traveled to Wancheng. Chan Master Daguan came up from the river;

[The Master] struck him with his staff and said, "Do you understand? Do you understand? The official said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "What is this 'originally empty' that is a dry piece of dung?
The official was suddenly enlightened; he simply nodded his head. From then on, his realization became stable and secure.
In the autumn of the Renyin year, he returned south and entered Fushan Heshengyan, where he met Song Yuanluku and Ou-yang Xiu (the "Sixth One" of the Liu family).

The site where he had preached the Dharma while playing chess had long been used for secular purposes. Mr. Ruan of the Dan-yu residence in Wan-cheng gathered his clan members and restored it, inviting the Master to reside there.

He renovated the stupa of Master Huiyuan and transcribed the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* with blood from his own body. Daily, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for the longevity of his mother.
In the year Wushen, at the invitation of Mr. Guan-wo Wu, the Grand Astrologer, he took up residence as the abbot of Mount Fu’s Great Avataṃsaka Monastery.
At the temple, he constantly took his fundamental practice as his Buddhist service. To the monastics from all quarters who arrived, he showed only the direct and immediate path.

He then compiled the causes and conditions of the various patriarchs entering the Way and had them carved into woodblocks for printing. Initially, Master Da had undertaken the carving of the Great Canon (Tripitaka), using Shuangjing Jizhao as the carving site;
the Master’s spirit shrine was also returned there. Desiring to fulfill his late teacher’s vow, the Master [Yuanwu] then departed. In the year Gengxu.

Upon arriving at the mountain, the Duke observed much mist and dampness. Below lay the ruins of an ancient *pūrvanivāsa* (transformed city), which was once the site of the meditation hall of Chan Master Furi Xuan of the Song dynasty.
The Grand Astrologer, Mr. Feng of Jiqu, had proposed restoring it as a location for storing printing blocks.

The Duke obtained a letter from his hand and showed it to the Left Provincial Governor, Mr. Wu Benru; Mr. Wu then inspected the site, demarcated the boundaries, and reclaimed it from various powerful landowners.

The hand [of the manuscript] was thus restored to its place as the Buddha-ground. Furthermore, he ransomed one hundred *mǔ* of fields from the Tàipíng Temple in Lín'ān to provide for the permanent endowment (*chángzhù*) of the monastery;
thus, the affairs of the Tripitaka collection had a place to which they could return. In the year Jiǎyīn, Wú Gōng established his provincial government in Shū.

Wú Gōng went to discuss the circumstances of the carving of the Tripitaka and subsequently ascended Mount Éméi to pay homage to Samantabhadra. In the spring of the year Yìmǎo, he departed together with Zhízhǐ Xu Gōng Ruògǔ.
Shu. In the autumn of this year, he returned to Jingshan. As the Master’s sacred shrine had already been interred, Lord Zhunin Zhu, the Minister of Education, paid respects at the Master’s stupa.
According to the pronouncements of geomancers, he learned that water lay beneath the site and proposed a reinterment. The Lord and the Master’s Dharma-protecting disciple, Mr.
Zhongchun Miao, traveled to seek an auspicious location and selected a new burial site on the southern slope of Pengbo Peak. This was in the winter of the Bingchen year.
I have come from Mount Nanyue to attend the funeral rites, exhausting the meaning of life and death within the Dharma gate.

Upon arriving at Jinsha, I composed a text for the memorial service, which was scheduled for the nineteenth day of the month of the Longzhi (Winter Solstice). When the assembly gathered, the cremation took place on that very day;
I personally offered the fire and requested the remains to be placed in the stupa, thereby repaying my lifelong friend and manifesting Master Da’s final segment of radiant light.

This was due to your efforts. There is a proverb that says, "Filial sons emerge from the tip of the staff," and you truly embodied this. When I returned to Mount Kuang, you grew weary of the burden of guiding others across the stream;
thus, you entrusted Jizhao to Master Gaofeng and established Huacheng as a permanent monastery for receiving guests from all directions.
He addressed his disciples, saying, "Beneath each of your kashayas lies a seat upon the earth; why do you linger here with such attachment?
In the seventh month of autumn in the year of Xin-you, he took leave of all his patrons and passed through the White Gate (Baimen), entrusting the affairs of the temple to the official Wu Benru.
In the tenth month of winter, he returned to Shuangjing. One day, leaning on his staff while standing below the hall, he looked toward the assembly and said:
"The antelope hangs its horns" [and vanishes]; he did not exceed twelve years. The multitude could not fathom it. When evening came, he burned incense and paid homage to the Buddha;
having bathed and changed his robes, he sat cross-legged in silence. At dawn, he suddenly passed away. This was the thirteenth day of the twelfth month of the *Xinyou* year of the *Tianqi* era.
His disciples, including [Name], performed the cremation and interred him at [Location]. The Master was born in the *Xinyou* year of the *Jiajing* era.
On the twenty-first day of the third month, at the age of sixty-one and with twenty-eight years of seniority as a monk, Master Da passed away.

Whenever I encountered Master Da, I observed that his gate was steep and inaccessible; I often thought that such a person would be difficult to find in the future. When I finally met him at Shuangjing, his countenance was pure and his frame was firm, possessing a towering and heroic spirit.
