He moves with the ease of one who has mastered the blade; his commands are as swift as he wishes. His demeanor is relaxed and composed; he acts without raising a sound or altering his expression.

In matters of escorting the dead to their rest and restoring them to life, exhausting his physical form and completing his life’s work, continuing his predecessor’s will and carrying out his legacy, he brings glory to those before him and surpasses all who follow.

He is truly a master of the final generation of disciples, one who does no shame to his very bones. I privately believe that the Master’s talent is sufficient to respond to the world, and his strength is sufficient to...
He bore the burden of the Way; there was no hardship or toil he did not fully undergo. In his conduct, he acted courageously upon seeing what was righteous, never shrinking from the blade or the saw.
He regarded gain and sustenance as like flowers in the sky or the moon reflected in water. At the moment of death and rebirth, he transcended it as if casting off worn-out sandals.
Alas! Were it not for a Great Man whose past roots were revealed and whose mind was in accord with the unborn, how could he have dwelt thus?
How could those who exist beyond the realm of form possibly be like this? Your disciple Yuanliang has prepared a detailed account and traveled to Mount Kuang to beg me for an inscription.
Reflecting on my bond of dharma, I have composed this inscription, saying: [The inscription follows.]
In the late autumn of the monastic forests, the great Dharma’s guiding ropes have fallen into decay. Amidst the cold of the year and the frost and snow, Zibo uses his light to illuminate the way.

Since his Way has been made radiant, the gateway of his school becomes increasingly steep; standing like a precipitous cliff, it possesses a vast and distinct character. Those who gaze upon it are struck with awe; those who draw near to it retreat.
A single staff of thorns—utterly without inhibition. When the lion in the cave bared its claws and fangs, the lion cub showed no hesitation at all;
beneath a single blow of the staff, it flipped over and leaped away, walking with great strides, returning by a path that was once again wondrous.

Bearing the burden upon his entire being, he spared no effort; the Dharma-treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were cast forth at the mere movement of his hand. The Wheel of Dharma turned inexhaustibly until it could no longer be turned.
When his role as a bridge and raft grew weary, he reached his ultimate end according to conditions. Finding rest in his temporary lodging, he dwelt within the realm of the city of *śūnya*.
All things are entirely for the sake of the eternal abiding of the ten directions. Before birth they did not exist; at the end they are likewise non-existent.

Not a single speck of dust can be established; it is fundamentally suchness as it is. Like a wild goat hanging from a tree branch—this is the clear pointing-out. Seizing up and acting immediately, one casts off the hand and returns home.
A single stupa stands solitary, erected in the midst of space. The Dharma-body is all-pervasive;
the sound of the wind and the color of the moon—Master Rui Guang, Lord of Mount Nanyue, inscribed this to the full extent of the Dharma-realm:
there is not a single thing that is not the Dharma-body. Among the gates of all afflictions, there is not a single practice that is not [the Dharma-body].

This is the work of the Buddha. How much more so for those who discipline the three karmas, concentrate their single mind, distance themselves from the mundane world, and diligently practice for the sake of the Pure Land!

Therefore, when our Buddha’s white tuft of light illuminates eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, the Bodhisattvas within that light seek the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions.
Is one such as Master Xiang of Nanyue not among those within that light?

He appeared, withdrawing his mindfulness to the mountain forests and single-mindedly and diligently seeking the Buddha-way. According to his records, the Master’s name was Faxiang, his courtesy name was Ruiguang, and his pen-name was Yinnan.
He was the son of the Zhou family from Sheng County in Yue. From birth, he was transcendent and expansive; though he pursued the Confucian studies, he did not succeed in the examinations.
Filled with a profound sense of world-weariness, he conceived the aspiration to transcend the mundane. He followed his uncle to the capital to visit the Elder Xiaoyan.
When the Elder pointed toward the ultimate reality, the Master said, "I am but a man of worldly toil; I do not yet dare to accept this responsibility.

The Elder replied, "The Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation is the most swift and essential path. The Master nodded in agreement. After some time, he returned south, resolved to leave the household life, and paid his respects at his home temple.
Master Kai of Xianan shaved his head at the age of thirty-two.

He visited Master Suanan of Qixia to receive full ordination and relied upon the lecture halls there for three years, after which he departed. He traveled north to the Great Capital (Beijing) to attend upon Master Bianrong.
Upon seeing him, Yi asked, "How do you practice? The official replied, "I have left the household life for the sake of birth and death;

I have been single-mindedly cultivating the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha. I wonder if this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Yong said, "There is no room for anything outside of mindfulness of the Buddha."
He sought the ultimate truth elsewhere. Having received the Master’s instruction, he prostrated himself. Empress Dowager Cisheng was performing great Buddhist rites;

she established a period of Pure Land practice and invited him to serve as the head seat (*śrāmaṇera*). When the three-year period concluded, he traveled to Mount Wutai and Mount Funiu, visiting various senior masters.
At that time, Venerable Baisong of Niu Mountain was an old acquaintance; upon meeting him, they conversed and their minds reached a profound accord.

He remained in a stone grotto, solitary as a shadow and cutting off all traces of his presence. For three years he lived on wild fruits; one day, while sitting in meditation, snow piled up to fill his bed and his fire was extinguished, yet his robes remained dry.
When an attendant went to see him, he was startled and ran to report this to Shishuang. Shishuang went to look and saw that the Master was in deep samādhi.
He struck a chime to awaken him and asked, "The smoke is cold and the ashes are cool; how do you perceive this state? The Master replied, "The mountain is originally stone; the ice..."

Originally it was water; now snow flies, filling the cliffs. [The Master] did not know why this was so. Song said, "This is merely a temporary cessation of worldly toil, resulting in a state of light ease.
If you become attached to this state, you will fall into a one-sided emptiness. Do not linger here; you should go forth on foot."
Upon meeting Nan, he stopped there. Nan gave him a bowl bag and instructed him, saying: "Zen practitioner, go south. Report that you are seventy-nine years old.
I, too, will not remain much longer; let us all keep watch over one another. Gong then took up his gourd ladle and straw hat and went straight to Mount Emei to pay homage to Samantabhadra.
He stayed at Dae'e Seok (Stone of Great Emei) for eight months, investigating with intense earnestness, yet his mind remained unsettled. Thereupon, he recalled pine and cypress trees.
Having read the *Record of Meeting Nanzhao*, he proceeded to the Southern Peak (Nanyue). Ascending the summit of Mount Zhurong, he gazed upon the ancient Great Brightness;

the mountains and forests were lush and flourishing, so he went there to seek a place to dwell. Not long after, the monk Churan of Mount Chidi invited him to preside over the reading of the Tripitaka.

The Master stayed for one night, when at midnight, amidst a hazy dream, a voice declared: "This is not where you shall reside; depart quickly. The following morning, he was about to leave for another location.
He went to visit the monk Da-kuan, who invited him to stay at Cedao Peak (Caidao Feng). The Master agreed. After traveling for three days, he found that the Tripitaka had been destroyed by fire.

The Master then took up the Dharma gate of *nianfo* (recitation of the Buddha’s name) as revealed by Xiao Yan, vowing to devote his entire life to this practice and intending to count his recitations by the number of beans.
Kwan-won volunteered to serve as the presiding master of the transformation ceremony and solicited forty-eight *dō* of beans. From that time on, the Master [Gong] set aside both body and mind;

his shadow never left the mountain. Day and night he applied himself with diligence, treating the beans as if they were pearls, maintaining pure mindfulness in uninterrupted succession until the end of his life.

Consequently, he was called "Bean-Child Buddha" (*Doe-er-bul*). While the Master resided on the mountain, he remained entirely free from external entanglements, yet his reputation and spiritual radiance became increasingly manifest, reaching the monastic robes of the ten directions.

His disciples returned to him from afar; the four requisites arrived without being sought, and the monastic groves were established without being built. At Mount Nanyue, where it had long been desolate, many came once they heard of Master Gong’s single stirring influence.
In his daily life, he constantly admonished his disciples: "You have shaved off your hair and beard, yet you do not realize the great matter of birth and death.
You merely lean against walls and rest against pillars, your karmic consciousness vast and茫然 (mángmáng—vast and bewildered). What is this that you call yourself? Is this not so?
"What our Buddha rebuked was those who wear patched robes while dwelling in seclusion, falsely claiming to be *āraṇyaka* (forest-dwellers), yet do not single-mindedly cultivate pure karma.
When the great limit of life arrives, with what will they confront Old Man Yama? Those who heard this were moved to tears.

Although the Master had severed all ties to the human world, the gentlemen of his time heard of him and looked up to him with admiration. When Liu Gong, the Regional Governor of Guangxi, visited the temple, he sent a letter.

He invited [the Master] to come for a visit, but the Master declined with great courtesy, saying he would not go. When Lord Lu, the Vice-Governor of Hengzhou, was performing a temple sacrifice, he decreed that those who failed to attend on time should be punished.
He then sent over thirty *shi* of grain to the Master. The Master said, "How could an old monk like me, for the sake of a single bowl of rice, gather such widespread resentment?"
He ultimately did not accept. Prince Ji of Changsha, who was devoted to the Master, dispatched an inner attendant to invite him. The Master said, "I, a mountain monk, am weary of traveling;
I have rested my shoulders here and have vowed to follow the example of Master Huiyuan until death, never setting foot among the laity. I dare not accept your command.

The Prince sent the aforementioned attendant again, bringing two copies of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, one copy of the Great Commentary and Sub-commentary (*Da shu chao*), and a hundred taels of silver for the support of his vegetarian retreat. The Master...

Receiving the imperial decree, he distributed the funds from the vegetarian feast throughout the mountain to broaden the King’s beneficence, while retaining the remainder to support the mountain gate.

The King consequently held him in even greater esteem. The Master received those who came and went without discriminating between the good and the bad, treating all with a single flavor of impartial compassion.

Seven men, including the great bandits of Jingzhou and Xiangyang, Jia Er and Tang Jiu, were captured and urgently sought refuge with him; they confessed their sins and repented, entreating him with deep sorrow.
To earn his livelihood, the official took pity on his sincerity and accepted him. He provided him with a *daojin* (Daoist cap) and ordered him to join the community in manual labor.

When the pursuing officials arrived, they saw that the official’s heart was filled with a profound aura of compassion; furthermore, they were moved by the sound of his reciting the Buddha’s name. Thereupon, they untied three pieces of gold from their waists and gave them to him.
Having prepared the vegetarian feast, he departed. The thief also transformed into an ascetic monk. In the year of Xinchou, there was a famine;
the community went without grain for three days and subsisted on gathered bracken. The Master prayed day and night to the Dharma-protecting deities.

A young monk appeared at the house of a donor in the mountains and delivered one hundred to several dozen *shi* of rice and beans. When the Master inquired about the previous monk, no one had seen him.
The Master resided at Side Dao Peak for over thirty years, where he cultivated pure practices with such diligence that he never ceased for even a moment.

He habitually slept on his side without ever touching a mattress and did not maintain a formal abbot’s quarters; instead, he sat alone in a single niche within the Buddha hall. He possessed no storage rooms or granaries, and his chest contained nothing beyond his basic necessities.
On the day of his passing, there was only a jar of black pepper and a few pieces of old cloth. He required no attendants for his final rites.

He did not act as a patron for conversions, nor did he form alliances with external supporters, nor did he associate with those in power or high status. His food was simple and coarse; he often made cakes from bran and chaff to satisfy his hunger.
When monks would throw their leftovers on the ground, he would publicly pick them up, roast them in the embers, and eat them.

Whenever he practiced walking meditation while reciting the Buddha’s name, he would invariably carry a hoe to wander about. Upon seeing any discarded filth, he would always cover it with earth. Someone once said to him: "Master..."
"Why are you so exhausted? The Master replied, "This is a place of pure stillness; I fear the mountain deities might see impurity.
Throughout his life, the Master had lived among the assembly, yet at over seventy years of age, he still had no dharma heir.

A layman from Linjiang named Fu, who had previously traded on the rivers and lakes, suddenly abandoned his wife and children to leave the household life on Mount Emei under the name Tongrong. He arrived in the winter of the Renyin year of the Wanli era.
"Enter. He transmitted the seal of the mind and bestowed the robe and bowl. A verse said: "What is the great meaning of the Westward Journey? Is it still seen even unto this day?
When nothing arises within the mind, how can there be anything seen? *Suru-siri svāhā.*" Rong then settled there to spend the remainder of his life.
The Master had previously attended to the assembly without weariness. One day, he requested a bath and paid homage to the Buddha.

He addressed the assembly, saying, "The melon seeds are ripe; at the very moment they fall from their stalks, there is no one in the hall who perceives it. At that time, Daorong was dwelling in Bifudong Cave.
He sent a messenger to summon [the Master], but upon reaching the foot of the peak, he heard the sound of music; entering the room, however, it was silent.
The Master sat in the full lotus posture. Zhizhou Rong paid his respects. The Master said, "I am about to depart. First, I entrust my alms-bag to you;
now, I leave behind this prayer-bead rosary and staff as parting gifts. Guard and uphold them well. After a long while, he had the Head Seat lead the assembly in reciting the Buddha’s name.

Sitting in the lotus posture, the Master admonished the assembly, saying, "Do not engage in empty pretenses or fabricate the strange to deceive and delude the people of the world. Focus solely on one thing: recite with sincerity."
The Buddha—having finished speaking—folded his hands, sat upright, and passed away at the hour of the Tiger on the sixth day of the second month in the Gengxu year of the Wanli era.
The Master was born on the full moon of the ninth month in the Renchen year of the Jiajing era; his worldly age was seventy-nine, and his dharma-age was forty-three.
The assembly made offerings to him within the hall for seven days, during which his countenance remained unchanged. His entire body was then interred at...

To the right of the peak, a stūpa was erected. Recalling when I was in the East Sea, Minister Zeng spoke of Master Yan’s asceticism and noble conduct, saying they were no less than those of the ancients;
at that time, I took note of this in my heart. Fourteen years after Master Yan entered nirvāṇa, in the year Guihai, I returned to Caoxi.
Master Rong presented a formal account and came to request an inscription for the stūpa. I stroked [the document] and...
The Preface sighs deeply, saying: "Alas! The time since the Sage departed has grown distant, and the gates of the Dharma have fallen into decay.

The established norms of the monastic groves are nearly swept away from the ground. Adrift like foam upon the waves, people are for the most part submerged in fame and profit, thereby losing their original authenticity.

The decline of the Way of the Dharma has reached this point. As for those of pure integrity and austere discipline, who maintain a single resolve throughout their lives and remain unchanging from beginning to end—"

One such as you may truly be said to have taught the Dharma with your very person. What need was there to wait for you to ascend the curved wooden seat, strike the gavel, or raise the whisk to manifest the ultimate truth?
Observing your coming and going through birth and death, entirely free from obstruction, were you not one who entered the state of non-arising through the mind of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation)?
I regret that I am unable to fully reveal the secrets of your inner realization; therefore, I compose this inscription for you. The inscription says:
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the Dharma-body universally responds; this engagement with all gates of worldly affliction constitutes wondrous practice.

How much more so when one maintains a single mind, with pure mindfulness succeeding one another, remaining unshakable from beginning to end, without substitution day or night! Alas for the age of the Final Dharma, where people pursue external objects and lose the truth!

How noble is our Master! For the sake of the Way, he has forgotten his own body. Having entered the thousand peaks, it was as if he were treading upon the edge of a blade; thus he attained the samādhi known as "Non-contention.
He turned away from external conditions and took beans for pearls; their radiance was vivid and distinct, and his mind and environment remained in a state of suchness.

His shadow did not leave the mountains; his traces did not enter the secular world. His austere discipline was lofty and imposing; his pure influence swept all around. The fourfold assembly came to take refuge in him, and he partook of rice and gruel according to circumstances.
With a single flavor and an even mind, each person prepared their own sustenance; through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, they entered directly into the state of non-arising.
Therefore, at the very end, he rose up and went forth. With a single body of bare discipline, not a thread of silk hung upon him.
For seventy-nine years, he cast everything down in its entirety; coming, he was unattached; going, he left no trace. Thus, I call him a true spiritual friend.
The shadow of the stupa stretches across the void; its radiance flows to Mount Nanyue. With the mark of the broad and long tongue, he speaks ceaselessly and fervently.
Where waters flow and winds stir, there is mindfulness of the Buddha and mindfulness of the Dharma. This is my public work, a precious raft for those lost at the ford.
Epitaph for the Founder and First Abbot, Master Gufeng Chun, of the Imperially Established Great Huguo Cishou Temple.

When the World-Honored One preached the Dharma, as discussed in the Tripitaka, it was said that manifesting bodies according to the capacities of beings is all the true mark (*dharmatā*). [He] plucked a flower...
Addressing the assembly: "Kāśyapa smiled" means that by touching objects one clarifies the mind; this is the direct transmission and pointing directly.
Those who studied the Buddha in antiquity who understood this may be said to possess the True Dharma Eye. As for the Chan Master Gufeng, he first appeared in the body of a layman.
In the end, he took the form of a bhikṣu. He benefited sentient beings according to conditions; no one could fathom his hidden resonance with the Dharma.
How could this be sought through the two truths alone? I have carefully examined the Master’s biography: his name was Juechun. He was a native of Xincheng in Baoding. His father was Song Qin.
His mother was Lady Zhang. From birth, his nature was such that he did not consume meat or alcohol; as a child, he delighted in sitting in the lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

Upon reaching adulthood, he took no pleasure in managing worldly affairs or engaging in productive labor. Although his parents forced him to marry, he remained skilled in contemplating emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and practiced the conduct of detachment from desire.
In each assembly, various good sons would convene a Dharma gathering for Prajñā and Perfect Enlightenment (*Samyak-saṃbodhi*). The Master was the eldest among them;
naturally gifted and quick-witted, at the age of twenty-seven, he abandoned his home to travel afar to the capital, where he ascended the altar to receive the lay precepts.
The Great Good Knowledge-holder, Master Baozang Cheng, was expounding the Dharma in the royal city. The Master went there to pay his respects and attained a profound resonance with the teachings.

He immediately underwent tonsure and took up the duties of a disciple. Although his master occupied the lowest seat in the assembly, even when performing tasks such as cooking or pounding grain, he never failed to take the lead with his own body.

Cheng Gong possessed qualities that made him worthy of being served as a teacher, and [the disciple’s] resolve became even firmer. After three years had passed, Gong finally commanded him to receive full ordination;
he then followed the two Dharma Masters Shouxin and Wugai to hear various sutras, including the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Complete Enlightenment*, and the *Śūraṅgama*.
Having attained a profound realization through the words, "When the four great elements separate, where is this delusory body?

he thereafter established Huayan and Yuanjue practice halls in every location he visited, never missing a single day for a year. The royal capital was moved by his transformative influence, as if Kapilavastu itself had been transformed.
Throughout the central regions and the outer dependencies, such [praise] continued for over ten years.
In the *Xinyou* year of the Jiajing era, Lord Huang of the Imperial Household Department and Lord Jiao of the Imperial Bodyguard reconstructed Puan Temple and invited the Master to reside there.
For nearly twenty years, the Master occupied only his private quarters, while inviting Dharma Masters Jiang, Daqian, Zhi’an, and others to propagate the two schools of Tiantai and Xianshou.
In the *Ren-shen* year of the Longqing era, the late Emperor first honored the Buddhist path and established the Jixiang (Auspicious) Dharma-assembly at Puan.

The Master presided over the altar and its rites; his sincerity moved the divine, and imperial favors were bestowed in abundance. All provisions for the vegetarian offerings were provided from the imperial treasury.
In the first year of the current reign, the two Imperial Mothers performed great Buddhist services to pray for the blessing of the state and the altars of soil and grain. All that was established...
The altar for the fast was mostly held at the Master’s residence. He had once been granted a brocade *kāṣāya* embroidered with the thousand Buddhas.
All those within the Imperial Scripture Workshop who performed Buddhist rites invariably followed him.

In the *bingzi* year of the Wanli era, the present Emperor, in accordance with the virtuous intentions of the Empress Dowager Cisheng Xuanwen Mingxu Huang Taihou, completed the construction of Daci’ou Monastery by imperial decree; he then immediately appointed the Master as its abbot.
The Abbot appointed him to ordain one śrāmaṇera as his disciple and issued an imperial decree for his works to be collated and included in the Great Canon.

The Master took charge of this project; whatever Buddhist activities he propagated and elucidated were entirely in accord with the Imperial Will. At that time, throughout the land, within the Dharma-gate...
Everyone recognized the Master as a great banner of the Dharma. In his daily life, he would receive the fourfold assembly, speaking only of the *Complete Enlightenment* (Yuánjué) with these verses:
"To know illusion is to be free from it; no expedient means are required. To be free from illusion is awakening itself; there is no gradual progression.

He also spoke of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*'s samādhi of illusoriness, or would cite and comment upon the "upward" kōans of the ancients to awaken and inspire them. In his leisure time, he would practice walking meditation.

Whether standing, sitting, or reclining, he would frequently utter exclamations of "Dududu" in private conversation; upon seeing or hearing this, those present would immediately alter their countenances.

No one recognized him as a practitioner of secret conduct (*mi-haṅ-pa*). Throughout his life, his movements never departed from his immediate surroundings, yet he widely disseminated the style of the lineage, such that no one could fathom its limits.
He was commonly referred to as a "Great Being in Fleshly Form. One night, he summoned his disciples and informed them that he was slightly unwell.
He sat upright for three days. Then, with a serene countenance, he gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name; following the sound, he passed away peacefully.
This was on the seventeenth day of the fourth month in the ninth year of the Wanli era. He was born in the Xunwei year of the Zhengde era and died in the Xinsi year of the Wanli era.
His worldly age was seventy-one, and his monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇerī*) was forty-odd years. He had fifteen disciples who received full ordination and over eighty grand-disciples.
Originally serving as the *Senglu Shanshi* (Director of the Monastic Registry) by Imperial Favor, he now presides over the abbotship of Cishou Monastery.

The Master’s entire body was enshrined in the rear garden of the temple. The Holy Mother lamented his passing and bestowed several measures of gold to construct a stupa as a monument to him. The inscription reads:
The Dharma-body is like space: it is neither sound nor form. It manifests forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water;

it is thus at every point of contact. What is real and what is conventional? Even the body of a bhikṣu is likewise like an empty valley. Such was the ancient style, yet it has given way to this age of semblance.

With a lofty and transcendent resolve, he performed great Buddhist deeds; both the ultimate and conventional truths were manifested together, and both form and spirit were wondrously perfected. Without leaving the bustling marketplace, he propagated the Supreme Way;
his spiritual resonance was manifest and clear, and the heavens and men were harmonious and reverent. Operating silently like the pivot of a wheel, dragons descended and tigers submitted.
The refined principles reach the Purple Palace; with sincerity, the Northern Dipper turns its favor. The Way of the Dharma flourishes; like a ball rolling upon a smooth board, harmony prevails.

As soon as the Buddhist temples (Brahma-shalas) arise and the jade palaces (Ling-gongs) are first established, the wind fills the entire realm, gathering like thunder and lightning. A single pipe brings forth spring; the reeds and ashes begin to stir.
The Great Earth radiates its brilliance—this truly begins from here. Who is this Master? Is he transformation or illusion? How could he be subject to the secret [seal]?

He passed away. Having practiced expedient means for over seventy years, the Master was gone in the time it takes to eat a meal; those who watched were left in foolish doubt, their feverish dreams yet unawakened.
With a snap of his fingers he returned to the void, breaking into a smile. In a deep abyss ten thousand fathoms deep, he cast but a single hook.
The stupa’s banner soared into the air; long pines were shrouded in mist. Amidst the moonlight and the sound of the wind, the true mechanism alone was revealed.
Epitaph for the Eighth Abbot of Longhua Temple on Mount Jintai, Master Zheng (Zheng’an) The master’s name was Guangzheng;
his courtesy name was Ruian. He was the son of the Sun family of Jintai. By nature he possessed many eccentricities;

even as a child, he did not conform to the ways of other boys, and those who saw him marveled at him. His heart delighted in Buddhist affairs, and from time to time he would murmur words concerning renunciation. Longhua...

Master Maogong of Rongyang served as the Left Director of the Sangha Registry (Senglü Zuǎnchàojiào) and was renowned for his exemplary conduct. Once, while attending a vegetarian feast hosted by the Sun family, he saw the Master at the age of seven, possessing an extraordinary spirit;
he therefore requested him to become a śrāmaṇera and subsequently ordained him as a disciple under his senior attendant, Jiansheng.
From his youth, the Master delighted in performing Buddhist services through vocal chanting and refined his three karmas, diligently practicing the six periods of daily meditation.
He constantly maintained his resolve to pursue the higher path. At the age of thirty, he ascended the platform to receive full ordination.

During the reign of Da-tong, the Dharma teachings flourished; he served with diligence and heard many essential points of the Dharma. In the first year of the Longqing era, the Grand Minister of Rites nominated him as the abbot of Longhua Temple.
The Master extensively opened the Dharma community, inviting masters of both the Chan and Exegetical schools and gathering scholars from all quarters to study and examine the Great [Scriptures].
He propagated the two fundamental tenets of the Shaoshi and Tiantai schools. As for Chan Master Daken Run, he was the one who revived the Cao-Dong lineage;

indeed, many who became masters and patriarchs in various quarters first gained their start here. When Chan Master Deng Miaofeng was in his early years, he sought out the Master on account of the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*).
The Master introduced him to high officials and nobles, whereby Miaofeng’s reputation for the Way became widely renowned. Master Miaofeng...

The gradual progression of the Dharma-gates likewise relies upon his support. His Majesty now reveres the Triple Gem, and among the renowned monasteries and masters throughout the realm, those who perform Buddhist rites mostly emerge from this master’s school;
they are generally hailed as a treasury of merit. In the spring of the Dingchou year,
The Master Miao lived in seclusion with me at Mount Qingliang. The Master was so devotedly enamored of it that he traveled to the Five Peaks, searching amidst snow and ice.
Before long, he took up his staff and traveled south to pay homage to the Great Being at Putuo, then entered Tiantai, where he lived in seclusion atop Tongxuan Peak.
For three years, he subsisted on bird droppings like a nesting bird, single-mindedly practicing the Samādhi of One Practice until he attained a profound realization.

He then took his leave and returned to Eastern Wu. There, he paid homage to the śarīra relics at Changgan. He sailed upstream along the Yangtze River, ascended Mount Jiuhua, and climbed Mount Kuanglu.
He befriended the Yellow Dragon and the White Deer, bowed to the Five Elders while gazing upon Mount Xianglu, and circumambulated the Mañjuśrī Sūtra Terrace three times.
Having cleansed his mind and attained profound insight, he found rest. He traveled to Huangmei to seek certification of his realization.

Continuing his journey, he gazed upon Wudang Mountain and reached Mount Heng (Nanyue), seeking the place where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* was realized. Upon returning, he entered the assembly at Funiu to undergo further refinement for three months before departing.
In the spring of the ninth year of the Wanli era (1581), the year of Xinsi, the Master was fifty-four years old. After staying there for a short while, Master Miao...
Together with me, he established the Great Assembly at Qingliang. Master [Zhixu] and Master Ping of Shuanglin, as well as Master Yun, all entered the Dharma society together.
In the spring of the Renwu year, when the assembly concluded, the Master again joined me in seclusion on Mount Taihang. By the beginning of winter, the Master returned to his former residence.
The following year, I too traveled eastward across the sea, vowing to return home together with the Master. This was the Jia Shen year.
By imperial command of the Empress Dowager Cisheng, I accompanied Master Miao to offer meals to the monastic community at various famous mountains in Qin, Jin, Yi, and Luo.
Thereupon, I passed through the Passes to visit Luyaya, crossed the river to ascend Mount Hua, and toured Chang’an.

I visited the Yanta Monastery to view the stone image left there, sought out the site where Kumārajīva translated the scriptures at the Caotang Hermitage, spent the summer retreat at Guifeng, gazed upon Mount Taibai and Mount Taiyi, and briefly traversed the Xiaoguan Pass.
He packed his belongings and headed east. Entering Mount Funiu once more, he visited Mount Song and Mount Shao to inquire after the direct transmission of the Patriarch.

He wept for Master Run and sought out Master Bai-ma before returning home. Not long thereafter, he again received the Imperial command to carry the Great Canon to Mount Tiantai and Mount Lu, and was subsequently dispatched to Mount Qingliang to report back.
The Master sighed deeply and said: "I am but a single, humble monk, yet several times I have been graced by the Imperial summons. He stroked [his beard].

Reflecting upon his virtue, [the Emperor] felt ashamed, wondering how he could ever be worthy of it. He consequently cited illness as an excuse to dwell in solitude, withdrawing from others and cutting off all traces of his presence.

Matters concerning the mountain monastery had long been entrusted to his disciples. Living in constant contentment, he held no interest in the world. Throughout his life, he had put himself last and others first, never regarding material things as a concern.

His precepts were like pearls and his mind like the moon; he was like autumn dew upon a cold sky. His appearance was ancient and his spirit was pure, like a tall pine tree or a solitary crane amidst the melancholy air.

He was indeed radiant. He was one who could be approached with affection yet not drawn too near; he could be treated with informal respect yet not neglected. It was difficult to find anyone who was not a paragon of the Dharma-eye;
he was truly a model for the monastic community of his era. Daguan Ke, whom I have taken as my teacher, once said to me:
"The Longhua of our school is like the mirror of Qin; it can truly reflect a person’s very liver and gall. Furthermore, it is like a wish-fulfilling gem wrapped in cotton—truly at one's fingertips."
He took them; there was nothing he did not find sufficient. At one time, his discernment was such as this. The Master had been afflicted by illness for a full year.

I went from across the sea to visit him. The Master took my hand, wept, and said to me: "Life and death are like dreams and illusions; departure and arrival are like night and dawn. This is not what I grieve over.
It is only that I cannot return with you, thereby failing the covenant made between us at the mountains and seas. Now, in a single moment, we part forever."

I pray that you will lead Master Wang to the Pure Land. As for those discarded fragments of this world—the various disciples who regard you as they did me when I was alive—do you not see that I am as good as dead?
Furthermore, he said: "The Dharma-gate has fallen into decline; this is what I grieve over most deeply.
Masters Miaoda and Er, and the various worthies such as Mizaigong, were all the most outstanding talents of their generation; yet now, I alone remain."
"May you, in your aspirations, forget the self for the sake of the Dharma. I pray that you will convey my thanks on my behalf. Not long after, he summoned his disciples and said:

"I have relied upon being a son of the Buddha, yet I feel ashamed that I have failed to contribute to the Dharma-gate. However, throughout my life, I have maintained this resolve, never daring to betray the Buddha's grace.
While I was alive, people called me insufficient; when I die, I shall have more than enough. You must exert yourselves. I am now departing; you must [follow my example]."

"Do not forget the Eastern Sea. Fashion a robe for me as a token of gratitude. Having spoken these words, he passed away on the twenty-third day of the fifth month in the seventeenth year of the Wanli era.
The Master was born in the Wuzi year of the Jiajing era; his worldly lifespan was sixty-two years.
His dharma-ordination years were thirty-something. He had two disciples who attained ordination:
his disciple Sun Jitan, who maintained the master’s funerary chamber and interred his entire body at the left side of Longxi Temple in Haidian, northwest of the capital.

In the tenth month of winter that year, Jitan, carrying out the master’s final command, traveled on foot across the sea bearing a set of his patched robes. When I heard the news of his passing, I sighed, "Alas! How tragic!"
"Are you alive or dead? Who is your teacher? [The Master] then recounted his life story in detail as follows, and then composed this inscription:

"The body that pervades the entire Dharma-realm cultivates the practices of Samantabhadra. Through the majestic spiritual power of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi, all things are brilliantly reflected together. At times he manifests as a dhūta practitioner..."
Whether dwelling in market stalls or amidst the dust of the marketplace and mountain forests, everything is nothing other than the work of the Buddha.

It is said that our Master, manifesting in the form of a bhikṣu, took the *Śīlanetra-sūtra* and the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as his guiding models. At the Yuanjue Monastery, there is a gathering from the ten directions; those who come should know this.
Without interior or exterior, like a wish-fulfilling jewel and resembling a treasury of merit, it produces wondrous benefits.

Though offerings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were brought up from the zenith, a single bowl of fragrant rice was seen; all who saw or heard of it received deliverance. It split open Mount Tiantai.
He trampled over Mount Lu; it was like the blooming of a lotus, like awakening from a great dream. Having traversed the entire world, he gathered the myriad realms within his bag.
Returning empty-handed, he had no money for trade. For over sixty years, through the nights and days of birth and death, he called out, but could not turn his head back.
Having first reached the other shore, he cast aside his skull and buried it in a mound of sand; a stupa marks the vast sky, its shadow sinking into the autumn waters.
This is the Master’s eternal body, manifest and clear as this.
Epigraphic Inscription for the Memorial Tower of Layman Xu Zhengguang at Longquan Temple on Mount Wutai.
Observe how the true realm is quiescent, yet the manifestations of its transformations are manifold; the paths of the holy and the mundane diverge, yet the traces of altruistic deeds remain.
There are distinctions [between them]. Thus, illusory manifestations take many forms, and shimmering lights assume ten thousand aspects.
As for those who rely on the power of aspiration to sustain the mind and employ *stūpas* to manifest their vows—this was seen in the case of the layman Zhengguang.

This layman’s surname was Xu; he was a native of Baoding County in Bazhou. His father was Shen and his mother was Lady Gao. From birth, the youth possessed extraordinary signs; at the age of one year...

She was able to recount events from her previous lives, and her deportment was as refined as that of a celestial being. In the thirty-fourth year of the Jiajing era, at the age of seven, she was selected by lot to enter the palace precincts.

She was enrolled in the Bureau of Inner Attendants (*neihan ju*) to study, promoted to an official of the bureau, and instructed in the rites of internal governance while presiding over the Secretariat (*bigu*).

Thereupon, she became proficient in the established precedents. At the commencement of the Longqing era, she was promoted to the *yuxian* (Imperial Presence). Diligent and prudent, she rendered distinguished service.

At the beginning of the Wanli era, His Majesty ascended the throne and recorded his meritorious deeds. [He] was promoted to the rank of *zhāizi* (tablet-bearer) for reporting internal affairs at the Qianqing Palace.
Serving through three reigns, he was reverently cautious and humble. He attended to the daily needs of the Empress Dowager, remaining vigilant morning and night.

He harmonized the central pivot of governance and assisted in the mechanisms of civil and military administration, exerting great influence. As his virtue and station grew ever more exalted, he placed deep faith in the Triple Gem throughout the capital.

Outside Chongwen Gate of the capital city, he established the Jianmingyin Monastery and printed and distributed one complete set of the Buddhist Tripitaka, appointing the śramaṇa Yongqing as its abbot.
Furthermore, at the former Luling Pass on the road to Wutai Mountain in Shanxi, he renovated Longquan Monastery.
He memorialized the Empress Dowager, who ordained the śrāmaṇera Yuanjian and conferred upon him the rank of Left Jueyi of the Monastic Registry, appointing him as the abbot of this temple.
Furthermore, to the north of Quyang County in Zhending, he reconstructed one Fengxiang Temple on a site of over three *qǐng* and several *mǔ*.
This was provided to sustain the incense and lamps of Longquan and to receive guests from the ten directions, including those from all the famous mountains and great monasteries within the realm.
Those who are graced by the merit of the Holy Mother do not fail to silently assist the Imperial Way and propagate her compassionate transformation.
As the single rain universally moistens all, sentient beings obtain blessings. Although the Layman dwells within the deep palace, his clothing is but plain cloth;

he willingly partakes of vegetarian food and constantly loathes birth and death, vowing to seek liberation. He attends court and reveres the rites, remaining unchanged through cold and heat, even to the point of drawing blood [to write].
He transcribed several fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna*, and the "Expedient Means" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
He erected a stūpa at the southeastern foot of Longquan Hill to manifest his power of aspiration and sustain his resolve.

May his merit flow through vast kalpas, quenching this fierce flame and forever dwelling in cool serenity; may he look forward to taking refuge in future lives and achieve completion in this single lifetime. Thus he intended.
The adamantine seed and spiritual sprout shall abide eternally within the field of merit. Alas! Is this layman one who has come directly to receive the entrustment?
Or does he perform the work of a Buddha by means of illusory manifestations as a human or celestial being?

How is it that his wisdom is so profound and his resolve so firm? Once his meritorious deeds were accomplished, he commanded his subordinate official Cheng Jin to hold a staff and prostrate himself before him.
The practitioner Haiyin requested that his deeds be recorded; thus, I composed this inscription for him:
"Heaven and earth, in their creative transformation, nurture the spiritual and produce the refined. Thus a sage was sent down—how could one distinguish left from right? Who was this sage?"
Only the son of Xu possessed the spirit of a true man; though his manifested form was that of a woman. As for this woman—what was she?
She was truly a grandmother in her internal instruction. Had it not been for her, who would have assisted the Sagely Mother? Serving through three reigns, her rank was among the Nine Ministers;

she aided in transformation and harmonized the primal source, leaving behind these great achievements. Vast is the wind of her compassion; brilliant is the sun of the Buddha. Throughout the land and under heaven, there is none who does not [revere her].
For the sake of the nation, in every place of practice and at every site of treasure, I only wish for adornment; who would distinguish between self and others?
Dwelling amidst the dust and toil of the world, my will seeks the Pure Land. Having received the Three Refuges, I universally cultivate the Six Perfections;

copying, receiving, and upholding the Mahāyāna sūtras and verses, I vow to cast off this body and ascend directly to the stage of Buddhahood. Alas for those dreamers in the long, dark night! How magnificent!

The man of realization regards death as life. Though his traces are bound to the royal palace, his heart dwells among hills and ravines. His firm integrity towers above the clouds, like a long pine or a solitary crane.
Like the artisan of Yan who created a living being, who is the borrowed and who is the real? The dragon maiden offering the pearl—her deed was as if divine.
The stupa stands as a mark upon the Great Wall, establishing peace and security for the capital region. May it offer prayers for the Emperor’s well-being, that heaven and earth endure forever.
Epitaph for the Founder of Pujian, Master Baozang Cheng.
The Great Master Baozang was named Zicheng. He was the son of the Liu family from Dezhou, Shandong. In his youth, he apprenticed in the smithing trade;
yet even amidst the tongs and hammers, he understood that one should apply oneself to the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation), following the method of the Buddhist goldsmiths. Thus he practiced.
Xin had been of age for some years when his father passed away early. His mother remained a widow, and by nature he was profoundly filial, exhausting all his heart and strength in providing for her.
At the age of thirty, he developed the aspiration for the transcendental life and received the tonsure under Master Tan at Zhonglou Temple in his home province;

he immediately established himself in Chan practice, training in the gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. As the Master intended to set out on a pilgrimage (*paryaṭana*), his mother was elderly and lacked support. The Master addressed her by her formal title and took up her burden.

He carried her away on his back and traveled far to the four quarters. Whenever he begged for food, he would offer it to his mother beneath trees or among tombs, celebrating her longevity with such joy that the offerings were no less than those prepared on a formal hearth.
Later, he went to the West Mountain of the capital, to the Hundred Flowers Valley, where he stayed for several years.

The local people held him in high esteem, and their offerings grew increasingly abundant; yet the Master kept nothing more than a single ladle of rice, having no other provisions besides. Thus it was.
He lived out his mother’s natural lifespan and was buried according to the *caitya* (cremation) rites. A *stūpa* was erected to commemorate his filial piety and righteousness;

it still exists today. Subsequently, he built a hermitage and resided at Eojapo on Dayu Peak. The high-ranking official, Duke Fu, assembled the community and invited the Master to reside at Puan Temple in the capital.
Not long after, a lay donor named Zhang established the Puji Hermitage.

Four *li* outside Fu Cheng Pass was the Yuan (Garden), where travelers from the ten directions were received. In the eighth month of autumn in the Gengxu year of the Jiajing era, the Great Lū (Mongols) invaded the capital.
The three sides of the imperial city were without gaps and suffered many routs and collapses; only the western wall remained under siege.
Just then, the Lū chieftain led several thousand cavalrymen of the Hu people, galloping directly to the head of the hermitage, where they tethered their horses and loitered about.

The chieftain suddenly entered the hermitage, followed by his retinue. The Master looked at them with a weary, foolish smile and scolded them, saying, "You slave chieftains, do not touch my things recklessly!
The Master had previously arranged fresh fruits on the steps; when the chieftain saw a persimmon that was like fire, he took it with delight and began to eat it.
The Master scolded him loudly, "This is not edible! The chieftain, fearing he would be betrayed, forced himself to eat it despite its bitterness.

It was bitter and astringent. The Master then took away the persimmon and gave him a *bimbi* fruit instead. The captive ate it and found it sweet; he shouted with joy, thinking that the Master had not deceived him.
Biting his finger, he warned the crowd, saying, "There is a man here among you; do not kill him recklessly," and then he stuck a command arrow into the ground and departed.
Shortly thereafter, a captive pursued the son of the Wang family into the hermitage. The man fled and hid beneath the Buddha statue. The captive—
He caught sight of it. Just as the blade was about to descend, the Master seized the captive with his hand, wrested the blade away, and threw it to the ground.
The man was ultimately saved alive. After a short while, the captives also gradually withdrew. Chan Master Daguanke often praised him, saying: "The Master faced the enemy alone;
with a single voice he commanded, directed, and rebuked them, saving tens of thousands of lives. This is truly the manifestation of a Great Heavenly Being."
The General himself came to preach the Dharma for him. How could this have been achieved by the strength of a single great general alone?

A virtuous layman from Hangzhou named Shao dreamed that the temple guardian was urging his master to accept offerings; he thus surrendered his heart in refuge and built a Maitreya Hermitage to welcome the Master.

The Master lived constantly without concern for food or drink, wearing robes made of discarded rags; his single alms bowl held nothing more than what was necessary. Whenever he received gifts or offerings...
He gave away all his rice and flour to relieve the poor until he was empty-handed, not even possessing a single grain.
He would not go to his own patrons for alms, but instead sat facing a wall at the entrance of his hut, enduring hunger. After some time, those who knew of his situation sent him offerings.

When the food was exhausted, they blocked the gate as before; this became their regular practice. Later, when the Puan Temple was completed, the Master returned to the monastery. His disciples gradually made progress.
Initially, Master Chun applied himself to his studies with great diligence, and the Master singled out Master Chun among the assembly for his hardships.

Whether in bitter cold or humid heat, he subjected him to menial labor and lowly service, always leading by example. Not even one in a hundred of these tasks was deemed acceptable [as too difficult]. There was no [task he would not undertake].
One who understood his meaning was the Master [Dao’an], who, as he was about to pass away, looked toward the assembly and said: "My possession of purity is like a tree having its trunk.
As for the flourishing and luxuriant growth of its branches and leaves, they provide abundant shade and shelter. Do you all understand this?"
Before long, he passed away without illness on the first day of the second month in the thirty-ninth year of the Jiajing era.
The Master’s worldly age was eighty-nine, and his years as a monk were fifty-odd.

After the Master’s passing, during the time of the late Emperor’s final testament, the present Emperor’s Holy Mother completed the construction of Cishou Temple and invited Master Chun to serve as its abbot.
The Abbot appointed his disciple Liaoning as his successor. After the Master passed away, he further appointed his grandson Benzai as the Abbot.
When Benzai retired from the monastery due to illness, he was succeeded in his duties by his disciple Yuansheng.
The Imperial Grace subsequently rebuilt Ci'en Temple for Benzai’s private use, so that he might rest in his old age. Such were the Master’s descendants and their lineage.
It is flourishing, just as you have said. Is this not indeed a sign of the profound and hidden retribution for virtue accorded by the Way of Heaven?

In the winter of the Jia-wu year of the Wanli era, while I was following my karmic conditions within the royal city, his grandson Liaojian and others came to me at Dazheng Temple requesting that I compose an inscription. Thereupon, I composed this inscription: [The Inscription] (Note: As the source text provides only the introductory prose and the concluding title for the inscription, the full inscription itself is not translated here.)
The Way of Heaven has no partiality; it ever favors the virtuous. With such brilliance above, how could it not be true? True, indeed, is that which is imperishable. Behold the body as having no self.
Were there no Perfected One who possesses nothing, how could one perceive its longevity? It is my Master alone who, through the accumulation of filial thought, has attained this.

Transcending the mundane and departing from the secular, his virtue is truly the foundation; manifesting through the gates of transformation, his merit is manifold. By means of diverse skillful expedients, he established these magnificent achievements;
because he realized non-arising, he therefore does not die. That the branches and trunk spread so luxuriantly is truly due to the seed.
Sheltering and protecting humans and devas, with its roots buried a thousand feet deep, this stupa stands majestically for a thousand autumns and ten thousand years.
This is the Stele Inscription for the Venerable Master Wuxia of Cihui Temple.
His name was Mingyu; his courtesy name was Wuxia. He was the son of the Liu family of Longju in An’uo, Western Sichuan. From birth, he did not care for...
He managed his livelihood through agriculture and industry. By nature he was stubborn and did not harmonize with worldly sentiments.

He married into the Wang family and fathered three sons. The eldest son was intelligent and profoundly filial; although the Master loved him dearly, he made no plans for the son’s worldly advancement.

He constantly took the Buddha as his primary concern, and whenever he made offerings to his two elderly parents, he invariably regarded vegetarian fare as the height of filial piety. His two parents...
This was his own peace. The Master held the transcendence of the mundane world and liberation from secular life as his constant concern, never setting it aside for even a moment.
When the two elders passed away, the Master was forty-six years old; he then resolutely abandoned his wife and children to wander among those beyond the secular realm.
At that time, his eldest son was twelve years old and followed him with longing. They reached Loutou Mountain in Bazhou and stayed with the Abbot Hai’an at Dongyang Sea.
The father and son both shaved their heads to become *śrāmaṇeras*. On the fifth day of the fifth month in the third year of the Longqing era, they were ordained with the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
From then on, while the Master took his eldest son on a pilgrimage, he supervised his studies and made him a disciple; thus, father and son followed one another.

He traveled ten thousand *li* on foot, visiting famous mountains and seeking instruction from masters of wisdom. His ascetic practices were peerless; he ate but one meal per day, subsisting on husks and vegetables without any grain.
Whether beneath trees or among graves, he remained content with whatever circumstances arose. From then on until the end of his life, his side never touched his mat.
At the beginning of the Wanli era, he visited Putuo, passed through Jinling, and reached the capital. He then toured Mount Wutai and stayed at Santasi.

At the temple, he venerated the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. The scripture contains six hundred thousand characters; for each character, he performed one prostration. Every day and night, he invariably performed three thousand bows.

He continued in this manner for three full cycles until the twelfth year. Subsequently, he went to Bifeng Temple in the capital and venerated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which contains sixty thousand or more characters.
For each character, he performed one prostration, never flagging day or night, just as before, for twelve years.

Za. His eldest son, who had become a śrāmaṇera, was also growing in both years and virtue. He frequently attended lecture halls to study and practice the *Avataṃsaka*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Śūraṅgama*, *Awakening of Faith*, and various sūtras and śāstras such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
He was skilled at elucidating and enlightening the ignorant, yet his service to his father grew increasingly diligent day by day.
At that time, everyone marveled, saying that there were few teacher and disciple like these; their reputation had already spread throughout both the inner and outer circles.

In the seventeenth year, the Eunuch Supervisors (Naegwan) and Grand Eunuchs (Taegwan), Wang Gong and others, wished to establish a *seongsa* (monastery) to invite the Master’s disciples as a center for propagating the Dharma, and also to serve as a place for the Master to retire in his old age.
They selected a site about two *li* outside the gate of Fucheng and donated funds to construct a temple for him to reside in.

When the temple was completed and they requested a name plaque, the Holy Mother (the Empress Dowager) commended them and bestowed the name "Cihui" (Compassionate Wisdom). The Great Ancestor [also] [honored it].
Li Gong of Baitangxuan recorded these events. One day, the Master said to his disciples: "I have been bound to this Sahā world for seventy-two years.
Now that I am overtaken by old age and illness, what benefit is there in remaining here much longer?

I shall return. You should hold the Dharma in your hearts and do not give rise to attachment. Thereupon, he ceased eating. For ten days, his recitation of the Buddha's name was unceasing, the sound of his voice being as [clear as before].
Zhong’s countenance appeared robust. His disciples asked him about the great matter of life and death. The Master merely said, "He-he he-he;
he-he he-he. It is not deluded thought; it is not true knowledge. After a long silence, he asked, "What do you say it is? He answered on his own behalf:
"A grain merchant at the Great Tong Bridge, originally a man from the south delivering rice, facing the moment of crisis."
He requested a bath and changed his robes. Sitting upright and holding his prayer beads, he recited the Buddha’s name with increasing urgency and lamentation, crying out repeatedly, “Buddha!

Buddha! Buddha! He then overturned the iron ox-cart to return to the Buddha-land; his voice ceased, and he passed away on the nineteenth day of the first month of the spring season in the year Yiwu of the Wanli era.
The Master was born in the seventh month of the Jia-shen year of the Jiading era; his worldly age was seventy-two, and his monastic seniority was two years.
Sixteen. On the [day] of the [month], his entire remains were enshrined in the pagoda at Huangcun.
His disciple Zhen Gui—now the Dharma Master Cihui—was with me when I held my almsbowl in the royal city and dwelt in the Maitreya Pavilion.

Gui maintained a record of his master’s actual conduct and earnestly requested me to compose this "Sea-Seal" (Haiyin) document to record these events. Although the Master was illiterate throughout his life, he found great ease and inspiration as the moment of departure approached.
Thus it is. Is this not one whose heel-cord has been severed, returning home along the very path? Thereupon, he composed an inscription:
"The mechanism of birth and death resides in but a single aperture. Welcome, welcome! The wooden man dons his cap; father and son are gathered in harmony."

Form and shadow look upon one another; what difference is there between the mundane and the supramundane? When we look back at Old Pang of old, who dismantled his home and scattered his estate, today it appears he did not quite let go.
How can this master compare? He is as if a single orifice were blocked; he stubbornly twists iron with forced strength.
Directly emerging from the cage. Pang did not marry his daughter; Gong did not abandon his son. With the same underlying intent, each attained their own advantage.
For seventy-two years, half-monk and half-layman; today’s splendor is sufficient in every way. A single stupa soars into the void.
The ten directions are eternally abiding; though the physical structure crumbles, the stupa remains. The Dharma-body is fully revealed.
*Epitaph for the Venerable Master Huàn of Miǎn’ān on Mount Sānjiǎo* I have carefully examined the formal record:
The Master’s name was Rúhuàn, with the style name Miǎn’ān. He was a son of the Lín family of Pútíán. His father was Huán. The Master was noble and unconventional.

Possessing an extraordinary spirit, he studied Confucianism from his youth. At the age of fourteen, he was enrolled among the students. In the village lived a student named Xia Zhishi, who was well-versed in the Buddhist scriptures;
the Master associated with him most closely. One day, the student said to the Master, "Your lips are upturned and your teeth are exposed."

"It is not a sign of longevity. The Master asked in astonishment, "What must be done for it to be so? Sheng replied, "I have heard that reciting the name of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara brings prayers no response;
simply maintain his title and the efficacy will manifest of itself. The Master then followed this practice with diligent devotion for two years, and his lips were indeed reunited.
At the age of nineteen, when the Japanese pirates invaded Min, both his parents perished in the conflict, and the Master wept bitterly.
He said, "Is the life of a human being truly like this? Why linger so long for one's hometown? Thereupon, he shook out his robes and wandered among the rivers and lakes for two years.
He then entered Mount Lu to attend upon Master Bianrong. Rong asked, "Virtuous One, where are you from, and what have you come here to do?
The Master replied, "I am a man from Min; I have come to seek longevity. Rong said, "Where there is growth, there must necessarily be..."
[The Master] said, "It is too short. Why not study non-arising (*anutpāda*)? He asked, "How does one study non-arising? I beg the Master for instruction.

Yunrong said, "Try first shaving off your hair and beard, setting aside all external conditions, and chewing over a single phrase that has no meaning or flavor. After a long time, you will reach a point of certainty; only then may I speak of non-arising to you.
The Master immediately shaved his head and received the tonsure, being given the name Ruhuan (Like an Illusion). He stayed there for a short while.
He then departed for Mayashan in Qishui to attend upon the Abbot Wuwai. After residing there for three years, he went into seclusion at Doufangshan for another five years.
He subsequently took up his staff and traveled north to the capital, where he visited various great masters (*jñānin*).
He relied upon the two Dharma Masters Xian and Li to hear the profound meanings of the various sutras; all the elders held him in high esteem. Later, there was a certain General Tian.
He was a man from Qi. Upon seeing the Master’s refined composure, he attempted to distract him with worldly matters. The Master laughed and said, "Would a sea dragon deign to enter a ditch?

He then took up his staff and returned to Jiufeng. Disciples gathered there in great numbers; the Master frequently used the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to clarify the essential points of the mind for the assembly.
Guo Zhengyu, a member of the Hanlin Academy, was residing at home due to the mourning of his late mother when he visited the Master at Jiufeng.
They took great delight in each other’s company. The Master (the Duke) then advanced and requested, saying:

"I have observed that those who discourse on Chan in this world often take staff-blowing, shouting, and sharp-witted repartee as the highest attainment, yet when one examines their actual conduct, these are merely peripheral matters.

If this is the case, it would be better not to pursue such things, but rather to uphold the scriptural teachings, refine the precepts, practice asceticism free from desire, and benefit all beings through compassion—this would be more excellent than what the Master does."
The Master said, "Indeed. This is not the fault of Chan, but rather the fault of those who study Chan. Alas!

As the distance from the Sage grows ever greater and the Dharma-gate declines, it is truly as you say; one might well shed tears for this. The Master disciplined himself with austere purity and had no personal attachments throughout his life.
Whatever he received, he would immediately give to others. Whenever he traveled, he carried nothing but a single alms bowl and three robes.
He went about barefoot, wearing nothing but straw sandals. Shen Jun, a high official of the Provincial Governor and Censor of Chu, was the Master’s closest friend.
When the disciples wished to acquire land for the incense and lamps, they presented the deed to Master Shen on behalf of the Master.

The Master rebuked them severely, saying, "If you do not diligently cultivate the field of merit within your own minds, why seek it from that petty district magistrate, Shen? The disciples did not heed him and requested the land privately. The Master became aware of this.
He then took up his staff and departed for Jiufeng. He traveled to Wugong and stayed at Jiyang Temple, where he closed his quarters and recited the Avataṃsaka Sūtra for three years.
He subsequently went to Sanjiaoshan in Tanzhou, the site where Mazu’s disciple Zongyin had founded a monastery.

Within a few years, it was transformed and renovated until it shone with new splendor, and his Dharma seat flourished greatly. One day, the Master said to the assembly: "Even at eighty, Zhaozhou still..."

"I am traveling on foot. Do my feet lack even a single pair of straw sandals? He then brushed his sleeves and departed for Mount Kuang-lu, entering Huanglong Temple where he stayed to lecture on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
When he reached the end of the second fascicle, the Master said to the assembly, "Let us set this aside for now;
furthermore, there is the 'final phrase' which I shall discuss with you all. Immediately thereafter, he manifested signs of illness and passed away six days later. The assembly...

Someone requested that he leave behind a verse. The Master said: "In departing from this world, I originally have no verse; it is but the deluded who seek traces in a dream. Space has no face or features; I ask space for its face and features. A disciple asked: "Regarding the Master’s sacred remains, may they be moved to Qishan? The Master said: [The remainder of the text follows: "Once moved, they will not remain; once returned, they will not stay. When the time comes, they will naturally go; when the time comes, they will naturally arrive. If you wish to know where they will go, look at the clouds in the sky. He then composed a verse: "The body is like a tree withered by frost, The mind is like the moon reflected in water. When the tree withers and the water dries, The moon and the tree both vanish. He then passed away. His remains were enshrined at Dongshan. Later, his disciples moved them to Qishan, where they remained until the Tang dynasty, after which they were moved again to Shuangfeng. They were subsequently moved back to Dongshan, where they remain to this day. The Master was seventy-three years old and had been a monk for forty-nine years. His posthumous title was Great Master Xuefeng. His stupa was named "Jingde" (Mirror Virtue). His Dharma heirs numbered one hundred and thirty-nine. Among them, twenty-five became patriarchs of various schools. The rest were renowned throughout the world. The Master’s teaching style was direct and unyielding; he did not permit students to harbor even a single thought. If anyone came seeking him, he would strike them immediately. He was thus known as the "Blind Ox. He often said: "If you can see me before I open my mouth, you may be my disciple. He also said: "If you can see me before I speak, you may be my disciple. He cherished the sufferings of this Sahā world and felt no attachment for the Land of Ultimate Bliss. "Why must one cling to the shadows of the past?

Tranquil illumination fills the three thousandfold world-system. Having finished speaking, he passed away. This was on a certain day of a certain month in the nineteenth year of the Wanli era. The Master was born in the *guisi* year of the Jiajing era;
his worldly lifespan was fifty-nine years, and his monastic seniority (*śramaṇa-varṣa*) was thirty-odd years. His disciples cremated him and subsequently [collected] his remains.

The stone was buried at a certain location on Mount Huanglong. Following his final instructions, the disciple Xingquan traveled to Guo, the Court Historian in Jiangxia, to request a record of his life and deeds.
In the ninth month of autumn in the Renchen year of the Wanli era, I was introduced to him by Guo, the Court Historian, and thus composed this stūpa inscription.
Having consulted the record, I have arranged the narrative and offer this inscription: [Insert Inscription Text Here]
The great ocean is vast and boundless; its flavor is entirely contained within a single drop of water. Sāgara swallows it, manifesting it as clouds and rain.

This single drop has neither interior nor exterior; it can be drawn up into the tip of a hair and dispersed throughout the sands of all worlds, falling in torrents and drenching the parched earth everywhere.

The three types of grasses and two kinds of trees—sour, sweet, bitter, and pungent—all grow and flourish, sprouting buds and developing trunks, provided they are not rootless and thus meet with ruin and destruction.
It is said: "My Master alone is the son of Sāgara; his poisonous breath overwhelms all, and those who touch him die."

Exhaling his breath forms clouds; contracting his breath forms ice. Sometimes cold, sometimes hot, he accords with the seasons and is honored accordingly. He takes the body as water and water as his life-force.

His transformations have no fixed direction, and his coming and going are indeterminate. Flowing or resting according to the terrain, he takes whatever conditions he encounters as his fundamental principle.
It is not like an illusion; how could it possibly accord with emptiness? Coming from nowhere and departing without attachment, he rides a yellow dragon backward, trampling the three peaks.
The waters of Tanzhou and the clouds of Kuangshan fill the six directions—this is the Master’s entire body.

The lineage of the Great Master Gaizu Xilin Weng, the Left Jueyi of the Nanjing Senglusi and concurrently the Abbot of Dabao’en Temple:
His ancestral name was Yongning, with the courtesy name Xilin. He was the son of the Guo family from Lihexian. Having left home at a young age, he paid homage to [the Buddha] at Ba...
Master Wúxiá was his teacher. Master Wēng was by nature upright and grave; his speech and actions were never frivolous. From his youth, he was esteemed by all.

At the age of twenty, he began reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which he continued until old age without ceasing. When Emperor Wǔzōng visited the Southern Capital, his imperial carriage halted at this temple.
The Grand Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, concerned that there might be no monk capable of receiving the imperial decree, carefully selected [him].
Neither was deemed suitable. Previously, the Elder had been on intimate terms with a monk named Huiyuan, known as Donglin; the two were of imposing stature and shared a profound mutual understanding.
When Qiao Baiyan served as Grand Marshal of the Army, he had long been on good terms with the Elder and subsequently recommended both men.
The Minister of Rites was greatly pleased and immediately appointed Yuan as the Right Jueyi of the Monastic Records and Weng as the Superintendent (Tiadian) of this temple.

When the Imperial carriage halted at the temple, the Emperor ascended the Great Hall the following day to pay homage to the Buddha. After the officials had finished their court audience, the Emperor issued a decree to perform a scripture-recitation ceremony and ordered that a draft of the formal petition be presented.
The Minister of Rites deliberated that a member of the Hanlin Academy was required for this task; the Venerable Ancestor replied, "The Buddha..."
The memorial has its own formal structure; it must be composed by a member of the monastic community. He then cited Master Huiyuan, who prepared a draft of the memorial and presented it.

Upon reading it, the Emperor said with delight, "Does my household have such a monk? The Minister of Rites immediately entrusted the Seal of the Monastic Registrar (Senglü) to Huiyuan to manage, and he began his duties.
When the Emperor reached the pagoda hall, he saw a hole in the ground and questioned the attendant in charge of the hall.
The monk asked, "What is this? Ying replied, "A golden well. The Emperor was displeased. The Patriarch knelt and reported, "This is a conduit for the breath.
The Emperor asked, "What use is it? The Patriarch said, "There is a Buddha-relic enshrined beneath the stupa;

this is left here to allow the passage of its vital energy. The Emperor’s mind was relieved. He established a seven-day dharma assembly, and those presiding over the ritual proceedings were all masters from afar.

Master Gong managed all internal and external affairs by following imperial decrees; everything followed the traditions of his ancestors, and when the Emperor traveled in person, there was not a single deficiency.

Consequently, the Minister of Rites held him in high esteem. In the tenth year of the Jiajing era, the assembly elected him as the abbot of this temple, where he oversaw the affairs of the mountain gate.
In the twentieth year, he was promoted to Right Jueyi in the Office of Monastic Records. Five years later, he was promoted to Left [Jueyi].

Regarding the meaning of "Awakening": Previously, the Buddha-dharma had not yet spread widely in the region south of the Yangtze River. Although the Master held official rank, he was deeply concerned for the Dharma-gate.
Whenever he saw that the monastic community was held in low esteem by the scholarly elite, he would sigh and say:
"Monastics do not study; therefore, they bring disgrace upon the teachings and defile the Dharma-gate. He first invited the late Master Yungu to reside in the Tripitaka Hall and instructed him...
Among those who practiced meditation, it was only then that they first learned of the existence of the Chan school. A few years prior, the late Master had retired to seclusion at Mount Xiqia.
Just then, the late Master Shouyu arrived from the south. At that time, Lord Lu, who served as the Director of the Ministry of Rites, said to the Patriarch:

"Recently, I observed the eminent monk Dharma Master Shouyu’s lectures; his explanations were exceedingly clear. You should invite him to the monastery to instruct and train the monastics. The Patriarch [agreed].
He immediately paid homage and invited his former teacher to reside in the Tripitaka Hall, where he established a permanent endowment for their sustenance.
He selected several dozen monks and personally led them daily to attend the lectures. From this point on, he first came to understand the Buddha-dharma.

When his former teacher Yungu was residing at Qixia, Lord Lu visited Mount She and, upon seeing him, held him in high esteem. Desiring to restore the monastery, he invited the Master to serve as its abbot; however, the Master remained firm [in his refusal].
He declined the offer. He then appointed his grandfather, Master Shan of Mount Song, as the abbot of Qixia.

From this, the monastery was restored, its properties reclaimed, and a Dharma community established as a forest retreat for receiving guests. Since then, the Way of Chan and the Buddha-Dharma have flourished greatly.
It is only now that we know of the "universal reception" (shifang jie dai) for travelers, all of which was initiated through the efforts of our grandfather. Previously...
The monastic community is largely steeped in worldly customs; they are unable to exchange even a single word with scholar-gentlemen.

The Elder [Wang] often remarked that while the Chan teachings constitute the primary vocation of monks, if they wish to master literary meaning and recognize the great principles of loyalty and filial piety, they must first enter through the Confucian path.

He therefore invited a Confucian teacher to instruct more than ten of us, including myself, in the Five Classics, the Four Books, and the works of the Masters and Historians. This is why I have attained a superficial...
He understood the meaning of the texts he read. Upon his tonsure, he immediately began studying and practicing Chan.

That Xuelang was able to revive the teachings of a generation was entirely due to the power of the Elder’s compassionate guidance and nurturing. For twenty-five years, the Elder held the seal of the Senglu (Bureau of Monastic Affairs), and all the monasteries uniformly served the Dharma with the utmost reverence;
even the smallest matters of the mountain gate, down to a single blade of grass or a single leaf, were not neglected.

How could I dare to treat it with such negligence? He regarded the permanent property of the monastery as his own eyes; thus, when the mountain gate flourished, the fortunes of the Dharma also thrived.

Every day, he led the assembly of monks to ascend the hall to offer prayers for the longevity of the Emperor. Whenever he saw a monk who was indolent and failed to attend, the Master would reprimand him sternly, saying:
"This hall is a celestial palace and a pure land. If you are so lazy and negligent now, how will you manage to seek even a single glimpse [of the Buddha] in the future?"

It is impossible to fulfill the rites. On the last day of the twelfth month in the forty-third year of the Jiajing era, the elder gathered his sons and grandsons to recount the conduct of his life and entrust them with his final affairs.
