He then patted my back and instructed me, saying: "I am eighty-three years old; it is time for me to depart.
There are many troubles within our household; were there not an elder for even a single day, it would be extremely difficult to sustain us."

"Although this boy is young, he possesses great wisdom and discernment. After my passing, all of you—members of this household, both great and small—whenever there is any matter, must stand before my image and defer to this boy’s leadership;
in this way, we may hope to ensure that no misfortune shall befall us.

From the late Master Gan-shan Hou and those below him, all responded with "Yes, yes," and accepted his command. On the seventh day of the first month of the following year, the Elder prepared his *kāṣāya*...
He toured the monastic quarters, offering his thanks to all the elders throughout the temple. For ten days he held the seal of the Monastic Registrar (Senglü).

He went to pay his respects to the Grand Minister of the Ministry of Rites and requested to resign on account of his old age; the Grand Minister comforted him and urged him to remain, but would not grant his request. Upon returning home, the Elder immediately sealed the seal.

The following day, he manifested slight illness and requested a physician to administer medicine. The Elder said, "I am finished. Ultimately, he took no medicine. I attended to the Elder during his illness.

The recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* continued without interruption. At midnight on the fifteenth day, he had the entire assembly, both old and young, surround him while reciting the Buddha’s name.
He supported his father-in-law in his arms as he sat upright, and then passed away peacefully. This was the sixteenth day of the first month in the fourteenth year.

The elder had never accumulated wealth; his simple chest did not contain more than thirty taels of gold. Yet the funeral expenses for the mourning rites were estimated at over three hundred taels—all of which had been borrowed.
Once the burial was complete, the entire household was left with no means to repay them.

My younger grandfather grew anxious about this, so he gathered the elders and the young before the portrait of the late patriarch to deliberate on how to resolve the situation. Thereupon, I stepped forward to take charge and proposed that we liquidate what the elder had left behind.

"His robes, alms bowl, and miscellaneous belongings—whatever can be appraised—shall all be valued and used to repay his debts. Should this prove insufficient, he shall liquidate his fields and pay them off in full.
Once he is free from these burdens, it will be easy for him to provide himself with food and clothing. The assembly agreed with this proposal.

He then established a vegetarian feast and gathered all the creditors, each holding their promissory notes. He distributed the principal and interest according to the documents, and the debt certificates were all burned in a single night.
Thereupon, he took charge of the gatehouse and its surrounding quarters; his descendants did not disperse. His younger grandfather first acknowledged that the Master was a man of discernment.
In the second month of that year, the abbot’s quarters were destroyed by fire. On the fifteenth day of the second month the following year, the Great Hall was consumed by flames.
By imperial decree, fifteen officials of this temple were appointed as head administrators and attendants to serve under the Judicial Office (Hōshi).

As this temple was designated as the Buddha hall for the Imperial Court, all provisions were supplied from the Inner Treasury; thus, the matter involved a grave legal code, and by law, the penalty was death.
All the monks of the temple were terrified and fled, but I alone went to the Judicial Office to oversee the salt and vegetables.
He provided thick gruel and rice porridge, carrying them back and forth while employing various means to protect and care for them, establishing methods to provide relief.

Finally, as his strength diminished, he sat down and punished the prisoners by withholding their rations; thus, the entire monastery was settled in peace. Everyone marveled at the Elder’s discernment.
The Elder was born in the *guimao* year of the Chenghua era and lived to the age of eighty-three. The present Xilin Hermitage is the retired residence he cultivated during his lifetime.
He was buried whole at Jiana Temple. At the age of twelve, he received ordination under the guidance of Master Mong-ung, who appointed Master Meijai Jun as his preceptor.
He was instructed in the scriptures and texts. At nineteen, he shaved his head. He attended upon his master for ten years;
the details of his daily conduct are mostly beyond my memory, though I do recall that every morning at dawn, he would engage in recitation and dedicate his merit toward the Western Paradise.
He never neglected his practice for even a moment. Whenever he moved about, one saw him upright and distinguished; his feet did not drag his robes.

With an iron-like countenance and a majestic air, he was never seen to so much as open his mouth with a smile. He served the two former masters, Yungu and Shouyu, as if they were great guests, showing them the utmost reverence and following all the rites of propriety.
Yet, when ordinary monks from various mountains came to visit, he would not see them unless they had properly adjusted their robes and caps.
In nurturing those such as myself and others in our studies, he was like a compassionate mother toward her infant. For over fifty years, I have cherished his ancestral kindness;

previously, while in the East Sea, I recorded the details of his life story quite extensively. However, having lost the manuscript due to the upheaval, and now being old, nineteen parts of it have been forgotten.
I earnestly consider that future descendants may not know the origins of their ancestors, and thus I record its general outline so that...
The Emperor issued an edict to his descendants, hoping that the statutes and precedents of his ancestral virtue would remain as if present in every generation.
The eulogy says: The Way of Heaven revolves in cycles, rising and falling with the times; the Way of the Law is likewise. Thus, when the Way is about to flourish—
It must have been that the time for the True Vehicle (Saddharma) had arrived, prompting him to reveal it; this was no mere coincidence.

When one observes that the Buddha-dharma in the region south of the Yangtze was in its nascent stage—like when the śarīra had not yet emerged—it is now filled with the rain of Dharma, a magnificent atmosphere of a Buddhist land. Who could have brought this about?
Although my grandfather did not formally assume the burden of the Way, the Way truly flourished because of him. Is this not a merit equal to that of a founding patriarch?

The Biography of the Great Master Yungu: The Master’s name was Fahui; his alternative style was Yungu. He was the son of Mr. Huai of Xushan in Jia County. He was born in the Gengshen year of the Hongzhi era.

From childhood, his aspirations were directed toward the transcendence of the world. He entered the monastic order at Dayun Temple in his home district under the tutelage of a certain master. Initially, he studied Yoga-tantra. Whenever the Master...
He thought to himself, "For one who has left the household life, the great matter of birth and death is most urgent. Why should I be preoccupied with the trivial concerns of food and clothing?

At the age of nineteen, he resolved his will upon the path and immediately ascended the dais to receive full ordination. There, he heard the Dharma-gate of the Minor *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Small Cessation-and-Contemplation) from Tiantai.
He applied himself with single-minded diligence to his practice. Chan Master Fazu of Fazhou succeeded to the lineage of Mount Jing; he was sequestered at Tianning Monastery in the prefecture.

The Master went there to seek instruction and presented the method he had been practicing. Fazhou said, "The essentials of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* do not rely on body, mind, breath, or the internal or external.
You have become detached from both. What you are practicing flows toward the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); how could it be the intention of the Western Sage? The student [realized this].
The Way must take the awakening of the mind as its primary focus. The Master [Zhaozhou] looked up with sorrowful longing and requested further instruction.

Zhiyuan bestowed upon him the meditation topic (huatou) of "examining the reality of Buddha-recitation," directing him to apply himself intensely to the cultivation of doubt. Following these instructions, the Master investigated day and night, neglecting both sleep and food.
One day, while receiving his meal, he did not even realize when he had finished eating; his bowl suddenly fell to the ground, and he experienced a sudden realization, as if waking from a dream.

He again requested further instruction and subsequently received formal certification (*inka*). Upon reading the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source), he attained a great awakening to the principle of "mind-only.
From that time forth, all the scriptural teachings and the *gong'an* (public cases) of the patriarchs became as clear to him as looking at old household items.

Thereupon, he concealed his brilliance within the monastic community and submerged himself in menial labor. One day, while reading the *Tanjin ji* (Tanjin Collection), he saw that the Great Master Mingjiao was protecting the Dharma.
With a profound resolve, he first paid homage to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara and recited the name ten thousand times day and night. The Master wished to emulate his practice;

he accordingly carried an image of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara upon his head and remained awake throughout the entire night, prostrating and walking in meditation without ceasing until the end of his life.
At that time, the Buddha-dharma and the Way of Chan were unheard of in the region south of the Yangtze River.

When the Master first arrived in Jinling, he stayed at the Vairocana Hall of Tianjie Monastery to practice the Way; those who saw him marveled at his extraordinary nature. Upon hearing of this, the late King of the Wei State invited him to the Conggui Hermitage in Xiyuan to provide for his needs.
While residing there, the Master entered meditative absorption for three days and three nights. Not long after, my late Grand Preceptor...

The Patriarch Xilin was the Director of the Sangha Registry and concurrently served as the abbot of Baoen Temple. He went to visit the Master and immediately requested that he take up residence in the Tripitaka Hall of that temple.
The Master sat upright in a single niche, completely without formal greetings or receptions, and for three years his feet did not cross the threshold.
No one knew of him. By chance, a person of high rank arrived on a tour; seeing the Master sitting upright, he deemed it a breach of etiquette and insulted him.
The Master took his staff and went to Mount Xiexia (Qixia). Mount Xiexia was the site where the founding patriarchs of the Liang dynasty first established their monastery.

Emperor Wu had carved the Thousand Buddhas Ridge, and successive dynasties had granted lands for offerings and sustenance. Yet the sacred precincts had fallen into ruin, and the halls had become dens for tigers and wolves.
The Master loved its secluded depth and consequently cleared away the bracken to build a hermitage at the foot of Qianfo Ridge. He never left the mountain, his shadow never departing from the peaks.
At one time, a thief plundered the Master’s belongings; traveling by night until dawn, he still had not left the hut.

When people captured him and brought him before the Master, the Master fed him with food and drink and gave him everything he possessed to take away. Because of this, those who heard of it were moved and transformed. [This was reported to] the Grand Chancellor.

Lord Lu Wutai initially served as the Director of the Ministry of Sacrifices. While visiting ancient sites of Buddhist practice, he happened to travel to Qixia Mountain, where he encountered the Master.

Finding the Master’s bearing to be extraordinary, Lu held him in high esteem. He stayed with the Master in the mountains for two nights and, wishing to restore the temple, invited the Master to serve as its abbot.
The Master declined firmly and instead recommended Master Shan of Mount Song to accept the appointment. Master Shan fully restored the temple to its former glory.

He expelled the local powerful families who occupied the manor houses and established them as the abbot’s quarters. He constructed a meditation hall and opened a lecture seat to welcome practitioners from the four quarters;
it was through the Master’s efforts that the monastic centers (*conglin*) of Jiangnan first began here.

Once the site of practice had been established, the number of visitors increased greatly, so the Master moved his residence to the deepest part of the mountain, known as Tiankai Rock (*Tiankaiyan*), where he remained solitary like a shadow, just as before. At that time, officials...
Laypeople, having been guided by Master Lukong, possessed considerable knowledge of the Way of Chan. Upon hearing of the Master’s reputation, they frequently came to pay their respects.
To all who sought instruction, as soon as they entered, the Master would immediately ask, "How are your daily activities?

Regardless of whether they were noble or humble, monastic or lay, he would invariably cast a meditation cushion onto the floor upon entering the room, commanding them to sit upright and reflect inwardly upon their own original face.
He would often remain silent throughout the entire day and night. Upon parting, he would invariably exhort them, saying, "Do not let the days pass in vain.
When they met again, he would inevitably ask about their subsequent practice and whether it had been difficult or easy. Consequently, those who were frivolous were at a loss for what to say.
Because his compassion was ever more earnest while his severity grew increasingly weighty, even though he established no formal school or system, those who beheld him were struck with awe.
He was so moved that he trembled though it was not cold. Yet the Master embraced everyone with an equal mind;

from the outset, he received people with gentle words and a low voice, maintaining a single flavor of equanimity and never once displaying harshness in speech or expression. The number of scholar-officials who took refuge in him increased day by day.

Even if he could not enter the mountains, whenever someone requested an audience, the Master, whose heart was set on transforming and guiding others, would also go to see them, traveling back and forth once a year.
Within the city, he primarily resided at Huiguang Temple. Whenever he arrived there, the lay followers would gather around him as if circling a flower-adorned throne;
yet the Master regarded them all as illusory transformations, never harboring a single thought of discrimination. Thus, those who drew near to him were like infants beside a compassionate mother.
When he left the city, he mostly stayed at Pude Temple, where the monk Yuegūhe (Emaciated Crane Yue) truly received his instruction.
Regarding his teachings: my late Grand Preceptor would frequently invite me into his private quarters, where we would remain for as long as ten days or a month.

Even during my childhood, I attended upon him closely and served him; he took a liking to me and instructed me tirelessly. When I was nineteen years old, I felt a reluctance to enter the monastic life.
The Master, perceiving this, asked: "Why do you turn your back on your original aspiration? I replied: "It is simply that I am weary of worldly life."
The Master said, "Since you know weariness with the secular world, why do you not study the biographies of eminent monks?

Among the eminent monks of antiquity, the Son of Heaven did not treat them with the etiquette due to a subject, nor did their parents raise them with the etiquette due to a son. Dragons and spirits paid them reverence, yet they felt no joy at this.

You should take up the *Chuandeng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) and the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) and read them; then you will understand. I immediately searched through my book chest and found the *Zhong* [volume].
There was a work titled *The Record of Broad Peaks* (*Fengguang lu*) in one fascicle. I presented it to my teacher, who said, "Taste this thoroughly, and you will know that the monkhood is noble.
From this, I resolved to shave my head and receive the precepts; I truly received my teacher’s guidance and inspiration at this time, which was the Jiayou Jiazi year of the Jiajing era.
In the winter of the Bingyin year, the Master lamented that the Chan Way had fallen silent. He thus gathered fifty-three people to establish a period of seated meditation at Tianjie Temple.

By his own effort, he drew me out from among them to join the assembly as a fellow practitioner, pointing out the path beyond the ordinary and instructing me to investigate the "critical phrase" (huatou) of "Buddha-recitation" with thorough scrutiny.
It was at this time that I first came to know of the matters of the Chan school; compared to the various monasteries in the Southern Capital, those following the Chan tradition...
There were only four or five people. Although the Master was advanced in years, his compassionate heart grew even more earnest.

He regarded even the youngest śrāmaṇera with eyes of loving-kindness and treated him with propriety. In all matters of movement, stillness, and dignified demeanor, he instructed him through personal guidance and face-to-face teaching.

With his gradual and skillful inducement, everyone who saw him felt as if they were being treated with personal intimacy. Yet, because his resolve to protect the Dharma was profound, he did not treat beginners lightly nor show them contempt.

Regarding the violation of precepts: among the monastics of various mountains, many were undisciplined. Whenever there was someone who reported a transgression of even a single rule of the Dharma, the Master would hear of it and go to provide rescue without waiting for a formal request;
he would invariably apply himself to the matter with earnest sincerity. The Buddha-Dharma is entrusted to kings and ministers as its external protectors;

this depends solely on their reverently embodying the Buddha’s mind. To insult the Sangha is to insult the Buddha. Upon hearing this, those present could not help but change their countenances and feel relieved, until they reached a state of certainty.
It was liberation alone that remained; yet, in the end, nothing of this was heard by others. Therefore, those who listened never found it troublesome due to its many details.
After a long time, all came to know that it arose from unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*). Before passing the examinations, Mr. Yuan Liaofan...

I attended upon the Master in the mountains. We sat facing one another in silence for three days and nights. The Master revealed to me the principle of establishing one’s destiny through the mind-only (cittamātra).

I received his instructions and served him; these details are recorded in my *Xingshen lu* (Record of Examining the Self). From this time on, the Master’s reputation as a teacher grew ever more eminent.

In the *Xinwei* year of the Longqing era, I took leave of the Master to travel north. As I departed, the Master admonished me, saying: "The ancient practitioners who traveled on pilgrimage did so solely to seek illumination regarding their own person."
Regarding the matters below: you should consider what you will say when meeting your parents, teachers, and friends in the future.
Be careful not to waste your money on straw sandals. Weeping, I paid my respects and took my leave. In the spring of the Renshen year, Lord Wu Moquan, Minister of the Board of Personnel;
Lord Zheng Danquan, Minister of the Board of Punishments; Lord Lu Wutai, Director of the Court of the Imperial Stud of Pinghu; and my younger brother Yun—[they all gathered].
Tai invited the Master to his former mountain retreat. Various gentlemen from time to time entered the inner chamber to inquire about the Way;

whenever they saw him, they invariably lit incense to seek further instruction, observing the etiquette of disciples. Chan Master Daguan Ke often accompanied Minister Pingquan Lu Gong and Chief Secretary Sishan Xu Gong to visit the Master and inquire about the essential principles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The Master then expounded for them the perfect interfusion of the four dharma realms.
Everyone marveled at this marvel, exclaiming that it was unprecedented. In his daily teachings to others, the Master specifically highlighted the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land of Mind-Only.

Throughout his life, he followed circumstances as they arose and never established a formal school or lineage. Whenever there was a Chan or lecture hall on any mountain, he would invariably be invited to occupy the abbot’s quarters.
Upon arrival, he would proclaim the regulations of Baizhang, striving to clarify the precedents and traditions of the former masters, without granting the slightest concession.

Jie was by nature calm, steady, and reticent; his speech emerged like an echo from a deserted valley. Sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he dwelt in the mountains in pure cultivation for over forty years as if it were a single day.
His side never touched his mat, and he spent his entire life in ritual recitation, never ceasing for even a single night.
During a time when the path of Chan was still in its nascent stage in the Jiangnan region, he moved freely through places of much clamor, remaining beyond dispute from beginning to end.
By this, his conduct may already be known. The Master resided in the village for three years, and those who were transformed by his influence numbered in the millions.
One night, the people of the four districts saw a great fire break out within the Master’s hermitage. When they hurried there at dawn to look, the Master had already passed away in stillness.
This was the fifth day of the first month in the third year of the Wanli era (1575). The Master was born during the Hongzhi era.
On the day of Gengshen, at the age of seventy-five and with fifty years of monastic seniority, his disciple Zhenyin and others performed the cremation and interred him to the right of the temple.

Since leaving my teacher, I have traveled throughout various regions; among the spiritual friends I have consulted, I have never seen one whose conduct was as level and sincere, and whose true compassion was so serene and composed as that of my teacher.
Whenever I give rise to such reflections, the teacher’s voice and physical form appear vividly before me.
However, my heart and mind were moved by the profound depth of the Dharma-milk; thus, even unto old age, I have been unable to forget it.

Regarding the Master’s origins and the circumstances of his entry into the Way, I had personally received his instructions on these matters; yet, as for that final stroke, I did not know where it would lead.
In the previous year of Ding-si, I traveled east to attend a vegetarian feast hosted by the lay practitioner Shen Dingfan at Qizhen Temple, where I paid homage at the Master’s stupa.

I subsequently raised funds to construct a pavilion for the stupa and established fields for offerings and sustenance, thereby fulfilling a portion of my single-minded aspiration. However, I have not yet fully understood the inscription composed by Mr. Liao Fan.
I have therefore compiled a general account of his life and conduct based on what I have seen and heard, to show it to future generations.
Alas, as the Master was the patriarch who restored the Zen Way, it is regrettable that his recorded sayings were lost; thus, there is no means to further propagate his profound mysteries.
Shi Deqing said: "The path of the single transmission of Bodhidharma, from the time of the Five Houses down to my own Ming Dynasty and after Mount Jingshan, the lion’s lute was about to fall silent.
Only our Great Master, following Chan Master Fazhou, continued the thread-like lineage.
Although he did not yet erect a great banner of the Dharma, at a time when the Great Dharma was in its chaotic infancy, he stood firm and exerted himself to revitalize it."
His path led people to realize there was a matter that transcends the mundane. His realization was stable and profound; his conduct was steady and sincere;

whether in motion or stillness, he never forgot the rules of discipline, preserving the formal statutes of Baizhang. Having traveled throughout all quarters, even if there were those who were accomplished masters, [he remained peerless].
There is nothing that can surpass him. Is he not truly the teacher and exemplar for humans and devas throughout this era? I, Qing, am ashamed of my dull faculties and inferior nature;

I have been unable to perpetuate the family’s reputation and have thus failed the luminous teachings. Nevertheless, as for my resolve to uphold the Dharma, I dare not forget it for even a single moment.
I respectfully record the general outline of the Master’s life here, so that future readers may gain insight into the ancients, as they say.
Biography of Chan Master Miaofeng Deng, Founder of the State-Protecting Holy Light Temple at Mount Wutai by Imperial Decree The master’s name was Fudeng;
his alternative style name was Miaofeng. He was a native of Pingyang in Shanxi, surnamed Xu, a descendant of the lineage of Xu Juju.
When the master was only seven years old, his parents encountered a year of famine and passed away without the means for burial; they were laid upon a simple mat of reeds.
Thus it was. Having lost both his father and mother, the Master entered the religious life at age twelve with a monk at a nearby temple, but he did not receive proper care.
At eighteen, he fled and, carrying a single gourd, arrived at Mount Dongshan in Pukhan Commandery.

There resided the monk Master Lang of Wanchangge Wan’gu Monastery. On the day the Master arrived, he begged for alms in the marketplace and stayed overnight in the pavilion. Moved by compassion, Master Lang took him in.
Not long after, King Shanyin went out on an excursion and, seeing the Master, marveled at him. He said to Master Lang, "You must look after this youth well;
in the future, he will surely become a vessel of great capacity. The Master then took him as his disciple. After some time had passed, the earth shook violently one night.

The civilian houses were completely collapsed, and the Master was buried beneath the debris; it was thought he would certainly die. Master Lang hurriedly searched for him and, fortunately, found him unharmed.

The King then said to the Master, "That you did not perish despite facing such great peril is no ordinary matter. Why do you not contemplate the great matter of birth and death with profound earnestness?
At that time, the Master was twenty-two years old, and he immediately resolved to travel far. The King said, "It is not yet time; for now, you should remain here."

At Seigan-ji on Mount Chūjō, he constructed a hermitage and had his teacher close the meditation gate. The teacher requested further instruction from Dharma Master Jin, who showed him the *Hokkai-kan* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm).
Within the closed gate, he practiced this meditative contemplation, standing like a crane day and night for three years.
His mind attained awakening, and he composed a verse to present to the King. Upon seeing it, the King said, "This boy’s insight is already like this;
if I do not break him now, he will surely become mad in the future. Thereupon, the King took an old shoe, cut out the sole, sealed it, and sent it to him, writing a verse upon it that said:
"This piece of stinking shoe sole, I have sealed and sent to you. It is for no other purpose at all, But solely to strike down your poetry-making."

The Master saw him; he prostrated before the Buddha and tied a cord around his neck. From that time on, he remained entirely silent. After three years, he broke through the barrier to go and see the King.
The King observed that he possessed the marks of a great man and was greatly pleased. He then said:

"Although you know the matter of your own fundamental nature, you have not yet heard the Buddha-dharma. I fear you might fall into false views. In the mountains of Jiezhou, there is one who lectures on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*..."

Regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Master was sent to hear it and was granted full ordination. At the age of twenty-seven, the King said to the Master, "As a monk, you have not yet left the mountain gates;
you are like a frog in a well. There are many spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in the south; you should go there to visit them.
When you return in the future, you may serve as my own traveling pilgrim. He then personally prepared for the Master the provisions and travel gear required for his journey.
He himself wore a woolen robe and socks, with a tattered blue outer garment draped over them. He handed these to him, saying, "This is to keep out the cold.

The Master accepted this instruction and immediately set out southward with only a single water gourd and a staff, traveling to consult various spiritual teachers. Upon reaching Nanhai, he paid homage at Putuo Shan;

returning to Ningbo, he contracted a seasonal illness and was nearly dead. While staying as a traveler, he could not find even a drop of water to drink, so he reached his hand down and took a bath in the river.
He scooped up some water from a basin and drank it; it was very sweet. When he examined it the following morning, it was extremely foul and turbid, and he vomited profusely.

Suddenly, he realized to himself: "When I drank it, it was very sweet; when I looked at it, it was very turbid. Purity and impurity depend solely on the mind. Immediately, his entire body broke into a great sweat.
His illness was cured; however, his entire body was covered in scabies and swellings. When he arrived at the Southern Capital (Nanjing), it was the winter month of the first year of the Longqing era.

At that time, our late Master was lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at Tianjie Monastery. I was serving as the Vice-Lecturer, while the Master held the post of *jingtou* (sanitation officer).
Every morning when I rose early, seeing that the latrine was clean, I knew at once that the attendant was no ordinary person. One night I went to observe him secretly and saw the Master holding—

I went to offer incense, sprinkle water, sweep the floor, and wash the tally-sticks and staff. Peering closely at him, I saw that he was merely a yellow-complexioned, sickly *dhūta*. I marveled at this. After some time, the Master fell ill and lay in the guest quarters.
I went to visit him and found his body covered in swellings and sores; he could not even raise his hand.

I asked after his well-being, and the Master said, "It is my karmic obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*). It is already difficult to endure this physical illness, but the 'gluttonous illness' is even harder to cure. I asked, "What do you mean? He replied: [The rest of the dialogue follows].

"What does this mean? I asked. The Master said, "I simply see people eating steamed buns during their vegetarian fasts; I regret that I have not yet let go of everything. I knew in my heart that he was a man of the Way.
The next day, I went to visit him carrying some cakes and fruit in my sleeve. I offered them to the Master with my hand, and he swallowed them with delight, feeling great satisfaction.
I smiled and said, "This is truly a man of the Way. We sat and conversed, and the Master said, "Whenever I hear your lectures, my mind opens and my understanding is clarified.
To possess such wondrous realization at such a young age! I replied, "This is not my primary concern. My intention is to follow you on a journey afar."
He devoted himself to investigating the supreme point of the Way. Before ten days had passed, he was unable to find a teacher and realized that Master Qianxing might become a burden to him.
When the Master returned, the King was greatly pleased and inquired about the persons and teachings he had encountered.

The Master described the virtuous predecessors and spiritual friends; regarding those at the stage of beginners, he included me as one of them. Consequently, the King also came to think of me. Once the Master had...
He returned, having no desire for the secular world. Thereupon, in the deepest recesses of Mount Zhongtiao, he cleared away the weeds and dwelt there alone with his own shadow as company.

For three years, he abstained from grain and subsisted only on water, attaining great awakening. He then took the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) as the seal of his mind, deeply entering into the principle of "mind-only.
King Ruzhong honored the Triple Gem; once the construction of a Buddhist monastery was completed on South Mountain, he invited the Master to reside there, desiring further to seek...

The Northern Edition of the Tripitaka was kept within the Imperial Palace, and the Emperor urged the Master to go there in person. Having resided in the mountains for a long time, the Master’s hair had grown long and remained uncut;
thus, he traveled to the capital along with an official on tour. At that time, I had already begun begging for alms in Chang’an.

While riding his horse through the marketplace of Yan, the Master happened to recognize me. Once we were settled in lodgings, he searched for me in the Western Hills; upon seeing me, he asked, "Do you recognize me?"
I gazed at him intently and saw that his two pupils were bright and piercing. Suddenly, I remembered that he was the sick mendicant from the celestial realm.
I said, "I recognize you. The Master replied, "You have changed your head and face. I said, "The original face is naturally present. The Master smiled and bowed; after the meal, we took our leave.
The next day, I went to visit him, and we spent the night talking together on the same bed, recounting in detail the circumstances of my quest for the Tripitaka. I...

He said, "Since parting from my teacher, there has been no day that I have not thought of him. I have come specifically to seek you out; I have merely been visiting the capital to satisfy my wanderlust for these days.
The Master said, "If you will not reject me, I shall serve as your vanguard to 'beat the dogs' for you.
They parted immediately. This was in the winter month of the Ren-shen year of the Longqing era. In the third month of the following spring, I traveled to Mount Wutai and resolved to dwell there.
Unable to endure the ice and snow, he returned once more to the capital gates to beg for alms. Left Grand Master Bo Yu, Lord Wang, said to me:
"The Dharma-gate is desolate, which is truly lamentable. Judging by your physical bearing and spirit, you shall one day become a teacher of devas and humans."
"I hope you will not wander aimlessly. My junior observes that among those of the present day, there is no one who may serve as a teacher for you;
setting aside Master Miaofeng, you have no other friend. I said, "I have had a pact with him from long ago. He said, "If we truly travel together, my junior should act as your guide.

In the autumn of that year, when the Master had completed the construction of the Tripitaka repository and was already packing his belongings, I arrived just then. The Master immediately ordered me to mount the carriage; before a single word had been exchanged, he departed.
They traveled together. Upon arriving at P’u, the King was greatly pleased to see them. Once the scriptures had been stored away, they remained there to observe the winter retreat;

this was the first year of the Wanli era, the year of Guiyou (1573). The Master constantly felt that the souls of his two parents had not yet found rest, and he wished to relocate their graves to a mountain.

Consequently, with the assistance of Lord Cha, the Regional Commander of the state, and Lord Hu Shun’an, the Prefect of Pingyang, each contributed toward the burial expenses. In the spring of the following year, Jiashu (1574)...
In the [Year of] Yue, my teacher and I retired together to Mount Wutai. On our way east, we passed through my hometown to perform the joint burial of my parents.

I selected a high and secluded plot of land to the east of the city for their interment and composed an epitaph for the tomb. Once these matters were concluded, I proceeded to Mount Tai. I chose a site at Longmen on the Northern Terrace to dwell;
amidst piles of snow and ice, I found several rafters of an old house where we took up residence together. Three years passed.
I have constantly reflected that there is no way to repay my two parents. Therefore, I made a vow to pierce my own blood and gild the characters to transcribe a copy of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

My teacher likewise pierced his tongue to transcribe a copy in vermilion ink; each was one volume. When the sutras were nearly finished, my teacher wished to establish an Unrestricted Great Assembly (*asaṃvara-mahāpariṣad*).

He subsequently went down the mountain to solicit funds and provisions, and within a year the necessary conditions were fully assembled. He intended to expound the Great *Avataṃsaka* in the ninth year of the Wanli era.

It was opened on a winter day in the *xinsi* year. Previously, the Empress Dowager Cisheng, for the sake of offering prayers for the late Emperor and to protect the Imperial Person, had repaired the pagoda and temple at Wutai Mountain.
When the construction was nearing completion, she requested that the Crown Prince dispatch an official to Wutai.
At that time, the assembly was already gathered at the new temple. I and the Master deliberated, saying: "In all matters concerning our disciples..."

This action was nothing other than repaying the fundamental debt to the state; it was appropriate that everything be dedicated to this cause, for it was truly the single-minded loyalty of a subject living beyond the secular realm.
The Master agreed. In the eleventh month of winter in that year, he inaugurated the assembly, which reached completion in the third month of spring in the following year, Renwu (1562).
The period lasted one hundred and twenty days, and monastics and laypeople from the nine borders and eight provinces attended.
The assemblies were held without interruption on the roads, and at every meal, the number of participants never fell short of several thousand.
When the assemblies concluded, he entrusted the remaining gold and grain to the permanent endowment of the monastery and departed forever with his single bowl, drifting away like the wind.

I traveled eastward across the coastal lands, while the Master went to Luya to build and dwell in a hermitage. After one year, seeking the karmic conditions for the birth of the Holy Mother, we two met once again.
Duke De obtained the Master’s favor; he visited Luyaya and was granted permission to construct Hua-yan Temple. In a short time, it became a great place of practice (*mahā-vihāra*).

At the summit of the mountain, he erected a single iron stūpa of the Ten Thousand Buddhas with seven tiers, seven stories high. Originally, Pu-ban Wan-gu Temple had been the Master’s mountain retreat;
there stood a thirteen-tiered stūpa for the śarīra of a holy monk of the Tang dynasty, three hundred feet high, as well as a Great Buddha Hall, all of which—
The temple was in a state of ruin. When the Great Marshal of the Region, Duke Wang of Jianchuan, saw this, he deliberated upon its reconstruction and invited the Master to reside there.
After three years, the pagoda and halls were completely renovated. Shortly thereafter, the Grand Intendant of San Yuan, Duke Li of Ku’an, requested that the Master build a bridge over the Wei River.
The Master went there for two years, and once the work was completed, he returned to Luya. Passing through Ninghua, he beheld a stone cliff rising ten thousand feet, as level as a single plane.
The Master was pleased with him and had a cave excavated, measuring three zhang and five chi in depth, breadth, height, and width.

He carved the worlds of the Flower Treasury and the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, and depicted images of ten thousand Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with such exquisite precision and subtlety that it became a great site of practice.
Not long after, the West Court of Xuanfu planned to build a bridge over the Great River; the Master responded to the summons, went there, and measured the site.
The waters were broad and the sands deep; thus, he constructed a bridge of twenty-three arches, which was also successfully completed.

The Master had long harbored the aspiration to cast three great clay statues with gilded surfaces and to construct three bronze temples to be sent to the three Great Sacred Mountains. In the spring of the Jihai year, he traveled to Luan’an with his staff to visit Prince Shen.
At that time, the Prince was preparing a gilded statue of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra to send to Mount Emei; the Master spoke of the bronze temple.
As for the matter, the King asked how much it would cost. The Master replied, "Each hall requires ten thousand pieces of gold. The King was delighted and wished to have one built at Mount Emei;
he immediately provided the necessary supplies and escorted the Master to Jingzhou, where he allowed him to supervise the construction himself, taking whatever funds were required from the King.

The halls were over ten feet high and wide, and they were inlaid with gold and carved with images of various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, so exquisite and peerless that nothing of their kind had ever been seen before in the world.

When the hall was completed, it was transported to Mount Emei. The Provincial Governor (Dazhongcheng), Lord Wang Jiyu, who was governing Sichuan, heard that the Master had arrived and invited him for an audience.

Upon questioning him regarding the essentials of the mind, they reached a mutual accord. The Lord then expressed his wish to assist in the project at Nanhai; consequently, copper was gathered in Sichuan and artisans were recruited from Jingmen.
When the work was finished and the vessel was being transported to Longjiang, the monks of Putuo resisted its arrival with great force, so it did not proceed there.
He then selected a site on Mount Hua in the Southern Capital and submitted a memorial to the Holy Mother requesting the construction of temple buildings for their enshrinement;

thus, a great monastery was established. The Master then commissioned the construction of the Five Terraces (Wutai), all of which were funded by the common people, and before long, these too were completed.
In the spring of the year Yisi, the Master personally escorted the Five Terraces [images] there and petitioned the Emperor regarding the establishment of Xiantong Temple at Taihuai.
The Imperial Horse Eunuch Wang Zhong was dispatched, and the Senior Attendant Eunuch Chen Ru was sent by the Holy Mother;

each carried treasury gold to inspect the site. They selected a location within the monastery and constructed a hall for enshrining [the image]. Construction commenced in the fifth month of the summer of the Bingwu year to establish a new edifice from the foundations.
Seven locations were laid out with bricks for the nine assemblies, featuring six tiers of halls before and after the main sanctuary, surrounded by multi-storied pavilions.
The structures rose in successive tiers, their scale magnificent. An imperial edict was issued bestowing the name "Great State-Protecting Holy Light Yongming Temple.
Upon completion of the construction, a Huayan Seven Sites and Nine Assemblies ritual site (*dōjō*) was established, attended by twelve hundred monastics from both the upper and lower assemblies.
He invited ten Dharma masters to expound the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, with all expenses provided from the imperial treasury.

The grandeur of this site of practice was such that it had never before been seen. When the Master first entered Mount Tai, because the roads were rugged and precipitous, he established bridges over the streams and paved the main road with stone for over three hundred li.
He repaired the bridge at Xiupian County and was granted the title "Pujie" (Universal Salvation). He then constructed [the monastery].

The Receiving Hall (*Jiedaiyuan*) serves as a place for travelers to rest their shoulders. Furthermore, outside Longquan Pass, at Rencao Stone, a tea hermitage was established, which was later granted the imperial title of Huizhi Monastery (*Huizhiyuan*).
Medicine was donated and tea was provided; annually, a certain amount of gold was bestowed.

Subsequently, the *Liangzhao Zang* (Dragon Canon) was granted in accordance with imperial decree, and a brick pavilion was constructed to house and enshrine it. Later, the Hall of the Seven Tathāgatas was built. Additionally, [a site] in Fuping...

He established Chōjū Village and constructed a temple hall for the sake of the Empress Dowager. The structure consisted of seven stories from top to bottom and enshrined a cast image of Amida Nyorai, three *jō* and six *shaku* in height.
The mountain gate, bell and drum towers, two corridors, and monastic quarters were all of grand and spacious scale.

Furthermore, he established it as a great place of practice (*dōjō*) and was granted the name Jiyū Enmyō-ji Temple; several *kō* of fields were allotted for offerings and sustenance, and the Master resided there.

When the five terraces were being established, they likewise depended upon external conditions. The Governor of Shanxi requested that he repair the vital road through Guo County and the great bridge over the Hutuo River;

the Prince of Jin requested that he repair the Great Tower Temple in the provincial capital. Once the halls and buildings were completed, he repaired the bridges of the capital city, which extended ten *li* in length, though the work was not yet finished.
In the ninth month of autumn in the year Renzi, the Master returned to the mountain due to illness and attended to his affairs there.
The Dharma-hall he had established was designated as a perpetual endowment for the ten directions, with each position filled by its appropriate person.

His former attendants were all ordered to return to their respective mountains, with not a single one remaining. At the hour of the Rabbit on the nineteenth day of the twelfth lunar month, he passed away with serene composure.
The Master was born in the Gengzi year of the Jiajing era and entered parinirvāṇa in the Renzi year of the Wanli era.

His worldly lifespan was seventy-three years, and his dharma-ordination age was slightly over forty. After the Master passed away, the Emperor heard of it and granted him a state burial, constructing a stupa to the west of Yongming.
He ordered that all the Master’s unfinished meritorious works be completed. The Empress Dowager bestowed one thousand pieces of gold and silk.
Five hundred [strings of cash] were provided for the funeral expenses. Initially, when Su Gong Yunpu, a Court Attendant, was inspecting Shanxi, he entered the mountains to visit the Master.
They discussed the essentials of the mind and reached a mutual accord; although many of their exchanges and dialogues occurred, they have not been recorded here.
When the Master fell ill, Su Gong dispatched a physician with medicine. Upon the Master’s passing, Su Gong composed an inscription for his stupa. He often said: "People regard Master Miaofeng as..."
As for the Field of Merit and spiritual friend, I truly do not know the extent of his transcendent realization. Alas! What kind of person was this Master?
Rising from a state of solitude and obscurity, he was ultimately able to perform the vast and great Buddha-work of a single age among devas and humans.

Since my early years, I have sought out the Master amidst those submerged in humble and lowly service; by the time I reached the age of thirty, I traveled as a wandering monk (*paryaṭaka*) with him, vowing to cultivate [the Way] with focused resolve.

Thus he traveled. Having parted from Mount Tai for over thirty years, his journey began with minor princes assisting in the Way and culminated with the Sacred Son of Heaven, the Sacred Mother, and various kings serving as *dānapatis*.
In all his constructions, the giving of the Dharma arose like clouds in response to his thoughts;
wherever he set foot, it became a precious monastery (*ratnārāma*). By what causes and conditions could such things be brought about? If it were not because his mind roamed [in liberation]...
Is it not the inconceivable power flowing from the ocean-like nature of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm that can manifest such a thing?
Since the Master first set out on his journey and took up residence in the mountains, he has possessed nothing beyond his single robe;
he has never had a single attendant follow him. All those he established were men who maintained a single, enlightened mind, yet he never once accepted offerings of gold or money.

He merely dipped his finger [in the offerings] and departed as soon as he had established himself, showing no lingering attachment whatsoever. Of the more than ten great monasteries he founded, not a single disciple remained to guard them.
When he stayed, he followed conditions with not a hair’s breadth of selfishness; when he left, he did so as if forgetting everything, without clinging to even a thread of silk.

He drifted like floating clouds gathering and dispersing, or like solitary cranes coming and going. Was he not one who had deeply realized that all is but mind, and whose very encounter with conditions was itself the ultimate principle?

The Master’s appearance was ancient and his bones were firm; he possessed the five physical defects. His countenance was stern and cold, and he was utterly devoid of worldly emotions and consciousness. Solitary and resilient, he was free from artificial adornment. Throughout his life, his ribs never touched his mat.

I am deeply moved by the power of his rigorous self-cultivation. Though his name is [Dao]— (Note: The final character "名雖道" appears to be a fragment or an incomplete phrase, likely referring to the Master's name ending in "Dao," such as Daoxuan or Daozhen.)

My friend, his heart was truly that of a teacher. Although we have been separated for over thirty years, he has constantly remained vividly before my eyes, as if I were in the presence of a master or a guardian.
Throughout my life, I have never forgotten my source; is this not surely the result of karmic affinity from past lives?

Alas, I am old and cannot offer even a single incense flower at his shrine. Because of the obstacles of worldly conditions, many in this age possess only the "fleshly eye," regarding him merely as a field of merit.
The Master, however, did not know that [the work] was being secretly composed.

Therefore, I have set forth a general outline of the Master’s life so that future generations may know that, throughout more than two hundred years of our Ming dynasty, he alone was the one who established meritorious deeds within the Dharma gate.
How difficult it would be to encounter such a person!
The eulogy says: When an ancient attained the single glimpse of the Vajra Eye, they were able to take the long river and turn it into cream and curd, and transform the great earth into gold;
this was not a matter beyond their capacity. Yet, within the emptiness of the Dharma-nature, [the Master] regarded these as nothing more than wild horses and dust motes—such was his self-perception.
I have often privately reflected that if one could possess even a semblance of the Master’s conditions, [one would surely realize this].

He integrated all teachings into a single principle and employed them as aids for practice. He established monasteries like Nālandā, where both the nature (Dharmatā) and characteristics (Dharma-lakṣaṇa) schools were established side by side, and meditation and purity were cultivated in tandem.
For over forty years, his feet never left the shadow [of his teacher]. In terms of his contributions to the Dharma-gate, he shall surely rival Qingliang and Donglin in grandeur.
At every turn, one beholds the magnificent adornments of the Flower Treasury Pure Land; moreover, it is not merely a matter of three mountains or ten peaks.
It is merely a matter of time. Alas, it is gone! Perhaps we must await the Master’s return once more.
The Dharma-way was revived by Master Xuelang, whose lineage descended from the White Horse coming from the West.
When the Image-Dharma flourished in the East, Kumārajīva and Vimalakīrti (Jingming) established its framework, while Huiyuan [expounded] the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Drawing upon its legacy, the Great Dharma first flourished and became clearly manifest in the Central Lands. During the Six Dynasties, it reached its height;
yet its true essence had not yet been firmly established. It was with Tiantai that the three contemplations were set forth to form a distinct school.
In the Tang dynasty, Xianshou first opened the tradition of the Huayan Dharmadhātu, while Qingliang alone excelled in its mastery. Xuanzang then expounded the principles of Vijñaptimātratā.

Kuiji specialized in this school. Consequently, the source of both the Nature (Xing) and Characteristics (Xiang) traditions, as well as the principle of the One Mind and Three Truths, began to flow widely across the land.
The holy teachings of our Buddha throughout his lifetime were like the great ocean’s hidden currents beneath the four continents;
now, their profound and subtle tenets were like the sun and moon raised high in the midst of the sky. From that time on, his writings proliferated in many directions.
The designations established are not uniform; yet there is none that does not explore its original source and subsume it back into the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

All together, they swim and play within the Tathāgata’s ocean of nature, hauling in the fish and dragons of the *dharmadhātu*. This is no different from beholding the white tuft of hair on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa or hearing the perfect sound in the Garden of Enlightenment.
Since the arrival of Bodhidharma from the West, the principle of the single transmission has been established, pointing directly to the one mind.

He did not esteem words and letters. Consequently, the Teaching became the Buddha’s eye and Chan became the Buddha’s mind; Chan and the Teaching drove side by side, proceeding together without contradiction.
From the time of the Sixth Patriarch downward, the Way of Chan flourished greatly, leading inevitably to criticisms regarding attachment and dogmatism, and the Teaching and Chan began to split apart.
Guifeng strove to pull them back but was unable to do so. Yongming unified the natures of the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings within the One Mind, designating it as the "School" (Zong).
The mirror reflects the entire body and great function of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, making them manifest and clearly evident.

Only when our Holy Ancestor ascended like a dragon did he sweep clear the realm and open the enterprise of ten-thousand-year peace; yet at the very beginning, upon arriving in Jiankang, his armor and weapons had not yet been laid aside.

He immediately held the Buddha’s teachings in high esteem. In the third year of the Hongwu era, he issued an imperial decree for eminent monks from throughout the realm to be stationed at Tien-chieh Temple.
He established a site for the Universal Salvation Rite (Pudu Daochang) at Linggu Valley on Mount Zhong, where renowned figures gathered in full.
The Emperor personally attended to hear the Dharma with joy, and the flourishing of the Buddhist path was no less than it had been in former times. How remarkable!

Magnificent indeed! Thus, within a single school, he established three teachings: namely, Chan (meditation), Lecture (exegesis), and Yoga. Through Chan, one awakens to one's own mind; through Lecture, one clarifies the Dharma-nature;
and through Yoga, one delivers those in the dark realms of the netherworld. Consequently, he constructed three great monasteries:
Tianjie for settling Chan practitioners, Tianxi for housing those of scholarly learning, and Nengren for housing those of Yoga. Their influence flowed vast and wide throughout the realm.

Regarding the "Chaozong" (The Source of the Lineage): Since the relocation from the north, the path of Chan has not been prominent; instead, only the lectures on this single school have gathered in the capital.
Consequently, the Dharma path of Jiangnan has gradually declined until it is no longer heard of.

During the Zheng and Jia periods, even among the lecture seats in the north, there were only the two great elders, Tong and Tai, who occupied the flowered throne in the capital, such that all scholars within the realm [gathered there].
Thus it was gathered. Yet scholars of the South were accustomed to softness and ease; [to them], this seemed as difficult as ascending to heaven.
Only my late Great Master, the Infinite Venerable One, followed his teacher from Huaiyin and went to rely upon him with a single alms-bowl.

For over twenty years, he drank ice and bit through snow, neglecting sleep and forgetting food, until he fully mastered the essential tenets of the Xianshou and Cien schools regarding nature and characteristics (*xingxiang*). Subsequently, he returned southward and arrived at...
The Prince of the Wei State in Jinling saw him and was moved by his presence; he subsequently became his patron (*dānapati*) and invited him to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

However, the chanting went unaccompanied and the listeners were few and far between. When Lord Lu, the Director of the Ministry of Sacrifices at Mount Wutai, went to visit him, he said to the late Master Xilin, his venerable grandfather:
"Recently, I encountered the eminent monk from the north, Wuji, who is truly a master of both humans and devas. Upon hearing..."
The exposition of these wondrous meanings deeply accords with the Buddha’s mind.

As I contemplate how to repay my debt of gratitude, I consider that this is the very teaching established by our Holy Ancestor for which the monastic community resides here; how could it be that we remain entirely without such instruction?

If you, Master, as the abbot, would truly invite him to return to the temple to extensively propagate the Way of the Dharma and enlighten the ignorant masses, it would be a great blessing for the Gate of the Law. The Master [Wenyi] agreed, saying, "Yes, yes. Immediately—
He exhausted all formalities and presented ceremonial gifts to earnestly invite him; this was in the thirty-second year of the Jiajing era.

Upon his arrival, the Master resided in the Tripitaka Hall of the temple, as it contained the hair-relic stupa of the Great Master Xuanzang, for which the permanent endowment provided annual offerings.
The Grand Preceptor then selected several dozen monks from the temple to attend at the Master’s feet, listening daily to lectures on various sutras. Nearby...

Among the elders of the various mountains, there were some who responded; after a long time, virtuous men from the capital gathered daily, providing the four requisites for his support, and the influence of his skillful transformation gradually spread.
At that time, there was a layman named Mr. Huang, whose husband and wife had long maintained the practice of fasting.
One day, the Master took his young son, Er-lang, to offer incense and food. Er-lang was none other than the Dharma Master Xuelang, later known as Master En.
By nature, the Master was transcendent and exceptionally bright, standing apart from the common crowd; he delighted only in playing and performing Buddhist rites.

When he entered the school for formal studies, the teacher’s instruction on reading and recitation barely caught his attention. Even when urged to study, he would merely look at him and laugh, showing no inclination toward it whatsoever.

On that day, a meal offering was prepared, as it coincided with the lecture on the *Eight Consciousnesses and Their Regulations* (*Ba Shi Gui Ju*). Upon hearing it once, the youth felt it resonated deeply within his heart and listened intently.
He remained there for two or three days. When his father returned and called for him, the youth did not respond. His father said, "Do you love leaving the household life?"

The Duke smiled and nodded his head. His father pressed him repeatedly, but he ultimately did not return. After his father had been gone for several days, the mother missed him deeply and urged her husband to go fetch him.
When the father arrived and entreated him again and again, the Master secretly tucked a pair of scissors into his sleeve and went quietly before the Tricīvara Stūpa.
He cut off the hair from the crown of his own head, held it up in his hand, and said to his father, "Take this and send it to my mother. The father wept bitterly; the Master looked at him.

He did nothing more than this. Consequently, he never returned home. When his father returned and informed his mother, she finally consented. At that time, the Master was twelve years old. From then on, he became a śrāmaṇera.
Moving among the assembly, he displayed the bearing of a great man. One day, during a communal meal, the Master arrived at the refectory first and took the seat of honor.
Shortly thereafter, the Head Seat (śrīpāda) arrived and shouted, "How can a young śrāmaṇera occupy [this seat]?"
Regarding this seat, the official asked, "Who is worthy to occupy this seat? The Master said, "One who has thoroughly mastered the Buddha-dharma.
The official said, "If that is so, then I shall occupy it. The Master asked, "What Buddha-dharma have you mastered? The official replied, "I ask you a question.
The Master said, "Then tell me, what is being taught upon this Dharma-seat today? The official responded spontaneously, grasping the essential meaning perfectly. The entire assembly was astonished.
He sighed and said, "This child is one who has returned for a second birth. Whenever the Master listened to lectures, [the boy] would play about;

yet when questioned, there was no meaning he failed to grasp. The year after the Master entered the monastic order, I was twelve years old and also entered the order. My grandfather, the Grand Preceptor, took me to visit the Great Master.
While the Master was sitting and playing in the Buddha Hall, he saw me and his countenance brightened with joy, as if we were long-time intimates.

People regarded us as fellow countrymen. However, I had followed [the Master] since childhood in reciting and chanting, yet I did not understand the meaning. The Master had resided in lecture halls since his youth;

his insights surpassed those of his peers, and the entire assembly respected and submitted to him. At the age of eighteen, he was granted a seat to serve as an assistant lecturer (*pofang*), and those who heard him were struck with awe and enlightenment.
Yet, by nature, the Master was unrestrained and paid little heed to such matters. When I was nineteen, I shaved my head; at that time, the Great Master...
At this temple, he expounded the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* in his *Xuántán* (Profound Discourse). I immediately received the precepts from him and listened to his lectures;
my mind was opened and enlightened as if through long-standing practice. At that time, he esteemed me as a vessel for the Dharma, and we became brothers in the Law, bound by unyielding harmony.
He had not yet mastered secular writing, so when I happened to compose a "Rhapsody on Dwelling in the Mountains," he pasted it upon the wall. His nephew, Dr. Huang...
When [his uncle] saw this, he looked at him with envy and said, "I am far inferior to this gentleman. The gentleman replied, "This is merely the art of carving insects;
what is it worth mentioning? At the age of twenty-one, [the Master] had already mastered the Buddhist teachings in their entirety.

From that point on, he resolved his will and began to study the secular classics, histories, the works of the hundred schools, as well as ancient prose compositions, lyrics, and songs, searching through them all without exception, immersing himself in them as if in play.

Han’s intention always preceded his brushwork. He studied under nearly every renowned scholar of the Three Wu regions; the verses and poems he produced were all so celebrated they became "minced meat" for the public palate.

Even a single letter or a solitary character from him was treasured as a secret rarity. He once said to me: "People say that if one does not read ten thousand scrolls of books, one will not understand Du Fu’s poetry.
I say that if one does not read ten thousand scrolls of books, one will not understand the Buddha-dharma. He constantly perused the *Avataṃsaka*...

In his *Great Commentary*, he states that upon reaching the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), a sage must have a broad mastery of the various secular schools of learning before being capable of engaging with the world to benefit sentient beings.
That the Master exerted such great effort in this area—could it possibly have been without purpose?

I studied Chan under my late teacher Yungu at Tianjie Monastery, and I was intensely determined to investigate the matter that transcends the ordinary. Whenever the Master saw me sitting in silent meditation, he would immediately scold me, saying: "What use..."
"How can one act as the local deity in a village of three households? he asked, repeatedly urging me to lecture. I replied, "Each person follows their own aspirations.
An ancient worthy said, "If one’s own nature is fundamentally realized, then looking back at written words is like pushing a door that falls right into its socket;
it is certainly not difficult. He said, "If you can truly do this, I shall treat you as my elder brother. From then on, I [dwelt] in the mountain forests.
The character *zhì* is pronounced with the *yì* rhyme. Having first read the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he learned of Mount Wutai and his heart raced toward it daily.
At the age of twenty-five, he resolved to travel north. He took leave of the Master at Xuelang Hermitage, who said: "Your physical strength is frail;

the bitter cold of the northern lands will surely be difficult for you to endure. If you must go, I shall take you along for now to wander through the Three Wu regions to exercise your sinews and bones."
"It would not be too late to set out after this. I said, "The Three Wu regions are merely a bed of pillows and mats.

Aware as I am of my lifelong habituation to softness and comfort, there is no place where I could not be employed; yet I am certainly unable to govern this place. This is truly my resolve. The Duke said:
"If you must go, wait until I have gathered some funds for travel expenses to prepare for wind and rain. He laughed and said, "Brother, how long do you think my life will last?
He replied, "How can one calculate this? He said, "Even if you could calculate the passage of years and months, brother—"
"How could I possibly endure the remainder of my days? The Master’s intention was full of lingering attachment and would not cease. I sent him word, saying:

"If you, brother, cannot set your mind at ease, try sketching it out briefly. Just as the Master was braving the heavy snow to enter the city, I immediately took up my gourd ladle and departed for good.
When the Master returned to the mountain and did not see me, he could not help but let out a loud cry of lamentation; from this, one may know the Master’s lifelong character.
I subsequently traveled north alone with my staff, while the Master also wandered his gaze across Mount Song, eventually returning after spending the winter at Mount Funiu.
He often remarked, "With my elder brother Qing gone, I have no friend. Upon hearing that I was in the capital, he set out in search of me with his gourd-bowl and straw hat.

Consequently, I traveled to other regions while you remained in the capital. When you heard that I had entered Mount Wutai with Master Miaofeng to dwell in a thatched hut, you immediately ascended the mountain.
Amidst the piles of ice and snow, you questioned me; during our night conversation, I probed into your resolve.
You said, "I see that this mind of yours is like ice; I vow to share in life and death with you. However..."
"I am mindful that our Master is advanced in years; what can be done? He replied, "It is not so. Each person has their own resolve, and each has their own karmic affinity.

If one examines your brother's affinity, it lies in propagating the Dharma to continue the life of wisdom, which is not comparable to mere austere seclusion. The Way of the Dharma in Jiangnan has long been submerged.
Fortunately, our Master, the Venerable Abbot, received the Buddha’s entrustment and opened the path there. Yet, looking at those under his guidance, it seems there is yet none [who can carry on]."
"One who can uphold the reputation of his family is truly a worthy son capable of fulfilling his filial duties. The future responsibilities for the Dharma path are no small matter;

moreover, as my teacher is in his twilight years, it is none other than you, brother, who can bring glory to the past and initiate the future. I pray you return quickly; do not linger long in another land.
The Master immediately prepared his horse to return. As he was about to depart, I instructed him, saying: "Brother, you have never previously considered the Dharma as your own..."
"Take responsibility. This time, take advantage of our Master’s advanced age to serve as his attendant; this will win over the hearts of scholars from all quarters.

When you ascend the dharma-throne in the future, it will be nothing other than the ancestral heritage of our house. Please do not decline out of excessive modesty. Once you have returned, you must stand firm and take the Dharma as your burden.
Those who have long practiced and studied will all step back in awe. Since the late Master began propagating the Dharma, he has expounded it three times."

In the *Great Commentary*, during the seventh lecture on the *Profound Discourse*, the Master fully grasped the essence of the Huayan Dharma-realm—the principle of perfect interfusion and non-obstruction—and immersed himself in the ocean of nature;

at that time, he was acclaimed as peerless. Having long admired the Chan school, when Master Dazhang opened the hall at Shaolin, the Master packed his bags and went to study under him, but eventually desisted. Subsequently, Master Xuan’an Ang arrived from Mount Shaoshi.

At Qixia, he took up and examined public cases (gong'an). He humbled himself to follow [the master] and, by deliberating upon the karmic conditions of the ancient worthies, he attained the essence of the single transmission.
When others felt shame over his conduct, he said: "Mañjuśrī was the teacher of the seven Buddhas; what harm is there in acting as the mallet-beater for Śākyamuni?
From that time on, whenever he uttered words, they were suddenly free from all constraints. Thereafter, he settled his mind in Chan contemplation and, regarding the late master...

Upon his passing, the Master occupied the honored seat, where ten thousand fingers circled him daily. Suddenly, he turned away from them and completely swept aside the conventional practices of philological exegesis.

He held up the original texts alone, directly probing the Buddha’s intent and pointing toward the meaning beyond words. He constantly taught his disciples to take contemplation through principle as their entry point;
consequently, the eyes and ears of the students were brilliantly renewed, like gazing into the vast sky after parting the clouds.

Like the sun and sky appearing through the mist, and the dragon’s thunder awakening the hibernating insects, all living beings were enlightened and revived; among those who heard him, there was none who did not marvel at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Prior to this, wherever lecture halls were established, they mostly followed conventional forms without literary elegance.

The doctrines taught therein were like someone clutching a post while rowing a boat—utterly lacking the mechanism for transcendence. Yet, upon his appearance in the world, it was like a mani jewel shining with perfect clarity, its five colors mutually radiant.
He responded according to the needs of each region; like a single rain that universally moistens all, the three types of grasses and two types of trees were all benefited by its nourishment.
He subdued some with compassion and broke others with majestic power. At one time, there was no scholar of exceptional intelligence who did not emerge from beneath his seat.

He preached the Dharma from beginning to end for nearly thirty years, always attracting a multitude numbering in the tens of thousands. Thereafter, he traveled at leisure through mountains and rivers, staff in hand.

Wherever he went, he followed conditions as they arose, at his own ease. By the water’s edge or beneath trees, he brandished his whisk in accordance with the Dharma-nature; like a dragon soaring or a tiger roaring, the wind stirred and the clouds followed.
Among the flourishing dharma assemblies of the past in both the North and South, nothing has ever equaled this.

Although my late master preached the Dharma for over thirty years, there were no more than two or three disciples who attained realization and emerged into the world, yet even they did not cause the teaching to flourish greatly. As for your disciples, they are capable of...

As for his disciples: he extensively propagated the teachings in all four directions. Among the masters of the Dharma seats in the south and north, all emerged from his school, with the exception of those at Yexi (three in total).
After Mingming Zongyi had passed away, the current generation—such as Chaosong and Jin-yiyu—soaked all in a single rain of dharma, loudly proclaiming the teaching throughout the Three Wu regions.
Yunpo Yu emerged late and shook the capital; Ruomai Zhi alone raised his banner in Jiangxi; Xin Guangmin propagated the Dharma in Huaibei.
Among those throughout the realm who called themselves preachers of the Dharma, there were none who did not point toward the Master’s gate as their ultimate refuge.

Were it not for possessing the power of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), how could such a thing be possible? Alas! How can this be fathomed by ordinary means? Whenever the Master withdrew from his seat, [the assembly would...]

He practiced the meditation of wall-contemplation (*bhittivipaśyanā*). Once, while dwelling in a thatched hut to cultivate stillness amidst the mountains of Changxing, he entered meditative absorption for two days;

the surrounding trees, forest, and dwellings shook as a result—something others could not have foreseen. By nature, he was open and even-tempered, never maintaining the formal barriers of social etiquette.
He did not avoid criticism or suspicion, taking contentment as his joy. His coming and going were carefree and serene, like a wild crane soaring through the void, casting off all constraints.
[The Master] was cautious. Chan Master Daguan harbored some resentment toward the Master (Xue Lang). I said, "The Master certainly does not know Xue Lang. I observe his causal ground:
he resolved his mind upon hearing the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and shaved his hair while facing the stupa of [Master] Zang. He is a man of rebirth, the very reincarnation of Kuiji.
Master Daguan nodded his head and said, "From this day forward, I shall no longer dare to look down upon this gentleman."—Recorded in the Ji year.

In the final years of the Jingtai era, the main temple was struck by a lightning fire; the halls and pavilions were reduced to ashes overnight. I and the Master stood facing one another and wept, saying: "Alas!
The Buddha taught that even when the great fires burn, the Pure Land is not destroyed. How could we have expected to perish together with it? How tragic, how difficult!
In this present age, if we abandon you, who else is there? Alas, his life was cut short while his merit remained unfulfilled.
"I am but a man of meager virtue and lack the power of the Way. From this moment forth, I shall resolve to practice cultivation;

in days to come, as my strength grows and my talents emerge, I shall ultimately fulfill this vow of restoration. For this reason, I have traveled north, firmly setting my will upon the great matter of birth and death.
In truth, for more than twenty years, I have never for a single day forgotten it in my heart—whether at Mount Wutai or the Eastern Sea, I have been like Zhang Liang."
From its inception until its conclusion, [this endeavor] was for the sake of Korea; unfortunately, it ultimately resulted in harm through our own actions.
Truly, great karmic conditions cannot be sought through mere idle fantasies. When I encountered misfortune and was sent away, passing through my hometown, you saw me off by the river.
We sat knee-to-knee at night and spoke of our original aspirations. I said: "The momentum of the undertaking has already been established; had we not met with this setback..."
"It shall be accomplished before long. For now, what can be done? I am departing. You, my brother, should wait for the right moment and take the initiative;

I shall personally go to beg for alms in the Southern Capital to awaken the ears and eyes of the masses. When I eventually return by the grace of Heaven, we may still deliberate upon our plans. The Master nodded his head in agreement.
At dawn on the eleventh day of the eleventh month of winter in the *wuchen* year of the Wanli era, I set out on my long journey. I calculated—

In the third year of the Ling era, the year Wuxu, the Master observed that the spire of his temple’s pagoda was leaning. He then resolved to repair it, and at once, those in authority provided their support.
Lord Zhu, the Palace Counselor, took the lead in initiating the effort. The Master personally led several hundred followers on a sequential alms-round through the city markets.
At that time, the hearts of the people were stirred with enthusiasm; those who gathered gold and money did so by the hundreds and thousands.

The plan was finalized and the great undertaking was launched. The pagoda was twenty-five *zhang* in height. The central shaft for the pinnacle of the pagoda measured approximately seven *zhang* in length;
when the scaffolding reached twice that height, it was lowered from the air like a mustard seed falling onto a needle—a feat of immense difficulty.

The Master’s mind was filled with extreme anguish, and he suddenly vomited several *sheng* of blood. At that moment, the shaft was inserted, and those on the scaffolding felt as if they were birds perched in their nests.
The tender branches have ultimately suffered no minor ailment; is this not brought about by the power of the mind? Calculating the expenses, they amounted to tens of thousands of strings of cash;
only three thousand taels were granted by the Holy Mother, while the remainder was drawn from among the common people, without moving so much as a single hair’s breadth of public funds.
