Born into a wealthy household, everyone regarded his disposition and habits as soft and indulgent, yet such was his steadfast conduct in middle age.
Regarding his ascetic practices, he established the Dashachaya Hermitage at Dajianling in Jiangdong. He personally carried water and provided for them daily without weariness;
as his disciples followed him, his preaching of the Dharma never ceased. Even those with frail bones grew increasingly robust through this practice.
Constantly contemplating the establishment of a "Ten Directions" alms-food association, he went to Wangting in Wu in his later years and opened a reception hall to welcome travelers and visitors.

He personally handled water and wood and took up manual tasks, leading his disciples in their labors. By day he provided them with meals; by evening he bathed them; and by night he preached the Dharma.
Bestowing both self-benefit and the benefit of others simultaneously, the scholars of the two regions of Wu flocked to him in faith and devotion.

Even those who were icchantikas turned into protectors of the Dharma. Before long, he manifested a slight illness. One day, he addressed the assembly, saying: "You must each well protect and maintain yourselves."
"I am about to depart," he said. "Disciples, I beg the Master for instruction. The Master replied, "It is like flowers in the sky; fundamentally they do not exist. What is there to speak of?
He asked, "Master, you yourself do not deny it; yet why use a sitting-casket and why use a coffin?

The Master said, "When one dies while sitting, one uses a casket; when one dies while lying down, one uses a coffin. As for the ceremonial gifts and the striking of the ritual vessels, do not prepare them yet. Having finished speaking, in a short while—
He requested a bath and changed his robes; then, sitting upright, he passed away. His disciples escorted his remains for burial at Xuelang Mountain.
On the day of his passing, a path of sorrow filled the roads, and those who studied under him felt as if they had lost their own parents.

The Master was born on the ninth day of the ninth month of the Jiaping year of Yisi (1565) and entered *nirvāṇa* on a certain day of a certain month in the Wanli year of Dingwei (1607). He was sixty-three years old in worldly age. [His] Dharma...

He was forty-five years old at the time of his parinirvāṇa. Although he had many disciples who received ordination from him, only Sūn Huìjīng—whose courtesy name was Yuándū—fully grasped the essential points of his teachings and was particularly adept in the Abhidharma school.
It was from him that the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (She dasheng weishi lun) was truly developed and elucidated. Alas, it is to be regretted that he died young.
As for the disciples who transmitted the Dharma and appeared in the world, they are as listed above; those who remained in obscurity are still many more. Alas!
I and you were once of the same clan, yet we have been separated for thirty years and have not reunited even in our old age—a thought that constantly brings forth eternal sighs.

Whenever I reflect upon this age, those who truly knew you were few; how much fewer, then, since your passing? Therefore, I have recorded the general outline of your life to serve as a record for the Dharma.
The Way is that upon which the restoration of the tradition depends. For now, let future students know that there is a long-standing provenance for the causal conditions of the Great Dharma.

The eulogy says: We have heard that when Bodhisattvas come and go among humans and devas, even as they retain afflictions to moisten their rebirth, they still experience the confusion of the "separation from the physical body" (the transition between lives).

Yet he did not possess the power of recollecting past lives; he could only verify it for himself within dreams. When the wise observe this through the lens of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), there is not the slightest discrepancy.
By virtue of the circumstances of your public renunciation, I know that you must surely be a person of "return" (*punar-āgata*). The actions of a supreme being are hidden and they sport in the world;
whether moving against or with the current, their ways are not fixed—how could they be fathomed by ordinary sentiments? The trampling of dragons and elephants is certainly not [for the common herd].
It is only fit for a lame donkey; it is no wonder that those with the physical eye disregard it.

Were it not for the power of long-accumulated vows, how could its light flow through the final age to revitalize the decline of a hundred generations? By observing his effortless liberation from birth and death, one can know this for certain.
Biography of Chan Master Master Langmu Zhi, the Restorer of Mount Fushan Dahuayan Temple in Huancheng. His name was Benzhi;
he was originally styled Huiguang. He was the son of the Li family of Qujing. He was originally a native of Jinling, later migrating [to the south].
He resided in Southern Duan. From birth, he was unconventional and stood apart from the crowd, harboring a resolve to transcend the mundane world.
To the south of Qu City lies Langmu Mountain, where his father had retired from secular life; he was known as Master Bāizhāi.

When the Master was twelve years old, he went to rely upon his father and subsequently shaved his head to become a *kū'wō* (a novice). Later, while traveling on pilgrimage, he encountered the scholar Huang Daoyue, with whom he conversed.
Seizing the opportune moment, he changed his name to Langmu (Bright Eyes). Baizhai took the Avatamsaka Sutra as his primary practice;

Gong, having been inspired by the teachings on "perfuming through hearing," immediately engaged himself therein. Constantly, he kept the great matter of birth and death in mind, resolutely aspiring toward the higher goal.
At the age of nineteen, he received full ordination. When Bai Zhai was about to pass away, the Master requested further instruction.

Zhai said, "How could I know that you would not long become a son-in-law? The Master was stirred with indignation; he immediately resolved to maintain his integrity and traveled north to the Central Plains.

He visited famous mountains and sought out spiritual teachers, his footsteps covering half the world until his spirit eclipsed those of eight or nine other regions. Regarding the Dharma traditions of the North and South—

The various great elders of the Gate—such as Dafang of Funiu, Yinzhong, Wujin of Nanyue, Dajian of Mount Lu, Bianrong of Jimen, and Yuexin—were all contemporary masters of both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings; they all entered his gate.
Having been refined through the crucible, the furnace, the tongs, and the hammer, he thus attained the essential point of both the *zong* (essence) and the *jiao* (teachings).

However, regarding the single matter of investigating one’s own person, he regarded non-awakening as his primary concern. Consequently, he established himself in meditation for twelve years until the light of the mind finally broke through.
From that time on, his spiritual eloquence became spontaneous and free. While traveling northward, he passed through Liu’an, where the Grand Officer, Lord Liu, acted as his patron.

Zhongfeng resided at the Huayan Aranya. Before long, he departed for Baixia. The Palace Attendant Zhong Gong of Yuchun was a man who treated others with arrogance and had little regard for the Dharma;
no one had ever dared to challenge his sharp wit. One day, he arrived at Tianjie Temple and asked the administrator, "In this world of the Dharma, are there any Chan practitioners?
The administrator pushed Gong out to meet him and requested that he inquire about Chan.
The Master asked, "Does Tiantai Temple reside within the mind or outside the mind? Gong said, "Set aside the temple for a moment; let me ask you, what do you take to be the mind?
Zhong remained silent. Gong said, "Do not speak of Tiantai; even the three thousand Buddhas reside upon the tip of this mountain monk’s whisk.
After a long while, Zhong bowed. From that time on, he first realized that there were people in the Dharma-gate.
Mr. Tao was well-suited for an official post in the Ministry of Rites, and they were in perfect accord with one another. When Mr.

Tao was demoted to the position of Vice Governor of Luzhou and was stationed at Liu’an, he established the Jingxin Vihāra (Mirror-Mind Hermitage) to await his arrival. Ninety *li* east of Wan is Mount Fu; this is where Master Huiyuan and Lord Ouyang once expounded the Dharma while playing chess.
There stands the ancient monastery of the Huayan Monastery, which serves as a center for the practice of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. It is a place of singular...
It had been destroyed and abandoned by the icchantikas. Grand Historian Wu Gong constantly lamented this, desiring to restore it but unable to do so.

Since the Battle of Feishui, the Master [Fahu] had arrived, his single staff trailing lightly behind him. Upon meeting and conversing with Grand Historian Wu Gong, they found their minds in perfect accord.

Prostrating himself twice, the Grand Historian addressed him, saying: "The 'Floating Across' (Fudu) is truly the fundamental vehicle of the Ninefold Canon; recently, Master Guting has propagated its transformation."

The site is the Flower Adornment (Avataṃsaka) Bodhimanda; it is here that the *kṣa* staff was once again erected. Now, that it has been carried away by those with power—what will become of this mountain?
Since Gu Ting was a man from Dīnnán, could he not have come as your very next incarnation? Is this not the fulfillment of a prior vow?
Upon hearing this, the Master was struck with amazement and said, "In my youth, whenever I faced the physical remains of Gu Ting, I would gaze upon them with longing and affection."
"No more of this. Furthermore, I have heard that the Dharma was first propagated at Fudu; I did not know it was this very mountain.

Thinking thus upon the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he realized it was the very origin of his renunciation of the household life, as if all were the fulfillment of a karmic bond from past lives. He then joyfully gave his heart’s assent.

Thereupon, he offered incense and prayed to the protective deities of the Dharma before departing with his robes tied around his waist. The Grand Historian still did not know where he was headed. The Master arrived at Huai.
Yin. Liu Zhongcheng Dongxing of Qinshui was stationed at Huai with his official insignia. Having long admired those beyond the mundane world, he encountered [the Master] by chance at Longxing Temple.
Observing the Master’s quick-wittedness, he rejoiced that it accorded with his own long-held aspirations; he subsequently took him into his residence as a guest.

During their leisurely conversations, they occasionally discussed the karmic conditions for crossing over [to liberation]. Liu Gong said joyfully, "This requires nothing more than the power of a finger-snap," and immediately issued an official edict to the prefecture.
He issued a decree to a single official, who intimidated and subdued the icchantikas, causing them all to surrender the fields of Wenyang to him.

This restoration of what had been in ruins for one hundred and fifty years was accomplished with a single word; was this not the power of his vow? Once the temple was restored, he subsequently traveled north to the capital.
At that time, the Divine Temple was commissioned by Imperial Decree from Empress Dowager Cisheng to distribute the printed Tripitaka scriptures. The Master...
He then received the imperial edict and, carrying the Great Canon, returned to Fushan.
From the year Wuxu until Renyin, within five years, the Huoguo Da Huayan Temple at Fushan rose majestically as if emerging from the earth; how could this have been the work of human effort alone?
Once the monastic community was established, he entrusted it to his disciple Yuan [name], moved by Lord Liu’s protection of the Dharma.
[The Emperor] granted leave. He traveled to Qinshui to offer his condolences. Prince Shen was a bulwark for the Buddha-dharma, the foremost among the Kṣatriyas.
Upon hearing that the Master had entered the country, he wished to have an audience with him. The Master said to the envoy: "The Buddha-dharma has been entrusted to the kings.

The śrāmaṇera was Huang Sheng of Qiantang. At the time of his death, he requested ordination; having assumed the form of a monk, he passed away while seated. Thus, he received the title of *śrāmaṇera*.
His secular name was Chenghui, and his courtesy name was Yuanfu. He had previously taken refuge with the Great Master Yunqi, whose dharma name was Jingming.

By nature, he was upright and did not conform to worldly ways; he did not engage in farming or business. While living among his fellow villagers, he frequently encountered opposition even from his own kin.

When meeting friends, he would simply sit alone, looking blankly with wide-open eyes. He was serene and had no worldly desires; apart from mountains, rivers, calligraphy, and painting, he had no other concerns.

When his father died, he was left with no remaining assets, yet he was barely able to support his eight family members. By nature, he was profoundly filial, serving his grandmother, his biological mother, and his adoptive mother.
He was thus distressed and unable to continue providing delicacies; he exerted himself in every way to fulfill his filial duties.

When his grandmother died, he lay bedridden with a grave illness, yet he strove with all his might to manage the funeral affairs and perform the rites to the utmost. His fellow villagers praised him for this. By nature, he was fond of giving.

When a neighboring woman was cold and had no clothes, he immediately took off his own garment to clothe her. When a neighbor was poor and had no food, he emptied his purse—which contained only a hundred coins—and gave it all to her.

His wife’s younger brother, having heard of him, remarked that he was solitary and stubborn, yet fit for entering the Way, and spoke of this to him repeatedly. Although he was pleased, he did not enter the path;

On Hearing of the Brief Biography of Zhongzi:
Zhongzi’s surname was Wen, his given name Qichu, and his courtesy name Ziyu. He was a native of Qiantang in Zhejiang and the younger brother of Qixiang, a filial and incorrupt official.
From childhood, Zhongzi had been prone to illness; therefore, he early on renounced the pursuit of the imperial examination curriculum. He had long harbored the resolve to transcend birth and death.
Having no desire for domestic life, he took refuge at Yunqi and received the Pure Land dharma-gate. He believed it with sincerity and practiced it with diligence.
When I went to pay my respects at Yunqi, his second son prostrated and said, "For the sake of the great matter of birth and death, I wish to shave my head and follow the Master.
I replied, "It is not so. The Buddha-nature cannot be constrained by the four great elements; how could it be bound by a mere hair?"
"How could I dare? Moreover, while one's parents are alive, it is improper to travel far away. Could a son of the Buddha be considered unfilial for doing so? Zhongzi then desisted.

Later, upon returning to Kuangshan, I learned that Zhongzi was critically ill and on the verge of death; my heart was deeply grieved for him. Furthermore, when I read the biography of his elder brother, [I felt even more sorrow].
He then said with great joy, "How true! He is indeed a heroic and valiant man. At first, the second son relied on the strength of his faith;

though he had been ill for a long time, his mental power remained very robust, and he was determined that rebirth would be no difficulty. Yet, when it came to the moment of crisis—the very threshold between life and death—his habitual tendencies manifested, and his mind became dazed.
Only then did he realize that his Pure Land practice had not been pure, and that he was still caught in the cycle of coming and going."
He could not remain still. He suddenly sprang up and cried out loudly, "Quickly, request my spiritual friends to recite the Buddha's name to assist me!

Once the spiritual friends had gathered, they recited the Buddha’s name day after day. However, his habitual environment remained dark and turbulent. He then called out again, "The root and trunk of birth and death—I know that no one else can pull them out.

He repented with bitter earnestness and sincere lamentation, never flagging throughout the night. Shortly thereafter, he realized for himself that his past karmic obstructions had melted away like ice;

He immediately ordered his hair to be shaved and donned the *kāṣāya* robe to assume the appearance of a *saṃgha*. Departing from the assembly in tranquility, he sat upright and passed away. Alas! How could this be the manner of an ordinary person?
How marvelous! We have often heard that Nirvana is the peaceful abode of all Buddhas; it is not something that cannot be realized except through kalpas of diligent toil.

It is like inscribing this upon banners and streamers: wherever the wind reaches, wherever its shadow falls, all who come into contact with it are able to leave suffering behind and attain happiness.
How much more so for those who practice it, uphold it, cherish it within their hearts, and take it as the seal of the mind!

Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If there are sentient beings whose habitual afflictions are difficult to eliminate, they need only single-mindedly recite this secret divine mantra of the Buddha’s *Uṣṇīṣa-raśmi-samcaya*.
The fire of lust will be instantly extinguished, like ice melting in hot water; by the mere thought of it, they shall be transformed into unsurpassed awakening. Alas!
All sentient beings take lustful desire as the very basis for their life and nature; now, if one merely upholds this—
Upon reciting the mantra, the life-root is instantly severed and one is forever liberated from birth and death.

How much more so, then, could those petty afflictions of greed, anger, ignorance, and pride not be transformed into the true seeds of unsurpassed Bodhi? The practitioner Ming-kuan has maintained this for many years;
he now requests the Elder Haiyin to transcribe this scroll, so that he may wear it upon his person for the rest of his life and recite it without forgetting. The Elder—

I admire his aspirations and conduct and assist him in his steadfastness; thus I have composed this writing and appended these words to it, intending it as a guide for his future career and an example for those who come after.
Postscript to the *Sūtra on the Eight Awakenings of a Great Man*:
In the past, when I resided by the sea, I would frequently write out this *Sūtra on the Eight Awakenings of a Great Man* for my disciples to recite.

Now, having come here, I have forgotten it. Yesterday, Master Daguan happened to show me a large-scale transcription of the text, calligraphed in the "baked-clay" style by the Great Master Yuansue’an, which had been carved into woodblocks.

I have long kept this manuscript hidden away in my chest, never having taken it up to show others. Now, the Venerable Jingxin of Xiao Jinshan has happened to bring this volume here and requested that I write some words of Dharma for it. Upon reading it, I was suddenly struck with the feeling of beholding an old possession from my past. I am Zhuhong. To be inscribed: The Way is originally one; there is no distinction between high and low. It is like the great ocean, where all rivers flow together. Yet, because people’s faculties differ, they each perceive it according to their own capacity. Thus, when the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī, he spoke of the Four Noble Truths; when he taught the Lotus Sūtra at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he revealed the One Vehicle. These were merely expedient means to guide beings according to their needs. Now, you, O Venerable One, have come from afar seeking the Dharma. I shall briefly set forth its essentials for you. First, you must realize that the mind is itself the Buddha. Do not seek the Buddha outside the mind, nor seek the mind outside the Buddha. When the mind is still, it is the Buddha; when thoughts arise, they are the functioning of the Buddha. There is no separate Buddha apart from this. Second, you must sever all delusive attachments. Whether it be wealth, status, kin, or fame—let them all be as empty as space. Only then can you attain liberation. Third, you must practice with diligence and perseverance. Do not be distracted by worldly affairs. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, maintain constant mindfulness.

This is what is called "constant cultivation. If you can abide in these three points, you will naturally accord with the Way. As for me, I am but an old man of the mountains, ignorant and lacking in wisdom. My writing is crude and unrefined; I offer this merely as a response to your request. May it serve as a small aid on your path. Respectfully written by Zhuhong. *Postscript:* This was written on the twenty-third day of the tenth month in the year of the Earth-Hare (1639). I hope that by reading this, you will feel as though you are seeing an old friend again. I have always kept this in my chest and have never shown it to anyone. Now that the Venerable Jingxin has brought it here, I have complied with his request. May it be auspicious. *End of Inscription.*
I was then inspired and transcribed this sutra once. Thereupon, I sighed and said: "This is sufficient evidence that the Way of resonance has been met;
it is simply the convergence of the proper time and conditions. When the Buddha preaches the Dharma for sentient beings, he waits only for the appropriate capacity. Therefore, it is said:"

I have long kept silent regarding this essential teaching and have not sought to expound it hastily. The reason I have never spoken of it before is that the time for its proclamation had not yet arrived.
When I first entered Guangdong, I did not see any monks who were fervently devoted to the Buddha-dharma. One day, however, I happened to visit Master Jinshan.
Thereupon, he took the various eminent gentlemen who had been invited and together transcribed one volume of the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*, requesting me to write a postscript.
From then on, several monastics and lay disciples transcribed the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*.
Consequently, I gave a complete lecture on it for the newly ordained śrāmaṇeras beneath the Bodhi tree; those who were able to hear this sūtra numbered no fewer than several hundred.
Indeed, the catalyst for this originated with the Venerable Master. This sutra is something rarely heard by any of the devas or humans in all the worlds;
throughout my life, I have delighted in bestowing this sutra upon others, yet here in this very place, the opportunity did not arise.
Now, through the Venerable Master, it has been brought forth once more—this matter is truly extraordinary. Why is this? Because of the Buddha...
In expounding the Dharma, one acts only in response to the capacity [of the listener], responding only when pressed by necessity.
It is like a great bell suspended on its stand, which resonates according to the strike. Thus, we know that this present causal occasion is no exception to this rule.

This is truly because all sentient beings lie dormant within this Great Treasury of Radiance, sinking into the dream of the long night; it has been a long time since they have first awakened to this truth. It is not otherwise.
Great awakening alone is insufficient to shatter the great dream; nor can one who does not shatter the great dream be called a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
It is not only those who can awaken others who are Great Men, but those who exert themselves with courageous vigor to awaken themselves are likewise Great Men.
This is precisely what enables one to attain great awakening and subsequently become a Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa); yet it is only by becoming a Great Man that one can attain great awakening.
To shatter the dream of eternal night through the awakening of a single thought—how could this be a trivial matter? Alas!
I observe that all sentient beings throughout the great earth equally receive this awakening and are none other than Great Men; they simply lack a Great Man to open their minds to it. I...
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, alone is titled the Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). At the single assembly on Vulture Peak, there were heroic and eminent figures;

from the breaking of the smile at the presentation of the flower and the wall-gazing at Shaolin, down to the six transmissions, five schools, and seventeen hundred followers, all are called those who have awakened themselves and awakened others—powerful Great Men. Yet they were all identical to ordinary people. Alas!

Indeed, all sentient beings are fully realized in Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). That they remain bewildered and fail to enter it is not because Enlightenment rejects those who seek to enter;
rather, it is because they are unable to awaken to these eight dharmas. Consequently, at the critical juncture of birth and death, they cannot cast off their burdens.
For this reason, they willingly endure sinking and delusion, hurrying through the realms of suffering, wandering in hardship and distress as transient guests.
One who acts as a lowly person cannot be called a great man.

That you, a superior man, could so magnificently trigger this pivotal moment—could this not be like the son of a wealthy family, fallen into poverty on a distant road, who at once conceives the thought of returning home?

Now, this *Sūtra on the Eight Awakenings of a Great Man* that I have transcribed is truly like a letter carried by a crane’s leg; by unfolding it, one immediately receives news from one's native land.

Try to unfold it from time to time, and do not for a moment forget your plan to return, so that the Compassionate Honored One may gaze upon you from the realm of eternal quiescence as you lean upon the gateway of Prajñā.
The Epilogue on the Vows of Śākyamuni and Avalokiteśvara:
The study of the Śākya clan takes the total embodiment and great function, extending to the full measure of the Dharma-realm, as its ultimate standard.
This is what is called the majestic spiritual power of Vairocana’s Sea-Seal Samādhi, which manifests with impartiality. Therefore, all Buddhas...

From its beginning to its end, all the bodhisattvas’ activities for benefiting sentient beings, down to conventional speech and the occupations for sustaining life, all flow forth from this samādhi. It possesses vast and inconceivable power;

the adornments of merit and wisdom are fully complete, whereby one perceives the wondrousness of the dharma-realm. Furthermore, all holy ones and ordinary beings are, without exception, encompassed within it.
This is how one knows that our Patriarch was one among those who attained samādhi.

The two treatises he compiled on Śākyamuni and Avalokiteśvara describe the realm of samādhi and transform it into skillful means for benefiting sentient beings; they further expound the dharma-gates of the teachings of a lifetime.
Moreover, they constitute the samādhi within samādhi—how could they ever be categorized by the mere words of worldly convention?
Ah! When the wise contemplate this, how could they not leap with joy into this samādhi? Alas, I, a mere youth, have likewise arisen from samādhi to offer praise;
how could this be fathomed or deliberated upon by ordinary sentiments?
Inscription for the Painting of Universal Mindfulness of the Buddha and Seeking Rebirth in the Pure Land:

Throughout kalpas of existence, worldly beings have long been submerged in the bitter sea of birth and death, cycling through the three miserable realms solely because their own minds give rise to delusive thoughts and afflictions, thereby creating all manner of karma.
Consequently, they find no time of escape. Thus, the Buddha taught the single gateway of the Western Pure Land.
To gather in sentient beings and lead them out of the miserable realms—this is the most sublime Dharma-gate. To achieve completion in a single lifetime:

the monk Haihui of Chu single-mindedly exhorts those throughout the ten directions who are truly subject to birth and death to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha with one heart, without any other distractions.

Because the afflictions of sentient beings are deep and heavy and their deluded thoughts are so numerous, all of which are the very roots of birth and death, many Buddhas are required to deliver many people.
Now we hear that you, Layman Dong, have carved a statue of Maitreya Amitābha welcoming [beings to the Pure Land], with approximately one thousand eight hundred circles covering its entire body;

Furthermore, it is prayed that those whom one exhorts to recite the Buddha’s name shall likewise reach the same number of recitations. It is further hoped that great-hearted patrons will [support this endeavor].

The distribution of paper seals is also similar in nature; however, when this merit is perfected, there is no doubt that both the donor and the reciter will together return to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
This concludes the Preface for the Fundraising Appeal for the Transformation City.
This grand undertaking of carving the Tripitaka is a momentous event in the history of the Buddha-dharma’s entry into China over two thousand years ago.
It enables immeasurable sentient beings in the age of the Dharma’s decline to plant the true cause for attaining Buddhahood;
even those in remote mountains and secluded valleys where the Dharma has not reached may now behold the complete collection of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s great deeds. This merit alone is truly...
This is the most rare and supreme undertaking in China. One who does not possess the power of great compassionate vows cannot give rise to such a mind;

yet one who does not possess the power of great resolve cannot successfully complete such an enterprise. Now that we have already passed halfway through, the expenditure has reached tens of thousands of units.
Thus, this is not the strength of a single person’s hands or feet alone. As for the location where the woodblocks were carved, the initial plan was five...
At Mount Tai, he suffered from ice and snow; subsequently, at Jingshan, he suffered from mist and dampness; neither was a long-term solution.

Finally, he moved to Huacheng, which can truly be called finding his proper place. The initial proposal for this was made by Palace Historian Feng; its restoration was achieved through the efforts of Vice Minister Wu;
and its successful fulfillment was due to Master Danguan Kai. All of these were the result of immense vows and power. However, the hall where the woodblocks are stored must have a high roof.

The racks were constructed so as to elevate them from the ground and allow air to circulate, preventing them from easily deteriorating. Once the wooden boards were completed and installed, the labor involved was such that it could certainly not have been accomplished by the efforts of a single person or a single force.
Now, observing the intent behind the memorials of the two gentlemen, Feng and Wu, they even went so far as to show no regard for their own heads, eyes, marrow, or brains;
what kind of bitter resolve was this! I have often said that there are those in this world who are truly people of an entire era. All...
Our shared aspiration has long resided within the Tathāgata’s treasury of radiant light; it is said that when conditions ripen, it manifests.
This monk who now begs for alms is much like one who carries an old bond to seek out a fellow aspirant.
We know for certain that those who are moved upon seeing him were all comrades from the past, and we shall surely meet again in the future. As for what he bestows, why should we calculate it?
Money, coins, silks, and fabrics! When one’s mind is equal in measure to this Dharma as empty space, then one’s merit shall likewise be equal in measure to the realm of empty space.
Inscribed for the Small Portrait of the Great Master Yunqi.
The Perfected Person has no body; they take the power of their vows as their body. The Perfected Person has no affairs; they take the benefit of sentient beings as their affair.
Thus, the body is not "mine," and affairs are not "done by me. This is why the body cannot constrain them and affairs cannot burden them.

Master Guan lived in this world for over eighty years, and the work he established for saving sentient beings was already more than half complete; had it not been known that he had not yet appeared in the world, [his legacy would have been even greater].
All that preceded was Master Cao’s means for engaging with people. Through this very gateway of the Dharma, he gathered in immeasurable sentient beings and shared in their cycle of birth and death;

one cannot know how many such individuals there were. Thus, although the Master came and went according to conditions and manifested through the illusions of birth and death, his Dharmakāya remained eternally present, enduring as long as the mountains and rivers. Postscript to the Text on Releasing Living Beings:
The teachings of the Sages govern the world through the Five Constant Virtues (*pañca-śīla*), with benevolence (*ren*) as the foremost. To refrain from killing is called benevolence.
The Buddha established the Five Precepts, placing non-killing first. Thus we know that the mind of the Sage takes compassion as its foundation. As the Sūtra says: "Filial piety is named..."
Regarding the precepts: these take filial piety as their foundation. Since all sentient beings who possess consciousness have Buddha-nature, to kill a living being is to sever that Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, it does not merely result in the cycle of mutual enmity and retribution;
therefore, throughout the long kalpas of birth and death, wandering through the six realms of existence, there is no destination one has not reached and no body one has not assumed.
Those beings you have killed can all be known as your parents, brothers, wives, children, and other close relatives from many past lives.
To now take their lives and eat their flesh—is this not nothing less than the devouring of one's own flesh and bones?
The Buddha took filial piety as his precept; therefore, know that non-killing is the greatest form of filial piety. How could it merely be a matter of sparing the lives of animals?
It is so. How tragic! The delusion of worldly people persists as they habitually practice eating one another without awakening; how painful this is!
Therefore, the Sage enjoined non-killing in order to preserve the Buddha-nature; this, moreover, is not merely a matter of worldly filial piety.
This Master Lianchi universally exhorted the release of living beings because he followed the mind of the Buddha.

If people can comply with and practice this, they will not only attain the Master’s intention, but it will be sufficient to fulfill the highest filial piety, perfect their Buddha-nature, and serve as the cause for attaining Buddhahood.
How could this be a trivial matter? This book has been carved to widely transform many; this is not merely to broaden [the teaching].
The Great Master’s mind truly expands upon the Buddha’s compassion; it is not the mere common speech of the world. One should believe it with firm conviction.
Preface to the *Record of Manifest Retribution for Killing Living Beings*.
The Buddha said: "All sentient beings, down to the most minute insects and living creatures, possess Buddha-nature.
He further stated: "Sentient beings have transmigrated through birth and death for immeasurable kalpas; there is not a single class among them that has not received a physical body.

Thus, it is evident that all those who possess life do not consist solely of the "life of wisdom" (prajñā-jīvita); they are all past kinsmen and causes, yet they remain deluded and unaware. Sentient beings are ignorant.
Deluded! Furthermore, it is not merely a matter of devouring; they also use the lives of others as nets for profit, nourishing themselves and their kin.
As for those who are killed, do they merely sever the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom? They also kill and harm the very causes of their own kinship.

What was previously said regarding retribution in a future life—now, observing this record, it is clearly manifest as immediate retribution before our eyes, witnessed and heard by everyone. This, then, is no mere theory.
He has killed his own wisdom-life and the cause of his own kin; he has truly killed his own body and hastened his own death. Why wait for the future?
How can one not be afraid! Contemplating this record, one sees that the Buddha said these are but the "flower-retribution" (the present signs), while the "fruit-retribution" lies in hell.
To be able to uphold and practice this is to pay homage to the Buddhadharma of the three periods of time.

How fortunate it was that the Most Holy Mother of the Late Emperor personally modeled herself for the Sacred Sovereign, bringing about a revival.
The propagation of the Buddha’s work has filled the realm for over forty years without ceasing for even a moment; this is likewise unprecedented in all history.
As for the "dragons and elephants" of the Dharma-gate, these five great masters have gathered together at one time.

Although their essential natures and functions differ, and their principles and phenomena are distinct, the means by which they uphold the religious teachings and open the eyes of humans and devas to serve as a beacon through the long night [of ignorance] is...
The Lamp of Wisdom has never failed to share the same path and tread the same tracks as the Buddhas and Patriarchs; how much more so when it stands majestic and sublime as a great banner of light!
I am fortunate to follow in the footsteps of these masters, yet I alone feel ashamed of my own meanness and inferiority, unable even to pick up a single blade of grass [to offer].
Third, I offer this praise: may its radiance not be obscured, so that it may illuminate the final age.

Inscription for the Scroll "The Dharma Thunder Resounds Afar," Presented to Master Kongyin of Wutai as He Spreads Enlightenment in Yunzhong (The following is appended from the *Drafts Left by Donghai*).

Before the Buddha appeared in the world and before the Patriarch came from the West, not a single speck of dust had been divided; the great earth was motionless, yet the myriad phenomena revealed the Dharma.
The substance of the body: empty space preaches the Sutra of No-Characters. Those who see it are blind; those who hear it are deaf.

To gaze upon this with eyes of compassion—there are those who cannot bear the sorrow. Suddenly leaping up, the shadow falls within this realm. Thus...
Facing death ten thousand times for the sake of life once, he shared both bitterness and sweetness. The *Tripiṭaka* masters were filled with anxiety until their broad and long tongues grew parched;
the "Old Lady’s" compassionate heart was moved to shed drops of blood from a single blow of the fist.

Thus, our Great Master, having no other choice, presided over the three miserable realms, manifesting his body among various species—sometimes stretching like a lion, sometimes turning back like an elephant king—taking what is not yet there as if it were already present.
Playing with the false brings about the true; it transforms humans and devas, overturning even the most eminent heroes.
Through this, the gate of ambrosia is opened, and the thunder of the Great Dharma resounds. Instantly, spring is brought to the cold valley, and sprouts gradually emerge.
The three types of grasses and two types of trees send forth tendrils and sprout branches; those with superior, middling, and inferior roots, bearing flowers and fruit, are beyond counting.
Thus, responding to conditions through provisional designation, the "knocking" and the "singing" proceed in unison, and the rhythm and beat form a command.
All of this is nothing other than meeting one capacity with another capacity, using a wedge to extract a wedge; how could there be any real dharma given to people?
Yet those who observe the scene later take the unreal for the real and cling to what is unsaid as being said. Consequently, their tongues become parched and their hearts bleed.
How tragic! The teacher exhorts with earnest repetition, yet the listener remains indifferent. Moreover, they rely upon this as the true master, thereby seeking to destroy their own perfection;
in the end, they receive not even a fraction of a reward, only to become entangled in the fetters of long kalpas. Why is this so?

It is because they take the non-existent for the existent and play with the false until it seems real; failing to recognize that gods and humans are illusory transformations, they cause even the heroic and eminent to fall into perversion.
[The Master] said: "The nectar of immortality and the poison of death both stem from this; by whom does birth and death arise? It is for this alone that my tears have never failed to fall. Alas!

Those who have sighed with frustration and sought such a person find them difficult to encounter. Only the Dharma Master, Master Cheng, is truly worthy of this role.
Having early paid homage to the King of Emptiness, he did not indulge in human artifice. Long transcending all realms of existence, he strictly purified the *vinaya*.

Amidst the turbid world, he moves with graceful ease; like a blue lotus, he stands tall and upright. In the silent, empty mountains, he is as majestic as towering ice and snow. With a chest full of gallantry and integrity, he is forged of living iron.

If it is so, only then can one repay the kindness of my Master. Let us join arms with you and wander together in the realm of the deathless.

The ancients regarded the matter of birth and death as paramount; therefore, they severed their attachments and renounced glory to climb mountains and wade through waters to seek out spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Seeking one another on the shores of suffering, emptiness, and profound stillness, they resolve their own fundamental nature and illuminate that which transcends the ordinary.
Before those with clear eyes, through a single raised brow, a flicker of an eye, or beneath a staff-blow or a shout, they suddenly burst asunder;

therefore, upon seeing these words, you felt such kinship with them. Otherwise, it would be like chewing on... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
"A soup of wood shavings; it is merely biting iron while eating rice. You, sir, are about to return to your native mountains, and I too shall return eastward to my cave-dwelling.

Otherwise, you will not only fail to honor your own spiritual nature, but furthermore—
Furthermore, this has even affected the Haiyin [Collection].

Following the postscript to Master Zhulin’s *Dharma Words for His Disciples on Shaking Up the School*, many Chan practitioners have come to disparage the teachings, while many who study the teachings remain ignorant of Chan. Consequently, Chan and the teachings have been treated as two separate, incompatible poles.

The masters of antiquity were ultimately unable to unify their ultimate aim. Even Guishan, who harmonized the various teachings and schools, still considered it like "seeing the moon through a gauze screen.
For over a thousand years, up and down through history, scholars have been unable to unify their direction of practice.
This is due to nothing other than a lack of authentic lineage transmission and the correct eye; it is for this reason that we must shatter the barriers. It is not that there is no Chan.

It is simply that there is no teacher. Because those of the Chan school lack extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), and because the teachings and the lineage lack the "correct eye" (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), this Great Way is therefore difficult to clarify.

When the Great Master Qingliang Zhulin sat upon his flowered seat surrounded by ten thousand fingers, he skillfully expounded the essentials of the Dharma and was hailed as the "Dragon of Meaning" of the age.
Yet in his daily practice, he did not enter the abstruse paths; observe the words he spoke to his disciples: [The passage continues with the cited teaching.]
This sentence contains the essential strategy of the Chan school. Were it not for the True Eye, how could one possibly produce such words and breathe forth such spirit as this?
Could such a heroic and robust expression be dismissed by those who merely rely on the mastery of written characters? Alas! Students have long fallen into the net of conceptual knowledge;
were it not for the Vajra King’s sword, it could not be severed with a single stroke. The Great Master used this to demonstrate and revitalize the school.
A student of the Way must surely act as the "grass for the household" (a servant of the Dharma); they will certainly not fail this significant karmic connection.
To regard this matter as mere ordinary entanglement is not only to miss the mark face-to-face, but it is also to gravely辜负 (betray) the profound grace of the Dharma.
Inscription on the Back of the Traveling Scroll of Attendant Zhenshan:
These are the words shown to traveling monks by eighteen eminent monks of the early Song dynasty. I venture to say that this is a single stream of the Zen source.
Since the time of Zhongfeng, the lineage has been silent and devoid of worthy successors.
Those who have descended from the Empty Valley have mostly been characterized by narrow-mindedness and pedantry, lacking the strategic mastery of the ancients—like a lion that has shed its shackles.

In the winter of the Jiawu year, while residing in the abbot’s quarters of Cishou Monastery in Dadu, the gentleman Yan Xiyun brought me the previously recorded verses he had transcribed. Having read them three times over, I sighed and said: "The eyes and the mirror of humanity."
It remains here, undestroyed. Alas, I regret that I shall not see the traces of the elders' own hands. Thus, I recorded it for preservation in the third month of the following year.
In that same year, during the tenth month, I departed from the capital as I was being sent to Lei-yang due to my involvement in a legal case.

My attendant, Fuxian, collected my *Haiyin* (Ocean Seal) manuscripts and, carrying them on his back, followed me across the mountain passes. We traveled together through the miasmic seas and the Cao region.
It has been fifteen years since [I left] Caoxi. In the first month of the spring of the Gengxu year, I joyfully relinquished my responsibilities at Caoxi and attained personal freedom.

Desiring to return home for a visit, on the fifth day after the Lantern Festival (Shangyuan), while aboard a boat on the Meng River, I was sorting through the fragments of paper from several years’ worth of accumulated drafts.
By chance, I recovered this scroll; reading it, I sorrowfully recalled that the ink of the calligraphy I had inscribed on that day had not yet faded.

"Qian! You have traveled ten thousand li; how could you have expected to suddenly find this old object? As the ancients said, 'If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you must observe the conditions of time and season.
Is this not the Buddhas and Patriarchs secretly bestowing their grace, receiving you through their spiritual power?
Otherwise, why would you have seen this from beginning to end? It is like emerging from the Fangwang Samādhi—just a snap of the fingers."
It was at the moment of clearing one's throat. Unfolding the scroll by the lamp, I was so filled with joy that I could not sleep; thus, I had the attendant, Zhong, transcribe it once more.
Alas, I am old and decrepit, truly unable to walk hand-in-hand with the elders. Yet, Shan is surely no less than the true attendant Sanyan;
his practice of traveling on pilgrimage is such that when the ancients casually dropped a word or half a phrase, it was like the sky covering all, as if...
The earth universally supports all; the old man picks it up with his hand as it comes.

To perform great Buddhist services upon the tip of a single hair is for those great elders to be like those who cover their ears while stealing a bell; this old fellow cannot help but add legs to a snake.

Good Attendant, tie them into a bundle and cast them into the vast ocean of the Eastern Sea—this would still be a hundred paces better than the Three Mountains. Otherwise, one cannot avoid failing one’s ancestors.
It is finished. Even calamities will reach one's descendants.
This is the postscript to the scroll of Chan Master Daguan sending three Chan practitioners on their travels.
From ancient times, those who have left the household life for the great matter of birth and death have been unable to resolve it for themselves; thus, they prepare straw sandals and climb mountains.
He crossed the waters and sought out a great spiritual friend (*mahā-kalyāṇamitra*) to seek definitive resolution. However, that great spiritual friend was like a lion crouching on the ground;

one could not dare to touch even a single hair on its body, for the moment one did so, one’s life-force would be instantly severed. Whenever he uttered a single word or half-phrase, it was as follows:
Like a thunderclap and lightning flash in a clear sky, it deafens the ears and blinds the eyes of men;

they are too preoccupied with saving their own lives to consider anything else, let alone dare to toy with the Buddha-dharma and the Way of Chan. Among these matters of benefit and harm, those who truly understand them are rare. Alas!

Over the past two hundred years, there have been many itinerant monks (*caryā-yogins*), but how many among them have transgressed this command? Now, such is the case with this certain practitioner of the third dhyāna.
He prided himself on his travels as a wandering monk (*caryā-pādika*), and his ambition was indeed commendable. Yet, having already met Master Daguan, he had merely bared his claws and fangs;
the root of his life remained unsevered, so he sought yet another teacher. Seeing this scroll, I laughed and said:
"For a third-time meditator to carry this scroll while traveling is like requesting the sword of the Supreme Palace to go hunt down bandits—without knowing what will happen at some future time."
Submission.
Following the inscription for the Memorial Text for the Great Monk Bianrong by the Master Taiduan:
In the past, Ji Zi of Yanling hung his sword at the tomb of Lord Xu, saying that he had made a mental pledge during their lifetime and was now notifying him of it.
After his passing, it was held that his righteousness would tower for a thousand ages. If this is the case regarding worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), how much more so regarding the supramundane?
For the ancients, regarding the great matter of birth and death, they severed their affections and took leave of their kin to visit spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*) and seek decisive discernment.

Whenever a single word provided enlightenment, the giver was like the sky universally covering all, and the receiver was like the earth universally supporting all; they met the essential point in a flash of lightning or a spark from flint.
In the interval between [this life and the next], the passions and defilements of birth and death burst forth like a crashing thunderclap; how could this be a mere coincidence?
Thus, the depth of his kindness is like a single drop entering the ocean—it must wither away along with it. How could it merely be valued as something that occurred before or after one’s life?
As I read Master Da’s “Text for the Memorial of Old Bian,” I was deeply moved. Alas! Even a single meal worth a thousand pieces of gold cannot repay such grace.
This is a marvelous matter. A single word remains undiminished throughout kalpas; how could it be anything trivial? Alas!

Master Bian has spent over sixty years delivering sentient beings, and his Dharma-giving is now nearly complete across the great earth. As for knowing gratitude and repaying kindness—how many such people are there in the human world?
Even if everyone were like Master Da, the causal ground for Great Penetration would not necessarily require as many kalpas as the "ink" (mo) kalpa.
This has been so from the past. Yet that which remains imperishable throughout the aging of these works relies upon a single word;
that which makes a single word imperishable is the presence of the ink dot. For an observer to perceive it thus may be said to be not failing the inherent nature of things.
The young bhikṣu Dàchuān, a servant of the Buddha, conceived the great resolve to offer a single alms-bowl to one hundred and eight thousand members of the assembly.
His practice was most arduous; therefore, when the elders and lay devotees heard of it, they were filled with joy and all praised him. Only...
In Gu Shifu’s song, there is the line: "There was Xiao Liang who sought to become a slave to the Buddha.

This was intended to highlight his ability to forget his own person for the sake of the Triple Gem, thereby casting aside the shame of those in the world who value themselves too highly—none being more so than Xiao Liang.
When Chan Master Daguan Ke saw this, he marveled at it; he then fully assumed the manner of a slave and composed a song to bring it forth. I have expanded this into three long stanzas.
He sighed and said: "Even if a yellow-faced or blue-eyed one were to encounter this, they would surely burst into laughter and fall over. How much more so for a mere 'nu-nu' (a slave)!

Since the matter above the Gate of the School does not involve the mysterious path and is peerlessly noble, even to take up residence in that nobility oneself is still merely being a servant or a slave;
it is called "falling from the summit. How much more so for all manner of conceptual thoughts and攀緣 (pān-yuan—clinging to conditions)! Flow...
This refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Nevertheless, young bhikṣu, why do you remain here? I recall that in the past there was a wealthy master whose nature was difficult to serve.
He had only one slave upon whom he relied. During the day, the master intensely desired to employ the slave, yet the slave could not endure it.
At night, the master dreamed he was the slave, and the slave dreamed he was the master; even then, [the master] intensely desired to employ the slave, and the slave likewise could not endure it.
Indeed, while dreams and waking are equal in nature, suffering and pleasure differ; how can this be considered strange?

Now, this bhikṣu intends to take a slave from the waking state and seek to become its master within a dream. Will those hundreds of thousands of followers he serves also be masters in the waking state, only to become slaves within his dream?
Alas! Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream from yesterday. Bhikṣu!

If you understand this, you can offer a single drop of water to the Buddhas and sentient beings of the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, and they will enjoy it without end.
Why limit yourself to a mere one hundred and eight thousand? By doing so, you are using a limited mind to arbitrarily delimit the immeasurable realm of the Tathāgata.
Preface to the Recorded Sayings of the Elder Shouchang:
Throughout his life, the Elder Shouchang’s conduct consisted solely of casting off his body and surrendering his life at the desolate shores of the empty mountains.
Tilling the soil, he has gained a full chest of breath, which he habitually scatters before the assembly of humans and devas.
It is like beating a poisonous drum, causing those who hear the sound to go deaf and those who are poisoned to die; yet how many are those who are poisoned?
Recall that in the past, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the Yellow-Faced Old Man led a troop of bewildered fellows, who day after day put on their robes.
Carrying his alms bowl, he passed through streets and alleys, begging for a single lump of cold rice.
Upon returning, after eating his fill, he washed his bowl, put away his robes, and sat in the lotus posture to engage in idle discourse.

In this manner, he made his living as a daily routine for over thirty years, while the great assembly of humans and devas remained bewildered, ultimately not knowing what he was doing. One day, by chance—
One day, he was seen through by Śāriputra, who then uttered this sigh of admiration: "How rare! O World-Honored One.

Seeing that his eyes were flickering between movement and stillness, the World-Honored One exerted his full strength and, in a sudden, chaotic manner, caused every trace of Śāriputra’s subtle doubts to be completely purified.

Only when the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) was utterly severed did it cease. Thus, Śūnyatā-janman (Subhūti) experienced a profound awakening; with a heart moved by urgency, he wept and wailed in grief, his lamentations and praises overflowing his lips.
At this point, the "Yellow-Faced Old Man" (the Buddha) felt his stifled breath ease slightly, finally not failing the single-minded maternal compassion he had shown from the beginning.

Now, observing that Shouchang’s mattock is very much like the yellow-faced one’s robe and bowl, these words— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content up to the point of interruption.]
To eliminate the entanglements of Mount Ling, one must know that this saying will spread widely, like the sound of a poison drum.
One does not know how many people will be struck by its venom; as for those who attain awakening and shed tears like Subhūti, one likewise does not know how many such people there can be.
As the proverb says: "Familiar faces fill the world, but how many can truly know your heart? Hereafter...
Those who read these words: if you attempt to understand them through verbal discourse, you will have failed Shouchang;

if you do not attempt to understand them through verbal discourse, you will have failed yourself. If you wish to avoid failing either, you must realize it at the very moment the pickaxe is raised, before it has even been lifted.
Only then will you succeed.
The Scroll on the Traveling Pilgrimage of Chan Master Bako:
Formerly, while Fazhao was engaged in his midday meal, he saw ten thousand Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest their forms within his alms bowl. He did not know for what reason this occurred.
He then asked a monk, "This is the realm of Manjusri’s transformation at Mount Wutai. Thereupon, he set out for Mount Wutai, vowing to behold Manjusri.

Eventually, he did indeed see Manjusri, who bestowed upon him the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation. [Manjusri said: "The Chan practitioner Zhaoke previously attained the samādhi of Buddha-recitation at Yunqi.
Now, if he wishes to go and seek Manjusri’s seal of certification, it will be appropriate. However, if he asks about the South..."
Regarding the assembly of methods: one must not be obstructed by the three triads of before and after; one should simply face them directly and set them aside.
Furthermore, as for the practitioner Zhaoke, when he first resided at Huangshan, he took the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as his primary practice—what is called "entering into a single mote of dust."

This is Right Concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Now, you have come from another region with the intent to clear away the dust and bring forth the scriptures, intending to "mow the weeds" upon the Western Lake.
Your intention requires that the Elder plant a single blade of grass. The old man, however, directly says this is not so.

Within the unobstructed *dharmadhātu*, whenever conditions meet, the essence is realized; it is complete in every place. One need only receive clarity within the mind—what further need is there for external things?

Preface and Postscript.
Preface to the *Platform Sutra*, shown to the Chan practitioner Zhijing:
From the time of the Buddhas and Patriarchs above, for the sake of the great matter of birth and death, they have appeared in this world;

there is none among them who did not utterly sacrifice their bodies and lives, undergoing every hardship and emerging from ten thousand deaths and one life. Consider our own Master, the Monk Śākyamuni.
Throughout vast eons past, for the sake of this Dharma, he has sacrificed his head, eyes, marrow, and brain more times than the sands of the Ganges.

Even now, having emerged from this [state], he still went to the Snowy Mountains to endure hunger and cold for six years, and underwent everything from eating horse- oats to being struck by golden spears—what has he not endured?
Up until now, you have merely gained the scent of forty-nine years of rice and gruel; yet you have not yet seen anything extraordinary.
Furthermore, at the very end, you have brought about a scene of ridicule that has circulated throughout the world to this day.
This is why the Blue-Eyed One came specifically from the West, taking it as a substantial reality, thereby deceiving Shen Guang into losing an arm. And so it reached his old age...
Lushu Hanzi was toyed with by a single word from him and was pierced into a black lacquer bucket, falling into a stupor that nearly killed him;

such instances are not limited to tens of thousands. Since Huangmei, at midnight, he cast down the stone from his waist and picked up a few fragments of tattered rags, regarding them as rare treasures;
yet he did not expect to be brought to the brink of death by them. Furthermore—
It is beyond measure. Moreover, having fortunately escaped from the thicket of the hunt, I am filled with shame at every turn.
Whenever I explain to others the places where I have failed throughout my life, even using the vast void as my mouth, I cannot utter a single word of it.
Thus, these anecdotes have spread throughout the rivers and lakes, and those who transmit them take them to be actual facts. How tragic! It is for this very reason that I [have written] this Dharma.

Above, he incurred the Imperial Wrath; truly, he emerged from the brink of death nine times. Fortunately, having been restored to life at the very point of despair, he was graced with the decree of banishment to Lei Yang.
In the winter of the Wanyili year (1615), he departed the Imperial Capital, traveling south through the snow.

Upon reaching Baixia, he was accompanied only by his disciple Zhijing, like a shadow following a form. When they arrived in Lei Yang, the miasmic pestilence broke out violently; of those who drank [the water there], ten thousand perished.
There is no such thing as a person who remains unharmed. Both I and my attendants were afflicted by a virulent pestilence, yet none of us died;

however, Jing was on the verge of death before returning to life. Had we not relied upon the empowerment of the Buddhas’ spiritual power and the sustenance of his own vows, it is certain that not a single soul would have survived.
When Jing’s illness had slightly abated, I immediately dispatched him back to Mount Lu to visit his teacher, and furthermore—
I borrow the light of ten thousand acres of lake and a thousand-foot waterfall to wash away my remaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Having nothing else with which to entrust you as I depart, I suddenly picked up this scroll from my desk and gave it to you. You will see that such news comes only after the ancients have undergone a "great death";
however, it cannot be attained by one who is not truly dead. You must maintain this state atop a solitary peak.
Before the ten-thousand-fathom cliff, try to find a place where you can set hand and foot; you must observe this closely.

If you can truly sacrifice your body and life as the ancients did, then not only will you not fail the old man’s affairs today, but you will also not fail the most supreme Vajra-seed planted throughout ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes. Strive diligently in this; do not forget what has been entrusted to you.
Entrustment. Recorded on the nineteenth night of the month of the winter solstice in the year Wanshi Bingshen (1608), before the lamp, upon the walls of the eastern suburb of Wuyang.
Preface to the Brief Outline of the Record of the Lankavatara Sutra.

The practice of dividing the scriptures into sections (*ke*) is an ancient tradition. Formerly, when Dharma Master Dao’an categorized the scriptures into three parts, his contemporaries ridiculed him for dissecting the meaning of the texts.

However, when the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* by Prajñākaragupta arrived, it was found that he indeed divided the complete scripture into three parts; at that time, people marveled that his approach was perfectly appropriate.
For every scripture possesses its own fundamental framework, and such divisions serve to lift the main themes and extract the essentials, enabling the reader to...
Thus, one grasps the essential core. It is hoped that by departing from words, one may grasp the meaning and enter into realization, thereby discarding the trap and the snare.
This is by no means a matter of dissecting the parts or following arbitrary conjectures.

Later scholars of doctrine, being ignorant of the intent behind departing from words, each rely on their own views to proliferate their arguments, thereby incurring the fault of slandering the Dharma and leaving students with no way to find a proper course. This is precisely [the situation].
This is what is meant by the saying: "The sheep was lost because of too many paths. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* takes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) beyond verbal expression as its primary tenet;

its text is vast and its meaning profound. Previous commentators merely categorized its passages without fully extracting its essential meaning, failing to elucidate the principle of the single, pervasive thread that runs through it.
Consequently, readers followed the literal text and missed the underlying meaning, such that they were unable to practice the three contemplations for cultivating the mind.
Although this has been expounded and circulated throughout the entire world from ancient times to the present, those who rely upon it to practice cultivation rarely understand its essential points;
thus, they fail to fulfill the Tathāgata’s instruction on the path of correct practice.

Now, I shall venture to provide a general discussion, intending directly to organize the principles for those who resolve to cultivate their minds, so that students may see the ultimate goal at a single glance. The brief outline is as follows:

First, I shall summarize the essential meaning to reveal the intent beyond the literal text, so that you may understand the source of the questions and answers, integrate them into a single coherent whole, and have them clearly manifest before your mind’s eye.
It is my hope that you may transcend words to grasp the meaning, rather than allowing the phrasing to become an obstacle.
Nevertheless, even this summary is already superfluous; future students must not consider it insufficient and attempt to add further elaborations.
Such a claim would incur no small measure of the sin of slandering the Dharma.
Written on the day of the Buddha’s Enlightenment in the first month of summer in the Wuxu year of the Wanli era, by the śramaṇa Deqing at the walls of Qingmen in Wuyang.
Postscript to the Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra:
The Buddha-nature within the bonds of affliction is like a pearl in one’s bosom, or water in the earth.

Although it is inherently possessed, it cannot be known without being pointed out, nor can it be obtained without being excavated. Thus, virtuous friends and spiritual teachers are those who point out the pearl; they are immeasurable [in their kindness].
This Dharma gate is merely a method of forced interpretation; how could it be the true Dharma?

The Tathāgata appeared in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition, namely, to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This "Buddha’s knowledge and vision" is none other than the Buddha-nature of sentient beings, which is the true wisdom of Prajñā.
Furthermore, this true wisdom has been inherently complete within each of us from the very beginning. Never...

There is neither increase nor decrease. It is just like a pearl at the bottom of a garment: it is inherently neither bright nor dim. Water within the earth has sources that are either shallow or deep;

this is because the Dharma itself has no suddenness or gradualism, yet there are differences in the ease or difficulty of awakening based on whether one's faculties are sharp or dull, and whether one's hindrances are thick or thin.

Those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence, whose hindrances are thin and whose merit is profound, understand it upon a single contact. This is the ease of awakening; therefore, it is so called.

This refers to the sudden [approach]. For example, when the Great Master the Sixth Patriarch heard the single phrase, "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere," he suddenly awakened to what is inherently present and immediately realized non-arising.
This was because the conditions for *prajñā* had matured over many kalpas; upon this single touch with the appropriate stimulus, he attained immediate and clear self-confidence.
It was like opening one's chest to see a pearl: it was originally inherent from the beginning and did not require seeking from without. How could such a thing be easily seen?
Alas! For human beings, the ground of ignorance is firm and solid, while the waters of the *dharmatā* grow ever deeper.

Since the labor of excavation has not yet been applied, it is truly difficult to seek a vehicle that may flow with the current back to the ocean of wisdom. Therefore, the Sage had no choice but to establish provisional teachings;

based on the five natures (*pañca-gotra*), he established the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and following the sharpness or dullness of faculties, he opened the gates of the sudden and the gradual. This...
The discourse on the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is still but the first step for those newly entering the Mahāyāna;
yet this sutra is specifically one of those eight divisions. That which is called "Vajra" is taken in the sense of its ability to sever.

It directly points to the Buddha-nature within each person—firm and indestructible—which suddenly cuts off ignorance, transcends all marks, and remains as suchness, unmoving. It is truly like the jewel within the garment...

The arrival is not obscure; it simply requires a person to point it out. Realization lies within oneself. Thus, the *sūtra* provides the method for knowing this, while the commentary merely employs the technique of analytical interpretation.

As for the state where one inhales a drop of water and attains refreshing coolness, where heat and affliction are removed and thirst is quenched, such that the mind is suddenly relieved and the spirit is liberated—this is known by the drinker alone; it is truly not something that can be pointed toward.
This was revealed by the person [who submitted it]. Master Sū Jǔdá possessed the seeds of *prajñā* from his youth; throughout his life, he was intensely devoted to this sutra.

Having associated with the Grand Historian Jiāo and other great spiritual friends, his self-confidence grew ever more profound. Upon obtaining this commentary, he regarded it as having acquired a most precious treasure.
He immediately had it carved into printing blocks to widely propagate the gift of the Dharma. Seeing this, I joyfully joined my palms in homage and praised him, saying: "Pāgoda..."
Dragon King, you are able to rain down a single drop of water to fill Jambudvīpa and moisten the parched and withered to bring forth a hundred things;
such is the transformation wrought by the power of karma. How much more so, then, that which is inspired and manifested by the divine wisdom of Prajñā!
By this, one knows that the merit of Master Su’s Dharma-giving is truly great.

rather, at the moment the World-Honored One raised up [the teaching], he was like a fine horse that gallops upon seeing the shadow of the whip. This is worlds apart from his state before opening his eyes. This verse is found in...
To speak of it from the standpoint of Śūnyatā-utpanna (Kōshō) is much like painting legs on a snake; yet, it is a joy to see Śūnyatā-utpanna’s true character.
If Śūnyatā-utpanna were to see the World-Honored One, it would be no different [from seeing him now]; it is merely like a phantom person clapping their hands in rhythm to a song.
For over twenty years, the Virtuous Attendant served the Old Man, and his daily expositions of this matter were no less than those at Vulture Peak. However, from...
Calamities and hardships are far removed from the state of Śūnyatā-janman (Kongsheng). If this mind were not like the realization of Śūnyatā-janman, how could it endure such manifold sufferings?
At this time, bound by demonic karma upon a single-leaf boat on the Fu蓉 River, I have written this during a cold night and entrusted it to you;
