In winter there was a great snowfall. The wind whirled it up and buried the house to a height of several zhang. Sitting together wrapped in our robes, we felt only that the night was long.
When we rose to open the door, it was blocked by snow. We hurriedly stoked the fire and fetched a lamp; looking at one another, we laughed, thinking we were about to be buried alive.
Just then, the master of the Northern Terrace (Beitai) went out to investigate and learned of our situation. He led dozens of laborers and provided tools and dry provisions.
He came to rescue me. We entered through a secret tunnel; once we had passed through the gate and met, our joy was so profound it was as if we were beneath the Yellow Springs.

For twenty years since my banishment to the regions beyond the passes, whenever I have thought of this, it has instantly dispelled the stifling heat and miasma—relying solely upon this single thought of a heart as cool as ice.
Recently, while I was living in retirement on Mount Kuang, I first encountered Master Han.

Master Jue pointed to the Five Milk-Tufts Peak to provide him with a dwelling. Master Jue was a direct bone-lineage descendant of Master Che. To me, Master Jue appeared as if he were Master Che himself.
Every time I met him, it was as though I were facing Master Che once more amidst the snow-cold cave.

In the first year of the Tianqi era, on the New Year’s Day, there was a three-foot snowfall; the myriad mountains were frozen solid, no different from being inside that cave. Since my departure from Wutai Mountain...
For more than thirty years, I have never seen such a scene; thus, moved by it, I composed this song.
I have sent it to Master Jue, so as not to forget Master Che’s companionship during the moments of life and death. Today, Jue carries on the illustrious reputation of the Huanglong lineage.

If one can realize that every single thing before one’s eyes has all emerged from one’s father’s endurance of cold and hunger, then how could the heat of affliction not be cooled, and how could the path of practice not be accomplished?
There is a proverb that says: "Founding an enterprise is not difficult; maintaining it is difficult.
If one knows the ancestral fields and weeds them at all times so as not to let them fall into ruin, then one will know one's own nature.
Our teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, sacrificed his body, life, and wealth;

for six years in the Snowy Mountains, he endured cold and hunger to obtain the four types of offerings to bequeath to his descendants. Every grain of rice and stalk of vegetable we consume in our daily lives is his legacy.
"All are drops of blood from every pore of my original teacher’s body. Reflecting on this, could one truly bear to let this life pass in vain?
That I have come to this through writing a poem on snow is much like seeing [the Buddha] because of meeting a fisherman.
"The great ocean’s waves and surges—may you keep this in mind. Written on the first day of spring in the first year of the Tianqi era, following the "Poems from the Army.
Leyang lies directly under the Southern Pole;东坡 (Sōngpó) inscribed it as "The First among Ten Thousand Mountains," which corresponds to what is called "the end of water and the end of mountains."
This is a geomantic site known as a "complete dragon" (*jinlong*). Therefore, many loyal ministers and righteous scholars of antiquity who were exiled resided here;
it was due to the influence of this vital energy (*qi*). Although the Duke of Kou (Kou Qianyi) lived there for but a short time, to this day the local elders speak of him with great admiration.

Formerly, when Dongpo (Su Shi) was exiled to Dan’er, Ziyou (Su Che) was also transferred there. Regarding these remnants of their history at West Lake, there is a shrine dedicated to the Duke of Kou, while that of Master Su remains [in Hangzhou].
There is a pavilion; the excellence of the mountains and rivers remains, and the scenery is as it was before. Yet, regarding the monks who come here for military service:
in the past, Daoyuan (Dahui) of the Song dynasty was exiled to Mei Yang, and Juefan was sent to Zhuya. Alas! Those two elders departed five hundred years before my time.

Now that I have received the imperial grace to be dispatched to this place, it is truly a marvelous event spanning over a thousand years. It is only in our Sagely Dynasty that monks are sent to serve as soldiers.
"Only our founding ancestor, National Teacher Nanzhou Heshan, incurred the wrath of the Emperor for protecting the person of Jianwen;
the Chengzu Emperor pardoned him but sent his disciple De Lu to be stationed here. He was soon released and returned home. It has now been over two hundred years since that time.
Recently, I too have incurred the offense of performing prayers for the state's prosperity and have arrived here. Is this not significant? Thus I spoke upon my arrival.
The master resided at an ancient temple west of the city, within the pavilion of Master Su [Shi]. There, scholars vied with one another to discuss Master Su as if it were but yesterday;
yet when they sought out the historical traces of Juefan, they vanished into obscurity. The climate and scenery of the southern heavens differ vastly from those of the Central Kingdoms;
the seasonal airs there do not conform to the patterns of the natural world. It is as if the pure Yang of the Qian hexagram transforms into Li; Li is the direction of fire.

All things manifest one another: they gather into intense heat and disperse into brilliant clarity. People perceive only the density of the scenery, failing to see the subtle wonder of its pervasive flow;
thus, in their compositions and poetic prose, they are unable to fully capture the subtleties of its creative transformation.
When I first arrived here, I encountered a severe epidemic; I consequently composed my commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* within these circumstances.

I considered myself to have deeply penetrated the mysteries of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, for it was indeed through this that I found true sustenance. Previously, I did not seek excellence in poetry; however, since coming here from the military, my poems have been circulated throughout the realm.
The wise all regard them as expressions of Chan (Zen), which is sufficient evidence that my mind and its objects have become integrated.

Rong: There are those who do not realize that this is so. From this, one also knows that the excellence of the poetry of the ancients lay simply in the genuineness of their feelings and the reality of their scenes.
When the Lord Marquis of Ziyuan produced his draft, I was commanded to write it down; I have recorded it here merely to serve as a cover for a jar.
He let out a laugh and inscribed these twelve verses following his "Poems Written While Lying Ill.

Regarding the śramaṇa serving in the military: there have been such instances in the past. For example, Chan Master Dahui was stationed at Mei Yang and preached the Dharma while wearing a scholar’s cap and gown.

The Venerable Jiyin was exiled to Chuyi Prefecture, where he annotated the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. These two great elders, through the samādhi of illusoriness, treated their hardships as if they were mere play.
Even when I was a youth driving away crows and birds, I already knew of these matters and longed to meet such men.
Unexpectedly, at the age of fifty, I too encountered this hardship. By imperial grace, I was banished to Lei Yang;
that place lies roughly between the two old masters. I felt ashamed that I was not their equal, yet I constantly reflected upon their refined spirit.

Upon first arriving at my place of exile, I immediately began annotating the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, for I was deeply moved by it. As for the time and circumstances of my stay there, I am unsure how they compare to those of the past.
How is it? With the very body of the Sangha and the life-force of the Dharma as your concern, you maintain them in a single thought, remaining vigilant and never forgetting.
You say that regarding the path of Chan and the Buddha-Dharma, you do not dare hope to reach the gates of those two elders;

yet, in firmly upholding the Dharma-gate with a heart of solitary loyalty, you truly possess the resolve to "chew snow and swallow felt," while your longing for the old self amidst the mountain forests is expressed through your poetry.
This is the true letter tied to the leg of a wild goose. In a thousand years, those who read this poem and seek to envision me—can they do so as I have envisioned the two elders?
Alas, I am old! I entrust this writing to my attendant Guangyi;
by holding this, one may clearly perceive the family precepts.

The essential point of the fundamental tenets of the Buddha-dharma, as expressed in these six verses of praise, does not transcend the single mind. Due to delusion regarding this mind, there arise impermanence and suffering.
Since suffering is fundamentally impermanent, its nature is inherently empty. Being empty, the self is fundamentally without self. If there is no self, who is it that could be born?

The deceased [said]: "This great treasury of the scriptures is the mind-seal transmitted by the Buddhas and patriarchs; it does not go beyond these six dharmas. In sum, they do not depart from the one mind.
If one is deluded regarding this mind, there is the suffering of birth, death, and impermanence.
If one awakens to this mind, one realizes non-self. Without self, one penetrates the emptiness of nature. With the emptiness of nature, birth and death are also empty. This is truly not..."
Apart from this mind, there exists a separate, sublime Dharma that constitutes true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Formerly, those with aspirations toward Chan were numerous;

for the most part, they sought the profound and the subtle outside the mind and sought the True Doctrine in the external world. Consequently, they missed boundless wondrous practices in their daily lives, mistakenly believing that the Buddha-Dharma exists elsewhere.
Little do they realize that it is present within our ordinary, everyday activities. It should be...
The activities of dependent origination—all their various manifestations—are truly the Buddha-dharma.

It is only because of the distinction between the existence of a self and the absence of a self that suffering and joy differ, and that the noble and the ordinary are distinct; this ultimately lies within the interval between delusion and awakening.
Since the self is the root of all sufferings, and as the Magistrate requested a writing on Chan discourse, I have recorded these six old poems of mine and noted them here.
This is for the time being; let it serve as a promissory note for the day when this Dharma-gate is realized.
Written after the poems of Lord Li, expressing my sentiments.

These ten poems on the right were composed on the full moon of the month of the Longzhi (Winter Solstice) in the year of Yisi. The following year, in the first month of winter in the year of Bingwu, at that time—
At Caoxi, I was delighted to undertake the reconstruction of the Patriarchal Temple, which has been completely renewed.

The Meditation Hall is the place where the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch, and the various great patriarchs of Nanyue and Qingyuan preached the Dharma and dwelt in retreat. Through the passage of generations, it had fallen into ruin, becoming a mere heap of refuse and a den for foxes.
Now, I have striven with all my might to restore it to its former design; its scale is now spacious and open, no less than it was in ancient times. And so it was recorded.
As for the assistance provided in the planning and execution, it was borne single-handedly on the shoulders of the Military Aide Lin and the Layman Jñānātus.

Reflecting upon this, I recall that in the past, when the East Sea was adorned with magnificent beauty and the Way of the Dharma was about to flourish, I was beset by calamity and exiled to the regions beyond the passes.
Who would have thought that I would again manifest such an illusory site of practice to gather an illusory assembly and perform illusory Buddha-works to deliver sentient beings?
Are sentient beings not like illusions? How much more so when they receive the imperial edict of grace, as the net of King Tang is cast wide open.

That which was the beginning of their initial binding is now the end of their liberation. This single cycle is complete and perfect, equal and without duality. As it is said: "Entering meditative concentration in the east and arising in the west;
entering right concentration within the body of a bhikṣu and arising from concentration within the body of a layperson. This is called the Net of Directions.
Regarding samādhi: it is not so. I have yet to forget the first thought of joy felt toward Master Li, the Imperial Censor.
Having just finished transcribing my sentiments in the form of a poem addressed to Master Li, I entrust it to you, Layman.

Through this, you may see that my humble resolve was neither overturned nor diverted by hardships, nor shifted by external conditions; it was not affected by differing forms or diverse destinies, nor did I harbor any reservations regarding coming or going.
To be thus unshakable by Māra—how could this be easily attained were it not for one who dwells upon the ground of patience and sits within the field of cessation?
This pivotal occasion is the secret legacy transmitted by the Elder;
it is utterly beyond the capacity of words to describe. Layman, will you be able to attain this?
Colophon to the Ten Poems on Dwelling in the Mountains (These poems were written ten days before his passing; they mark the end of his brushwork).
These poems were likely composed at Wuru Peak on Mount Kuang during the spring of the Renzi year. The attendant Shen Guang requested that this scroll be inscribed with them.
The old man was weary of his brush and inkstone, so he set it aside on a high shelf. It was only upon returning to Cao that he finally wrote them.
While traveling along the banks of the stream, he entrusted it to his attendant Guangshou to bring back; it had been kept hidden for a long time.

In the ninth month of autumn in the year Guihai, Guang sent a letter from Xingzhou to inquire after him and urged that the collection be completed. At that time, the Old Man was suffering from pain in his feet and found answering correspondence to be a hardship.
Guang took advantage of an interval to request it repeatedly. The Old Man then thought, "I am old now; I fear this will become a debt for the future," and so...
I have hurriedly transcribed this with all my strength to return it. One might say that out of pity for a three-year-old child, he did not begrudge even his two eyebrows;
is this not truly a compassionate heart? If one were to view this merely as poetry or calligraphy, one would be failing his kindness by far.
Written on the first day of the tenth month of winter in the year of Guihai.
Epilogue to the Verses on Contemplating Illness by the Elder Zibo:
The Elder Zibo habitually demonstrated the meaning of "no-nature" (wu-xing) to others with the ease of one who handles a spinning ball;

those who witnessed it could not help but feel their hearts startled and their eyes dazzled. Since the time of the great masters Xueyan and Zhongfeng, those who have truly understood this teaching have been few indeed.
How lamentable! The Way has fallen out of step with the times, and his lifelong aspiration to revitalize it remains unfulfilled.
This was the source of this old man’s bitterest regrets. Alas! The sage has passed away; how can later generations and juniors ever again behold the standard of the ancestral school?
When the Chan practitioner Haemo of Mount Emei presented me with the "Verses on Contemplating Illness," I beheld them and could not help but weep tears of sorrow.
After several instances of opening and closing [the scroll], the traces of his hand remain as they were. One should treasure this as a seed of radiance.
This was written following the discourse of Fan Li.

A Request for a Eulogy on the "Diagram of the Return of the Ladle to the Lake. It was upon this that I was moved to compose these words.

I have often remarked that when ancient literati evaluate historical figures, their works—such as those of the Three Sus—are brilliantly clear; yet why is it that they generally do not touch upon this matter?
From this, one knows that seeking a true friend across a thousand years is difficult even for the ancients, whereas hoping for a meeting as close as morning and evening is what they longed for.
It was no mere coincidence. Fan Li’s heart was indeed difficult to perceive; yet, by bringing it forth through my words, Fan Li will surely close his eyes in peace.

What difference is there between past and present, or coming and going? I say that when a man of integrity dwells in this world, one who harbors a vision that transcends the mundane will certainly not be easily recognized or known by the world.
Thus, as for the dragon and the qilin, even every child of three feet in height throughout the world [knows them].
To know them as divine and auspicious is merely to dispute over what one has not seen. If a dragon were to appear at dawn, people would take it for a snake;
when a qilin first emerges, it inevitably brings calamity upon the foresters. What is there to wonder at?
During my ten years of residence at Caoxi, I have encountered both dragons and snakes; yet I could not avoid a single disaster. At that time, there was a man from Kuang who...
The siege had lasted for twenty days. On the day of Jǐyǒu, at the season of Cold Dew when frost descends, I was stirred by inspiration during a clear night.

I thus wrote it down, recording my intention as follows.
Inscription on the Back of the Song for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Since my youth, I have known how to recite this song; it may be said that I have deeply entered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
Every time I unroll the scroll, my spirit leaps forth involuntarily, and immeasurable joy suddenly arises within me. I have often transcribed it to bestow upon others.
As for Dao, I have recently come to Caoxi to restore the monastic site as the Sixth Patriarch;

Unforeseen, demonic monks have created internal obstacles, destroying the Dharma-gate through perverse delusions and instigating litigation against the government offices, which has caused me to reside in the prefectural seat for the past two years. At present, I am here...
Among those who have taken refuge to protect the Dharma, there is only the layman Huang. For two years and a single day, he has been constant morning and evening without interruption;
through freezing cold and scorching heat, he has rushed about without failing by even a hair’s breadth. Because of this, I am reminded of the late Chan Master Juefan, who was sent abroad;
when his close acquaintances and friends were startled like birds or scattered like fish, only Hu Qiangzhong remained to attend to him, escorting him all the way to Shaoyang.
Yang. The Master composed a preface to distinguish it. Even now, as I read his writing, I can imagine what he was like as a person.
Now, with this body of mine wandering through exile and hardship, standing all alone in a field of defilement, disgrace, and contention, there is a layman who has provided me with a wooden tongue;

As Jun was about to depart, I composed a song for the practice of reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* to entrust to him, so that he might chant and study it to form a karmic connection of Dharma-joy.

Furthermore, while I was exiled beyond the Ling Mountains, my close friends and relatives were cut off from me, as if separated by the heavens. Written in the summer of the Jihou year of the Wanli era (1609). Daidu.

The Elder of Cishan Temple, Master Uicheon (Hakgong), came specifically to offer his condolences beneath the pines of Caoxi. At the mere sight of him, grief and joy welled up within me simultaneously;

he was like a person from another age. I recall how, in the past when I was begging for alms in Chang’an, I passed through your honorable residence at Xuangming and there washed away the dust of the world.
Now that I am here in this burning house of the scorching wilderness, whenever I reflect upon those times, I am suddenly transported into a state of pure coolness.
This land is now but dust and soil; if one wishes to seek even a drop of water to wash one’s body and mind, how could it be easily found?

At the beginning of autumn, I had business in Duanzhou and invited the Master to travel with me. We ascended the Baoyue Terrace to enjoy the cool air for ten months, after which we returned to Wuyang.
There we ate fresh long-yan fruits, returning home satiated. Truly it was a source of joy. As we traveled by boat, a north wind blew, making it difficult to go against the current.
Seshu: The Master brought out this scroll and requested that I write it. I then transcribed this song.

Upon my return, the Master said, "I shall instruct all my disciples so that each one becomes like the monk upon the Pāṇḍava Rock, making the recitation of the *White Lotus Sūtra* their daily practice.

Not only will they not fail Xiu Ya, but even for me, an old man eight thousand li away, it will be as if I am still here by the bright moon beneath the pines, leaning my ear to listen to the recitation."
It is the right time. Following the *Qianziwen* (Thousand Character Classic) calligraphed by Master Xuelang En:

He admired the practice of *mokusen* (dry meditation). His elder brother was resolute in his pursuit of learning; regardless of whether he was focusing on the teachings of the Buddhist vehicles (*kyōshō*) or immersing himself in the garden of arts, he was widely inquisitive and possessed a powerful memory.
He never grew weary even during eating or resting. Holding his brush and practicing at the pond, he did so day and night without interruption for more than twenty years.
When he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, he far surpassed his predecessors; yet in calligraphy and composition, he also excelled, earning the title of one of the "Two Wonders.

For over two hundred years in our Ming dynasty, no one of such outstanding virtue among the monastic community has had their finger raised twice [to refute him]. He is someone for whom I have felt lifelong admiration and with whom I have served with reverence.

I am ashamed that my merit is slight while my karma is heavy, leading us to be separated until old age. It is a pity that at the age of sixty—the year of *er-shun*—my elder brother has ultimately... [passed away].
A thousand autumns have passed. Alas, I have merely dragged out seventy years of life without contributing anything to the Dharma-gate; what benefit is there in this stolen existence?

While I was living in seclusion at Mount Nanyue, the monk Shi brought this scroll to me. Upon seeing it once, I could not help but feel moved by sorrow; reading it three times over, I sighed deeply. Alas!
The man is gone, yet the traces of his touch remain as if he were still alive. Beholding this, it is as if I am facing Jiguo in person.
The Postscript to the *Bisheng* (Notes on the Brush) by Layman Gu Baocang states:
"The layman Gu Baocang of Jinling, whose given name is Yuan and courtesy name Qingpu, was from his youth a man of exceptional talent and refinement.

In poetry, calligraphy, and painting, he did not adhere strictly to ancient rules; rather, he applied his brush with spontaneous confidence, achieving a celestial resonance that was utterly transcendent. Nevertheless, it was truly rooted in the ancient methods."
He came to see me one day and said, "In calligraphy, four parts must follow the ancient methods and six parts must express one's own intention;
only then is it sublime. Otherwise, even if every stroke can imitate the ancients, it will ultimately result in 'slave-calligraphy' (nu-shu) and is not worthy of esteem.

In his middle years, he devoted himself to the principles of Chan, attaining great realization and insight. Nevertheless, he never disparaged the cultivation of causes simply because he had attained the principle. In his later years...
He joined with renowned monks to establish the Western Society (Xifang Hui). His observance of the precepts was so rigorous that none could equal him.

At the time of his death, he sat upright and closed his eyes; the entire household smelled the fragrance of lotuses, which did not dissipate for three days. The layman once personally wrote several quatrains, which I now record here:
"Ten meditation cushions, nine already worn through; Whose parched well is it, where the snow is hard to fill? Now..."
The samādhi of phenomena being established as phenomena: sound and form reach the ear without obstruction. Pine-fire soup steaming, its fragrance fills one’s robes;
amidst snowy cold, the noble man has long been hungry. A bright pearl is not exchanged for a jar of yellow radish broth; the luster of spittle vies with the brilliance of the sun and moon.

Who among those feasting from tripods knows the toil of day and night? At every turn, the total mechanism is ready for you to examine with care. The fishing pole does not betray the autumn that is like brocade;
on both banks, yellow chrysanthemums strike the oars with fragrance. In short robes and with a long spade, one grows old at Shimen;

a simple vegetable platter easily passes the mornings and evenings. A hundred years of clever ingenuity have been worn away; I am ashamed that people still transmit these traces of ink and powder. Two Knives upon a Bowl.
Shining upon the snowflakes. In my youth, I once grew drunk at the house of Lu Zhujia. Though I have pondered and reflected, I have yet to fulfill the ambitions of a man of honor.

With hair turned white, I dwell by the capital gates learning how to plant melons. In my snowy cottage, cold pickles mark the passing seasons; though gold passes through the scales by the bushel, there is no need for boastful praise.

If one says that achievements recorded on bamboo and silk are difficult to decay, this too is merely adding flowers to one’s eyes. Vines and leaves, green moss, grow long enough to clothe the body. Chrysanthemums...
Flowers fresh, wine fills the ladle with fragrance. Should any of these times’ people visit Layman Pang, ten thousand trees and clouding vines guard his thatched hall.

With hair disheveled, he was once a man who received the prediction of enlightenment; clad in grass robes, his idle body dwells wherever it may be. For ten years, old friends have shattered the dust of worldly toil;

together they offer incense and lamps to repay the springtime of the wild temple. Amidst the clouds, green mountains and ancient cypress groves stand; their branches and boughs are like houses, providing shelter.
"Frosty winds. A man with ambition casts his lot; the alms-bowl remains faintly in his hand. This is recorded in Jiao Xi’s *Bisheng*.
When I was a child, I heard that when Master Baodang was first a student, his spirit was most bold and unrestrained, and his talent was swift and agile.
In middle age, he suddenly abandoned all that he had studied and began a lifelong fast before the embroidered Buddha image. He constructed...

His family members and women never appeared before him, and his acquaintances were cut off from visiting him. He truly resembled a *dhūta* ascetic in the deep mountains.

Every night at the fifth watch, he struck a large wooden fish-drum and recited the Buddha’s name in a loud voice. The layman’s house was near the market, where there were many butchers. There was one wicked...
A young man, whenever he heard the sound of a wooden fish, would immediately rise to slaughter livestock. One day, being late, he rebuked his wife.
His wife said, "The practitioners strike the wooden fish to recite the Buddha's name; when you hear it, you do not realize you should cease killing, yet you blame me?

The young man immediately broke his knife and staff, changed his heart to do good, and at that time, many butchers likewise turned their hearts around. A gentleman remarked, "I shall embrace the wooden fish."
"Beating all night long—how many dreamers does it startle back to wakefulness? At the age of nineteen, I followed the venerable master Xilin of Changgan to leave the household life.
My late teacher Yungu was a Dharma-eye of his generation; while residing at Qixia, he maintained an exceptionally close relationship with you, Layman.

"What kind of person is he? The Master said, "He is a Pang Gong of the present age. One day, while strolling casually with his peers through a pine grove, they caught sight of a practitioner entering the mountain gate.
His appearance was clear, ancient, and most elegant; he moved with the leisurely ease of a solitary crane soaring through the sky, transcending the mundane world.
When they drew near to observe him, his eyes did not blink, as if he were indifferent to the affairs of men.
"Worldly indeed! I said with surprise and joy, "Who is this person who possesses such great virtue? An acquaintance replied, "This is the Layman Ratnaketu.
I wished to pay my respects but was apprehensive; thus, I followed him to observe his destination.
I saw him enter through a side gate of the temple’s corridor and prostrate before the Śāriputra Stūpa of the Tathāgata. I watched him secretly. Five...
His body was upright and diligent; his earnest devotion was beyond words. Upon observing the pagoda and the hall, they rose towering into the clouds, their five colors vividly brilliant.
As the light reflected back, it appeared as if inlaid with precious gems. Suddenly he realized that this realm was surely not of the human world, yet he still did not know why this was so.
Later, I asked my late teacher Yungu, who said, "This is the layman’s contemplation of this."
He created a visualization of the Western Pure Land, intending it to support his contemplative practice. Thereafter, he entered the inner circle of disciples under his former teacher.
When the time of his death arrived, he spent several days and nights facing his former teacher and a small number of eminent monks, reciting the Buddha’s name together.

He suspended a Western Pure Land image within his chamber. While I was among the assembly performing Buddhist rites, a member of the layman’s household reported that the fragrance of lotuses could be smelled throughout the entire house.
The assembly was all struck with wonder and joy, yet the layman remained serene and showed no change in expression.

These accounts recorded in the *Bisheng* (Notes on the Brush) were all witnessed by me personally. The layman had several sons who were all students, yet they were not [fond of] worldly affairs... [text ends].
He had faith in the Buddha. Upon reaching this point, he wept before his father’s bed and, prostrating himself, entreated him, saying:
"Father, you have now transcended birth and death and dwell in the Pure Land; do you not think of your children and grandchildren? Will you not bring about their deliverance?
Why have you left no word of instruction for us? The layman smiled and said: "Do you all think that I am living or that I am dead? Have you not observed the sun? The sun..."
It rises in the east and sets in the west; does it truly set, or does it not set? My birth and death are just like this.
Having picked up my brush to write these words, I cast down the brush and passed away with serene composure. This was what I personally witnessed and recorded.

The Proclaimer says:
This volume, titled *The Ten Thousand Dharmas Return*, was written by the Layman Nangao.

From the time of the Buddhas and Patriarchs above, there has never been a substantial dharma given to others; it is merely a single blow delivered within the delusive dreams of sentient beings' false conceptions.
It shatters with a resounding *keng*! Suddenly awakening from the dream, one’s eyes snap open; looking back at the realm of the dream, it is utterly unobtainable.
To direct the mind toward this state of unobtainability is itself a dream-like affair.
Viewed in this light, how could there be a single dharma that can be grasped by the emotions? Thus it is said: "Not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata."
This is what is called Avalokiteśvara. Thus it is said: "Free from marks, free from names, not falling into any categories.
If one calls this "one," then one falls—and falls again. Layman Nangao has secretly conformed to this Way and has enjoyed its mastery for many years.
Yet, mindful that those who truly understand it are rare, he specifically takes up this ancient kōan and frequently brings it forth.

This was shown to others so that they might know for themselves where the matter falls. If an observer can quickly take it up before the Layman has even raised the point, they are still only halfway there.
If one further dwells upon the "oneness" of all phenomena, it is much like telling dreams to a fool.
Master Hui-an had long studied under the Layman and frequently entered the abbot’s quarters; having heard him speak of non-duality...
This Dharma gate has already been thoroughly practiced and mastered. Now, tell me: is this koan the same as or different from Vimalakīrti’s silence?
Investigate! [End of] the Preface to the Verses on the *Complete Enlightenment* (Yuanjue).
Grand Historian Mr. Zou had long studied the teachings of Yangming. His son, Zi-yin, inherited the lineage and the dharma-robe.
In the spring of the Gui-chou year, he came to see me at the Green Gate in Wuyang and inquired about the essential meaning of the Westward Transmission.

I instructed him to completely cast aside all habitual tendencies and intellectual views from his mind, and to sit in silence for seven days before I would administer the medicine. Upon hearing this, Zi-yin suddenly attained realization and forgot [all conceptualization].
The purport of these words is that, having previously fallen into the gateway of shadows and reflections, he suddenly leaped back to his original state.

When I reached Mount Nanyue, I received a letter from your elder brother, Ziyin, which spoke of your awakening and liberation; it further mentioned that you had recently passed away through misfortune.
I was grieved at heart for a long time. Later, when I retired to live in seclusion on Mount Kuang, nine years later in the winter of the Xinyou year, your son...
I have received a copy of the *Verses on Perfect Enlightenment* composed by Master Yu Hou.

Upon reading it, I know that although Ziyin has passed away, he remains steadfastly within the Great Luminous Treasury (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*). It can be said that he has deeply planted the primary cause of Prajñā.
Had Heaven granted him more years, the extent of his further progress would have been immeasurable. What a pity!
Postscript to the Epitaph for the Venerable Master Huan-yu.
The Venerable Master Huan-yu previously attended upon our late teacher, Master Yunguk. He was born in the same year as I.
In the year of Xinsi, we met at Mount Wutai; I observed that his countenance was pure and emaciated, so frail he could hardly bear the weight of his robes, yet his mind was as vast as—
The Earth possesses the power to sustain all sentient beings; thus, it can forget its own self for the sake of others, never for a single moment harboring the mark of selfhood (*ātman*).
This is evident in his treating sick monks as if he were a skilled physician, even to the point of cutting his own flesh to provide medicine.

Once, while I was sitting amidst ice and snow, I was about to die of cold and hunger, but the Master rescued me and brought me back to life. Therefore, I regard the Master as a King of Physicians (*Vaidyarāja*).
It has been more than thirty years since we last met, and twenty-three years since you entered *parinirvāṇa*.
Previously, for the sake of the project to carve the Tripitaka, I left your sacred relics at Jizhao on Shuangjing.

In the winter of the Bingchen year, as I arrived there on account of Master Da’s enshrinement in a stupa, your senior disciple, Master Gao, also took this opportunity to inter them. Thus, I was able to perform the divination for you.
The bones of the earth have entered the soil. Alas! This is a most extraordinary matter; could it not be due to past karmic conditions?

Reading the "Epitaph for the Master's Stupa" composed by the Layman Tongguan, I felt as if I were sitting within a Vajra Cave in conversation with him once more. Thus, I composed a poem to offer him this elegy:
Who knew of the cold crags and the hunger and cold? Only by relying on the Master did you revive after your death.

Today, as the Five Peaks cast their shadows upon the stupa, it is as if we are still sitting here in conversation. I reflect that this mountain has been a Dharma cave for the Southeast, where eighty-eight generations of masters have preached the Dharma within its midst.
What prior affinity do you possess, that following the Great Master Da, you have attained ultimate peace and rest?
In this regard, I feel ashamed that I and you were born of the same lineage but shall not die of the same lineage; how could I ever obtain this single mound of earth to cover these withered bones?
I imagine that when you emerge in the world in the future, I do not know who will be the master of that age.
Should you possess the memory of past lives, you will surely see this old man lighting a lantern on New Year’s Eve as I write these words.
Inscription for the Reception Hall of Qianfo Temple at Jinnazhiping, Mount Lu.

Mount Lu is the foremost among the scenic wonders of Jiangzuo. Since the founding of the mountain by Master Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty, and through the Dharma-preaching sites of the various patriarchs of the Tang and Song dynasties, it has been uniquely preeminent throughout the world.
The shape of the mountain resembles a blue lotus floating upon the water, and Jinnazhiping is situated therein like—

He sat upon flower petals. Formerly, this place was overgrown with wild brush; recently, Dharma Master Gongqian arrived and dwelt alone in a thatched hut, casting his solitary shadow against the cold cliffs.
His disciple, Monk Lianxufang, exerted himself with all his heart and strength to serve him. Whenever he went to beg for alms in the provincial city, [he would return with provisions].
Day by day they went forth and night by night they returned; they traveled through the wind and slept under the dew. They experienced every form of hardship, hunger, and cold.

Within ten years, they had cleared the wilderness and reclaimed the land, and finally constructed dwellings. When Master Qian passed away, Master Lian upheld his legacy, sacrificing himself to establish the community, which eventually became a great monastic center.
For thirty years, he shared both joy and sorrow with the assembly, sleeping and rising together with them, down to the smallest grain of rice.

He tended the leafy vegetables and did not perform his duties for private gain, but led by personal example. Even now that he is old, he sits upon long benches with no private sleeping quarters at all;
he has truly attained the manner of the ancients in guiding the assembly. Thus, monastics from the ten directions come to him as if returning home.
Yet the Master does not use "Buddha-dharma" or "Chan Way" as a banner; he relies solely on the single flavor of impartial compassion through the Dharma-gate.
He made this his primary concern. He never used the consumption of porridge or rice, nor the rhythms of his breath, to drum [his fame] across all quarters or to flaunt his own capabilities.

This was because he had profoundly attained the samādhi of non-self (*anātman*). Therefore, among those who drew near to him and rejoiced in his virtue, there were none whose hearts were not transformed by their profound observation and inspiration.

Each year, the number of those who took food from him counted in the thousands; yet the Master remained serene and free from worldly attachment, regarding the four requisites of life as no cause for personal anxiety, nor did he focus exclusively upon them.
Regarding the master of the transformation [the abbot]: though he resides within the monastic groves, there are few who lack the aspirational mind;

none fail to volunteer their services, running about to beg for alms in order to solicit offerings from the ten directions. Through the resonance of such a reputation, the annual provisions have never been lacking.

This, moreover, deeply accords with our Buddha’s supreme teaching of acting in accordance with conditions. In this age of the Dharma-ending period, when various monasteries are being established, some individuals may point out difficulties.
This is indeed a rare occurrence. I, an old man, have just now come here to share in this joy; my praise is inexhaustible.
Moreover, I observe these practitioners returning from their almsrounds, never failing in the slightest regard for cause and effect, and never betraying the faith of the donors.
Looking in all directions, among those who manage the affairs of monasteries, there has never been anyone as truly sincere as these. This is surely due to the genuine heart of the presiding master.
This was brought about by what he had perceived, so that the dragons and devas responded; it was no mere coincidence.

The old man’s sense of gratitude is inexhaustible, and thus he has written this in general terms to inform all the donors. As for the four kinds of offerings and the giving of the seven treasures as vast as Mount Sumeru, even these could be accepted and digested;
there are surely great-minded Bodhisattvas present for such matters, which is not something the old man dares to take for granted.
Inscription on the Back of Master Zhulin’s Scroll from Mount Tai:
In the past, the Old Man dwelt within the Golden Realm, where he alone shared a close bond with the Old Han of the Bamboo Grove.

As he was about to depart, he entrusted this broom of discarded refuse to him with earnest instructions, charging him to serve as his attendant in the meditation hall. It has now been thirty years since that parting.
In other years, when I was an old man, I was exiled to the scorched wilderness; more than twenty years have passed since then.
Although we are separated by ten thousand *li*, my out-breath and in-breath have never been even a hair’s breadth apart from this old fellow.
Now, suddenly seeing this scroll, the body of the Old Man of the Bamboo Grove emits light and shines upon the eyebrows of this old man. Who would say that this old fellow has entered extinction?

Little do they realize that the Fangwang Samādhi (Net of Methods Samādhi) is to enter meditative absorption in the East and arise in the West, or to enter absorption at Mount Tai and arise at Mount Kuang;
this is precisely the daily fare of this old fellow. Now tell me, when Zhulin arrives, he will surely sweep the floor for everyone as before.
Disciples, take this up for daily use in all places, and do not allow it to soil the broom handle.
This is the beginning of knowing and repaying kindness.
Regarding the inscription on the wall by the youth Shen Dayu:
all sentient beings inherently possess Buddha-nature, which is named *prajñā*. It is endowed with great radiance and is eternally aflame, never obscured. This is truly because of [the absence of]...
It begins with ignorance; therefore, one is obscured and lacks awakening. Because ignorance is profound and thick, one perpetually slumbers within birth and death without realizing it.
Thus, when a Bodhisattva practices, using only the light of wisdom to shatter ignorance, that is precisely the moment of emerging from birth and death.
Therefore, those who cultivate the mind are said to be practicing the path of Prajñā. As for the people of the world, their wisdom is bright...
As for those who possess benefit, it arises from within Prajñā; they manifest as loyal subjects and filial children because their nature is so constituted.
Even to the point where one perceives neither the signs of going nor coming regarding birth and death, this is because of the constant radiance [of wisdom]. Observe the youth Shen Dayu:

having entered the world at the age of eight, his various deeds and actions were all the result of practicing Prajñā in previous lives. Thus, at the moment of his death, his single thought was brilliantly clear.
The constant light is never obscured; this prajñā manifests at the very moment of impending death. This is sufficient proof of the powerful and victorious force of prajñā. Alas!
Beholding this, how could one be considered a person subject to birth and death? Yet parents regard such a one with eyes of attachment.
To turn back this *prajñā* and make it the root of birth and death—is this not to be ridiculed by the youth?
Originally seeking liberation through insight, one instead encounters further entanglement; the young man has indeed come with many expectations.
On the sixth day of the third month in the Ding-si year, his father, Layman Erhou, presented this transmission to him. The Elder Master Hanshan inscribed this upon it. Therefore:

The King was the nephew of Duke Sima Gongmei. Duke Gongmei’s elder sister married into the Zhang family and gave birth to Anren (the Lady), who died young. Lady Wang raised her from infancy.

At a tender age, she was introduced to a female teacher to study the *Shijing* and *Shujing*, and she became skilled in calligraphy and painting. She served her mother, Lady Kang, with filial devotion.

She had been a widow for twenty years, yet she remained respectful and compliant as if it were but a single day. By nature deeply filial, although born into a family of great wealth and status, her disposition was simple and unadorned;
she did not concern herself with cosmetics or finery. In her mother’s old age, she served her with even greater diligence in her devotion to Buddhism.

She paid homage to the Great Master Daguan; Lady An devoted herself to vegetarianism and took pleasure in giving. Lady Wang, the Imperial Consort, commanded the brothers of Sima Gong to attend upon Lady An.
He treated [others] as his own children. Of the family assets he divided, numbering in the tens of thousands, he gave them all away to serve as fields of merit.
He turned his heart toward the Pure Land like a lotus blooming among men. In his later years, he drew blood to transcribe one scroll of this sutra.

At the time of his death, he instructed his entire family to recite the Buddha’s name aloud day and night; he passed away peacefully. While I was exiled to the regions beyond the passes, Kāṅ-jūn’s younger brother, Jìxiū, [recorded this].
He has been my friend in the arts beyond our immediate circle. Recently, having entered Guangdong, Ji-xiu sent a letter entrusting me with a preface for this scripture transcribed by An-ren.
Upon beholding her handiwork, I see that it is dignified and meticulously calligraphed;

its brushwork emulates the ancients, not a single hair’s breadth being careless, and it is utterly devoid of any trace of softness or sentimentality—this is indeed difficult even for a man of stature to achieve. As I stroked the scroll and read it three times over, I sighed deeply and said:
This is indeed the overflowing radiance of the mind. Now, *prajñā* is named wisdom; it is that which all sages and ordinary beings alike are endowed with and receive in common.
When the Buddhas realize it, it becomes the adamantine ground of the mind (*vajra-citta-bhūmi*), manifesting as the wondrous functioning of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
When sentient beings are deluded by it, it becomes the root of birth and death, giving rise to discursive thought and worldly toil. While their nature is identical, their manifestations differ. If...

If one wishes to transform afflictions and delusive thoughts into the wondrous function of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), it cannot be accomplished without relying on the supreme power of Prajñāpāramitā.
Therefore, it is said: "If there are those who can believe in this sutra, they have already deeply planted roots of goodness under immeasurable billions of Buddhas.
From this, we know that Ananda’s dwelling in the world throughout his life was like a lotus flower growing in the mud without being defiled by it.
They were deeply devoted to the Triple Gem and faithfully upheld this sutra, receiving and maintaining it without doubt.

Were it not for the fact that they had practiced Prajñā over many lifetimes until it was thoroughly matured, how could they have been so diligent? How tragic it is that worldly people all possess this numinous and enlightened wisdom!
Bearing this physical body of flesh and blood, many have indulged solely in greed and anger, creating boundless dark karma and thereby sinking into the miserable realms.
Who can sprinkle drops of blood into the ocean of wisdom so that they flow as one with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*)?
The Vajra is named for its indestructibility; the *prajñā* of letters is the eternally abiding Dharmakāya, luminous and radiant.
Resplendent and radiant, its brilliance shines without end. What is called the "Vajra Seed" remains unpolished through kalpas;
how could it merely serve as a family treasure?
Written after the Memorial for the Restoration of Bao Guo Temple in Nanxun by Imperial Historian Zhu.
The Baoguo Ancient Monastery in Nanxun, Huzhou, was first established during the Song Dynasty. Over five hundred years have passed, and its main hall has long been in ruins.

Both monastics and laypeople pass by without concern, and there is no one to lead the restoration. A novice monk of this temple made a vow to rebuild it, swearing to sever one of his arms to fortify the resolve of the assembly.
The Imperial Historian Zhu composed a preface to elaborate upon this intent. A monk from the monastery brought this account to Mount Jing.

I have read this three times over and am deeply moved by it. It suggests that while the imperial tombs of emperors and kings mostly fall into ruin and desolation, Buddhist monasteries, though dilapidated, still remain standing.
One can infer from this the same fate that awaits places like Jingu Valley and the Bronze Horses. As the proverb says: "A thousand-year field has eight hundred masters.
Among all these people, who is able to preserve their ancestral holdings for several hundred years? Or rather, is there one who has descendants capable of doing so?

Is this not like a śrāmaṇera who abandons his worldly estate, weighing the relative importance of each? A sutra states: "The Buddha-field is firm and solid, composed of vajra, and guarded by nāgas and devas;
disciples inherit it. Tracing its origin, one finds that it was all acquired through the collective donation of wealth and resources, which remains undiminished for a thousand autumns.
When comparing this to the longevity of a worldly estate, the distinction is crystal clear. All people...

One knows that this śrāmaṇera severed his arm and vowed to establish a Buddha-field; yet few realize that this single arm of the śrāmaṇera is the eternal, imperishable legacy preserved by the donors of all generations.

If a wise and enlightened gentleman can relinquish non-essential wealth to place it upon a firm foundation, then for a thousand or ten thousand years thereafter, his merit will remain imperishable—relying on the śrāmaṇera’s single arm to preserve it is even more excellent than that.
How much more so for one whose merit and capacity are as vast as space? The Master said: "These desolate tombs rely upon Buddhist temples to endure for long;
truly, this is the Eye of the Dharma. I know that when a man of realization utters the first note, the multitude rises to respond in harmony.
Behold how this golden temple was established, like the Lord of Devas plucking a single blade of grass—which is none other than a novice monk manifesting a thousand hands and eyes.
...and so forth.

Following the two inscriptions for the Bronze Hall of Longchang Temple on Mount Hua, I, [the author], reflect that my friend Master Miaofeng entered the Way early through the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm). Therefore, all the foundations he established throughout his life were derived from the Universal [Vow].
The noble vows and practices flow forth from the heart of the *dharmadhātu*. Setting aside other merits for a moment, one may observe the circumstances regarding the bronze pavilions.

Since Mount Emei, Putuo, and Wutai are the bodhimandas of the three great bodhisattvas and the most supreme places for benefiting sentient beings in this land of China, a bronze pavilion was cast for each to enshrine their honored images. As for the South Sea...

Due to unforeseen circumstances, it was subsequently established on Mount Hua in Jinling. This was primarily owing to the blessed majesty of the Sacred Ancestor, and through the profound compassion of the Holy Mother and the Sovereign, who acted as patrons by providing the gold for its construction.
Thus, it has come to stand alongside the Three Mountains; such a convergence of conditions is truly rare.

Its adornments are wondrous and beautiful, and its halls and chambers are vast and expansive. However, due to the shifting influence of my own karmic forces, I have not yet been able to [complete this task].

Upon visiting and paying homage, I observed that the epigraphs for the two officials, Imperial Historian Jiao and Director of the Ministry of Rites Huang, display the *samādhi* of the writing brush so perfectly that a jeweled world-system (*ratnarāja-kṣetra*) appears within a single hair-tip; how could one not believe this?
Though the three calamities may encompass all things, their karmic deeds remain serene, sustained by the power of their vows; they shall surely be equal to the Dharma-realm itself.
Inscription for the Scroll of True Compassion and Attainment of Filial Piety through the Ullambana Sutra:

The Sutra says: "The Greatly Filial Honored One Śākyamuni repaid his parents' kindness over successive kalpas. This is because during the many lifetimes when Śākyamuni practiced the path, every instance was an occasion for repaying his parents.
Thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "Filial piety is called the precepts. This means that being filial and obedient toward one's father [is the foundation of all virtue].
Mother... and so on, up to all sentient beings. Now, the precepts are the foundation for attaining Buddhahood, and filial piety is, in turn, the foundation of the precepts.
Thus we know that when the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas deliver sentient beings and rescue them from all suffering and affliction, they do so by cultivating the practice of filial obedience.

For throughout kalpas of birth and death, as sentient beings emerge and submerge within the six realms, undergoing the casting off of one body and the taking up of another, there is not a single class [of being] who...
There is no single being who has not previously been one's parent. Furthermore, it is only when all sentient beings have been delivered that one attains the realization of Bodhi;
therefore, every sentient being delivered from suffering represents the fulfillment of the filial path by the Bodhisattva.
Moreover, how could this be discussed in terms of a single lifetime or a single body? This is evident even in the case of the one person saved by Maudgalyāyana.

The mother who gives birth has not yet exhausted the filial piety of the Tathāgata. His teaching includes the Water and Land Assembly (Shuilu Zhaihui), established for the purpose of repaying one's parents.

It encompasses all beings within the Dharma-realm—whether moving in water, on land, or through the air—even those in the three miserable paths and the six realms of existence—none of whom are excluded from the aspiration to emerge from their suffering and delusion.
Although this is a teaching of the Semblance Age, it is the fundamental source of the Tathāgata’s great filial piety. [Written by] the monk Li Huan of the Capital.

I bow my head to the Great Muni, the savior and protector of sentient beings. Appearing in this defiled and evil world, you are like a lotus flower emerging from the water.
The thirty-two marks of excellence are all adorned with merit; therefore, those who behold them rejoice as if gazing upon their own compassionate parents.
Truly, they are equal and without distinction from the minds of sentient beings; thus, through skillful contemplation, they manifest solemnly at the tips of the fingers.
The threads of sentient beings' delusive thoughts weave together the forms of the evil realms. Amidst these delusions, the Buddha manifests subtle and wondrous marks.

With his hand he draws out the threads of delusion, and with his needle pierces the fine silk of light. With every stitch one beholds the Dharmakāya; in every thought-moment, one attains perfect enlightenment.
Within these conditions of harmony, one suddenly perceives the inconceivable. Thus it is known that the dharma-realm is empty, yet the seeds of Buddhahood arise from conditions.
I vow that all sentient beings, through the needle and thread of their own delusive thoughts, shall perceive the Dharma-body in every thought-moment, so that none fail to attain Buddhahood.

The Vairocana Buddha manifests subtle and wondrous marks upon the tip of a single hair; like flowers in the sky, like reflections in a mirror, they become even more manifest when one seeks to hide them, appearing as soon as they are withdrawn.
Thus we know that our Master’s radiance is immeasurable.
In Praise of the Buddha:
I bow my head to the Pure Dharma-body, the mass of immeasurable radiance, the most supreme Lotus King, thus hailed as the Sage among Sages.
Within the ocean of profound quiescent extinction, you manifest subtle and wondrous marks; dwelling serenely in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, you gather and transform all sentient beings.
With a single mind, one universally seals the minds of all sentient beings. Therefore, the mind of sentient beings is itself the Tathāgata.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three have fundamentally no difference. To see the mind is to see the Buddha; to recollect the Buddha is to recollect the mind.
Upon beholding this extraordinary countenance, one awakens to the nature of reality. Thus, from the tip of a single hair, this rare phenomenon is manifested.
By paying homage, recollecting, and briefly taking refuge, one suddenly attains the fruit of eternal abiding.
While walking in meditation, the Tathāgata praised me, saying:
"How is it that our Great Master has manifested his body? For the sake of sentient beings, he acts as a guest among hosts. [Behold] the mark of his broad and long tongue."
Like wind moving through space, the sound of thunder awakens the masses from their long night of ignorance. Coming from nowhere and going nowhere, they seek to see my Teacher. Thus it is, thus it is.
Furthermore, there were two disciples who followed him as the Tathāgata sat in meditative seclusion.
[The Buddha] asked, "Why do you practice walking meditation? A thought suddenly arose: "In order to deliver sentient beings. The Venerable One followed him.
To catch the wind and grasp shadows. Though all sentient beings have been delivered, the feverish dream has not yet awakened.
*Praise for the Sandalwood Vairocana Buddha* (with preface):
Yunyi, grandson of an elder from Qu’a, styled Tunan, traveled for official service to the South Sea and happened upon sandalwood incense.
A single branch, over a foot in diameter and approximately eight feet long, was considered a rare wonder of the world.
Delighted, he purchased it with the intention of emulating the precedent of King Wutian; he brought it back and enshrined it at the Guangfu Monastery in his district.
The bhikṣu Tongtan carried it on his shoulders, and it thus became the wondrous form of Vairocana. He constructed a pavilion to house it and further requested a complete set of the Great Canon.
Together they achieved this magnificent adornment. At another time, while I was resting in old age at Mount Nanyue, he respectfully presented a letter requesting a eulogy.
Although I had not yet met the Elder in person, I rejoiced that his meritorious deeds were inconceivable; thus, I briefly recounted the facts and composed a eulogy for him, saying:
The *candana* from the seashore is beyond price; even a mere grain the size of a *zhu* is worth a great trichiliocosm.
From where has it been brought to the land of Zhendan? All who hear its fragrance are filled with joy. Now there was an elder who encountered it by chance, without seeking it.
Wishing to emulate the King of Udyāna in creating an image endowed with wondrous marks, he surrendered his heart and offered it; may he attain Buddhahood immediately.

Selecting the ground for the offering, he subsequently obtained vast merit. At that time, there was a bhikṣu possessed of great power of faith who conceived a resolute mind of devotion and adorned [the image] with various exquisite ornaments.
Possessing the thirty-two marks, a person emerges from his hand, as if descending from Tuṣita Heaven. He manifests majestic spiritual power, perfecting the Vairocana of great merit;
his immeasurable radiance pervades all places, like the splitting of a single atom through skillful means.
At that moment, the great thousandfold sutra-scrolls surged forth. The Buddha is originally without marks, yet he manifests according to the mind;
the Dharma is originally without abiding, yet it takes form in response to conditions. Through the aspiration of the elder and the vow of the bhikṣu, the Three Jewels of the world thus appeared.

The Dharma-realm receives the perfuming; those who touch it are freed from defilement. All who take refuge therein suddenly empty all realms of existence. The Dharma-body is eternally abiding, and the land is abundant and joyful.
Beings with scales, shells, or feathers alike receive liberation; even blades of grass, weeds, and minute dust motes all return to the Flower Treasury World.
Therefore, I, the Tathāgata, appear as the most supreme among the honored ones.
Homage to the Tathāgata Blazing Radiance,
the King of Blazing Radiance, who universally illumines all the suns, moons, and four heavenly kings within the dust-motes and lands of the ten directions.
Below. All sentient beings receive benefit. Sentient and insentient beings are of one essence, together entering the Tathāgata’s net of light.
Within the pores of the body and mind, even down to a single atom, all are brilliantly illuminated without exception.

The dreams and deluded minds of sentient beings are entirely the Tathāgata’s treasury of radiance. Therefore, the seven luminaries and the four remaining [planets], as well as the twenty-eight [lunar mansions]...
The various elements are distributed and together form the embodied beings with their characteristics. Birth and death, coming and going, are all quiescent.

The suffering of sentient beings is the very mind of the Buddha; the Buddha is the ocean of afflictions of sentient beings. Because these two are without distinction, suffering and pleasure transform according to thought.
Excellent, O Son of the Buddha, you accord with the Buddha-mind and are able to uphold the secret seal of the Tathāgata.
In every thought-moment, they constantly radiate great light, capable of shattering the darkness of afflictions from time immemorial.

All wondrous functions manifest before them as they flow into the ocean of the Tathāgata’s great vows. May all who see, hear, or praise them be led entirely to the ground of eternal bliss and nirvana.
Having awakened from sleep, Maitreya’s eulogy concludes;
all day long he wanders the streets. His two feet never rest; when weary, he sleeps beneath a tree. His belly is as black as ink. By whom was he called awake?
His dream-talk has not yet ceased. His entire body is exhausted and his bones ache; he yawns to left and right.
They cannot be eliminated by stretching them out. These village monks are too lazy to sever their own tendons;
how can they be called Maitreya?
A traveling Maitreya praises himself as he carries a staff slung across his shoulder, bearing a leather bag filled with a bundle of broken, tangled things, treating them as rare wares for sale.
Whenever he meets someone, he begs for a single coin, unaware that these are all debts from a future life. Pointing toward the estate beneath the Dragon Flower tree, he says:
"When the accounts are settled, there will still be a balance remaining."
The Praise of the Open-Bosomed Maitreya:
How remarkably wide his mouth is! He laughs without ceasing. His open bosom reveals a bare belly; one suspects it is because he fears the heat.
This is the Praise of the Cloth Bag Monk.
Observe closely: it is not present within the breast; look at it: it is not absent from the hand.
Born with such a cumbersome burden, one instead laughs at others for being muddled. With a staff slung across the shoulder, the feet are free and unrestrained.
Had one not been toyed with by this "little child," one might truly be called a heroic and fierce man.
Praise of the Pratyekabuddha:
Upon the Panṭa Rock, beneath the long pines, he realized the non-arising of phenomena with perfect clarity; the waters flow and the flowers fall.
—Praise by the Three Great Sages.

The three Great Beings manifest their bodies according to the species they encounter: appearing as gods among the gods and as humans among humans, just as the moon dwells in the sky while its reflection falls into all waters.
Though the water may be clear or turbid, the moon remains neither here nor there. With the Perfection of Wisdom as their mother, they thus have many sons.
Loving-kindness can bestow happiness according to one's wishes; its great vows are inexhaustible. The true scripture is beyond words;
the mind of the Great Being is like empty space.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva praises the moon within the Golden World-realm, the snow upon Mount Wutai, the lion cub amidst the clouds, and the thunderous tongue in the void.
Who recognizes that the old man who waters his oxen is originally Nectar-Extinction (Amṛtānala)? He sits in solemn repose within the Vajra Cave, as if crouching in the den of a fierce tiger.
A single cup of crystal tea briefly clears the fever of afflictions. I ask: how many people are within this cave?
That "three by three, before and after" is no idle speech.
Furthermore:
Dwelling in the stage of quiescent extinction, he raises the great Dharma banner and beats the drum of lethal venom; those who hear it find their minds subdued.
He is the teacher of the seven Buddhas and the father of all sentient beings; like a lion king, he strides with broad and majestic steps.
The Great Being Samantabhadra praises the Lotus Sutra in its half-finished scroll: Upon Mount Emei, the moon is a single orb; the world glistens like silver. His crown is white as snow;
from ten thousand ravines, the pines howl in the wind. All these are his broad and long tongue, which can overturn the entire Dharma-realm at will. Like flowers in the sky, they arise and perish.

Buddha-fields enter the tip of a single hair; the ten directions are placed upon eyebrows and eyelashes. Fragrant elephants gallop and stride with ease, while they trample blind donkeys and lame turtles beneath their feet.
Furthermore:
I prostrate to Samantabhadra, whose body is the Dharma-realm. Within the lands of every mote of dust and hair, he sits, lies, and walks.

In the emptiness of the nature of phenomena, great clouds spread everywhere; because they are all-pervasive, there is ultimately no coming or staying. Thus, his subtle and wondrous marks are never hidden nor manifest.
If there is one who sees it, it must be with the Universal Eye. Mounted upon the Great Elephant King, its body is purely white; because it is fundamentally unstained, it is truly pure and clean.
All sages and ordinary beings are not separate from a single pore; pervading the entire body and extending throughout it, they surge forth like the tide of the ocean.
The Great Being contemplates me, and I contemplate the Great Being; as emptiness merges with emptiness, we have been non-dual from the very beginning. Therefore, I pay homage.
O Great Dharma-realm of Emptiness, may we meet at all times and in every place.
Furthermore, you are called the Body of the Dharma-realm, the essence of the myriad practices. Within the lands contained in a single pore, what is there that cannot be accommodated?
Like an elephant king roaming, you are unimpeded throughout the ten directions. I prostrate to you, who are as vast and sovereign as space.
Eulogy for the Illustration of Samantabhadra Washing the Elephant:

Taking the Dharma-realm as his body, there is nowhere he does not go; were he to deviate from this King of Elephants, he would instead become entangled in worldly affairs. The elephant’s form is pure white.
Originally free from defilement, there is no reason to wash it; doing so would only increase the specks of dust. Water does not wash water, and white does not stain white.
If one seeks these two, they are found to be entirely without differentiation. Why trouble yourself with this "servant"? It is a waste of effort; there is a place where it does not reach.

Your perspective is still obstructed. As I view it, the present manifestation is the most excellent. When both man and elephant are forgotten, and both the holy and the ordinary are swept away—furthermore, since the body of the elephant is pure white, where could dust ever stain it?
It is only when grit enters the eye that its filth spreads throughout the whole body; wash it with water.
On the contrary, it increases its filth; it is naturally pure without being washed. One does not know the reason for this: the water does not increase in purity, and purity does not depend on water;

the two do not reach one another. Since the beginning, it has been thus. The samādhi of the Great Being is perfectly interfused with the Dharma-realm; why then concern yourself with these defilements?
Thus, obstacles arise. To retain them is not defilement; to discard them is not purity. This dharma-gate of illusion is called "Non-contention.
Samantabhadra rides upon his elephant, extolling the vast strides of great practice;
he traverses the ten directions, appearing everywhere within the pores of the skin and the motes of dust. Whether walking alone or sitting alone, he is ever present.

What is this so-called "lightness and agility"? If one must rely on the power of another, one immediately falls into a state of distress. With lotus flowers beneath one's feet and coiling through the nostrils—this is not merely a matter of being toppled by others;
body and life depend upon one another, and such coming and going has long been practiced. Though it may seem that one is burdening others, [it is otherwise].
"Rest now, my feet.
O Great Being Samantabhadra, you who empower this elephant with your praise:
O Great Being, whose body is the Dharma-realm, whenever there is one who upholds this sutra, you immediately manifest your form; this is not due to supernatural powers."
Nor is it for the sake of mere display; rather, it is intended to cause sentient beings to awaken with sudden intensity.
The Eulogy on the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara Image says:
"I have heard that the Great Being fundamentally has no abode, yet dwells only within the thoughts and minds of sentient beings. Since sentient beings are themselves the Great Being,"
The mind—how could it be inverted if it does not perceive? If you say that the Great Being’s mind is inverted, how can he transform those who are themselves inverted?
If sentient beings were not inverted, why would the Great Being need to labor so hard to preach the Dharma? Alas! Humans lack the light of wisdom;
they are like those lying drunk in the bright daylight, wandering through various dream-like paths of fear, trembling with terror and dread.
Terrified, they cannot escape; though they drive themselves to flight, they find no refuge. It is like a thirsty deer rushing toward a mirage;

the more it runs, the thirstier it becomes, until its mental and physical strength is exhausted. Yet, even while in this dream, it does not realize its state. To the observer with clear eyes, compassion arises;
yet the dreamer, despite being rebuked with all their might, remains unaware of the suffering and instead gives rise to anger. Furthermore, they continue to see pursuers in their dreams.
Terrified by what lies ahead and fearing what lies behind, he calls out with all his might. With one cry, he suddenly raises his arms and rises. From this single awakening, he looks upon the dream;
only then does he believe that the delusions arise from his own mind. Such a Great Being is able to save others from suffering; for the most part, he is like one whose eyes have been opened.
Even if he can always accord with the needs of sentient beings, those who harbor doubts will instead give rise to further alarm and fear. If a person is willing—
Temporarily turning back the light is still superior to the thousand hands and eyes of a Mahāsattva. How excellent, O Son of the Buddha! Why this perversion?
If you do not seek within yourself but seek elsewhere, yet see your own mind in the very place where you seek, then I shall also be called Avalokiteśvara.

Furthermore, the Perfected Person has no name; it is only in people that there are names. Seeing colors within the ears and hearing sounds within the eyes, the six functions are but one, yet even this "one" does not stand.
Pervading the world and pervading space, there is nowhere they do not enter. As the bright moon hangs in the sky, its light seals the myriad rivers.
Like dewdrops on the tips of blades of grass, each perfectly round; upon the tip of a single hair, they manifest subtle and wondrous bodies.

Seated within a speck of dust, they turn the Great Dharma Wheel. Amidst masses of fire, mountains of swords, iron beds, and copper pillars, with a single cry, these places suddenly become a pure land.
He makes no distinction between the pure and the defiled, nor does he differentiate between male and female. If one wishes to seek him out, it depends solely upon oneself.

Furthermore, I have heard that the Great Being manifests billions of transformation bodies; when one sees them with the eyes or hears them with the ears, one does not know which is the true one. When suffering arises, one simply cries out.
When one calls out, there is no one who receives; one does not see coming or going, nor does one know who might save them. Now I reflect: the Great Being is without self.
At the gates of the six sense organs, whatever touches is like fire; fire does not burn fire, and dust does not stain dust, for there is neither "this" nor "that."
He is named Avalokiteśvara.

Furthermore, the body of this Great Being resides within the minds of sentient beings; it interpenetrates without being mixed and remains distinct without being divided. Therefore, when I have a need, [I call upon him].
He responded according to the sound: "It was not that a Great Being came; it was truly my own self-realization. I did not know suffering, so how could I have sought it?
To know the locus of suffering is itself the reversal of the flow. Once my flow has been reversed, the Great Being is myself. Thus, I seek myself by means of myself."
What is there that is impossible?
Furthermore, I observe that the body of a Great Being is fundamentally free from all marks; because it is fundamentally free from marks, he is able to manifest manifold bodies.
It is like a mani jewel, which manifests various colors according to conditions.

Therefore, from Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to sentient beings of the six realms, and even to forms of diverse species—there is nothing that does not enter [into it]. How could there be any discriminatory views regarding male or female bodies?
If one beholds the body of the Great Being, it is equal and without dual characteristics; realizing that the nature of phenomena is empty, its radiance is like the full moon.
It can cause the darkness of afflictions to be instantly and entirely dispelled. Therefore, by relying upon the Great Being, I am suddenly delivered from the suffering of birth and death.
Praise of Avalokiteśvara as the Moon in Water:
His body is like floating clouds; his mind is like the moon reflected in water. He responds without moving; he speaks without words. When called upon, he gives voice.
Though one seeks it, it cannot be found. Yet, for all who seek it with earnest longing, there is liberation.
Furthermore, the form of the moon in water, the appearance of flowers in the sky, the sound of an echo in a valley, and the mani-jewel—these are encountered everywhere.
He immediately manifests his form; coming and going through the six realms without distinction between darkness and dawn. A single piece of mind and body exists only for others.
Which master could you seek out, and where?
Furthermore:
Like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water, like a flash of lightning in the vast void—when touched and stirred, the image appears in an instant.
Furthermore, unstained by a single speck of dust, it is laid bare throughout the ten directions; with the eyes and hands of one's entire body, there is no need for shifting or evasion.
Furthermore, the mind is fundamentally without objects; for whom, then, would it engage in arduous contemplation? When someone comes to question it, even the mind itself does not know.
Moreover,
The Great Being is without mind, yet like an echo responding to a sound, whenever there is one who seeks, he responds immediately to every call.
Furthermore, with a formless body, he accords with the seeking minds of others, manifesting everywhere; thus he is named Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, the flow of water reaches the ocean, yet the moon does not leave the sky; responding without deliberation constitutes the dhyāna of mastery.
Moreover,
The mark of formlessness—its marks do not reside within me; they manifest in accordance with conditions, like fire meeting fuel. The thirty-two manifestations are but minor matters;
what could prevent the appearance of hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, or billions?
Furthermore, the body and mind of the Great Being are identical to those of sentient beings; therefore, whatever he aspires for arrives in accordance with his resonance.
Moreover,
The Perfected Person has no form; true compassion is soundless. When resonance and response intersect in the Way, the sands become white and the water clear.
Furthermore, taking wisdom as life and all beings as one's own heart, seeking out sounds to rescue those from suffering, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, his body and mind are transparently clear, like lapis lazuli; both surface and interior are pure, like the moon reflected in a pond.
He responds without being moved and arrives without being sought. For this reason, my teacher is named "Inconceivable."
Furthermore, he speaks without sound and responds to those who seek him, like an echo answering a call or appearing before a precious mirror.
Thus he is called Avalokiteśvara; the samādhi he cultivates is named "True Purity."
Furthermore, with a mind of quiescent extinction, one manifests subtle and wondrous signs; like the full moon in the cool void, its radiance is immeasurable.
