A single robe covers his head; with palms joined, he bows his head low.
With a single robe covering his head, all conditions are transcended through sitting. With palms joined, he prostrates; thus he receives the teaching with faith.
Second, when a subduing lion seizes a lion cub and leads it away with vigorous strides,
and a powerful, majestic lion exerts its strength to snatch the cub back, would it not hurl the other back?
Third, he stands alone with his staff raised and his fists clenched, walking solitary strides;
one staff supports the void, and two fists grip the bones. His spiritual power is boundless as he chants "Namo Buddha.
Fourth, three or four people sit together in the manner of preaching the Dharma.
Speaking without a tongue; listening without ears. The sound of the Dharma is like thunder, yet no one is willing to believe it.
For kalpas they sit silently and upright, yet amidst their deluded thoughts, they do not perceive it in the midst of their busyness. At the very moment of sitting in silence, it all appears at once.
With the six dhyānas as his patched robe, he was like space; with a backbone like iron, he sat and cut off the ten directions, yet he ended up with a dot on his forehead.
Seven times he held up his bowl.
With both hands I hold up the almsbowl and present it to you on its full platter. Examine it closely: what is there within?
These eight great bellies are so vast that their expansiveness is difficult to conceal; their legs are so long that they cannot be shortened. You harbor your own aversion; it is not my fault.
In the latter part of the ninth month, while viewing the sutras, the moonlight was as bright as day. My aged eyes were not fatigued; I rose to recite the scriptures to briefly dispel my weariness.
I spread out ten sitting mats and sat down.
He spreads out his sitting mat and casually lets down a single line; he does not sit in meditation, but instead yawns with his whole body.
With an eleven-bag pack slung loosely over his shoulder and a clumsy staff in hand, he travels as a wandering monk in such a manner—truly loathsome and strange.
Twelfth, the Hand Holding the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel (Cintāmaṇi):
holding a wish-fulfilling jewel with the hands stacked one upon another; wearing a *kāṣāya* robe merely to conceal his ugliness.
Thirteenth, the One Holding a Rosary and Reciting the Buddha’s Name.
The Buddha himself thought to himself: "Where could I hide? Since I am seeking me, why should it not be possible?
With fourteen broken reeds, one crosses the boundless ocean of suffering;
with feet that find no firm footing, one relies on this single leaf to reach the other shore.
Furthermore, the ocean of suffering is boundless; yet one takes a lotus leaf for a boat and relies upon others for one's life. Being old, one knows no shame;
the aggregates are empty, yet one cherishes the body; the mind is empty, yet it possesses a substance. Such perversions as these—do not say you do not recognize them!
A wish-fulfilling gem in hand, reed leaves upon his heels; in a state of frantic bustle, when will he find rest?
Fearing the monsters of the sea, he treads upon the vajra; clenching his fists and glaring with bared eyes, as if seeing a tiger.
Emitting light from mid-air, treading upon scriptures with his feet, and laughing at the long and short of others—how can such a person be called a monk?
To measure the ocean with a conch-shell or seek spring on the tip of a branch; if one does not see [the truth] face-to-face, how can they be named an Arhat?
Turning over the seas and moving the mountains; stretching out a hand and drawing back a foot—such sovereign spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*), who would dare speak of them?
Treading firmly upon the ground oneself, watch him enter the water; steady and secure, he is nothing short of extraordinary.
The nature of the divine dragon is fundamentally untouchable; because its pearl was first taken away, it did not dare to oppose him.
Within the great ocean, he immediately found a shallow place. By calling upon Avalokiteśvara, he was at that moment rescued and protected.
He would not accept his own ease, but was dragged along by others. Though he is old and decrepit, he does not know how to be at ease.
Covering his head with his patched robe, he is so happy he nearly dies; let him have all his supernatural powers, they are still not equal to yours.
Eulogy for the Twelfth Patriarch, Rāhula:
Clutching his robe, he crosses the water;
a wandering monk encountering water on his way. The path has gone astray; there is nowhere to turn back or avoid it. He must simply pass through.
Second, as for those who can cross over carrying others versus those who cannot:
one with great courage is not afraid, while one with small courage is afraid of falling. If you are fortunate enough to be willing to carry them, both parties will be well.
Third and fourth, those who first reach the other shore shall use their staffs to receive those who cannot yet cross.
He has surpassed nine-tenths; he lacks but one step. Relying on his staff, he gains great strength.
Having already reached the other shore, he looks back at his companions; with a single pull at the ultimate limit, what skillful means is this?
Fifth, having stepped into the damp ground, the boy twisted his clothes without knowing their depth;
he walked on impulsively until his garments were soaked through, thereby burdening others with the consequence.
Sixth, having reached the foot of a tree, he took off his clothes and prepared himself.
His garments were disheveled and he was drenched in mud and water; though he had merely dragged himself along, he had to laboriously adjust his dress once more.
Sitting beneath a tree with bare feet, he cleared away his drowsiness by sneezing, expending all his energy.
As he sat idly dozing, his nostrils pointed toward the heavens; a single sneeze suddenly awakened him.
8. When the spirit is exhausted and weary, one looks upward and dozes;
though the mind is fatigued, both eyes remain open. Observe those who are dazed: they are utterly dull-witted.
9. Tying the skirt.
While crossing the water, he feared being entangled by it; having escaped, he would be caught again, thus wasting his energy in vain.
Then, leaning on his staff, he sat with legs spread wide upon a stone.
His spirit became expansive and clear, and forgetting all fatigue, he felt ten times more joyful.
Eleventh, sitting idly, he uses a *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem) to scratch his own itchy spots;
others do not know of it, for the gem is in his hand, allowing him to scratch as he pleases.
Twelfth, leaning on a staff and sitting upright, he looks back at the practitioner’s bundles, robes, and bowl.
Having reached a place of rest, why do you not let go? To burden yourself with such wrappings is truly pitiable.
Venerable Bunat praises those whose bodies are covered in rags; he wishes to mend them anew, never wearying of the labor of needle and thread.

Furthermore, there is a single piece of tattered rag-robe, patched a hundred times and mended a thousand times. With every needle and every stitch, it is truly arduous work; each needle must pierce through, and one will not rest until it has.
Even if it is finally mended, it is fit only for covering one's head.
The Venerable who studies the sutras does not understand for himself; instead, he pores over old paper. Within the realm of purity, he turns it into mere dregs.
Furthermore:
Born unable to read, yet forced to look at the sutras, my ears are deaf and my eyesight failing; to whom shall I speak them?
The Sanskrit manuscripts have stood for many years, their pages riddled through by woodworms; the characters are indistinct, all of them full of errors.

In the *Praise of Venerable Dragon-Tamer*, it is said that those who are excessively wrathful cannot be captured by force; one must instead employ single-minded compassion and focus the visualization with concentrated attention.
Furthermore:
The black dragon was fast asleep; the Master stole the pearl while it slept. Had he encountered it while awake, how could he have hoped for a peaceful end?
Venerable Subhūti, who subdues tigers, praised him as being difficult to tame and possessing peerless, fierce power; yet he surrendered his entire body, exhausting all his spiritual might.
Furthermore:

"The claws and fangs are already bared, yet the fierce spirit has not yet been unleashed; had it not been for my Master, the marketplace would have been nearly startled."—In Praise of Venerable Tiaoshi.
The claws and fangs of the Dharma-cave—dare anyone dare to touch them? My Master’s supernormal powers regard them as mere playthings.
The Venerable who floats upon the ocean praises the boundless sea of merit;
its vast currents flow on without ceasing until one directly ascends to the other shore. Upon a single leaf of the blue lotus, this body is no longer a body.
Bearing the *khakkhara* staff, the sky and water join at the heavens. This markless mark—emptiness is not outside of existence, and beyond water there is no flow.
Who can let out a single shout to sever both ends? Treading through the vast void, kicking over the blue seas, the thread snaps from the heels.
With a mind free from obstruction,

the Venerable Who Crossed the River praised those who have transcended the stream of ignorance; yet they remain halfway there, for their delusive thoughts are not yet severed— like a gourd bobbing upon the water.
To cross the stream by cutting it through, one may naturally transcend; why then rely again upon a single leaf of the *pāṭala* tree?
Though the hollow substance of the plantain is subject to rapid decay, it is not something borrowed from another. To do so would be nearly a source of shame.
The heels are not yet steady; the earthen vessel is not firm. Swaying and drifting, one is fortunately able to preserve both.
To go alone and simply rest—why turn back? If you seek a companion, you will find none who is not petty.
Palm-leaf scriptures rest in his hands; azure eyes gaze into the void. Striding tall and solitary, our Master is like a dragon.

The Venerable Who Burns Incense praises him for never ceasing in old age and never slackening in youth; he stirs the embers and burns incense without letting a single breath go idle. Originally, there was nothing to do.
Seeking busyness for oneself—how can one reach the Land of No-Birth?
*The Dream-Wandering Collection of Old Man Hanshan*, Volume Thirty-Four;
*The Dream-Wandering Collection of Old Man Hanshan*, Volume Thirty-Five.
Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and his disciple Tonghyeong;
revised by the Disciple from Lingnan, Liu Qixiang.
Eulogy on the Great Master Dharma Crossing the River:
Coming ten thousand li from the West, for what purpose was it truly? When old Xiao first beheld him, there was still doubt within his breast.
A single word did not meet the occasion; shaking his sleeves, he departed. Having broken off a single stalk of reed, he wished to lay it across the great earth.

For nine years he sat facing a wall; all was silent, devoid of any intent or interest. He won back the arm of Shen Guang, which has been transformed into a mass of radiance throughout his entire being.
When meeting him, there is no need to inquire about one's future path; a man of true character naturally possesses the ambition to soar through the clouds.
Furthermore, he did not come in vain; there was a matter in his breast. Failing to meet the right person, he swallowed his words and endured his indignation.

Raising himself up, he departed at once, without a backward glance. Like the vast Yangtze River, he cut across the current to cross over; taking a single reed, its five leaves floated through the air.
This serves merely as a substitute for my feet; how could it be a supernatural power? My future path is yet undetermined, and I know not where I shall go.
Who would have expected that, before the cliffs of Shaoshi, I would again fall into nine years of deluded thoughts?
Furthermore:
Having come specifically to seek one who understands, we met yet did not meet; a single word failed to strike the vital point, so he withdrew and departed.
Crossing the vast Yangtze River by breaking off a reed, his heels did not touch the ground. Had it not been for Shaoshi Cliff, he would have nearly suffered a great loss.
Fortunately, I have found a child of sincere heart; with this, I may briefly conceal my shame. It deceives all those who come after, whom they call the "Meaning of Coming from the West.

Furthermore, in the *Banying Zan* (Half-Shadow Praise), it is said that his appearance resembles a hawk, and his mind is like a pouncing hare. It is not that he has no body, but he does not wish to reveal it in its entirety.

Furthermore, you came back from the West in such a great hurry and returned so swiftly, your spirit exhausted and your countenance abashed; you have ended up with nothing but a single broken shoe, which moreover has leather but no lining.
When you go back to see your mother, what words will you have to report to her? Aha!
"Ha! To bend when one should not bend—this only causes descendants to weep into the void.
Furthermore, this matter is the common lot of every person; why labor to come from the West specifically? It was simply said that they sought profit by means of their capital; who would have known?"
Upon returning, one encounters suspicion and doubt; going back, there is boundless melancholy and longing. Only upon reaching home does one regret returning empty-handed.
Furthermore, regarding the praise for the embroidered image:
originally it has no face or features, yet the needlework is needlessly expended; when threaded together, not even a single hair is lacking, even though it is but the whole body.
One obtains only half. In the halls of King Liang’s palace, or by the crags of Shaoshi Mountain, there is absolutely nothing like this.
All these calculations and deliberations—people say this is the Patriarch coming from the West; I say it is the manifestation of compassionate concern.
Furthermore, Master Dharma’s eulogy reveals a heart of sincere toil:
"Having come from afar for a great matter, yet failing to meet one who is 'in the person,' it truly lacks all meaning."
For nine years he sat facing the wall; the ice was frozen solid and the snow had grown old. Without a man who could sever his own arm, this mind would never have been resolved.
It was only because he was in such a frantic hurry at the beginning that today he finally knows it was too early.
Furthermore, his journey has been exceedingly long and his heart has suffered greatly. Having failed to encounter a true master, he was frequently subjected to contempt and insult.
Now that his Way has become radiant, its bounty spreads ever wider; his life, as precarious as a thread suspended from a single reed, has secured descendants beyond counting throughout the heavens.
The entire earth turns in total refuge; this is the true patriarch of our teacher.

Furthermore, there is a matter in my heart that I cannot restrain from expressing: when he came from the West with his ten thousand-mile journey, who was the one who understood? A single word did not meet.
Facing the wall for nine years was not merely the act of Shen Guang; it nearly came to utter ruin. The sea of suffering is boundless, with waves that toss the heavens.
To attempt to grasp it is to fall; to step upon it is to perish. Five leaves float in the void, yet the single flower remains unchanged. Thus we know our Master.
To this day, they remain as if present.
Furthermore, his spirit overwhelms heaven and earth, and his mind encompasses the six directions. That he traveled ten thousand *li* to the west specifically for this purpose was no small matter.
He was unwilling to accept it, simply because he disliked being probed. A single word that did not hit the mark, and he crossed the river;
how could one ever avoid getting one's feet wet when crossing water? For nine years he faced the wall in solemn stillness; he deceived Shen Guang until an arm fell off.
To this day, blood flows across the great earth, and all his worldly possessions have been cast away. People say this is the direct pointing and single transmission; I—
The Way is the livelihood of those who dwell in leisure.
Furthermore:
"Blue-eyed barbarian! Blue-eyed barbarian! Having come from a hundred thousand miles away, for what purpose do you come? A single word did not meet [his] mark, and he hurriedly broke his reed."
He turned his head away and paid no heed—this truly puts me to shame. In the stone chamber of Mount Song, ice and snow withered all around;

for nine years he faced the wall, his mouth silenced like Lu. Neither sorrowful nor indifferent, how solitary was his heart! Suddenly he opened both eyes, yet they were both blurred and dim. When asked, "Who is the disciple standing here?
had he been about to open his mouth, his body would have perished. One arm fell off, yet his heart and gall were revived; drops of blood flowed across.
Filling the rivers and lakes. Tell me, who is without this matter? I ask you: why do you not go to the end of it?
Furthermore:
Arriving specifically for this purpose, seeking someone but finding no one, he hurriedly broke off a reed and withdrew at once before the cliffs of Shaoshi.

It is utterly devoid of flavor; it relies on a divine light to faintly exhale its breath. It stubbornly leaves behind a single pair of stinking leather shoes, provoking descendants to loathe their fragmentation.
How could this compare to when one had not yet arrived? The bright moon in the vast sky is free from even a trace of obscuration.
Furthermore, his departure was too swift and his arrival was too early; those who understood him were few, and he needlessly increased their remorse.

Had it not been before the cliffs of Shaoshi, this mind would likely never have been resolved. Although it is said to be a direct pointing and a single transmission, it ultimately remains a mere circling about the gate.
The descendants have propagated this to this day; the family legacy remains in great disarray. Heh! The east wind blows through the spring on the treetops;
fallen flowers cover the ground, yet no one sweeps them up.
Furthermore, the eulogy for the Great Master Dharma of the Stone Grotto:
In the stone grotto of the Azure Cliff, he faced the wall for nine years. This was not because he lacked a mind; it was simply because he did not recognize [his own nature].

It was utterly tedious and left one with no definitive point. He waited until Shen Guang’s snow reached his waist, when a single word out of the blue brought all to ruin. Thus, the flowers of the five petals bloom.
The great earth is springtime; yet until now, thorns have grown before our very eyes. Furthermore, in praising [this state]:

having come with empty hands, what object could there be to wrap up? To treat it as private property or stolen goods is to become smeared with lethal poison, such that one cannot disentangle oneself from it.
To this day, he remains burdened by his grievances.
In praise of the living body of the Great Master Huineng:
When the first yang returns, the warmth gradually approaches; When the three yangs are complete, all things are in spring. When the first yin first arrives—
The flowing fire [of summer] coagulates within; the three yin energies begin to intersect. Grasses and trees suddenly wither. Even the powerful forces of creation cause such decay and flourishing;

how much more so for that which is birthless? Moment by moment, they infuse one another: through existence one enters emptiness, and as the four elements all melt away; through emptiness one enters existence.

Where there is existence, there is imperishability; when both existence and emptiness are forgotten, one accords with the Vajra-nature. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all the Constant Samādhi Light (Saddharmaprakāśa).
Therefore, my Master is the King of the Dharma.

Eulogy for Great Master Yongming (With Preface) When I was young, I read the *Mind-Affirmation* (*Xin fu*) and the *Secret Instructions on Mind-Only* (*Weixin jue*), and I immediately knew that the Master was a banner of radiant light.
Subsequently, from my late teacher Yungu, I heard it said that the Great Master daily performed one hundred and eight kinds of expedient practices; I had taken this to be...
These were merely matters of ordinary diligence that I privately admired and practiced. Consequently, I observed them without omission, considering this to be the skillful employment of the mind.
Approaching old age, I traveled to Jingci Temple on West Lake, entered the Zongjing Hall, paid homage at the memorial tower of the Great Master, and inquired into his conduct.
My disciple Dahe produced his *Record of Personal Practice*, which I opened and examined with clarity.

He remained silent, overcome with emotion, and sighed, saying: "This vast, boundless, and subtle practice of the Dharma truly cannot be sustained even in its slightest degree by one who lacks a diamond-like mind and the vows of Samantabhadra;
how much less so for one who attempts to reveal the core of the Mind and fuse the ocean of the teachings."

He reveals the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) to encompass the myriad dispositions of sentient beings. Were it not for the three wheels being in accord with the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), how could one possibly reach its threshold?
Qing sighed in admiration at its inconceivability and, bowing his head, offered this eulogy:
I prostrate to the Great Master, the Banner of Radiance, who universally illumines the pure treasury of the Dharma-realm;

who, mounting the wheel of great vows, manifests the three karmas and uniquely opens the true eye for all sentient beings; who personally transmits the secret seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, harmonizing the ocean of teachings within the single mind;

who smelts and refines both the holy and the mundane beyond the reach of comparison, and enters instantaneously into the ocean of samādhi of ultimate reality through hundreds of thousands of wondrous practices.

Revealing that all is but mind, the myriad virtues converge in the single True Reality (*ekasatyatā*). Contemplation naturally brings forth the Three Jewels; in this land, only the Master is able to protect the Dharma.
For this reason, both the Han and the barbarians look up to him in total devotion, all entering into the sphere of his compassionate mindfulness.

Whether flying or submerged, moving or stationary, nothing is left uncared for. He even takes upon himself the suffering of others; were it not for the contemplation of quiescent equality (*śamata-samatā-vipaśyanā*), how could this be?

One is able to realize that there is no distinction between self and other. How tragic are the ignorant and deluded ones of the Final Dharma! They do not know that they are all entirely encompassed by the power of vows.
When this Mirror of the School is suspended to illuminate the myriad dharmas, what dharma before one's eyes is not the Buddha’s work?

Even this single virtue of releasing living beings immediately leads one into the gate of Vairocana’s Dharma-realm. One’s own mind first enters the minds of sentient beings; how then could those beings escape?
Pure Land. Taking the lakes and mountains as my brush and inkstone, I am unable to depict even a single pore of the Master.
May all who joyfully witness or hear of this together realize the great power of mind of our Teacher.
A Brief Biographical Eulogy on the Spiritual Portraits of the Patriarchs.
Regarding the Dharma-body śarīra of the Patriarch Senghui:
its radiance shines universally across the great earth; there is no place where it is not present. Now, there was a supreme person.
Following the light, they came and earnestly entreated him to appear.
When the Brahma-realm was first opened, the *Zan* (Eulogy) for the Monk Fotudeng of India states:
"The movements of this Supreme Person are unfathomable; his body is permeated by radiance, and his functions are naturally distinct. He enters and exits the imperial court."
Like one who has grown familiar with seagulls, he departs with effortless ease by the path he came.

Master Huiyuan of Donglin on Mount Lu praised vast aspirations and lofty sentiments, directing his mind toward the Pure Land. He first established Donglin Temple as a preliminary step; there, the clear sound of the lotus-water clock resonates.
Its resonant melody flows down to the present day; among all who hear it, there are none whose hearts do not turn in devotion.
In the eulogy for Master Baozhi, it is said that the Perfected One moves in hidden ways, his traces unknowable: from where did he come? He was the offspring of a hawk, wandering through the world.
No one can fathom it. To strip away the mask of the face—why even bother to speak?

Great Master Fu praised the Way as being not in the crown, Confucianism not in the shoes, and Buddhism not in the *kāṣāya*. There is no "this" or "that"; it is simply a matter of being able to remain unborn.
The mind of discernment—this very person is the patriarch of the Three Teachings. Master Zhāng'ān praised his influence upon the Dharma and transformation, saying:
"Like clouds and dragons, like wind and tigers; wherever a banner is raised, there must be its corresponding ranks. Such is the teaching and contemplation of this single school.
Reaching Master Dàchāng, he entered the ocean of extensive learning; his source was distant and his stream long.

Dharma Master Fǎzhì praised him as the founder of one school of the Tiantai tradition. He distantly revered Nāgārjuna, and his teachings and contemplations were so clear that many who encountered them attained awakening. For five hundred years, [this lineage has flourished].
When the net was not yet spread, he truly gave birth to my teacher, who greatly shook its main ropes.
This is the Vairocana Consecration Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, praised by the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra;
it is the Seal of the Mind. When the true command is fully upheld, Buddhas and demons obey, while dragons and spirits flee in haste.
Subtly eliminating a hundred anomalies, the wise thereby attain great mastery.

In the Venerable Master Xianshou’s hymn to the Great Dharma-realm Net, the sages and ordinary beings are arrayed, yet there is but a single main cord; only the Master can pull it. He leads the flow of ten thousand streams.
All return to the ocean of the nature of reality; the five teachings are gathered therein in their entirety, unchanging through all eternity.

The National Teacher Qingliang praised him as one who upholds the Great Seal of Wisdom, encompassing the entire dharma-realm and entering the gate of *dhāraṇī*. Possessing the four kinds of unhindered mastery, his physical stature was nine chi tall.
He dwelt in this world for a hundred years as the gate-teacher to seven emperors; his deeds were inconceivable.

While Guifeng Chan Master took up the brush to win the rank of a marquis ten thousand *li* away, my teacher cast it down and directly transcended birth and death. We now travel together in the ocean of nature.
The seal of the true son is the gateway into the Dharma-realm; thus he is called a "Sublime Sage.

National Preceptor Fazhao praised the Great Being Manshushri and longed to behold him even once; therefore, he first appeared within the almsbowl in the Golden World, and upon entering the gate, [he was seen].
As if returning to an old acquaintance, he points directly to the Land of Ultimate Bliss as the place of refuge.

When the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang praised the eastward flow of the Great Teaching, its Dharma had not yet spread universally; thereupon, a *arhat* risked his life to go and retrieve it, so that the radiance of Prajñā might shine forth.
The School of Characteristics (Xiangzong) was grandly inaugurated; it serves as a vessel for crossing the sea of suffering, providing boundless benefit and salvation.

Master Kuiji praised the profound and subtle doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra*); its meaning is deep and mysterious. Only you, Master, have propagated it so that it shines like the sun in the sky. You shall surely ascend from Tuṣita Heaven.
I report in advance to Maitreya: [this teaching] does not come from within [the mundane]. How could one know its secret?
Master Daoxuan praised the Tathāgata’s establishment of the teachings:
"The Three Studies serve as the teacher; that which is brought forth by Samādhi and Prajñā takes the Precepts as its foundation. Thus did the Great Dharma flow eastward.
This teaching had not yet flourished until the eminent figures of Nanshan emerged and once again shook its fundamental principles.
Master Xingxiang praised the schools of both Exoteric and Esoteric Buddhism;

through the principles of the prophetic scriptures (*kengwei*), the Great Divination (*dayan*) was perfected, and Yin and Yang were brought into harmony. Thus, both mundane and supramundane dharmas were established.
There was nothing he did not master thoroughly. The practices of the fifth stage were witnessed within his teacher.
Master Nanyue Huairang’s eulogy: His spirit and bearing pierced the heavens;
his mind was empty and immeasurable. He seized the waters of Caoxi to stir up waves and billows; he put the "horse colt" to sleep.
A single brick was raised; he strode across it with a kick, and all who were touched died.
Zen Master Xingxi of Qingyuan praised him as naturally noble and beyond all ranks;
a single word met his potential, like a bee finding honey. This is the single stream of Caoxi.
The branching veins spread and flow; from this, descendants emerge like thunder rolling and lightning uncoiling.

The Great Master Wuxiang of Yongjia praised his solitary standard as a golden staff, alive with the vigor of dragons and tigers. Were it not for Old Lu, how many times would he have suffered humiliation? If one can realize it before a word is spoken—*yanqian*.
They traveled for one night and departed. Even though they have transcended, they are still but descendants.
Zen Master Daoyi of West River praised Magu as being like a dragon:
"The gait of an ox, the gaze of a tiger; one hundred and thirty people, all treading the earth with a single foot. The Dharma flows toward the West River."
A hundred rivers flow eastward; a single drop spreads everywhere. It moistens this withered and parched state.

Chan Master Shitou Xiqian praised the *gaozao*’s Buddha-nature, saying it originally has its cause: "If you seek it for even a moment, you will immediately attain its truth. He sat perched upon the stone.
The path is extremely slippery; even those who are able to walk upon it may take a tumble.
Chan Master Dazhu Huihai of Yuezhou praised himself:
"One holds one's own precious treasury, yet seeks it elsewhere. With a single word pointed out, its application is free and at ease. In Yue, there is the Great Pearl."
Perfectly luminous and penetrating, it shines forth in every direction.
Not falling into any conceptual mold, Zen Master Tianhuang Daowu’s eulogy says:
"Not dwelling there, from where did he come? Upon seeing Shitou, he opened wide with his eight characters. He used this to instruct others.
It is only valued that one knows it exists. To pick it up amidst inversion is like the hand of one who plays with a ball.
Zen Master Lingyou of Mt.

Guishan in Tanzhou praised Baizhang for his "cliff-like wall," where those who came looked on from afar in awe; only the Master entered directly, and as he stirred the fire, his mind was opened. He became a water buffalo.
Moving among those of different kinds, Yangshan’s discernment shattered the reputation of this father-and-son lineage.

Master Daolin of Niaoke in Hangzhou was praised for coming upon the light of the sun and abiding in his own nature; thus, as soon as he emerged, he attained natural and wondrous enlightenment, dwelling in a nest atop a tall pine.
The human path is perilous. One merely observes others without examining oneself.
Under Mount Daxiong in Hongzhou, there was a great beast, Master Xiyun of Huangbo;
with a single roar, it deafened those who heard it—a mechanism as swift as a crashing thunderclap.
With eyes like flashing lightning, the teaching style of the West has from this point become exceedingly perilous.

When Zen Master Linji Yixuan of Zhenzhou praised his teacher Huangbo as a lion, its claws and fangs had barely been revealed when the pivot of Dayu was like a hawk seizing a rabbit; three blows beneath the ribs.
A slap on the cheek! Just now you met his edge; this was not out of recklessness.
Chan Master Dongshan Liangjie Wuben of Duanzhou praised one's original face, saying:
"One touch and it is seen. Regarding the teaching of the insentient, it seems there is still something lacking. Once he had seen Yunyan...
Overturning the old molds, one must see the reflection upon crossing the water before beginning to penetrate through.

Praising the extraordinary capacity of Chan Master Caoshan Benji of Fuzhou—his traces left no name behind—and his transcendent vision that recognized [the truth] at a single glance: the five ranks are empty and profound.
The fundamental purpose is subtle and dense; for this reason, even to this day, it remains as black as lacquer.
Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun of Fuzhou praised [this state] as "that which is familiar is difficult to forget.
His habitual tendencies toward vegetables and bamboo shoots, and his heart’s intoxication upon hearing the sound of bells, sutras, and chants—his staff was like a dragon.
A friend’s mouth is like iron; therefore, one must step forth and naturally transcend.
Zen Master Yunmen praised him, saying:
"As soon as he saw Muzhou, [Muzhou] shut the door and pushed him out. With a shove of the body, he suddenly broke a leg. From that moment, he turned his way."
He covers heaven and earth; even before Xuefeng saw him, they were already in accord at heart.

Chan Master Fayan praised him as "all things being spontaneously complete, with nothing to look back upon or wait for. Amidst the myriad phenomena, he stands forth majestically and alone, maintaining a single flavor of equanimity.
The present moment is it. As soon as one engages in thought, one falls into the secondary.
Chan Master Shengnian of Shou Shan in汝州 (Ruzhou) composed a commentary on the seven-fascicle Lotus Sutra;
having held it for a long time, with a single word of letting go, one immediately knows what is inherently possessed—this is the teaching that is not taught.
Lifting it up, he looked at it; then, shaking out his sleeves, he walked away. How refreshing!
Chan Master Tianyi Yihuai of Yuezhou praised [this act] as the manifestation of innate compassion.
Coming to settle an old debt, once he saw the fish, he released them with his own hands. Out they went from the net of the mundane world.
He immediately ascended the stage of awakening; the carrying-pole broke, the bucket fell off, and empty space was pulverized.
Chan Master Chuyuan Cimeng of Shishuang in Tanzhou praised Xihe’s “contrary mechanism”:
those who see him do not recognize it; when encountering it personally, one has one's mouth covered and one's nostrils knocked out. His mechanism issues forth with lightning speed.
Liberated and beyond restraint, those with clear eyes call him a true lion cub.
Chan Master Hui Nan of Huanglong in Longxing Prefecture praised the Lion of Xihe, saying:
"The style of this father and son is such that they wield the Great Sword (Ta’a) upside down; who would dare face their blades? Should one encounter them, they strike with a single blow."
When the sentiments of both sages and ordinary people are exhausted, the three barriers within the room are fully raised as the orthodox command.
Chan Master Fānghuì of Yángqí in Yuánzhōu praised those who shoulder the Great Dharma and maintain the monastic groves:
meeting on a narrow path, a single word reveals the mind; in future generations, his descendants shall continue this legacy.
Pervading the world, its source is distant and its flow long; its roots are deep and its branches vast.
Chan Master Shouduan of Baoyun Temple in Shuzhou praised [the Buddha]:
"For a long time he held the bright pearl, keeping it as a rare treasure; yet upon meeting a true master, with a single laugh, it fell away. To see through the place of laughter—"
I too burst into laughter. Whatever comes to hand is none other than treasure.
Regarding the verse by Chan Master Wuzu Fayan of Qizhou, which reads:

"Going out the door is inauspicious; he immediately bumps into a man carrying a wooden board. Whenever he meets someone, he asks; it only serves to cover his eyes. Fortunately, he encounters a master."
With a single blow, it was shattered; as his head turned back, he finally realized his words had fallen short.
Master Huiji Yongming Yanshou Zhijue of Hangzhou, through the power of his great vows, appeared as an auspicious sign for the Dharma.
The gateway of total retention opened, and all practices were fully perfected. He hung the mirror of the single mind.
It brilliantly illuminates all things; the Buddha-sun is at its zenith, leaving no hidden corner unlit.

Tianmu Gaofeng Chan Master praised the peril of Xueyan’s “Snowy Cliff,” which stands ten thousand fathoms high like a sheer wall. Only the Master ascended it and found its shortcut; such was the danger of the "Gate of Death."
Furthermore, it rises even higher than the cliffs; thus, those who gaze upon it feel as if they were ascending to heaven.
Master Chan Tianmu Zhongfu praised the cave at Tianmu:
"A true lion cub within the cavern; as soon as its claws and fangs are revealed, all beasts flee in terror. Upon the solitary peak, it stands majestic and awe-inspiring."
The ocean of Dharma is vast and boundless; therefore, my teacher is called the King among the Sangha.
Furthermore, he dwells upon the high peak of Tianmu, penetrates the iron walls of space, and breaks through the heavy barriers of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. This small temple...
The cognition of the dust reveals the body and mind as an illusion; unfolding the power of concentration of a nāga, it shatters the nest of birth and death for sentient beings.
Even if one should encounter it, there is nowhere to be found.
Chan Master Qianyan’s eulogy:
"Where is the Buddha? he asked. Seeking him, he could not find him. A mouse overturned the cat's bowl; suddenly, [the Buddha] appeared, leaping into the void as if into empty space.
His responses were like echoes following sounds; they were not of this mundane sort. For how many times had he nearly sunk into deluded thoughts?
Chan Master Foyin praised him for his textual habits, which have been manifest since birth. He speaks of Chan with a ready tongue, never falling into conventional traps. He pre-arranges his smile.
Not knowing what to do, he passed away with a broad smile. This very moment is it.
Zen Master Wuzhun of Jingshan offered a single phrase that struck the vital point;
the ten directions were penetrated, his tongue rolled like thunder, and monks gathered like clouds. He entered the inner court twice.
Leading ten thousand chariots, he does not rely on external power but depends entirely upon the True Command.

When the world and its Way flourish together, the True Man responds to the destiny of the age; like clouds and dragons, wind and tigers, they cannot be restrained. It is as when true gold emerges from the ore.
The ancient mirror gives rise to radiance; once its brilliant clarity has emerged, its illuminating function is boundless.

Chan Master Baiyun Jue sat upon the White Cloud Peak, his thunderous tongue rolling like waves upon the ocean of nature and his principles arrayed like stars in the heavens, commanding the spirits and deities to hasten forth.
Secretly extinguishing demonic afflictions, a single point of cool clarity that dispels miasmic fever—what a fine master! His bearing is perfect;
were it not for this full beard covering his mouth, people would surely have taken him for Kāśyapa on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Praise to the Vajra Stūpa:
I prostrate to the Vajradhvaja, the mass of the radiance of Prajñā, who is the mind of all sentient beings; therefore, you are called the Mother of all Buddhas.
Pervading as far as the atoms of the universe, you are able to perform deeds of benefit. How wonderful is the person of sublime wisdom! From the most subtle mental conceptions, [you manifest].
This most supreme banner was erected, resembling the Lotus Treasury; the banner stands upon motes of dust, with a single character inscribed upon each mote.
Within every mote, a world is complete; within every character, radiant light appears. Thus, within this single banner, in each and every cluster of motes of dust, [all worlds are contained].
Fully endowed with the conditions for prajñā, neither increasing nor decreasing, one knows that the minds of sentient beings are each individually complete.
When I observe this body of mine, it is no different from this supreme banner. In the subtle mind used daily, everything relies entirely upon the power of prajñā.
If one gazes with devotion for even a single thought-moment, everything is fully possessed; if not separated from the mind in every thought, all merits will be perfected.
The eulogy on the diagrams of the Three Teachings is "three in one," like a child wearing a flower-patterned cloth shirt; it is "one in three," like a melody-less tune played on a flute.
The bamboo flute of Confucius: speaking lies without shame on one's face, deceiving others with a heart as black as lacquer.

Do not say that liver and entrails can be of two kinds; who can discern the true message? A whole chest of heart-matters is altogether difficult to speak; the blood of the cuckoo dyes the spring mountains wet.
The Emperor Lord of Wenchang extols the essence of creation;
it manifests as literature, shining brightly through the long night. As the sun and moon alternate in their illumination, there is nothing that does not reach its ultimate limit within this.
It is tranquil and profoundly still. When someone strikes it, it produces a sound like that of a bamboo flute—deep and inexhaustible, like a valley that seems full.
The Sovereign emerges from the movement of thunder; this is what is called the Ultimate Spirit.
Eulogy on Laozi Riding His Ox:
Purple Qi comes from the East; the Blue Ox departs toward the West. This was not for the sake of seeking out men—what, then, was his purpose?
Eulogy on Laozi Crossing the Pass.

The mind dwells in the Great Antiquity; the Way stands apart from the decadent customs of the age. It is luminous yet does not dazzle; it is empty yet does not bend. To achieve emptiness and maintain stillness, one must minimize thought and diminish desire.

With tranquility and detachment, the spirit is pleased; all things are swept away until nothing remains. While the multitude of heroes compete with one another, busily engaged in the pursuit of worldly affairs, [the sage] remains aloof.

While the Central Plains were boiling like a cauldron, he looked back longingly toward Western India. Hardly had he mounted his green ox when purple vapors ascended; the Lord of the Pass knew beforehand that the True Man was about to arrive.

Prostrating himself to receive his instructions and gazing upon him with devotion, he requested the revelation of the profound mysteries. Thus, five thousand words were bestowed, in which the Way is perfected and virtue is complete.

He did not place himself before things, nor did he initiate calamity. His way was one of humility and selflessness; he knew contentment and knew when to stop. He mingled with the world and harmonized his light, such that no one could discern his traces.
Thus he was praised as being "like a dragon," serving as the Recorder beneath the Pillar.

Confucius extolled the teacher of the hundred kings, the mandate of the thousand sages, the social order of ten thousand ages, and the true nature of all living beings. He bore this burden with singular strength, leaving nothing unfulfilled.
Were it not for my Master, a man of boundless capacity, who else could have eternally ensured that human relations remain upright?
Pang Zu’s countenance was like that of an infant, and his vital energy was like that of a newborn. He inhaled the wind and dew, consuming only the rosy clouds.
When a peach on the Pangu tree ripens once every three thousand years, he was still remembered as a child, plucking its blossoms.

Eulogy for Lü Chūnyáng: The universe is held in his hand; the myriad transformations are born from his body. He received the ultimate refinement of the Three Powers and attained the pure essence of the Two Qi.
Carrying a blue serpent, he wanders freely without hindrance; beholding a yellow dragon, his wondrous realization became true. In the morning he roams Penglai Island.
He took up residence at Mount Kunlun in the evening; his longevity was equal to Heaven and Earth, and his virtue was comparable to the warmth of spring.
He is truly what is called a sage among men, and indeed a deity among immortals.
Eulogy for the Marquis of Hanshou Ting:
Majestic as if alive; luminous as if present. Resplendent is his solitary loyalty; noble is his spirit and resolve. Vivid is the vitality upon his countenance.
A mass of resentment within the breast; everywhere one meets those who manifest their form out of affection. Most likely, they have not yet settled their heroic debts.
The Reverend Yufeng of Mount Qingliang praises his half-shadow as "a crescent moon, a single drifting cloud, snow-old and ice-dry, clear water with shallow sands"—people transmit this as his "nose."
Ancestors and descendants. I say these are the companions of Mañjuśrī. Eighty years of ascetic practice are inexhaustible; hundreds of thousands of kalpas are perfected in a single thought.

Who knows that an old enemy from a previous life has come to this human realm to repay a long-standing debt? Late in life, he found a husband who was neither worldly nor non-worldly, yet produced a countenance that was neither true nor false. Heh! Today, a smile once again— *Note: The original text contains a play on words and paradoxical phrasing characteristic of Zen (Chan) discourse.

"Ancestors and descendants" (*zǔ ér sūn*) refers to the lineage of transmission. "Mañjuśrī’s companions" suggests those who share in his enlightened activity. The phrase "neither worldly nor non-worldly" (*sú bù sú*) describes a state beyond conventional dualities. The final "Heh! (*yí*) is a classic Zen exclamatory particle used to punctuate a sudden realization or a turning point.*
Meeting: We shall wait until the first assembly at the Dragon Flower to see him.
Master Baofeng’s eulogy says: "Is it true? Is it not true?
Without form, yet not non-form; like colors within a pearl, like an image in a mirror. He has roamed throughout the great trichiliocosm."
No trace remains; throughout the ten directions, walls and barriers offer no obstruction. Having struck down the iron ox of Shanzhou, he broke the bamboo staff of Qiongzhou.
In the northern mountains, cold winds drive the snow; in the southern lands, warmth brings forth the first blossoms.
When meeting him, he refuses to reveal his full mechanism, saying only that both "existence" and "non-existence" are slanders. Pray tell, where is that master who has no handle to grasp?
It is said that this is the Venerable Baofeng before the Gate of the Son of Heaven.
The Great Master Zibo praised him, saying:

"The net of the Dharma-realm has been torn asunder; its cords were not being stretched taut. Now the Great Master has appeared, exerting his strength to uphold the framework, and he sits enthroned within the lion’s den."
He fells the sandalwood tree; his prowess has not yet been fully displayed, yet his claws and fangs are already bared. He beats the drum of lethal poison and pours out the nectar of immortality;
those who drink it become intoxicated, and those who hear it go mad. Within the nature of quiescent emptiness, he unleashes the thunderbolt tongue—like rushing thunder and rolling lightning.

Upon hearing this, their spirits were struck with awe. With a mind as vast as the great earth, bones as firm as adamant, sinews within their eyes, and no attachments within their chests, Linji did not die and Huangbo still lives.
Who knows that the Great Master did not accept such titles? He strode forth with wide steps across the great square.
He abides by no fixed rules; with a single turn of his body, he hurls himself over the peak of Mount Sumeru. With one punch, he shatters the realm of non-arising.

Furthermore, sitting alone on a solitary peak, he opens his breast to conceal the ocean. "Tut! He awakens the fish and dragons, causing ghosts and monsters to vanish in secret. He stands firm, supporting all as he pleases.
The two eyes are empty; the worlds of the ten directions are without obstruction or concealment. Do not say that the spring breeze is the same everywhere;
the ice withered and the snow aged, yet the cold cliff remains.
Furthermore:

The eye that settles heaven and earth is like a suspended precious mirror; those who approach it cannot escape its discernment of the beautiful and the ugly. Grasping the Great Aśoka sword upside down, he bestows it upon others without stinginess.
When demons and heretics encounter it, they lose their bodies and forfeit their lives. He performs a fist without hands; the fist does not reside in the hands.
Though tongueless, it understands speech; yet speech does not reside in its mouth. Its beard and eyebrows are slightly visible, and its form appears to exist;
yet if one probes its interior, it cannot be dissected.
Furthermore: His face is like the moon; his heart is like iron. With short hair and a long beard, his majestic spirit is uniquely distinct. When the fist is clenched, both eyes become empty;
as soon as the backbone is straightened, all conditions cease. He smashes the diamond circle and perfectly accomplishes the extinction of ambrosia throughout the ten directions.
The world is without obstruction; a single ray of divine light leaves no space for idleness. Meeting him suddenly, one’s nostrils sting;
the pain within the heart is difficult to describe.
Furthermore, with blood and sweat covering his entire body, like a lion tearing through its snares, he has severed the roots of emotion and cast off his heavy burden.
Though he maintains a formal exterior, within he is free of all boundaries; with eyes wide open, he sees only this man.
The Great Master Yunqi came by the power of his vow to dwell in this Sahā world; he opened the gate to the Pure Land, fulfilled his debt of compassion, and erected the banner of radiant light.
He received the Vajra Precepts and spent over eighty years benefiting sentient beings; at the time of his passing, he attained the state of empty non-obstruction.
If you recognize the mind of our Master while dwelling in this world, then you shall be named Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, I observe that the Great Master’s entire body is vibrant and alive; from every pore, radiant light streams forth. His countenance cannot be seen—how could it be depicted?
Even if one were to paint it, it would ultimately fail to capture him. He sits in meditation like space and preaches the Dharma like the wind.
To catch the wind and grasp shadows is to fail to find their tracks; to hear the wind in the air and see the shadow in the water—how many deluded people there are who nod off while wide awake!
Furthermore, they take emptiness as their dwelling and wisdom as their life. Entering the minds of sentient beings, they practice the conduct of Samantabhadra.

Without distinction between scales and shells or feathers and down, all enter equally into the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). With a single flavor of compassion and tenfold purity—if one were to ask my teacher:
This is a most profound Dharma gate. Within it, samādhi is clarified as being without contention.
Furthermore, the mind is like the moon in the sky, its form like a reflection in a mirror. This is my Master’s [teaching] for forty years, in accordance with the assembly.
He is a true model for all living beings.

Furthermore, his countenance is tranquil and his mind is profound; there is no distinction between inner and outer, nor any coming or going. To him, the hundreds of thousands of samādhis are but flowers in the eye.

All gates of practice are like bird tracks in the sky; one does not believe that they are manifested within the myriad phenomena. How foolish it is for such a person to seek them at the tip of a hair!
Ehi! This is the Master Wuming’s eulogy on the *yuanxiang* (perfect circle).
For a long time I have heard the name "Ignorance," yet I have not seen the face of Ignorance. Suddenly emerging from a great mountain, we see one another from across a thousand li.
My livelihood lies upon the pickaxe; I preach the Dharma like a flash of lightning. I draw a bow without a string, accustomed to using the arrows of Shigong.
As soon as he shoots at anyone, they flee at the sound of the string. Suddenly he strikes a stubborn stone; the arrowhead and feathers sink right in.
He hurls out an iron ball; those who see it are left speechless. This is my teacher’s old face;
looking at it, one may only realize it before words are spoken. If you ask about the direct and supreme function, the clouds and mountains fill the eyes, making them impossible to distinguish.
Eulogy for Master Wúbiān:

The ocean of lands is boundless, yet not a single speck of dust can be established within it. Wherever his feet tread, causes and conditions converge; wherever he goes, he dwells amidst the monastic groves.
Everyday tea and rice; those who come are fully satisfied. They manage their affairs as they please. With a single step, they reach Wujiang;

as soon as the monastery banner is raised, dragons and elephants gallop forth without hesitation. Clouds arise at Shuangjing; the moon shines bright in the Single Transmission. Who is it that shouts out?
The Master answered its resonance; upon the tip of a single hair, he manifested the Jewel King’s realm. For eighty-eight generations, all have been utterly silenced.
The Way-functioning employs the full mechanism, yet it relies on the Master’s single nudge. As for that half of the nostril—has anyone ever touched it?

In the Golden Realm, the Master Kongyin of Mount Qingliang constantly follows the myriad multitudes; yet while he alone guides his disciples, he secretly exerts a great function. The five peaks stand high.
As he walked in meditation, his gaze turned toward the world; the wind roared through ten thousand ravines as the sound of the Dharma spread far and wide.

He wandered upon the ocean of nirvana and sat amidst groves of various blossoms, sporting like a lion, yawning and stretching his limbs. His fame reached the ninefold imperial palace, the winds of purity swept across the universe, and beings from the ten directions took refuge in him.
Like the ocean absorbing water, his form did not mirror his mind; true to himself, he did not mingle with the mundane. We see only his outer skin—who can reach his very bone?
Now that the Dharma-banner has fallen, the net of the teachings is no longer secure. May the Master shake its mainstay, weaving it like the silken threads of heaven. The sage has passed away.
Silent and desolate for a thousand years, Heaven has truly given birth to you, Master. Your physical form remains unchanged upon the thousand-fathom cold cliffs and the ten-thousand-year ice caverns.
I dwell before you; you tread behind me. I am driven by karma; you are sustained by your vows. Though our conditions—heat and cold—differ, [our connection endures].
Within this, nothing shifts. The kalpa-fire blazes forth; ice withers and snow ages. Once the illusory cataracts are cleared away, the flowers in the sky are also understood.
Floating clouds disperse entirely and the azure heavens are high; a single bright moon shines lucidly in the void. I ask you, O person within the Vajra Cave:
how many are these threes before and after?
Furthermore, the *Half-Body Praise*:
The questioner asks, "Old man, from where have you come? He does not know for what reason his face is covered in dust. Though frozen by a thousand feet of ice and snow, he cannot die;
he leaves behind half of himself to cause people to wonder. How strange! The bell beneath the lion’s neck—he ties it on himself.
How truly marvelous is this realization!
Dharma Master Shaojue praised him, saying:
"He takes the Dharma as his body, wisdom as his life, the triple world as his home, and sentient beings as his nature. As for his form..."
His skeleton is like withered wood; his samādhi is free from contention. The burning house is but cold ashes, and the toil of worldly dust is an icy pit.
He takes cities for mountain forests and enters right concentration through speech.
Thus, he speaks with fervor without ceasing, for the ocean of wisdom flows forth so profusely that it cannot be restrained. It is no wonder, then, that this master’s mouth does not stay still.
In praise of Dharma Master Lingche:
His bones are rugged and prominent; his mind is vast and empty. His nostrils are high and noble; his eyebrows stand out sharply. He is as serene as a clear azure pond with its blue lotuses.

He stands as upright as a tall pine or a solitary crane; his tongue does not move, yet his speech is like thunder. People of the time should not say he is without words. Elder Ziguang praised him, saying:
"From the Vajra Cave, he has come to the city of Rājagṛha. He has no other business at all; he acts solely for the sake of sentient beings, serving as a grove for their single bodies."
When rice gruel arrives from the ten directions, all who come eat together; there is no distinction between host and guest, for with a mind free of self, one performs the myriad Buddha-activities.

Encountering conditions, one immediately acts according to the principle; it is equal and non-dual. Yet if one seeks its truth, that truth does not reside here. Simply look at what is manifest before you.
He is truly a son of the Buddha.

Great Rest (Daxie) praised those of early years, saying they knew how to leave secular life; it is only in old age that one can truly renounce the world. To take *upāya* as one's wondrous practice is to follow the Buddha.
Taking worldly affairs as one's livelihood, within this world of five turbidities, there is not even a trace of hindrance;
within the pure realm, there is only a single lotus flower. This is truly the foremost master among the assembly of upāsakas.
The Elder Master Dingzong praised him, saying:

"When he was young, he entered Qianfoyan (Thousand Buddhas Cliff) and immediately took up residence there. He never left that place, whether sitting or standing; people did not know the reason for this.
Although eighty years have passed, he is still at the very first step. Only when one enters the Forest of Miscellaneous Flowers is it truly the path home."
Praise for the Master of Xueqiao Mountain: He sits firmly atop Mount Shuangji;
he squeezes out the essence from the balance-beam and pestle; he shatters the diamond circle and crunches the iron thorn-fruit.
Time and again he perished of cold and hunger only to be reborn; thus he has just managed to win a breath of leisure. This is no innocent bystander, but a vengeful enemy who has slain his own father.
For those who are deeply attached, death is urgent. Having lost but a single life, they nevertheless cast it hither and thither, fleeing to the peaks of Shuangjing.
Unable to sweep away their tracks or extinguish their traces, they reveal this very form; this too is like dust in the eyes.
Even if snow were piled upon frost, one must know that there is still the blazing sun in midsummer. Try to see the reality: frowning brows.
Turtle-shaped nose. Amidst the cries of the cuckoo, the rain is like mist. The east wind blows the fallen flowers into disarray;
barefoot and with disheveled hair, one descends into the emerald heights. Meeting thus, who is truly an old acquaintance?
The encomium for the Abbot Huaihui of Lingxiao Peak says:
Coming from the midst of space, he seeks to dwell in the place of reality; thus he heads toward Lingxiao, yet follows a separate path, his body already within the void.
If your feet have not yet left the ground and you wish to leap beyond, you must first shatter them to pieces. Clouds and mountains fill the eyes; entanglements are not few.
Though they offer no obstruction, they nonetheless wind around one. Bringing nothing with you, you need only let go. Do not allow even the slightest thing to remain.
Only then does one see its greatness. It is not sought outside; it is not found through others. Originally present and manifest before one, all is true reality. Cognitions and views vanish;
the profound and mysterious cannot be established as something fixed. In a single thought-moment, one passes straight through silver mountains and iron walls.
Master Nayun was praised for having a spine like iron and a mind like space. His single robe was like a cloud; his myriad affairs were like the wind. Early in life he entered the chamber of Fangshan;
late in life he upheld the lineage of Qingliang. Growing ever more robust as he aged, he remained serene without exhaustion. This is not [the work of] the ten thousand... within the cave.
Among all people, who could possibly match such lofty footsteps? Therefore, though I contemplate them, they remain unseen;
though I attempt to depict them, they defy description. Vague and indistinct, he resembles an old man tending oxen by a pond.

Master Xugu’s eulogy: Outwardly he was like drifting clouds; inwardly, he was like the spirit of the valley. His mind was the eternal abode, which he took as his body. Seventy-nine years were like a dream;
hundreds of billions of kalpas were like a single lifetime. He has preserved a single plot of pure ground to be passed down from generation to generation.
Grandson, grandson. E! On the coral tree, the bright moon is propped up; at the bottom of the sea, the Persian chews ice at night.
Master Yue'an praised him for not coming when he emerged and not going when he sank. Throughout his life, they met face-to-face, yet no one could find him. The clouds race away.
The movement of the moon; a boat traveling while the shore rushes by. Aha! With one long cry, autumn fills the sea and sky. At midnight, the golden crow crows as dawn breaks.
—Praise by Master Xueling.
The face is like the full moon; the bones are like ice and snow. Looking at them, they appear rugged and tiered; within them, there must surely be jagged peaks and precipices. Aha!
White clouds cut across the horizon as the morning peaks turn green; the cuckoo cries until the spring mountains are drenched in blood.
Danju Kai praises him: His skeletal frame is rugged and imposing;
his mind is vast and empty; his spirit is lofty and dignified; his faculty is lively and agile. That "half" cannot be captured by brush or ink. Buddhas and patriarchs appear disheveled;

sentient beings are entangled in complexity. He risks his life and casts himself forward, bearing the burden with single-minded strength—this is the one stroke that does not fail the ancestral transmission.
Self-praising, I have failed to penetrate the teachings; practicing Chan, I have not yet had a glimpse. I am entirely dull-witted and ignorant, as clumsy as the world at large.

My capacity is as vast as space, and my iron-like will is unyielding. I am glad that I have already entered this cold mountain cave, fully prepared to let go of myself and rest. Suddenly, I encounter a gale...
Driven by black winds, he was cast down into the realm of rākṣasa demons; hurled into a great smelting furnace of red-hot metal; and tossed into the burning house of the southern lands.
Relying upon the sustaining power of the Buddha, this life was recovered. His face is covered in dust and wind, yet his inner heart remains as pure as ice and snow.

This is not a matter of practicing ascetic itinerancy; it is mostly the recompense for past karma. Among all things, this single piece of bitter resolve is difficult to speak of when opening one's mouth to others.
One must wait until the Dragon Flower Assembly; only then will it be clearly understood.
Even if one were to attempt to depict it, it would not be one's own innate flesh and blood.
Furthermore:
Sitting upon Mount Laṅkā, perched on a flat rock, listening to the sound of the ocean tide, he entered the realm of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Having long ago come from the Golden Realm (*Suvarṇabhūmi*), in his old age he mistakenly became a traveler in Lei-yang. Following horses and donkeys, eating in the wind and drinking from the dew, he traversed every hardship.

Amidst the conflagration and the mountain of swords, I am glad that the clash of arms has been stilled. Grateful for Your Majesty’s grace in granting me release once more, I have recovered my single life-force.
Turning my back, I ascend straight to the crest of ten thousand peaks; day and night I strike sleep without ceasing.
The myriad demons’ minds are emptied, and the ears of all Buddhas grow hot. If people of this age ask about the pivot within this state: upon the mountain of Dinghu, the clouds are ever white.
Furthermore, his form resembles a fragment of cloud; it does not abide in the great void. Coming and going without intention, it passes once with the wind.
Seated atop the high peak of Dinghu, he laughs at the pillar of Caoxi. Let the waves of the bitter sea roll as they may; he has confidence that his own liver and entrails are cast of iron.
Looking back at the blazing heat of the burning house, how can it compare to the depths of the white clouds?

Furthermore, having long been accustomed to being a monk, I am now deficient in my renunciation; my habitual tendencies are difficult to forget, and I am unable to accomplish my spiritual practice. Fortunately, I have entered the Holy [Path].
The Son of Heaven is a great smelter with a red furnace, casting a single iron arhat. He hurls it into the burning wilderness of the house of fire;
it is much like a cauldron of boiling water and glowing coals. It smelts until every bone and muscle is molten, leaving behind only a single fragment of the compassionate heart.
I deeply realize that this great kindness cannot be repaid; to repay it, one must rely on a sincere vow.
Furthermore, though my mind is not that of a householder, my form remains mixed with the secular world. There is a pearl within my eyes, yet nothing within my breast. This is when I hear his name.

It is neither right nor wrong. After meeting face-to-face, one shouts and clamors. No matter how many hundreds or thousands of ways others may try to depict it, there is but one single point they cannot paint.
Furthermore:
Neither lay nor monastic; neither real nor false. His liver and gall are as ice and frost; his physical frame is but chaff and dross.
With a single flavor of simple-mindedness, he possesses a myriad forms of carefree elegance.

Were it not for the unconventional forging of the Sage Emperor, how could he have accompanied the General’s warhorse? Behold his distinct spirit; it truly does not belong to the realm of "zhi-hu-re-zhe."

Furthermore, as for leaning on a staff or wielding a long spear, using a bowl as a basin or a *dioudou* gong as a vessel—these are all one and the same way of life; how can one distinguish between beauty and ugliness?
One need only observe the moon reflected in water or flowers in the sky; beyond this, what else do I possess?

Furthermore, having loved the life of renunciation since youth, one is taught by elders to return to secular life. If you do not constantly accord with worldly conditions, it will only be said that there is something obstructing your chest;
thus, for the sake of briefly revealing your original face at the gateway of light and shadow, you have needlessly exhausted yourself over your hair and beard.
Scratching and itchy; the physical form delights in being free from constraints. One turn of Laṅkā, one stick of incense—wherever one goes, life’s livelihood is sufficient according to one's lot.
Furthermore:

The mind does not reside in the hair; the form does not reside in the Sangha. As a person, he is not worth speaking of; as a name, he is not worth praising. He possesses nothing worthy of being taken up;
in every respect, he is loathsome. Only this one alone is capable of the Dharma-gate of forbearance.
Furthermore, they love mountains that are not high and water that is not deep; as monks, they do not shave their hair, yet as laypeople, they do not wear crowns or turbans;

in civil matters they do not recognize characters, and in military affairs they do not discuss strategy. They possess no substance worth taking up, yet they vainly hold to their reputation. This useless-headed master—only...
It is fitting to demote him to the ranks of Lei Yang; let him follow behind the donkeys and horses. This one move is most effective.
Furthermore, walking alone and sitting alone, he is free and beyond reproach. Indifferent to all affairs, he would not even become a Buddha. Ten thousand *li* to Lei Yang.
With a single throw, he passes through. If anyone should encounter him and ask who he is, he replies: "The first seat within the Tuṣita Palace.

Furthermore, his mind does not dwell in the Way, yet his form does not enter the secular world; his feet have no entanglements, and his mouth has no constraints. He is like the wind moving through space.

Like an echo responding to a valley, I am of one flavor of dull ignorance, yet buried in a thousand ways. Fortunately, by relying on a single branch of the Bodhi tree, my life’s needs are fulfilled a thousandfold and ten-thousandfold.
Furthermore, having left home at a young age, he returned to secular life in his old age. He feigned innocence and acted foolishly; he has skin but no bone.
Unfamiliar with spiritual cultivation, he was entirely unrestrained. One day, he specifically offended the Emperor’s majesty and was banished to Leyang to serve as a footman. Now...
He evaded his duties and went to Caoxi, where he studied under Shitou while pounding rice and grain.
Furthermore:
"This old fellow is shameless; what manner of being is this? He does not feel pain when struck, nor does he feel an itch when scratched, nor does he feel shame when reviled."
To slander this would be unjust. Sitting like a stump, one fails to understand Zen; with nothing but random thoughts, there is no portion for becoming a Buddha and obstacles to becoming an Ancestor.
It is best to consign oneself to the armor of non-action and act as an old army commander.

Furthermore, they are unknown by name among the laity and do not count among the monastics. They are not permitted within the ranks of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, nor do they dwell within the realm of sentient beings.
With empty hands they brandish spears; naked they display their banners. Fearing death, they enter the earth but find no gate; seeking life, they ascend to heaven but find no path.
Everyone says this master has no skill; who knows he is a great adept who does not recognize characters?
Furthermore:
with frost-white hair disheveled and an ice-cold heart, he clamps his mouth and ties his tongue, yet moves like thunder and rolls like lightning, acting as east, west, south, and north.
The man from the north has endured hundreds of thousands of millions of hardships; they call him a "foolish monk" and hail him as an "iron man.
As he gazes upon his own reflection on the shores of the miasmic sea, do not say that this man has no companion.

Furthermore, sixty years have passed since his appearance in the world; he has spent three thousand days in military service and twenty autumns dwelling in the mountains, yet in the end, he remains without any foundation.

Because as a monk he does not understand the practice of cultivation, and when engaging with the secular world he lacks any restraint—what kind of karmic conditions are these? Who could possibly create such a thing?
Worms and insects! Most delightfully, you possess a heart of utter delusion, treating the lineage of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as if it were your own private household affairs.
Your afflictions are boundless and the ocean of suffering is shoreless; having weathered every storm and wave, you follow along in the ranks of the deluded.

You cast yourself headlong into thorny thickets and play your games amidst fields of spears and halberds. Even now, you refuse to turn back your heads—will Old Man Yama not surely give rise to resentment?

As for this "qi" (vital energy), one might wait for Maitreya’s descent to be enlightened; alas! At such a time, it would be too late. *Du!* The night rain falls on the spring mountains as the cuckoo cries;
with every call, it urges people to return home.
Furthermore, his appearance was decrepit; within him there was emptiness. He did not abide in the realm of Buddhas and Patriarchs, nor could he be accommodated among the ranks of sentient beings.
He did not comprehend various conditions, and not a single dharma passed through him. He simply took ordinary tea and food as the means to establish the tradition of the school.
To have wasted one's deluded mind to no avail is to incur endless affliction.
It would be better to be exiled to the realm of non-arising, where one lies in high repose beneath the white clouds and embraces the bright moon until the end of time.
Disregarding all else, one may thus vaguely become a truly authentic "Dolt."

Furthermore, he came for the sake of the Sixth Patriarch and departed because of Master Rang. Although his coming and going appear hurried and frantic, the Dharma-gate is fundamentally without abiding.
He did so solely to uphold the lineage of father and son; it was not that he gave rise to idle vexation. Thus he endured every hardship.
Having broken the bamboo whisk, he has earned a face covered in dust; yet he takes this as the ancestral meaning of the West’s arrival.
Ultimately, it is but a single diamond-like mind, still remaining to spread once more across the land of Caoxi.
Furthermore, to be dull-witted and ignorant, with nothing in mind and utterly devoid of skill, being nothing but a single flavor of stupidity—how could such a person be the eyes of gods and men?
Originally, this rice-eating monk has only one extraordinary quality: like the bright moon rising over the mountain peaks.
Huzhi. Furthermore, once while looking into his alms bowl, he saw ten thousand people within it. He asked if this was Mañjuśrī, but was teased by him until they reached Mount Wutai.
Having personally received his profound respect and heard him preach the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, it was as if opening my eyes to find myself dreaming;
I suspect this old man was my own former self, returning today once more to stir up a ruckus.
Furthermore, for seventy years I have wandered through the human world in dreams, following various monasteries and engaging in the empty-flower rituals of Buddhism.

Disregarding danger and death, I have been utterly devoid of caution or restraint. One morning, I offended the Dragon’s countenance; pressed by this, the void was crushed to powder and I was cast ten thousand *li* away.
In the scorched wilderness, he continues as ever to play his part upon the stage; only when the bow is broken and the arrows exhausted will he finally draw breath.
Looking at it with a direct eye now, he has ended up with nothing but a deep, sound sleep.
Furthermore, when the moon hangs over the tall pines and its reflection sinks into the autumn waters, there is a form that can be glimpsed, yet nothing can be compared to it. It cannot be approached;
how could it ever be grasped? Drawing upon the long winds from ten thousand *li*, one lets a single reed float across the vast waves. This is very much like...
Before the cliffs of Shaoshi, this is not within the city of Vairocana. Pure and transcending all dust, it is utterly free of dregs. The earthen ox roars its cry;
the pestle’s tip blossoms with flowers. Let others recognize it as filling the universe, but how many can truly take it up in their very being?
Furthermore, it is like an image reflected in a mirror, like clouds drifting across the sky, like echoes in an empty valley, or like the tracks of fish in still water. Those with eyes do not see it;
those with ears are as if deaf. Since there is nothing by which it can be praised, how can it be described? To call it "a single thing" is itself a misnomer.
This is precisely what makes him "Dull-Witted Elder" (Ham-wong).
Furthermore, he is majestic and imposing, lucid and profound; he maintains no secret chambers or stratagems, and is entirely without boundaries or limits. His spirit overwhelms heaven and earth.
His eyes gaze toward the Milky Way, yet he has fallen into the gateways of worldly affairs; he does not emerge from beyond the realm of Vipaśyin.
Whether layman or monk, the carrying pole never leaves his shoulder. If he is neither a slave nor a master of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, he is surely a petty peddler at the site of enlightenment.
Had he not entered the red furnace of the great smith, who would have known him to be an iron man?
Only when Maitreya descends to be born shall this heavy case be settled.
Furthermore:
The ice and snow on Mount Wutai have withered; the waves of the Eastern Sea are treacherous; the miasma of the scorched wilderness is deep; my karmic affinity for Caoxi is thin.
Waiting only for my heart to grow weary and my strength exhausted, I shall run back to the Southern Peak, naked.
Upon the seventy peaks, I sleep soundly; when I awaken, both eyes are wide and vacant. Leaning against a tall pine, I gaze alone as a single wisp of white cloud rises from the secluded ravine.
Furthermore, not belonging to either the holy or the ordinary, from where does this original face come? It emerges from the tip of a hair; when the water is clear, the moon shines upon the face;
when the clouds part, the mountain reveals its bones. If you wish to know the silent depth and the thunderous sound, it is much like an echo transmitted through a valley. There is someone...
If asked about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, simply say to them: "This very mind is Buddha.
Furthermore: broad face, narrow mouth; brows horizontal, nose straight. No matter how you try to depict it, it is entirely devoid of vital breath; its literary brilliance has not yet been revealed.
At that time, who knows the ultimate point? One does not come upon the path of humans and devas. I ask you: where have you ever known such a person?
Furthermore, within this old man, there is emptiness and not a single thing; he is neither sage nor ordinary, neither mind nor Buddha. He uses a staff made of rabbit horns to scoop up [the water].
The traces of the moon in the water. A rope made of tortoise hair binds the bones of empty space. To call it "Hanshan" is to turn one's back on it; not to call it "Hanshan" is to offend it.
If you examine this closely, it is just like a withered stump or a firewood log, yet it possesses a kind of distinct alertness.
In the end, it cannot be captured by brush or ink. *Du-du-du!* When the moon sets, it does not leave the sky; when the bird returns, it goes to the tree.
He stayed overnight on high.
Furthermore,
he sat amidst the ice and snow of Mount Wutai, listened to the surging waves of the Eastern Sea, drank the miasmic poisons of the scorched wilderness, and lay down in the south.
