At the high peaks of Mount Yue, he brandishes the bamboo whisk of Double Path; at Yunqi, he blows upon the cloth-hair. Behold these traveling monks:
it is just like the moon rising above the pine treetops. If you ask about the strategic maneuvers of a Great Man, there is not a single trace to be found.
If you seek the very core of a monk’s realization, there is not a hair’s breadth to be grasped. There is only one set of liver and gall: their pain and itch do not reside in the skin and fur.
Repeatedly feeling and probing, carefully scratching and searching, one cannot find it; though pressed hard, it is difficult to disturb. But tell me, what is it ultimately like?
*Ei!* A monkey wailing in the moonlight of a frosty night at the Wu Gorges—its heart-rending cry causes dreams and soul to vanish.
Furthermore, forty-seven years ago, I once dwelt in the heart of the river. Now, having passed seventy-two, I have come for a second time.
Like clouds moving through the sky, I ultimately know not the reason for this. Meeting those who were there in former times, I ask them for the path home.
To discern that the body is like a dream or an illusion is the first step. If you ask for the final word, look at the lanterns and the pillars;

again, contemplate the eulogy on the sea chart, the massive boulders, and the tall pines. Amidst the vast waves and dark ravines, they seem ever higher when looked up at and ever broader when gazed upon. Within them stands a single person.

His spirit was expansive and clear. At times he listened to the sound of the tides as they expounded the Universal Gate (Pumen), personally realizing the true liberation of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*).

Furthermore, while traveling on foot, he praised the ringless *khakkhara* staff; his straw sandals had no laces, so he traveled throughout the ten directions wherever his feet led, whether in the mundane or supramundane realms.

The two are not alike. A water-moon is the site of practice; a flower in the sky is the work of the Buddha. If you ask about their livelihood, it is thus, it is thus. As for the portrait eulogy of Minister Hu:
he is neither monk nor non-monk, neither layman nor non-layman. He has one and the same heart, yet two different physical presences. If you ask whether he is a lay official or a bhikṣu—
It is just like raw rice being made into porridge. Meeting on a narrow path this morning, it remains as "two or three" becoming "six.

Whether north, south, east, or west, it makes no distinction; when touched, it is like a nail driven into wood. Wandering back and forth at the head of the path of birth and death, one knows not where to find a place of rest.
I only wish that we may be born together in Tuṣita Heaven; with this mind, a thousand and ten thousand wishes will be fully satisfied.

Eulogy for the Portrait of Wang Zongbo: A breast as vast as the moon amidst the waters; a field of vision like empty flowers. An iron-and-stone liver and entrails; a spirit and bearing like wind and clouds.

I recall him before entering the womb—he was not this sort of clumsy, worldly fellow. There is no place within him to be sketched or modeled; upon closer inspection, he appears somewhat strange and extraordinary.
At first, it was not fitting for me to remain silent at Vaiśālī; today, I have come to repay my long-standing debt. Amidst the toils of worldly existence, I turn the inexhaustible Dharma wheel;
upon the tip of a single hair, I manifest hundreds of thousands of samādhis. Sacrificing self for others, I trade gold for a clod of earth.
The people of that time all said he was a high official; I say he is named Avalokiteśvara.
*The Dream-Wandering Collection of Old Man Hanshan*, Scroll 35 and Scroll 36.
Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and his disciple Tonghyeung;
revised by the Disciple from Lingnan, Liu Qixiang.

Verses on the机缘 (Kaiyuan) of the Buddhas and Patriarchs (Thirty Cases) When the World-Honored One Śākyamuni was first born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth, and walked seven steps.
Taking a step, he looked around in the four directions and said, "In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored.
Later, Yunmen said, "Had I seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow and fed him to a dog, so as to ensure peace throughout the world.
Langye Huijue said, "One may truly say: 'Dedicating this very body and mind to every dust-mote world—this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.'"
The verse says:
As soon as the head emerges, one is already in a flurry; Vainly opening a wide mouth to speak of one's conduct and retreat.
Knowing only how to vomit forth the affairs of one’s own heart, One instead provokes others to speak of one’s faults and virtues.
Because Devadatta slandered the Buddha, he fell alive into hell. The Buddha commanded Ānanda to inquire of him, saying, "Are you at peace within hell?
He replied, "Though I am in hell, it is like the bliss of the Third Dhyāna Heaven.
The Buddha again ordered Ānanda to inquire, "Do you still seek to leave? He replied, "I shall leave as soon as the World-Honored One comes."

Ānanda said, "The Buddha is the Great Teacher of the Three Realms; how could he have any portion [of karma] that leads to entry into hell? Since the Buddha has no portion for entering hell, how could I have any portion for exiting hell?

He spoke in verse: The Buddha is the Great Teacher of the Three Realms; How could there be a portion for him to enter hell? Since the Buddha has no portion for entering hell, How could I have a portion for exiting hell?
What difference is there between hell and heaven? Where one receives deep grace, that is home. When human life is contented, that is joy;
why use idle sentiments to scrutinize another?

The World-Honored One, because of the brahmin Kālakafijasta’s exercise of supernatural power, used his left and right hands to lift up two *sāla* trees—each as large as a carriage—and brought them to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to offer to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Brahmin, you should let go. The brahmin replied, "As you command. The Buddha said, "Let go.
The brahmin let go of one tree with his left hand. The Buddha said again, "Let go. The brahmin let go of the [other] one.
The Buddha held up a flower with one hand. The Buddha spoke again, saying, "Let it go. Zhizhe said, "Both my hands are already empty;
I do not know what else there is to let go of. The Buddha said, "I am not instructing you to let go of this flower.

You should let go of the six internal sense faculties, the six external sense objects, and the six consciousnesses in between. When there is nothing at all that can be discarded, that is the place where you escape birth and death."
Zhi suddenly attained great enlightenment. He spoke in verse:
"Carrying it forth, he raises weapons on level ground; Setting it down, he leaves him with no recourse.
Reaching the very end where waters cease and mountains end, Even if there were not a single thing, one would still find it too much."
In the past, when the World-Honored One arrived before the Many-Sons Stūpa, he commanded Mahākāśyapa to share his seat and sit beside him, then encircled him with his *saṃghāṭī* robe.
He then declared: "I have the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye; I entrust it secretly to you.
You must protect and uphold it, transmitting it to future generations so that it shall never be severed. He spoke in verse:
Clearly revealed, the great earth stands forth in majesty. How could a single piece of *kāṣāya* conceal it? When one speaks of "mystery," it was never mysterious;
the tongue extends everywhere, vast and manifest.
Mañjuśrī, while at Vulture Peak, the assembly where all Buddhas gather, he saw a woman sitting near the Buddha’s seat and entering into samādhi.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, “How did this woman come to sit so close to the Buddha? The Buddha replied:
“You need only awaken this woman and cause her to rise from samādhi; you may ask her yourself.

Mañjuśrī circumambulated the woman three times and snapped his fingers once; even when he had lifted her up as far as the Brahma Heaven, he was unable to bring her out despite exhausting all his supernatural powers.
The Buddha said, “Even if there were hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs, they still could not bring this woman out of her concentration. Below here, beyond—”
In lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers, there was the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhā, who was able to bring this woman out of her samādhi.
In a brief moment, Vimalaprabhā arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling. The Buddha commanded him to bring this woman out of her samādhi, and Vimalaprabhā immediately stood before the girl.
He snapped his fingers once, and the woman then emerged from her meditative absorption. The verse says:

The woman before the Buddha had lost her way; it was not that Mañjuśrī’s power did not apply. Though one might possess hands capable of seizing dragons and catching tigers, they are no match for beating the drum and playing the lute.

*Sixteen Sublime Contemplations of the Pure Land*, Verse on the First Contemplation:

Third Ground Contemplation: Contemplate ice as lapis lazuli.

Fourth is the contemplation of the trees: contemplate the ground of lapis lazuli as being jeweled trees;

form the thought of a jeweled pavilion, where the reflections of the jewel-adorned pavilion appear in infinite layers. Within this, immeasurable devas assemble; celestial music plays spontaneously without being struck.

One contemplates the marks, signs, and radiant water-moon body of one Buddha and two Bodhisattvas, just as a lost child beholds its compassionate parent; from this moment on, recognize them as your mother.

In the tenth visualization of Avalokiteśvara, one visualizes the form of the Great Being (Mahāsattva). One should imagine the Buddha standing upon his crown, with the body of the Great Being vast and boundless.
From the light at the crown of his head, emanated Buddhas appear as numerous as motes of dust. One should minutely observe the sentient beings contained within each of his pores.

This is the "Verse on the Original Abiding Dharma" composed for the eightieth birthday of Chan Master Wunian of Huangbo Mountain (with an introduction).
In the third year of the Emperor’s reign, the second month of the spring in the year of Guihai, on the seventeenth day, it was at Huangbo...
This is the four hundred and eightieth year of the Master Chan Master Wunian of Mount Shan. The Master alone, from his youth, set his will upon the supreme path;
he early awakened to his own mind, opened the true eye at the crown of his head, and raised high the banner of fearlessness.

The Dharma-gate accorded him great respect, and practitioners flocked to him like the wind. There were none who did not point toward the primary meaning, leading them to enter the ground of self-confidence.

Truly, you are a bridge across the dharma-ending age and a wisdom-torch for the long night. While the lineage of our school has fallen into desolation, it is thanks to you, Master, that its family reputation has been upheld alone.
Although I, of dull wit, have not yet had the honor of beholding your countenance, our minds’ radiance illuminates one another without a hair’s breadth of separation.
Through the Dharma, I have long since forgotten my emotions and am free from the distinctions of self and other.

Alas, now that I am old, I regret that I cannot once more take up the fly-whisk to form a karmic connection for the joy of the Dharma. Now, fortunately, I encounter the anniversary of your teacher’s birth.
The officials, lay devotees, and the assembly of monastics and laity from the ten directions each brought offerings and offered words of celebration and praise.
Upon hearing this, I, the one of dull wisdom, was filled with joy. I privately remarked: "Those who have realized non-arising are free from the mark of a life-span;

they cannot be shifted by the four marks of existence. How can they be approximated by worldly conventions? Thereupon, I spoke these verses on the Dharma of Original Abiding and respectfully dispatched them.
The attendant, holding incense and flowers from afar, offers this expression of praise. Thus, by means of a single drop of water, he extols the great ocean;

through a mere crack, he beholds the vast void. This is not intended to exhaust its boundless measure, but is merely to manifest a humble sincerity in the spirit of making a Dharma-offering. He then spoke a verse:

The self-nature of all phenomena is eternally quiescent; it is profoundly still and unmoving, like empty space. The myriad things of the world and the ten thousand images are all sealed by this single Dharma.
Before the Buddha appeared in the world and before the Patriarchs arrived, this primordially abiding Dharma was without lack or deficiency.
Even blades of grass, dust, and a hair possess their own complete essence; even white oxen and black slaves know that it exists—how much more so for sentient beings!
Each is fully endowed and equal to the nature of all Buddhas. This equality of self-nature is without arising or ceasing;
how, then, could it be subject to the transitions of the four marks? It neither comes nor goes, having no beginning and no end. Therefore, it is called the "primordially abiding dharma.
If a person awakens to this essence as suchness (*tathatā*), they transcend at once, abruptly severing the views of ordinary and sage. When the True Eye opens, birth and death are empty. Delusion...
Awakening to the two barriers, they are opened up at once; those who have already passed through the barriers walk with arms swinging free.
Treading alone upon the Great Way without hindrance, they roam with sovereign ease like a lion; they are not something a jackal can ever follow.

Having torn away the thatch-roof covering of the five aggregates, they sit with open chest upon the bare ground in utter composure. Such a person is called one liberated through fearlessness; from this point on, they always rely upon the fundamental source.
The Dharma abides; only the Master has realized this primordial, abiding Dharma. He sits alone atop the highest peak of Huangbo, towering and immovable like Mount Sumeru.
All the myriad phenomena join their palms in reverence. The sun and moon traverse like flashes of lightning; the mountains and rivers of the world are but reflections in a mirror.
This is because when the mind is empty, the body is also empty; all dharmas are merged in unity, without arising or ceasing. Therefore:
When a single mote of dust merges with space, it becomes one essence with the void; all subtle motes are likewise so.
The body and the motes of dust are equal and non-dual. Since the body and the motes of dust have entered the emptiness of the Dharma-realm, their intrinsic nature is equal to the void.
This emptiness is the primordially abiding Dharma. Those who enter this Dharma possess immeasurable life.
Within emptiness, worlds arise and perish at will; all sages and ordinary beings come and go. This Dharma is an unmoving characteristic, eternally abiding.
This is the life-span of the great earth and its sentient beings. Since sentient beings are identical to the Buddhas, how could my teacher be different from them? I only pray that my teacher...
Constantly manifesting through transformation-birth, one realizes and enters the immeasurable life of sentient beings.
This admonition for the seat was shown to Huang Sheng.
Desires must not be indulged; the will must not be dissipated; one’s nature must not be made perverse;

the mind must not be left unrestrained; the body must not be allowed idleness; study must not be erratic; principle must not be obscured; thought must not be reckless. Do not be indolent and let your spirit wander abroad;

do not be addicted to cravings and lose yourself within. Dwell in tranquility and serenity, and your hundred limbs will remain free from ailment. Unmoved by external enticements, your spirit shall reign supreme.
This "Admonition on Steadfast Resolve" is shown to Jiang Sheng:
Do not wallow in the turbidity of worldly desires; do not be oppressed by disordered thoughts; do not be haughty like drifting clouds; do not pursue the snares of the world.
You should steady your resolve through simple living, hoping to concentrate your spirit and cultivate tranquility. Let your diet of coarse herbs be plain...

I have lived in seclusion; the mountains and waters are pure, and I enjoy them alone. I unfold the profound *I Ching* to exhaust the mysteries of transformation; I peruse the *Spring and Autumn Annals* to reflect upon the past;
I recite the *Nanhua Jing* to dispel my sorrows; and I strike the western grave to shatter my obstructions. I view the ways of the world as a mirage in the sun;
I hear right and wrong like echoes in a valley; I regard all things as the limbs of insects; and I look upon this body as a mound of rat droppings. Wealth and honor mean nothing to me.
What is sought? Gain and loss among men turn over like the palm of a hand. It is luminous before one’s eyes; it is manifest above.
Without artifice, without apprehension—what daze, what bewilderment! The form is like a wooden cock; the mind is like the Elephant-Net. Confucius said:
“Neither resentful nor covetous—how could one not be excellent? This is what is called the excellence of the long.
I admonish you:
all love and hatred arise from the obstruction of the self. If the obstruction of the self were empty, radiant light would be immeasurable.

When the mind arises following external objects, and thoughts move according to emotional attachments, both mind and object are forgotten, and the distinction between things and the self vanishes. There is no beauty or ugliness in things; it is through the self that right and wrong are judged.

When my mind does not arise, what use are external objects? Observing movement and stillness as equal, viewing the noble and the humble as one, and regarding the ordinary and the sage as level—this is called the inconceivable.

An Admonition for the Body: I respectfully address you, O body. What are you? You are a composite of the four great elements; internally and externally, you are empty and false. You are like a mass of foam or a plantain tree, like dust motes or a mirage in the wilds.
You are a dense forest of manifold sufferings, a vast wilderness of birth and death. Those who remain ignorant of this are many; those who truly recognize it are few.
When a single breath does not return, one becomes a mere excrescence or a heap of refuse.
O heart, admonish yourself:
why do you act thus? In its state of vacillation and profound obscurity, it serves as the standard for all things and the spiritual essence of humanity; it is luminously clear and never obscured.

Ever alert and constantly awake, it is the treasury of good and evil and the courtyard of the sages and saints. Do not allow yourself to be obscured by desire; do not let yourself be entangled by delusion.
In tranquility and solitude, the spirit will naturally find peace.
An Exhortation to One’s Nature: Your essence is perfectly luminous; your form is subtle and profound. It neither moves nor transmigrates; it is without marks and without appearance.

Like the moisture of water, like the dryness of fire, it remains unchanged through all transformations and lies beyond the reach of names and words. Whether departing or staying, past or present, leisurely or busy, tranquil or restless—[it is ever thus].
Standing alone in its transcendence—this is called the True Way.
This admonition on life asks:
from where do you proceed? It is truly through Heaven’s regard. Whether long-lived or short, in poverty or success, listen to what one encounters. Be neither malicious nor covetous.

Free from resentment and free from malice; dwelling like a quail and feeding like fledglings, appearing as dragons amidst clouds or leopards amidst mist—truly, such is your spiritual nature. Floating and sinking follow their own destiny;
rest contentedly and await it, without harboring external longings.
Inscription for the Mother and Son (with Preface):

Because the Pure Cause led to the propagation of the Dharma, it incurred difficulties. It offended the wrath of the Sagely Son of Heaven, whose voice was like thunder. I privately reflected on my old age...

His mother, upon hearing this, would surely have been struck with such terror that she would have died of shock. Yet, he was instead granted the grace of clemency and did not die; he was instead dispatched to serve as a frontier guard in Leiyang.
On his way there, he passed through his hometown and met his aged mother by the river. At the mere sight of one another, they rejoiced and conversed with laughter;
her voice was clear and resonant, and there was not the slightest trace of lingering grief in her heart. He then asked his mother: "When you heard of your son’s death and rebirth, were you not—"
He sighed and said, "Life and death are matters of fixed destiny. I myself do not grieve; why should I grieve for you?

It is merely that people's words are inconsistent, leading to a lack of decisive insight regarding reality, which gives rise to doubt. He sat with them in attendance until dawn, when he made his final parting.
His elderly mother entrusted him with these words: "You must take good care of yourself through the Way; do not worry for me. Now..."
"I shall also part from you forever. She joyfully set out on her way, showing no sign of looking back.
I was thus moved by how such is the nature of motherhood throughout the world; could it not utterly exhaust all sentiments regarding life and death? Therefore, I composed this inscription for her:
[Inscription follows]
The bond between mother and child is like a magnet attracting a needle; this wondrous, natural nature is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected.

When I look upon my mother, it is like fire emerging from wood: once the wood has been consumed, the fire itself has no self. To be born without attachment and to die without awareness—this is the way of things.
When one first beholds my body, it is like the son of a barren woman.
To clarify the mind and inscribe this teaching for Ding Youwu:
the true nature is a profound abyss, like still, clear water. When the monk Ai strikes it, the waves of affliction arise; once they have arisen, they do not cease.
The self-nature is turbid; afflictions and ignorance further increase this lack of awakening. Taking that with the notion of "I" is like mud entering water;
being moved by that is like adding grease to a fire. That disturbs my true nature, and from that disturbance, the false self arises. If the false self did not arise, [there would be no delusion].
Even the kalpa-fire that burns the world can be turned into ice. Therefore, the Perfected One first empties the mark of self (*ātman*).

If the mark of self is empty, from what could those [afflictions] arise as obstructions? The merit of forgetting the self lies in steadfast endurance. As soon as habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) arise, one must suddenly awaken with fierce alertness.

In the very place of this awakening, one realizes a single thought turning its light back upon itself; tracks are swept away and traces are severed. At that moment, there is purity and coolness (*śītalatā*); in this purity and stillness, one stands forth solitary and independent.
Tranquil and serene, the spirit finds delight; no external thing can rival it.

Contemplating the mind, one realizes the body is not the self; like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water, the mind is observed to be without marks, its radiance pure and bright. When not a single thought arises, this is true contemplation.
Vast, spiritual, and serenely illuminating, it is perfectly identical to the Great Void. It encompasses all wonders; it neither goes out nor comes in, being without form or appearance.

The hundreds and thousands of skillful means all converge in this single aperture. It does not rely on physical form or vital energy; where form and energy obstruct, do not mistake them for reality—do not cling to delusive thoughts.
Deluded thoughts give rise to strangeness; observe this mind closely and it is empty and void, containing nothing. When a fleeting emotion arises, one immediately feels dazed and confused.
If one quickly turns the light back upon itself and exerts effort to illuminate it once, the clouds disperse like a clear sky and the white sun shines brightly. Thus, no internal thoughts arise.

External objects do not arise; however, whatever possesses form is not the original reality. When a thought arises, one awakens to it immediately; awakening is the act of illuminating and shattering it.
When an object appears, one sweeps it away; sweeping it away is letting it pass. Good and evil objects transform according to the mind; so too do the forms of ordinary beings and sages.

They appear in response to thought. When reciting mantras and contemplating the mind, it is like a polishing compound for a mirror: once the dust and grime are removed, even this [polishing agent] does not adhere.
The vast and great supernormal powers are fully possessed within one's own mind; one may roam at will through pure lands and celestial palaces. There is no need to seek the Truth elsewhere.

The mind is fundamentally the Buddha. If it arises in the realm of heat, it matures naturally within that very place of arising. Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, every single thing is wondrous;
remaining undeluded in every encounter—this is called the essential core of the mind.

The Master’s Inscription on the Nature of Humanity: Human nature is originally vast, transcending all physical forms and vessels. It is only because of the existence of the "self" that obstructions arise spontaneously. When habitual defilements become thick, one is burdened by external things;
when inquiry and study are not broad, one is frequently self-righteous; and when the perception of principle is not clear, one becomes arrogant and relies upon one's own temperament.

To slight the internal while valuing the external, to pursue external objects until one loses one's will, and to let carnal desires ravage one’s life—failing to know what to avoid or refrain from, abandoning oneself and forgetting the truth—who can such a person be called wise?
The man of realization maintains an empty mind; responding to conditions without obstruction, he flows with the times, playing at the world like a dragon or a serpent.
Neither gain nor loss startles him; nobility and meanness concern him not. He composes his spirit in tranquility and serenity, reflecting deeply with few anxieties.

He exerts himself in what he has not yet mastered and is careful regarding what he has not yet attained. He studies non-action and practices non-activity. He listens as if there were nothing to hear and looks as if there were nothing to see.
Turning the gaze inward to reflect, moment after moment does not abide; all delusions are extinguished, and the essence is singular without duality.

This is the secret of the "Teacher of the Mind" for ordinary people. Seek it within yourself, and there will be ample room for its expansion. To fail to contemplate in this manner is called self-abandonment.

To realize that all is non-substantial is to inscribe ten thousand miles of travel; yet at every step, all is non-substantial. It is because people do not realize this that they do not move even a single inch.

In a hundred years of human life, every thought-moment passes away without staying. The deluded act with reckless presumption, unable to distinguish the new from the old. Good and evil alternate and shift like a ring without end.
One knows not its limit. Who causes it to be so? The causer does not know. It grows ever new and ever more bewildering.

The heels find no footing; every step taken results in exhaustion. Having been exhausted for a long time, one loses what was originally possessed. A hundred strange transformations emerge, yet their ugliness is not seen.

Taking delusion for awakening, the entire world is mistaken; like the haggard lady Maqiu imitating the beauty’s smile, one remains complacent in self-delight. In a fleeting moment, as one approaches the mirror, there is a sudden and violent realization:
simply let the wild mind rest, and there is no need for the application of powder. Naturally beautiful and charming, the brows and eyes are clear and bright.

The original face is flawless in its slightest detail; regardless of beauty or ugliness, it requires no carving or polishing. Simply allow it to remain as it is, and it naturally returns to its primal simplicity.
Whether one is aware or unaware, whether one knows right from wrong—cast both right and wrong away, and all things will return to their common source.

Inscription on Dreaming and Awakening: Good and evil have no fixed origin; with a single mind, one turns back toward the source. Between the sage and the ordinary person there is no separation; there exists only dreaming and awakening.

To enter the dream from the state of awakening, delusion increases and becomes heavy; to enter awakening from the state of the dream, one is liberated in this very moment. When both dream and awakening are seen as non-existent, there remains only silent, numinous awareness.
Neither born nor extinguished, what is there to worry about or think? The hundreds of thousands of illusory transformations exist only within a single thought.

When a thought arises without awareness, it is like a flash of lightning across the great void. If afflictions are not bound, karma will not arise. Attachment and aversion, when made firm, are truly the root of birth and death.
The retribution of cause and effect is as swift as a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound. If the root does not sprout, from where can the branches grow?
There are many kinds of karma, yet killing is foremost among them. To love life and loathe death is common to all; though their physical shells differ, their Buddha-nature is the same.

Simply observe with equanimity; the thought of killing will naturally become empty. When the mirror of the mind is buried under dust, one must use awakening to erode the thick layers of habitual defilement.
As light naturally penetrates through gradual polishing, thoughts arise and are immediately recognized; as awakening reaches the state of non-arising, the mind and its objects become vast and empty.
To pursue deluded thoughts is ultimately of no benefit. Examine and contemplate with clarity: birth and death are swift;
the coming and going of samsara is a profound, dark dream. One merely revolves according to karma. If there were no birth, one would not be attached to birth. One must awaken from this dream.
Viewed with an awakened eye, one is binding oneself without a rope. Moment after moment, turn the light inward; thought after thought, reflect back upon the mind.
Simply not following after emotions—this is called the essential mystery.

To forget conditions and cling to mental states distinguishes the wise from the foolish; by nature, clarity and obscurity differ. The distinction between the ordinary and the sage truly lies in one’s orientation—whether one turns toward or away [from the truth].

It is like a minister serving his sovereign or a son attending his father: a single moment of refined sincerity admits no lingering glance or hesitation. To linger is to shift; to shift is to create delusion.

Having been deluded for so long, the spirit grows weary by the day; yet if one does not shift from this state, awakening will follow. Once awakened, one no longer looks back. Standing alone and profoundly still, its wondrous function is eternally present.
Responding to conditions like an echo, dwelling in the world like space, it wanders freely through the transformations of things, suddenly shedding the cage of worldly entanglement.
Neither emerging nor entering; neither going nor coming. Worldly phenomena are like flowers in the sky; one’s disposition is like the moon reflected in water.

Contemplating the world, one inscribes upon it that this illusory body of the four elements is fundamentally nothing at all. The ignorant cling to it, fettered by love and hatred, while the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind remains as it is.
All-pervading and pure, yet delusions accumulate through ignorance and inverted views increase as sickness. Like a thirsty deer chasing a mirage, the more one pursues, the thirstier one becomes;
upon seeing through this, one simply rests, only then realizing it was an error. The playful exercise of spiritual powers is not separate from daily life—whether noble or base, beautiful or ugly.

Let them manipulate as they please. The person of great attainment views from a vast perspective; all is clearly and transparently understood. Union and separation, sorrow and joy—these cannot be found at all.
The realms of the six sense-objects are like gathering treasures in a dream; infinite craving and seeking vanish upon a single awakening. As for sounds and forms, [they are likewise empty].
Wind and moon travel through space; therein they do not cling. How could this be blindness or deafness? Using this to dwell in the world, what hindrance could there be?
Though the body is that of an ordinary person, it is named Avalokiteśvara.
The six sense organs serve as the medium for karma, and the mind serves as the seed of karma. From these six faculties of emotion, greed rushes forth and craving surges up;

the eyes flow toward forms and lose their true clarity, the ears flow toward sounds and abandon their fundamental hearing, and the tongue, though not failing to perceive flavors, is truly full of false speech.
Indulging one's whims and following one’s passions, the winds of consciousness drum within; habitual tendencies arise and resonate through the apertures like the sound of reeds, their origin unknown.
Those who hear them are struck with alarm. As words exit the mouth and enter the ear, love and hatred arise; once the sound has vanished, the calamity begins.
It is like poisonous mushrooms suddenly growing from dung struck by lightning; the fool who eats them mistakenly brings about the end of his life.

The nose unites with the body to form a single consciousness, yet both are entirely mundane dust. The body abounds in faults and evils, while the mind is the pivotal mechanism that flows along the currents of the sea of poison.

Driven by these [external objects], their true sovereign is swept away. Therefore, although worldly people are born, they are as if not born. If one can turn back and observe, each will attain the refined truth.
When the refined truth is restored, the six sense faculties become non-existent; they are like clouds floating in space, or echoes emerging from a valley.
Not constrained by form, not hindered by mind, far transcending the dust of sensory objects, one is sublime and autonomous.
In the Inscription on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation:

Recite the Buddha while recollecting the mind; recollect the mind while reciting the Buddha. The Buddha is not external to the mind, and the mind is not a material thing. It is the luminosity of self-nature.
Mind after mind illuminates all; the tracks of delusive thoughts vanish. The physical form is like an empty valley; the Pure Land is never far from before one's eyes.
Lotus flowers constantly adorn the two feet. Why wait until after death to be reborn?
This very state is the Samādhi of Universal Radiance, appearing right before us, neither emerging nor entering, requiring only a single exhalation of the person present.
The true mind is by nature luminous;

it is only because of the obscuration of desire that it becomes dark. This innate essence is dissipated by following emotional attachments. Now, wishing to rectify it, one must eliminate desire and restrain the emotions.
Once the single reality is restored, all delusions will no longer arise.

The intent of sincerity is the very root of delusion. Riding upon emptiness, one digs deeper day by day; though one examines its source closely, it remains hidden within the unconscious. To awaken is to be free from delusion;
when delusion ceases, that is the Real. When utmost sincerity is unceasing, one’s goodness becomes profound.
The Inscription for Self-Cultivation:
The body is the vessel of desire; the indulgence of the passions is the root of it. Intoxication by wine and infatuation with beauty are pitfalls that trap the person.
If one is deluded by desire and does not turn back, the body and mind will lack stability. To have this life in vain is truly to waste it.
An Inscription on Governing the Family:

The essentials of governing the family are frugality and diligence. When righteousness and propriety are abundant, one naturally becomes pure through simplicity. Diligence and frugality are passed down through generations;
simplicity and purity settle the will. This is the secret of sages and worthies for dwelling in the world.

The Six Wondrous Epitaphs (with Preface) The Master of Xueqiao Mountain built a hermitage at the foot of Chaoyang Peak on the Double Path. Because a thousand peaks pointed toward it like fingers, he named it "Thousand Fingers. The front peak embraces it closely, curving like a horn; I have named it "Qilin Horn" and used it as a metaphor. Six Wondrous Epitaphs 1. Epitaph for the Qilin Horn 2. Epitaph for the Thousand Fingers 3. Epitaph for the Great Snowy Peak 4. Epitaph for the Morning Sun 5. Epitaph for the Dragon Gate 6. Epitaph for the Tiger’s Den **Epitaph for the Qilin Horn** The Qilin Horn is the most prominent among the peaks. It rises majestically from the earth, its form resembling a horn. Its summit is sharp and its base broad, like the horns of a qilin. It stands alone, towering above the myriad peaks, as if it were the head of the mountain range. When the clouds disperse and the mist clears, one can see the sun rising from behind it, casting a golden light upon the surrounding peaks. This is why I have named it the Qilin Horn. **Epitaph for the Thousand Fingers** The Thousand Fingers are the peaks that surround the hermitage. They stretch out in all directions like fingers pointing toward the sky. Their shapes are varied and their heights differ, yet they all converge toward the central peak. When the wind blows through the valleys, the sound of the trees is like the rustling of many voices. This is why I have named them the Thousand Fingers. **Epitaph for the Great Snowy Peak** The Great Snowy Peak is the highest point of the mountain range. It is covered in perpetual snow, white as jade. Its summit is vast and its slopes are steep, like the wings of a great bird. When the sun shines upon it, the snow reflects its light, creating a brilliant spectacle. This is why I have named it the Great Snowy Peak. **Epitaph for the Morning Sun** The Morning Sun is the peak where the first light of dawn appears. It is situated to the east of the hermitage, facing the rising sun. When the night passes and the darkness fades, the first rays of light break over its summit, illuminating the world. This is why I have named it the Morning Sun. **Epitaph for the Dragon Gate** The Dragon Gate is the narrow pass leading to the higher reaches of the mountain. It is steep and precipitous, like the gate of a dragon’s lair. Those who wish to ascend must pass through this gate with courage and determination. This is why I have named it the Dragon Gate. **Epitaph for the Tiger’s Den** The Tiger’s Den is the deep valley where wild beasts dwell. It is secluded and remote, hidden from the eyes of men. Here, the tigers roam freely, unafraid of the world. This is why I have named it the Tiger’s Den. These six epitaphs are inscribed upon stone tablets to commemorate the wonders of this mountain. May they serve as a reminder of the beauty and majesty of this place. May those who visit here find peace and inspiration. May they remember the virtues of the Master of Xueqiao and the spirit of this sacred retreat. May there be peace and prosperity for all beings. May the Dharma flourish and spread throughout the world. May all who encounter these epitaphs gain insight and wisdom. May they be guided toward the path of enlightenment. Amen. It is solitary. In front of the hermitage is a pond, commonly called "Washing the Inkstone" (*Xiyan*), likely because Su Dongpo once visited this mountain three times;
I have changed its name to "Coming Moon" (*Laiyue*). An ancient sage who illustrated the Way said: "When the pond is formed, the moon comes of itself.
Above the pond is a study hall, which I have titled "Washing the Moon" (*Xiyue*) to symbolize the state of mind and heart. Behind the hall is a spring, the taste of which is sweet and crisp.

It was rich and pure. I inscribed its name as "Exceeding Milk," for according to the words of the ancient sages, the water at the beginning of the kalpa tasted sweeter than milk because it originated from the Vajra-limit (*vajrakoṭi*).
Since this water from the mountain peak must have a source that deep, it may serve as a metaphor for the Dharma-lineage;
one who wishes to know the root [should look here]. Behind the hermitage is a rock which I named "Great Rest" (*mahāviśrāma*), signifying that an *āraṇya* is the place of true cultivation.
The place of practice is the field of quiescence; it is the ground of great rest. This scene is natural, and thus it is titled "The Six Subtleties. At the beginning of the scroll, it says:
"Penetrating and reaching everywhere in the six directions and four quarters. This is intended for those within this realm so that the old man may not be bound by the subtleties.
One must simply seize both simultaneously; therefore, it is called "penetration and reaching. Each person must act accordingly.

Inscription: To keep one’s resolve unforgetting. It is not a realm of conceptual encounter; it does not fall within the reach of words or thought. This is something realized spontaneously by host and guest alike.
—Qianzhi An (Thousand-Finger Hermitage)
A thousand peaks stand tall, pointing directly at this hermitage. This hermitage is like space; it is utterly without obstruction or enclosure.
When asked about the master of the hermitage, he neither comes out nor enters. To any who come to inquire, he gives a single shout from within the void.
A herd of qilin horns rushes and gallops; a single qilin is sufficient unto itself. What the qilin values lies in the uniqueness of its horn. A single stone resembles a qilin;
ten thousand trees are like its fur. How laughable is the rider who cannot move even a single hair!
The moon in the pond next month originally does not come; the water also does not go. They suddenly meet, and one knows not the reason why.
The sky at the bottom of the water and the moon within the pond—their aspects of coming and going cannot be described at all.
Washing the Moon: The moon is inherently free of dust; the water is naturally pure. From where could one wash it? Seeking it, one finds nothing.
When the moon falls into the water, the water contains its reflection. Alas for the onlookers; their feverish dreams have not yet awakened.
To select milk from within the spring water, one must be a king of geese; here, there is no need for such selection. It depends on skillful tasting. Not even a drop is permitted to enter the mouth;
one must first know the flavor. Only those who know the flavor drink it with hearts intoxicated.
The Great Resting Stone does not run ill; why must it rest? Its great resting is because it is fundamentally quiescent.
Seated in full lotus posture within this state, unmoving and unswaying, it extends its broad and long tongue as the pines and winds cry out at night.

Inscription for the Prajñā Pavilion (with Preface) The pavilion derives its name from the study of this scripture within it. It serves as the retreat of the lay practitioner Zhu Lu, styled Wangzai, of Wumen.
Lu was a man of singular character; Wangzai passed the provincial examination for the jinshi degree and served as the Commandant of the Prefecture. [Wangzai] spat upon the pavilion...

Mian abandoned his wife and children and retired in seclusion at Mount Tianmu. After some time, he passed again through Shuangjing and resided in this pavilion, where he read the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and experienced great awakening.
I had come from Mount Nanyue specifically to attend to the final circumstances of Master Da;
thus, I was able to reach this mountain. Upon seeing me, the Layman (Jushi) rejoiced and took up the role of a disciple. I sighed and said: "It is not..."
He possessed great power. As for those who delight in the bliss of *nirvāṇa*, how could they suddenly cast off worldly entanglements to reach this state?
For this reason, Zhu was named "Great Power" (Dàlì), the King was titled "Great Gold" (Dàjīn), and he inscribed the name "Prajñā" upon his pavilion. He then composed an inscription to commemorate it.
The inscription reads: [The inscription follows.]
Alas for this hall! Its radiance penetrates through and beyond; within and without are perfectly clear and bright, entirely free from bondage and attachment.

At the gates of the six sense-faculties, all is perfectly penetrating and vast emptiness; both the mundane and supramundane worlds are cast away at once. The flavor of this hall is tranquil, serene, and profoundly still.
The master within the pavilion experiences joy in body and mind; all sensory afflictions are like a mass of fire reduced to mere embers.
This dharma-gate is called "Ineffable."
Inscription for the Vimalakīrti Chamber (with Preface) The layman Guan Juexian was born and raised in Wumen.
At an early age, he took refuge in the Triple Gem; he did not maintain a wife or children, nor did he engage in the cultivation of property.
He constructed but a single chamber, which he named "Vimalakīrti," in order to welcome those from the ten directions. Since there is no dharma that can be preached...
He performs the work of a Buddha solely through fragrant food. An old man passed by his room and, having been moved by this, requested an inscription for it. The inscription reads:
"In the city of Vaiśālī, firm and dense, though situated amidst the marketplace, there is no trace of dust. Within it dwells a lay devotee."
He sleeps alone in a single room; the door does not admit drafts, and the six windows are empty and silent, with only the ten directions present.

Those who occasionally gather like clouds to inquire about the Dharma receive only his silent response. He does not request fragrant meals, but partakes of alms-food as circumstances provide. He does not borrow a seat.
Using the open ground as one’s mat, wherever there is a secluded space, not even a speck of dust shall stand. Body and mind are both forgotten; the world is cast away all at once.
Ten thousand entanglements are discarded together, and all conditions suddenly cease. To be amidst the dust yet transcend the dust—this is the foremost.
Inscription for an Iron *Ruyi* (with Preface) Having parted from the Master of Mount Xueqiao at Shuangjing, he presented me with an iron *ruiyi* and an incense casket as offerings. Moved by this,
I have composed this inscription.
This very *cintāmaṇi* shall take the place of my heart and mouth; I am unable to speak, so I borrow your skillful roar.
Your words are not in vain, yet my Dharma is not existent. Since both have departed, even "one" is no longer maintained. Only the fragrance of the Dharmakāya shall be your companion.
Entrusted to this vajra, it is used to ensure its imperishable transmission.
*The Collected Works of Old Man Hanshan from His Dream Excursions*, Volume Thirty-Six;
*The Collected Works of Old Man Hanshan from His Dream Excursions*, Volume Thirty-Seven.
Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and his disciple Tonghyeong;
revised by the Disciple from Lingnan, Liu Qixiang.
Verse 1 (of seventy-two):
The Verse on Mind-Only.
Pure, wondrous, and inconceivable, The perfectly realized true mind, Vast and endowed with majestic power, Manifests immeasurable phenomena.
Its essence is free from all defilements, yet it does not abandon the conditions of the defiled and the pure. In both the mundane and supramundane realms, it accomplishes manifold wholesome deeds.
These manifold deeds are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent. Because they are non-existent, they are said to be the very same as the true and eternal.
Thoroughly realizing that the nature of karma is empty, one is not deluded by illusory arts; neither clinging nor loathing, one contemplates with truth according to reality.

Where it arises, there is no birth; one should contemplate its own inherent emptiness and stillness, understanding that there is no limit of before or after. A single thought-moment is like Mount Sumeru.
In movement and stillness, it is equal and like suchness; the winds of sensory objects cannot move it. It is the wondrous, eternal bliss of quiescent extinction, pure as a lotus flower.

Though it enters deeply into the mud of worldly toil, it is unstained by the defilements of the mundane world. Cherishing this wish-fulfilling jewel, one lacks for nothing according to whatever is sought.
The light of the divine illuminates the darkness, universally awakening all sentient beings.
Living in the mountains, I ask those who dwell there: "What is the purpose of living in the mountains? "Three meals of congee every day, and stretching out both legs to sleep."
A solid rock serves as the meditation seat; clouds and mists form the canopy and bedding. A gentle breeze whistles through the secluded pines, revealing the meaning of the Westward Journey.

It sweeps away blossoms from amidst the clouds and scrapes clean the cataracts from the eyes. In a single thought, center and periphery are severed; there is no longer any boundary between before and after.
Upon awakening, both eyes are empty; looking back at the events of the dream, they are like grasping at the moon reflected in water—which only results in dull stagnation.
When both the mundane and the holy are cast away together, one is finally liberated from the burdens of birth. To bring forth not a single thing is still but the secondary meaning.
Having broken through to the state of non-action, I have finally fulfilled my intention to dwell in the mountains.
To the Zen practitioner Daze, who has come from across the passes and seas to pay his respects three times, I show this:
"From ten thousand miles away, for whose sake do you come? You come back again; for what purpose? It is like searching for one's own toe inside one's boot—it is originally not to be found elsewhere.
If you seek it outwardly, you will run to the ends of the earth; coming and going again and again, this Dharma originally has no abiding place.
I ask you, monks of Caoxi: can there be a tree of Bodhi? If you do not obtain even a single branch, you have spent your efforts in vain selling your coarse cotton cloth.
To the Chan practitioner Daomaiyuan:

there is no secret method for practicing Chan; it simply requires that you be cut by the urgency of birth and death. Let birth and death hang upon your eyebrows, and never let this mindfulness cease for even a moment.
Grasp the vajra-ring; make your backbone as firm as iron. Strive with all your might to pursue it forward until the life-root is severed.
Erroneous thoughts will suddenly vanish from their tracks, and body and mind will be cast off in an instant. To see the person of original nature is like driving a stake into empty space.
Only by breaking through the black lacquer bucket is there great rest.
[This was written] while inscribing a diagram of the Ganges for the Chan practitioner Hengyi-lin.

When the Buddha dwelt on the banks of the Ganges, he constantly preached the Dharma facing the river. When he reached points where the Dharma is inconceivable, he immediately used the sands of the river as a metaphor.
If one were to count grains of sand, they would still not exhaust the Buddha’s intent; it is only through this Dharma-body that the true meaning is revealed.

The Dharma-body is eternal and unchanging; though it flows along with phenomena, its nature does not shift. Although it may be defiled by all manner of impurities, its essential nature is eternally pure.
Even until the fires of the kalpa blaze forth, its ultimate essence remains undestroyed; therefore, the Dharmakāya is eternal, its self-nature being without birth or cessation.
O Son of the Buddha, recognize this meaning and awaken to the Svabhāvakāya; like the sands of the Ganges River, its nature remains eternally one throughout all kalpas.
This is called the Vajra-ground; the Son of the Buddha dwells securely therein.
Contemplating conditions through verses, he observes this body as having arisen from beginningless time through inverted false imaginings, cycling through the six realms of suffering.

In the midst [of delusion], one’s nature returns to the realms of humans and devas for immeasurable kalpas. When deluded thoughts do not cease, suffering is boundless; when deluded objects are not seen as empty, karma is like the ocean.
If one can momentarily turn the light back for even a single thought-moment, one will immediately ascend to the other shore. Deluded karma accumulates like Mount Sumeru;
the egoism of "I" and "you," and the suffering of right and wrong, become solidified. These form the Iron Ring Mountains of birth and death, persisting through hundreds and thousands of kalpas.
Once born, one cannot escape; yet the boiling cauldrons and glowing coals were originally non-existent. They arise solely from the single thought of a mind of anger.
If one eliminates them at the very moment they arise, the golden lotus within the fire is true liberation. The present environment is like flowers in the sky;
it cannot be compared to reflections in a mirror or the moon in water. Worldly people are deluded and lack the eye of wisdom; they mistakenly take this to be real—a perverted view.

Falsely taking the four elements to be one’s body, and making the six consciousnesses and the three poisons one’s masters, one is unaware of greed, anger, and egoism, falsely rushing about through the various realms of suffering.
One’s own nature is inherently pure—this is Amitābha; unstained by the six sense objects, it is the Land of Lotus Flowers.
When not a single thought arises, birth and death are empty; manifest in daily life, this is true Ultimate Bliss.

To teach the practice of *nianfo* (mindfulness of the Buddha), one must first understand that the very purpose of *nianfo* is to transcend birth and death (*saṃsāra*). One must first recognize the mind of birth and death: delusion and craving are the roots of birth and death;
if these roots are not uprooted, liberation is difficult to attain. Delusion and craving are themselves the mind of *nianfo*; therefore, one uses *nianfo* to sever them.
Delusion and craving—if one can sever them moment by moment, then Amitābha will manifest fully in every thought.
This itself is true diligence; it must not be forgotten for even a single instant. The Pure Land resides within the pure mind;
do not seek it elsewhere outside.
The Verse on Perfect Clarity concludes:

The mind-light of perfect clarity is fundamentally immeasurable; it is only because of those superficial, floating eyes that it is obstructed. When separated by paper, one cannot perceive external objects;
yet when turned inward, how could one ever see the five viscera? It is like the bright sun shining in the void, while a person remains in a dark room.
One born blind and one in the dark may both possess two eyes, yet how could they not communicate with the sunlight?
These four elements of mine are like a thatched hut; the mind within the body is like a bird in a cage. Who can strip away the thatch and seal this dwelling?
Radiant illumination is fundamentally inexhaustible. If one can see for oneself that the light of the mind is full, it is clearly and eternally bright without the need for eyes. This is...
The light of neither-arising-nor-ceasing does not flow along with the four great elements. How fortunate you are today that Heaven has looked upon you with compassion;

it has specially removed all obstructions so that the celestial light is complete. You need not lament not seeing it during the day, for it is just like having eyes while sleeping in the dark of night.

It is the same when one has eyes while sleeping at night; the luminous clarity of the mind’s light is naturally so. If one leaves behind both light and darkness to see one's own mind, that luminous clarity will suddenly manifest, transcending birth and death.
Who in the world knows the excellence of being sightless? An ancient once lamented that he was not blind sooner.
Suddenly casting off the four elements, the radiant light is complete; this is the wish-fulfilling jewel of our own house.
Ascending Mount Kun to Show My Fellow Travelers:
A single fist-sized stone within the city of Mount Kun is as vast as Mount Sumeru containing a mustard seed.

When I came and took up my staff to ascend it, I suddenly entered the eye-socket of a tiny gnat. To those of this age, it appears as nothing upon a single glance; the fourfold assembly looks on in confusion.
Startled, he hurriedly came to question the person in the air. Still, [the person] pointed out that very same one from before.
"The beam collapsed and crushed Tan-sheng," [he said].
To show this, he presented a verse: "The rafter collapsed and crushed Tan-sheng; Tan-sheng was crushed—why did he not die? If the beam had reached his body, his body would have [perished]."
Shattered! If the body reaches the beam, the beam does not avoid it; since both have arrived, why do they not interact? Let us inquire into the reason for this non-interaction:
the state before one’s eyes is not like a beam. Why, Master Tan, do you first feel such distress and alarm?
If you wish to be free from alarm, watch the dog being driven to leap over the wall.
To demonstrate the root of merit and wisdom for the practice of purifying the Buddha-land, one need only contemplate the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha.
If one maintains this constantly in the mind, moment after moment without interruption, and if each thought is most clearly distinct, then one will personally behold Amitābha face to face.
Simply contemplate that the Pure Land is right before you; in every activity of daily life, it is present everywhere.
Though lacking, the Buddha-lands are fully encompassed within a single thought-moment; this is the true expedient for rebirth.
It lies solely in the state of clear and distinct awareness; one must not give rise to further discriminatory views.
Contemplate the body as a body like a water bubble; appearing for a moment, it does not endure long. Fools mistake it for a pearl, yet though they grasp at it, it does not fill their hands.
How much more so within this [body], where excessive greed serves as a den of sin. It must be viewed only with the eye of wisdom: what ultimately exists therein?
Contemplating the mind, this mind is fundamentally formless; it cannot be seen even when looked upon. Its arising and ceasing are entirely without end, as swift as lightning in the sky.
Deluded thoughts pursue worldly toil, like thirsty deer rushing toward a mirage. How lamentable are those of past and present! They all suppress the noble to become the base.

I show you that the ocean of illusions is boundless and has no end; when will the toil of worldly afflictions and deluded thoughts cease? You should know that worldly phenomena are like lightning in the void;
you must believe that human life is like a bubble upon the water. Only by gathering the single mind and returning to the Pure Land can one rely entirely upon the myriad practices.
True cultivation: Before one's eyes, all is the path to Bodhi; in every thought-moment, one constantly boards the vessel of Prajñā.
The Elder Wuxiang, having seen you when you were in your early sixties, has now been parted from you for nearly ten years. How have you fared? Time is limited; do not let it pass in vain.
Awaken! Eradicate boundless delusions thought after thought. Water the lotus of the pure land with the water of dhyāna; weed the field of the mind with the sword of wisdom.
Pass through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas as entirely empty; do not allow this present life to drift into further falsehood.
Showing that Immersed Life Produces Virtue (Two Poems) When one lies damp in bed, illness is certain;
yet the eel, by its very nature, does not die. Each thing has its own inherent suitability; what cause for sorrow or joy in suffering and pleasure?
Things are fundamentally without anything desirable; it is people themselves who desire them. Just as sweet and bitter tastes differ, those who relish them consider them extraordinary.
To Master Liu-yi (Two Poems): Worldly affairs suddenly seem like a dream;
human sentiments are empty as clouds. Who would have known that within the dusty marketplace, one whose mind is still is already apart from the crowd?
In outward conduct, how could I not depart from worldly custom? With a mind empty of self, how could I remain at home? Just look at the turbid waters; from their depths, lotus flowers emerge.

To show this to Pumen, the Chan practitioner did not shrink from the hardships of traveling on foot, traversing mountains and rivers for ten thousand *li*. Now that he has reached the road to Caoxi, who will repay him for the debt of providing lodging without charge?
To Zen Practitioner Guishan Jinshan (Three Poems) White hair brings sorrow that is hard to dispel;
The road through the red dust is impassable. My body dwells within the realm of men, But my heart resides amidst ten thousand mountains.
Day after day within the dust of worldly toil, morning after morning in the arena of love and hate; one knows not for what reason, yet busies oneself solely for their sake.
The sea of suffering is deep and bottomless, while the affairs of this floating life have their limits; one knows not within the three realms where the home of return lies.
A Gift for Chan Practitioner Benjing:

Building a Hermitage Seated alone amidst a thousand peaks within the white clouds, I am too weary to don my hundred-patch robe. In stillness, I listen to the sound of flowing water; At leisure, I watch the white clouds drift by.
To demonstrate the character "upright" (áng) is to show that there is no self;

one must not be self-exalting. When pride and arrogance rely instead upon one's own spirit, one should humble oneself until reaching the state of non-existence, thereby entering the Ground of Cool Serenity.
The ocean of wisdom, Shanzi Haiyue, gathers a multitude of treasures;
its supporting pillars are solely coral. The bright moon comes and goes at times, its coolness matched by the night pearl.
To Chan Practitioner Shijingtang:
A single bowl follows a solitary staff; at the three mountains, one gathers the conditions for the assembly. A mere drop from the waters of Caoxi has paid in full the debt for the straw sandals.
To Mr. Liu: Four Rests.
One flavor, always content; much seeking is entirely mistaken. Eating rice and vegetables, drinking water—this alone completes one’s life.
*The Eight Views of Puti Chan* (With an Introduction) Puti Chan is located at Shimen in Jiahe.
It was established by the lay practitioner Yan Shengsheng for the sake of Master Xing of Zhihe.
The Summer Retreat. I passed through here on my way to Jingshan, and thus composed this verse:
Without having reached Mount Bodhi, how could one know the realm of Bodhi? Only those who dwell within the mountains can, forgetting words, realize it within their own minds.
The verdant city is encircled by lush greenery, resembling a vajra-ring where neither Buddha nor Mara can enter; within it all is void and empty.
An Ancient Avalokiteśvara Image.
Avalokiteśvara has before and after; the Dharmakāya has neither past nor present. Because he has severed the mind of coming and going, he is able to constantly rescue those in suffering.

The Arhat’s pine stands tall and solitary like a single pine tree; it is the majestic manifestation of the true form. If you ask about the mind of Nirvāṇa, the bright moon shines upon the branch tips.
In the Lotus Bay, lotuses grow from the mud; their nature is inherently fragrant and pure. Behold the person within the flowers, sitting upright in silence.
The Fish-Releasing Pond.
A single mind of non-arising fully manifests the place of releasing life. May all those with scales and shells tread the path of non-arising.

The bubble arises, the stupa arises, yet the bubble is fundamentally unarisen; the bubble ceases, yet originally it was not extinguished. Only the seamless stupa remains, its light illuminating the moon in the cold sky.

The *huán* tree is able to eliminate afflictions because it is afflicted by them; the *huán* tree loves its own growth. Upon seeing these *huán* seed beads, one suddenly gives rise to the thought of detachment from affliction.
*Shanju shizhong* (Teaching the Assembly While Dwelling in the Mountains), Twenty-five Verses.

Sitting alone by a single incense burner, carefree and forgetting all myriad concerns. Gazing quietly at the ants below the steps, for whose sake are they so busy? In profound stillness, one departs from cognition;
in brilliant clarity, seeing and hearing are extinguished. The moon beyond the heavens at the third watch; a single fragment of cloud atop the ridge.
The affairs of the world are a single game of chess; at every move, one contends for victory or defeat. Before black and white have yet been distinguished, how many are able to awaken?
Within the pure and luminous treasury, a single thought suddenly arises; the boundless ocean of birth and death is entirely born from within this.
The road through the red dust is even longer; the green mountains have no time for idleness. I ask those who pass to and fro: who recognizes the excellence within the mountains?
Deeply clear is the blue lotus flower, dwelling in the mud yet unstained. Radiant is the world-transcending mind, like snow within a crystal cup.
The puppet appears at night; the onlookers give rise to joy and admiration. It is only fitting that one remains intoxicated within the heart; it is difficult to restrain the sober eye from seeing.

When the four elements and various conditions combine, delusion distinguishes between the beautiful and the ugly. Try looking at this illusory person: from where could consciousness and emotion possibly arise?
A single mote of dust contains a world; do not doubt its capacity for total inclusion. Do not say that the mote of dust is small; you should know that the world is empty.
On the path before the withered tree and the cliff, the traveler becomes lost upon reaching it. You must ascend the summit of another peak and climb yet another flight of stairs.
The trees on the bank hang over a crumbling precipice; withered vines dangle above a deep ancient well. How can one endure the gnawing of two rats? All the more so when assailed by a rushing torrent.
Within this blazing house on fire, there is no escape from the feverish afflictions. When one lets go for a single thought-moment, one suddenly attains the ground of cool serenity.
The whole world desires much and seeks much; seeking much only gives rise to further affliction. Only the mind of contentment is the wish-fulfilling jewel.
The Pure Land is a manifestation of one’s own mind; it is the fragrance of the lotus-natured ground, ever present before one without obscuration—this very state is the Western Paradise.
Delusive thoughts lead to the realms of samsara; a pure mind is the field of liberation. When you turn the light back to reflect within, you face-to-face pay homage to the King of Emptiness.
Chasing after it, one runs toward a mirage; walking on, one enters a pit of fire. If you can but open a single eye, you will realize at once that there is no birth.
The worldly path is fraught with many entanglements; empty fame is what most distresses man. Only when the threads at one’s heels are severed can one be permitted to leave the red dust of the world.

Though one may find inspiration in mountain forests, how often can one truly endure such solitude? If one does not reach the place of true rest, it will ultimately become nothing more than a subject for idle talk.
The mark of self is truly difficult to shatter; another’s faults are very easy to find. Examine yourself idly throughout a lifetime, yet in the end there is no basis for it.
The Buddha of original nature and innate truth is entirely ensnared by delusive thoughts. If one can simply see through this once, one realizes the state of the Golden Immortal on the spot.

The myriad dharmas are created solely by the mind; in a single thought-moment, a thousand paths may diverge. If one does not know the place where [thoughts] have not yet arisen, the sea of suffering remains truly boundless.
In the state of profound stillness where conditions are forgotten, when every moment of mind is let go—there is no other intent in the West; it lies only in self-realization.
A single drop of water from the great ocean possesses the flavor of a hundred rivers; the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is inherently identical, yet the ignorant perceive it as diverse.

In the human way, a hundred years are long; in my way, a hundred years are short. On a pillow, one dreams for three watches of the night, yet before the eyes of the awakened have even turned, the dream has ended.
A single patch of vacant ground is mostly overrun by weeds; If one can clear them away from time to time, that is the mind emerging from the dust.
Ten Verses for the Assembly (Six-Syllable Verse):
The thieving heart and its schemes are utterly extinguished; A useless way of life is established. Gathering up infinite delusive thoughts, They are exchanged for...
A single lotus flower;

the four great elements support a mere skeleton. The heart-mind is solitary and still within the cold void; there remains only a single, continuous breath, like a thread of tortoise hair binding the long wind.
Let us say that a hundred years are like a dream; who has ever truly opened their eyes? Even if one exhausts every clever stratagem, in the end it is all but folly.
A pity that this pure and cool mind-ground, without cause, erupts with greed and anger; when the fire of lightning strikes within the heart, it burns everything to ashes.
The self-nature is primordially true.

The body is a provisional combination of manifold conditions; the four great elements enclose a single void. Movements and actions are called the "True Ruler," yet one does not know who dwells within it.

One creates the trap-mechanisms oneself; who shall face the forest of blades and the cauldrons of fire? You may think you find joy before your eyes, but how can you know the long suffering that follows after death?
Your appearance is the very image of one who has transcended the mundane; your robes are like lotuses risen from the water. Let us examine what lies within your breast—do not let it be so.
Deluded thoughts provide a slight obstruction;

like silkworm cocoons, they spontaneously create their own entanglements. Who causes the moth to burn itself in the lamp? One intends to seek light through clever means, yet one knows not that the power of karma draws one along.
Names are merely provisional designations and not real; praise and blame entering the ear are like the wind. Try calling me a "thief-grass" (a useless weed);
it is like someone idly reviling empty space. Swing your arms within a thicket of thorns;

withdraw your body from the field of right and wrong. You will thus attain an infinite, cool detachment. Such is this— [Note: The original text appears to be a fragment of a Zen or Chan discourse, likely concluding with a term such as "this kind of person" or "this state," which has been omitted in the source.]
Completely unyielding toward others.
(Verse 2, 308th poem). Reading the "Chapter on the Four Marks" of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* within the meditation hall.
The sounds of my bell, drum, gong, and cymbals never cease; with every sound, day and night, they proclaim non-arising. How pitiable are those intoxicated by dreams and who harm their own lives;
as they gaze at one another in the mirror, their tears flow down in torrents.
Human forms are jagged and towering, rising like an iron city; the forest of knives and trees of swords is cold as ice. Who knows that fire shall break forth from within this mountain of ice?
Once the mountain of ice is consumed, the fire itself will cease to arise.
The iron gates of sentient beings are tightly closed and difficult to open; the myriad locks are a bitter misery indeed.
How strange that these moaning guests of the long night do not know for what reason they have come here!
A single blood-stained staff for those who cling to the mark of a self is utterly heartless; when it strikes, it must bring an end to birth and death.
Only when the pain reaches the point where the heart aches and the nose stings will one know that the King’s Law is most clearly defined.
Leaving the city walls, I pass through the Chang'an market; four verses on Chang'an’s wind and moon.
The wind and moon of Chang’an are the same in ancient and modern times. The purple roads and red dust have no end to their paths. Most intimate of all that calls to men:
A single crowing of the cock and the five-watch bell.
The essence is like empty space, naturally at ease; not even a speck of dust can obstruct ten thousand layers of mountains.
How pitiable are those travelers under the bright sun and blue sky, their eyes wide open, sighing at the hardships of the road.
Whirling winds and gathering rain come all at once; countless travelers cannot open their eyes. Suddenly the rain ceases and the clouds disperse entirely;
the vast void is from the beginning free of dust.
A dry city in the void, wild horses, and people; before one's eyes, it resembles a village of mist. One must enter the city to see for oneself:
sounds and forms are originally not real.
Passing through Tangsi Temple on Mount Wu, I met the Chan practitioner Mingtong, who was paying homage to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

In response to this, I showed him that wherever one goes, the mountains and rivers are the very essence of reality: "The entire great chiliocosm is contained within a single speck of dust; when leisure allows, it is split open and lightly extracted.
Do not say that Mañjuśrī is merely a wise man."
Passing through the Iron Buddha Hermitage, I present this to the Censor Zou Erzhan:
On the riverbanks, green mountains stretch on without end; Before the gate, flowing waters are pure and free of dust.
Opening the door, I suddenly see the master of the hermitage— He is truly the indestructible Vajra body.
To the novice Zhao Li, he showed the original intent of leaving home: for what purpose? To sever affection and bid farewell to kin—how could this be a trivial matter?
If one does not seek liberation through the *kāṣāya*, the gate of the pines will instead become an Iron Ring Mountain.
Inscription on the Wall of Dongshan Temple:

Dongshan lies but a few feet away, merging into the misty heights. In the deep forest, the sun shines through as the rain falls in fine spray. The sounds of the flowing stream harmonize with the clamor of the marketplace.
What meets the eye is clearly the ultimate teaching.
On a wall in an inn midway on my journey, I saw a verse by Master Da, along with its title:
"You reached Caoxi and I did not come; I reached Caoxi and you had already left.
Coming and going, there is fundamentally no mind— Who would have known we would meet upon this narrow path?"
The stone for refuge was, without cause, tainted by a single thought of foulness. From this point on, the burdens of the physical form were no longer light.
For ten years, in the places where hunters spread their nets among the thickets, the stones filling one’s eyes were all non-arising (*anutpāda*).
I command my junior disciple Dayi to read the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:
its jade thread and golden needle are not easily passed through. Cease seeking the azure sky by questioning the bright moon. The path to the profound barrier is severed and there is no news;
when you go out and meet people, do not transmit this recklessly.
Question: When Grand Councilor Ding Youwu was ill, who in the world knew his body within that illness?
Only Vimalakīrti sat alone and beheld the partial truth. Let the great wisdom of his torrential eloquence be as it may;
a single silence reveals the springtime of the myriad phenomena.
The two attendants of Shiguo Hongfu Hall have returned to their former mountain;
though ten thousand waters and ten thousand mountains lie between us, they have come to inquire after me. That first step from the heels is most intimate;
do not let them stumble and fall over the precipice, for even if they emerge their heads, they will have already lost the truth.
Vast and boundless, mist and water—how lonely the view! Why do I ask passersby whether [the person] is here? Turning my head, ten thousand mountains pierce the very bones with their clarity;
yet the spring colors still fill the level marshes.
Presented by me to the Venerable Yinting upon his request to take the Tripitaka back to Yanxiang Temple in Nanxiong:
Ever since the time Nanquan crossed the ridge, The imperial ink at Caoxi remains fresh and dripping. Now, once again, these precious cases are carried forth;
I wait to see the rain and dew descend upon this scorched land.
Seeing off the Chan practitioner Go as he returns to Jihwa:
A single leaf floats upon the vast, boundless expanse; misty waters stretch afar, making it hard to find the ford. Returning to his mountain home, the vitality of life is full;
amidst the depths of a hundred flowers, birds sing out in spring.

I see that you have indeed crossed waters and climbed mountains; how magnificent! Wearing straw sandals, you came from afar from Jingting Mountain. Upon entering the gate, a single smile dispensed with the distinction between host and guest.
Do not say that Vimalakīrti’s mouth was closed.
**Inscription on the Buddha’s Austerities at the Snowy Mountains** Ten thousand peaks and ice connect root and branch in frost; A single body and mind are chilled to the very bone.
Were it not for reviving once more from within death, How could one possibly dry up the consciousness and emotions?

Without cause, he has cast aside the station of the Golden Wheel; he has specifically caused great doubt to arise among those on earth. This is a matter of profound secrecy within the nine-layered palace;
from of old, it was not permitted for outsiders to know.

Lightly casting off Tuṣita, he entered the royal palace; a single glance and a turn of the head—his thoughts were inexhaustible. He rushed toward ten thousand mountains and a thousand fathoms of snow;
his body was buried, with not a breath of wind passing through from any side.
The mind was like ice and frost, the bones like firewood; for six years of freezing hunger, his mouth could not open.
Who would have known that upon suddenly beholding the morning star, he attained a smile so full it filled his cheeks?
Reply to the Letter of Congratulations from Magistrate Dingzhai:
A single phrase newly encompasses heaven and earth; A thunderclap in the clear sky clears away the smoke and dust. Where the arrowheads meet, there is no room for evasion;
