Meeting on a narrow path—this is an old friend.
The blue lion and white elephant ride amidst the clouds; golden hue and silver light emerge from the same source.
If you ask for the essential meaning of non-arising, it is the wind and rain roaring through the tall pines in the empty mountains.
To Mr. Ou Yuzhong, who transmits the scriptures at Heli Monastery:
This Way is profound and subtle, like a single thread; it relies entirely upon the power of faith to be sustained.
Were it not for a piece of adamantine ground, it would be difficult to cause the leaves of Bodhi to shine with brilliance.
Seeing off Dharma Master Lètián as he returns to Mount Kuānglú:
The mountain colors and lake light open like a single mirror. Mañjuśrī has mistakenly descended into this midst.
Do not let the lion lightly snap its tongue, For fear it might shake the ancient lecture platform of yore.
A Gift for the Western Monk from the West:
A blue-eyed barbarian from the West has come; He once broke a single stalk of reed while crossing the river. Now his shadow remains within the stone chamber;
I ask you: does he exist in a former life, or not?
For five years, I have thrice knocked at the Zen barrier of Master Benlai. On this day, he seeks his teacher and does not return;
it is likely not at the White Gavel in Doushuai Monastery, but rather he has gone to Mount Wutai to listen to the Dharma.
I escorted the Chan master Ruzheng back to Mount Wutai with a sandalwood image;
amidst the red clouds and scorching sun of this vast wilderness, the golden light pervades the ancient site of enlightenment.
Were it not for Mañjuśrī’s own manifestation, who would know that every place is Qingliang?
The pure Dharma-body of sandalwood from the seashore, with its boundless marks and signs, conceals itself within a speck of dust;
now clearly carved out for all people to behold—this fresh phrase strikes the vital point face-to-face.
I recall Master Dajian, with whom I shared the dharma seat thirty years ago; since we parted, news has been cut off from our distant lands. Suddenly I hear he now dwells amidst a thousand peaks;
I imagine his mind is already empty as he perceives the wondrous fragrance.
The incense and lamps at Caoxi’s stupa are as if they were lit all at once;
his descendants keep watch through the silent night. The offerings of tea and soup seem just like those made during his lifetime;
he has not betrayed the stone that fell upon his waist in years past.
Exhorting the disciples of Caoxi:
these ten verses, chanted in harmony by a thousand monks, resemble the assembly at Vulture Peak. That the great multitude relies upon this teaching is no small matter;
were it not for having received the direct entrustment, how could one pass through the Patriarch’s barrier?
The physical body is present right now, just as it was when born. Morning and evening, with tea and soup, let sincerity emerge. The bells and drums clearly and constantly preach the Dharma;
there is no need for bitter words or repeated admonitions.
The seeds of the field of merit must be planted deeply; cause and effect are like facing a bright mirror.
Though you have reached the Mountain of Jewels ten million times, this time you must not return empty-handed once more.
Labor diligently in your tasks; do not shrink from toil. One may recall how, in years past, a stone fell upon one’s waist. When a single breath ceases, ten million kalpas pass;
if roots of goodness are not planted, suffering shall be difficult to dispel.
Do not let your life pass away in negligence; the light of time passes like an arrow and is truly startling.
I fear that once the breath has vanished from the three-inch space of the mouth, when will you ever again traverse the Jewel Mountain?
The grove of merit and virtue must not be treated lightly; at every step, one must maintain clear awareness.
Do not allow yourself to stumble and follow after others, lest you become like a blind man walking again in the night.
A single rafter or a shard of tile is formed through manifold conditions; do not treat the fat and marrow of faithful offerings with contempt.
Do not, in your greed, covet another’s donkey-dung tethering stake, lest you casually exchange away your own pair of eyes.
Faith and sincerity are more precious than Mount Sumeru; not even a grain of rice or a stalk of firewood may be treated with deceit. Behold those with fur and horns:
they repay their karmic debts from former lives within the bitter hells.

Fortunate to be born in the Middle Kingdom and early to leave the dust of the world; wearing the *kāṣāya* and distancing myself from my six kin, I enjoy the pure blessings of the Gate of Emptiness—how can I repay the kindness of the Patriarchs?
From youth one can maintain a mind directed upward; though starting from a mere hair’s tip, it will eventually grow to a thousand fathoms.
One must simply endure the hardships of frost and ice before finally attaining the quality of timber to emerge from the Deng Forest.

Showing that the novice Caoxi, Nengxin, possesses profound wisdom and thorough understanding; having washed away all impurities and mastered the texts, he has now begun transcribing the Avataṃsaka Sūtra—seven verses on this occasion.
He shatters minute particles to bring forth the Great Scripture; the boundless oceans of lands reflect one another. The sound of pines and the song of birds are clearly manifest.
It is said: It depends solely on the person to listen with focused intent.
The Buddha-realm is layered and immeasurable; how could the samādhi at the tip of a hair be ordinary? One must know that when the hand is raised, the entire body is revealed;
at every point of contact, the light of the Sea-Seal is fully manifest.

As they fly one after another, their geese’ shadows fall upon the cold void; whether upright, vertical, horizontal, or slanting, they simply follow the wind. Do not seek wondrous practices from Samantabhadra;
first, you must recognize the true host.
When will the Vairocana pavilion open? A mere snap of the fingers awaits the awakening of Sudhana. Suddenly one beholds the inexhaustible treasury within the pavilion;
how wondrous are these successive realms of the Buddha!
Worship Mañjuśrī on the eastern side of Fucheng; seeking true knowledge, one arrives at the edge of the sea. The fifty-three patriarchs are harmonized as one;
there is no need for the toil of traveling vast distances.
Even if the ocean waves were used as ink, they would surely dry; if the brush were as vast as Mount Sumeru, it would not be difficult to lift.
To delineate the Flower Treasury World of Vairocana—who can behold even its very first character?
Paper, ink, and written words are all not real; the true scripture lies entirely in the splitting of a single atom.
If you can cause every character to manifest in radiant clarity, do not say that Mañjuśrī is the wise one.
I send these greetings from Wanwo Temple to Master Ilsan;
it has been twenty years since we last inquired after one another’s health. Though we have met again as if in our first encounter, I now gaze afar at the moon over Zhongtiao Mountain;
there is but its pure light alone illuminating my bamboo-thatched hut.
Entrusted to High Attendant Chang:
Recalling the Past When we parted in Chang’an, we spoke of old; In the falling snow, we clasped arms at the parting ways.
Now, ten thousand *li* beyond the scorched wilderness, A single thought of pure coolness—you alone know it.
I present this to Master Yi of He-lin, who has long dwelt beneath the Bodhi tree. From time to time he walks and circumambulates the tree in contemplation.
Looking back to the day when the tree was first planted, I recall that his own hands once applied the sealing clay.
Presented to Yan Xingyuan, the Physician:
The myriad herbs on the Snow Mountain grow lush and verdant; Picking them up at random, he employs them with skillful mastery. He is no ordinary physician of the state;
How could he allow them to lie in wasteful disarray, resenting the spring breeze?
Presented to the Elder Taeho:
We met long ago within the Diamond Mound; with snow-white hair disheveled, his spirit remains more majestic than ever.
Still intoxicated by a single cup of glass-like tea, I vaguely recall the old man who tended the cattle.
Seeing you off, Attendant Xian, as you travel to Mount Wutai and inquire after Master Kongyin:
From the burning house you have entered the Cool Land; ten thousand li, do not say the road is long. If you should meet Mañjuśrī, ask after his news:
How many monasteries remain now within the excavated valley?
Passing by the Bodhi Tree at Fahsing Temple, I pay homage to the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch.

Under this ancient Bodhi tree we have met once more; though a thousand years have passed, our spirits remain the same. The sound of bells and drums has faded, yet the fragrance of incense never ceases;
why do you, my descendant, seek the traces of the profound?
As I see off Chan practitioner Jiai on his journey to visit various teachers, I entrust him with a single bowl of Caoxi water to sprinkle throughout all quarters as the five flavors of Chan.
Do not say that old Hanzhuang has no Dharma to speak; even now, it is not worth half a coin.

I send you, O awakened and lucid master, to pay homage at Potalaka, where the waves do not stir and the white flowers bloom on the mountain. The face of the Great Being is like the full moon in the cold sky;
if you encounter him before the cliff, you must listen to the Universal Gate with reverent devotion.
I rejoice in my nephew Faxing’s extensive travels;
I recall the year we parted from home and left our ancestors. You must still be as you were before birth.
From this place where we meet across ten thousand li, a single smile traces back to our karmic ties from past lives.
Question: Wandering among the rocks of Yang, one asks about illness;
inquiring after the sickness within the body at Vaiśālī—among these, which can be scrutinized as truly real?
One need only strip away the layers of heavy darkness until, at last, the harmony of the great earth’s spring is revealed.
Sengxing comes to visit Master Laiyi on his pilgrimage:

The vast expanse of misty waters stretches boundlessly. Turning back, the mountain city lies behind him through a hundred layers. He journeys thus solely to seek a teacher and inquire into the ultimate matter:
"Virtue Cloud is not upon the Wondrous High Peak."
Recalling the Thousand-Buddha Temple at Dadu, I remember of old the terraces of a thousand flowers and seven jewels. Each flower and each leaf was a Tathāgata;
I know not whether the Buddhas amidst the flowers these days can still sound the Dharma-thunder as they did in years past.
To Zen practitioner Nengzhe:
You have reached Caoxi without straying from the path; your journey before your eyes is not yet far. Try looking back toward where you first departed:
the fragrant grasses stretch on and on—where is home?
I visited Layman Wang at Qingliang to discuss Chan together on a snowy night; it has now been twenty years since that parting. I have constantly remembered the true countenance of Vimalakīrti;
how many times has the bright moon become full in the cold sky?
Once again at Faxing Temple, Master Xijiong returned from his pilgrimage to Putuo;
for three years he has not sat upon the Bodhi tree. A single thought constantly suspends the lamp of Prajñā. Do not say that the dhūta practitioner is too weary to preach the Dharma;
it is simply that his karmic conditions for the Way differ from those of the monks in the hunting forests.
A Verse on the Lankā Chamber, Sent to the Layman Tianyu Kong:
The surging sea of poison is vast and boundless; At night, the rākṣasas make this their home.
Only here lies the priceless jewel of Laṅkā, Its radiance shining day and night upon worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The body of eight facets radiates light and is most perfectly round; though the vajra be sharp, it cannot pierce it.
At all times, it is enshrined within the palace of the mind-king, illuminating and shattering the three thousandfold world system and the great chiliocosm.
Snow Tea from Caoxi was sent to Master Zhen of Jinnshan, who had plucked a branch of its earliest spring leaves.
Sent to this crane-boned, ailing master, he brewed a cup and tasted it for himself;
was it like the time he first visited Zhaozhou?
In the spring of the *jiachen* year, having received orders to return to my post, my boat moored at Zhijiang.
The two masters Yi and Heng, along with Qinan, Yuzhong, Zhongqian, and other disciples came to visit me. Thus I composed this verse:
Tethered for a time to a solitary boat beside the willow shade, Sitting in stillness, it is just like the Jetavana Grove. Beneath the Bodhi tree, I am ever in attendance.
The assembly marveled that Dao was able to come and inquire about the sound of the Dharma;

he demonstrated that the mountains, rivers, great earth, and all things down to a single mote of dust are the work of the geomancer Liang Sheng. Only when the Dharma-eye is perfectly clear does one first see the truth; from this point on, one seeks the place of ultimate rest.
Abiding thus, he would never allow such a person to be buried and lost in the mundane world.
He showed this to Imprint Master Zong of Mount Luofu.
Beneath Mount Luofu, the winding Ganges River flows; the *Jetavana* grove by the riverbank resembles Potalaka. If you ask about the flower within, contemplate it yourself.
Look: the bright moon falls upon the clear waves. Presented to Zhou the Physiognomist, who wanders the rivers and lakes with a mere blade of kua grass at his waist.
His art of divining the spirit and mind comes from Huchou; If anyone asks him of prosperity or decline, he simply says: In the end, it all depends on the clarity of one's own heart.
Matter: A single segment of true light resides within the two eyes.

To reveal one's nature is like the matter of a Chan practitioner from Ji who traveled south to study with Sudhana; seeking out spiritual friends, he wandered for a long time, yet at the summit of Mount Miao, no trace remained.
Traces. Do not say that Mañjuśrī pointed them out in error.
To the Zen practitioner Shenglín of Pútuó:
beneath Mount Pútuó, in the village of Báihuā, the sound of the tide preaches the Universal Gate day and night. I ask you: where does your hermitage reside?
There was. I merely heard that the parrot announced it was dusk.
I heard that Master Xinglai had received full ordination at Yunqi; upon his return, I sent him a verse of inquiry:
"A single staff, alive like a dragon, has long been his companion as he ascended Tianzhu Peak. He has now gone to Yunqi himself to hear the Dharma."
Afterwards, all conditions may suddenly become empty at once.

On a summer day in the mountains, with a bamboo bed and a ceramic pillow, the pine breeze is sufficient; one’s midday nap is deep and intoxicating, and in dreams, the four limbs and hundred perceptions all arise as empty.
Guest: I do not know who the host is.
In the still night, the sound of the bell;
the bell’s sound resonates through the clear night in the cold void. A single strike is like the wind blowing through ten thousand apertures. It is no idle urging for the dragon to listen.
Dharma. One should mostly awaken the host and show that the Great Way of Taihe Zhou has always been right before one's eyes;
yet instead, people seek withered meditation in the realm of death. Who knows that in daily life, it is present at every turn?
All phenomena are entirely the supreme conditions of non-arising.

How can the power of the Way compare to the power of karma? Within this, one must carefully contemplate what is raw and what is ripe. When encountering circumstances at the critical moment, one can respond with flexibility;
thus, the frantic madness of deluded wandering is suddenly stilled.
Showing the Elder Yuantong the Total Retention:
A single stream from Caoxi flows to the West River. Mazu suffered a headache—who could have healed it?
If you seek the "life-giving medicine" from Yuantong, the story of the dead cat’s head is most worthy of contemplation.
I tell Gong Sheng Boqi that traveling thousands of miles to seek out a kindred spirit is simply to look for this mind among others.
Only when you meet face-to-face and behold one another in person will you realize that all your past searching was in vain.
To Chan Master Ciming Xian:
With a single staff you have come from afar from Many Treasures Stupa; seeking the Way southward through misty waters, you alone floated your bowl.
On your return journey, should you pass by the road of Caoxi, beware the slippery moss after the rains—do not tread upon it.
Written on the occasion of revisiting Yangcheng in the summer of the Wushen year:
Thirteen years have already passed since I left Xiancheng; In the human world, sixty years have now elapsed. Looking back upon the mundane realm, it is like a dream;
I know not what karmic conditions will ultimately determine its end.
In those years, with a single bowl, he traveled through all quarters; wherever he reached, famous mountains were his sites of practice.
Having consumed the rice-less meals provided by donors, even now the price remains a matter for deliberation.
Five terraces, a thousand feet of snow covering the head; one might think that with the cold ashes extinguished, all is over.
Who would have thought that from a single spark of fire, the great earth is scorched and flows forth once more?
In the Eastern Sea, he once braved ten-thousand-li surging waves; thundering like crashing lightning, the wave crests shattered the rocks.
Lightly riding a single leaf upon the wind, he went straight to the Three Mountains to fish for the six giant turtles.
The attendant of the True Position has reached the very limit of the hundred-foot pole on the precipice; to move even a single step is most difficult.
He is simply taught to let go and turn the body over, not to be viewed as a mere wildcat or an ox.
To Chan Practitioner Shiyue:
Reciting the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the misty waters of a hundred cities appear as if they were heaven. Where shall we meet to inquire of Samantabhadra? I imagine you have passed atop Mount Miaofeng;
I do not know if you have ever recounted these causes and conditions.
Showing the virtue of the rice-head:
When will Deshan’s alms-bowl arrive? Changsha’s removal of the rice—do not guess recklessly. Do not borrow from the Fragrant Accumulation Heaven above;
the matter by the hearth is truly marvelous!
I entrust this to Master Miaofeng of Mount Wutai, in a world of glass and a palace of crystal. Golden hues and silver radiance are identical everywhere.
Solely treading the steps of the golden-maned lion, he wanders through the eight directions where not a breath of wind can pass.
With bones like frost and crane, hair as white as silver—who could recognize this as the final incarnation of Mañjuśrī?
Since the moment we parted from within the pit, not even a single atom has separated us until now.
Carrying my staff across my shoulder, I wander through oceans of lands; boundless realms are gathered within a single speck of dust. At leisure, I split open a mote of dust to look;
the empty flowers have all fallen away, leaving only my two eyes.
A thousand-fathom cold cliff, a hundred-foot ice sheet—back then, we sat together facing this jagged precipice.
Now, in the realm of coolness within the burning house, there is one Vimalakīrti and one monk.
Sent to Master Kongyin of Mount Wutai:

I think of you from afar as you sport amidst the groves of various flowers, Sitting alone in the shade of precious sandalwood trees. Without moving the faculty of your tongue, you constantly preach the Dharma;
Ten thousand people at times hear your voice like the sound of the ocean tide.
First, I cast my body into the surging waves of the miasmic sea; amidst the蛮烟 (man-yān) and poisonous mists, I ate my fill. Returning home, I thirstily drank the waters of Caoxi;
they were no less refreshing than a bone-chilling coldness.
At Caoxi, the host of Zisun Zhuang reports:
One night, with the eastern wind, the purple shoots grew plump; boundless spring colors reached his thatched gate. Peach blossoms fill the eyes, yet no one asks;
who can recommend the principle beyond the "Facing South" (Danyang)?
Resting branches, hidden within the white gate; deeply secluded, a single branch finds peace. Mountains and waters delight the mind as worldly thoughts fade away.
Having once entered the inner chamber of Vimalakīrti, hundreds of thousands of samādhis reside upon the tip of a single hair.
To Zen practitioner Gao:

Closing the retreat, the six windows are tightly shut so that not a breath of wind passes through. For what purpose do you hide your body within this? Try it at the place where Mañjuśrī snapped his fingers;
there, you must directly force open the great void.
Presented to Chan Master Rong upon his appointment as the abbot of Zhongxiao Temple by Grand Marshal Guo of Taishou:
Originally from a land of pestilence and miasma, In three lifetimes you have again forged karmic ties with a high official.
In the chamber of Vimalakīrti, there is not a single word; Do not say that silence is not Zen.
Manifesting the intent of the Hall Master Xiuhuai, these three mysteries of the upward path cause doubt at every step. Who can know that single phrase prior to words?
Unless one lets go completely from the edge of a precipice, one will bring shame upon the two brows given by one’s mother.
Inscribed for Master Guifeng of Mount Ling:
The assembly at Mount Ling remains vividly present; Cypresses and pines fill the Deer Park like gathering clouds.
Since the Dharma-body constantly preaches the Dharma, The bells and drums clearly announce the arrival of dusk.
Sent from beyond the kalpas of the Eastern Sea by a Dharma Master who personally received the entrustment on Vulture Peak, this Dharma assembly is now opened upon the seashore.
How many times have the hosts of Māra from the summit of Laṅkā Mountain come to this lecture hall to hear the sutra?
To the practitioners of Nan Chan, I show this:
when asking about the body within the illness of Vimalakīrti, who knows that it is one among the sick?
Twice a day of gruel and rice, three meals of medicine—when these are consumed with clarity, the intent is most intimate.
Entrusting myself to Layman Lài Gǔxiān, who observes a lifelong fast in a single room and serves the King of Emptiness; from time to time, he burns the incense of Prajñā within his mind.
Far off, I imagine the place where he sits in full lotus posture as the days grow long, quietly listening to the birds’ songs as they emerge from the mountain light.

I send this message of thanks to the Layman of the Blue Lotus, who ever remembers the body of the Layman of the Blue Lotus; in dreams and in spirit, he often faces the person within the mirror. I know that you have deeply realized the state of non-arising;
you trust in yourself to dwell amidst the dust without being stained by the dust.
Having weathered all storms while dwelling on Mount Dinghu,
I have long since trained this mind to forget artifice. Turning my back, I enter directly into the midst of a thousand peaks,
sitting and watching as idle clouds drift through the day.
Master Mingzong once received the signal from Tuṣita;
having once accepted the golden razor, his Dharma-eye was opened. Now, in these present times, he transmits the proclamation, teaching nothing but to cleanse the dust from level ground.

When I parted from you, Master Yunji, with knees pressed together by the riverbank, I turned my head; the green mountains entered my dreams and thoughts. I ask the thousands and hundreds of beings at the Flower Terrace:
how many among you know that single phrase prior to words?

Master Jichao, you have donned the clouds and girded yourself with the moon, weathering wind and frost; on these long, clear nights, your crane-like dreams stretch far. Having finished reading the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the incense seals burn fine and slow;
I know that you have nothing left to contemplate.

Master Fayu has long manifested from Vulture Peak to respond to the capacities of those present. When someone asks, clouds arise and flower-rain falls. Do not say that the Dharma assembly is now silent;
for you, Master Xuezhong, have become the refuge for the multitude.
Manifesting the sign of *zhongfu* (the hexagram of sincerity), he shows how to transcend worldly conditions through meditation;
look at this, for when one returns from breaking through, it is no easy matter to bloom a lotus flower within the fire.
One must thoroughly wash away both the sense organs and their objects, lest one enter that womb again.
To the Zen practitioner Wuzhijian:

The Buddha-nature is luminously clear and fundamentally unobstructed; it was only from a single prior thought that you went astray. Having long since lost your footing, you have sunk deep into the sea of birth and death;
this time, do not fail the lotus flower.
The Chan practitioner Weimi has arrived from afar at Mount Funiu with his alms-bowl bag. Crossing the ridges, the cold plum blossoms are in full bloom. If you ask for the intimate verse of Caoxi:
"There is no tree of Bodhi; the mirror is not a stand."
To the Chan practitioner Nengzhi Han:
With a shaven head and square robes, your body is adorned with the eight auspicious signs. The original intent of leaving the household life was to transcend the mundane world;
yet if you allow yourself to be buried by the light dust of afflictions, when you emerge once more, you will have already lost the truth.
I entrust this to Chan Master Zhan, who dwells at Mount Funiu;
once he held a single almsbowl and traveled to Caoxi. How could he have shunned the arduous journey as he walked alone with his staff?
I hear that in a place deeply hidden among ten thousand mountains, the setting sun slants down as birds vie to sing.
An Inscription for Guo Cigong’s “Thusness” Hermitage:
In the past, Śrāvastī once opened the Jeta Grove; Now you, sir, again conceive the heart to spread the golden ground.
Where the Dharma King thus fully upholds the teaching, Only Mañjuśrī is granted the appreciation of its true sound.
In response to Guo Yunsu’s former inquiry at Caoxi regarding the Supreme Vehicle: "The esoteric intent of the West belongs to Nan Neng;
do not say that Vimalakīrti was one who kept his mouth shut—he was no ordinary monk with hair on his head back then."
An Inscription for Guo Shuzi’s Taiyi Nangquan Pavilion:
The clear pool reflects the moon’s deep, shadowy image; The "pouch" of water embodies the heart that delivers all across rivers and lakes.
If one asks where the roaming fish find true glory, Perhaps even the banks of the Hao River do not truly understand them.

Chan practitioner Hongfan bows in gratitude before the precious throne of a thousand flowers; having already sought the Three Mysteries from Linji, he now comes further to inquire about the path of Caoxi.
Clouds fill the green mountains, and the moon fills the heavens.
Entrusting this to Dharma Master Yunna:
at Dangyang, he split open a single atom. He personally employs the staff as he idly lifts it; under the moon at night, the tiger is beneath the cliff.
Taking refuge is still like the person of former times.
A monk departs to create a sandalwood image and returns to Chaling;

a branch of South Sea sandalwood incense. The Dharma-body manifests wherever it may be; his twin brows meet as he is welcomed back beneath the silent shade of pines, appearing just like the time when he held up the flower without speaking.
Presented to Mr. Guo Lingxi:

Maintaining a long fast, you embroider the Buddha to worship the King of Emptiness; The burning house is transformed into a field for selecting Buddhas. At night, you trim the bright lamp until the mind is utterly still;
There is no need to imagine the Western Paradise through the lotus flower.
Leaving for Mount Nanyue, Ten Poems on Parting from My Disciples in the Dharma Community of Lingnan.
One fall into the dust of the world, twenty years have passed; To meet again, one must surely believe it was a karmic bond from before.
Since the robe and bowl were brought southward, Today we once more take up the Zen of Direct Pointing.
This matter is clearly present within one’s own person; there is no need to seek outside for understanding or success.
If you can simply turn the light back upon every contact, do not allow yourself to be trapped by worldly toil.

The Great Way has from the beginning been devoid of fundamental reality; it is mostly due to discrimination that one forcibly distinguishes between the distant and the intimate. One must directly see through the face given by one's mother;
only then is one a person of distinction amidst the dust of the world.
Having drunk the miasmic vapors to the dregs, my teeth still shiver with cold; I no longer recall the hardships of the roads traveled before.
From here, deep within the dense embrace of ten thousand mountains, I shall behold the five-colored clouds and mists from within my very seat.
For twenty years I have galloped through pestilential lands; as the years passed, I did not realize my hair had turned white as frost. Now I depart upon a single-leafed skiff;
my traces shall surely be hidden within ten thousand gorges.

For long I have mingled my traces among the dust and toil, harmonizing with the light; I was merely busy picking up and pointing out this very matter. A thousand-foot fishing pole has been nearly worn away;
turning my head toward the sea and heavens, all is once more vast and boundless.
First, take refuge and circumambulate the Dharma altar. From time to time, seek peace for this mind. Do not say you will depart three thousand li away;
the bright moon is in the center of the sky, to be beheld face-to-face.
At that time, grasping the fishing line, one beholds the pure heart. Having finished singing the bamboo-branch song, how many can truly understand?
Returning in a small boat through the frosty night, where shall one seek the bright moon amidst the reeds?
In the cold sky, the cries of solitary geese ring out clearly; from now on, their tracks shall fall upon the Five Lakes.
Boundless mist and waves harbor my sorrowful thoughts; a single sail upon the horizon is the path home.
For the sake of the Dharma, one would rather endure the length of distant roads; how could it be said that the miasmic seas constitute the edge of the world?
Repeatedly taking a single drop of Caoxi’s water, he irrigates the five-leaved flowers that came from the West.
The Dream-Travel Collection of the Elder Hanshan, Volume Thirty-Seven;
The Dream-Travel Collection of the Elder Hanshan, Volume Thirty-Eight.
Compiled by the Attendant Fushan, Daily Record.
Compiled by the Disciple Tonghyeung;
Revised by the Disciple from Yeongnam, Liu Qixiang.
Verse One.
Ten Verses for Zi-yin, Son of Zou:
This matter is manifest and utterly without concealment; it is revealed everywhere under heaven and across the earth, majestic and open.
If a man does not suddenly pierce the adamantine eye, he will look directly at the essence of reality as if facing a blank wall.
Seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are all but empty flowers. While the cataract has not yet been removed, what one sees is distorted.
One must wait for the clear sky and the pure eye before realizing there is a distinct and excellent way of life.

Within the field of sound and form, how could this be by mere chance? One brings upon oneself thorns that pierce the heavens with bitterness. Who can cast a single throw and turn their body out [of the trap]?
Only then will one believe in the Zen of spontaneous freedom.
The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous, its original source being true; from the beginning it has been pure and bright, utterly free from even the slightest speck of dust.
Not allowing delusive defilements to lightly obscure or obstruct it, one is immediately a person of transcendent and great power.
The mind of the Way is fundamentally not separate from the ordinary; it is busy with the affairs of welcoming guests and receiving visitors. Try to examine the pivotal mechanism within this:
how could it have ever moved so much as a single hair’s breadth?

Within the mountain of the five aggregates lies the field of tranquil extinction; the six windows are vast and open, where light arises in the night. One need only call forth the master within the hut;
do not allow dullness and torpor to shroud and conceal him.
The profound radiance of the mind is fundamentally free from delusion; it is only because of emotional thoughts that they drift apart. Simply observe where they arise and there will be no trace;
let the cries of the monkey go on day and night as it pleases.
The sky of one's nature is clear of clouds; the lunar orb stands solitary. Why need one inquire whether body and world exist or not?
If only the traces of worldly attachments are severed, there is no need to labor to inscribe one's name upon the rivers and lakes.
Worldly conditions pursue one incessantly; when will they ever cease? Abandoning the mountain home to seek elsewhere, the bright pearl beneath the robes remains buried;
on the long road, one needlessly harbors only poverty and sorrow.
A flash of lightning in the vast void leaves no trace; how can likes and dislikes be allowed to march in formation? I shall tear asunder your mother-born true face;
would I ever allow it to be buried and wasted for the rest of my life?
I recall once sending a letter to Yuan Sheng, in which I asked about the Dharma from afar regarding the Supreme Vehicle. I knew that samādhi could be entered through written words,
yet I did not know if he remembered the monk from those bygone days.
To Zen practitioner Suiten:
It is no easy matter for a teacher and disciple to meet. The message within this state is difficult to put into words.
At the place where one walks upon the summit of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, it is not a mere empty deception of Sudhana.
I show Tanfu that he once followed the Bestowal of Prophecy toward Mount Ling; today he comes again to strike at the barrier.
To ask about the matter of the Flower-holding on that day—how could the Dhūta have easily revealed his countenance?

I tell Zhong Shengheng that it has already been ten years since you passed by Caoxi; that we have met as fellow practitioners is entirely due to our prior karmic ties. Why must Mr. Ruan weep on his lonely journey?
There is, after all, the supreme Chan that has come from the West.
Pointing out the way, the mind of awakening is revealed;

the light alone stands bare beyond the physical form. If one can penetrate the Patriarch’s intent, the opportune words lie before them. I imagine you have long been steeped in the lotus-drip of meditation at Mount Kuang;
thus I have come once more to unravel these old causes and conditions.
To Zen practitioner Changda:
The single stream from Mount Heng to Caoxi has been transmitted down to us. It is said that even the bright mirror is not the stand itself; the adamantine true eye is shared by all people.
You must open it within the phrase "grinding a tile."
To the Chan practitioner Zongxuan:
The five aggregates are illusory and originally empty; to seek them with intent is like trying to catch the wind.
Try this after your entire body has dissolved away—you must recognize the true host.

I, Yongzhi, a humble mountain master of Nanyue, dwell in a single-thatch hermitage deep within ten thousand mountains. Morning and evening, amidst the clouds and mists, I offer this small discourse for your contemplation: "Most especially, the sound of the stream cannot be kept out;
day and night it speaks in a continuous murmur."
Seventy years spent dwelling on Nanyue Mountain have passed in dreams; my traces upon the rivers and lakes were all in vain.
Now, having fortunately attained this field of leisure, do not ask how things were in the past.
My heels have trodden through every corner of the Water-Cloud Realm; yet I have not left the ancient site of the Qingliang Monastery. My physical strength gradually declines and my heart grows weary;
to sleep in peace and eat to satiety is my way of withdrawing from the world.
The place of great rest is extraordinary; when delusive thoughts dissolve, the world is forgotten.
All seek true Sukhāvatī elsewhere, yet who knows that the present moment itself is the Western Land?
One perceives only the mind of birthless quiescence; how could delusive thoughts dare to invade it? The sense organs and their objects are all but shadows of empty flowers;
why seek Buddhas and Patriarchs elsewhere?
Observing the place where the mind arises, one realizes it is birthless; within a flash of lightning, the eyes become doubly clear. I ask: what is accomplished by that which came from the West?
Nowadays, people only know how to hasten their journey.
When Shishi asked the monk Mijie of Luling, "How are the prices of rice in Luling lately? Mijie simply replied, "It has ceased entirely.
If one can but lightly chew a single grain, Only then will one know that the Buddha-dharma is not at all much.
To the Chan practitioner Du Yan:
The Chan of Master Ma’s single stream from the West—though one hears it was long lost to transmission—do not say that polishing a tile can serve as a mirror;
naturally, one does not fall by the wayside.
To the Chan practitioner Dingshui:
Having long relied upon the lotus seat to seek the true exposition, the bell and drum are distinct—every phrase is profound.
If you ask for the definitive meaning of the Westward Transmission, it has never been transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs from the beginning.

When the Chan practitioner Shiliangkong received guests at Wuchang and heard that a Buddhist monastery was being opened on the riverbank, he remarked as the wind-swept travelers were crossing the ford:
"How many know that the one fishing at Huating is three inches away from the hook?"
Inscribed at Fangjue’s Vigata-mala Hermitage:
Within this hermitage, as small as a mustard seed, not a speck of dust remains; From the beginning, there has been nothing with which one can associate.
Contemplating in stillness the ground of quiescent extinction and cool clarity, One suddenly beholds the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma-body.
Inscription for the Kṣānti Hermitage:
Self and others are like space, ungraspable; The boundless great ocean is but a single bubble. Look only at where it arises—there is no trace;
Let suffering and joy cease right here and now.

To Zen practitioner Tianyuan, I show that the matter within one's own person is exceedingly clear. There is no need to seek a teacher or undergo the hardship of a long journey; simply realize it directly before your very eyes.
Who is it that sees forms and hears sounds?
The six meanings of Chan are revealed;
do not deliberate upon the great matter of birth and death. To speak of it arouses sorrowful thoughts that can break one's heart. For immeasurable kalpas we have utterly missed the mark;
how could we now bear to betray the Empty King?
I address this to Dharma Master Ruomai, who dwells in a hermitage beneath Lotus Peak. Day after day he is in close company with the five elders among the clouds;
as the waterfall falls from the void scattering jade-like flakes, it is as if host and guest are engaged in conversation.
I tell you, Zen practitioner Changyuan of Yunju, your original purpose in entering the world was to investigate this mind; it was not to seek fame or to have your name hung in the monastic groves.
When you reach the state of no-mind through the primary koan, do not seek it outside of that source.
Entrusting this to the Abbot of Haihui:
The ocean-assemblies of the ten directions are one’s home; coming and going along the path, the way is never mistaken. Having eaten one’s fill of fragrant food, turn back and depart;
once you have left the gate, the misty waters stretch beyond all bounds.
In response to Master Yu’s transmission of his new commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra*:
The single assembly at Vulture Peak has required deliberation for over forty years; now, after long concealment, it is revealed in its entirety.
Clearly, it resides within a mere hair’s breadth.
The gate is tightly shut, blocking all passage; with much hesitation, one sighs at the end of the road.
Were it not for the power of a light, effortless snap of the fingers, how could one know that within lies a capacity as vast as space?
When the impoverished son returns and beholds his father, this mind is entrusted with total confidence and free from doubt;
even if the entire treasure store were handed over to him, he would not know it at all unless it were overturned and revealed.
The infinite oceans of lands are all a single lotus; it is a pity that those of the past merely counted the sands. You have personally pierced through this at the tip of a hair;
from this day forth, you shall forever ride the white ox-cart.
To Zen Practitioner Su Po (With Preface):

The Zen practitioner previously attended upon me at Caoxi. Having recently returned to Wumen, the two Dharma Masters Chao and Yu, noting that I and Master Ruoshi Xuelang were brothers in the Dharma gate, commissioned the Zen practitioner to carry a letter and travel far to the south.

Yue, you have welcomed me to spend my final years here. Moved by the lofty friendship of these two gentlemen and mindful of the great effort the Zen practitioner has undertaken from afar, I have composed two verses to record my sentiments.
I once paid homage at Caoxi and traveled through pestilential lands; I took refuge, circling the meditation seat three times.
This single phrase of non-arising is perfectly clear—do not say that it was concealed at that time.
From afar, I hold this single sheet of a friend’s letter; specifically, I come to this empty mountain to inquire about dwelling here.
Entrusting my entire body and mind to you alone, I need not ask how my remaining life will unfold.

In response: The dharma-gate and spiritual resonance between the two Dharma Masters, Chao and Yu, are extraordinary and beyond the mundane. From now on, the fragrance of their kinship shall pervade the green mountains.
I intend to go to the summit of Tongxuan Peak, where we may face one another in wordless silence upon a single meditation platform.
The mountains and waters of Wumen are most secluded and pure; the two lofty peaks of Lang have long been renowned.
If we may find our pact with the mists and clouds to grow old together, we shall sleep in peace and eat our fill for the remainder of our lives.
Shishufu shows a Chan practitioner from afar toward the thousand peaks to inquire after Lan Can: "The cold snot from his mouth has not yet dried; the yellow tubers have just been roasted in the fire.
Even if he were to offer them before you, they would not be easy to eat."
The Chan practitioner Dazhi, with his bamboo staff and straw sandals, has crossed ten thousand mountains; from afar he came from Nanyue to knock at the pines of this gate.
The path of Shitou is slippery and difficult to traverse—do not say that traveling to study under masters is a matter of casual ease.
Inscription for the Scroll of Meeting at Different Peaks:
Gazing south from the city wall, the misty waves stretch to the horizon. What is the matter when they meet upon the mountain peak? It is not that Sudhana lacks a face;
it is simply because his spiritual friends were deceptive and contradictory.
I inquire after the Honorable Master Heng, whose specialized wisdom is dedicated yet simple:

you have long observed the four great elements as being like bubbles and shadows. Where can the demons of illness find a place to hide their tracks? The ancients possessed their own methods for peace and leisure;
they resided solely within the single thought of non-arising.
I show you that the Zen practitioner Shiruo travels to the ends of the earth seeking this mind; from the beginning, he has always sought it outwardly.
Even before he has stepped out the door, one must believe that the weeds along the path are already deep and vast.
In a letter to Xu Meng’uo, I inquire after your body while you dwell in the illness of Vimalakīrti. When the gate of non-duality opens, the true nature is revealed.
Only after having eaten one’s fill of fragrant rice and forgotten words can one truly believe that the Way becomes intimate once free from emotional attachments.
To show that the nature and capacity of the mind-hearing practitioner are originally like space: seeing forms and hearing sounds are like trees passing through the wind.
Provided only that the floating clouds are entirely dissipated, how could a single thing ever adhere within it?
To show the true Chan practitioner of samādhi who has traveled all over the various regions visiting Mount Emei:
he would do well to let his mind rest; thus his name will not be in vain as it hangs upon the monastic forests. Returning home, his face is covered with the snow of Emei;
amidst white clouds and green mountains, where can he be sought?
At Jingshan, I showed the attendant that the flash of lightning or the spark from flint is not the truth; meeting in a fleeting moment, one must not yet presume intimacy.
If the original message is severed, the entire great thousandfold world-system manifests the whole body wherever one is.
If the Chan practitioner from Yanyue had traveled from Huangmei to Nanyue and further visited Shuangjing, [the Master] would have shown him the way with a verse:
"Traveling far to Nanyue to seek traces of practice, / Joyfully finding a single thread of connection at Huangmei, / We shall meet again elsewhere on Wufeng."
In this place, amidst ten thousand snow-clad mountains, stands an old man with white hair.

To the Zen practitioner Wuxia, who has come from afar leaning on his staff to the depths of Shuangjing: meeting you on this distant peak is like finding a true kindred spirit. Should an old friend ask after my remaining life—
The matter: ten thousand layers of clouded mountains, a single mind.
To Layman Shinianxi:
Having traveled through a hundred cities across rivers and lakes in search of the Way, when you encounter a true teacher, what shall you do? Go further into the depths of the Five Peaks.
Seek! You must know that the Buddha-dharma fundamentally has nothing more to it.
To show diligence, consider the Zen practitioner who travels from Shuangjing to pay homage at Mount Emei;
wading through waters and climbing mountains, for whose sake does he do so? If you but see the true face of Samantabhadra—
Look! Do not let this pair of eyebrows be in vain. To the Hall Master of Mount Jing, I show the single transmission of the Buddhas and Patriarchs:
the azure cliffs and verdant bamboos of the ancient forest; you should know that the true command is ever renewed.
In this place, the bells and drums constantly proclaim the wondrous sound of the Dharma.
Who knows that my master, like a phantom, suffered from cold and hunger in the frozen ravines? Only after death did he return to life, thanks to his teacher. Today, at Wufeng, we peer into the stupa.
The reflection was so vivid that it seemed as if we were still sitting face-to-face in conversation.
To Master Ren’an, he showed that his body and mind were a single expanse like a crystal pitcher; try looking within it to see whether there is anything or nothing—delusive thoughts bring no news.
Severance. Why seek further effort beyond this?
At Guo Puti Hermitage, I joyfully encountered my Dharma friend Zhihe, who was originally a person beneath the Bodhi tree.
Upon arriving, I suddenly saw my former self; the sound of the stream constantly speaks of non-arising.
The Dharma. It is a pity that people of this age do not listen with true sincerity.
Meeting beneath the tree, we share an old karmic affinity; I do not know how many lifetimes have passed since we parted. Entering the gate, a single smile brought our minds into accord;
only then did I believe that wordlessness is the secret transmission.
Shi Xun asked Nan Chan:

"What is the most supreme cause for attending to the sick and transcending the world? To see through the body within illness right before one’s eyes, And to know the point where another's pain and itch are interconnected— Among the myriad practices, no thought is more true than this.
To the Chan practitioner Shimude:

The Sea-Eye of the Sūtra-collation has from the beginning been free of even a speck of dust; the Great Radiant Treasury is where one may find rest. You need only examine it carefully from the beginning;
were even a tiny speck of dust to settle upon it, you would immediately lose the truth.
It is shown that Chan Master Feixuan once followed the structural principles of Ci'en’s teachings; casting aside his fishing rod, he has wandered through all quarters.
If you now recognize your mother’s true face, there is no need to labor your mind questioning the Dharma King.

Passing through Amṛta Reception Temple, climbing mountains and wading through waters, I was entirely lost on my way. I did not know whether the village ahead existed or not; suddenly, as I went straight on, I encountered a shower of nectar.
Upon touching but a single drop, my parched withered state was broken.
To the Zen practitioner Shishōzoku, who maintains the esoteric practices of the Vidyādhara:
the fierce flames of delusive thoughts flow on. The nectar of *amṛta* must be poured at the gateway of the crown;
only when one realization of a single drop of the teaching permeates every pore is this truly the secret cultivation of a Vidyādhara.
At the Chamber of Serene Simplicity, shown to the Layman Yunshan:
Within this chamber in the marketplace, it is as cold as ice; Sitting cross-legged, the midnight lamp burns brightly. When true adepts come and go, they fill the hall;
Everyone knows him to be a monk living at home.
To the Layman Lianxi:
When delusive thoughts arise, let them cease in that very moment. Once there is not a single thought hanging upon the mind, the forgetting of artifice is itself the true Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
Why need you seek Sukhāvatī elsewhere?

Inscription on the Ink-Light Pavilion of Master Da’s Scriptural Transcription I have heard that the lotus pen brings forth life from beneath it; The luster of the ink still illuminates the empty clarity. Leisurely, I come to inquire of the Lord within the flower:
From my ears, the sound of preaching fills me like autumnal tides.
To Cao Sheng Xiqing:
For a man of character who sets his resolve, how could it be ordinary? He has endured every hardship, from piercing his thigh to hanging himself by the beam.
Only ensure that the six sense-faculties are free from defilement, and you shall surely find the light of the mind arising within yourself.
While traveling to Mount Fushan, I heard the Zen practitioner Zhideng reciting the Lotus Sūtra at the foot of Wondrous High Peak;
I have therefore inscribed this upon the wall:
A lotus flower upon the water, a sūtra upon the tongue— A single hermitage, deeply locked, amidst ten thousand peaks of green. The pines and winds constantly proclaim it day and night.
He spoke thus: "It is a pity that people of this age do not understand what they hear.
To show the true successor:

a śrāmaṇera’s life and death are impermanent, separated by but a single breath. It is well to direct one's will toward the green mountains; one need only refrain from dwelling in the red dust of the world."
Through karma, one wins a lifelong leisure beyond the mundane world.
On Mount Kuang, I rejoice at the visit of Grand Councilor Chen Chishih;
ten thousand layers of green mountains are but a single mind. Everywhere before one’s eyes is a forest of clouds—there is no need to ask further about the West.
O mind! At times, waterfowl proclaim the wondrous sounds of the Dharma.

When Master Xiuxiu Liu closed himself within his retreat at the Ten-Thousand-Fathom Peak of Mount Jinlun, sitting alone atop that peak, he let go of body and mind—this was the total upholding of the Way. Yet, even silver mountains and iron walls must be pierced through.
Penetratingly clear—there is no permitting of knowledge.
I shall escort the Chief Seat Wuxinrong back to Jingkou and remain at Kongsan to spend my remaining years.
Why have you returned from the East to board the Dharma-ship? Wait well for the solitary moon at the gate of the sea.
Above. One phrase of the *huatou* was completed for me by the old monk Yuan.

He instructed the Chan practitioner Daben, who had thoroughly penetrated the mind of ten thousand kalpas of mundane existence; returning, he gazed afar toward the depths of the white clouds, where the sound of pines rolls like waves beneath Golden Wheel Peak.
Urgent! Daily listen to the wondrous sound of the Dharma of non-arising.
To reveal my original intent:
the practitioner’s body and mind have long dwelt amidst the white clouds. For what reason do you follow conditions like a drifting tumbleweed? Gather yourself and return; let it all go completely.
Below, the mountain peaks are high as he lies sleeping in the crimson sun.
To the attendant Xing Su, he shows:

cast away body and mind; you are a King of Dharma. There is no need to inquire about your future course or whether you will remain in seclusion; it suffices that you can recognize your mother-given nature.
The mountains, grasses, trees, and forests all emit light.
To show the sudden benefit to Zen practitioners traveling to Mount Wutai, I carry a single staff, a traveling mat, and a gourd.
Do not decline to pay your respects for the sake of ten thousand miles’ distance; should you happen to encounter a feast gathering for Mañjuśrī, [partake].
One day, he said: "Stop teaching; do not pour foul water over people's heads.
To those who have realized the wisdom of the second Zen personage, Huilin, I say:
students need not strive in bitter pursuit. When delusive thoughts are extinguished, one attains freedom. Simply don your robes and dwell in leisure."
Look! This unceasing flow of mind from mind—whose stream is it?
In the silent, empty mountains, all conditions are severed. Do not study the "five flavors" of Chan found in various quarters; those who practice need not seek the "upward direction.
Simply being able to let go, one is naturally so.

To the practitioner Hengyi, I show that this matter has never been sought outside. Seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving all have their source; simply know that they manifest in every instance of daily life.
Do not fall into the second move of following conditions.
To Zen student Kewen:

The arising and ceasing of flowers in the sky have no beginning; yet how can it be helped that everyone looks with cataracts in their eyes? You must believe that nowhere in the clear sky can they be found;
O man of integrity, do not let yourself be deceived by them.
To the Chan practitioner Juchu:
Seating yourself amidst a thousand peaks, you do not inquire after Zen; incense and sutras are your natural conditions.
If you can have no other concerns beyond these, you will naturally find the Land of Ultimate Bliss within the midst of dust.
When the senior monk Xingjiong arrived from afar to inquire after me, I showed him this:
"We have followed one another through the sea of suffering for twenty years; once again we come from Mount Lu to pay respects to the Silent Meditation Master.
Looking at one another, let us not ask about the affairs of our remaining lives—the clouds and mists of the Five Elders are right before our eyes."
The Chan practitioner Nianyun, following the command of his ancestors, has received guests from Wujiang; now that he encounters his sixtieth birthday, I offer this verse to celebrate him:
"The path to awakening within the dust opens at the Cloud Hall; Body and mind spread everywhere, filling the ten directions. A single piece of the patriarch’s permanent abode."
O Earth, may you grant that we forever serve as a bridge across the kalpas.
Behold the brows of the child;

the fire-houses of this world blaze fiercely and are not easily cleansed. The six sense-faculties are consumed and scorched—how pitiable is such life! Yet, if one can for a single thought-moment become like ice, [the fire will be extinguished].
Cold! This is the first stage of transcending the mundane.
Accompanying Master Mei to lecture in Yangzhou, I happened to board a single reed-raft and cut across the river’s current.
The Dharma drum roared like thunder upon the further shore; Countless multitudes of living beings opened to the Great [Dharma].
Dream. Upon returning, the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the hair-tuft between the brows) has never been withdrawn.
To the lay practitioner Zheng Baisheng, [I say]:
when you let go of this single piece of body and mind, it shall be made transparent like lapis lazuli, both within and without, such that not even a speck of dust can cling therein.
In every situation, in daily life, head after head knows only itself.
To the Hall Attendant of Caoxi, Mian Wuan Gong, I say:

"Constantly think of the monk from Xinzhou with his hair still on his head; he did not know a single character—what ability could he possibly have? With a load of firewood upon his shoulders and around his waist..."
Shi: "I have extensively obtained the endless lamp of the Westward Transmission.
The site of enlightenment need not be sought elsewhere; it resides solely within one's own single thought-moment.
If one can fully manifest one's own nature, why worry that the ocean of Dharma does not flow forth?"
To show the practitioner of emptiness-meditation:

the original intent for leaving the dust of the world lies in the mountain forests. At forty, I have heard nothing and am ashamed of this heart; now I rejoice that the thread at my heels has been severed.
Deep within the ten thousand peaks, one should be even deeper still.
To the Zen practitioner who bows to Mount Emei as the boundless Dharma-realm: wherever you encounter it, the meaning is most intimate.
Yet if you turn toward the summit of Mount Emei, clouds and mists fill your eyes and further bewilder the mind.
Gazing westward, Mount Emei’s snow is like silver; Samantabhadra sits upright within a single mote of dust.
He encompasses all infinite oceans of lands, manifesting a body of joyful appearance according to conditions.
He showed the smith forging a bell:
heaven and earth as the furnace, the myriad phenomena as the bronze. Melted together, they form the many apertures that roar with the long wind;
a single sound resonates through the three thousand worlds, awakening those within the great dream of the human realm.
I tell you, young man Li:
the light of time in this floating world is truly not much. As for the matter within your own person, what have you accomplished?
If you do not seek your place of rest in this life, you will continue to follow conditions and fall into the river of craving.
To show the simple practitioner begging for alms:

in distant mountains and deep valleys, one begs for food from afar. Carrying a single bowl alone along the long and winding path, do not allow weariness or aversion to arise from its twists and turns;
you should instead contemplate Huangmei’s stone falling upon his waist.
In the past, Master Wuyin sat upon a lotus throne and circumambulated the King of Emptiness; from his words, the fragrance of Prajñā was constantly produced.
Now, facing the ocean of lands within a single pore, he meets people and has no need for detailed deliberation.

The Chan Master Huanzong has had this edition of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra printed, cleaving open a single atom to reveal the Great Scripture. Its dharma-gate is like a lattice of pearls reflecting one another;
it clearly brings forth the Lotus Treasury World, awakening the dream-eyes of all who encounter it.
Presented to the Elder Nun Xiangshan, Master of Fengshui:
The vast earth and mountains enter the eye as empty space; A single staff wanders alive like a dragon.
Clearly pointing out the path of non-arising, It directly connects with the lineage that came from the West.
To those practitioners who possess the essence of Chan:
Zhaozhou’s “Mu” is the barrier of birth and death. With cold eyes, look upon these iron walls and silver mountains;
simply perceive them as they were before birth, and you will naturally not be deceived by your own tongue.
To Chan practitioner Shi Yue: At the Qingliang Hermitage, I have offered tea and willow branches;

nectar is sprinkled upon the parched and withered. A single drop, once it touches, revives those tormented by heat and affliction. To point directly at the essential meaning of the Westward Transmission:
when you meet someone, simply ask, "Will you drink some tea?"

Entrusting this to Master Wuyi of Boshan, our hearts and aspirations are not separated by even a hair’s breadth. A thousand li of clouds and mountains are seen face-to-face. This is the most intimate place where I think of you:
the bright moon shines cold upon people at night deep.
Showing how Elder Shouchang turned rubble into a great Dharma ground: "Do not let the ancestral fields fall into ruin. One should reflect on the lines about braving rain and piercing the cold;
a single grain of rice or a stalk of firewood can break one's heart.
To Chan practitioner Qiyan Mi of Shouchang:
A lion cub in a pit has long been well-trained; its rolling, tossing, and turning over are not easily discerned. Do not let the tracks of wild foxes draw near;
remember well that time when its fangs were bared.
To the Zen practitioner Wan Shi:
Burying oneself where the eight directions are windless, only when the thieving mind is utterly extinguished does one see true merit. Exert yourself toward that which precedes birth;
only then will you know the sun is red beneath the ocean floor.
The old monk Bixia has traveled extensively through other lands and has now returned;
he sits upon his home mountain within the monastery grounds and opens the gates. For the monks who enter the gate, there is nothing else to do:
drinking tea and washing the bowls—how truly marvelous!
To the Chan practitioner Xuanshu, I show that the matter of one's own person must be clearly understood. Hold fast to a single thought-moment without following a set course.
Simply ensure that deluded attachments are exhausted, and you will be taught how the water of the mind naturally becomes clear.
I show that for the old monk Guizong of Qiyang, every thing he encounters is the manifest light of Prajñā;

it constantly radiates through the six gates, never concealed. If one can sever the roots and objects of perception in this very thought, then in daily life, sitting upright, one dwells in the Great Dharma Field.

Showing that for those whose minds are in the mirror of wisdom, the vision of light does not reside in the sense organs; from of old, no darkness has been able to obscure it. The three thousandfold world-system is like looking at fruit in the palm of one's hand;
Nalakalpa personally ascended this Dharma-gate.
Manifesting the six aspects of reality, like the earth element, Master Kun closed himself in retreat to gather and restrain body and mind;
he kept his door firmly shut. Amidst the dust of the world, he was no different from one dwelling in deep mountains.
You should now cast away all deluded thoughts and from this point forward diligently seek the supramundane.
Shishi Jianshen attendant, recall how in the past you carried the water jar and followed my staff of *lei*. How many times did we go to Caoxi for the sake of the Dharma?
Now you have come directly into the midst of a thousand peaks, seeking once more before the hall for guidance from one lost.
Manifesting clear understanding, he again pays homage at the Five Milk Springs;
having formerly completed his pilgrimage, he paid respects at Qingliang. Upon seeing Mañjuśrī once, he returned to his native land.
Not knowing how many of the thrice-three assemblies there were, he has come specifically to request that you expound upon them once more.
Zheng Baisheng asked again about the Five Breasts;

because of this, I show him that he came yesterday from Mount Lu to inquire about the Dharma. "Does one fully grasp it in a single phrase? There is no such thing. It is simply a matter of not forgetting the path back home, and one will naturally transcend the realms of the holy and the ordinary.
I heard that Shen Langqian has closed his door within the city and sent me this message:
"A single room for dwelling in the marketplace is as vast and open as space; where ordinary beings and sages intersect, they fall into this midst.
Only the master remains eternally still and silent, cutting off the ten directions so that not even a breath of wind can pass."
To Zen Practitioner Huikong of Mount Guanyin in Danyang:
Outside the gates of Jetavana, this is the very ford of delusion; travelers pass through its winds and waves with great frequency. Hold high the lamp of wisdom so it is ever unclouded;
you must directly penetrate even a single mote of dust.
To Zen practitioner An-du:
The illusory sea is boundless, its waves yet unrestrained; one must rely entirely on the oars of wisdom to steer the boat of compassion.
Sailing lightly through the midst of the stream with the tall cassia as a mast, one shall reach the very shore of Bodhi.

While sitting with Jin Zhengdu at the Jīvana Monastery for a meal, I recall our past parting and reflect upon it with constant mindfulness. Our affinity for the Dharma must surely resemble that of Vimalakīrti;
with whom are we conversing on non-duality? Who is this person so close to us?
To the Chan practitioner Yuguang at Putuo:
For a long time beneath White Flower Mountain you have sat in full lotus; within the moonlight upon the water, a single thought stands alone.
Even if the ten directions were all severed at once, the sea would dry up and the rocks crumble, yet it would remain as if nothing had happened.
In response to Master Xin Guang:
A single room in the empty mountains, sealed by white clouds; the bird-path is profound and subtle, entering ten thousand layers.
This is not a direct road leading beyond the heavens—how could one know that with every step, all traces of movement are severed?
To Attendant Shen Guang:
You have been separated from your compassionate parents for twenty years; you sought to understand what existed before your parents were born, yet now you again dream of returning home.
From now on, you must sever the conditions of attachment.
To Layman Yao Xingyang:
Your mind dwells amidst the dust, yet you vow to transcend it. You must simply not fail to recognize the person who is originally so. Constantly, at all times, contemplate the place of refuge;
amidst the flowers of the Eight Treasures, there shall be your future rebirth.
To reveal this old monk’s increasing years:
in this turbid world of floating life, do not ask about age. The Dharma-body cannot be shifted across the three periods of time;
one need only have the constant radiance manifest in a single thought, and the adornments of the Flower Treasury World will be present before one's eyes.
Showing the attendant Huaguan how to lift the tea and offer the water requires true knowledge. Whether moving or still, in every turn of action, look to see who it is.
You must do so at the point where he called out three times right before one's eyes; do not let this pair of eyebrows be in vain.
The rhinoceros fan—bone and hide intact. Hurry, call it here; you do not know how to wield it. A single word is as painful as three blows of the staff.
How many can understand the returning fist beneath the ribs?
Shishi of Xin'an addresses Chan practitioner Yanshan Benyuan:

You must understand that renouncing worldly attachments is the cause for transcending the world. Do not allow even a speck of dust to settle upon the ground of your mind. You must, in every thought-moment, turn the light back to illuminate within;
do not obscure the pure Dharma-body of your own true self.
The perfect clarity of a single thought leaves nothing hidden; wherever one encounters conditions, all is the tranquil light.
Picking up a single speck of dust contains the entire Dharma-realm—where else could one seek the Western Paradise?
To Master Chongxu at Jikim Temple:
Lake and mountain hues shine before my bed; The pavilions and towers are like lotuses emerging from the water.
I recall afar the place where my old friend enjoyed his pastimes, Sitting in peaceful meditation amidst the flowers under the bright sun.
Sent to Master Liaoxin of Huangbo Mountain:
Zen from Huangbo is the most difficult to investigate; as soon as one relies on words and explanations, one falls two or three steps behind. Only the wind and light deserve a single slap;
to this day, the mountains and waters still murmur their discourse.
Entrusting himself to Mount Fan, he manifests as a minor king according to conditions; his mind is like a lotus flower, unstained by dust.
Seated in deep palace chambers, he constantly preaches the Dharma, directly causing those who have not yet realized their original nature to awaken.
To Layman Yuan:
This body has always been but a guest; Now, with a casual wave of the arm, one finally returns home.
Looking back at the path of rushing through the red dust, How does it compare to resting the mind within the white lotus?
For the Zen practitioner Shimyeonghae:
Beneath the *kāṣāya* robe, how could this be ordinary? Not seeking the mind for oneself is most lamentable.
Drifting through vast eons until this very day—this time is truly the moment for earnest deliberation.
To the Zen practitioner who has realized the mind through nine years of seclusion:
these nine years of sitting in austere retreat are like the time on Mount Song when he faced the wall.
Though there may be snow three feet deep reaching his waist, how many know the single phrase of "settling the mind"?
The manifestation of nature pervades all;
the man carrying the load and the millstone at his waist resemble those of Huangmei. Since when did he open his true eye at midnight?
Simply believe that from the beginning there has never been a single thing, and you will know that even the bright mirror is not a stand.

Seeing Chan practitioner Kewen depart for Shaolin to pay homage to the Patriarchs—where the snow before the "Severing the Arm" cliff still glows red—I wonder: who can transmit this single stream that came from the West?
If he but attains the Dharma of settling the mind on this journey, he shall once again stir the wind of the founding Patriarch of yore.
Master Niao Song,
who originally descended from Tuṣita to strike the gavel, shall surely return to sit upon the lecture platform. When the day of the Compassionate Honored One’s descent arrives,
we shall know that you are once again restoring your former foundation.
To Chief Seat Rong:
The West River’s boats of constant traffic have ceased their coming and going; Since our parting, letters and news have utterly vanished.
Only the moon upon the pines before your bed— Its shadow falls before you as the night deepens.

I address the layman Sun Tunan, who has long been adrift upon rivers and lakes with no fixed trace. Since we parted, you have already lain amidst a thousand peaks. Who would have known that you have shattered all worldly dreams?
There remains only the silent night bell of the empty mountains.

To show the profound folly, I use the word "dumbness" to indicate that the Great Way coming from the West is fundamentally beyond words. One who delights in following this folly and dumbness may trace back to the true source;
one must directly investigate until reaching the state where conditions are forgotten, only then will one believe in the Gate of Non-duality at Vaiśālī.
To Chan Practitioner Sanbai:
When will you take up your staff and pass through Donglin? Entering my room, we shall again discuss the mind that transcends the world. Do not fail the autumn night moon over a thousand peaks;
its pure light shines alone upon these deep, silent shadows.
To the attendant Guangkai who upholds the Lotus Sutra:
I personally heard this one [verse] from the ink-black kalpa ago; at that time, a great causal connection was already established. From now on, I shall again unravel the phrases of many lifetimes;
with every word, the mind opens and the lotus blooms upon the tongue.
Revealing the ancient Dharma-body of Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna to the practitioners of the Ocean-Treasury,
he surges forth from the void to manifest before all people. If one can realize that within this very place there is neither arising nor ceasing,
then every dharma is seen to be, from the beginning, nothing but the Truth.

This shows that Zuo Fu, the filial son of Jiangzhou, was fundamentally a person of filiality from many lifetimes past. He constantly maintained a single thought of mindfulness to serve his compassionate parents.
If one seeks to attain Buddhahood through the Way of Filial Piety, no practice among the myriad deeds is as true as this mindfulness.
To the Chan practitioner Mingming:
You have come from afar for the sake of the Dharma to Mount Kuang; through many mornings and evenings you have knocked at the gate.
If one asks about the essential meaning of the Westward Journey, white clouds fly away and then fly back again.
To the Zen practitioner Minghua, I give the name Daoguo (Fruit of the Way):
A single reed came from the West, and the flower of the five petals has bloomed; From this point on, the seeds of the Way will sprout of their own accord.
If you simply diligently irrigate them with the water of wisdom, The realization of Bodhi will certainly not fail.
To Elder Jianyin of Guizong, who shoulders the True Dharma in ancient monasteries:
One must employ a vajra-like mind for protecting the Dharma. Once the radiant manifestation of the whole body is attained, every single thing and every object will be known by its true nature.

I showed the Chan of Pure Practice transmitted through generations in the home of Layman Wang and his son; once they had sought the true dharma from me in the miasmic seas, they have now returned to Mount Kuang.
Seeing them again is just as it was before we parted.
The Chan practitioner Mochu of Wuyi traveled from afar to pay his respects and request my presence, but due to illness I did not go.

Thus, I have shown him this verse for one who comes from afar for the sake of the Dharma: Coming from afar for the sake of the Dharma, you have reached Mount Kuang; Your longing and devotion are earnest, as you come and go again.
Do not say that this old monk is too weary to preach the Dharma— The white clouds do not allow me to leave the pine gate.
Adorning the flower seat and surrounded by the devas, they await your radiant arrival to open the dharma assembly. Do not say that the Dharma-body has never moved;
its faculty of the tongue has already pervaded the three thousandfold world system.
Sent to Zen practitioner Guanzhiyun:

Carrying a single bowl, you have traveled far to other lands; wherever you go, following conditions as they arise, that is the site of enlightenment. Do not say that worldly toil is not the work of the Buddha;
it is from the sea of suffering that you set sail upon the compassionate vessel.
To the Chan practitioner Xianjing:
You should realize that the prajñā-light is inherently perfect and luminous. At the gateways of the six sense-faculties, there is no concealment or obstruction.
If you can manifest non-arising in every thought-moment, then wherever you touch, it is a field of liberation where the mind is absent.

Eight Verses for Zen Practitioners When a person’s single thought-moment is maintained with essential precision, it is a state of vivid, solitary clarity, never obscured. There is only that one stroke prior to birth;
from the beginning, it was not permitted even for the Old Barbarian to know it.
The great matter of birth and death is most worthy of sorrow; to begin one's efforts now is already too late. Seek liberation solely within your own mind;
there is no need to seek it further elsewhere.
Wandering through birth and death for so long, I have endured constant hardship; not yet awakened to the state of non-arising, I have never paused. I vow that this very body shall attain liberation;
do not let me turn my head back once more into the depths of darkness.
The perfectly luminous single nature is devoid of even the slightest speck of dust; it is only because of past errors that one fails to recognize it as real.
If one simply severs the hindrance of afflictions, one will naturally behold the person of original essence.
The waves of the ocean of desire surge in an endless flow; who will turn their head once toward the other shore? One must hoist the light sail high and depart;
until the source is reached, one shall not cease.
Worldly conditions are endless and suffering is boundless; yet with a single thought of turning back, one arrives home.
Once you recognize your original true face, you will know that you have not brought shame upon this *kāṣāya*.
This mind need not be sought outside; it rests solely within one's own single thought-moment. View body and world simply from the perspective of emptiness;
they are just like a single bubble floating upon a tranquil sea.
At the gateways of the six sense organs, the six objects of perception abound; throughout the world, everyone is at their wits' end.
If you are willing to constantly illuminate and penetrate them with every thought, then naturally, in your daily life, you will not follow after them.
Six Verses on Cultivating the Pure Land:

When all conditions have vanished, one is severed from both the distant and the near; How can these aged eyes allow even a speck of dust to settle? Do not let the lotus-water clock cease its flow through the six periods of the day;
Within the flowers, the body of the future has already been secured.
Initially, it was through affectionate attachment that one was reborn in this Sahā world; to reach the Pure Land, one must emerge from the river of craving.
To obtain a lotus flower as one’s parents, one must rely entirely on seeing Amitābha Buddha in every thought-moment.
Seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are all the constant radiance; the lotus of the mind’s ground silently exhales fragrance.
If the six sense faculties are free from defiled attachment, then naturally, everything one encounters is the Western Land.

A single ray of white tuft-light between the eyebrows covers and conceals all Buddhas and sentient beings. If one can simply cause it to manifest before them at all times without obscuration, the lotus-heart-ground will naturally produce its fragrance.
The five turbidities and defiled labors are to be loathed and abandoned; the Pure Land of the West is one's destined destination.
One must simply ensure that the light manifests in every thought-moment, and then one shall behold the blossoming of flowers in the pool of seven treasures.

The Pure Land is originally not to be sought elsewhere; when a person’s single thought seeks to know rest, and one looks back at the place where delusive thoughts dissolve—that is the first step toward the Western Land.
Great snow covers ten thousand mountains; ice and frost freeze the very roots. A single piece of mind and body is chilled to the bone.
Recalling those six years of hunger makes one’s nose involuntarily sting with emotion.
In response to Grand Councilor Liu Sanwei:
From a thousand li away, amidst clouds and mountains, you perceive this mind; I shall briefly offer these words to Donglin.
If you do not fail the Lotus Society’s pledge, The secluded appointment at the White Hermitage may yet be sought.
