The layman Huayu brought the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and sent his nephew Jue to request [its transmission]. Consequently, he sent this:
"Within a single mote of dust, there are infinite Buddha-lands, adorned with the wondrous and peerless treasury of flowers.
If one can cause their radiant light to manifest in every thought-moment, one is truly a person liberated through following conditions."
It is shown that for those traveling the path of birth and death, suffering is longest; one should gladly seek an efficacious remedy from a spiritual friend.
If one can cast aside worldly concerns and proceed with ease, one must turn toward the Gate of Emptiness and pay homage to the Dharma King.
Zen practitioner Yunzhen has come from Mount Wutai to visit the old traces within the Diamond Enclosure at Shuangjing.
Since we parted, clouds and mountains have separated us by ten thousand layers. Tonight, snow fills the vast sky for a thousand miles;
it was here, in years past, that he once sealed the mountain cave entrance.
The Dream-Wandering Collection of the Elder Hanshan, Volume Thirty-Eight;
The Dream-Wandering Collection of the Elder Hanshan, Volume Thirty-Nine;
Daily Record by the Attendant Fuxian.
Compiled by the Disciple Tonghyong;
Revised by the Southern Disciple Liu Qixiang.

In this swirling torrent of the mundane world and the vast expanse of the human path, how many heroes have been utterly deceived! Pleasurable sights and joyful affairs—poetry and wine can dispel one’s sorrows;
though the lute and books are elegant, they still fall short by a single move. The Golden Valley and Orchid Pavilion are now but ruins.

Even if one possesses empty fame, it has already been shared with others; when meeting a monk beneath the bamboo, what remains before one's eyes? This is not merely a matter of stealing moments of leisure, but a hollow pretext.
Thus we know that the foremost move for transcending the world is most precious, yet alas, people of this age are ignorant and fail to perceive it.

Within the field of the five desires, amidst various evil conditions that are like boiling water or a crackling fire, to be able to give rise to even a single thought directed toward birth and death is as difficult to attain as a lotus growing in fire.
If one does not deeply cultivate a sense of weary detachment and fear, and seek the path of liberation, it will remain impossible.
It is unavoidable that one will be roasted and boiled.
The intelligent men of this world, from birth, know only the pleasures of worldly fame, achievement, wealth, honor, and attachment to wife and children;
they believe that such is the extent of human life in this world, unaware that there exists something far greater than this.
The reason why the heroic sages of antiquity were able to transcend birth and death was none other than their singular ability to see through this.
The Buddha said: "Under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I truly received no prediction of enlightenment. Had I received a prediction, that would have been an attachment to a self."
Even in becoming a Buddha, one still fears attachment to a self; how much more so in the affairs of birth and death!
One should only wish to empty all that exists and by no means fill what does not exist. These words are not merely the secret lineage transmitted within the house of the old Layman Pang;
they apply to all Buddhas and patriarchs as well.

What was known by the former sages has been transmitted from one to another: that deluded thought (*vikalpa*) is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). If deluded thought possessed an intrinsic nature, then Buddhas and patriarchs would have no way to emerge.
"Moment by moment" (*kṣaṇe kṣaṇe*) is a designation for arising and ceasing. Only those who realize non-arising (*anutpāda*) truly perceive the moment.
These words might seem to doubt that the entire world could be enlightened.
Yet, through the Samādhi of Illusion, the Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening, one can transcend the stage of No-More-Learning in a mere snap of the fingers.

If this Dharma is so swift and miraculous, consider the public case of Master Yangshan’s dream of ascending to Tuṣita Heaven and striking the gavel, and his subsequent banishment to the Iron Encircling Mountains along with Mañjuśrī.
Are these identical or distinct? It is laughable that the World-Honored One went specifically to the palace of Māra to preach the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, as if there were no other pure lands.
All illnesses arise from ignorance and craving; when ignorance and craving do not arise, inverted perceptions are extinguished—this is called Nirvāṇa.
"All phenomena are unarisen; this is what I call the meaning of momentariness. That which arises is simultaneously subject to cessation;
this is not taught for the sake of the foolish. Could this be taught to the foolish?"

Dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows; dew, lightning, and mirages; reflections, the moon in water, a city of the gandharvas, and plantain trees—these ten metaphors constitute the foundation for entering the Way.
Those who understand them are rare.
"When deluded thoughts arise, Nirvana manifests; when afflictions stir, the Buddha-way is perfected.
This Dharma can only be known and seen by those whose five eyes are perfectly clear.
When the three inches of breath have ceased, who is the master? After a hundred years, one is but a hollow name. These words were spoken by the Tathāgata twenty... [years ago].
No discourse on shattering attachments surpasses this.
Zen Master Zhenxie Liao’s poem on lying ill with sickness says: "Only after falling ill do I realize the body is suffering;
when healthy, I was mostly busy for the sake of others. Truly, these words are true!
"In nature, there is fundamentally no water or fire; cold and heat arise spontaneously. This was a poem written by me during an illness when I formerly lived upon the sea.
Now, residing abroad, my illness has suddenly recurred, appearing just like its former manifestations. Indeed, illness does not change because of a difference in location.
The mind is not shifted by external circumstances, yet its aesthetic appreciation naturally differs;
it is difficult to explain this to others. Su Dongpo said: "Whatever one has a fondness for will inevitably have its own obscurations.

I read the *Jū Danni Ji* (Collected Works from Dwelling in Dan’er) and learned that Ju Fan later arrived overseas and visited his former residence to inquire about his past affairs. An old woman replied: "The Prime Minister Su could do nothing about it..."
He was fond of composing poetry; how could even an old woman still know of his fondness for it?
Is this not a form of self-deception? When Dongpo was first exiled and reached the regions beyond the passes, he enjoyed the delicious lychees and remarked:

"Eating three hundred lychees a day does not hinder one from being a permanent resident of Lingnan. When I first heard this, I thought it was mere affectation. I have lived here for nearly... [text fragment]
It has been six years now. Whenever I encounter this work anew, I unconsciously recite it hundreds of times over.

Throughout my life, I have loved the various calligraphic inscriptions of the Jin and Tang dynasties and have often refined myself in their elegant style; yet I had never even considered the four masters of the Song dynasty.
Now that I have been exiled overseas, I frequently recall the flavor of Su Dongpo’s days in Danyang, within the *guāngláng* bower.
I feel that my calligraphy has approached this [ideal]. Xianzhi said, "How could outsiders know such things? These words are truly full of flavor.
The subtlety of calligraphy is indeed not easy to describe. Although there have been many who practiced calligraphy since antiquity, their words were all incomplete.
Only I have said: "Like a wild goose crossing the vast sky, its shadow sinks into the autumn waters. If this were spoken by a Chan master, it would be thorough and ultimate.
This is a phrase that overturns everything. If a student can penetrate this, they may study the supreme vehicle of the scriptural Dharma.
When people of old discussed poetry, they all compared it to Zen; little did they know that poetry is itself true Zen. Tao Qian (Jingjie) said:
"Picking chrysanthemums beneath my eastern fence, I leisurely behold the Southern Mountains. The mountain air is exquisite at sunset; flying birds flock together."
The conclusion says: "Within these words lies a true meaning; wishing to discern it, I have forgotten my speech.

To treat such phrases as mere poetry is like a young child reciting "Shang Daren" (The Great Man) and "Qiu Yiji" (Qiu is the second person). Among the poets of the Tang dynasty, this applies only to the words of Li Bai.

They created their own "mysterious subtlety," claiming they could discourse on the Way without knowing meditation (*dhyāna*). If Wang Wei had spoken more of the Buddha’s words, later generations would have vied to praise him as a skilled meditator;

yet, in essence, was it not simply meditation? It was merely "meditation in words and letters" (*wenzi chan*), unlike those such as Tao Qian and Li Bai, who achieved mastery beyond the realm of words and letters.
When I was young, I read the "Rhapsody on the Goddess of Luo" by the Prince of Chen-si, which describes her as "flitting like a startled wild goose, graceful as a gliding dragon.
I took these merely as descriptions of the Goddess of Luo and used to say privately that while the startled wild goose could be seen, the gliding dragon remained unknown to me.
Formerly, when I lived by the sea, one morning at dawn, the morning glow filled the sky; though the sun had not yet risen, it was red, and for ten thousand *li* there was not a single cloud. The sea—
The sky was a uniform expanse of color. Suddenly, he saw a fragment of cloud arise in the vast void;

the seawater flowed backward and surged toward the heavens, appearing like the Milky Way suspended across the nine heavens—a sight he deemed most marvelous. A moment later, he beheld a dragon winding through the clouds;
its head, horns, and scales were as distinct as an object held in the palm of one's hand. It descended from the sky into the sea, its graceful, sinuous form beyond words for its exquisite beauty.

Among worldly things, there is nothing with which it can be compared; thus one comes to realize that the words of the ancients were not spoken in vain. Reflecting further, I see that this applies not only to dragons:
the Buddha’s benefit for sentient beings is complete in its majestic deportment, and is therefore called the "conduct of a Great Man," likened to that of a dragon or an elephant.
Knowing when to stop is my teacher, the Buddha, the Sage. Having left the household life to study the Way, he then stayed at the Snowy Mountains to practice.

Upon attaining Perfect Enlightenment, he took his seat within the Bodhimaṇḍa to preach the Dharma; for the Snowy Mountains are a place of cool serenity. It was my thought that sentient beings dwelling there together—
The five desires are entirely the fires of affliction, burning and boiling day and night, blazing without ceasing. Yet we individuals alone desire to escape them;

this is not possible unless one places oneself in a state of total severance, buries this body and mind amidst ten-thousand-fathom snow and ice, subjecting them to a piercing cold that reaches the very bone, and through such freezing and hunger, undergoes a great death and subsequent resurrection—otherwise, what else can it be?
By quelling the fierce flames, one is spared from being consumed and melted away. Alas! My Master halted his practice here at the site of Bodhi-enlightenment and declared:
"This ground is composed of vajra; it is a place of ultimate solidity. The Dharma he taught therein is the Dharma-gate of the Ocean of Nature.
To begin with, the Ocean of Wisdom has no inherent nature; through delusion, it becomes karma and consciousness. Therefore, it is called the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).

The ocean is the eternally abiding realm, yet it is stirred by the wind. To awaken to this is to realize it as enlightenment and wisdom; thus it is said: "The nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect;
its perfect limpidity is the primordial subtlety of awakening. This meaning reveals that all sentient beings share the same source of *dharmatā*.

It is only through delusion that distinctions arise between movement and stillness, or confusion and awakening. It intends to lead us to observe stillness within movement and to illuminate awakening within confusion. Not...
To be unswayed by the delusions of Māra and externalists, and unmoved by the winds of sensory objects—how could this be possible without relying upon the ground of supreme firmness?
Otherwise, how could one destroy heterodox views and establish the Great Enterprise?
Therefore, my Teacher relies upon this to preach the Dharma. Viewed from this perspective, that which my Teacher relies upon is what he desires for all people to rely upon together. Thus...
I have set my mind upon Nārāyaṇa. Nārāyaṇa signifies firmness; he dwells facing the great ocean, solemn as a gateway to the Dharma.
His abode is named "Ocean Seal" (Sāgarāmudrā), radiant with samādhi. It is said: "In stillness, know where to rest. If we humans rest here, it may be called resting in its proper place.
Furthermore, it is said: "Virtue in a neighborhood is what makes it beautiful. If one chooses not to dwell in virtue, how can one obtain it?
I understand. Furthermore, it says: "The warbling yellow birds rest upon the corner of the mound. In their resting, they know where they should rest;
can a human be less than a bird? I shall repeat these words three times.
The Discourse on Abiding in Poverty states: "To be poor without flattery, and rich without arrogance—arrogance leads to the loss of wealth, while flattery results in the surrender of poverty.
Therefore, it is better to be poor yet joyful. When one is poor yet joyful, there is nothing that is not joyful. This is why Yanzi lived in a humble lane.
The square-walled hut of Yuan Xian, the coarse hempen robe of Zi Lu, and the plain white sash of Duke Rong—how could these not be instances of finding joy where there was nothing to enjoy?
If one attains such joy, then even the whole world cannot change it. Alas!
This is why Xu You, Wu Guang, Nie Que, and Poyi adopted lives of total renunciation, severing all worldly ties. Confucius also said: "I eat plain vegetables and drink water..."
Water. Bending my arm to serve as a pillow, joy is found within it. Wealth and honor obtained through unrighteousness are to me like floating clouds.
This is the essence of learning.

He once said that there are three essentials for studying: "If one does not know the Spring and Autumn Annals, one cannot navigate the world; if one is not refined in Laozi and Zhuangzi, one cannot forget the world; if one does not practice Chan, one cannot transcend the world. These three encompass the studies for governing the world and transcending the world. To lack even one is partial; to lack two is narrow.

As for those who claim to be men of distinction while lacking even one of these three— [The text continues: ...they are merely people who have not yet attained the Way. They may be called scholars, but they are not yet practitioners of the Way. They may be called practitioners of the Way, but they are not yet sages. They may be called sages, but they are not yet Buddhas. Why? Because they have not yet fully realized the principle of the Middle Way. Therefore, one must study all three exhaustively. Only then can one be called a complete person. Only then can one be called a true man of the Way. Only then can one be called a Buddha. Thus, the three essentials are the foundation for attaining Buddhahood.

If one lacks them, one will surely fall into error. One must not be negligent in this regard. One must strive with all one's heart to master them. This is what is meant by "the three essentials of learning. Those who understand this are few; those who practice it are even rarer. Those who preach it are rare indeed; those who embody it are the rarest of all. May you all take this to heart and apply it diligently. Do not let it be lost. This is my final exhortation. Thus ends the discourse on the Three Essentials of Learning. May all beings attain enlightenment. Namasté.
It is merely a matter of emulating them. Nevertheless, one must not fail to know the essential point. The essential point is the fundamental principle (*zong*).
Therefore it is said: "Words have a fundamental principle; affairs have a sovereign. If words lack a fundamental principle, they will proliferate without a governing thread.

If affairs lack a sovereign, they will become fragmented and increasingly chaotic. If learning lacks an essential point, it will be dispersed and yield few achievements. For this reason, a student must certainly not fail to—
It is essential to apply oneself diligently. However, the essence of these three lies in a single mind. The essence of applying oneself to the mind lies in Zen meditation (*chán*).
The essence of Zen meditation lies in forgetting the world. The essence of forgetting the world lies in adapting to the times. The essence of adapting to the times lies in mastering change.
The key to mastering change lies in perceiving principle. The key to perceiving principle lies in stabilizing the will. The key to stabilizing the will lies in abiding by one’s lot.
The key to abiding by one’s lot lies in diminishing desire. The key to diminishing desire lies in self-knowledge. The key to self-knowledge lies in cherishing life.
The key to cherishing life lies in attending to the internal. The key to attending to the internal lies in single-minded focus. Once this singleness is attained, one attains Heaven.
The principle underlying this has been established. When one engages with the world in accordance with this principle, there is nothing that is not forgotten and nothing that is not possessed.

When there is neither forgetting nor possessing, then all things are not forgotten and all things are possessed. All things are not forgotten; all things are possessed. All things are not forgotten; all things are possessed.
Thus, there is no entry into the world where one does not find fulfillment. Therefore it is said: "Heaven and Earth were born together with me; the myriad things and I are one.
To integrate all things and make them one's own—can this be anything other than the Sage? Alas! It is ultimate, it is exhaustive;
its wondrousness reaches its peak within the single mind, leaving no phenomenon unaccounted for. For this reason, a student must certainly know the essential point.
To pasture the mind, tranquility lies in emptiness; to maintain the mind, it lies in equanimity; to employ the mind, it lies in illumination; to awaken the mind, it lies in non-attachment.
The essence of the mind is fundamentally empty, yet worldly desires intermingle, and delusive thoughts accumulate until not a single gap remains. Thus, the vital energy becomes stifled.

The substance [of the mind] becomes obscured; it flickers and blazes, yet finds no peace. Therefore it is said: when objects are withdrawn, clarity emerges; if they are not withdrawn, there is no voidness.
Without voidness, there is no clarity; without clarity, there is no peace. Thus, settling the mind depends upon voidness.
The mind is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*), equal within and without. That which is unequal arises from heaviness and lightness. For this reason, the ignorant value the external.
The wise value that which is internal; the sages value the forgetting of both. Those who value the external fall; those who value the internal become artificial; those who forget both are equanimous.

Being equanimous, there is nothing that does not hit the mark; therefore, maintaining the mind lies in equanimity. The substance of the mind is fundamentally luminous, such that there is nothing it does not illuminate.
It is because of its being turbid and obscured that there is something it does not illuminate. Observe the people of the world: day by day they increase their turbidity and obscuration. Although...
In the end, there is simply nothing with which to reflect oneself. Therefore, the application of the mind lies in illumination. The mind is fundamentally not deluded;
it becomes deluded only because it loses its power of illumination. Once delusion is dispelled, illumination itself vanishes. Thus, the realization of the mind lies in forgetting.
Contemplating the mind, contemplating the mind—this is the foremost and most subtle dharma-gate. Now, the mind is the sovereign of the single body and the root of all practices.
If the mind is not clear, those who desire the body to be upright and their conduct to be correct will be rare indeed. Therefore, regarding all the various [phenomena] in the world...
Suffering and affliction all arise from deluded thoughts and inversion. If inversion does not arise, then birth is non-birth.
Where there is non-birth, though there is birth, it is without birth. Where there is birth without birth, then thought is also without thought.
If there is no thought, how can inversion arise? If there is arising, it is not right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). Right contemplation is such that there is nothing incorrect.

Reading the *Zhuangzi*, I see that the True Lord (Zhenzai) is fundamentally formless and transcends the dust and dregs of the world. Yet, suddenly, through a single moment of delusion, one rushes headlong into this skin-bag, like a monkey wrapped in furs;
left and right, one finds no ease. Rising or sitting, one must offer sycophancy; hungry or thirsty, one demands to be served.

One busies oneself for the sake of fame and profit; one exhausts one's fields and gardens by mortgaging and selling them. Yet there is another kind of folly: using one’s face to seek the love of others.
Applying cosmetics to this stinking skin is just like being a malevolent ghost or monster. Everyone does this for the sake of others, thereby inviting debts from future lives.
How lamentable are those of both ancient and modern times! Who would dare to be startled by this truth? Only the Master of Lacquer Garden (Zhuangzi) possessed a slight understanding of its flavor.
Yuan Shan spoke of me on a summer day in the year of Yichou; having been unexpectedly defiled by a madman, I stayed at Dongguo while holding my ink-stone, whereupon this fan emerged.
This book was written because I spoke as it came to me and recorded it.
When a great fire rages and flows across everything, melting metal and scorching stone, few who dwell between earthen jars and window-frames do not suffer from being burned or boiled.
Alas for humanity! Were one merely to obtain my skin and bones to sustain themselves, then in their eating, breathing, and daily activities, they would have only to obey my command.
The joy of coolness would instantly arise from their armpits; the state of scorching heat would immediately dissipate from their flesh;
swarms of mosquitoes would retreat at a mere gesture; and the suffering of biting would vanish away through a simple arrangement. Furthermore...
How can one boast of being born with wings to ride the cool breeze, or ascending upon floating clouds to roam the six realms? Alas!
When a single cool gale arrives, they are cast aside and abandoned; when frost and dew first arise, they are regarded as mere superfluous things.
Is this not because they act without a master and achieve their function without dwelling upon it? How could anything else possibly compare to this?
To speak of solitude is easy;
to practice it is difficult. To attain it within one's own mind is even more difficult than practicing it in conduct.
Thus, regardless of how one navigates worldly affairs—whether rising or falling—the ancient heroes and sages, some of whom emerged...
In some instances, the outward conduct is manifest while the inner mind remains hidden; it is truly difficult to discern them by following their traces alone.
Were it not for one who possesses the eye of transcendent power and holds the mirror of perfect illumination, how could one possibly grasp their true form? Alas!
This is why the madman of Chu sang as he walked before Zhongni, and Xu You shook his head at Yao and Shun. Nevertheless, was it that those two men were right, and...

Is it that the Three Sages were wrong? Rather, each was right in their own way. To take such partial correctness as ultimate attainment originates from the Great Way, yet remains but a shadow and an echo.
Those who loathe shadows while harmonizing with echoes find it difficult to speak of the principle of profound stillness (*moji*).
For the gentleman who turns toward the Way, there is a place for rest and dwelling therein.
In his sincere exposition for Tanzhi, [the Master] said:
"Your mind is neither sincere nor clear; your nature is neither tranquil nor settled; your essence is neither concentrated nor complete; your spirit is neither coagulated nor detached."
If one's resolve is not singular, it will not be steadfast; if one's vital energy is not nurtured, it will not be harmonious; if anger is not restrained, it will not be rectified;

if desire is not blocked, it will not diminish; if learning is not discussed, it will not be broad; if questions are not debated, they will not be understood; if integrity is not established, it will not be firm; if conduct is not maintained, it will not be vigorous.
Therefore, the learning of the gentleman consists in valuing what others slight and augmenting what others diminish; taking up what others discard and attaining what others lack.
Thus, his Way becomes great and his virtue expansive; his person is at ease and his reputation is honored, standing loftily without rival.
Zeshan Shuo heard from Zhuangzi that it was said: "To hide a boat in a ravine or to hide a mountain in a marsh may be called secure;
yet a man of great strength might carry them away on his back while the ignorant remain unaware. This means that wherever there is something hidden, there is something being carried away.

If there is nothing stored within, then there is no burden. Nevertheless, while taking "having nothing stored" as the ultimate state, my humble opinion is that one who has something stored within is superior to one who has nothing.
Thus it is said: "The mountains harbor jade and the vegetation flourishes; the rivers hold pearls and the banks do not wither.
Is this not because there is something stored within, which causes radiance to manifest without? Therefore, the gentleman prizes the art of concealment.
The vessel resides within the body, awaiting the proper time before it is employed. Furthermore, because the accumulation of a mountain is vast, it is high and possesses all manner of beauty;
because the accumulation of a marsh is deep, it is low and attracts all manner of virtue. There is a further reason why these serve as metaphors for the gentleman.

Awakening from a dream, he spoke of the illusory man who had mounted a single leaf and moored upon the shore of the illusory sea; he was about to dwell with the vast multitude in the boundless wilderness to find rest.
Just then, a certain Mr. Floating-by happened upon him and asked, "Alas! How strange! I have observed..."
Your difficulties are inexhaustible. When I gaze at your form, it drifts like a cloud; when I look upon your countenance, it is as cold as ice.

When I strike at your core, it is utterly empty; yet when I approach you, you are warm. To unravel your nature, you are profound and deep; you are sealed as if in silence, floating as if riding upon the wind.
You resemble a human being, yet you are not a human being. What dwelling place do you have? What business brings you here? You are a phantom man!
He had no response; he was only silent and still, without cognition or consciousness, without showing or speaking.

[The Master] shared his rest with him—sitting, lying, eating, drinking, rising, moving, waking, and sleeping—for ten days without interruption. The Master’s mind was scorched and his will dissolved, as if he were about to undergo transformation along with him.
Just as the Master was about to depart, he addressed the illusory man, saying: "I am but a person of the winds and waves."
"I wish to borrow your boat and oars to float across and reach the other shore; may I rely upon you, Master? Do you have no intention [to help]?
He replied, "Wait. What kind of talk is this? Have you not seen those who dream? During their long night of sleep, they are inevitably steeped in intoxication and plunged into darkness.
Their spirits are clouded and bewildered, their souls are agitated and terrified. Their bodies are as if dissolved like a corpse, yet their minds are like wandering ghosts."
Before he had even moved from his seat, a hundred strange phenomena arose; before a single moment had passed, a thousand ages seemed as vast as eternity.

Reaching a state of profound obscurity and vast emptiness, he wandered about looking in all directions—sometimes ascending to the peak of the Infinite, sometimes gazing down upon the unfathomable abyss.
A venomous dragon lies ahead; a fierce rhinoceros follows behind. To advance is to tread upon peril; to retreat is to be pressed into danger.

There is no fissure into which to enter, and though one ascends, it feels as if one is falling. One must grasp at withered branches and pluck at decaying vines, while bees and wasps glare with their eyes and vipers and scorpions bind one's feet.
At such a time, the mind is exhausted and wisdom is stymied; there is no way to escape.
There is no skill to liberate them, and there is no one to rescue them. When they cry out, with whom can they find kinship?
Why are they so filled with such terror and anxiety, manifesting various forms and colors while uttering groans? Even for those who possess awareness, how can they ever find peace?
It is only when one suddenly shouts in indignation and leaps up, awakening with a great realization, that upon looking back at the dream-event, it appears as if vague and indistinct;
yet, though sought, it cannot be found, and though spoken of, it cannot be fully grasped. This must surely lead the awakened one to laugh and let it go.
Alas! Is this true only for those in dreams? It is so for the entire world. First—
I shall now attempt to apply this self-awakening to awaken all those within my dreams.
It was the winter of the Gui-mao year, eight years after I was exiled; while wandering from Caoxi, I happened to beg for food along the Ling River.
To the west of the water, there happened to be an elderly man with thick eyebrows and white whiskers who visited me at my lodging. Observing his majestic appearance, I knew him to be a recluse.
When I inquired about his practice, he said it was that of Qibo and Huang Di. From this, I knew him to be a man of great attainment.
Someone said: "There is an ancient saying: 'If one succeeds, one becomes a good minister; if one does not succeed, one becomes a good physician. I say this is not so;
rather, it is that if one succeeds, one becomes a physician, and if one does not succeed, one becomes a minister. Why?

For the duty of a minister is to harmonize yin and yang and preserve the primal qi, to regulate the myriad things and show benevolence to all living beings, to bring the sovereign to a state of great tranquility, and to set the world at peace."
Furthermore, to bring peace is their duty; yet it is not necessarily fulfilled. Even if it were fulfilled, the merit would not necessarily be forgotten.

This is because they place themselves before others and the world behind them, offering loyalty through their own interests. Moreover, they must outwardly rely on the authority of the sovereign and utilize the hands of the multitude to accomplish their task.
How much more so when they remain ever-vigilant amidst the fields of gain and loss, right and wrong, honor and disgrace until the end of their lives.

Though one may labor in their practice, the Way is not necessarily illuminated. Day and night they toil busily, exhausting their spirits and scorching their minds, even to the point of harming their lives and injuring their natures;
yet many remain unenlightened until old age and death. How can such people be considered realized? As for physicians, however, it is quite the opposite; this is their very vocation.
He takes his mandate as his responsibility, benevolence as his heart, righteousness as his substance, and all things as himself.
He makes the removal of evil his task, rectifying the vital breath his principle, the Classics his standard, and expedient means his application.

Therefore, in his governance, he brings the sovereign of the mind to tranquility and places the four limbs in a state of harmony. Whenever encountering danger or treading upon hardship, he exercises his independent judgment.
He possessed wisdom and maintained a character of independent integrity; he was not confused by the clamor of the masses nor did he avoid the influence of the wicked.
In times of various emergencies, his advances and retreats were always appropriate. He took the Great Mean as his standard and supreme stillness as his priority.

When his efforts bore fruit, he did not calculate the profit nor claim the merit for himself. Is this not one who acts without presiding over the act and achieves merit without dwelling upon it? It is no other.

Among those who have attained the ultimate realization in the world, how could they be involved in this? Viewed from this perspective, the merit of forgetting oneself is great; the reputation of forgetting profit is lofty.
For those who do not forget, there is manifest reward and hidden retribution; for those who forget both, the signs are subtle at first but become evident later.
Thus one can know that for those who forget their own merit, the future will surely be great. Alas! If people could truly grasp the art of the skilled physician...
If one governs a state with this mind, what state would not be well-governed? If one manages external things with the mind that forgets the self, what thing would not be accommodated?
When things are accommodated, there is universal inclusion; when the state is governed, there is universal goodness.

This is the achievement of the sage and the capable task of the man of virtue. Thus, while the methods differ, the success is one; while the names differ, the reality is the same. Furthermore, why [should they be distinguished]?
To manifest or obscure [the truth] based on their relative merits, and to rank the noble and the humble according to their spiritual insight—this is how it is done.

Since you, my lord, hold these practices in high esteem and regard medicine as a divine art, I have thus discussed the secrets of medicine to supplement your travels, hoping that those who observe them will [understand].

It is not that you alone know the art of medicine; rather, through medicine, you advance toward the enterprise of a gentleman, intending to apply it to the world and the state so that all may behold the transformative influence of Xuanyuan and Huangdi. You, sir, are a man of profound understanding.
If one understands your heart, there will be nowhere to which you cannot reach.
This Guanglou (Light Pavilion) is said to be located at Hexi (Cranewell Creek) in Qu’a. It was the site where the Great Master Zibai propagated the Dharma.
The layman of the He family gathered his clan to serve the Master with the utmost reverence. There was an elder named Yunfeng who, in the previous Dinghai year, constructed a pavilion to house him.
In the third year of the Zongzhen era, the year Bingshen, the Great Master passed away.

Twenty years later, when a full decade had elapsed since his nirvana, the old man traveled from beyond the Ling Mountains to the Shuangjing Monastery to attend the occasion of the Great Master’s enshrinement in the stupa.
Taking a path along the stream, the elders and lay devotees saw the old man as they would their own teacher; grief and joy mingled within them as they offered him a vegetarian feast.
For several days, there was the son of an elder, Maoqian, who had received this light but had not yet realized its inherent presence.
He prostrated himself and requested an explanation, his resolve never wavering. The old man joyfully said to him, "This Great Master uses this tower as his broad and long tongue.
Furthermore, the entirety of the ten directions is the Light of Constant Quiescence; all sentient beings employ this light through the gates of their six sense faculties."
The head illuminates heaven and earth. Therefore, the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the sun, moon, and stars; grasses, weeds, humans, and animals;
and all things with scales, shells, feathers, or fur—none fail to manifest from within this light. Thus, the pavilion is this very light, and this light is the pavilion.

It encompasses the myriad phenomena, integrating and subsuming them all without exception. Those who dwell in this pavilion revere and serve the Triple Gem, paying homage and reciting the name in devotion.

Relying upon this, from the sound of the *qing* bell and the names of the Buddhas, even to the company of wife and children, eating and resting, rising and sitting, throughout the twelve periods of the day, whether turning or walking, bowing or looking up, laughing, joking, or rebuking—in all movements and expressions, there is nothing that is not the wondrous function of this light.
Even when dreams and delusions arise, they are still the manifestation of this light. If one can, for a single thought-moment, know where to return, then this light...
This is indeed what has always been possessed by our own house; it is naturally free and not obtained from without. Thus, it is already fully realized.

How can one allow oneself to be oblivious to all these enjoyments and willingly remain a person outside the light? If you can truly see in your daily activities with earnest humility and skillfully apply this insight, you will not fail the inherent nature.
Not only does the Great Master’s Dharma-body abide eternally and preach inexhaustible Dharma-gates, but you too shall do so.
When these words fill the ears and penetrate the heart, one can immediately transcend the toils of worldly existence and dwell uprightly in ultimate bliss.
Why then look for this tower apart from the light itself? This statement by the old man is much like lighting a lamp beneath the sun, or adding legs to a snake—it is superfluous.
You, sir, must understand this.

Regarding the meaning of the insentient Buddha-nature, I was staying at Kuangshan to nurse my illness, having closed my quarters to decline all external entanglements. At that time, Kong Yizi knocked on the door and requested an audience, saying:

"I am a man who begs for alms among the people, and I have heard gentlemen discussing the meaning of Buddha-nature; some do not believe that insentient things preach the Dharma. There were others as well.
This refers to the Buddha-nature of sentient beings, which each possesses individually, like bubbles upon the great ocean.

For those who do not believe in its perfect and complete fulfillment, I pray that the Great Master will resolve their doubts. I said: "How stubborn! This meaning is profoundly deep; it is difficult to understand and difficult to enter."
Those who have not previously cultivated the seeds of the highest faculties will find it difficult to believe this. Even that which they perceive is indeed what the Buddha taught;

it is simply not a discourse of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). If one does not verify and believe the Mahāyāna of definitive meaning, nor consult with an enlightened spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), then for one who has not yet realized the principle of "mind-only," it is rare that such an interpretation does not arise. Thus it is said: "The insentient speak."
The Dharma has explicit teachings. The "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"For example, among the devas there is a great Dharma-drum named 'Awakening. Whenever the sons of the gods act with negligence, a voice issues from the void, proclaiming:
'You should know that all sensual pleasures are entirely impermanent, false, and inverted; they last but a moment...'"
It is subject to decay and transformation; it merely deceives the foolish, causing them to become attached. Do not be negligent!

If you are negligent, you will fall into the various evil realms, and later regret will be of no avail. Having heard this, the devas gave rise to great sorrow and fear; they felt shame and remorse, repenting their ways.
Furthermore, how could the sound of the celestial drum possess a sentient being, yet be able to preach the Dharma and awaken the devas? This extends even to the Cloud-Palace of Radiance.

The jeweled nets each produced wondrous sounds, reciting verses in praise of the Buddha; this continued even to the point of speaking from every atom and speaking from every world-system. Furthermore, who provided the faculty of speech for these?
It was the devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, who possess no discursive thought (*vitarka*) or investigation (*vicāra*) nor any verbal expression, yet produce sound solely from within their light.
Each performs its own function. Furthermore, as for the sound within the light, how could it possibly issue from a mouth? These are all actual proofs of the insentient preaching the Dharma.
Moreover, in the Chan school, Xiangyan heard the sound of bamboo being struck and clarified his mind; Lingyun beheld peach blossoms and awakened to the Way.
From what mouth of a virtuous spiritual friend did these teachings enter them? It is further said: "Sentient beings are Buddhas..."
The nature [of all things] is individually and fully possessed by each. This is also taught within the scriptures;

however, it is a discourse that conceals the true aspect for the sake of those with inferior capacities belonging to the three vehicles, and is not the ultimate expression of the One Vehicle’s supreme principle. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"I now universally perceive the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment within every body. Now, Vairocana is but a single Buddha, yet [he is present] in all sentient beings.
Birth is not for a single person alone. If the Buddha-nature of sentient beings were possessed individually and separately, then every sentient being would each become a Buddha;
this would mean that multiple Buddhas are simultaneously perfected.

If there is only one Buddha, and yet [the nature] is possessed by each, why then speak of "all sentient beings" attaining perfect enlightenment within their own bodies? Furthermore, it says: "How marvelous! How marvelous! All..."
Sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata. Now, the virtues and marks of the Tathāgata constitute the entire body of the Dharmakāya.

Since sentient beings possess these, how could it be said that they possess them only partially? The Third Patriarch said: "Perfectly identical to the Great Void, there is neither deficiency nor excess.
This means that every person shares the same essence as the Buddha; it does not merely refer to the Buddha alone. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "All sentient beings..."

All have realized perfect enlightenment; it is not that they merely possess it. Thus Ānanda said: "I and the Tathāgata each possess the jewel-like enlightened mind of awakening, which is perfectly complete.
This is what is meant by: 'The Dharma-body of all Buddhas enters my nature; my nature, in turn, merges with that of the Tathāgata.'"

The single moon universally appears in all waters; all the moons in the waters are subsumed within the single moon. It is like a thousand lamps in a single room, their lights intermingling and reflecting one another.
Regarding such a perfectly complete and vast Dharma-gate, those of the Two Vehicles who sat here in the past were as if blind and deaf.

It was only natural that they would have narrow views, be startled and terrified by these words, and fail to believe them. Alas! Among those who study the Buddha-dharma according to conventional truth, there are many...
One merely practices oral and auditory understanding, yet lacks the genuine work of true investigation and realization.

Without having awakened to the vast, perfect, and luminous essence, whatever one perceives is nothing more than the shadowy reflection of the conscious spirit—vivid and alert—which one mistakenly identifies as a substantial reality.
Furthermore, one clings to this physical body of flesh and blood, sealing it as the "self-characteristic. In truth, one has not yet opened a single eye; thus, the seeds of birth are produced.
These are merely various forms of conceptual discrimination; they take provisional teachings as definitive meaning and regard their own views as the ultimate.

Now, there is no need to debate whether insentient things preach the Dharma or not, nor whether the Buddha-nature is possessed by each individually or not. Have you not heard the verse from the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*?
"If a person wishes to know the principle of true emptiness, The True Suchness within the mind pervades that which is external. Sentient beings and insentient things..."
They share a single essence; everywhere they are identical with the true *dharmadhātu*.

Simply keep this verse within your breast, and at all times during daily life—at the gates of the six sense faculties, wherever you see forms or hear sounds—seal everything with this single seal. After a long time, through constant practice, inner and outer will naturally become one as a single whole.
Sentient and insentient beings will be forged into a single piece. One day, there will be a sudden, expansive awakening. This is...
Only now do I realize that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth all together turn the fundamental wheel of Dharma;
that scales, shells, and feathers everywhere manifest the Samādhi of the Manifestation Body (Rūpakāya). There is no dharma outside the mind—before one's eyes, it is all green mountains.

Reaching this point, I finally believe that Zhaozhou sometimes took a single blade of grass and used it as a sixteen-foot golden body, and sometimes took a sixteen-foot golden body and used it as a single blade of grass.
Usage. An ancient worthy addressed the assembly, saying: "Does the great assembly see?

Right now, all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the patriarchs of successive generations are simultaneously emitting light from the tip of this old monk’s whisk and shaking the earth. This is to receive illumination within the mind; it does not depend on the external.
Why then seek Chang’an inside the Han-yuan Palace? When Kongyizi heard this teaching, he was filled with joy.
They leaped for joy, paid their respects, and withdrew.
Regarding the "Four Vows of the Fast," the four vows are:
"I vow to deliver all sentient beings, who are boundless; I vow to sever all afflictions, which are inexhaustible; I vow to master all Dharma gates..."

The four vows—"I vow to study all the teachings; I vow to save all sentient beings; I vow to master all dharmas; and I vow to attain the unsurpassed Buddha-way"—are what is uttered by my disciples who practice as Bodhisattvas.
Yet, a Bodhisattva is not a distinct class of person, but rather an ordinary person of great resolve who, amidst the toils of worldly affliction, aspires to seek upward toward Buddhahood.
As it is said in the teachings: "If you wish to seek the fruit of Buddhahood above..."
One must descend to transform sentient beings. To transform sentient beings, one must first resolve to sever afflictions (*kleśa*).
To sever afflictions, one must first extensively study the various Dharma-gates (*dharmaparyāya*). Therefore, these four matters exist in mutual dependence.
Sentient beings are the counterparts of the Buddha; afflictions are the root of sentient beings; and the Dharma-gates are the medicine for treating afflictions. By means of sentient beings...
"Life is boundless" means that afflictions (*kleśa*) are inexhaustible. Because afflictions are inexhaustible, the Dharma-gates are likewise immeasurable.
That which is difficult to deliver, one vows to deliver; that which is difficult to sever, one vows to sever; that which is difficult to learn, one vows to learn.
Once these three are accomplished, although the Buddha-way is unsurpassed, it can nevertheless be realized. These are what are called the Four Great Vows. There is a great [significance] to this.
Only the mind can give rise to this great vow. Only one who possesses the great vow can establish a great enterprise, achieve great merit, and attain great renown.
All of these are supported by great practice; they are not empty vows.
These four [aspects] do not require seeking from without, but rather seek only within oneself. How is this made clear? Because the original nature of our own minds is...

The Buddha and sentient beings originally possess no dual substance. It is because of the single thought of "self" that this self is established; once the self is established, all those who oppose it are regarded as "others.
Each other is likewise a self, and when these many selves aggregate, sentient beings are formed. That upon which sentient beings are fundamentally based is affliction (*kleśa*).
When afflictions are stubbornly clung to, the mark of self (*ātman*) becomes even more firm. When the mark of self is firm, others do not cease to exist, and the self...
If one passes away, people do not remain. When people do not remain, afflictions become empty.

Thus, if the afflictions of my own mind are exhausted, I shall look back upon "self" and "others" as being like flowers in the sky. If I am like a flower in the sky, then seeking sentient beings is like gathering flowers from the sky to produce fruit from the sky;
searching for them in this way, they are ultimately unobtainable. This is what is meant by the exhaustion of afflictions. And...
Sentient beings are empty; this means that they are saved not by being delivered [by another], but by saving themselves.

This is because [the self] and its characteristics are both non-existent. Yet, among all the people in the world, there is none who does not possess a self. Those who possess a self do so through afflictions (*kleśa*).

When afflictions prevail, it is not the true mind. Now, afflictions are merely emotional attachments. If one were to sever these afflictions while using a mind characterized by affliction to do so, this is—
This is like borrowing the enemy's troops and providing the bandits with grain. To enter emotion with emotion is like throwing fire into fire; this is called "increasing the excess.
If one seeks to sever desire through such means, it cannot be achieved. Therefore, one must inevitably study the Dharma-gate. As for the Dharma-gate:
This is the method for manifesting one's true nature; it is the instrument for eliminating afflictions, namely the Dharma of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The Dharma of Emptiness is the mind of the Buddha; that which is clarified through it is the practice of the Buddha.

Those who study the Buddha take their own human mind to embody the mind of the Buddha, and take the affairs of daily life to emulate the practice of the Buddha. Thus, they learn by means of the Buddha-mind within their own minds.
To practice the Buddha-way within one’s own mind, to sever the afflictions within one’s own mind, and to deliver the sentient beings within one’s own mind—this is like ice melting in boiling water;

it requires no further effort. Thus, while these four vows are indeed difficult [to fulfill through external means], if one seeks them inwardly, nothing is not fully present within my own heart, for I do not depend upon anything external.
If one knows that nothing is depended upon externally, then for us, in the present...
In this preceding body, there was a self. Looking closely, there are the brothers, wife, and servants of one's own family;
looking afar, there are the people of the world, the state, and all classes of living beings—all are sentient beings. Turn back and seek within your own mind in your daily activities:
if you act with a mind of affliction (*kleśa*), then even your own six sense-faculties will contend with one another, let alone bringing order to the family or the state.

Is it not so that the world is brought to peace? If this single thought-moment manifests before you and you engage in affairs by means of the dharma of emptiness, then every moment of affliction will be transformed into the light of wisdom.
Illuminating sentient beings, they will all together return to their own nature, and thus you will be of one essence with the Buddha.
In this way, afflictions are empty and sentient beings are exhausted; sentient beings being exhausted, the Buddha-way is perfected.

All people are brothers and all things are kin; there is a vast and great impartiality. How could one wish for such a state to be established in vain? Viewed from this perspective, the Dharma that transcends the world is accomplished within this very world.
From this day forward, whatever we do—whether it be to serve our sovereign or to benefit the people—[should be undertaken with this realization].
There has never been a single matter or a single action that did not emerge from the Four Great Vows; there is nothing therein that is not the practice for attaining Buddhahood.
How could it be merely a matter of practicing empty words and valuing outward appearances, or simply entrusting one’s ears and eyes to them? This is how I have set my aspirations;
will there be anyone who attains realization through this?

The doctrine of spiritual resonance explains that the Buddha taught all the causes and effects of good and evil within the world, with their retributions following like a shadow follows a form; there is not even a hair’s breadth of deviation.
Yet those in the world who do not believe call it empty talk. As for the Confucian Sage’s teaching on the acceptance of fate, there are those in the world who do believe in it.
Every time they perform divinations, they rejoice when seeking auspicious matters and fortune, yet they loathe hearing of calamities and misfortunes;
this is an extreme delusion. They fail to realize that birth and death, day and night, and the cycle of the three periods of existence are as ordinary as events from yesterday or this morning.
Let me illustrate this with a recent example: it is like inviting guests for a banquet; regardless of whether the items set upon the table are refined or coarse, [one must accept them all].
Whether coarse or abundant, whether frugal or lavish—every form must be prepared and made ready in advance, so that when the time comes, everything may be displayed with each item complete.
If there were even the slightest deficiency, it would surely not be perfect; this is an immutable principle.

Throughout a human life, the duration of one's primary retribution—the body and life—and the secondary retribution—the family, property, wealth, fame, status, poverty, richness, nobility, or meanness—all down to the finest hair, are entirely determined by what came before.

The cultivation of meditative concentration in this life—those things currently experienced and enjoyed—do not come from without; they are entirely what one has created oneself and what one receives for oneself. Thus it is said:

"If you know the causes from past lives, you will see that what is received in this life is the result; if you know the fruits of the future, you will see that what is being done in this life is the cause.
Worldly people rely on their own intelligence, talent, and skills, believing they can thereby achieve fame, office, wealth, and honor; yet they fail to realize...
Success, fame, wealth, and honor are not brought about solely by talent and wisdom;

rather, they arise because I cultivated meditative concentration in previous lives and, in this life, these factors coincidentally converged with my talent and wisdom. Therefore, to rejoice upon obtaining them is delusion.

Furthermore, when the wealth, honor, success, and fame that I inherently possess are destroyed by others, to feel resentment toward those people and harbor deep hatred for the event is utterly [misguided].
I did not realize that the extent of my karmic fortune was limited to this. As for those things that have been destroyed, none were rightfully mine to possess;

or perhaps they were lost because I fell short of what was required of me. To then become anxious and, in turn, resent Heaven and blame others—thereby creating a grievance that remains unresolved—is a mistake.
Thus, we know that the "acceptance of fate" (*an-ming*) of the Sage Confucius is precisely this.
Regarding the causality of our Buddha: if one knows how to accept one's lot with peace, then poverty or wealth, gain or loss—all are entrusted to prior determination;

all are created by oneself. Thus, whether one is in straits or success, long-lived or short-lived, these are all the natural course of one’s own destiny. If one clearly believes in cause and effect, [one will not be disturbed].
Thus, all that we enjoy and utilize in this present life was cultivated and perfected by us in previous lives;

it originally could not have been granted by another, nor could it have been achieved through intellectual power alone. Even that which is attained through talent and wisdom is likewise our own inherent portion.
Being thus, why should one calculate gain and loss, wearying the mind with anxious thought, and vainly accumulating enmity and gratitude?
In this regard, if a person of wisdom truly believes in the retribution of cause and effect, they need not calculate their past gains and losses;
rather, they should utilize all that is presently available in this life to plant the field of merit for the future.
This is like a farmer of the world who selects fertile soil, plows deeply, weeds easily, and sows the seeds at the proper time, so that what is harvested in the autumn will be abundant.
Some count by the tens and hundreds; this is again clear and manifest. It simply depends on the field where one sows, for there are differences between fertile and barren soil.
The Buddha taught that making offerings to the Triple Gem—the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—is the field of excellence; serving one’s parents with filial piety is the field of reverence;
and relieving the poor and uprooting suffering is the field of the mind. I wish that the wise men of the world would not necessarily calculate [the merit].
Regarding past gains and losses, one should simply cultivate the field of merit for the future.

If one can indeed economize on useless and excessive expenditures and restrain the wealth spent on the luxury of body and speech, planting it within the three fields of merit, then not only will the adornment of future blessings and virtues increase, but in this present life as well, one’s person will be at ease and the mind joyful; such a person shall be foremost among those of fortune.
If one can plant blessings in the three fields of merit, further apply the mind to the Buddha-dharma, dispel delusive thoughts through mindfulness of the Buddha,
transform greed and anger through compassion, tame the violent through gentleness and harmony, and subdue arrogance through humility and radiance—
this is the practice of a Bodhisattva of great resolve. Layman, if you can indeed believe this, you should...
He is titled the Most Supreme Heroic Man.
Zhang Xiaozu’s *Ganlu* states that I once read in the *Fangwai zhi*:
"When the primordial chaos first divided and human beings first came into being, their bodies possessed radiance. They could fly...

They possessed mastery over their movements. They inhaled the wind and drank the dew; they did not cultivate the five grains. Springs gushed forth and dew descended, condensing into a substance like fat, called "earth-fat" (*pṛthivī-rasa*).
Its flavor was like *ghṛta-manda* (the finest essence of clarified butter); people who ate it found it sweet, relishing it without satiety.

Their bodies gradually became heavy and they could no longer lift themselves up; thus the earth-fat diminished and the five grains arose. Once the five grains arose, the earth-fat ceased to exist. As for the people—

When people first began to eat grain, the apertures of their emotions were bored open and the fire of desire arose. Consequently, the pure qi became turbid, the dew was no longer sweet, and the springs did not yield sweet water.
It was only when sage emperors and enlightened kings appeared that the heavenly virtue harmonized and the pure qi was preserved; thus, sweet dew descended and sweet springs gushed forth.
At such times, these phenomena served as auspicious signs and portents, as spiritual wonders and blessings. They moved the hearts of men and responded in heaven, originating from—

Consider this: such auspicious omens today are the constant norm of antiquity. In the eras of Yao and Shun, they occurred frequently; during the Three Dynasties, there were no records of them, nor were they mentioned in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
It was not until the reign of Emperor Wu of the Western Han that they began to be used to designate years, and from then on, they have appeared in every successive dynasty.

In the eighth year of the Hongwu era, when the Sacred Ancestor proceeded to the斋宫 (zhāigōng) to sacrifice to the Supreme Deity, sweet dew descended upon the tips of the pines at the Round Altar (yuánqīu).
It congealed on the branches and hung there, shaped like pearls and as sweet as molasses.
Thereupon, he commanded his ministers to gather it and eat it, and ordered them to compose poems, songs, and treatises to record the event. The Worldly Temple (Shìmào) was likewise so; thus we know:
The auspicious omen of the sweet dew appears through the virtue of a sovereign; it has never been heard of descending upon the wilds.

Now, Zhang Ziming Qiuliu of Longshan, through his profound filial piety, has moved Heaven so that sweet dew descended upon the locust trees in his courtyard. Its fragrance and flavor were extraordinary, and it did not dissipate for ten days.
What is the reason for this? Let me attempt to discuss it: Filial piety is the constant pattern of Heaven and the righteousness of Earth. It is the way of the people...

In the practice of filial piety, when the virtue of filiality reaches its height, the qi of harmony and centrality is nurtured. When the qi of harmony and centrality is nurtured, the qi of purity is maintained.

When the qi of purity is maintained, the heavenly virtue is attained. When the heavenly virtue is attained, auspicious omens respond; thus, sweet dew descends and the spring of nectar wells up. Now, filial piety is one and the same;
from the Son of Heaven down to the common people, it fundamentally possesses no dual nature. It is only that the mind is perfected and...

One whose vital energy (*qi*) is sufficient responds swiftly; this remains true whether the response is immediate or long-term. Therefore, I say that regarding Zhang Zi’s filial piety, there are aspects he himself did not realize;
thus, while the auspicious responses manifested over such a long duration, those who explained them had yet to reach the full depth of the matter.
Alas! The human mind has been submerged [in delusion] for a long time. Yet, there is none who does not possess this physical form;
and possessing this form, there is none who does not possess this nature (*xing*). When this nature is fully realized, filial virtue becomes complete, and auspicious omens respond.

Thus, when a person such as Master Zhang manifests a single act of filiality within his household, a hundred acts of filiality arise in his village, and ten thousand, a hundred million, a billion, and ten trillion acts of filiality arise in the state, extending even further.
If, throughout the world, people do not fall short of the sages and affairs do not fall short of antiquity, then the world and the state may ascend to the highest excellence.
All shall merge in the vast indistinctness and equally enjoy the bliss of Huaxu.

I would surely say that the dew is all sweet and the springs are all sweet as nectar, such that one drinks and eats according to one's needs without waiting for songs of praise or drumming the belly; what need then would there be for auspicious omens?

The disciple Liang Sishang, whose courtesy name is Bujian (Non-Transmigration), prostrated himself in homage and requested that his name be inscribed. I named him Bujian, intending to capture the essential purport of Master Zhaolun’s treatise.
When I was young, I read the *Zhao Lun*; reaching the passage, "The whirlwind topples the mountains, yet they remain eternally still; the Yangtze... [and so forth].
The rivers rush in competition yet do not flow; the wild horses gallop and flutter yet do not move; the sun and moon adorn the heavens yet do not revolve. One is dazed, knowing not where they point.

In the *jiashu* year of the Wanli era, while traveling on foot to the region of the Yellow River, I stayed for the winter retreat with my Dharma friend Miaofeng at the Daoyuan Hermitage in the northern mountains.
While collating and carving the woodblocks for this treatise, I suddenly attained a profound realization. Upon opening [the text]...
Behind the curtain, he saw wind blowing through the leaves, fluttering and filling the sky. He then realized it for himself, saying, "Master Sengzhao truly did not deceive me.
Whenever he would mention this to others, they all said, "Within that which moves, there is that which does not move.

I laughed and said, "If that were so, it would be a case of 'non-transmigration of principle,' rather than what Master Sengzhao called 'the non-transmigration of things. However, since he spoke of 'identifying with things' (*jiewu*),"
It does not migrate. How could it be that one abandons phenomena to seek principle, or relinquishes movement to seek stillness?

The Master Liang speaks of the four marks [of existence], yet there are no myriad things that are not subject to migration by these four marks. That which does not migrate is not something that ordinary sentiments can fathom or discern;
only Master Sengzhao has seen into its very core. Now that Master Liang has turned his heart toward the Dharma-gate, he is surely one who aspires to this.

Is it not so? If one attains the wondrous state of non-transmigration, then in daily life, amidst all manner of movement and stillness, leisure and busyness, adversity and favor, suffering and joy, gain and loss, toil and ease, profit and decline, praise and blame—and even wealth and honor versus poverty and low status, up to the great matters of calamity and death—one will clearly perceive not the slightest trace of coming or going. This is none other than the emanation-body of Śākyamuni.
