Huang Yongzhong said that Huang Sheng Yuanheng was my given name, and I styled him Yongzhong; I shall therefore provide an exposition for him. Now, the "Middle" (Zhong) has no substantial body. How could it...
It may be used; by observing it with a balance, its internal nature becomes self-evident. Yet the balance is the standard of equality for the world and the criterion for all things;

it is that which people must necessarily trust, such that its reliability is as clear as a wordless explanation. Alas, while people know the balance is trustworthy, they do not realize this applies to themselves.

Yet they do not realize that the application of the Mean lies herein. It is like an ordinary person who knows that food can satisfy hunger, yet does not know that it is the flavor that brings satisfaction;
because they prize the subtle flavor, they reject the coarse food. Therefore it is said: "Only through refinement and singleness may one truly hold fast to the Mean.
If one does not know the flavor, one does not know refinement; if one does not know the Mean, one is not skilled in its application. Only when one can employ the Mean does [true mastery] begin.
This was titled "Discourse on the Meaning of the Name 'Jiaka'" by Huang Zhizhi.
Ou Xingji came from afar to visit me; seeing that this youth had been diligent and arduous in his studies, I admired his resolve and thus bestowed this name upon him.

To say "jiā kě" (excellent/approved) means that all instances of "kě" (acceptable/approved) are interpreted as merely acceptable. To be merely acceptable implies there is something incomplete; this is incorrect.

For when a person has a desire in their heart, they will indulge in it if it is acceptable, and grow weary of it if it is not. Furthermore, the indulgence and desires of the heart do not cease until they are fully satisfied;
there are even cases where one desires to reach completion yet does not stop—how could this be called "merely"? This is true for both ancient and modern times.
Such a person, though situated within the realm of the "acceptable," does not perceive that which is acceptable.

Only in the Chan school’s supreme path is there the "seal of mind upon mind," which is termed *yinke* (confirmation/authorization). In the case of a sage, this is called "neither acceptable nor unacceptable.
Yet, as for "no unacceptability," it means there is nothing that is unacceptably so. Thus, all people and things in the world, the world and its time, and time and...

Life possesses that which is firm and unchanging. If one knows this unchanging Way, then poverty and success will be of one realm, danger and ease of one accord, and emergence and retirement of one moment. In this way, there is nothing that is not possible.
If a person can see through to this possibility, then wherever they go, it is simply what they encounter. Mr. Ou knew this realm; thus his name was true to his reality.
The Ultimate Limit. How could the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) be considered small?
The scholar Shi Xiu composed an explanation of his own name;
Zheng Sheng Shangzhi asked me for a name. I named him Shi Xiu. This is because one must be resolute in the Way (dharma), not merely a practitioner of cultivation.
This is insufficient to exhaustively encompass the Way (*dharma*). Yet the Way resides within each of us; it is inherently complete from the beginning, lacking nothing and having no surplus.

It is simply because we are obscured by material desires that we lose what is innate to us, leading to the six sense-faculties vying with one another and the six organs failing in their respective functions.
This is something those who are ignorant and unworthy cannot attain; even for those who are resolute, or even for the virtuous, there may be excess in their practice, as well as for the wise.
This refers to the excesses of knowledge. It is for this reason that the Sage establishes a standard of compromise (*zhézhōng*):

he restrains what is excessive and extends what is insufficient, returning all to the substance of the Great Mean and Ultimate Rectitude (*dàzhōng zhìzhèng*) so as to perfect that which is inherently possessed and not lose one's original nature (*tiānzhēn*).

Therefore, it is called "cultivation" (*xiū*); it is not that there is some cultivation apart from this. Thus it is said: "The cultivation of the Way is called instruction. From this, we know the Sage...
To teach one person another does not truly benefit that person.

Rather, one should shape them according to what they have been endowed with and inspire them in accordance with their own aspirations, so that within the interval of daily seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, and inside the midst of rising, sitting, eating, and resting, there is nothing that is not the ground where original luminosity is uniquely revealed.
Because they are obstructed by the suffering of long-standing habitual tendencies, [the teacher] therefore...
That which it clarifies is to penetrate its obscurations. For example, when the eye is obscured by forms, one penetrates it by means of forms;

when the ear is obscured by sounds, one penetrates it by means of sounds; when the tongue is obscured by tastes, one penetrates it by means of tastes; when the nose is obscured by odors, one penetrates it by means of odors;
when the body is obscured by tangibles, one penetrates it by means of tangibles; and when the mind is obscured by cognition, one penetrates it by means of cognition.
This penetrates them, washing away their long-standing habits and bringing forth their fundamental luminosity. It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is cleared, its brightness appears.
Yet the mirror’s brightness was originally inherent; it is not augmented by the act of polishing.

Because that which they practice is the Way, one must employ focused resolve to awaken it. If one lacks a single-minded and indomitable resolve, one will inevitably be overcome by habitual defilements. And...
The sun flows into the depths of darkness; it recedes so far that one does not know how to return. Such a person is not fit to be called human, much less worthy of being termed a scholar (*śi*).
Therefore, I say: the scholar is noble in his resolve, and resolve is noble in its cultivation. This is my discourse on the cultivation of the scholar.
An Explanation of the Epithet for Xu Zihou, composed by Xu Sheng Tianzai. Xu Sheng Tianzai performed the ritual of requesting an epithet. I conferred upon him the epithet "Zihou" (Thick as a Son).

Thereupon, I wrote this explanation: "Heaven is the original nature of our being. As for the term 'Carrying' (*zai*), its meaning is derived from the capacity of nature to carry all things. As the *Chunqiu* states:

"Attaining Zhong (central harmony) and He (harmony), heaven and earth find their proper places, and all things are nourished. Now, Zhong is the substance of human nature, while He is the virtue of human nature.

When a person can fully realize their nature, its substance becomes pervasive and its virtue expansive; thus they are able to establish heaven and earth in their proper positions and nourish all things.
This is the inherent principle of the specific allotment of one's nature. However, although this nature is originally possessed, if it is not... [the text continues].
If one’s cultivation is not sufficient, one cannot reach the utmost vastness to exhaust the subtle and minute.

Therefore, I have selected those passages that emphasize "thickness" (substantiality), intending to deepen what is cultivated so as to reinforce that thickness; only then can one sustain and carry all things without omission. Thus it is said:
"If the accumulation of wind is not substantial, it lacks the power to support great wings. If the accumulation of water is not substantial, it lacks the power to support a great ship."

One lacks power. Yet, although the inherent virtues we naturally possess are vast by their very nature, unless one has cultivated them deeply through accumulation, one will lack the power to shoulder great responsibilities.

Therefore, among the heroes of antiquity who were endowed with exceptional talent, there were none who did not subject themselves to rigorous austerity and diligent resolve to sharpen their instruments, so as to await the great tasks of the world and the state.
By this means, one establishes a great enterprise that shall remain imperishable for a thousand years; thus its light illuminates a hundred generations and its bounty flows without end.
This is what is meant by "the source being distant and the stream long"—the ultimate degree of thickness.

Because one's nature is the foundation of heaven, earth, and the myriad things, if one can fully realize that nature, one may participate alongside heaven and earth, thereby fulfilling the capable service of a true man. One is able to...
When one’s task is completed, one may truly be called a human being; otherwise, one will decay along with all other things.
How then could such a person be called a "great man" (zhūngfú)? Therefore, the sage dwells in the substantial rather than the thin, and abides in the real rather than the ornamental.
To discard ornamentation and take up reality is the Way of the Substantial. Thus, I have named you Zǐhòu (Substantial). May you exert yourself in this!
Allow me to explain the meaning of the word "to contain" (*rong*).
Heaven and earth are most vast; there is nothing among the myriad things that they do not contain. Yet, you say, "Contain me. Is it that I alone am unable to be contained?
Nevertheless, there must be a reason for this. As an ancient said: "Who says heaven and earth are wide? When one steps out the door..."
Only that which possesses obstruction cannot admit others; it is not that heaven and earth cannot accommodate me, but rather that I am unable to accommodate heaven and earth.
Therefore, the sage encompasses all things without regarding them as his own.
Not regarding things as one's own is non-self (*anātman*). Where there is no self, there are no objects. Where there are no objects, there is neither object nor adversary.
When there is neither object nor adversary, object and self are forgotten. When object and self are forgotten, all objects become the self.
When all objects become the self, the self merges with the myriad things. Because of this merging, it is able to contain the self; this is the perfected work of the sage. Only...
Those who have forgotten artifice resemble this. Therefore, I bestowed the style name "Ruzhong" (Loyal to You) upon Elder Li.
Xie Ruzhong’s *Exegesis on Style Names* says:
"The youth of Zhanggong named Shangjia requested that I provide him with a style name; I named him Ruzhong. This means that filial piety is extended [to all].
Loyalty is indeed that which the superior prizes. That the child was born because of Bing (the third branch) indicates this: Bing is the image of the ruler’s virtue;
it is bright and yang, firm and upright, outwardly firm yet inwardly supple—this is the substance of virtue. Therefore, it is called "supple and admirable."
This means that the yang is strong and the yin is weak; the ruler is strong and the minister is weak. This is the correctness of the superior and the subordinate, and the harmony of Heaven and Earth.
Because the great arrives and the small departs, the yang seeks the yin and the yin enters the yang; therefore, in the hexagram, it is Li, representing fire.
In humans, there is the mind and the eyes. The essence of the mind overflows into the eyes; the eyes look out while presiding over the mind. Thus, the internal and external are one.
Therefore, a ruler’s seeking of ministers is like the mind’s relation to the eyes; a minister’s service to the ruler is like the eyes’ relation to the mind.
In this way, the internal and external are unified and their functions do not differ. When virtue is harmonized, success is achieved; hence, such a state is praiseworthy. Otherwise, it is not.
Then one is already in peril. What is called "hearing with the ears and seeing with the eyes" means that the Lord of Heaven has lost its governance and the five organs have failed in their duties;
to seek excellence under such conditions—is it not difficult? Thus we know that a minister serving his sovereign is like the eyes obeying the commands of the heart;
this is the height of loyalty. Therefore, I take his excellence and further praise it, for through loyalty, one may indeed be firm.

How admirable! I observe that this youth possesses a spirit that transcends his years and a physique of noble vigor; his temperament is harmonious and his mind is serene. He has the natural endowment of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*).

As the saying goes: "The great man does not lose the heart of an infant. In truth, he already embodies the characteristics of a great man, as is evident in every aspect of his demeanor and physical presence—even in the way he plays childish games like Confucius did as a child.

C'en... [text fragment]... The provided text ends abruptly. Based on the context, it likely refers to the famous anecdote where Confucius played at building cities with mud while his mother looked on, which was interpreted as a sign of his future greatness.
The sacrificial vessels and ritual implements were set out, and the ceremonial decorum was established. Is this not because Heaven has bestowed something, and man is able to bring it to completion?
This month, Master sent the young boy to enter the Elementary School; he immediately gave him this name, and I conferred upon him the courtesy name Yizhong.
Master desires that I write this for him to preserve with care, as a formal contract for the young boy.

Regarding the explanation of the character "Jue" (Awakened), it was given to the man surnamed Fang Yimin. His father had traveled to Hengzhou for official service, where he paid me his respects and inquired about the Dharma of transcendence.

Consequently, he requested a dharma-name, which I bestowed upon him as "Fuxin" (Blessed Mind). This was because the mind is the foundation of the field of merit and the place where all virtues converge, much like fertile soil.

It gives rise to the hundred grains. [The child] requested a name once more, and was named Jue-zhi (Awakened-to). This is because "Buddha" means awakening. An ancient worthy said: "The mind itself is the Buddha.
Since this mind is fundamentally the Buddha, it becomes a sentient being due to delusion; this is the transformation of awakening through delusion.
In our daily lives, the single thought-moment of the present: if one awakens, every thought is a Buddha-thought; moment after moment, it is always thus.
Awakening constitutes the eternally abiding Buddha; non-awakening leads to eternal fall into the path of delusion and the loss of one's original existence.
It is like a person with eyes dwelling in a dark room who sees nothing at all—this is what is meant by being "upside-down and blind" while remaining unaware of it.
Since the mind is the field of merit and awakening is the seed, if one does not awaken in daily life, it is as if having a field that is not plowed; how can this be?
Is it not because one hopes for the harvest of autumn? Therefore, I say: awaken to it. To awaken to it is the root of planting merit.
If you, my friend, are able to awaken, you will not fail the inherent nature; this is the greatest of blessings.

If one reads the "Discourse on Penetrating Hearing" by Master Dashi and the words of Penetrating Hearing, one will find that he follows Mañjuśrī’s selection of the "perfect penetration," taking the ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara as supreme, and further takes the "mind-hearing that penetrates the ten directions" of Samantabhadra as the standard;
one [the former] through the perfection of the ear, and the other [the latter] through the penetration of the mind. If...
From the standpoint of Old Han, look at how the void and the eyebrows are intertwined; he speaks the Dharma everywhere, and the myriad phenomena all hear it.
Thus, the three great Bodhisattvas are left utterly embarrassed, and even Zibo’s words find no ground upon which to rest.
Only when one penetrates this point can one be said to have "heard through the caverns."
The Hall Master Tianxiang requested the Elder Haiyin to change his name to Wuyin (No Concealment), as his former name, Minggui (Bright Cinnamon), was too close to the mundane.
The Elder smiled and replied: "Names are merely provisional designations; moreover, the Truth cannot be named. Whatever can be named..."

[The Master] said, "All these are merely worldly ears. Thereupon, [the disciple] took his leave. One day, he happened to visit the master’s quarters and said, "Last night, I dreamed that you were changing my name.

When I asked for the name, why have you forgotten it? The old man laughed again and said, "Birth-and-death and nirvana are both like a dream from yesterday. Furthermore, all that can be named is but the talk of a dream. Know this well..."

If phenomena are like dreams, then all names and words are nothing other than dream-events. If one contemplates phenomena as being like dreams, then the Buddha-dharma is constantly manifest before one.
For this reason, it is termed "No Concealment" (*Wuyin*), intending to capture that which is clearly present before the eyes:

within the mutual engagement of the six sense faculties, everything is nothing other than the Buddha-work. This is just as Lingyun attained awakening upon seeing peach blossoms, or Xiangyan upon hearing bamboo strike.
This is to clarify the mind. All of these are those who have attained actual realization at the very gateway of sound and form.

When the Wayman of the Valleys relied upon Master Haitang and requested that he point out a shortcut for him, Haitang said: "As for what Confucius said, 'My disciples, do you think I am hiding anything from you?
I hide nothing from you,' how would you, Grand Historian, explain this in your usual way? The Master prepared to respond, whereupon Haitang—
He said, "Not so, not so. One day, while attending the hall and walking in the mountains, the rock-peonies were in full bloom.
Master Tang asked, "Do you smell the fragrance of the *mugicha* flowers? He replied, "I do. Master Tang said, "I have hidden nothing from you.
At this, he was suddenly enlightened and prostrated himself, saying, "The Master’s heart is so earnestly compassionate; this worldly fellow has attained it through the dust of fragrance."
Regarding "entering through awakening": Hall Master, do not say that one enters through the dust of fragrance; this may be called "nothing hidden.
Is there anything else hidden? Confucius also said: "There is no action of mine in which I do not share with my disciples; such is Qiu."
San. Regarding the "Explanation of the Character 'Vast' (虛懷)," composed by Master Zhulin of Wutai. In the year Wuma, the year following his passing, his disciple Daqian traveled from afar to Kuang...
[The monk] Shan requested me to compose an inscription for his stūpa. The Master had received his training at Bichun Temple on Mount Xishan.
Bichun was a preeminent monastery within the royal capital; its provisions were abundant, and it was the foremost place where monks enjoyed the most excellent sensual pleasures.

Yet the Master was able to renounce this and depart for cold cliffs amidst ice and snow, to draw near to his spiritual mentors and devote himself deeply to the Buddha-dharma. He was a disciple of Zhulin.
There were those numbering in the hundreds and thousands; yet Master Gong alone kept in mind the imperishability of the final radiance. One can thus know that his intent was to value the fundamental.
When I sat in conversation with him and probed what he held within, he was focused on contemplation of principle and meticulous in his observance of the monastic discipline.
Thus, his aspirations are far superior to those of the mediocre people of the mundane world; I highly commend him.

His original style name was Yuguang (Excelling Light), but I found it too ostentatious and therefore changed it to Xuhuai (Empty-mindedness). This was intended to signify that he possesses a humble mind capable of receiving benefit.
This is because sentient beings have long been slumbering in the cycle of birth and death without awakening, solely due to their immersion in the five desires.
Habitual tendencies have become dense and thick; afflictions fill the breast. Thus, whatever actions one undertakes all serve as provisions for karma.
Because one clings to what one possesses without transforming it, accumulated defilements grow ever deeper. As defilements deepen, karma becomes increasingly heavy.

When delusion accumulates without end, the path of suffering grows ever longer. Since there is ultimately no reflection or repentance, how can there be any light? To investigate the reason for this: its...
It is not the fault of the mind being non-empty. When the sages empty themselves to wander through the world, it is because they are able to relinquish that which they grasp.

Once what is grasped is relinquished, the mind naturally becomes empty. When the mind is empty, objects naturally become still. With the mind empty and objects still, both self and others are forgotten.
When the self is forgotten, there is no mind capable of grasping; when objects are forgotten, the objects grasped are severed.
Thus, when one seeks it within the mind and its objects, it is utterly unobtainable; this is the ultimate in emptiness.
When one’s state of being is such as this, one stands transcendentally alone, roaming together with the Dao. What single thing could then constrain one, or what speck of dust serve as a burden?

Yet, by entering the non-existent through the non-existent, one’s wondrous practice accords with the profound mystery. Casting oneself across for the sake of all beings—this is what is called "non-arising."
To manifest various dignified demeanors while abiding in the meditative attainment of cessation—this is the sage’s capacity for engaging with the world.
Furthermore, how could it be merely a matter of tireless humility? It is, rather, that which is luminous yet does not dazzle.
Regarding the name Nie Yingru:
Nie Sheng studied under the Chan Master Daguan, whose given name was Yingru.

Observing his name, I thereby understood that what the Master bestowed upon the student was the most supreme Dharma-gate. Thus, I shall provide an explanation for it. Now, "Rú" (Suchness) is not a mark.
The discourse on "resembling" (si) refers directly to the fundamental substance of our own being. What is called *tathatā* (True Suchness) is but another designation for the One Mind.
Now, "true" (*zhen*) means not false, and "such" (*ru*) means unchanging; thus it is named *tathatā*.
Because this mind is luminous and vast, as tranquil as empty space, its essence is quiescent, such that even as days pass and months come, and as darkness and light alternate...
They succeed one another: clouds drift and birds fly; the wind stirs and dust rises. The four seasons revolve in a cycle, day and night without interval.
All manner of transformations arise and cease without stopping, yet the essence of emptiness remains steadfast, tranquil, and unmoving.

We human beings receive this nature of True Suchness (Tathatā) and rely upon it to form our bodies, yet we are carried away by deluded thoughts, fluctuating through honor and disgrace, sorrow and joy, and likes and dislikes.
Anger, illness, calamities, and misfortunes—even unto the succession of birth and death—manifest as various transformations that act as obstacles.
This is because while one's own essence is inherently suchness (*tathatā*), it is now not so. Therefore, the Chan Master, based on what is originally inherent, guides them by saying:
"You should be such. Thus it is called "being such" (*yingru*); it means that although one is inherently such from the beginning, one is currently not so, and desires to return [to that state].

It is inherently present; there is no need to seek it externally. One should simply accord with this "thusness" (*tathatā*). If one truly accords with this original thusness, how could there be anything further to accord with?

Thus we know that for us, the distinction between the holy and the ordinary is not separated by anything else; it lies precisely between delusion and awakening, between according with thusness and not according with it.

To not accord with it is to be ordinary; to accord with it is to be holy. As the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "That which is called 'Tathāgata' is the meaning of the thusness of all phenomena. For this reason...

Contemplate this: it is not only that the essence of the mind is fundamentally suchness; rather, all dharmas—from the immediate perspective of one's own body, there are the four great elements and six sense organs, and when minutely analyzed, the thirty-six constituent parts—whether internal or external—are all suchness.
From the distant perspective of external objects, there are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth;
the scaly, the shelled, the feathered, and the hairy; the grasses, trees, and even the finest motes of dust. To the very limit of every phenomenal form within the world, all are suchness.
There is nothing that is not thus. Therefore it is said: "The lush green bamboo is entirely True Suchness (tathatā); the dense yellow flowers are none other than Prajñā.
Viewed through this lens, all phenomena are fundamentally such-like (yǐrú). Since all phenomena are such-like, what room is there for likes and dislikes, or for emotional grasping and rejecting?
How could one then be obstructed by the karmic activities of birth and death? This is what is meant by: "The myriad realms are fundamentally..."

The world is tranquil, yet people create their own clamor. If a person can turn things around, they are identical to the Tathāgata. When things turn [the mind], both mind and objects are as such (tathatā).
When both object and self are forgotten, the holy and the ordinary are equal. Birth-and-death, coming and going, are like dreams and illusions;
what connection do they have with our essence of numinous awareness? Therefore, those among us who are resolved to transcend birth and death should conform to this suchness.
Therefore it is said, "One should respond thus. You must recognize this.
Why is the word "rare" (希有) explained?
It is because of the arising of life. To be earnest in one's orientation toward the Way—such that a person can truly orient themselves toward the Way—is indeed rare. If one can truly...

To behold the Path of Seeing is even more rare. Once, while I was reading the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, I reached the point where Subhūti addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "How rare!
I felt great doubt about this. Upon examining the passage prior to that exclamation, there was nothing particularly extraordinary, nor were there any profound or mystical words;
it merely described how the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, ate his meal, walked for meditation, washed his feet, and spread out his seat.
That is all; there is nothing else particularly extraordinary about it. What did Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti) see that caused him to exclaim with such wonder?

This statement has remained unrefuted by the Buddhas and patriarchs in their commentaries for over a thousand years. Suddenly, however, it was seen through by Śūnyatā-utpanna at the very place where the World-Honored One had practiced.
Unconsciously, you let out such a cry! What is so rare? Indeed, what have you seen that is so rare?
If it is like Subhūti seeing through the Buddha’s state, or seeing through one's own home, this is merely a matter of everyday life and livelihood.
Furthermore, what dharma could you point to as a rare dharma, or what matter as a rare matter? If [you have not yet...]
Pay close attention. People merely compete in praising and extolling [the Dharma] based on the appearances of words and letters;
I fear that if they turn their heads and look back one day, what they see will no longer appear marvelous. Why did He-sheng request a dharma discourse?
Since this old man has no dharma to speak, I have spoken thus by following his request.

Regarding the explanation of the name "Fragrant Forest" (Xianglin): The Elder Zhanshan was named Zhenxiao. His teacher bestowed upon him the style name Xianglin and requested that I provide an explanation for it.
When I resided in Wuyang, I saw a Western ship carrying sandalwood arriving; when I inquired about its place of origin, they said: [The remainder of the text follows.]
This is a land that produces incense. It is extremely hot and teems with giant snakes. These snakes are naturally venomous, and their heat cannot be dispelled;
they rely solely on this incense to alleviate it, coiling themselves upon it to obtain coolness. Because of the snake's venom, the incense also becomes more potent.
Furthermore, its trees grow solitary, and where they grow, no other vegetation thrives; the incense alone forms a forest. Thus, the ancient masters said:
It is said: "Sandalwood is utterly devoid of common timber within; now that Master Da has been praised for his filial piety at Xianglin, how could his title be without significance?
Consider our original teacher, Śākyamuni, who appeared in the world and taught the three trainings of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. He focused exclusively upon the precepts.

Although there are many categories of precepts, he uniquely revered the Brahma Net Great Precepts (*Brahmajāla-sūtra*). These precepts are the teaching for Bodhisattvas; they are not for those who lack the adamantine mind.
I am unable to uphold them. Upon humble inspection of the Sūtras that open the chapter on precepts (*śīla*), I see that they take filial piety as their foundation.

Thus, the Sūtra says: "Filial piety is called the precept. This means being filially obedient toward one's parents; being filially obedient toward teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem; being filially obedient to the Dharma of the Ultimate Way; and being filially obedient toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, the Vinaya records the categories of precepts: there are five hundred enumerated in brief, while in detail there are three thousand modes of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*). Eight...
Among the myriad subtle practices, the Buddha uniquely points to filial piety as the root.

His intention is that if a son of the Buddha can fully fulfill this filial piety, then all categories of precepts will be completely possessed within a single mind. Is this not like the solitary growth of sandalwood?

When the three poisons and the heat of afflictions scorch and roast the body and mind, there is no means of rescue or relief; yet by relying upon the precepts, one attains coolness. Is this not like the sandalwood?
Can it not eliminate the great venom of a serpent? Filial piety arises from the mind-ground of sentient beings' feverish afflictions (*kleśa*);

its own essence is pure, thereby eliminating those afflictions. When afflicted by defilements, the light of the precepts becomes perfect—is this not like sandalwood growing in a land of poisonous heat?
Its own essence is cool, yet it produces its fragrance precisely because of that heat and poison. When one filial piety is perfected, all [virtues] are complete.
His precepts were perfected; as his precepts were perfected, his filial piety became ever more sincere. Like a sandalwood grove, he was thus called "Fragrant Grove" (Xianglin);
is it not fitting that this was used as his name? This is the Master Da’s speaking without having spoken; my own words would be but a superfluous addition.

Jianbai wrote this preface for Master Shou, who served as the abbot of the capital monastery. His noble aspirations were directed toward the ultimate, and he delighted in associating with spiritual friends.

Although he had not yet traveled across a hundred cities, whenever eminent and virtuous elders from various quarters arrived, he would rejoice in their presence; thus, he may be described as one who "sits in practice" while visiting and attending upon them.
My Dharma brother, Master Gumei, was deeply esteemed by him [the Master]. He once bestowed upon him the name Jianbai (Firmly White).
I therefore offer this explanation on his behalf: When Buddha-nature is within the bonds of saṃsāra, it is like a mani jewel fallen into a latrine or a lotus flower situated in the mud;
it is neither obscured by the defilement of afflictions nor sullied by the mire of the five desires. This is because its own nature is celestial.
Yet, its fundamental nature is thus pure, clear, luminous, and pristine. Yet people see only defilement and fail to recognize the radiance of the *maṇi* jewel;
they see only the mud and fail to recognize the fragrance and purity of the lotus.
Consequently, they are submerged in the toil of worldly dust and do not realize the perfect clarity of their own nature. You, sir, were born amidst the dust, yet you remain steadfast and noble.

The aspiration to transcend the mundane world sets the heart upon the Land of Ultimate Bliss and brings about weary detachment from birth and death. This is the fruit of a single moment of solitary clarity, which constantly illumines in response to conditions;
it is precisely through this that one performs Buddha-work within the midst of worldly toil and transforms a defiled realm into a pure land.

How could such a state be merely characterized by the categories of "solidity," "whiteness," "identity," or "difference"? Nevertheless, if the aspiration is not ground, it will not be firm; if the mind is not washed, it will not be pure. For us, people...

If one's resolve is not firm, it must be polished with patience; if the mind is not pure, it must be washed with precepts. When patience reaches the state of non-arising, the precepts return to their own nature.
This self-nature is inherently pure; this is what is meant by "polishing it without wearing it away. If it is polished without being worn away, [it remains as it is].
