If the retribution for such [meritorious deeds] is already as profound as this, how much more so for the field of merit that is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—how could its virtue possibly be conceived?
Now, to the north of Gaozhou and south of Shendian, lofty mountains pierce the Milky Way and steep ridges span the heavens.
It serves as the throat of the lands beyond the sea and the gateway to Lopang. In former times, the wheels of travelers' carriages could not pass side by side there.
Today, as one travels for trade, how could one venture alone? Truly, this is a perilous path for the pursuit of fame and profit; it is indeed a den of thieves and bandits.

It is only thanks to the years since the Jia-long era, following the defeat of the rebels by the Imperial Army, that these treacherous roads have been transformed into level highways and this obstinate local custom has been turned toward the Imperial Wind. Although there is the toil of wading and climbing on the journey, and yet—

In their coming and going, they lack the caution one would have toward wolves or jackals. Yet, because this is a scorched frontier in a hot region, where miasmic vapors and misty fogs prevail, compounded by a stifling, steaming toxic air;

and furthermore, because it coincides with the surging of hot springs, travelers from the ends of the earth tread as if upon fire and into boiling water, while soldiers on distant garrisons and those on campaign walk as if amidst a spreading conflagration or treading upon cauldrons.
Shouldering one another and following in close succession, they barely manage to ride upon the hem of a sleeve...
Clouds formed; they ascended the crags and clambered through the forests, truly sweating as if it were raining. Their lips grew parched and their tongues dry;

they longed for a single ladle of water like those in a great drought yearn for clouds and rainbows. With throats burning and entrails withered, obtaining even a drop was like a person suffering from consumption drinking ambrosia.
How much more so when traveling a hundred *li* for a single rest station, exhausting the day to obtain but half a meal; the servants sweat blood while the carriage and horses are drenched in rain.
With no kinsman in sight, this suffering has no one to whom it can be told. All of this arises from greed for fame and pursuit of profit, seeing gain and forgetting one’s own form.

One knows only how to pick up earth and call it gold; who understands how to cast away a brick to draw forth a jade? Furthermore, as for those of lowly status on the frontiers and the Miecili [Mleccha] tribes—
As for the people of this land, they customarily worship spirits and honor licentious shrines; the common folk hold life cheap and take pleasure in killing and theft.
Though it be but a cubit of cloth or a peck of grain, they will recklessly seize it from others; yet how could they joyfully bestow even a single grain of rice or a small coin upon themselves?

Thus, their seeds of Bodhi grow increasingly parched and withered, while the sprouts of their roots of goodness daily lament their own decay. For this reason, their evils become ever more evil. And...
The poor become ever poorer; delusion leads to further delusion, making transformation increasingly difficult.

Fortunately, we have recently encountered the various high-ranking officials of the administration, who practice universal love and benevolence to aid humanity and benefit all things. By means of this Way, they awaken the people, continuing the legacy of the former sages and opening the path for future learners.
They have established Buddhist temples throughout the prefectures and counties, planting the supreme banner of the Dharma and raising the crimson standard.
In the Jeta Grove, he performed inconceivable Buddha-works; he may truly be called an extraordinary vessel and a precious raft for those lost at the crossroads.
This mountain monk [Name], having encountered hardship while propagating the Dharma, was graced by imperial favor with an exile to Lei Yang.
Cast into ten thousand *li* of remote wilderness, I took up arms at Dianbai and ascended the Ridge of Bitter Vines, parched and exhausted.
Originally, while longing for the nectar of immortality, I was lingering on a perilous path when I happened to see two groups of bhikṣus building a dwelling by the roadside.
Taking a bowl of fragrant tea, I respectfully presented it before their horses' heads. I joyfully drank it while weeping; moved by deep sorrow, I felt a surge of grief.
Who would have known that in this land of pestilence and miasma, I would unexpectedly encounter companions from Tiantai? Thus, we briefly rested amidst the trees, and then...
He inscribed this upon a stone (at that time, there was an inscription for the Tea Hermitage written upon the wall). From this, he made a vow:

"I pray that in this place a great monastery may be established, so that by means of these practical matters one may clarify the mind, and by relying upon tea one may expound the Dharma. Since then, the years and months have passed.
Suddenly, after two years had passed, in the summer of the Wuxu year, I encountered Master Wan, the Judicial Commissioner of Gaizhou, by chance in the city of Xianyang.
As we conversed on the matters of the Vulture Peak, when he spoke of this [temple], he sighed greatly in wonder, exclaiming, "How marvelous!
He then requested that I serve as a bridge for the protection of the Dharma, daring to ask that I act as a compassionate donor to restore its transformation-city, leading [the way].

The multitude turns toward the place of jewels; yet, wishing to transform a defiled land into a pure realm and replace tiles and stones with grass and thatch, one need not necessarily strive for the intermingling radiance of gold and emerald.

It is sufficient to ensure that both the Dharma and material sustenance provide relief. However, considering that such merit cannot be achieved by a single effort, it is essential to gather many people through shared conditions.
For this reason, I respectfully compose this brief memorial to announce it universally throughout the ten directions, entrusting it to virtuous men and women.
[Name], I prostrate before you, Illustrious Official. I inquire after the health of the Elder, the merchant travelers, and the high-ranking officials and scholars.

I humbly pray that you will give rise to the vast and great mind and regard this as a rare encounter. For every person is a Buddha; it simply requires one’s own willingness to accept this responsibility.
Every dharma is true; what thing is not an act of giving? Whether much or little, whether refined or coarse, even a drop of dew may suffice.

By adding a stream, even a light speck of dust can fill a mountain. Although the three chariots outside the gate were provisionally established as a skillful means to guide them, it was truly an act of compassion to cause them to penetrate directly the path that transcends all.
Simply by breaking open the bag of stinginess, one suddenly beholds the adorned Buddha-land.
Those who have passed go, and those who come find rest; here, I offer you a single bowl. Within the cup of Old Zhao, radiance floats.
The radiant white snow: those who thirst drink it and those who hunger eat it. Lu Tong forcibly swallowed seven bowls; from beneath his armpits arose a refreshing breeze.
It removed the heat of affliction to attain coolness, and relieved fatigue to eliminate exhaustion.
Furthermore, using the water of the Dharma to irrigate the seeds of Bodhi, it causes the spiritual sprouts to grow; planting roots of goodness within Prajñā.
This field has successfully borne the fruit of sainthood. From this point on, his mind is free and unburdened; whether departing or staying, he moves with effortless ease.

This may truly be called a dojo of ultimate bliss, a Buddhist practice of joy. He spreads the vast and sweeping breeze of compassion, completely clearing away the mists and fogs of the pestilential sea;
he hangs the perfect orb of the Buddha-sun, shattering the illusory dreams of the dark alleys. Thus, for those of icchantika...
May those who have committed the evils of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, and those who are perverse and rebellious, not fall into the ghostly realm of the rākṣasas.

May the virtue of one person lead to the virtue of many, so that goodness fills the borders. May the peace of one family lead to the peace of many families, so that the entire world is brought to security.
May all together ascend to the land of benevolence and longevity, and collectively witness the transformation of a flourishing and harmonious era. By these merits, we pray for the Emperor.

May your life span be boundless. With this body and mind, I shall requite Your Majesty’s infinite grace. May it be known that blessings are not established in vain, nor are these matters spoken of in idle discourse.
I only pray that you will grant your approval; there is no need for further hesitation. Respectfully submitted.
Written on the first day of the middle month of autumn in the Wuli E-xu year (1618) at the Lupo Hall in Xiancheng.
Petition for the Reconstruction of the Tàipíng Bridge and Pǔjì Temple at Nánxióng Prefecture:

It is submitted that this renowned district on the southern frontier serves as a slender thread connecting the life-veins of both the Chinese and the barbarians. This ancient ford of Tàipíng, where a flying rainbow spans the waters, guards the strategic throat of the hundred Yue territories.
Among the merchants and travelers within the realm, there are none who do not pass by this way; and as for the rare treasures from beyond the seas, they must inevitably traverse it.

Alas! In this vast ocean of delusion spanning kalpas, upon whom can one rely for the precious raft? Amidst the turbulent waves of the sea of suffering, by what compassionate vessel may one cross over?
We reverently consider the Taining Zhenqiao Pujisi Temple: its regulations were established in a former age, and its legacy honors the sages of old.

Facing south, it welcomes the Ling River, solemnly resembling the Ganges at Śrāvastī; behind it lies Mount Meikui, appearing just like the Jeta Grove in Kapilavastu. It commands the southern region...
The source of the ocean commands the magnificent vistas of a formidable pass; it is truly a bridge and ferry for all eternity, and a most advantageous crossing upon the long journey.
Yet, as days follow months and rains grow thin while winds wither, the world changes and time passes; the beams collapse and the rafters rot.
Illusory flowers easily fade, and mirages are difficult to retain. Thus, the Triple Gem remains hidden and unmanifested, and though the hearts of the multitude turn toward it—
There is no longer any place for reliance. Now, fortunately, we have encountered a benevolent ruler on the throne who wishes to reform the old and establish a new era.
The mind of this noble gentleman is set upon rescuing what is biased and mending what is decayed. I, a mountain monk named [Name], dare to grasp the sounding-stick to raise my voice;

may the scholars, commoners, and men of high attainment hope to receive his influence and carry forth its resonance. Since human nature is inherently good, it must surely respond and achieve penetration when moved by such inspiration. Thus, although the Buddha—

When transformation responds to those with whom there is a karmic affinity, how could it fail to manifest spontaneously without being sought? For this reason, I respectfully hold this brief memorial and announce it far and wide to the ten directions.

I humbly entreat those of wealth and status to exert their strength to repay the kindness of past lives; I entreat those of poverty and low station to apply their labor, hoping thereby to plant the seeds for future fruition.
May it be that wherever the bags of stinginess are torn open, the diamond seeds shall reveal their radiance; and when the waters of craving have dried up...

With the vessel of Prajñā, one ascends to the other shore; neither bound by the past nor constrained by worldly commerce, the seed of Bodhi is fully realized by all, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss is accessible to every person.
Let it not be said that merit is merely like the sands of the Ganges; rather, rejoice that the mind has returned to the Treasure Abode.

Their achievement transcends the outflows, and their virtue bears measureless bounds. We pray for the Emperor’s longevity as enduring as mountains and rivers, and may his radiant influence spread throughout the ages.

Throughout the realms of the sun and moon, may all who encounter the falling frost and dew submit to the breeze of compassion. Wherever ships and carriages reach, may all gaze upon the sun of wisdom with reverent devotion.
Such benefits as these cannot be fully extolled. I request that your honorable names be inscribed here, hoping they shall endure imperishably.
A Memorial for the Reconstruction of Jetavana Monastery:
I humbly submit that throughout the worlds of the ten directions, every place is a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); those with the eye of wisdom can perceive this.

The eighty thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) are, in their various forms, none other than the Buddha’s work; those who have realized the mind know this of themselves. How much more so when there exists the precedent of covering the ground with gold—let us follow this model.
This constitutes the ancestral tradition of the ancient Buddhas. I have often reflected that the noble counsel of leaving behind one’s sash is precisely the standard for officials.

However, affairs follow their opportunities, and the Way relies on individuals for its propagation. Such auspicious times are difficult to encounter, yet this favorable condition has coincidentally come together.

This ancient monastery of Jetavana was founded during the Tang Dynasty, as recorded clearly in the annals; it has long been a place of veneration and solemn rites. It is a regret that the mountain spirits failed to preserve it.
Suddenly falling into a thicket of brambles, he relied upon the protective power of the Dharma to regain his awareness; in an instant, his blocked path was cleared.

This son who had previously committed the five heinous crimes was nearly left without refuge by the Buddhas and Patriarchs; now, by the grace of the Three Heavens, both spirits and men have fortunately found a place of reliance.
Yet, the temple buildings are dilapidated, the golden images wither amidst the wind and rain, the incense and lamps have vanished, and the sounds of the *brahman* remain silent through day and night.

I, this mountain monk Rujian, have come by chance to beg for alms. Hanging my staff by the Ling River, I have established a vihāra on the Ganges and opened a bamboo grove at the foot of the city wall.
Yet I fear that a great mansion cannot be completed by a single tree; it must rely upon eminent worthies to combine their collective strength so that the task may be easily accomplished.
To pluck a mere blade of grass and fashion it into a Buddhist sanctuary is, by its very nature, the forging of the Lord of Heaven. To dissect the subtle...
Dust has been cleared from the sutra scrolls; this excludes only the abbreviated works of Samantabhadra.

We humbly entreat you all to lend your hands and eyes, each vying in spiritual powers, gathering the small to form the great, proceeding from the minor to the major, until even ghosts and spirits must yield their transport, no longer rivaling Mount Sumeru.
Suddenly, gold and azure hues intermingle in splendor, perfectly forming a Pure Land; its transformation follows the mind, and its enjoyment is within one's own grasp.
This serves as a sign of karmic retribution, and its merit shall endure imperishably.
Preface for the Rebuilding of the Universal Vow for Buddhahood Stūpa at Lake Center Temple for the Release of Living Beings:
The Buddha’s great compassion universally delivers all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma realm, so that they may all attain Buddhahood. Thus it is said:
"If even a single sentient being has not yet attained Buddhahood, I shall not take up Bodhi. This is the vow of the Buddha to deliver living beings. *Prajñāpāramitā*...

If it is said that immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings are all brought to nirvana, yet in reality not a single sentient being has attained nirvana—this is the true realization of these sentient beings attaining Buddhahood.

Throughout antiquity and the present, many have practiced with the aspiration to become Buddhas, yet few actually bring boundless sentient beings to liberation in the present moment. This is because each person harbors thoughts of waiting for [the future].

It is only after one has attained Buddhahood that one can truly deliver sentient beings; yet, little do we realize that the very act of being able to deliver sentient beings with a Buddha-mind in this present moment is the wondrous practice of true Buddhahood.
Among all practices for the vast deliverance of sentient beings, none surpasses the single gateway of releasing living creatures (fangsheng).
In the past, the Great Master Tiantai—and following him, the Great Master Yongming—while serving as officials, once...
Purchasing living beings with government funds to release them so that they do not die is something everyone currently knows.

From that time until now, only Master Yunqi has been able to emulate the conduct of these two masters. Furthermore, West Lake has anciently served as a sanctuary for the release of living beings (*fangsheng chi*).
Now, we have merely dredged the three ponds, constructed embankments to form a lake, and taken but a fraction of its former extent.
Furthermore, since ancient times, West Lake has been a place for song and dance, truly a "wine-pool" and a "meat-grove. Now, within this lake, there are these three pools.
The sentient beings released therein fill its waters; this is the Land of Ultimate Bliss manifested from the ocean of karma.
Yet, those who pass by that pond on their multi-storied ships, amidst song and dance, never once reflect or look back. This is just like being in a state of drunken sleep.
Whether the mind is pure or defiled, suffering or joy follows accordingly—how could it be otherwise? It is like the difference between "wei" (only) and "a" (not); how far apart can they be? Its...

In the pond lies Huseongsa Temple. The temple has three pagodas; though the temple has been built, the pagodas have not yet been constructed, for the embankment has not yet been able to hold back the water.
I visited the pond to partake in the merit of the occasion and praised Master Hyeonjin’s compassion, lamenting that his work had not yet reached completion, which left me with great regret.
That night, as I lay down to sleep, I dreamed that I was walking along the embankment; the sand beneath my feet was so fine that every grain was square and flat.
Every one of them bore the character for "Buddha. As they followed me, they did not dare to set foot upon them.
I said, "If you all know that the great earth is the Buddha, there is no place to set your feet; this is precisely the time for your practice.

Thereupon, I addressed the assembly, saying, "If these grains of sand were gathered to form a Buddha-stūpa, then both the donor and the recipient would ascend together to the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Upon awakening from this, he reflected deeply.
Thereupon, he conceived the aspiration for universal salvation (*pudu*), vowing that those living beings he had released might be liberated from suffering and attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, if one regards these wriggling creatures as Buddhas, how much more so should one regard the people before one’s eyes, who are the most sentient and most enlightened?
How can they be viewed merely as ordinary beings (*sattva*)? Why not wish that these beings, who are so easily saved, should first achieve Buddhahood?
With such thoughts and through manifold vows, one delivers those many sentient beings;
thus, not only does that which is delivered become more vast, but by uniting the minds of the multitude to maintain this pond, that which is maintained becomes increasingly firm.

Is such a practice and vow not precisely the contemplation that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are equal and without distinction? Therefore, the method of universal transformation was established, and people offer ten...
Money. With one coin, chant the Buddha’s name a hundred times; unify the minds of the multitude upon a single Buddha. By gathering many people, three stupas are completed.
What is bestowed is small, yet what is accomplished is great; this constitutes an ocean of merit and a mass of blessings.
This is to use sand-counted Buddhas to deliver sand-counted sentient beings; its power is even greater. Is this not the most supreme of Buddha-works?
If one were to arise from this inspiration with the intention that, in the future, this entire lake shall become a lotus pond,
then all sentient beings of this region— whether noble or humble, rich or poor— would together be reborn in the Buddha-land of Ultimate Bliss.
Would this not be a sublime practice?

Petition for the Reconstruction of Longhua Temple The mountains and waters of ancient Hangzhou are ethereal and exquisite. During the Song Dynasty, monasteries were established like stars in a constellation, their bells and drums resonating with one another.
Among them, Longhua Temple is situated to the southwest of Nanping; it was founded by the Great Being (Mahāsattva) Fu during the Liang Dynasty, over a thousand years ago. Sima Guang...
"Your Excellency, there was once a shrine here in the past, but now it has all fallen into ruin.

This site not only possesses the excellence of mountains and waters, but also serves as a vital thoroughfare between Putuo and Tiantai. It is a place that must be passed by those traveling from the ten directions;
indeed, with temple banners of Qiantang standing side by side, it is not easy to find a place to rest one's weary shoulders while on pilgrimage. Previously, San-kong of Mount Fuyou..."

Furthermore, when I arrived, I took pity on it. A lay practitioner from the riverbank, Hong Yunquan, had invited [the master] there; though the construction had not yet been completed, the assembly was always full.
After a short time, however, the project was suspended. Then, the Chan practitioner Guangkun conceived a vast mind and vowed to establish it as a monastic center for receiving guests.
In the spring of the Ding-si year, I happened to pass by and beheld the subtle and majestic adornment of the Buddha image. Once again—
A deep longing arose within me. I paced back and forth across the terrain, turning my back on the imperial camp and facing the Qiantang River; it was the most excellent spot.
When traveling monks from the ten directions arrive here, their strength is exhausted and their spirits weary; they seek a moment’s rest but cannot find it.

If they happen to gain a place to set foot and settle their bodies, even a drop of water moistening their lips feels like being drenched in clarified butter or drinking sweet nectar. To dedicate this merit is supreme.

This is indeed a most excellent condition. Furthermore, seeing that the Zen practitioners are filled with compassionate urgency, and that the lay devotees who have suddenly resolved to act each leap with joy, this constitutes the supreme cause.
However, the scale of the temple project is vast and the expenses are immense; the time required is long and the number of tasks is great.
Were it not for vast *dāna*, it would not be easy to fulfill the fundamental vows of a practitioner of *dhyāna* by performing inconceivable Buddha-works.
Moved by this, I offer praise and veneration, and provide this guidance for all officials, elders, laymen, laywomen, and virtuous sons and daughters.

If one can indeed give rise to a rare and extraordinary mind, conceive the thought that such an opportunity is difficult to encounter, and tear open the sack of stinginess to adorn the Buddha-lands, then with these impermanent riches one performs an indestructible deed.
Thus, by relinquishing one’s body and home, they are guarded by dragons and spirits for ten thousand generations without end.
Compared to the worldly pursuits of owning land for a thousand years only to have eight hundred different masters, how could this possibly be measured? It is beyond comparison.
How vast is the difference between heaven and earth! How much more so when one creates the causes and conditions for the Pure Land and establishes the seeds of Buddhahood for the future.
One may hope to become a foremost member of the retinue during the three assemblies under Maitreya’s descent; is this not the supreme and most excellent merit for transcending the world?
For every person possesses the Buddha-nature, each is endowed with past causes, and thus the conditions of today are surely destined to be realized.
Do not fail to seize this opportunity and let it pass. How could one bear to return empty-handed from a mountain of jewels?
It is for all those possessed of wisdom to suddenly give rise to immeasurable joy and swiftly exert courageous effort.

A Vow for Transcribing the Avataṃsaka Sūtra with Gold Using Blood Drawn from One’s Own Veins I bow my head to the Great Awakened, Unsurpassed Honored One, who pervades the entire Dharma-realm throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time;
whose wondrous adornments are like lotuses, and whose pure lands are as numerous as atoms. You manifest bodies everywhere to expound the ocean of purity—the perfect *sūtra*.

The definitive exposition of the nature and characteristics, which transcends all marks of letters—within the seven locations and nine assemblies, to Mañjuśrī and the great bodhisattvas, to the number of field-dusts of spiritual friends, and to the pure assembly of noble monks: I now prostrate with my three karmas to ultimate emptiness.

Relying solely on your unconditioned compassion, please illumine my true aspiration. Reflect upon me, who since beginningless time have wandered through various births and deaths, transmigrating through the realms of suffering like a great whirling wheel of fire;
the number of times I have cast off this body and taken up another is beyond the power of thought to conceive.
The various evil karmas I have committed are known only to the Buddha’s own wisdom. Now, relying on the power of the Triple Gem, may I be counted among the ranks of men;

though my six sense-faculties are fortunately complete, my consciousness remains largely shrouded in darkness. Yet, by virtue of subtle roots of goodness from past lives, may I soon emerge from the ocean of affection and craving.

It is like entering a dense forest of worldly existence, or like avoiding drowning only to leap into fire. Internally, through the permeation of the power of goodness, one vows in every thought-moment to remain detached;
externally, moistened by the rain of the Dharma, the pure sprouts suddenly emerge. Yet, because the habitual tendencies of defilement are so rampant, they occasionally wither and dry up once more.
How excellent is this great spiritual friend! You have bestowed upon me what was like the gift of Devadatta;

through this great causal condition, I have attained liberation from the heat of affliction and shall together return to the realm of cool serenity to pay homage to the Honored One Mañjuśrī, dwelling joyfully in the most profound and tranquil place of *araṇya*.
The mind is like a monkey, constantly leaping upon the signs of sensory objects; when the power of prajñā is weak, it is difficult to withstand the army of birth and death.
For these reasons, as I observe the various activities of conditioned existence, I prostrate to the Lotus Treasury, the perfectly wondrous and supreme vehicle.

I vow to give rise to a heart of reverent devotion and shall carry this upon my head for as long as I live. Having heard of the conduct of Samantabhadra, which is vast and inconceivable, among the six ways of upholding it, writing it down is the foremost.
Even if one were to use bone as a pen and blood as ink for as many eons as there are motes of dust, [the merit would remain unsurpassed].
Accumulating such scriptures, equal in measure to the great trichiliocosm—having heard such a vow, it is difficult to find its peer.
Taking blood as ink and blending it with gold, I shall transcribe this great scroll, a single word that is an ocean of Dharma gates.

By this supreme cause, may the ocean of suffering find its ferry. May every drop of the blood from this body accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), merging into the Flower Treasury Ocean (*Ghanavyūha-samudra*) to universally moisten the realms of sentient beings.
As I hold this in my hand and write it, may my mind attain mastery over every stroke and dot.
May this illusory body forever attain the vajra-body; may the body be like a mountain of purple gold, most sublime and peerless in its majesty.
May those who hear its name or behold its form give rise to great joy in their hearts; may hands like a mass of great jewels constantly produce worldly and spiritual wealth.

The seven treasures and the four requisites shall all be filled in every variety. Throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm, may all sentient beings—those who are impoverished or afflicted by illness—have all their needs fulfilled according to their wishes. May it be so that when I attain Buddhahood, my land is utterly pure.
Those of the pure and singular Supreme Vehicle have no suffering in the evil realms; they constantly turn this wheel of Dharma until the very end of kalpas throughout all dust-like worlds.
I, however, am born in the age of the Final Dharma; the power of my faith is meager, and I am ever accompanied by the veil of ignorance, making it difficult to escape the karma of birth and death.
If my roots of goodness are not yet matured and I should fall into the cycle of saṃsāra, may I rely on this most excellent cause to avoid falling into the various evil realms.

May I always be born in pure buddha-fields, never departing from the presence of the Triple Gem, and may I swiftly awaken to the emptiness of self-nature, transcending all outflows in a single moment.
In all that I do and all that I undertake, may I forever be free from the obstacles of the three poisons.

Sustained by my power of aspiration until the very end of the future, may this scroll of mine not be destroyed by the three calamities. When Maitreya is about to descend to be born, light shall issue forth from this sutra.
It universally illumines the worlds of the ten directions, and the earth shakes in six ways. After Maitreya has descended to be born, he first sits beneath the Dragon-Flower Tree;
this sutra emerges from the earth, leaping up into the void, and from every word issues a wondrous sound, proclaiming my original vows.
A multitude of a million devas and humans all acclaimed this rare event. At that time, I was within the assembly, and for their sake, I expounded the meaning of ultimate reality.
Whenever a Buddha appears in the world, during the first three weeks, he invariably expounds the Great Avataṃsaka Sūtra; I was the foremost among those present to receive the teaching.
Although my body is illusory and false, it was born from my father and mother; relying upon these deluded faculties, I shall accomplish deeds of true reality.
May my father be like the pure Brahmā and my mother like Queen Māyā; when the Buddhas descend to be born, may they emerge through me, my father, and my mother.
The Master has long delivered me from suffering; his grace in the Dharma is most supreme and honored. May he be my guide within the assemblies of all Buddhas.
My friend is most sincere and true; may he lead me upon the right path. May this friend be like Mañjuśrī, acting as my foremost spiritual mentor (kalyāṇamitra).
Through the great power of faith in *dāna*, they generously bestowed vast wealth and resources. May these wise ones forever be free from the suffering of stinginess and attachment.

When the Buddhas appeared in the world, they were the first to request the teaching of the Dharma; they did not spare their bodies, lives, or wealth as they extensively cultivated all manner of wholesome deeds.
I perform such practices, relying upon all those who uphold [the Dharma]. May these worthy sages never be parted from me throughout all my births.
Wherever I may be in any Buddha-land, may we together cause the Buddha-Dharma to flourish and spread. May all who see or hear of me praise and extol it.
All subtle and detailed roots of goodness and causes and conditions Return together to the ocean of Flower Treasury. I have made such vows, vast and inexhaustible;
Reaching to the end of future time, my ultimate mind shall be perfected.
In the *Text on Releasing Living Beings*, it is said: "Life arises of itself; why then release them? Furthermore, why is releasing living beings considered a Buddhist practice?

Pei Xiu stated: "All that possesses blood and breath must possess consciousness. All that possesses consciousness shares the same essence. Therefore, it is said: "The wriggling and moving [beings]..."
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; because this nature is itself the Buddha, one who kills a living being is, in effect, killing the Buddha.
It is not that they say "I am killing the Buddha," yet by killing a living being, one lacks compassion and thereby severs the seed-nature of the Buddha.

Although those wriggling creatures are regarded as fit to be killed, one fails to realize that within oneself there exists the originally inherent, luminous Buddha-nature—how could it ever be destroyed?
It is severed by the mind that refrains from killing, which is the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*). Compassion (*maitrī*) is what is called benevolence (*ren*);

compassion is the inability to endure [the suffering of others]. This heart of non-endurance is the very beginning of benevolence. Therefore, seeing life one cannot bear to see death; hearing their cries, one cannot bear to eat their flesh.
The first proclamation of the sages and worthies—how could it belong to the Buddha alone? The Confucianist, because he abides in his proper station, merely keeps a distance from the kitchen;

the Buddhist, because he practices compassion through equality, extends it to all beings. However, those who practice the release of living beings differ in their adherence to signs versus the forgetting of signs.

Consequently, among those who emulate this practice, there is no lack of the faults of releasing life only to kill it later. Therefore, the Dharma values the forgetting of signs; its subtlety lies therein.
Adapting to conditions, the fundamental essence has no fixed abode; its function is to loathe that which is tainted by outflows.

If the fruit can encounter conditions and immediately manifest the essence, then every sight will give rise to spiritual vitality, and every occasion will become a Buddha-activity. In every object and every situation, there is the gate of joyful relinquishment; in every thought and every mind, there is entirely the realm of compassion.
Why, then, must one be bound by formal conventions to cling to achievements, or establish time limits to strictly enforce rules?
Ah! Master Mingchan has long harbored this aspiration. If you fulfill it through this practice, your compassion will spread daily and the scope of your transformative influence will broaden daily.
If you maintain it for ten years, there shall be immeasurable youths who will offer you worship; what cause for doubt could there be?
A Memorial Text for Land Minister Wutaishan Jushi: Alas!
Having received the secret entrustment of Mount Ling, you came to this turbid world to benefit sentient beings. In coming, you did not come;
thus you did not reveal your original face. In departing, you did not depart; you left behind only a heart of raw iron.
For over eighty years, he has played his part wherever he encountered the stage. His boundless, wondrous virtues find their ultimate principle whenever he meets a Buddha.
He serves the sovereign with the heart of a Buddha, regarding the sovereign alone as the Buddha; he loves all beings with the true mind, regarding all beings alone as the True.

Thus, throughout his life, his highest pursuits never departed from the edge of his official head-wrap; and at the final moment of departure, he entrusted the ultimate word to his children and grandchildren. It is only...

Your Excellency currently holds the office of a high official, yet you are not one whose nature is that of an official; I am ashamed that I have become a bhikṣu, yet I do not possess the true marks of a bhikṣu.
Although our paths are distinct, in truth, we are both alike in supporting our families.

Moved by Your Excellency’s departure—having set out yet not yet gone—I have dispatched this half-sheet of letter from Lingnan, so that within the midst of the empty and the non-empty, I may draw forth for you a single drop of Caoxi.
Water. I prepare this offering of nectar and present it to the Honored One of Empowerment. Alas! Like a tranquil lake reflecting the full moon, I behold the pure Dharma-body;
as celestial music fills the void, you extend your wondrous, broad tongue. May I receive this flavor of the Dharma to reflect upon my own deluded mind.
May you graciously accept this offering. *Shangxiang*.
A Memorial for the Grand Councilor, the Late Lord Hugu Shun’an.
Alas, how painful! Is the Lord alive? Is he dead? I have sought the reason again and again, yet I cannot find it.
Suddenly I heard the announcement of your passing; it was as if you yourself had said you were dying.
Yet, upon reading your poem written while changing your bedding, I saw that you clearly informed others that you would not die, though no one understood. Only I clearly knew that you were not dead.
I spoke of it, fearing that others would not believe me. Alas, how tragic! I reflect that I and you met by chance amidst the great transformation of the universe.
For more than thirty years, it has been as if a single day; this is truly extraordinary. At first, I met you on the wilds of Shouyang;
upon seeing you once, our minds were in perfect accord. Suddenly, I spoke to you of uniting fortune and calamity, and equalizing life and death;
at that time, you were already serene, and it resonated deeply within your heart. Subsequently, you sought me out again on Mount Qingliang, where you sat in the full lotus posture.
Beneath a cold cliff a thousand *chi* high, amidst ten-thousand-year accumulated snows, he conversed with laughter while chewing hard ice and eating *qiūlěi* (grains).

To him, vast eons were but a single breath; at that time, Master Gong already harbored thoughts of ascending to heaven and parting the mists, possessing a transcendent desire for a far-reaching departure.
Yet, I did not yet know his secret. Not long after, I visited Master Gong at Yanmen, where we sat together in the carriage courtyard.
Their gate was as if situated in a secluded valley. They shared a single bed and blanket for three months without parting.

Day and night he would expound upon the threads of his discourse, at which time the Master already understood them clearly, attaining silent realization within his heart. From this, it became known that he regarded official rank and robes as mere dust and grime, and his physical existence as nothing more than the wings of a cicada.
He then made an appointment with me atop the Eastern Sea, where we would consume the morning mists and build our towers.
We remained there for some time. Eventually, you indeed allowed me to escape the fetters of the mundane world, while I, in turn, enabled you to forget the distinction between leaving and staying.

At that moment, we sported together within the light of the Sea-Seal Samādhi; the vast waves stretched for ten thousand *li*, a brilliant, uniform azure, as if gazing into a precious mirror or treading upon lapis lazuli.
Seated upon a lotus flower in a pure land, one was unaware that this body even existed.
Heaven and earth—these external things existing within this body—their joys were truly far from ending.

Yet, in an instant, the Lord of Heaven grew angry with me for recklessly boring into the Chaos, dispersing the uncarved block and diluting the primal simplicity; he thus punished me with nine deaths and banished me to a pestilential land.
At that time, I took my final leave of you, sir. You thought I would surely die, and intended to commission a portrait to summon my spirit.

Yet suddenly ten years have passed like a single breath. From time to time I know of you; you contemplate me with longing amidst the cold clouds, and your accumulated tears for me flow like a long river.
But you do not realize that I and you have been roaming together as if it were only yesterday, our brows still meeting face to face.
Awakening from sleep, there was not even a hair’s breadth of interval between my dreaming and waking. Alas, how tragic!
In the fifth month of this year, the Master sent a short letter to comfort me from ten thousand *li* away. I dispatched an attendant to inquire after the Master in the seventh month;
my poem expressing my longing for him said, "He resembles the body of Vimalakīrti while ill. When the letter arrived, the Master had already manifested his illness. The Master took hold of me...

I write this to recite my poem for you; your spirit remains present before my mouth. Within one month you have passed away, yet through this I console you with our shared life, as if you were bidding me farewell face-to-face forever—this is truly extraordinary.
When I bid you farewell in the past, it was not like your bidding me farewell now.
It makes me think of you and weep for you; is this not like your thinking of me and weeping for me? As for your life...
It is no mere coincidence. Yet, you possessed lofty insight and harbored extraordinary talent; your loyalty lay with the state, and your heart was set upon the common people.
While your life span has come to an end, your talent remains unexhausted; your physical form has dissolved, but your mind has not. As your poem at the time of death says:
"The spiritual root ever shines beside the moon’s radiance. Judging by this, one views life and death as [one].

Night and dawn; a thousand autumns are but as a single day. May your spirit roam the vast void, listen to the celestial music of the Jade Palace, and dwell in the Great Prefecture, where you shall be a companion to the flying immortals and enjoy infinite longevity. To you, the past will seem like mere refuse;
who would have known that your present joy would be so utterly transcendent compared to former times? Since you are at peace, what cause for sorrow remains for me? Alas! How lamentable!
May you accept this offering.

This is the text for the sacrifice to the Great Master Daguang, composed in the forty-fourth year of the Wanli era, the year of Bingchen, on the tenth day of the eleventh month (the *gengzi* day of the new moon). Beyond [these ten days]...

The ninth day, the Bingxu day. The former Sha-men Haiyin, whose virtue has been humbled by your teachings, respectfully presents this offering from the Gandha-kuṭi to pay tribute to the spirit of the Venerable Zibo, the Great Master Daguan. He says: Alas! When the Master was born, he was not born;
he came by the power of his vows. When the Master died, he did not die; he departed in accordance with liberation. Thus he comes and goes.

He does not fall into common sentiments. How could birth and death be the same as worldly truth? During his stay in this world, he maintained the adamantine mind and sat firm upon the ground of solidity.
For over thirty years, his daily fare was the family meal; his backbone was pure steel.
Regarding the seventeen hundred cases of stale and rotten vines, his nostrils were full of the remnants of mucus. He toppled Maitreya and Śākyamuni, and did not yield to Deshan or Linji.
He was supremely compassionate toward others; when the moment arose, he had no hesitation or concealment.
He vowed to protect the Dharma as if it were his own eyes, and sought the Great Matter as if he had lost both parents. Refusing to harmonize with worldly sentiments was his true practice.
Sitting in meditative stillness amidst the moonlight upon the water, he walked alone within the shadows of empty flowers. When he first visited me at Donghai, he suddenly cast off his physical form.
When Hai and I met again at West Mountain, he searched my very marrow; even before my calamity had taken shape, he fully disclosed my hidden secrets to me.
Now that my misfortune has already manifested, he intends to wash away my stains for me.

Furthermore, to fulfill our long-standing agreement at Caoxi and to seek an audience at the imperial capital, he braved the sweltering heat upon the roads, hoping to catch a glimpse of my shadow and echo.
In his every movement and pause, he established various methods, hoping to deliver me from the nine deaths. Alas!
In his practice of the Dharma, the Master truly harbored the heart of Cheng Ying and Chu Jiu;

in his regard for me as a close friend, he was surely beyond the comparison of Guan Zhong and Bao Shuya, or Chen Lin and Lei Hu. While I bear the light punishment of Imperial benevolence, the Master’s concern for my heart remains unabated.

I was banished to the regions beyond the passes, while my Master waited for me upon the riverbank. At our first meeting, grief and joy welled up within us together, as if we had risen again from the Nine Original Plains.
As I bid my Master a final farewell, I was willing to become a restless spirit in the fiery lands;
my Master exhorted me to maintain a peaceful mind, hoping that the dark door of the underworld might open once more. Shedding tears, I stood at the brink of departure.
As we parted on the road, the Master took my hand and, filled with sorrow, remained silent. At that time, though separated by mountains and rivers, the days and months have sped like arrows.
I know in my heart that the Master has not forgotten me, and he repeatedly cautioned me against negligence.
Sustained by the power of his vows, the Master swore never to betray his original resolve; thus, he withdrew the radiant brilliance of the Great Axe and did not wish to let it loose.
Amidst the dust and dregs, I hope that the Jade of He will surely be recognized; I spare no effort, even at the risk of lightly casting away the Pearl of Sui.
As I am about to knock upon the nine-layered gates of Your Majesty, suddenly a whirlwind rises from all sides. The land and seas surge with waves; dragons and snakes fall prostrate in disarray.

Jade and stone are burned together; the banner of the Dharma collapses. You, Master, have ascended the broad highway of the Eightfold Path, yet you suddenly encounter the Long Serpent and the Great Boar.

The August Heaven truly beholds his innermost heart; it is only that he has displayed himself before the vulgar and base. Fortunate that this mind remains pure and white, he shall briefly unfold its hidden depths.
The Master is indeed vast and open; what sorrow or joy can there be? Whether encountering the adverse or the favorable, he acts as the occasion requires;
in life and death, he plays freely. Why do past burdens persist in pursuit? Truly, prior karmic conditions are firm and fixed. Alas for the five turbidities...
It was unbearable. Relying solely on the single path of practice, he washed his face and sat in the lotus posture;
then, he passed away in profound stillness. Alas, how painful! Since the Master did not allow himself to be disturbed by calamities or misfortunes, why would he concern himself with coming and going?
He simply cast off his hands and went forth, entirely without deliberation. It is only because the Master took the *vajra* as his heart that he remains indestructible.
The essence of this [teaching]. My disciple has returned from serving his master, having settled his residence at Shuangjing. When I heard the news of his passing, my heart was shattered;
gazing toward Chang’an, I shed tears until they seemed to fall away. I wished to personally pay homage at the reliquary chamber, yet I am bound by the constraints of karmic ties.
I intended to return to life to comfort the spirit of my master, but suddenly years have passed like the shifting of stars and frost. It is not that this heart...
Though there was a brief respite, it was merely because the conditions were not yet favorable to me. Recently, fortunately, my original aspiration has been fulfilled;
I am finally able to set forth these words to deliver my final judgment. Alas, how painful! Why does the Master die while I live? Why do I not come while the Master remains in unrest?
Though our physical forms differ, we share this same heart. Though separated by the realms of darkness, we shall ultimately be united. We swear to return together.
Ah! Fulfilling our profound vow, the Silent Radiance is bright; the Master dwells in peace. I prostrate myself, expressing my sorrowful longing.

As the fragrance of the Accumulated Array spreads, may the nectar be sprinkled. The Master, responding to the opportune moment, we pray you will come. With radiant light shining forth, I wait in earnest anticipation.
Alas! May you graciously partake.
A Memorial Text for the Great Master Yunqi Alas!

The Master was fundamentally unborn, nor does he have anywhere to go. Yet, by the power of sustaining his body and in accordance with causes and conditions, he saw the waves of the ocean of desire surging and the flames of the burning house blazing.
The Master unfurled the wheel of his vows and came specifically to provide salvation. He revealed the nature of worldly toil, that we might return early to the source.
O Compassionate Father! Once one has ascended the path to enlightenment, one walks like a white ox; one regards worldly affection as spittle and views kin as enemies.
Who would not be startled by such a swarm of flies? Taking the Dharma-realm as home and all sentient beings as one’s dwelling, one views all things with equanimity—without duality or distinction.
Opening the gate of ambrosia, you point the way back to the Pure Land; those with scales, shells, feathers, and fur all flock there together at once. O Compassionate One!
With the Dharma-eye, he cleared away the cataracts from the root of his precepts; using the diamond probe, he scraped away defilements and removed the darkness.

Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, he brought the three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices to complete purity. His body became the eyes for the multitude, and his mind became a great dwelling;

those who came from the ten directions had their delusions and madness suddenly stilled. For over forty years, the banner of the Dharma stood high, and the single rain universally nourished the medicinal herbs.

All trees, upon receiving but a single drop of moisture, have their branches and leaves flourish together; whoever attains this will ultimately achieve fulfillment. I observe my Master as being like a lion king:
while he lies high within his den, the multitudes run about in terror. I also observe my Master as being like a medicinal king-tree:
all who come into contact with him are certain to be cured of chronic ailments. Alas! In this age of the Dharma’s decline, the sun of wisdom has long been submerged. My Master, regarding...
Through the long night, you have held aloft the great lamp of wisdom. The Buddha originally has no self-centered mind; his mind is entrusted to the Master. The *sattva* has no independent practice;

his practice is entrusted to the Master’s sustenance. Therefore, the Master appears in the world. Being of one flavor and free from self, he dwells for a hundred kalpas—how could this not be possible? Alas!
The Master manifests through conditions; when conditions cease, he departs. I lament these blind masses who have lost their refuge and reliance.

For this reason, I have traveled thousands of miles from afar, bearing fragrant incense and prostrating my five limbs to pay homage to the Master in the realm of tranquil light. Moved by compassion for those of the same essence, the Master recognizes me as one who understands his music.
May you behold my sincerity; may you come and accept this offering. Alas! May you partake with honor.
*Memorial for the Sacrificial Offering of Gold and Bamboo to Continue the Fragrant Lineage of Master Gong:* Alas!

Master Gong held the wheel of vows and was born into this world of endurance (*sahā-loka*). Having early encountered an enlightened teacher, he suddenly severed the bonds of affection and gave rise to firm resolve.
He stabilized his mind to repay the debt of compassion. Retiring to the empty mountains, he endured hunger and cold.

Reverently upholding his master’s instructions, he personally bore and carried out their weight, vowing to provide for the ten directions with impartiality and without obstruction. He cleared away thorns and brambles to establish a monastic grove, and drove off foxes and hares so that the chanting of the Dharma could resound.
Disciples arrived like clouds, and devas and dragons stood guard in attendance. Grain was piled as high as mountains, providing ample food for all who came.
As vast as space and as boundless as the earth, those who dwell here have no external attachments. Endowed with the power of diligence, they remain untiring until old age.

Regarding this single body as a mere lodging, they leave behind not even a trace. Intending to take one’s hand and return together, how could one have expected that the other would depart first without waiting? Raising themselves up, they simply go.
What is this joy? The Bequeathed Vajra Banner remains eternally indestructible; the Dharma-body is profound and serene, its tranquil light sovereign and free.
Only the spirit is not obscured—may it behold this lamentation. Alas, how tragic! May you still partake of this offering.
**A Text on Forming a Society for Nianfo to Cultivate the Forty-Eight Vows and Be Born Together in the Pure Land** I humbly submit that the Land of Purity is but one's own mind;
every place is a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Amitābha is one’s own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); every person is fully endowed with it.

It is only because of the obstructions of worldly toil and the disputes of self and others that we perceive mountains of earth and stone filled with impurities and filth, thereby obscuring our original [nature].
This body of innate purity obscures the perfect wisdom and radiance within each person, so that not even a single hair’s breadth of it appears.
Throughout the day, the consciousness of karma remains vast and indistinct, while the winds of external objects sweep on day after day. People only know how to enjoy what is before their eyes;

who understands how to cultivate the causes for the life hereafter? Therefore, Amitābha Buddha, the Master of my Land of Ultimate Bliss, when he first resolved his mind upon the path of practice, grew weary of this Sahā world.
He established forty-eight vows, vowing in each one to deliver sentient beings; he cultivated the sixteen contemplations of the mind, making every thought a Buddha.

He caused everyone to know that the mind is the Buddha—how could one seek it elsewhere? He enabled each person to realize that the fulfillment of vows is itself the truth, so that all return to their own nature (*svabhāva*).
He toppled the high mountain of self and others, causing the precious ground to become as level as the palm of a hand; he shattered the shackles of worldly toil.
Like an illusion or a dream, a lotus flower arises, vast as a wheel. My mind is pure, and that land is manifested and perfected.
Do not wait until later to reflect; the fruition lies only in the present moment. Without distinction between male and female, all shall realize Bodhi.
Whoever possesses the karmic affinity shall ascend to the Jewel Ground. Yet, even though Maitreya is born by nature, he must still receive his prediction at Vulture Peak; thus, it is naturally so.

Kāśyapa, one must also adorn the Buddha-lands. One should deeply lament that beings dwell amidst the five turbidities; life cannot be preserved for even a moment, yet sinful karma is manifold, making it difficult to escape suffering for long kalpas.

Though fathers may be compassionate and sons filial, each looks only after themselves; though elder brothers may be affectionate and younger brothers respectful, how can they substitute for one another?
Even if there be wealth, status, and splendor, in the end it all becomes but a single dream. Reflect deeply upon this.
Reaching this point, it is truly lamentable. Therefore, I have made a vow to cultivate the causes, desiring to achieve completion within a single lifetime.

Since one knows that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, how could one still harbor former attachments? Having realized that one's own mind is the Buddha, one need only directly accept this.
To churn the long river into cream and butter depends originally upon the person; to transform the great earth into gold truly arises from [one's own realization].
I pray that your mind may become like the Buddha’s; this is itself the Buddha-mind. Since both cause and effect are true, you shall surely realize the true fruit.

By making a single vow, all beings within the four modes of birth and the nine realms of existence shall together emerge from the wheel of suffering. By bestowing a single drop [of compassion], those in the eight difficulties and the three miserable paths shall [be liberated].
All shall return to the Land of Bliss; when the flowers bloom, one beholds the Buddha, like the fragrant intimacy between mother and child.

When delusions are exhausted, one returns to the source, as pure and bright as ice and frost. With a single mind made pure, myriad virtues converge; the great earth, mountains, and rivers all become the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
A Text for the Ritual of Concluding the Memorial Service for Master Chekong of Mount Kuanglu:
When the Master came, what was his purpose? What did he do? When the Master departed, what was his mind? What were his concerns?
Manifesting in the body of a bhikṣu, he sat and cut off heaven and earth; letting out a lion’s roar, he startled and drove away the foxes and rabbits. One should seek me at Mount Qingliang.

Clouds filled the streams and mountains as he returned once more to his former hermitage. The moon was full over his thatched door, yet he still held the pearl of the nine bends, waiting for his Master while it passed away in darkness.
How could he have departed so suddenly? His mournful voice has now reached us with the news of his passing. Alas!
It leaves me with a mouth that finds it difficult to open; harboring grievance, there is no one to whom I can appeal. For though we were born together, we do not die together;
though we return to the same source, we do not dwell together. Fortunately, Mount Kuanglu is high, its Dharma-body universally covering all; Lake Penghu is clear, its Samādhi manifest and evident.
Although the banner-pole has been overturned, I am fortunate that the pillar has been propped up, suddenly causing the Five Elders to cry out in long-drawn tones.
A thousand peaks dance in unison; white deer mourn in the wind; yellow dragons weep in the rain. The more it rolls up, the more it unfurls; the more it seeks to hide, the more it reveals.
This is something to be praised, not lamented; something to be laughed at, not wept for. Alas! Master, please rest for a while.
Listen to the final word! Smash through the *sambhogakāya* realm (*sambhogakṣetra*), overturn the Pure Land, and come once more to encounter this fierce master.
He will seize you by the collar and hold you fast, refusing to let you go as the teacher departs. May the spirit alone enjoy the offering.
A Brief Sermon at the Memorial Shrine for Layman Zeng Jiulong.

On the twenty-sixth day of the fifth month in the thirty-sixth year of the Wanli era, on the occasion of the fifty-seventh day (the third anniversary) of Layman Zeng’s passing, his fellow members of the society each held incense and paid their respects, requesting Master Hanshan to deliver a brief sermon for the layman. The layman listened.

"Do you understand? The Buddha taught that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, cessation is bliss. Layman, do you understand?
During the thirty-seven years you have lived in this world, were the various actions you performed impermanent at the very moment they were being done?
Were they impermanent after they were done? Or are they impermanent even up until this very day? If you say they are..."
If this day were impermanent, one would fall into the view of annihilationism. If you say that it is impermanent after the action has been performed, then it does not depend on the present day.
If it is impermanent at the very moment the action is being performed, then the entire world would be impermanent; why then speak only of the layman? Layman, do you understand?
If you realize that this "action" is impermanent, then impermanence itself has no inherent nature. Who, then, undergoes birth and extinction? There is no birth.
If it is extinguished, how could there be birth and death? Layman, if you understand this, then today is the very time to experience the bliss of tranquil extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*).
Those who pity you do so because they all still harbor views of arising and ceasing.
This is the text for lighting the pyre for the cremation of the Master.

The nature of fire is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true fire. Meeting on a narrow path, there is certainly no place to hide. We respectfully venerate the Venerable Master Zibo, the Great Monk Daguan.
Having come to the human realm by chance, you have unfortunately fallen into the mundane world. Now, with naked strength, you have completely cast it off.
A daughter’s birth-gown, its radiance shining forth to reveal one’s original face. Shouldering the True Dharma, forged from pure steel upon the shoulders.
Acting thoroughly for the sake of others, liver and gall cast from raw iron. On the path of birth and death, proceeding straight forward and coming straight back.
At the gateway of present affairs, half-open and half-closed. For over sixty years, the breast and mind have been like pines, waters, wind, and moon. A thousand...
Seven hundred cases—rabbit horns, tortoise hair, and a staff. Even if one possesses the last-ditch elegance, one cannot avoid hiding the head and exposing the tail.
Having cast aside this thief’s private property, who would have thought it would fall into the hands of the Chan Master Hanshan?
Today, before the assembly of humans and devas, I specifically bring it forth in the open light. Does the great assembly see it? (He draws a circle with his torch and says: The staff lifts it open.
Clouds over the Double Peaks; from every pore emerges the treasury of radiance. Cherish this, all you people, and look with clear eyes!
Only now do you truly believe there are no obstructions.
