Preface to the Re-examination of the *Daxue Gangmu Jueyi* by the Disciple from Lingnan, Liu Qixiang:
At nineteen, I abandoned my brush and inkstone; at thirty, I entered the mountains and severed all ties with writing. At fifty, I was censured, yet I was graced by imperial favor.
I have been exiled beyond the frontier for fourteen years now. While coming and going to Wuyang with my alms bowl, my sons have mistakenly praised me as one who speaks with wisdom;

from time to time they visit me to inquire about the Way, yet I am ultimately unable to respond. It is as if I were someone who comes empty-handed but departs with something real—I am ashamed, I am ashamed.
Occasionally there are those who look upon me through the lens of Chan, but I am like a mute person eating bitter *huángpò* (Buckthorn) fruit. The autumn of the Jiyou year.

One day, while I was out begging for alms, the sons [of a certain family] prepared fragrant offerings at their Dharma assembly. I was able to indulge in a hearty meal; these sons were truly my disciples.
When the meal was finished, they requested further instruction, but I could do nothing but belch out the scent of rice and gruel. They departed with a sense of shame.
As I returned to Caoxi by boat, I thought of how these sons had satiated me for no small number of days, yet I had ultimately failed to repay them. This is why I recall Yan Hui’s question.
As for those who request this from me, I can only respond with a sigh. Even if I were to speak, my words could not be exhaustive;
and even if they were exhaustive, they could not fully satisfy the hearts of all. It is not easy to find discourse that pleases everyone.

Since the food of the various schools is difficult to digest and my belly still feels full, and since I have slept soundly on this boat, when I heard the attendant reading the *Great Learning*, it disturbed me and gave rise to doubt. Therefore, I took up a scripture...

Chapter. Examining the *Jiangmu* (Outline), he establishes questions and answers to resolve [the meaning] for himself, further citing the "Yanzi Wenren" (Yan Hui Questions about Benevolence) chapter to synthesize them.
It is like the whirling of a butcher’s knife; he completes the study in two half-noon intervals. To read it as mere strings of characters that do not form sentences is not to grasp the text.

Reflecting deeply, I have studied the books of Confucius since childhood, seeking the direct pointing to the mind-dharma (*citta-dharmatā*). It was only to Yanzi that the true transmission was uniquely bestowed.
This is the secret instruction. As for the rest, I have drawn the bow but not released the arrow. Previously, you did not know the Heart-Seal of the Sage;
now it has been fully revealed within these two hundred and five words. How subtle! How subtle! Is it that you have no eyes? Alas, alas! This year I am sixty-four.
Only now do I realize this; it may be called too late. Fearing that I might die and my teachings ultimately vanish into obscurity, I have hurried to inform my sons.
Some of you are already half my age, while those not yet half my age have fortunately heard this; for them, it may be called early.

Like a fine horse that covers a thousand *li* in a single breath upon seeing the shadow of the whip, or like the king of geese that distinguishes milk from water—could these not be considered the very essence of rice gruel?
This was merely inspired by a single meal; I hope you, my sons, will uphold this to nourish the hungry throughout the world.
I do not dare claim it is a matter of vast charity. Written on the second day before the Mid-Autumn Festival of the Jiyou year. By Fang.
Written by Waidéqīng aboard a boat at Xuyáng Gorge.
The Way of the Great Learning lies in illuminating the luminous virtue, in bringing the people near, and in resting in ultimate goodness.
"The Great Learning" refers to the learning of those of immeasurable greatness. The word "Way" (dào) signifies method. By means of...
Those whom people in the world perceive as small are all petty men;

they cannot be called great men because what they have studied consists only of minor methods—such as the various schools of thought and their wondrous schemes and eccentric calculations—which are nothing more than one-sided views.
Even if one masters them, one will achieve nothing more than the status of a petty man. If one were instead willing to turn inward and seek that which is inherently possessed within oneself...
As for the nature of the mind: once it is awakened to, one is immediately a great person (*daren*). Because that which is studied is great, it is called the "Great Learning" (*Daxue*).
The methods of the Great Learning are not many; they do not require extensive knowledge or broad vision, but are simply accomplished through three matters.
First, one must awaken to the substance of one's own mind; hence it is said, "To manifest the luminous virtue within oneself. Second, one must...
I wish for every person in the world to attain enlightenment equal to my own. May everyone cast off their former views and knowledge to initiate a new undertaking;
free from both self and others, may we all share in the peace of the era. Therefore it is said: "To be with the people is primary;
next is to cultivate oneself and then serve the people. One must not act with negligence or stop halfway. Everyone must do so.
Only when one reaches the ultimate point can one finally cease their efforts; therefore it is said, "To abide in ultimate goodness.
If one can truly master these three matters, one becomes a great person. As for the two instances of the word "clearly" (ming), one must understand them with complete clarity.
Furthermore, the second character "ming" (bright) refers to the brightness of radiance; it points to the substance of one's own mind.
The first character "ming" has two meanings. If it is explained in terms of the virtue of brightness regarding one's own practice, it is the brightness of awakening and clarity.
This means that the virtue of brightness is one's own inherent nature, yet one has merely followed along with it without realizing it—this is precisely [the meaning].
How fascinating! It is simply that one says one has lost one's own head and, though seeking it everywhere, cannot find it.
One day, suddenly awakening, one realizes at once that one’s original head is autonomous; it was never lost.

The self-nature of every person is originally luminous, vast, and autonomous—not lacking even a single hair’s breadth. It is only because one is deluded oneself that one turns outward toward the houses of others.
Investigate this thoroughly until you reach a clear understanding. Study every word of what he says, thinking that by mastering them, they will be of practical use.

Yet, were you suddenly to awaken to your own original nature—radiant, luminous, and lacking nothing in the slightest—this would be the realization of the enlightened virtue (mingde) that has always been inherent within you.
Therefore, it is called "luminous virtue. Having awakened to this enlightened virtue, one stands firm in this very moment.
This is what constitutes a sage. This is explained from the perspective of one’s own cultivation.

If, however, it is explained from the perspective of governing the people, the first character "ming" (明) refers to the clarity of illumination; it carries the sense of informing and instructing, as well as the meaning of revealing and manifesting.
It is like hoisting the sun and moon into the midst of the sky—this is the clarity of the Great Illumination (*dà míng*). Both of these meanings must be fully penetrated.
Che asked, "What is ultimate goodness? The Master replied, "From antiquity until now, everyone has known and seen it;
they simply understand that one walks upon the two paths of good and evil. They merely instruct people to reform their wickedness and move toward goodness.
This is but an old-fashioned way of knowing and seeing—what is extraordinary about it? Little do they realize that the two poles of good and evil are merely external opposites."
The Dharma is fundamentally unrelated to my own original nature and essence.
Therefore, when worldly people who commit evil can be transformed into good, and good people can likewise change into evil, it is evident that goodness is not something to be relied upon.
Because goodness does not reach the ultimate state, whether one is good or not, the student cannot stand firm; this is because they have not yet arrived home.
It is a place of departure, not a place where one can rest. Viewed in this light, these are all merely the habitual tendencies of past cognitions and views.
What is now called "ultimate goodness" refers to the realization and clarification of the true essence of one's own nature, which is fundamentally neither good nor evil.
It is simply a single expanse of radiance, without interior or exterior, without past or present, without person or self, and without right or wrong.
No. What is called "standing alone and unchanging" allows not even a single point of attachment. It is vast and free from the slightest speck of dust.
If one uses good to destroy evil, then while evil departs, good remains; this still leaves a layer of separation.
Even this very word "good" is originally but a guest-dust, not the original host. Therefore, it is not the ultimate place of rest. One need only [discard] both good and evil.

Forgetfulness. When the traces of self and others are severed, there is no dependence and no obscuration by ignorance; there is no coming and no going, neither moving nor wavering—this is precisely the moment of arriving home.
Reaching this state, one does not perceive within oneself any virtue that can be made clear, nor does one perceive among the people any populace that can be renewed.
All is blended into a single entity; this is the realm of the Great Man (Mahātman). There being no goodness by which it may be named, it is simply called "Namelessness."
"Ultimate Goodness. Only when one knows this can it be called "knowing where to rest.
After knowing where to rest, there is concentration (*ding*); after concentration, one is able to be still.

The character *ding* in this section refers to the fundamental substance of one's own nature (*xing*), which is quiescent and unmoving, profoundly and eternally concentrated, and does not depend upon cultivation.

Regarding "subsequent concentration": it is because practitioners do not realize that the fundamental substance is inherently and eternally concentrated. Consequently, they go off to practice concentration through forceful effort.
They merely take the views and knowledge they have cultivated throughout their lives and seek concentration within the dual extremes of good and evil, or upon the mind of arising and ceasing.
This is like a monkey entering a sack or pressing a gourd down upon water; seeking concentration in this manner, one will exhaust the years.

One cannot attain concentration. Why? Because illness lies in employing a mind of arising and ceasing, maintaining views of good and evil, failing to penetrate the fundamental substance, and being exclusively entangled with delusive thoughts—what is called "mistaking a thief for one's son. This is simply a great lack of knowing how to rest.
If one can truly comprehend the fundamental substance, it is immediately still and silent; this is the concentration of self-nature, not a concentration obtained through forced effort.
Take, for instance, the Great Master Huineng. When he instructed students on how to apply the mind, he asked:
"Neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—what is your original face? At that moment, the student was cut through in two by a single stroke;

they immediately beheld their own nature, and their deluded mind was suddenly stilled. From then on, they sought nothing else, finally realizing that what they had always possessed was originally not...
This movement is precisely what it means for the mind to have "stopping" (*zhì*) and subsequently attain "concentration" (*dìng*). It is further said:
"If you simply do not deliberate upon either good or evil, you will naturally perceive the substance of the mind. This is precisely what it means for the mind to have "stopping.

Therefore, students value knowing where to stop; when one knows where to stop, concentration follows naturally. The character *jìng* (stillness) is different from the character *dìng* (concentration). Concentration...
This is the essential substance of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This "stillness" is spoken of in contrast to external turmoil and lack of stillness;
it is far removed from the true essence of concentration. Why? Because the student’s deluded thoughts have been flying about in one direction, and the mind finds no moment of rest.

They merely strive to forcibly suppress [thoughts] within their perceptions and views, attempting to make the mind still through effort. Unaware that they are seeking stillness with increasing intensity, they...

Distracted thoughts will only burn more fiercely, and one will certainly be unable to attain stillness. Why is this? It is because one seeks the mind with the mind; the more one seeks, the further away it goes.
How, then, can a single moment of rest be attained? This is because one enters by seeking from the outside, like a person calling at a door that does not open.
Instead, one quarrels with the gatekeeper. This quarreling continues until the very end; if the true master does not appear, the conflict will ultimately never cease.

If the master can open the heavy gates wide from within, then the gatekeepers will flee so swiftly they leave no trace, and the seeker who truly beholds the master will find that the very desire to see him has also come to rest.
It is extinguished and no longer exists. This means that the point where the wild mind ceases is what constitutes stillness (*jing*).

If one does not truly perceive the fundamental substance, one will ultimately never be able to attain stillness. Therefore it is said: "Only after achieving concentration (*ding*) can one become still. The character *an* (安) carries the meaning of being secure, stable, and at ease.
It is like the "peace" in "accepting one's fate" (*anming*); it refers to being self-sufficient and seeking nothing further. Because [the mind] has been consistently...
Seeking stillness, one finds none; discursive thoughts proliferate, and the pursuit of objects never ceases. This mind has not possessed a single moment of peace.
Now that the fundamental essence has been realized, the restless mind has come to rest. Self-nature is inherently complete, lacking nothing and possessing nothing more than what is required.
It is profoundly settled and secure, joyful and autonomous. Such tranquility and happiness are attained precisely where the deluded mind comes to rest.

Therefore it is said: "Only after being still can one attain tranquility. The character *lǜ* (consideration) here does not refer to the consideration of discursive thought or mental deliberation, nor does it refer to the consideration of anxiety;
rather, it refers to the consideration of non-consideration. Thus it is said: "The *Yī* has no thought and no consideration."

"Quiescent and unmoving, yet responsive and penetrating all affairs of the world. It is also said, "A hundred deliberations lead to a single principle," and again, "Without deliberation, it is universal.
This very word "deliberation" (lù) refers to the state prior to awakening, when one seeks exclusively through deluded thoughts and mental calculations.
Even regarding a single matter, one may engage in a thousand thoughts and ten thousand deliberations, yet in the end, it is of no use; one cannot even reach it through such excessive deliberation.
Formerly, I was prone to excessive deliberation; my mind was constantly troubled by shifting anxieties. Now that I have attained awakening, this mind is peaceful and sovereign.
Every movement of thought and every stirring of intention is perfectly fulfilled and penetratingly clear. All things in the world are vividly manifest before me.
Such states are not obtained through clever discernment or intellectual calculation; rather, they are the luminous radiance of the very essence of one’s own mind.

However, it is because [the mind] is fully endowed [with this capacity]. Thus it is said: "Only after being at peace can one deliberate. The character *de* (得) here does not mean the attainment of gain or loss;
rather, it signifies the absence of leakage. The Sage responds universally and adapts to every situation;

he illuminates all human sentiments without a single hair's breadth of error, penetrating to the very source and ensuring that every action accords with the proper measure (*zhongjie*). Therefore, it is called "attainment" (*de*); it is not a matter of having something acquired. Part One.

When one has not yet clearly realized the luminous virtue (*prabhāsvara-guṇa*), one exclusively employs deluded thoughts and calculations, weighing and deliberating; even if one succeeds in this way, it cannot be attained. Why? Because it is not real.
Now, by means of the radiance of one's own nature (*svabhāva-prabhāsvara*), all things are observed simultaneously and illuminated together.

The diverse dispositions and states of all beings universally return to a single principle; thus, one can bring them to completion in their particularity without omission. This is not a matter of having something to acquire; it is simply because [of non-attainment].

It is through deliberation that one deliberates; it is through non-attainment that one attains. Therefore it is said: "Only after deliberating can one attain. This means that it is not a matter of accidental coincidence with the proper measure, but rather that attainment results specifically from deliberation.
The first section, "Those of antiquity who desired to illuminate their bright virtue throughout the world," explains the sequence of root and branch,
priority and posteriority, in order to verify the actual efficacy of illuminating one's bright virtue and bringing order to the people.

Speaking in terms of the process of self-cultivation, taking "illuminating one's own virtue" as the root and "transforming the people" as the branch means speaking from the fundamental source down to the peripheral details.
Now, speaking in terms of the perfection of things, we speak in reverse, proceeding from the branches back to the root.
This is because, starting from the single mind and the knowledge of where to rest, one proceeds until one reaches the stage of "deliberation and being able to attain."

Thus, all things and affairs in the world are contained within my own mind. Now, desiring to employ this enlightened virtue that I have already realized to reveal it to all people in the world, I wish for everyone to awaken together.
Indeed, the character *yù* (欲) is synonymous with the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*);
it means that since I have now realized this nature of enlightened virtue, and this nature is what is equally bestowed upon all people in the world.
As for those who share this same endowment: how could one bear to know it oneself and yet abandon others?

Therefore, I wish to reveal it to all people under heaven, so that they may awaken to it together and realize it together. However, I fear that those who would fail this vow might find it too remote and vast, making it difficult to achieve swift results.
Furthermore, the world is so vast; how could it ever be traversed in a single stride? Thus, I shall provisionally begin with a single state.

It is about to depart. This is what is meant by "knowing the near within the far. If one state provides an example, then the whole world will be easily transformed. In the past, Yao had his capital at Pingyang;
Shun presided over the hundred affairs of state; Tang ruled from a territory of seventy li; and King Wen ruled from a territory of one hundred li.

All were ancient sovereigns who desired to illuminate their bright virtue throughout the world. Who did not follow according to the power of their vows? Therefore, I say: it is through desire and vow.
This is the power [of the teaching]. The person is the foundation of the world, the state, and the family. As the text proceeds further on, it ultimately concludes with the cultivation of the person.
Thus, we can see that the cultivation of the person is a matter of vital importance; yet, this one matter is the most difficult to comprehend.
How could it be that by merely restraining this physical body of flesh and blood so that one is cautious and dignified—like a youth appearing before a master—is this sufficient to govern a state?
How could it be that by making every part of one's person presentable in appearance—like a performer on a stage—is this sufficient to bring peace to the world? Therefore, one must cultivate oneself.

This is entirely a matter of the work performed upon the mind. For instance, when Yanzi asked about benevolence (*ren*), Confucius told him that "to overcome oneself and return to ritual propriety (*li*)" is benevolence;

this is precisely the true manner of cultivating the person. He then further told him: "If for one day you can overcome yourself and return to ritual propriety, the whole world will turn to benevolence.
This is the actual practice for truly governing the state and bringing peace to all under heaven.

If one does not believe that this "overcoming the self" (*keji*) is the actual practice for cultivating the person (*xiushen*), how could it be that when Yanzi asked for its specific details, Confucius immediately instructed him in the "four prohibitions"?
Furthermore, these four prohibitions are all matters of cultivating the person.

Overcoming the self is the work for realizing benevolence (*ren*) within the mind-ground. To overcome the self for the sake of benevolence is precisely the manifestation of luminous virtue (*mingmingde*). Throughout the world...

Returning to benevolence (*ren*) is precisely the transformation of the people. To practice benevolence depends on oneself; this "self" is the true self, which is the ground of ultimate goodness (*zhishan*).

Thus, Yanzi’s discarding of his keen intelligence, the rejection of his physical limbs, and his "fasting of the mind" (*xinzhai*) and "sitting in oblivion" (*zuowang*) were all the actual effects of relying on the self—the ground of ultimate goodness.
In a person’s body, that which constitutes an obstacle is nothing other than seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving. What is...
This refers to seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting—all of which are the established perceptions held by every person throughout the world since ancient times.
To practice benevolence, one must completely eradicate all these old perceptions and begin anew with a different way of life;
it cannot be entered while still carrying along the habitual views of the past. By means of the old...
All that you have seen, heard, known, and perceived since the past are contrary to propriety; they are chaotic and inverted, and not a single hair’s breadth of them is of any use.
Therefore, [the Master] gouged out his heart and plucked out his gallbladder to extract this single word: "Do not" (wù).

"Do not" is a term of prohibition and expulsion, meaning that one must completely eliminate all former modes of seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting, and absolutely forbid their recurrence. To violate them again is...
This is a most severe prohibition. Upon hearing it, Yanzi immediately attained realization;
he then cast away his cleverness and discarded his physical form, setting everything aside to sit alone. Sitting, he forgot;
forgetting until there was nothing left to forget, he sprang up and leaped about. All his former perceptions, hearings, knowledges, and sensations were no longer like they had been.
The person of former times is as if they have newly fashioned for themselves another human body;
is this not, then, a new person? Since one is oneself new, one should extend this newness to transform the people.
Yet there was no one among the people who was not moved by this transformation and renewed themselves. This is what is meant by the saying:
"If for a single day one can overcome the self and return to ritual propriety (li), the whole world will turn to benevolence. This is precisely the effect of cultivating the person.

Were it not so, how could the cultivation of the person be considered the foundation for governing the state and bringing peace to all under heaven? The mind is the fundamental substance; it is the host. The intention is discursive thought and deliberation; it belongs to the guest.

This is the distinction between mind (*citta*) and thought (*manas*). Now, to rectify the mind, one must first sever all deliberations and discursive thoughts of the faculty of thought (*manendriya*) all at once, like cutting through a tangled skein.
When not a single thought arises, the substance of the mind (*cittatattva*) becomes pure and singular, free from delusion;

therefore, [discursive thought] is called a "thief. For the mind becomes deviant because the faculty of thought is insincere; now that the ground of thought is free from delusion, the mind will naturally [become upright].
This is correct. Therefore it is said: "To rectify the mind, one must first make the intention sincere. Knowledge (*zhi*) and intention (*yi*) are the distinction between the true and the delusory.
Intention is delusive thought (*wangxiang*); knowledge belongs to true knowing (*zhengzhi*).

True knowing is the luminous virtue of the fundamental substance (*benti*), yet it has been consistently obscured by delusive thoughts so that it cannot manifest. Consequently, true knowing remains dark and obscured, while delusive thoughts prevail.

"Expedient means (quán). It is like a treacherous usurper who uses the Son of Heaven to command the feudal lords. Now, if one wishes to execute the wicked and depraved, one must request the sword from above;
nothing less than the true mandate will suffice to destroy such usurpation. Therefore it is said: 'If one desires to make one's intentions sincere, one must first bring about knowledge.
Knowledge is the true master. For a long time, one has been in a state of delusion and unconsciousness. What is now called 'bringing about' (zhì) is synonymous with 'reaching' (dá)."
For example, it is like a loyal minister who intends to eliminate a treacherous official. He does not dare to act on his own authority;

rather, he must first present the evidence of that official’s villainy to his sovereign, causing the ruler to awaken to the truth. This is why it is called "causing" (zhì). Once the true sovereign has awakened, the treacherous official can no longer harbor his malevolent influence. Therefore, it is said:
"If one wishes to make one's intentions sincere, one must first cause one's knowledge to reach its fulfillment. "Things" (wù) refers to external objects.
Regarding "things": those that consistently act as opposites to me are the objects grasped through seeing, hearing, knowing, perceiving, viewing, listening, speaking, and acting.

When one knows, this is true knowledge; it is the light of wisdom (*jñāna-prabhā*) of the inherently luminous self-substance. This single character "knowing" (*jñā*) is the source of both delusion and enlightenment.
Through delusion, one internally transforms true knowledge into discursive thought (*vikalpa*); thus, the intention is not sincere, and because it is not sincere, [it does not accord with reality].
Clarification: Because one externally grasps at the true object as something desirable, things do not transform. Because they do not transform, they become obstructions.

Thus, this single character "knowledge" (*zhi*) serves as the fundamental root of the internal and external mind-objects, and of truth and falsehood, delusion and awakening. As the ancients said: "The single character 'knowledge' is the gate of all wonders;
it is also the gate of all calamities. Now, to eliminate disorder and rectify what is right, one must rely internally upon...
By the power of true knowledge (*tathatājñāna*), one destroys deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*); externally, by employing the illumination of true knowledge, one dissolves deluded objects.
"Gearing" (*ge*) refers to the "gearing" of Yu toward the Three Miao tribes, meaning that through the resonance of utmost sincerity (*zhicheng*), they were transformed and returned to him.

This is what is meant by "utmost sincerity penetrates metal and stone and moves hogs and fish"—this is "gearing. Furthermore, because one knows that the true and the deluded are different, one therefore employs [true knowledge].
It is also different. Furthermore, there are two types of "resonance" (*ge*). When false knowledge employs deluded thoughts, objects and the self obstruct one another;
this resonance is the resonance of conflict, as in the expressions "to engage in confrontation" or "the mind battles with the sun.
When true knowledge employs ultimate sincerity, objects and the self resonate and communicate with one another; this resonance is the resonance of sympathetic response, as in...

It is said that what is obstructive is not the mind itself, but rather its attachments. For instance, the braying of a donkey, the croaking of frogs, and the grass before one’s window are all objects of sound and form;

they stand in opposition to us and act as obstructions. Yet, there were Confucian scholars of the Song dynasty who attained awakening upon hearing a donkey bray, frogs croak, or seeing the grass before their windows.
Sound and form are one and the same; what previously opposed us has now been transformed into ourselves.

This is the wondrous realm of the mind. When things are transformed into cognition, they become one with the self. As for this principle of resonance and response (*gan-ge*), what cause for doubt could there be? Question: If true cognition has no object to confront it, how can it resonate and respond to things? Answer: True cognition is, in reality, transparent throughout both internally and externally; thus, there is no object to confront it. Yet, the principle by which it resonates with things is most difficult to express in words. The *I Ching* says: [The Supreme Ultimate produces the Two Forms.]... "Quiescent and unmoving, yet responding so as to penetrate the affairs of the world. "Quiescent and unmoving" refers to the substance of knowledge (*zhiti*). "The affairs of the world" refers to external objects (*wuwai*).
"Responding so as to penetrate" refers to the investigation of things (*gewu*). This so-called "responsive penetration" does not mean that true knowledge physically penetrates into the objects;
rather, it is because true knowledge is vast and unobstructed, such that no object stands before it. [This concerns] the true and false mind.

The objective realm cannot admit of two simultaneous standpoints. External objects are like darkness, while true knowledge is like the bright sun. When the sun rises once, all darkness is instantly extinguished;
this is likely what is meant by "resonance and penetration" (gantong) in terms of the point of transformation and dissolution. If one uses darkness to sense light, then light becomes darkness;
now, using light to sense darkness, then darkness withdraws of its own accord and light stands alone. Therefore, although there is resonance, fundamentally there has been none.
They meet one another, yet the emphasis lies in illumination. The substance of things is fundamentally empty; because of deluded grasping and attachment, obstructions arise.
Now, when true knowledge shines alone, the place of liberation becomes transparently clear, such that no object can confront the mind.

With this true knowledge that is quiescent and unmoving, one penetrates the illusory nature of objects which have been non-existent from the beginning. Thus, knowledge does not depend on external stimuli but arises spontaneously.

Illumination. Things do not require mediation to be harmonized; they are mutually unobstructed. How subtle! How subtle! Therefore, for the student, the sole priority lies in true knowledge (*zhēnzhī*).
Once true knowledge is established, luminous virtue (*míngdé*) becomes naturally manifest, without the slightest trace of contrivance.

This is why the discipline of the Great Learning speaks of "illumination" and "knowledge"; the principles of cultivation, regulation, ordering, and bringing peace are all manifestations of this very thing.
Question: At the outset, you spoke of "establishing the guiding principles," "clarifying virtue," and "bringing the people to rest in the ultimate good. These are clearly three distinct matters.
Yet, in this specific section, you speak only of "clarifying virtue throughout the world" and ultimately reduce it to "extending knowledge and investigating things.
If these are one and the same matter, what is the intended meaning? Answer: The Sage’s intention here is most subtle; no one throughout the ages has been able to comprehend it. Within this...
Regarding these eight matters, they all hinge solely on the single character "knowledge" (zhī). This "knowledge" is precisely luminous virtue; it is the fundamental substance.
As previously stated, the first character "luminous" (míng) carries two meanings. This is what I have previously explained as "extending knowledge" (zhìzhī) and "investigating things" (gēwù).

Thus, one employs the single principle of the previously realized awakening. The work of cultivation already resides within "stopping" (zhǐ). The character *zhǐ* is the substance of knowledge that is "tranquil and unmoving.
The character *zhī* (knowing) in "stopping by knowing" (*zhǐzhī*) is the first instance of the character *míng* (illumination), which constitutes the work of cultivation.

This section has already reached the ultimate point of "extending knowledge" (*zhìzhī*). Once the substance of knowledge is perfected, then the tasks of "sincerity of intention," "rectification of the mind," and "cultivation of the person" are accomplished.
It is finished. Thus, "cultivating one's own bright virtue" (*mingmingde*) and "transforming the people" (*xinmin*) are clearly two distinct matters.

Now, when one wishes to "make one's own bright virtue manifest throughout the world," one employs the second [hexagram] to reveal the meaning of illumination; consequently, "extending knowledge" (*zhizhi*) and "investigating things" (*gewu*) may also be discussed in terms of transforming the people.

Furthermore, "knowing where to rest and thereafter having stability" constitutes "establishing oneself"; that is, once one knows where to rest, then— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
One's own heels have already been firmly planted. To contemplate before acting, one can attain [realization]; this is what is meant by "having reached" (*yata*).

This means that regarding all phenomena, one has attained thorough penetration without omission; when not even a single hair’s breadth of obstruction remains before one's eyes, then every dharma is true.
Is this not indeed "having reached"? The reason for being established and the reason for having reached are both dependent upon the power of true knowledge. Therefore, now...
In the practice of becoming a new person, one takes the true knowledge already realized within oneself and extends it to reach all things.
Once all things have received the singular illumination of this true knowledge, they are like snow falling upon a red-hot furnace or frost dissolving under the scorching sun.

Without awaiting transformation, they transform of their own accord. Therefore it is said: "To attain knowledge lies in the investigation of things. When things transform of their own accord, this is called "investigation" (*ge*).
Once those things have been investigated, my enlightened virtue naturally shines brightly upon the world;

the people do not await renewal, yet they renew themselves. This is what is meant by "establishing the person and reaching others. In this way, the enlightened virtue that renews the people is simply—
This is one matter. As for the three fundamental principles, they are one yet three, and three yet one. Therefore, these eight matters are simply to fulfill the single phrase:
"to bring forth illustrious virtue over the world. Furthermore, proceeding from the family and the state before reaching the world is to know the near through the far;
this is most clear. Question: How does one investigate things (*gewu*) so as to be able to bring peace to the world? Answer: Tell me, first of all—how?
What is the object to be investigated? It is none other than heaven, earth, and the myriad things; they are all contained within this very scope.
How could one seek some other object to investigate apart from heaven, earth, and the myriad things?

If investigating things were insufficient to bring peace to the world, how then could Confucius have said, "In a single day, if one overcomes the self and returns to propriety, the whole world will turn to benevolence"? Furthermore, tell me: what is this "world" that turns to benevolence?
"What thing? Where does one who returns to benevolence ultimately go? "Study, study! Question:

"Regarding 'extending knowledge and investigating things' (zhì zhī gé wù) and 'overcoming the self and returning to ritual so that all under heaven return to benevolence' (kè jǐ fù lǐ tiān xià guī rén), how should these be understood? Answer: "Overcoming the self is precisely extending knowledge;

returning to ritual is precisely investigating things; and all under heaven returning to benevolence is precisely the investigation of things being perfected. Question: "I, a student, do not understand. Answer: "The self is the thing."

To achieve this is the perfection of knowledge (*zhìzhī*). To restore ritual propriety (*lǐ*) is for oneself to undergo transformation. Is this transformation of oneself not precisely the investigation of things (*gèwù*)?

When all under heaven turn toward benevolence (*rén*), what a state of great peace! This is called the perfection of things (*wùgé*). Question: What is the distinction between rectifying the mind (*zhèngxīn*) and perfecting knowledge (*zhìzhī*)?

Answer: Rectifying the mind refers to the "four prohibitions" (*sìwù*). One must first sever all that is contrary to ritual propriety regarding seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting; thus one can cultivate the self and rectify oneself.

One cannot transform others. If the focus on "attaining knowledge" (zhìzhī) lies solely in "investigating things" (géwù), then for the person of great attainment, this [investigation] constitutes the greatest merit.

Therefore, in the *Great Learning*, the emphasis is placed on attaining knowledge. Question: Regarding the principle of the sequence between "investigating things" and "things being investigated" (wùgé).

Answer: In the preceding eight matters, the character "prior" (xiān) is used; however, they all ultimately converge upon the final emphasis on "attaining knowledge. This refers to the process of cultivation (*gōngfū*). Now, following from "things" (wù)...

In the progression of the teachings up to "rectifying the mind" and "regulating the family," the inclusion of the character "to rectify" (*ge*) is intended to highlight the character "knowledge" (*zhi*).
This serves to demonstrate that the seven subsequent matters are all the efficacy of this very knowledge. Students must focus their attention upon this character "knowledge.

As stated previously, "extending knowledge and rectifying things" means responding to things in order to fully realize one's knowledge; thus, this character "rectify" (*ge*) refers to the act of responsive resonance (*gan-ge*).

Regarding the term "ge" (to reach/arrive). When it is now said that "only after the objects are reached does knowledge become ultimate," this means that one relies upon objects to verify the substance of knowledge.
The intent is that if there is even a single hair’s breadth of an object that has not been fully digested, then knowledge has not yet reached its ultimate state.
One must desire for all objects to be fully digested before this true knowledge can be perfected. In this sense, the "ge" in "wu-ge" (objects reached) refers to "lai-ge" (to arrive at).
The character *gé* in "the manifestation of the divine" (*shén zhī gé sī*) precisely signifies the meaning of "all under heaven returning to benevolence.

Only when all things have come to be manifested (*gé*) is this the verification of knowing. Therefore, regarding the investigation of things (*gé wù*) and the manifestation of things (*wù gé*), students must seek a clear understanding.
If all things have been manifested, then one proceeds with this single path of manifestation until it reaches the entire world; only then—
Set down your hands. The Sage’s intent is clear and plain; it simply requires that you produce genuine practice to see its ultimate result.
Question: From the Son of Heaven down to the common people, all must take the cultivation of the self as the foundation.
Since you say it is simply a matter of "knowing," how does this return to the cultivation of the self? Answer: It is not from the standpoint of the cultivation of the self.
One begins from here; it is not said that one acts within empty space. Therefore, the Sage clearly showed you:

"To overcome oneself and return to ritual propriety (*li*), and the whole world will turn to benevolence. "The self" refers to one's own person; it is the most intimate thing to me, unlike external objects.
To "overcome the self" means that my cultivation of knowledge must first be applied to this single thing that is my own person. If one were to...
Once you have mastered this object yourself, what difficulty could there be in mastering Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things?

Therefore, it is universally held that cultivating the self is the foundation. Question: There are three meanings of "ge" (to master/understand): *hange* (obstruction/resistance), *kange* (resonance/response), and *raige* (coming/approaching).
Answer: These three meanings all originate from a single person. Please allow me to clarify this through an analogy. Formerly, the wife of Qi Liang was skilled at wailing; when her husband died...
He wept for him. When he first began to weep, the villagers detested the sound of his crying and loathed the man;

thus, upon hearing his wailing, they would cover their ears, and upon seeing him, they would close their eyes, because his weeping was different from that of others. Yet his wife did not cease her weeping out of concern for the villagers' loathing.
After he had wept for a long time, the villagers unconsciously came to feel grief and sorrow for him as well.
They wept. By weeping, they forgot their loathing. When their loathing was forgotten, their hearts turned toward pitying him.

His wife, too, did not cease weeping because she pitied herself for his sake; she continued to weep until she could no longer stop. After a long time, everyone throughout the neighborhood became skilled at weeping.
When everyone was skilled at weeping, they forgot their own grief and pain, and no longer saw that man as an object of aversion.
Regarding the practice of wailing: if everyone is skilled at wailing, and they wail for a long time, it will become a custom throughout the entire neighborhood.

Once the custom is established, everyone will consider themselves naturally capable of wailing. When everyone considers themselves naturally capable of wailing, they will regard the wife of Qi Liang as just like any other woman;
they will not distinguish her from themselves and will interact with her intimately and closely. Thus, there would be no one who does not forget [the propriety of mourning]. Furthermore, Qi Liang—
When the wife weeps, she does not weep for her husband; she weeps for Heaven. Heaven is that upon which one relies for a lifetime;
when it is lost, one cannot help but weep. To wail with grief is the lifelong regret. Because one knows that Heaven allows no escape, the weeping likewise does not cease.
How could it be stopped merely because others loathe it? Even if the entire neighborhood...
People questioned him day after day, yet his weeping grew even more sorrowful. It was likely not that he intentionally desired to elicit pity from others;
how could questioning possibly have stopped it? Even if a blade were held before him and a cauldron of boiling oil behind him, no amount of intimidation could have halted it.
Why is this? Because beyond this world, there is nothing left to weep for. As for those who initially loathed him because of his weeping, it was because—
His grief was exceptionally different from that of others; it was a state of profound agitation. After he had wept for a long time, everyone else felt pain as well.
This was because the intensity of his grief pierced the hearts of all present, so that everyone felt pain for themselves rather than feeling pain for Qi. It was a matter of being moved and affected.
It is likely that over time, the people of Tongli became accustomed to wailing until it formed a local custom; thus, they did not realize that the practice of wailing out of grief originated from Qi.

Furthermore, their behavior was merely an imitation of Lady Liang. This, then, is what is meant by "coming to resemble. Although these words concern a minor matter, they can serve as an analogy for matters of great importance.
This is the *Deciding Doubts Regarding the Outline of the Great Learning* composed by the Great Master Hanshan.

While the Master resided at Caoxi, many scholars who had studied under Confucian masters came bearing their brushes to seek his instruction. The Master, manifesting himself in the form of a civil examination candidate (*juzi*), preached the Dharma for them.
This year, having traveled to Wumen, he presented this work to Qian Yi, saying: "In my old age, I still dabble in brush and ink; yet there remains..."

Childlike innocence (*tongxin*) is surely not a matter for beneath the patched robe. What do you say to this? I further heard that Zhang Zishao studied under Guishan in his youth and caught a glimpse of the "centrality of the unmanifested.
Upon visiting Jingshan, he engaged in a dialectical inquiry based on the principle of "investigating things and things being investigated," whereby he suddenly grasped the subtle essence.
Among those celebrated for their integrity in the late Song dynasty, he was ranked first.

As for Xiao Shao: looking at him from the present day, when he vigorously debated at the Imperial Lecture Hall, he was later exiled to Hengpu. There, holding his book as he stood leaning against it, his double lotus posture (sitting cross-legged) was clearly visible.
Compared to the youthful vigor of his earlier integrity, that [later state] was almost like the tracks of a wild goose in the melting snow.
Could this have been possible without having attained a profound realization at Mount Jing? Those who act as Xiao Shao does today possess aspirations that differ [from those of the past]. Their...
To proclaim the True Dharma by means of worldly truth is one and the same. When Bian Que heard that the people of Qin cherished their young children, he became a pediatrician.
Since the world today prizes the birth of sons, the Great Master manifested in the form of a son-seeker to preach the Dharma for them.
How could this not be a matter beneath the monk’s robe? Zishao once said: "Whenever I hear of the Elder of Mount Jing..."
The causes and conditions thus raised are like a thousand doors and ten thousand gates opening at a single step.
If those who take the imperial examination today can contemplate in this manner, then the Great Master’s adamantine eye will be manifested, point by point, from the tip of their brush.
In the fourth month of the Ding-si year of the Wanli era, the disciple Qian Qianyi of Yushan, wearing a cloth cap,
respectfully inscribed this while burning incense for the forty-fourth volume of the *Record of Dreaming Wandering* by the Elder Master Hanshan.
[The forty-fifth volume of the *Record of Dreaming Wandering* by the Elder Master Hanshan.]
Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and his disciple Tonghye;
revised by the Disciple from Lingnan, Liu Qixiang.

In the preface to the *Lao-Zhuang Yingxiang Lun* (Treatise on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi), it states that the various patriarchs of the Western Regions composed treatises to refute the attachments of non-Buddhists; therefore, one must be well-versed in both one's own and others' schools. In this land...
From ancient times, among the masters of the various sūtras and śāstras, there has never been one who was not proficient in both their own and others' schools.

As for those of our school who are but late learners, they settle for narrow ignorance; they are oblivious to the fact that all things share the same essence, regarding them instead as disparate entities.

Unable to harmonize the teachings and contemplation, they find it difficult to benefit the common people. Among these, there are those who have only recently begun their faith and cannot deeply penetrate the scriptural canons, suffering under the burden of mere names and superficial characteristics.

It is difficult to comprehend. As for his passionate devotion to Laozi and Zhuangzi as the source of his literary compositions, when it comes to the ultimate aim of his discourse, there are none who do not gaze out at the vast ocean and sigh in wonder.
Upon examining the various commentaries by other scholars, each follows their own partial views, making it difficult to reach a definitive judgment.
However, upon seeing the *Kouyi* (Oral Explanations) and its supplementary texts, which extensively cite Buddhist scriptures, every single word [reveals...]
It is appropriate to say that the entire Tripitaka emerges from this; yet those who are deluded take this as a matter of necessity, which fills me with deep lamentation.
While I sat in silent meditation by the sea, I happened to read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Lotus Sūtra*. Subsequently, someone requested instruction on the principles of Laozi and Zhuangzi;
thus, I allowed my discourse to branch out to these matters to resolve my own doubts. This was not intended to seek renown.
Regarding the True Person (the Buddha), I consider this to be a discourse that must necessarily be followed.

Furthermore, I lament that since ancient times, those who have sought to refute the original teachings have mostly administered medicine, yet few have been able to open up the chronic ailments of the *gāohuáng* (the incurable region of the body). It is not that their prescriptions were not skillfully applied;

it is simply that they failed to diagnose the source of the disease. Therefore, I have used the contemplation of mind-only consciousness (*cittamātra-vijñapti*) to provide a definitive resolution, like a *maṇi* jewel.
The perfect illumination reveals the five colors in their vivid clarity; as an empty valley transmits sound, all echoes respond accordingly.
If one contemplates all phenomena solely through mind and consciousness, then those phenomena do not emerge outside the realm of shadows and echoes. Therefore, this is discussed by way of names.
In discussing the source of the teachings, I have observed that among the world’s various craftsmen and artisans, those who reach the pinnacle of mastery cannot transmit it through words;
nor can those who attempt to emulate them acquire it through words. How much more so for the subtlety of the Great Way—it cannot be bestowed or received by means of mouth or ear.
It is not through language and written characters that one attains it; rather, it lies in the subtlety of mental awakening. Thus, it is not only in Zen meditation that sublime awakening is valued;

even regarding worldly wisdom, eloquence, the arts of governing the world, and the occupations for sustaining life—there is not a single dharma among them wherein one does not attain its subtlety through awakening.
Being subtle, it cannot be reached by words. Therefore, our Buddha, the Sage, said:

When preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one speaks exclusively of the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), yet regarding the "Wondrous Dharma" (*saddharma*), not a single word has been uttered; it is merely said to be "thus" (*evam*).

As for those who have awakened to the Wondrous Dharma, they simply say that one who is skilled in preaching the Dharma—even mundane speech and activities for sustaining life—all conform to the True Dharma.
Thus, the noble ones of the fifth stage of the *Avataṃsaka* are well able to penetrate the worldly.
As for this study, it encompasses everything from the arts of Yin and Yang and the calculation of omens, to ancient charts and seals, medical prescriptions, and poetic compositions;

there is nothing he does not master thoroughly. Only then can one engage with the world to benefit sentient beings. Therefore, the Great Being of Equal Enlightenment manifests forms within the ten realms;

according to whatever body or teaching is required to deliver them, he immediately manifests that very body and teaching to bring them across and liberate them. Viewed from this perspective, the Buddha...
How could the Dharma be utterly devoid of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and how could conventional truth be entirely non-Buddhist?

It is simply because people do not awaken to the subtlety of the Great Way that they arbitrarily demarcate the distinction between "internal" and "external. How could the Way be such a thing? Observing those throughout antiquity who have defended the boundaries of the Way:
when it concerns this [tradition], they say, "That is a heterodox path (*tīrthika*"); when it concerns that [tradition], they say, "This is a deviant sect."
Viewed from a grand perspective, these are like the pairing of the noble and the lowly, or like drawing boundaries within the vast void; they are not the light of the sun and moon.
All of this stems from failing to awaken to the wondrous nature of one’s own mind, thereby merely augmenting one's frivolous discursive proliferation (*prapañca*).

Indeed, the sages of antiquity had nothing else to offer; they were simply those who awakened to the wondrous nature of the mind. All their verbal teachings issued forth from that wondrous awakening within the mind.
They flow forth, manifesting in varying depths according to the capacities of sentient beings. Therefore it is said: "There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm;
there is nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm. For this reason, if we do not awaken to our own minds, we will not know the mind of the sages.
To fail to understand the mind of the Sage while merely imitating his words is like the joy and sorrow of a spectator at a performance:
though they appear joyful, they are not truly joyful; though they appear sorrowful, they are not truly sorrowful. For their grief and joy do not originate from within themselves.
To claim that grief and joy originate from oneself when they do not—this is what I observe in those who interpret the words of the Sage according to the [Confucian] tradition.
In this treatise on the mind and dharmas:

when I was young, I took Confucius as my teacher, yet I did not know Confucius; when my teacher grew old, I did not know he was old. Having reached maturity, I took the Buddha as my teacher, yet I did not know the Buddha.
I withdrew into deep mountains and vast marshes to practice stillness and contemplate the mind. From this, I came to know that the three realms are but...

Mind. All phenomena are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Since one observes that all is but mind and consciousness, then all forms are reflections of the mind, and all sounds are echoes of the mind.
Thus, all sages are the most prominent among these reflections, and all verbal teachings are... [echoes].

As for that which accords with the resonance [of reality]: because all phenomena are manifested solely by the mind, worldly speech, the activities of livelihood, and so forth, are all in accord with the True Dharma.
Since there are no phenomena apart from the mind, every phenomenon is truly real. Those who are deluded grasp at them and thus find them not sublime;
if one awakens to one's own mind, then there is no phenomenon that is not sublime. When both mind and phenomena are sublime, only the sages are capable of this.

In discussing what to accept or reject regarding our Buddhist scriptures, it is evident that they all originated from the Western Regions and were produced through translation. Yet, while the arrival of these scriptures began during the Han dynasty, it was not until the Western Jin that they flourished greatly.
Among the translators of the Jin, Kumārajīva alone is acclaimed as the most eminent; and among his disciples, those born...

Sengzhao, Daorong, Sengrui, and Sengsi were the "qilin" and "phoenixes" among the monastics, yet Kumārajīva obtained their service. Regarding Sengzhao, Kumārajīva even said: "In my understanding, I do not yield to you;
in literary composition, however, I must bow before you. This was because Sengzhao was particularly adept at the *Laozi* and *Zhuangzi*.

Nevertheless, while all Buddhist scriptures are proclaimed from the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha], when they reach this region [China], the language often differs; thus, for a single scripture, there are several...
There have been those among the translators who, giving rise to doubts based on their shallow understanding, failed to realize that the underlying principle is in fact unerring;

it is merely a matter of the skill or lack thereof in the translator’s literary expression. Thus, whenever the *Tripiṭaka* emerged from the hands of Kumārajīva, the prose was invariably elegant and refined, for he was supported by four sages.
Consequently, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, with its profound principles and dense diction, exhaustively captures its subtle wonders—not through mere words, but...
The literary style of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* is elegant and refined; its principles are self-evident. As for Sengzhao’s *Four Treatises*, they are seamless and holistic;

unless one possesses the "right Dharma-eye," they are certainly difficult to clarify. Thus, those who are deluded reject them, rightly regarding the Emptiness school as mere superficial talk akin to that of Zhuangzi, Laozi, and Mencius.
Master Qingliang Guanding was a Bodhisattva of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; when it came to his commentaries...
The *Avataṃsaka* school frequently cites the *Treatise by Zhaolun*, invariably referring to him as "Master Zhaopeng" (肇公) out of respect. I have once ventured to reflect upon this:

had Zhaolun’s views been incorrect, how could Kumārajīva have permitted him to sit in his presence? Had Kumārajīva’s own vision not been clear, how could he have accorded such honor to the translation?

And if Zhaolun’s treatises were not canonical, how could Huiguan have allowed them to be spoken of? Although there have been many doubts raised regarding these matters throughout past and present, they have generally not been addressed.

Why is this so? When examining the *Huayan Sūtra Commentary*, one finds that it frequently cites the words of Laozi and Zhuangzi in great abundance; yet it is said that [the author] takes their phrasing but not their underlying intent.
Guifeng, however, maintained that these two schools were unable to provide a fundamental account of human nature, an argument for which Zongjing was particularly prominent in his refutation.

Nevertheless, the aforementioned masters were all great bodhisattvas of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) who erected the great banner of the Dharma; why then do their views differ so greatly regarding what to adopt and what to reject?
Let us attempt to discuss this: it is likely that each has his own specific focus. For the language of the Western Regions is plain and direct, lacking literary ornamentation.

Furthermore, there is much redundancy. As for the learning of translators, if they are not proficient in both traditions, the text will often be vulgar and crude, which greatly hinders the underlying principle.
Indeed, among the words of the sages of China, apart from the Five Classics which are bound by worldly instruction, the only other work that conveys the Way is the single book of Laozi.
However, Laozi’s words are ancient and concise, profound and obscure, difficult to clarify. To bring them forth—
Among those who wielded the Way of the Old Master (Laozi), there was only Zhuang Zhou alone. Jiao Xian had a saying: "Laozi having Zhuangzi is like Confucius having Mencius.

This statement is indeed credible. Yet, since Confucius praised the Old Master as being "like a dragon," by means of Mencius we come to see Zhuangzi; would this not be to pay him homage from the north?
I have once privately remarked that, throughout the entire span of the past and future across the Middle Kingdom, even reaching back to the time of the Sage, [there has been no one to equal him].
Among those who possessed a vision that transcends the world, there is none other than Zhuang Zhou alone who has cast off the "Old" (Laozi).

As for words that carry the Way, vast and sovereign, apart from the Buddhist scriptures, there is only the single work of Zhuangzi among the various masters and hundred schools for one who investigates the study of heaven and humanity.
Even if such a person did not exist in China, for ten thousand generations thereafter, people would not have known of the True Man. China.
This book does not exist [in its original form]. For ten thousand generations to come, it may be that no one will know of this wondrous treatise. This is because our Buddha-dharma is vast and subtle;
translators employ difficult terminology to convey it, so that the underlying principles must necessarily remain hidden, as is the case with the *Laṅkāvatāra*.
Therefore, the reason for the excellence of Kumārajīva’s translations was simply that he had four sages to assist him. Master Guān has said: "Take..."

That he adopted the phrasing without adopting the underlying meaning is indeed for a specific reason. Had there been anything in this land that surpassed the words of Laozi and Zhuangzi, Sengzhao would certainly have discarded them without a second thought.
Viewed from this perspective, the reason Sengzhao’s commentaries and treatises employ [their] phrasing is that he took the *Lotus Sūtra* as his primary authority;
it is therein stated that "one who skillfully teaches the Dharma uses the language of worldly convention (*saṃvṛti-satya*) to support the activities of livelihood."
All these [teachings] accord with the True Dharma; they are the deeds of those who have profoundly penetrated the true nature (*dharmatā*).

As for Guifeng’s *Zhongjing lu* (Mirror of the Canon) and Yuan’s [Zongmi’s] distancing himself from it: when Confucius composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, he relied on the mandate of the Heavenly King to bestow rewards and punishments.
Do these two masters not likewise exercise the authority of the Dharma King to issue praise and censure? As for Qingliang, he merges seamlessly with the *dharmadhātu*, leaving nothing...
There is nothing that is not possible; thus, to take and yet not take is each governed by its own principle.

Therefore, when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* describes the thirty-two manifestations of Avalokiteśvara, it says: "If one should be saved by means of the body of a Brahmin, he immediately manifests that body and preaches the Dharma for them.
As for the two sons of Miaozhuangyan, however, it says: "Your father has faith in and accepts the teachings of external paths."
They were deeply attached to the Brahmanical dharma, and even the two sons regretted being born into this family of heterodox views.

Indeed, the Laozi and Zhuangzi of this land are the equivalents of the Western Brahmans. Yet, while [the Buddha] manifested his body here to preach the Dharma for them, he immediately dismissed them as followers of heterodox views.
Why is this? It is simply a matter of whether one is attached or unattached. This is according to the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* on Perfect Penetration.

Being unimpeded, one is not obstructed from manifesting a body and preaching the Dharma. However, because Miaozhuang deeply gave rise to attachment, he became a follower of external paths and heterodox views.
Therefore, when the Sages teach people, they only break their attachments and do not break their methods.
Thus, those who are attached to sounds and forms do not possess right view.
On the Study of Learning:
Whenever I see scholars perusing sutra commentaries, if they suddenly encounter a citation from the secular histories or records, it is like a tiger blocking their path;
they are invariably struck with alarm and fail to proceed. Yet, when instructed to study those works directly, they say, "Those are merely the words of outsiders," and cast them aside.

They do not turn their heads to look back. Furthermore, I have often observed that when scholar-gentlemen discuss the words of Zhuangzi, they invariably cite Buddhist teachings as a mirror for comparison.
Should a single phrase happen to be appropriate, they even say, "The entire Great Canon of the Buddha is entirely derived from this. Alas! Can this truly be called "thorough understanding"?
When these two are compared, one who studies Buddhism without being versed in the hundred schools of thought not only fails to understand this [Zhuangzi], but...
He understands the *Zhuangzi* yet remains ignorant of the Buddha-Dharma; he interprets the *Zhuangzi* and claims to have exhausted the Buddhist scriptures.

Not only does he fail to understand the Buddha’s intent, but he also fails to understand the intent of *Zhuangzi*. This is why [the meaning] is so difficult to clarify. Thus it is said: "Those who view the small from the perspective of the great do not grasp it fully;
those who view the great from the perspective of the small do not see clearly. I have often exhorted myself with three matters, saying: "If one does not know spring..."

Autumn. If one cannot navigate the world, one does not understand Laozi and Zhuangzi; if one cannot forget the world, one does not practice Chan; if one cannot transcend the world, one has not attained realization.
Knowing this, one may be spoken to regarding the study of learning.
In the *Lun jiao cheng* (Discourse on the Vehicle of the Teachings), it is asked: "The sages of the three teachings originally share one principle; is this indeed so? It is replied:

"If one contemplates through the lens of 'the triple world is mind-only' and 'all phenomena are consciousness-only,' then not only do the three teachings originally share one principle, there is not a single thing or a single phenomenon that does not do so."

The Dharma is not established by this mind. If one contemplates through the impartial *dharmadhātu*, it is evident that not only are the three sages fundamentally of one body, but there is not a single person or a single thing that is not manifested by the majestic spiritual power of Vairocana’s *Sāgaramudrā-samādhi*.
Therefore, it is said: "While the characteristics are not destroyed, they arise through conditions; defilement and purity are eternally distinct, yet they do not abandon their causal conditions."

Yet they are immediately the truth; the holy and the ordinary are equal. It is only in what is provisionally established that there are differences between the circular and the sequential, and between the provisional and the real regarding persons and dharmas.
As for the circular, all phenomena are but the one mind; defilement and purity are interfused, without obstruction or hindrance.
As for the sequential, the ten realms, the five vehicles, and the five teachings differ in their principles and phenomena, causes and effects, and their degrees of depth and shallowness. What is...
The "ten realms" refer to the four noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings. The "five teachings" refer to the Hīnayāna, Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect [teachings].
The "five vehicles" refer to humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; the Buddha is the supreme One Vehicle.
Nevertheless, these five vehicles each have their own cultivation and progress, with the distinctions between cause and effect clearly delineated and without confusion. As for humans...
This refers precisely to that which covers and encompasses the space between heaven and earth—the realm within the four seas governed by sovereign rulers.
Tracing its fundamental practice, it takes the Five Precepts as its basis. As for what is called "Heaven," this refers to the various heavens of the Desire Realm governed by Śakra Devendra;
tracing its fundamental practice, it takes the superior grade of the Ten Wholesome Paths as its basis. The various heavens of the Form Realm are governed by Brahmā; the Formless [Realm]...

The various devas of the realms are sustained by the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*). As for the basis of their cultivation, it consists of the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*), with the mundane meditative absorptions (*sāsrava-dhyāna*) and the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti*) as its foundation.
These two constitute the cause and fruit within the realm of desire and form. This is what is referred to as the practice cultivated by the *śrāvakas*.
Taking the Four Noble Truths as the foundation is what is practiced by Pratyekabuddhas; taking the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination as the foundation is what is practiced by Bodhisattvas;
and taking the Six Perfections as the foundation—these three constitute the causes and effects of the realm beyond. The Buddha, however, perfectly awakens to the single mind.
It perfectly accords with the three virtues (*triguṇa*), which, when subsumed, form one; thus it is called "perfect fusion" (*yuanrong*). When expanded, they form five;

thus it is called "gradual progression" (*xingbu*). This principle is fully recorded in various sutras. Viewed from this perspective, the teachings of the five vehicles are all the Buddha-dharma, and the practices of the five vehicles are all the Buddha-practices.
This is truly because the capacities and dispositions (*indriya-bhājana*) of sentient beings differ in magnitude.
The sages established their teachings with varying degrees of depth, all of which were expedient means devised in response to the capacities of beings;

this is what is meant by the principle that "teachings do not skip over levels. From this it is proven that Confucius was a sage of the human vehicle (*puruṣayāna*); therefore, he governed humanity by emulating Heaven.
Laozi was a sage who mounted the Way of Heaven; thus he was pure and free from desire, departing from the human realm to enter the celestial.

The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas were sages who transcended both humans and devas; thus they loftily surpassed the three realms and distantly leaped beyond the four modes of birth, abandoning the human and celestial worlds without entering them.
The Bodhisattvas were sages who transcended the two vehicles; they emerged from the human and celestial realms yet entered the human and celestial realms, and thus they come and go.

He saves those within the three realms and delivers those born through the four modes of birth. He emerges from the truth to enter the mundane; thus, the Buddha is the saint among both the holy and the ordinary.

Consequently, he can manifest as both holy and ordinary: appearing as a celestial being when among the heavens, and as a human being when among humans. Even to the point of manifesting diverse forms among different species, there is nowhere he does not enter.
Now, as for this ability to be both holy and ordinary—how could it be something achieved by the holy or the ordinary? If one observes according to reality:
Thus, there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma; the three teachings are none other than the sages. Whether persons or dharmas, they are all subsumed within the one mind;
whether phenomena or principles, they are without obstruction or hindrance. This is what is called the Buddha. Therefore, perfect interfusion does not obstruct sequential manifestation.

The ten realms stand in dense array; yet their sequential unfolding does not obstruct their perfect fusion. Within this single, equal limit, how could there be any distinction between self and other, or any debate over right and wrong?
Thus it is said: "Sometimes the Four Truths are taught using the language of the borderlands; sometimes they are taught using conventional worldly language.
This refers to those among humans and devas who, following worldly convention, speak of the Four Truths. Considering those two sages, were they not indeed our Buddha?
"Did he not secretly dispatch two men to serve as precursors for the Buddha-dharma? This shows that both the person and the dharma are expedient means (*upāya*).
It is because, at the gateway of transformative manifestation, the characteristics of cause and effect are not destroyed. The studies of the Three Teachings all serve to guard the minds of learners.
From the shallow to the profound, and from the near to the far: for this reason, Confucius wished that people would not become tigers."
The wolf is the behavior of a beast. Therefore, one must assist it with benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and wisdom, temporarily causing it to abandon evil and follow the good.

Proceeding from the state of a thing to that of a human, one cultivates the teachings of the former kings, clarifies the authority of rewards and punishments, and composes the Spring and Autumn Annals to clarify the traces of order and chaos.
Thus one rectifies the human heart, establishes the hierarchy of high and low, and institutes the distinctions between ruler and subject, father and son. By means of this—
It establishes the regulations of human relations; its laws are strict and its teachings are earnest. It accords with human nature and is easy to practice.

Yet, it was only during times when human desires flowed out uncontrollably that those [in other lands] found it urgent and difficult to implement. In my view, were it not for the Master Kung (Confucius), this would not have been so in the Middle Kingdom.
Yet among humans, those who do not become barbarians or beasts are few indeed. Nevertheless, while such may be the outward traces of the Master Kong, how could his mind have been entirely so?
Moreover, he spoke these words clearly: "Do not harbor arbitrary conceptions; do not be compulsive; do not be stubborn; do not be self-centered.
Observing his heart in saving the world, was he not one who, relying upon the Bodhisattva vehicle, expounded the methods for governing the world?
Indeed, it is for good reason that the Sūtras call him "The Youth of the Confucians" (Routong). Yet, scholars fail to perceive the mind of the Sage and assume his Way is merely as they perceive it.
Thus, they cling to the traces of the former kings to seek fame and office, solidifying their attachment to the self (*ātman-grāha*).
They indulge their greed and desire, creating burdens for their lives, until they even take benevolence and righteousness (*ren-yi*) as tools for banditry, inciting attack and...
The calamity of contention exists; therefore, Laozi lamented it, saying: "This is the fault of exalting the sage and employing wisdom.
If one were to cut off sageliness and abandon wisdom, the people would benefit a hundredfold. If one were to split the measures and break the scales, the people would not contend."
How grave is the harm caused by greed and desire! Therefore it is said: "If one does not see that which excites desire, the mind will not become disordered.

Thus, its teaching is to distance oneself from desire and maintain purity through stillness and concentration to hold the mind; not to occupy oneself with external things, but to remain tranquil and non-active.
This is the way of Heaven. It causes people to learn this, leaving the human realm to enter the celestial. Because these words are profound and far-reaching, one must study them.
This [truth] is difficult to clarify; thus, Zhuangzi arose to expound it with great vigor. Because people’s stubborn attachments were deep-rooted, his words were correspondingly urgent.
That he reviled Yao and Shun and disparaged Tang and Wu was not mere hyperbole; it was a call to sever the pursuit of sagehood and abandon cleverness.
That he traced the governance back to the High Antiquity and placed the Way beyond Fuxi and Huangdi was not idle talk; it was an extreme expression of the truth.
This was done because [such views] were harmful. To disparage Confucius was not to disparage Confucius himself, but rather to disparage those who merely follow the traces of Confucius's teachings.

Furthermore, these were not literal statements, but rather words intended to shatter attachments; thus it is said: "Fictitious parables account for nineteen-twentieths; words of authority account for seventeen-twentieths."

They reprimand and instruct to urge one toward detachment; they cause the form to be discarded and wisdom to be merged, intending to lead people away from the human realm and into the heavenly realms, solely for the purpose of removing the burden of greed and desire.

As for the meticulous investigation of worldly affairs and the thorough mastery of human sentiments—breaking through the sturdy gates of self-clinging, crossing the great boundaries of the living, employing parables in profusion, drawing analogies and classifying expressions with precision and clarity, and reaching into the profound, subtle, and mysterious depths—[it is all for this same end].
He is inconceivable. This man expounds the teachings for humans and devas while possessing unimpeded eloquence; is he not one who manifests in the body of a Brahmin to preach the Dharma?

How vast is his mastery of the *līlā*! He treats the mundane world as mere chaff, regards birth and death as illusory transformations, liberates himself from worldly burdens, and dwells in carefree sovereignty—such is the measure of his transcendence of the world.

How lamentable! I have often thought that in the aftermath of the five Hegemons’ usurpations, scholars of retired status indulged in reckless polemics, clogging the path of benevolence and righteousness.
Had it not been for Mencius arising to open it wide, I believe the world and posterity would have been left in the barbarian garb of the *zuo-ren*.
Amidst the extreme of the many heroes devouring one another, when the entire age was dazed and blinded, losing its life to external things and the fire of desire galloped on without returning.

Such individuals have been many. Had it not been for this old man who rose up and rolled up his sleeves amidst them, even if there were high-minded and pure scholars in later generations, they likely would not have known that official rank and emolument are shackles. As for their merit in benefiting the world, how could it be compared?
Furthermore, his cultivation entered through stillness and concentration, while his writings emerged from *samādhi*. For those who come after...
