To fathom a person with a one-sided view, or to read their books with a turbid and confused mind, is to remain茫然 (mángrán)—bewildered and ignorant of where to turn.
If one merely observes the words without seeing the mind, it is only natural that one would be struck with alarm and fail to enter [the teaching].
Moreover, they themselves have said: "After ten thousand generations, one may encounter a Great Sage; those who understand his interpretation are..."
We encounter them morning and evening. Yet, as for that Great Sage whom they seek—if it is not the Buddha, who else could it be?
If one intends for them to serve as the vanguard for my Buddha in shattering attachments, these words may indeed be trusted.
But if worldly people do not even enter into them, how could they ever enter into the Buddha-dharma?
Regarding the methods of practice,

although the specific practices of the five vehicles within my teaching differ, their cultivation of the mind all takes *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) as the foundation. Therefore,
the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of my teaching include those of the Mahāyāna, the Hīnayāna, and the human and celestial vehicles— these four.
The Chan school has the eight dhyānas and the nine supernormal powers and clarities (*abhijñā*).

Confucius also said, "Only after knowing where to stop does one attain stability," and further, "From sincerity comes clarity"—this refers to the person who rides upon *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Laozi said, "Always being without desire, observe its subtlety;
always having desire, observe its boundaries. He also said, "All things arise together; I observe their return. Zhuangzi likewise said:
"It is better to rely on clarity. It further says: "The sage does not follow [the senses] but illuminates them through Heaven. It also says:
"People do not use flowing water as a mirror, but use still water as a mirror; only that which is still can bring rest to all things that seek rest. It also says:
"Great stability maintains it, such that the hundred bones and nine apertures are all encompassed within its existence. With whom, then, would I feel intimacy? It also says: "It is all its..."

Take it for yourself: who is it that becomes angry? As for the reclusive retirement of the Yellow Emperor, the "mind-fast" (*citta-śīla*) of Yan Hui, the elder’s parable of catching cicadas on a pole, and Confucius’s discourse on awakening from a dream—all these represent the practice of stillness and concentration (*samatha-vipaśyanā*).

They all involve relinquishing the physical form and discarding the intellect, becoming free from desire and pure. This is what is meant by "disgusting the lower realm of suffering, coarseness, and hindrance, while rejoicing in the higher realm of purity, subtlety, and detachment," hoping thereby—

Leaving behind the human realm to enter the heavens: according to what is clarified in the teachings, this refers to one who abandons birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is born in the first dhyāna (*prathamadhyāna*).

Therefore it is said: "When the universe [of the mind] is profoundly settled, the light of heaven (*devaprakāśa*) emerges. This is the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calming and insight) of the celestial vehicle (*devayāna*). The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states:

"Among all those in the world who cultivate the mind, if no attachment or defilement arises and they do not remain in the desire realm, such a person, by virtue of their mindfulness, [attains] the body..."

They become companions of Brahmā (*brahmacārin*). Furthermore, it is said: when the habituation to desire has been eliminated and the mind free from desire manifests, such a person is able at that time to practice the virtues of Brahmā and is called a "Brahmā’s Retainer" (*brahmapurohita*).

Again, it is said: through pure precepts augmented by clear awakening, such a person is able at that time to preside over the assembly of Brahmās as a Great Brahmā King (*mahābrahman*). Again, it is said: these three superior classes cannot be overcome by any afflictions.
"Pressing on. Although this is not yet the true, correct Samādhi, within the pure mind, the various outflows (āsrava) do not move; this is called the First Dhyāna.
Proceeding until the mind is clarified and unmoving, where profound stillness gives rise to radiance, it becomes increasingly superior as one passes through the Second, Third, and Fourth Dhyanas.

When refined vision appears before one, one can mold and cast without obstruction, reaching the ultimate point of all subtle movements and exhausting the nature of form and its essence, thereby entering [the state of non-outflow]."
It is boundless; it is called the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*). This is its proof. Viewed from this perspective, as for the teachings of Laozi:

if one considers what constitutes the "great affliction," nothing is worse than having a body; therefore, he sought to extinguish the body to return to non-existence. If one considers what causes the most toil to the form, nothing precedes the possession of knowledge;
therefore, he sought to relinquish knowledge to dissolve into the void. This bears a resemblance to the Two Vehicles (*Dvayayāna*), yet they appeared in an age without a Buddha. Thus we observe.

In his transformations he knows non-existence; in his appearance he resembles a Pratyekabuddha. Yet, when one traces the source of his fundamental tenets—namely, emptiness and spontaneity—he belongs to the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika).

When one observes his compassionate mind that rescues the world, with both humans and devas turning toward him in harmony, and his simultaneous illumination of both existence and non-existence, he again resembles a Bodhisattva.
This is indeed a provisional discussion. It is precisely what is meant by "manifesting in the body of a Brahmin to preach the Dharma. However, to judge according to the ultimate reality, it is...
Those who, belonging to the vehicles of humans and devas, cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) with diligence and enter the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) are such persons.

The reason they are able to save the world is that the Great Brahmā King serves as the lord of the Sahā world, presiding over the universe and preaching the ten wholesome dharmas (*daśa-kuśala-dharma*) to deliver sentient beings.

According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) serve as the Great Brahmā Kings; even down to the assembly of Brahmās, all are those who practice the true path of the heavens.
A person who, by means of the Human Vehicle, cultivates the practices for rebirth as a deva—this is precisely such a case; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, I say that the profound discourse [of the *Zhuangzi*] thoroughly investigates the boundary between Heaven and humanity; it is no idle or superficial talk.
Discourse on the Fundamental Source of Practice:
To begin with, the ten realms manifest from within the single mind; thus, the four classes of noble beings and the six paths of ordinary beings are all but echoes and shadows of this single mind.
How much more so is this true for humans and devas? When investigating the stages of cultivation and progress, they truly originate from the human realm.
He stood upon it. This demonstrates that the human being is the root of both the ordinary and the sage. Thus, Pei Xiu said: "Spirits and ghosts suffer the bitterness of deep obscurity;
birds and beasts harbor the grief of wild flight and solitary howling; the asuras are in the midst of rage; and the devas are immersed in pleasure."
One can rectify the mind and its deliberations and advance toward Bodhi; only the human path is capable of this.
Viewed from this perspective, apart from the human path there is no means to establish the Buddha-dharma, and without the Buddha-dharma there is no means to exhaust the single mind.

Thus, the Buddha-dharma takes the human path as its foundation, while the human path takes the Buddha-dharma as its ultimate goal. Therefore it is said: "That which Bodhi takes as its object is suffering."
It is said that if there were no sentient beings, there would be no Bodhi; this is what is meant.
What is called the "human way" refers to the constant daily life of the people among rulers and ministers, fathers and sons, and husbands and wives.

If, for a moment, ruler acts as ruler and minister as minister, father as father and son as son, without conscious effort or deliberate knowledge, free from greed and competition, like a person created by illusion—this is [the state of] the sages.
If those of the highest virtue were to assemble in one place, this very world would become the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
What need, then, would there be for a separate land of sages? Alas, human beings are born because of craving and die because of craving.
These cravings that govern birth and death consist of wealth, form, fame, food, and sleep. From these five things, the mind of greedy attachment arises, leading to conflict and strife.
The calamity of strife leads to a situation where the ruler is not a ruler, the minister is not a minister, the father is not a father, and the son is not a son.

Even the rewards and punishments of the former kings were insufficient to restrain such minds; instead, they merely satisfied one’s own insatiable desires, thereby binding oneself to immeasurable suffering in the future.
Therefore, our Buddha took pity on them and said: "The cause of all sufferings is rooted in greed and desire. If...
Having extinguished craving and having no place of dependence, he manifests his body within the three realms and shares in the sufferings of the people;
thus, he teaches the essential path for departing from desire and escaping suffering.

Furthermore, that he does not dwell in the heavens but is born among humans is precisely to demonstrate that the characteristics of cause and effect across the ten realms are all established upon the human realm. However, since he now dwells in the human realm, he must not...
This is because they do not understand the Way of humanity. Therefore, our Buddha, the Sage, was not born from emptiness alone;
he took Śuddhodana as father and Māyā as mother to demonstrate the existence of sovereign and parent; he took Yaśodharā as wife to demonstrate the existence of husband and wife.

He took Rāhu as his son to demonstrate the existence of father and child. Furthermore, he necessarily abandons his parents to leave the household life to show that it is not out of a lack of loyalty to sovereign or kin;
rather, he severs the affection for sovereign and kin and casts aside national glory without looking back to demonstrate that fame and profit are burdens;
he casts away his wife and children and distances himself from them to demonstrate the harm of greed and desire; and he enters deep mountains to practice austerities to demonstrate...

This is the practice for transcending desire. First, he practiced the four universal bases of mastery (*kṛtsnāyatana*) of the non-Buddhists to demonstrate that one must leave the human realm to enter the celestial realms.
That he then abandoned these to realize the path of Perfectly Complete Enlightenment demonstrates that the practices of humans and devas are not worthy of esteem.
After attaining Buddhahood, he entered the royal palace and ascended his father’s coffin; he went up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother.
By thus demonstrating the Way of the Buddha, he showed that filial piety is not abandoned. By preaching the Dharma based on the human realm, he showed that the human path easily leads to Bodhi.
By employing kings and ministers as external protectors, he showed that while dwelling in the world, one does not transgress worldly laws. This is what our Great Master demonstrated.
They manifest as models for saving sentient beings and establish a grand standard of sincerity for future generations. Alas!
We who are disciples of the Buddha do not know the mind of our Buddha; dwelling in the world of men, we do not understand the affairs of human relations.

When discussing the Buddha-dharma with them, we speak of *tathatā* (Suchness) in a vague and abstract manner, and of *buddhatā* (Buddha-nature) in a muddled and superficial way. When discussing worldly laws with them, we are confronted by every single matter...

Facing a wall, he was almost as ignorant as a block of wood. When I discussed the Vehicle of Teachings (*śāsana-yāna*) with him, he said, "These are but branches and leaves; they are not worth admiring.
When I spoke to him of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), he said, "The conduct of a Bodhisattva is not something I dare to practice.

When I spoke to him of the Four Noble Truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*), he said, "That is merely the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); it is not worth pursuing. When I spoke to him of the Four Dhyānas and Eight Samādhis...
He said: "Those are merely the practices of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). What is there worth mentioning?

When one speaks with them of the Way of Humanity, they are utterly ignorant of the distinctions between ruler and minister, father and son, and the practice of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom. Alas!

These people do not know what it is they seek, yet they aspire to the lofty and yearn for the distant, using mere words and hearing as their only resources, while remaining entirely unaware of our Buddha."
To save others and lead them beyond the world, one takes the practice of detachment from desire as primary. Thus it is said: "Detachment and tranquility are the most supreme.
Since I was born into the human realm and did not transcend the path of humans, I first studied under Confucius to understand that human desires are the root of all suffering;
I resolved to practice detachment from desire, and thus in my youth I studied under Laozi and Zhuangzi to contemplate that the three realms are but mind alone.
"All phenomena are consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) is the influence of knowing that the ten realms are nothing but mind. Therefore, one takes refuge in the Buddha.

As for the ultimate aim of this treatise, the "Great Way of Non-being" (*wúxū dàodào*) venerated by the Old Master (Laozi) is precisely what the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* refers to as "darkness becoming space," the essence of the eight consciousnesses.
This is the essence of clarity. Yet, we sentient beings are deluded regarding this wondrously luminous single mind, thereby becoming the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Based upon this, the seven consciousnesses arise as the root of birth and death, and the six consciousnesses become the foundation for creating karma.

These transform and give rise to the phenomena of the sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world within the cycle of birth and death. Thus, the ten realms of beings—both sages and ordinary folk—are all universally inseparable from this.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is merely the distinction between grasping and the destruction of defilement and purity.

Because ordinary beings of the desire realm do not know that the objects of the six sense-fields and the five desires are transformations of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), they rely on the discrimination of the six consciousnesses to give rise to craving and attachment.

They cling tenaciously without relinquishing it, thereby creating various karmas and undergoing various sufferings—what is called the "overflowing of human desires. For this reason, Confucius established benevolence (*ren*).
Ritual propriety, righteousness, and wisdom serve as dykes for transformation and instruction, ensuring that thoughts are not depraved and that one temporarily abandons evil to follow the good.

As for defining social roles and rectifying the hierarchy between superiors and subordinates, such methods do not transcend the realm of conceptual discrimination; this refers to what is called the practice of stillness and concentration.

To verify this through the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*): this serves to sever the deluded and false thoughts of discrimination belonging to the first six consciousnesses, thereby removing the harm of contention.
Yet, that which is ultimately sought as the "Sublime Path" takes the seventh consciousness as its point of reference and ultimate destination.
This refers to what is called the "Source of the Way of Life. Thus it is said: "The continuous generation of life is called the *Yī* (Change). This is precisely it.
As for Laozi’s taking "emptiness and non-being" (*xūwú*) as the wondrous Way, he says: "The Valley-Spirit does not die"; again, "To die and yet not perish is longevity";

and further, "That which generates life does not itself take birth. Moreover, his teaching takes the renunciation of sages and the abandonment of wisdom, the forgetting of form and the elimination of desire, as its practice.
Taking the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) as the ultimate goal, this school surpasses even Confucianism.

Observing the profound pulse of the life-force (*jīngī*), it shatters the attachments of the discriminating first six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) and subdues the mechanism of arising and ceasing in the seventh consciousness (*saptama-vijñāna*).
It recognizes the essence of the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*)—that which the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* calls "formless and void" and "subtle, refined thought"—as the wondrous Way.

This is the source. Therefore it is said: "Vague and indistinct—within it there is an image; indistinct and vague—within it there is a substance. This consciousness is the totality of ignorance (*avidyā*);
because one does not penetrate it through contemplation, it is said: "Profound and dark—within it there is an essence.
Because this substance of consciousness undergoes inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation, it is said: "Mysterious within the mysterious. And...

It is called the "Sublime Way" (*miao dao*). Since heaven, earth, and the myriad phenomena all manifest from within it, it is said to be "the root of heaven and earth" and "the gate of all subtleties.
One does not know how it comes to be so, yet it is so; thus, Zhuangzi calls it "spontaneity" (*ziran*).
Furthermore, Laozi was a native of China who had never seen the Buddha-dharma, yet his profound contemplation reached such heights—this may indeed be called swift and incisive.
They possess sharp faculties. If they were to behold my Buddha but once and receive his seal of confirmation, would they not suddenly realize the true state of non-arising?
It is for this reason that I intend to travel west across the shifting sands; how could it be without purpose? Generally speaking, this consciousness is profoundly hidden and difficult to fathom.
Before the Buddha appeared in the world, the ninety-six heterodox schools of the Western Regions took the Six Teachers as their masters; the treatises they established—
In groups of hundreds, there were many who attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Furthermore, their scriptures did not stop at those of the Laozi and Zhuangzi of this land.
When my Buddha appeared in the world, at the single assembly on Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*), the eminent and heroic sages were all formerly disciples of those six teachers.
Moreover, upon seeing the Buddha, they did not awaken with a single word; like fine horses that gallop upon seeing the shadow of a whip, was this not so?
The former effort was not without purpose; it was simply that the mind of perverse attachment had not yet been forgotten.

Therefore, seeing the Buddha now occurs only within the space of a transformative instruction, intended solely to shatter that attachment. Thus, when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, there are originally no redundant words;

he merely strikes down and breaks through the attachments of sentient beings as appropriate to their circumstances. This is what is meant by "using one wedge to extract another": fundamentally, there is no substantial reality.

Regarding the Dharma and its transmission to people: at the assembly of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, the Buddha minutely analyzed and sequentially interrogated and debated [the disciples] to shatter their attachments to causality and spontaneity, and to sever the doubts of ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and those of the two vehicles. As for those who study these teachings:
I do not understand this. You merely say, "Those are people of the Western Regions," while "these are people of the Eastern Land.

There may be distinctions between "those" and "these" among humans, but how could there be two natures of Buddhahood? Furthermore, our Buddha is the teacher of the three realms and the father of the four modes of birth;
how could his preaching of the Dharma be intended solely for the people of that region, while here, ten thousand *li* away, it is utterly absent?
[If you say] it is divided, nevertheless, all sentient beings rely upon the eight consciousnesses;
how could it be that only the sentient beings of that region possess the sentiment of a firm attachment to a self, while the sentient beings of this region do not?
Thus, regarding this eighth consciousness, those non-Buddhists may grasp it as *amūrta-tattva* (the principle of the unmanifest) or they may grasp it as the *ātman* (self).

However, some grasp this as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), while others grasp it as the divine self (*ātman*). By means of meditative concentration they cultivate the mind and are reborn in the Brahma heavens, where they grasp this state as the fivefold present nirvana (*pañca-dṛṣṭa-nirvāṇa*).
Others exhaustively investigate emptiness and do not return, entering the formless realm heavens (*ārūpyadhātu-deva*).

There, they suppress the generative impulse of the preceding seven consciousnesses so that they remain unmoving; they then advance to contemplate the nature of consciousness, reaching the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), where there is nothing further to perceive.

There is a passage which states: "The realm of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is the ultimate limit. This refers to those who cultivate the mind within the realms but have not yet transcended the nature of consciousness.
Thus it is said: 'Those who study the Way do not recognize the Truth, for they continue to identify with the conscious spirit.

This has been the root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas; fools mistake this for their original self. This refers to such people. As for the Śrāvakas outside the realms, they have already..."

Having extinguished the delusions of views and afflictions within the three realms, they have severed the suffering of birth and death in the three realms and realized the bliss of unconditioned nirvana.
Yet, they remain ignorant even of the names of the eight consciousnesses, while still regarding this as *nirvāṇa* and claiming it to be their ultimate place of refuge.
Moreover, having personally received deliverance through the Buddha’s teachings, they still require my Buddha to spend forty years of exhortation [to correct them].

He criticized the merit of [mere] elimination and refinement. Even at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he still harbored doubts regarding the Buddha’s intent, believing that he had been delivered by means of the Hīnayāna.
Although Bodhisattvas of the stages (*bhūmi*) do not discard this consciousness until they have reached the seventh stage, their *vipāka* (maturation) is still not yet empty.
Viewed from this perspective, the eight consciousnesses are the root of birth and death; how could they be anything but profound? Therefore—

He said: "All practitioners in the world who are unable to achieve unexcelled Bodhi, and instead become merely Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, or even become followers of external paths, gods, Māras, or the retinues of Māra, do so because they do not know the two kinds of roots.
The first is the root of beginningless birth and death; it is this very thing that you now share with all the multitudes."
First, that which takes the攀緣心 (攀緣心; *pān-yuán-xīn*, the mind that clings to objects) as its own nature. Second, the fundamentally pure essence of beginningless nirvana.

That which you now possess—the original luminosity of the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-tattva*)—which is able to give rise to all conditions, yet is itself left behind by those very conditions: this is precisely what is meant by the latter.

Alas! Laozi was born into the world of men during an age when the Buddha had not yet appeared, yet he was able to exhaustively investigate the source of transformation and observe it with such profound depth.
Considering his diligent efforts, they were truly no small feat; however, he merely failed to break through the nest of birth and death. An ancient worthy once said:
"Confucius assisted in the precepts (*śīla*), because he was strict in governing the self; Laozi assisted in meditative concentration (*samādhi*)."
Their mastery in the forgetting of self—the learning of these two sages—is complementary to that of the Buddha; it is by no means in vain. To speak according to the facts:
those who cling to Confucius involve themselves in causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), while those who cling to Laozi fall into spontaneity (*ziran*).

In essence, neither has escaped the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-svabhāva*), for they are unable to reach the ultimate realization of the One Mind. The Buddha, however, transcends mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*); therefore, it is said: "Fundamentally, it is not..."
It is through causes and conditions, not by way of inherent nature, that one finally penetrates the source of the single mind.

This is the distinction between worldly and world-transcending dharmas. What the Buddha refuted did not stop at this alone; even the three vehicles of the world-transcending path are all contained therein.
When worldly people see only the *Zhuangzi*—which reviles Yao and Shun, disparages Tang and Wu, and censures the disciples of Confucius—they take it as something startling.

This is different. If one hears the World-Honored One rebuke the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), regarding them as withered sprouts and ruined seeds, and pity the bodhisattvas so deeply that he regards them as icchantikas who have abandoned the Buddha-dharma—how then should one understand this?
Nevertheless, when the Buddha rebukes the two vehicles, it is not that he rebukes the two vehicles themselves.
The censure of those who cling to the traces of the Two Vehicles is intended to cause them to abandon the Small and proceed toward the Great.

As for the so-called severe disparagement of Confucius, it is not a disparagement of Confucius himself, but a disparagement of those who study the traces of Confucius; it is intended to cause them to sever their attachment to the Sage and cast away their reliance on wisdom.

In essence, all of this is termed the discarding of emotional attachments and the breaking of fixations. If, indeed, emotions are forgotten and fixations are relinquished, one will then walk hand-in-hand to roam within the wondrous.

This is the very heart of the Way. One is currently so preoccupied with the joy of supreme bliss that there is no leisure for it; what need is there, then, to concern oneself with such deluded confusion?

Bodhisattvas on the stages of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra manifest their bodies among those who smear themselves with ashes, worship fire, lie upon thorns, or throw themselves upon needles, acting as their teachers and elders.
If it were not for the Buddha-dharma, how could they be led to enter the Buddha-dharma?
Ah! Thus, regarding the banners held by those six masters, nothing short of the Buddha is sufficient to uproot them.

In my view, as for the grand pronouncements of Laozi and Zhuangzi, nothing short of the Buddha-dharma is sufficient to verify their direction. It is indeed true that such playful discourse cannot be resolved or escaped even by veteran teachers and long-standing scholars;
now, through the contemplation of mind-only consciousness, it is seen that they do not transcend the realm of shadows and echoes.
Thus it is.
The initial conception of this treatise dates back to the winter of the Wuli year (1588) of the Wanli era, when I was living by the sea.

While begging for alms in the royal city, I once engaged in a late-night discussion with the Layman Dongguan on these matters; the Layman clapped his hands in great delight. This was in the summer of the Gengyin year (1590).
On that day, I first took up my brush. Having been hidden away for a long time, it had not yet been brought forth.
In the winter of the Jiawu year, I traveled to the royal capital at the leisure of circumstances, intending to seek further instruction from the historian Jiao Ruowei; however, this was not to be.

In the spring of the following year, the Yiwu year, I encountered hardship while propagating the Dharma, and my draft was already left behind on the sea. I therefore dispatched an attendant to retrieve the surviving fragments.
I recovered it from within [the collection]. In the autumn, by imperial grace, I was dispatched to Lei Yang.
Master Daguan, traveling from Mount Kuanglu on foot, waited for me by the river. In the eleventh month of winter, just as I was crossing the river, I met the Master at Lupo Hermitage.
Sitting together that night, he brought this forth. Upon reading it once, the Master sighed three times, saying: "This is sufficient to dispel long-standing delusion. Immediately...
I instructed my disciple Ruqi to carve [this work] in order to broaden the gift of Dharma, but I firmly refused him.

In the summer of the Wuxu year, while I was staying in Wuyang, I established a retreat by encircling the walls with my disciples. There, I expounded the essential tenets of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* for the assembly.
My disciple Baogui saw this and, filled with joy, vowed to exert all his strength to complete it so that the work might reach its conclusion. Alas!
If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the causes and conditions of time and season.
These few words of mine are truly insufficient to weigh the importance of a Dharma gate. Conceived ten years ago, they were perfected ten years later;
composed in the land east of the Eastern Sea, they are now being practiced in the land south of the Southern Sea. Is this not due to the convergence of karmic conditions?
Is it merely a coincidence? It is the Way and the times; how can one force it? Nevertheless, this was composed upon contemplating Laozi and Zhuangzi;
therefore, I have titled it "Discourse on Names. Written on the eve of the New Year in the Wuli Wuxu year by the Chan monk Qing of Mount Hamsan.
Written in the Laṅkā Hall.

Since my illness, I have been burdened by worldly affairs; it was only recently that I began reading the *Great Composition: A Comprehensive Gazetteer of Caoxi*, as well as works such as the *Treatise on the Shadows and Echoes of Laozi and Zhuangzi*.
I am deeply moved and filled with admiration. As it is said: "If one does not know the Spring and Autumn Annals, one cannot navigate the world."
Those who know Laozi and Zhuangzi cannot forget the world; those who do not practice Chan cannot transcend the world.

As for Confucius, the sage of the human vehicle (*puruṣayāna*); Laozi, the sage of the celestial vehicle (*devayāna*); and the Buddha, the sage who can be both sacred and ordinary, and both human and celestial.
Such matters as these are principles that remain unchanged for a hundred generations. Qi-yuan bows his head again in prostration.
This is the preface to the *Commentary on the Dao De Jing*, clarifying its fundamental tenets.
That which the school of Laozi venerates takes "voidness" (*śūnyatā*) and "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) as the wondrous Way.

This is precisely what the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi Sūtra* refers to as "the total absence of discrimination," that which is "neither form nor emptiness," and what those such as Kauśika mistook for the "dark principle" (*tattva*).
This is exactly what is meant by the "substance of the eight consciousnesses' empty obscurity. Because this consciousness is most profoundly deep, subtle, and difficult to fathom.
Were it not for a Buddha, one would be unable to fully exhaust its meaning. To transform this [state] is precisely the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

When Bodhisattvas realize this, they employ *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to break through it; yet there remains a partial realization (*bhāga-prativedha*). As for the Śrāvakas who do not know this, they grasp it as *nirvāṇa*.
The non-Buddhist Brahmins of the Western Regions who do not know it, cling to it as the "Dark Principle" (*tamas-tattva*). This is regarded as...
Emptiness and spontaneity are the wondrous Way. Thus the Sūtra says: "Those who practice cannot achieve unsurpassed Bodhi, nor even become Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
they may instead become devas, non-Buddhists, Māras, or the retinues of Māra."
All this arises from not knowing the two kinds of fundamental roots and practicing erroneously, like boiling sand in the hope of producing a fine meal;
even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, one will ultimately never succeed. What are these two? The first is the root of beginningless birth and death.

Thus, you who now, along with all sentient beings, take the攀緣心 (攀緣心; *pān-yuán-xīn*, the攀緣心 or攀緣心—the mind that clings to and discriminates objects) as your own nature, and [the other] which is the beginningless body of Nirvana, fundamentally pure and clear:

this essence of consciousness (*shí-jīng*) which is fundamentally luminous (*yuán-míng*), capable of giving rise to all conditions (*yuán*), yet that which is lost amidst those conditions—this "essence of consciousness, fundamentally luminous" is precisely the "Mysterious Dao" (*miào-dào*) of Laozi. Hence it is said: "Profound and dark... (*yǎo-yǎo míng*).
It is dark and obscure, yet within it there is an essence. This essence is profoundly real. Because its substance is the ultimate void and the ultimate magnitude, it is not form (*rūpa*);
because it can give rise to all conditions, it is not emptiness (*śūnyatā*). One does not realize that heaven, earth, and the myriad things are all manifested from this consciousness.
This is called the "spontaneous" (*zìrán*). Because it arises from inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation, it is called "wondrous" (*miào*).

Because its ultimate essence is unmixed, it is called "true" (*zhēn*). Though heaven and earth perish, this substance does not perish; though the human body is extinguished, this nature eternally persists;
therefore, it is called "constant" (*cháng*). All changes of the myriad things emerge from this; therefore, it is called the [source] of heaven and earth.

The faculties are the gateway to all wonders. Whenever one encounters terms in the scriptures such as "true permanence," "mysterious subtlety," "voidness," or "the Great Way," one should verify them by means of this seal;
then they will naturally have a point of reference. Otherwise, one will be as lost as if trying to catch the wind or grasp a shadow.
Therefore, I present this first. When reading the texts, there is no need for me to repeat it again.

Regarding the clarification of the intended direction, my humble opinion is that those who study Laozi and Zhuangzi must first thoroughly examine the Buddhist teachings (*śāsana*) and gain a profound mastery of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.

Only by harmonizing these with our Buddha’s treatises on the shattering of attachments will they not be deluded by the texts of the other [traditions]. Thereafter, one should diligently cultivate the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is the method.
Only through mastery and subtle application of mind can one truly perceive this old man’s arduous and earnest effort.

Yet, one must see with absolute sincerity that the body is the root of suffering and that intellect is the source of entanglement. Only when one is naturally able to cast off form and relinquish intellect will one know the place of ultimate bliss where this old man truly enjoys himself.
Furthermore, you must thoroughly penetrate every worldly affair and discern every human sentiment.
Having thoroughly penetrated this, one dwells in the world with an open mind; before one's eyes, there is not even a hair’s breadth of obstruction.
Only then does one see that this old man was truly carefree and joyful, vast and sovereign, appearing as a man of no affairs.

Subsequently, when he could not help but respond to the world, he did so without expending a single bit of effort, remaining upright and governing through non-action (*wuwei*). Observe the reason for his teaching.
The words of Confucius can thus be understood. The entire work of Zhuangzi is a commentary on Laozi;
therefore, what I, the humble one, have said—that Laozi has Zhuangzi as Confucius has Mencius—is to know that what these two masters spoke were all truthful words, not grandiose claims.
Thus it is said: "My words are very easy to understand and very easy to practice, yet none in the world can understand them, nor..."

They are indeed capable of practice; yet when people of the world discuss these two masters, they do not focus at all on their own personal cultivation and realization, but instead attempt to approximate them through mere words and phrases—“zhi-hu-ye-zhe.
Consequently, there is a vast discrepancy between themselves and those masters.

Furthermore, while some may adopt the mannerisms of the "scholarly eccentric" (xueshu kuang), I have yet to see anyone who has entered [the Way] through the practice of stillness and concentration (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). This is because...
It is said that those who truly understand me are rare. Those who hope to be close to my two sons should contemplate in this manner.

Regarding the *Laozi*, which elucidates the methods of cultivation, commentators of the past have generally taken "emptiness and non-being" (*xūwú*) as its primary tenet; yet, when it comes to seeking the actual entry into the Way, [they fail].
Regarding this practice, one may feel utterly bewildered and find no place to begin.

Therefore, in the first chapter, I stated that within "there is no contemplation" (*wu guan*), the single word "contemplation" (*guan*) is the essential for entering the Way, so as to enable students to enter easily. Nevertheless, the merit of contemplative observation (*guan zhao*) is the greatest;
the sages of the Three Teachings all pointed this out to people. Confucius said, "Only after knowing where to rest does one attain stability," and he further said:
"Explain clearly the luminous virtue. Here, "knowing clarity" (*zhīmíng*) carries the sense of thorough awakening.

When the Buddha speaks of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), there are the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of the Three Vehicles, as well as those of the Human and Celestial Vehicles, which differ in their degrees of depth.

For instance, Confucius represents the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of the Human Vehicle, while Laozi represents that of the Celestial Vehicle. Nevertheless, although the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of these three teachings differ in depth, if one examines their essential point...
In treating these illnesses, both [the medical and spiritual traditions] take the initial destruction of self-attachment as the first step of practice.

This is because for all people in the world, the single word "self" serves as the root of their ailment; whether wise or foolish, virtuous or base, they are busily engaged in the field of fame, profit, and official rank, devising schemes for a hundred generations of descendants.
They exhaust every bit of their ingenuity, yet it is all ultimately for the sake of the single body.
Regarding this plan: as the Buddha taught, the cause of all sufferings is rooted in craving, which arises entirely from the notion of "self.

Laozi also said, "He values great calamity as his own person. Because he regarded Confucius, the Sage, as the master of the teachings for name and instruction, [he addressed himself] to those of middling and inferior learning.
He did not dare lightly speak of destroying the self-clinging (ātmagrāha). Only when addressing Yanzi did he say "overcoming the self" (*keji*);
for all others, he spoke merely of rectifying the mind, sincerity of intention, and cultivation of the person.

Yet, once the mind is rectified, the intention sincere, and the person cultivated, to apply this within the relationships of ruler and minister, father and son, and to fully exhaust one's sincerity therein—this itself is the Way. This is what is called the teaching of names (*mingjiao*).
This is indeed so. As for the principle of "severing sageliness and discarding wisdom" and "non-self," these belong to the stage of self-realization (*svasamvid-bhūmi*);
I dare not lightly mention them to others. I merely draw the bowstring without releasing the arrow. As it is said: "If one were as saintly as the benevolent, how would I dare to claim such?
And again: "What knowledge do I possess? I have no knowledge. When a vulgar man questioned me, I was as utterly empty as space."

Furthermore, as for the ultimate effort made on behalf of others, it is said: "overcome oneself" (*keji*), and it is said: "no arbitrary will, no obstinacy, no rigidity, no self-centeredness" (*wuyi wubi wugu wowa*).

These four phrases reveal one's innermost being; yet, "self" (*ji*) refers to private bias, "arbitrary will" (*yi*) refers to the arising of thoughts, "obstinacy" (*bi*) refers to the expectation of results, "rigidity" (*gu*) refers to the clinging of the mind, and "self" (*wo*) refers to one's own ego.
"Overcoming" (*ke*) means to exhaustively eliminate them, while "not" (*wu*) means to prohibit and cut them off.
This discourse teaches people to completely sever the four afflictions of desire, status, fame, and wealth, as well as the sicknesses of fixed views and self-attachment.

The Sage wanders through the world with an empty mind; silent and unmoving, he responds in accordance with things as they arrive, and his resonance immediately brings all things into communication. His use of the mind is like a mirror:
neither welcoming nor sending away, there is no sticking when things come, and no trace when they depart. Body and mind are both forgotten, and he does not compete with things. This is the Sage.

This is the nature of the human mind. The reason why people of the world cannot be like the sages is simply due to the maladies of the four—intention (*yi*), necessity (*bi*), stubbornness (*gu*), and selfhood (*wo*).
Consequently, they lack autonomy; every movement is suffering. Confucius observed that the root of the world's maladies lies herein, and thus he sought to sever them utterly.
This very teaching is precisely what Buddhism and Daoism take as their primary tenet: non-self (*anātman*).
Furthermore, the character "wu" (do not) is itself the work of severance; it is the most potent tool for application.

It is just like the prohibitions and edicts of the Legalist school which say "you must not," ensuring that there can be no transgression whatsoever, such that even a single offense leaves no room for pardon.
It is simply that students do not understand this. As for the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, although it is vast and expansive, its essential point is...
It merely issues forth to shatter the coarse and subtle dual attachments to self and dharmas among sentient beings.
Once these two attachments are shattered, one immediately ascends to the stage of Buddhahood. Thus, all the texts of the Tripiṭaka are instruments for shattering these two attachments.

The attachments to be shattered are none other than the "four maladies" of Confucius, which are themselves but coarse attachments. Yet worldly people do not realize this; they mistakenly believe there exists something else that is profound and mysterious. If...
Master Laozi transcends the world by one step; therefore, he speaks specifically to shatter attachments.

He seeks to have people relinquish their intellect and cast off their physical forms, distancing themselves from desire to achieve purity. Yet, the "intellect" he asks them to relinquish is precisely private intellect—that is, the insistence of the mind.
The "form" he asks them to cast off is precisely the solidified self. The "desire" he asks them to distance themselves from is precisely personal selfishness. As for "purity," it is a vast emptiness.
Unobstructed, like the vast void, it is precisely the "Great Publicity" (Dagong) of Confucius. Thus we know that the heart-mind teachings of Confucius and Laozi have never failed to accord;
it is only in their pedagogical methods and in their establishment of barriers to protect worldly ethics that they could not help but differ.

This is because Confucius was dedicated solely to governing the world, while Laozi was intent upon forgetting the world, and the Buddha was intent upon transcending the world. Nevertheless, although they ultimately differ, their...

This is truly the first step. In all cases, the primary focus is the destruction of the attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*). The practice enters through both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Regarding the clarification of essence and function, some say:
"The sages of the Three Teachings all instruct people that they must first destroy the attachment to a self; this is the essence of non-self."

They are the same. How, then, can their application differ? Is there not a distinction between those that govern the world, those that forget the world, and those that transcend the world? The answer is: both essence and function are identical;
there is only a difference in degree—shallow versus deep, small versus great. Suppose, for instance, that Confucius truly possessed a self...
This is merely for the sake of one’s own private interests. How can it govern the world? If the Buddha and Laozi truly sought to transcend the world, this would be for their own salvation;

how then could they benefit living beings? Thus we know that it is only through non-self (*anātman*) that one can govern the world, and it is only through benefiting living beings that one realizes non-self.
In reality, these two are one. As Confucius said: "Tranquil and unmoving, yet responding and thereby penetrating all under heaven."

Therefore, function is manifestation; clarity is sincerity. Sincerity is the essence; from sincerity comes form, which is function. Rectifying the mind and making the intentions sincere is the essence;
cultivating the person, bringing order to the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world is function. Laozi’s "Namelessness" is the essence; "acting through non-action" is function.
It is so used. Confucius said, "Only Heaven is great; only Yao took it as his model. Vast and boundless, the people were unable to give it a name.
He further said, "Was it not Shun who ruled through non-action? Moreover, the world has taken Yao and Shun as its progenitors."

How could this be called having a "conditioned existence" (saṃskṛta)? It is precisely because of non-self (anātman) that one regards all under heaven as oneself; hence it is said: "Yao and Shun were merely the same as other men.
Since all people share the same substance, the only thing that differs is the presence of selfishness (*ātma-grāha*) acting as an obstruction.
Because the human mind is identical to this [universal] mind, when minds are identical, there is no formal obstruction. Therefore, he was diligent in establishing the teachings for them.

Transformation is what governs the world; this is how one navigates the secular world from the standpoint of non-self (*anātman*). Laozi, however, says: "He who constantly uses goodness to teach others does not discard any person.
Since no person is discarded, everyone can become a Yao or a Shun. This demonstrates that it is only through non-self that one can benefit living beings.
As for what is said in another text: "Acting without being a ruler; when the work is accomplished, [there is no claim of]..."

In the words of those who dwell [in this world] and so forth, all take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as the great function for governing the world; how, then, could they ever have forgotten the world?
As for the Buddha, his essence encompasses empty space and his function pervades the realms of the sands of the Ganges. He manifests bodies according to the various types of beings, saying:
"I attain perfect enlightenment within the bodies of all sentient beings," and further: "Only after delivering all sentient beings shall I achieve the Buddha-way. Furthermore...
He said: "If one could cause even a single sentient being to resolve upon Bodhicitta, I would endure the sufferings of the hells in my own body without weariness or fatigue.
Yet, do the beings thus transformed not exist within the world? Since one engages with the world to deliver sentient beings, how can this not be called 'engaging with the world'?
Furthermore, if one does not tire of the pains of hell for the sake of a single person, is this not the height of earnest dedication?"
If there were no such category [of beings] who do not manifest their bodies, how could there be a fixed name for them? Liezi once said:
"In the West, there is a Great Sage who inspires trust without speaking and transforms others through non-action. How could this be the result of having a deliberate intention to act?
Thus we know that the substance of non-self and the function of benefiting sentient beings are identical among these three sages; it is only the scope of their application that differs in magnitude.
Confucius rectified and maintained the worldly way, proceeding tentatively from the individual person to the family and the state, and subsequently to all under heaven;
therefore, his transformation was limited to the Middle Kingdom. Furthermore, he required every person to become a Yao or a Shun, for his ancestral model was Yao.
It was Shun. Because Laozi observed that the hearts of people at that time were corrupted and superficial, he sought to restore the Great Antiquity;

since the one from whom he claimed descent was Xuanyuan (the Yellow Emperor), his discourse on each point was unlike anything ordinary. Thus, he perceived that the Way is vast and difficult to accommodate.
Therefore, [the Buddha] went far away to the shifting sands. If it were the Buddha, his teaching would have been spread throughout the trichiliocosm;
it would have been so vast and great that no one would have been excluded. As for the Sage praised by Zisi, he said: "All those who possess blood and breath do not fail to revere and love him.
From this we know that the substance and function of Confucius were never not great; it was simply that he was constrained by the circumstances of his time. This is precisely following...

This is the method of the pivot; thus, it accords closely with human nature. This is the distinction between essence and function. Alas, scholars of later generations are each bound by their respective doctrines:
those who practice Confucianism are拘 (constrained), those who practice Daoism are狂 (reckless), and those who study Buddhism are隘 (narrow-minded).

These are the defects of scholars, all of which stem from the harm of clinging to a self (*ātman*). If one were truly able to shatter this clinging to a self, then one would break down the barriers and immediately enter the Great [Way].
It is settled.

As for elucidating the ultimate destination, I have privately considered that if the Sage Confucius had not known Laozi, he would certainly not have been at ease; and if he had not known the Buddha, he certainly would not have been.
It is not troublesome. If Laozi had not known Confucius, he certainly would not have spoken repeatedly of governing through non-action (*wuwei*).

If he had not known the Buddha, he certainly could not have taken compassion as his treasure. If the Buddha had not passed through the world, he certainly would not have taught and transformed sentient beings within this world.
In my humble opinion, Confucius and Laozi are simply transformations of the Buddha. This is the view of the followers of Buddhism in later generations.

If you do not understand old age, you will simply go straight ahead and look into the void; every dharma before your eyes will become an obstacle, and in every matter you will fail to attain liberation.
If you do not understand Confucius, yet single-mindedly employ the Buddha-dharma to engage with the world, you will certainly remain ignorant of worldly ways and human sentiments;
you will speak of the mysterious and the wondrous to everyone, like one selling a dead cat’s head. One.
It is utterly useless. Thus the Patriarch also said: "If preaching the Dharma does not meet the capacity of the listener, it is ultimately but idle talk.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In some borderlands, the Four Truths are preached. This shows that the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma has never been a matter of merely praising the abstruse and the mysterious.
Nevertheless, to save sentient beings by following worldly conventions—is this not precisely Confucius’s mind for governing the world? Furthermore, the Sūtra...

It is said: The noble ones of the fifth stage, when traversing the world to deliver sentient beings, must master all worldly scriptures, arts and crafts, medical prescriptions, miscellaneous treatises, calligraphy, painting, seals, and insignia—indeed, there is no variety of phenomena they do not thoroughly study. Only then can they act in accordance with the capacities of others. Therefore it is said:

"The speech of conventional truth and the activities for sustaining life all accord with the True Dharma. Thus, the Confucians take benevolence (*ren*) as their foundation, while the Buddhists take the precepts (*śīla*) as theirs.

It is the root. If one says, "Filial piety and fraternal respect are the root of benevolence," and compares it to the Buddha’s teaching that "filial piety is called the precepts," their essence is one and the same.
Viewed in this light, how could the Buddha have no methods for governing the world? Because Confucius excluded the barbarians, his teachings circulated only within China;
because the Buddha spoke of the Four Truths using the dialects of the borderlands, the barbarians all followed him.
This is why their manifestations differ in scale. Thus we know that among the sages of the three teachings, what they share is the mind;
what differs is their outward trace (*li*). To seek the mind through its traces is like measuring the ocean with a seashell;
to dissolve the traces within the mind is like a mustard seed containing the void. When mind and trace are forgotten, all rivers flow toward the source, and the hundred streams become of one taste.

Hanshan’s Preface states: "That which possesses things cannot be used to speak of the Way. The myriad phenomena are in a state of flux; they do not 'exist' in themselves. It is man who makes them exist.
If man did not exist, what would the myriad phenomena have? All who possess things must pursue those things; those who pursue things are close to [losing their true nature]."
The deceased person: the person has perished; who then can be united with the Dao? As for things and persons—how extreme this is!

One who forgets things is not yet sufficient to attain the Dao. Now, one who does not possess things realizes that things are empty. When things are empty, there is no need for deliberate forgetting, and yet one forgets.
To say, "I have forgotten things," or "I have forgotten things"—if there is something that can be forgotten, it is not [the Dao].
Truly forgotten, it is therefore said that they are insufficient to bring about the Way.
Those who sink into emptiness are not yet sufficient to exhaust the Way. For when the mind is not empty, it exists because of external objects;

when objects are empty, the mind becomes empty of its own accord. When both mind and objects are empty, the mind exists as non-existence; when both objects and mind are empty, the objects exist as non-existence.

There is nothing. If this is so, what could possibly cause stagnation? Yet, if one insists on taking emptiness as emptiness and regards the attainment of emptiness as the ultimate, this is to sink into emptiness;
how can such a person exhaust the Way?

Forgetting and not forgetting are both forgotten. When even the act of forgetting is forgotten, one is necessarily bound by duality; when even the act of forgetting is forgotten, it is difficult not to be bound by duality.
Alas! How profound this is! How can one attain that which is without forgetting yet without not forgetting, without duality yet without not being dual?
And when speaking with him, he forgot about both [of us]. Now, as for those who attain the Way:

when amidst the dust of the world, they must say that movement changes their physical form; when they have left the dust, they must say that stillness changes their realization. That which changes through movement is like a spark from a flint-stone;

that which changes through stillness is like a rushing torrent. The stone-spark seems to exist, yet the torrent— (Note: The source text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on the *Zhuangzi*, specifically the "Qi Wu Lun" chapter. The final sentence is incomplete, but the translation reflects the extant portion.)
To say that the flow is like stillness, or to attempt to change this, is to fail to comprehend the source of movement and stillness, and the root of arising and ceasing.
That which is moved by external objects is invited by the self. Were there no self, who could be moved? Observe how the long wind rages between heaven and earth;
trees are broken and the hollows shriek, yet what does this have to do with the Great Void? Therefore, the Perfected Person is without self and remains empty.
This is because it is ultimate. Because it is empty, it is unmoving.

The substance of the mind is originally true; it becomes delusory through habitual defilement. Therefore, the essential method for realizing the Way is simply to remedy these habits. The essential method for remedying habits is as follows:
It relies solely on wisdom. Try observing one who melts ice: when fire prevails, the ice easily dissolves; when wisdom is profound, habitual tendencies are easily exhausted.
When others believe and I do not, it is not that they do not believe, but that my faith has not yet reached them. When I believe and others do not, it is not that I... [do not believe].

Lack of faith means it is not worth trusting. Therefore, I trust with a faithful mind; when people trust in words of faith, and those words ultimately accord with the mind, then there will be nothing that is not believed.
A shift of a mere ounce can overturn a weight of a thousand *jūn*; a single instance of partiality robs one of the great public nature that is inherently possessed.
This "partiality" is a cataract obscuring perfect luminosity and the very root of birth and death. Therefore, gain does not lie in small matters, nor does loss lie in great ones;
it is in the realm where neither is seen nor heard that the Sage exercises caution and trepidation.
One toils for profit; one toils for fame; one toils for achievement; one toils for the Way. Although their toil is the same, the reasons for which they toil differ.
Thus, there may be profit without fame; there may be fame without achievement; there may be achievement without the Way.
As for those who possess the Way, when the Way is perfected, nothing is not complete.
Terrestrial fish do not forget the moisture that moistens them; caged birds do not forget the preening of their feathers. This is because they have lost their natural state and long to return to it.
If a human loses their natural state and does not think of returning, they are inferior even to fish and birds. How tragic!
Those who pursue profit are urgent; those who pursue the Way are slow. Profit brings benefit to sentient beings, while the Way is flavorless.
To find flavor in what is flavorless is to turn slowness into urgency. As for this flavorlessness, who would savor it? Those who savor it are called True Men.
The mind is originally as clear as a deep pool; yet, by inhaling external objects, it becomes turbid in its nature, giving rise to various states of confusion and agitation.
As distress and delusion arise, one must trace their root back to their source: the fault lies in attachment.

When a single film obscures the eye, empty flowers arise in confusion; when a fine speck of dust settles upon the body, discursive thoughts fly about in disorder. Once one realizes that the film has no flowers and dissolves the dust to sever all thoughts, [the mind is restored].
That which is most subtle is great; that which is most minute is significant. The subtle is easily treated with levity; the minute is easily neglected.

The multitude does not recognize this, yet the sage remains cautious and vigilant. Because of this vigilance, the Way achieves great success and its merit becomes manifest, remaining faultless for ten thousand generations.

Objects have nothing inherently desirable; it is because people desire them that they become desirable. Desire arises from attachment; attachment necessitates grasping; grasping necessitates entry [into the cycle of rebirth]; once one has entered, one is submerged.
Once submerged, the self becomes small while objects become large; life becomes light while objects become heavy; and the person perishes while the objects remain.

Those who lived well in antiquity did not concern themselves with external things; thus they were without desire. Even if ten thousand forms were arrayed before them, it was as if Xi Zi were attempting to sell her beauty to a deer.
I observe those who dally with tigers and wolves; though they dally with them, they remain constantly fearful, for they dread being devoured by them. Thus they are ever afraid.

As for sensual desire in relation to human beings, how can it be compared to tigers and wolves? People not only dally with it but treat it with playfulness, and when it has consumed them entirely, they feel content in their hearts.
To remain complacent and unaware of this fear is a grave error. Tigers and wolves devour the body; lust and desire devour one's nature.
Lust and desire pose no rival to humanity. Therefore it is said: "Fortunately, there is but one [rival].

If these two were to coincide, then among all people under heaven, none would be able to practice the Way. In my view, the best way to oppose desire is through wisdom; assist wisdom with disenchantment (*nirveda*).
When one feels weary, fear arises; when one fears, one distances oneself; when one distances oneself, one becomes dispassionate; when one is dispassionate, one forgets.
For one who has forgotten, the body is regarded as a puppet and flavors are viewed like chewing wax. What desire could there be?

That which is difficult is easy; that which is easy is difficult. The multitude fears what is difficult and neglects what is easy; the sage fears what is easy and reveres what is difficult. Therefore, there is nothing the Way does not encompass;
there is nothing its Virtue does not broaden; there is no achievement it does not accomplish; and there is no reputation it does not establish.

The world universally regards fame and achievement as imperishable. Believing these can be attained through the mind, they weary their minds; believing they can be attained through the body, they weary their bodies.

Yet, though one exhausts oneself, it is not certain that anything is planted; and though something is planted, it is not certain that it will endure. Alas! Apart from the Sage, who is able to ensure endurance?
What does not endure is subject to decay; how then can there be endurance? That which I call "imperishable" is different from this.
This is so. To know my own imperishability is to know true imperishability.
Glorious fame is a pursuit of fame; glorious rank is a pursuit of rank. Once one has pursued them, what further disgrace could be added?

Therefore it is said: "He who stands on tiptoe cannot remain standing. He who cannot remain standing lacks a foundation. Without a foundation, how can he maintain his anxious vigilance over the gain or loss of name and rank?
How glorious is this!

Yet his wealth was not great because of his accumulation; for where there is accumulation, there is loss, and thus it was not great. His nobility did not reach the highest degree because of his loftiness.

Where there is height, there is depth; therefore, one does not arrive [at the ultimate]. Thus we know that the person of great attainment has no accumulation, and thus his wealth is the greatest of all.
He has no height, and thus his nobility is unsurpassed.

To conceal one's traces is not true seclusion; though the traces are hidden, the mind may not have forgotten them. To rely on fame is not true manifestation; though the name is prominent, the Way may not be realized.
Therefore, such seclusion is not authentic, and such manifestation is not great. What I call "seclusion" and "manifestation" is different from this.
What I call "concealment and manifestation" refers to being concealed within the essence (*tǐ*) and manifested through its function (*yòng*).

When the essence is concealed, it is vast and empty like the Great Clarity (*tàiqīng*), and all phenomena are stilled. When the function is manifested, things appear vividly and instantaneously, and the single Way is perceived as a whole.

Thus, whether encountering adversity or favor, one acts according to what is appropriate; in failure or success, they remain one and the same. Alas! One who dwells in this state is truly a Great Perfected Person (*zhēnrén*).
The commands of one's lord and father cannot be evaded; how much less so the Great Mandate? Consider those who rely on petty skills yet fail to comprehend the Great Mandate:

they are constantly dissatisfied in their ordinary lives, and when faced with the prospect of being cast aside, their hearts leap and kick in agitation, resorting to impassioned rhetoric to demand recognition from the world.
Alas! This is an error. To the eyes of a man of realization, it is like a person intoxicated by wine in the middle of the night.
He went forward and struck his forehead against a pillar, clutching a cloth drum and crying out for help from Heaven. Nevertheless, the cloth drum remained there;
one who knows their fate would not take it up.
To regard skill as secret is not true secrecy; to regard the Way as secret is true secrecy. I have often observed those who play with crossbows:

they stand trembling, yet after a hundred shots, they hit only a few times—this is what is called "skillful. How much more so for one who is not skillful! One who is truly skillful in the Way can grant respite to all things;
without even discharging an arrow, there is nowhere for things to escape. Therefore, nothing is greater than this secrecy; nothing is more powerful.
Thus it reaches its consummation.
Heaven and earth circulate in a cycle of a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes; birth and death follow their constant laws, yet no one can fathom them.
Failing to fathom these constants, people pursue external things and forget their true nature. The sage returns to these fundamental things, and thus he prospers.
What others discard, I take up. Thus, what others possess, I do not possess; what I possess, others do not possess. It is not that others do not possess these things;
it is because they do not know they possess them that they do not possess them. If they were to know they possess them, how would I differ from them?
When dust and grime soil a finger, one must wash it before feeling refreshed. Yet, when greed and anger harm one's virtue, one does not know how to remove them;
this is to regard virtue as less than a single finger. A soiled finger suffers only a temporary blemish, whereas virtue harmed by such passions loses its very nature.

Those who carry heavy burdens suffer; those with much knowledge toil. When suffering accumulates over time, the body is injured; when toil reaches its limit, the mind becomes exhausted. Once exhausted, one perishes.
The reason for this exhaustion is that one’s affairs lie outside [the self]. Therefore, those who value life attend to what is internal and not to what is external;
they follow themselves and not others; their will is set on preservation and not on loss.
Transformation and adaptation are difficult to discuss. No one fails to consider it right to pursue profit and avoid harm, yet I am truly not so.
Furthermore, there are instances where benefit and harm are placed before one and cannot be avoided; this is transformation. How does one achieve adaptation? The common person follows them;
the gentleman examines them; the sage accords with them. To accord with them is to have no possession of them. Because he does not possess them, [he is free].
It does not exist. People call one who steals physical objects a thief; yet that is not the ultimate theft. I call one who possesses a thieving mind a thief; this is certain.
As for such theft, the stealing of physical objects is not necessarily complete: if there is resistance, one will not enter; if one enters, one will be caught; and once caught, [the matter ends].
There is no room for death; once dead, what is there to steal? As for thieves, their thieving intent is inevitably lost when they face extreme urgency, yet they enter even more deeply.
Even if they are captured and spared with their lives, they are often released again, and moreover, there are those who encourage them. Be cautious! Be cautious!

When the Way flourishes, it is supple; when virtue flourishes, it is humble; when things flourish, they are broken. Thus, the more supple one is, the stronger one becomes; the more humble, the more radiant; the more prone to breakage, the more one perishes.
Those of antiquity did not treat things as objects, and therefore they endured long.

Those who are secretive about their affairs have loose minds; those who are secretive about their minds achieve success in their affairs. Thus, the more secretive one is regarding affairs, the looser the mind becomes;

the more secretive one is regarding the mind, the more successful the affairs become. For one whose mind is not cleansed, there is no way to attain such secrecy. Therefore, the sage prizes the cleansing of the mind and withdraws into concealment within the profound mystery.
A single thorn in the skin causes it to twitch and brings no peace; when many thorns are in the heart, how can there be peace? A thorn in the skin causes the skin to fester;
a thorn in the heart causes the heart to perish.

Great majesty is awe-inspiring. Observe that which brings about the sternness and slaughter of heaven and earth; this is great majesty. Though the myriad things are numerous, who among them can withstand it when it flows forth?
Therefore, when a person possesses majesty, they receive it from Heaven. The majesty of Heaven is supremely impartial;
the majesty of man manifests this impartiality. The majesty of Heaven loves all things; the majesty of man governs the preservation of life.
To transform others is without merit; to transform oneself is meritorious. When one has attained the fruit of self-transformation, others will be transformed spontaneously.
Indeed, when one observes the countenance of a person of virtue, it causes the intentions of others to dissolve—this is truly so.
It is easy to govern what is contrary, but difficult to govern what is compliant. What is contrary has its counterpart; what is compliant lacks awareness.

Therefore, those who possess true knowledge regard encountering the contrary as ambrosia and fear compliance as the poison of a *viṣa* bird. This is the height of vigilance. Because of this vigilance, they maintain their integrity without loss. Such is the nature of vigilance.
Is this not one who has perfected virtue?
The substance of the mind is originally luminous, yet the dust of the passions grows ever thicker; as the dust thickens, the mind becomes increasingly obscured.

Therefore, the sage employs wisdom and does not employ passion. Thus, those who attain the Way use wisdom to eliminate passion. When passion is forgotten, wisdom vanishes. This is the forgetting of passion.
This is how one draws near to the Way.

Wisdom is vast while affairs are minute; in skillfully mastering affairs, nothing surpasses wisdom. Therefore, as for the vessel of wisdom, it blunts sharp edges and untangles entanglements, finding no disadvantage.
Try observing a flake of snow falling upon a red furnace, or clear frost dissolving a scorching sun: it prevails over them by virtue of its nature.
Therefore, as for those who have achieved self-mastery, who can resist them?
Others employ great cleverness, while I employ ultimate simplicity; others lose through cleverness, while I gain through simplicity.
Thus, those who excel at practicing the Way discard cleverness and adopt simplicity, and there is nothing they do not attain.
Those who comply with me bring joy; those who oppose me provoke anger. Joy and anger alternate and shift; likes and dislikes compete to arise. Thus one's transgressions increase day by day.
If one traces the origin of this, it is rooted in a lack of awareness. This lack of awareness is precisely what leads to the forgetting of one's original nature.
To indulge the mouth and body, to exhaust the ears and eyes, and to clash with external things—people call this "joy. But what joy is there? There is no suffering greater than this.

To cast aside the physical form, to extinguish the mind and intellect, and not to rank among worldly things—people call this "suffering. But what suffering is there? There is no joy greater than this.

Therefore, for those who seek joy through suffering, their suffering deepens day by day; for those who endure suffering for the sake of joy, their joy increases day by day. Thus, one should emulate the Way.
People abandon that to take up this.

Heaven and earth accomplish their transformations without toil; the sage achieves his success through toil; the multitude carries out their affairs through toil. When affairs are completed, one rests;
when success is achieved, one withdraws. Therefore it is said: "When success is achieved and affairs are completed, the body withdraws—this is the Way of Heaven."
Those with much wealth are arrogant; those in high positions are haughty; those with many merits are boastful; those with great ambitions are frantic; those with superior talents are insolent;
those of profound virtue are humble; and those who embody the true Way are compliant.
Failing to understand that conditions are merely provisional, one recklessly gives rise to grasping and rejecting. The winds of consciousness fan them into being, surging and rolling without ceasing.

It is like the ocean waves: when the water is clear, waves arise because of the wind; if the wind does not arise, how could the waves be produced? If consciousness does not arise, how could the myriad conditions exist?
Therefore, for one who has realized the Way, non-arising is not understood as something that arises; rather, understanding itself is non-arising.
Excellent! The source is not distant, the stream is not long, the Way is not vast, and the merit is not solidified. Thus, the virtue of the Sage permeates all living beings.
Its merit flows through ten thousand generations because its Way is great. When one possesses the Great Way, who could possibly destroy it?
The eyes encompass heaven and earth, yet a speck of dust can obscure their clarity. The mind contains the vast void, yet a single thought can obstruct its breadth.

Thus we know that a single thought-moment is the root of birth and death and the foundation of calamity and misfortune. Therefore, the sage maintains the precepts by knowing the subtle and perceiving the minute.
One who has self-confidence will be believed even if others do not; one who lacks self-confidence will not be believed even if others do.
One must have faith in this. Therefore, one’s own faith is rooted in sincerity; human faith is easily deceived. Sincerity is called refinement (*jing*);

deception is called sinking (*lun*). Wisdom illuminates while consciousness deludes; from delusion arise a thousand differences, whereas illumination remains solitary and independent. Thus, those who attain the Way use illumination to illuminate delusion.
Value wisdom, not consciousness.

Observe the common people walking through a marketplace: if they stumble into a hollow and lose their footing, they will inevitably startle and wave their arms, vowing never to do it again, because they loathe the soiling of their shoes.
Yet today’s gentlemen dwell in a state of inferior virtue with complacency, neither startled nor making a vow.
This is to belittle oneself before the common people and to treat one’s own Way and virtue as mere dross. How tragic!
Everyone knows that change is change and acts accordingly, yet they do not know that within change there exists that which does not change.
If one truly knows this non-changing, then change will be unable to alter them. If one does not know this non-changing, then even though—
How could that which is unchanging ever fail to change? Please observe the Sage: his body follows along with all phenomena and moves silently through the four modes of birth;
though things arise in profusion, he neither welcomes nor rejects them. This is to abide in the unchanging while manifesting change.

What transformation is there? If such a person’s form is like withered wood while their mind is like drifting dust, and though all external things have ceased their traces they still groan, this is no transformation.
When has it ever not been transforming?
Sleeping, resting, sitting, and reclining are the means by which the body is at ease. Ceasing all攀緣 (pān-yuán, mental clinging/external distractions) is the means by which the mind is at ease.

When the body is at ease, the will becomes lax; when the mind is at ease, the will becomes refined. Therefore, those who nurture the Way forget their physical form and take the mind as their teacher; thus the Way becomes constant.
Heaven and earth are great because they can contain all things; rivers and seas are deep because they are skilled at receiving all waters;
the sage is honored because he accepts impurities and endures insults. Thus, the more the sage is accommodating, the greater he becomes; the more humble he is, the more honored he becomes.
Therefore, his Way extends through a hundred kalpas and his blessings flourish for eternity, such that none can contend with him.

To regard the people as one's own people, and to approve of the good while disapproving of the evil, may not always be impartial. To regard the people as one's own heart, to love the kind and grieve for the cruel, is without exception true.
Therefore it is said: "Heaven and earth share the same root; the myriad things are one body. This is what is called universal benevolence.
Those who see forms are blind; those who see the seer are enlightened. Those who hear sounds are deaf; those who hear the hearer are acute of hearing.
