Therefore, when form and seeing are complete, and sound and hearing are exhausted, there is nothing that is not integrated. Sound and form are both non-existent; seeing and hearing have no abiding place. This is what is called Great Penetration.

When manifold thoughts proliferate incessantly, there is no means by which to realize the Truth. If one attempts to stop manifold thoughts with manifold thoughts, the more one stops them, the more they will not cease.
If one uses a single thought to stop manifold thoughts, then without stopping, they cease of themselves.
What I call "a single thought" is non-thought (*amanyana*). One who can contemplate non-thought may continue through every moment of thought, yet in the end, what thought is there at all?
Although this is so, in reality, there is no such thing as "non-thought," for [the notion of it] is superfluous. Indeed, one does not realize that it is a wedge.
The substance of the mind is fundamentally void; delusive thoughts do not exist. If one realizes that delusions do not exist, then even though they appear, they are non-existent.
If one does not realize that delusions do not exist, then even though they are non-existent, they are as if existent. Therefore, delusive thoughts are like flowers in the sky; their root lies in—
The cataract of the eye: one clearly perceives that the flowers seen by the cataract are not non-existent. The essence of emptiness is eternally quiescent.

Now, as for those who, while at rest, seem to perceive things through internal illumination, yet find nothing exists when engaging with external phenomena—it is simply because mind and object have not yet merged, and the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) have not been fully understood, resulting in lingering obstructions.
Therefore, for one who is constructing the Way, if they do not understand these sensory objects, even if their mental conceptions are both present...
To cease is still to incline toward quiescence; therefore, one does not grasp at the ultimate Way.

Its essence is quiescent while its function is illuminating; the function never loses its essence, so it is quiescent within illumination. The essence is not separate from its function, so it is illuminating within quiescence.
Therefore, its essence is as tranquil as the great void, while its function is as illuminating as the midday sun. Thus, amidst ten thousand transformations, nothing is diminished;

there is no depth that it does not reflect. It has no beginning before and no end after; ten thousand kalpas are but a single thought-moment. The six realms are unified in one void; humans and things follow the same track, whether large or small.

It remains identical in form; it does not change through day and night, nor does it migrate through death and birth. This is what is called "permanence. Yet, one who realizes this is like a human being who has become a celestial being—what fault could there be in such a person?

The phenomena are minor, but the principle is great. Phenomena have a thousand differences, yet the principle is of a single flavor. For one who is proficient in the principle, phenomena have nothing beyond it;

whether hidden or manifest, existing or perishing, there is no duality between them. Therefore, the person of ultimate attainment becomes increasingly still the more they move; there is nowhere they do not dwell.

It cannot be attained through a mind of non-existence, nor can it be sought with a mind of existence. To have a mind of existence is to cling to existence; to have a mind of non-existence is to be attached to non-existence.
Since both of these are incorrect, one must transcend them and stand alone. Thus, the Great Man has no counterpart, because there is nothing that can correspond to his state of mind.
Contemplate that things exist, yet the mind is empty and phenomena are empty. Thus, if mindfulness is like a melting void, one will be sovereign in encountering conditions;
the mind is like a round mirror, ever tranquil in its coming and going. One who excels in this does not depart from the ordinary, yet dwells uprightly in the sublime realm.
The great forgetting is not forgetting; there is nothing that is not forgotten. For one who intentionally attempts to forget, the more they try to forget, the more it becomes manifest.

Those who cling to such notions have not yet realized the Way. Once the Way is realized, why would there be anything left to forget? Therefore it is said: "Fish forget each other in water; people forget each other in the Way."
The swimming fish does not know the sea; the flying bird does not know the sky. Ordinary people do not know the Dao. If they were to know it, how could they remain ordinary people?
It is my view that one who truly embodies the Dao has a body like that of a fish or a bird and a mind like the sea or the sky; such a person is close to it.

In one movement and one stillness, in one word and one silence, in the raising of eyebrows and the twinkling of eyes, or in drinking and pecking—whether turning left or right, there is no moment when he does not observe.
Having observed for a long time, his conceptual thoughts shatter; suddenly, he attains it spontaneously. That which is attained spontaneously is known by oneself alone; no one else can recognize it.
The work of Heaven and Earth does not neglect a single blade of grass; the moisture of the vast ocean does not discard a single drop;
the essence of perfect luminosity is never separate from a single thought. Thus we know that the importance of this single thought is truly profound.
The true mind is ultimate and great; this body is ultimate and minute.

Therefore, one who clarifies the true mind looks back upon this body as being like a fragment of cloud floating in the vast emptiness—coming and going as it pleases, carefree and without dependence. Because there is no dependence, one dwells in the world as if on loan.

To act is to have something to do; to be incapable of acting is to have nothing to do. To act is to be capable of doing something. Therefore, the sage acts through non-action (*wuwei*) yet there is nothing he does not do.
What I call the sage’s non-action means that although he acts, he does not claim the action as his own;
it is not like cold ashes or withered wood, which are utterly incapable of acting.
The great void roams within my mind like a single bubble upon the ocean; how much more so, then, are heaven and earth within the great void?
How are the myriad things within heaven and earth? How is this body within the myriad things? And how are external objects within this body?
Ah! How small it is! Because it is small, it is great. Heaven and earth are silent;
the myriad things are one. Abiding in silence and knowing oneness, all affairs are completed. One who dwells in this Way is never errant.
Because it is without error, all actions and movements are never lost. That which is not lost is called the True Man (*zhēnrén*).

He is transcendent and beyond all dependencies, in great harmony with all things. Now, where there is difference, there is duality between self and object; where there is duality between self and object, there arises opposition of forms.
When there is opposition of forms, nothing is more grievous than this. How can such a state be severed? In my view, those who excel at attaining the Way value both.

Forgetfulness. When both are forgotten, then things and the self become one. When things and the self are one, then the opposition of forms is forgotten. Once the opposition of forms is forgotten, who is there to depend upon?
Because it is free from dependence, it is great; because it is great, it is universal. This universal sameness is what is called the Sage. Therefore it is said:
"Only the Sage can take the myriad things as his own."
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are of one flavor, pure and true. If the mind is perfectly luminous, heaven and earth are void and still.

Therefore, for one who attains this realization, externally there is nothing encountered by the eyes that can stir the emotions; internally, upon turning back to observe, one realizes there is not a single thing. In this state, all is empty, and emptiness leaves no trace.
Though things are spoken of in vain, the body dwells within the mundane world while the mind transcends the realm of forms.
When stillness reaches its ultimate limit, the mind attains penetration; when words are forgotten, one realizes the essence through embodiment.

Therefore, for those who have attained such penetration and realization, their minds are like suspended mirrors, their mouths are like tied tongues, their forms are like withered wood, and their vital energy is like frost and snow. Alas! What kind of person is this?
I wish to roam with them.
His form resembles that of a hunched cripple; his interior is deep and hollow. His eyes seem not to see, and his ears do not hear.
He is dazed and bewildered; people look upon him and think he is a fool, like one who has lost his soul and knows not with whom he is joined.
I beg to take him as my teacher.
All that exists in the world is as remote and elusive as a dream. Within the dream it is not non-existent, yet after awakening, what remains?
Therefore, if one does not awaken, how can one transcend existence? If one does not transcend existence, how can one leave the world?

What I call "leaving the world" is not leaving the world; it is leaving the world while remaining in the world. One who leaves the world while remaining in the world is called a Perfected Man (*zhiren*).
To know that the conditioned has its beginning and the ultimate has its end is to employ knowledge through wisdom and to direct the ultimate through skillful means.

Skillful means involves engaging with existence; in engaging with existence and confronting change, there have been those throughout antiquity who underwent ten thousand transformations without losing their correctness, for the root remained intact.
Now, those who do not establish a foundation yet boastfully shift their views are like those who seek to untie others while binding themselves;
people will surely spit upon them, and even small children will laugh at them.

Direct penetration is called "sudden"; gradual cultivation is called "gradual. Direct penetration reaches the truth; gradual cultivation eliminates the false. If the truth is not reached, the false is not eliminated.
If the false is not eliminated, the truth does not reach its ultimate state. Viewed from this perspective, is the false not a veil over the truth?
Is it not a harm to the Way? Is it not a burden upon virtue?
Perfectly interfused and all-encompassing, vast and mutually penetrating; phenomena and principle are entirely one, their concealment and manifestation unfathomable.

The one contains the many and the many enter the one; by raising the one, all are gathered, yet they are not hindered from being arrayed side by side. Small and large are no different, and ordinary beings and sages are not separated.
Ever merging and ever illuminating; ever arising and ever tranquil. The mind is inconceivable, and words are beyond deliberation.
In the ordinary course of daily life, there has never been any deficiency. One always dwells within it without the need for arduous travel—this is what is called the ultimate.

Great words convey the Way; small words convey names. Ultimate words transcend words. Those that convey names are near; those that convey the Way are distant. Those that transcend words are pervasive.
Therefore, what is near is easily befriended; what is distant is easily disparaged; what is pervasive cannot be fathomed.
Because it is ultimate, it cannot be fathomed. To abide in that which cannot be fathomed is called "divine transformation" (*shenhua*).

A single palm does not produce sound; there is no resonance without emptiness. When conditions are severed, there is no speech. Viewed from this perspective, speech exists only because it depends upon something else.
Nevertheless, when one speaks of the "speechless," that very speaking is itself the speechless. That which is speechless is that which speech cannot reach.
In my view, the way to truly attain the speechless is by relinquishing speech. Once speech has been relinquished, that which is speechless is realized.
It is so. What more need be said? Fu Guangzhai of Liaocheng remarked:
"Regarding what the world calls 'books of the masters' (*zishu*), are not those of Laozi and Zhuangzi their ultimate expression?

The words of Laozi are concise yet their meaning is profound; the discourse of Zhuangzi is extraordinary yet his thought is far-reaching. Those who discuss the Way in later ages have looked to them for refuge."
From Xunzi and Yangzi downward, none are sufficient to be compared [to him]. Is this brief account not of the same order as Laozi and Zhuangzi?
His prose is magnificent and pure, yet its underlying meaning is difficult to express in words; perhaps even Laozi and Zhuangzi have not reached such heights.
A skeptic says: "You are mistaken. How could Laozi and Zhuangzi ever be equaled? I reply: [It is so.]

Laozi and Zhuangzi are indeed unsurpassed; yet, regarding what they call the "Valley Spirit" and its harmonious unity, or the "Mysterious Pearl" sought by the Doubting Beggar, these seem to be words that have not fully exhausted the subject.
Furthermore, they appear to be those who wish to speak but find it difficult to do so, for the Way is truly infinite and boundless.
The Sage of the West had no dharma to preach, yet he preached the Dharma—this is how he spoke of it.

It is exhaustive. Thus, by examining Laozi and Zhuangzi, one knows that the various other philosophers have not reached this exhaustiveness; yet by examining the Sage of the West, one knows that even Laozi and Zhuangzi have not reached this exhaustiveness.
Their fragmentary words derive their essential meaning from the Sage of the West, while their literary style resembles that of Laozi and Zhuangzi.
Therefore it is said: "In some respects, even Laozi and Zhuangzi have not yet reached [the ultimate]. Nevertheless, there is also this...
These are "discursive words" (*xu yan*). Where there are words, there is discursiveness; therefore, they are called "discursive words.

To take these words and seek therein that which was not spoken is dependent upon the person. Otherwise, one might say: "Hanshan is a man of the present age; how marvelous could his discursive words be?
They not only fall short of Laozi and Zhuangzi, but even fail to reach the level of the various other philosophers (*zhuzi*)."

Although I have been able to grasp the essential meaning throughout my life, I have lacked the capacity for memorization.

I am able to recall the entirety of the discourse, beginning with its titles and recording its general outline.

Use the seal of the teaching as your standard, taking the objects and conditions encountered in daily life as your verification.

If you can simply remain light and detached toward these objects, without a mind of attachment or obstruction, this is precisely where you gain power through the functioning of the mind. You should be able to examine yourself by means of these objects and conditions;
it is not necessary to rely entirely upon the words of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) as the ultimate truth.
"Fix your teeth upon the critical phrase (*huatou*). This is not for the purpose of clarifying the phrase; rather, you borrow the phrase to give rise to doubt and sever delusive thoughts.
In your investigation, you must investigate apart from the phrase itself. Only when you have brought down this doubt will you gain power.

As the Ancient Sage said: 'Three inches away from the hook—why do you not speak? The predecessors have already set their minds upon this. When doubt reaches the point where it transcends the realm of intellect and emotion, it goes beyond words."
When there is no passage through time and one is pressed to the limit of exhaustion, a slight glimmer of light flashes forth; this is called the "Lightning Flash Samādhi.
At this point, you should press forward rather than rejoice. If you mistake this for the goal, you will consider a small attainment to be sufficient.
Your very body will then be covered by that speck of light, and you will no longer be able to emerge from it. Even if you eventually emerge later on, you will have become its servant. (8)

Within consciousness there remain latent habitual tendencies from many lifetimes; when subtle seeds suddenly manifest in a place where one cannot reach them through effort, it is necessary to rely on the power of mantras to eliminate them.
Question: Regarding the difference between wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*): the very first moment of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is wisdom.

As soon as one turns toward a second thought, it becomes inferential cognition (*anumāna*) and falls into conceptualization. Furthermore, it is said that what comes with attachment to emotion is consciousness;
what does not come with attachment to emotion is wisdom. To "bite into the head of the phrase" is precisely to seize the path by which emotional consciousness arrives, so that it does not arise.
The second thought:
realizing and awakening is also not a particularly difficult matter. If you maintain the breath for three months, you will certainly see results.
First, you must not harbor a mind that anticipates awakening; as soon as you wait for awakening, you are merely waiting for someone else to awaken, and this itself is an obstruction.
Once the "head-board" is set, one can no longer enter through the effort of practice. It is also said: "This matter must be undertaken by a person of courageous spirit.
Those of sharp faculties are born with innate wisdom; having encountered the conditions in this life, they realize it immediately. There are those who do not rely on inquiry."
As for "entering," it simply requires that you maintain it and break through to liberation. The Sixth Patriarch was such a person.
What about those of dull faculties? They must simply accept it themselves. Though those of dull faculties lack skill, they gain strength precisely from their dullness.
Bite down firmly on the critical phrase (*huatou*). It is applicable at all times; even when ascending a mountain of knives or a mass of fire, it remains applicable.
This is precisely the place where one attains meditative power (*samādhi*). If there is even the slightest evasion, you will fall headlong into ruin.
A person practicing Chan must not sit upon pure white ground; this is a pitfall for a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas.
I wish to expose this for the sake of the assembly, and therefore I have composed this "Song of the One-Sided Board."
The eye of the teachings and the eye of the school are originally not two eyes. Master Yongming extracted the words of the teachings in their entirety to provide a seal of entry.
He feared that people might consistently set foot upon the pathless margins of meaninglessness; if one lacks the eye of the teachings, one will fall into false views.

In my commentaries on the *Vajracchedikā*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Śūraṅgama*, and other sutras, I have submerged the meaning from where the realm of emotional consciousness cannot reach.
He picked up what had burst forth by the roadside and intended to use it to instruct the Patriarch.

"The student must realize this for themselves," he said. While at Donghai, one night as he sat in meditation, body and world both became empty. The Sea-Seal (Haiyin) emitted light, and the mountains and rivers shook;

within this realm, he attained the wisdom of correspondence (*saṃprayukta-jñāna*). Shortly thereafter, he awakened to the crucial points of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which suddenly appeared vividly before his eyes. He was seized with urgency.
I lit a candle and wrote it. My wrist could not rest for long; by the end of the fifth watch of the night, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* had already been transcribed as if it were suspended in a mirror.
An attendant came out to wait upon me and, seeing the remaining candle on the desk, was struck with wonder.
The Bodhisattva’s sole concern is the benefit of sentient beings; yet, without employing the various worldly dharmas, one cannot adapt to their capacities to bring them benefit.
In studying the Buddha-dharma, one first gives rise to the mind of great compassion, making the destruction of self-grasping the primary objective.
Regarding ancient public cases (gong'an), if people of the present day attempt to measure them with their deluded thoughts, they will not even meet the point of the needle's tip.
Even if they were to understand or explain them, they would still lack power within their own domain.
It is easy to enter through movement; it is difficult to enter through stillness.
Those who enter via external knowledge and views lack power; those who enter by inwardly realizing their own nature gain power.

Question: What is it like to attain realization through conditions? There are two kinds of conditions: those of seeing and hearing, which involve the possibility of regression; and those of objective realms, which do not involve regression.
This is because they differ in terms of being illusory or real.
Sentient beings have the patience of desire; those of the Two Vehicles have the patience of arising; Bodhisattvas have the patience of non-arising; and Buddhas have the patience of cessation.

Only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are correct, yet there also exist the knowledge and vision of Bodhisattvas, the knowledge and vision of those of the Two Vehicles, the knowledge and vision of sentient beings, and the knowledge and vision of externalists—all of which are confused and erroneous.
Therefore, through various skillful means, the World-Honored One seeks only to bring about complete understanding.
With single-mindedness, one enters into right knowledge and vision; this is called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
To fully realize that the mind of arising and ceasing is quiescent is itself to fully realize birth-and-death.
What is "pointing upward"? There is only this: letting go.
The words of the Patriarchs are alive in every sentence; when a student treats them as substantial phenomena, they become dead in every sentence.
For daily practice, it is sufficient simply to see through deluded thoughts so that you are not driven by them; there is no other place for the mind to apply itself.
"If everything is empty and does not descend, how can one act? One simply realizes that it is provisional; thus, all things can be emptied and all things can be lightened.
What business does a Bodhisattva have dwelling in ultimate bliss? I must pull him out."
The phrase "Mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha" is fundamentally the same as any other *huatou*. Yet nowadays, people immediately take it to mean going to the Western Paradise.
All things are illusory; everyone knows this. However, one must have a firm resolve regarding the functioning of illusion itself, only then will one not be swayed by it.
While at Haiyin Temple, I happened to contemplate the kōan of the Sixth Patriarch coming at midnight to behead him.

I then desired to train in that power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Every night, I would open the door and practice visualization, thinking: "If someone were to come seeking to borrow my head, I would joyfully give it away.
I did this tonight, and I did it again tomorrow night. After some time, I felt that a power of stable vision had arisen within me. Suddenly, one—
At night, he reported that a thief had entered. I said, "Simply call him in. I sat upright by the bright light of a candle, free from any sense of fear or trepidation.
When the man reached the door, he crawled on his hands and knees, not daring to enter; he was a large, burly man. I called out to him, saying, "There is nothing here to be found."
He ordered that two hundred coins be taken from the treasury and given to him. Had there been no one previously to take charge, he would have been left in a state of frantic distress.
While staying on Mount Wutai, the clamor was like that of a million men in a fierce battle; there was not a single moment of peace.

One day, while listening to a spring at a place of extreme turbulence, after a short while it suddenly could not be heard. As soon as he raised the thought, "Why is it heard again? it was audible once more.
He then sat for several days at the place where the water was most turbulent. After he had sat for a long time, the sound of the water became silent;
from then on, although the sound of the water never ceased, it was as if it could not be heard. Thereafter, he dwelt peacefully in the mountains, no longer moved by clamor or noise.
While he was in Donghai, he encountered an imperial official sent by the Empress Dowager bearing several taels of silver.

He did not dare refuse it, yet he considered that he could not accept such a gift indiscriminately. Reflecting that the local region was suffering from famine, he thought the funds could be used to extend the Empress Dowager’s bounty.
The official would not permit this, so he informed the official that each county where the relief was received should compile a register and return it to him.
He replied, "It shall be so. Later, when the two palaces heard of this, they were greatly pleased. When the time came for the disaster, they ultimately relied on the power of this single act.
Thus one knows that in matters of wealth, one must not act with negligence or expediency.
When I was in Lingnan, the local people were not yet familiar with me; their demeanor remained aloof and they could not be made to feel at ease.
There was no one with whom I could establish intimacy. Whenever a small child wished to approach me, I would immediately become fearful and move away.

One day, I practiced the method of taming lion cubs, forcing myself to lie down and draw near to them affectionately, giving them fruit and melons. Day by day I became more familiar with them, until finally they no longer feared me. From that time on—
People do not avoid or shun me; day by day they come to treat me with intimacy.
When I first went to visit a certain military governor, I held my petition beneath the courtyard eaves. For a long time he did not order me to leave.

My mind understood that he should have called my name for me to report my presence, yet I could not bring it to my lips. It was as heavy as a thousand-jin weight; there was nothing I could do about it.
At that time, Fen announced his name and said, "I, so-and-so, come to seek an audience," whereupon he rose and departed. The next day, when he came for an audience again, he acted in the same manner;
this continued for an entire year without the slightest concession. Those around him remarked, "How can this man of arms know how to break conventional rules to attend upon a virtuous teacher?

Finally, on the day they were scheduled to visit the Provincial Governor together, the General Headquarters prepared a boat and provided offerings of vegetarian meals and fruit, treating him as a guest of honor.
He invited Guo Zhou to pay his respects. Bowing, he gestured for him to take the seat of honor and said, "It is not that I am unable to accommodate you, Master;
rather, I know you possess a spine of pride, and I merely wished to bring us together. They conversed joyfully with knees pressed close as they took their leave.
He then sighed, "Among the lay officials, there are truly those with profound resolve. What need is there to ask about Wu?"

If one does not read with careful attention and thorough realization, one will not grasp its practical application. When I was annotating the *Laozi*, I reached the passage: "The Way of Heaven is like drawing a bow.
For several days, I could not find a point of convergence for this analogy. I then borrowed a bow and a string from someone else, strung them, and hung them on the wall.
Whether sitting or lying down, I watched them. After two more days, I suddenly realized that the character "draw" (*zhāng*) corresponds to [the downward pull of the bow].
An Explanation of the Character "Chi" (Relaxation). When a bow is relaxed, the back (*fǔ*) is too high and the tip (*shāo*) is too low; thus, it is useless.

When it is drawn for use, one suppresses the high and raises the low, diminishing the back and compensating for the tip so that the upper and lower parts are balanced and equal, enabling one to hit the mark.
The Way of Heaven employs totality through movement; it primarily governs giving rather than receiving, which is precisely what is appropriate. This is profound.
Regarding the two lines concerning "lightness as the root," I have also deliberated upon them for several years and did not dare to offer a hasty interpretation.

On the very day I was traveling southward, sitting alone in my boat, my state of mind was desolate; yet, the interpretations of lightness and heaviness, stillness and agitation, suddenly dawned before me.

Only then did I realize the true purport of the Great Sage’s words. It is clear that one must experience it personally before seeing it; thus, one cannot claim that the words set down on paper lack truth.
This is the flavor [of the work]. Thus, the *Daode jing* was completed after thirteen years; it was not produced in haste.

When I compose a scripture, I must invariably concentrate my spirit and enter into contemplation, so that my realization accords with the Buddha-mind and the subtle spark of inspiration suddenly bursts forth of its own accord.
On the paper appended to this: if one engages in conceptual deliberation, it will not be of practical use.

Our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, manifested his birth in a royal palace, left home at the Snowy Mountains, practiced austerities for six years, awakened to the Way and attained Buddhahood, and preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings in the Deer Park.

When the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world, there were ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders in the western regions, each establishing their own schools and all claiming to be masters. However, when the Buddha attained enlightenment and began preaching the Dharma, [they were eclipsed].
Each of the various non-Buddhists took refuge and left the household life to become disciples of the Buddha. Relying on the teachings, they practiced and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Therefore, those present at this single assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, numbering more than one thousand two hundred and fifty people, were all members of the ranks of non-Buddhists.
At that time, those who had faith in the Buddha took refuge in the Buddha and the Dharma, relying on the teachings to practice accordingly.
Those who do not believe will give rise to alarm and doubt, and even undergo various demonic harms and slanders,
falling into the evil realms in numbers beyond counting. Thus we know that in lands where the Buddha-dharma has not yet spread,
whether one is wise or foolish, virtuous or unworthy, though there may be differences in their doubts and beliefs, they all remain unaware of me.
This is the fundamental intention of the Buddha’s appearance in the world, as well as the sequential rules for the expedient means of saving sentient beings.

Therefore, I shall now briefly describe the sequence of expedient means for transforming sentient beings, so that those who have not yet heard or believed in the Buddha-dharma may know that our Sangha’s dharma-gate for transforming beings cannot be entered through a single matter, a single practice, or a single door. Thus it is said:

The gates of skillful means are manifold, yet the source to which they return is non-dual. To summarize: throughout forty-nine years, [the Buddha’s teaching] followed the sequence of capacities—great or small, shallow or deep;
this is what is meant by "teachings do not leap over stages. You should understand this thoroughly and not dismiss it as mere common talk.
A single Buddha appears in the world for the sake of one great causal event: namely, to reveal and instruct sentient beings in the Buddha-nature.
Knowledge and vision. To cause them to awaken and enter [this truth], there is only this one matter and no other.

What is called "the one great matter" means that one must cause sentient beings to know that birth and death constitute the one great matter. The Buddha’s knowledge and vision is precisely the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by each and every sentient being.
It is due to delusion regarding this Buddha-nature that birth and death are produced; now, one must bring forth [liberation].
Regarding the suffering of death, one must take the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as the primary meaning.

Is this not precisely why the Buddha appeared in the world to point directly to the human mind and see one's nature to become a Buddha? Thus, the path of Zen practice for awakening the mind did not depend upon the arrival of Bodhidharma from the West;
indeed, the Buddha appeared specifically for this very matter. Yet, alas, sentient beings have passed through kalpas [of ignorance].

Since that time, greed, anger, ignorance, craving, afflictions, and evil views have become so deeply entrenched in delusion that [beings] are unable to suddenly be shown the Great Dharma of awakening the mind.
Therefore, the Dharma of the One Vehicle was taught by being differentiated into three.

For this reason, there is the establishment of the gradual progression of the Three Vehicles—namely, the Small Vehicle, the Middle Vehicle, and the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, there are those who are unable to endure even the teachings of the Small Vehicle.

Thus, the five precepts and ten wholesome actions are established as the causes for the good fruits of human and celestial rebirths, and furthermore serve to avoid falling into the sufferings of the three miserable realms—those of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Therefore it is said: "If the five precepts are not maintained, the path to the human and celestial realms is cut off. Now, as disciples of the Buddha, we must respectfully uphold them.
Buddhism takes the salvation of sentient beings as its primary task.

If one does not employ gradual expedient means to guide and lead them into the Way, but instead suddenly reveals the Great Dharma to them, it will conversely cause them to give rise to groundless doubts and slanders, leading them to incur the sufferings of the three miserable realms for themselves;
thus, they would take the finest *amṛta* (clarified butter) for poison. This is the fault of failing to provide skillful guidance. Therefore, we now follow...
As ordained by the Buddha, laymen are called upāsakas and laywomen are called upāsikās.
They should observe the five precepts to cultivate the wholesome fruits of human and celestial rebirth. These are the five precepts for the laity:

First, abstaining from taking life (this precept brings about the retribution of longevity in the future, as well as the harmony of one's family and dependents, and the flourishing of one's descendants in the present).

2. Refraining from Stealing (Taking what is not given is all termed stealing. This precept brings about the retribution of attaining great wealth and abundance in future lives, with food, clothing, and necessities in plenty, and all requests fulfilled according to one's wishes).

Third, abstaining from sexual misconduct (to harbor lustful desires for those who are not one's own wife or concubine is called sexual misconduct; this precept brings as its retribution in future lives the attainment of a chaste and virtuous spouse, mutual affection between father and son, and harmony among one's kin and relatives).

The fourth is the precept against false speech (if one speaks what is untrue or incites discord between two parties, it is called false speech; by observing this precept, one will in future lives attain wisdom that surpasses others, one’s words will be truthful, and all who hear them will believe, following their instructions as they practice).

Fifth, abstaining from drinking alcohol (alcohol can cause confusion and disorder of the nature, incite madness, and give rise to calamity; it is the root of all evils. This precept brings about the retribution of attaining clear and penetrating wisdom in the future, with insight and vision that transcend the ordinary).
The above are the five precepts.
When our Buddha appeared in the world, he specifically established this teaching for laypeople in the secular realm at the outset, so that people might rely on these precepts to cultivate the causes;
thus they will not fail this life, avoid falling into the evil realms, and be able to bring about future lives without losing their human form, attaining long-term [benefit].

Longevity, great wealth, and numerous descendants; the flourishing of one’s household and the reward of exceptional civil refinement—those who now hold high office and noble rank, those who possess abundant riches and prosperity, and those who are intelligent, sharp, and successful—all come from the practice of the Five Precepts.

Indeed, these Five Precepts are identical to the Five Constant Virtues of the Confucian school: not killing is benevolence (*ren*); not stealing is righteousness (*yi*); and not committing sexual misconduct is propriety (*li*).
Furthermore, not drinking alcohol is wisdom; not speaking falsely is faith. Thus, there are aspects of the Buddha-dharma that benefit the royal way:
by transforming people through the Five Precepts, litigation and disputes will cease, punishments and penalties will be reduced, families will be well-ordered, and social customs will become pure.
This is my [view].
This is the ritual for the transformation-birth (*upapāduka*) established by the Buddha at the very beginning.
Now, worldly people do not understand the Buddha-dharma and utterly lack a heart that delights in goodness; instead, they give rise to views that slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

This is merely to willingly indulge in ignorance and delusion, and to bring suffering upon themselves. Furthermore, there is a certain class of people who, although they are able to eat vegetarian food, yet...
They do not know the path of correct practice according to the Buddha-dharma; they follow non-Buddhist outsiders who advocate non-action (*avikṛta*);

they show no reverence for the Buddhas, the patriarchs, Heaven, or Earth; they are unfilial toward their parents; they do not burn incense or prostrate before the Triple Gem; they are devoted solely to a single flavor of perverse conduct.
These are heterodox teachings. Blindly leading one another, they gather to engage in idle talk, claiming it to be the transmission of the Dharma.

They have no knowledge at all of the path of authentic practice, yet they instead slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Stubbornly clinging to their views and refusing to be transformed, these are the most foolish of people;
they are truly pitiable. Now, [I] respectfully...

This is precisely what the Imperial Decree intends to prohibit. I only pray that the eminent gentlemen of the present age will distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, and between right and wrong.
Whenever you encounter such individuals, you should immediately provide them with instruction, leading them to abandon error and return to the truth.
This not only protects the Buddha-dharma, but also serves as an aid to it.
This is the transformation wrought by the King. Yet, whether one studies the heterodox or the orthodox, it all stems from a single thought of a virtuous mind.
It is a pity that, failing to recognize what is heterodox, one falls into error. Now, if you know it to be wrong, why not abandon those heterodox followers and become a truly virtuous person?
To be a virtuous citizen in a sagely age—
this is the aforementioned Five Precepts, which constitute the cause and effect for cultivating the human path in Buddhism. Furthermore, the Ten Paths of Wholesome Action are established as follows:

Regarding the causes and effects of humans and devas, what are called the ten wholesome actions consist of three bodily unwholesome karmas—namely, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. If one abandons these three unwholesome acts, they are termed the three wholesome paths of action.

Second, there are four evil karmas of speech: namely, false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech. If one abandons these four, they are called the four paths of wholesome action.
Third, there are three evil karmas of mind: namely, greed, hatred, and delusion. If one abandons these three, they are called the three paths of wholesome action.
The ten non-virtues mentioned above are things that ordinary people practice daily without realizing it.
If one can now sever these ten non-virtues, they are termed the "ten virtues," which serve as the cause for rebirth in the heavens; such a person is called one of pure goodness.

These ten virtuous dharmas are precisely the Way of rectifying the mind, sincerity of intention, and cultivation of the person in the Confucian school. If one can truly cultivate this, then in the present life one will become...

When the noble become virtuous, they will certainly experience rebirth in the celestial palaces of the next life, receiving supreme and wondrous bliss. This is a practice that is ten thousand times true.
Why, then, are worldly people so deluded as to remain ignorant of it, instead devoting themselves exclusively to heterodox paths in their pursuit of gain?
Is this not to betray one's own mind?

The aforementioned five precepts and ten wholesome actions are the teachings specifically established by our Buddha for laypeople in the world. They require that people cultivate the causes according to these, so as not to lose the blessings of the human and celestial realms.
These are words proclaimed from the golden mouth [of the Buddha], a discourse free from falsehood. If one does not follow this cultivation, in total...
This is a false path; it is not the correct practice. To wholeheartedly endure hardship in cultivation yields no benefit whatsoever, but instead increases the fruits of suffering.
This is called "using suffering to abandon suffering," and our Buddha has already deeply lamented this.
The doctrines of the five schools and six volumes currently prevalent in the world are those of outsiders and heterodox persons.
They falsely claim to be masters and steal the words and phrases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, intermingling them with vulgar, worldly speech to delude the ignorant masses.
These are precisely those whom the current imperial decree prohibits for subverting the truth with heterodox paths;
they are all of this ilk. Since laypeople already possess a desire for goodness, why do they not...
Having taken refuge in the Triple Gem, yet inevitably falling into this false dharma— how can such a person be considered wise?
Furthermore, observe the good men of the present age who have already been able to take refuge.
Regarding the Triple Gem, relying on one's own mundane wisdom and views of being clever and sharp, one gives rise to the inferior mind of Māra.

One treats the five precepts and ten wholesome actions with contempt and fails to practice them; instead, regarding the preference for meditation as the "Supreme Vehicle," one does not cultivate the three karmas.
Thus, having read only a few cases of the Patriarchs' ready-made koans and memorized them in one’s breast, one flaunts a sharp tongue and constantly employs intellectual maneuvers.
Feng: When one attains a subtle realization for oneself and takes this to be correct, one is entirely unaware of what is wrong.

Furthermore, such a person slanders the Mahāyāna sūtras, claiming that they are not worth adopting because they are merely words. They also mock monks of genuine cultivation and authentic practice as followers of the Hīnayāna.

They give rise to all manner of false views and do not believe at all in the laws of cause and effect, sin and merit. To the point of arrogance, they even show contempt for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Monks, you fail to realize that you have fallen into the pit of the karmic obstacles of ignorance and delusion.
With wife and children gathered around you, you are scorched by the confluence of manifold sufferings and afflictions; yet you recklessly point to this present world as the Way.

Such ignorant people are truly objects of great pity. Since you possess even a single thought directed toward the Ultimate, why not make it authentically real and establish a firm foundation for yourself?
Regarding this effort: it is said that "a hundredth part of speaking is not equal to a single part of practicing.
To speak such idle words is like a poor man who falsely claims to be an emperor and brings his own execution upon himself—how lamentable! I earnestly exhort the virtuous gentlemen of the world.
Those who are intelligent and of sharp faculties, and who are determined to transcend birth and death, should examine their own capacities.
While Zen meditation is indeed a supreme practice, it was taught by the Buddhas and Patriarchs specifically for those of the highest caliber. You should each examine yourselves:
Are you truly of the highest caliber? Can you truly achieve sudden awakening in every instance? Can you truly [attain it] in this very moment?

Will you then be able to bring an end to the cycle of birth and death for a hundred kalpas? If your faculties are not of the highest grade, you should instead assess your own strength and single-mindedly cultivate the gate of the Pure Land.
Dedicate your merits toward the West, vowing to be born in Sukhāvatī and forever abandon the sufferings of Saṃsāra.
This dharma-gate has been practiced as a cause since antiquity; the number of monastics and laypeople who have relied upon it to transcend birth and death is beyond counting.
This is what is meant by "Ten thousand practice, ten thousand depart. It is the most stable and reliable, the great Dharma-gate that is not mistaken by even a single hair's breadth.
As the Patriarch said: "There is only the shortcut of cultivation: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. By means of this Dharma-gate...
This is entirely without error. If you can set aside both body and mind and practice according to this, the rules for what ought to be practiced are briefly indicated below.
First, regarding the single gate of the Pure Land:
it is often discussed by scholars and officials, yet they claim it is established solely for those of middling or inferior faculties; this is most certainly not the case.
Know that this gateway universally encompasses the three faculties and leaves no capacity untapped; it is most vast and expansive, yet also simple and easy to practice.

Indeed, among the ancient patriarchs, there were many who, after attaining realization of the Way, turned their minds toward the Pure Land—such as the great patriarchs Yongming and Zhongfeng, who were by no means alone.
However, in the practice of *nianfo*, there are superior, middling, and inferior levels.
Because the three faculties (indriya) differ, the nine grades of the Pure Land also have distinctions based on those faculties.
Furthermore, there are three types of Pure Lands: first, the Land of Constant Quiescent Light; second, the Land of Real Reward Adornments;

and third, the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder. This last refers to the Land of Co-residence for Ordinary Beings and Sages. Moreover, because the causes cultivated for these three lands are different, [the results vary].
The experiences realized therein are each distinct; let me briefly describe them.
First is the Land of Constant Tranquil Light, which is what the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* calls the "Great Treasury of Luminosity.

Within this realm, the holy and the ordinary are equal, and the environment and its inhabitants are inseparable. It is solely the Buddha’s Dharma-body, profound and eternally tranquil—the very Dharma-body realized by all Buddhas.

This realm is the dwelling place of those who, following only the various patriarchs above, have attained sudden enlightenment into the Dharma-body through a single thought and have entered the Buddha-realm by wondrously harmonizing with its identical essence.
This is precisely the Pure Land for those of the highest capacity; how could it be lightly regarded as being established for those of middling or inferior capacity?
Second is the Land of True Reward Adornments. This is the Flower Treasury World (*kusumagarbha-lokadhātu*) with its twenty tiers;
it is the wondrous land of infinite adornments, commensurate with the measure of the Dharma-realm, brought forth through the cultivation of countless eons by me, Śākyamuni Buddha (Vairocana).
This refers to what is taught in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra regarding the infinitely layered adornments of the world-systems. This is the realm where the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) Buddha dwells;

it is a pure land specifically for the sake of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) who turn the Great Wheel of Dharma. It is not accessible to those of the two vehicles, such as the Śrāvakas.
Neither seen nor heard—these are precisely those who received their predictions at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Having awaited the cultivation of causes over many kalpas, they shall eventually experience this portion of the Pure Land herein; it is by no means an ordinary realm that can be reached with ease.
The third is the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder, also called the Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages. This is precisely the nine grades of distinction;
it is the transformation land of Amitābha Buddha. Within the Flower Treasury World (Huazang Shijie), there are twenty tiers.
From the first tier, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field surrounding it, small at the bottom and large at the top, like an inverted stupa.
From this point upward, the dimensions double at each successive level until reaching the thirteenth layer.
This Sahā world, however, is the central principal realm among these thirteen layers. The Land of Ultimate Bliss is equal in size to the Sahā world;
it extends from the center to the western edge of the flower petals. Therefore, it is said that it lies beyond ten trillion Buddha-lands, situated side by side with the Sahā world.
As for this: among all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, only the Sahā world is defiled and evil.

Filled with earth, stones, and various mountains, and teeming with the impurities of the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties where all sufferings converge, it is called "Endurance. Because its sentient beings are stubborn and most difficult to discipline and transform, I—
Although Śākyamuni Buddha transformed and guided humans and devas through the ten wholesome paths, they remained within birth and death and had not yet escaped saṃsāra.

Furthermore, if one were to engage in Chan meditation to awaken the mind, sudden enlightenment is difficult to achieve. Therefore, he established the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, which is called "transcending the three realms horizontally" by relying upon [the Buddha's power].

Through the power of the vows made during Amitābha Buddha’s causal stage, he vowed that if there were sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who could recite his name yet fail to be born in his land, he would not attain buddhahood.

Relying upon this power of the vow, anyone who recites the Buddha’s name will certainly be welcomed by Amitābha and born in that Pure Land; therefore, birth there is easy. Furthermore, this Pure Land is opened into nine grades.
Regarding the grades: if one has practiced Chan and awakened to the mind, yet is unable to forget the state of mind and its objects, they will be reborn in the highest-of-the-high grade.

If there is one who practices the Buddha-remembrance with single-mindedness and without distraction, they will be reborn in the high-middle grade. If there is one who has not yet awakened through practicing Chan, but whose recitation of the name is pure and diligent...

If one adorns oneself with the myriad practices, one will be born in the upper or middle grades. If one cultivates the myriad practices, upholds Mahāyāna sutras, and single-mindedly recites the Name while aspiring for rebirth, one will be born in the three middle grades.

Those who diligently observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, focus their minds on mindfulness of the Buddha, and make vows of dedication—whether monastic or lay—mostly attain rebirth in the three lower grades.
Although these individuals have not yet severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), [they are nonetheless assured of rebirth].

By merely attaining birth in that land, one beholds the Buddha, hears the Dharma, and dwells on the stage of non-retrogression, never again falling into the cycle of birth and death within the triple world.
From this point, if one makes a vow to return to the triple world to deliver sentient beings, one will come and go with mastery, unbound by the afflictions of birth and death.
Therefore, Master Yongming said: "If one merely attains the sight of Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment?"
This is what awakening is. This single Dharma-gate can be accomplished through a lifetime of sincere devotion.

Once born there, one is instantly liberated from birth and death and forever escapes the cycle of saṃsāra. Given such a direct and expedient Dharma-gate, why would one fail to practice it, or even slight it?

Now, while it is difficult to resolve birth and death through Zen meditation, it is easy to resolve birth and death through the recitation of the Buddha’s name; it requires only a single thought-moment of the person.
This is truly a sincere and earnest plea. Since antiquity, those born in the Pure Land have been immeasurable and innumerable;
yet, though they are seen by the eyes of the world, people do not believe it. If this is so, what other teaching could one possibly trust? I now exhort you, O wise and intelligent gentlemen:
you should trust your own minds and must not mistakenly believe in false doctrines. Even within the Dharma gates, there is the practice of cultivating both Chan and Pure Land together.

There are many such individuals. As Yongming said regarding the practice of nianfo and chan, or chan and nianfo—what is known as "possessing both Chan and Pure Land"—such a person is like a tiger with horns:
in this life they serve as a teacher for others, and in the future they will become a Buddha or Patriarch.

This is indeed the most supreme practice. It stands in a relationship as vast as that between heaven and the abyss to those who falsely claim to have realized the Way and thereby fall into the great transgression of false speech.

It is because all sentient beings, having become deluded regarding their inherently existing Buddha-nature, have fallen into the cycle of birth and death within the three realms and transmigrated through the sufferings of the six destinies.

That they remain submerged for long kalpas and fail to attain liberation is entirely due to greed, anger, ignorance, and craving, which serve as the basis for various evil karmas such as lust, killing, stealing, and falsehood; thus, from body to body, they are driven by sexual desire.
To rectify one's destiny and nature: throughout birth after birth, parents, wives, children, and the six classes of kinsmen and relatives bind one with the ties of affection.
Burned by the great fires of the three realms, there is not a single person who can escape them.
Therefore, my original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, within the Land of Constant Quiescent Light, gave rise to a heart of great compassion to rescue those in suffering, and relinquished...
Delighting in the Dharma by its very nature, he descended from Tuṣita to the imperial palace and entered his mother’s womb. He renounced his parents, wife, and children;
he severed the deep and heavy bonds of worldly affection; he suddenly cast aside the rank of a Wheel-Turning King and fled into the Snowy Mountains to shave off his hair and beard.
For six years he endured freezing cold and hunger, practicing asceticism until he attained enlightenment and became a Buddha.
This is the very model of one who leaves the household life for the sake of transcending birth and death. Even after attaining Buddhahood, he again encountered demonic harms;

he underwent the calamities of the golden spear and the horse-barley, enduring all manner of hardships with patience. He was prepared to sacrifice his own body and life, suffering through the countless afflictions of demonic adversaries.
For forty-nine years, he preached the Dharma; it was nothing other than a single thought of compassion, intended solely to deliver sentient beings and rescue them from suffering.
This was his only concern, and there was no other matter besides this.

Therefore, among the one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples at the assembly on Vulture Peak, all were men of singular brilliance and heroic resolve who had studied the practices of the Buddha and each had renounced [their worldly attachments].

Having departed from the worldly attachments to parents, wives, and children, he relied upon the Buddha for practice, fully realized the nature of such attachments, and attained liberation from birth and death, realizing the fruit of Arhatship.
Just as Ānanda was the younger brother of the Buddha, he likewise followed him into the monastic life and underwent suffering alongside the assembly;
this is my [disciple].

This is the model for the disciples whom the Buddha delivered through ordination. During the Buddha’s lifetime, there were disciples who had entered the monastic life under him but did not know the methods of spiritual practice;
therefore, the Buddha established precepts based on specific incidents to cause them to cease evil and guard against wrongdoing.
Because they attain correct cultivation, those who have first left the household life are called *śrāmaṇeras*. For them, there are the ten precepts;
upon becoming a *bhikṣu*, there are the two hundred and fifty precepts. When women leave the household life, they are called *bhikṣuṇīs*, for whom there are the five hundred major precepts.
This extends even to kings, ministers, officials, and lay devotees (*gṛhapati*), whether they are householders or renunciants.
When the fourfold assembly advances to cultivate the Bodhisattva Great Precepts, there is the Brahmajāla Sūtra, which expounds the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts.
These various precepts are the family law of our Buddha-dharma gate;
therefore it is said: "If a person receives the Buddha-precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas. If...
Those who belong to the Sangha yet do not receive the precepts are called "shaven-headed thieves. They have stolen the Buddha’s kashaya robe and trade upon the Tathagata;
they are not disciples of the Buddha. This is why serving the Dharma within the Sangha is so difficult. Furthermore, when the Buddha was in the world, the human lifespan was one hundred years.

The Buddha’s lifespan was originally to have been one hundred years; however, because he perceived that the disciples of the Final Dharma lacked merit, he remained in the world for only eighty years, leaving behind twenty years of unexhausted merit for the benefit of future generations.
Therefore, the offerings of the four requisites made by present-day disciples are all the utilization of a single portion of the merit from within my Buddha’s white-hair light (ūrṇā-kośa).
This is equivalent to the donor’s gift of a single grain of rice or a stalk of grain.
Even a gift as small as a blade of vegetable is a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) left by the Buddha.
Yet, those who have now entered the Dharma gate and become monks do not know who the Buddha was, nor do they know for what purpose they exist.
They do not know why they abandoned their parents, left behind their wives and children, shaved off their hair and beards, and dwell in monasteries rather than in secular homes. Furthermore—

Not knowing that they neither plow nor weave, they do not understand from where their food and clothing come. They merely claim that they themselves possess such capability that they can transform offerings from donors;
yet they remain ignorant of the donor’s faith, which is as difficult to digest as fat or blood.

In the future, they shall drag plows and pull harrows, with bits in their mouths and saddles upon their backs—such will be the bitterness of their retribution. Thus, the great masses are all collectively bewildered and distressed.

As for those who know: if they were to enjoy themselves in this manner, it might still be tolerable if they were able to roughly maintain their observance of the precepts, uphold the sūtras, practice mindfulness of the Buddha, and preserve their fundamental duty.
Yet, how much more so when they are entirely ignorant of the nature of the Sangha, do not receive the precepts, and let their bodies and minds run wild?

They pursue worldly relatives, enter and exit [the monastery] without restraint, and do not avoid scandal or reproach; they even go so far as to violate the Dharma and transgress prohibitions. Completely...

Those who do not know what is wrong are, moreover, of more than one kind. In the end, they do not know for what purpose they have left the household life, for what purpose they have abandoned the secular world, or for what purpose they have shaved off their hair and beards.
Not only are they ignorant of the matters of spiritual practice, but even regarding the burning of incense and bowing to the Buddha, they remain unaware.

The heart that reverently serves the Triple Gem is utterly forgotten; one drifts through a lifetime, living and dying in a drunken stupor, entirely unaware of the path of authentic practice for those who have left the household life.
Even when such a path is seen, it is instead regarded as wrong. This is most pitiable. The Buddha said:
"The three miserable realms and the hells are not yet the ultimate suffering; the true suffering is to lose oneself beneath the *kāṣāya*."
The body begins as suffering; in short, it is simply that you do not know what a *saṃgha* is. Therefore, the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections* says:
The Buddha said, "You bhikṣus, every morning you should rub your own heads. If you are willing to rub your own heads, then..."
Reflect upon yourself: why is it that you lack both hair and beard? It is because you do not know the rules for leaving home according to the Buddha-dharma;

thus, the teacher does not become a teacher, and the disciple likewise does not become a disciple. The distinction between superior and inferior is severed, and you roam in the company of birds and beasts.
You know only the urgency of food and clothing, yet you have no awareness at all of the matter of birth and death, nor do you fear what lies ahead.
Regarding the sufferings of the three miserable realms, the world has allowed such customs to become the prevailing norm, treating them as ordinary matters.

There are even those who leave their hometowns to wander about seeking their fortunes, yet they know nothing but the communal meals of monasteries; they remain utterly ignorant of the Buddha-Dharma and the Way of Chan.
This is truly most pitiable. Alas! The time since the Sage departed is remote, and the Dharma-gate has fallen into decay. One...
It has reached this point; it cannot be saved. Nevertheless, even in a village of ten households, there must be those who are loyal and sincere.
How could it be that among the various mountains today there are no men of heroic spirit and talent?

If in each region there were but one or two who were willing to resolve their minds and exert themselves, there would naturally be an opportunity for transformation. Therefore, for now, I look only to you, O Abbot, [to take up the burden].
All you who possess the aspiration for the Way should reflect and turn back; you must contemplate the great matter of birth and death and resolutely reform your past errors.
Arouse a single thought directed toward the Path. At the very beginning of this resolve, you must first seek out a virtuous teacher (kalyāṇamitra) and receive the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera.
If you maintain these ten precepts without transgression, you may then advance to the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu.
Examine each and every precept in meticulous detail, even until you proceed to receive the Brahma-net Bodhisattva Great Precepts.

For the Buddha established his teachings with the three trainings—precept, concentration, and wisdom—as the foundation for attaining Buddhahood; that is to say, concentration arises from the precepts.
From concentration arises wisdom; these constitute the three trainings in the outflow-free (anāsrava). The various characteristics of the precepts are fully recorded in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra;

please examine them for yourselves rather than having them listed here in detail. Once you have received the precepts, whether dwelling alone or in a community, you must certainly recite the code of precepts before the Buddha every half-month.
Should there be any transgressions, one must repent before the assembly and reform.
To renew oneself, one’s body and mind become pure and karmic obstacles are eliminated; this is the essential means for escaping suffering.
Since upholding the precepts constitutes the foundation of spiritual practice, one should draw near to the Buddha-dharma.
Even if one cannot leave one's home to attend lectures elsewhere, one should personally resolve to single-mindedly recite Mahāyāna sūtras, such as the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, *Awakening of Faith*, *Śūraṅgama Samādhi*, and other Mahāyāna sūtras, the seeds for the causes and conditions of prajñā are planted.

However, if there are those whose resolve is dedicated exclusively to the single gate of the Western Pure Land, they take the recitation of the Buddha’s name as their primary practice (*maulī-pratipatti*) and the recitation of Mahāyāna sūtras as their auxiliary practice (*anukūla-pratipatti*).
One should make vows and dedicate merit during the six periods of the day and night, seeking liberation from the miserable realms of birth and death.
Only in this way will one not fail the immense karmic conditions for leaving the household life, nor will one spend this life in vain.

If there are those of superior capacity who resolve to abandon worldly affairs and, taking up the mendicant’s staff, seek out a spiritual mentor (kalyāṇamitra) with the intent to investigate the great matter of birth and death beneath their own very feet—then, simply...
One must maintain a single thought-moment and seek nothing further outside of this; this is the vessel for the most supreme vehicle (Ekayāna).
Yet, if one simply gives rise to the heart of resolve, there will certainly come a time of clear realization and awakening; it depends on how each individual’s faculties and aspirations are.
Although the aforementioned practices of observing the precepts, cultivating meditation, reciting sutras, and chanting the Buddha's name cannot bring about sudden enlightenment by themselves...
O mind, do not let this time pass in vain; do not fail the very opportunity for which you have left the household life.

If you remain indolent and indulge your passions, you will achieve nothing until death—is this not a cause for great sorrow? To let this present life go to waste and fall into the three miserable realms means that one knows not when one shall emerge from them again in the future.

The methods of practice for householders and renunciants as described above, though differing in depth, are the teachings expounded by our Buddha during the first twenty years of his appearance in the world.
However, the Buddha taught the Dharma for forty-nine years.

The Dharma taught consists of three vehicles, namely the Small, the Middle, and the Great. During the first twenty years, he taught only the doctrine of existence, which is called the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
This teaches that there is the suffering of birth and death within the three realms from which one may emerge, and that there are two vehicles of nirvana to be sought.
There are the causes and effects of the good path for humans and devas; there are the causes and effects of the three miserable realms resulting from evil karma.

All phenomena are truly existent; therefore, they are called the Dharma of the Four Truths (*catur-ārya-satya*). "Truth" (*satya*) means reality. The Four Truths are: suffering (*duḥkha*), accumulation (*samudaya*), and cessation (*nirodha*).

The Path consists of four factors. First, it is truly and substantially that there is suffering to be experienced. Regarding the "origin" (*samudaya*): it refers to the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, and craving.

It is said that these afflictions are the cause of all sufferings and are capable of summoning the fruit of suffering; therefore, it is truly and substantially that there is a collection of afflictions that can be severed.
Regarding "cessation" (*nirodha*): it refers to the partial emptiness of *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles outside the three realms, because it transcends [samsara].
One realizes this bliss of *nirvāṇa* at death; therefore, it is said that there truly exists a *nirvāṇa* to be realized.
As for the "Path," it refers to the method of practice cultivated by those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

It consists of revulsion toward suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the aspiration for cessation, and the cultivation of the path—namely, the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) and the five meditations for settling the mind (*pañcavipaśyanāsthiti*), which involve contemplating the impurity of the body, contemplating sensation as suffering, and contemplating the mind as impermanent.
There is the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). Furthermore, there are contemplations of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and so forth;

these are called the methods for transcending suffering practiced by those of inferior faculties. This is termed the teaching of the Hīnayāna. Moreover, there is a class of practitioners with moderate faculties and limited sharpness who are termed followers of the Madhyamāyāna (the Middle Vehicle).

For them, the four truths previously mentioned are expanded upon to explain the doctrine of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*), namely: ignorance conditions volitional formations (*avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*); volitional formations condition...

Consciousness. Conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form. Conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases. Conditioned by the six sense bases is contact. Conditioned by contact is feeling. Conditioned by feeling is craving. Conditioned by craving is grasping.
Conditioned by grasping is becoming. Conditioned by becoming is birth. Conditioned by birth are old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.

These are called the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). These twelve links encompass the causes and effects of the three periods of time: namely, two links in the past are the cause; [the remaining ten are the effect]. Unconditioned...
The "clearly understood" refers to the five present factors of the fruit, namely from consciousness through sensation; the three present factors of the cause, namely craving, grasping, and becoming;
and the two future factors of the fruit, namely birth and aging-and-death, including sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. "Conditioning" means leading forth;

it refers to the cycle of cause and effect across the three periods of time, which exists through mutual conditioning and leading forth. This is for a person of medium faculties to contemplate these twelve links of dependent origination.
There are two gates: the gate of saṃsāra and the gate of cessation. That which proceeds from ignorance through to old age and death is the gate of saṃsāra.
If ignorance ceases, then all twelve links of existence cease; this is the gate of cessation.

By contemplating these in both direct and reverse order, one realizes non-arising and attains the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha’s solitary awakening. This is the Dharma of the Middle Vehicle. These are the teachings of the Two Vehicles.
He taught for twenty years as a provisional means because their faculties were dull and inferior, rendering them incapable of receiving the Great Vehicle.

Following these twenty years, as their faculties gradually became more open and receptive, he then taught the Dharma of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) practiced by Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas—namely, giving (dāna), ethical discipline (śīla), patience (kṣānti), diligence (vīrya), meditative concentration (dhyāna), and wisdom (prajñā). These six constitute the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva path.

What is thus cultivated is called the Mahāyāna. If one cultivates these six perfections solely to deliver sentient beings below and to seek the fruit of Buddhahood above, this dharma of the six perfections takes Prajñā as its sovereign.
Therefore, during the second turning of the wheel, the Buddha taught the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras for twenty-two years;
these sūtras are the most numerous. Of those that have come to this land, there are eight versions of the Prajñāpāramitā, totaling six hundred [fascicles].

Volume. This sutra exclusively discusses the wisdom of the *prajñā* of true emptiness. It shatters the views of existence regarding both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa held by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
It extensively expounds the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), as well as the dharmas such as the four noble truths and the twelve links of dependent origination;

all of these take the *prajñā* of true emptiness as their ultimate standard. It refines away previous attachments to the view of existence, just as in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which is entirely [composed of] *prajñā*.
As for its ultimate principle: the emptiness adhered to by the two vehicles of the past was a partial emptiness, namely an emptiness of annihilation.
This present Prajñā, however, is the true emptiness of the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*).

Since the Buddha taught the three contemplations of emptiness, provisional existence, and the middle way as the sublime gateway to attaining Buddhahood, this single volume of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* alone expounds exclusively upon the contemplation of emptiness; therefore, it serves as the entry point.
This is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna and the sublime dharma for the practice of Bodhisattvas. In the Sanskrit language it is *prajñā*, which here is translated as "wisdom.
Therefore, when Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings, they take wisdom as their primary guide; as it is said: "Without wisdom, skillful means are bondage;

with wisdom, skillful means are liberation. Now, although this single gate of the contemplation of emptiness is contained within the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā* scriptures, it is in fact the most direct [path].
Essentially, it is contained within the fourteen lines of the Heart Sūtra; the entirety of karma is already encompassed therein.
Furthermore, this single scroll of the Heart Sūtra is condensed into the single phrase, "perceiving that the five aggregates are all empty," which exhausts its full meaning.
Within this single phrase, if one applies oneself to the practice, it rests solely upon the character "perceive" (zhào). This is the most concise and essential dharma-gate.
However, regarding the practice of the Chan school, the initial effort of applying the mind consists solely of the single character "zhào" (illumination).
This dharma-gate of this one character was what our Buddha waited thirty years to preach.

Judging from this, how could the method for cultivating the mind be something easily explained or easily practiced by ordinary people? This dharma-gate of one character is what is called "teaching the bodhisattvas."
This is indeed the Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
It is the fundamental intention of the Buddha’s appearance in the world: to directly cause all sentient beings to attain Buddhahood, with no other purpose whatsoever.
Thus, the teachings of one lifetime spoken over forty-nine years now constitute the Great Canon of the Tripitaka; they are all for the purpose of learning and realization.

In the Buddha’s Dharma-gate, though there are the six perfections and myriad practices with their various and numerous approaches, the primary intent is simply that the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) constitute the foundation for attaining Buddhahood.
These three contemplations are emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*upāya*), and the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*).

Throughout the entirety of the teachings of a single lifetime, it is only these three contemplations that are explained; from the preceding teachings up until those of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it is only then that...
Having just spoken of the single gate of the contemplation of emptiness, one thereby knows that the Dharma is not easily explained, nor is it easily entered.

Yet, during the assembly at the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, those of the two vehicles who were present and heard the teaching all considered Prajñā to be beyond the scope of their own wisdom and did not partake of it at all;
how much more so for those who had personally received the Buddha’s teachings for thirty years, yet still did not believe or enter?

Nowadays, ordinary people of evil karma speak of emptiness at every turn, falsely proclaiming the dharma of emptiness, asserting that there are no Buddhas and no patriarchs, and that there is neither cultivation nor realization;
they then claim for themselves to be individuals of the highest capacity. Are these not truly great liars?

Only after the Buddha had already taught the contemplation of the true emptiness of *prajñā* did he then teach the contemplation of the provisional. This gate of contemplation is what is expounded in the sutras.

This refers to the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, which expounds the Dharma-gate of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). That is to say, delusion regarding the Tathāgatagarbha is termed the *ālayavijñāna*.
Based upon this *ālaya*, it possesses three divisions that transform to give rise to the sense organs, the body, and the receptacle world.
All mountains, rivers, the great earth, sentient beings, and the provisional phenomena of the world are but shadows transformed by consciousness, like images within a mirror.
It is like the moon in water: it exists, yet is not real; therefore, it is called "provisional. Question: For what reason did the Buddha teach the contemplation of the provisional?
Answer: Because those of the two vehicles previously clung to *nirvāṇa* as being substantially existent, they fell into a biased emptiness.
Therefore, the Buddha taught the true emptiness of *prajñā* to destroy the view that clings to existence, and thus caused them to contemplate *prajñā*.
