Regarding the true mark of ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), there is another class of bodhisattvas who delight in the superiority of emptiness; they cling to mere emptiness and are unable to engage with existence, refusing to deliver sentient beings.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that the bodies, minds, and worlds of all sentient beings are all manifestations of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) and are entirely conventional phenomena.
By means of this dharma-gate of consciousness-only, he harmonizes emptiness and existence, intending to reveal that which is "identical to emptiness" (*śūnyatā-svabhāva*).

The existence of these [phenomena] is precisely the emptiness of their existence. By directly contemplating *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) to realize *tathatā* (suchness), this constitutes the dharma-gate for bodhisattvas prior to formal instruction to emerge from emptiness and enter the provisional in order to save sentient beings.

Therefore, regarding this single contemplative gate, it is taught in profound and esoteric sūtras such as the *Ghanavyūha*. When this sūtra was being expounded, those bodhisattvas of great capacity were already able to believe and accept it, whereas those of lesser...
Those rooted in the Two Vehicles do not dare to enter the secular world to benefit sentient beings.
Therefore, the Buddha preached the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, wherein the layman Vimalakīrti manifests living among the laity with a wife, children, and retinue.

Using the pretext of inquiring after his illness as a cause and condition, he engages in dialogue with Mañjuśrī on the Dharma-gate of Non-duality, thereby rebuking the followers of the Two Vehicles and inciting them to develop the resolve to enter the secular world to save sentient beings.

This teaching is named "Refuting the Partial and Rejecting the Small" and "Praising the Great and Extolling the Perfect. It serves as an inconceivable Dharma-gate for those of the Lesser Vehicle, intended to dispel the narrow and inferior views of the two vehicles.
This is the profound compassion and great mercy of our Buddha, employing various skillful and expedient means to lead those of lesser faculties into the Mahāyāna.

This is indeed so. One thus knows that the Bodhisattva’s work of engaging with the mundane world to benefit sentient beings is truly beyond the capacity of those with inferior roots and weak faculties.
Even after more than forty years of the merit of his teaching and transformation, such skillful means and spiritual power are still required.

In these present five turbidities, those caught in the ocean of suffering of afflictions and birth-and-death speak of emptiness at every turn, discourse on Chan and the Way, and constantly take the "point above" as their own responsibility.
They hold the True Dharma in contempt, fear neither cause nor effect, and lack self-reflection; how can they be so deluded and arrogant? Observe me...
The Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) for benefiting sentient beings involved how much arduous effort; he did not dare lightly speak a single word of teaching people to become Buddhas.
Yet nowadays, people constantly claim to "surpass the Buddhas and transcend the patriarchs"—if this is not delusion, what is it? Should one not be fearful of this?

Since my Buddha appeared in the world and preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, the various sutras he compiled comprise a great canon; yet from beginning to end, he has spoken only eight characters:
namely, "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. From the start until now, this has already been so.
After forty years, he finally explained the meaning of the single phrase "all phenomena are consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
Yet, he still did not dare to reveal the principle of "mind-only" (*cittamātra*), for mind-only is the ultimate standard of all phenomena.

Since the time of the ancient masters, the great disciples had already heard the Dharma-gate of consciousness-only; therefore, from this point onward, he preached the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to reveal it.
The Dharma-gate of "The Three Realms are Mind-Only" seeks directly to lead people to awaken to this single mind as the ultimate principle.
By subsuming the two preceding types of emptiness and their provisional designations, and by dissolving the two truths, all are brought back to the single mind.

Only then is the single mind made complete and fused into the Middle Way, which constitutes the finality of principle. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Quiescent extinction is called the single mind; the single mind..."

This is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. That which is termed the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is itself the *tathāgatagarbha*. It is neither empty nor existent; it points directly to the one mind.

Transcending names and severing all marks, it dissolves the distinction between the holy and the ordinary. It does not belong to the gradations of cultivation or realization. To suddenly contemplate the nature of this storehouse is called the realm of self-awakened noble wisdom.
One directly abandons all攀缘 (*pán yuán*, objectifying/dependent) deluded minds; one simply realizes that false thoughts have no inherent nature.

One immediately awakens to non-arising; this is the Dharma-gate of the Sudden Teaching. The Patriarch Bodhidharma transmitted it to the Second Patriarch, Master Ke, taking this sutra as the seal of his heart.
Therefore, this sutra alone reaches those of the highest faculties, while those of the two vehicles are excluded from its scope.
Under the gate of the Patriarchs, those who first study Chan must transcend mind, intellect, and consciousness in their practice;
they must transcend the realm of deluded thoughts and seek to exit the paths of ordinary beings and sages. This is precisely taking this sutra alone as the ultimate principle.
This teaching expounds the supreme rule of the one mind. More than forty years have passed since I have extensively revealed it through various means, traversing countless methods.

Chapter: Now, as this sutra is being expounded, even those of inferior capacity find their portion utterly severed. As for the monastics and laypeople of today, their eye of the teachings is not yet clear;

they have no path for cultivation and remain in blind ignorance. Within their own minds, they engage in the攀缘 (pān-yuan—clinging to objects) of deluded thoughts, entirely unaware of the number of times these arise and cease.
Day and night, they have never experienced a single moment of cool clarity. Therefore, one must transcend the mind and intention toward the higher [truth].
With a single point of attachment, they take it as their own responsibility; yet they have not even dreamed of the "critical phrase" (huatou), and thus they open wide mouths to speak of Chan.
How can their self-deception be described? They may be called people utterly devoid of shame; how can they not stand in awe?
Moreover, today there are not only ignorant laypeople who talk recklessly; even the junior monks within our own Dharma gate have heard nothing at all.

Regarding the Buddhist methods for cultivating the mind, they have no understanding whatsoever of the practice of mental application; they merely indulge in discursive thoughts for as long as they wish.
Lacking any correct insight (samyag-dṛṣṭi), they claim to have realized the Way and consider themselves sufficient. This, moreover, is whom they deceive and whom they mislead?
Be cautious, be cautious! Be careful, be careful!
It was only forty years after the Buddha’s passing that he revealed the Dharma-gate of One Mind.
This sufficiently demonstrates that the Dharma is not easily taught, not easily practiced, and not easily realized.
Only our Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared in this world specifically for the sake of the one great cause and condition.

This "one great matter" refers to the Buddha's knowledge and vision possessed by sentient beings. Because sentient beings inherently possess the Buddha's knowledge and vision, they are now deluded regarding it.

Yet they possess the knowledge and views of delusive thoughts regarding birth and death. Throughout kalpas, they have been lost in confusion and unaware of it—like a destitute son who carries a jewel while begging for alms, needlessly enduring toil and hardship.
Therefore, the Buddha gives rise to great compassion of the same essence and appears specifically in the world to reveal and instruct them.
He causes sentient beings to awaken to and enter into the Buddha’s innate knowledge and vision, just as one points out what was already there.
It is like the jewel within the garment of the impoverished son; it merely causes him to know of its existence so that he may come to enjoy its benefits.

Now, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is precisely what is described in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* as "the single mind," which is termed "the holy wisdom of self-awakening. [The Buddha] never dared to speak of it all at once.
Because he observed that the faculties of sentient beings were dull and incapable of receiving this Dharma, he long kept this essential teaching in silence and did not strive to proclaim it hastily.

Only after forty years had passed, when their capacities had been refined through various methods of training and his work of transformation was nearing its end, did he preach the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to reveal the gateway of the One Mind, establishing it as the ultimate expression of principle. Following this, he then preached the *Dharmapada*.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* reveals the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in order to manifest the ultimate realization of phenomena; this is the sequence of the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.
Only when both principle and phenomena are fully realized does one reach the ultimate limit of the single mind.

Therefore, it is only upon reaching this point that those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) finally believe in the Buddha-mind with certainty and without doubt, and also awaken to their own inherent Buddha-nature, which they had previously failed to perceive.

It is lost. For example, it is like a destitute son who has long fled to another country and has only now returned to see his father. He also believes that the father’s family estate was originally his own;
with hearts that trust one another and a mutual understanding, he is capable of inheriting the family estate, and thus the elder entrusts it to him.

It is often said that this single *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is like the written testament by which the elder entrusts his family estate; it is the ultimate means for the Buddha to benefit sentient beings.
This was his fundamental intention. Therefore, the Buddha bestowed individual predictions upon all his disciples, declaring that they would certainly attain Buddhahood in the future;

he even stated that among all who have heard the Dharma, there is not one who will not become a Buddha. Thus, this Great Matter of Cause and Condition (*mahā-kāraṇa*) has been completed, and it is for this reason that it is designated as the Final Teaching (*paryanta-śāsana*).
Not long after this, he entered *nirvāṇa*. However, during the single occasion of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he had already exhausted [the purpose of] my...
The Buddha’s fundamental intention in appearing in the world to benefit sentient beings is fully realized in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

This scripture elucidates the meaning of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) in order to gather those whose capacities were not yet exhausted by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and to shatter the lingering doubts of his disciples that remained unresolved prior to this teaching.

For the Buddha declared that among all who hear the Dharma, there is not one who will not attain Buddhahood; he did so out of concern that his disciples might harbor the notion—previously heard—that even those of indeterminate nature (*icchantika*) lack the capacity for faith.
People might harbor doubts, thinking that certain individuals are not permitted to attain Buddhahood; therefore, this sutra teaches that even icchantikas possess Buddha-nature.

Thus, by taking the butcher Guang'e as an example—who simply set down his butcher's blade and performed the work of a Buddha—it is shown that those with any degree of understanding will ultimately achieve Buddhahood without any doubt.
Only in this way is the purpose of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world fully realized through this single act of transformation.
The task of benefiting sentient beings has now been completed; therefore, he enters into nirvana.

As explained above, this constitutes the ritual for the transformation of living beings throughout the beginning and end of my Buddha’s appearance in the world, and the dharma-gate for the gradual cultivation of causes. Although...
Observing that sentient beings inherently possess Buddha-nature, each fully endowed with it, there is none who does not aspire to attain Buddhahood.

However, because their afflictions are thick and their karmic offenses are deep-rooted, they are unable to immediately receive the Great Dharma; therefore, the One Vehicle Dharma is taught by being differentiated into three.
This is the reason for the establishment of the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles. Thus, prior to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, there were only the three [vehicles].
The *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* are the provisional teachings of the vehicle; they are the true teachings of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Therefore, Tiantai judged them to be teachings that "open up the provisional to reveal the real. Thus we know that what was taught during the forty years prior were all provisional arrangements, made because the capacities of sentient beings were not equal.
What has been explained above varies in its sudden and gradual approaches, yet it serves generally as both teaching and doctrine.
Now, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* suddenly reveals that the one mind is the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata; is the teaching, then, not the Chan (Zen) school?
As for the World-Honored One himself saying, "In forty-nine years, I have not spoken a single word," and finally plucking a flower to show the assembly—people...
The assembly of hundreds of thousands of devas was utterly bewildered and knew nothing; only Mahākāśyapa alone broke into a smile.
The World-Honored One then said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvāṇa; I entrust them to you.

This is the essential principle of the separate transmission outside the teachings. From this point, it was transmitted twice to Ānanda, continuing through the forty-seven patriarchs of India and reaching the land of the East.

Two or three [generations] later, when the Dharma came from the West, it was designated as the Chan School. It does not rely on words and letters, but points directly at the human mind so that one may see their nature and become a Buddha;
this is called the Dharma-gate of Single Transmission. Thus, from Caoxi downward, there arose two branches and five schools.

The *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) records seventeen hundred people, all of whom were Great Beings who realized the mind. Whatever sayings or phrases they left behind are termed *gong'an*. By means of these—
Chan is fundamentally beyond words; yet, these few phrases have been preserved as evidence for the seal of the mind, much like legal documents in a worldly court.
It is not intended that people take these as the actual Dharma, nor that they be circulated through speech and hearing to serve as one's own profound and mysterious views. However, I...
The Buddha has already expounded a great treasury of teachings. As for the Dharma-gate of the single mind (*ekacitta*), what is there that it does not encompass?

Why, then, must the "Plucking of the Flower" be taken as the essential core? It is because the principle of the single mind is free from the marks of verbal expression, free from the marks of names and words, and free from the marks of mental conditioning.
Although those who have heard the teachings in the past may have realized their original mind, they were still unable to remain free from these marks.
Therefore, the final act of holding up a flower was a provisional means intended to dispel the habitual tendency toward verbal expression;

it was a treatment for the ailment of clinging to names and words, serving as a golden probe. People today do not understand that the essence of both teaching and Chan is the single mind, which is the Buddha’s skillful means for transforming and delivering sentient beings.
Each person arbitrarily clings to one extreme, considering it to be absolute truth, and thus remains in attachment.
The teaching is not meditation; those who cling to meditation do not possess the teaching. Now, those who cling to the teaching while rejecting meditation have certainly already erred for themselves;

yet those who cling to meditation while rejecting the teaching err even more severely. Because those who cling to meditation stubbornly hold to their own ignorance as being right, they falsely identify with their own views and consider them their own realization.
They disparage the definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna as mere "words," thereby leading [themselves] to the ultimate [delusion].
There is no success. Even more pitiable is the observation of this present age of the Dharma’s decay (*mofa*). The lecture halls have already declined and there are no great masters or craftsmen;
thus, clever youths lack the wisdom born of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*). Even those who are determined to aspire upward toward Zen meditation lack the firm resolve for the long term.
Relying on teachers who lack the "eye of wisdom," they merely follow their own emotions and act with reckless arrogance, thereby leading themselves to fall into error.

Such cases are numerous. This is truly a matter for great lamentation. Furthermore, there are monastics who falsely consider themselves to have realized the Way, deceiving and deluding the ignorant laity while greedily seeking offerings.
To those who take refuge in them, they immediately instruct them in the practice of *chán* (meditation) as the "supreme point" (*xiàng shàng yī zhù*).
Those who believe them find that before their *huàtóu* (critical phrase) has matured, their delusive thoughts run rampant, boiling with feverish agitation.
They then take this as correct and consider themselves to have attained enlightenment regarding the eight stages; consequently, they fall into erroneous views.
Such a thing is more harmful than anything else. This is especially something one must not fail to recognize with fear and reflect upon.

In my humble view, it is not that Zen practice should not be undertaken, but rather that one’s practice lacks authenticity, and that one lacks the long-term, resolute will [to persevere], falsely claiming to have attained enlightenment and thereby erring.

There are very many such people. In my humble opinion, if one merely studies the teachings but cannot practice Chan meditation, or if one practices Chan meditation but lacks determination, it is in every way inferior to focusing the mind exclusively on the Pure Land practice;
at least this will not allow one’s life to pass in vain. The wise can discern this for themselves.
I ask that each of you reflect upon this, and I hope you will not deceive or mislead yourselves.
I have observed that among officials and scholar-gentry, those who have attained realization through Zen meditation have not been few since antiquity;

as recorded in the *Lamp Records*, they were by no means limited to a single individual. Among the officials of the present age, there are many who are determined to protect the Dharma and regard Zen meditation as the supreme path.
This is not like ordinary cases of uniformity, for there is certainly a reason for it. Indeed, in the past, there was a Master... [text continues].
Among those who enter the gate to study Chan, there are those who, though not yet fully awakened, have made vows to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma;
there are also various patriarchs who possessed the power of great vows to deliver sentient beings, as well as Bodhisattvas appearing in the world to save it;

and there are also those who, having previously been among the monastic community, failed to penetrate their investigation due to being led astray by worldly studies, and thus now appear in the world despite being within the realm of conventional truth.
Amidst the dust and toil of worldly existence, the seed of *prajñā* from past habituation has long been present; its radiance breaks through and cannot be concealed.
Thus, it manifests as literary works, fame, and worldly achievements, serving as external supports for the Dharma.

These various skillful means (*upāya*) differ in their functions, and the corresponding practices (*caryā*) are likewise not of a single kind. Some are dedicated exclusively to the upward path, while others focus solely on merit.
Regarding practitioners:
there are those who establish the Three Jewels and vow to protect the Dharma; there are those who act solely for their own sake regarding birth and death;

and there are those who cultivate practice out of loyalty and filial piety. These various modes of conduct are all the Bodhisattva path; one must not view them with a single standard based merely on whether they are practiced within the Sangha.
Nevertheless, among the monastics, there are those who do not understand the two schools of Chan and Teaching. There are those who practice asceticism and the dhūta observances;

there are those who specialize in the cultivation of Pure Land practices; there are those who follow the gates of authentic practice; there are those who assist in the propagation of the Dharma through circumstantial Buddhist activities;
and there are those who recite and transcribe scriptures as a means to seek the gates of practice. All of these are within the Buddha’s...
Among those within the light of the white tuft who seek the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions, one cannot judge them all by a single standard.
Therefore, among officials, anyone who possesses a profound heart for protecting the Dharma is sufficient, even if they possess only a single virtuous practice from among the monastic community.
Furthermore, it is not strictly necessary for every individual to practice *chán* (Zen meditation) in order to constitute the correct practice.
Although practicing *chán* is indeed sublime, in reality, it is not something that those of inferior capacity can achieve.

Yet, during the Buddha’s lifetime, among hundreds of thousands of humans and devas, there was only Kāśyapa alone who attained realization. When Bodhidharma came from the West, he obtained only the Second Patriarch. As for the Yellow... [text truncated]
Among the seven hundred or so followers of Master Mei, only the Sixth Patriarch alone had his mind certified. How could this be a trivial matter?

If one were among the monastic community, even possessing a single practice that could serve as the true business of the Dharma-gate and could transform and teach sentient beings, that person would be a Bodhisattva.
Therefore it is said: "All various practices are the path of the Bodhisattva. If even a single matter can be adopted, one has already transcended to the vehicle.
Rice porridge and meals flow by constantly; those who let time pass in vain are indeed countless. As it is said: "If one takes the long from the short, no person is discarded;
if one takes the short from the long, no person remains whole. From ancient times, both in the mundane world and the world-transcending realm, a "whole person" has been difficult to find.
This is as explained in the preceding entanglements, and so forth.
Regarding the sequence of the ritual for the Buddha’s miraculous birth: does the Buddha not desire that people achieve sudden enlightenment to their own minds and become Buddhas in this very moment?
However, because the faculties of sentient beings are dull, he cannot help but employ skillful means to guide them. As the ancients said:
"If monastics cannot realize their own minds, they should at least apply themselves to the teachings so that their time does not pass in vain. As for me, however—

This refers to the present-day monastics: even if they cannot engage in Chan meditation or study the scriptures, those who are able to uphold the precepts, recite the sutras, perform meritorious deeds, and protect the Dharma are said to be millions of times superior to ordinary demonic types.

Among laypeople, those who can simply observe the fasts, recite the Buddha’s name, and assist in promoting the Three Jewels are all practitioners of true conduct; this is what all the Buddhas hope for.
Furthermore, may the eminent and enlightened scholars of all quarters take confidence in this; pray do not regard these humble words as delusory.
Beyond the formalities of transformation, it is appropriate to manifest them for the multitude of practitioners.
In the winter of the Gui-chou year, the Elder traveled from Guangdong on foot to Mount Nanyue.
On his way, he passed through Yizhang, where more than twenty virtuous men, including Kuang Shaozhen and others, welcomed him at the Scripture Hall.

With great devotion, they prostrated and made offerings, requesting his instruction. He briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma and departed after staying for one night. Subsequently, the Elder...
The Linghu Hermitage was established as a place for the recitation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
In the sixth month of the summer of the year Yimao, Shaozhen and others traveled from afar to pay their respects.

It happened that the Elder was then expounding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for the assembly; they listened with sympathetic joy and were filled with great delight. They offered incense and requested instruction.

Regarding the essential method for practicing while remaining at home, the Elder showed them this way: "One should reside in deep mountains or remote areas where no spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) pass by.
Although there may be many lay faithful there, they have not heard the True Dharma.
Now, each of you should diligently uphold the five precepts as your primary practice. These five precepts were specifically established by our Buddha for those living at home."

The virtuous man says: "These five precepts are identical to the Five Constant Virtues of the Confucianists: benevolence (*ren*), righteousness (*yi*), propriety (*li*), wisdom (*zhi*), and faithfulness (*xin*). Therefore it is said:
'If the five precepts are not observed, the path to the human and celestial realms is cut off. For this reason, a virtuous layperson should reverently uphold them.

Once one has upheld the five precepts, one must not listen to or believe heterodox teachers or heterodox teachings that recklessly preach the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and deny cause and effect, leading to nihilism."

Those of the Buddha-seed who have created karma for the hells should simply rely exclusively on the Buddha’s teachings and cultivate the Dharma-gate of the Western Pure Land with single-minded devotion, taking the recitation of the Buddha's name as the primary practice.
Indeed, among all the gates for guiding and receiving sentient beings, the Pure Land gate provides the most extensive benefit;

throughout ancient and modern times, those who attained rebirth through the recitation of the Buddha's name have been very numerous. However, this depends primarily on being diligent and focused; it is not a matter of mere formality.
Once or twice a month, recite the Buddha’s name several thousand times; in this way, one performs the primary practice.

First, one must resolve the mind, deeply loathing this Saha world as suffering and aspiring with determination to leave it behind. One should maintain the visualization of the Western Pure Land and of being born there by transformation within a lotus flower.
Moment after moment, one must fix the resolve to be reborn in that land and personally behold Amitābha Buddha, taking this as one's fundamental vow. Every day...
Morning and evening, you must establish a fixed practice. Recite either the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Amitābha Sūtra*, or the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha Dhāraṇī*.
You must certainly recite the Buddha’s name and dedicate the merit toward the Western Pure Land, vowing to be reborn there. Make this your constant rule.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, regardless of whether you are busy or idle, active or still, hold the single phrase "Namo Amitābha Buddha" within your heart.
Mindful of it at all times, with the thought-continuum uninterrupted, even within sleep and dreams, one does not forget or lose it.
When this is thus forged into a single mass without any interval or break, it is called the Samādhi of Single Practice.

When this mindfulness becomes fully matured, one is not interrupted by any objective conditions or circumstances; whether eyes are open or closed, the single sound of "Amitābha Buddha" manifests clearly before one.
All worldly attachments—parents, wives, children, and various delusory thoughts of affection and karmic concerns—are entirely consumed and purified by a single recitation of the Buddha’s name.
In this way, one’s own mind attains purity. As the sutra says: "When the mind is pure, the buddha-field is pure.
Reciting the Buddha's name in this manner and applying the mind in this way, when the time of death arrives, [one will have] solely...

If one recites the name of Amitābha Buddha even once while it is present before one’s eyes, with single-mindedness and without distraction, one will naturally behold Amitābha Buddha coming personally to welcome and guide one.
In the space of a single thought-moment, one shall attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

From this point on, one shall forever escape the suffering of birth and death, ascend loftily to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and be born by transformation from a lotus flower; this is what is meant by "reciting the name for a single lifetime."
Such is the efficacy of the Buddhas. If one does not attain rebirth through such single-minded devotion, then the Buddhas would be guilty of speaking falsehoods.
To pass the years in indolence, reciting "Namo Amitābha Buddha" with the mouth while lacking actual practice in the heart, is to deceive and defraud oneself.
Is this not indeed a time for manifest proof? Sons of good family, having already given rise to faith, you must practice accordingly;
by all means, do not deceive yourselves.

The Buddha taught that the birth and death of sentient beings accumulate over long periods of days and nights, revolving through kalpas without ceasing or resting.
This is due to the攀緣 (pān-yuán, object-dependent clinging) of moment-to-moment delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*), which has never for even a single thought-moment found temporary cessation.
Because delusive thoughts are not severed, birth and death are endless; it is precisely because of this that the swift wheel of long kalpas never halts or rests.

The Buddha taught various methods for restraining the mind, all of which serve as a foundation for the wheel of cessation (*nirodha*). Although these dharma-gates are numerous, because sentient beings have heavy defilements and obscured consciousness, it is difficult for them to be gathered and entered [into the path].
Therefore, the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha is the most swift and essential.

As it is said: "By recollecting the Buddha and being mindful of the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future. This is because of the various deluded views of sentient beings.
All [phenomena] belong to birth and death; only the vision of the Buddha is permitted as the dharma for transcending birth and death.

Yet, the vision of the Buddha must arise from mindfulness (*smṛti*). Since deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*) occur without interruption day and night, one specifically employs the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) to sever them.

Out of ten people, only eighteen are called "exalted sages. Thus, those who truly practice the recitation of the Buddha's name are not many.
To regard the recitation of the Buddha's name as an inferior practice today—is this not a failure to truly understand it?

In recent times, only Niusan has taken the recitation of the Buddha's name as his practice, styling himself "The Refiner of Demons. Yet, he was so harsh in his discipline that even day and night... [he could not endure it].

[The practice] was discontinued. Confined to only three winter months, and since people’s circumstances were not uniform, it was difficult to maintain for long. Recently, Yunqi strongly advocated for *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation).
Although he practiced it four times daily, there was sleep during the night, which required the trouble of calling out to rouse others; thus, the method lacked subtlety and precision.
Now, the Dharma Masters Foshe and Xuanjin have each resolved to request [the recitation] throughout the twelve periods of the day. This...
The Dharma is indeed profound and subtle; yet, regarding movement and stillness, as well as eating and drinking, it seems difficult to unify these practices.
If one manages them with proper measure and establishes methods that are appropriate, this is yet another excellent regulation for both ancient and modern times.

I requested further instruction from the Elder, who consequently established a set of regulations so that various affairs would not be cumbersome and the minds of people would be unified. This is a subtle and wondrous practice; thus, he formulated this system.
The regulations are set forth as follows. In establishing a Buddha-recitation assembly (*nianfo hui*), the scale varies according to the number of participants and their aspirations;

it may be extensive or limited. If resources are abundant, there will be many halls; if resources are meager, there will be but one hall. The same principle applies to the personnel: regardless of whether the number of people is large or small, they shall be divided equally into six shifts.

Each shift consists of two sessions for both day and night, with incense sticks distributed in rotation. Participants shall leave their seats in turn to perform prostrations and recitations, and engage in circumambulation and repentance.
Repent of this. As for the rest, all should sit in stillness, silently reciting what they hear or practicing the gates of contemplation according to their aspirations.
This approach emphasizes stillness over movement; it is neither cumbersome nor chaotic, yet the sound of the Buddha’s voice continues uninterrupted.

Thus, delusive thoughts will not arise. Like calling out to one another, one remains neither drowsy nor distracted. Upon entering [samādhi], movement and stillness are as one, and self and others are non-dual, remaining constant both in waking and in sleep.
Always remain thus, without rising from your seat, and you will suddenly behold Amitābha. This is the first wondrous practice of spontaneous fulfillment (*yīruì*).
As for food and drink, you should likewise regulate them according to the Dharma, striving to ensure that the internal and external are one and the same; then, both self and other will be forgotten.
When both right and wrong are extinguished, there is nothing more wondrous than the profound stillness and silence of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

The old man has contemplated this Dharma deeply, yet he feels ashamed that his feet have not yet found firm ground; his heart’s desire remains unfulfilled. Therefore, he specifically reveals it to serve as a vanguard.
In the future, when many people observe and hear of it, it will surely be established everywhere, and the Pure Land will spread throughout China.
There is hope in this. In the Zongjing Tang (Hall of the Mirror of the Source), a covenant for a practice-and-realization dharma-assembly was established.

It states that while the Buddha’s entire Great Canon of Teachings enumerates all various practices, they are all ultimately subsumed under cultivation and realization as the final goal. As it is said:
Based on the one mind, all practices are established; through these myriad practices, one returns to realize the one mind. Thus it is said:

"There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm, and there is nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm. To examine the origin of the Dharma-realm: it belongs neither to delusion nor awakening, nor to the holy nor the ordinary.
It is simply because of the non-awakening of ignorance that one is deluded regarding this one mind. From delusion to further delusion, one creates various karmas. From [self...]

One takes upon oneself the suffering of saṃsāric birth and death. As for what is called "cultivation and realization," it consists merely in purifying the three obstructions of one's own mind and returning to the fundamental nature of that very mind;
therefore, it is termed "realization. It is not that there is a realization existing separately apart from cultivation.
Therefore, the secret instruction for people to practice according to the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is that one must first realize the single mind and purify the three obstacles.
Because the mind is difficult to realize, contemplation is established to penetrate it; because the obstacles are difficult to remove, repentance is established to purify them.
This is precisely the Perfect School of the Dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, which honors Samantabhadra as the eldest son of Vairocana, and through the ten great vows, [establishes this path].

The repentance of karmic obstacles is placed at the forefront. Therefore, from ancient times until now, even when Tiantai personally realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sutra, he still revered the methods of repentance as the sublime practice.
As for the existence of ritual manuals, even Master Yongming—himself a person of the Pure Land—still strictly adhered to and diligently practiced them;
how much more so should others do the same? Alas! In this Dharma-ending age... [text ends]
The Sage has become increasingly distant, while the defilements of sentient beings have grown heavy; their accumulated delusions have become ever deeper.
Since they lack the merit of realization and investigation, and further lack the practice of repentance and the expiation of transgressions, by what dharma can they hope to transcend birth and death?

Only Master Yongming, who fused the entirety of the Great Canon into the principle of Mind-Only, composed a work of one hundred fascicles titled *Zhongjing* (The Mirror of the Source), which endures to this day.

The Hall preserves the *Zhengci* (Pure Compassion). Its text extensively elucidates the single mind (*ekacitta*), like raising the sun and moon in the midst of the sky to illuminate the profound depths of all phenomena.
If students can personally practice it, they will penetrate and see their own minds without waiting for further awakening;
there is no essential method for realization that surpasses this. Regarding the Master’s lifelong personal practice, his daily recitation consisted of one [copy of the] *Lotus Sūtra*.
Ten thousand copies [were made]. He took up the *Tiantai Fahua Chan Yi* (The Ritual for the Lotus Repentance of Tiantai) and practiced it according to the Dharma, making it his constant practice.
Consequently, while he was still dwelling in this world, the Lord of the Underworld depicted his portrait so that others might gaze upon and pay homage to it.

This was because he was one who had transcended birth and death and realized the reality of "mind-only. Today, his writings are still in circulation and his hall remains intact; who could [fail to acknowledge this]?
Is he one who came later to inquire about him? This Dharma Master Xuanjin He is his direct successor.
Having left home from childhood, on the very day he was tonsured at that monastery, he immediately asked about the Great Master’s name and what kind of person he was;

he subsequently resolved to pay homage to his stupa. Could this not mean that he had previously attended upon him as a servant? The Great Master’s stupa has already crumbled, and his hall has already...

The ruins were restored by your lordship’s capable efforts. That the Great Master’s radiant brow-light has once again been released among the mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees is not without cause.

Now, as various conditions have gathered in small measure, your lordship desires to clarify the purport of the Mirror of the School and to cultivate the practice of repentance and realization with refined diligence.
You intend to assemble twelve true Dharma companions to emulate the Perfect [Assembly].

Regarding the path of awakening, I vow to practice for a long period. Dividing the year into four seasons, I shall dedicate twenty-one days in each season to the method of repentance, following the ritual of the *Lotus Sūtra Repentance*.
On other days, I will daily peruse the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) to realize that all is but mind.

Should doubts arise, I shall clarify their meaning for the assembly. Without relying on peripheral branches, I shall take only the direct and immediate approach as my primary investigation, hoping thereby to attain its true fruit.
He took those who had entered the period of training as his exemplars, intending to lead the disciples of this mountain to become fledglings of Zen.

He would refine their wings so that they might take flight together; when the Dharma-nature is realized in its vast emptiness, one ascends to the heavens of enlightenment and makes the sun of wisdom shine brightly—this is the purpose of this undertaking.
As for the regulations for the retreat (jie), they were established according to practical necessity, striving to be simple and easy to practice, authentic and free from artifice.
Thus, one treads upon the ground of reality. However, regarding the four requisites of life, one’s strength is insufficient to sustain oneself;
consequently, one cannot emulate the Tathāgata’s practice of begging for alms day by day while dwelling in retreat. Nor does one dare to hope for the ritual of offerings sent by devas and humans.
Yet, when examining names against reality and resolving to provide support, one places hope in a donor who has awakened such a resolve. Now there is a layman, Tan...
If Meng Xun exerts his strength to lead the way, then all who have a karmic affinity will respond with joyful acclamation.

Since all phenomena arise from conditions and the seed of Buddhahood emerges through conditions, although the conditions of this day are near, the distant path to attaining Buddhahood truly takes this as its initial expedient means. Upon hearing this, the people were filled with joy, and so...

If one breaks through this initial point, then the ultimate fruit lies simply in all those who share the same conditions, the same practice, the same activities, and the same mind, exerting a single surge of courageous power.
It is by means of this that the mundane mind of birth and death is exchanged for the supramundane mind.
Using wealth acquired through sinful means to nourish the life-force of meditative concentration and wisdom—what wise person would not consider this and act accordingly?
If one gives rise to even a single thought of doubt, one will miss the opportunity for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas before one's very face.

**Preface to the Collection of Dream-Wanderings** Compiled by the disciple Tonghyŏng of the Gate; revised by the disciple from the South, Liu Qixiang.
The collection is titled *Mengyou* (Dream Excursions). As for what is taken [from it]: it is said that the triple world is a dream-dwelling and this transient life is like a dream.
Adversity and favor, suffering and joy, prosperity and decline, gain and loss—these are merely events within a dream. Thus, these words record the realms traversed during a dream.
Furthermore, poetry is the most intimate expression of a state of mind; in short, it is all but the language of dreams. Some may say: "The Buddha prohibited frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).
If even ordinary prose is already excessive, how much more so is poetry, which is the height of frivolity?
Moreover, poetry is rooted in emotion, whereas Chan is the method for transcending emotion. If this is so, does it not fall into the trap of emotional conceptualization? I reply: Not so. The Buddha—
It is said that birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday; therefore, even the Buddhas and Patriarchs are but people within a dream.
The entire Tripitaka and the seventeen hundred koans are nothing but drowsy talk—how much more so in this case? As for monks who compose poetry, it began with Zhiyuan of the Jin dynasty;
by the Tang dynasty, there were over thirty such *śrāmaṇeras*. At the beginning of our Ming dynasty, there was one from Chu...
[The lineages of] Shi, Jianxin, Jitan, Yichu, and other great masters were subsequently unheard of.

During the Jiajing and Longqing eras, when I was a child, I knew only one person, Qian Tang Yuzhi; however, his poetry has not been transmitted. As for Jiangnan, it was I and Xuelang who first revived it.
Xuelang applied himself with intense devotion, traveling throughout the various renowned families of the Three Wu regions to refine his craft through mutual study.

The discussions never ceased for even a moment, so that the sound of their voices vibrated throughout the land. As for me, I had long since abandoned my brush and inkstone, becoming addicted to dry meditation (*śuṣka-dhyāna*).
Wandering with a single bowl through the clouds, and later dwelling in silent, empty mountains, I spat out all former habits until not a single word remained in my breast.

From Mount Wutai to the Eastern Sea, over the course of twenty years, whenever habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) might suddenly erupt, I would discard my drafts accordingly. This has been the case for many years.
I am fifty years old. Once, while propagating the Dharma, I encountered misfortune and was summoned to prison, nearly facing death nine times.
Subsequently, by imperial grace, I was released and exiled to the borderlands of Linghai. I regarded this as falling into a perilous path in a dream; thus, my reflections began to take form.
I have observed that many of the finest ancient poems originate from those on military campaigns or travelers in exile, for their emotions are genuine and their circumstances are real.
Furthermore, monks who have followed the military service throughout history are not often seen. In the late Tang dynasty, there was Guquan; in the Song dynasty, there were two: Dahui and Juefan;
and in the Ming dynasty, there has been only myself. Guquan died in the midst of the army, and what he left behind is only a single verse spoken at the moment of his death, which says:
"Today is the sixth day of the sixth month; Guquan’s retribution for his sins is complete."
"Either go to heaven, or enter hell. Having spoken these words, he passed away. When Dahui was exiled to Meiyan, his expressions were those of Chan discourse;
when Juefan was banished to Zhuya, there appeared the *Lengyan ding lun* (Treatise on the Pinnacle of the Śūraṅgama).
The collections of his poetry are not numerous either. Yet, reflecting on my own path, I feel ashamed before the virtues of my predecessors;

the circumstances I have encountered exceed theirs, and the times have long passed, such that what I have met is no longer comparable to the past. In the second month of spring in the year of Bingshen, I first arrived at my post of command.

For three years, there had been pestilence and famine, and bleached bones covered the wilds. It was as if I were sitting within a śītavana forest; fearing that people would die without their deeds being known to the world, [I resolved to record them].

He thus completed the *Lengqie Biji* (Notes on Laṅkā). While serving at the military headquarters as a General-in-Chief who held the halberd, he dwelt within the camp’s ramparts, intending to emulate Mahāmati by wearing a scholar’s cap and gown while preaching the Dharma.
He constructed a *cangana* (meditation hall) within his felt tent and occasionally performed the Buddha-work of dreams and illusions with his assembled disciples.
Thereupon, he used golden drums as bells and chimes, banners and standards as *dhvaja* and *patākā*, and signal gongs as alms bowls.

The basin: he takes the long halberd as his *khakkhara* (staff), the three armies as his dharma-companions, the military ranks as his monastic regulations, the war cries as the sound of the ocean tides, and the audiences of inspection as his ritual recitations;
with all demons as his kin, it is truly a great site of practice (*mahā-maṇḍala*).
Therefore, among what he speaks—whether dharma discourses or verses of praise—there is much that pertains to the supramundane Dharma, while his poetry is as follows:

This was spoken solely to conform to worldly conventions. Although he had not yet ascended the Dharma hall, sat upon the flowered throne, or wielded the mallet and brandished the whisk, he remained amidst the toils of worldly existence, blending with the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and suddenly entered the gate of non-duality (*advaya-dvāra*). This was certainly no less than [the assembly at] Vaiśālī;

it merely lacked one goddess scattering flowers. His teachings were not uniform because his audiences were not uniform; they were medicines prescribed according to specific ailments, and thus could not be considered fixed standards.
Regarding the ultimate barrier of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, it is in truth a Dharma-gate spanning a thousand years of past and future—a singular and extraordinary dream-like causal nexus.
Furthermore, upon being granted leave to return to my original robes and retiring to Mount Nanyue and Mount Konglu, it was as if I were wandering in a dream through Tianmu.
For over twenty years, the attendant Fushan has accumulated [merit] day by day and month by month, while the disciple Tongjing has resided there from the beginning.
I have compiled these "Milk" [sayings] into a volume. Previously, when seekers came forward, I did not dare to bring them forth, fearing they might stain the pure realm.
Now, Haiyin, a disciple of Master Xinyang of Mount Yan, has requested that I first publish them in sequence as poetry.
I know that those with clear eyes will view them as bird tracks in a cold sky or fish traces in autumn water; yet if one seeks them through words and language, it is like looking through a cataract.
This is like seeing flowers in the sky before one's eyes; in the end, it cannot avoid being a dream within a dream.

On the first day of the first month of the spring season in the year of Xinyou, the first year of the Tianqi era, the reclusive elder of Kuangshan, the old man Hanshan, Shi Deqing, wrote this within the Kumu Hermitage.
On the March: An Expression of Feelings, Ten Chapters, Four Lines Each The wild swan soars aloft;
it flies and cries out. Alas for its search for companions; it laments this distant journey. (1) The fire-clouds flow like rivers;
the white sun is like a flying arrow. Far-off on the march, not returning—whom will there be to think of me? (2) Washing my ears in the spring water, I gather the *wei* roots.
To satisfy hunger. How could I be without heart? Who is that person? (3) The purple mushrooms are radiant; the white stones are brilliant.
My longing for that person extends from night until dawn. (4) Who says that a drop of water can pierce stone? Who says it can dispel sorrow?
My heart is like a loom. (5) One might say it can be cooled; one might say the wind can be tied. Sorrow comes from within; one knows not whence it arises.
(6) Tall and stately are the long pines; monkeys and cranes dwell therein. Vast and drifting are the white clouds; my heart follows them away. (7) Hunger and thirst come upon me;
food and drink are easily found. Alas for that drunken man! It is difficult to remain the only one sober. (8) There is wine, and there is fine flavor.
Truly they were my companions; now all is profound and silent. The honored vessels have long been empty. (9) Alas for those travelers, who come and go looking at one another;
they knock upon the reason, yet none know the cause. (10)
Poems on Feeling the Times, Fifteen Chapters in Four Lines Each (With Preface).

Recently, reports have come from all quarters that for several years there have been floods and droughts, compounded by locust plagues. The people live in constant terror, unable to wait until evening for the morning’s provisions.
The officials have requested that Your Majesty take pity on them; thus, both internal and external government treasuries have simultaneously released gold and grain.
Relief was granted. The various officials, admiring his virtue, each donated one year’s salary to assist. This was unprecedented; moved by it, they expressed their feelings in verse:
"Heaven loves life; why does it inflict calamity? These people seek peace and security; why is it not so? (1) The vast and surging flood...
Water. Yu then brought it under control. When excessive rain flows out of course, who can resist it? (2) Dew falls in thick drops; timely rain is like a gruel.
Not a single cloud arises, and our people are filled with dread. (3) When the rains fail their season, the people are exhausted;
how much more so now that this drought-demon *huabie* acts as a malevolent spirit! (4) Locusts fly, obscuring the heavens; why is this so? They devour the fat and consume the marrow.
It causes the people to look on with resentment. (5) That which the people hold dear exceeds even their own parents; they exchange their children for food—these words are truly bitter.
(6) O Great Heaven, you love these people; the lives of these people depend upon Great Heaven.
(7) The imperial benevolence is vast and great; it bestows gold and grain. Who can spit water to make Heaven rain down millet? (8) Thus one honors Heaven.
May rain and sunshine fall in due season; let me grieve for my people, so that the benefits bestowed may be even more extensive. (9) The means for recompensing merit are governed by the High Heaven;
were it not for our shared kinship as fellow beings, who could provide for them? (10) Distant indeed was the High Antiquity, when auspicious grain grew of its own accord;
alas for this degenerate age, where sowing and planting do not yield a harvest. (11) All living creatures—how they crawl and struggle—I truly regard as my own kin. O lofty and sublime Heaven, I...
We all share this under heaven. (12) How could one obtain fertile lands without exhausting the people's strength? Where is the Sovereign of Xuanyuan? Let them rest and eat as they please.
(13) The people of the Broad Road exist at all times; who would say that the transformation of the era of Tao Tang was not enduring?
(14) The times have passed and cannot be turned back; the suffering of the people is great and cannot be delayed. (15)
On Recalling My Feelings (Composed in the Garden) The Great Mass is but a mote of dust;
the vast ocean is but a single drop of water. Within this boundless universe, the cycle of succession and replacement never ceases.

The man of realization takes a sweeping view: spanning thousands of millions of years from past to present, he surveys it all as if before his eyes. The worthy and the foolish can be counted on one’s fingers;
beauty and ugliness are not worth mentioning, and right and wrong can hardly be compared. Confucius valued knowing one’s destiny; Laozi prized forgetting the self.
O my Great Hero, Honored One, you have transcended birth and death. The world is like a bubble on the water; body and mind are like dust and dregs.
Illusory transformations are merely such as these—what cause for worry or joy over honor and disgrace? Let delusions be as empty flowers at will; this is all I perceive.
At the Jingtu Hermitage in Luling, while receiving a vegetarian feast from the lay devotees led by Wang Xinghai, I recalled Governor Wang’s verse on “A Grain of Rice from Luling”:
“A single grain of rice from Luling is worth more than Mount Sumeru; Mount Sumeru may yet be shattered, but this grain never perishes.”
It transforms into fragrant *piṇḍapāta*, serving as sustenance for the Pure Land. Picking it up, one eats it with an open mouth; once satiated, one forgets a hundred hungers.
It is like eating diamond dust, which ultimately penetrates through the skin. In this land, lotus flowers abound, their myriad wondrous fragrances wafting abroad.

One person sits upon each flower, with attendants following one another from left and right. Their radiance outshines the sun and moon; in a single snap of the fingers, they transcend incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Yet, among the flowers, one seat is vacant; this lingering absence tires my thoughts.
Preface to "Delighted to Meet Master Wang Tangnan Again in Luling" At the age of twenty-five, I once traveled to Qingyuan, where I met the Master;
at that time, he was fifty years old. Now, meeting him once again, [I am filled with joy].
Already more than half a century has passed, yet he remains as if from days of old. Because the elder has cultivated pure deeds with a devoted mind, his complexion is like that of an infant.
Moved by the past and mindful of the present, I joyfully compose this verse as a gift.
A human life lasts one hundred years plus twenty-five days. One first encounters half of that half; then one meets five-tenths of it.
You have already passed three-quarters of it, yet you appear exactly as when first seen. Your face has the complexion of an infant; your bones are like those of a *vajra*.
Visualize the mind entering the lotus; sounds emerge from the celestial drum. Sitting upright upon the terrace of the seven treasures, one walks among the trees of manifold fragrances.
Without departing from the body of the five aggregates, this is itself the pure land. Shatter the *piṅgala* jar, and you will immediately behold the Lord within the flower.
Though we are parted from you, it is precisely a place of meeting.
The Heart of the Six Poems on Verse.
When the garuḍa reaches the end of its life, its flesh and bones completely dissolve and vanish; only the heart remains, unchanging, perfectly luminous and brilliantly radiant.
The dragon king takes it as a jewel, which pierces through all darkness. When turned by a wheel-turning monarch, it fulfills all wishes and is able to rescue one from every peril.
How is it that, though dwelling among humans day after day, one does not perceive it?
The nature of impermanence is fundamentally non-constant, yet it does not fall within the realm of numerical categories. Like clouds in the sky, its very essence is eternally abiding.
Sages and ordinary people are all but travelers; there are no two paths for coming and going. Whether born or not born, it is neither new nor old.
For one who sees clearly with the eye of wisdom, what else is there to long for?
In a nightmare, one enters a great mass of fire; filled with fear and trembling, one suffers in extreme distress. At that very moment of agony, a drop of water brings cool relief;
yet when the water is exhausted and the fire flares up again, what is the use of such longing and lamentation? When one awakens and looks upon reality, who was it that was grieving before?
Empty Mount Sumeru spans the vast void; the great earth floats upon the fragrant sea. The six sense-objects obscure the sky of one's nature, while the four elements pervade the Dharma-realm.
When the kalpa-fire blazes forth, this very thing—neither destroyed nor unchanging—need not wait until all is consumed before it becomes free from obstruction.

The non-self is like a single body of water that produces various flavors; though it possesses sour, salty, bitter, and pungent tastes, it is because its original nature is tranquil that it can accomplish all things.
If one were truly not compliant, how could one be willing to follow another? Only those who are non-compliant—who else could recognize this path?
Birth-and-death does not circulate within birth-and-death; circulation is not birth-and-death. If there were truly no circulation, birth-and-death would have no end.
Contemplate the nature of circulation: circulation ceases in the very moment. Not perceiving a mind that circulates—this is truly transcending birth-and-death.
The world is scorched by the heat of suffering; how could my mind remain cool? It is simply because there is nothing with which to be contacted that I can abide in peace as usual.
Like fire-cloth (agnimandala-vastra), it gains even greater luster when subjected to fire. Beholding those petty people, who would dare to confront them with such confusion?
On a moonlit night, I passed through the Three Gorges, my small boat carrying the bright moon.
Following the current, it raced along with the surging waters; the reflection of the sail seemed to shift and turn, yet the moonlight has neither coming nor going.
The nature of mind is fundamentally quiescent and extinguished—wherein then do birth and death reside? That which one dwells in is itself eternal bliss; everything else is but dust and ashes.
Four Poems on Contemplating the Pure Land Alas for this Sahā world!
Most are born as humans burdened by anxieties. When sorrow comes, a hundred thoughts knot together, Entangling and exhausting their physical forms.
The multitude of sufferings gather within this fragile body; its putrid stench attracts the blue flies. Confused and deluded, one knows not for oneself, busily wandering from dawn until dusk.

Clarity and purity diminish day by day; submerged in the world, one exhausts the spirit. How can one cleanse the defilements of the emotions? Only when returning to the truth all at once can it be done.
I bid a long farewell to this great burning house; from now on, I shall take leave of the clamor and dust of the world. Roaming at ease in the pure land, my joy shall be truly boundless.
I have heard that in the far western reaches there is a realm named Sukhāvatī, its palaces exquisitely adorned and draped with nets of jewels and strings of pearls.
Devas and humans gather in a great assembly; their radiance shines and dazzles one another. Gardens and groves are spread with various flowers;

celestial music scatters from the air. Lotuses bloom in ponds of eight virtues; fragrances drift through seven-jeweled pavilions. A gentle breeze blows at the eaves; golden bells chime amidst the clouds.
The various birds sing in harmony; the Dharma-sounds are proclaimed at will. If ordinary minds hear this but once, all shall be liberated on the spot.
Ultimate Bliss is not remote; though it is said to be ten trillion lands away, if one can purify oneself for a single thought-moment, it is right before one's eyes.
The lotus grows from the mud; coolness gives rise to blazing flames. Potsherds and rubble become jade and agate; jeweled groves emerge from thorns.

Through mindfulness, the barriers of mountains and rivers are crossed; through contemplation, deep stagnations are dissolved. Ascending the steep path to the level way, the faculties of the mind realize the First Ground.

Who would have known that within the subtle and secret, both the pure and the defiled, as well as suffering and pleasure, are fully present? Try observing flowers in the sky: their arising and ceasing leave no trace.
The cause of suffering arises from hatred and attachment; pleasure is obtained through purity. It is like a person in a dream: whether noble or base, these states are not to be sought externally.
Emotions and perceptions have no beginning; suffering and pleasure are not preordained. Behold those clouds in the clear sky—suddenly appearing and vanishing.

The ignorant cling to them as real, laboring with joy and grief as they pursue external objects. The man of realization prizes brilliant illumination, clearly understanding that there is nothing to be grasped and purifying long-standing habits.

Once awakened, one is never again deluded; the profound abyss is eternally serene and still. I pray that, riding upon the light of the white tuft between the brows, you may dwell peacefully in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Gathering pearls, the path is bright with shimmering moon-jewels produced from the depths of the deep abyss; as they are scooped up from the void, fish and dragons alike are startled into rising.
The *jiāorén* (sea-siren) embrace one another and weep; their shed tears suddenly become rain. A fishy wind blows upon the distant shore as the whale-waves surge ten thousand *lǐ*.

Dense nets hang like clouds in the sky, while light sails unfurl like the wings of a *péng* bird. With a single rip, the River Lord (*Chuánhòu*) is made sorrowful; with a second strike, the Sea Lord (*Hǎirùo*) is moved away.

I have exhausted my efforts in splitting the bellies of oysters and clams, yet I could not obtain the marrow of the azure or crimson dragon. How might I obtain a wish-fulfilling jewel to bring back and report to the Son of Heaven?

A divine radiance burst forth in the middle of the night; the Dragon Countenance was filled with great joy. Whatever seven treasures were sought followed accordingly, and all four seasons became bountiful and beautiful.
Successively aiding the orphaned and the poor, bringing benefit and joy without end; using this to reward the merit of victory in battle, transmitted as the blessing of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

Ceasing this service of rebuking the scales [of authority], I shall briefly find release from my weary thighs. The vast ocean does not toss its waves; the ditches and channels clear away the dust and silt.
I pray that Your Majesty’s longevity may be as vast as the waters of the Eastern Sea.

You chant the transformations of the dragon, which have no beginning or end; with a single breath you create clouds and rain. Your nourishing moisture benefits all living beings, falling in torrents upon the earth below.
In an instant it pervades the nine realms; in a moment it blankets the entire world. How can this compare to the insects in the sand, which share the same fate as all things—stinking and rotting?
The tiger’s long howl resounds through the empty mountains; The mournful wind shakes the forest trees. The autumn rains fall with a whistling chill; The night ghosts wail in bitter sorrow.

The rank and stench of the vulgar merely brings self-conceit; their coarse hides and fur they find fit for consumption. How can these compare to the ease of the "reclining mouse," who drinks from the river only until its belly is full?
A Gift to a Wandering Monk of Caoxi (With an Introduction):
When Lord Zhu, the Surveillance Commissioner of Nanxiao, first took up his post, he felt deep sorrow at the desolation and ruin of the ancestral temple. He devoted his utmost efforts to restoring it.
For the time being, I shall style myself a wandering monk of Caoxi. Moved by this sentiment, I compose this verse in his honor:
I came from Caoxi as a wandering monk; I originally departed from Caoxi. Having borrowed [this name] for long without returning, I suddenly recall the path to Caoxi.
I have immediately fallen into the body of a high official; as ever, I dwell nowhere. Amidst the spontaneous great transformation, how could the clumsy and ignorant be able to restrain me?
I still remember the words spoken at our parting: "Bodhi originally has no tree. Because of this, I am not deluded by people. Upon contact with every sight, there is much awakening and realization.
Following circumstances, I have arrived at my native land; ten thousand mountains are filled with mist and fog. Before even entering the gate of Caoxi, this mind was already as it was before.
How much more so upon seeing those of former times—my feelings flow forth in poignant sorrow. Raising up my *quxuan* robe, it is just as when it was first entrusted to me.
He hammers to pieces the stones that weigh upon the waist; he opens wide the treasury of jewels. He draws forth the wish-fulfilling pearl and alone boasts of the elder’s wealth.

According to what is bestowed, the three carts appear; the children are suddenly struck with terror. With a single shout, he makes ghosts and spirits weep; with a few words, he drives away the foxes and hares.
The *māra*-sprites suddenly hide their tracks; dragons and snakes joyfully intertwine. Walking through the field of quiescent extinction, one comes and goes relying on staff and sandals.
Piercing through the clouds at the bottom of the ravines, one treads upon the dew atop the withered grass. Even shards of tile and rubble all radiate brilliance; the sacred source never runs dry.
Who knows the sequence of former and later bodies? Host and guest gaze at one another. I pray you take up the whip of *upāya* and drive long on the steps of the white ox.
In response to Professor Dong Guo’s visit to Caoxi:
You came to Caoxi; you entered the path of Caoxi directly. Suddenly meeting you upon the stream, seeing you for the first time, it was as if we were old acquaintances.
A single smile opens the eye of the mind; host and guest forget formalities. Sitting knee-to-knee as the night deepens, they lay bare their innermost sincerity.
Their lofty aspirations are as bright as ice and snow; their pure words resonate like jade and gold. Looking down, the six realms appear empty; their tall frames are fit for a thousand-mile stride.

At the end of the year, I set out on a journey afar; in the realm of ultimate truth, there is neither going nor staying. Grasping your hand as you departed, I lingered alone by the bridge over the stream.
When the disciples from the Green Locust Grove came to visit me, I had closed my gate and they left without meeting me; I present this to them now.
Within this blazing house of fire lies a single patch of cool ground. Though it was bestowed by the Elder, it is truly a gift from the Sovereign.
Dharma companions joyfully visit one another; their lofty aspirations reveal what was hidden. They see clearly the heart before a word is spoken, reaching directly to the state of non-arising.
What need is there to inquire of Vimalakīrti? Herein, truth is indeed non-dual.
The Imperial Historian Dong Xuanzai painted this "Diagram of Mountains" as a gift for me; I compose this poem in response while at Wutai during the three summer months.
Trees in the twelfth lunar month of Jiangnan; a solitary figure amidst clouds in the void; the remainder of my life like dew upon a blade of grass.
Cold and heat have no inherent origin; north and south are matters of going and staying at will. Wherever one finds oneself, there is sufficient coolness; what is there to long for in this?
Written on the boat from Wuyang to Caoqi on my fiftieth birthday, the first day of the tenth month in the Gui Mao year:
Today I am fifty-eight; tomorrow I shall be fifty-nine. The future is inconceivable; what exists in the past?
The phenomena of the world are like flowers in the void; praise and blame are but ugliness in a mirror. One does not push for the sheep- or deer-cart, but delights in following the ox and horse.

I am ashamed that my knees are worn through by the reeds [of long kneeling], yet I find it strange that willows have grown from my elbows. My hair is disheveled, lacking the restraint of a crown; my face is thick with dust and grime.
Having defeated the army of birth and death, he shattered the mortar of ignorance. Exhausting his grandmotherly heart, he laughs until the void’s mouth splits.
Neither the two banks can contain him, nor is the middle current his domain to guard. He comes and goes at the mercy of wind and waves; in leaving or staying, he is utterly beyond peer.
Gazing toward Chang’an from the edge of the heavens, I turn my head once toward the cold void. Turning my head, I ask the people of this age: who is a true friend to me?
At Fangguang Monastery, at dawn I don the clouds of Mount Nanyue; at dusk I lodge within Fangguang Monastery. A lofty path winds deep into the distance; a thousand peaks lock in profound seclusion.
Sitting solemnly upon a blue lotus flower, he has suddenly entered the Cool Land. The flowing springs harmonize with the sound of pines, as if in dialogue on non-duality.
Simply sever all worldly thoughts; do not ask about the meaning of the Westward Journey. How could one merely perch upon branches to fulfill the ambition of dwelling in the mountains?
I shall rest this plantain-like body; tears and spittle are but the affairs of empty flowers. From now on, I bid farewell to the dust of the world, forever severing the fetters of human existence.
Traveling to the Southern Peak, I ascended Mount Zhurong.
My heart yearned for the mountains of Nanyue for forty years; those seventy peaks at the edge of the heavens have always remained before my eyes.

I am ashamed that I lack wings; how much more so when bound by the constraints of this physical form? Recently, fulfilling the promise made with an old friend, I have finally been able to indulge in carefree wandering.

Girding my robes, I ascended Mount Zhurong; a single glance reveals the empty heavens and the blue sky. The Xiang River stretches like a roll of fine silk, while the stars and constellations appear as if wrapped around its waist.
The distance to heaven is less than a foot; in a trance, one follows the flying immortals. Looking down upon the myriad phenomena, they appear small; the world is like a pellet.
One’s body has already entered the void, with clouds and mist floating beneath one's feet. If one rides the cool wind to depart, from this point on one transcends the mundane world.

Turning my head back, I contemplate the ancients: what karmic affinity has there been across three lifetimes? A single drop of water from Caoxi has transformed into a drenching rain, moistening the parched and withered earth so that spiritual sprouts may emerge;
the Dharma drum awakens those lost in the darkness of delusion. How is it that within the Lion’s Den, foxes and hares are now allowed to lurk?
The Brahma palace is vast and empty; the lamp of wisdom flickers, unlit. Who shall hold aloft the candle that illuminates the heavens, to shatter once and for all the slumber of the long night?
I linger about, overcome with sorrow, drinking tears like flowing springs. How might one of great supernatural power, with a mere snap of the fingers, transform this great trichiliocosm?
Instantly, the land became composed of the seven treasures, with golden lotuses carpeting the earth. Beholding the clouds gathering in the sky, all the sages and worthies assembled there.
To the mountain man Kuang Muyi of Nanyue:
I have come from Caoxi, intending to grow old among these mountains. The spirit of the mountain has not deceived me; before my eyes, the clouds and mists are magnificent.

I have traversed and surveyed the ancient sites of enlightenment; golden sand falls amidst the dense bamboo. At the place where Lan Can once roasted yams, no trace of his secluded path remains to be examined.
I look back with longing upon the Master who ground bricks: had he not attained Buddhahood so late? Within the Lion’s Den, who could dare to challenge the King’s tusks and claws?

The rain of the Dharma has not moistened for long; the sacred sprouts have withered away. Alas, why did I arrive so late? Facing the wind, my regret and distress increase. Fortunately, I have met one who feeds on the mists of immortality;
we shall pledge to transcend the mundane world together. I wish to sit with you in the deep crags, exhausting the profound subtleties of the mysterious teachings.
I cherish this noble mind, which is truly able to decline worldly turmoil. Before the Lotus Society has yet opened, you have again taken the path back to the East.

This is surely because your feelings for your kin have long been entangled within your breast; now you depart briefly from the clouds and mountains, yet this heart of yours remains ultimately unresolved.
I board a boat upon the river; you hide among the leopards in the mountains. Thinking thus of Li Yehou, I fear that your leisure may not be preserved.
I shall leave but the clouds by my window, waiting for me to return and sweep them away.
Traveling east from Mount Nanyue along the river, I bid farewell to Fang Juezhi and Zi Jiang.
We met upon the waters; let us form a bond as friends of the mountains. May we pledge to lie together amidst the white clouds, spending our final years in retirement.
The spirits of the mountains did not detain me; I grasped my staff and took leave of their profound seclusion. You too are one weary of wandering; your aspirations lie beyond the mists and clouds.

Having hidden your spirit within the gateway of myriad wonders, you have long desired to renounce worldly turmoil. Yet, as your innermost feelings are bound to your sovereign, you have not yet allowed yourself to indulge your heart’s desire.
Now I board the vessel of compassion, hoisting sail to traverse the vast and boundless ocean. Though I shall part from you, our karmic conditions are not yet exhausted.
If my life does not end prematurely, I shall once again take up a blade of grass; wait until your marriage is complete, for it will still be early when I return.
Parting from Mount Heng, I dispel my self-reproach;

lying in the empty forest, my resolve was not firm. Once again I prepare my oars for the journey back to the East; drifting away, I bid farewell to the clouds and mountains, yet my lingering attachment still binds my heart.
Of the seventy peaks of Mount Heng, I longed to explore them at leisure; that I departed as soon as I arrived leaves the mountain spirits to lament my departure.
It is already late that you have returned; how soon it was that we parted! I am originally a man of the mountains; I have long been satiated with my dwelling among hills and ravines.
My staff and sandals are born of mist and clouds; as I sit and lie down, deer circle around me. Dust finds no place in my eyes or ears; the light of my mind is free from the cycle of dusk and dawn.
The four great elements are like an empty valley; the six sense organs are severed from all turmoil. Wherever one goes is a deep mountain—why must one cling to withered stumps?
I ask those who dwell among the mountains: when will this stillness-bound state come to an end? Only by shattering the crystal flask does one finally realize the excellence of following conditions.
In Wuchang, I met the two Chan practitioners Shilang and Minyue as they were returning to Sichuan to visit their parents;
they thus instructed me, a wandering monk: "Suddenly meeting a traveling guest, one asks about the matter of traveling; looking at each other, there is nothing to say."
A single cloud over Mount Kuanglu; a thousand feet of snow on Mount Emei. Such is the heart of the wandering monk: coming and going like the moon reflected in water.
Reflecting thus upon the affection between mother and child, my every thought is never separated from her. Now returning to receive her joyful countenance, it is as if we have never parted at all.
