Serve the imperial decree, not the sweet; inquire of the cold, not the heat. Splitting open the mother-born face, one then beholds the non-arising and non-ceasing.
Only this is the time for the traveler to arrive home.
It is shown that the son of hearing and the illness within illness both arise from the existence of a self (*ātman*).
Because of this self, afflictions (*kleśa*) accumulate; afflictions are nourished by delusion and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and thus the wheel of birth and death (*saṃsāra-cakra*) does not cease.
The faculty of emotion is like a shuttle; deluded thoughts interweave. Woven together, they form this illusory and false body, where all manner of suffering accumulates.
Seeking the expedient means to escape suffering, one must swiftly brandish the sword of wisdom. Severing the threads of deluded thought, the faculties and their objects are instantly stilled.
In a single thought, one realizes non-arising; the four elements each return to their source. Since the self cannot be found, from where can illness be sought?
Returning to Kuangshan (with a preface):

In my youth, my aspirations were for distant travel; at thirty, I settled in the mountains, and suddenly twenty years have passed. Unexpectedly, I have been blown by the winds of karma into this place.
It has been more than twenty years since the ocean of illusions; yet this single thought of mine has not left the ice and snow of the cold crags.
Recently, I was fortunate enough to return late to Mount Kuang to fulfill my desire for retirement, as I am now seventy-two years old. Alas, alas, this floating world!
How brief is human life! Beholding this remaining span of existence, it is like the setting sun over the western mountains—a fleeting glimmer for but a moment.
Thus, I composed a poem to record it:
In this floating world, there are not even a hundred years; I have wandered in dreams for more than seventy. The illusory sea is vast with its surging waves; The further shore has no fixed direction.
A single reed follows the celestial wind, drifting and wandering wherever it may go. It has traversed the eight wildernesses, encountering many perils and obstacles along its path.

My spirit is spent and my body weary; I shall erase my traces to pursue a distant ideal. Mist and clouds have become the knots of my dreams, while mountain crags and caves have long been neglected by my heart.

Only in my advanced years did I finally fulfill my aspiration; shaking out my sleeves, I returned to Mount Kuanglu. Having transcended the karmic ties of this turbid world, all worldly thoughts have withered away.
A thousand peaks embrace secluded ravines, far removed and distinct from the human realm. The Seven Sages stand in the midst of the clouds, and the Five Elders frequently beckon me.
Brows and eyes meet from time to time; with carefree laughter, there is much joy and amusement. Sometimes the bright moon arrives, a single mirror suspended in the void.
Its clear light enters my thatched hut, illuminating my countenance so it relaxes. With white hair facing the green mountains, my form and shadow are like a vessel of ice.
Sitting dejectedly upon a stone seat, day and night in the double-lotus posture, he looked back to the time before birth: fundamentally, there was not a single thing.
Having realized that all is but illusory conditions, why be constrained by birth? From this point on, he shed the tangle of entanglements and ascended high to the capital of eternal bliss.
The Great Historian Jiqian received [this] at Mount Lu, where peaks rise to the clouds.
The rivers and lakes stretch far to the horizon; from the earth, blue lotus flowers emerge, their branches and leaves shimmering with fresh beauty.

I look back upon those people in the land of China, who transcend and remain aloof from the mundane world. For fifty years, they have appeared in my dreams, yet the auspicious conditions for our meeting have not been fulfilled.

By chance, riding upon a cloud in the sky, I followed the wind to the region of Wu and Kuaiji. Here, the mountains and waters of the southeast are beautiful, and I find solace among many excellent scholars.

Upon first beholding this man of pure heart, my spirit was as if intoxicated; before a word was spoken, my innermost being was laid bare. His refined discourse penetrated the subtlest depths, and facing him, we forgot our physical forms.
We were clearly liberated from all constraints and inhibitions; his brilliant, white resolve for the transcendent life is truly worthy of a vow in the vast void.

The ocean of suffering is now surging with great waves; I pray you provide a ferry to cross it. Taking my leave at the bridge over the river, I shall finally fulfill my vow to return to the mountains.

With a long bow, I depart for Mount Kuanglu, concealing my traces in its profound and remote depths. There, the Five Elders and the Seven Sages shall be my constant companions, gazing upon one another day and night.
I clear away the brambles to lie in the empty mountains, with mist and clouds as my robes and coverlets. Beholding this *bāzāo* body, I cast it aside like a drop of spittle.
I look afar with longing at those who have not yet returned home; my thoughts race through dreams and slumber. How can I mount a long rainbow and, riding the wind, arrive in an instant?
For a time, I bid farewell to the ties of the mundane world and entered the samādhi of true reality.
Returning to the Patriarchal School, I ascended Mount Jinyun to pay homage at the Śarīra Stūpa.
As I climbed Mount Jinyun, I took a single glance and saw that heaven and earth were narrow; the myriad mountains rushed like ants, and Penghu Island was as small as a lacquer tray.
Ten thousand ravines roar with the long wind, blowing down the moon from the edge of heaven. At night’s stillness, looking down upon the world below, the lamps flicker on and off of their own accord.
Once my body has entered the void, all conceptual thoughts suddenly cease. I think afar of the World-Honored One who saves; his Dharma-body pervades all things.
The śarīra came from the West; the Sage established the three karmas. A stūpa was erected upon the mountain peak, adorned with gold and iron.
Thereupon, a great man was moved to build a monastery and relinquish his residence, which thus became a banner of radiance; from this point on, the conditions for the Dharma were established.

For over a thousand years, spanning from past to present, this cool place has dispelled the scorching heat. Alas for that realm of sentient beings! The four marks of existence have turned into kalpas;

the meditation halls lie abandoned amidst thorns and brambles, and the golden and azure glories have become mere rubble. The groves have been felled by the axe, yet a solitary pine stands alone, towering and resilient.

The roots and stumps were half-gnawed and severed; the branches and twigs were on the verge of withering. Who would have expected that a Sage would arrive, offering blessings and bestowing the moisture of his grace?
By this, the restoration was foretold; the Dharma-thunder resounded like that of former sages. The bark and bone grew day and night; dense and luxuriant, they regained their luster.
The Vajra-mind of fruition is fulfilled; from this point, the wilderness is cleared. The Dharma-treasury descends from heaven; the Dragon-light illuminates the mountain caves.
Buddhist temples arise like clouds; the fourfold assembly increases in joy. Only now do we know that pure and impure lands transform according to the differences of the mind.
In Donglin, I recall the past;

from my youth, I have been devoted to the ambition of traveling afar. From early on, I have admired the Master of Donglin: the green mountains open the White Society, where all the high worthies reside.

I lament the passing of moments as I observe the lotus-water clock, practicing pure cultivation through the six periods of the day. With pure mindfulness, I sever all worldly thoughts, making the Land of Ultimate Bliss my destination.
His lofty spirit vibrates through a thousand years; I raise my head, bound by thoughts of the distant past. His radiant countenance seems as if before my eyes; he follows me even in dreams.

Only now, in my declining years, do I ascend these heights; beholding the scene, my lingering sorrow increases. Wild woods shroud the crumbling walls; the weeds and brambles spread thick and tangled once more.
I linger at the site of the Three Laughs, where moss and dew-blossoms flourish. In the portrait hall, the assembly of eminent sages is arrayed; their noble precepts appear as if before my eyes.
Ancient steps are locked in cold mist; white lotuses bloom in the foul pool. Fragrant valleys emit pure resonance, as the terrestrial pipes and celestial winds blow.
Hills and mounds undergo change and transformation, yet the Ultimate Way remains unaltered. If you, Master, have unfulfilled wishes, why delay your return?
Should this grove be restored to its former state, your lofty traces may still be pursued. The mountain spirits have long offered protection; their divine power ever resides herein.
I have already resolved to end my life here. From now on, I bid farewell to this turbid world.
A Poem on Gratitude for My Fortune, in Response to Yuan, the Prefect of Nankang (with an Introduction):
Yuan, the Prefect of Jiujie, governs the commandery of Nankang. The mountains and lakes of Mount Kuang and Lake Nan all come under his transformative care; not only...
The people of this land cherish his virtue. Even the recluses dwelling in crags and caves appear as if they were seated upright within the center of a white-hair mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*).

This ancient monastery of Qixian had long fallen into overgrown weeds; yet, in a single stroke, he raised it up and restored it, further constructing the "Cloud-Climbing Bridge" (*Nieyun Qiao*) to facilitate passage across the perilous path.
These are the imperishable, magnificent deeds of this sacred mountain. Fayun’s founding was truly moved by the protection of the Dharma.

Preface to the Record of Chenghui Monastery A single word is sufficient to endure for a thousand ages; thus, this inscription is carved upon stone to mark its completion. These humble words serve as an expression of gratitude.
Mount Lu rises high into the clouds, where heaven and earth concentrate their refined essence. A thousand peaks stand arrayed against the layered heavens, while blue lotuses embrace the horizon.

In the past, many were those who consumed the mists of immortality, concealing their forms and nourishing their profound secrets. Since the arrival of Master Yuan, the forest has been opened and a true covenant established.
Noble worthies gather like clouds, vowing to cultivate purity and transcend the world. The mountain hues reflect the lake’s radiance; man and his environment grace one another.
I recall in the past, when the assembly of dragon-elephants was as numerous as stalls in a marketplace. I look back upon that Elder of Xiqian, whose tongue was like a cauldron boiling over;

amidst the striking of mallets and the raising of fly-whisks, he pointed directly to the meaning of the Western Arrival. Who would have known that beneath a thousand years, the workings of creation have shifted in secret?
The jeweled steps fall amidst the wild brambles; the devas abandon the thorns. Though the elder grasps a single blade of grass, he has not yet seen the Truth.
How much more so when the jackal howls—it can never rival the lion’s play. The bells and chimes are silent and still; the mountains are empty as spirits and ghosts weep.

By the grace of Heaven, a supreme person arrived; on Vulture Peak, he received a personal prediction of enlightenment. Manifesting in the body of a high official, he performed Buddha-work according to conditions.
Like the rain of Dharma moistening the parched and withered, like sweet showers nourishing all vegetation, his single adamantine mind was spread far and wide like the great earth.
These people are like infants, gazed upon by a compassionate mother. She spits out her food rather than swallow it, adjusting and removing all that is harmful.

Within the mere blink of an eye, there is hardly anyone who does not secure their livelihood. Sitting in the spring breeze from a thousand miles away, the desolate village knows no sound of barking dogs.

Suddenly placing the people with teeth [in a state of peace], they stand solemnly as in the age of Ge Tian. With leisure from governance, there are many secluded moods; seeking mountains and exploring spiritual wonders, they behold this Jetavana Grove.
Moved by this sight, they conceive the resolve for its restoration. With a single stroke, they wield the chisel; the vermilion rafters rise like the wings of clouds.
In no time the Brahma-palace was completed; it appeared as if the heavens themselves had descended. His supernatural power still had surplus, yet the adornments seemed not yet fully prepared.

Across the precipitous ravine he spanned a flying bridge, like a long rainbow girding the azure verdure. In the jade-like abyss lay dragons and serpents, their forms and shadows appearing as if looking back and forth.

The Five Elders and the Seven Sages—beard and brow fall like clouds. You have established a perilous path upon the compassionate vessel; those who travel it come and go without exhaustion or stumbling. I look back with longing upon the grace of your salvation;
how could this concern only those dwelling within the mundane realm? Whenever I receive even the remnants of your cough or spittle, jade-like fragments sprinkle my liver and lungs.

Upon the *wanye* jade, excellent verses are engraved; upon a fragment of stone, the weight of a bronze bell or cauldron is entrusted. Merit and virtue are recorded on famous mountains; may you assist the sovereign and be enshrined among the ancestral sacrifices.

Woodcutter’s songs mingle with the sounds of the Dharma; recitations and prayers shall continue for ten million years. In the empty valley, clouds and mists accumulate, all of which become vessels for offerings.

Moved by this rare opportunity in this world, I compose this brief verse to express my innermost thoughts. I pray that you may preserve your long life, bestowing blessings eternally upon all of heaven and humanity.
In "That Which I Long for":
Since parting from you, we have been separated by thousands of li; my longing for you flows on unceasingly like a stream. The flowing water rushes eastward and never returns.
I return; my mind is like a ring without end. Raising my head, I gaze at the vast sky; the vast sky is infinitely boundless.
I wave my hand to summon the bright moon; the bright moon has its time of arrival. Though light and shadow may look upon one another, it can be gazed upon but cannot be grasped.
How might I obtain a countenance like the full moon, so that upon seeing it once, my heart’s face would be opened?
An Ode on Viewing Mr. Hou’s Paintings of Mountains and Water Mr.

Hou’s poverty surpasses that of the guests at the Yi Gate. Who among those who hold the reins has ever passed his dwelling? Only in his thoughts upon the art of painting does he enter the divine realm;
His refined elegance is truly enough to be called "madness to the utmost. A single room, utterly empty, is as pure as ice and snow; Mists and clouds occasionally drift toward his brush-hair.
O Master Kong, wild deer run through the air from time to time; the mountain spirits are startled night after night in the darkness. By day, the gates remain closed and swept clean;
though fine meats are lacking, he is satiated by the mist and clouds. He takes up a brush and ink as if they were clarified butter (*sarpis*);

yet people of the age find his appearance strange. Sixty-six cycles of the *jiǎzǐ* have passed in recent years; half the time spent in seclusion he has suffered from hunger. A single cubit of cloth...
A pint of grain is traded for fine wine; clear springs and white rocks only provoke derision. Sometimes I stand alone on the street corner;
seeing people, I feel a flush of shame before they have even spoken. Everyone says my impoverished bones are as soft as mud; who would believe my iron-like heart is as firm as steel?
The waves of the Three Rivers and Five Lakes surge vast and wide; a thousand crags and ten thousand gullies vie for their wondrous forms.

Idly unrolling silk and wielding the brush with light strokes, all at once they are gathered upon the tip of the brow. Entering the mountains to seek out the wooden stake, one sees it beneath a pine tree and calls out joyfully.
When drinking tea, one only regrets that a thousand vessels are too few; when asking about the Dharma, there has never been so much as a half-syllable. An old man has lost his belly.
The tongue is long; it swallows and spits out the light of the ten-thousand-li bright moon. The stars are scattered, with nothing to gather them up. You would be fit to serve me as a traveling pouch.
I shall keep you and lie down for a while among the mountains. Flakes of white cloud form a canopy over the blue sky.
When thirsty, drink from the clear stream; when hungry, chew the purple *zhī* fungi. Let the seas dry up and the rocks crumble—what does that matter to us?
A Song for the Tánhuā Monastery, based on the逸史 (Yìshǐ) of Jìyuán; by General Dū Jiāngtáoyīng.
In my past travels through the kingdom of Miàoyán, I beheld with my own eyes the *tánhuā* flower, white as snow.
Beneath the flowers stood the bodies of the great Bodhisattvas, their countenances radiant with a golden hue. These flowers do not bloom in vain; they appear but once every thousand years.

The embryo is contained within. When the Perfected One is about to manifest his blossoming, he first sends forth [his light]. He comes alone for the sake of this great matter of causes and conditions.

This great matter of causes and conditions is not of a single kind; with thousands of millions of bodies, he delivers all across the world. To the three vehicles and the eight classes of beings, he responds to their thoughts with all-encompassing presence.

Throughout the ten directions and the dharma-realm, he reaches wherever the mind turns. At times he manifests in the body of a Great Heavenly General, his majestic wind blowing from all eight sides like a celestial deity, extending for ten thousand *li*.
Moving with sweeping strides, he is without rival; he sweeps away the calamities of the comet and clears all smoke and dust.

His transformations are boundless and most rare, like the blooming smile of the *buddhāvatamsaka* flower. Under the moon he plays the flute and the phoenixes arrive; on horseback he brandishes his halberd and the lion roars.
The moment it opened, it became an auspicious omen for the human realm. The person and the flower-spirit were non-dual. The person emulated King Jeta’s heart in spreading his gold upon the ground;
the flowers performed the meritorious work of creating a garden. The General employed martial prowess without departing from dhyāna;

he constructed a small vihāra beside the Jeta Grove. Facing the flowers, his mind entered the realm of non-arising; with his door closed, his body dwelt in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Every trace of the impulse to kill was entirely...

The wisdom that subdues demons: the wondrous fragrance and color reveal the meaning from the West. Seeing forms and hearing scents, the Dharma-realm is empty; on the spot, one enters the samādhi of battle.
Enveloping the transformations of nature, he is the Lord within the flowers. His literary brilliance traverses past and present; his "Spring" edict unleashes thunder and lightning.
As wind and clouds shift their moods, he drives dragons and tigers. The gardens are vast and the flowers remain unharmed—this is the essence.
The dwelling is but ten feet square; heaven and earth, past and present, are empty within a mustard seed. The world and its mountains and rivers are reflections in a mirror.
A *tathāgatagarbha* flower entering the mirror is all the more spirited; the general, too, is but a person within the mirror.

Ten thousand *li* suspended in space, as if facing one another face-to-face—how can listening with the eyes compare to seeing with the ears? I, too, am a chronicler beneath the flowers of Jetavana; from time to time, I irrigate the Chan [mind].
That water—the creeping weeds of the five aggregates have long been cleared away; the illusory body of the four elements has lost its support.

Cast into the scorched wilderness like a public proclamation, amidst the boiling cauldrons and glowing coals there is no turning back. Suddenly, one beholds the former master among the flowers, who sends word:
do not forget the path by which you came.
Song of Mokam (With Preface) The Zen practitioner Jeong Tae changed his pen-name to Mokam (Dry Wood Hermitage). The layman Nangao presented him with a gift, which prompted me to write this playfully.
Mokam. Mokam. A lion’s den before the crags of Sangnyeong Peak; its gnarled branches are strangely curved and impossible to grasp.

Frosty leaves spread like clouds, how blue and lush they seem! From afar they look like withered stumps, fit for nothing; yet when approached, their parched state is as if one were truly practicing meditation.
If an old man of snow sits within his hall wearing these, what need is there for Manjusri’s three-by-three arrangements before and after?
I am already worn out and the ocean of my consciousness has dried up; I sit with you now in this hermitage of withered wood.
The Crows Cry at Night:
Snow accumulates in the cold forest as the white sun sets in the west. Compassionate crows caw and caw upon the branches; the owls in their nests dare not settle.
Starving and unable to find food, their hearts are filled with bitter grief. How dense is the hunter’s net! The flesh of the hungry crow is not... [to be eaten].
Having eaten enough, for what purpose do you entangle yourself, seeking day and night? Failing to repay the kindness of nursing, how can your heart’s longing be satisfied?

Mother and child separated, neither is whole; moreover, the mother has died and returned to the Yellow Springs. Her cries of lamentation never cease, like those of the cuckoo, leaving her son to harbor resentment for all eternity.
O weeping crow, weeping crow, truly pitiable! When the hunter was suddenly slain, the owls and hawks were destroyed. Clearly...
How manifest is the Way of Heaven!
A song while wandering Mount You:
a solitary island amidst the sky gathers azure mists; it is just like a lotus flower floating upon the fragrant sea. Rock grottoes and stone treasures cluster like blossoms.
The filaments are like the interlacing pearls of Indra’s net. I have come from afar to ascend the Flower Treasury Realm; once my two eyes are opened, there is no obstruction.
The surrounding rows of trees cast layered shadows, as distinct and vivid as mustard seeds within a jar. Palace halls span the void like reflections in the clouds;
the Dharma-body is unmoving, as stable as the green mountains. The fragrance of flying flowers drifts in dark incense, wafting upon me in gentle breezes.

The man feels cold beneath his heavy patchwork robe. He drags his staff and pushes aside the mist within the crags. Wondrous rocks tower and jut like a spread of chess pieces; pointing them out is like counting a row of stars.
A single spray toward the blue sky scatters flying spittle. The stone gate and its stairway pass through a hair’s breadth of space;
one must lean sideways against the sheer cliff, for there is no room for feet. Even the passage of monkeys and birds is not easy; how could it exhaust my strength?

Climbing through the vines straight up to the summit of Mount Sumeru, the lake’s radiance beneath one's eyes spreads like brocade. Before the feet have left the ground, the body already contains the void;
looking back, it is as if a reflection in a crystal pitcher. Turning slightly, I pass once more by Huisheng Rock; how wondrous are its stone corridors and grottoes!

Our distant ancestor, through the game of chess, skillfully expounded the Dharma; the black and white stones, before their moves were made, leave people to wonder. Crossing the stream, I ascend toward the west.
Lotus Stone: Blossom after blossom of golden lotuses emerges from the earth; I wander about but see no one within the flowers. I hear only the long and broad tongue of the pine wind;
I turn to pay homage to the sixteen-foot body at Jingu Valley. Vast and luminous, there is no place for even a speck of dust; The kalpa-fire blazes fiercely, yet this remains unharmed.
Only then do I believe that the azure cliff is my original reality. I wish to clear away the brush and dwell in a stone grotto; [The rest is missing.]
Birth borrows this to conceal its traces; if one could obtain peaceful sleep, the white day would be high.
Body, mind, and the world are all cast aside—how can one abandon this and follow elsewhere? A single leaf floating in space is entirely a lodging; it is better to return quickly before long.
Do not let the monkeys and cranes constantly remember you. The Flower Treasury (Huazang) has always been your ancestral home; having traveled through the ten directions, you now emerge.
It cannot be. He conceals his body and suddenly enters a single mote of dust. Who among men knows the news here?
(With an introduction to the "Song of the Board-Carrying Fellow"):
At Mount Jing’s Dharma Cave, since the time of Dahui, the Way of Linji has continued its lineage of wisdom-life, generation after generation.

There is a lack of people. Lately, the Chan school has become desolate; its resonance has long been silenced. Recently, however, there have been practitioners engaged in investigation who have filled the mountains;
among them, some have had a sudden flash of realization, with the Truth manifesting before them, thereby attaining great mastery.
What a pity! You sit upon pure ground, refusing to let go, regarding this as something extraordinary, unaware that you have instead created a hindrance to the Dharma.
In the teachings, this is called the *jñeyāvaraṇa* (the cognitive obstruction). Thus, the ancients said:
"Even if you reach the state where you are like the bright moon in a cold pond or the sound of a bell in a silent night—unimpaired by being struck at will, and yet touching the waves..."
Not dispersing [the mind] is still merely a matter of standing on the shore of birth and death. As the saying goes: "It is easy to set foot within a thicket of thorns;
it is difficult to turn one's body outside the curtain of night-bright light. This is called clinging to the tip of the staff and sinking into stagnant water.

Since even this is not permitted as a place to settle, how much less can one who has not yet attained a glimpse of reality—having merely coincidentally obtained the lightning-flash samādhi—consider themselves to have attained anything? They are merely playing with consciousness.
Is this not the "shadow of a deity"? This—attaining a small measure through Zen meditation and being satisfied with it—is a universal malady throughout past and present.

Fearing that it might fall into worldly discourse and mislead many people, I have composed this "Song of the One-Carrier" (Damban Han) in response to those who requested instruction, to show them its meaning.
The song says: [The Song follows]
The board-carrying fellow! The board-carrying fellow! How can he be so shamelessly deceived? He seeks only to lighten his shoulder, heedless of the trip at his heels.
Even if he carries it back to before birth, he has already been obscured by it for half the journey. This single board!
A cangue upon the neck; every bone and muscle of the body belongs to him. If you do not quickly cast him off, he will be a true enemy for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Walking, he burdens you; sitting, he burdens you. Clearly an obstacle, why do you not realize it? It is only because from the beginning you mistook him for the real thing;
thus, within the pure gates and clean households, he gives rise to demons and sprites. Whether eyes are open or closed, he is seen; by day, he is too...
A flash of lightning flickers in the void; a city of Gandharvas appears in the sky. Foolish children mistake it for a celestial palace. To attain lightness, one must let go.
What price is there to quarrel over a stinking dead frog? Black beans are brought to trade for one’s eyes.
One must distinguish the true from the false among fish-eyes. There is a path, best traveled: level and vast as the surface of a pond. But do not...
Linger by the flowers and willows; take it for granted that next year you shall enter the imperial capital. Sacrifice body and life as if they were the great earth;
there is no need to avoid oxen, horses, camels, or donkeys. If you can truly cast yourself over Mount Sumeru in a single throw, the forest of swords and mountain of knives will be like child’s play.
If you cherish others, you will be harmed by them; complications arise largely from the burden of excessive concern. Once the glass bottle is shattered, [great...]
The earth, mountains, and rivers are all pulverized. I exhort you: do not carry them. The marrow within the skull dries up on the spot;
the body divides and shadows disperse in hundreds of billions of forms. From this moment forth, one shall not enter the pass of birth and death.
I have heard that Shen Langqiu has closed his door within the city of Gusu; I compose this song to send to him.
The burning house blazes fiercely, yet the dream has not yet awakened; amidst the dust, there lies a single realm of pure coolness.

One sees only the towering flames licking the sky, while the practitioner’s single thought remains like an ice well. The clamor of the marketplace rushes like ten thousand galloping horses, day and night without ceasing—what is this?
As for "acting": when the faculty of hearing is stilled and the mind does not arise, all that is seen is but a provisional manifestation within emptiness.

A wife and children face one another like conjured beings; looking back at oneself, one is like a body reflected in a mirror. All day long they meet yet do not recognize one another; where in these two eyes could even a speck of dust find entry?

Sometimes the spirit wanders through the Flower Treasury World (*Avataṃsaka-dhātu*), and with a single stroke of the brush, the blockages within the breast are cast away. (Lang was skilled in painting.)
The reflections of mountain and water are layered upon one another; interlacing and encompassing them, there is no obstruction.

At times, one sits within a land of lotuses, where the ground is as level as the palm of a hand and strewn with golden sand. Amidst the ponds of eight virtues, the lotuses bloom; a single touch of their fragrant breeze awakens the mind.
The single chamber of the abbot’s quarters has no walls or partitions; its measure encompasses the *dharmadhātu*, vast and empty like space. Thus do the ocean-assemblies of the ten directions gather.

Enter within; sit in meditation and do not trouble yourself with traveling on foot. Mount Lu rises ten thousand fathoms high, suspended in the great void, as if you were dwelling in the same room as me.
Neither going out nor entering, neither coming nor going—tell me, at this moment, what is your state of mind?

Poem on Serving in the Military (With Preface) Having encountered misfortune while propagating the Dharma, I was graced by imperial favor with an assignment to Lei Yang. In the second month of spring in the year of Bingshen, I entered Wuyang;
on the tenth day of the third month, I arrived at my place of exile. At that time, the region was suffering from famine and pestilence, having been so for three years.
For years there has been no rain; corpses lie scattered along the roads, and the sight of weapons fills the eye. Epidemics break out uncontrollably, and the dead and wounded cover the fields.
The state of such misery and tragedy is truly beyond description. As I traveled along my path, these sights stirred deep feelings within me.
I have spontaneously composed several five-character regulated verses (*pañcapadī-vṛtta*). Having long indulged in the stillness of emptiness, I have not attended to brush or inkstone;

thus, the diction is vulgar and fails to form proper stanzas. Yet, as the sentiments and circumstances are vividly realized, they can surely be considered no mere flowery rhetoric. I record these briefly to mark the events of this particular moment.

The marshes of Chu are no scorched frontier; I feel ashamed to be the only one awake as I wander and chant. The miasmic smoke turns a thousand ridges black, yet the wild grass remains green through all four seasons.

When the typhoon strikes, the autumn waves rage; humans shrink from it, yet the spirits of the fierce ghosts thrive. From of old I have always been a wanderer; today I am even more like a drifting duckweed.
Who can endure this burning house? One should naturally seek the cool and refreshing. The heavens seem low as they lean toward the sun; the trees are ancient, unaware of autumn.

How tranquil is the heart like the moon over the sea! How light is the thought like a cloud drifting in the void. Yet I pity those who dwell nowhere; once again, I find myself cast upon this scorched island.
The old accounts speak of the Road of Leiyang; now I pass west of Dianbai. A thousand mountains merge in miasmic vapors, and a single staff wanders through the mist of pestilence.
On this final journey, I follow my humble bundle; for the remainder of my life, I trust to my horse’s hooves. How can I bear it, deep within the trees, where everywhere the partridges cry?
Traveling afar along the paths of practice, one may rely only on solitary clouds. All who have homes are but guests; those free from worldly burdens are monks.
When the poisonous mists intoxicate the heart and the scorching winds steam through the bones, I recall my former haunts as clearly as if I were treading upon thick ice.

Wandering as a pilgrim is my original vocation; carrying the staff and satchel is truly what I am capable of. My heart hangs upon the moon ten thousand miles away; on my shoulders I bear a single rattan cane.

I fret over eating when confronted with barbarian tongues; I rejoice in meditative stillness when meeting worldly monks. To subdue demons, one need not speak of swords; today, at last, I have begun my ascent.
Leaving the world, I once again serve in the military; who would pity the hardships of the road? A long spear serves as my mendicant’s staff; my short hair cannot support a crown.
The cool, dewy air lingers over the Three Isles; the scorching heat oppresses the hundred tribes of the south. When I turn my head toward the southern heavens, the setting sun is Chang’an.
The August Heaven covers all without exception; how could it be that its reach excludes the distant frontiers? My life is short and winding, yet the path through this world is long and arduous.
I only know that my heart remains like snow, though I suddenly perceive my hair has turned as white as frost. Wherever I may be buried, I shall never forget the grace of Your Majesty.
Formerly dwelling in the realm of Cool Serenity, now I have ascended to the Heaven of Heat and Affliction. The climate differs between warmth and cold;

the terrain varies between north and south. Ten thousand *li* share one bright moon; a thousand mountains are separated by twilight mist. Though wild geese from the frontier may carry letters, they cannot pass beyond the Geese Peak.

From my childhood I followed the path of pure deeds; now, nearing old age, I have cast off the black robes. Is it that Your Majesty’s grace has grown thin? It must be that the ways of the world have turned contrary.
Vapors and mists are seldom seen on my travels; ice and snow are rarely met with by my eyes. Do not ask about the affairs of the road ahead; my home-mountain lies within reach wherever I turn.
Rising at dawn to observe the celestial signs, the Milky Way and the light of day divide. The tide swallows the sun of the Vermilion Phoenix; the mountains vomit forth clouds of the Poisonous Dragon.
Drifting and adrift, I return to my companions of gulls; lingering here, I recall the herd of deer. Who knows that this world-fleeing guest, in his old age, has begun to study the ways of the army?
On this day at the edge of the world, I lament my own hardships and perils. The sea wind brews a stench of rain; the mountain mists harbor a poisonous smoke.
On the dreaded road, I follow behind others; through the slush, I press forward ahead of the horses. Only now do I realize the bitterness of travel: it mostly falls upon the border guards.
Traveling abroad, I mourn the Cold Food Festival; amidst the clash of arms, my years grow old. Having survived nine deaths, my mind remains as it was before birth.
I think of Shanfu for the northern campaign; I recall Ma Yuan for the southern expedition. Where does the flute play its *plum blossoms*? Listening until the end, I cannot sleep.

Exiled from the land of Jambudvīpa, I have reached the furthest reaches of the desolate wilderness at the edge of the sea. Cloud-forms carry flying crimson birds; the tails of stars drag vermilion serpents.

Long has it been since I abandoned my staff in the forest; though I brandish my halberd, the sun has not yet slanted. From the southern heavens to the northern frontiers, everywhere there is the sound of the Hu flute.

A single bowl follows me from my teacher’s camp; I travel alone like a drifting tumbleweed. My physical form rides upon the wild horses of the wilderness, while my heart’s intent is entrusted to the soaring wild geese of the void.
Clouds emerge white from Cangwu, and mists steam as the sun rises red over the sea. I have long since cast aside this life; I need not wait for this moment to realize its emptiness.
In this fleeting world, I am content to be a guest; weary of this life, I lament this body. Though the tongue remains, it is ultimately bitter; yet if the Way is present, how can one be called poor?

Thirsty deer vie to rush toward a mirage; hungry crows habitually draw near to humans. Though the great transformation of blue seas and yellow sands has not yet occurred, where is there that is not filled with flying dust?

A single breath remains, yet further life is but a burden; the road ahead spans a thousand mountains. Asking the way, I meet a herder tending his horses; clutching my scroll, I am like one who lost his sheep.

My inner heat has burned for three autumn days; my heart is chilled by the frost of the sixth month. Having traversed these paths as if treading into a cauldron of boiling oil, how could I dare indulge in negligence or recklessness?

The traces of illusion originally have no abiding place; upon encountering a mountain, one should immediately return. Because I observe that the path ahead is narrow, I perceive this life to be increasingly fragile.

At times I harbor the hunger of those between the mulberry trees; constantly I bear in mind the starving of the old woman who fed me. What I find joy in is having no month of the year to worry about; I do not hope for someone to send me cold-season clothes.
Sitting alone in this floating world, my body stands apart from it all; A weary life within a transient inn. Who can, with a single eye, Open wide the emptiness of the ten directions?
The cool moon flies across the azure sea; The morning breeze disperses through the green groves. Seated at ease on a low stool in the *kijū* posture, My carefree spirit knows no bounds.

Returning late to the camp gates, I mingle with the mundane world in hopes of forgetting the traces [of my former life]. Facing the military array, I recall the image of the tethered sheep. My vanguard endures the *tṛṇa* grass; I bared my left shoulder and adjusted the *kāṣāya*.
The setting sun intoxicates the river’s surface; returning clouds obscure the hues of the trees. My movements and stillness are like those of a weary bird, gradually lowering its wings toward people.
In the year Gengzi, four poems on current affairs:

Tigers and leopards roam throughout the central lands; star-drawn carriages gallop day and night. The imperial edict contains no words of lamentation, yet among the people there is sorrow for those turned away from the corner.
I journey afar to explore the lair of the black dragon; I delve deep to split the branches of the fragile wood. Heaven and earth are but a moment’s glance up and down;

my brows are knit with despair. The clear seas have just achieved victory; the campaign against Zhuya has finally ended. Red-feathered arrows fly from the Jianmen Pass; Qiang troops rush along the gallery roads.

The Emperor listens to the counsel of "embracing and softening" distant lands; the royal army feels shame at the thought of war. The barbarians ought to be bound with long cords, yet we do not see anyone requesting such cords.

Yellow dust fills the eyes, obscuring all; shoulder-length hair hangs down in disarray. The path home across the rivers and lakes is remote and dim; the gulls and herons beside us seem suspicious of us.

I contemplate today’s salvation; I look to this moment for security or peril. From of old, the *diao* and *er* head ornaments have been held in high esteem; how can I not feel ashamed of such private favor?

In life, people find sweetness in their own clumsiness; yet the drums of war boil over like a cauldron. Gold and pearls are joyfully accumulated, while the humble *jiancao* grass fears the relentless pursuit of taxes.
Who among the statesmen can bring stability? The will of Heaven cannot yet be relied upon. When shall the southern breeze begin to blow, so as to wash away this scorching heat?

Passing through the Three Gorges, ten thousand ravines rush downward; a thousand mountains stretch on in purple and emerald hues. The sail flies amidst the rain of the Three Gorges; the traveler enters the autumn of the ninth month.
On the traveler's road, beyond floating clouds; my heart for home falls before the setting sun. My life has not yet come to an end; the Yangtze and Han rivers shall be my remaining years.
Having stayed overnight at Qingxi Station, I composed the lines: "Grass insects cry out on the broken embankment; sandbirds roost upon the cold marsh.
I have therefore continued these into a full poem.

Tracing the current upstream, I follow a distant islet; my journey leads me beside a solitary pavilion. The moon hides behind the mountains as their contours grow faint; fish lurk beneath the water, its scent pungent.
Grasshoppers chirp along the broken bank; sandbirds roost on the cold marsh flats. I feel deepest pity for those adrift and lost; in this floating life, the dream has not yet awakened.
In response to Zhu Shuxiang’s gift of a mottled bamboo meditation desk:
Half a bed for the stillness of dhyāna, I rest my cheek upon it amidst white clouds. Its hollow heart especially loves me; Its lofty nodes alone pity you.

Gently wiping away tears that mingle with the Xiang River, I carefully edit these words while weeping over the "Writings of Chu. These are most fitting for tempering my ailing bones; from now on, I shall sever all connection with the dust and vapors of the world.
Military Officer Lin has followed me into the mountains;

his warhorse has grown old through his service, and the winds and mists have turned his hair white. His bones are weary from the enmity of iron armor, and his heart grows cold toward its love for green mountains.

In the Zen of wooden chips, one is detached from flavors; with tea and incense, affairs are entirely at leisure. Delighting in dwelling together amidst white clouds, how could one be willing to leave the pine gate?
Reconstructing Caoqi, I enter the mountains to gather timber; a single stream winds and meanders as it enters.
Flanked by peaks on both banks, the waters turn back. Onlookers suspect we dwell in the era of Qin; the monks appear as if they have come from Central India.

Bamboo and trees reach the clouds in their growth; fields open out following the contours of the land. Who would have known that within the bends of the Five Ridges, there is likewise its own Mount Tiantai?

The timber, a hundred feet tall, sprang from a mere shoot; its solitary root emerged from the weeds. Having endured the bitter suffering of smoke and miasma to the end, it has heard nothing but the mournful cries of cranes.
Used for great purposes, it should not be broken; fashioned into this form, how could it be a calamity? I only pity tonight’s moon, which shines in vain upon the moss and lichen.

Seated on Little Golden Mountain, the Moon Treasury illuminates the floating Fragrant Temple; jeweled banners surge from the Brahma palace, the blue conch reveals the precious topknot, and the full moon manifests the compassionate countenance.
The world is as level as the palm of a hand; the river’s flow is as pure as the void. One should pity those driven along this path, all of whom fall within the Dharmakāya.
Along the desolate road, the distance is neither far nor near; the winding course seems like a double journey. The earth turns with the flow of the river; men travel upon the bird-path.

A solitary wild duck vanishes amidst the clouds; a single sail is light upon the treetops. Turning my head toward the road to Chang’an, I find it difficult to hear the cry of the wild geese at the frontier.

At Taiping Station, I urge my horse toward the postal inn; this long road is one I have traveled before. Throughout the day the mountain mists are white; in the tenth month, the scars of the forest fires are green.
The face flushes with betel-nut and wine; the spirit grows dull amidst the briny mist of the sea. From the solitary city, the *jia* and drums stir; their tragic grandeur is unbearable to hear.

Traveling at dawn, the waning moon hangs above the city walls. The mournful *jia* pipes deepen the traveler’s sorrow. The north wind blows through my shortening hair; the cool dew drenches my heavy robes.
Wildfires connect the military camps; beacon fires darken the watchtowers of the frontier garrisons. A solitary cloud lingers indistinctly; its carefree drifting is like that of a floating speck.

On the road to Huazhou, the hills and ridges wind through the vast wilderness; their winding turns are beyond reckoning. The roadsides resemble the Pass of Hangu, and the inhabitants seem like those of Wuling.
The deep forests harbor tigers and leopards; the distant heavens summon hawks and falcons. For what reason, upon these dusty roads, does a lone old monk hasten along?

Having traveled alone through Huazhou for ten thousand li, my grief grows ever deeper as the path extends. The mountain hues breathe the air of pythons; people speak with the warbling tongues of *jué* birds.
A traveler’s lodging for this day; a heart of ice and snow for a lifetime. Though there be trees reaching the heavens, they cannot compare to the Jetavana Grove.
Passing through the mouth of a deep valley by the Stone City, I see the horizon from the treetops. The wild expanse retains the lingering light; the desolate city is girded by the setting clouds.
Driven by hunger, I forgot my fatigue; desiring speed, I found the road longer than expected. At twilight, I sought shelter in a mountain inn; sleeping peacefully, it was as if I had reached home.

Transverse mountains and fortresses—low hills descend into the ravines; a single stream flows to the winding village. The level plains open up at the frontier of the tropics; garrisons line the borders.
The people’s lives are empty of years; the seasons have lost their measure of cold and warmth. Do not say that the ends of the earth are far away; the sun rises first at Fusang.

Reaching the palace of the sea-monsters, the long journey fatigues one's feet; entering the vast expanse, one arrives at level plains. The terrain reaches its limit in the Southern Ocean, where the luster of pearls connects to the Northern Dipper.

Distant mountains lie low, their peaks joined by trees; the great ocean stands level with the heavens. From afar they appear like wings of hanging clouds; sails unfurled, they are ships gathering treasures.
In the spring of the Gui-mao year, Da-lian composed this upon witnessing the phenomena of the southern lands:

the climate and scenery here are strange. The affairs of the year are altogether difficult to predict. When the twelfth month ends, insects do not hibernate; when spring arrives, birds seem unaware of it.
Bean blossoms open as old pods fall; banyan leaves shed from new branches. Recalling the snows of Mount Yan, it seems the warmth of spring holds a partiality for them.
Spontaneously Composed on a Spring Day:
In Qiong Hai, spring accumulates its gloom; the sultry heat hides deep within lingering mists. Sai-lan incense turns to pestilence; bitter bamboo grows thick in dense forests.
Do not inquire after the affairs of this weary life; simply look at the mind that stands on the brink of death. Loathing the burden of my hair and beard, day by day I long to pull out my pins.
The boat is launched upon the autumn waters where lotuses abound; a single leaf of a small craft is light. The calm current is like my old home; drifting and wandering is the path home.
Scattered rain drives away the sweltering heat; a cool breeze stirs ripples like fine silk. Coming and going as I please, I no longer heed the cries of the partridges.
From midstream I gaze upon Feilai Temple;
on both banks, mountains cast their shadows down. A thousand peaks seem to pour into the void; above the clouds soars Vulture Peak, while beneath the water appears the Dragon Palace.
Fine petals of heavenly flowers fall like rain; the earth’s pipes resound with long-lingering winds. A swift current threatens to moor my boat; a small space will not suffice to contain it.
*The Dream-Wandering Collection of the Elder Hanshan*, Scroll Forty-Seven.
*The Dream-Wandering Collection of the Elder Hanshan*, Scroll Forty-Eight.
Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian and his disciple Tonghyeong;
re-edited by the disciple from the South of the Pass, Liu Qixiang.
Dream-Wandering Collection, Volume Lower:
Rejoicing at the Snow on Ling River (With Preface).

Since ancient times, there has been no snow in Lingnan; in the twelfth month of the Gui-mao year, I happened to pass by Ling River and, seeing it for the first time, was filled with joy and recorded this.

A drizzling rain sprinkles the thatched gate; the sound of cold gradually fades. At first I suspect it is the emaciated shadow of a plum tree; I cannot believe it is snowflakes flying. It weighs heavily upon the leaves of the banana plant;
it lightly mocks the garments of the *bìlì* creeper. For eight years my dreams have been weary with longing; today I rejoice to behold its radiant splendor.
The Chan practitioner Kongjian has traveled from ten thousand *li* to bid me farewell;
for seven years he lingered in the land of fire. Now he dwells by the banks of the Ganges, yet his heart remains drawn to this distant stream.
There is this body capable of bearing its burden; there is nothing that can be conceived by thought. Before the cliff-tree where my arm was severed, I again hear the fragrance of the cassia seeds.
Having returned from Caoxi to my military post, I have surrendered my form to follow the Great Transformation.
Whether departing or staying, how could the mind allow for such deliberation? Even if driven across the scorching seas, I shall remain as one sitting beneath the Jewel Forest.
The roots of theft are shallow; the source of the Way is deep and its traces cut off. Gazing to the horizon at the color of the cold void, floating clouds stretch from antiquity to the present.
Ascending the Mingchang Pagoda in Qiongzhou, the great earth floats upon a fragrant sea;
a solitary pinnacle rises as a Brahma-banner. The divine Vulture Peak appears in the waters and heavens; the venomous dragon is subdued within the fiery cave.
The sun and moon hang like mirrors in the sky; heaven and earth are lit by a lantern through the night. Gazing at the clouds, I snap my five fingers; floral rain falls upon the empty window.
On a summer day in the year Bingwu, I went from Caoxi to Qianzhou to beg for food.
Crossing the mountain pass, I fell ill due to the heat and stayed at General Chen Wenji’s pond pavilion, where I observed fish playing in the fresh water and listened to the clear cries of gibbons.
The cranes and deer that respond to the whistling moon rely upon man as if they were in the deep mountains; sitting together at night, moved by emotion, I compose these five poems.
The General’s office is desolate and cold; I linger here as a guest at leisure. I am too lazy to compete with worldly affairs; my tranquility surpasses the abundance of white clouds.
Waving the whisk, I am too weary to train the deer; by the pond, I practice my love for the swan. I know not what else awaits me deep within the secluded valley.
By day, the heat blazes like fire; at night, I sleep soundly as the air grows cold. Awakening from my dream, I return to the Moon Palace; in thought, my heart enters the Ice Basin.
Drums and horns resound at the gate of the chariot-pole at dawn; the Milky Way fades as the light of day breaks. Having awakened, I loosen my hair; with sorrow I gaze upon my bamboo-slip hat.

In the waters of the pond, I harbor thoughts of rivers and lakes; the joy of the swimming fish I have not yet forgotten. Forever I long for the great abyss, entrusting my profound reflections to the banks of the Hao River.
The new moon sinks like a fine hook; the weeping willows draw out the long line. With the wind and rain breaking forth tonight, how many scales and shells are cast upward?

It is easy to abandon the various burdens of worldly dust, yet difficult to dissolve this body of great suffering. In my coming and going, I allow myself to blend with the common folk; for old age and illness—how can they spare anyone?
The teeth of oxen and horses are about to fall out; the hearts of monkeys are not yet pure. The six sense-faculties are like warring fiefdoms;

one knows not with whom to be intimate. In old age, one is driven by idle thoughts; in life, one is impelled by the force of karma. In vain, one uses three inches of breath to bind together a hundred-year frame.

Medicine and stone are not the essence of life; the heart-fast of *xinzhai* is surely no folly. I only grieve for the sufferings of the human world, and thus vow to become a servant of the Buddha’s house.

Walking the mountain, the narrow path winds through the slender waist of the peak; clear waters flow with trailing lengths of moss. Wind-swept pine seeds fall, and dew-drenched rice flowers exhale their fragrance.
Village dwellings with blue lotus buds; people’s homes are simple wooden huts. If you have not yet reached the Peach Blossom Spring, there is no need to ask the fisherman.
Descending High Peak at dusk, I encountered rain and stayed overnight at Lotus Temple.

At twilight I descended from High Peak; the mountains are deep and the summer heat remains intense. The air steams like the days of the Three Fests, while a cool spray falls upon the pines of the forest.

The wind blows fiercely, hastening the cold rain; from the clouds rises the stench of the reclining dragon. Haste to return and dwell in the Flower Treasury (Huazang); the bell of the Upper Hall awakens one from the dream.

A single expanse of Lotus Temple reaches through the fragrant sea; a thousand peaks embrace the City of Transformation. Blue lotuses unfurl their delicate petals; the moon of wisdom shines with lofty brilliance.

The world is far removed and all conditions have ceased; the mind is at ease and the five turbidities are lightened. Even as fine dust might be shattered, one realizes here and now the state of non-arising.
Two Poems on Crossing the River after Rain and Returning to the Mountains by Boat:
Sudden rain drives away the scorching heat; the crisp air of early autumn arises. The riverbank sand is submerged by the water; the moon by the river walks beside the traveler.
The toil of life is like a mass of foam; the sentiments of travelers are like drifting clouds. Gazing at bubbles and reflections by the stream, I perceive this body as increasingly light.
A single leaf rides upon the wind; a small boat follows the current back. The mountains coil and turn like ants; the river winds and curves like a ring.

My body merges with the empty clouds; my mind dwells at ease amidst the moon reflected in water. Ten thousand peaks have returned to their rest in tranquility; in profound stillness, I close the pine gate.
The crow-path leads to a deep temple; the mountain market gathers like clouds.
The Flower Palace opens beside the water. My regulated life does not abide in idleness; leaning on my staff, I have happened upon this journey.
Rice awaits the offerings of donors; lotuses require the planting of the community leader. Within this pure ground, it is fit to construct a platform for expounding the sutras.

Returning late from begging for alms, the setting sun is especially favored in its clarity; on the path home, the cold makes the journey even slower. A mind at leisure never tires of the clouds; weary birds surely understand my intent.

The paths of the world are ultimately endless; this weary life truly has its appointed time. Looking back from within the ten thousand peaks, who is there chewing the purple-stemmed *śrīveṣṭaka* fungus?

On the night of the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment, when the morning star rose above, it was just as when he first awoke from his dream. The Snowy Mountains still stand before his eyes, and the Bodhi tree is now hanging down its branches.
Gazing afar, I imagine his emaciation from hunger; I reflect upon the deer that offered its milk. For six years, the cold pierced his very bones; who could have known the bitterness of his heart?

At night he set forth across the river in an empty boat, drifting wherever it led. The waters were utterly free of obstacles; the moonlight appeared even more beautiful, and the sound of the river grew increasingly tranquil.
Floating clouds are matters external to the body; white hair is the face seen in the mirror. Do not say that your drifting has lasted long; ahead lies your old mountain home.
The boat passes the Zhenyang Gorge without stopping, for you are but a traveler.
An empty vessel drifts with the whirling tumbleweed. A thousand-fathom bank lines the river; half a sail catches the wind amidst the rain.
Gathering stones, they fly like swallows; riding the current, it is as if treading upon the void. The intent to find the ford through eternity lies entirely within the flux of coming and going.

Lodging in Yingzhou, I laugh at myself: what kind of person am I? Wandering aimlessly, I suffer in my quest for the ford. Let me try to rub this three-inch breath of life—can it bind this hundred-year body?
The great earth is entirely filled with exiles; the toil of life gathers but dust. Behold the moon upon the river:
how many people has it ever shone upon? Two Poems on Bitter Rain in Spring:

In these scorched frontiers, cold and heat abound; we rely upon this season of clarity and harmony. How lamentable that this rain, falling night after night, shall bring the fullness of spring to an end.
Easy to shatter are dreams of mountain passes; hard to restrain is the traveler’s heart. The peach blossoms and the waters of the third month have, since antiquity, led one astray at the ford.
Drop by drop, the mind finds no order; thread by thread, the thoughts grow more intricate. A single boat is lost upon the distant marsh; my two eyes grow dim before the vast sky.
The trees of a thousand villages have already perished; once more, the wind blows through ten thousand apertures. Grief adds to the newly accumulated waters, surging amidst the turbulent rapids.
Intending to spend my final years at Mount Nanyue, I first arrived at Hudu and conversed with the Master Zangliu under the night sky.
In my old age, I rely upon this secluded excellence; truly, I hope for a forest of the Way. The conversation of this night spans a hundred years; this heart of mine remains as it was through kalpas.
Snow covers Mount Heng white; clouds bury the waters of the Xiang deep. My time for retirement has now come to an end; I shall no longer trouble myself with seeking out visitors.

To my sons, while ill, I show this: my aversion to the world has become a chronic habit. How can I bear that illness acts as a demon? I already know my remaining days are few, yet I see this body still full of ailments.
Medicine and stone suffice for the Fragrant Accumulation; moaning shall serve as the *karmavācanā*. If Mañjuśrī were to ask, how could one silence remain?

On the Occasion at the Xiang River: The spring rain has passed over Xiao and Xiang. A light sail hangs against the morning frost. In the swift current, the Stone Drum turns back; With fresh waters, we cross toward Hengyang.
The colors of the mountain peaks appear near at hand; the lake and sky stretch far into the distance. Who would have known that within this sea of dust, everywhere there are ferries and bridges?

At Bridge Mouth, the setting sun drenches the lake and sky. The moon shines upon the sands as it rests in the boat. Birds settle in the trees bordering the water; human voices drift through the forest mist.
This floating world is but a single night’s stay; how many more years remain of this life? Why, on these declining days of old age, do I still linger by the banks of the Chu River?
Having passed Lake Longxu, I stayed overnight at Lake Tuzikou;
it is shallow and not difficult to cross. The wind-swept sails are not yet easily set; the sandy paths twist like sheep’s intestines, and the bird-winged shores rise in jagged tiers.
The earth folds as the twin wheels turn; the sky is empty as a single mirror hangs suspended. Looking back at the place where I rest, the new moon shines upon my蛾眉 (yúméi) brows.

Beyond the Heavenly Heart Lake, the myriad mountains connect with the earth’s veins; the various waters pour into the Heavenly Heart. Vast and surging is the Great Universe (Qiānkūn); deep and profound are the rising and setting sun and moon.
The sails fly along with a solitary bird; my gaze reaches into the level forests. If I were to follow you on your small boat, where in the misty waves could I seek you out?

In Longyang County, the pink battlements hide within the morning clouds; the solitary city lies beside the water’s edge. Along the embankments, willow colors abound; surrounding the outer walls are peach blossoms.
The heavens are distant as the yellow cranes fly; the river is clear as the white sands flow. One knows that Wuling is not far away; at the ferry crossing, one sees the fishermen’s homes.
Four Poems on Paying Homage to Deshan:
The Master occupies the command of the Empty King; I come now, ashamed of my late years. Gazing afar upon those of a thousand ages past, I see ever-present a single lamp suspended.
The bird speaks the preceding phrase; mountain light is Zen beyond the categories. With an iron staff in hand, he scrapes away the drool of wild foxes.
Having shed all traces of finicky attachment, he comes to study with an ancient master. The staff strikes the lion’s bone; from its tongue, the *pāṭala* flower emerges.

The radiant form contains the autumn moon; the sacred shrine is hidden by the evening clouds. Within the chamber, on a space no larger than a square foot, how many dragons and snakes have been distinguished?
Leisurely resting the alms bowl before the hall, the lion treats the colt with disdain. Where one cannot turn back even upon facing each other, there is the moment of bowing the head in silence.
Failing to clarify the final word, he instead leaves us in doubt to this day. I ask about the matter of the three years: by what means was it known so early?
With the Vajra-eye upon his crown and the *liji* thorn within his breast, a single phrase roars like a thunderclap, sending heroes fleeing across the four seas.
The Patriarch’s intent is presented before the pivot; ordinary sentiments are instantly emptied. The Gate of the School possesses the hand that gives life and takes death;
its true wind is seen with chilling majesty.

Ten Poems on Dwelling in the Mountains Heaven and earth preserve my Way; in mountain forests, old age grows more intimate. When at leisure, I open my azure eyes; a single glance encompasses all the yellow dust.
Joyfully attaining the state of non-arising, I dissolve this body of outflows. How many follow illusory shadows? All are but people coming and going.
My hair is not as white as my mind; my form is like withered wood. When all conditions have ceased in the midst of stillness, looking back for a single thought-moment, I am solitary.
Heaven has already accepted my rustic simplicity; in Chan, one should transcend both existence and non-existence. This remaining life is like the setting sun; every step is the path home.
The principle of existence is fundamentally without abiding; fleeting light cannot be grasped. Who can take these new sun and moon and exchange them for their former countenance?
Sitting alone, I hear only the birds; opening the door, I see nothing but mountains. When illusory conditions have completely ceased, why seek further seclusion?

Having grown weary of mingling with the world, I return to the mountains, intent on resting within myself. How often have I planned for a thousand years? It was only for the sake of one person that I remained.
Vastly expansive, it forms the void of kalpas; from tiny droplets, a great torrent accumulates. If one contemplates only the principle of purity, the body and the world are both like floating things.

The body is already difficult to rely upon; its fragmented parts each have their own causes. For a brief moment, the four elements join together, but in the end, they are merely an aggregation of subtle dust.
The myriad sounds contain emptiness and stillness; all conditions reveal their fundamental truth. From time immemorial, within sound and form, many have been led astray.
This hut, though but a small measure in size, allows for freedom of movement within its bounds. Clouds and mists arise at its doors and windows; stars and moon hang from its courtyard and eaves.

As mindfulness of the breath deepens, the mind becomes increasingly tranquil; as defilements vanish, the objective world remains as it is. When the southern breeze enters the hall, a whistling sound fills the six empty windows.

Having eaten my fill, I have no further concerns; I sleep soundly by day, with no sense of time passing. I am not at all aware of the shift between darkness and light, nor have I heard the tolling of bells or drums for many days.
Surrounded on all four sides by azure peaks, I lie my whole body amidst white clouds. Who says that the power of tea is so robust that it can dispatch the armies of the sleep-demon?
Having no intention for the world of men, my spirit roams the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Only this "leakable" child remains, who is ashamed to let loose his blind, ignorant dhyāna.
I alone envy the wings that seize the wind; they can support many lotuses emerging from the water. Looking back at those worldly guests, who among them is not bound by the sleep of entanglements?
This nature is originally without attachment; why then is it not free? It is only because of the arising of governing attachments that it is subjected to the flux of the world.
Failing to recognize the shadow of flowers in the sky, one pities the bubbles upon the great ocean. Only by opening the eye of purity can one clearly see within the tip of a single hair.
Brandishing the fly-whisk is my original affair; what can be done with a mind so idle? For now, I shall employ the power of diligence to subdue the demon of sleep.

In profound stillness, the celestial pipes resound; slowly and far away, the ripples of flowing water pass. From the beginning, there has never been a single word; surely he would not have reproached Vimalakīrti.

Departing from Nan Yue, my face bears the hues of mist and clouds; I walk with a sense of inner shame, doing so merely to fulfill an old promise—how could it be for the sake of pursuing fleeting fame?
Let the monkeys and cranes cease their lament for parting; the pine wind does not pause its sound. Only the broad and long tongue remains, preaching non-arising day and night.
The boat travels as the Xiang River connects to Ba and Han; the solitary sail enters the land of Chu. A single cloud hangs low over the distant trees; the bright sun shines upon the slanting stream.
Living in this world is always like staying on temporary lodging; do not inquire after the years of this fleeting life. Even if one follows the path back home, it is like a boat at a river crossing.

Setting out at dawn from Xiangtan, setting out at dawn from the bend of Qingtan Creek, I raise my oars and drift with the current. The sails fly along with departing birds; the banks turn as they follow the moving boat.

The trees are so distant they seem to mark the end of heaven; the river is so empty it appears that the earth is floating. Mount Dongting seems but a few inches away as we draw closer to Yueyang Tower.

Borrowing the wind from the pavilion, the course of Heaven shifts the mandate of the fiery reign; all vie with one another in this autumn of the "stags" (the struggle for power). Who knows that this recluse lying amidst the clouds has lent his own sinews to serve as the first strategic calculation?

The imperial enterprise was settled in three parts; heroic ambition was requited by a single fire. The east wind harbors a thousand-year-old resentment; the waters of the Jiang and Han flow on and on.
Passing Jia-yu, the boat halted to stay the night at Pu-shui. At the break of dawn we passed Jia-yu; dew rests upon the small city walls, and the river holds the sparse shadows of trees.
The heavens hang as if near at hand; the waters stretch afar as if resting upon the void. A single reed-raft rides the wind away, drifting and floating wherever it may lead.

Setting sail from Wuchang, I have beheld the sights and traversed the Xiao and Xiang rivers. Riding the current, I passed through Wuchang; the mountains and rivers are majestic at Hankou. Clouds and rain once deceived King Xiangwang.

Tracing distant paths like soaring yellow cranes, light sails are hoisted against the setting sun. My life’s journey follows the flowing waters; there is no need to inquire whether I am active or in retreat.

Passing through Huangzhou, seven marshes stretch out, commanding Jing and Xiang. A single expanse of water reaches to the heavens. The river current turns at Red Cliff; mountain hues embrace Yellow Ridge.
In composing this rhapsody, I extol the Fisherman; in singing my way along, I recall the Madman of Chu. Formerly I longed to wash my feet; now I am already at the Canglang River.
*Six Poems on Returning Joyfully to Kuangshan* This mountain was where I dwelt in a former life;
these woods have opened up from this very day. Having mistakenly entangled myself in worldly burdens, I have departed; now, I rejoice that I rely upon my past affinities to return.
The skeletal peaks stand gaunt; my mind at ease, a hundred thoughts have turned to ash. Smoke and mists now suffice; why need one ask of Mount Tiantai?

To withdraw from the world, one is originally free from vexation; dwelling in the mountains, one never tires of depth. Dense clouds carry rain even in fair weather; secluded ravines are perpetually shrouded in shade.
A fawn with its mother sleeps upon the lush grass; crows returning home gather in the evening woods. A bright moon falls from the mountain peak, piercing through the mind of a lifetime.

Having shed my entanglements in my declining years, I hollow out my heart to easily enter meditation. Having lived on by stealth until this day, I feel a sense of serene joy for these remaining years.
Long have I borne my debts; now they are all repaid. My noble affinity is surely not yet exhausted. When my spirit sinks into this mound of earth, a blue lotus shall spring forth from that very spot.
The old mist and clouds of my former lordship—having returned, I have reached home at once. Clouds arise like rolls of silk; mountains embrace me as if they were lotus flowers.

Deeply asleep, I forget the distinction between dusk and dawn; in my deluded meditation, the years and seasons pass by. This is the place where one may find rest for their feet, requiring nothing more than a single *kāṣāya*.

White hair reflects my withered face; I rely on the mountains to conceal my form. For the remainder of my life, I await only transformation; when this single breath ceases, all shall return to stillness.

Meditation is so intense it makes speech difficult; the clouds are so deep they easily conceal the gate. Perfect penetration enters the flowing stream, resounding with a constant, murmuring "chan-chan" day and night.

Old age and indolence suit one another; the physical form dissolves and the vital breath fails to sustain itself. Seeing and hearing are entirely like a dream; rising and sitting are suddenly like being dazed.
The sun and moon pass from morning to evening; flourishing and withering follow the seasons. What remains is but a single thought: silently entering the state of no-thought.

Sitting at Night to Enjoy the Cool Air (Three Poems) Delighted by the fresh clearing of the night, the crisp air of autumn arrives. After the rain, the forest leaves grow heavy; as the wind passes, the mountain clouds become light.

In meditative concentration, one contemplates non-self; Through hidden cultivation, one grows weary of existence. Sitting, one gazes at the moon in the empty realm, Vividly facing its solitary brilliance.

The ten thousand sounds are silent and voiceless; The source of the mind is as clear as water. Incense smoke from the brazier drifts thin through the night; The mountain moon enters the window with clarity.

The insects dwelling in the grass find particular stability; the cranes sleeping upon the clouds are not startled. As I sit deeply, all conceptual thoughts cease; suddenly, I hear the dawn bell tolling.
There is no need to shun the scorching heat; coolness surely has its time. Clouds fly and the mountain colors fall away; thunder stirs and the sound of rain follows.
Do not resent the heavy dew that shortens the grass; do not complain of the autumn wind’s delay. Simply sit beneath the pine trees and wait for the favorable breeze to blow.
Wall-observation: Sitting upright, contemplate the mind with clarity. Its source is not easily found. When it moves, its traces appear; where it arises, it is profoundly deep and mysterious.

In profound stillness, the sound of knocking on emptiness echoes; A continuous stream of chirping emerges from the fledgling’s throat. One should know that the marks of thought-free detachment Belong entirely to neither floating nor sinking.

On Illness (two stanzas): Suffering and its accumulation are the causes of birth; This body of great affliction is difficult to sustain. Support relies solely upon the bones; Movement and turning do not depend on the person.

A single breath is as thin as a thread; this remaining frame is as insubstantial as dust. From the beginning, all things have been merely borrowed; in the end, with whom can they be truly intimate? For long I have loathed the body as a burden;
how much more so now that it is assailed by old age and sickness? I am ashamed of my shallow meditative concentration, and I perceive ever more clearly the profound source of this illness.
Having realized the Dharma and transcended all marks, one contemplates emptiness and perceives this very mind. Desiring to transcend the path of birth and death, do not seek it outwardly.
After the communal meal, he walked in meditation, demonstrating that even after eating, one should practice walking meditation.
Following the current without questioning the distance, his feet were like severed silk threads and his body was as light as a fragment of cloud.

Stepping forth, the mountain’s radiance pierces through; returning, the moonlight is bright. There is no need to trouble yourself by entering the room again; simply listen to the sound of the night bell.

Autumn deepens, autumn deepens, and the cold air grows heavy; it is most fitting to wrap oneself in one's robes. As man ages, his bones grow more resilient; though the pine withers, its branches become even more extraordinary.

The yellow flowers show little sign of life; white hair marks my departure from worldly affairs. Sitting alone after forgetting all ties to conditions, I am left with only this vast silence known to myself.
Arriving at Guangzhou in the second month of the Bingshen year, I lodge at Huazhou Temple.
Having traversed the ends of the earth, my journey still feels far from over. Countless are the mists and fogs of the Hundred Yue lands; only by crossing these perils do I realize the ocean of dust.

Vast! When the Way is exhausted, one sees the lightness of birth and death even more clearly. For a time, I dwell within the radiance of the water-moon; by chance, I walk upon the ground of lapis lazuli jewels.
Having reached the shore, the boat has now been cast away; for whom do the bells and drums of the upper realms resound?

Ding Youwu, King: Since we departed from our excursion through the various wonders of Xingyan and have not yet returned, I compose this verse to express my longing for those sights and the pursuit of the extraordinary at Rangsu Qiu.
How much more so now that I encounter Xiao Shi as a fellow traveler! A thousand mountains closely follow as if on the wings of a pair of dragons;
ten thousand ravines vie to rush toward a single leaf-boat. Within the caves, who can find the cinnabar? Amidst the clouds, how many *zhi* and *shu* herbs remain?
At that time, I gathered my things; do not look at those playing *qi* beneath the pines—half a game can cause one’s hair to turn white.
Setting out for Lei Yang, I paused briefly at Xiao Jinshan;
human affairs are mostly hollow and full of error. I sought to still my mind by the heart of the river; there was a temple, yet it would not allow a monk to stay even for a moment.

Dwelling here, one who has left home should vie with cranes in their return to the wilds. Benevolent clouds darken to cover the chamber of the Unborn; fragrant mists leisurely permeate the traveler’s robe.
For those lost at the ford for a thousand ages, the precious raft is suspended; if you are willing to halt amidst the swift current, you may take refuge.
Master Ji traveled far from Mount Lu to inquire of Caoqi;
from afar he turned toward Caoqi to ask about the mirror-stand. Upon entering the gate, a single glance caused his smile to unfold. His body arrived like the idle clouds of Mount Lu;

his mind brought with it the white snows of Mount Yan. Having traversed the paths beyond the heavens to the very end of birth and death, he has fully inscribed the changing seasons upon the mountain ridges.
Head Plum. My old friend, may you simply possess such thoughts as yours; this constant concern has long since reduced me to ashes.
In the year Jiachen, I returned to garrison duty at Caoxi upon receiving the imperial summons;
the misty clouds and mists have always been remote from the dust of the world. How could I dare claim a true love for forests and springs? As I grow old, my heart is like a fire that has gone out.
