A tree grows from its withered remains, as if a second spring had dawned. Heaven and Earth do not permit those who have fled to Chan; the rites and laws cannot forget those who have transcended the world.
Only the companions of monkeys and cranes in the solitary mountains frequently follow my pure dreams to keep company with my idle body.
In the past, I traveled with Master Miaofeng to Wangu Temple in Hedong; now hearing that it has been renovated, I compose this to express my sentiments.
Forty years ago, I once begged for alms beside the Jetavana Monastery by the Ganges, where Mount Zhongtiao surged forth like a blue lotus.
The topknot: clouds rise from Mount Hua, the blue waves surge; the city walls of a thousand homes return to Śrāvastī. The Dharma-body unfolds thrice to transform the Sahā world.
When shall I again bear the dragon-subduing staff and perform the *kaṭhina* ceremony once more before Magu’s seat?

Ascending the Wujing Water Tower, one passes through clouds over the gorges and across level fields. Having traversed the very source of the stream, one beholds the vast expanse of the marketplace. A single thread of river flows toward the great ocean;
on all four sides, mountain hues embrace blue lotuses. The tower stands upon the cool land where water meets moon; when a person enters this abode of emptiness, they naturally—
Abiding in heaven, it resembles the Peach Blossom Spring, a place to escape the Qin; yet those who come and go there are not merely fishermen.

In Duanzhou, I bid farewell to Magistrate Feng Yuancheng—may you serve in the imperial court or roam the lakes and rivers, each following his own destiny. That we have met here is surely no mere karmic bond of this life. May you employ compassion well in your official duties.
He practiced the Chan of worldly peace and mastery. Having attained the ground of a Khenpo with its attendant emoluments, there remained no further traces of defilement to serve as latent tendencies.
A *dharma-flower* bloomed for three thousand years; now, rejoicing, it opens once more at the edge of the Northern Dipper.
Suffering from the persistent rain on my boat, I thank you, Master Zhong, for visiting me.
Amidst the overcast clouds that do not part even by day, I rejoice deeply at the arrival of an old friend. Pine blossoms alone permit the brewing of wine for one who frowns;
in the Lotus Society, how could one decline the talent of composing a rhapsody? One should view worldly affairs as merely pointing at a horse to show it; this mind does not speak of comparison.
Cold ashes. Sitting and listening to the city wall flute at dusk, light breezes carry the falling plum blossoms one after another.
On the river, moved by sentiment:
wind and rain howl across the river, and upon the boat, I see but a drifting soul wandering in emptiness. Returning from a dream, I rest atop the pines where clouds dwell.
Cranes, I watch idly as the gulls play upon the sands. There is no need to trouble the northern geese with letters; worldly affairs have long since been consigned to the eastward-flowing current.
Two-thirds of my hundred-year span have already passed; even if there remains a life, it is all but a floating bubble.
On my way south, I encountered rain; a north wind blew the rain dark upon the mountain city.
At the end of the year, still far from home on the edge of the world, I continue my distant journey. I long to hide from the world among the ranks of deer and roe.

On this perilous road, my heart breaks at the sound of the *shējū* (partridge) bird. For ten years I have drifted like a lone gourd-buoy across the miasmic seas; in a single night, the frost has fallen twice.
Gray hairs have grown upon my temples; I spurred my horse through the mud to seek lodging in the wilds. Unable to bear looking back, the evening smoke stretches across the sky.
I send these words from Yan-du’s Cishou Temple to the Elder Bieshan.

For many years we have traveled together with but a single bowl; through the long nights I would don my robes to listen to the dawn bells. At every meal, I have always remembered the Fragrant Accumulation Heaven.

In the realm, he constantly recalled Mount Sumeru while walking in meditation; the miasmic heat was secretly dispelled as his heart harbored snow. He silently marked the passing years by planting pines with his own hands.
May he sweep the lotus lion-throne so that I may once again raise the school of the ineffable truth.
The Dharma-nature of the Summer Retreat is as clear and alert as a public banana grove;
how could this grove compare to sitting in the Jeta Grove? To borrow a cool breeze for a moment to dispel my vexation. How many green leaves have been provided for Huaisu’s brush?

Deep shade still covers the Hall for Translating Scriptures (the Hall where Master Fang served as scribe for the translations). To protect living beings, one is not permitted to go out for alms in the morning. Practice...
I shall surely close my door again during the day; having heard that from the beginning there has never been a single thing, I now face all day long the ineffable silence.
When Zou Ziyin came to visit, I showed him this for his inquiry into the Ultimate:
"The matter is clear; it is fundamentally not delusion. As the wind rises in the courtyard at dawn, it blows through the green pines.

Bamboo: After the spring mountain rains, the long green *qílí* grass grows lush. Only when at leisure does one realize all conditions are stilled; only after awakening does one know that all things are equal.
Most intimate of all is that which calls to people: the single crow of a cock that shatters the dream at the fifth watch.
After De Shan paid homage to the Patriarchs, he passed by Dingwang Ling;

that one blow of his staff distinguished the holy from the mundane. This true, essential function transcends both seeing and hearing. For a thousand autumns, the incense and lamps have occupied the royal aura;
for all eternity, the mountains and rivers are covered by clouds of compassion. In the empty forest, deer still follow the whisk; in the Pure Land, lotus flowers have already blossomed.
It belongs to you. A staff leaning against the spring breeze, I stand waiting once more; the sunset’s purple and azure hues are swirling in dense profusion.
Having completed the construction of my hut east of Lake Hengyang, Liu Cun, Chizhong, Hengying, and Yuanlai came from afar to console me, and we thus spent the year together.
For a year our spirits have been joined in thought, consumed by longing; now we meet with joy at the end of the year. Your small boat has come from a thousand li through the snowy night;
you bring a single branch of lotus seeds for the Pure Land. My aged frame is but a thing of long-past utility; from this moment on, the days and months shall be new acquaintances.
Do not say that the community of Mount Kuang has perished; it may well be expected that the society shall be re-established here once more.

Two Poems on Departing for the East to Attend the Feast at Huayao Monastery At the ancient site of practice west of Śrāvastī, I happened to pass by three times to pay homage to the King of Emptiness. Having contemplated the mind, I have entered the realm of Mind-Only;

To preach the Dharma, I shall ascend once more to the Hall of Good Dharma. Fragrant food can satisfy the many gathered masses, Yet the finest cream of clarified butter is granted only to those who are sharp of faculty.
Roots and flavors: while people have not yet grasped them lightly and cast them out, perhaps they may come again to raise them up once more.

The Jetavana Garden opens toward the Great Western River; there, lotus flowers spring from the earth as the most fitting dwelling. The Buddha-land far transcends all external forms; the Dharma-body is as tall as the four heavens.
If you come for but a moment, please ascend the lotus throne; if you dwell long, you should send frequent messages of faith.
Leaning on my staff of withered branches, I regret that our visits must come to an end; alas, it is unbearable to turn back and gaze upon this scene once more, filled with profound sorrow.

Passing by the Mei Xue Tang (Hall of Plum and Snow) at Huayao Temple—the former residence of Master Sun’an, whose skeletal frame was even more refined amidst the plum and snow—I took a leisurely stroll after the midday meal as I passed through the hall. Fragrance wafted from the stone chamber as the flowers first bloomed.

Letting go, the shadow enters the ice-clear pitcher and the moon shines all the brighter; At the crag where his arm was severed, old traces remain; In the flute, longing for the man, one recalls the new melody.
If one were to ask now about the meaning of the Westward Journey, Who could recognize the path of his departure—those single sandals?
Beyond the Nine Peaks lies the ancestral abode of Master Wunian, a Brahma-palace hidden amidst mists and clouds.
Outside the gate, the red dust of the mundane world is far removed. The mountains themselves open up a Pure Land from their nine peaks;
monks sit upon thousand-petaled lotuses. Radiance floats over the stone chamber where Imperial calligraphy remains; its reflection falls upon the various heavens.
Guarding the crimson silk. If one asks about the definitive meaning of the Westward Transmission, it is clearly and fully entrusted within a single *kāṣāya*.
Having stayed in the abbot’s quarters of Jiufeng, I entrust this to Elder Wenyuan:
from afar, toward the famous mountain, you pay homage at the Dharma altar; may you pray that the Patriarch may settle this mind. The night moon of Jiufeng invades the person.

I declare: The pine wind from ten thousand ravines pierces the bones with cold. The lamp of wisdom, once extinguished, has again blazed forth its flame. Leaving behind only the robe and bowl, to whom shall they be entrusted?
You should know that on the day the Lord of Devas took refuge, the lion’s roar was still not finished.
Leading my disciples, I went to the suburban garden for the vegetarian feast of Wang Zhangfu in Hanyang;
from afar, I visited the banks of the Han River. It was just like the time when the assembly gathered at Vaiśālī. We ate our fill of fragrant food, a celestial offering;
we delighted in profound discourse, like the refined lyrics of the city of Ying. The level fields were once the pattern for cutting robes; the tall willows now droop with fresh rain.
Exposed branches; wind and rain, the night deepens and the mind becomes tranquil. In its cool clarity, one wonders if one is sitting in a pond of lotus flowers.
For two nights, Tenguang Zhashang received guests at this ancient site amidst a thicket of thorns.
Twenty years of toil—on whose behalf was he so busy? Now that the hall is opened, dragons from the four seas arrive.
The Elephant: Chanting the Brahma-hymns at the three times, one pays homage to the Dharma King. Within this realm, the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) is fully realized.
From between his brows, he constantly radiates the white tuft of light; having relied upon him, one enters the land of Mind-Only. What need is there to further proclaim the Ultimate?
Passing through Qu’a, I joyfully encountered Magistrate Wang Dongli;

his mind dwells upon the blue lotus emerging from the water. His carriage and horses seem as if he were still dwelling among the mountain forests. Like flowers in the sky or reflections in a mirror, the dust of the world is utterly stilled;

like the solitary moon over the cold river, his intent grows ever deeper. I imagine you received the prediction of enlightenment directly from Vulture Peak; surely this is your former abode in Vaiśālī.
A Connoisseur of Sound. Meeting face-to-face, a single phrase of non-arising— Clearly manifest before one’s eyes, there is no need to seek it.
Ascending Mount Lingxiao on Jing Mountain, I climbed alone to the high peak, leaning on my staff of *lǐ*.
The pervasive azure-green mist grows increasingly mysterious and dim. The two eyes of the Westward Transmission are like the Peng bird.

Wings [of the mountain] stretch eastward for a thousand peaks like horse hooves; the precipitous ravines have long been called the Lion’s Den. The empty forests shall forever allow the Elephant King to dwell.
Now, as I wish to preach the Dharma of non-arising, the mere flick of the fly-whisk causes the ten thousand phenomena to bow low.
I entrust this to Commissioner Cai of the Five Peaks:
you once formed a noble karmic connection at Caoxi. Since our parting, the Chan of the Patriarch has grown cold;

yet when you speak of non-duality, I think of Vimalakīrti, and whenever you discuss birthlessness, I recall Master Dadian. Who would have known that these official documents were but manifestations of a high-ranking magistrate?
True Commentary: Before the Hall of the Withered Tree at Xuefeng, tonight because of you, the moon wanes and then waxes again.

Joyfully returning to Mount Kuang after long travels throughout the rivers and lakes, weary of wandering; it is only upon reaching old age that one finally finds refuge in the green mountains. The physical form has already been cast off like a flower in the sky.
Shadows. All worldly affairs flow away like a passing stream. In silent stillness, my idle body has the clouds for companions; with windswept white hair, snow covers my head.
There is no need to calculate how many years remain; in a single thought of non-arising, vast eons come to rest.
Forest-viewing by the sea, Lord County Magistrate Chen Chishi, Great Participant, visited this mountain;
I recall those days at the White Society on Mount Kuang. On this day, your noble carriage is most worthy of pursuit. Upon entering, one can immediately forget worldly anxieties;
having arrived, there is no need at all to knit one's brows. My body is drenched by the clouds of ten thousand valleys; I sit waiting for the moon amidst a thousand peaks.
The scenery is slow to change; one night of pure conversation has become a place of excellence. Since antiquity, heaven and earth have known the weight of the heart.
Few are the country folk who, having left home at a young age, no longer remember their family. Reflecting on past events, all is worthy of lamentation; I still think of my old friends as children.
Facing it, withered trees find it hard to bloom their old-time flowers. Willow branches by the river hang with the morning dew;
the mountain hues before the gate bear the morning glow. Only these scenes remain year after year; there is no need to inquire further about the passage of time.
Seeing off Master Xiuliuyi as he returns to his home mountain:

For twenty years you have diligently accompanied me through pestilential lands; again you followed my staff and bowl as I wandered through all quarters. To seek the mystery, you ascended directly to the summit of the Golden Wheel;
to enter the chamber, you relied once more upon the Great Dharma Hall. Though you have the intention to return to your home mountain, how could old age find delight in springs and rocks?
I am able to forget [this]. Should my remaining years not yet have filled the ditches and ravines, I look forward to dwelling together with you in the field of nirvana.
Heart-light, Dharma-nephew, holding the hand-written manuscript of my elder brother En-xiong from Xuelang, was moved upon reading it:

"When you arrived, I suddenly recalled the feelings of an old friend; in the end, the vow for transcendence is difficult to forget. Upon first seeing these bequeathed words, they are as if we were face to face."

Looking at his face, I reflect deeply that our laughter and conversation seem to span many lifetimes; I know he has ascended the high throne in Tuṣita Heaven. To enter directly into Bodhi—how could one calculate the distance?
If we should meet again as we did in days of old, would he not be willing to let his companions walk the same path with him?
On the Mid-Autumn Festival, I rejoice that Chen, the Minister of Sacrifices, has come to visit me in the mountains.
From afar he inquired after the herds of deer and wild boars in this empty valley; with his carriage, he entered the ravine as the sun set.

We opened our robes and spoke in detail of our innermost thoughts, brewing tea and burning incense until the hour of night. Rejoicing in the bright moon, my mind was like a mirror; I observed the affairs of the world and saw them vanish in an instant.
Like clouds. If a student asks about the meaning of the Westward Journey, I have nothing at all to hand over to you.
To the assembly:
My lifelong traces follow the conditions of past karma; I am ashamed and startled, not yet liberated. A single mind of leisure follows wherever it may be.
I see it: unbidden white hairs shift in the darkness. I know for myself that every coming day is but a day subtracted. Who would believe that adding years is actually diminishing them?
Turning my head toward the home-mountain after returning, I shall sleep upon a stone pillow amidst ten thousand peaks.
Shoujue Xiumiu, Layman: You have long been one who manifests a physical body;
your adamantine mind-ground is pure and free from dust. Having long cultivated the means to transform living beings, you have awakened to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Though dwelling in the world, you are like one who has transcended it. Māmakī’s Dharma-gate is not silence; Pánggōng’s wife and children were not...
For my kin, my spirit has already entered the Lotus Treasury; what need is there to ask about the longevity of the Great Chun tree?

These ten poems on dwelling in the mountains record the traces of my life’s journey, drifting east and west as it may. In my old age, how could I choose where to perch like a bird seeking a tree? Even if my backbone were as stiff as—
Iron! Alas, how my shinbones are as soft as mud. Idly watching clouds rise from the precipitous ravines, I sit leaning against a thousand peaks and listen to the birds’ cries.
There is no need to further pick at words beyond the ordinary; the sounds and forms before one are the complete presentation.

Structuring a hut of grass upon a cliff, it can barely accommodate a single body within one small cell. Yet, once the source of the mind has returned to profound stillness, one may leave worldly affairs to their own stupidity and delusion.
When the sun has risen three spans high, one still lies in high repose; the chamber is sealed by clouds, allowing no entry for visitors.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs have directly caused all traces to be severed; why need there be a succession of three times three?
Looking back, the five turbidities swirl in dense mists; the crowds clamor like gnats in a jar. Before a single thought arises, delusion and enlightenment are severed;
as soon as a single atom is established, the holy and the mundane are divided. The green mountains naturally allow me to hide my ineptitude; who can save this burning house from its conflagration?
I crane my neck toward the vast sky with my two azure eyes, yet the entire great earth is but drifting clouds—this is unbearable.

How lamentable that past events are but a journey through dreams; like flowers in the sky seen by cataract-ridden eyes, they cannot be sought. The path of the mind is surely like the moon emerging from dispersing clouds;
let the physical form be as a bubble floating on water. With but three inches of breath remaining for this life, to grow old amidst a thousand peaks is worth ten points more than worldly success.
From now on, my traces in the human world shall be severed; no longer will joy or sorrow rise upon my brow.
My practice in seclusion has now fulfilled my original aspiration. From time immemorial, I have dwelt in the mountains, never wearying of their depth.

Beyond the void, let a thousand peaks stand as they will; how could my eyes tolerate the intrusion of a single speck of dust? The pine wind occasionally preaches the Dharma of non-arising; the flowing water eternally sounds the zither of antiquity.
What need is there to laboriously raise the whisk upon entering the room? To grasp the truth at the moment of encounter depends solely on being a true connoisseur.

In secluded crags, orchids and fragrant herbs abound with their lingering scent; the gentle breeze of the pines wafts forth a hidden fragrance. By briefly borrowing from this perfumed cultivation, one opens the ground of nature;
it is more excellent than pouring down sweet nectar to irrigate a withered gut. With every thought, one enters directly into the Lotus Treasury;
in every moment, the light of Prajñā is ever-bright. Once contentment is attained, one ascends to the Tuṣita realm; what need is there to labor elsewhere seeking the Western Land?

In the depths of spring, bamboo shoots sprout in the cold valley; once more, I see the tips of the pines gradually putting forth blossoms. A single bowl awaits the arrival of guests to provide the midday offering;
the assembly of monks waits with single-minded devotion to taste the new tea. Empty and devoid of supernatural power, there are no celestial meals from the gods;
yet abundant and adorned are the five-colored clouds. I ask the guests of song and dance in Chang’an: when have you ever let your dreams fly to this mountain home?

For three winters I have sat in withered meditation, wrapped in my patched robe; now joyfully beholding the spring light, it is most pitiable and lovely. In the earthen cauldron, wild vegetables are being prepared as an offering;

in the hearth, the pine fire gradually fades to smokeless embers. The green mountains, covered in snow, reveal their faces anew; my white hair, shielding against the cold, has already reached my shoulders.
Fortunate to be a cloud-dwelling guest in this era of peace, I burn incense morning and evening to pray for the longevity of the Yao dynasty.
Old travels are hazy, as if from a former life; every memory of my past conduct stirs a secret alarm. The green mountains of this day are the dreams of that time;
the white community of now is the covenant of the past. To respond to circumstances, I use only a scale without stars; for the joy of old age, I keep only a broken-legged cauldron.
If you ask for the definitive meaning of the Westward Journey, it is the single stream of Caoxi, overflowing with water.
For what reason did you love leaving home in those days? It is hard to forget the old, worn-out kashaya robe. It was simply because many debts from past lives remained unpaid;

it was not that a single thought went astray from the beginning. Half a lifetime of karmic conditions is like a dream or an illusion; a hundred years of deluded thoughts are equal to flowers in the sky.
Returning home, there remain only the green mountains; how could one bear to trade gold for sand?

Lying ill upon my meditation cushion, dust gathers daily upon the incense table. Old age and sickness find no place for this world-transcending body. The sound of the spring enters my dreams, piercingly clear to my ears;
the moonlight reaches my bed, its chill penetrating me. My idle mind does not unite with external conditions; of pure karma, there remains but one.
Meditate on the Truth. Ultimately, one must know the place of ultimate destination. The lotus has already blossomed as a kinsman for the future.

To repay Lord Lu Jingye, how many times did your noble carriage pass through these empty mountains? Having traversed a thousand peaks, you have directly broken through the barrier. Even with a tongue, one could not repay this profound intimacy.
Truly, forgetting artifice is enough to face this aging countenance. Flying snowflakes come to illuminate the cold; gazing into the blue clouds, my thoughts grow even more serene.
I recall from afar the place where you sit upright at the military camp gate; Mount Lu often appears between your two eyebrows.
To Chan Master Jingguang of Yangshan:

Since you first returned from seeking the Dharma at Mount Lu, months and years have passed and news of you has been rare. I see that you have already entered the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), while I know you constantly participate in the higher-level teaching.
After the rain falls and the clouds part, the mountain’s bones grow lean; as spring deepens and the sun warms, the bracken sprouts.
The sprouts are lush. When shall I once again strike the bed with my staff and display the cassock brought from the West?
*Six Poems on Dwelling in the Mountains (with an Introduction)*:
While I was in retreat, I resided as if in the deep mountains; hence, these verses were composed.
A firewood block burns for a thousand years; it supports a single-plank bridge. The paths of men and worlds are cut off; the hermitage master is serene and listless.
White snow rests before the eaves; though it falls day after day as of old, it is not that you have no mind—how else could we dwell together forever?
The bright moon hangs in the cold sky; its light penetrates to the bottom of the cold pool. Above and below are fundamentally one and the same; when viewed, there is neither "this" nor "that.
The flowing water is not sound; the bright moon is originally not form. Sound and form do not relate to one another—who can realize this realm?

From where does the wind come? It causes all manner of echoes to stir within the rocky caves. Yet when one listens in stillness, there is fundamentally no sound; how, then, can there be arising and ceasing?
My body stands amidst a thousand crags, and the path ahead is impassable. In this solitude, who is my companion? Only these few pine trees.
The boat moors at Zhujiang;
the moonlight is as pale as water. The tide is calm, its chill like that of the void. A lone boat lies across the wild crossing. The person exists within the realm of being and non-being.
Four Poems on the Meditation Hall in the Army.

In the morning one hears the sound of war-drums; in the evening one listens to the resonance of the golden chime. Though movement and stillness differ, they are appreciated only by those who understand the music.
Banners and pennants shroud the floating clouds; the shadows of streamers reflect the morning sun. Observe the mechanism of life and death: the military arts are not as subtle as Chan.
The Dharma drum resounds through the Dragon Palace; its roar shakes heaven and earth. How does this compare to the wind passing through myriad apertures, sighing forth the breath of the Great Mass?
Once I sat by the Eastern Sea, where terrifying waves raged like crumbling mountains; now, hearing this thunder that shakes the heavens, it enters my ears and my mind becomes even more tranquil.
Entrusted to You, Wang Jinwu:
Meeting by chance, we suddenly part; a reunion again will surely be difficult. My thoughts of you are like falling snow; my dreams fly to the cold gates of Jimen.
Rejoicing at the Arrival of a Friend.
The meeting of human lives is as fleeting as a stormy evening; when we were yet unacquainted, it was like a day within the clouds.
Spontaneously composed in four stanzas:
The willow flowers are blown by the wind, drifting east, west, south, and north. Is it that they love to follow others? No, for their own essence is originally non-existent.
The pheasant is confined within a pen; its fine grain is no small matter. How does it compare to one dwelling in the mountains and forests, satisfying its needs for drink and food as they arise?
The leopard hides in the mists of the Southern Mountains, yet it constantly fears the encroachment of nets. It is solely because of its fur and skin that it becomes a burden to its own body and mind.
A lamp’s oil illuminates the night’s journey; while others benefit, one suffers loss. How could one not cherish oneself? One’s physical nature is what has been naturally bestowed.

I recall the bamboo grove and lotus pond at my home mountain, where ten thousand bamboos fluttered in the clear rain. Two ponds drew from the stone spring; thirty years have passed since we parted. Day after day I remember planting the lotuses.

Jongshan (Qiongshan) is a wondrous realm where incense is the national treasure; Zhuyai (Zhuya) has mountains made of jade. People cross over from the sea of dust, appearing as if they have emerged from the Celestial Gate.
Mount Wuzhi.
A single leaf floats beyond the heavens; a thousand mountains fall within a mirror. Who can wield five fingers to cleave through the vast void?
Golden grains float upon the spring like golden dust; the spring flows with white jade nectar. I have come holding a single bowl, sufficient to offer to the King of Space.
In Mingchang, the pagoda opens the Dragon Canon upon the sea of jade; incense banners emerge from the Brahma heavens. Behold now within this burning house: blue lotuses spring up from the earth.
Two poems on General Liu’s invitation to view the Jade Dragon Spring.
The clear spring is as cold as jade; the noble trees are as dense as clouds. The people possess the joy of the era of Fuxi and Huangdi; their hearts are one with the herds of deer and wild boars.
Since what year was the primordial chaos pierced? Here on this spot, the deep spring has opened. Men stand within the realm of emptiness; the mountains emerge from within a mirror.
Four Poems on the Depth of Ink Fragrance Green grasses spread like sash-bands;
Solitary orchids form fragrant girdles. In the empty pavilion, I sit alone; My mind has already reached the age of Xi Huang.
The color of the bamboo invades the eaves with green; the lotus flowers reflect red upon the water. When the cool dew falls deep at night, the person stands amidst the hidden fragrance.
The hibiscus blooms like brocade; the yellow chrysanthemums layer like coins. In this state where the intoxicated eyes perfume the heart, there is the sublime and spontaneous dhyāna.
The snow presses the plum to unfurl its buds; spring urges the grass to sprout its shoots. Who among those observing the signs of life before their eyes can recognize them within this mountain home?
Sent to Li Sheng of Jiaodong: The road of ten thousand *li* is not far; my heart remains empty and at ease. I know not how many layers of gates separate us from those who think of me.
Holding the civil to the left and the martial to the right, Grand Councilor, fallen leaves fill the thousand mountains with rain;
a single cloud drifts across the cold sky. Raising my head, I cast my gaze abroad for a moment—where could there be a place where I do not think of you?

On Pines, Two Poems The tree grows old, yet its heart grows ever more crimson; The maples wither, yet their leaves turn even redder. How pitiable, amidst the frost and snow, There stands alone a single branch of pine.
Its frost-bitten trunk is aged like dragon scales; Its wind-swept branches are long as horse-tails. A clear, resonant roar issues forth; A rustling sound fills the empty hall.

Two Poems on Plum Blossoms In the monasteries, autumn has already deepened; All the myriad trees are withered and scarred. Only the cold plum tree remains, Sending its fragrance flying amidst the snow.
The hue of snow heralds the arrival of spring; The cold fragrance is even clearer at night. A single cry from a secluded bird Suddenly causes my dream-soul to hasten forth.

Five Poems on Bamboo Coldly soaring, a thousand feet of jade; Purely sprinkling, a grove of frost. Though my worldly heart be heavy, Beholding this, I suddenly forget it all. Majestic is its form that soars above the clouds;
The wind arises, and the dragon roars through the night. Frost and snow do not know the passing of years; Truly, you are my friend through the cold season.
The frost-covered trunk is as cold as jade; the wind-swept branches resonate like a lute. A night’s rain in Xiao and Xiang shatters the traveler’s heart.
When the leaves fall, the roots remain firm; with an empty heart, the joints grow even higher. As a cold breeze sweeps through the grove, it accompanies the pine waves on this clear night.
The spring clouds over Qi’ao are azure; the night rain at Xiao and Xiang is cold. In the empty window, a person listens in stillness as the *langgan* bamboos rustle and sigh.

Three Poems on Rejoicing in Rain: Cool rain falls upon the scorching heavens; a driving wind shakes the forest trees. A light thunder rolls at the eaves, its deep resonance like that of an empty valley.
The primal yang is like a fierce fire; all beings are as if being forged in a furnace. Suddenly the wind and rain arrive; where has the scorching heat gone?
The mountains are empty and the springs grow colder; the summer heat neither comes nor goes. As the wind and rain arise with a whistling sound, my very hair and bones feel refreshed and clear.

Six Poems Composed in the Mountains Dust-secluded from the three thousandfold world-systems, The mind transcends the eighteen dhyānas. As the bell chimes forth in the clear night, I listen through to the end and cannot sleep.
Sun and moon do not know how they pass away; This mind should surely merge with emptiness. Sitting alone at times upon the mountain pavilion, It is as if I were dwelling in the vast primordial chaos.

The branches suddenly stir with the onset of spring; the vital energy of plants and trees is fresh and bright. Amidst stillness, I observe the transformations of time, my mind forgetting the years of outflows.
I pluck pines from the Jewel Forest and draw water from Caoxi’s stream. Returning, I brew tea amidst the falling snow; this flavor is beyond compare.
The cold hues of ten thousand mountains have broken; Warm earth-gas gives birth to spring. Flowers fall upon the Caoxi waters;

Who would be willing to ask for the ford? At leisure, I strike sleep during the day; The pine wind blows through me without end. Where does the sound of the wooden fish come from? In my dream, its resonance is yet more distinct.
I have casually drawn a single drop from the Caoxi Spring. A thousand pines reach toward the Milky Way; people stand within the realm of emptiness, as if amidst a painted landscape.
Two Poems for the Monks in Charge of Affairs.
Before the Cliff of Severed Arms, the snow remains; even now, the blood is still thick. At the Stone beneath the Waist of Huangmei, how many can there be who grind it?
Amidst the accumulated snow and bitter freezing cold, the groves are entirely withered and frozen. When the first yang-energy begins to stir, spring is already revealed upon the branches.
When Professor Dong visited Caoxi, I presented him with this verse on "A Drop of Water from Caoxi":
Wandering through rivers and lakes, it follows you as drenching rain; It sprinkles everywhere upon the parched and withered.
In summer, King Ch'i visited me;
the heat was as virulent as fire. The scent of tea was cool as ice. Who would have known that within this world, none could surpass the monk, save for the indolent?

Two Verses Sent to Chief Seat Wuxin Rong A single expanse of Jiangnan snow, Coming to clear the miasmic heat of the southern seas. Now you cross the mountain ridges; The cold hues linger upon the tips of your brows.
A seven-foot rattan cane reaches over my head; three meals fill my gourd ladle. When, amidst the ten thousand peaks, shall I lie weary and sated upon the clouds?
Facing the moon, the solitary pine on the snowy ridge grows old; at Caoxi, the dripping water is cold. Who knows that tonight’s moon is still the one I beheld in days of yore?
Four Poems on Passing by Xiao Jinshan One visit after another, ever new;
I return again and again without weariness. It is only because I crave the Buddha-sun That I frequently pay homage to the body of the Dharma King.
The green mountains never change; the flowing waters go and return. Only the moon between the pines sheds its clear light upon the green moss.

The fisherman’s fires are white in the deep night; the shore chickens clamor in the clear day. The river is empty and the world of men is cut off; through the long days, I keep my thatched gate closed.
The fish and dragons are secure beneath the steps; the gulls and egrets are at leisure upon the sands. A mere span of water divides us, yet it cuts off ten thousand layers of mountains.
I rejoice that Mr. Gongliang has returned from Beimen.
(Five Poems) In human life there are no hundred years, and when meeting you, half was already past. Suddenly we part again after three years; how can one calculate such unions and separations?
Yesterday I boarded a boat upon the void; last night, suddenly, wind and rain broke out. This morning, I joyfully encounter you—how remote and dreamlike it all seems!
Upon the grass-tops of the frontier, the color turns white; the maple leaves of Mount Yan turn crimson. Only the hue of the cold snow remains, yet you still linger at the tip of my brow.
Along the postal roads, rows upon rows of willows; across the rivers and lakes, ten thousand miles of waves. Coming and going, emptying years and months—who among us has not wasted time?
The half-moon over Mount Luofu, a single drop of water from Caoxi—partake of these together with you; their flavor is neither here nor there.
I rejoice that Master Xinqing has arrived;
you have come down from Mount Bai to comfort me with the heat of this southern land. To behold you in this burning house is as joyful as facing the snows of Mount Yan.
Master Zhaoqing once wrote:
"In the long summer, the fire-clouds are red; in the fifth month, the lychees ripen. Sitting with you by the Zhujiang River, day after day we strike the cold jade."

In Response to Master Qing’s “Nostalgia for My Former Hermitage,” Where I Lived Next Door to You: The water and bamboo shared our pure common interests; A single parting has spanned thirty years; Beholding one another now, we have both grown old.
Three Poems Sent to the Two Lords of the Zong Clan, Zhen and Song, of Puban and Xiangyuan.
A vast expanse of Yellow River water flows from afar across the heavens; surging eastward, it enters the sea. I ask, when will it ever turn back?
Two peaks rise from Mount Hua, their jade-green heights cold against the high sky. From afar I hear the resonance of celestial music; surely they are performing at a sacred altar for the immortals.
The colors of Mount Zhongtiao are green; morning mists disperse like fine silken brocade. I know there is one who has forgotten the world, sitting alone contemplating the beginningless.
Dreaming of Traveling to Tiantai (Two Poems) Suddenly I arrive at Mount Tiantai and meet an old man amidst the clouds. I imagine he is a man who fled Qin; his countenance is so exceptionally fair.
Flying up to Mount Huading, I suddenly hear the cry of the celestial rooster. Gazing afar at Mount Penglai, I lift my beard and let out a long, resonant whistle.

Recalling old dreams, I sit beneath the Dragon Flower tree; I have heard the lingering tolls of the Changle Bell. Now awakened within the empty valley, ten thousand ravines roar with the sound of pines in the wind.
The old monk Làn-cán dwells in a mountain hermitage hidden within a small valley;
his mind is as empty as a mustard seed and his robes are void. He sleeps indolently upon the rocks beneath the pines, sitting steadfastly atop the highest peak.
Setting out for Leyang, I bid farewell to Master Tan by the river;
parting at Fuyong River, the autumn waters grow ever more azure. My homeward boat ascends the cold current; my thoughts as I travel back and forth are like the warp and woof of a loom.
On the Moon:
Its light is as if submerged in the deep sea; Its hue in the cold void seems non-existent. Who knows that within a single glance, It has illuminated the path of delusion for a thousand ages?
On Clouds:
A single speck like a fine veil spreads and fills the vast void; one knows only what has already arisen, yet does not see the initial moment before it was born.
I have composed three verses on the trial of the inkstone:
"The gentleman loves and wears jade; its warmth and smoothness reflect his virtue. This stone surpasses it even further; its true treasure lies in brush and ink."
The ocean of phrases flows for ten thousand li; the peaks of the brush are a thousand fathoms of snow. All arise from within this, as flakes of jade fly forth at every moment.
Vast and sweeping are the clear waters of the Jiang; towering and rugged is Mount Zishan. Who knows that the intent of a thousand ages resides, fundamentally, within the primordial chaos?
Two Poems on Huacheng Hermitage The mountain colors shift from dawn to dusk;
beneath the shade of banyan trees, the ancient path is quiet. How many travelers pass to and fro? The red dust of the world swirls in vain.
A well was dug upon the high plateau; the earth was deep and water hard to find. When the labor was brought to its ultimate conclusion, a spring gushed forth, flowing without ceasing.

In a stone-chamber or a small room, one harbors the depths of a secluded valley; in intimate friendship, one encounters the ancients. Though there remains but a square inch of space within, there is nowhere for the clamor and dust of the world to settle.
By the Chan practitioner Mingchan, tea is offered.
This mind fundamentally does not dwell; the bare feet are originally free from dust. Now drawing water from the source, it cools those afflicted by the heat of affliction.
Jichen, Head Seat of the Hall, recalls the place where you planted tea:
the entire garden was nourished by the spring rains. When shall we sweep the pine needles and, facing one another, brew a pot together?
Sent to Chan Master Zongyuan of Xitang:
At Caoxi, the spring waters rise; At Mount Heng, the geese return. I recall you sitting in meditation through the night; The moon rises late at the pine gate.
Composed upon the Meditation Hall of Longxing Temple.

The royal aura gathers at the mountain peaks; the sound of the scriptures penetrates the imperial palace. At this Dharma assembly, the assembly of noble "elephants and dragons" prays for the wind of Yao’s virtue for ten thousand generations.

Entrusted to the Imperial Mausoleum: Heaven and Earth opened the Emperor’s enterprise; the sun and moon revolve over the rivers and mountains. With diligent offerings of incense and lamps, morning and evening we gaze upon the Sage’s countenance.
Twenty-one Poems on Painted Miniature Scenery Flowing clouds cover the spring mountains;
A light chill freezes them as if they would split apart. From where have you come to tread upon the green? As you return, the moonlight is white.

Fragrant trees grow long at the start of summer; light boats glide upon the azure lake. Carrying my lute, I seek an old friend; where shall I find him amidst the deep clouds? A solitary figure crosses the broken bridge;
a small boat floats beneath the frosty moon’s white light. Turning my head to gaze at the cloud-covered mountains, I feel at ease, separated from the dusty marketplace.
Smoke-shrouded trees and spring clouds are green; the river sky and setting sun are red. Knowing not where one has been drunk, one returns toward the bright moonlight.
In the night, a lone boat amidst wind and rain; the grasses and trees are hazy with spring. A dog barks in surprise at the thatched eaves—it must surely be someone crossing the river.
Fine clouds drift over the river pavilion; the solitary village is tranquil in the bright sun. A small bridge spans the wild waters, cutting off ten thousand layers of mountains.

I sit in meditation amidst the peach-blossom groves, dwelling in seclusion far from the dust of the marketplace. It is simply because the spring colors are beautiful; it is not for the sake of fleeing Qin.

Tall trees hold the cries of new cicadas; deep forests shroud thatched cottages. A broken bridge spans the shadows of passing figures; white clouds fill the mountain valleys. Waterfalls cascade beyond the cold sky;
a solitary pavilion stands amidst water and rock. With long days and nothing to do, we have formed a companion to gaze upon the spring mountains.
The autumn waters are as green as jade; distant mountains are as solid as rouge. At nightfall, the fish do not eat;

for whom, then, are the baited hooks set? The chilly forest is thin and sparse; the water over rocks flows clear and murmuring. Amidst ten thousand miles of white clouds, we face one another, having utterly forgotten all worldly passions.

Myriad trees shroud the drifting clouds in density; a thousand mountains grow cold under the setting sun. The gate of my humble dwelling remains shut through the long day; only with wine companions do we gaze upon one another at dusk.

Distant trees merge with the clear mist; the river is empty and the thatched pavilion is chill. We wander and chant together by the marsh’s edge; only then do I realize how difficult it is to remain alone sober.
Ancient trees and weathered pines are old; clear springs and white rocks are strange. Carrying my lute, I seek out a kindred spirit; from afar, I gaze upon the tavern flag.

Sitting on the river pavilion, I forget all artifice; leaning on the railing, I watch the evening glow. A person stands poised at the riverbank, as if waiting for the moon to rise before returning home.
Clouds white, a stream of silk hangs from the heavens; the river clear, its waters merge with the sky. Hand in hand we seek our drinking companions, together passing to the east of the stone bridge.
Autumn mountains, their vapors thin; crimson trees, brightened by the morning frost. A single expanse of lake and sky stretches wide; in vain we wait for the moon’s clarity.

The mountains resemble the Terrace of Heaven; the flowers bear no trace of the springtime of the Qin era. A fisherman sits by the mouth of the stream, yet he does not see the traveler seeking the ford.
Scarlet clouds obscure the four fields; layered ice breaks the myriad trees. Braving the cold, I visit an old friend, treading through the snow that blankets the continuous mountains.
Ten thousand mountains hold accumulated snow; tall trees break under the light frost. Where does the cold plum blossom bloom? Its fragrance beckons a solitary monk.
The autumn mountains are clear after a fresh rain; the distant waters are pale and boundless. The dwelling of a reclusive hermit by the lake lies serenely beyond the dust of the marketplace.
The Dream-Traveling Collection of the Elder Hanshan, Volume Forty-Eight;
The Dream-Traveling Collection of the Elder Hanshan, Volume Forty-Nine.
Compiled by the Attendant Fuxian as a Daily Record.
Compiled by the Disciple Tonghyeong;
Re-edited by the Southern Peak Disciple Liu Qixiang at Huanpu.
We met before the Southern Peak; sitting together, we faced the Mid-Autumn moon. We gazed at its clear radiance throughout the night, suspecting it to be the snow of Mount Yan.
Leisurely ascending the peak of Mount Yu, I beheld the smoke and fires within the city. Myriad dwellings were as dense as clouds; lotus flowers bloomed blue, petal by petal.

Ascending Alone to the River-Boundary Tower I ascend alone to the River-Boundary Tower; On all four sides, the mountains are like woven brocade. Within them dwells one who feeds on the mists of dawn; Facing each other, we do not know one another.
Gao-shan Temple (Mount Gaoshan)
The mountain city rests upon the river’s flow; a Buddhist temple rises amidst the clouds. As the bell tolls, ten thousand doors open; people dwell within the lotus.
O Yu Creek, O Yu Creek, how do you compare to me? I am not as foolish as you. Your flowing springs resound day and night, their dharma-preaching voice ringing out clearly.
Huayan Monastery is near the Ganges River; the monks’ robes belong to Śrāvastī. The sound of the sutras blends with human speech, all of which speaks of non-arising.
Two Miscellaneous Verses.
The white crane soars toward the heavens; carefree, it follows its own coming and going. A pity that this unimpeded body does not know the path of birth and death.
Ants crave the scent of meat and fat; they follow the vapors to call out for companions. In their frantic haste, they never pause for a moment; yet what can they truly gain?

Spontaneously Composed in Two Stanzas The reflections of a thousand peaks are my dharma companions; My life’s sustenance is but a few acres of fields. I know well that within the world of men, It is difficult to form such karmic affinities here.

The green mountains wait for me to return; Originally, I sought a profound resonance with them. Who would have known that the mind of the one who comes, Is so often at variance with stillness and motion?

Thirteen Poems on Dwelling in the Mountains A single cloud floats in the great void; In an instant, it pervades the entire earth. Try to look before birth: Pure and clear, without a trace of obscuration.
The myriad realms are fundamentally quiescent; It is because of the mind that arising and ceasing occur. If not even a single thought arises, Where can one find movement or stillness?

Through the long night there has been no lamp or candle; the extended path is entirely shrouded in darkness. How pitiable are those who slumber in intoxication—when will they awaken from this great dream?
It is easy to enter the green mountains, and pure karma is not difficult to cultivate. Only in the Dharma for subduing the mind does the hero yield a single move.

A single pillow for the dream of yellow millet; a thousand autumns of labor with dripping sweat. One knows only that these things are eternally imperishable; who would believe that in a mere turn of the head they become empty?

The snow ages the ancient, dark pines; the monk is at leisure by the water and stones, pure and clear. Sitting thus, one forgets a hundred anxieties; looking out, one perceives the body’s own lightness.
The scorching summer heat is unbearable for man. A pure breeze comes from beneath the bamboos; with its whistling coolness arising, my very hair and bones suddenly feel refreshed and elegant.

When the wind stills, the cicada’s cry grows urgent; as the dragon returns, the air carries a pungent scent of rain. Taking advantage of the coolness beneath a lofty tree, I idly transcribe the *Go-kyō* (The Scripture of the Swans).
Clouds deepen the wild temple; the aged monk loves to lean on his staff. Returning late from begging for food, he worries about threading the ten-li of pines.
A crisp air enters the sparse woods; the autumn colors of ten thousand mountains are beautiful. Greedy to gaze at the clouds above the stream, he forgets the path by which he came.

Sitting alone beneath the tall pines, my mind is at ease, like that of the Great Antiquity. With the sentiment of the high mountains and flowing water, who else could truly be a connoisseur of this music?
The sun and moon fly like birds; heaven and earth turn like a rolling ball. The ephemeral life is spent amidst the bustle; who will look upon it from within stillness?
A bowl of lamp-light burns long and bright; facing it at night, the mind grows even more still. How many people, drunk and asleep, find their madness unabated within their dreams!
Twenty Poems on Mountain Dwelling (Hexasyllabic Verse):
A few rafters for a hut beneath the pines; before one’s eyes, green mountains on all four sides. The sun and moon rise and sink without staying; white clouds...
Coming and going, always at leisure;
amidst the snow, the plum blossoms first bloom. A hidden fragrance drifts in the deep night; sitting alone before a cold lamp, suddenly it pierces the nostrils open.
A few flecks of white cloud do not depart; a single orb of bright moon flies in. It accompanies my solitude amidst the mountains, laughing at the dust and toil of the world.
A single heart of coldness on a snowy night; several strokes of a frost-bell that shatter dreams. Incense has burned out within the brazier; before the window—
The moon rises over the solitary peak;
a face filled with the piercing chill of clear frost, and a head of hair flowing white and sparse. Empty flower-phantoms have fallen away from the world;
the illusory cataracts before the eyes have entirely vanished.

The sound of the spring water murmurs into the ears; the clear intent of the Patriarchs came from the West. Without moving the root of the tongue, he speaks constantly—what need is there to sigh again at its wonder?
In the secluded valley, the orchid fragrance is rich and full; in the middle of the night, the moonlight is bright and pure. A single segment of this refined atmosphere surges forth, without cause.

Breaking through stagnant meditation, in a single thought one forgets conditions and enters profound stillness; solitary luminosity shines alone in wakefulness. One sees through the lightning flashing in the void, which is not the same as the fireflies flying before one's eyes.

Clouds disperse across the vast sky after the rain; snow melts and spring arises in the cold valley. One only feels as though the body has been washed clean, unaware that the mind has become as pure as ice.
Though my decrepit frame should pity its own frailty, upon reflection, I find the spirit grows ever stronger. At midnight, my spine is like iron; at all other times—
A single thought is like frost;
all the dust of the empty valley has vanished, leaving only a solitary patch of idle clouds to accompany me as I wave my whisk at the foot of the pine.
It is fitting that many deer gather in herds here.
Characters are but cataracts in the eye; Chan practice is but floating dust upon the mind. Cast both inner and outer away at once, and the entire great thousandfold world is your whole body.
Amidst the unceasing tolling of the bell in the still night, dreams upon the stone bed are all empty. With eyes opened, one knows not where one is—just listen.
The sound of pines fills the ears;
the pure, empty mirror reflects all. When spring arrives, the waters fill Lake Penghu, illuminating the very face of Mount Lu.
The moon is like a bright pearl upon the brow.
The six periods measured by the lotus-drip incense are still too short; the hundred measures of long-incense are but a makeshift arrangement. Day and night flow on in true permanence;
may your consciousness and spirit soon take refuge in a flower-womb.
A single cloud seals the mouth of the valley; a thousand peaks cleave through the void. Within lies a cottage of budding wood; it is deeply hidden.

The old mountain man with white hair laments that while the green mountains remain forever, his own white hair changes with every passing moment. All are but transient travelers within the dust of the world;
who among them is a person at ease beyond the realm of things?

The mountain colors harbor the melancholy of lingering rain; the pine sounds choke with the chill of clear frost. The monk seeking alms is like a weary bird; the蛾眉 (ebí) moon wears fresh makeup upon it.
The light of the world is like that of the water-moon; body and mind are as bright as lapis lazuli. One merely sees the ice melting at the bottom of the ravine, unaware—
In early spring, the flowering branches;
beyond the gate, green mountains in full bloom. Before the window, yellow leaves rustle and fall. Sitting alone, there is nothing to say;
looking back, all delusive thoughts have vanished.
On the Occasion of Being Aboard a Boat:
The sky and water merge as one; a single-leafed boat floats upon them. Behold now, this body and world are equal to drifting bubbles. The cry of wild geese shatters the dream of conditioned arising;
The bright moon shines over the reeds at the ancient ferryhead.
Mount Dagu wears clouds for a skirt and mists for a sash; the moon bows like a furrowed brow. The rivers and lakes fill the eyes, yet few are true companions.
The cold current reaches the bottom, washing the heart clean. Do not ask who this lord of yours may be.
The pagoda atop Mount Gushan floats within the void; it is a body of water-moon, a single mote of dust set within the great emptiness. To the eyes of the traveler, it adds but more dross;
how many men can recognize it for what it truly is?
The glass palace and crystal pavilion of Baotuo Temple on Poyang Lake;
on every side are green mountains and jade railings. Within stands one who constantly preaches the Dharma;
he has drunk dry the West River, leaving the night tides cold.
Passing by Tongjiang, I offer this elegy for Minister of Ceremonies Zeng Jianzhai:
Beneath the dragon-flower trees we once met; Each night we conversed of the heart until the dawn bell rang. Today I seek you on the banks of Tong River;
In vain I hold my blood-tears as I shed them upon the spring breeze.
Two Poems in the Style of "Fisherman's Lyrics" by Qingjiang The water is clear and the sand white;
the moon is like a hook. Its reflection falls into the heart of the waves, yet the line is not yet reeled in. Countless wandering fish cannot swallow it;
In vain, they leave the fisherman to harbor deep sorrow.
A single-leaf light boat turns with the waves; at the Five Lakes, wind and moon provide a sufficient meal. The soul’s dreams ever linger in the deepest depths;
most bitter is the water growing colder once detached from the hook.
My boat stops at Hengpu;
the Five-Clouds stream flows into Nan’an. Ten thousand layers of mountains wind back, and sixty-six rapids lie ahead.
Traveling until the waters end and the mountains exhaust themselves, I gaze upon countless plum blossoms atop the ridges.

Ascending the walls of Nan’an, lotus blossoms surge forth from every turret; their fragrant stamens hold the smoke of ten thousand households. One’s own form is within the mirror, yet people do not recognize it;
how could one seek the various heavens elsewhere?
Crossing Mount Dayu, Two Poems A single path winds through clouds and mists;
the gallery road is deep. The plum blossoms and pine rain create a dense, somber atmosphere.
I turn my thoughts back to those travelers of old who journeyed by night— how can they compare to my heart as I cross the ridge this morning?
Cold plum blossoms are in full bloom atop the ridge; Clouds embrace the branches like an ancient *kāṣāya*. Try once more to lift up the staff;
Its fragrance follows the celestial wind across the sea’s edge.
Two Poems on Visiting the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi A drop of water from Caoxi originates in a numinous abyss;
It flows into the vast blue ocean, its waves lapping against the heavens. How many fish and dragons undergo transformation therein?
Yet that single stream at its source remains refreshingly clear.
The woodcutter’s axe has barely been cast when the stone falls upon his waist. At midnight during the Huangmei period, all is silent and desolate.
Since I took up my single bowl and returned south, from that time on, the spirit of the descendants has grown increasingly arrogant.

Two Poems on the Road to Guangzhou Traveling south through misty waters across a hundred cities, The spiritual friends I meet are all without affection. Just as I press closer, wishing to stay for a moment,
They point toward the road ahead and depart elsewhere.
Neither bank nor midstream can contain it; a small boat chases the waves, surrendered to the heavenly wind.
One must simply hoist the solitary sail and go forth, for one has confidence that the waves of grace are the same everywhere.

Arriving at my military post in Leyang, miasmic vapors and mountain mists drift day and night; the breath of dragons and serpents exhales, mingling with the clear currents. Having arrived, I find this to be entirely a land of non-arising;
yet, the more I see it, the more I realize that the Emperor’s grace is not easily repaid.
Two Poems Dedicated to the Silent Master of Shaolin On the summit of Wueru Peak, the vegetation is deep;
In spring, flowers bloom, filling the forested slopes. The snow accumulated on the peak remains a thousand feet high;
Who can equal the heart of that man who severed his arm in former times?
The Qingliang Assembly concluded, and we returned once more to Chang’an. Each time we met, there was joy; yet after parting, one looks toward the south and the other toward the north.
We gaze upon each other from afar—one through the scorching winds of the south, the other through the driving snows of the north.

Setting sail upon the Pōra River, my single sail drifts eastward as the sea waves grow calm. Flutes and drums sound as if echoing from the heavens. Gazing afar, the Three Mountains appear to descend from beyond the sky;
one knows not that they are but reflections within a mirror.
I entrust this to Master Zhen of Xiao Jinshan:
May the divine wind blow you up to Mount Sumeru; at midnight, riding the tide and carrying the moon, you shall return.
You shall sweep the rocks upon Mount Laṅkā and wait for me to come once more to transcribe the scriptures.
Three Poems on Little Gold Mountain Ten thousand li of vast waves flow ten thousand li; who has used a mere fist-sized rock to anchor this central isle?
Had it not been for the three tiers opened by Yu’s excavation, fish and dragons would naturally have nodded their heads in agreement.
The crystal palace leaves no trace of dust; fragrant mists swirl as the dew grows thick. The bright moon floats in the sky above my drifting boat;
deep into the night, fish and dragons lie coiled beneath the steps.
Mountains float upon the water’s surface, temples rest in the void; Pavilions and towers stand amidst the vast, ethereal mists. These are not human worlds created by illusion;
They must surely be Brahmā-kings’ palaces surged forth from heaven.
Three Poems Sent to Master Miaofeng of Hedong The colors of Mount Shouyang rest upon the river’s flow; you, Master, dwell at the very summit of Zhongtiao.
Before Magu’s seat lies Changjing’s staff—its refined aura even now makes the ghosts and spirits sigh in sorrow.
The Yellow River flows from heaven along its single course, entering the Central Plains to wash away the ashes of calamity. Grasping the vital pass, it beholds the Zhizhu Rock;
its compassionate ferry is beyond mere talent for crossing the river.
Having traveled to the ends of the earth, the road is difficult; may I feast at will upon the poisonous mists and scorching winds.
Suddenly remembering the thousand-fathom snows of Longmen, I abruptly raise them up, and my heart is struck with piercing cold.
Reply to High Attendant Gao’s Gift of a Single Incense Coil:

This famous incense comes from the Upper Realm; Sealed in a letter, it has been sent afar to this scorched wilderness. In my dreams, I hear the clanging of *diao-dou* drums, mistaken for bells and chimes;
Rising at night, I personally burn it as an offering to the Dharma King.
In my heart, I recall my former dwelling at Longmen on Mount Wutai, where for ten thousand years ice and snow embraced my sprout-like hut. It has been more than twenty years since we parted;
tonight, beneath the bright moon atop Xuedou Peak, I know not who dwells here in peace.
I recall Mount Kuang from afar—I recall the Five Elders’ Peak of Mount Kuang. Thick white clouds lock away ten thousand pine trees; the cold sky’s moon shines upon the waters of Lake Peng.
The sound of waterfalls flies over the chiming of several bells.

Embracing Mount Kuang’s Heavenly Pond and the Pavilion Floating on Emptiness, the master of this pavilion in mid-air is like one who dwells freely amidst the flowers. At midnight, the Heavenly Pond bathes the bright moon;
I know not at this moment with whom it is intimate.
Five Sheep Delighted by the Arrival of Master Tanziwen from Jimen (Two Poems) The snow of the Western Mountains engulfs Jimen in cold;
I recall once sitting by the hearth as the night drew to its end. Since our parting, it has been as if worlds apart;
meeting again now, I suspect it is but a vision within a dream.

The scorching winds of the south and the driving snows of the north—neither can be relied upon. How could this burning house be anything other than the great earth frozen as ice? Do not be startled by the changes in our hair and beards;
this mind has always been that of a monk from Mount Wutai.
Recalling My Home Mountains and Former Haunts (With Preface):
It has been more than thirty years since I left my home mountains. Now, having been banished to the regions beyond the passes, I have encountered my Dharma brother, Master Ke.
I have written three verses to console my nephew Guangyuan; upon returning, I hung them on the old wall so that one might see how the illusory traces of human life are thus.
A ten-thousand-bamboo grove surrounds my old hermitage, and on the upper floor, I still hang the books I have read through. In a dream, I saw that the four eaves were green and unchanging.
Altered. In vain remains the bright moon shining upon the courtyard steps.
The old traces of my travels upon the streets of Chang’an have been swept away by the winds of morning and night until not a speck of dust remains. Since our parting, thirty years have passed;
I know not how many times I have emerged from the void.
I recall how, in our childhood, we gathered together on the sand; hundreds and thousands of us played and laughed like blossoming flowers.
Though wind and frost have caused our appearances to change, this memory remains entirely as it was, as if we had never left home.
This temple was consumed by fire, and I too traveled far away. For a long time I have harbored the intention to restore it;

now I hear that my venerable brother has already renovated the precious stupa, yet the halls and buildings still lie amidst the thorns and brambles. This thought moves me deeply, and I send this poem from afar.
The kalpa-fire blazes forth, recalling years past; the precious stupa is like a lotus born amidst the flames.
Now that the udumbara flower appears once more, when shall we behold the Tuṣita Heaven again?
Sitting alone upon a seven-petaled lotus, a single stick of incense burns; the day is long, and I sit cross-legged leaning against my simple bed.
The dust of the marketplace lies deep beyond my door for a thousand feet, left entirely to the busy traffic of wheels and hooves day and night.
**Three Poems Sent with Liu Yizhe Returning to His Hometown, Also Addressed to My Old Friends** For three years in the miasmic seas we shared this same heart;
Our physical forms were entirely beyond the reach of rising or sinking. You return alone, carrying the autumn river moon;
In the bottomless cold waves, my thoughts grow even deeper.
My body toils on its own while my mind remains at ease; in this humble hut, the hunting party is as green as the distant mountains.
Should an old friend inquire after my news, simply tell them that I linger here, my hair already streaked with white.
The worldly path is rugged and difficult to traverse; how few can truly perceive this as a transient life.
When you return, should you pass by West Lake, please observe the nature of the lotus flower emerging from the water.
Entrusting my thoughts to Master Xugu amidst the army:
The meditation board has been lightly cast aside for the sound of drums and gongs. Sitting cross-legged upon a saddle is not at all fitting;
Deep in the night, the moon shines beneath the camp gate, Just like when we sat facing each other in the shade of the pines.
Two Poems on Huaitian Terrace Mountain At Tiantai, clouds and mists abound beside the sea; Half my life has passed in vain through dreams and fantasies.
When shall I once more drag my sky-reaching staff To rouse the deluded monk from his demon of quiescence?
The moon shines twice as bright atop Mount Kōmyō; the waters beneath Shakyō Bridge are exceptionally clear.
To be able to hold even a single drop from these and bring it to this scorching sea is far superior to the blooming of a *t'an-hua* flower within a cup.
A Verse on the Four Seasons at Caoxi:

The Patriarch’s intent is manifest at the tips of the hundred grasses; In the spring forest, flowers bloom and birdsong is profound. This morning, after the rain has passed, the mountains are as if washed clean;
On every branch, red and white blossoms have not yet shed their dew.
The four mountains are dense with thick, lush green shade; beneath the window, the wind comes from the pines by the water’s edge.
Just as I am snoring in midday sleep, about to drift into a dream, I suddenly hear the sound of a single bell from the long corridor.
Plowing with knives and sowing by fire is the best remedy; when autumn arrives, every household is fragrant with late rice. When you cannot let go, take it up and carry it away;
how does that compare to Old Yan in Shaoyang?
Deep in the night, I have just brewed tea amidst the falling snow; this natural flavor is most worthy of praise. Yet there is another extraordinary quality:
the full moon bathes the plum blossoms throughout the forest.

Two Poems on Reciting Amidst the Army Iron armor is Heaven’s decree to serve as my tattered fur robe; I joined the army originally not for the sake of becoming a marquis. My body has passed through the scorching sun like a furnace and forge;
My haughty bones have now been tempered until they are supple.
Casting off the black robes to don military attire, one finally realizes that following conditions is itself the site of enlightenment.
Even if the blazing heavens were like a raging fire, it could not extinguish the cold heart-mind of ice and snow.
Mr. Chen studies at the ruins of Tianning Temple;
having left the secular world, he dwells within the Jetavana Garden. Sleeping at night, he must surely be close to the Buddha. His dreams and soul are suddenly shattered by the tolling of the bell;
only then does he realize he was originally a seeker of the Dharma.
Haichuelou:
A single pavilion abides where sea and sky meet; within its vast expanse, it contains infinite void. Rising at night, I open the window to release the bright moon;
the shimmering ripples and rosy vapors fill my robes.
Master Liu studies his books by the heart of Shihu;
his mind is like cold spring water, his countenance like ice. In his secluded dwelling, he does not yield to the monks of the rocky crags. At night, he boils a drop of water from the source;
he frequently asks for fire to share in illuminating the Buddha-lamp.
To Master Yunqi:
With long eyebrows and white hair, you have long dwelt among the clouds; occasionally waving the fly-whisk, you surround the herd of deer. From afar, I send a single incense pellet of sandalwood;
I imagine you holding it up before the Dharma King and burning it as an offering.
To the Layman Tu Chui, who dwells in the house of Vimalakīrti near White Flower Mountain: Mist and waters are hazy; the Sea-Seal is cold. I hear that Mañjuśrī has gone east again;
I know not with whom he partakes of the fragrant meal.
To Master Feng Kaizhi, Imperial Historian:

A Request for a Preface to the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra I recall in the past, when we two conversed beneath the thousand-petaled lotus; The precious robes were cast off long ago, leaving only tangled, coarse hair. Upon Mount Laṅkā lies a cluster of mani-jewels;
On what day shall the casket of a hundred treasures be opened once more?
Reading the final verse of Great Master Daguan:
"A single thought has never been concealed from the beginning; The whole body does not fall into the field of right and wrong.
Try looking at how he lets go and lightly brings it forth— Only then will you believe this master’s burning heart."
I recall my old dwelling on Mount Wutai;
snow still lingers atop Yue Dou Peak. Since we parted, news has been long and sparse.
Amidst the dusty dreams of the southern lands, I pass by a solitary wooden bridge, staff in hand.
Six Poems Sent from the Army to Attendant Censor Huang Yu and Li:
For ten years I have wandered through the scorched wilderness on military horses; I often recall our shared travels beneath the light of Haiyin.
Seeking a foothold amidst the great mass of fire, it is in parting from you that I find the truest coolness.

Gathering and dispersing like floating clouds, they cannot be relied upon; yet this mind of mine has not ceased its longing since the moment I parted from you. The two orbs of sun and moon pass like swift birds;
their coming and going never pauses, hastening my dreams and thoughts.
The great ocean and the long river flow as one stream; misty waves vast and boundless are all like empty space.
Though ten thousand mountains may serve to separate them, they are just like flowers falling from the void into a mirror.
The void and the great earth may perish; how could this mindfulness belong to either annihilation or permanence? I ask you now, within the chamber of Vimalakīrti:
where have all existing things been placed lately?
You first waited for the dew-drops at the Zichen court; from afar you grasped the *Laṅkāvatāra* to inquire into the silence.
After the attendant had eaten his fill of fragrant rice, not a single grain has been digested to this day.
Worldly affairs are as empty as space; how could there be a place in heaven and earth where green mountains do not exist?
I know that the place where you perceive with the true eye does not lie within the realm of sounds or forms.
Beside the water fields, in front of the gate of Imperial Censor Zou of Nangao, lies a single patchwork robe of merit.
At times, he breaks off pine branches to sweep away the dust. The mountain colors and the sounds of the stream constantly preach the Dharma;
one knows not who among them is truly responsive to the teaching.
Inscription for Ziyun Hermitage at Xianglu Peak Beneath Xianglu Peak, the purple clouds are deep;
Pines, bamboos, and tiered cliffs cast shadows in broad daylight. The gate borders the long river, which connects to the mountain stream;
Its clear currents wash away the worldly mind.

A summer day in the mountains is like being scorched by fire; the daylight is especially long. Thirsting for the cool shade beneath the Bodhi tree, a breeze passes through the void, carrying with it the fragrance of lotuses from somewhere unknown.
In my heart, I cherish Mount Jiuhua, where the lotus blossoms beautifully upon the waters of the Nine Rivers; a single stretch of clouds and mists hangs over its sixty-six peaks.
Turning my head toward the miasmic lands under the bright moon at night, I find myself, for no reason, with a pure dream suspended from the cold pines.
Master Yi came from Hengyang to visit me;
from afar he sought the ford at Caoxi alone. The autumn waters at the head of the creek are pure and free of dust.
He brings with him a sliver of moonlight from Mount Heng, which still illuminates the men of the hunting party from years past.
To Layman Liu Cunchi of Tacheng:
How can meeting be compared to not yet having met? Having come here, the news is that spring is at the mountain pass. The moonlight of Mount Heng is the water of Cao’s Creek;
looking through to the very bottom, you are an old friend.
My boat stopped at Luojiang to visit the monk Master Zhong, but I did not meet him;
I once sat on the riverside pavilion waiting for the snow to melt. The spring waters of Luojiang are as swift as the tide;
now, gazing at the moon before Bailuzhou, it still seems to accompany my former solitude.

Having been granted grace and returned to the mountains, I have been a monk for fifty years since my youth. In old age, I have intentionally mingled with worldly ties; from now on, I shall cut off all paths to the ends of the earth.
Henceforth, I shall sleep through the white days among a thousand peaks.

Sitting in the night, dew sprinkles upon the secluded orchids, their fragrance striking the nose; the wind blows through my hair and bones, bringing a coolness born of the night. Having sat for some time, my mind is already perceived as snow;
the moonlight makes one suspect it is frost upon the earth.
Two Poems on Passing through Fǎxìng Temple on a Summer Day Beneath the Bodhi tree, the breeze dispels the heat;
Before the Prajñā terrace, the rain brings coolness. With a single cup of clear tea, all discursive thoughts are extinguished;
Where else could one seek the Western Paradise?
The Bodhi tree was planted here in its prime; the original aspiration was to await the arrival of a sage. After a thousand years, the robe and bowl remain as they were;
who will ascend the old lecture platform to preach the Dharma?
In the Hall of Withered Trees at Xuefeng, before the Hall of Withered Trees, it is as cold as ice. In years past, half a thousand monks sat here.
Thinking back on that ground of cold ashes, on what day shall the midnight lamp be lit once more?
Two Poems on Paintings The mountain colors of Flying Peak veil the luster of the lake; Mist-shrouded trees, after a fresh clearing, bear the glow of the setting sun.
From afar I hear the bells and drums of the Tuṣita Realm above; Their echoes fall faintly through the mid-heavens.
A single expanse of misty waves and fifteen bridges; clouds, mountains, and falling leaves, desolate at evening. A solitary city half-submerged by the waters of the Wu River;
on the water dwellers listen for the tide at night.
As I was being sent to Lei Yang, I took my leave of Master Tan by the river;
we met again at Mount Yu when the sun was still low. I wished to pluck which branch of the plum blossoms? Suddenly, driven by the autumn wind, I crossed the fiery seas.
Parting from you is not like meeting you.
Longing for my old dwelling, I rest peacefully where I once lived by the western bamboo grove; beneath the bright moon at the head of the stream, how many times have I leaned on my staff?
I often imagine the night deepening as the dew falls upon the pines, unaware that the monkeys and cranes are calling out to whom.
Sent to Master Danguan Kai of Fushan:
How is the matter of the Nine Bands of Fushan? Looking back on those years, the chess pieces have already rotted away. I ask:
at the place where you sit in meditation deep in the night, Of whom is there more—white clouds or bright moon?
As my boat passes Little Golden Mountain, I record my reflections:
I have often thought of this place three times during the past half-month; yet suddenly, we have been parted for another five years. On this day, I sit once more upon the mountain peak;
the clouds of virtue (De-yun) are not at all what they were before my birth.
Recalling the Plums of the Mountains, Two Poems At Caoxi, whenever the plum blossoms reach their full bloom, it is as if one were sitting in the world of Gandhavyuha.

This winter, however, due to the interference of demons, I was drawn away to the banks of the Fu Rong River. Looking toward the mountains from a mere few dozen paces away, I am unable to sit and enjoy the fragrant offerings. A poem.
I recall it thus:
Cold plum blossoms open atop the snowy peaks; slowly, heavenly flowers fall upon the lecture platform.
Would that the fragrant realm of Upariṣṭha could send a single alms-bowl, bearing it all here for me.
The plum blossoms scent the trees until they form a forest; their fragrance permeates people, bringing joy to the heart. Beneath the trees appear spread lion thrones;
who can understand the sound of the wind as the tide?
I have received two letters from my disciple Jiang Wuyu at Donghai;

one arrived by air and was a single sheet of paper—a letter from an old friend. It has traveled ten thousand *li* from afar to inquire after my well-being. I reply that my relatives and acquaintances have all perished;
with frost and snow filling my hair, I am even more sorrowful for myself.
For fifteen years I have sat in this miasmic land; facing the sea and sky, I could not forget [my homeland].
Often I gaze upon the mid-night moon across ten thousand *li*, as if we were traveling together once more at Haiyin Temple.

In the ancient Buddha’s pine forest, the shade of the pines is dense and pure, free from dust. The mountain colors and cloud-light are the Dharma-body itself. Day and night, the wind and waves are the broad and long tongue;
one does not know who it is that hears them through to the end.
