The dawn bell tolls as the Milky Way reveals its clarity and the sparse stars grow pale; in the eaves of the ancient temple, hundreds of spirits dwell. A single strike of the morning bell startles one from the great dream;
I know not who among them can truly claim to be awake.
The ancient stupa on the plains—of what era does this pagoda enshrine the various devas? Tradition says it dates from the Daye era of the Sui dynasty;
now the moss has stripped away the seals and the broken inscriptions are gone, while the plains are covered with wild grasses upon the field where gold was spread.

Sent from Yuan’an, I imagine the Dharma Master seated upon the lotus throne to expound the teachings; the four heavens overspread the Dharma hall, and the dragons and elephants within the assembly are as pure as such.
May you remember this old man with vermilion beard in the scorched wilderness.
Entrusting this to Dharma Master Caotang:
Having returned from the miasma-filled seas to the seat at Baolin, you constantly cherish the old companions of the Dharma cave.
Gazing afar at the single moon over Mount Yan, it is entirely the heart that traverses the world according to conditions.
Four Poems Spontaneously Composed While Dwelling in the Mountains The affairs of a hundred-year life are within empty flowers; A single body and mind dwell amidst water and moon.
I alone permit myself this place, deep and secret among ten thousand mountains, Where I sit in meditation through the long days, closing the pine gate.
The world of swirling red dust is a long journey; I know not for what reason I wander in a foreign land. Turning my head, I gaze daily toward my distant home mountains;
before my eyes, empty clouds stretch across the setting sun.
In the midst of the clamor, who would dare withdraw in haste? Since ancient times, the green mountains have separated the city’s dust. Do not say that the Peach Blossom Spring has no path to enter;
the falling flowers and flowing waters are themselves the known ford.
Day and night, mist and clouds guard the verdant peaks; together with monkeys and cranes, I await the forgetting of artifice. Do not say that these green mountains have no master of leisure;
it is simply that the man of leisure refuses to return.
Seeing off Zen Practitioner Yin-zhi as he returns to Shu:
A single staff, cold and clear, passes through the miasmic lands; To the west of Mount Wu, his thoughts stretch boundlessly.
Upon the peak of Mount Emei, the new autumn moon— I know that when you gaze upon it, you will have reached the upper reaches.

Two Poems Inscribed on the Title of General Du’s *Dharma-flower* Hermitage The martial drums and pipes fall silent at the imperial headquarters; beneath the *dharma-flower* tree, he sits in tranquil meditation by day.
Who would have known that the day the Khan returned to his sovereignty was precisely the year the General shattered existence?

Bells, drums, and *huqia* pipes—all constitute the site of practice; amidst the shadows of banners and pennants, one sits and burns incense. I think of you, whose power shatters the fortresses of the myriad demons;
you have vowed that with a mind emptied of self, you shall behold the Dharma King.
Seeing Master Ci return to Mount Wutai—thirty years have passed since our last parting at the mountain.
The snow and ice before my eyes remain as they were. You have come to recount in detail the matters within the caves;
once again, we have bound together the unfinished karmic ties of many lifetimes.
Entrusting this to Master Kongyin:
I recall in the past, at Mount Tai, amidst ice a hundred feet thick, sitting opposite you with our bones starkly prominent.
Reflecting now on those events of over thirty years ago, they seem like a dream, as if they never even occurred.
Two Poems on Parting from Caoqi To resolve the matter of the ten-thousand-li stream of Caoqi: My heart’s longing often touches the hilt of my great sword.
Recalling how blood once soaked the waist-deep snow, For a thousand ages it causes people’s pain to never cease.
I have come on foot from Caoxi; sitting here, I watch the mountain colors as my smile unfolds. From now on, we part for a thousand peaks;
the songs of birds and the sounds of the stream cannot fully express our grief.
Two Poems on Rejoicing at the Snow upon Arriving in Hengyang On the peaks of seventy mountains, the snow is intensely cold; Having arrived here, I see deeply the peace of this mind.
Reflecting back on the places of frantic toil within the burning house, I view them all now as reflections within a crystal pitcher.
A phantom body amidst the fivefold heat; for twenty years I have wandered through the winds and dust. Now I return to a single expanse of Xiangxiang snow;
originally, I am one whose very bones are cool and clear.
Twenty-eight Poems on Dwelling in the Mountains:
Throughout my life, I have harbored a passion for the mist and clouds. In my youth, I traveled as a wandering monk; at thirty, I dwelt amidst the ice and snow of Mount Wutai for eight years.
Subsequently, I resided by the Eastern Sea for twelve years. Now, having reached the age of fifty, I am beset by worldly karma.
The wind blew me down into this miasmic region nearly twenty years ago. Alas, how brief is human life! In the blink of an eye, I have already reached seventy years of age.
Like floating light and illusory shadows, how can anything endure for long? Recently, by the grace of the Emperor, I was granted leave to return to my original robes.
I came specifically to Mount Nanyue to plan for my final years, but as circumstances did not yet align, I have instead settled at the ancient [site] in Hudu.
The site of the meditation hall was established with the assistance of various donors to facilitate the summer retreat.
It commenced on the full moon of the ninth month of the Jia-yin year and was completed by the end of the twelfth month.

Though finished in a hurried and makeshift manner, from this point forward, my entire being has finally found a place of rest, like a long-traveling guest returning home to cast off a heavy burden. How free and unburdened I feel!
"How joyful it is! As thoughts arose, I dictated them on the spot and commanded my attendant to record them, so as to preserve these profound sentiments.
This is not poetry; I simply wrote down whatever came to mind whenever inspiration struck, without any particular order."
Having borrowed a branch for rest at Jetavana, from now on no matter how difficult the road may be, the sun rises three poles high and one sleeps soundly;
looking upon each other, there is no need to urge one to eat more.
Snow presses upon my humble gate as I huddle by the brazier at night; though this body is here, it is as if non-existent.
Unaware of where the days and months have gone, I turn my head and find the years of this world have already passed.
A small hermitage amidst the shrubs, with a stone bed for a seat and grass for a niche;
its door closed like that of Vimalakīrti—do not ask about the three before or the three after.
The form is like withered wood; thoughts are like ashes. Snow fills the crown of the head; frost covers the cheeks. It is not that old age alone causes one to loathe the world;
there is simply no place for dust to settle within the eyes.
Body and mind set down, there is ample leisure; my life in declining years rests amidst the ten thousand mountains. Do not allow the white clouds to lightly leave the valley;
better to follow the bright moon and guard the wooden gate.
A cold lamp illuminates my solitary shadow, faint and thin; In the drafty hut, the wind blows snow upon my robes.
Suddenly I recall the place where I sat in meditation on Mount Wutai— A single wooden door amidst ten thousand years of ice.

The cold’s power pierces the bones amidst snow on a thousand peaks; Fury assails the person like wind through ten thousand apertures. With my patched robe covering my head, I have just awakened from sleep;
I do not realize that I am within a state of desolation.
The hundred thousand worlds are like the shadows of flowers in the sky; this single body and mind are like the moon’s reflection in water.
When all skillful means are exhausted, the news is cut off; therein, there is no place for thought or deliberation.

The earthen stove is cold without fire, and the stone couch is freezing; the incense in the earthen cauldron has faded as the night draws to a close. All sounds have subsided and the mind is even more tranquil;
I wonder if my body is now being viewed within a mirror.

On all four sides, the shadows of fine trees spread in lush profusion. Beneath them lies a small cottage, deeply concealed. The sound of carriages and horses is unheard, and human tracks have been severed;
with the door closed, he sits alone in full lotus posture throughout the long days.
Cold rain falls in a drizzle as the wind fills the forest; the lotus-drip clock ticks through the long, deep night. Who knows that throughout the world, dreams are difficult to awaken from?
All are but the luminous *prajñā* mind.
Sitting alone deep into the night, I practice withered Chan; I stir the cold ashes, yet the fire will not ignite. Suddenly, I hear the bells and stone chimes ringing from atop the tower;
A single clear resonance fills the frosty sky.
Snow fills the universe, and all phenomena are renewed; within this world of white silver, one conceals the body. Sitting thus, one suddenly enters the Treasury of Radiance;
here, from the beginning, there has been no speck of dust.

The calm lake reflects the cold garments of water-lilies and lotuses. The green mountains above the lake are utterly free from the fray of right and wrong. All traces of the mundane world have vanished;
white clouds, gulls, and birds alike have forgotten their artifice.
Sitting alone by the thatched gate hemmed in by snow, The cold forest’s every branch snaps like jade. At dawn, the colors of the green mountains have suddenly vanished;
Though the plum blossoms are fully bloomed, I remain utterly unaware.

Spring has passed and the human day (*renri*) arrives; the snow has just cleared. The new moon shines over the sparse forest, its shadows even more clear. Rising at night, I push open the window to gaze into the vast expanse;
Countless stars and constellations hang from the rafters and eaves.
Clouds part and the four fields stir with spring light; from where does the plum blossom send forth its hidden fragrance?
Grasping my staff, I wish to seek it out in the secluded valley, yet a single branch leans askew against the eastern wall.
A single cloud seals the pines of ten thousand valleys; before the gate, the flowing stream gurgles day and night.
Without distinguishing day from night, it provides for his snoring sleep, until a bell from across the ridge startles him from his pleasant dream.
Deep in spring, after the rain has passed, fallen blossoms fly. Gently, the heavenly fragrance rises upon my patched robe. A single heart of leisure has nowhere to rest;
Leaning on my staff at the mountain peak, I watch the clouds return.
Trusting steps, surging forward, following wherever they may lead; this physical form is just like a pine tree in the snow.
Having arrived by chance, one stands but a moment at the head of the stream, then follows the idle clouds over to another peak.
Deer and elk roam the empty mountains—whom can they follow? They yield themselves to the lush grasses and tall pines.
Though the red dust of the world holds dreams difficult to awaken from, how could such worldly things ever reach the ten thousand peaks?
With white hair hanging low, facing the green mountains; my body dwells amidst a thousand crags and ten thousand gullies. In the silent pines-gate there are no passing guests;
only the white clouds come and go in leisure.
The green mountains remain unmoving, as they are in their suchness; morning and evening, the clouds and mists roll and unfurl as they will.
Though the red dust of the world may be ten thousand fathoms deep, not a single speck has ever reached this thatched cottage.
Solely seated in full lotus amidst the depths of ten thousand peaks, Vivid and luminous, a solitary thought stands alone. The body is like the bright moon suspended in the cold void;
Only its clear reflection remains, falling upon rivers and lakes.

Having awakened from sleep, I called my servant to brew tea at once. In the bamboo stove, the boiling water surged like falling snow. Before the banners were even raised, the demons had already retreated;
only then did I believe there are true masters within the monastic groves.
Weary, I lean against the empty window, sitting and gazing at the mountains; a thousand peaks of purple and azure emerge from among the pines.
Though clouds may come and go at their own will, how can they compare to the even greater leisure of the *tathatā* (suchness) body?
Moonlight and the sound of pines are both seen and heard; the Zen mind and deluded thoughts distinguish the holy from the mundane.
To dissolve them back into the single thought of the unborn—how can this meaning be conveyed to you?
The autumn waters of the level lake soak the cold sky; ancient trees, struck by frost, shed crimson leaves. On the stony path and across the small bridge, human traces have ceased;
a single hermitage is deeply locked away amidst white clouds.

I have entrusted myself to the old monk Shun’an for over thirty years, practicing indolence and ease. My life’s path is cut off at Mount Zhurong. With a body as light as a crane’s bone, do not speak of old age;
look at the thousand-foot pine I planted with my own hands.
Residing in seclusion like Kǎoshǔ of the Wèi state, he is truly a monk living at home. His single room is as pure as ice in the sixth month;
even if he were to exhaust all existence through the perfection of emptiness, the mountains and waters would still remain suspended upon the ridges of his brows.
Parting from My Friends in the Lake-East Society: Two Poems The *tánhuā* (dharma-flower) hermitage lies to the west of the Bamboo Grove;
Remote from the market, it is the most fitting place to dwell amidst the clamor of the world. Diligently sweep the steps before you where clouds lie upon the ground;
When you return, do not let the weeds grow rank and wild.
I have come by chance to close the wooden gate beneath the pines; seeking you out to invite you away from this world. Who would have thought you would follow the flowing stream once more?
As I part from you, my heart clings to the clouds and mountains.
Two Poems on Being Held Back by Wind at Yueyang Beyond the Yueyang Tower, the lake merges with the sky; Below the tower, boats moor for the night upon the sandy islets.
The wind-driven sails of those coming and going cannot be detained, Yet the mountain colors alone remain as they were before.
The north wind blows waves that strike the mountain city wall; a single light sail blocks my onward journey. I suspect you stayed behind to gaze upon the moon over Lake Dongting;
hence it is strange that it shines so brightly right by my side as a traveler.
Passing through the golden sands, one reaches Yunlin in a mere moment;
from Yunlin, it does not seem far away. Upon arrival, the cold and refreshing air is desolate and sparse;
with the gates closed, mist and clouds are not allowed to escape, and how many worldly thoughts are easily dispelled!
Spontaneously Composed upon Visiting West Lake:
On all four sides, lake and mountains are seen as in a mirror; The tower-ship is deeply submerged in the cold, azure waves.
Unaware that one’s body is but a reflection in a crystal pitcher— How laughable, this state of drunken indulgence, the dream not yet ended!

Joyfully returning to Mount Kuang in my declining years, I dwell amidst the green mountains, grateful for the Lord’s grace. Mount Lu lies facing south, reclining as it receives the morning sun. The Seven Sages and Five Elders gaze at one another from afar;
the sound of the spring water is like a profound discourse on the Gate of Non-duality.

Two Poems in Commemoration of Master Chěkōng of Huanglong on Mount Kuāng In the past, I lived with the Master among the snow and ice of Mount Wutai for three years. It has been more than thirty years since we parted.
Now that I have retired to Mount Kuāng in my old age, I have come to pay my respects at the Master’s stupa and offer these verses of lamentation.
I recall the past, when we sat together at Qingliang; Falling snow and ice hung like tassels upon our brows. Since parting, I have dreamed of that heart-wrenching place;
This single, unbearable fragment of feeling is known only to myself.
The shadow of the stupa circles, embraced by ten thousand pines; The Dharma-body unmoving, it soars above a thousand peaks.
Knowing that you constantly preach the Dharma of non-arising, The songs of birds and the sounds of the stream harmonize with the dawn bell.

In the snowy night within the mountains, snow embraces a thousand peaks as I alone close my retreat. A cold lamp illuminates my aged face deep into the night. My heart has turned to ash, severing all dreams of the red dust;
who would believe that such leisure exists in the human world?
While reading the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, I happened to compose this in a dream:
A light leaf-boat and a single fishing pole; The fragrant bait at the hook has never been exhausted. One must plunge straight into the deep sea to haul in the catch;
Do not linger on the shallows of reeds and sandbars.

Two Poems on Longing for My Hometown I left my hometown when I was twelve years old; it has now been sixty years. Recently, while staying in the mountains, a fellow villager sent me a message from afar.
In response, I composed these two poems.
Tall willows before the gate reflect in the clear pond; I often recall the time when we children played in the water. Over sixty years have passed like a dream;
how many times has the longing for my old garden stirred within me?
A range of green mountains winds along the river's course; my home stands by an ancient ferry crossing on the bank. Having left my native land since childhood, I am now old;
yet this heart remains unbroken, as flowing and vast as the water.
I long for the Lord of the Dragon Flower Assembly, the one with whom I share a karmic affinity beneath the Dragon Flower tree.
Once parted, it is difficult to seek our former intimacy again. How many times have my dreams and soul flown through the night moon?
Even if we were to meet, it would all be but an illusion.

Entering the mountains, one goes straight into a thousand peaks without wearying of their depth; in the most secluded and remote places, one may find peace of mind. Let the moss grow thick at the pine gate;
from this time on, seek him where men have vanished.
Two Poems Sent in Response to the Visit of Master Mian Wuan from Caoxi Hall It has been ten springs since we parted at Caoxi;
I often long for even a single drop of that fragrant water to moisten my lips. In dreams and spirit, I sometimes sit beneath the shade of the pines;
I only fear that this present life may already be my final incarnation.
The plum blossoms atop the stream emit an unceasing fragrance; several times the fragrant mist has soaked my robes.
Every year when I reach the place where I once viewed the flowers, it is as if I were sitting in the Dharma Hall back then.
Two Poems on Seeing Off Master Xi of Qinglin as He Travels to Mount Nanyue I recall in the past ascending seventy peaks,
Leaning against the heavens, gazing beside the sun, and caressing the long pines. Having explored every wondrous crag and remote ravine,
You go now to seek the traces of my staffed footsteps.
Deep within ten thousand peaks, the azure clouds are cold; there you once built a thatched hut to study the ways of Lan Can. The cow dung embers for roasting yams are still buried there;
you should stir the earthen stove and look.
Spontaneously composed:
The sea is tranquil and clear, not a single thing exists; in the cold void of the deep night, the moon’s orb stands alone.
Beholding the ten-thousand-li expanse where the finest clouds have parted, I realize of myself that my ice-cold heart dwells within a jade pitcher.
Five Additional Poems Rejoicing that my Mother has Sent My Brother to Heaven Our kinship is as dear as a shared stem;
The Emperor’s grace has bestowed this life upon me. If there is a day when I may return, I shall still be able to serve my compassionate parent.
I recall my hometown, where I lived on the shaded slopes of Mount Gui; it is just like a bend in the Ganges. I remember back when I was a child:

bathing in the river during the heat, with willow trees casting thick shade along both banks, and the lush green of the Southern Mountains facing my door. I planted a peach tree with blue blossoms there myself—I do not know if it still stands today.
Before my gate is a small bridge; when I was young, I saw the current sweep it away and wished to build a single-log footbridge. Though the path is long, I have not yet accomplished this.

I recall my childhood friends with whom I studied together—sharing the same bed and even the same blanket. Who would have known that since our parting, we have each grown old, looking now nearly sixty years of age?

I recall instead the time when we gathered sand; in our play, we often caused each other distress. I remember only the faces of those children; I could not have believed that we would now grow old and frail.

A stupa stands tall before the tomb; in front of the stupa, there are further overlapping halls for the various devas. The masonry is broken and piled up, leaving not a single gap across the breast-like expanse.
To the left near the hall, there is a monk’s quarters, as small as a fist used to prop up the chin. In the lower right corner, there is the housekeeper’s kitchen.
Filth and impurities had accumulated; the two arm-pits were like monastic dwellings, and the sagging, dilapidated rafters were like a thicket of brambles.

It forms a complete layout. This removed the filth and impurities from the western corner of the Ancestral Hall.

The management was conducted according to plan, exactly as it had been designed. Thus, the ancestral hall was renovated so that its lofty structure is magnificent to behold.
Two subsidiary halls were established in front, intended to enshrine the images of the various masters of the five schools of Nanyue and Qingyuan.

As for the surrounding buildings of the main gate, numbering fifteen bays, they were intended to house the descendants of the patriarchs of the *Lamp of the Dharma*, just as the seventy disciples were enshrined as secondary offerings to Confucius.

In selecting monks for their conduct to nurture human talent, the monastics of this temple have, until now, lived in comfortable manor-like dwellings; they engage in planting, cultivation, and animal husbandry no differently than the laity.

Within the temple, the hundred rooms all have their doors bolted shut, and upon entering, there are no traces of human presence, save for those few who attend to the incense and lamps in the ancestral hall.
The monks and the abbot’s staff numbered only a few dozen; consequently, the mountain gate was left to the whims of scoundrels who acted with impunity.

As for the entering and exiting of the monastic community, they all avoided shadows and hid their tracks—this is truly lamentable. When the Master first arrived, he made the cultivation of talent his foremost priority.
