There were many who were thus subjected to arbitrary deductions regarding their dwellings. Recently, powerful local figures nearby have also set their sights upon these properties;
they colluded with corrupt officials of the yamen to fabricate mutual accusations, using the pretext of "connivance" to file complaints against the provincial governors and prefects.

Using this as a pretext, they expanded their ruse to alarm their superiors, striking terror into their hearts and ears until it was taken as truth. They then submitted a formal petition to the military headquarters;
once the order was issued, the entire monastery complex was demolished. Monks who did not conform to the regulations were expelled.

At that time, those executing the order were unscrupulous; trusting their own biased perceptions, they regarded the site as a source of extraordinary profit and personally entered the mountains to trample it down.
Investigation. Whenever he arrived at a village estate, he would appraise its value; by paying half, one was exempted from further liability.

Consequently, the temple monks were all ensnared in this net, and having already lost half their assets, the calamity continued to spread like creeping vines, leaving them no leisure for even a moment’s peace.

In the second year since the Master had crossed the mountain range, which was the year of Dingyou, he first went to pay his respects to the Provincial Governor and Grand Marshal, Lord Chen. Because...
He was able to generally express the circumstances and sentiments of the assembly of monks, whereupon the decree was suspended and he fortunately escaped [punishment].

He immediately intended to have the Master go there to rectify the situation, but the Master, as he was currently in the midst of his monastic duties, did not dare accept the command. The following year, Wuxu (1638), Zhou Gong, the Commissioner of the Salt and Salt-Production Department, was appointed to oversee the affairs of Nanxiong and Shaoguan and wished to rescue [the community].
He entrusted the Master with the task of revising the *Tongzhi* (Comprehensive Gazetteer). Not long after, Zhou departed to offer congratulations at the imperial court. Jihai (1639).

When Lord Zhu, the Governor of Nanxiao, took up his duties, he styled himself a "pilgrim-monk of Caoxi. Deeply lamenting the state of decay, he exerted great effort to invite the Master to bring order to the monastery.

In the year of Gengzi, the Lord also departed for the New Year’s audience at court; before leaving, he gave personal instructions and ordered the temple monks to earnestly entreat the Master to accept the summons.
Consequently, in the ninth month, the Master entered the mountains. Seeing these people acting with such license and disorder, he [reflected upon] his ancestors...
This is a malady at the very core of our hearts. If it is not cured, the life-force of the Sixth Patriarch will ultimately be difficult to save.

Thereupon, we shall alter the geomancy: the main road to the mountain gate shall be filled in from east to west and relocated to the edge of the stream, with the direct exit to the waterway serving as the thoroughfare.
In this way, the former market stalls will all be enclosed within the mountain gate, and those who come and go—
"It is inconvenient for lodging and eating; yet there is ultimately no means to remove it.

After three months had passed, at the end of the year, he went to visit the Grand Councilor (Zhefu Dasisima) Dai Gong and fully described the nature of the harm it caused. The Duke said, "This is the responsibility of those who protect the Dharma.
Simply issue an edict and charge the local officials to strictly supervise its removal. This was a matter for a single district magistrate.
He left it to them. On New Year’s Day, he traveled through the county, sitting and waiting to drive them out until not a single person remained.

All the shops and stalls were demolished, not a single tile left behind. Thus, the filth and impurities that had accumulated at the mountain gate over more than a hundred years were cleansed in an instant, and the harm caused by the monks was forever ended.
Once the shops were demolished and the market streets were empty, the Master then proceeded to the west.
He converted the butcher shops on the street into a *dan-kuo-tang* (lodging hall for travelers) to receive practitioners from the ten directions who visit the ancestral temple.

On the eastern street, he established a public guesthouse (*kung-kuan*) to serve as a place for the official of the *Wengyuan* district to halt his carriage upon entering the commandery. As for the mountain gate and the road—
At first, it was but a single thread; yet to the left, market stalls were lined up, extending directly to the center of the path. Consequently, they were all demolished.

The stone archway, which had previously stood above, has now been moved to the edge of the stream. The obstructions have been cleared away so that the sights face one another like a taut line, forming a magnificent view.
The source of this harm cannot be fully described, yet its roots were deep and difficult to uproot; now that it has been completely severed in a single stroke.
I have recorded this here to serve as a mirror for future generations.

Having restored the monastic lands to settle the community of monks and having expelled the master of wandering scoundrels, all the fields, mountain estates, and houses previously defrauded [of us] are now held by him.

Regarding these bonds: this class of people is attached to them and will ultimately find no final resolution. I considered that this was not a virtuous or long-term strategy, and therefore established a vegetarian feast in the Patriarchal Hall.
I invited all the guests and hosts; each produced their bonds for mutual comparison. Those whose principal remained intact but whose interest had not yet reached its full amount were compensated.
Those whose interest exceeded half [the principal] were excused from further payment. As for those who had already recovered their principal...
Those who had accumulated heavy burdens, as well as those whose mouths were filled with empty luxuries, were dismissed.

Thereupon, he burned all their deeds and returned the fields, mountain estates, and houses entirely to their original owners. From this point on, external troubles finally ceased, and impoverished monks were able to dwell in peace without disturbance.
At that time, some people feared the Master would incur resentment; the Master said, "No."
However, although ordinary people may be unvirtuous, they must all possess a fundamentally good heart.

If one explains matters clearly and thoroughly, each person will recognize their own error, and there will be none who do not submit their hearts. Thereupon, the ruffians gradually withdrew; yet, in the end, no further trouble arose.
He strictly observed the precepts and fasts to encourage pure cultivation.
Previously, many of the temple monks had failed to observe the precepts and fasts; they kept livestock for breeding and slaughtered them at will.

Consequently, whenever officials from the provincial, prefectural, or county levels entered the mountains, the responsibility for providing supplies to the local *li* and *jia* units was invariably imposed upon the temple monks, and the labor conscripts relied on this to their advantage.
To satisfy their own palates, they employ one [offering] above while consuming ten times that amount below;
thus, the lives of sentient beings harmed and the wealth squandered exceed all record each year, and the burden upon this temple is likewise without end.

Furthermore, those who come do so with the intention of honoring the patriarchs, yet to have raw meat and pungent delicacies arrayed before them is most certainly not a pure offering, nor is it an act of benevolence.
This was his original intention. However, as abuses had accumulated over a long period, it was difficult to reform them.

Initially, it was fortunate that Zhou Gong, the Governor of Hai-men, initiated the process of lifting prohibitions and reforms; he approved the petition submitted by the Master. Subsequently, when Yu Gong, the Acting Governor, took office, he strictly prohibited slaughter. This is recorded in the local gazetteers;
consequently, whenever officials were to be supplied with provisions, the custom was to provide vegetarian offerings. Since the Master’s arrival...

This was the beginning of the mountain [monastery]. However, it was feared that because the two monasteries were so majestic and imposing, such a practice would be difficult to implement consistently.
It happened that Governor Zhizhi Gu entered the mountain to offer prayers for his parents; the local magistrate then urgently supervised the matter according to established custom.

The governor issued an edict regarding fasting and purification, and from then on, this became a fixed and permanent rule. Once this matter was implemented, it not only protected life but also refined and solemnized the pure regulations, thereby saving... [the text ends here].
Expenditures of wealth and resources were beyond calculation each year, yet the permanent endowments (*sthavira*) were also spared from the burden of suffering.
Consequently, those among the monastics who upheld the precepts increased day by day, and the monastic groves became pure and serene; this was all achieved through this single act.

Furthermore, you graciously sent your kinsman to the mountains to instruct the monks, forbidding the raising and slaughter of livestock, and transforming the fish ponds into lotus pools. From that time on, the mountain gate suddenly—
The outlook was transformed.
To supplement the permanent endowment, he reformed the rental taxes.

When the Master first entered the mountain, he examined the records of the annual accounts for the permanent endowment in the Patriarchal Hall and saw several sheets of promissory notes, all of which—

In the loan contracts held by the Patriarch, interest rates of seven or eight percent were recorded. When the Master questioned this, the presiding monk replied, "This is because the monastery's provisions are insufficient;
we borrow these funds to provide for our needs. The Master was deeply pained by this.

Upon further inquiry regarding the monastery’s assets, he asked, "Where do the rents and taxes from the existing incense-lamp estates and fields go? He immediately assembled the community to conduct a thorough investigation.

Regarding the incense and lamps for the Patriarchs, there are the "Yellow Nest" (Huangchao) and "Wet Source" (Yongyuan) bowl-replenishment funds, as well as various plots of land established by this mountain itself.
When the annual total is calculated, the rent amounts to approximately four hundred taels of gold or more. What expenses could possibly be deducted such that one would say they are insufficient?
The assembly said: "Each village has its annual quota; it should simply be collected by the administrative monk on duty through rotation, and he should be authorized to remit the funds.
Upon investigation, however, it was found that the administrator and the tenant farmers were colluding to commit fraud, resulting in arrears and incomplete payments.
There was only empty reputation, but no actual benefit; this is why the monastery’s assets are seen to be increasingly depleted."
The Master then selected from the assembly ten monks who were upright, impartial, incorruptible, and capable to manage the affairs of the monastery.

He ordered them to take an oath before the Patriarch, pledging their blood in a written covenant not to misappropriate even a single hair’s breadth of property. He summoned the tenant farmers from each village and established fixed regulations, setting annual quotas for the delivery of produce to the temple.
Furthermore, he established a treasury office and appointed four *jian-si* (administrative superintendents) to oversee the permanent assets (*chang-zhuang*) and manage their custody.
Regarding income and expenditure: a total accounting was then made for each village to determine the exact amount of silver to be collected annually.

The revenues were calculated and allocated for the various expenses of the temple according to fixed regulations, which were codified into a formal charter. Nothing was omitted, even in the most minute detail; after all expenditures were met, there remained a surplus.
From this point forward, not only would the temple’s permanent assets (*changzhu*) be abundant, but the Dharma-benefits for the Patriarchs would be as secure as before.
The rain falls universally, and thus one shall not become a seed for the hells. The regulations and rules of the pure code are listed separately as follows.
Imperially Bestowed Caoxi Nanhua Chan Temple establishes permanent endowments and re-establishes the Changsheng Treasury.
The clear regulations and standards for recording the receipt and disbursement of funds and grain are hereby inscribed.
Indeed, when our Buddha, the World-Honored One, dwelt in this world, he initially led the assembly only by carrying his alms bowl and practicing the method of begging for food;
originally there was no accumulation, so how could there have been permanent property?

Subsequently, because elderly and sick bhikṣus were unable to go begging, they instructed their co-resident bhikṣus to take the food obtained from begging and bring back half of it to provide for them; this was called *piṇḍapāta* (distribution of alms).
This refers to the practice of setting aside portions of one's food to protect and sustain the path of practice; this is recorded in detail in the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Even after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma of the Western Regions remained no different from when the Buddha was still present.

When the teachings flowed eastward, from the Yongping era of the Han dynasty through to the Tang dynasty, successive emperors, renowned ministers, officials, and lay elders each donated their own wealth to establish monasteries for the support of the Sangha.
The Sangha is regarded as a field of merit; yet, all too often, temple abbots claim it as their own private property.

Many are greedy and corrupt, violating the Dharma and encroaching upon the community of monks, showing no fear of the law of cause and effect—until we reach the grandson of our Sixth Patriarch Master and disciple of Mazu.
Master Baizhang first established the Pure Rules (Chingui) and instituted the system of permanent endowment (changzhu).

All offerings and profits, as well as fields, money, and grain, within the precincts of a monastery were placed under the charge of designated stewards; thus, the one who presides over the temple is called the Abbot (zhuchi).

With the propagation of the Dharma as the primary concern, the general outline is thus governed. To assist and support the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) and aid in the promotion of the Dharma transformation, two orders of administrative officers (*zhíshì*) are established.

These include the *dūjiānsì* (General Supervisor) and the *jiānsì* (Supervisor), who are responsible for managing the monastery’s permanent property (*chángzhù*). Assisting the two *zhǔchí* (Abbots), they oversee the annual accounting of money and grain;
their respective storehouses for expenditures and receipts are administered by what is known as the *kūsī* (Office of the Treasury). This office is located within the *jiān*.

Within the temple, those who are public-spirited, upright, and outstanding among the assembly are appointed to oversee these matters. Fearing that they might be unable to manage the tasks alone, an assistant abbot (*fuji*) is established to assist them.
As for the temple estates, there is a steward (*shōshu*); furthermore, when collecting rents and taxes, there is a collector (*kanshū*).
These positions are filled by selecting from among the assembly those who are impartial, honest, capable, magnanimous, and benevolent. They are responsible for handling the disbursements.
As for the dispensers, there are also those who manage the affairs of the mountain gate on a monthly and annual basis to attend to officials and patrons.
Whenever anything required is to be disbursed, they must report to the abbot; upon receiving his authorization and verifying the official note, they shall clearly record it in the treasury ledger.
To ensure thorough inspection, the property of the monastery remained without the slightest discrepancy. Thus, the monastic community was like a single body:
the abbot was the head, and the administrative officers were the hands, feet, eyes, and ears. They depended upon one another for function, and none could be absent.
Therefore, whenever any matter concerning the mountain gate arose, those above and below shared a common purpose, whether great or small.
It possesses power, such that it is like seeing with the eyes, hearing with the ears, grasping with the hands, and running with the feet; there is nothing that does not obey its command.
This is why the monasteries flourish and the Dharma teachings prosper, why external aggressors do not invade and internal obstacles do not arise.

This is the model for Buddhas and Patriarchs in saving the world, and the standard precedent for monasteries since antiquity. Why is it that since recent times, the Way of the Patriarchs has declined?

Alas! The monastic communities have fallen into decay and ruin. Although the former sages have left behind their instructions, people are utterly ignorant of them. Take my own Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi as an example:
he was the source of the Chan school, and his monastic community was the preeminent among all under heaven. The offerings of incense and lamps were no less than in ancient times;
yet now, the permanent endowments are utterly destroyed, and the monks are so foolish, deluded, and dull-witted that they do not even know what these things are for. I—[continue]—*

Having suffered persecution for propagating the Dharma, he was graciously granted leave to reside beyond the mountain passes. In the second month of the spring of the *wanshi* (Ming) *bingshen* year, he visited the Great Master Huineng.

Beholding the Master’s skeletal remains, which remained as solemn and lifelike as if he were still alive, yet seeing that the mountain gate was so desolate as to be almost unbearably pitiful, he lingered there for a long time, weeping.
Furthermore, the monastic community had been decimated, and the local authorities were summoning [the survivors].
The pursuit was as urgent as a shooting star. Day and night they hounded us, such that more than half of our families had sold their lands and properties.

Consequently, the ancestral temple fell into ruin, nearly reduced to nothingness. Fortunately, we were graced by the compassionate relief of the Grand Councilor and Minister of War, Mr. Chen, who slightly eased the burden. Subsequently, under the administration of Mr.
Zhou, the Commissioner of the Salt and Monopoly Department, who concurrently governed Nan and Shao, the abuses regarding the provision of wine and meat for official functions were largely abolished.
Subsequently, Master Zhu of Nanxiao severely rebuked the transgressions of the monastics and, by strictly prohibiting the killing of livestock, exerted great effort to save them.
He then commanded the assembly of monks from the entire mountain to repeatedly entreat me to enter the mountain and take charge of its affairs.

In the winter of the twenty-seventh year of the Wanli era (the Jihai year), the Master personally and earnestly urged me; then, in the first month of the spring of the following year, the Gengzi year, he again commanded the temple monks, Zhen...
Quán, Xíngyù, Jìngtài, Huìshān, Yuànrì, and others carried this letter and traveled to Wǔyáng to urge me to enter the mountains.

At that time, I was still amidst military service and had not yet been able to comply with their request. In the fourth month, the Duke went north on an official mission to offer congratulations for the imperial accession;
I saw him off at Língzhōu, where he personally and earnestly exhorted me repeatedly. It was not until the ninth month of the autumn of that year that I finally took up my staff and set out.

He entered the mountains. Upon arrival, he first selected a certain number of monks to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). They gathered together in the hall twice daily to recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Next, he selected several novices who were capable of being taught to study the scriptures; these were divided into the three types of training.
From among the assembly, those whose learning and conduct were somewhat superior were chosen as instructors. Finally, he examined the geomancy and topography of the mountain gate.

In general, those elements that were subject to conflict, injury, or suppression were removed; those that were ruined were restored. The gate of the spiritual source was sealed, and the "elephant-trunk" (the mountain’s vital point) was nourished to strengthen the ancestral temple.
The path to the mountain gate was cleared, and the stone pavilion was relocated to receive the primal qi (*yuanqi*).

Within three months, the appearance of the site underwent a dramatic transformation. Previously, inside the mountain gate, rascals had been secretly residing and occupying the temple grounds by force. Now, [the situation was rectified].

Inns and shops, taverns and butcher stalls, have artfully established systems of debauchery and gambling, colluding with local bandits to deceive and harm the temple monks; they are as predatory as jackals and tigers.
This has become a long-standing custom that is difficult to break, acting as a great internal parasite for which I harbor secret anxiety.
In the twelfth month of this year, I traveled once more to Duanzhou to pay my respects to the Grand Commander of the Circuit, the Great Minister Dai Gong, and requested—

He ordered them to be driven out. Immediately, he commanded that they be sent down to Qujiang and issued a three-day deadline to completely expel them from the borders, not permitting even a single person or a single shop to remain.
Thereupon, the bandits vanished from sight, and the temple sites and market streets previously occupied by them were all returned to the permanent endowment (*sāṃghika*).
I then used this opportunity to block the "piercing-heart" roads to the east and west; to the left [of the road], I established...
The public guest house was established as a place for Wenyuan and all passing travelers to halt their carriages; its plaque read "Coming from Three Lives.

To the right stood the Ten Directions Guesthouse for Overnight Lodgers, intended to welcome monks from the four quarters as a place to suspend their staffs; its plaque read "Awakening in a Single Night.
The main thoroughfare was moved to the edge of the stream so that those coming and going could each find their proper place, and no longer be confused with one another.
The monastic groves were purified from this point on, and the assembly of monks could sleep in peace thereafter.
On the third day of the first month of the New Year in the following year, the Year of Xinchou, I received an official dispatch from the Provincial Governor (Zhìtái) to attend to local affairs.

Furthermore, I requested that the Inspector General, Lord Li, be recognized as a patron (*dānapati*) for the restoration of the monastery. In the seventh month, the Lord entered the mountain to pay his respects.

The Patriarch [Huineng] was pleased to grant three hundred pieces of gold as funds for the reconstruction of the mountain gate. Thereupon, I, the temple administrator, conducted a thorough investigation into the offerings, incense, lamps, and estate rents provided for the Sixth Patriarch.
Regarding the annual yield obtained from these sources, not even a hair’s breadth had ever been entered into the permanent endowment (chángzhù) of the monastery;
it had all been embezzled by those in charge of its custody. This had become a long-standing custom. Consequently, I first attended to the matter of Taiping [Temple].
Regarding the estate rents: the annual tax silver for the twenty-ninth year of the Wanli era has already been assigned to the permanent endowment (changzhu).

A fixed schedule of three periods—spring, autumn, and winter—has been established for its expenditure during the current year. Now, the "Yellow Nest" and "Ten Thousand Goodness" bowls are to be supplemented.

Furthermore, the various estates of this temple that have been successively established shall all be returned to it; these were previously collected and are now restored for the purpose of covering expenditures in the coming year.
With the exception of the rents and taxes from the twenty-ninth year of the various estates, which have already been settled, starting from the thirtieth year:
This was established as a permanent regulation. Furthermore, it was investigated that this temple formerly possessed a "Longevity Treasury" (Changsheng Ku), which is now being reinstated.

All monastic rents, taxes, and offerings from patrons shall be deposited and stored within this treasury. In accordance with the precedents of the Pure Regulations (Qinggui), administrative officers shall be appointed to oversee the treasury;
specifically, four Monks-in-Charge (Jiansi) shall be selected from among the mature and experienced members of the assembly to manage all income and expenditures.

Regarding those who are incorruptible: they shall fill the ten quarters of this temple. Originally, there was one *duguan* (general manager) and nine *dusi* (temple administrators), who were originally assigned to perform labor services:
receiving high-ranking officials, providing supplies for the prefectures and counties, and procuring pepper, tea, *zōng*, *lǐ*, fruits, and bamboo shoots.
Furthermore, the permanent rents and levies of the past have all been embezzled by these individuals, which is truly lamentable.
Now, ten monks who are diligent and experienced in affairs shall be selected to fill these positions. All necessary expenses shall be apportioned equally per head;
each monk shall contribute a small amount from his own portion, which will be collected in advance and deposited in the treasury to await the occasional demands of the superior authorities.
It is necessary to avoid further trouble and disturbance. All revenue collected from the various estates shall be deposited in the treasury;
these shall be disbursed and paid according to the established regulations for land taxes and labor levies, ensuring that no amounts are withheld, delayed, or embezzled.

As for the expenses incurred by superior officials when entering the mountain to receive them, if fixed rules have been established, they shall not unfairly burden the administrative staff. Regarding the Buddhas and Patriarchs...
The use of incense and lamps in the halls has established regulations, so that the intent of performing devotional rites and making offerings to repay one's fundamental debt may not be lost.

As for the monks who serve as attendants, they toil and run errands throughout the year; they shall also receive compensation for their labor, ensuring that hardship and ease are balanced and that no cause for lamentation or resentment arises.
Furthermore, the fullness or deficiency of the rents collected shall be examined and adjusted accordingly, thereby manifesting the distinction between diligence and indolence.

The four items mentioned above are all deducted from the monastery’s treasury. However, the tuition fees for the training of novice attendants are paid solely by me, with the exception of the Confucian teacher, for whom I provide the funds myself.
As for the monastic teacher, his compensation comes from the reduction of the robes and bowls of the Patriarchs kept beneath the stupa;

this is intended to train and nurture the śrāmaṇeras so as to increase their sense of shame and remorse in future lives. There are fixed regulations for this, and such is the practice of the permanent endowment.

Regarding funds and provisions, there shall be no provision for waste; regarding those in charge of administration, there shall be no opportunity for self-theft; and as for the monastic community, there shall be no regulations concerning the granting of favors to lay patrons.
Thus, the permanent assets of the monastery may be secured for the long term. Furthermore, all the monks and novices of the entire temple, both great and small, [shall be included].

If everyone were to fully observe the precepts, they would avoid the reproach of defiling the ancestral monastery; furthermore, by saving on the expenses for wine and meat, they could provide for their own clothing and food.
Thus, when clothing and food are sufficient, ritual and righteousness flourish; even a defiled land can be transformed into a pure Buddha-field.
The restoration of the Caoxi ancestral monastery and the re-establishment of the monastic discipline depend entirely upon this single undertaking.
The great pivot of the Dharma’s destiny is of no small importance.

With the exception of the aforementioned faults that have corrupted the Dharma, which shall be left unaddressed, all matters of business shall be reformed from this year, the thirtieth year of the Wanli era, and established as a permanent standard.
All those in charge must exert themselves and ensure its diligent implementation; you are not permitted to remain negligent over time, nor to harbor unscrupulous monks.

If there are those who, in vain, give rise to scheming and calculating thoughts that destroy the Dharma, or who arbitrarily alter established regulations—if such persons exist, they shall be scrutinized by the divine eyes of the Patriarchs, the Spiritually Penetrating One, and the Dharma-protecting Kṣetrapāla.
Their offenses will certainly not be pardoned, and the retribution will be clearly manifested.
Even for those wicked and thieving individuals who destroy the Dharma, they shall encounter the royal law in their lifetime and fall into the Avīci Hell after death. Therefore—
The results were manifest; there was not even the slightest discrepancy.
From now on, all those who serve as heads of affairs should frequently and earnestly examine their own minds, so as not to inadvertently incur bitter retribution or bring guilt upon themselves.

At the inception of the treasury, the rents and taxes of the current year were all collected and deposited for the following year, while the current year’s expenditures were drawn in advance with no funds remaining. I have already made preparations.
Three hundred and twenty-five taels of silver shall remain in the treasury as a reserve fund to serve as the principal for the permanent endowment.
Subsequent expenditures shall be met from this fund, with the expectation that future rents and levies will be used to replenish it year by year.
The following regulations to be implemented are hereby set forth for perpetual observance as a fixed rule.
The roster lists: First, four office-holding Monks of the Abbot’s Office (Jiansi) shall be appointed.

They shall exclusively manage the treasury, handling the income and expenditure of the monastery’s funds and grain, procuring necessary utensils, and presiding over the major affairs of the mountain gate to assist the Abbot.
In all matters, they shall deliberate with a unified mind; among them, one person shall be specifically assigned to...
Appoint a manager to store and manage all monies, grain, and miscellaneous goods; in this way, there will be accountability.
Appoint one person within [the monastery] to oversee the collection of rents and taxes, so as to root out abuses before they become widespread and to serve as a standard for the community.
Appoint one clerk for the storehouse office to exclusively manage the registration of income and expenditures in ledgers, so as to facilitate audits and prevent negligence.
Appoint one head of the household;
this is according to the old regulations. He shall exclusively manage the village households (*li-jia*), the corvée labor, and the grain taxes, continuing as usual.
The *gui* (regulator). This is the ancient position of the Vice-Abbot (*fu-si*).
There is one person for this office, who is the ancient *gui-du-zhi-shi* (regulatory chief administrator); he is the head of the administrative staff (*zhi-shi*).

Today, this office is charged with acting as the *zhuang-zhu* (estate manager), leading the entire monastery and collecting rents and taxes from the various estates, while overseeing the execution of all duties.
Regarding the temple tax-exemption (ji-ryō-sa): the deputy head of the household (*fuko-chō*) is also called the *chokusai*.
The chief administrator (*doshi*) is of the ninth rank; this is the ancient equivalent of the *chiji* (administrator).

They assist the chief supervisor (*dokan*) in collecting taxes and exemptions, take turns serving as the month-on-duty official (*chiketsu-gatsu*), and manage all major and minor affairs of the mountain gate. These ten administrative offices (*jūshitsu*) are currently...
In accordance with the ancient regulations of the ten quarters of this temple, each quarter shall take turns by rotation, with a change occurring at the end of every year.

Consequently, those who have served previously were often individuals lacking integrity, and many were unable to manage affairs of great importance. Now, we shall specifically select those whose talent and capability stand out from the crowd to serve in these positions.
When the time arrives for the annual replacement, the Abbot and the Chief Administrator (Jian-si) shall continue to examine their merit and diligence.

Those who leave the community shall be replaced as before; those who are unfit, or who have other obligations and cannot respond to their duties, shall be immediately replaced by those who are public-spirited, upright, and mature.

Should there be those who fail to observe the pure rules, who defy the law for private gain, or who collude with tenant farmers to ruin the permanent property of the monastery, delay the payment of rents and taxes, or who, out of greed for small profits, oppress and exploit the tenant population—[they shall be removed].
If there are those who exploit the assembly of monks and thereby harm the great principles of the Sangha, the general manager and the prior shall not tolerate or conceal such acts.

They must immediately report the matter to the abbot, sound the bell to assemble the community, and before the presence of the Patriarchs, clearly testify to the offender’s crimes. For minor offenses, appropriate punishment shall be meted out, followed by reform or dismissal;
another capable person shall be selected to replace them without waiting for the end of the year. For grave offenses, the case shall be presented to the authorities according to the law.
Punish them in order to warn the rest. The abbot must not permit indulgence or favoritism, lest great harm be fostered.
Be cautious! Be cautious!
First, an explanation of income and expenditure: Income consists of five items:
annual offerings and interest from the Patriarchal Hall; silver hats and ritual implements; annual rents and taxes from the various monastic estates;
contributions from visiting officials; and voluntary donations from patrons. Each of these shall be solicited and managed for the purpose of repairs and construction.
[He] shall construct [buildings], provide funds and provisions for the monastic assembly, and impose fines upon offending monks. All such items— including money, grain, fragrant oil,
and silver for official buildings, properties, fields, and lands that ought to enter the public treasury— as well as the value of materials purchased from the storehouse,
goods belonging to deceased monks that should enter the public treasury, and fields, houses, and buildings acquired by the monastery, shall all be accounted for accordingly.
Regarding the inventory of household goods and documents, each item shall be listed individually and recorded in the ledgers for the purpose of inspection.
For each category, two receipt books shall be prepared; the abbot and the administrative office (kūsi) shall each hold one copy.
Whenever there is anything to be received, it must be collected in the presence of the assembly at the Patriarch’s Hall (zǔdiàn).
For all the various manors, there are specific upper and lower deadlines for the annual rent and taxes each year.

In advance, the General Manager shall direct the Temple Administrator to jointly urge the various tenants, holding the Village Head (Tianjia) collectively responsible for collecting the silver and ensuring full payment. [The Administrator] shall personally go to the Ancestral Hall, where he shall hand over the funds to the Abbot and the Chief Monastic Officer (Jiansi).

The Chief Monastic Officer shall supervise the collection, using a standard weight and balance to ensure the transactions are clear and transparent. The Secretary shall then record these details in the ledgers.
The abbot shall sign the seal. Immediately within the treasury, take one treasury receipt and, together with the abbot’s collection ledger, record the amount of silver upon it;
affix the seal across the joint of the documents, and further have each person sign their flower-mark (signature) beneath their respective title as an attendant official.
Only the official land registers shall be used as the standard. No one in charge of affairs is permitted to grant private allocations.

If it is discovered that any rental has been granted without an official stamped receipt, this constitutes collusion; such individuals, including the abbot and the heads of departments, shall certainly be reported to the authorities and punished according to the law.

During both the spring and autumn seasons, lay patrons from the ten directions come before the Patriarch to present incense, offerings of silver hats, flower vessels, silver coins, *kāṣāya* robes, and other items;
these are collected by the stupa master and recorded in the register by the abbot.
At the end of the year, the various categories of the annual inventory shall be clearly enumerated and audited. Those items that ought to be retained shall be stored as before.
Items for use in the Patriarchal Hall shall be transferred to the storehouse and managed according to established regulations.

At the appointed time, it is imperative to assemble the assembly of elders to inspect and verify the items in their presence; the *tazhu* (stupa master) is not permitted to conceal anything or collude with the administrative officers.
[The official] shall investigate and determine [the matter], and punish those who embezzle or misappropriate official property.

Regarding all offerings made by officials, funds raised for construction and repairs, grain for monastic feasts, rice for monks, and all other items belonging to the permanent endowment (sangha-property), one must establish ledgers according to the prescribed format and record each item in detail, collecting them in accordance with the Dharma. Do not...
If there are items that ought to be collected but are not recorded in the ledgers, the scribe, the supervisor,
and those who colluded in the fraudulent practice shall be held accountable for their crimes.

For all items such as silver, grain, and other goods to be disbursed for use, the Head Monk (Dōji) serving as the month’s director shall prepare a draft according to the prescribed form and first present it to the Abbot (Jūji) for approval.
Once the Abbot grants permission for the disbursement, the draft shall be recorded in the disbursement ledger.
Furthermore, the ticket shall be filled out with both the sequential number and the amount of silver disbursed; these two sections must be joined together and sealed with a private seal.
Additionally, the characters "zhun zhi" (authorized for disbursement) shall be written in the blank space. The attendant on duty, holding the ticket, shall go to the treasury to receive the funds.
The treasurer’s clerk shall record the details of the ticket in the disbursement ledger, and only then may the abbot’s assistant issue the silver according to the specified amount.

If there are no official records, seals, or tickets, it shall be considered the responsibility of the lineage branch (Chang-zhi). If the amount is small, the head of the branch shall assemble the community and impose a proportional fine;
if the amount is large, they shall be sent to the authorities to be punished according to the law.

If funds were not for public use but were spent by the abbot acting out of personal interest, or by the monthly administrators and custodians who collectively issued unauthorized tickets to disburse money and goods—regardless of the amount—if such acts are discovered, [the offenders shall be punished].
He was charged with the offense of embezzlement.

A "Longevity Treasury" (Changsheng Ku) was established exclusively for the storage of accumulated reserves. The *jian-si* (superintendent) was appointed as the official in charge of managing funds and provisions;

many people were not permitted to enter indiscriminately. Therefore, a *jian-si* chamber was also established as a place for formal consultations. Whenever it was the turn of the month for duty, the administrative affairs were managed [there].

The *sengding* (monastic supervisor) must reside exclusively in the quarters for one month. He shall oversee all internal and external affairs of the monastery, both large and small, and manage the disbursement of money, grain, and goods.
At the end of the month, he shall provide a clear settlement and prepare a single small monthly report booklet, which he shall submit to the Abbot.

Upon verification and finding it accurate, the Abbot shall sign it with the two characters "Not Erroneous" (*bùchā*) and forward it to the Treasury Office (*kūsī*), so that it may be categorized at the end of the year.
[This is] for the purpose of ensuring that [the records] are not confused or erroneous.
At the end of each year, on the first day of the tenth month—the date for the change of incumbents—the abbot and the assembly shall first calculate the accounts of the year’s income and expenditure.
On this day, the prior, the secretary, and the administrators of the ten offices shall each hold their ledgers.
Register. All assemble in the Patriarchal Hall. Invite an elder skilled in calculation; one person shall oversee the counting while another shall chant the numbers.

Before the eyes of the assembly, they shall count together clearly and transparently. Once the total is determined, it shall be handed over to the secretary to compile a formal document. Within this, it shall be recorded:
"Now, for the year of [year], the total rent and grain collected by the permanent endowment of this temple amounts to [amount]; donations amount to [amount]; [name]..."
The quantity of goods is as follows. For the current period, expenditures for specific items and miscellaneous expenses total such-and-such an amount;

the remaining inventory is such-and-such an amount. There may also be outstanding rents or taxes totaling such-and-such an amount. Each item shall be listed individually, and a comprehensive ledger shall be prepared in four identical copies.

One copy shall be sent to the Patriarch’s Hall to be stored within a casket; one copy shall be sent to the Central Monastery (Zhongxing Changzhu); and one copy shall be deposited with the Administrative Office (Kusi).
These were established as permanent standards; the same applied to items such as pepper, tea, and areca nuts.
The annual allocations for these fixed items are listed below.
The total number of items for the settlement and payment of grain and labor taxes is fifteen.
These are levied according to the fields in accordance with established precedent; annually, they amount to approximately one hundred taels of silver or more.

Should there be newly added land, or in the event of an intercalary month, the labor services and levies will increase and never decrease. However, this shall not apply in the event of tax exemptions.
Thus, there was little and not much:
for the incense and lamps of the Buddha Hall, ten taels of silver were provided each year;
for the offerings of incense and lamps at the Patriarchs' Hall, fifty taels of silver were provided each year.

For the maintenance of the Dharma and the monastery, there shall be offerings for the fasts on the first and fifteenth days of every month, totaling twelve taels of silver annually; no amount is allotted for intercalary months.
For the reception of superiors and visiting officials by the abbot, the established annual precedent was eleven taels, to which an increase has now been added.
Four taels.
The Head of the District (Hùzhǎng) shall entertain the official; according to the annual custom, ten taels [were previously allotted], with an increase of two taels.
For the four Monastic Administrators (Jiànsì) and the one Librarian/Secretary (Sīkù Shūjì), each person shall receive three taels of silver annually for their vegetarian meals.
Six *qián*. Together with the silver, this totals eighteen *liǎng*.
There are ten *duguān* and *dūsuì*; for their annual vegetarian meals, there is three *liǎng* six *qián* of silver, totaling thirty-six *liǎng* of silver.
One new mountain steward shall be appointed to guard the trees of the ancestral mountain, repair them, and cultivate them.
Each year, he shall be granted a stipend of one *liang* and five *qian* of silver for his food.
The six officials—the Abbot and the Karmadāna—lead the assembly daily to perform recitations in each hall;
each person is provided with two bolts of cloth and five *qián* of silver, totaling three *liǎng* of silver.

Two senior attendants and one assistant servant shall guard the official residence, strike the bells and drums to announce visitors, and await orders from the permanent establishment to perform their duties.
Each person shall receive an annual wage of one liang and two qian of silver; the total for all is three liang and six qian of silver.

To revitalize the ancestral temple, the Wujin An (Inexhaustible Hermitage) has been rebuilt. Each year, thirty taels of silver shall be allocated for offerings and the maintenance of the incense and lamps.
This is an extra provision, established from the personal donations received by the Founding Patriarch himself;
it is not comparable to the offerings made by others. Future masters, administrators, and custodians must not treat this lightly, lest they incur grave consequences.

Caution! Be cautious! Be cautious! As for this sum of silver: since the meditation hall was renovated in the thirty-fourth year, this silver has been placed within the hall to serve as provisions for the Sangha of the ten directions; it has no connection whatsoever with the hermitage.

Whenever the two provincial courts (the Provincial Governor and the Censor-in-Chief) enter the mountain, with the exception of the three locations where the Abbot of the Pagoda, the Head of the Monastery, and the Head of the District households receive the superior officials, all other officials— including those from the Prefectures and Counties,

the Inspecting Censors, the Traveling Censors, the Commandant of the Prefecture, the Merit-Appraising Officials, the Central Army Officers, the Garrison Commanders, and the Patrol Captains— must likewise do so.

Regarding officials of equal rank, as well as messengers and laborers dispatched by ordinary superiors, they shall continue to follow the established regulations by being assigned to the ten administrative offices to receive guests collectively;
the permanent monastery funds are not permitted to cover these expenses.

Regarding the entry, exit, and movement of officials from Wengyuan County, they shall exclusively attend to administrative duties during their assigned month. For the reception of vegetarian meals, the established regulations are as follows:
for the Head Official (Zhengtang), one coin of silver per meal; for the Assistant Officials (Zu'er), seven fen of silver per meal.
For Confucian scholars: for each meal, five fen of silver. For the Gong (Gentleman): for each meal, three fen of silver.
Regarding the above four regulations, after the manager has received the guests, he shall immediately prepare checks and present them to the Abbot for the seal to be affixed;
they are then to be drawn from the treasury. If the guests do not belong to this county, the old regulations shall still apply.
The instructors for the children’s recitation of the scriptures consist of three teachers. Each year, they receive a total of ten taels of silver and two bolts of cloth each;
each bolt is valued at twenty-five cash. All of these are provided.

The ancestral master’s robe and bowl are taken from within [the treasury] and prepared by the current stupa-keeper. For each person outside [the monastic community], one pair of shoes and a silver discount of two cents are provided;
this item shall be disbursed from the permanent treasury (changzhu ku).

Should there be no funds available in the Ancestral Hall, it shall be drawn from the Changsheng Treasury according to the precedent for the Monastery Supervisor (jian-si), to be disbursed in installments rather than in small, piecemeal amounts. As for the provision of meals, they shall follow [the standard].

Regarding the number of residents in the meditation hall and the aforementioned regulations: the incense, lamps, and fields of the founding patriarch shall continue to be pooled for communal use as a permanent, fixed standard.

Future abbots, head officers, and administrative officials are not permitted to harbor ulterior motives, greedily consume the monastery’s assets, act according to private interests or whims, or arbitrarily increase or decrease these provisions, even if the annual ancestral offerings are fully met.

Once the aforementioned expenses have been deducted, if there remains a surplus, the administrative officers shall not be permitted to invent pretexts or establish new categories to arbitrarily appropriate these funds.
Expenditures are only allowed for the repair of the monastery gates, the travel and incidental costs of the officers, or matters pertaining to the common property of the community;
such withdrawals are permitted only when absolutely unavoidable. However, one should strive to economize on all other items.
People should regard the permanent endowment (*sāṃghika*) as substantial and enduring; by no means should they give rise to the desire for minor profits, thereby inviting hell for themselves.

An ancient worthy said: "Regarding the property of the permanent endowment, if the presiding administrators and those who manage its income and expenditure can skillfully economize on frivolous expenses, then the funds and grain will be inexhaustible.
From this point forward, year after year, there will be accumulated reserves."

Others managed the affairs according to the Dharma, so that the community flourished day by day and month by month; there has never been a monastic grove (*saṃghārāma*) that did not prosper, nor a wheel of the Dharma (*dharmacakra*) that did not turn.

Having received my Patriarch’s command, I have undertaken the task of restoring what was collapsing and rescuing what was in peril, and upholding the sagging disciplinary code—this is no small matter.
All administrative officers must strictly adhere to this; do not neglect even the slightest detail. Alas! Be mindful! Property belonging to the Sangha is precious down to the smallest fraction.
It is, indeed, the seed for the field of merit for donors and the very blood and fat of their faith.

How could one ever treat it with levity, deceive, or steal from it? As the ancient masters said: "Property belonging to the Sangha is like the poison of the *hebi* bird; were one to ingest but a single grain, it would tear one's liver asunder."

Their heads are shattered; their entire bodies are festering and putrid. Therefore, those who hold positions of authority, if they understand cause and effect, will thereby create celestial palaces and pure lands.
Those who do not understand cause and effect will instead create immeasurable hells, with iron beds, bronze pillars, and glowing hot iron balls.
Their suffering for ten thousand kalpas will not end merely with being born as beasts with hair and horns, or having to wear iron collars and carry heavy loads.
The saddle is merely for the repayment of past debts. How much more so, then, should one stand in awe of the rigorous majesty of the royal law and the surveillance of the divine spirits?
All you who serve here should deeply reflect, contemplate, and keep this in mind.
Established on the first day of the first month of the spring in the year Renyin, the thirtieth year of the Wanli era.
To alleviate the burden of compensatory levies, the original estate of Wengyuan was exempted from empty-tax obligations;
this estate was originally donated by the local villager, the surnamed Xie.
To provide for the offering of incense and lamps, the Sixth Patriarch established an annual endowment of one hundred and twenty taels of silver.
In the sixth year of the Wanli era, Lin Huan, who had traveled abroad for study and was a personal friend of the local Magistrate Wang, sent [the Patriarch’s remains] to be enshrined in this temple.

He harbored a desire for the temple’s property that he had not yet fulfilled; consequently, he slandered the District Vice-Governor, claiming that all the profits from this estate were being diverted to the monks.
The Vice-Governor, having been misled and while presiding over the affairs of the prefecture, subsequently divided sixty taels of silver from the original capital of the estate.
To offset the empty grain levies imposed on the egg-producers of Qujiang, a formal petition was submitted to the two courts and the provincial authorities to establish this as a standing regulation.
Consequently, sixty taels were allocated for the maintenance of the temple. Furthermore, due to the persistent malfeasance and arrears of the tenant farmers, the temple monks suffered incessantly;

they repeatedly appealed to their superiors, even spending over a thousand taels of gold, yet ultimately could not escape the burden. Later, during the tenure of General Liu, a proposal was deliberated and approved.

The Prefecture submitted a detailed report stating that the taxes from the Hanguang salt factory were deducted from the surplus funds within the military provisions of the Commandant’s office to compensate for the monks’ burden;
this practice remained unchanged until the arrival of the Salt Monopoly Commissioner in the Gengzi year of the Wanli era.
The factory tax was then assigned to the Imperial Eunuch Office. When this was reported to the Military Commissioner Dai, he granted permission for it to continue as before.

Subsequently, the Tax Supervisor personally dispatched officials to collect the taxes, which left no surplus to be deducted. Master Shi learned of this and went in person to the Military Commissioner’s office to explain the situation.
He requested that the local county authorities investigate whether there were any impediments to compensating for the loss, and that the monks of the temple not be further burdened. The county...
After repeated investigations, nothing further was found. Consequently, it was proposed to levy a tax on small grain-boats plying the rivers and streams leading to various mountains;

this yielded twenty-six taels, which was still insufficient. Subsequently, an investigation was conducted into the mountain villages facing Mōnglǐ, where there was formerly a plot of "poisonous" (gǔdú) land that had not been subject to taxation.
This land was then leased for thirty-four taels to bring the total revenue to the required amount. A formal report was prepared.

The proposal was submitted for approval. From this point forward, the harm to the mountain gate (the monastery) was permanently blocked; all of this was due to the power of the Grand Councilor [Zhitai] in protecting the Dharma.

Now that these burdens had been averted, the tenants of the original estate were found to be wicked and obstinate; furthermore, because the estate was in a different county, they were difficult to control.

Previously, these fields had caused trouble within the monastic community, leading to expenses incurred in pursuing the land. Consequently, it was deliberated among the assembly that the aforementioned estate lands should be sold.

It was deemed convenient to redeem the temple’s nearby fields by paying their value. This was reported in full to the military headquarters (junmen), which issued an official dispatch (pibi) to the provincial administration (bendao).

The regional government and the county authorities deliberated and found this arrangement convenient. Since the time of our ancestors, the community has cultivated these lands for generations as if they were their own private property; they have neither relinquished them nor sold them separately.

Out of sincere desire, they requested that the land be re-measured and added to the ancestral holdings, so that they might perpetually maintain the temple’s estate without substitution. Thus spoke Xu Gong, the Second Magistrate of Qujiang.
While serving as the magistrate of Wenyuan, he convened all the tenant farmers for a land survey. It was discovered that there were indeed surplus fields and lands;

consequently, in addition to the regular tax quota, he measured and added a new increment of fourteen taels and some odd coins in silver. He submitted a formal petition to his superiors, which was approved in detail.
He then engaged in farming with the community of cultivators. Every year, they would agree upon a date for the delivery of the harvest to the storehouse.

At that time, the abbot and the assembly of monks deliberated on increasing the rent and taxes, concluding that since this was due to the Master’s efforts, it should rightfully belong to the Master as the restorer of the monastery's permanent endowment.

Consequently, they combined the previous offerings for the incense and lamps at Wujin’an with these new revenues and assigned them all to the Meditation Hall to serve as provisions for its support, establishing this as a permanent regulation; of all matters, this was the sole instance [of such a change].
In truth, the Buddhist monastic community has suffered ceaseless harm. Previously, we were fortunate that Lord Liu of the Zhitai [Academy] exercised provisional measures;
ultimately, we were graced by Lord Dai, who forever severed these afflictions and ensured future blessings. Thus we know that the Buddha-dharma is entrusted to kings and ministers:
were it not for reliance upon the great power of external protection, how could it be preserved for all eternity? The records of this case are fully maintained in the provincial and county archives.
Furthermore, the ancestral mountain of Caoxi was protected from encroachment;
its shape resembles that of an elephant, with its head, tail, and all parts clearly defined. The current range behind the mountain constitutes its entire body.
As for Zisun Zhuang (Purple Bamboo Estate), it was one of the twelve fruit and flower gardens where the Patriarch frequented during his lifetime.
This is the first [account]. Previously, there were seven abbots who governed the monastery; it was known as "Little Nanhua" and had existed for a long time.

In the first year of the Chenghua era (1465), Shaoguan began to open up the fields and roads and establish the well-field system (*jingtian*). Consequently, the entire mountain was swallowed up by powerful landowners.

At that time, the monk Man Cangsheng submitted a memorial to the Imperial Court, requesting that the Provincial Surveillance Commissioners (*fuzhan*) conduct an investigation to restore the original holdings. Thus, the purple robe was conferred upon him.

Sun Zhuang was the first to be punished for this. Later, because many monks were undisciplined, the neighboring residents began to encroach upon and exploit the land, causing such harm that the monks could no longer find peace there.
Consequently, they each returned to their respective temples and abandoned these properties.

During the twentieth year of the Wanli era, the local bully Jiang Yingdong feigned the purchase of monastic lands to occupy the entire area of the rear mountain for geomantic purposes, leading to further complications.
The Elephant’s Back and Zu Mountain were divided; furthermore, logging operations gradually encroached upon the interior lands.

The Master lamented with a heavy heart, saying, "From this point on, the ancestral mountains will be entirely lost to the private holdings of the common people. He then exhorted the assembly of monks to go and petition the military headquarters.

Having received approval from the provincial government, the Prefectural Administration personally investigated the matter. Subsequently, they were granted an audience by Wan, the Acting Tongpan of Zhaoqing Prefecture, who personally [conducted the inquiry].

He went into the mountains to conduct a survey and establish boundary stones, thereby determining that the aforementioned fields should be reclaimed by the monks to eliminate the source of future calamity.
The Master personally solicited two hundred taels of silver to redeem the aforementioned fields, including the subsequent mountain sites and timber.
All of these were collectively dedicated as a permanent endowment for the meditation hall (*candang*).

Not only was the ancestral mountain thus preserved, but it became the eternal foundation for the meditation hall. However, because the Master acted in this way, resentful monks joined forces with outsiders to cause harm.
Nevertheless, he ultimately established a stele with firm resolve, making it a Vajra Banner (*vajradhvaja*).

To establish the meditation hall for the purpose of consolidating the fundamental basis, the Master once addressed the assembly, saying: "The existence of a meditation hall within a monastic community is like the existence of schools within a state."
This is a place for nurturing and cultivating talent. Since ancient times, those who have governed states have regarded the storage of talent as their foundation;
the Dharma-gate is likewise so. Since Bodhidharma came from the West, the robe and bowl remained at Caoxi.
At that time, among the disciples under the Sixth Patriarch, there were over thirty who realized the Way, with Nanyue and Qingyuan as the foremost. That Baolin Chan Hall was...

This is the place from which all the patriarchs originated; thus, among those recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp) throughout the world’s meditation halls, more than one thousand seven hundred individuals all emerged from the single lineage of Caoxi, just as the disciples of Confucius emerged from the banks of the Shu and Si rivers. This, then, is the meditation hall of this very mountain.
This is indeed the fundamental site of the Chan school. Alas, as the years have passed, the monastics have failed to maintain it, and the meditation hall is nearly lost to oblivion.
Upon its original foundations, there are seven miscellaneous monk’s quarters and two incense-storage kitchens.
Consequently, the latrines and pigsties each came to number nine, as the pure jewel-grounds were transformed into manure and filth. The Master felt profound sorrow for this;

he reflected that for a Buddhist monastery (conglin) to endure for a hundred years, it must be established through the cultivation of people. He now selected śrāmaṇeras to train them into mature adults.
He thought that if one trains them but does not sustain them, it is like a farmer who knows how to sow but does not know how to weed—the end result will be difficult to bring to fruition. If...
"If there is no meditation hall, upon what shall future generations rely? Reflecting on this day and night, I have labored with a heavy heart and great anxiety.

Having thoroughly examined the suitability of the site, I have used my own robes and bowl, as well as funds saved from my meager diet, to accumulate several taels of gold. With these, I have searched for and purchased a vacant plot of land."
The monastic quarters were each relocated; they were paid for and rebuilt separately, and the vacant space of the meditation hall was cleared.
Measuring every inch, ten parts were traded for one to ensure the area was perfectly level and square. Exhausting every ounce of effort and heart, a new meditation hall was constructed.

Although it does not entirely follow the old regulations, its scale is already complete. Furthermore, I reflected that if one followed the conventional patterns of other regions, it would certainly not...

It was able to endure for a long time. Consequently, he established the Ten Directions Hall outside the mountain gate to receive those coming and going, while the inner hall remained solely for the resident monks of the temple to cultivate future generations of disciples and focus their minds on pure practice.

Fortunately, as these regulations were established, the monks within the hall were numerous and impressive to behold, making it a truly solemn site of practice. Once the meditation hall had been established, the Master [addressed] the matter of food...
Finding this difficult to accomplish, he then took thirty-one taels of silver from the rent for Zhongxing Monastery— which had previously been provided for offerings—
and fourteen taels of newly increased rent from Wengyuan, and petitioned to redeem the original price of the fields, lands, and mountain tracts of Zisun Estate.
Some two hundred taels were spent to purchase a plot of land at Huangshan and Chaisan for an unspecified amount of silver.
Furthermore, the owner’s own purchased Zhandanlin Hall was exchanged for two monastic quarters behind the Xiangji Kitchen;

these were all consolidated and returned to the Zen Hall to serve as the foundation for the permanent endowment (*sangha-rāma*) from its re-establishment to its conclusion. Including the expenses for construction, this single site alone— [The text ends here.]

He donated a thousand *qian*. All of this was provided through the collective effort of the military forces. From that time on, the monastic community’s food and clothing became sufficient, and rites and righteousness flourished.
Therefore, whatever the monks in the hall currently enjoy using was all the blood, heart, and sweat of the Master from those days.
How could those who later live in peace and comfort not know their origin? If the monks wish for their own sustenance to be sufficient and are further able to consume the food of the Dharma...
By filling [these gaps], the life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs may rely upon this to remain eternally secure.

The above enumeration of the incomplete causes and conditions is appended in accordance with the regulations of the ten chapters of the *Tanzing Tongzhi* (Comprehensive Record of the Platform Sutra) as established by the Great Master; thus, I have excerpted [the relevant material].
The general outline of these matters is likewise divided into ten sections, intended to reveal a single hair from the whole body.
As for the subtle gates of practice, which all transcend the reach of thought and deliberation, they cannot easily be enumerated in their entirety within the span of eight years.

Through the toil of such hardship, his spirit was utterly exhausted. Of what has been accomplished, seven-tenths is the merit of its original founding and three-tenths is the merit of its subsequent restoration.
As for this one great hall that remains unfinished, it is the work left incomplete by the Sixth Patriarch himself.
He had long desired to manage its completion, but his strength fell short of the task. In the third month of the spring of the Wushen year, in Lingxi—
Wen Suofeng observed that the Master had entered the mountains to visit him. He stayed overnight in the hermitage.

During the night, he dreamed of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, who appeared in a towering form with features of perfect dignity and grace. Upon seeing him, Wen prostrated and praised his majestic beauty.

He heard the Great Being say: "That which is not adorned is what is called adornment. Wen attained a realization. When he awoke, he was filled with great joy. At dawn the following morning, he went in...
The Duke paid his respects to the Buddha and visited the Great Being (Mahāsattva).

Upon seeing that the rear pillar of the main hall was rotting and on the verge of collapsing, and that the three statues of the Great Beings were likewise in a state of great peril, the Duke pointed this out to the Master and asked, "Why do you not repair this? The Master replied, "I have long harbored this intention."
"It is simply that my strength is insufficient. The official asked, "How much do you require? The Master said, "I will not dare undertake it for less than three thousand *jin* of gold.

The official said, "Please feel free to take on the responsibility. The Master replied, "If the donor truly gives rise to the great mind, it will be accomplished in the space of a cough or a snap of the fingers."

The Duke said, "Truly, this is not something that can be accomplished by a single effort; let us plan it gradually. Upon returning, the Duke went to see the Grand Councilor and Commander-in-Chief, Dai Gong, and informed him of the situation.
Dai Gong said, "When a child is about to fall into a well, a person of benevolence will surely crawl forward to rescue them."
"How much more so when a great mansion is about to collapse—how perilous is the state of the Buddha and the sages! This is something that a benevolent heart cannot bear.
He then spoke to Lord Feng, requesting that the Master consult with him in person. Upon hearing this, the Master was delighted; he prepared architectural plans and went to visit Lord Dai.

Studying the plans, he calculated privately, saying, "If it were as the Lord has described, it would still not be enough. The Master said, "Buddhist works are like clouds in the sky; they are simply..."
"This is merely the unfolding of conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Your Excellency has already provided the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) for it.

The Master said, "Matters concerning the Dharma cannot be constrained by worldly laws, nor can they be expected to achieve completion quickly. It would be inconvenient if you, Excellency, were to exert yourself alone;

rather, it must be accomplished through the collective will of the assembly. It will suffice simply to rely on the power of the Dharma to provide guidance. Thereupon, they deliberated on the composition of ten prefaces.

The news spread throughout the provincial governors, intendants, prefects, and magistrates, each of whom contributed. Before long, the military governor and the two provincial intendants, along with the prefects and magistrates, each donated a thousand taels of gold.
The Master personally traveled to Western Guangdong to seek large timbers, taking full responsibility for every task upon his own shoulders.

In the first month of summer in the following year, Jǐyǒu (1609), the timber was fully transported to Mónglǐ. The Master returned to the mountain and convened the assembly to deliberate on selecting an auspicious day.

The construction work began. Since the obstructing monk’s quarters had to be moved first to the vacant lot to serve as a storage area for the dismantled materials, one or two unruly monks deemed this inconvenient and incited the crowd to clamor and riot as if they were in rebellion.
The Master thus suspended the work for three days. He sat in silence within his hermitage, reading the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and then said:
This was precisely my own fault for clinging to signs. I nevertheless completed the *Vajra-Resolution of Doubts* (Jingang jueyi jie) in three days, whereupon the crowd ceased their agitation.
The instigator grew anxious; having no other recourse, he falsely fabricated a report that the Master had embezzled several taels of gold from the temple and demolished several halls.

The Tathāgata Ratna was no different [from others]; he was no different from today even when the Great Master had not yet entered parinirvāṇa. That was his time.
Just as at Yongjia, upon seeing him once, he immediately realized the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); though they tried to detain him for one night, it could not be done.
Nan Yue and Qing Yuan both attended upon him for over ten years, attaining various kinds of samādhis and subtle gateways that were inconceivable.
Thus, he manifested the radiance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs like the clear sun rising in the sky; even now, his Way fills the world like the scorching sun of midsummer.
Among those who encounter it, there are none who do not sprout shoots, develop trunks, blossom with flowers, and bear fine fruit, which further disperse as countless seeds of the Vajra.
All of this is the merit of meeting a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) but once. —The Stupa of Caoxi.
The master’s attendants served him morning and evening with washing and rinsing, tea, soup, gruel, and meals, no different from his time in this life.
From the sounds of the bells and drums at dawn and dusk, the Master’s broad and long tongue was constantly engaged in preaching the Dharma without ceasing for even a moment.
Those who attended him witnessed this with their own eyes and heard it with their own ears day and night, never for a moment obscured. I wonder, among the various attendants, were there any who...
Is there one who has realized non-arising like Yongjia? Is there one who possesses a wondrous realization like those of Nanyue and Qingyuan?
If such exist, they appear all at once like the udumbara flower; if they do not, they remain forever unseen, just as the udumbara flower never appears.

Since it is said that a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) is like the udumbara flower, then all those who attend upon them, prostrating at the six times of the day and drawing near to offer worship, perform the work of irrigation.

Alas! Once the spiritual root is present and the seeds of wisdom are deeply planted, if the labor of irrigation is perfected and the conditions of time arrive, why worry that the udumbara flower will not manifest all at once? The Elder is currently staying in a temporary lodging.
Within the hall, he wrote a letter and entrusted it to the Abbot of Caoxi, instructing him to preserve it as a testament for the future blossoming of the flower.

He showed this to the monks of Caoxi, explaining that Caoxi is the source of the Dharma-lineage of the Chan school throughout the world, and that its mountains and rivers are the most magnificent in all the regions south of the Ling Mountains. Thus...

This monastic community has been preeminent among all quarters since the passing of Master Mazu Daoyi. From the two great elders of Qingyuan and Nanyue, branches grew and trunks sprouted, providing universal shade for humans and devas.
Through a single word or half-phrase, or even within the blink of an eye or a flash of a brow, those who attained transcendence from birth and liberation from death were beyond counting.
Since then, this mountain has remained desolate for nearly a thousand years. Is this not indeed...?
Is it that one cuts down the branches while leaving the root intact? Although his Way is said to be formless, in reality it is manifested through form;
that it rises and falls with the times is indeed its inherent principle. If one seeks the source of the Five Houses from afar, their roots are not two.
The intent behind their establishment also lies in accordance with what is appropriate. From the Song dynasty to the Yuan, great masters such as Gao Feng, Duàn Yá, and Zhōng Fēng were all...
The power to uphold the family’s reputation and the mechanism of thunder and lightning have not diminished from the flourishing era of the Zen forests.

Since the rise of the Ming dynasty, this tradition has gradually declined. One cannot hope to find those who possess true practice and actual realization; even those who aspire toward the path above are exceedingly rare.
Yet, in other regions, there may still be one or two who know this Way. As for Caoxi, it remains the true home of the lineage.
These descendants of his lineage alone do not recognize what the *kāṣāya* robe is, nor for what purpose the shaving of the head is intended.
Is it not only that man has deviated from the Way? Even the excellence of the mountains and rivers, and the lushness of the monastic groves, no longer resemble those of former times.
How much more so when they are beset by evil demons and various calamities arise? Is this not because the Way rises and falls with the times, while the mountains and rivers remain as they were?
Do we share in each other's joys and sorrows? In the spring of the Bingshen year, I was graced by imperial favor with a dispatch to Leyang;

on my way, I passed through the mouth of Caoxi and was thus able to pay my respects to the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch. It happened that I arrived just as the monks were finishing their meal of boiled rice;

the cauldrons were still bubbling and the heat had not yet subsided. I stood there in tears for a long while before departing. In the autumn of the following year, the Grand Marshal and Provincial Governor, Lord Chen, [sent a message...]
He thought of the Caoxi Chan school as being like the Zhu-si [tradition] and wished to place me among them to serve as a caretaker.
At that time, I felt ashamed, considering myself a blemish upon the Dharma-gate, and declined out of fear of bringing disgrace to the ancestral temple.

The following year, Zhou Gong, the Governor of Haimen, assumed administrative control of Nan and Shao; his mind was in accord with that of Lord Chen. I continued to firmly decline, but he merely commanded me to take up the pen once again.

He compiled their aspirations. Duke Zhou departed after entering to offer his congratulations. Observing that [the new official] was alert and mindful, he prayed for the Duke to govern with integrity.
The Duke styled himself a "pilgrim-monk of Caoxi. Not many days after he took office, bandits were suppressed and litigation ceased; the people enjoyed great harmony.
At the mountain gate of Caoxi, all that had fallen into ruin was restored at once, as if the Great Mirror (Huineng) had once again grasped the corner of the *kāṣāya*. As for what occurred previously—
Even those monks whose consciousness failed to recognize [the truth] all had the radiance of their Buddha-nature brilliantly manifest.
Is this not what is meant by "sentient beings come to sow the seeds, and in that ground the fruit is subsequently produced"?

For a long time, you, Sir, have desired to serve as an attendant to Dajian (Huineng), hoping to offset the transgression of destroying the Dharma through the labor of burning incense and washing the alms bowl. I felt ashamed for a long while. You, Sir, having entered—
As he was about to depart, I had the elder monks of the temple lead the assembly in paying their respects.
