The Master first sent a letter, and then met with me face-to-face to offer repeated and earnest exhortations. I am moved by this journey of his; he does not regard it as a matter of official duty, but rejoices in becoming the master of Caoxi.
This is him manifesting the body of a lay official at the gateway of illusory transformation to perform the work of a Buddha.
It is surely because the Way of the world is flourishing together that these mountain colors and stream sounds can manifest the Dharma-body and emit the mark of the broad and long tongue.
This humble body, burdened by sin and defilement, does not dare to tread upon the jeweled flowers or beat the poisonous drum;
I have merely written this to entrust it to future monks, serving as a cause and condition for their attainment of liberation and for their entry into the Hall on a future day.
The Deed of the Hall. On the full moon of the third month in the year of Gengzi, [I entrusted this] to the two superintendents, Sulim Yoo and Mokam Tae of Caoxi.
In the spring of the year Bingshen, I crossed the ridge and passed through Caoxi to pay homage to the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch; gazing upon his sacred remains, they appeared as if alive.

I imagined that at that time, he must have been seated upon a flower throne, surrounded by ten thousand fingers [of disciples] no differently than now. Yet today, the halls and buildings are dilapidated and the groves are withered;
this auspicious site of the Jewel Forest has been turned into a den for foxes and hares. After lingering there for a long while, I departed. Not long after, [the following occurred].

External demons flared up and the monastic community encountered calamity. Out of compassion for them, I sought out the local officials and government functionaries to serve as great protectors of the Dharma.
Governor Chen Gong and Lord Zhou of the Salt and Monopoly Commission both exerted great effort to revitalize the situation;

thus, the demonic winds subsided slightly, yet the strength of the monks was already utterly exhausted. At that time, there were among the temple’s monks those such as Sulin Yu, Muan Tai, and Haiyue Shan.

I observe that several individuals, including Xiang Hanquan—who served as the abbot during the Zhongxing era—have all vowed to sacrifice their lives and bodies to uphold the ancestral legacy and ensure the safety of the monastic community.

Day and night they toil with diligence, laboring with a devoted heart and comprehensive concern to seek those capable of providing even a single day’s refuge to the ancestral temple; their resolve is most earnest. Consequently, the assembly has...
Sincerely taking refuge and receiving the precepts, he immediately invited me to enter the mountains. Out of deference to this sacred kindness, I did not dare to give a light refusal;
yet, though my body had not yet entered, my mind was already as firm as a vajra. In the Jihai year of the Wanli era, Observation Commissioner Zhu of Nanxun and Shaoguan...

Taking it as his own responsibility to uphold Caoxi, he exerted all his efforts to personally invite [the Master] to come. In the winter of the Gengzi year, he finally accepted the invitation and entered the mountain.
Within three months, all neglected affairs were restored; he eliminated long-standing pests, selected the monastic community, established a school for doctrinal study, and conferred the precepts.
In a single moment, the transformation was complete. He then re-established the monastery’s scale and greatly opened the Way of the Patriarchs. Before five years had passed—
That the work has reached completion with more than half accomplished is truly due to the silent inspiration of our ancestral spirits and the hidden protection of the devas and nāgas.
Yet, the single-minded sincerity of those such as Yu—his true heart and genuine practice—is no less than the weeping of Wei Baoxu before the court of Qin;
what is thus invoked cannot be denied. I have resided here for over five years, yet I have spent more than half of that time in constant travel, all for the sake of managing these affairs.
The labor of this task has been such that you all have served me as if for but a single day;
yet I regard you all as my own children. Recently, I was graced by an imperial edict of amnesty; though my body had not yet removed its robes, my mind was already liberated.
At that moment, the disciples were each filled with joy; they burned incense and prostrated themselves, holding scrolls and requesting words. Thereupon, I took up my brush and showed it to them.

It is said: "The minds of all Buddhas and sentient beings are without distinction. This so-called non-discriminating mind is precisely what is called the adamantine ground of the mind (*vajra-citta-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, this single mind is realized by all Buddhas and they preach the Dharma; it is awakened to by the Patriarchs and they deliver sentient beings;
it is cultivated by Bodhisattvas and they attain the Way; it is grasped by Śrāvakas as *nirvāṇa*; and it is clung to by non-Buddhists."
Yet they slander the Dharma. Sentient beings are deluded by it and thereby create karma; those in the three miserable realms are obscured by it and thereby undergo suffering.
Ordinary people use it daily without knowing it; we humans respond to conditions through it.

You who are disciples of the Buddha and descendants of the Patriarchs—whatever actions you undertake, there are none that do not flow forth from this very mind. Simply follow the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
To engage in the work of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one must remain ever-present in mind and never allow even a single thought-moment to degenerate;
proceeding thus, it will remain uncorrupted through kalpas and become the adamantine ground of the heart, the primary causal seed for attaining Buddhahood and becoming a Patriarch.

Conversely, if one opposes or turns away from this, then even if one wears the *kāṣāya* robe, while the mind remains fixed on the path of karma, proceeding thus, one will surely fall into the realms of suffering.
It is the cause of suffering, and it is also that which does not destroy the fruit of birth-and-death for long kalpas.

Therefore it is said: "The dharmas of the upper and lower realms within the triple world are created solely by this one mind. To follow it is to be a sage; to turn away from it is to be an ordinary person.

How could this be empty talk? You and several others share this same mind; if we were to join with the thousands of people on the mountain, they too would share this same mind. If this mind is employed in this way...
Because it is directed toward the Buddhas and Patriarchs, it is like a vajra; thus, its future enjoyment will likewise be like a vajra.
However, if one employs it for a single body and schemes for oneself alone, regarding a mere patch of dung and soil as a place of joy, one’s enjoyment is like that of a miserable insect.
Though the mind works ceaselessly, in the blink of an eye, when a single breath does not return, one enters the three miserable realms—the bitter fruit [of such actions].
It is inexhaustible; moreover, through kalpa after kalpa and birth after birth, its enjoyment shall never be exhausted. This is because there is nothing else [to rely upon].
It is simply that one does not understand this mind, which is the true seed for becoming a Buddha or a Patriarch, and the field of merit.
Since receiving the precepts from me, Yù has vowed to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for as long as he lives. Furthermore, this sūtra is my Sixth Patriarch’s...
This is the Master’s own mind-ground. If you can maintain it without forgetting and internalize it within yourself, then for kalpas to come, its enjoyment will be inexhaustible.
With this very body and mind, you shall dwell eternally at Caoxi. Therefore it is said: "The Buddha-son dwells in this place; this is the Buddha’s enjoyment.
He constantly remains therein, walking, pacing, sitting, and reclining. You all clearly see this now.
On this day, the Elder has transformed Caoxi into a Pure Land and driven away the hosts of demons to become Dharma companions.
If you truly believe in the wondrous nature of this mind, then all of you shall transcend birth and death and realize Bodhi in less than a single thought-moment.
If it be otherwise, you will continue as before to wander through the three realms of suffering and drown in the sea of misery. Pay heed to this!
I, Zhirong, a śrāmaṇera, have come south by imperial grace.
The various Dharma protectors invited me to reside at Caoxi. Upon first entering the mountain, I made the cultivation of talent my foremost priority.
I therefore selected several śrāmaṇeras and invited eminent masters to instruct them, so that they might practice their fundamental studies and train in dignified deportment.

He established rites and recitations, and set up a meditation hall for the summer retreat (*an-shu*). He regulated the community with pure rules so that the assembly was as unified as a single finger.

However, due to the pull of karmic conditions, the Elder could not remain in retreat. At times he preached the Dharma for them, and subsequently invited a virtuous *ācārya* to preside over the community.
After several more years, the scale of the establishment was completed and the appearance of the mountain gate was transformed. The Elder once remarked that regarding the Buddha-dharma...

It is noble that you have heard [the teachings] and cultivated them into seeds. For a long time, the region south of the Ling Mountains has lacked the熏習 (xūnxi—perfuming/habituation) of the Buddha-dharma; because they lack these seeds, it is difficult for faith to arise.
I constantly pray that fifty-three monks of the teaching order shall each transcribe one copy of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

First, this is so that the vast conditions of the Dharma may serve as the most excellent seed. Second, it is so that the power of borrowing and transcribing the scriptures to sustain and uphold them may assist the initial [stage].
He practiced mental contemplation as an auxiliary to the provisions for entering the Way. Previously, he had been distracted by internal demons, and his vow remained unfulfilled.
Among those present was a śrāmaṇera named Zhirong, who was the first to resolve his mind on the matter, vowing to transcribe the Great Sūtra. The old man greatly admired his aspiration.
The initial transcription was not even half-finished, yet the śrāmaṇeras under the supervision of the Office of Learning simultaneously resolved their minds to transcribe it;
those who have now completed the work number seven. Alas! How can one limit or measure the spiritual capacities of human beings?

In the past, our Teacher Śākyamuni was once an ordinary person during a former kalpa, when he and a thousand companions heard the names of the fifty-three Buddhas and simultaneously resolved their minds to practice the Way.
Thereafter, each of them successively became one of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa. Because my teacher possessed such courageous power through his vows, he was foremost among the multitude;
furthermore, when he was one of the sixteen princes, he heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which served as the causal seed for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Thus, he attained Buddhahood in each of the eight directions. How much more so for the *Avataṃsaka*, which is the great scripture of the unimpeded dependent origination of the perfect and sudden Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of the One Vehicle!
It is thus: what is called "transcending the stages of the eight difficulties" is the realization of the fruit of vast kalpas in a single lifetime;

what is called "a single character encompassing the sutras of the Dharma-realm" is a single practice that gathers the boundless ocean. Furthermore, with every dot and every stroke, the light of the mind flows forth and great function manifests before one.
If the person is not deluded regarding this fruit, then there is no need for further investigation of karmic conditions; rather, through contemplative practice...
One is self-sufficient within the ocean of all dharma-gates; there is no need for the arduous journey through a hundred cities to sit and consult with spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Is this not the most supreme condition for the Dharma? If the sutras you have transcribed are fully present before you, and you read, recite, receive, and uphold them for the rest of your life, what need is there to seek the Buddha-dharma elsewhere?
This is precisely the flow of the Sixth Patriarch’s Dharma-transformation, encompassing the seventeen hundred spiritual teachers.
You may simultaneously and universally manifest the Samādhi of the Tip of a Hair. You should cultivate such contemplation.
Do not allow the dust of worldly habits and emotional attachments to obstruct the eye of wisdom. Exert yourself! Exert yourself!
To Supervisor Muan Ang of Caoxi:
Though the trees of Mount Denglin are numerous, those that have become fine timber are few; though the products of the vast ocean are many, those truly called treasures are rare.
Confucius said, "Talent is rare; is it not so? Even though our Buddha preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, he merely designated ten great disciples as being foremost in their respective fields.
Yet, among the hundreds of thousands of humans and devas who attained the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, only Kāśyapa was in accord with his mind.
Even those who have transmitted the Way through the ages and are called the "true bone-lineage descendants" are not easily found. I, [the Sixth Patriarch]...

The Great Master Zu preached the Dharma at Caoxi, with no fewer than a thousand monks beneath his seat. According to the *Platform Sutra*, there were forty-three individuals who attained realization of the Way;
yet those specifically renowned were only five or six. Those who extensively propagated the Way were exclusively the two great elders of Nanyue and Qingyuan.
Master Yue served the Patriarch with such diligent devotion that he never left his side day or night for more than...
In the nineteenth year [of his reign], he passed away together with Qingyuan during the lifetime of the Patriarch.

Thus, from the very beginning of the monastic communities, whenever a virtuous teacher (śāstr) ascended the hall to preach the Dharma, their primary concern was to find worthy disciples. They took the diligent devotion of these two elders as their family precept.
While such people are difficult to find, those who can serve as teachers and exemplars for a hundred generations are even more difficult to find. —The Elder.
At the outset of his crossing of the ridges, he passed through Caoxi and paid his respects to the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch.
He observed that the mountain gate was in ruins, nearly reduced to nothingness, and that the entire community was in a state of alarm, having no one to rely upon.

Therefore, wishing to establish a monastic center to provide stability for the great assembly and preserve the thread-like lineage of the Patriarchs, he selected from among a thousand monks those named Yu, Quan, Shi, Tai, and Shan.
Among these five men, those who wished for the Elder to be their refuge were like infants longing for a compassionate mother.
Their resolve to preserve the monastic groves was no less than that of Bao Xu in his effort to save the state of Chu, and their entreaty to me was no less than the wailing at the court of Qin.
Thereupon, the Elder, moved by their sincerity, came forth and took it upon himself to shoulder the task of restoration.

When they were held accountable, corruption and abuses were eliminated and all affairs were properly conducted. He selected monks from the assembly who were learned in the rites and the chanting of the Dharma;
among them, he chose three who were capable of serving as models for the novices and were worthy to be called "Teachers of Instruction. Having appointed them, they served for several years.

Examining the subtleties of their mental dispositions and the integrity of their conduct, one finds that their words and deeds correspond with one another; thus they enable later students to follow the path of former masters.
Among those who cherish the ancestral way and protect the monastic groves, there is but one person, the Supervisor Ang. Of these three individuals, who would not say they are peers?
Yet their inclinations and conduct are not uniform, and their aspirations and actions are not identical—like weights on a scale, some are heavy and others light.
He has been before my eyes and ears for no small number of days; he perceives right and wrong as clearly as one distinguishes black from white.

I have personally witnessed his conduct, following the method of Confucius for observing men, and I have scrutinized him for more than a few days. Therefore, when the various superintendents requested my words, I joyfully granted them at once.
Yet these three volumes alone I have kept hidden for five years, not daring to give my assent lightly—not out of stinginess, but because of the gravity of the matter.
This is the Dharma. For at the time of transmission between ancient masters and disciples, they did not grant permission recklessly;

had they uttered even a single careless word, they would have lost not only the person, but also the Eye of the Dharma. That it is difficult to know others has been a source of concern for the sages and wise ones. As it is said:

"The human heart is more treacherous than mountains and rivers, and more difficult to fathom than Heaven. Even Heaven has the orderly succession of the four seasons, yet as for humans, their sentiments are deep and their natures profound.
As for appearance: those who possess outward dignified decorum while harboring snakes and tigers within are not easily known. A saying goes: "A fierce wind reveals the sturdy grass;
in times of upheaval, one recognizes the loyal minister. If everyone could be called loyal and filial, then there would be no such thing as "loyal ministers" or "filial sons" in this world.

Indeed, such abundance is not what is remarkable. It is because they are rare that their difficulty is perceived; and because of this difficulty, it is not easy for those who would be loyal ministers or filial sons.
I have often remarked that although Xuan Meng claimed to have obtained worthy men, those who risked death to establish the orphan were none other than Cheng Ying and Chu Jiu.
Although the state of Chu was said to abound in talent, those who sacrificed their bodies to restore Chu were none other than...
First, there was Shen Baoxu. Alas! For us who are śramaṇa sons of the Śākya, our very bones, flesh, liver, and entrails have all been transformed by the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Our birth and death, our ascent and descent, are likewise turned by the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Yet, those who seek to achieve a single-mindedness like that of the ancient heroes are rare; for they cherish their own karmic bodies and thus create [delusions].
It is an instrument of suffering. Yet they do not spare their bodies or hesitate to sacrifice their lives, accepting it with a willing heart.

To seek someone who can, in a single thought, realize their error and be able to embody the legacy of the Patriarchs—such a person is difficult to find. Thus we know that as long as there are no thieves in the house, the family will not be destroyed.

If a state has no treacherous ministers, it shall not perish; if a person commits no evil deeds, their life shall not end in ruin; if a scholar does not undergo arduous practice, their fame shall not spread;
if there is no perversity in goodness, the Way will not reach its height; if the mind lacks firm endurance, the Way will not become great.
Thus we know that although good and evil differ, were one not to rely on a firm and indomitable resolve, one could not bring the reality of that good or evil to fruition. If one lacks this...

That the reality of good and evil and their corresponding retributions do not fail to coincide is not something to be taken for granted. As the saying goes: "Accumulate goodness and you achieve renown; accumulate evil and you bring about your own destruction.
Accumulate water and it becomes the sea; accumulate earth and it becomes a mountain. Knowing this, Master Ang need not worry that those who are evil will naturally accumulate [their own retribution];
rather, he should worry about whether he himself has accumulated the path of loyalty and integrity beneath his own person. —Confucius.
The Master said: "Do not worry that others do not know you; strive to become someone worthy of being known.

If the Sixth Patriarch knew you possessed this mind, he would simply urge you as the old man has urged you. What further method could there be? To provide one would fall into the obstacle of superfluous speech.
In the second month of the spring of the Bingshen year, I, Haiyue Shan, the administrative monk of Caoxi, visited Caoxi to pay my respects to the Great Master the Sixth Patriarch.

Seeing that the incense burners were sparse and the monastic community was in decline, I lingered there for a long time. A monk, assuming a dignified demeanor, came forward to prostrate and questioned me.
[The Master] replied: "I have received your message with great respect. Observing his sincerity and upright integrity, I was pleased and said to him, 'This is truly a monk of the original character.
In the following year, the year of Dingyou, demonic winds arose in competition, and this place of practice nearly fell into ruin.

With the monks having no refuge, Master Shan and several of his peers came to Wuyang to visit me and requested that I confer the precepts upon them. It was then that I first learned [of these events]."

The one who had previously paid his respects was Master Shan. In the winter of the Gengzi year, when I accepted an invitation to enter the mountains, the Master led his disciples to attend upon the ancestral master’s stupa.
Observing the sincerity of their offerings, they were no different from the time when the ancestral master was still alive.
I sighed and said: "That the ancestral temple remains undecayed for a thousand years depends solely upon the descendants' single heart of filial piety.
Thus the World-Honored One said, 'Filial piety is called the precept. This is precisely what Confucianism calls 'filial piety as the root of benevolence'; it is the very foundation of this Way."
Furthermore, during the initial retreat (*varṣā*) while residing in the mountains, whatever tasks were undertaken were carried out with the collective resolve of the assembly;

yet, it was Master Shan who most frequently bore the burden of toil and resentment. His anxiety, diligence, and self-motivation, as well as his circumspection and reverence, were as upright as those of a filial son toward a compassionate father.
There was no matter—whether sorrow or joy, illness or pain—that did not concern him. Thus we know that his heart in serving the Patriarch was no different from his service to [his own kin].
Therefore, I have entrusted this to the permanent endowment. With a mind equal to that of the assembly, we have united our strength and forgotten ourselves to sacrifice for the Way.

That the monasteries are now restored and the Dharma teachings are flourishing once more is surely due to the silent inspiration of the Patriarchs' spirits; it is truly the result of the filial sincerity of Shan and the others moving the divine response.
As the saying goes: "If there were not the right person, the Way would not manifest in vain. I often reflect that I am not one whom the Master could have taken under his care.
I have received [your invitation], yet I cannot go to Caoxi. It is not that Caoxi did not come to me; it is simply that without me, there could be no "today.
This is not merely a matter of your filial piety and respect, for without them, my heart would have no way to be bound here.

Furthermore, the merit of reviving the monastic community cannot reach its ultimate fulfillment or maintain its integrity from beginning to end without pure sincerity. Altogether, this is a matter of great significance and destiny; it is truly no accident. I am fortunate indeed.
When the construction of the ancestral temple was completed, on the twentieth day of the eighth month of the Bingwu year, I was graciously granted an imperial edict permitting me to become a monk.
Judging by these events from beginning to end, it is evident that my coming here was not without cause;
nor were you all born into this world without cause to encounter such an occasion. I imagine that in days of yore, when the Way of the Patriarchs flourished...
At the time of my flourishing, there were over thirty disciples who had awakened to the Way; you all were merely those who performed the tasks of sweeping and attending upon me.

Otherwise, how could you have had the karmic affinity to see me and draw near? Long ago, when the World-Honored One was under the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, he preached the Lotus Sūtra for his disciples;
ultimately, until the appearance of Śākyamuni, they all emerged from one and the same assembly.
Each and every one shall receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.

Through the karmic conditions of the past and the realization of the present, how could there be even one person lacking in the future assembly under Maitreya at the Dragon Flower Tree? Therefore, maintain this resolve to illuminate the ancestral Way;
take it as your duty to protect the Triple Gem, cherishing the welfare of all such that even a single stalk, a single leaf, a drop of water, or a piece of firewood may be of benefit.
Within the forest of the sangha, those who possess the path of the Dharma are the very seeds of the vajra and the true cause for attaining Buddhahood.

They enable all beings to look up to them in reliance for eternal kalpas and serve as that upon which the ten directions depend; they are thus identical to the eternally abiding Dharmakāya of the Patriarchs. How can one not exert oneself?
I send this to show the venerable elder of Caoxi as he resides at the ancestral temple.

I have taken this opportunity to propagate the Great Matter of the Sixth Patriarch’s appearance in the world, desiring that all may cultivate the causes for transcendence and plant the conditions for the Pure Land. Unforeseen, however, circumstances have diverged midway.
The winds of Māra have brought about destruction, and the "lion-insects" have wrought havoc, causing me to fail in my original resolve.

Although I have once departed from the Patriarchs and abandoned the great assembly, even now, though I dwell on the shores of solitude, I have never for a single thought-moment forgotten my fundamental vow.
Subsequently, although his studies seemed to show a resolve directed toward the higher path, he lacked a wise teacher or virtuous friend to introduce him to the way of practice.
Among the assembly of elders, there was one who understood the old man’s heart and felt a poignant concern for the great matter of birth and death.
Furthermore, there is no elder upon whom we can rely for refuge, nor can we gather together in one place to perform Buddhist services in unison.
Alas, as the days and months flow like a stream, senility gradually encroaches and the time of death approaches.

On the road to the Yellow Springs, lacking the provisions for the journey, by what Dharma can we escape the retribution of suffering in the three miserable realms and the hells? When these words are spoken, they are truly tragic and painful. Ancient...
People say: "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. To practice with urgency is already late.
Because of this, the old man reflected deeply and repeatedly, yet found no one capable of making a definitive decision for the assembly.

Just as the Hall Master came to visit, he was exactly suited to the old man's heart. Therefore, he earnestly instructed him to return to the mountain and reveal the old man's intention to the community of elders.
Old [text]: "If we are truly to transcend birth and death, we must all assemble in one place to form a *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) society.
We shall collectively cultivate pure karma and together emerge from birth and death, vowing to deliver one another in succession.

If even one person among the community should first pass away, we shall provide mutual support to ensure their rebirth in the Pure Land. Would this not be the foremost and most supreme causal condition? This is precisely it."

These remaining years have already surpassed a hundred kalpas and a thousand lifetimes spent in vain. To accomplish the work of the Way, one must gather in a place that is most essential, pure, and undisturbed.
While the meditation hall is currently occupied by junior students reciting sutras, its activities seem somewhat distracting and complex.
Only the Wujin-an (Inexhaustible Hermitage), where the elders practice, is supremely tranquil; all things are spontaneously present there. It would be better to settle here.
To establish a Hall for Pure Practice (Jingye Tang) is to accomplish a most sublime undertaking;
it will not only ensure that the old man’s arduous efforts are not in vain, but will also serve as a recompense for the merit of the patrons. Regarding the regulations for cultivation and progress:

although the ancients practiced mindfulness of the Buddha during the six periods of the day and night with diligent devotion, such intensity may prove difficult for an elder to sustain. Therefore, one should take the four periods of the day as the standard.

Regarding the two daily periods of practice: at both times, one shall kneel and recite one fascicle of the "Chapter on Vows and Practices" (*Pranidhāna-pāramitā*), chant the Buddha’s name one thousand times, and make vows for the dedication of merit.
This shall be undertaken without limit as to time and without restriction as to the number of participants; however, one must select only those who are mature, possess firm faith, and are sincere.

Forgetting the distinction between host and guest, dissolving the sense of self and other, severing all notions of right and wrong, and refraining from frivolous discourse, one shall single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name. No visitors shall be admitted; one shall focus exclusively on this.
Serenity is paramount; this is the true forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) and the place for authentic practice.
If the great assembly can truly perceive the old man’s heart, believe his words with certainty, and practice according to the Dharma, it will be the moment of liberation from birth and death.
It will mean that you shall never be separated from the old man throughout all future lives, and you shall always be born as Buddhas.

Previously, when listening to the sound of the Dharma together, the person who organized the assembly and the location for the summer retreat were both managed by the Hall Master of the Listening Hall;
this was precisely the fulfillment of the Elder’s instructions regarding the diligent cultivation of the Way.
Furthermore, within this great assembly, each of you must exert yourselves. As the ancients said: "One cannot walk by holding another's hand;
only when one is personally willing can there be true intimacy. This means that if you simply possess the heart of willingness, you will certainly not be deceived. Cherish this and exert yourselves!
Sent to the disciples of the Caoxi Meditation Hall:
When the Elder first established [this hall] for the sake of the Patriarch, the assembly did not understand the Elder’s intention.

Today, after the Elder has passed away, regarding all matters concerning the welfare of the mountain gate as well as the establishment of the meditation hall, you all take delight in entering the hall.
The summer retreat (*an-gyo*). This reveals the bitter resolve of the old man. If you understand the heart of the old man, then you shall understand the heart of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
You must now reflect that it is impossible for the old man to provide further instructions as he did before.

Nevertheless, the conditions of gathering and dispersing are unavoidable even for the Buddhas and Patriarchs; it rests with you, his disciples, to recognize this kindness and repay it by following the teachings.
Regarding practice: although it is after the Buddha and the patriarchs have entered parinirvāṇa, it is no different from being in their presence and drawing near to them while they were in the world.
Therefore, when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, his great disciples asked him, "After the Buddha’s passing, what shall we take as our teacher?
The Buddha said, "You should respect the *prātimokṣa*; this is your great teacher. In the Sanskrit language, *prātimokṣa*—this...
It is said: "This is the precepts. The Buddha often said: "O bhikṣus, if you can observe my precepts, though you be a thousand li away, you are as if at my side.
If you do not uphold my precepts, even if we face one another, it is as if we were a thousand li apart.

These are the words of our Great Teacher, the Buddha, spoken from his own golden mouth; how could they not be followed? Moreover, in this age of the Final Dharma, the time since the Sage has passed is far removed. If a disciple of the Buddha...
Sons, if you do not uphold the Buddha’s precepts, what ground will you have for spiritual practice? Upon what can you rely to escape the bitter sea of birth and death?
As I depart, I have specifically preached the Brahmajāla Sūtra Precepts for you;
I do not know whether each of you is able to maintain them with firm resolve. The Buddha ordained that bhikṣus recite this sūtra of precepts every half-month, as if following the Buddha himself.
Listen closely to the ritual procedures for the *karmavācanā* and do not allow them to be violated. At every thought-moment, examine and observe your three karmas and six sense faculties;
do not permit transgressions to arise in secret, nor may you violate the root of the precepts. This itself constitutes true practice.
By progressing along this path while seated, there is no need to seek out distant enlightened masters, which would only increase your hardship. If you [proceed] in this manner...

If you have not yet been able to maintain [the precepts] firmly, you should from this time forth, according to the Dharma, every half-month, recite the *Brahmajāla Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Precepts*—its ten grave and forty-eight light rules—before the Buddha.
Each and every article of the precepts must be clearly and thoroughly memorized.

Should you violate even a single rule, then on the day of the recitation, you must invite a preceptor (*ācārya*) to serve as witness, and the assembly shall successively examine one another regarding such transgressions. Violation...
One must repent before the assembly and never permit such transgressions again. In this way, one may reform and renew oneself, and the work of the Path will be accomplished.
Regarding the offenses committed, in addition to repentance, the assembly shall deliberate and establish clear regulations and penal examples for compliance.
These may serve as the standard practice, following the revised articles left behind by the Elder in the past. The assembly shall study the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra.

Once you have reached maturity, you should commit to memory the Forty-two Sections Sutra, the Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teachings, the Śūraṃgama Sūtra, the Lotus Sutra, the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, and other such scriptures to serve as the seed of the Buddha.
As for the single matter of Chan practice, you should follow the instructions of the Sixth Patriarch to Huiming regarding the koan:
"When you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil, what is the original face of the person? Keep this deeply within your breast.
Investigate this from time to time. After a long while, there will naturally come a moment of realization.

Only in this way is it the great causal condition for continuing the life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. If you can follow these words, then I, an old man, am as if constantly dwelling at Caoxi;
you yourselves need not travel about on pilgrimage.

In the year of Gengzi, while serving as a novice at Caoxi, I was invited by the local authorities to manage the monastery there; I accepted. Upon my arrival, I found that nearly all affairs were in a state of ruin and could not be undertaken.
Reflecting on the way to govern, I considered that the cultivation of talent is like the nurturing of timber. Consequently, I selected several novices and established a school for them.
The students invited guest masters to instruct them in ritual decorum and to recite both internal and external scriptures.

Once they had gained some degree of faith and inclination, they were tonsured and established in the meditation hall to follow the pure regulations and receive the precepts. Day and night they performed prostrations and recitations;

at this time, the śrāmaṇeras first understood the vocation of renunciation, all of whom grew weary of plowing and digging and came to admire pure cultivation. I have labored with a devoted heart for ten years...
Over the years, he has become somewhat worthy of admiration, so [the master] eventually abandoned him. Now that he is old, he dwells in seclusion at Mount Nanyue.
The śrāmaṇeras who were previously transformed by his teachings did not deeply understand the old man before; now they reflect upon him with deep thought, even seeking to serve him for a single day.
"A single word of instruction is difficult to bestow. The novice [Name], though once a mere child, now among the assembly has finally realized he is but an old man;
that his heart’s desire to draw near to you could not be fulfilled, he has therefore prepared this written petition to seek your guidance from afar.

Upon hearing this, the Old Man was both moved with sorrow and filled with joy. In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, he feared that if he remained for too long, sentient beings of meager faith would become numerous."
With reverence and faith, he then ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, causing the multitude to look back upon him with longing;
thus, every person conceived the thought that such a meeting was difficult to encounter. Had the Elder remained at Caoqi for long, how could all these people have felt such yearning as they do today?
If a śrāmaṇera contemplates the Elder, it would be better to contemplate the Buddha or the Sixth Patriarch. If you contemplate the Buddha, you should...
When you come here, there will surely be a time when you see the Buddha; if you are able to see the Buddha, that is precisely the moment of transcending birth and death.
Reflect on the Sixth Patriarch: he was originally but a wood-seller. How did he come to receive the offerings of humans and devas today?
Consider further these offerings today: they stem from his casting aside the affection for his mother and fleeing to the assembly at Huangmei to carry stones.
The rice was pounded; it came from amidst toil and hardship. Reflect again on the Sixth Patriarch: at the third watch, he entered the abbot’s quarters of Huangmei and received the robe and bowl.

By what realization did he alone attain this among a multitude of five hundred? Furthermore, every person possesses a single bag of stinking skin; after three or five days of death, it becomes putrid and foul beyond use. Why is it that the Sixth Patriarch’s physical frame— *Note:
The text appears to be an excerpt from a Zen discourse (likely a *kanbun* commentary) discussing the nature of the body and the transmission of the Dharma. The final sentence is left incomplete.*
This physical body has remained as if alive for a thousand years. What kind of practice could have rendered it so firm and indestructible?
The śrāmaṇera contemplated this point minutely and one by one, yet his contemplation did not penetrate it.

He simply read the *Platform Sūtra* thoroughly and investigated its meaning deeply. He investigated again and again, but was unable to grasp it entirely. He then focused solely on the phrase: "Originally there is nothing at all..."
The phrase, "Where do things gather dust? remains stored within my breast. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
whether drinking tea or eating rice; carrying firewood or drawing water; or welcoming guests and attending to visitors—at all times, in every place, and at every turn, I maintain this inquiry.
I must see for myself right before me: "Originally there is not a single thing. What is this? How is it that they do not gather dust?
This is the scene of dust and ashes. If one can apply the mind in this way, it is called "investigating Zen" (chan).
If you investigate until you reach a state of self-confidence free from doubt, then you will truly see the countenance of the Sixth Patriarch; only then will you know the old man’s nostrils.
This is precisely the moment when a novice monk has truly left the household life and transcended birth and death. If you are unwilling to turn toward your own mind...
To seek one's fundamental nature through mere hardship is but empty contemplation; what benefit is there in this?
Hitherto, the śrāmaṇeras have known only to receive the elder’s personal instructions, merely practicing formal deportment, movement, stillness, and the recitation of texts.
From this day forward, I shall provide the śrāmaṇeras with such instruction as they have requested: to apply yourself with single-minded effort is alone the way.
This is the Elder’s sincere instruction. The Elder is old; this is his final teaching.
If you miss this day, then even if you were to travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions to visit wise teachers in the future, it would all merely be their own private business.
Be careful not to regard these words of an old man as mere empty talk.

This is an instruction on the emptiness of phenomena for the selection of a temple director by a disciple of the Buddha in the Dharma-ending age: to cultivate the four practices of ease, namely, rectifying one’s body, rectifying one’s speech, rectifying one’s mind, and great compassion.

One cultivates based on this compassionate mind; this constitutes sublime practice. Furthermore, regarding these four practices, the "sphere of action" (*caritra*) and the "sphere of proximity" (*upāsana*) serve as the initial foundation.

As for the sphere of action, it means that at every step one does not depart from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). As for the sphere of proximity, it means that in every thought-moment one does not depart from the Three Jewels.

I observe that among the bhikṣus of the Final Dharma, those who are able to practice in accordance with this [teaching] are few; indeed, they know only the service of the temple as being most intimate.
Because these śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya do not understand the essentials of spiritual cultivation, they allow their bodies and minds to drift aimlessly and fail to restrain the three karmas.

Consequently, they constantly commit transgressions and evils, so that their sinful karma deepens daily and it becomes difficult to escape from birth and death. Therefore, one must be able to seek out and consult wise teachers from afar.
Furthermore, it is not necessary for one to be able to follow [the Buddha] step by step or to draw near to him mind-to-mind;

rather, solely serving the Triple Gem and maintaining incense and lamps day and night is to not forget the Buddha. Ringing the bells and drums at dawn and dusk to assemble the community for chanting and recitation is to not forget the Dharma.
To remain in harmony with the great assembly and to attend to them throughout the six periods of the day is to never forget the Sangha.

To sit, lie down, or practice walking meditation without leaving the Buddha hall is for every step to be a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). If one can purify one's own mind, then even a single incense offering or a single flower becomes the true body of the Buddha;
raising a hand or bowing the head becomes a sublime practice. Thus, without moving from one's heels, one has visited all teachers.
Knowledge is surely the most supreme cause and condition. For peaceful and blissful practice, nothing surpasses this.
Let the practitioner exert themselves throughout their entire life; what need is there to seek the Buddha-dharma elsewhere?

Shishi [the Sixth Patriarch] told the landowner Caoxi Ji that the Sixth Patriarch’s residence at Baolin on Mount Caoxi could not accommodate a vast multitude. He therefore requested from the local resident Chen Yaxian a piece of land the size of a *kāṣāya* robe;
this encompassed the four borders of the entire Caoxi region, and the Zisun Estate situated behind the mountain was one corner of that *kāṣāya*.

Furthermore, the monastic dwellings once occupied half the temple grounds. After a long time, the monks increasingly forgot their origins; external insults gradually encroached, and powerful families began to consume the land.
Their mountain fields and farmlands mostly fell into the hands of the wealthy and influential, such that the monastic estate was ruined by eight or nine-tenths.

Once the "Dragon of the Ancestors" turned his back on them, they lost everything. Now, the local residents have already begun harvesting timber within the monastery's interior, and it will soon be seen that they are further encroaching upon it.
At Zhuyi, when the old man first arrived at Caoqi, he fully understood the underlying circumstances. He then said to the assembly, "The local land is the foundation of a monastic community.
Moreover, the cassock of our Patriarch remains as it was; the ancestral graves of Master Ya-xian still exist."

"Therefore, it is called our ancestors' fields. How could we allow them to be lost? He then assembled the community and appealed to the Provincial Governor (Zhi-fu) to order the local magistrate to clear up their ancestral lands and rectify their boundaries. The multitude were all bewildered and did not know what to do;
even those who did know were too intimidated to speak. Only Master Ji, having lived there in the past, pointed out everything clearly with his hands.

The haughty and powerful man’s spirit was thus broken. The elder then solicited funds to redeem the fields, mountains, and groves that had originally belonged to the temple, providing them entirely for the sustenance of the Baolin Chan Hall and to support the monks living behind the monastery who were intent on practicing the Way.
He intended thereby to redeem the thread-like pulse of the Sixth Patriarch’s lineage. Consequently, Master Ji was appointed as the head of the estate.
The Master assisted the Elder in restoring Caoxi, managing the monastery’s finances, grain, and all affairs with meticulous order.
If one can maintain this, then a thousand years will be as a single day. It has been nearly ten years since the Elder departed from Caoxi;

all the established regulations have fallen into disuse, with the sole exception of the Meditation Hall, which Master Āṅ continues to maintain as it was before. Furthermore, Layman Jizhuang maintains a pure and sincere heart, never forgetting his original resolve;
he regards the Elder as being right by his side and protects every inch of the monastery's property, down to the finest detail. All is as it was.
This is for the protection of one’s eyes. An old man like myself feels ashamed that I lack the karmic affinity to fully promote the ancestral Way.

Consequently, I reflect upon how in the past Huanglong displayed a look of unease; when the Head Seat asked him about it, he replied, "I have not yet found someone to serve as the *jian-shou* (storekeeper). Thus we know that the ancients were thus.
I have appointed one person to oversee the collection [of funds]. Having reflected deeply on this matter, I realize that the responsibility of the estate manager is no small task.
Since ancient times, all states have found it difficult to find worthy talent; the same is true for monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*).

At Caoxi, when the Elder resided there for ten years, he refined his monks through training until he could find only two people to serve as the head of the meditation hall and the estate manager. Furthermore, there were two others...

If there are three people who can act as his assistants and supporters, then virtue will not be solitary, affairs will be easy to carry out, and the ancestral master’s place of practice may be preserved without misfortune.
When the Hall Master came to visit the Elder on Mount Kuang, Master Ji inquired after him and sent this scroll to request instruction.
What more need be said by the Elder? Truly, since our Buddha appeared in the world, there has been nothing [that was not for the sake of others].
These are two distinct matters; they concern nothing other than the two tasks of protective mindfulness (*anuparigraha*) and entrustment (*parindana*).

As for protective mindfulness, it is because one desires to find a person to continue the life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*). As for entrustment, it is because there is something to be handed over as the family legacy of the Buddha, just as a householder entrusts his family estate to his son.
Thus, the various patriarchs of successive generations have all followed the Buddha’s intent, their resolve being fixed upon wisdom.
It is simply that the mandate must not be severed. Now, the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is entrusted to the single stream of Caoxi.

Caoxi’s primary concern lies in obtaining capable men; obtaining such men depends upon their being provided for; this provision depends upon the four requisites; and these four requisites depend upon those who provide them.

If those who hold office are worthy individuals, then the multitude will have a place of refuge, the Way can be realized, and the monastic communities can be revitalized. Thus, the Dharma-way may flourish;
when the Dharma-way flourishes for the benefit of all, the wisdom-life of the Buddhas and Patriarchs will continue in succession without interruption throughout the eternal future.
This truly depends upon this very day. To be able to protect this wisdom-life is itself a profound repayment of the Buddha’s kindness. Such as this is what is called...
Truly, you are a son of the Buddha! Master Ji may indeed be said to have been able to repay the kindness and virtue of the Patriarchs.

From this day forward, you should contemplate the Sixth Patriarch even more deeply. Regarding the public case of Master Huiming at the head of Mount Dayu, keep it within your breast and apply yourself with renewed doubt.
Doubt after doubt, until you reach the point where doubt can no longer persist; then, suddenly, the mass of doubt will burst asunder, revealing—
The original face—this alone may be called being a true bone-and-flesh descendant of the Sixth Patriarch.
Compared to those who merely protect their ancestral fields, this may be described as taking one step further atop a hundred-foot pole. This koan is the very life-vein of the Sixth Patriarch;
if there is even a single person who penetrates it thoroughly, then the Sixth Patriarch dwells eternally in the world and has not entered parinirvāṇa.
Indeed, these are ancient relics that have lain dormant for a thousand years. I, an old man, have now brought them forth once more.
If their value is enhanced through this encounter with you, they shall thereafter constantly radiate light, illuminating heaven and earth.
You must stake your very life and body upon this, firming your resolve so that you do not succumb to even a single moment of indolence. Strive toward this!
The Dream-Travel Collection of the Elder Hanshan, Volume Fifty-one and Volume Fifty-two.
Compiled by the Attendant Fushan and the Disciple Tongjiong. Daily Records.
Haichang, Fayi, Jinzhao, and Jinguang have preserved and displayed [these records].
Regarding the Baolin Monastery of Caoxi, Master Ang, the Hall Director,

noted that although Lingnan had been connected to China since the Han dynasty, it was only during the early Tang period— after more than six hundred years— that it first became known for its cultural achievements.
The Sixth Patriarch arose from Xinzhou and received the robe and bowl of Huangmei, transmitting the Way of the Direct Pointing that came from the West.
At that time, people first came to know the existence of the Buddha-dharma. He opened the BaoLin Monastery at Caoxi as a site for the Way and preached the Dharma therein.
From then on, his Way shaded the entire universe, and all the Chan schools under heaven took this as their beginning. How magnificent it was! After the Sixth Patriarch passed away, his [flesh...]

Although the physical body [of the teaching] remained, the Dharma center gradually declined. By the time the Song dynasty had lasted over three hundred years, the monastic communities were in a state of extreme ruin.
At that time, there was Zen Master Zichao, who rose up and greatly revitalized it; from this, his Way was restored once more.
As for those recorded in the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), such individuals have not been seen much since the time of the Sixth Patriarch.
Thus, although the Way and its Dharma have spread throughout the ten directions, those who devote themselves to the fundamental ground are few.

Without a master to provide guidance and transformation at the monasteries, the monks have taken up worldly occupations and have utterly forgotten their original purpose; this is indeed only natural. From the Song dynasty down to...
In the Wanli era of our dynasty, another five hundred years will have passed. The ruin of this place of practice will be even more severe than during the Song;
the monks will have no leisure to dwell there, and the Dharma caves will all become the lairs of foxes and rabbits. In the year of Bingshen, the old man arrived outside the passes.
I was able to pay my respects at the ancestral temple and, beholding its dilapidated state, departed with great heartache.
Five years later, in the year Gengzi, all the Dharma protectors, taking the path of the Dharma to heart, urgently desired for the Elder to go and rescue it from its decay.
Upon arriving, he made a vow to sacrifice his body and life, resolving to be a loyal minister and filial son to the Sixth Patriarch. At once, everything was renewed. Hundreds...
The discarded was abolished and all was restored; this relied upon the spiritual protection of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and was not the work of human effort alone.

At that time, there were nearly a thousand monks in the assembly, yet those who feared the instability of the monastic community numbered only a few. As for those who sought to ensure the ancestral Way would not decline, they were even fewer still.
Later students lack the eye [of wisdom]. As for those who could not firmly uphold the banner of the Dharma, you alone were lofty.
As for one who understood the old man’s resolve to restore [the tradition] and his heart sworn to die for it, you alone were such a person. Alas!
This shows how difficult it is for the Dharma gate to find a true successor. At that time, when the old man first entered Caoxi, he selected various monks whom he might instruct.
I instructed him. When I searched among the assembly for one of like character, there was none but you alone.
During the eight years that the Elder resided here, regarding all the plans he devised for the long-term welfare of the mountain gate, the assembly remained utterly bewildered;

yet, as for those matters concerning which he applied his mind, leaving nothing out, whether great or small, there was none but you alone. Furthermore, when the "lion-insect" (a corrupt monk) destroyed the Dharma and the faction of Mara vied with one another in their machinations...
Furthermore, several of those previously mentioned as being at the site of the *dōjō* were likewise caught in the net, leaving them no leisure to seek their release.

Among those who sought to protect the forest with diligent effort, who grieved over the collapse of the ancestral Way, and who deeply understood the kindness of the Elder’s establishment, there was only you alone.
At that time, had it not been for you acting as a stabilizing pillar in the midst of the chaos—
[If I had not] flowed [here] and protected you with meticulous care, Caoxi would certainly not exist today.
When I, the old man, abandoned it and departed, the meditation hall was without a master and nearly devoured by "lion-insects" (corrupters).

Had you not stepped forward to support it, not only would the site of practice have been destroyed and later students left without refuge, but the old man’s lifelong, painstaking efforts toward its restoration would ultimately have been cast away like flowing water.
How can one hope for the Way of the Patriarchs to be revived once more? For this reason, it has been ten years since the Elder departed from Caoxi.
These days, you have tirelessly and sorrowfully contemplated the Elder’s return, hoping for a renewal of the Dharma-way;
every thought is imbued with grief, never for a single moment forgetting him. When the Elder went to Nanyue, you followed him there; subsequently, the Elder—
I, Ren Yi, grew old at Kuangshan. My son Xun has come from afar;

seeing that his heart of gratitude grows ever more sincere and his anxiety for the Way deepens day by day, he both hopes for the elder’s return and looks forward to the arrival of a Perfected Being (*zhiren*).
His sincerity is truly difficult to describe in words—it is like that of the loyal ministers and filial sons of antiquity who worried for their country and family, or the noble women of integrity.
"A wife who vows to die rather than harbor a second heart is not in error. Just now in the mountains, the old man detained you for a long time;
your heart of deep sorrow led you to request further instruction more than once. The old man therefore showed you this, saying: 'Your resolve is indeed admirable, yet your thinking has gone too far.
You have not yet heard that the Great Way does not perish; even Buddhas and patriarchs [are no exception to this]...'"
It is difficult to escape the conditions of time and circumstance; the convergence of these causes and conditions is certainly not brought about by human effort alone.
Furthermore, consider how one’s fortunes rise and fall in accordance with the times—it is truly impossible to force such things, and even such individuals as those are not easily found.
Observe closely that since the Sixth Patriarch entered nirvana, a thousand years have passed; his Way has spread throughout the world, flourishing in every monastery.

Those who have transformed a region are not few; yet, when seeking one who has taken the ancestral temple as his cause and managed its internal regulations according to the family dharma, there was only Song Zichao.
Five hundred years after Zichao, those who were determined to serve the Way of the Patriarch and strove to rectify the collapsing order were only this old man.
Moreover, within the thousands of people at Caoxi, if one seeks those who grieve for the Patriarch...
The Way. You alone, O elder, are one who knows this. Such a person among those of the Dharma gate—one who cherishes this truth—is surely not easily found.
Now, the Elder has shown you the most supreme Dharma gate: namely, that "seeking others is not as good as seeking oneself.
Furthermore, before the Sixth Patriarch appeared in the world, he was merely a wood-seller. It was because of his long-accumulated merit...

The spiritual root had been nurtured through long-term cultivation; upon hearing a single phrase from the sutra, he suddenly awakened to his own mind and thereby obtained the robe and bowl of Huangmei.
Is this not the very Bodhimanda of Baolin today, which was once the load of firewood on the Sixth Patriarch’s shoulder?
He came from the side of the waist-stone used for pounding rice; thus there is such vast and great radiance, pervading heaven and earth.
Every word and every phrase of the Chan school flows forth from the side of the waist-stone on the firewood shoulder-pole.

To this day, the offerings of incense and lamps are no different than when he was alive. His physical body is firm and indestructible, no different than if he were currently preaching the Dharma. As it is said:
This blessing also came from the side of the firewood shoulder-pole and the waist-stone; how could it have been obtained by having a mind to seek it from others?
Since you already possess such resolve and are concerned for the ancestral Way, why must you seek someone else to respond to it? He is already a man of stature.
I am the same. As for that segment of Prajñā-light realized by the Sixth Patriarch, everyone possesses it; not even a hair’s breadth is lacking.
Now, you should only worry about your own mind not being awakened; there is no need to worry about the failure of a monastery to flourish.

If one can fully awaken to one's own mind, then one can churn the long river into cream and butter, transform the great earth into gold, take up a single blade of grass and make it a sixteen-foot golden body, and treat that sixteen-foot golden body as a single blade of grass.
One will naturally possess great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), transforming things according to the mind and acting as one pleases, with nothing being impossible. Thus it is within me.
Everything is already complete. Why do you labor under such delusion, hoping that others will come to manage the affairs of your household?

In ancient times, when people sought to awaken to their own minds, this was prior to the Sixth Patriarch; everyone attained awakening through a single word in the moment, with no talk of "applying effort.
After the Sixth Patriarch received the robe and bowl from Huangmei, he gave his instruction to Huiming at the head of Dayu Ridge, saying: [The text continues with the teaching].
"Humanity is one: this is the public case (gong'an). Hereafter, it is simply a matter of applying effort; this is the manner of practicing Chan.
From now on into the future, I instruct you to cast away all at once that former habit of worrying about being too tall or too short, and that mind of looking toward others."
Simply set aside body and mind; stake your very life upon it. With this single thought-moment alone, seek only to awaken to the nature of your own mind.
Take the koan "Hui Ming" and hold it across your chest; deepen your state of doubt.

Throughout the six periods of day and night—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whether welcoming guests, attending to others, or engaging with affairs; whether amidst tea or rice—grasp it.
Lift the spoon and pick up the chopsticks; do not let anything pass unexamined. Whether doubt arises or subsides, you must resolutely see your own original face.
Alternatively, take up the "head-word" (huitou) of "Buddha-recitation," asking: "Ultimately, who is it that recites the Buddha's name? You must see this one.

When such doubt reaches the point where it resembles a silver mountain or an iron wall, and at the very place where one cannot doubt, the life-root suddenly snaps and the mass of doubt bursts asunder.
One’s own original face manifests immediately before one;
at that moment, one finally knows that the person who recites the Buddha’s name is like seeing one’s own father at a crossroads—there is no need to ask anyone else. As the ancients said: "Good..."
For those who cultivate the Way, the work may take a thousand days, or perhaps ten or five years, or two or three decades;
or they may fail to attain realization throughout their entire lifetime. Such a person may vow to emerge again in a future life, or even after two, three, or as many as ten or more lifetimes.
For one whose original vow remains unclouded, though the duration of birth and death is long, within the Constantly Quiescent Light there is ultimately no coming or going.
Consider this: your years and strength are still robust. If you can truly resolve your will and begin from this very day, then whether it takes ten or twenty years, you may attain enlightenment;
even in this life, my original vow shall be fulfilled. Even if you do not realize it now, by virtue of this practice of investigation, the seeds of *prajñā* remain;
should they sprout again, they will still serve as a living resource for the present. Even if it is far off...
In no more than four or five decades, with a single somersault, it will be as if it were right before one's eyes.

At that time, to settle the affairs of one’s own house—what difficulty could there be? To neglect this and not worry about it, while worrying instead about other matters, is entirely a waste of mental effort.
"Deluded conceptualization is of no benefit. Not only is it of no benefit, but it further increases the boundless ocean of suffering in birth and death.
Is this not the height of great folly? This statement by the Elder is like striking the head of a stone man with a staff; such is the way to practice."
Thus, the Old Man is constantly present within your eyebrows and eyes, emitting light and shaking the earth.
He has established the Dan-guo-liao (Guest House) at Caoxi as a *rong-tang* (hostel) for the monastic community,
serving as a lodging station for wandering monks from all directions who travel ten thousand miles on pilgrimage.
Trudging through mountains, braving wind and rain, treading upon snow and ice, and enduring the hardships of hunger and cold, one wanders alone along the long road with no knowledge of where to stop.
Thus, one looks toward a grove of trees to seek a night’s rest, like a destitute child longing for his parents’ home.
Even if one should reach such a place, if the host is not the right person and remains indifferent—

Pay heed! If those who are hungry are not given food, those who are thirsty are not given drink, those who are weary are not given rest, and those who are ill are not given peace, then how shall their hearts of sorrow and suffering find anyone to whom they may appeal?
From antiquity, the establishment of monasteries to receive guests from the ten directions has been deeply rooted in this insight. In every direction and along every path, there are...
Step back. There may be neighboring peaks or nearby markets where one might not find a proper place and must seek it elsewhere;

however, as for the Caoxi Monastery in Lingnan, where the living body of the Sixth Patriarch remains present, it is a destination that monastics from across the realm must inevitably travel to pay their respects.
They will journey several thousand li, crossing the mountain ranges alone and solely for this purpose—how much more so when one must brave...
This is a land of miasma and pestilence, a place from which nine out of ten travelers perish. Having arrived with feet blistered like cocoons, how could there not be provisions for their reception?
Before the Elder reached Caoxi, he heard that those who came as *śramaṇas* had no place to dwell or rest their shoulders;
even when they sought a single drink or a single meal, it was impossible to obtain. Consequently, they all turned back immediately, leaving their alms-bowls behind.
The monks’ quarters were all closed with their doors shut and would not admit him; he was thus able to obtain only a few *sheng* and *he* of rice, yet there was no means for cooking or boiling it.

He gathered firewood by the stream and sometimes obtained a single meal before departing. The old man grew concerned about this and went to the butcher shops and wine stalls, clearing them away to establish a reception hall for monks from the ten directions.
He built a separate kitchen to facilitate their meals, and everything required was supplied from there.

The inner hall must be made fully sufficient so that those who are hungry may eat, those who are thirsty may drink, the weary may rest, the sick may receive medical care, and the unclean may be washed.
Let them remain for as long as they wish and come and go as they please; thus, the sea of karma becomes a land of bliss.
However, it is not easy to find even one person to serve as its master. Furthermore, there are those who, by means of this very [establishment], create a hell for themselves. Compared to this...
This is a comparison. There may be "lion-worms" gathering here to create demonic disturbances; those who lack the power to subdue them are for the most part not at peace.

Recently, Master Ang arrived and said that he has recently obtained Master Rong as the Hall Master of the Guest Quarters (*danguo tang*). Everything is proceeding as it should, fully meeting the intent behind its establishment.
It has been three years, yet it feels as though it were but a single day. Hearing this, the Old Man was delighted and said, "This old man..."

This is the result of the power of human aspiration. One should constantly contemplate the practices of the Bodhisattvas, taking the consolation and comfort of sentient beings as the fundamental principle.
One should regard all sentient beings such that those who are older are like fathers and those who are younger are like brothers, serving them all with a heart of filial piety and obedience.
How much more so for those within the Dharma-gate, who share the bond of a single essence—a relationship beyond comparison with anything else. If one can indeed...
To serve them with reverence through a heart of filial piety and obedience is to take the Buddha-mind as one's own mind.

The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* is the Dharma-gate of the Buddha’s own mental ground; it begins by declaring that "filial piety is named the precept," which refers to being filially obedient toward the Three Jewels.

Be filial and obedient toward your teachers and monks; be filial and obedient toward the Dharma of the Ultimate Way. If you can receive these precepts, you will immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.
Thus, filial obedience is the root of the precepts, and the precepts are the root of attaining Buddhahood. To be able to practice this conduct is to establish the foundation for becoming a Buddha;
there is no need to seek the Buddha-Dharma elsewhere. The Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "The Bodhisattva practices giving..."

To sentient beings, whether it be their heads, eyes, body, flesh, hands, or feet, whenever there is one who comes to beg, they give it away accordingly and depart. Furthermore, they rejoice within themselves, saying:
"Those who come to beg are all my spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).

They are friends for whom I have not even requested [teachings], yet they are able to bring about immeasurable merit and cause my resolve for bodhi to become firm. Viewed from this perspective, those who now come from the ten directions...

These are all friends whom I have not invited myself. If Master Rong can, with a heart of filial piety and obedience, reverently make offerings so as to fulfill the categories of the Vajra-precepts and thereby establish the seeds for attaining Buddhahood—then this single practice will fully encompass all practices.
What, then, is there in the profound and wondrous Buddha-dharma apart from this? If Master Rong can truly believe this old man, from now on... [he shall] deeply [trust].

To exhaust one's body and life in making offerings to the ten directions with firm resolve and without retreat is equivalent to a bodhisattva giving away their head, eyes, hands, and feet to sentient beings;
there is no difference between them. In seeking the wondrous path of the Buddha, what could possibly surpass this?
If you are still not convinced, take the Sixth Patriarch’s single phrase, "Originally there is nothing," and hold it firmly within your breast. After a long time, [the truth will manifest].
Once you have recognized your own original face, at that moment you will have threaded the nostrils of the Sixth Patriarch all through as one.
Then, you will see that picking up a single blade of grass is itself the establishing of a Buddhist monastery.

Fearing only that the wandering monks from the ten directions might not arrive early enough, how could there be any weariness or exhaustion? Alas, I am old; I regret that I can no longer serve as the Sixth Patriarch.
The Patriarch acted as the master to his servant; you, sir, are able to embody this principle, which is precisely to act on behalf of the old man by constantly turning such a wheel of Dharma.
To the novice Da-yi of Caoxi:
An old man has retired to Mount Kuang. Master Ang, the Hall Master of Baolin Temple, brought the novice Da-yi here from afar to seek instruction.

They paid their respects. The elder then showed them [the remains] and said, "You should reflect upon what cultivation and what merit you have performed to be born in this remote land and become descendants of the Sixth Patriarch, able to draw near to the physical body of the Patriarch morning and evening, no different from his manifesting in person to preach the Dharma."
How utterly foolish you are! You are like one born blind who does not know that the sunlight is shining upon you.
For what reason and by what merit have you encountered this old man, who used a golden probe to scrape away the cataracts and open your blindness?

Only now do you see the sky and the sun, yet you still do not realize that it is the sunlight shining upon you. You all should reflect that before the Sixth Patriarch arrived at Huangmei, there were only the new...

This man from the prefecture was but a wood-seller; yet upon hearing the single phrase from the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, "one should abide nowhere," he suddenly severed the roots of birth and death accumulated over kalpas.
How could this have come about through mere study or training? It was truly due to the seed of the Buddha-nature.

Every person is fully endowed [with the Buddha-nature], yet it has not encountered the conditions for its manifestation; it is like a seed in the earth that has not yet received the nourishment of rain and dew.
I, an old man, have consistently pointed this out directly to you. All manner of skillful means are the work of providing rain.

However, because the roots of your afflictions are deep, it is difficult for the sprouts of the seeds of wisdom to grow. That you have come from afar today to request further instruction is still due to the moisture provided in the past.

This is indeed meritorious. From now on, you must cause the seeds of wisdom to sprout; take the single phrase "non-abiding" realized by the Sixth Patriarch as your point of convergence for inquiry and investigation.

When your mind suddenly attains illumination, at that moment you will not only have brought an end to birth and death throughout kalpas, but the nostrils of the Sixth Patriarch himself will be entirely in the hands of all of you.
Whether he is held fast or let go, it depends solely upon yourselves. It is like this:
This is no different from personally attending the Sixth Patriarch as he preached the Dharma; why wait for an old man to further entangle himself in complications and exhaust his compassionate heart?
Although the Old Man is not at Caoxi, you should simply take this one public case (gong'an) of our own house and explain it to your fellow practitioners, the novice monks.
Everyone must practice their cultivation in this manner; it must not be otherwise.
Relinquish it all at once. This is precisely how an old man dwells permanently on this mountain, preaching the Dharma for you all from time to time.
This matter is no mere child’s play; it requires a single-minded resolve of total death. You must apply yourself with a lethal blow, risking your very life-roots.

If you are like those who trade three in the morning for four in the evening, or who are cold in one moment and harsh in ten, not only will the seeds of wisdom fail to grow, but they will never sprout at all.
Furthermore, I fear you might become a withered sprout or a rotten seed. It is thus: not only would you fail the old man, but you would truly fail yourself.
You must by no means let time pass in vain; for when the great limit arrives, once the human body is lost, it will be difficult to recover for ten thousand kalpas.
You should reflect deeply and exert yourself; do not be negligent.

It was shown that it was only with the novice of Caoxi that the Dharma of the direct pointing, transmitted solely from West, was realized. The robe and bowl were passed down six times to Caoxi, and the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye spread throughout China for over a thousand years;
all say this is the single lineage of Caoxi, like the Zhurong stream among the disciples of Confucius.
Si. Indeed, the Dharma gate involved here is no trivial matter. When I formerly resided by the Eastern Sea, I often lamented that the Chan school was in decline;
surely its source must be obstructed. I once discussed with Master Daguan my desire to go there and dredge it, planning to meet at Mount Kuanglu.
Not long after, I encountered difficulties while propagating the Dharma. Since I had not been able to fulfill our plan, Master Daguan went there alone first. Upon arriving—
At that mountain, I saw that the monks there were all like commoners from the countryside. We stayed beneath the eaves for two nights before returning.

Not long after, I encountered misfortune due to my propagation of the Dharma and was banished to the regions beyond the ridges by imperial decree; at that time, I considered it to have been encompassed by the spiritual power of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The Master waited for me on the river and said to me, "I have already explored Caoxi. This was the sixth [chapter].
The Patriarch was reborn, yet he could not restore [the tradition] once more. I said, "It depends entirely upon the strength of one's vow.

When I crossed the mountain pass and resided there for five years, in the year Gengzi, those in authority—whose hearts were set on protecting the Dharma at Caoxi—exerted great effort to invite me to go.
Upon my arrival, I began with the Patriarch’s Hall and proceeded to the various triple gates; all neglected matters were restored simultaneously. As for the monks, regardless of their seniority...

These śrāmaṇeras were for the most part young woodcutters and cowherds; they established a separate meditation hall and formulated its pure regulations, ordering each to follow their original occupations.
There were over a hundred such individuals. Alas, their affinity for Prajñā was not deep;

although the old man earnestly demonstrated the great principles of the Buddha-dharma, those who could truly receive and uphold them were rare—it remained merely a matter of outward decorum. Thus spoke the old man.

He labored with great effort for eight years. When the temple monks, who were adherents of the *icchantika* view, created difficulties, the Old Man ultimately took his leave and retired to Mount Nanyue.
The novice monks followed him in succession without ceasing, like children who have lost their mother’s milk;

among them was the attendant Ruojue, who had previously waited upon him at Mount Nanyue and now waits upon him at Mount Kuang. He then offered incense and requested further instruction. Moved by compassion, the Old Man said to them: "You all..."
