To be born in a remote borderland where one does not hear the names of the Triple Gem is one difficulty. To have the good fortune to encounter an elder who provides guidance is another blessing.

Although you possess the conditions to receive this transformation, that you ultimately cannot penetrate deeply into the Buddha-dharma is simply because you have not yet planted the seeds for the conditions of *prajñā*.
If you all keep me in mind without forgetting, then once the faculty of faith is established, you will eventually attain the Buddha-dharma.
It is at such times that one enters. That is to say, if you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the causes and conditions of time and season.

Since you now know how to cast off worldly entanglements and have transcended them to dwell beyond, this constitutes the correct cause for entering the Way. Furthermore, you should draw near to spiritual friends.

To know what is difficult means that one should not, with deluded thoughts and a frantic mind, let the opportunity pass before one’s very face; this is precisely what it means to know what is of true value.
If one distances oneself from worldly ties and considers oneself free from constraints, yet allows the body and mind to drift aimlessly, engaging only in empty vanity, one has missed the mark.
To indulge in the pleasures of mountains and waters merely wastes the money spent on straw sandals; what benefit is there in this? Does it not only serve to further increase the suffering of karma?

If you can now truly be willing to sacrifice your body and life to seek the Great Dharma with resolve, for the sake of the great matter of birth and death, and investigate the Ultimate by taking advantage of your current physical strength and vigor for twenty or thirty years, you must directly seek to manifest your own nature. If you do not awaken...
Cease. To establish one's practice in this manner is the true practice of a renunciant.

Only then will you not fail the kindness of the Elder’s guidance, nor fail the karmic conditions for encountering a spiritual friend throughout thousands of lifetimes and ten thousand kalpas, nor fail the purpose of your renunciation.

To draw near to the physical body of the Sixth Patriarch is no different from being in his presence during his lifetime. Furthermore, you must make a vow: may I propagate the Patriarch’s Way to save the Dharma.
This is the standard for preserving the Dharma-gate. To harbor such intent and resolve is to be a true bone-and-flesh descendant of Caoxi.

If, however, you continue to pass your days in indolence, clinging to ignorance as being right, then even if you go to visit famous mountains, pay homage at the ancestral halls, and follow along at monastic sites to share in the joy of the Way, these are merely the tracks of common, worldly folk—the conduct of those of the lowest sort. Even if you were to travel them all to their end...
Though you are at a famous mountain, you still possess the bones and flesh of an ordinary person with no progress whatsoever.
Are you not, then, betraying yourself and the great karmic conditions of hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas? Reflect deeply; be careful not to deceive yourself.
Inscription on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* Copied by My Disciple Chaoyi, Following Its Original Copy:
This was written by me in the first month of winter in the year of Renyin while at Mount Potalaka.

It records the circumstances and the sequence of events regarding the initial resolve of my disciple Shixing, who commissioned his own disciple, Chaoyi, to copy this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* after the original had been lost. As for myself, since I first received [the teachings]...

He crossed the Endu Ridge and preached the Dharma in Wuyang. After several years of teaching and transforming others, among those in black robes who were sincere believers and took refuge in him, there were only a few individuals under the Bodhi tree.

Among these few, only the two, Master Yi and Shixing, shared the same aspiration and practiced together, jointly resolving to cultivate the Great Mind and transcribing the Great Dharma-nature. Before they had even completed half, both died prematurely; only Master Yi ultimately finished the task.

Regarding that karma—alas! It is not only the difficulty of first generating the resolve for enlightenment; even once the resolve has been generated, it is far more difficult to encounter the necessary conditions and thereby fulfill one’s aspirations.
Therefore, within the assemblies of the Dharma, our World-Honored One spoke extensively of the difficulty of faith in the Dharma, as when he said:
"Suppose the world were consumed by the fires at the end of an eon; to enter those flames carrying dry grass upon one's back without being burned would not be so difficult."

"After my parinirvāṇa, if one upholds this sutra and explains it for even a single person, that would be difficult. From this perspective, it is clear that the difficulty does not lie solely in believing the Dharma;
rather, the difficulty of upholding the Dharma is ten thousand times more arduous.

Now, consider this region of Nan Yue, situated at the frontier of the sea, whose customs are far removed from those of the Middle Kingdom. It was only with the arrival of Bodhidharma that the Buddha-dharma first began here."
Regarding maritime travel: in the past, when [the ship] rested at Wuyang, the Great Master Buddhabhadra arrived bringing the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.

He first established the ordination platform at Faxing Temple. Subsequently, the Great Master Jñānabhadra planted a Bodhi tree beside the platform, serving as a precursor for the Great Master Huineng.
Nearly a hundred years later, the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi arrived bringing the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*. Prime Minister Fang Gong...
When it came time for the dictation of the text, Master Lu rose from amidst his woodcutting axe. Thus, the Buddha-dharma also first flourished during the Tang dynasty;
its roots sprouted in Xinzhou, blossomed at Faxing Monastery, were deepened at Caoxi, and spread throughout the realm.

From this we know that while cultural refinement gradually reached the regions south of the ridges from China, the Way of Chan actually originated in those southern ridges and spread to China. This...
Thus, we rely upon one another for mutual utility, serving merely as a bridge and ford for crossing over the world. It has been twelve years since I crossed the mountain ridges.

Lamenting the desolation and filth of the ancestral path, I have sought to uphold the family tradition of Caoxi. With this body of mine, worn out by transgressions, I have faced the edge of a hundred-fold adversity;
that I have fortunately remained free from harm until now—for six years—has been due to the grace and spiritual power of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. All...

In general, there was an order of events. At the very beginning of the establishment of the Dharma-way, those who were personally under my tutelage during the Dharma assemblies were limited to only two individuals:
Chao Yi and Tong Heng. This sufficiently demonstrates the difficulty of teaching and transforming others, and indeed the most difficult of difficulties is finding such people.
Yi personally paid his respects to me; I then departed for Leiyang, traveling through pestilential regions to take charge of Caoxi, journeying back and forth in constant haste.
Having no day of leisure, I diligently followed these instructions. I closed my door and swept away all distractions, making it my daily task to transcribe the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Furthermore, with whatever strength remained, I sought out the original site of the Sixth Patriarch’s ordination platform, redeeming it and restoring it.

In my spare time, I led my fellow practitioners to hold ceremonies for the release of living beings (*fangsheng hui*), which became a regular monthly observance. Gradually, this practice reached the coastal regions and was adopted as a standard tradition.
The Dharma-methods were indeed initiated by me, yet those such as Yi were able to propagate them.

Now that I have completed the restoration of the ancestral temple, I hope to retire there to bring my remaining life to its conclusion. Yi has also followed me to travel extensively throughout his life;
thus, it is not only difficult to initiate the aspiration for enlightenment, but even more difficult to bring it to completion. Yet, what was difficult for the ancients is uniquely easy for you, sir.
This is not due to the roots of goodness accumulated over many lifetimes; for those whose affinity for Prajñā is deep, how could it be so easy to reach this state?

When one turns back to contemplate the true nature, a single breath not coming is already an eternal kalpa. If one seeks now for the conditions of seeing, hearing, and sympathetic joy—the various kinds of superior circumstances present before us—how could they ever be obtained again?
Thus, while the resolve to awaken is the same, their past vows differ; therefore, [this difference] arises.

Death takes divergent paths; the realm of the unseen is forever separated from this world. For those of us who are resolved upon the great matter of birth and death, there is ample here to inspire reflection and realization.
Yi and Xing simultaneously requested instruction, and I have recorded this scripture. These words of praise for the Dharma [conclude the work].
This has already been fully set forth at the beginning of the preceding section; therefore, I shall not elaborate further here in this brief record.
I have merely presented the difficulties regarding the beginning and end of the ultimate cultivation of the resolve for enlightenment in this manner.
Preface to the Copy of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* by the Zen Practitioner Shixing Our World-Honored One,
Vairocana Tathāgata, having first attained perfect enlightenment at the site of Bodhi, expounded the Great *Avataṃsaka*,
titled the *Sūtra on the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm*. He spoke of that which all Buddhas have realized and which sentient beings possess within themselves.
This is the Dharma-gate of the Nature. Therefore it is said: "How marvelous, how marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata;
yet because they cling to deluded thoughts and inverted views, they do not realize them.

If they were free from deluded thoughts and inverted views, then all-knowledge and teacherless knowledge would spontaneously manifest before them. It is further said: "I now, within the bodies of all sentient beings..."
In the middle [period], he attained equal and perfect enlightenment and turned the great wheel of Dharma.

Therefore, that which is elucidated by this sutra has as its essence the pure, single-flavored, impartial great wisdom that perfectly illumines the dharma-realm; it encompasses all holy ones and ordinary beings, the environments and inhabitants, and the sentient and non-sentient.
All are entirely equal. Whatever karmic actions all sentient beings perform do not transcend the self-nature *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas.
All deluded thoughts, ignorance, greed, hatred, delusion, and craving are themselves the true wisdom of *tathatā* realized by the Buddhas.

All mountains, rivers, and the great earth; all creatures with scales, shells, feathers, or fur, whether wriggling, crawling, or flying—all are the universal manifestation body (*vairocana-sarvarūpakāya*) of Vairocana.
Thus we know that in our daily lives—whether turning, walking, bowing, or looking up; coughing, spitting, or swinging our arms;
even down to eating, drinking, resting, and rising—all are the wondrous conduct (*pranidhāna-caryā*) of Samantabhadra, never departing from the ocean-seal (*sāgara-mudrā*) of the Tathāgata Vairocana.
This is samādhi. How much more so for those who cultivate right practice and perform pure deeds? It is only that we fail to recognize it in our daily lives. Alas for these people!

Deluded regarding this innately possessed wisdom, they flow through the currents of ignorance and karma, sinking and drifting in birth and death, wandering through the six realms of existence and undergoing all manner of sufferings, countless as the sands of the Ganges—how many hundreds of thousands of millions have they endured? I know not.
For kalpas as numerous as the atoms of worlds, they have never known to reflect upon or examine themselves.
Therefore, our Great Master, out of impartial great compassion, renounced the bliss of the dharmas of his own nature and appeared in the world.
He stood forth within the three realms to guide them, entering deeply into the burning house just as an elder rescues his children. Yet, the father’s heart toward his children does not stop there.
My sole hope is merely to escape calamity and misfortune; my true aspiration is that my family estate be left entirely intact. This is my original intention.

Therefore, at the very beginning, I shall preach this sutra, suddenly revealing the equal Dharma-realm and directly pointing to the self-nature Dharmakāya of all sentient beings, so that they may instantly attain immeasurable Dharma-bliss.
Thus it is said: "It is as if within a single minute particle there were contained a great thousand-fold world-system scroll."
Suppose there were a wise person who clearly perceived all that is written within the events of a trichiliocosm;
they then split open a minute atom, extracted this scripture from it, and presented it to sentient beings to bring them benefit. Now, as for that single minute atom:
The minds of sentient beings are characterized by delusive conceptualization. The great chiliocosm scroll is the inherent merit of the self-nature of sentient beings.
The person of clear-sighted wisdom is the Great Compassionate Lord, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. To split open a minute particle of dust is to shatter the delusions and inversions of all people.
The method for splitting open a minute particle of dust is precisely the entirety of the sūtra teachings spoken by the Buddhas.
However, the Dharma has both sudden and gradual aspects. While other sutras all provide a gradual analysis, this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the method for a sudden revelation.

It displays the vast treasury of the Buddha-dharma realized by all Buddhas, desiring that sentient beings see it with a single glance and, in a single thought-moment, suddenly attain immeasurable enjoyment. Viewed from this perspective, the kindness of our Buddha [is immeasurable].
The virtue bestowed upon sentient beings—how could it be anything but profound and vast? Alas!

Since the advent of the Buddha-dharma, this sutra has circulated throughout the world, and many have seen or heard it; yet how few are there who can truly comprehend the benevolent grace of the Buddhas?

After my Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, all the successive patriarchs who transmitted the mind-seal of the Buddha and directly pointed out the buddha-nature of sentient beings were my compassionate fathers and sons who upheld the family estate.
Only our Great Master Bodhidharma came to this land by sea specifically for this purpose;
he sat facing a wall at Shaolin, coldly remaining seated for nine years, and was harmed by others.

After searching four times, he found only one person, the Second Patriarch, and immediately withdrew to travel west. The Dharma was transmitted through six generations until it reached our Great Mirror Meditation Master (Dajian Zenji).
Rising from among the woodcutters, upon hearing a single phrase of the sutra, he at once went to Huangmei; there he carried grain for pounding and wore a stone belt around his waist.
Having finally obtained his robes and alms bowl, he traveled south. Yet he suffered various injuries at the hands of wicked men and took refuge among a band of hunters for seventeen years.
Later, when the time for the final causal conditions arrived, he briefly borrowed the words of the wind and the banner to shake the realms of humans and devas.
Only then did he shave his head and don the robes beneath the Bodhi tree of Dharma-nature, beginning to preach the Dharma at the source of Caoxi.
The head [of the lineage]—the seventeen hundred masters of knowledge—flowed forth from this single stream.

These vast merits all originate from the single thought of my Great Master’s endurance of suffering. Are they not, indeed, the loyal ministers of the Dharma King and the true sons of the Compassionate Father?
To this day, the foundation of the ordination platform remains, and the Way-tree under which his hair was buried still stands.
All those who dwell beneath his protective shade find peace within the shelter he provides.
Among them, there is not a single person who seeks to recognize the Master’s kindness or reflects upon the hardships he endured while providing food and clothing. How tragic!
This may be called "using daily without realizing it. I, too, am the unworthy recipient of the Master’s grace during this age of the Dharma’s decline.
The disciples were assembled. When Kōbō Daishi suffered persecution and was exiled to Ra-yang, he crossed the mountain pass on the Bingshen year and visited Caoxi to pay homage to the Great Master.

The Master’s skeletal remains were solemn and appeared as if alive; lamenting that the Dharma-way had fallen into desolation and that social customs had collapsed, he wept for many rows of tears for a long time before proceeding to his place of detention.
That autumn, he returned to the walls and ramparts of the Qingmen barracks in the capital city.

In the spring of the following year, those who died of famine and pestilence were so numerous that white bones covered the fields; those who collected and buried them numbered in the tens of thousands.
He then established a *tīrtha-yāna* (ford-crossing) *dharma-śālā* and invited a multitude of monks.

In the following year, Wuxu (758), during his leisure from bearing arms, he led several disciples under the trees and expounded for them the Dharma of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness. Subsequently, he composed a commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
[The work] was completed. I expounded [the teachings] for him. Furthermore, I went beneath a tree and preached the *Sutra in Forty-two Sections* to the śrāmaṇeras;
thus, those who listened increased day by day. My disciple Chao Yi Shixing held incense, prostrated, and said to me:
"I wish for you to transcribe one copy of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* with your own hand, to serve as a bridge across the sea of suffering. I was filled with joy and offered words of praise. (2)
The disciple then closed the door and burned incense. Beginning in the *gengzi* year of the Wanli era, he took up his pen to commence the work;
however, by the following year, *xinchou*, Shixing suddenly passed away. The scriptures he had transcribed amounted to only twenty-seven fascicles. His grandfather was Chaozhen.
Furthermore, he entrusted his life to the master Mingzhan, whose true nature is reality, to complete his studies and fulfill these supreme conditions. Alas!
How tragic it is that sentient beings wander through the realms of suffering, coming and going within the six paths for as many kalpas as there are grains of dust and sand.
Among them, those who encounter the Buddha-dharma and are able to give rise to faith are like a blind turtle in the great ocean encountering the hole of a floating log. How could this not be so?

How easily attained! Now that you have truly been born in this age of Dharma-Decline (*mofa*), by relying on this supreme cause, you may travel through the celestial realms of the Flower Treasury (*Huazang*) without moving a step;

upon setting down your pen, you shall behold the ocean-like assemblies within the atoms of all lands. You will pay homage to Vairocana in this very moment and perfect the ocean of practices over many kalpas.
Thus, your birth is no longer in vain, and your death will not be a mere fleeting passing. How much more so when one rides this ferry!
Is it not to cross over and travel to the realm of neither birth nor death?

In the first month of winter in the year of Renyin, I was about to set out on a journey to Leiyang when Chaozhen brought me a scripture written by Xing. He requested a single word from me to record this event.

I hope that those who see or hear of this in the future will, because of it, give rise to faith; should they but turn their light back for a single thought-moment, they will immediately emerge from the vast [samsara].

Transcending birth and death throughout kalpas—this is the true nature. Furthermore, from the tip of a single hair, one manifests the mark of the broad and long tongue to preach the Dharma-gate of the self-nature of sentient beings;
this does not diminish Vairocana’s sitting beneath the Bodhi tree.
This very state is the eternal abiding of the Dharmakāya.
Postscript to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* Written by Various Śrāmaṇeras of Caoxi How magnificent is this scripture of the Dharmadhātu!
It was originally expounded by our own Honored One, Vairocana Buddha, when he first attained perfect enlightenment.
Seated at the Bodhimanda of the Dharma in the Āraṇya, upon the adamantine ground of the mind, he entered the Samādhi of the Ocean Seal and proclaimed it in accordance with his true nature.

Perfectly interfused and unimpeded, this is the dharma-gate of vast majesty and sovereign power. Across the seven locations and nine assemblies, without arising from one’s seat, one ascends to perfect the ten bodies.
Arrayed like stars throughout the dharma-realm, sentient beings within every atom and land—both their environments and their physical forms—speak in unison, blazing forth in an uninterrupted stream.

This is an inconceivable Dharma. The Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi, who held the seal of the mind transmitted in a single line, left behind his robe and alms bowl to remain as a guardian upon this mountain.
This is precisely the Vajra Ground of the Bodhimaṇḍa of the Dharma; his physical body remains present here.

This is precisely the eternal abiding of the Dharmakāya of Samantabhadra. The sounds of bells and drums, uninterrupted from morning until evening, are themselves the blazing preaching of the Dharma throughout the motes of dust within the Buddha-fields.
Alas! Those disciples sitting in the assembly are like the blind and the deaf; they have long since missed the truth before their very eyes.
Having previously received the Sage’s compassion in being tamed from ten thousand *li* away, his kindness is so great that it is difficult to repay. Therefore—
"I vow to sacrifice this body and re-establish the Dharma-hall as a means of repaying my debt of gratitude to the earth. My disciples were entirely unaware of this matter;
they were no different from the deaf and blind. Thereupon, I selected several young śrāmaṇeras and taught them to practice calligraphy, having them transcribe the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
My intention was to rely on the causal conditions of this Great Dharma to serve as the seeds of the Vajra. Indeed, it was not...
Over the course of several years, those who have resolved to transcribe [the scriptures] can be expected to number ten. The Hall Master, Master Āṅ, was formerly the teacher I invited to Mount Kuāng;
he has now brought this work here. Upon seeing it, I sighed and said: "This is precisely the scripture produced from the splitting of a single atom.
Observing its strokes and dots, they all flow forth from the Vajra-mind. How much more so for this youngest of śrāmaṇeras!"

"May those who wish to transcribe this by piercing their own blood know that this is precisely the 'unlearned wisdom' (asvikṣā-jñāna) and 'spontaneous wisdom' (svayambhū-jñāna) spoken of by our Buddha, now manifest before us.
Moved with gratitude, I shed tears; it is only a pity that I cannot serve as the ultimate guide for these śrāmaṇeras.
Nevertheless, let this alone be the sprinkling of my own heart's blood. From this point forward, may all who see or hear [this]..."
With joy, I resolve to arouse this aspiration so that its conditions may be inexhaustible until the very limits of the future.

I shall cause every disciple of Caoqi to enter this Dharma-gate, such that this Dharma is proclaimed amidst the dust, proclaimed throughout the lands, and proclaimed among sentient beings—blazing and turning constantly.
This is precisely Śākyamuni preaching the Dharma in the present; the Sixth Patriarch dwells eternally here. Thus, even in death, I shall not perish.

How can one not rejoice? I have respectfully recorded these initial causes and conditions to show them to future generations, to serve as a means for awakening the mind-ground, and furthermore, as the broad and long tongue of this old man.

Inscription on the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna* Written in Blood by a Śrāmaṇera of Caoxi I formerly resided at Caoxi to revive the ancestral Way and nurture the śrāmaṇeras, hoping that the legacy of the West would not fall into decline.
Within less than ten years, there appeared to be a transformation in the community. Among them, a certain śrāmaṇera conceived the resolve to prick his own blood and transcribe this scripture.
He took the "Universal Worthy’s Practices and Vows" (Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna) as his lifelong recitation and practice. The old man sighed deeply and said:
"The śrāmaṇera is one who recognizes the Dharma; he is thus able to draw blood to transcribe this sutra and perform such a great feat that is difficult to accomplish.

For the dependent origination of the Dharma-realm makes no distinction between delusion and enlightenment, nor does it belong to the categories of sage or ordinary person. As long as there is great dedication, all returns to the ultimate reality."

It is said that the mountains, rivers, and great earth together turn the fundamental wheel of Dharma; even scales, shells, feathers, and fur universally manifest the Samādhi of the Manifestation Body.
How much more so this blood from one’s own body, which flows from the Dharma-realm and enters into this sutra—how could it not be called the true nature of reality?
If a śrāmaṇera writes it thus and recites it thus, never flagging until the end of his life, then his mind...
The mind does not depart from the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices; at every step, one does not leave the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha) Bodhimanda.

One need only believe with earnest conviction and without doubt; beyond this, there is no other Buddha-dharma. If this is so, then even an elder who praises it in accordance with the Dharma has not yet exhausted the measure of its merit.
If, however, one is personally ignorant of one's own fundamental mind and acts in opposition to the Dharma, then even if one were to see the Vow face-to-face...
Your Majesty, this merely further increases the karmic consciousness.
Regarding the constant regulations for masters entering the mountains: from the twenty-eighth year, on the twentieth day of the ninth month, [the master] arrived at the temple.

Beginning on the seventh day of the tenth month and ending on the ninth, for three days, the monks of all ranks throughout the temple—both great and small—were selected to remain in the Hall to recite sutras and study their texts.
On the ninth day, the Lotus Hall (Hokke-dō) was established. At the third strike of the bell at dawn, everyone was to proceed together to the Buddha Hall;
the arrangements were not to be delayed, and all were required to wear their *hien* robes neatly and carry their respective items.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in its entirety shall be recited by at least two people together, completing it all at once without any omissions or errors.
On the thirteenth day, three centers for doctrinal study (*yixue*) shall be established.
The East Gallery Hall opens at noon on the thirteenth day of the tenth month;
the West Gallery Hall opens at the hour of the tiger (3–5 a.m. on the thirteenth day of the tenth month;
the Yanshou Hall opens at the hour of the snake (9–11 a.m. on the thirteenth day of the tenth month.
Regarding the Pure Rules for the Ten Directions' Permanent Endowment at the Bao Lin Chan Hall of Cao Xi:

it was our Sixth Patriarch Master alone who, while preaching the Dharma at Cao Xi, drew all the monastics of the world to him; there, the Patriarch established the practice of *an-ju* (the summer retreat).
To accommodate a vast multitude, this establishment of the meditation hall (zen-dō) was the very beginning.

When Master Baizhang instituted the monastic codes (rituryō) to regulate the many, this was the origin by which the Pure Rules (shingi) were first established. From that time on, every monastery (sōrin) throughout the land has possessed a meditation hall to practice these Pure Rules;
they are known as the "Ten Directions Permanent Abode" (jippō jōjū), and though there may be thousands upon ten thousands of such places, [the principle remains the same].

Just as the head, eyes, hands, and feet are mutually indispensable for a single person’s body, so too has the Caoxi Chan Hall been neglected for a thousand years since the time of the Sixth Patriarch.

Over such a long period, it has fallen into ruin; the monks of this monastery have dispersed like scattered smoke and fire, their dwellings no longer unified, and the pure regulations have ceased to be observed.
Even when monks from the ten directions come to pay homage to the Patriarch, they find themselves in such a state.
They were utterly bewildered and had no refuge. Although the ancestral temple was established, the practice of pure cultivation no longer existed; they even became indistinguishable from commoners.

How could this be the fundamental source of the Chan lineage? This old man, having received the Imperial Grace to cross the mountain passes, has been sustained by the profound resolve of those who protect the Way and the Dharma.
Unable to bear the decline of the ancestral temple, he commanded the monastery monks to invite me here.
I organized the site. Upon my arrival, I devoted my mind and will with single-minded resolve, making the restoration of our ancestral Way my primary concern.
Aside from repairing the temple buildings, I cleared the old grounds of the Baolin Monastery, where the monks' quarters had become overgrown and obstructed.

Consequently, I donated funds to purchase a separate plot of vacant land and relocated seven monk's cells there to establish a new precinct. Furthermore, I constructed an inner Chan Hall to provide a stable residence for the resident clergy.
The assembly established a hall outside the main building to receive those coming and going from the ten directions.

Apart from the incense and lamps maintained by the monastery, they separately donated their own funds to redeem the Zisun estate, its fields, gardens, and lands, establishing them as provisions for the community; this was named the "Ten Directions Permanent Endowment" (shifang changzhu).
Once the summer retreat was settled and the four requisites were fully provided, [the masters] feared that those residing in this hall might fail to discipline themselves and advance in the Way.

Furthermore, the presiding officers within the hall may be unfamiliar with the monastic regulations of the ancient masters; their conduct may be erroneous and their words and deeds may contradict the Dharma, thereby bringing ruin upon the Buddhist teachings.
This not only fails to honor the original intent of those who founded this institution, but truly betrays the will of the dragons and devas who protect the Dharma.

Regarding daily affairs and matters of routine, I have briefly established the following articles for reference. Both guests and hosts should observe them with diligence to ensure the long-term stability of the community.
I have glorified the ancestral Way so that the Dharma-gate may not decline and the path of practice may be perfected.
As an old man, I have looked up to continue the thread-like lineage of the Sixth Patriarch and have also somewhat fulfilled my original vow. All you disciples must strive to uphold it.
Be careful not to treat this with levity.
The Buddha taught that there are two kinds of permanent property (*śāśvata*). First is the "permanent property of the permanent," which refers to the present-day monastery;

it is presided over by an abbot (*sthavira*), who is called an elder (*sthavira*) and serves as the leader of the monastery. Second is the "permanent property of the ten directions," which refers to the present-day...

The Meditation Hall. A Hall Master is established to preside over it. As he serves as the leader for practitioners from all directions (the ten directions), those who reside in this hall—whether internal or external—are all addressed as "those from the ten directions.
This is because they have resolved to practice and their aspirations transcend the mundane world; they are not comparable to worldly people.
Its regulations and etiquette follow the precedents for the abbot (*zhuchi*).

However, while there is a distinction of superior and inferior between the abbot and the assembly of monks, if one presides over the meditation hall (*candeng*) with equal access to both Dharma and sustenance, then a relationship of teacher and disciple exists, and such a person is titled "Hall Head" (*tangtou*), as is the case today at Shaolin.
If one merely manages the affairs of the meditation hall, they are titled "Hall Master" (*tangzhu*), and stands in a guest-host relationship with the assembly.
This is their portion. Indeed, all the monks currently within the hall rely upon them for their daily practice of the Path and for the four requisites of life;
they depend entirely upon them for all matters, both great and small, within the monastic community (saṃghārāma). While the assembly merely stands with hands folded, this is no trivial matter.
Therefore, you must show mutual respect, maintain harmony between the inner and outer circles, and hold the Way as your primary concern.
Do not engage in groundless speculation to seek out faults. The rites, laws, and monastic regulations you observe already possess established precedents;
you must strive to remain content with your lot and uphold what has been accomplished, rather than arbitrarily adding to or subtracting from them.
The establishment of the meditation hall (zen-dō) is not a trivial matter; the responsibility of the hall master (dōju) is exceedingly grave.
As the eyes of the ten directions, he points toward a single individual and must ensure that his words and conduct are upright and pure to meet the expectations of the assembly.

Therefore, those who occupy this position must strive to maintain a heart of compassion, a vast and expansive heart, a gentle and harmonious heart, a heart of forbearance, and a humble heart, acting with the mind of a bodhisattva’s practice.
Like a bridge or like the great earth, only when one is capable of bearing the burden of sentient beings can it be called "sublime conduct" (*miao-xing*).
Therefore, in daily life, whether eating or drinking, one must share both joy and suffering with the assembly; one must not act privately or set oneself apart from the group.

Even regarding a drop of water or a stalk of vegetable, one should hold the community in mind and never act solely according to one's own will, lest one incur censure and reproach. If the monks of the assembly commit a transgression, one should report it to the board in the hall.
First, handle matters with gentle words and skillful means; do not hastily utter violent or coarse speech, nor indulge in arbitrary scolding.
Do not oppress the tenant farmers so as to invite resentment and slander. Regarding all administrative affairs, you must carefully deliberate upon the merits and faults of those involved.
One must not recklessly employ unsuitable persons. Regarding the permanent assets of money and grain, one should economize on superfluous expenditures and must not spend excessively.

If an expense is deemed necessary, it should be discussed in advance with the head of the community regarding its feasibility. One must consult the accounting records and clearly itemize all disbursements;
one must not act solely according to one's own whims.
Regarding the annual budget for the Hall, which consists of the permanent endowment rents and taxes, it falls short by more than one-third each year.
There is no actual revenue to speak of; it relies entirely upon the collective practice of the assembly to invoke the protection of dragons and celestial beings.
This burden rests solely on the shoulders of the Hall Master to solicit donations. Should there still be a deficiency, the assembly should simply...
Share equally in both the sweet and the plain; do not seek excessive abundance or beauty, nor lend money on credit to burden the permanent property (*sangha*).

Those who perform manual labor toil with heart and strength, working diligently throughout the year. During the two seasons of winter and summer, single-layered cloth must be measured and provided to assist their resolve for the Path.
However, as the annual budget of the permanent property is insufficient, it is truly difficult to establish a fixed rule. This depends upon...

The Hall Master must employ various means to provide for them; otherwise, the practitioners cannot be settled in peace. Regarding the single monks within the hall, it is only right that they be treated with equality;
however, due to limited resources, it is difficult to manage this, and to borrow funds would only bring further burden upon the permanent property of the monastery.

It is difficult to sustain for long. If it occurs during the August assembly, the circumstances are not certain; moreover, there may be a fear that funds have been borrowed in advance, which must be repaid immediately.
Now, according to all available offerings and profits, first deduct and repay what is owed.

The remainder shall be distributed among the assembly members according to their respective shares to assist in the conditions for the Path. No fixed rule can be established for this. If there is still a surplus, it shall be set aside for storage.
By being based on reality and remaining constant, one shall not fall into emptiness or vanity; thus, it may endure for a long time.
Should there be a donor who focuses their intent upon giving, they may act according to their inspired resolve, as this does not belong to the regular routine.

The annual accounting for the Hall depends entirely upon the August assembly. When the donors have gathered, all offerings made for the monks' meals—such as rice—are to be entered into the storehouse.
As for any silver coins, one casket and one ledger must be established; a secretary and one person appointed as a witness shall jointly manage them.
Any silver received in lieu of rice must be recorded in the ledger in accordance with reality, with the witnesses present to verify it.
The funds shall not be diverted for other purposes or embezzled. The silver contributed for the vegetarian feast must likewise be recorded in the ledger and accumulated;

it shall be disbursed daily before the assembly. The secretary shall maintain a separate expenditure ledger for the purpose of audit and inspection. The Hall Master (Tangzhu) is prohibited from making private withdrawals or expenditures.
Any silver offered for the recitation of sutras or the performance of repentance rites must also be entered into the ledger to await the conclusion of the assembly.

The funds shall be distributed collectively among the assembly; no one within the hall may claim them as their own property. Because all members, both inside and outside the Dharma hall, must exert themselves with a single mind, no individual may exercise exclusive control.
If there are funds for tea and fruit offerings sent from outside that are designated for the Hall Master, the Hall Master may personally retain them.
However, regarding items sent directly to the hall, such as banners, ritual texts, and materials for Buddhist services, these shall be the exclusive property of those within the hall.

If the donor is single-minded, then it shall be taken publicly as agreed. Should anyone violate this precedent and dispute the matter, they shall be punished according to the rules of the Pure Regulations (Ching-kui):

based on the nature of the dispute, they shall be fined double the amount involved for the preparation of one vegetarian offering. Those who do not comply shall not be permitted to dwell together with the community.
The monks seated in the hall are all those who have been nurtured and raised by this temple; they reside not far from their own monastic community and are in close proximity to their kin and friends.

Yet, fearing that one may find it difficult to forget familiar surroundings, they must not constantly use various pretexts to return to their private quarters, indulging their whims and acting recklessly by drinking alcohol, gambling, wandering about, or engaging in idle play.
Nor should they arrive at the hall in a state of drunkenness, thereby defiling the divine spirits or showing contempt for the sacred.

Regarding the rules of propriety: one who violates them shall undergo a period of solitary confinement (*baiban*) under the supervision of the Hall Master. For serious offenses, the offender shall not live in communal residence;

for minor offenses, they shall be penalized by kneeling before the assembly while burning a single stick of incense, repenting and reforming their transgressions. Should they fail to comply, they likewise shall not live in communal residence.
The monastics residing in the hall have all been nurtured by these elders to illuminate the ancestral Way; you must take cultivation as your sole purpose.
Each of you should diligently observe the precepts and discipline the three karmas, subduing transgressions and refraining from creating further karma.
You must not gather in groups to engage in idle discourse that deludes upright people and initiates trouble, nor should you entice those who are unrighteous.
To destroy the permanent property or to steal the utensils—those who violate this shall sit together with the offender.
All affairs within the hall, as well as the annual budget and provisions, are to be borne entirely by the Hall Master alone.
For one person to shoulder so many duties is truly difficult to manage perfectly in every detail. Should there be any lapses or errors, the assembly should likewise show understanding and empathy;
they must not demand perfection or reprimand him for every fault, nor point out shortcomings to incite dissenting opinions.

If there are indeed transgressions, one should convene with the head of the quarters (ban-shou) to discuss the matter privately within the abbot’s quarters (fang-wang), engaging in a frank conversation to offer counsel.
Correct. One must not hastily utter coarse words that would injure the essence of the Way.
All monastics who have traveled from afar to the ten directions shall rest in the outer hall or the *danguo* (guest) quarters; they must enter the hall to pay their respects.
The head of the board (*ban-shou*) shall then lead the assembly in returning the bow to express thanks. The guest prefect (*zhi-bin*) shall serve tea, but [the guests] must not sit.

Do not harbor pride; take upon yourself the offenses of the ten directions. If they are learned Dharma masters or eminent, virtuous monks, you should inform the Hall Master to invite them into the inner hall or private quarters for the summer retreat, or to remain through both winter and summer.
You must devote your whole heart to honoring and making offerings to them with reverence.
The assembly must inquire after the essentials of the Dharma morning and evening; one must not treat them with negligence or contempt, lest one’s transgressions increase.
If those staying in the guest quarters (*dangguo liao*) for three or five days require their midday meals, these shall be provided from the inner treasury.

The Hall Master (*tangzhu*) must constantly attend to these matters and inspect them, ensuring that nothing is lacking. An attendant for the quarters (*liaozhu*) should be appointed to oversee the reception of guests. If, within the inner hall, one encounters...
When a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*) is being prepared, the monks of the next hall should also be requested to participate in the communal labor (*pǔqǐng*).

The administrative affairs of the Meditation Hall (*cān-táng*) are extremely simple; the collection of rents and taxes is handled solely by the Head of the Board (*bǎnshǒu*), or perhaps the Hall Master (*tángzhǔ*) collects them personally, so there is no need to appoint many attendants.
However, one person—the Guest Master (*zhīkè*)—is indispensable, as he must respond to and manage visitors.
Regarding the reception of guests: one must welcome the monastics from the ten directions. This duty requires the employment of the right person;
if such a person is lacking, the monk on duty in the hall shall act as substitute. When a guest arrives, they must be courteously retained and served tea.

If a patron arrives specifically for this purpose, the Hall Master must be informed so that they may be received with due ceremony, ensuring their faith is not discouraged. If it is a monastic from the ten directions, they too must be properly distinguished.
I inform you, wise and foolish alike: do not be negligent regarding coming and going.
As for the public affairs of the monastic community, matters shall not be distinguished as internal or external; all shall be treated equally through communal labor (*fǔqǐng*).

This is the universal rule throughout the world, from ancient times to the present. Now, regarding the provisions for the mountain monastery, the donors provide the meals personally; as for the temple lands, the tenant farmers manage them themselves.

Regarding the *sō* (sending): when gathering firewood, the practitioners enter the mountains; beyond this, there are no heavy labors, only the transport of wood to the streamside and the tending of vegetables in the garden.
If a communal work (*fusshō*) is held in the hall, only one person on duty shall remain to watch over the hall;
the rest must all attend together and may not evade service. Any who violate this rule shall be punished by kneeling for the duration of one incense stick.
In the monastic communities throughout the world, regardless of whether they are internal or external, those belonging to the Dharma share a single essence.

Those who reside within the halls rely on laborers to assist their spiritual practice, while the laborers exert their strength to support the practitioners' cultivation. In truth, it is the laborers who bear the greater burden;
unless one possesses a firm resolve for the Way, one cannot endure such ascetic practices for long. For the most part, this is not comparable to the kind of service performed for secular purposes.
Furthermore, regarding all matters pertaining to the permanent affairs of the monastery, the head of the meditation hall (ban-shou) shall lead the assembly and direct their actions;

each must comply and is not permitted to resist or disobey. As for private matters of individuals, unless there is a long-standing relationship of intimacy, one must not privately compel or employ others.
Even when there are many people engaged in tasks, if they cause commotion, disputes, excessive consumption of food, or partiality—[the head shall intervene].
Regarding those who commit various transgressions during the communal meal: if there was previously a *dianzuo* (steward), they were subject to his regulations;

if there was no harmony, they were subject to the disposition of the *tangzhu* (hall master). According to the examples set by the *qinggui*, their dismissal or retention was left to his authority. Should anyone be seen committing a fault within the hall, [the hall master] must address it accordingly.
Furthermore, one must report this to the Hall Master (Tangzhu) to have it adjudicated. One is not permitted to speak with coarse words or insults directly, thereby provoking disputes.

Whether a course of action is acceptable or not depends entirely upon the Hall Master’s thorough understanding of the circumstances; it cannot be determined by a single-sided perspective. Therefore, regarding the temple residents...
It must not be used for private purposes;

it is intended for the comfort of those who perform their duties below. The Hall Master (Tangzhu) shall take exclusive responsibility for its inspection. It shall remain within the hall, and no personal favoritism is permitted.

I have strongly retained my close friends for fear that they might engage in unlawful acts or damage the permanent endowments (*sāṃghika-vastu*), thereby implicating those who recommended them; should such matters come to light, they would face punishment by association.

All those currently in the hall are monks of this monastery whom I have nurtured and raised. Now that the monastic community (*saṅghārāma*) has its affairs in order and its scale is established, [the time has come].

Observation: There may be junior members from the parent temple who have long lacked virtue and conduct, who do not submit to the instructions of their teachers and seniors, and who seek only leisure and self-indulgence under the pretext of entering the hall; such individuals must absolutely not be permitted to enter.

Or, having already entered the hall, they fail to observe the pure rules and precepts, acting recklessly according to their own whims and refusing to join the assembly in chanting and recitation, devoting themselves solely to [selfish] maintenance.

If there are those who are indolent, or who are frequently absent from the monastery, and furthermore indulge in drinking alcohol and eating meat without any sense of shame, merely relying on empty reputations while neglecting actual practice and thereby disturbing the community and the assembly—the head of the hall (*ban-shou*), the *yuè-zhòng*, and the *zhǔ-zhǒng* shall jointly petition the abbot.

The abbot shall then immediately dismiss them from the hall, not permitting them to remain for long, lest they harm the virtue of the assembly. Should they fail to comply with this, [punishment shall follow].
The abbot shall govern according to the Dharma; be careful not to yield to personal sentiment, lest it breed future harm.

Throughout the monasteries of the world, there are naturally the Baizhang Qinggui (Pure Rules of Baizhang), which serve as an eternal standard. However, regarding the meditation hall of this very mountain...
Although his fame spread throughout the ten directions, it was not comparable to that of other regions.

When the Elder first entered the mountains, he earnestly reflected that the ancestral Way was in decline and that the monastics had lost their fundamental practice. With the goal of restoring the tradition, he took human talent as his primary concern;
thus, he first provided stipends to instruct and train the śrāmaṇeras. Once they had been tonsured, he established meditation halls to teach them the practice of cultivation. He donated...
I have provided clothing and provisions for his support and sustenance, undergoing all manner of hardships in raising him.

This was done solely to honor the Sixth Patriarch above by continuing the lineage of the Way, and to receive the ten directions below by illuminating the monastic community. Now, alas, this old man is of meager merit and cannot fulfill his original vow;
he must depart midway and relinquish his charge. Therefore, I appoint the Hall Master of the Ten Directions to act as the old man’s representative.
It is laborious; however, there are still many deficiencies among all the items required for use.

Although the Hall Master may embody the elder’s heart and aspirations, he lacks the elder’s spiritual power (*mārgabala*), and it is feared that omissions will occur and things cannot be carried out with complete thoroughness. The head officers and administrators of this monastery...

Venerable elders and the great assembly, each of you should understand and be patient. You must reflect that if a patriarchal monastery lacks a meditation hall, it cannot be called a true *dharma* site;

if it lacks a hall master, it cannot receive guests from the ten directions or sustain a large community. If these matters pertain to our own temple, we cannot help but conform to worldly conventions.
Otherwise, it will soon fall into ruin. Therefore, between the abbot and the hall master, there must be the relationship of host and guest;
each should cherish the Way. Host and guest must each fulfill their respective duties and must not act arbitrarily or impose harsh demands that would harm harmony.
To do so would destroy the monastic community and betray the intention of the Elder who founded it, thereby incurring transgression.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "If you incur the reprimand of the dragons and devas, you must be careful to observe the precepts.
The above conditions are very numerous and cannot be fully detailed; although the matters listed here do not conform to ancient regulations, [they are nonetheless essential].

This is undertaken to earnestly remedy the ills of the times. If one can follow and practice each of these instructions within this Bao Lin Monastery, then the flourishing of the ancestral Way will depend upon this very effort.
I hope you will not regard this as ordinary and treat it with negligence or indifference, thereby failing the intent behind its establishment.
All those present in this hall should each exert yourselves.
The twelfth day of the eleventh month in the forty-first year of the Wanli era.
Written by the Elder Master Hanshan, Deqing, at the Baolin Chan Hall of Zhongxing Caoxi, for the common property of the ten directions.
Preface to Master Han’s Record of the Restoration of Caoxi:

In the year of Gengzi, while I was serving as the military commander of Nanxun and Shaoguan, I reflected upon how the Dharma-ending age had caused Caoxi to fall into obscurity, and how the Buddha-realm had nearly become a marketplace.
I therefore expelled all butchers, liquor vendors, and ruffians, along with the chickens, pigs, geese, and ducks they kept.

He commanded the monastic community to forever abstain from wine and meat; when guests arrived, they were served only tea or vegetarian meals, so that the site might truly be called a pure *dharmadhātu*.

Because he was a flesh-and-blood Bodhisattva who had not, for countless kalpas, created the evil karma of Avīci hell, the monks at first felt apprehensive, but soon thereafter they praised him with great joy, as if emerging from boiling water and fire and being drenched with cool, refreshing water.
These words were recorded among my miscellaneous writings from my travels in Yue. At that time, Master Hanshan was expounding the Dharma in Wuyang;

monks and laypeople from near and far looked up to him as they would to a dragon or an elephant. As I was about to enter the capital to offer congratulations on the Emperor’s longevity, I reflected with concern that the habitual tendencies of the various monastics would be difficult to cleanse, and that the Dharma at the end of the age might soon sink into oblivion.
I therefore requested the Master to come and preside over this mountain. I [departed] from Wuyang.
I went in person to pay my respects. [The Master] said, "This single plot of land at Baolin is a great matter of cause and condition for all eternity.
Who other than you, Master, could shoulder this responsibility? The Master responded with assent. He saw me off to Lingzhou and we parted.

From then until the present year of Xinyou, I have again come to Guangdong on the mission of planning the coastal defenses and passed through Baolin. More than twenty years have slipped by like the mere bending and stretching of an arm.
It has been nearly eight years since the Master departed from Baolin. Beholding what has been newly constructed, the layout is orderly and the atmosphere is solemn and majestic.
The monastics are all disciplined; donning their black robes, they chant the sutras.

Looking back at those of old who wore loincloths, carried hoes, were preoccupied with eating and drinking, and whose eyes did not recognize the characters of the scriptures—it is as if one has suddenly undergone a transformation of the womb and shed the bones, as if existing three lifetimes prior. Thus, one yearns for and admires the Master.

I hope to return again one morning or evening, not unlike an infant yearning for its compassionate mother. Thus, he requested several lines from me to send to Kuānglú, where he was urging Master [Zhao] to come.
Before long, I received the Imperial Grace and was summoned back to the secondary capital. My returning boat drew near to Qīngxī.
The temple monks arrived three stations short of Caoxi, bringing a letter from the Master as well as the *Record of Caoxi* they had compiled.

Upon opening the envelope, the first thing they presented was a passage on "dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows" with which they sought to examine him. This was clearly because they were deeply moved by the impermanence of coming and going, parting and meeting within the mundane world.
As they further perused the record, they found that all its various accounts consisted of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Now, since it has been stated that one has entered into the midst of delusive thoughts and all things are illusory, then Bao Lin and Cao Xi must also be illusory;

even the monasteries, the remains, the robes, and the alms bowls—all these cannot but be illusory. Why, then, employ such systematic cataloging of trivial and minute details to trouble the monastic community?
Furthermore, does the *Shilu* (Veritable Record) not treat the property of the monastery as a matter of monastic discipline?
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are eternally abiding dharmas; yet that which is called "dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows" refers to non-abiding dharmas.
Only when there is eternal abiding can there be non-abiding; only when there is non-abiding can there be eternal abiding and non-abiding.
When there is both eternal abiding and non-abiding, one can then speak of neither abiding nor non-abiding. It is solely through eternal abiding [that this is realized].
Yet, while dreams, illusions, and emptiness do not obstruct existence, it is only through constant non-abiding that the existence of all phenomena does not obstruct emptiness.
Because the monastic community dares not treat the Dharma with contempt and enters into it without becoming mired in it, this is recorded in the true annals compiled by my teacher.
That which is discussed as dreams and illusions, and that which is experienced as coming and going, separation and union, emptiness and existence, encompass one another without mutual obstruction.
This is precisely the original intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and also the inexhaustible intent of the ancient worthies.
I shall dwell for a few kalpas with you, Master, within this realm of dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows, and we shall deliberate further. May you, Master, provide a turning word in response.

Completed by Zhu Yiyou, Junior Censor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices in Nanjing and native of Western Zhejiang, during the first month of autumn in the *Renxu* year of the Heavenly Opening (*Tianqi*) era.
*The Collected Works of the Elder Master Hanshan from Dream Journeys*, Volume Fifty-two.
*The Collected Works of the Elder Master Hanshan from Dream Journeys*, Volume Fifty-three.
Attendant Fuxian; Disciple Tongjing; Daily Records by Hai-chang;
Dharma Heirs Jinzhao and Jinguang; Compiled by the Elder Hanshan himself:
Autobiographical Chronicle and Real Record, Volume One.
In the year of Bingwu, the twenty-fifth year of the Jiajing era, I was born.
My surname is Cai; my father’s name is Yan’gao and my mother’s is Hong. Throughout her life, my mother had cherished the service of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara.
Initially, she dreamed that the Great Being, leading a young boy, entered her door; she received him and embraced him, whereupon she became pregnant. When the child was born, it was white—
He was born on the twelfth day of the tenth month of that year, the *jǐhài* day, at the *bǐshēn* hour, under the *jǐchǒu* branch.
This was the twenty-sixth year, the *dīngwèi* year.

When I was one year old, I suffered a stroke that nearly killed me. My mother prayed to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara), who then granted her permission for me to renounce the world and become a monk.
She registered my name at Changshou Temple in our district and subsequently changed my milk-name to "Shangheshi" (Preceptor).
In the twenty-seventh year, the Wushen year,
when I was three years old, I often sat alone and took no pleasure in playing with children. My grandfather would often say of me,
"This child is like a wooden post."
The twenty-eighth year, Jiyou;
the twenty-ninth year, Gengxu;
the thirtieth year, Xinhai.
In the thirty-first year, the Renzi cycle, when I was seven years old, my paternal uncle doted on me. My parents sent me to join the village school.
One day, my uncle died and lay upon his bed. When I returned home, my mother deceived me, saying, "Your uncle is sleeping; you may call him to wake up. Thereupon, I called out to him.
After several cries, my aunt was overcome with grief and wept, saying, "O Heaven! Where have you gone?
I was startled and suspicious of this, so I asked my mother, "My uncle’s body is right here; where else could he have gone? My mother replied, "Your uncle is dead."
I asked, "After death, where does one go? and I began to harbor this doubt most earnestly. Not long after, my younger aunt gave birth to a son.
When the mother went to see him, I followed her. Seeing that the infant was already as large as this, I asked the mother, "How did this child enter your womb, Aunt?
The mother clapped her hand once and said, "Foolish boy! Where did you enter [my]..."
"Did you enter your mother’s womb? He again questioned him with urgency. Consequently, the doubt regarding death and rebirth remained unresolved within his heart.
In the thirty-second year, the Gui-chou year.
When I was eight years old, I went to study while living with relatives across the river. My mother warned me not to return home, yet I returned once every month.
One day, having returned, I was so attached to my mother that I refused to leave. My mother grew angry and whipped me, driving me toward the riverbank.
Still refusing to board the boat, she became enraged; she grabbed my topknot and threw me into the river, then turned her back and departed without looking back.
At that time, his grandmother saw him and hurriedly called out for help to raise him up. She sent him back home. His mother said, "This is an unworthy child;
why should I keep him instead of drowning him? She beat him and drove him away, showing not the slightest lingering affection.

At that moment, I privately remarked to myself that my mother’s heart was cruel, and from then on, I no longer thought of home. My mother would often stand by the river weeping, and my grandmother scolded her. My mother—
He said, "You must certainly sever your attachments before you can truly read books.
In the thirty-third year, Jia-yin, when I was nine years old,
I was reading in the temple and heard a monk reciting the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra, which he said could save one from the sufferings of the world.
His heart was filled with great joy. He then questioned a monk to seek out its origin and read it in secret; he was immediately able to recite it from memory.

His mother had been devoted to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and whenever she burned incense and prostrated herself, he would invariably follow her. One day he said to his mother, "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva has a single sutra.
His mother replied, "I do not know of one. He then recited it for his mother once; his mother was greatly [impressed].
Master Xi said, "From where did you obtain this? Your voice reciting the sutras also resembles that of the Old Monk.

In the year Yimao, the thirty-fourth year [of the sexagenary cycle], when I was ten years old, my mother was extremely strict in supervising my studies. Finding it burdensome, I asked my mother, "What is the purpose of reading books? My mother—
He said, "To hold office. I asked, "What kind of office? His mother said, "Start from the bottom; if you have ability, you can reach the rank of Prime Minister.
I said, "Once one has become Prime Minister, what then? His mother said, "Resign.
I said, "It is a pity that after a lifetime of toil, it all ends in resignation. What is the use of such a thing? I think one should simply be someone who never resigns."
The mother said, "A son such as you is truly unfilial; you can only become a 'lodging monk' (guàtā sēng). I asked, "What is a lodging monk?
What merit is there in it? The mother replied, "A monk is a disciple of the Buddha who travels throughout the world."
[The Master] was free and at ease; offerings were available everywhere. He said, "Doing this is exactly right.
His mother said, "I only fear that you lack such merit. He asked, "Why would one need merit? His mother replied, "In this world, those who become provincial champions (zhuangyuan) are common enough.
But those who leave the household life to become Buddhas and Patriarchs—how could they be so common? He said, "I possess this merit; I only fear that my mother does not [recognize it]."
"I can give it up. His mother said, "If you possess such merit, I shall indeed be able to give it up," and she took note of this in secret.
In the thirty-fifth year, the Bingchen year, when I was eleven years old, I happened to see several traveling monks approaching with gourds and bamboo hats slung over their shoulders. I asked them:

"Mother, who is this person? The mother replied, "He is a *tāta-saṃgha* (a monk). I felt a private sense of joy and looked at him. When the monk arrived, he set down his burden and leaned against a tree.
I then asked after his health and invited him for a meal. The mother said, "Please sit," and she hurriedly brewed tea and prepared the meal with great reverence.
After he had finished eating, the assembly of monks rose; the monk immediately took up his burden, lifting it with a single hand. The mother quickly stepped aside and said:
"Do not thank me," the monk said, and he departed. I remarked, "How discourteous is this monk? He does not even thank me for the meal. My mother replied, "If you thank him, there will be no merit.
I thought to myself privately, "This is precisely why this monk is so eminent. I must keep this in mind. Thereupon, I resolved to leave the household life;
it was only that I lacked a convenient way to do so.
In the thirty-sixth year, the *ding-si* year, I was twelve years old.
Having read and mastered the meaning of the texts, my local clan and kin all held me in high regard. I was generally disinclined toward worldly affairs;
when my father arranged a marriage for me, I refused and stopped it. One day, I heard a monk from the capital speak of the Great Master Seonil of Bongeunsa.
"Upādhyāya, there is a man of great virtue. My heart desires to go and follow him. He informed his father, but his father would not permit it.

He informed his mother, who said, "In raising a son, one should follow his aspirations; let us simply allow him to achieve his goal. She then sent him forth. That year, in the tenth month, he arrived at the temple.
Upon seeing him, the Grand Preceptor (Taishi-weng) was delighted and said, "This child’s bone and spirit are extraordinary. If he is..."
"A secular monk? What a pity! I shall invite the Master to teach him to read and see how he develops.
At that time, Grand Master Wujie was beginning his lectures at the Sanzang Hall of the temple; the Patriarch took [the boy] along to visit him.
It happened that Zhao Dazhou was present, who, upon seeing him, said with joy, "This child is destined to be a teacher of gods and men," and then stroked him.
A questioner asked, "You love to hold office, yet you wish to become a Buddha. I replied at once, "I wish to become a Buddha. Zhao Gong said, "This child must not be underestimated;
you should instruct him well. When he went to listen to the lectures, although he did not understand what was being said, [he remained attentive].

Yet my mind was filled with resentment. If there were those who knew [the truth] but could not attain realization, at that time, my elder brother Xuelang—born one year after me—had entered the monastic order under the Great Master one year prior.
Seeing me, he looked at me and laughed; people of the time considered us to be "brothers from the same womb.
The opening of lectures on the Buddha-dharma in Jiangnan began with the Great Master Wuji. At a young age, I entered...
Regarding the Buddha-dharma, it began with Xuelang.
In the thirty-seventh year, the Wuma year, when I was thirteen years old, the Grand Preceptor Zu selected among his grandsons those who were learned and practiced; Jun Gong was chosen for me.
The Master first taught him the Lotus Sūtra, which he completed by heart in four months.
In the year Jiwu (1679), when I was fourteen years old, he circulated various sūtras, all of which I was able to recite from memory. The Grand Master said, "This child is worthy of instruction."
"One must not let him go astray. Thereupon, he invited a master proficient in literature to instruct him.

In the thirty-ninth year, Gengshen (1560), when I was fifteen years old, my Grandfather, the Grand Preceptor, requested a Master to teach me the curriculum for the civil service examinations. I began my studies immediately.
Since he was capable of being taught, I had him read the Four Books all at once.
That year I fell frequently ill;
in the fortieth year, the Xin-you year, when I was sixteen, I completed the Four Books and recited them from beginning to end without missing a single character.
In the forty-first year, the Renxu year, I was seventeen years old.
During that year, I lectured on the Four Books, studied the *I Ching*, as well as the temporal arts, classical prose, and poetry and fu;
I was immediately able to compose poems and write essays, such that among the youths of the time, none could surpass me.
In the forty-second year, Guihai (1623),
when I was eighteen years old, the Imperial Commissioner for Education was exclusively lecturing on Daoxue (Neo-Confucianism) and treated candidates for the first degree as mere singing boys.
They moved in groups of several dozen, singing as they followed their ranks; there were even those who sought advancement through such means.
I felt great shame for this and consequently desired to abandon my studies. That year, due to illness, I declined the invitation and did not enter the library.
In the forty-third year, the Jiazi year, I was nineteen years old.
My fellow students at the academy had all achieved success in the examinations, and some urged me to go and take the test as well.
At that time, the Great Master Yungu—a true possessor of the Eye of the Right Dharma—was residing at Mount Xixia; my late grandfather had long supported him, so I went there.
Whenever he came, he would invariably stay for ten days or a month. I served him with great diligence. It happened that Grand Master Yun left the mountain;

hearing that someone had urged me [to leave], I feared he might have the intention to depart. The Grand Master earnestly instructed me on the transcendence of the world through Zen meditation, revealing the wondrousness of awakening to the mind-ground.
He recounted the various patriarchs of the *Denglu* (Transmission of the Lamp) and the *Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks), commanding me to go and read them. I...
He opened his book chest and found the *Extensive Record of Zhongfeng*. Before he had finished reading even one fascicle, he felt great joy and exclaimed, "This is what my heart has been longing for!
He then resolved to leave secular life and immediately requested his grandfather to shave his head and grant him the tonsure.

He completely burned away and discarded all that he had previously studied, focusing his mind exclusively on investigating a single matter. When he had not yet grasped its essential point, he concentrated his mind on the recitation of the Buddha’s name, continuing day and night without interruption.
Not long after, one night in a dream, he beheld Amitābha Buddha appearing in person, standing in the air at the place where the sun was setting.
He gazed upon the features of the Buddha’s face and the radiance of His eyes, seeing them with perfect clarity. I [received this account].

He performed his prostrations with deep reverence, his grief and longing never ceasing. He further prayed to behold the two Bodhisattvas, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, who immediately appeared in half-form.
From that time on, the three sages were vividly present before his eyes at all times, and he gained confidence that his practice could be successfully accomplished.
That winter, a dharma hall was established in the meditation hall of his home temple, where he invited Great Master Wujie to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*’s *Xuantan*.

I immediately received the full precepts from him. Following his lectures until I reached the "Ten Mysterious Gates," I suddenly attained a clear realization of the principle of the inexhaustible, perfectly interfused Dharmadhātu—the state where the ocean-seal of all phenomena eternally abides.

Deeply admiring the character of Master Qingliang (Zongmi), I therefore chose for myself the style name Chengyin (Ocean-Seal) and requested his correction. The Great Master said, "Your aspiration is to enter this Dharma."

As for the name "Gate": because one sees that on Mount Qingliang there is solid ice accumulated in winter and flying snow even in summer, with never a trace of scorching heat, it is thus called "Qingliang" (Cool and Refreshing).
From this point on, the landscape of ice and snow where one walks and dwells will naturally appear before one's eyes.
I vowed my life’s resolve to dwell therein. There was not a single matter that could satisfy my heart; the thought of renouncing the world never left me for a moment.
In the forty-fourth year, the year of Yi-chou (1765).
I was twenty years old. On the sixteenth day of the first month of that year, my Grand Preceptor passed away.
The previous year, on the eve of the New Year, the Preceptor had gathered all his kinsmen and said, "I am eighty-three years old;
my departure is imminent. Of the eighty-odd disciples I have ordained, not one carries on my lineage. He then patted me on the back.
He said, "I have looked forward to this boy reaching maturity, but now it seems he cannot. Although he is young in years, he possesses the insight of a mature man.

After my death, all matters, both great and small, regarding the temple quarters shall be decided by him; do not treat him with contempt because of his youth. The assembly sighed deeply and received his charge.
On the seventh day of the New Year, the Master prepared his robes and toured the various quarters one by one. Each...
He took his leave. The assembly all marveled at this. Three days later, he attended to his final affairs and manifested a slight illness.
When the medicine was offered, he refused to take it, saying, "I am departing; what need is there for medicine? He then gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name for five days and nights.
Holding a rosary in his hand and cradling it in his embrace, he passed away with serene composure. This was because throughout his life, the Master had maintained the *Vajra* [Sūtra].

Even at the time of his death, he did not cease reciting the sutras. The Grand Preceptor, who had resided as the Abbot for thirty years while serving as an official in the Bureau of Gratitude, passed away on the eighteenth day of the third month;
at that time, the abbot’s quarters caught fire, which everyone marveled at as a miraculous sign.
In the tenth month of winter that year, the Great Master Yungu established a period of Chan practice at Tianjie Temple.

He assembled fifty-three men of renowned virtue from throughout the land and opened the dharma-gate of seated meditation (*zuo chan*). The Great Master exerted every effort to urge me to go and follow him;
the Junior Preceptor (Weng) granted permission, and thus I was able to join the assembly. At first, I did not know the secret of applying the mind and suffered greatly. Then—
He offered incense and requested instruction. The Master gave him an opening teaching on the koan of "Investigating the Reality of Nianfo.

From then on, he applied himself to this investigation with unwavering focus. Within three months, it was as if he were in a dream; he no longer perceived the presence of the assembly, nor was he aware of his daily activities.
The entire community regarded him as one possessed of great resolve. After only a few days, because of his application...
His mind was too hasty. Suddenly, he developed a carbuncle on his back; it became red, swollen, and enormous. The Master found this very distressing.
I donned my *kāṣāya* and, with earnest and piteous prayers before Weituo, said: "This must surely be the pursuit of a life-debt from past karmic retribution.

I pray that you permit me to recite ten volumes of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. I request leave for three months to complete my period of meditation; thereafter, I shall repay this debt. When [the illness] reached...

During the latter part of the night, being utterly exhausted, I ascended the meditation platform and fell into a deep sleep; I was unaware even when the period of seclusion ended. Upon waking, I had forgotten it.
When day broke, the Master asked how my ailment was. I replied, "I am well. When he looked at me, I had already fully recovered.
The entire assembly marveled at this, and thus I was able to complete the full term of retreat. Even after leaving, it was as if I had never been away.
While sitting in meditation, I would walk through the marketplace as if seeing not a single person; at that time, everyone considered this strange.
In Jiangnan, people had never known Chan before, and it was Master Yungu who first established the Chan path there.
Among the young monks practicing Chan, I was the only one. At that time, the temple monks’ attire followed secular fashion, with many wearing bright, flamboyant colors.
I completely discarded all my accustomed clothing and sought out only a single *nāṃsa* (patchwork robe) to wear it. Those who saw me considered it strange.

In the forty-fifth year, the year of Bingyin, when I was twenty-one years old, I emerged from the period of meditation. On the eighteenth day of the second month of that year, at the hour of the horse (noon). Great...
The rain fell like an overturned basin. Suddenly, a great thunderclap descended from the pagoda, and fire erupted from the pagoda hall. Before long, the main hall was consumed by flames.
By the time of the Shen and You watches, more than one hundred and forty rooms, including the various halls and painted corridors, were reduced to ashes and embers.
At that time, my late grandfather served as the abbot. When the matter was reported to the throne, an imperial decree was issued to the Ministry of Justice, and they were arrested in succession.
