There were eighteen fellow practitioners. Fearing that they might be implicated, the monks of the entire temple each fled in different directions.

However, the administrative monks of the temple had no one with whom to deliberate on the matter. I stood forth alone to rescue them by force; I personally carried salt and vegetables to the prison to provide for them.
The temple was twenty *li* away from the Ministry of Justice, yet I traveled back and forth three times without weariness.
Yue, meanwhile, employed various means of protection and care, so that those involved in the matter were ultimately spared from death.
At that time, he and Master Xuelang En both resolved upon the will to restore [the site], saying: "This is a great causal connection;
it is not easily accomplished by one who does not possess great merit, fortune, and wisdom. We must both risk our lives in practice, waiting for the opportune moment. At that time...
He immediately resolved to travel far away. Shortly thereafter, his younger grandfather passed away;

as there was no one to support the patriarch’s household, and since the Master’s father had previously passed away leaving no savings, all funeral expenses were obtained through loans without any private funds.

Consequently, many debts remained unpaid, and we were forced to divide our residence. Realizing that it was impossible to maintain the estate, I reflected upon the final instructions of my late grandfather, the Grand Preceptor (Taishi).
I therefore devised a plan to fully repay all the outstanding loans; as for the remainder, it was distributed among the disciples, each of whom took up their own vocation.
Thus, the temple buildings and gates were ultimately preserved. That winter, I followed Master Wujie to Tianjie Temple to hear the *Lotus Sūtra*. Because of this—
Zhiyuan intended to travel afar. He frequently observed the monks from various quarters, seeking one who could serve as his companion. After a long time, he had still not found such a person.

One day, seeing that the rear hall was exceptionally clean and pure, he thought to himself that the *śayanāsana-pālaka* (the monk in charge of cleanliness) must be no ordinary man, and so he went to inquire after him.

Upon meeting him, he found he was merely a monk suffering from jaundice and swelling; yet every morning, when the master rose, all tasks were already fully completed, for it was unknown at what hour he had performed the sweeping and cleansing.
Therefore, I could not sleep. I secretly walked along the corridor to observe him. Just as the assembly was dismissing the session, he had already finished his cleaning.
After several more days, I saw that it was still unclean, yet the man was nowhere to be seen.
When I questioned the attendant, he said, "The janitor is ill in the guest room. I went to see his condition; it was truly pitiable. I asked him, "How are you, Master?"
"No," he replied. "The physical ailments caused by karmic obstructions are already difficult to bear, but the sickness of gluttony is even harder to endure. I asked why this was so.
He said, "Whenever I see others practicing vegetarianism, I long to cast it all aside as well. I laughed and said, "This is merely the chronic illness of craving food."

Knowing that this man was genuine, he prepared some fruit cakes, tucked them under his arm, and went to see him. He asked the man’s name, which was Miaofeng, and learned that he was a native of Puzhou.
The master immediately made an appointment with him to travel together as companions. A few days later, he went to see him again.
Thus he was not seen. I knew him in my heart, yet fearing that he might be burdened by me, he moved in secret.
In the first year of the Longqing era, the year Dingmao, when I was twenty-two years old, I specifically appointed Master Zhong of Xugu as the abbot of the temple to save it from its state of ruin.

Subsequently, due to a fire incident, the monastery’s permanent assets were burdened with debts totaling nearly a thousand *qian*. All these matters passed through my hands, and the community was at a loss as to how to manage them.

I devised a plan, setting a three-year limit for the full repayment of the debt. In that same year, I received an official summons from the Ministry to establish a school of righteousness (*yixue*) at this temple to instruct the monastic community;
I was requested to serve as the teacher, imparting lessons to one hundred and fifty novice monks.
Regarding others: because of this, I again examined the records of the Left Historian and the ancient prose and poetry of the various masters.
In the second year, Wuchen (1628), I was twenty-three years old.
That year, I resigned from my duties at the library and returned to reside at Gaozuo Monastery, using the room at the gate—
Thus it was with accumulated weight.
In the third year, Jisi (1539), I was twenty-four years old. That year, Jinshan invited me to serve as his tutor. I resided there for one year.
In the fourth year, Gengwu, I was twenty-five years old. That year, I again accepted the invitation from Jinshan.
In the fifth year, Xinwei.
I was twenty-six years old. Because my home temple had been destroyed by fire, I resolved to restore it;
intending to cultivate practice to nourish the Way and await the right time, I set out on a long journey that year. First, I traveled with my elder brother Xuelang En to Mount Lu.
Upon reaching Nankang, hearing that the mountains were infested with many tigers and disturbances, I did not dare ascend them. Consequently, I caught the wind and traveled to Jixian, where I toured.
When Qingyuan saw that the temple was in ruins and the monks were all wearing their hair long, he felt a profound sense of regret and resolved to restore it.
He then addressed the local authorities and selected those under forty years of age to shave their heads; more than forty men were thus recruited.
During the summer, he returned from Qingyuan to attend to his late master’s affairs, settling everything with due propriety. In the eleventh month of winter, he departed with but a single bowl.
On a distant journey, as he was about to travel north, Xuelang stopped him, fearing he would not be able to endure the bitter cold. "For now, you might as well go to Wuyue;
there are many fine mountains and waters where one may delight the eyes and ears. Xuyi replied, "The habitual tendencies of us humans are such that we cling to what is soft and warm."
Only when one reaches a place where no further aid can be given does it become easy to exercise self-restraint; [otherwise], it would be like [traversing] the land of Wu and Yue as if on a bed.
Thereupon, with a single bowl, he departed for a long journey.
In the sixth year, the year of Renshen (792).
At the age of twenty-seven, I first arrived in Yangzhou. Heavy snow blocked my way, and I fell ill.
After a long time, I went to beg for food in the marketplace, but I could not even enter the gates. I wondered to myself why this was so;

I quickly examined myself and realized it was because I had two small silver coins tucked in my waistband that I could rely upon. Thereupon, I saw monks and Daoists in the snow who were unable to obtain alms. Immediately—
He invited everyone to a tavern and threw silver coins at them; they finished their meal in a single sitting.

The next day, he went out into the streets and entered one or two gates before he was finally able to call out for food, whereupon he obtained it. He said to himself with joy, "My strength is sufficient to treat ten thousand *zhong* of grain as light as a feather."
He inscribed his alms bowl, saying: "The means to regard ten thousand *zhong* of grain as light. He inscribed his patched robe, saying: "The means to regard the entire world as light.
Then he composed this inscription for them: "You entrust me with your form; I entrust myself to you with my mind.
Thus, a single body is naturally sufficient through this, and the myriad things are truly rendered light by it. Just as I am about to trail the sleeves of the long wind and don the white [robe]..."
The folds of his robe were like the wings of a great swan when he raised them, and like the scales of a hidden dragon when they flowed.
He wandered at ease through the universe, departing and dwelling among the mountains and forests. Why should he display the splendor of crimson and purple?
He sought only that which neither frost nor snow could invade. In the seventh month of the autumn of that year, he arrived at the capital, yet had nowhere to set foot.
In this place, I wandered for alms all day long but was unable to obtain any food. At dusk, I reached the tea warehouse of Xitai Pingcang and obtained but a single meal.
I took up lodging at Yijiao Temple by the river canal. The next day, when Director of the Left, Mr.
Wang Boyu, learned of my arrival, he invited me; this was because he and Mr. Cigong Zhongyan were fellow members of the literary society. Thus, I was able to stay there.
After ten days, I visited Dharma Master Mahāzhong and followed him to the Western Mountains (*Xishan*) to listen to the *Miaozongchao*.

There was a poem by my elder brother Huaien of the Western Mountains expressing his expectations for the end of the session. When it concluded, Mahāzhong invited me to stay through the winter to hear the *Fahua* and *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Weishi), with Dharma Master An serving as the expounder.
We also studied the three-membered syllogism (*trirūpa-hetu*) of Hetuvidyā. In the eleventh month, Master Miaofeng came to visit me.
He arrived. His beard and hair were long, and he was dressed in coarse cloth garments. He first announced, "A salt merchant has come to visit.
Upon entering the gate, the Master asked, "Do you still recognize me? I looked at him intently and saw the Master’s two eyes;

suddenly, I remembered that he was formerly the head attendant (jingtou) during my illness at Tianjie Temple. I said, "I recognize you. The Master said, "Your head has been changed and your face has been transformed. I...
[The Master] said, "The original face is naturally free; let us share a smile and have no time for anything else. He then asked where [the visitor] was staying.
[The visitor] replied, "I shall come to visit you tomorrow at Longhua. That night, as they sat together, [the Master] asked about his appearance, "Why is it like this?
The Master said, "Because I have lived in the mountains for a long time, my hair has grown long and remains uncut. Just now, because of the donor, His Highness the Prince of Shanyin, I..."
One of them was from a Brahma palace; he had come specifically to invite [the Master] to the Inner Treasury. When asked about his circumstances, he said:

"I have come specifically to seek the Master, and furthermore to behold the splendor of the imperial capital and to consult with a spiritual friend (jñānin), so as to sever all future delusive thoughts. The Master said:
"There has been no moment since we parted that I have not thought of you. I had supposed that there was no karmic connection between us; now, fortunately, you have come.
I wish to accompany you on your alms-rounds, acting as your vanguard to drive away the dogs. After conversing throughout the night, they laughed together at dawn and parted.
He then went to visit Master Bianrong, where he prostrated himself and requested the Master’s instruction. The Master remained silent, merely gazing directly at him.
I visited Master Xixian. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? I replied, "From the South. The Master said, "Do you remember the path by which you came?
I said, "Once passed, it is simply over. The Master said, "You, however, have a clear understanding of where you have come from.
I prostrated, stood in attendance, and requested further instruction. The Master gave me several words of guidance regarding the ultimate Way (*shangxiang*), and we parted.

In the first year of the Wanli era, the year of Guiyou (1573), when I was twenty-eight years old, I traveled to Mount Wutai in the first month of spring. First, I sought out the *Qingliang zhuan* (Biography of Qingliang) and followed its traces to explore the mountain.
Upon reaching the Northern Terrace, I saw Hanshan and asked where that mountain was; the monk pointed it out, and indeed—

It was extraordinary and beautiful; he silently took it as his name and composed a poem to record it. There was a line that read: "Let go of those who follow you, and for now, let this serve to stifle the workings of the mind.
Because he could not endure the bitter cold of the ice and snow, he was unable to remain there and once again entered the capital to travel eastward.
While begging for alms, he reached Mount Pan, where at a stone grotto in Qianxiang Valley, he saw a monk who did not speak; he, too, [remained silent].
He did not inquire further; instead, they gathered firewood together, drew water, and went begging for alms.
Sima Wang sent a letter inquiring after him, saying, "I fear you have become a starving man in the eastern suburbs. In the autumn, he entered the capital again, accompanied by Ou Zhenbo from Lingnan.
A few years prior, we had not met and I had only sent him letters. Now, having become a State Scholar (Guobo), he was in urgent need to see me; therefore, I returned.

In the second year, Jiashu (1514), when I was twenty-nine years old, I traveled to the western mountains of the capital during the spring. Among the renowned scholars of the time were the two Wangs and the two Wangs.
Together with Ou Zhenbo of the South Sea, they all gathered in the capital at one time. One day, he visited Wang Changgong of Fengzhou;

upon meeting, [Wang] underestimated me because I was young. I treated him with haughty courtesy as host and guest, but he immediately began to instruct me earnestly on the methods of composing poetry.
I stared at him blankly and eventually took my leave without uttering a single word. He was displeased, and so...
This was said regarding Cigong Linzhou. The next day, Cigong came to visit. Upon seeing him, he immediately said, "Last night, my elder brother lost one of his eyes.
I asked, "Do you yourself possess the single eye? He bowed with joined palms and said, "The younger brother has met [the master].
We both laughed heartily and returned home. Cigong said to his brother, "Elder brother, you have lost to Vimalakīrti."
I understood this and presented him with a poem, which contained the lines: "One may know Wang Yishao for his principles; in fame and reasoning, he yields to Master Zhigong.
One day, while Wang Cigong and I were living together and reading the *Zuozhuan*, he said to me:
"Your natural endowment is exceptionally extraordinary; you possess a great spirit for literature. Your elder brother is a literary paragon of the age. Why do you not..."
[Zhi]ye said, "Is this to establish the reputation of a single school? I laughed and spat, saying, "Keep your knees for yourself, elder brother;
one day you shall pay homage to an old monk and receive the meaning of the Western Transmission. Next Gong was greatly displeased and returned to inform Sima Gong.
Gong said, "It is true. I observe the integrity of Master Yin’s character; in the future, he shall enter into the lineage of Dahui."
The Master of Feng’s Studio said, "How could I possibly concern myself with such trivialities as written words? I only fear that drifting aimlessly may lead to error.
Upon seeing the poem I had written on a fan for Cigong, which contained the lines, "In this world and body, I am like two cicada wings;

in heaven and earth, I am but a single hair on a horse's tail," he showed it to Cigong and said, "Is this truly a monk of mere words? He then specifically prepared a vegetarian feast and invited [the Master] for another day.
I was sitting together with Master Miao when the Duke said to me, "The Chan school is desolate and deeply lamentable; you, my young disciple, must take this to heart.
Judging by your capacity and character, your future achievements will be no small matter. Why wander aimlessly?

I replied, "This poor monk has come specifically for the sake of the great causal conditions to visit and consult with wise teachers. For now, I am merely traveling to broaden my perspective on the present age."
"Regarding this person, it was merely to exhaust his delusions of future days; it was not a casual wandering. Furthermore, as he is about to depart," the Master said, "I truly believe so.
I observe that among those of today, there is no one who could serve as your teacher. If it were not for Miaofeng, you would have no friend.
I replied, "In the past, I already sought him out from among the multitude and once entered into a covenant with him as fellow practitioners. Therefore, [he has gone] north..."

I came seeking you, and did not expect to encounter you here by chance. The Master said, "How extraordinary! If these two gentlemen truly set out on their journey, I, your humble servant, wish to serve as their guide.
At that time, Master Miao was returning with the Tripitaka scriptures;
Sima Gong therefore presented him with two *kanhe* (certificates of authorization) and composed a letter to send with me. One day, the Master hurriedly summoned me and asked, "Miaofeng is departing."
"Why do you not see me off? I replied, "Please walk slowly. He said, "I know that you do not wish to follow in the footsteps of others;
however, this is far from the case. The ancients were not ashamed of minor details, but were ashamed that their achievements were not manifest throughout the world.
I only hope that one day you will accomplish a brilliant feat for the Dharma."
Furthermore, why concern oneself with such petty deliberations over whether to leave or stay? Moved by these words, I bowed in thanks and resolved to depart.
I went at once to see Master Miao, only to find him already seated in his carriage. Seeing me arrive, he asked, "Are you going? I replied, "I am going.
He immediately climbed into the carriage and departed without bidding a single person farewell. In the eighth month of autumn, they crossed the Mengjin River and saw King Wu inspecting his troops.
At that site, there was a poem in mourning for him which said: "A single stone and a weathered stele lean against the riverbank; In years past, it was here that the lords of men gathered.

May the royal framework remain as firm as heaven and earth, Flowing on forever like the Yellow River. Passing the place where Bo Yi and Shu Qi struck their horses to refuse the throne, he offered this lament:
"To renounce the state and cast aside glory—his resolve was profound; Now only the ancient temple remains, with its cypress trees standing dense. Shouyang..."

The mountain scenery is as clear and serene as this; it still evokes the heart that once struck the horse’s hooves [to urge the Master forward]. I then entered Shaolin to pay my respects to the First Patriarch.
At that time, the Master Dajian Run had recently taken up residence at the monastery. I went to visit him, but did not meet him.

I left the mountain to view the ancient city of Luoyang, the Platform for Burning Scriptures, and Baima Temple, whereupon I pursued Master Miao. In the ninth month, I arrived in Hedong and met Master Shan.

The winter months arrived, and I remained there to spend the season. At that time, the Prefect, Lord Chen, extended an invitation to Master Miaoyan and myself with great sincerity, commissioning us to carve the *Zhongwu Jijie* (Collected Explanations from the Mid-South) of the *Zhaolun*.

I served as the proofreader. Previously, I had not understood the purport of the "Whirling Gale Overthrows Mountains" passage in the *Bujian lun* (Treatise on Non-Regression), and I had harbored doubts for a long time.
Upon reaching this point now, I was still bewildered—until we reached the section concerning the Brahmin.
Having left home to become a monk in his youth, he returned with white hair. A neighbor saw him and said, "Is that still the same man from before?
Zhì replied, "I resemble the man of old, but I am not the man of old. Suddenly attaining clear realization, he said, "Truly, all dharmas are fundamentally without coming or going.
He immediately descended from his meditation seat to prostrate before the Buddha, yet there was no appearance of movement; he lifted the curtain and stood upon the steps.
Earlier, when a sudden wind blew through the courtyard trees and flying leaves filled the sky, he perceived no sign of movement at all and said:
"This is like a whirlwind that topples mountains yet remains eternally still. Later, when he went out to relieve himself and found no sign of flow at all, he said:
"This is like the great rivers rushing together yet not flowing. Thereupon, his doubts regarding coming and going, birth and death, were completely dissolved like ice melting away. Thus it was.
There is a verse that says: "Birth and death come day and night; The river flows and flowers wither. Only today do I know: The nostrils point downward.
The next day, Master Miao met him and said joyfully, "What have you attained?
The master replied, "Last night I saw two iron oxen fighting by the riverbank and plunging into the water; to this day, there has been no further news of them. Master Miao laughed and said:
I was glad to have the capital for dwelling in the mountains. Before long, Chan Master Faguang of Niu Mountain arrived at my invitation from Shanyin.

I had long admired him; upon meeting him, I rejoiced at the opportunity to sit and study under his guidance. Our dialogue was harmonious in its spiritual resonance, and I requested further instruction.

He instructed me to practice by departing from mind, intellect, and consciousness, leading me beyond the paths of both ordinary beings and sages. I studied deeply until I attained his essential meaning.

Whenever I saw the Master engage in discourse, his voice resonated like the sound of celestial drums. At that time, I realized that those who have awakened to the ground of the mind produce speech and breath that are truly distinct.
I was profoundly moved by his character. One day, I found a poem of mine inside my bag.
He read it and sighed, saying, "From where did these excellent lines come? He then laughed and said, "They are indeed excellent, yet one 'hole' remains unpenetrated.
I asked, "Has the Master penetrated that one hole? The Master replied, "For thirty years I have been seizing dragons and catching tigers;
today, a rabbit has bolted out from the grass and taken a leap. I [did not respond].
[The Master] said, "The Abbot does not possess the hand that seizes dragons and captures tigers.

As the Master raised his staff, just about to strike, I immediately seized it and stroked his beard with my hand, saying, "You say this is a rabbit; it is actually a shrimp. The Master laughed and withdrew.
One day the Master said, "You need not go elsewhere. I hope you will remain here with me at Old Vufu; this is what I desire."
I said, "Observing your master’s Buddhist dharma and his eloquence, they are no less than those of Dahui. Yet, when you are at ease, you seem to have the manner of one who is mad;
your chanting never ceases from your hands or mouth—what does this mean? The Master replied, "This is my 'Zen illness.
When I first attained awakening, verses flowed forth like a stream, uninterrupted day and night. Since then, I have been unable to stop it, and thus it has become an illness."
[The Master] said, "I heard this. I asked, 'When this illness first broke out, how was it treated?

The Master replied, 'Once this illness breaks out, if one cannot see through it oneself, one must have a person of great insight strike one severely with a staff, causing one to fall into a deep sleep.
Upon waking, it will naturally vanish. At first, I regretted that he did not possess a "poisonous hand" [to strike me]. Toward the end of the year, the Master knew..."
I departed for Mount Wutai at the beginning of the new year. He then presented me with a poem to see me off, which contained the lines:
"The lion from among the clouds comes to gaze; let the hidden dragon within the cave go free. He asked, "Do you understand this? I replied, "I do not."
The Master said, "I only wish that you would not grasp at a dead snake. I nodded in agreement. For a long time, there had been no master of the Way of Chan;
it was only upon meeting Master Guang that I first understood the strategic maneuvers of the School.

When the Ruler of Shanyin inquired after my parents' well-being, he presented me with two hundred pieces of gold as funds for their support until their passing. I declined, saying, "When I first set out on this mendicant path..."
My feet are such that I cannot even save myself; how then could I dare trouble my parents? For this reason, I yielded to Master Caizhao.
In the third year, the year of Yihai, when I was thirty years old, I set out from Hedong with Master Tongmiao in the first month to ascend Mount Wutai, passing through Pingyang. Master...
This was his hometown. Because his master had been poor since youth, he encountered a year of famine during which his parents died; there were no coffins or funeral implements for their burial.
At this time, Shan-yin and one or two officials of the provincial government assisted him. I selected a high and spacious plot of land for them to be buried together.
I composed his funerary inscription. The Master’s secular surname was Xu; he resided in the eastern suburb of Pingyang. He was likely a descendant of the Xu Juju of the Spring and Autumn period.
Lord Hu, styled Shun’an, was a native of Donglai. Hearing that I had arrived, he stayed outside the city walls, wishing to see me but unable to do so.
When I was about to depart, the Lord sent me a postal pass. I said, "For a practitioner on pilgrimage..."
"It is merely a straw sandal. Why do you value it so highly? When I was about to depart, he followed after me. We met at Lingshi, and together we proceeded to Huicheng.
He stayed for several days to converse with me, and then dispatched attendants to escort me to Mount Tai.

On the full moon day of the second lunar month, I took up residence at Tayuan Temple; the master of Dafang then selected Longmen on the Northern Terrace as my dwelling place. This was the best [location].
It was a secluded and precipitous place. On the third day of the third month, he cleared out several rafters of an old house from amidst the snowdrifts to dwell there.
At that time, seeing the myriad mountains blanketed in ice and snow, the very scene he had long yearned for, his body and mind were refreshed and serene.
It was as if entering the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Before long, Miaofeng went to wander in the realm of the dead, leaving me alone to dwell here.

I maintained a single-minded focus, remaining silent when people came and merely observing them with my eyes. After a long time, I viewed people as if they were wooden stumps, until I reached a state where not a single character could be recognized.
At first, great winds blew frequently, and the myriad apertures roared in fury; the ice melted and the water in the mountain torrents flowed.

The surging and rushing was like thunder; amidst the stillness, he heard a sound like the appearance of thousands of armies and ten thousands of horses setting out for battle, which he found deeply disturbing.
He therefore questioned Master Miao, who said, "The object arises from the mind; it does not come from without.
He then recalled an ancient saying: "If for thirty years one hears the sound of water without shifting the faculty of the mind, one shall realize the state of Avalokiteśvara."
Yuantong: On the stream above my dwelling was a bridge made of a single log. Every day I would sit or stand upon it.
At first, the sound of the water was distinct and clear; after a while, I heard it only when I gave rise to a thought, and ceased to hear it when I remained unmoving.
One day, while sitting on the bridge, I suddenly forgot my own body, and the sounds became silent. From that time on, all clamor was stilled, and they no longer disturbed me.
I eat barley bran mixed with wild vegetables daily, using rice to make a broth to accompany it. Initially, people brought three bushels of rice, yet after half a year there was still a surplus.
One day, after finishing my gruel, while walking in meditation, I suddenly became established in stillness;
body and mind vanished, leaving only a great treasury of radiant light—perfectly full, profound, and tranquil, like a great round mirror reflecting mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
The earth appeared as reflections within it, and upon awakening, all was luminous. Seeking his own body and mind, he found they were utterly unobtainable.
He then spoke this verse: "In a fleeting instant, the wild mind is stilled; The internal faculties and external objects are both transparently clear.
Turning over, I strike through the vast void; The myriad phenomena of the universe arise and cease from within. From this point on, both internally and externally, all was serene and still. No...
Furthermore, the sounds and forms of the world became obstacles; yet, from the moment of that previous encounter with doubt, they were instantly dissolved.
By the time I looked at the cauldron, it was already covered in dust. Because I was alone and without companion, I did not know how much time had passed.
In the summer of that year, my elder brother Xuelang came north to visit me. Upon reaching Mount Tai, he could not restrain his profound sorrow and took leave after staying for two nights. Winter.
I constructed a single wooden hut to dwell in.
In the fourth year, *bingzi* (1636), when I was thirty-one years old, in the third month of spring, Great Master Lianchi visited me while traveling to Mount Wutai; he stayed for several days.
Day and night we conversed, and our minds were deeply in accord. Since my own awakening that year, no one had come to seek instruction;

thus, I opened the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to verify my realization. Previously, I had never heard this sutra expounded and understood none of its meaning at all; therefore, I now simply illuminated it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
As soon as even a slight thought or consciousness arose, it could not tolerate deliberation. In this manner, eight months passed. Then—
The essential purport of the entire scripture was thus clearly understood, leaving no room for doubt.

In the seventh month of autumn, Lord Hu, the Governor of Pingyang, was transferred to the military command of Yanping and came to visit me in the mountains. In my quiet chamber, I subsisted on nothing but wild oats and a gruel of wild vegetables.
At that time, it was intensely hot down below; his attendants went to the stream to strike ice from the water and chew it. Upon seeing this, the Lord said:
It is a separate world altogether. Since I arrived here, worldly thoughts have been like this ice.

In the tenth month of winter that year, the head of the pagoda temple, Dafang, was falsely accused; the provincial authorities proposed sentencing him to exile and forcing his return to lay life, which nearly brought the monastic community to ruin.
Master Cherkong of Mount Lu came and lived with me; he happened to witness these events and suffered greatly.
I said, "It is no matter. Thereupon, I went in person to visit Master Hu. Braving the heavy snow, I went;

when I saw him, Master Hu said with delight, "I was just thinking that the great snow in the mountains would be difficult to endure, so I have already written a letter to send someone to welcome you. It is fortunate that you have come at this very moment."
This was truly moved by his sincerity. Nevertheless, he eventually took leave of his host. The site of the ritual arena remained intact, and [the host] earnestly requested that I stay for the winter.

Morning and evening, I inquired after the Way, and he spoke to me of its fundamental principles. When the High Duke of Kaifu was transferred to govern Dai Commandery, he learned that I was at the official residence and said to Lord Hu:
"My family has a garden and pavilion where many poems have been inscribed; I wish to request a poem from a man of lofty talent."
Lord Hu promised him. He addressed me with these words: "I said, 'There is not a single character within my breast; how could I possibly compose poetry?
I refused his request with all my might. Lord Hu then took a collection of ancient and modern poems and placed it upon the table to stimulate my poetic inspiration."
I happened to open [the book] and was just beginning to contemplate when, suddenly, my mental faculty stirred; thus, verses flowed forth rapidly and could not be restrained.
When Master Hu left the hall and returned, I had already composed twenty or thirty stanzas.
I suddenly realized this and said, "This is the demon of literary habit. I immediately stopped and took one verse to fill the blank space. However, the faculty...

It could not be stopped. Unconsciously, all the poetry, books, and prose compositions I had previously studied—everything that had ever entered my sight—manifested all at once, filling the void of space.
Even if my entire body were a mouth, I could not exhaustively utter them; furthermore, I no longer knew what constituted my own body or mind.
Looking inward in silence, I was in a state as if about to take flight. It was indescribable.
"What can be done? The next day, when Lord Hu saw Lord Gao off, I sat alone and reflected, saying:
"This is precisely what the Chan Master Zhengfaguang called a 'Chan sickness. Now that I am in this state, who can cure me?
If there is no other way, only deep sleep might dispel it. Thereupon, I closed the door and forced myself to lie down. At first, I was quite unable to do so; after a long while...

His "sitting-in-forgetfulness" was like being asleep. A youth knocked at the door, but it did not open; he struck it repeatedly, yet there was no response. When Master Hu returned, he inquired urgently about this.
He then ordered the window to be broken open and entered, where he saw me sitting upright, wrapped in my monastic robe. He called out to me, but I did not respond; he shook me, but I did not move.
Previously, a Buddhist offering table had been set up in the study room, upon which there was a mallet. Master Hu picked it up and asked:
He asked, "What is this object for? I replied, "When a monk from the Western Regions enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and cannot be awakened, one uses this to strike him;
he will then awaken immediately. The official suddenly remembered it and said, "Has the Master entered absorption?
He quickly took the striker and struck it against my ear several dozen times. Only then did I begin to faintly awaken; opening my eyes and looking about, I could not tell where my body was.
"It is a dwelling place. The Master said, "I am going. The Teacher immediately closed the door and sat down; it has now been five days. I said, "I do not know.
It is merely the first breath. Having finished speaking, he sat in silence and observed with clear attention, yet he ultimately did not know what this place was, nor from where it had entered.
Upon looking back at the mountains and reflecting on his past travels as a wandering monk, everything was [clear].
It is merely a matter within a dream; sought for, it cannot be found.

Then those former disturbances that pervaded all of space will vanish like rain dispersing and clouds gathering, leaving the vast sky as if washed clean—all becoming utterly still and devoid of any image. Thus, the mind is empty and the environment is tranquil.
That bliss was beyond compare. He then said: "When stillness reaches its ultimate limit, luminosity penetrates through; in silent illumination, it encompasses empty space.
Returning to observe the world, it is like a dream. Truly, the Buddha’s words do not deceive me.

At the end of the year, intending to return to the mountains at the start of the new year, he spoke to Lord Hu about how the trees and forests of Mount Yanlin were being ruthlessly felled by unscrupulous merchants. [The Bodhisattva...]
The site of the *dōjō* was about to become entirely barren and treeless. The Duke prepared a memorial and petitioned for a strict prohibition against its destruction.
Thereafter, whenever the state constructed various monasteries, they all relied upon the timber restricted by this decree; otherwise, there would have been no material from which to take.
In the fifth year, Dingchou,
when I was thirty-two years old, I returned from Yanmen in the spring. Reflecting upon the boundless kindness of my parents and mindful of the many obstacles to the Dharma,
I saw the Vow Text of the Great Master Si of Nanyue and consequently resolved to perform [the practice of] piercing [my body].
Gilding the script with blood-gold, he transcribed one volume of the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*. Above, he established a supreme connection with Prajñā;
below, he requited the boundless kindness [of his mother]. He conceived this intention in the spring of that year. Previously, the Empress Dowager Cisheng...
To preserve the state, monks were selected to recite scriptures. I presumptuously included my name among them.

When the Emperor heard that the scripture-copying was underway, he immediately granted gold-colored paper to assist the project. In the fourth month of the following year, the copying of the scriptures began.
Master Chekong had traveled to Mount Kuang; I composed ten poems to see him off.

In the sixth year, the Wuyin year, when I was thirty-three years old, I applied myself with great diligence to copying the scriptures. Regardless of whether a stroke was large or small, for every single brush mark I made, I would recite the Buddha’s name once.
Whenever monks or laypeople came to visit me while I was traveling the mountains, I invariably had my attendant announce their arrival; although I was [engaged] by hand...
He did not cease his writing; yet he never failed in his responses. To anyone who came to inquire after him, he would invariably converse for several words.
When it was high-ranking guests or old friends, he would certainly invite them to sit upon his meditation seat; he would converse with them without fail, and this did not hinder his writing.
Even when copying from an original text, he did not miss a single character. Every day was as usual, without even a trace of agitation or stillness. His neighbors...
The various senior monks privately considered this strange. They led several followers to come and verify it, intentionally causing a disturbance.
When the writing was finished, they read it and found it to be truly reliable. Thereupon, they asked Master Miao, "How is it that Master Yin is able to do such a thing? Master Miao replied:
"My friend has merely mastered this samādhi. Since I have resided on the mountain, from the time I began transcribing the sutras, I have frequently had auspicious dreams.
On the first night, I stayed at the Vajra Cave; the stone gate was inscribed with the name 'Great Prajñāpāramitā Temple.
Upon entering, I saw that it was as vast as space, with halls, pavilions, and towers of incomparable magnificence. In the main hall, there was only a great couch."
I sat down and saw the Great Master Qingliang reclining upon his bed, with Master Miao standing in attendance to his left. I hurried forward to enter, prostrated, and stood to his right.

I heard the Great Master’s instruction on the initial stage of the contemplation of the perfectly interfused realm of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which describes how Buddha-lands mutually penetrate one another, how principal and attendant deities intermingle, and the phenomenon of coming and going without movement. As he spoke of this realm, it was immediately—

He beheld it manifest before his very eyes. He realized for himself that his body and mind were interpenetrating and interfusing. Having finished showing this, Master Miao asked, "What kind of state is this?
The Great Master smiled and said, "It is the state of no-state.

After waking from the dream, he saw for himself that his mind and objects had become transparently fused, and he was once again free of doubt or obstruction. On another night, he dreamed that his own body ascended into the void, rising higher and higher.
It was boundless. When one looked down, the ten directions appeared utterly empty; only the ground stretched out like a mirror, as translucent as lapis lazuli.
From afar, there was only a vast, great tower, its dimensions equaling the void.
Within that tower were contained all the people, affairs, and activities of the world, down to the smallest matters of the marketplace. One entered...
There was nothing outside. Within the pavilion, a high seat was set up, glowing with a purple-red flame-like color;
I thought in my heart that it was a vajra-jewel throne. The pavilion was adorned with inconceivable and wondrous beauty. I felt joyful and wished to draw near, yet I reflected in my mind:
"How can there be such impurity within this pure realm? As soon as I had this thought, the pavilion immediately—
It was distant. He then reflected to himself: "Purity and defilement arise from my own mind alone. The pavilion immediately became near.
After a short while, he saw a multitude of monks standing in attendance before his seat; their stature was tall and grand, and their dignity was beyond compare.
Suddenly, a young bhikṣu emerged from behind the seat, holding a volume of scripture, and descended to present it to him, saying: "Upādhyāya, this is..."

While he was preaching this sutra, he specifically commanded that it be bestowed upon me. I received it; upon unrolling and examining it, I found it was written in golden Sanskrit characters which I did not recognize.
I then placed it within my breast. Thereupon, I asked the Venerable One who he was, and he replied, "Maitreya. I rejoiced and followed the bhikṣu upward.
Upon reaching the steps of the pavilion, I closed my eyes, collected my thoughts, and stood there. Suddenly, I heard the sound of a *kṣaṇḍa* (gong). Opening my eyes to look, I saw—

Having seen that Maitreya had already ascended the seat, I immediately paid my respects and gazed upon his face; it shone with a radiant purple-gold hue, the like of which does not exist in this world.
Having completed my prostrations, I thought to myself: "He has come specifically for me; thus, I am the one for whom he is the intended audience.
Thereupon, I knelt long and took up the scroll to unroll it. I heard him say: "Discrimination is consciousness; non-discrimination is..."

Discriminative cognition is defiled by depending on consciousness; wisdom is pure by depending on gnosis (*jñāna*). Where there is defilement, there is birth and death; where there is purity, there are the Buddhas.
Upon reaching this state, body and mind suddenly become like a dream, and one hears distinct sounds resonating from the void, which clarify the ground of the mind.

Not a single word remained [in his memory]. Upon awakening, he realized that the words were still ringing in his ears. From this point on, the distinction between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) became perfectly clear to his mind and eyes.
Furthermore, he came to know his destination: it was the pavilion of Maitreya in the Tuṣita Heaven.
On another night, a monk appeared in a dream to inform him, saying, "Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva has prepared a bath at the summit of the Northern Terrace; please go there. He followed accordingly.
Upon arriving, I entered a vast hall filled with fragrant incense, where the attendants were all Brahman monks.
They led me to a bathhouse, where I removed my clothes and entered to bathe. There I saw a person already in the pool; looking closely, I realized it was a woman.
My heart felt aversion and I did not wish to enter. The person in the pool then intentionally manifested her form, so that I knew it was indeed she.

It was a man. He entered to bathe with me; he scooped up water with his hand and poured it over me from head to toe, washing down into my five internal organs as if rinsing a meat bucket, scouring each of the five viscera until nothing remained but a single skin.
It was like a crystal cage, transparent and radiant through and through. At that time, someone in the pond called out for tea.
[The monk] saw a Buddhist monk holding a human skull, half-split like a melon; looking at it, the brain matter was dripping profusely, and he felt profound revulsion.
The monk then used his finger to scoop out some of it and showed it to me, saying, "Is this not impure? He immediately put it into his mouth and ate it;
thus he took it as it was found and ate it, finding it as sweet as molasses. Once the brain had been entirely consumed, there remained only blood and water.
A man in the pond said, "You may give it to him. The monk then handed it to me. I received it and drank it; its taste was like nectar (*amṛta*).
As I drank, it flowed down through the pores of my entire body in a single stream. When I had finished drinking, the Indian monk rubbed my back and struck me once with his palm.
I immediately awoke, at which time sweat flowed from my whole body like water, and my five internal organs were completely clear.
Indeed, from this point on, my body and mind were as if washed clean; their lightness and agility were beyond compare. Such being the case, auspicious omens abounded.
In short, everything was an exchange with the various sages. I constantly recalled the Buddha’s words: "One who frequently has such auspicious dreams shall always encounter good fortune."
In the seventh year, the Jīmō year (1619), I was thirty-four years of age. In the autumn of this year, the construction of Daciśou Temple in the capital was completed.
Initially, the Empress Dowager, in order to offer prayers for the late Emperor and to protect the Imperial person, had intended to construct temple buildings at the Five Terraces (Wutai Shan).
Regarding the construction of the Lirbao Pagoda, an edict was issued to the administrators stating that Mount Tai was too distant from the capital.
Consequently, an auspicious site near the capital was selected to build the Daci’ousi Temple. The work was completed this year.

Upon reporting this to the Empress Dowager, she remarked that it did not fulfill her aspiration for Mount Tai. She then commanded the Emperor to dispatch eunuchs along with three thousand laborers and craftsmen once again.

He came to the mountain to undertake the construction. At that time, the Imperial Court was first engaging in Buddhist affairs, and as this was the first time an inner court official had been dispatched abroad, there were fears that the project might not reach completion, thereby harming the Dharma-gate.
I personally provided protection and support, ensuring that from beginning to end it proceeded without mishap.
In the eighth year, the Gengchen year, I was thirty-five years of age.
In this year, by special imperial decree, a land survey and tax assessment was conducted throughout the empire, leaving not even a square inch of land unaccounted for.
Mount Tai had never before been included in the official registers; local officials and corrupt individuals there had sought to conceal it, intending to shift the tax burden onto other districts.

Five hundred *shí* [of grain] were allocated for Mount Tai. Repeated official inquiries were made regarding the lands, yet throughout the entire mountain, its groves, and its hermitages, there was not a single person who could find peace.
From this time on, Mount Tai became a den of foxes. Thus it was recorded in the assembly of the elders of the various mountains.

I informed him, and he comforted me, saying, "Do not worry, masters; we shall plan for this gradually. Thereupon, I employed various expedients and submitted a full report to the authorities, ultimately securing an exemption from the land survey.
Not even a single *sheng* or *he* was added [to the tax burden], and the monastic complex at Mount Tai was thus preserved in its entirety.
In the ninth year, Xinsi (1061), when I was thirty-six years of age, this year I established an *anāvaraṇa* assembly (*wu zhe hui*).

At the outset, Master Miao also drew blood to transcribe the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, sharing my aspiration to establish a perfect and complete site of practice named the *Anāvaraṇa* Assembly. Master Miao...
Fundraising was undertaken, and once the funds and provisions were fully assembled, five hundred monks of great virtue were invited from the capital.
All the requirements for the ritual site were prepared. It so happened that the Emperor issued an edict to pray for an heir to the throne;
he dispatched an official to Mount Wudang, while the Empress Dowager dispatched an official to Mount Wutai. As for this very temple, I, as a śramaṇa, considered all that was to be done...
All Buddhist services are performed for the sake of praying for blessings upon the state and providing secret support to the imperial governance.
Now, praying for the Crown Prince is the very foundation of the state; nothing is greater than this.

I pray that all matters concerning the ritual site currently being prepared may be entirely consolidated into this single matter of seeking the heir, and not be treated as a trivial concern for one’s own private self.
This was merely a name. Master Miao did not understand its meaning. The Emperor sent an inner messenger, who likewise failed to grasp the matter; his only concern was to curry favor by flattery.
I strongly disagreed with this and remonstrated against it, thereby offending him. Ultimately, however, he followed my proposal. Shortly thereafter, a sorcerer from Jiangnan caused an uprising.
Those who harbored resentment immediately sought to use this as an opportunity to slander me and destroy the monastic community (*daochang*). Nevertheless, because...
Regarding the matter of seeking an heir for the state, it was ultimately preserved, remaining free from peril from beginning to end. In this year, the stupa was completed.
I then inscribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in gold characters and enshrined it within the stupa’s treasury. There is one scroll of a vow-text.
Having personally raised funds to complete the construction of the *Huazang Shijie* (Flower-Treasury World) revolving bookcase, I established a ritual site (*dōjō*) within it for its practical use.
Regarding all necessary items—ritual implements, vessels, provisions for the fast, fruits, and everything else—the Master was as if ignorant of them while in the capital;
I managed and prepared them all single-handedly. For ninety days and nights, my eyes did not close. When the tenth month arrived and the appointed time drew near...
Master Miaoshu led the more than five hundred monks he had invited, who assembled in one day.

With over a thousand people both inside and outside the monastery, the provisions for the summer retreat—including tea, rice, and vegetarian meals—were provided with such order that nothing was missed or disordered, yet no one knew where they came from.

All who witnessed this were struck with awe. When the Water and Land Buddhist rites were first inaugurated for seven days and nights, I did not consume even a grain of rice within those seven days, drinking only water. Yet, the performance of the rituals was never deficient;

the offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas were changed every day across five hundred tables, following the proper sequence without fail, and it was unknown from where these provisions came. Those who observed this were filled with wonder.
I considered this to be the movement of the divine; I also knew it myself to be the empowerment of the Buddha’s power.
In the tenth year, the *Renwu* year, when I was thirty-seven years old, during the third month of spring, I lectured on the *Huayan xuantan*. Within the hundred days, I constantly...
At the Upper Hall, there were a thousand monks; from the ten directions, monastics and laypeople gathered like clouds, numbering no fewer than ten thousand daily.
They took their single meal together as if seated in one hall—neither jumbled nor chaotic, with not a sound of shouting or knocking heard.
All was directed by me alone; others had no part in it. Those of wisdom do not know how this came to be. Throughout my life...

My vital energy was exhausted here. When the three-month assembly concluded, I took all the remaining money and grain in the treasury—approximately ten thousand units in total—and entrusted it entirely to the administrators of this temple to serve as permanent property.
Master Miao and I then departed with nothing but our alms bowls, wandering off into the distance. Master Miao went to Luya, while I, due to illness, went to Zhending.
While staying at Jangseokyan for my retreat, I composed a poem containing the lines: "The carved cliffs pierce the heavens, surely narrowing the sun;
the severed precipices have no path, only flying ladders. In the eighth month of that year, the Crown Prince was born.
I returned to Jungbongsa Temple on Mount Jungbuk and wrote the preface for the re-engraving of the *Chungbong Gwangnok*. I then entered the winter water-retreat (*sui-jae*) in the Stone Chamber.
In the eleventh year, the Guiwei year, when I was thirty-eight years old, in the first month of spring, I completed my retreat at Shuizhai.

However, because Mount Tai was merely a hollow reputation, and it is difficult to dwell long beneath a great name, I subsequently crossed over to the shores of the Eastern Sea and first changed my title to Hanshan. At that time...
Consequently, I no longer thought of returning to Chengyin. Initially, when my monastery was destroyed by fire, my resolve was set upon its restoration;

thus, I practiced with a view toward curtailing external conditions. However, having resided on Mount Tai for eight years, I perceived that there were significant opportunities [for advancement], and fearing I might lose the right moment indefinitely, I retired to the Eastern Sea—this was my original intention.
On the eighth day of the fourth month of summer, I arrived at Laoshan. At first...
When Master Miao was away on a journey, as I could not travel alone, he appointed his dharma-kinsman Dezong as my attendant.
Initially, while reading the *Huayan* commentary on the "Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas," I encountered the passage stating:
"In the Eastern Sea there is a place called the Nārāyaṇa Cave, where from time immemorial various bodhisattvas have dwelt. The Qingliang commentary states:
In Sanskrit, *Nārāyaṇa*; here translated as "Firm and Solid" (*jiānláo*). This refers to Mount Láo (Láoshān), located in the region of Qīngzhōu comprising Dēng and Lái, as recorded in the *Yǔ Gòng*.
There exists a cave there even today. Out of admiration for it, I made a special journey to Mount Láo and indeed found the site.
However, as it was unsuitable for habitation, I explored the deepest part of the southern slopes of the mountain, where one’s back is turned toward...
Surrounded by many mountains and facing the vast ocean, it is exceedingly marvelous and extraordinary; truly, it is not of this human world.
The place is named Guanyin Ān (Avalokiteśvara Hermitage); it was an ancient monastery, now of which only the ruined foundations remain.

Upon examination, it appears that during the early Yuan dynasty, the Seven True Men emerged from the East and, utilizing the power and prestige of Emperor Shizu, took possession of many Buddhist temples and converted them into Daoist cloisters. As for Emperor Shizu...

Upon his return from the western campaign, the monk submitted a memorial to the throne, and many [monasteries] were ordered to be restored; however, because Laoshan was situated in a remote location off the coast, it had not yet been reached.
I took delight in that place’s seclusion and obscurity, for it is truly a sanctuary for those fleeing the world and seeking solitude.
It was my aspiration to dwell there. Initially, I spread a small mat beneath a tree for seven months, after which I obtained the residence of a local man named Zhang Daxin.
The scholar cleared away the weeds and built a thatched hut to dwell in. He entered the mountains for a period of one year; no people came or went, and his heart was filled with great joy.
At that time, at Ling Mountain Temple in Jimo, there was Dharma Master Guifeng, a preeminent leader of the region, who delighted in meeting him.
The twelfth year, the Gengshen year.
I was thirty-nine years old. In the seventh month of autumn, the Holy Mother, in recognition of the labor involved in praying for an heir at Mount Wutai, sought out three administrators;
these were Master Dafang Miaofeng and myself. The two masters had already arrived and received [the appointment].
An imperial gift was bestowed. However, as I could not be found when he came to visit me alone, he sought me out with great persistence.

He then commanded Rui’an, the incumbent of Longhua Temple—the former master—to visit me in person. Upon learning that I was on the sea, the Duke arrived, staff in hand, and delivered the Emperor’s compassionate decree in full.
I humbly declined, saying: "If I may be permitted by Your Majesty’s grace to remain among the mountains and seas in my old age, I shall accept this gift."
"It is already much; what more could I seek? Gongfu replied. The Imperial Will was not yet satisfied. He subsequently sought out a site to build a temple on Mount Xishan.
The Emperor repeatedly dispatched an inner messenger (neishi) to urge him to go, but I ultimately declined and did not accept.

The inner messenger returned with a report of my firm resolve to remain in the mountains and lie low. The Imperial Will took pity on me and, upon learning that I had no dwelling, [sent further instructions].
He immediately issued three thousand *kǎn* of gold and dispatched the aforementioned messenger to deliver it for the purpose of repairing his thatched cottage.
When the messenger arrived, I tried to dissuade him, saying, "My cottage of a few rafters has more than enough comfort; why do you need so much?
The messenger insisted, as he did not dare disobey the imperial command. I said, "In antiquity, there was the matter of a forged edict used to relieve the hungry; now, in the mountains..."
The harvest in the eastern provinces was poor this year. Why did you not extend your sagely compassion to the starving people?

Instead, you ordered the monks to lead the envoys to distribute [relief] throughout the various prefectures to the monastics, the elderly, the orphaned, and those in prison. Each person was required to take the official seals and registers and report back;
Your Majesty was greatly pleased and sighed with admiration without ceasing. Later, when I encountered misfortune and was brought before the Pacification Commissioner, he interrogated me.

The Emperor remarked that a sum had been drawn from the Inner Treasury. I replied that I would request an inspection of the expenditure records of the Inner Storehouse. Upon investigation, the Emperor found that these funds were used solely for this one matter of relieving famine;
there was not a single cent remaining for any other purpose. Consequently, the Emperor’s suspicions were entirely dispelled.
In the thirteenth year, the year of Yiyou (1605), I was forty years old.
People from the East had never before known monks; as I resided in the mountains, the Huang clan was the most prominent, and their sons gradually drew near to me.
The one currently referred to as the heterodox Luo Qing was, in fact, a member of this mountain [clan].

He was a native of Chengyang in the lower region. Having grown up in a land of non-Buddhists (tīrthika), his teachings were widespread throughout the East, and he was entirely unaware of the Three Jewels.
While I resided here, I gradually guided and transformed him; after a long time, he became a master and elder among them.
He led his followers to come and take refuge. From this point on, they first came to know that there was the Buddha-dharma; this was the beginning of my founding [of the tradition].
In the fourteenth year, the Bingxu year, I was forty-one years old.
In this year, the Tripitaka was promulgated. Previously, at the beginning of our state, the Tripitaka had been carved [into woodblocks], and it reached this region.
Regarding those various scriptures composed that had not yet been included in the canon: by imperial decree of the present Sovereign’s Holy Mother, they were now to be supplemented and added.
Once the carving was completed, the Emperor issued an edict to distribute fifteen sets of the Tripitaka throughout the famous mountains of the realm;
first, four sets were bestowed upon the four frontiers: Laoshan in the East Sea, Putuo in the South Sea, Emei in West Shu, and Luyaya on the northern border.
At that time, the Holy Mother repeatedly summoned me due to circumstances regarding Mount Tai; however, being unaware of this, I did not accept the summons.
She then sent a complete set of the Tripitaka to the East Sea. Initially, I was unaware of this matter.

Upon arriving at Laoshan, there was nowhere to settle it, so the local officials of the provincial and circuit administrations provided for its enshrinement. Seeing that it bore an imperial edict, I [accepted it].
I went to the capital to express my gratitude for the imperial favor.

Recently, by the grace of His Majesty, it was commanded that all my kinsmen contribute offerings to repair the temple and provide for its maintenance, and I requested that its name be changed to Haerin Temple. While I was in the capital, I heard that Master Daguang had come to visit me at the seaside;
I immediately hurried back home and pursued him at double speed. Just as I reached him, the Master was leaving the mountain, so we returned together.
He lingered for twenty days and presented me with a poem containing the lines: "Leisurely dwelling upon the sea, my name has mistakenly fallen among the mountains of Shandong.
In the eleventh month of winter that year, I had been constantly burdened by labor since the year of *xin-si* (1801) and had found no rest;
thus, I was deeply fatigued. Only now that my meditation hall was first completed have I finally attained a place of settled peace, allowing both body and mind to relax.
Below. His bliss was beyond compare. One night, while sitting in meditation, he rose at night and saw the ocean deep and the sky clear; the snow and moon mingled their radiance.
Suddenly, body, mind, and the world sank away into stillness, like the falling shadows of flowers in the sky.
All was a vast, luminous treasury of light, where not a single thing existed. He then spoke this verse: "The ocean is deep and the sky is clear; the snow and moon’s light."

Within this, the conduct and concealment of ordinary beings and sages are severed; with the vajra-eye piercing through, the flowers in the sky fall away. The great earth returns entirely to the field of quiescent extinction.
He then returned to his chamber, took up the *Lengyan Yinzheng*, and upon opening the scroll, he immediately beheld your body and your mind.

"The external world, including the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—all are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind. Thus, the entire contemplative object of this sutra became clear to my heart and mind.
I immediately set pen to paper and composed one fascicle titled *The Hanging Mirror of the Śūraṅgama*. Before even half a candle had burned down, it was finished.
At that time, the meditation hall was just opening its period of silence; I summoned the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) into the room to read it aloud for me.
To me, it was like hearing the words of a dream.
In the fifteenth year, the Dinghai year, at the age of forty-two, I renovated the temple buildings and began to open the hall to preach the precepts for the assembly. From that time on—
Monks from the four quarters arrived there daily. For the sake of the lay devotees, I gave a direct exposition of the Heart Sūtra.
In the autumn of that year, Vice Minister Hu took leave to return to his estate; he brought along his nephew, whom he sent forth to leave the household life as an attendant.
I named it *Fuxian* (Merit and Goodness).

In the sixteenth year, Wuzi (1648), when I was forty-three years old, some students read my *Lengyan Xuanying* (Hanging Mirror on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) and requested [a commentary], saying: "This sūtra’s mind..."
The *Guānmíng* (Contemplation of Clarity) has not yet fully digested its terminology; I fear that later students will find it difficult to enter.

I hope that each word will be dissolved back into the contemplative mind—this would be a most magnificent gift of the Dharma. I have already conceived the idea for the *Tōngyì* (General Commentary) and established its fundamental principles, though I have not yet committed them to draft.
In the seventeenth year, Jichou (1689), I was forty-four years old.
That year, I read through the Tripitaka and lectured on the Lotus Sūtra and the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith for the assembly.
Since my departure from Mount Wutai, I had occasionally felt the desire to visit my parents; however, fearing that I might fall into worldly attachments, I tested myself for a time.
One night, while sitting in meditation, he suddenly opened his eyes and uttered this verse: "Smoke and waves daily soak the cold void; Fish and birds roam together within a single mirror.
Last night, the moon beyond the heavens suddenly sank; Its solitary brilliance must now mingle with the black dragon.
He then urgently called his attendant and said, "I can now return to my native land to see my two elders. This was preceded by...
On behalf of Ba’en Temple, he requested a complete set of the Tripitaka. In the tenth month of winter, he arrived at the capital;
the Emperor immediately ordered that the collection be provided for his journey. In the eleventh month, he reached Longjiang at his home temple.

For several days, the precious pagoda emitted light. On the day the scriptures were welcomed, the light from the pagoda formed a bridge leading northward to meet the scriptures, through which the monks walked.
Furthermore, while the sutras were being installed and the ritual arena established, a radiant light appeared daily without ceasing.

Those who came to gaze upon and prostrate before it numbered over ten thousand, regarding it as a rare and auspicious omen. When the old mother heard that I had arrived, she first sent someone to inquire on which day I would reach home.
I replied, "I am here for the affairs of the Imperial Court, not for my family. If the old mother wishes to see me," [she may do so].
She was as joyful as if we had never been parted; she could only be trusted for one night’s stay. Otherwise, I would not return.
When my old mother heard this, she said, “To meet again after being reborn is a joy beyond measure—how could there be any sorrow?
One night would suffice, let alone two. When I returned and met her, my old mother was so delighted that she fell over in laughter. I considered this most extraordinary.
As they sat together at night, an elder of the clan asked whether she had come by boat or by land. The old woman replied immediately, "Why ask whether I came by boat or by land?
The questioner asked, "From where have you come? The old woman said, "I have come from the midst of the air.
I was struck with wonder and said, "It is no wonder that back then this old woman was able to abandon me. Thereupon, I questioned the old woman further.
[The son] asked, "I wonder if you have thought of me since we parted. His mother said, "How could I not think of you?
[The son] asked, "Mother, how do you console yourself? His mother said, "At first I did not know. Once I learned that you were at Wutai, I asked the masters there, 'Where is Wutai?
They replied, 'It is beneath the Big Dipper; it is precisely where your noble son resides. From that night on, I have performed prostrations."

“Regarding the Northern Dipper: if one recites the name of a Bodhisattva, one no longer harbors such thoughts [of fear]. Now, when it is said that you are dead, one neither prostrates nor entertains such thoughts anymore.
That I see you now is because you have come as a manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Tomorrow, while I am selecting a burial site for my two parents at the ancestral cemetery, my father is already eighty years old; I shall joke with him, saying: ‘Today, I am burying my old man alive.’”
"Son, check back another day," she said. I took up my spade and struck the ground, but my old mother snatched it away, saying, "I, an old woman, will bury myself;
why trouble others? She struck the earth herself dozens of times. Three days later, she bid me farewell with the same joyful countenance as before, never once frowning.
Only then did I realize that my old mother was no ordinary person. Thus it was at Jimo.
The youth Huang Shanazhan, styled Ziguang, was the younger brother of the current Grand Minister (Dasi). When I first arrived at the coast, he was nineteen years old;
he immediately took refuge in the Triple Gem and requested instruction. I taught him the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which he mastered through recitation within two months.

From then on, he maintained a vegetarian diet. Although his parents rebuked him for this, he did not waver in his resolve. He applied himself with earnest intent to investigation and study, resting [only] on his side...
He did not come to the seat. At that time, as I was returning south, Guang thought to himself: "I was born in a remote land and for kalpas have not heard the name of the Triple Gem.
Now I have fortunately met a Great Good Spiritual Friend who acts as my uninvited friend. If he does not return, we shall lose our refuge.
He then faced the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, broke his own arm to light a lamp as an offering, and prayed to the Bodhisattva.
I urged him to return home early. Thereafter, he suffered from painful inflammatory sores and sat in a state of perilous concentration day and night, reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
After three months, he was healed. Upon his recovery, he saw that the scars on his body had formed the image of a Great Bodhisattva;
its eyebrows, eyes, body, and robes were as distinct as if they had been painted. Even his mother and wife were unaware of this. He constantly sought to leave the household life, but I dissuaded him.
He did not permit it. Then [the monk] said, "I, your disciple, shall perform a somersault; how could you, Master, possibly stop me?
From this, one knows that even in the land of the Mlecchas, the seed of the Buddha has never been severed.

Initially, I resolved to rebuild this temple and dwell on Mount Tai, for the conditions were already ripe; however, as the expenses would amount to several hundred thousand, it was not easy to speak of. Therefore...
He waited upon the sea for the opportune moment. Now that the conditions were nearly ripe, he took the opportunity of returning to the Southern Capital on a mission to deliver the Tripitaka.
Having fully obtained the details regarding the origins and history of the temple, he returned to report his findings to His Majesty the Empress. He further submitted a memorial, stating:

"The scale of the project is vast and the expenses immense; it is difficult to undertake lightly. I pray that Your Majesty will daily reduce your food and drink by one hundred *liang*, and accumulate these savings over three years."
The age [of the project] may now be set forth: ten years of work shall bring it to completion. His Majesty was greatly pleased and immediately issued the command;
thus, in the twelfth month of that year, the accumulation of materials began.
In the eighteenth year, Gengyin (1710).
I was forty-five years old. In this year, the temple buildings were completed. During the spring, I transcribed the *Lotus Sūtra* on behalf of the Holy Mother.
At that time, a local official wishing to seize the site for a Daoist ritual ground conspired with a heterodox practitioner wearing a yellow cap;
they falsely claimed to occupy that Daoist cloister and gathered a crowd to lodge a lawsuit before the Provincial Governor, Lord Li. The Governor had already become fully aware of the situation.
I felt deep resentment at this matter. He was sent down to the Laizhou Prefecture for thorough investigation; I personally presided over the hearing and strove to save him.
Several hundred unruly elements raised a tumult in the prefectural city, surrounding me like a siege.
At that time, there were two attendants with me, whom I dismissed to go elsewhere. I then walked slowly alone amidst them. One of the ringleaders held—
A copper plaque [emerged]; a sharp blade came forth from its sheath and was brandished before me, intending to kill me.
I looked at it with a smile and said, "If you kill a person, how will you deal with yourself? His spirit was disheartened, and he immediately withdrew the blade.
We walked together outside the city for about two *li* and were about to part ways when the frantic crowd suspected that he, as their leader, had an interest in me. Immediately—
He intended to assault him. I silently calculated that if his crowd charged with a single drumbeat, the man would be in peril; what could be done?

I hesitated, intending to depart, but he immediately seized me by the head and brought me to his lodging. He closed the door, stripped off his clothes, and sprawled about, laughing and chatting as if nothing were amiss.
We took melons and fruits and ate them together. At that time, the entire market was in a commotion, crying out, "The Daoist master has killed a monk!"
When the Prefect heard of this, he immediately dispatched many officials to arrest them all. The group was terrified and, bowing their heads, all begged for their lives.
I said to them, "Do not fear, nor do you need to argue; simply listen to what I have to say.
When they arrived, the Prefect asked, "Did these madmen kill the monk? I replied, "Not yet. When we first came to arrest them, the monk was still with them."
The leader said, "We were merely sharing some melons and fruit. The Magistrate asked, "Why did you cause such a commotion? He replied, "It was simply a market bustle.
The Magistrate wished to place him in a cangue, but he said, "I intended to disperse them; to put him in a cangue would only serve to bind them even more firmly.
The Magistrate understood and ordered the local authorities to drive them all away. Within three days, the frantic crowd was completely dispersed. From this point on...
This matter was thus settled. In this year, I composed the *Liaoying lun* (Treatise on the Shadows and Echoes of Laozi and Zhuangzi).
In the nineteenth year, the *Xinmao* year, at the age of forty-six, my Holy Mother commissioned a sandalwood statue of Vairocana Buddha and began its construction.
The Great Hall. In the autumn of that year, my disciple Huang Ziguang passed away while seated in meditation.
In the twentieth year, the Renchen year, I was forty-seven years old.
In the seventh month of the autumn of that year, I arrived in the capital to visit Chan Master Daguan.

In the past, during the Jin dynasty, there was Master Wan. Fearing that the three calamities at the end of the kalpa would destroy the Buddha-dharma, he carved stone scriptures and enshrined them within a stone chamber.
His pagoda complex had been sold by the monks; the Master redeemed it and wished for me to compose a record.
I arrived just as he was overjoyed. Upon meeting him, we immediately went together to Shijing Mountain, where I then composed the inscription for Master Wan’s pagoda.
The temple records, the record of the re-concealment of the śarīra relics, and the previously composed *Haiyin* manuscript—
these I spent forty days and nights discussing with Master Da, an event that remains a marvel of my life.
In the twenty-first year, the *guisi* year, I was forty-eight years old.
That year, there was a great famine in Shandong; corpses lined the roads.

All the provisions for vegetarian meals stored in the mountains were distributed to provide relief to the people living nearby. When this proved insufficient, I took advantage of a passing boat to travel to Liaodong to purchase grain.
He provided several hundred *shí* of beans to relieve them; consequently, among the people of the four villages along the mountain frontier, not a single person died of hunger.
In the twenty-second year, the Jia-wu year.
I was forty-nine years old. In the third month of spring that year, the Duke Zheng Kunya, the Provincial Governor of Shandong, entered the mountains to inquire about the Dharma;
I spoke to him of expedient teachings. In the tenth month of winter, I went to the capital to offer congratulations on the Emperor’s birthday and remained there to pass the New Year.
He requested that I administer the precepts at Cishou Temple. At that time, I was engaged in the project of restoring my own temple.
Knowing that the Holy Mother’s provisions were already ample, he requested that the undertaking be commenced.
At that time, as the Emperor was deliberating on an expedition to punish the Japanese for their invasion of Korea, [the request] was temporarily set aside and postponed.
