including the postscript, volume two,
twenty-three years, the year of Yiwu (1635).
I was fifty years of age. In the first month of spring, I returned from the capital by sea and immediately encountered misfortune.
Initially, for the purpose of distributing the Imperially-bestowed Tripitaka, four palace eunuchs were dispatched to deliver it. These men arrived first at the East Sea.

Previously, the Emperor had been parsimonious with his resources and had always held the palace eunuchs in low esteem, as he considered their requests for Buddhist services to be excessively frequent. At that time, by chance, the inner court...
He intentionally provoked the Sage’s wrath, which was about to extend to the Holy Mother. The ministers on both sides feared for their safety.

It happened that an official of the Inner Authority, harboring resentment, had sent a messenger to deliver scriptures; he wished to have the messenger executed and intended to use this as a pretext to incite a rebellion.

Consequently, they falsely spread rumors through a former Daoist master and ordered eunuch guards of the Eastern Factory to disguise themselves as Daoists, strike the *dengwen* drum, and present their petition.

The Emperor read this and was greatly incensed; he issued a decree extending punishment downward, and because of the circumstances surrounding the delivery of the scriptures, [the monks] were implicated as well.
Upon hearing the report, I said to the assembly: "The Buddha does not abandon even a single sentient being, even if they dwell within the three miserable realms.

Now, in this land of the Mlecchas in the Eastern Sea, the names of the Triple Gem have never before been heard. Yet, for twelve years, I have taught and transformed them; in the third year, the red..."
My son, you all know how to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. As for those who have abandoned heterodoxy to return to the Right Path, they are found in every neighborhood and every household.
My wishes are fulfilled; what regret could there be in death? My only cause for heartache is that my vow to restore this temple remains unfulfilled.
He then departed from Jimo. The soldiers, officials, elders, and children of the city all came out en masse, weeping as they followed him in farewell;

this clearly demonstrates the transformative power of his influence upon the people's hearts. Upon arriving at the capital, he was ordered by imperial decree to be interrogated by the Zhenfu Commandery.
The officials first received the imperial decree, intending to summon [the monks] all at once.

They prepared funds for travel to the various famous mountains where the Holy Mother had appeared, amounting to no fewer than several hundred thousand [coins]. They subjected them to severe torture and interrogation. I said:
"I am ashamed to be a monk and have nothing with which to repay the grace of the state. Now, why should I begrudge a single death that would only wound the majesty of His Majesty?"

How unfilial! To pander one's will and recklessly seek profit, and to serve the sovereign’s whims at the expense of the fundamental social order—this is utterly contrary to the heart of a minister or son who loves his ruler.
What will history say of such a person? One must resist this with all one's might.
He had previously solicited alms from the assembly, receiving over seven hundred pieces of gold;

upon examining the internal treasury records and the registers of prior relief efforts in Shandong, the Emperor’s suspicions were finally dispelled. Consequently, mother and son were restored to their former relationship.

Subsequently, a memorial was drafted, and by the Imperial Majesty’s compassionate consideration, [the monk] was sentenced for privately establishing a temple and dispatched to Leizhou for military service. I, however, [was spared].
In the third month of that year, he was imprisoned. At all the monasteries within the capital, sutras were recited and repentance rites performed for his protection.
Among the monks (nàzǐ), there were those who burned incense and cauterized their arms, while others maintained a vegetarian fast by water and chanted mantras to provide additional guardianship.
Zheng Dàsīmǎ of Ānsù, the son of Gōngzǐ Fànxi, was then serving in the Jīnwǔ Command; though they had never met before, he specifically prepared a banquet to host him.
In the morning, the gentry and officials requested his release, even to the point of weeping as they pleaded for his innocence. Such was the devotion of the people of that time to the Dharma.
He remained in prison for eight months; during this time, the only one who provided him with food and offerings was his attendant, Fushan.

In the tenth month of winter, he was dispatched southward. Many civil and official elites followed him on their journey, some in informal attire and others on pack mules, to see him off at the ferry crossing.
As for Ji: on the day he departed from the capital, Fushan and two or three fellow monks accompanied him. In the eleventh month, they arrived at Nanjing.
On the riverbank, he took leave of his aged mother and composed the "Inscription on Mother and Son. He then took his orphaned nephew Kejiu with him.
Initially, while at Shijing Mountain with Master Daguan, he reflected that the Chan school was in decline; he considered Caoxi to be the very source of Chan.
"If the source is inevitably blocked, one must set out together with determination to dredge it. Before the Master arrived, he had already gone to wait at Mount Kuang.
When I was beset by calamity, the Master was residing at Tianchi; upon hearing the report, he was greatly alarmed and said, "Master Han has passed away!"
"Thus, the vow of Caoxi remains unfulfilled. The Master then traveled ahead to Caoxi; upon returning to Liaocheng, he heard that I was about to depart, so he returned to Jinling to await me.
When I arrived, we parted at the Lubo An (Traveler’s Lodging) on the river.
The Master intended to exert all his efforts to clear my innocence, but I said, "The command of one's sovereign is the duty of a minister and a son."
"The matter is no different; how much more so for fixed karma! Master, please do not speak of it.

At the parting of ways, he clasped my arm and said, "Upon hearing of your difficulties at Tiantai, I immediately made a vow before the Buddha to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* one hundred times to ensure you remain free from harm.
My heart is your tongue. I responded with repeated expressions of gratitude and took my leave. The Master then composed the "Discourse on the Banished Guest" for me.
In the twenty-fourth year, Bingshen, when I was fifty-one years of age, I passed through Wenjiang in the first month of spring to visit the Censor-in-Chief Zou Nangao.

Wang Xinghai of Luling, who had recently passed away, paid me his respects by the river and requested that I provide a commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. In the second month, I crossed Mount Yuling and arrived at...
At the summit of the ridge, he observed the place where Huiming had seized the *kāṣāya* and composed a poem in his memory:
"When I recall those nights of travel in the past, how can they compare to my heart as I cross the ridge this morning?

Seeing that the road was rugged and the travelers were sweating profusely, he then instructed a practitioner to establish a tea hut at the summit. Another practitioner urged him to repair the roads; before long—
The year was a smooth path for him. Upon reaching Shaoyang, he entered the mountains to pay homage to the Patriarch and drank from the Caoxi waters, composing this verse:
"A single drop of Caoxi water originates from the numinous source; It flows into the vast ocean, its waves lapping against the heavens. How many fish and dragons undergo transformation therein!"
The single stream from its source still flows with clarity; yet seeing that the ancestral temple was in such a state of decay it was beyond description, he departed in sorrow.
Upon reaching Wuyang (Guangzhou), he appeared before the Great General in prison attire. The General released him from his bonds and treated him to a meal of vegetarian offerings.
He took up residence at Haidao Temple. There, the Grand Councilor Zhou Haimen led several dozen of his disciples to visit him. While they were seated together in conversation—
The Duke of Zhou raised the question, "One who penetrates the way of day and night possesses knowledge," thereby posing an inquiry.
Among the assembly was one called Lao Dao Zhangzhe (the Elder of the Way of Old Age), who replied: "Every person possesses awareness. When responding to affairs during the day, it is this awareness;
when dreaming at night, it is likewise this awareness. Therefore it is said: 'One who penetrates the way of day and night possesses knowledge. Zhou [the Duke]...
The Duke said, "The great assembly all speak in this manner, yet in my heart I am not certain.
He then asked me, "Venerable Chan Master, please instruct me. I replied, "From which scripture does this phrase originate? The Duke said, "It is from the *Xici* (Appended Phrases) of the *I Ching*.
The Duke recited several lines. I said, "This was the Sage’s instruction to people: that awakening does not belong to birth."
"This is the one move that ends death. Zhou Gong clapped his hands in approval and said, "Truly, this old Chan master’s instruction is intimate and direct.
The assembly was all at a loss. When they questioned him further, Zhou Gong said, "'Death and life' is the way of day and night. One must penetrate both day and night."
Thus, it was not subject to the constraints of day or night. The assembly sighed in admiration.

Previously, various Dharma protectors had sent letters to the Grand Marshal of the Regional Government, Lord Chen, requesting that postal couriers provide transport; on the tenth day of the third month, they arrived at Leizhou.
I joined the ranks and resided in an ancient temple to the west of the city. On the first day of the fourth month of summer, I began my handwritten commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
At that time, there was a great famine, pestilence broke out violently, and it did not rain for years; the deaths and injuries were beyond description.
I felt as if I were sitting in a śītavana cemetery, yet through the empowerment of the Dharma, I remained at ease. During this drought, the well water had withered away.
Only his virtuous attendant followed him. Every night at midnight, he would wait until he obtained a jar of water to sustain him for the entire day.
When the starving man saw it, he found even a single drop to be like celestial nectar. Within and without the city, corpses lay exposed in heaps.
In the seventh month of autumn, I, together with the *xiao-lian* Ke Shifu, exhorted the assembly to collect and bury tens of thousands of skeletal remains.
We then established a ritual site for salvation (*ji-du daochang*). Immediately, Heaven sent down heavy rain, and the water on level ground reached three feet deep;

from this point on, the pestilential vapors were dispelled. In the eighth month, by order of the Prefectural Government, I returned to Wuyang and occupied the military training grounds (*yu-yanwu-chang*), where I traveled back and forth and composed [this work].

Poems on Military Service. Twenty pieces. Initially, upon passing through Kūteng in Dianbai—the gateway for bandits of the southern ridges—I composed an inscription there and established a tea hermitage.
The Right Vice Minister of War Ding of Yuzhang was exiled to Guanghai due to false accusations;
he had long admired me, and thus we became inseparable friends.
In the twenty-fifth year, the *dingyou* year, when I was fifty-two years old, during the first month of spring, there were many casualties in the capital city and many skeletons lay exposed.
I ordered people to collect them, burying several thousand in total. Thereupon, I established a Universal Salvation Ritual (*puzhi daochang*) for seven days and nights.
Ding Youwu served as his assistant. Previously, the people of Yue were ignorant of Buddhism; from this time forth, they unanimously came to know and take refuge in it.
In the fourth month of summer, the *Lengqie Biji* (Notes on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra) was completed.

Because various scholars had taken refuge [in the Dharma] yet had not yet entered into the principles of Buddhism, he therefore composed the *Zhongyong Zhizhi* (Direct Pointing to the Mean) to elucidate them for them. At first, the high officials viewed me as a monk of transgressions.
He made it very easy for me. Marshal Chen Da was like a mountain at the military gate; his discipline was extremely strict, and no one dared to seek a private audience.
Although I had not yet gone to see him, he dispatched people to wait upon me with great diligence. In the ninth month of that year, I went with the Right Guard to pay my respects.
When we reached the gate and sent word of our arrival, he stopped us. That evening, he came in person to bow to me on my boat, bringing a tea box and sitting down with me.

When he spoke, he struck the wooden sounding-block three times, and everyone was struck with wonder and amazement. Later, he praised him before the various high officials, saying, "He is a qilin or a phoenix among monks.
Consequently, even the Three Ministries issued an edict for them to go and pay their respects. From then on, everyone knew that the monk was a person of great importance.

In the twenty-sixth year, the Wuxu cycle, when I was fifty-three years old, in the first month of spring, Fan Gong Youxuan, the Attendant Censor, was banished to Leizhou for his proposal regarding the establishment of the heir apparent.
He first visited me at Wuyang; at that time, I was collating a manuscript of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. The official asked me about Leizhou.
"What is the scenery like in Yangfeng? I took up a scroll of the sutra and showed it to him, saying, "This is the scenery of Leyang.

The official marveled at this and immediately drafted a preface to solicit donations for its carving into woodblocks. When Zhou Gong of Haimen served as the Judicial Commissioner of Guangdong, he came and went to consult me on the Way.
Because [the work] encompassed Nanxiao, it was included in the *Xiuxi Caoxi Zhi*. Formerly, the local scholars were unaware of Buddhism;

however, as Zhou Gong (Yangming) propagated his learning, these students gathered together and came to me to inquire about the Way. Among them was Long Shengzhang, who, upon hearing my discourse, found it extraordinary.
Upon returning home, he told his friends Wang Sheng Anshun and Feng Sheng Changli: [...text continues... *Note: This is a partial translation based on the provided fragment.*
Hearing that the Chan Master from the North was expounding the Dharma most wondrously, the two sons both came to seek his instruction. I revealed to them matters of the Ultimate;

they believed with deep conviction and without doubt, vowing to apply themselves earnestly to investigation. Originally possessed of virtuous conduct, the two led others to take refuge [in the Triple Gem], and the number of followers increased daily.
From this time on, they first came to know of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Thereafter, the transformation through the Dharma spread greatly.

[The hall] was opened. This was the fruition of the power of three lifetimes. Recalling Master Da’s vow to bestow the scriptures, that summer he began constructing a meditation hall amidst the piled-up walls.
Intending to don the ceremonial cap and robe of Great Wisdom (Dahui) to preach the Dharma, he gathered dharma companions who had traveled from afar.
Together with several dozen disciples from the Bodhi Tree Hall of Fǎxìng Monastery, including Tōng'àn, Chāoyì, and Tōnghuǐ, he recited the Lotus Sūtra and expounded it for the assembly.
Upon reaching the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa," he attained a sudden and profound realization of the Buddha’s intent.
The essential point is this: for everyone in this Sahā world, the Flower Treasury (Huazang) is right before their eyes.

Yet, the necessity of the three transformations is specifically for those of inferior faculties, serving merely as a gradual introduction to a single aspect. The ancients generally treated the final six chapters as the "Circulation" (liutong) section;

they too had not yet grasped the Buddha’s true intent. Consequently, I have composed the *Fahua Jijie* (Beating the Beat of the Lotus). Right-Wu is impetuous by nature and possesses a spirit of noble indignation; he understands [this].
He revered the Sangha but did not understand the Buddha-dharma. As he was about to depart, I sent him off on a boat, applying once more the hammer and tongs of rigorous inquiry.

Thereupon, he suddenly attained great awakening. I thus bestowed upon him the style name "The Layman Who Realizes His Errors" (Juefei Jushi) and presented him with an inscription; I further composed the "Inscription for Clarifying the Mind" (Chengxin Ming) to serve as a warning to him.
In the twenty-seventh year, Jihai (1659),
when I was fifty-four years old, I completed the carving of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* notes in the spring. I lectured on them once for the assembly and then printed more than a hundred copies,
which I distributed widely to the Dharma-teachers and protectors of the Dharma throughout the realm, so that they might take note.
Though I dwell amidst hardship and adversity, I have not forgotten the affairs of the Buddha. The customs of Yue are indeed fond of killing;

on the occasion of the Zhongyuan Festival, everyone sacrifices living beings to their ancestors. When the time arrives, the livestock piled in the market are like stacks of firewood—how truly pitiful it is!

Consequently, I organized an Ullambana Assembly and lectured on the *Xiaoheng Chao*. I exhorted people to provide vegetarian offerings for the monks and to release captive creatures on this day, using only vegetables for sacrifice. Thus, [the practice was followed].

Those who did so were very numerous. Thereafter, for all major occasions such as funerals and ancestral sacrifices, on the birthdays of one's parents, or for prayers of averting calamities, people would invariably perform prostrations, repentance, and the release of living beings (*fangsheng*), maintaining a vegetarian diet.
Before long, societies for the release of living beings had emerged everywhere; this was one mechanism through which the Buddha-dharma brought about transformation.
In the fifth month of the summer of that year, the Grand Marshal of the Provincial Government, Lord Chen, moved his military command to [the region].
Upon arriving at the provincial capital, before he had even paid his respects to a local official, the official first sent someone to wait upon me.
Shortly thereafter, he ordered more than a hundred pieces of the finest foodware to be brought out. None of those under him knew what they were for.
When the vegetarian feast was prepared, he requested that I specifically use these new vessels; thus, everyone came to know how highly he valued them. Not long after, he invited me...
I took my leave to return home. That autumn, salt-tax commissioners were dispatched everywhere, and the region from then on faced increasing troubles.
The Minister of Rites, Yang Fusuo, of Huizhou, who shared a profound affinity with me in the Dharma, had previously returned home due to mourning.

This autumn, I went to visit him; upon my arrival, he had already passed away at his burial site. On the following morning, as I was about to enter the mountains, [I encountered] his spirit... (Note: The final sentence appears incomplete in the source text.)
I had already arrived at the city. I went immediately to view the enshrouding and sought a coffin.

While on the way to Chaoyang, I encountered the Governor Ren Gong, who was accompanying the Provincial Inspector in Huizhou; he invited me to visit West Lake and ascend Mount Baihe, where东坡 (Sudō) once dwelt, before returning home.
Upon my return, I intended to close my gate and withdraw from worldly affairs.
In the twenty-eighth year, the gengzi year, I was fifty-five years of age.

At that time, the salt-tax commissioners had first arrived; they were cruel, tyrannical, and violent, such that both officials and commoners could no longer endure it, and the region was thrown into turmoil.
Furthermore, there was the alarm of the Japanese incursions, and the hearts of the people were filled with dread. I immediately dispersed my disciples and closed the gates.
[The official] cut off all traces [of the matter]. The people of Yue have long suffered from the white-canoed grain transporters (*baicuo*) of the Min Sea, fearing that rice prices would soar;

at that time, this was considered a cause for unrest. The new Commander-in-Chief was a native of Min. While his son’s vessel was anchored at sea, it happened that the Grand General was about to depart on leave.
The Imperial Tax Commissioner (*seoshi*) had long harbored the intention to encroach upon him, and upon finding several white-canoed vessels by chance, he used them as a pretext.
When the Great General, acting as the prince’s escort, incited the citizens to a great clamor, several thousand people gathered in an instant.
They hurled bricks and stones, nearly shattering the prince’s boat, and surrounded the military headquarters, brandishing spears with great urgency.

At that time, the officials of the Three Departments, the Prefectures, and the Counties all went to the military gate to perform the rites of submission; not a single regular official remained in the capital city.
In the end, there was no one to provide salvation; the situation had changed in the space of a breath.
The Great General was in peril and, having no other recourse, dispatched his central command to my barrier to seek deliverance. I strongly refused, saying, "I possess no divine arts.
The central commander knelt and wept, saying, "If you, Master, do not consider the bond between host and guest, do you at least not consider the living beings of this land? I—
Hearing this, I was struck with alarm. I immediately broke through the pass to visit the tax commissioner.

I spoke to him with composure and exhorted him to change his ways, seeking to enlighten his mind. Upon hearing my words, the commissioner finally attained realization; he then ordered that the people be pacified by their own accord so as to disperse the chaotic crowd.
I went ahead of them and addressed the multitude with bold words, saying: "What you are doing now, gentlemen, is merely because you wish to eat cheap rice. Now, having committed [these offenses]..."
"The Great Dharma shall meet its end," he said. "There is now this base rice; who will eat it? When the multitude heard this, they were struck with astonishment.

Shortly thereafter, the imperial decree reached the military headquarters, and the siege was immediately lifted. The city subsequently found peace. The elders were moved by his words and wished to honor him as a sacrificial priest.

At that time, the three high officials were dining at the military gate when they received the report that the people had risen in rebellion; they all dropped their chopsticks and rose from their seats.
When they returned and the region had already been restored to peace, everyone knew it was due to my efforts.
Upon hearing this, Overseer Ren sent me a letter saying: "If Master Han does not come out, what will become of the local area? Now that Master Han has come out..."
"What will become of Master Han? I also knew for myself that from this point on there would be no days of peace.
That autumn, Lord Zhu, the Governor of Nanxiao, invited me to enter Caoxi. Seizing the opportunity, I entered the mountains and became a servant to the Sixth Patriarch.
The new Provincial Commander-in-Chief, Lord Dai, knowing that I could settle the turbulent people, held me in deep esteem and desired to see me; he thus issued an edict.
The Great General took me to pay him a visit. Upon meeting him, he received me with great courtesy and invited me to a formal meal.
When I expressed my intention to depart for Caoxi, the official then pledged to act as a protector of the Dharma, whereby I was able to find peace of mind.
In the twenty-ninth year, the *xinchou* year, when I was fifty-six years of age, in the first month of spring, I visited Caoxi.

Thieves and scoundrels from all quarters had gathered at the mountain gate, openly engaging in butchery and liquor trade to such a degree that the place was utterly defiled; this corruption had persisted for over a hundred years, and their graves generally occupied [the sacred grounds].

At Zusan, the monastic community had largely encroached upon the mountain lands, and moreover, they colluded with outside hooligans to extort and deceive the temple monks; none dared to look at them squarely.
I sighed and said, "This is a disease of the heart and belly. If it is not removed, then this will become the site of the Sixth Patriarch’s Dharma seat."
"In the end, it will surely turn into a fox den; ultimately, there will be no way to save it. Even if I were to remain here, what would it avail?
After reflecting deeply and repeatedly, I went to inform Lord Dai, the Provincial Commander-in-Chief. The Lord said, 'It shall not be difficult. I shall endeavor to carry this out for you.
He immediately issued an order to the local magistrate to maintain a defensive watch and drive them all out within three days."

Not a single person was left behind; the dwellings were all demolished until not a tile remained. From this point on, the defilements that had accumulated at the Caoxi mountain gate were washed away in a single day.
The official then invited me to stay for a meal, where we sat and conversed. The official remarked, "The Sixth Patriarch was indeed tainted by worldly vulgarity."
"I have already washed it for you, sir. "The people of this region are currently drowning in misery;
Great Bodhisattva, what compassion do you have to save them? I asked, "How so? He replied, "There are over a thousand ships, all of which are led by great pirates of the sea.
Now, under the pretext of official collection, they use their power to extort resources. When the collection period ends, they do not return, but instead commit acts of violence."
"Plundering at sea continues without end, yet the law cannot restrain it; this is the first [problem].
Furthermore, local mining operations employ forced labor with such violence and arrogance that they dig up people’s graves and destroy their livelihoods.
Everywhere, the common people suffer harms even more severe than those from plundering; consequently, the people have no peace of mind. What can be done about this? I replied: "This..."
"This is not easy to speak of; let us plan it gradually for now. He took the envoy, Master Li, as his disciple, who possessed considerable faith.
That autumn, they went to Caoxi to offer incense to the Sixth Patriarch. They stayed in the mountains for several days, and upon hearing the Dharma, he was greatly delighted.
I therefore exhorted him to become a patron (*dānapati*) for the restoration of the Patriarchs' Hall; he responded with great resolve and took up the burden. Then, he secretly initiated [the plan].
He said: "The harm caused by mining to the local region is extreme; it is certainly not the intention of Your Sacred Majesty.

Let strict regulations be established immediately for the mining boats, and let those who exceed the permitted time for their journeys be punished. Once the mining operations cease, all levied labor services must be abolished.
Simply order the relevant authorities to remit the annual quota of tribute; thus, the people will not be disturbed in the slightest. Is this not feasible?
The officials received these instructions with utmost deference and implemented them with all their might. Consequently, the regions of mountains and seas were suddenly brought to peace.
The Duke was deeply moved by this and wrote a letter to thank me, saying: "Only now do I realize the vastness of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' compassion.
Because of this, my resolve to protect the Dharma becomes even more earnest. It is thanks to this that I am able to find peace at Caoxi. This is it.
In the autumn of that year, he restored the ancestral temple, altered the topography and roadways, selected monks for ordination, established a school of doctrine to nurture śrāmaṇeras,
instituted the regulations for the administrative treasury, audited rents and taxes, and redeemed monastic properties that had been encroached upon.
Within a single year, all neglected affairs were fully restored.
In the year of Renyin, the thirtieth year [of my life], I was fifty-seven years old.
That year, I reconstructed the Patriarchs’ Hall, reinforced the rear dragon (the geomantic ridge), and altered the path.

I converted a butcher’s quarter into a guesthouse for monks from the ten directions, cleared the divine way, relocated the monastic quarters, expanded the meditation hall, and established new regulations.
Proclamation.
In the thirty-first year, the year of Gui-mao,
when I was fifty-eight years of age, in the eleventh month of winter, Chan Master Daguan was in the capital and encountered the "Seditious Book" incident.

Regarding this misfortune: when I was subsequently imprisoned and interrogated, it was because they considered me responsible; thus, he too was implicated. Knowing in my heart that I could not escape, I remained composed and waited.
By the grace of the Imperial Majesty, I was pardoned. The capital’s monastic community granted me passage.
In that year, my attendant Shin-kō (Shingō) entered the priesthood.
The thirty-second year, Jiachen (1724).
I was fifty-nine years old. In the first month of spring, on account of Master Da, I traveled to the Censorate.
An official decree ordered me to return to my military post, whereupon I departed Caoxi and went to Leizhou. There, I recalled what Master Da had said regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Regarding the causes and effects of the seven realms of existence, there were none among the scholars of the secular texts who could provide a correct interpretation.

I remarked, "The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) is precisely a book that elucidates cause and effect," and subsequently composed the *Heart-Method of the Spring and Autumn Annals* (Chunqiu Zuoshizhuan Xinfa).
In the thirty-third year, the year of Yi-si (1865),
when I was sixty years of age, in the third month of spring, I crossed the Qiong Sea to visit Dongpo’s Guanglang Hermitage and Bailong Spring.

I sought the remains of Chan Master Juefan but could not find them. While staying at the Mingchang Pagoda Temple, I composed the "Preface to the Heart-Dharma of the Spring and Autumn Annals and the Zuo Commentary.
I traveled to famous mountains and wrote the "Record of Exploring Wonders at the Ocean of Jewels" and the "Record of the Golden Grain Spring.
Gazing at the prefectural city at night, it appeared desolate, as if devoid of any human presence; only the western part of the city wall possessed a slight trace of vitality. Thereupon, I remarked:
The gentlemen said, "A calamity is about to befall our city; we must urgently perform rites of expiation. People regarded this as mere delusion.

Yet, when I had been crossing the sea for only half a month, the earth shook violently. The eastern wall of the city, including its gates, collapsed, and all the official residences within the city were leveled.

The Mingchang Pagoda fell down, crushing everything, and the multi-storied pavilion where I resided was completely destroyed. When I set out on my journey, the scholar-officials were already suffering.
He detained me. I refused to stay. If I do not go, I shall likewise be reduced to ashes and dust.
On a moonlit night, I crossed the sea to view the magnificent scenery of Qiong; I considered it a celestial capital, one of the Ten Islands. The fourth month of summer.
The Provincial Governor issued a mandate for me to return to Wuyang. In the seventh month of autumn, I arrived at Caoxi;

when I left, the Patriarch’s Hall had already been demolished, and construction work had not yet ceased. Upon my return, however, six or seven tenths of it was complete. The costs for labor and materials amounted to nearly a thousand taels of gold, yet there were no funds whatsoever.
I converted two female imperial messengers into lay patrons, and they fully reimbursed the expenses. That year, I also renovated [the temple] in Wuyang.
The Changchun Hermitage served as the administrative office for Caoxi and was the place where offerings were prepared for the Sixth Patriarch.
In the tenth month of winter, the attendants Guangyi and Guangshe were ordained.

In the thirty-fourth year, Bingwu, when I was sixty-one years of age, in the third month of spring, I crossed the mountain pass and arrived at Nanzhou to await Ding Youwu and to thank Prime Minister Zhang Hongyang.
This was because, during the time of my ordeal, the Prime Minister held the rank of Vice-Prime Minister and was aware of the difficulties I faced. At that time—
The details were most thorough. We joined forces at that time to rescue him. My heart was moved by this; thus, I went to express my gratitude to the Master.

He received me with joy and recounted the past events, then invited me to offer a vegetarian feast at the Jianyunlou Pavilion by the river, requesting that his fellow countrymen join us in conversation.
The Duke said, "Everyone knows Master Han as one of the great spiritual benefactors (*kalyāṇamitra*) among the monastics, yet they do not know that he possesses immense hidden merit for the state.
When the assembly heard this, they were struck with awe and questioned the Duke. The Duke spoke of the general outline of these matters, and everyone in the hall was moved.
Upon returning to Wenjiang, he visited Imperial Censor Zou and stayed there for several days. Then he went to Zhanggong to visit Master Chen Er. He was about to—
The army remained at the headquarters for a month while he was ill. He composed twelve poems on his illness titled "Returning to Caoxi.
In the eighth month of autumn, the Emperor’s eldest grandson was born, and an imperial amnesty was proclaimed for all those serving in the garrisons who were aged, infirm, or involved in errors.

The Emperor decreed that they be heard together and clearly adjudicated for release, as this was established by precedent. Thereupon, he went to inform the Military Commissioner (Junmen), who authorized an investigation and subsequent report.

The Leizhou Circuit Inspectorate investigated and determined that they were eligible for amnesty. The Ministry of Justice compiled the records accordingly; pending the formal memorial to the throne, the prisoners were released.

In the thirty-fifth year, the Dingwei year, when I was sixty-two years old, in the third month of spring, I took my leave to return to my native place. The military headquarters issued an edict to Shaogou, assigning me to Caoqi.
While residing in the mountains, I was able to preach the Dharma for my disciples; in this same year, I annotated the *Daode jing*.
The scripture was completed. When I was young, I studied the *Laozi*. Because its language was archaic and its meaning profound, I investigated its purport thoroughly and attained some understanding.

A lay disciple requested that I write a commentary on it. I began to focus my intent in the year of Renchen; only when I had investigated each point to the point of complete penetration would I set pen to paper.
If there were even a single character that I doubted or could not fully comprehend, I would by no means let it pass lightly. It was through this that I applied myself with diligence.
Fifteen years had passed since it was carried away during my travels; it has only now been completed.

In the thirty-sixth year, Wushen (1608), when I was sixty-three years old, I discussed the restoration of the Great Hall at Caoxi. In the second month of spring, Lord Feng Yuancheng took charge of the project.

The official from Lingxi Dao came to visit me and stayed overnight in the mountains. During the night, he had a dream in which the Great Being (Mahāsattva) manifested his form, leaving him deeply moved.
At dawn, while performing prostrations before the Buddha in the hall, he noticed that two beams were decayed and crumbling. Startled, he said to me, "Why do you not repair this?
I replied, "The work would be vast and the expenses great; our strength is insufficient. He asked how much it would cost, and I answered with such-and-such an amount.
Gan said, "It is no difficulty; let me try to do it. Upon his return, he informed Governor Dai Gong. The Governor said, "This is perilous!
When one sees a child about to fall into a well, one must surely crawl forward to rescue them. How much more so for a Buddha or Bodhisattva to remain unmoved by such a crisis—this would not be human!
He then inquired as to the expenses required, and Gan immediately reported the Master’s words to him. The Governor said:
"Not yet. He then referred the matter to the Governor of Nanxiao, requesting that he be invited for a face-to-face discussion.

When I went to see him, the official expressed his resolve to undertake the reconstruction entirely at his own expense. I told him, "If you were to expend public funds, it would likely be inappropriate.
If we follow the established precedents of our school, I request that we raise the funds through a collective appeal. The official then commissioned the Provincial...
The West Road official prepared twelve ledgers for the three departments, each province, and each district, placing one slip in each. Donations were made according to one’s inclination;
they were all consolidated at the provincial level and unified into a single account, with no need to distribute funds to individual monks. In this way, it was effortless yet easy to collect.
The official followed this method, and before a month had passed, nearly a thousand taels had been gathered. I personally traveled to Western Guangdong to gather the great [teachings].
When the timber arrived at Duanzhou, the Provincial Governor detained it to repair the Baoyue Terrace; he then separately commissioned an official to procure the materials.
In winter, the Baoyue Terrace was completed, and I composed a record for it. All the timber had been accumulated on the banks of the Duan River and was transported there in succession.

In the eleventh month of winter, bandits from Annam broke into Qinzhou. Lord Dai petitioned for the imperial army to launch a distant expedition to suppress them, but the proposal was subsequently reviewed and rejected.
The thirty-seventh year, Jiyou (1259).
In the second month of spring, when I was sixty-four years old, I returned from transporting timber along the Duan River.
Stalled by the wind at Lingyang Gorge, I visited Duanxi and wrote the "Record of a Dream Journey to Duanxi. Once the timber transport reached Mengjiang, I returned to the monastery.
Just as we were gathering the assembly to manage the affairs, one or two unworthy individuals among them proceeded to commit offenses and act in opposition.
Consequently, they incited the multitude to riot like rebellious subjects. Seeing this, I sighed and said: "This is my grave transgression against the Buddha's teachings;
it is the fault of my attachment to forms. While the crowd was clamoring and shouting, I sat alone in the hall, burning incense and reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

Previously, I had merely recited the text without truly understanding its meaning. Upon reaching this point, I suddenly attained a realization and composed the *Jingang jueyi* (Resolving Doubts about the Diamond Sūtra).
When the draft was completed, the assembly remained silent; those who were unworthy did not believe me, and my heart grew increasingly fearful.

I consequently appealed the matter to the Provincial Surveillance Commission (*Anyuan*), which authorized the local magistrate to adjudicate the case. At that time, I immediately departed the mountains in a light-hearted manner to attend to the proceedings by boat.
I lived by the Fuyong River for two years until my travel funds were exhausted. The Vice Governor, Mr. Xiang Chudong, was stationed at Hanguang with his military pass;
he invited me to go there. During the journey by river, we encountered a storm and our boat was wrecked. Upon arriving, I fell gravely ill and nearly died.
The Governor summoned physicians to rescue me with all their might. When I returned to the prefecture, I lay ill in a guesthouse for nearly a year.
The year was the thirty-eighth, Gengxu. I was sixty-five years old.
That year, I lay ill in a guest house. In the seventh month of autumn, the Provincial Inspector arrived while touring his jurisdiction.
The district magistrate’s inquiry reached me. When the judicial officer heard of this, he was just beginning his investigation, yet he instead held me accountable for the crime.

The Provincial Inspector strongly disagreed and refuted him, stating: "This man has rendered great service to the Sixth Patriarch; what he previously donated was for the sake of the permanent endowment."
Now, while corrupt monks have profited, you instead condemn them; can this be called the Dharma-gate of equality?

Furthermore, I personally investigated this through the fundamental principles of the Way with rigorous scrutiny. Consequently, I went in person to the mountains and examined the monk’s submitted statement point by point.
It was entirely false and without merit. As for the accusation that he embezzled over eight thousand taels of gold from the monastery’s permanent property, I [initially]...

The regulations for the permanent treasury office were established, and numbered tickets were issued. For all matters concerning the receipt and disbursement of money and grain, the administrative monk (jian-si) and the secretary maintained these records;
every expenditure, down to the smallest fraction, was based upon these numbered tickets as proof to ensure nothing was issued arbitrarily.

When the time came for official inspection and audit, these numbered tickets served as the standard, and there was not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy between what was recorded and what was actually given. At that time...
From high and low, internal and external, they finally believed that I was not being deceitful, and the matter was cleared.

The local authorities were deeply incensed with the monk and repeatedly requested that I remain in the mountains; however, my heart was already weary, so I declined their request with all my might and took up residence at Changchun Hermitage in Wuyang.

In the thirty-ninth year, the Xin-hai year, when I was sixty-six years of age, I resided at Mount Dinghu in Duanzhou during the third month of spring to convalesce from illness. Having initially received the imperial pardon, I awaited the formal title;

however, as there had previously been no review by the Provincial Surveillance Commission (An-yuan) regarding the decree, the matter has been delayed until now. Furthermore, I have received orders for a re-examination.

Ming. He began to annotate and circulate [the work], allowing it to be studied at one's convenience. At that time, various scholars relied upon him to request instruction, and he composed the *Daxue jueyi* (Decisions on Doubts Concerning the Great Learning).
In the fortieth year, the Renzi year [1592].

At the age of sixty-seven, while residing at Changchun An and lecturing on the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Regulations for the Eight Consciousnesses* for my disciples, I composed the *Direct Explanation of the Hundred Dharmas*.
However, because the phrasing and meanings of the *Lotus Sūtra* were so closely interwoven as to be indistinguishable, students found it difficult to comprehend;
therefore, I subsequently wrote the *Categorized Sections*.
In the forty-first year, the *guichou* year, when I was sixty-eight years old, I resided at Changchun Monastery.

During the summer, while I had lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-samantabhadra-bodhi-citta-uttaratantra-sūtra* (The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment) for only half its length, I developed a carbuncle on my back.

The physicians were unable to cure it, and I nearly perished. The Great General, Duke Han Chongwang, [came to my aid].* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The full historical context indicates that Duke Han Chongwang sent a physician named Liang Jizhen to treat the illness.*
He was asked to attend to his final affairs. A man from Yue named Liang Xingshan was a wine connoisseur who had long been renowned for treating wounds.
He happened to arrive and examine him, saying, "It is grave; if you wait even a moment longer, there will be no saving him. Fortunately, rest your mind and you shall suffer no harm."
He then applied a medicinal ointment made solely from pure herbs, which took effect with every touch, as effortless as rolling a ball.

The recovery was achieved according to his schedule, and by winter he was fully healed. I composed a text to express my gratitude to him. This carbuncle had originally manifested when I first sat in meditation;
recognizing it as the result of karmic retribution, I requested leave to recite the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and engaged in the practice of calligraphy.

Whenever he recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, [the pain] would suddenly subside; it would cease according to his prayers. He subsequently went to Guangdong, where he failed in two successive attempts at the examinations.
This affliction had plagued him for forty-eight years. At the onset, he happened to forget about it and did not realize it was a carbuncle, whereby it developed into a major illness.
That his karmic retribution was being settled is proven by how it manifested upon his person without fail. (10)
Yue recovered from his illness. Previously, he had made a vow with Zeng Yibü Jinjian of Hengyang to retire together at Mount Nanyue, and they had exchanged dozens of letters regarding it;
yet, he had not been able to do so. Now, having received a letter requesting his presence, I took up my staff and went there.
Thus, I departed from Guangdong. When I first arrived in Guangdong, several dozen disciples of Faxing followed me; after some time, they gradually dispersed.
Luo was the only one among Tong and Heng who was exceptionally transcendent. Throughout the storms, hardships, and illnesses that followed him, Luo never left his side.

Now that he was about to depart, neither would abandon him, wishing to accompany him. Heng still had some worldly ties, so he delayed for a short while; eventually, he took up his staff and traveled along with them.
In the eleventh month of that year, he arrived at Hudu. Previously, his disciple Fushan had taken the attendant Shenguang and returned north to visit his relatives;
now, after only a few days, they too arrived in pursuit.
The forty-second year, Jia-yin. I was sixty-nine years old.
In the first month of spring, I traveled to De-shan to pay homage to the Patriarch; there were four poems written on this occasion.
I visited Master Feng Yuan-cheng at Wuling and met with Minister Long of Zhu-ling, who received a vegetarian feast from the Prince of Rong at Da-shan Temple.
The assembly of monks requested to receive the precepts. Lord Feng, together with his fellow practitioners, each contributed funds to repair the Tanhua Hermitage.
In the fourth month of summer, he returned to Hudu; there he heard that the Holy Mother had passed away. He immediately established a Daochang for requital of kindness.
Upon receiving an imperial edict, he performed the tonsure before the spirit casket to express his gratitude and resumed his monastic robes. Thereupon, he wept bitterly, saying: "Alas!"
Ah! The donor has departed; the aspiration of our original temple is fulfilled. How could one wait for a second coming?

Regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I first conceived the intent to compose a *Tongyi* (Comprehensive Commentary) while in the Eastern Sea. It long remained stored in my heart, as I lacked the leisure to describe it.
Only this past May did I finally take up the pen; the draft was completed in fifty days. In the eleventh month, the hermitage was finished, and there were poems on dwelling in the mountains.
I ordained my attendant Cili.

In the forty-third year, the year of Yimao (1675), when I was seventy years old, I lectured on the *Lengyan Tongyi* for the assembly during the spring; in the fourth month of summer, I composed the *Fahua Tong*.
Regarding the meaning: although there were two sections, the entire text had not yet reached full coherence; therefore, I reworked it. The draft was completed on the fiftieth day.
I then compiled the *Abridged Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*. In the eighth month of autumn, I traveled to Mount Nanyue, and on the Mid-Autumn Festival, I ascended Mount Zhurong.
On the ninth day of autumn, Lord Feng was transferred from Wuling to serve as Governor of Hunan.
After returning from a visit to Fangguang Temple, Provincial Commissioner Wu Gong Shengbai came to visit me in Hudu. We discussed the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and Mr. Wu was greatly delighted;
he immediately raised funds with his subordinates to carve the woodblocks for its printing. He also paid homage to the portraits of the eighty-eight patriarchs and offered great praise. Thereupon—
He commissioned painters to copy a small album of portraits and requested that I compose a biographical eulogy for each.

Not long after Lord Feng had departed for his post, he invited me to travel to the Nine Doubts Mountains. In the tenth month of winter, we arrived at Lingling and stayed through the winter at Yu Creek.
In the forty-fourth year, Bingchen, when I was seventy-one years of age, I returned from Lingling in the first month of spring; Fang Yimin had also just returned from his official travels.
Located to the east of Lake Hu, it was named Fuxin (Blessed Mind) Temple.

In the year following the passing of Master Daduan, my disciple Dayi requested that the sacred reliquary be returned to the south. The monastic and lay disciples enshrined it at Jizhao Monastery on Mount Jing;
now, twelve years have passed. I have not forgotten the profound significance of our dharma connection and previously intended to visit in person.
I had sent one condolence message, but I had not yet dispatched the incense. Upon hearing that the funeral was imminent, I felt compelled to go.
As I was about to depart, the monks of Huayao Temple invited me to a vegetarian feast to ensure the continuation of the Dharma lineage. I visited Meixuetang to pay my respects to Master Sun’an.
In the fourth month of summer, I left Hudu; there is a poem titled "A Verse to Dispel Ridicule upon Leaving for Nanyue" by Kuang Muyi, Fang Yimin, and He [Yuan].
Zhongyi and several disciples escorted me to the city of Zhangmu. In the fifth month, I arrived at Wuchang, where I met with the Censor-in-Chief Duan Huanran;
we paid homage to the Great Buddha and toured Jiufeng. In the sixth month, I reached Xunyang and visited Donglin, composing a poem on my reflections regarding antiquity.
He ascended Mount Kuanglu to pay his respects to Chan Master Chekong and spent the summer heat at Jinnazhiping, where he annotated the *Zhao Lun*.
Seeing that the mountain was secluded and magnificent, he conceived the intention to retire there; however, after searching everywhere, he found no place to dwell.
In the seventh month, he traveled to Guizong Temple, climbed Jinfeng Peak, and paid homage at the Śarīra Stūpa, composing a poem. A monk escorted him as far as Wuru Mountain.
The Tranquil Chamber: I ascended to survey the site; though the land was not extensive, its surroundings were quite secluded. I therefore accepted it.
The lay practitioner Xing Laici of Jiangzhou, a disciple of Master Da, wished to serve as a patron by providing the gold for the ground.
Consequently, I conceived the intention to spend my final years there. Chen Dacanshi Chishigong of Fuliang arrived at the mountain to visit me.
Hearing that I had the intention to dwell at Mount Kuang, he also wished to act as a protector of the Dharma.

In the eighth month of autumn, I left the mountain and went to Huangmei, where I paid respects to the Fourth and Fifth Patriarchs. I visited Lord Wang Sima and entered Mount Ziyun, staying there for ten days.

Lord Wang pledged to serve as the patron (*dānapati*) for the construction projects on Mount Kuang. After bidding him farewell, I went to Xiangcheng to visit the Grand Historian Wu Guanwo in the Wu region.

The Vice-Director was originally from Ruru. He wished to establish Ruyi Hermitage to remain there, but he traveled to Fushan, crossed the river to ascend Jiuhua, and reached Jinsha at the beginning of the tenth month.
There, he joined the Wang clan’s ancestral assembly and was welcomed by Dongchan’s Layi Yao, with whom he resided.
Recently, I went to Shuangjing. Yan Sheng, a lay practitioner (upāsaka) from Shimen, awaited my arrival at Wujiang and escorted me to his home.
The gentleman provided all the provisions for the vegetarian feast to accompany me on the journey. On the nineteenth day of the month of the winter solstice, we arrived at Jizhao Temple.
To perform the cremation rites for the Great Master, he first composed a written text to offer as a sacrifice. He fixed the date for this day with such precision that there was no deviation.
Those who understood him marveled at this. On the twenty-fifth day, he personally gathered the sacred remains and enshrined them upon the Mañjuśrī Terrace.
The disciple Fa’ai (Fakai) subsequently erected a stūpa, for which I composed an inscription to fulfill the lifelong principles of the Dharma-gate.
I remained there to pass the year. At that time, I gave a small public discourse (*xiao-can*) to the monastics in the meditation hall on the essential points of Chan practice.

Master Fakai requested instruction on the *Abhidharma* school (*xiangzong*), so I expounded upon the common teachings regarding the nature (*xing*). To those who sought further instruction, each spoke [according to their needs].
There is a discourse on the Dharma, composed as a "Song of the One-Carrier" (Damban). It was written by the disciple Tong’an Xianbie, together with Du Chao, Yi, and the various sons Fushan;
and by the Dharma-grandsons Shen Guang, Guangyi, Guangshe, Cibang, and Xing.
In the forty-fifth year, the Ding-si year, when I was seventy-two years of age, in the first month of spring, I traveled to Shuangjing to pay my respects at Yunqi.

At that time, over a thousand disciples, both ordained and lay, had been waiting in the mountains for a long time; they remained there for twenty days, attending the nightly small *sēn* (informal sermons) to hear the Dharma. Each [of them]...

Everyone was filled with joy. Disciples, upon hearing of Master Lianchi’s lifelong secret practices, were moved to tears, remarking that I had revealed what others did not know, and thus requested me to compose an inscription for his stupa.
Upon my return, Dharma Master Xuanjin Hekong, along with local magistrates, lay devotees, Imperial Censor Jin Zhongcheng, Minister Yu, and Elder Weng... [and others] joined in the request.

I respectfully address the assembly. I requested that he remain at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci Temple, where thousands of practitioners gathered daily for him to administer the Great Precepts and compose the *Record of the Zongjing Hall*.
Distinguished Dharma masters from various mountains and regions assembled by the lake to inquire about the Dharma, each posing challenging questions and debates;
it was regarded as the most preeminent Dharma assembly in the southeast, the likes of which had never been seen before.
He then traveled to the famous scenic sites of Lingyin, the Three Zhus, and the Western Hills. He offered praise for the practice of releasing living beings at the Three Ponds and then departed.
The local officials and lay devotees (upāsakas) of the city provided boats for the release of life and saw him off upon the lake.

They also submitted a formal petition requesting him to remain at Yunqi, proposing an agreement for a three-year stay; however, he eventually set out on his journey. All the writings composed during these travels are recorded below.
Master Xuanjin Hegong discussed his travels with Mengjun. They compiled these accounts into four volumes titled *Dongyou ji* (Collection of Eastern Travels) and had them carved for printing.
Upon returning to Wumen, the Dharma Masters Chaosong and Yiyu invited him to Mount Hua.
There he visited various scenic sites such as Tianchi, Xuanku, and Tieshan. He was joined by Hanshan, Zhao Fanfu, Yan Tianchi, Xu Zhongrong, Yao Mengchang, and Wenwen.
It began. Xu Qingzhi and various lay devotees (*gṛhapati*) made offerings in the mountains. Feng Yuancheng and Shen Xuanzhu, two officials, held a vegetarian feast at their home.
As they were about to depart, the disciple Dongwen informed them that Han Yue had been waiting for a long time.
Qian Taishi Shouzhai personally went to welcome him as far as Changshu, where they stayed overnight at Yushan. Taishi saw him off at Quhe River. [Hui] He.
Knowing that his father, son, and nephew were waiting at Sanli Hermitage in Ben’ou, he invited them to remain in the garden for the summer retreat (varṣā), but they declined his earnest request.
He escorted them as far as Jingkou; after receiving the vegetarian offerings from the monastics and laypeople of the Three Mountains, he immediately returned to Kuangshan.
On the first day of the fifth month, he passed through Bai-xia and stayed one night on the riverbank, where he met with one or two old friends, before setting sail.
In the west, on the fifth day, I arrived at Wuhu. Liu Yan-shou, the Director of the Ministry of Works, treated me with great kindness and invited me to stay.

He recounted his record of a strange dream and spoke of his meeting with Cui He-lou, the Director of the Ministry of Personnel, by the river. On the sixteenth day of the fifth month, my boat reached Xingzhu, where I arrived at Gui-zong.
I took up residence there for a short while; at that time, Mr. Wang Gong, the Grand Secretary, had already prepared the necessary funds to have a quiet chamber built for me.
On the fifteenth day of the sixth month, the disciple Fuxian began the construction of the Wuru site;
by the end of the tenth month, a single chamber was completed and he was able to dwell there in peace. He then began lecturing on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* for the assembly.
The disciple Chaoyi sealed himself in a retreat at Mount Jinlun.
In the forty-sixth year, the year of Wumao (558), I was seventy-three years old. That year, I renovated the Buddha Hall and the Meditation Hall.
In the third month, Chen Chishi of Fuliang entered the mountain and joined with Zhongsu Bao Gong and I, Xia Gong, to form a group of ten friends who assisted with the funds for the construction.
In the twelfth month of winter, the temple hall was completed.

In the forty-seventh year, the Jiwu year (1479), when I was seventy-four years old, on the first month of spring, my disciple Tonghyeong arrived; we then opened the hall and began the ritual chanting.

Huayan. For a long time, he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and various other sūtras and śāstras for the assembly.

He appointed [Master] Hyeong as the head of the community. In the seventh month of autumn, he dedicated Wueru Mountain as a permanent endowment for the support of the elderly throughout the ten directions.

On the full moon of the eighth month, I closed my retreat and retired from affairs, emulating Master Huiyuan by carving incense every six hours to mark the passage of time, and focused my mind single-mindedly on purity.

I have often reflected that the Huayan school is on the verge of being lost. Regarding the commentaries and sub-commentaries of Qingliang, many fear they are too voluminous and extensive, and that their own mental faculties are insufficient to grasp them;

consequently, the world has for the most part set them aside. However, since the *Zongjing lu* (Compendium of the Essential Teachings) is the very source of this tradition, and considering that Qingliang was the patriarch of all writings in this land, I felt that if these were abandoned, the core of our school would be lost. My resolve, therefore, is simply to clarify the meaning of the commentaries.
He extracted the essential themes so that readers might understand them easily; he titled this work "Outline" (*Gangyao*).
During his time in Guanzhong, beginning with his editorial revisions and critiques there, he lectured on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith* for the assembly in the winter.
