The Master repaired an old stupa, gradually fulfilling his vow. Once, while he was attending a lecture at Tianjie Monastery, the latrine was spotlessly clean with no sign of human presence.
He thought to himself, "The one in charge of the eastern cleansing must be no ordinary person. He went to inquire and found a yellow-faced, sickly monk whose gaze was piercing;
he then made an appointment to visit him. At dawn the next morning, the monk had already departed—this was Miaoxin.

This was Master Feng Deng. The Master, considering that the habits of the Jiangnan region were soft and indulgent, felt it appropriate to enter a land of unbearable bitter cold—where there is winter ice and summer snow—to discipline himself through hardship.
He thus set out for the north with a carefree spirit.

Amidst a great snowfall, he begged for alms in the marketplace of Guangling, saying, "A single bowl is sufficient to put ten thousand measures of grain to shame. Upon reaching the capital, he donned the robes of Miaofeng.

Hae came to visit; his hair and beard were disheveled like those of a merchant from the He-shuo region. The Master, observing the pupils of his eyes, recognized him, and they looked at each other and smiled.
He then visited Master Jeong-byeon Yuam, who said nothing, but merely stared straight ahead with wide-open eyes. He also visited Master Hwa-am.
Yan asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From the south. Yan said, "Do you remember the path by which you came? He replied, "Once passed, it is simply over.

Yan said, "You, however, have a clear understanding of where you come from. Xiu traveled to Mount Pan and reached the stone chamber on Thousand Images Peak (*Qianxiangfeng*), where he encountered a silent monk (*buyu seng*).
They subsequently spent the summer together gathering firewood and drawing water. This was the first year of the Wanli era, the *Guiyou* year (1573). The following year, [he departed].

Accompanying Miaofeng, they spent the winter at Puban, where they read the "Treatise on the Non-Transmigration of Things. Upon reaching the section on the Brahmin’s renunciation of the world, [Hui]yuan suddenly realized the profound meaning of the whirlwind that topples mountains.
He composed a verse, saying: "Death and birth are like day and night; The water flows and the flowers wither. Only today do I truly understand."
His nostrils pointed downward. As soon as Feng saw him, he immediately asked, "What have you attained? The Master replied, "Last night I saw two iron oxen in the river fighting;
they plunged into the water and have not been heard from since. Feng said, "I am glad you now have the capital for staying on this mountain.
He then went to meet Chan Master Faguang of Niu Mountain to seek instruction through formal sitting and inquiry. When Faguang raised his voice, it was like the sound of heaven.
Gugu deeply resonated with this. He composed a poem to see Master off on his journey to Mount Wutai, saying: "A lion rides through the snow to behold;
a hidden dragon is released from the cave. Do you understand this meaning? I wish for you not to grasp at a dead snake."
The Master resided at Longmen on Mount Beitai. His dwelling consisted of a few rafters of old wood, situated amidst ten thousand mountains in ice and snow.

At the transition between spring and summer, melting ice surged and crashed; within the stillness, it sounded like the galloping of ten thousand horses. He asked Miaofeng about this, and Miaofeng cited the words of an ancient:
"For thirty years, hearing the sound of water, he did not shift his faculty of mind; thus he realized the perfect penetration of Avalokiteśvara. The Master [was moved].

He did so. Every day he would seek out a rickety footbridge spanning a stream and sit perilously upon it. At first, the sound of the water was distinct; after a while, however, he suddenly forgot his own body.

All other sounds fell silent, and the noise of the water no longer distracted his ears. One day, after finishing his morning gruel, he was walking in meditation when he suddenly became fixed in stillness.
A radiance like a great round mirror appeared, within which the mountains, rivers, and the great earth were reflected as images. Upon awakening, he realized this.

His body and mind were serene and still, such that nothing could be apprehended. He expressed this in verse. While traveling through Yanmen, the military commissioner Hu invited him to compose a poem.
As soon as he began to contemplate, his throat became choked with lines of verse; everything he had previously memorized and all his learning manifested instantaneously before him.
It was as if his entire body were a mouth, yet he could not exhaustively utter it all. The Master said, "This is what is called 'the illness of dhyāna' (chanbing) by Dharmakīrti."
He thought only deep sleep could dispel it. Wrapping himself in his robes, he sat in the full lotus posture for five days and nights.

When Master Hu shook him, he did not move; only after striking the small bell several times did he emerge from samādhi. Sitting in silence, he looked back and observed that even his inhalation and exhalation were like a dream;

dwelling in the mountains and traveling on pilgrimage were all matters occurring within a dream, and his bliss was beyond compare. Upon returning to the mountain, he pierced his own flesh with a needle to transcribe the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
He would apply his brush to chant the Buddha’s name without ceasing his verbal responses; his mouth recited while his hand drew, all with such vivid clarity that a neighboring monk marveled at him.
Leading his own disciples, the monk came to provoke him, but they all departed after offering praise.

He once dreamed that he and Miaofeng were attending upon the Great Master of Qingliang as he revealed the initial stage of the "Contemplation of the Perfect Interfusion of the Dharma Realm. As the Master expounded it, the very scene of that realm appeared before him.
He appeared again in a dream, ascending the Maitreya Pavilion and hearing the Dharma being preached, which said: "Discrimination is consciousness (*vijñāna*); non-discrimination is wisdom (*jñāna*).

Relying on consciousness leads to defilement; relying on wisdom leads to purity. Defilement entails birth and death; purity is the state of all Buddhas. From this point on, the distinction between consciousness and wisdom became perfectly clear to his mind and eyes.
After the Master had established the prayer altar for the succession of the Dharma, he subsequently withdrew far away to the fortress of the Eastern Sea.
The Mountain [Monastery]. By imperial decree from Empress Dowager Cizheng, the monk Ruian of Longhua Temple was dispatched to seek it out.

When the envoy returned and reported that he could not bring it back, the Empress granted him three thousand taels of gold from the inner treasury. He again firmly declined, and the messenger did not dare return with the report.

The Master said, "In antiquity, there were instances of issuing forged edicts to relieve famine. Since there is a poor harvest in Shandong, let this be used to extend the Imperial benevolence to the starving people."

"Is this not also permissible? The messenger returned with the register of the alms and reported it. Empress Dowager Cisheng sighed with emotion and led the entire palace in the distribution of gold to build a temple, granting it the name Haiyin.
The Master went to the capital to express his gratitude and requested the Tripitaka for Baeongsa Temple.
The Emperor commanded the Master to carry [the scriptures] back as an offering, using the occasion to return home and visit his parents.

For several days, the temple pagoda emitted light. On the day the scriptures were welcomed, the light crossed northward like a floating bridge; the scriptures traveled amidst the light within the pagoda.

Upon his return, the Master submitted a detailed report on the entire process of the "Gratitude" (Bao'en) mission, stating: "I wish to reduce my daily provisions by one hundred *jin* of gold; in ten years, this task may be accomplished. Thus it was done with compassion.
The Emperor granted his permission. In the year of Yiwu (1095), however, the persecution of those in yellow caps arose.

The Master had resided on the mountain for thirteen years, skillfully expounding the Dharma so that the lands of Mlecchas in the Eastern Sea all turned toward the Triple Gem; yet the followers in yellow caps proceeded to encroach upon and seize the monastic precincts.

He submitted a memorial of slanderous accusations, and by imperial decree was arrested and sent to the palace prison. Previously, Empress Dowager Cisheng had placed great faith in the Buddhist vehicle and dispatched imperial envoys everywhere;
however, palace eunuchs had instigated slander, constantly claiming that such activities were wasteful and extravagant, yet the Emperor did not inquire into these matters.

Nevertheless, these rumors spread somewhat to the outer court, and the relevant authorities consequently treated the Master as a "rare commodity," wishing to use him as a pretext for further incriminations.
The Empress Dowager and her attendants personally oversaw the proceedings, with offerings from both before and after totaling several hundred thousand taels of gold.

Despite the most exhaustive forms of torture, the Master remained entirely silent. Eventually, he calmly looked up and replied, "Your Excellency merely wishes for me to falsely plead guilty; that is all."
The case has been finalized. Where will you place the Holy Mother? To the authorities, the hundreds of thousands you have adjudicated are but a mere trifle.
Our Sovereign is of pure filial piety; he surely will not, on account of such trifles, allow his heart to be wounded by grief for the Holy Mother.
After the case is concluded, fearing there would be no way to offer her consolation, where will you turn for refuge once you have brought this case to its ultimate end? O Master!

His tongue protruded and could not be retracted; he was then placed under formal indictment. The charges listed were solely for providing three thousand *jin* of gold to relieve the famine, a fact verifiable by the records of the Inner Treasury.
Both Empress Cisheng and the Emperor were greatly pleased. However, because he had privately constructed a temple, he was sentenced to military exile in Leizhou;
this was not the Emperor’s true intention. When Master Daguan Ke was in urgent distress during the crisis of his teacher, he was about to set out for the capital gates when he encountered [him] at...
On the riverbank, the Master said, "This is the decree of Heaven; how could it be transgressed? He then composed a "Discourse on the Banished Guest" for his teacher and took his leave.

The Master crossed Mount Yuling, entered Caoxi, and reached Wuyang. There, wearing the crimson garments of a convict, he presented himself before the Governor of Yue and was enrolled among the ranks at Leizhou.

In that year, there was a great epidemic; the dead lay piled one upon another like pillows. [The Master] led the multitude to bury them and performed an extensive *prajñā* assembly for their dedication.
A heavy rain fell, leveling the ground by three feet, and the miasma of the pestilence was instantly dispelled. Minister Zhou led his students to come and strike at the Master’s gate.

When they raised questions concerning the Way of penetrating day and night, the Master said: "This is the Sage’s instruction to people; it is essential to realize that [the Way] does not belong to..."

"Life and death are but a single matter. Lord Zhou sighed deeply and struck his palm in appreciation. Feng Changli and others—filial sons and eminent scholars from Yue—heard of this and came to take refuge.
The Master modeled himself after Dahui, wearing a scholar’s cap and gown while preaching the Dharma. He constructed a meditation hall amidst the city walls and lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*.

When he reached the chapter on the manifestation of the jeweled stupa, the Sahā world and the Flower Treasury World appeared vividly before his eyes. Many were awakened to the truth. He resided there...

In the fifth year [of the reign], he was finally able to take up residence at Caoxi. He reclaimed the encroached fields and expelled those occupying the monastic quarters; what had been butchery shops and wine taverns flourished as a precious monastery (*ratnārāma*).
Monastics and laypeople gathered in great numbers, and the methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* were practiced in tandem. Thus, the Way of the Great Mirror (*Mahādarśana*) was vigorously restored.

In the summer of the Jiayin year, while the Master was in Hudu, the Empress Dowager Cisheng passed away. By imperial decree, he went to wail in grief, whereupon he resumed his tonsure and returned to his monastic robes.

In his second year [of retirement], he contemplated the meaning of birth and death within the Dharma-gate of *Daguang* (Universal Observation). He traveled to Shuangjing to attend the funeral rites and perform the *caibi* (cremation) ceremonies.
There, he offered admonitions regarding the maladies of Chan practitioners in the Wu-Yue region and composed the "Song of the One-Sided Plank" (*Dankan Ge*).
He visited Yunqi to pay tribute to Master Lianchi Hong, extolling his secret practices to serve as an example for students. Returning from Wumen to Mount Lu, he established a hermitage at Wufeng.

Beneath the Milk-Peak (Nanyue), he emulated Master Huiyuan by carving a water clock with six dials and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land. After four years, he returned to Caoxi.
In the third year of the Tianqi era (the Guihai year), Master Xuanhua arrived for a visit upon being summoned to court; they conversed at great length for two nights.

The Master remarked, "Your physical vigor does not seem more than a hundred years old; you could sit in meditation for another twenty or so summers as easily as snapping one's fingers. The Master smiled and said:
"The old monk’s worldly ties are nearing their end. How could this illusory body be worth lingering over? Five days later, he indeed manifested a slight illness.
When Zhang Jun, the Governor of Shaoyang, came to inquire after him, the Master firmly declined medical treatment; he sat and conversed as usual.
After the visitor had departed, he bathed, burned incense, assembled the congregation to bid farewell, and passed away while sitting upright on the eleventh day of the tenth month at Caoxi.
The water suddenly dried up, and hundreds of birds wailed in grief. At night, a light shone as if illuminating the heavens. After three days, he was placed in the shrine;

his face turned crimson, his beard and hair grew long, a slight sweat appeared at the tip of his nose, and his hands and feet became as soft as cotton. The monks were startled and announced that the Master had returned to life.
Lord Xiao said to me, "I am old and infirm, yet I have traveled twenty thousand *li* to the capital. What could I possibly do there?

Heaven seems to have sent me here merely to serve as a witness for the Master’s final moments. Alas, how profound his words! The Master was tall and imposing in stature, with a majestic and dignified presence.
Wherever he went, he benefited all beings and aided living things; his skillful means were so adept that they were like the warming sun and the moistening rain, bestowing their grace upon all.
No one was aware of this. When Shandong suffered another famine, the Master emptied his granaries and personally traveled by boat to Liaodong to purchase beans for relief.

He thereby saved the people of the surrounding mountains from emaciation and death. A tax collector had a feud with the Provincial Commander of Guangdong and incited the city merchants to cause a disturbance using white-hulled boats.
They gathered in a mob and surrounded the Commander’s residence; the Master spoke calmly and persuasively to the tax collector to dissolve the siege, but they would not budge.
The sounds and sights [of the region] were such that the capital city attained peace. A thousand pearl-ships ceased their harvesting and did not return.

While plundering upon the seas, the labor of mining was particularly disruptive and chaotic. When the Superintendent of Pearl Harvesting visited Caoqi, the Master received him through the Dharma and gradually explained the benefits and harms of mining.
Consequently, the pearl-ships ceased their harvesting and did not enter the sea; furthermore, the quota for mining was assigned to the relevant authorities.
In the year [X], the Provincial Governor, Lord Dai, sent a letter of thanks, saying: "Only now do I understand the vastness of the compassion of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The Master told me that while he resided at the Northern Terrace, there was a great snowfall several *zhang* high, such that one could see the hairs on one's head in the darkness of night.
He sat firm, awaiting his end, his body and mind radiantly clear. At dawn, the monks of the pagoda temple dug through the snow to enter and found him—"

He carried [the manuscript] for about one *li* through a snow cave before emerging. While he was being interrogated and tortured in the imperial prison, he suddenly entered a state of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
Though subjected to flogging, caning, piercing, and burning, he remained as unyielding as wood or stone. After more than a year in Leyang, he heard his attendant urgently calling him;

he was arrested and subjected to such cruel torment that his skin was nearly stripped from his body. This is the origin of the composition of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra Notes*. The Master traveled eastward until—
At Lêng-yen Monastery in Chia-hsing, surrounded by a multitude of people, there was a servant who appeared as if he were insane.
He struck his forehead incessantly, saying, "I am the scholar Chung from the western part of our monastery. Having died, I still remain in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Hearing that a Bodhisattva in human form has appeared in the world, I have taken possession of this servant's body to seek liberation. The Master preached the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts for him and asked whether he had attained liberation.

He said, "The liberation is complete. Suddenly, he awoke from his stupor. That the Master erected the great banner of the Dharma to serve as the eyes for humans and devas—how could this have been by mere chance?
The Master’s worldly lifespan was seventy-eight years, and his monastic seniority fifty-nine years. He had a vast number of disciples who received ordination before and after him.
Among those who followed the Master even into prison and served him with food and clothing was Fushan. From beginning to end, they remained in mutual reliance within Yue.
As for those who were excellent in bestowing [teachings] and whose penetration was brilliant, transcendent, and reaching the further shore:

the noble scion of high station who gouged out his own arm to light a lamp in order to seek the Way of a Master, and upon whom the image of a Great Being appeared amidst the scabs of his wound before he sat in liberation and departed—that was Mo Huang Na Shan.
Among the gentlemen who took refuge [in the Dharma], Feng Chang Li served as their leader. Also present were the Censor Wang An Shun and the Xiaolian...
Liu Qixiang, Chen Dixiang, Ou Wenqi, Liang Sxiang, and Long Zhang were all disciples of Changli.
Among the master’s writings are the *Notes on the Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Essentials of the Avataṃsaka*, the *Hanging Mirror of the Śūraṅgama*, and the *Beating the Beat of the Lotus Sūtra*.

He authored several fascicles of commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*; a treatise on the "Echoes and Shadows" of Laozi and Zhuangzi;
a commentary on the *Daode jing*; direct expositions of the *Daxue* and *Zhongyong*; and the *Heart-Dharma of the Zuo Zhuan of Spring and Autumn*, as well as several fascicles of the *Mengyou ji*.
Alas! Regarding worldly literature, how could our Master necessarily fail to equal the ancients? Yet there are things he did not reach.
These are merely dregs and refuse. As for your realization of the ultimate truth regarding the supramundane meaning, how could it necessarily fail to accord with the ancients?

Should there be points where it does not accord, these too are but the superficial skin and hair. It is only that you, Master, having long ago mounted the wheel of your vow, have entered the sea of afflictions through great compassionate wisdom.
By the power of fearlessness, he dwells within the stream of birth and death, manifesting his body according to conditions and responding to sentient beings as they arise.
In his final act, his entire being is fully revealed, so that five hundred years hence, people may know there exists this Great Matter of causal connection.
How could this be grasped through words, emotions, or intellectual views, nor be measured by conjectures of its brevity or length? Therefore, reading the Master’s writings is not as [effective] as—
"Listen to the Master’s words! Listen to the Master’s words! Yet, even this is not as good as following him in person with one's staff and almsbowl.
By examining his life from beginning to end, one can truly know where his vows and powers reside. I, Qianyi, am of inferior and dull faculties;

yet, having been blessed by the Master’s prophetic prediction, I have recorded this upon stone based on the chronological biography and the formal life account. My words are more verbose than they ought to be, for I desire..."

This is to demonstrate the protocols for the Dharma-ending age and to inspire right faith in sentient beings. The inscription says: Human life appears and disappears within the world of the five turbidities.
The path of birth and death stands as a formidable barrier. How steep and high this barrier is! Who would not fall back into decline?

Like a lion’s vigorous spring, he leaps across in a single bound; like crossing a river by burning his boats, he halts his chariot and restrains his horses. With a single alms-bowl he flies across; who could stand as my opponent?
Amidst ice mountains where all is dormant and snow pits where one is buried, the ice melts and the frost dissolves; the waters flow and the flowers bloom.
The fourfold radiance shines forth, penetrating upward to the celestial gates. Honor, fame, profit, and sustenance—these are not what my mind dwells upon.
Though thunder and lightning rage with fury, my nature does not shift. Amidst shackles and wooden stocks, my preaching of the Dharma blazes on. From Juefan at Zhuya to Miaoxi at Meizhou.
Ten thousand *li* from the Yangtze River’s warm currents, what do you seek from me? With a *kundika* as your vessel, you cross the plains with spear in hand and staff in girdle;

shattering your form and discarding your robes—therein lies an ancient precedent. The legacy of the Great Mirror is profound, its spiritual illumination unclouded; the garments of Quxu appear like painted embroidery.

The Master’s manifestation was like clouds emerging from a valley; touching the rocks, they spread from a mere skin-thickness, yet rain falls before it can be gathered. When the clouds return and the rain is hidden, the mountains and rivers remain as they were.
Who can grasp the fleeting light to peer into the Great Void? His merit is towering and majestic; his words and phrases are brilliant and radiant.
Behold this physical body: it is equal to the one reality, both real and illusory. Mount Kuang does not come; Caoxi does not go.

The light of the stupa shines brightly, forever illuminating the path to awakening. Written respectfully on the first day of the ninth month in the seventh year of the Tianqi era (Dingmao), by the disciple Qian Qianyi, wearing a cloth cap from Chushu.
The Biography of Master Hanshan:
The master’s name was Deqing. He was a native of Quanpao and surnamed Cai. His mother, Lady Hong, dreamed that the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara) entered her door accompanied by a young boy.
She carried him in her womb and subsequently became pregnant. Upon his birth, she was clothed in white and had double amnion sacs. She was by nature disinclined toward worldly life;

at the age of twelve, hearing that Master Xilin possessed great virtue, she wished to go and follow him. Her father would not permit it, but her mother said, "In raising a child, one should follow their aspirations."
He was then sent into the monastery. At that time, Wujie was lecturing on the sutras at Xilin; he was one year senior to Master Xuelang Chang.

Having previously relied upon Wujie, when he saw the Master, it was as if they had a karmic affinity from a former life. At nineteen, he followed Wujie to listen to his profound expositions on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, reaching as far as the "Ten Mysterious Gates."
At the Sea-Seal Monastery, a place where all things abide eternally, he realized the principle of the non-obstructive, perfectly interfused Dharma-realm.

Deeply admiring the character of Master Qingliang (Chengguan), he took the name Chengyin for himself. Whenever there were lectures or assemblies, he would secretly observe the monks to see if any might be suitable as companions.

One day, seeing that the rear quarters were exceptionally clean and orderly, he thought the head cleaner must surely be no ordinary man; yet when he went to visit him, he found it was actually a monk suffering from jaundice.
Every morning he would rise early to ensure that all tasks were completed. Not knowing at what hour the sweeping and cleaning took place, he stayed awake to observe it.

Thus, when the assembly was just breaking from their evening meditation session (cham), the cleaning had already been finished. After several days, the head cleaner fell ill. The Master asked after his health, and he replied:
"The burden of my karmic illness is already difficult to bear, but this 'gluttonous illness' is even harder to endure. Whenever I see the serving of the midday meal, I feel regret."
He did not set them down together. The Master took some fruit and snacks from his sleeve and gave them to him personally. He asked for his name, which was Miaofeng. He was a native of Puzhou.

Because they had agreed to accompany one another on a long journey, Miaofeng departed after several days. Six years later, when the Master arrived in Chang’an, a man claiming to be a salt merchant came to visit him.
He had long hair and beard and wore coarse cloth garments; as soon as he entered the gate, he asked, "Do you recognize me?"

The Master examined his two eyes and suddenly recalled that he had once been the monk Jingtou in the celestial realm. He said, "I was requested by King Shanyin to bring the *Neizang* (Inner Treasury) here.
The Master followed Miaosheng to Hedong; King Shanyin remained there to observe the winter retreat and commissioned the carving of the *Zhao lun*.

Regarding the *Buxian lun* (Treatise on Non-transmigration), he had not yet clarified the meaning of the passage concerning the whirlwind that topples mountains. Suddenly, while reading the section on the Brahmin from childhood...
He left home to become a monk and returned with his hair turned white. A neighbor asked, "Is that former man still here? Zhi replied, "I resemble the former man, but I am not the former man.
At these words, he attained sudden and clear enlightenment. When the Master was seven years old, his uncle died.
His aunt embraced the corpse and wept, crying, "O Heaven! Where have you gone? The Master stared in astonishment and asked, "If my uncle's body is here, where has he gone again?"
He said, "I am dead. He wondered, "When one dies, where does one go? Doubting this, he went to visit his second aunt’s son shortly thereafter.
Seeing the infant, he asked his mother, "From where did you enter your aunt's womb? His mother clapped her hand and said, "From where did you enter your own mother's womb?
Again, he was deeply perplexed by the matter of death and rebirth; it remained vividly in his mind.
[This matter] had been held within [his heart], but now it was like ice melting away. The next day, Master Miao asked what he had attained.
The Master said, "Last night I saw two iron oxen by the river fighting; they entered the water and have not been heard from since.
Master Miao laughed and said, "I am glad you now have the capital for staying on a mountain. At that time, Chan Master Faguang was at Mount Funiu.
At the King’s residence, [the Master] was shown the practice of transcending mind, intellect, and consciousness, and departing from the paths of ordinary beings and sages.
The Master deeply grasped its essential meaning and would often sigh, saying, "Master Guang’s discourse is like the sound of a celestial drum.

One day, he searched for and read the Master’s poems, then said with a laugh, "How did you come by such fine verses? He laughed again and said, "They are indeed fine, yet one 'aperture' remains unpenetrated. The Master asked:
"Does the Master have the skill? he asked. The Master replied, "For thirty years I have been seizing dragons and catching tigers, yet today a rabbit has bolted out from the weeds, giving me a start.
The Teacher said, "The Master does not have the hands of one who seizes dragons and catches tigers.
He [the Teacher] took up his staff and made a gesture as if to strike. The Master seized him and stroked his beard with his hand, saying, "You say it is a rabbit; it is actually a frog."
Guang smiled and departed. One day he said to the Master, "There is no need for you to go elsewhere; I wish to grow old together at Mount Funiu. This was his way of expressing their mutual regard.
The Master then ascended Mount Wutai with Master Miao. Guang sent him off with a poem, which read: "Riding a lion through the snow, come to behold me."
"The dragon hidden in the cave has been released; let it go. When asked for the meaning of this, he replied, "I wish for you not to grasp at a dead snake.
The Master remarked, "For a long time, there have been no teachers of the Way of Chan. Only now that I have met Master Guang, do I first understand the strategic maneuvers of the School.

The Master of Dafang then selected Longmen on Beitaishan as a place of residence. Great winds frequently arose, and the myriad apertures roared in fury; the Master took this clamor as a sign of his spiritual progress.

He asked Master Miaoshan. The Master said, "The objective realm arises from the mind; it does not come from without. He added, "An ancient said that for thirty years he heard the sound of water without shifting his faculty of thought;
this is how one should realize the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara. At first, the Master sat daily by a bridge over a stream.
The sound of the water was as clear as ever. After a long time, whenever he stirred his thoughts, he heard it; when he did not stir his thoughts, he did not hear it.

One day, he suddenly forgot his own body, and both the sounds and the self were stilled. From then on, all clamor became silent, and he was no longer disturbed by them. Someone sent the Master three *dǒu* of rice.
He ate barley bran mixed with vegetables daily, using the rice to make a gruel which was delivered to him. This continued for more than half a year.
While walking after finishing his meal of gruel, he suddenly entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*). He no longer perceived body or mind;

there was only a great treasury of radiant light (*mahā-prabhā-kośa*), perfect, tranquil, and still, like a great round mirror in which the mountains, rivers, and the great earth were reflected. Upon awakening, he spoke this verse:
In a fleeting instant, the wild mind of a single thought ceased; internally and externally, the sense organs and their objects were all transparently penetrated.

Turning over, he struck through the vast void, and the myriad phenomena of the universe arose and perished. At that time, he was thirty years old. Having attained awakening, there was nothing further to request instruction upon.

He then opened his copy of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*; since it was something he had never lectured on before, he simply illuminated it with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), giving rise to only a slight movement of the discriminating consciousness.
It was beyond the reach of conceptual thought. Thus it was for eight months; the essential purport of the entire scripture became perfectly clear within his mind.

One night, he dreamed that he entered a Vajra Cave, where a stone gate bore the inscription "Great Prajñā Temple. There he saw the Great Master Qingliang reclining upon a bed, with Miaoshan attending him on the left.
The Master [the dreamer] hurried forward to prostrate and stood to the right. The Great Master then revealed to him the initial entry into the Dharma.

The contemplation of the realm of the perfect fusion of the *dhātus* refers to the mutual entry of Buddha-lands, the interpenetration of principal and satellites, and the phenomenon of coming and going without movement.
As soon as this realm is described, the realm itself manifests; one knows for oneself that body and mind are mutually interfused and enter into one another. Master Miaosheng asked:
"What realm is this? The Great Master smiled and said, "It is the realm of no-realm.

Again, he dreamed that he stepped upon the void and ascended, entering a vast and lofty hall where he beheld and paid homage to Maitreya. He heard him say: "Discrimination is consciousness (*vijñāna*);

In Lamentation for the Passing of Chan Master Han’gong: By Xiao Yunju (Former Minister of Rites from Guangxi).
Oars struck against the shore of Shuanglin as the evening gate was knocked; An old friend grasped my sleeve, our hearts in perfect accord. A year of parting at Longhua—
Meeting: When the geese’ letters from ten thousand *li* are cut off, He ties his thatched hut on Mount Lao and returns to the North Sea;

Flowers bloom on the Yu Ridge upon the southern branches. The land of Hengyang is narrow, yet the *kāṣāya* robe is vast; The clouds of Mount Kuang are deep, as he shifts his staff and bell. The mirror of the high terrace is originally empty—contemplate one’s own nature;
The wind and banner suddenly stir—is this not the Master? How many times have cool moons doubled my clear dreams? A single night spent in autumn...

Facing the wind, one knows through contrast; leaning on the armrest, he discusses the Way and gathers profound meanings. Wielding his brush, he reveals the ground of realization and sweeps away all doubts.
Long free from attachments, his mind is ever settled; though empty, his compassion causes his head to hang low once more. As autumn deepens, fallen leaves forget the fatigue of speech;
at midnight, hearing the bell, he speaks of the peril of the mind. He often laments that the worldly heart is ever suffering; yet when reaching the Chan platform, the path turns toward the fork.

The Dharma words were worthy of respectful assent; the journey home was pressed by haste, hence the lingering delay. In old age, one knows such a person as this will be difficult to encounter across the lakes and seas;

having met with such a karmic opportunity, we part so suddenly and unexpectedly. As the wild geese pass over Cold Mountain, the autumn shadows fade; as the horse neighs by Cao River, the sound of its departure is mournful.
When the letter arrived, conveyed by a messenger from the north, the *kalyāṇamitra* heard the news of his passing and tears flowed down his cheeks. The pillar of the Dharma-gate has collapsed.
Rare indeed are those of true substance. Once the boat has vanished into the ocean of awakening, there is no turning back. The butterfly, fluttering in its sleep, has just entered the dream;
the dragon, soaring aloft, where would it go? Since our meeting, a thousand kalpas have already passed; as you depart through transformation, what need is there for a single word of praise?

I have forgotten myself, not out of greed for formless beauty; I contemplate emptiness, yet do not marvel at the wonders of form. Looking back, the mountain peaks and the temple atop the forest trees—this is but a dream.
I imagine the poems within the casket of the Tide-Sound; in perfect stillness, how could there ever be parting or staying? His majestic demeanor remains unchanged from before;
I only fear that his dharma companions will become few. To whom shall the alms bowl be entrusted and the robe passed on?
A Lament for the Great Monk Hanguang (With Preface) By Wu Zhongwei (Former Left Vice-Governor, native of Haiyen) The Great Master Hanshan was a dragon and elephant of the Chan school.

Once again, while serving in my humble capacity in the region south of the passes, I traveled by way of Caoxi and prostrated before Nanhua. The ancestral image was barely shielded from wind and rain;
though timber lay piled high like mountains, the tortoise was exposed and the crane had flown away, and the colors of the painting were peeling off.
After lingering there for a long time, I sighed with deep regret and inquired as to the reason. An elderly bhikṣu replied, "This is the unfinished task of our Great Master Han."
He sat in meditation for seven days. As the golden ground was nearly completed, slanderous intrigues arose from the three realms, causing the Wheel of Dharma to be suspended midway.
Having finished speaking, he suppressed his grief, overcome by sorrow beyond measure. I, deeply moved by his intent, said to him: "If you truly desire the Great Master, I shall summon him for you.
The bhikṣus were all filled with immeasurable joy; they prostrated themselves on the ground in thanks and departed. Thus it was once again...
Traveling a thousand *li* on blistered feet, he earnestly requested [an audience]. Beginning from such-and-such month of this year, he entered Caoxi once again;

thus, the assembly of monks had already visited the Great Master three times, and I too had sent three letters to him. On the day he planted his staff (arriving), a letter of dharma-inquiry was bestowed upon me.

Bound by the constraints of my official duties, I have not yet been able to offer a reply. I constantly think that when I return north in the future, I may perhaps have the leisure to attend to his transformation [of beings].

the forest wind and moon conceal the lamp at the head of the bed. As the mist of the grain-rain festival vanishes, the samādhi is settled.

Later tea; in the age of the Dharma’s decline, having been revived, it falls once more. Pausing in sorrow beneath the twin trees, I alone sigh deeply. The prophecies of the Southern School mark a thousand years;
at this very site of the Way, he again settled into meditation. The stream of the Dharma remains in the heart for infinite awakening;

the Patriarch has departed, the robe is hidden, and the transmission shall not be repeated. The *bhiṣu* weeps until his tears sever [the ties] beneath the yellow leaves; the spirit is buried, the *kṣepaka* (chain) is white.
At the edge of the clouds, one should preserve the *Śāsanāntima-sūtra* alongside the Buddha; it is as if one has obtained a treasure ship amidst the midstream.

The robe comes from white wool, the body ever pure; the teaching unfolds from the blue lotus, the tongue again enfolded. How many scriptures have been translated to the end upon golden tablets? The patriarchal lineage is completed in silver-hook calligraphy.

It still makes me wish to listen to Hanshan.

I know that you, Master, were originally an ancient Golden Immortal.

The imperial decree to return from the fiery seas was a great act of sovereign grace; many were the demons subdued amidst crocodile waves and serpent clouds. Let it be—what need is there for the numinous mountain?
Through the power of the Way, only the auspicious marks remain as one listens to Amitābha.

To manage a thousand things is to dwell in a single cave. How shall one study Caoxi and Mount Lu? Had I known earlier that wind and moon were still being carried on a rack, there would have been nothing left to shoulder when the fire consumed them all.

the three ridges of the waist and spine are naturally perfected. The townspeople amidst the red leaves have eyes like blood; the disciple amidst the white clouds—[one...]

A letter from the lay disciple Haiyin of Mount Yushan, Qian Qianyi, to the Great Master Han at Caoxi. This letter is addressed to the Great Master Han at the Caoxi Pagoda.
To the Abbot and all the senior elder brothers of the monastery: I respectfully consider that in the year of Jiashen, the Great Master’s true body returned from Wueru to Caoxi;
it has now been thirteen years since then. Having repeatedly endured the turmoil of war and chaos, I have survived by the grace of a thousand deaths and a single life, barely maintaining my breath.
I have secluded myself among the grass and soil, unable to pack my bedding and carry my bowl to personally sweep the pagoda and the temple grounds.

Furthermore, being unable to purify my heart for the sake of prostration, I offer this incense from afar. Looking up, I am ashamed to have failed in repaying your arduous labors; looking down, I am guilty of neglecting your prophetic charge.
My body cramped like one walking on eggshells under heaven, my sighs and shame know no end. Yet, having served you through many lifetimes, I take refuge in you for the rest of my days.

The memory of spreading my hair [for your feet] has not been forgotten from past causes; I have long yearned for a compassionate mother who lost her child. This matter is such that even the ink of the ocean could not exhaust it, nor could the fires at the end of an eon...
Ashes. My Great Master must surely, within the eternal realm of quiescent light, again extend his compassionate pity and secretly bestow his empowerment upon me.

Since the banner of the Dharma collapsed and the final age began its decline, the lion has passed away while the jackals howl; the dragon-elephants have fallen silent while the demonic foxes flourish.
Every household claims to be Linji, and every individual calls himself Deshan; masters are as thick as thatch, and the transmission of the fly-whisk is as numerous as [the blades of grass].
Furthermore, they construct false narratives, showing contempt for the holy Sangha. Regarding Zibo, they say he had no formal lineage;
regarding the Great Master, they say he was merely a scholar of doctrine. Gathering the deaf and leading the blind, they delude the age and deceive the people.
There has never been a time when the Dharma-gate was more ruined than it is now. The entire world drinks from the medicine of a mad well, yet there is one...
People are not insane; the entire world fears the head reflected in a clear mirror, yet there is one person who does not fear it, standing alone and unsupported with wind and snow at his door.

This one person is perhaps one of the Four World-Protecting Kings or a Muditā-malla, who has lent his hand as this man to serve as the Tathāgata’s messenger, charged with clearing away the outer māras so that the lineage of the Buddha—our Great Master—shall not be severed.
With a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, he universally bestows fearlessness; yet how could he have no high expectations for future generations?

He and the various elders, as well as myself—though we differ in our status as monastics or laypeople—are all equally disciples who emerged from the gate of the Great Master and have alike received his final testament. Living in this present age, [we must uphold his legacy].
Following the waves and drifting with the current, you sit idly by as this person runs madly in a storm, waving their hands and closing their eyes, yet you do not rescue them.
How can you then claim to be a true child of the Sea-Seal (Sāgaramudrā)?

When demons are strong and Buddhas are weak, when the secular is valued and the Way is slighted, when the eye of wisdom is meager and the City of Dharma daily collapses—O Venerable Elders, how can you not be struck dumb by my words? Now...
What I most earnestly wish to request of you is this: in recent times, the collected works of Zibo and Yunqi have both been circulated in the world.
However, as for the *Mengyou ji* (Dream Wandering Collection) of our Great Master [Zhuhong], the edition contained in the Jiaxing Canon consists solely of his recorded teachings (*fayu*).

Other writings—such as correspondence, prefaces, and biographies that elucidate the Great Dharma—exist only in their catalogs but not in their actual texts. I have heard, however, that the Great Master’s posthumous manuscripts still exist.
Stored away at Caoxi, these volumes are exceedingly numerous. I now specifically request that you open them and hand over their contents, bag and all.
You should then rectify errors and excise redundancies, so that this world may behold the complete jewel rather than regretting having seen but half of it.

This is the eye of the Buddhas and patriarchs, venerated by those as numerous as the atoms of the universe; it must by no means be delayed until later, lest we incur the regret of its being lost to oblivion. Furthermore—
The Great Master composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals: The Heart-METHOD of the Zuo Commentary*, which is a treatise elucidating the law of cause and effect.

He often said that when he was revising his drafts by the lamp and candle at Caoxi, as he sought out the definitive judgments [of the texts], his very soul could be summoned back and the hairs on his body would all stand on end.

Due to the temporal conditions of this present age, it is precisely now that this book must be revealed and elucidated, so as to transform the stubborn and halt the taking of life, to rescue those drowning in the turbidity of the *kalpa*, and to honor the Great Master’s past entrustment, which was by no means trivial. How can the responsibility for its circulation be evaded?

I humbly entreat all the venerable elders to exert your collective strength in searching for and gathering [the texts], collecting every fragment of paper and single character with the utmost diligence.
Nothing was omitted or left behind. The gong and mallet were struck to assemble the multitude, who were summoned before the True Body (śarīra) of the Great Master.

This is the brilliant radiance of the Dharma-vehicle and the ocean of teaching for a thousand autumns; it is not merely the private good fortune of this one disciple at the Master’s gate. The Master’s five...
I, who have unworthily served as a scribe at the Nurturing Pagoda Monastery, recall that the late Chancellor of Nanhai once composed an inscription for it, which was engraved upon stone at Nanhua.
Regarding the deeds concerning his return to the reliquary from the year Jia-shen onwards, the mountain gate should possess a formal record.

Undaunted by my own meager talent, I wish to examine these facts and compose a second stele to supplement the monastic chronicles. At the age of seventy-five, I vow to [complete this] in the western regions.

This year, I take refuge in the Buddha-dharma. I shall reconcile the differences between the Tiantai and Xuanzang schools, shatter the divergent attachments to *svabhāva* (nature) and *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics), propagate the Bequeathed Teachings, and widely protect the True Vehicle.
May I strive throughout the remainder of my life so as not to fail the Great Master’s profound intention in bestowing his hand upon my head in entrustment.
Once this collection of writings is completed and some progress has been made, I shall compose a formal memorial to inform the Great Master in the netherworld.

This is a matter of utmost confidentiality. Bear this in mind with constant mindfulness. At present, however, there is truly no leisure for such matters. Gazing afar at the twin peaks, I burn incense and pay my respects.

Though the distance between the mountains and the sea is vast, it feels as if we were sitting together upon the same mat. Amidst the cold of heaven and the freezing of night, I have carved these words through ice.

At a time when this school was in decline, the Great Master stood alongside the two other great masters, Yunqi and Daguan, as a pillar of the triad.
